# PREFACE
### TO THE
# R E A D E R.

->To the Truth, virtue, and knowledge-loving Reader:<-

1. §. In these pages, I offer you a treasure of very many jewels, which primarily belong to the furnishing and adornment of your soul and understanding.

God's word, the principal fountain of all these, was to me an Ocean—so deep, and unfathomable to my limited comprehension, and filled with treasures of Divine wisdom, valued far above gold, silver, and rubies—that I frankly confess I have not been able to reach its bottomless depths, but have only skimmed something from its surface. Should anyone believe they can penetrate to the abyss with their own intellect, let them begin the work; yet I flatter myself that I have drawn so many and such matters from that sea, and presented them in these pages to be accessible to everyone, that he—if he be but truly earnest, of whatever state or calling he may be—will be able to store away something, like a little gem, in his jewel-box.

2. §. Old and new things will occur to the Reader during reading and reflection: presented by no means with the intent that they must be blindly accepted, but rather to be ruminated upon, tested, and brought to the touchstone of a pure and hallowed judgment. In this way, one may obtain material for reflection and intellectual play, and thus arrive at some true and enduring profit.

3. §. When I gave proper attention to the Title of my work, I noted that "shadows, examples, etc." <note>This refers to "typology," the theological study of how Old Testament persons or events foreshadowed the New Testament.</note> must be treated according to the promise. Having observed this as was proper, I thought it would not go against my plan or purpose, nor be to the detriment of the matters appearing in this work, nor cause any displeasure to the Reader, if I were to insert here and there the opinions and remarks of various men of rank and name in this my preface concerning the meanings, examples, and related matters.

4. §. I sense from the Christian Reader that he will have noticed that the Divine Scripture is sown with improper and figurative modes of speech, shadows, prototypes, teaching-models, allusions, and whatever other name one might give them. If Christ is the end of the law, the body of the shadows, and the Spirit of the prophecies (*Colossians 2:17, Hebrews 8:5 and 10:1, Revelation 19:10*), then it follows naturally that the law, the legal ministry, and the things serving it must also be exemplary. And so the Lord Herman Witsius <note>Herman Witsius (1636–1708) was a highly influential Dutch theologian known for his work on covenant theology.</note> in *Economy of the Covenants, page 448*, said by no means outside the mark: *If there were no spiritual mysteries and exemplary meanings in the legal ministry, then one might regard them as childish and ridiculous, and not as becoming of God.* For if one were to take away Jesus and the spiritual meaning from the law, from legal matters, and from the ministry, what else would remain but a bare letter, an empty carcass, and bodily exercises without spirit and refreshing soul-life?

I further maintain as certain that the events, or histories, of Abraham, Sarah, Hagar, Ishmael, Zion, Sinai, the struck rock, the manna, etc., besides the literal sense, also have a higher, secret, and spiritual meaning—even though Paul and others in their letters might not have given us the clearest transfer of each of these matters everywhere. Instead, they have shown here and there only a footing and ground, and in some matters the manner in which we must also spiritualize other things and translate them to a higher meaning. For so says the Lord Herman Witsius in *Economy of the Covenants, page 488, etc.* and in *Sacred Miscellanies, page 395*:

> "Let no one think that those things which Paul cites alone contain mysteries, or that one would spend labor in vain in searching out other things: for so that we might not think and believe such a thing, Paul has testified of all the institutions of Moses that they are shadows of Christ Jesus, *Colossians 2:17, Hebrews 10:1.*" and subsequently, "One must not think that those few mysteries revealed to us in the New Testament represent and exhaust the entire secret teaching of all the old institutions and mysteries in such a way that all the rest would have been given in vain..."

<summary>This preface introduces a theological work focused on Biblical typology, arguing that the Old Testament "shadows" and "examples" contain deep spiritual treasures and mysteries centered on Christ.</summary>
<keywords>typology, Herman Witsius, shadows, Old Testament law, spiritual interpretation, biblical metaphors, covenant theology, jewels of wisdom</keywords>

„ if they had no hidden meaning, and could be understood by no one as types and anti-types. <note>original: "voor- en tegenbeelden"</note> See *d'Espagne* part 2, Chapter IX. *page 86.*

5. §. Indeed, one often sees that when the work of creation is viewed, expressions are borrowed from the history recounting it, which, through spiritualization <term>vergeestelykinge: the practice of interpreting biblical events as allegories for the soul's inner life</term>, are applied to something higher that pertains to the soul. Serving as a small proof of this are *Psalm 51:10 <note>The Dutch text cites verse 12 following a different numbering system</note>: Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.* 2 Cor. 4:6; 2 Cor. 5:17; Eph. 2:10; and 4:24; etc.

When one perceives such things, one surely has grounds to judge that there must lie something in the six-day work of creation regarding its own spiritualization, and that one does not err when one seeks to follow the trail of God's Spirit and his holy writers. See *Witsius, Economy <note>original: "Wits. Oecon." refers to Herman Witsius's "The Economy of the Covenants between God and Man"</note> page 491.* etc.

6. §. And so as not to wander far and wide into the matter of personal types <term>voorbeelden: historical figures seen as "types" or prophetic symbols of Christ</term> such as Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Jonah, and others, I shall mention, as if in the distance, the spiritualization of Naphtali, according to *Witsius, page 461. etc. Economy*: „ What can the released hind <note>Referring to Genesis 49:21</note> better signify than a great multitude that runs somewhere with great zeal; above all, toward the fountain of life, for the Holy Spirit often compares believers to a deer, *Song of Solomon 2:7; Isaiah 35:6.* Whom, indeed, could one more fittingly understand by him who gives beautiful words than Jesus Christ, upon whose lips grace had to be poured out, *Psalm 45:2.* Why should one not wish to believe that Jacob, when he predicted the lot of his sons, spoke of the same?

7. §. It would lead too far afield if I attempted to provide the Reader with a sample of everything, and to show in what manner various ancient Teachers have translated and spiritualized different things, persons, histories, etc.; however, I must provide some examples so that the Reader may notice that it is quite an old, known, and tested path which I have followed in this work.

*Augustine once said that the kingdom of Israel, and all the kings of God's people, are a great prophecy of the kingdom of God the Savior. Justin, in his book against Trypho the Jew, Cologne Edition pages 313-314-338-361-364, applied himself to find and demonstrate a type and anti-type in Moses' staff, in Jacob's marriage to Leah and Rachel, and in the red thread given to Rahab by the spies. And Irenaeus, Book 4, Chapter 2, asserts that the journey of Israel out of Egypt toward Canaan served as an example of the journey of the church, which would consist of Gentiles. And thus he also spiritualized, in Numbers 12, the marriage of Moses to an Ethiopian woman, Book 4, Chapter 37; and also the case of Tamar, Genesis 38, Book 4, Chapter 42.*

*Tertullian, in "Against the Jews," Chapter 10, acts in a similar manner regarding Isaac standing ready to be offered, and regarding Joseph, in "Against Marcion," Book III, Chapter 16, and "Against the Jews," Chapter 9.*

*One can see how Melanchthon on Matthew 27, page 567, and Calvin on Genesis 37, have dealt with the spiritualization of Joseph and bringing him over to his anti-type.*

8. §. And why should I not insert here what the great Franciscus Junius has provided in his *Commentary on Psalm 2, pages 632-634, Parallels Book I, Chapter 6*: „ The land of Canaan is a type of our inheritance, and Canaan's Kingdom a type of the holy kingdom, by whose power we shall be brought to our heavenly inheritance, and the Kings governing Canaan's kingdom are types of Christ. And subsequently, he speaks in a broader explanation thus: „ The types of the ancients consisted either of persons—namely: Judges, Kings, Priests, and Prophets; or of things—such as the Tabernacle, temple, the ark, the altar and the ornaments, and such like; or properly of deeds—like offerings, sacrifices, first-fruits, the flood, the passage through the Red Sea and Jordan, and many more. The learned world knows that I could produce an extensive list of old and new Writers, if I were only inclined to make a task of it here; but by naming only a few, I shall let an entire army stand still.

Our learned Annotators <note>The "Kanttekenaars" were the scholars who provided the official marginal notes for the Dutch "Statenvertaling" Bible</note>, for whom the Christian world holds a singular respect with great reason, have in many places in their remarks given evidence that they thoroughly understood types, allusions, and such matters. It will not be necessary to write out their very words, as they can be found in their notes on *Gen. 22; Num. 4; on Num. 18; Num. 11; Judges 16; Num. 58; Hosea 3; Num. 4; Psalm 45; Num. 2; Jonah 2; Num. 10:20; Revelation 17; Number 28;* and in many other places.

And with a very broad pronouncement on this, Munsterus <note>Sebastian Münster, a famous 16th-century Hebraist</note> in his Preface...

And so that I do not exceed my scope, I further point out to my reader that the study of examples <term>voorbeelden: also known as "types," these are historical people or events intended by God to symbolize later spiritual truths</term>, spiritual applications, allusions, and whatever else may be of this nature, is not new, but already old. It has been beloved and practiced by prominent pillars and lights of the church; in which exercise some have expressed themselves more broadly, and others here and there from time to time, showing themselves not at all a stranger to this practice; such as Roelof Pieterse, in his *Praise of Christ and the Church*, Taylor, Robinson, Burman, Bierman, Herminkhuizen, Botsak, Bauman, etc. See Gomarus on *Matthew 11:23.* Rivet regarding Joseph, on *Genesis 41 and 46.* Witsius in *Economy & Miscellanies.* <note>Referring to Herman Witsius's *De Oeconomia Foederum* (Economy of the Covenants) and *Miscellanea Sacra* (Sacred Miscellanies)</note>

9. §. Furthermore, it will (as I see it) not be out of place for me to provide the reader with what the learned have judged should be observed in the treatment of these types, in which I shall be as brief as the matter will allow.

That which Gulichius has noted in *Prophetic Theology, Sacred Hermeneutics, Part I. pages 83-92, 93* <note>Latin: *Theologia Prophetica* and *Hermeneutica Sacra*</note>, I think, will provide the reader with taste and pleasure.

That due to the very close relationship and fellowship found between the head, Christ, and the body and its members—yes, mutually between the Jews—it should by no means seem strange that one prays and speaks for the other, and that they sometimes replace one another. „ For, says His Honor <note>referring to Gulichius</note> regarding this fellowship between the head „ and the members, so it happens that not only David, but also Christ, joining himself „ through a communion with his members, imitates their speech: for an „ intercessor who presents the desires of others to a king, if they are „ just, or if they are the known will of the one who explains them, seems to „ demand for himself what he requests for those he loves: and Christ demands our „ goods for himself, because he is our head, and we are his body. All the „ benefits of God which are bestowed upon the elect and believers, Christ receives „ in them, as in his members, *Psalm 68:19. Ephesians 4:8.* Let the reader refer „ to Mr. Vitringa, *Sacred Observations, Book 6. Chapter 20.* <note>Latin: *Obſervat. Sacr. Lib. 6. Cap. 20.*</note>

10. §. And although some matter or person might be considered as a type, it does by no means follow in respect to every typical thing or person that all the circumstances with which the thing or person is clothed are typical for this reason. And regarding this, one must take heed of what Campegius Vitringa has noted on *Isaiah, part 1, page 156, and part 2, page 539*; *that one must transfer the principal characteristics and the most emphatic sayings to a higher mystical sense.* <note>original: "hoogeren geheimzin"</note> For it often happens that many and various things are told of that which serves as a type which belong only to the type itself, and should by no means be transferred to the antitype <term>tegenbeelt: the New Testament reality that fulfills the Old Testament "type" or shadow</term>. Therefore, one must very attentively note what is actually and essentially intended to constitute the actual comparison according to the meaning of God's Spirit, or not. See Spanheim in *Evangelical Doubts, part 2, pages 479-633.* <note>Latin: *Dubia Evangelica*</note> Witsius, *Economy, page 490.* Glassius, *On Types, page 331, Canon 2.* <note>Latin: *De Typis*</note> Tako Haio vanden Honert, in his *Treatise regarding Melchizedek, defended, page 692.* etc.

11. §. The learned have also noted that there are divine oracles <note>original: "Godtsſpraken"</note> and prophecies which have a composite, joined, and twofold sense, and therefore also a twofold fulfillment and literal sense, of which the first takes place in the type, and the second in the antitype—of which the latter is always the most excellent. For example, *Hosea 11:1* compared with *Matthew 2:15*, is applicable to both Israel and Christ. See Spanheim, *Evangelical Doubts, part 1, pages 100-101-295. part 2, page 501.* Witsius, *Economy, page 490.*

And because the spiritual sense is the most excellent, and many persons and things have a typical regard to Christ and to that which descends from him, the head, down to his members, one becomes aware through accurate treatment of the types and antitypes that there is far more excellence in the antitype than in the type; because in the antitype is found the spirit, the substance, the essence of the matter, but in the type, only the letter and shadow. See Glassius, *On Types page 331. Canon 3.* Witsius, *Economy page 490.* Spanheim, *Evangelical Doubts, part 2, page 370:* Gulichius in *Prophetic Hermeneutics, part 1, page 15. Paragraph 37.* Saldenus in *Leisure, page 277.* etc.

12. §. Furthermore, I note that some view as typical that which has been done and occurred in an unusual manner, whether according to divine command or through unusual divine influence, having some resemblance to Christ,

It was beloved and put into practice by prominent pillars and lights of the church. In this exercise, some have expressed themselves more broadly and extensively, others only now and then here and there, showing themselves to be not at all a stranger to this practice; such as Roelof Pieterse, in his *Praise of Christ and the Church*, Taylor, Robinson, Burman, Bierman, Herminkhuizen, Botfak, Bauman, etc. See Gomarus on *Matthew 11:23.* Rivet regarding Joseph, on *Genesis 41* and *46.* Witsius in *Economy & Miscellany.*

9. §. Furthermore, it will (I believe) not be out of place for me to provide the reader with what the learned have judged should be observed in the treatment of types <term>voorbeelden</term>, in which I shall be as brief as the matter will allow.

That which Gulichius has noted in *Prophetic Theology, Sacred Hermeneutics Part 1, pages 83-92, 93*, will, I think, appear to the reader with taste and pleasure.

That due to the very close relationship and communion which is found between the head, Christ, and the body and its members—yes, mutually between the Jews—it should by no means seem strange that one prays and speaks for the other, and that they sometimes replace one another. „ For, says His Honor regarding this communion between the head „ and the members, it so happens that not only David, but also Christ, joining Himself „ through a commoning <note>vergeenzaminge: a rare term for identifying or unifying oneself with others</note> with His members, imitates their speech: for an „ intercessor, who presents the desires of others to a king, if they are „ just, or if he knows the will of the one he explains them to, seems to „ demand for himself what he asks for those he loves: and Christ demands our „ goods for Himself, because He is our head, and we are His body. All the „ benefits of God, which are directed to the elect and believers, „ Christ receives in them, as in His members, *Psalm 68:19. Ephesians 4:8.* Let the reader refer to Mr. Vitringa, *Sacred Observations, Book 6, Chapter 20.*

10. §. And although some matter or person might be considered a type <term>voorbeeldt</term>, it by no means follows regarding every typical matter or person that every circumstance with which the matter or person is clothed is typical for this reason. And concerning this, one must observe what Campegius Vitringa has noted in this regard in his work on *Isaiah, part 1, page 156, and part 2, page 539*; namely, that one *must transfer the most important characteristics and the most emphatic sayings to a higher mystery.* For it often occurs that many and various things are told of that which serves as a type, which belong only to the thing that is a type, and must by no means be transferred to the antitype <term>tegenbeelt: the New Testament reality that fulfills the Old Testament type</term>. Therefore, very careful attention must be paid to what is actually and essentially there, which is directed—or not—to constitute the actual comparison according to the meaning of God's Spirit. See Spanheim in *Evangelical Doubts, part 2, pages 479-633.* Witsius, *Economy, page 490.* Glassius, *On Types, page 331, Canon 2.* Tako Haio vanden Honert, in his *Treatise on Melchizedek, defended, page 692,* etc.

11. §. The learned have also noted that there are oracles and prophecies which have a composite, joined, and twofold sense, and therefore also a twofold fulfillment and literal sense, of which the first takes place in the type, and the second in the antitype, of which the latter is always the most excellent. For example, *Hosea 11:1* compared with *Matthew 2:15*, is applicable to both Israel and Christ <note>Hosea 11:1 says "Out of Egypt I called my son," which historically referred to the nation of Israel, but in the New Testament is applied to the child Jesus</note>. See Spanheim, *Evangelical Doubts, part 1, pages 100-101-295, part 2, page 501.* Witsius, *Economy, page 490.*

And because the spiritual sense is the most excellent, and many persons and things have a typical regard for the Christ, and for that which descends from Him, the head, down to His members, one perceives by a careful treatment of the types and antitypes that there is far more excellence in the antitype than in the type; because in the antitype is found the spirit, the reality, and the essence of the matter, but in the type, the letter and the shadow. See Glassius, *On Types, page 331, Canon 3.* Witsius, *Economy, page 490.* Spanheim, *Evangelical Doubts, part 2, page 370.* Gulichius in *Prophetic Hermeneutics, part 1, page 15, Paragraph 37.* Saldenus in *Leisure Hours, page 277,* etc.

13. §. It was noted above in *Paragraph XI* that one sometimes encounters a composite meaning, where the literal sense applies to the example <term>voorbeeld: a "type" or historical foreshadowing</term>, and the spiritual sense applies to the counter-image <term>tegenbeelt: an "antitype" or the spiritual fulfillment, usually Christ</term>. From this principle, one sees that the type and the counter-image appear with one and the same name, while maintaining a single literal sense, yet also possessing a hidden, spiritual, or more sublime application. See *Spanheim* in *Evangelical Doubts, Part 2, page 506.* *Saldenus* in *Leisure Hours, page 279.* As an example, *Exodus 12:46*, *not one of his bones shall be broken*, literally refers to the Passover lamb, but spiritually to Christ. Likewise, through the name "David," we literally understand the king in Israel, but spiritually, the Christ, who is represented by David. *Jeremiah 30:9. Ezekiel 34:23, 24; 37:24, 25. Hosea 3:5. Isaiah 37:35; 55:3. Amos 9:11. Acts 13:34; 15:16.* etc. See *Campegius Vitringa on Isaiah 55:3.*

14. §. Furthermore, nothing is considered typical <note>original: "voorbeeldig"</note> that is in any way contrary to the rule of faith, to the holiness of God and men, or to the truth of the statement. On the contrary, it would contain something absurd if one attempted to interpret it without any relative regard to Christ and His works. See *Gulichius* in *Prophetic Theology, Part 1, Sacred Hermeneutics, page 6, Paragraph X.* *Saldenus* in *Leisure Hours, pages 265-271.* Also *Rivet* on that passage.

15. §. Subsequently, that which—through a pleasant and clear deduction—can be proven to belong to Christ outside of the Tabernacle service, and which contains a mystery that contributes exceptionally to true wisdom and godliness, should also be regarded as typical. It should be noted that it is not clearly stated in all places, regarding all persons and things, what is a type of this and what is not. For what else should one think of Abel, Enoch, Noah, Melchizedek, Joseph, and many others?

16. §. Thus, various things and persons can be regarded in their capacity as being typical, even though it is not emphatically written that they are "types." This is the case when there is not only some similarity between persons and things occurring in the Old and New Testaments, but also when the transfer of a name from one thing to another, or from one person to another, is clearly observed. This is seen in how the name of the Passover Lamb, of David, and of the Mercy Seat <term>verdoendekzel: the golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant, representing God's throne of grace</term> is transferred to Christ. See *Gulichius* in *Preface to Prophetic Theology, page 12, Paragraph 29; page 13, Paragraph 30. Glassius, Part 2, page 330. Saldenus in Leisure Hours, page 263.* etc.

17. §. To wrap up the matter more closely and briefly: the Jewish Tabernacle service, with all its belongings, was typical.

18. §. Out of caution in commending this study, this precautionary rule has also been used: that one must not regard all things between which some similarity is perceived as types and counter-images. Rather, this should only occur when a person, thing, or deed appearing in the Old Testament is, according to the intention of the Lord’s Spirit, transferred to Christ, His cause, and His actions. See *Spanheim, Evangelical Doubts, Part 2, page 518.* And *Gomarus*, in *Theological Works, Volume I, pages 299-423; Volume II, page 174*, says: *“One must not establish any prophetic types unless the Holy Scripture leads us in this; and it is also certain that in some historical things of the Old Testament something hidden and typical is enclosed; yet which things these are must be drawn from the explanation of the Prophets and the Apostles, and by no means be dipped from the fountain of our own brains.”* Very sweetly and emphatically, *Cocceius* said on *Isaiah 22*: *“Whenever the Holy Scripture does not show that we must observe the image of another thing in some matter—even though the various things explained by Scripture might possess some similarity—we cannot firmly establish that this is a figure or type of that, except insofar as the equality is demonstrated from the comparison of the Holy Scriptures, etc.”* See *Hendrik Groenewegen on the Catechism, questions 6 and 66.* and *Gulichius, Sacred Hermeneutics, Part 2, page 81.*

19. §. *Herman Witsius* in *Economy, page 589* would seem to want to go a bit broader when he writes:

> "to which it has a similarity with the type, then it is established with right and

> "unless someone thought it better to suggest that the
> "similarity perceived between an artistic painting and the painted subject
> "was caused more by chance than by the intent of the master artist,
> "which is outside of and against all reason."

21. §. Next, I will also say a very few words regarding the Parables, and that which pertains to this work of mine.

The famous Mr. Campegius Vitringa, in his *Treatise on the Evangelical Parables*—which make up a significant portion of Jesus Christ’s Gospel teaching—can be consulted on pages 1–2, etc. Likewise, Salomon Glassius in *Sacred Philology* <note>original: "Philol. Sacr. Lib. 2. pag. 1. Tract. 2. Sect. 5."</note>, who has set forth the description of a <term>Parabel: a parable</term> in this manner: that it is a similitude or comparison in which some matter is aptly feigned and narrated just as if it had truly happened, and is compared with some spiritual matter, or applied and transferred to the same, in order to signify its meaning. Yet, Mr. Campegius Vitringa, judging that this description lacked something, added the following: that parables contain a narrative, not of all sorts of things, but of common things, or those known in the common intercourse and social life of men; this is done to teach and clarify other excellent and more hidden matters that are harder to understand. For in a parable, two things—one of which is less noble and more common, and the other more excellent and of a more sublime nature—are compared with one another through a fictional story in such a way that the first brings light to the latter. Therefore, we judge that one may best describe a parable in this way: that it is a narrative of a common matter, known in general use, as if it had happened, for the purpose of clarifying a matter that is more sublime and less known, by comparing the one with the other. See also Johannes d’Outrein’s *Introduction to the Parables*, page 4.

22. §. And regarding the distinction between a parable and an <term>voorbeeldt: an example or "type"</term> or <term>figuure: a figure</term>, Campegius Vitringa also gives a very precise account on this:
> "p. 2. A parable is thus distinguished from an example and a figure <note>original: "Typus & figura"</note> in that those usually signify either specific things or true events
> "that are or have been in the world; whereas a parable is an entire narrative of a
> "happened event which is generally feigned, and is aptly transferred by the wit to learn, instruct, exhort, or reprove. Although
> "it can also happen that the matters narrated in the parables as having happened
> "may indeed have truly occurred among men, since parables are borrowed from the common usage of men. Yet a teacher using parables pays no heed to that; since he brings forward such matters—which might truly have happened among men—as if they were feigned and invented, insofar as it serves
> "his purpose, which is the very soul of the parable."

And his Reverence, proceeding further, shows how a parable is distinguished from an <term>allegorie: an allegory</term> or figurative way of speaking, writing thus: "In the same way, a parable is distinguished from an allegory, as the latter presupposes a matter that truly happened and is
> "described in history. And a parable differs even more from a History and an example,
> "both of which concern things that truly occurred, which frequently do not
> "signify anything more sublime or excellent than the event narrated." See also d’Outrein in his preface to the parables of the New Testament, pages 4, 5–6.

23. §. That parables and similitudes have been used through almost all ages to teach something ingeniously in a pleasant and meaningful way is abundantly known from the Divine secret-scroll <note>The Holy Bible</note> and from the writings of the Egyptians, Arabs, Jews, Greeks, Romans, Tyrians, etc. See one or two samples of this in the Divine Word: Judges 9:8, 2 Samuel 12:7, Isaiah 5:1, 2, etc. In the New Testament, there are also several. That such was the custom of the Heathens <note>Non-Christian nations of antiquity</note> I shall attempt to show with Huet’s *On the Origin of Fables* <note>original: "de Orig. Fab: pag. 9."</note>. And certainly, it can hardly be believed how inclined these peoples are to poetry, how ready to invent, and how fond of fables. All their speeches are strewn with figures; they express their thoughts only through figurative sayings; their theology, philosophy, and especially their ethics and politics are swaddled in the wrappings of fables and parables. And speaking of the Egyptians, he says: The <term>betekenisbeelden: hieroglyphs (literally "meaning-images")</term> of the Egyptians sufficiently show how that people was infatuated with mysteries. Almost all things were shown among them through other forms, and they had turned the habit of expressing all things through images into an art; for the matters of their religion, as if covered under a wrapping, were not opened to the common people except under a veil of fables.

And regarding the Persians, etc., his Reverence writes: As for the Arabs, if you look closer at their works, you find nothing in them but improper and far-fetched expressions. 21. §. Next, I will also say a few words regarding **Parables**, and that which belongs to this work of mine.

The renowned Mr. Campegius Vitringa, in his *Treatise on the Evangelical Parables* <note>original: "Verhandeling van de Evangelische Parabelen"</note>—which make up a significant portion of Christ Jesus's Gospel teaching—can be consulted on pages 1–2, etc.; as well as Salomon Glassius in *Sacred Philology* <note>original: "Philol. > " p. 2. And his Reverence, continuing, shows how a parable is distinguished from an **allegory**, or figurative speech, writing thus: "In the same way, a parable is distinguished from an allegory: as the latter assumes a matter that truly happened and is described in history. Let this be enough for my purpose regarding this matter.

24. §. I well know that others before me in their writings, here and there—and most having made a start in this regard piece by piece—have granted me not only the lead but also the material for this work of such great scale and heavy undertaking. If anyone then thinks lightly of my labor, let him grant me only to be the echo of these men.

> ->We pluck the final voices and words of those before us,<- <note>original: "Carpimus extremas voces & verba priorum"</note>
> ->Of the ancients: we who write now are the echo.<- <note>original: "Priscorum: qui nunc ſcribimus, echo ſumus."</note>

> ->[*We follow the sound of those who wrote before us.*<-
> ->*For us, only the echo has remained.*]<-

The state of this century is such that I can easily foresee that I would not satisfy everyone: and what mortal has ever been found capable of it? I knew well that I had not looked through everything to its deepest foundation with the utmost accuracy. I notice that it has sometimes happened to me, as it also happens in respect to others, that one allows oneself to be carried away by the name and prestige of learned men, without bringing everything to the test and touchstone with the greatest precision. Often, one also presents the thoughts of other men, not with an aim to examine and weigh them oneself, but to share them with the Reader where it is appropriate, letting them be worth to the Reader as much as they may.

Let everyone use his judgment and keep his freedom: even if he does not agree with all my views, I will not call him a blockhead in my heart, nor regard him as biased. Everyone has his judgment, freedom, and choice, and I have mine: never have I sought out any <term>last</term> <note>A wooden model of a foot used by shoemakers to shape leather; the author is saying he does not try to "tailor" his work to fit everyone's specific prejudices.</note> to prepare shoes for every person's feet upon it.

I confess, I am a man, I am subject to error; but I know that by fate all are subject to it with me. If there is something defective here and there in my work, or something to be criticized here and there, may one cover it and overlook it in love, being mindful that no perfect work can come forth from imperfect men. Otherwise, if someone wishes to reject everything, let him let me keep what is mine, and give certain proof that he understands the art more perfectly, and bring something more exquisite to light.

25. §. I have made use of the thoughts of many writers and learned men in this work in such a way that I have tried to present their thoughts, as far as possible, honestly with their own words: not because I lacked matter for speech, but because in many occurring matters I had nothing that was better. I have added little or nothing to strike through anyone's opinion. Everyone writes, I thought, according to his ability; everyone has his judgment: and in a work of this nature, as this is, I judged it more fitting to present the thoughts of many, than to make of the work a rebuttal and a satire.

I intended to pick out from the writers that which served my plan and purpose, letting each keep what is his, along with his due honor, so that while I praised some writers, I might make them known, in case they might not be known to some. At least, many men do not have the writings of all learned people: it is also not convenient for everyone to buy or read all books: therefore I believed I was not deceiving myself when I thought that I would do the reader no disservice when I brought together the labor and thoughts of many learned men in this work with much effort, as far as I understood it to belong to the matter and my intent.

26. §. I have submitted my written draft, for the purpose of compiling this <term>Dictionary</term> <note>original: "Woortboek"</note> from it, to the judgment of many learned Gentlemen, Professors, and Ministers, and to the subscribers...

# PREFACE.

...[undertak]ers of the work granted the freedom to let my manuscript be brought before the eyes of such learned men as they might please; which undertakers also by no means neglected to solicit written testimonials from learned men.

Meanwhile, something negative reached my ears from the sidelines, though for the most part from people who had never seen the work, its arrangement, or its substantive content up close: from people who gladly wished to be seen as wise and learned, and, swollen with windy wisdom, imagined they were bringing forth heavenly revelations and oracles. Such people, and others with them, claimed the work was too extensive and that it ought to be much shorter and more concise; some spoke of it as if it were merely a book of notes. There were those who attacked the style. In their opinion, the work ought to have been composed in a high-flown style and proud language, since the world nowadays is fastidious and refined. Many also exerted their utmost strength to help stifle the work, had it been possible for them; and it is not unknown to me from what principle of envy and with what intentions this occurred. Just as I also have grounds and reason to think regarding such people that they themselves, being unable to do without the work, will yet show on many occasions that they have seen and read it closely.

But, what may seem strange to anyone, hardly had this class of people heard that the work was undertaken and about to be brought to the press, than they changed their tune: everyone had their remarks. Furthermore, they no longer balked at the extensiveness; but Reader (who would not be highly provoked?), then they began to say that quite a few necessary things had been overlooked, many things from antiquity not cited, merely to shorten the work; various texts had been passed over which also ought to have been mentioned and clarified, and whatever else the spirit of fault-finding could bring up. Behold here the inconstancy of men. It was said outright, *the Author ought to enlarge the work by another two or three hundred sheets.*

27. §. Leaving these people to themselves, I prefer to thank, before the whole world, the Lords Professors and Ministers who have been pleased to occupy themselves with reading through my manuscript pieces and to deign to favor me with their kind testimonials, both oral and written. Among these, I have a great obligation to the Gentlemen Johannes Hagelis, Wigbold Muilman, Henricus Velse, Johannes Regnerus Kelderman, Johannes Hermanus Brender à Brandis, etc., Ministers in Amsterdam, The Hague, Utrecht, and Dordrecht, because their Reverences occupied themselves and deigned to accurately look through my transcripts, to let their remarks reach my hand, and also to give me the opportunity for these and other further thoughts and considerations of the same.

And I neither will, nor can, conceal that I have a singular obligation to Mr. David van Hoogstraten <note>David van Hoogstraten (1658–1724) was a prominent Dutch physician, poet, and scholar known for his work on Dutch grammar and Latin literature.</note>, Doctor of Medicine and Assistant Rector of the Latin School at Amsterdam, the Phoenix of contemporary poets and champion of pure language-lovers, because his Reverence kept a careful eye on my work and took upon himself the trouble of translating many Greek and Latin verses, cited from ancient writers, into Dutch rhyme; and for enduring the burdensome correction of the printed sheets, which was utterly impossible for me due to the great distance.

28. §. Believe truly, beloved Reader, that I could have expanded my thoughts much further, which perhaps would not have been untimely in various places, had I not dreaded even the appearance of sought-after long-windedness. I also comforted myself somewhat by thinking: *a.* man’s lifespan is short, and distractions are many. *b.* A single man cannot bring a major piece to its perfection. *c.* I imagined that once I laid the bridge, blazed the path, and brought the structure to some height, some capable and favorable minds would later appear who, from the treasury of their well-worked collections, would wish to provide us with abundant material and opportunity to bring this work to greater perfection. *d.* To which end I would already set myself, if anyone during my lifetime and with sufficient strength came to my aid in this regard, as I would very gladly attempt to fill in what is missing by way of a supplement.

29. §. Furthermore, I do not expect that anyone will want to attack and nitpick <note>original: "muggeziften"—literally "gnat-sifting," a Dutch idiom for pedantic hair-splitting.</note> one word or another, or the spelling; and if it should happen, I shall endure it, and leaving every man to his own taste, concern myself little with it, and follow my habit, continuing only to strive that I may be understood. And this is enough for me, insofar as it found approval with Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" of the early church.</note>: *we shall have no dispute over words, so long as the syllables lead us to the same sentiment.* And Cicero in the third book to Herennius <note>Referencing the *Rhetorica ad Herennium*, a classical text on oratory formerly attributed to Cicero.</note>, *when the matters are understood...* <note>The author leaves this quote unfinished as he moves to the next page.</note>

<summary>In this preface, the author defends his work against contradictory critics who first called it too long and later too short. He expresses gratitude to the scholars and ministers who supported him, particularly David van Hoogstraten for his help with classical verses and proofreading.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the preface of Martinus Koning’s dictionary. It transitions from the previous page's discussion of critics who claimed the work lacked certain antiquities or historical details.</meta>

# PREFACE.

[antiquities] be understood, *then we are easy about the words*. <note>A Dutch idiom meaning that if the meaning is clear, one should not fuss over the specific vocabulary used.</note> It would truly be a poor reward for my tenacious labor and many nights spent awake if people were to show displeasure at the mere shell of the words. However, if anyone finds pleasure in doing so, let them wear their teeth down, for I know that such shadow-boxing usually occurs not so much over the essence and weight of the matters, but rather over the words themselves.

30. §. But before I make an end to this Preface, I have deemed it necessary to inform the Reader that, although this Dictionary of mine did not come out at its strictly appointed time, such a delay is to be attributed neither to me nor to the printers. I have provided them with sufficient manuscript from time to time, and they have already progressed far in the printing of the third volume of this work, as can be seen at the house of the publishers. Therefore, the actual and true reason for this delay is that one cannot strictly limit and define artists <note>original: "konstenaars," likely referring here to the engravers responsible for the book's illustrations</note> in all their parts—and all the less so when it is perceived that they, mindful of their honor, do not come forth with botched engravings, but strive to give the utmost pleasure to lovers of art.

Meanwhile, the world owes no small debt of gratitude to the two Brothers, the noble undertakers <note>referring to the publishers/financiers</note> of this Dictionary, without whose request and encouragement I would have let it remain resting among my other writings. I am particularly obliged to them for bringing it forth so neatly and elegantly, whereby the slight delay in publication is richly compensated.

31. §. And since it has come to my ears that there are some who have tried to give the world the impression that I might have made use of Mr. Ruimich’s Emblematic work, <note>Ruimich published an illustrated book of emblems or moral allegories shortly before this work.</note> which appeared some time ago, I find myself compelled to openly oppose this manifest untruth. I testify that it is no less than twenty years ago that I commenced this Dictionary, and that it has lain finished in my possession for a good seven years; and these two Brothers, the undertakers of the same, had already agreed to the printing of this work lying by me before I knew that a Mr. Ruimich or his Book of Emblems existed in the world.

32. §. Lastly, let it serve as a preliminary notice that the Subscribers shall receive the Frontispiece, the Dedication, and the necessary Indexes with the final two volumes.

33. §. I shall make an end, having expressed my meaning in these letters, hoping and praying to God that He may sanctify you, beloved Reader, to the knowledge and pursuit of His truth. I testify that my labor shall have carried away its best reward when I perceive that I have edified you and given you true pleasure; with which I remain your servant seeking your salvation in Christ,

->MARTINUS KONING.<-

*At Nieuwpoort in Holland*
*the last of May*
1722.

# A.
### See ALPHA.

<margin>Eel named *Anguilla*, because of its similarity to certain snakes.</margin>
The **EEL** has been described by *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar known for his work on animals in the Bible.</note> and *Hofmann* as being named <term>Tzelachah</term> / <term>Tzalachat</term> / <term>Alchat</term> <note>original: "צלחה / צלחת / אלחת", Hebrew terms discussed by scholars as potentially referring to the eel</note>; in Greek <term>egchelys</term> <note>original: "ἔγχελυς"</note>, and in Latin *Anguilla*.

In Latin, the Eel seems most likely to have been named *Anguilla* because it has some commonality with the snake, called *Anguis* in Latin, regarding its slipperiness, its writhing movements, and the general shape of its body.

<margin>Where it is mostly found.</margin>
It is found and caught in the sea, as well as in the mouths of rivers, though more abundantly in inland waters. *Pliny* and others record that it is neither found in the cold Danube, nor can it live there.

<margin>Eel described.</margin>
It is somewhat round, stretched out in length, ending in a pointed and somewhat flat shape; it is slippery and smooth of skin. From this arose the proverb used to express something that lacks full certainty and that one could very easily lose or miss: <margin>What is meant by "having an eel by the tail."</margin> *one has a slippery eel by the tail*. For this reason, in order to be manageable and held firmly, it is rolled in sand.

<margin>Birth and reproduction.</margin>
Whether the breeding of eels occurs through eggs, or if they are born from the dew, and how the matter stands in this regard, I shall leave to the investigators of Nature <note>The author refers to "naturalists" or early scientists who debated spontaneous generation vs. biological reproduction.</note> to settle.

<margin>An unclean fish.</margin>
Although eels have small fins to some extent, they nevertheless have no scales, and are therefore a species of fish that, according to Divine Law, is unclean. *Leviticus 11:9, 10, 11, 12.*

<margin>Cannot tolerate murky water:</margin>
According to what we find in experience, this fish cannot thrive or live well in murky water, even though it may love loose, slippery, and marshy grounds.

<margin>Nor can it endure thunder.</margin>
It cannot well endure thunder, which stirs the bottom and makes the water murky; it is because of this that they are mostly caught, which gives rise to the proverb: *It is good fishing in murky water.*

<margin>Unhealthy food.</margin>
Eel-meat is considered by many to be a very delicious food, <term>the greatest of delicacies</term> <note>original: "τῶν ὄψων μέγιστον"</note>, although because of its tough sliminess, it is by no means considered among the healthiest by *Galen* <note>An influential ancient Greek physician.</note>, *Beverwijck* <note>Johan van Beverwijck (1594–1647), a famous Dutch physician and author.</note>, and many others.

Among the Egyptian follies and superstitions, it is noted among other things that they worshipped eels as gods. The comic poet *Anaxandrides* says:

> <term>You hold the eel to be your greatest God,</term> <note>original Greek: "Τλὼ ἔγχελυν μέγιστον ἡγῆ Δαίμονα"</note>
> <term>While we hold it by far as the greatest of delicacies.</term> <note>original Greek: "Ἡμεῖς δὲ τῶν ὄψων μέγιστον παραπολύ"</note>

<margin>Egyptian idolatry and superstition regarding the eel.</margin>
->[*You hold the eel as your greatest God.*<-
->*We hold him, for the sake of lovely delight,*<-
->*As the noblest of all table dishes.*]<-

See *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Vossius, a renowned 17th-century Dutch scholar.</note> *On Idolatry, book 4, chapter 29*; *Herodotus* in *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus's "Histories".</note>, and *Antiphanes* in *Athenaeus*, who in his comedy wittily mocks them for this reason; whose words Hugo de Groot <note>Also known as Hugo Grotius, the famous Dutch jurist and scholar.</note> has thus translated in his excerpts:

> <term>Then they say the Egyptians are clever in other matters,</term> <note>original: "Tum rebus aliis ajunt esse Ægyptios / Solertes"</note>
> <term>as well as in this, that they equate the Eel to the Gods.</term> <note>original: "tum quod Anguillam equiparant Diis."</note>
> <term>Indeed, she is far more precious than a god.</term> <note>original: "Quin verò longè eft illa dis pretiofior."</note>
> <term>For the Gods grant themselves to us for prayers alone;</term> <note>original: "Nam folis precibus nobis fe indulgent Dii;"</note>
> <term>But as for her, when you have given ten solid drachmas,</term> <note>original: "At illam, drachmas folidas cum dederis decem,"</note>
> <term>Or somewhat more, one is finally scarcely allowed a sniff.</term> <note>original: "Aut plus aliquanto, olfacere vix tandem licet."</note>
> <term>Such great sanctity does that animal possess within itself.</term> <note>original: "Tantam habet in fe animal illud fanctimoniam."</note>

->That is:<-

> *That the Egyptians are great clever-clogs, I have heard tell,*
> *Since they place an eel among the Gods.*
> *Indeed, they have set a much higher price upon it:*
> *For the Gods listen to our prayers for nothing:*
> *But if you want to have an eel to use for your food,*
> *Then you must blow hard into your purse, and then you may only just have a sniff.*
> *Such a great sanctity does that animal contain.*

<column-break/>

<margin>No intentional mention of these fish in God's Word.</margin>
It does not occur to me that God's Spirit has anywhere spoken of this intentionally or with any emphasis, or made any allusion to it by way of comparison. However, I can allow that one may regard the eel—being slimy and smooth, without a covering of scales, keeping itself in the marshy mud, unable to endure murky water or the bursts and cracks of thunder—as a symbol for many and quite various kinds of people: such as

<margin>However, one can make an application of it,</margin>
To people who are entirely natural, not having the Spirit, and being stripped of the covering of Jesus' righteousness— <margin>To natural men.</margin> <note>In 17th-century theology, a "natural man" is someone living only by human instinct and reason, without divine grace or spiritual rebirth.</note>

<meta>This page continues the entry for "Aal" (Eel), focusing on its metaphorical use in emblems and proverbs regarding social unrest and unreliable character, before transitioning to the new entry "Aangezicht" (Face).</meta>

...righteousness, and all the true adornment of the Holy Spirit: people who swim along the bottom, people who are of this earth, whose portion is in this life, who mind earthly things. *Psalm 17:14; Philippians 3:18, 19.*

<margin>Easily startled and terrified.</margin>
Of people who, lying in the world with heart, mind, and thoughts—and as if drowned in it—nonetheless cannot endure the "troubled water" of necessity, disturbance, and adversity; they become despondent and are easily captured and mastered.

Of people who, though they live in the mire of sin and the filth of fleshly movements and lusts, and even wallow in them (*Isaiah 57:10*), nonetheless cannot or will not endure the "thunder-speeches" and "lightning-bolts" of threats from the Law, or sharp rebukes (*Amos 5:10*). Instead, they run, flee, and because of the pangs of conscience, can find no resting place. *Proverbs 38:1; Joshua 48:22 and 57:31; Romans 2:9.* <note>The author uses these biblical citations to compare the slippery, mud-dwelling nature of the eel to the spiritual instability of sinners.</note>

<margin>Tolerating no rebuke or threat.</margin>
Of people who are not only rarely found or spoken with at home (which is why it is said, *He is as hard to catch as an eel by the tail*), but upon whose words, promises, nature, and so forth, one can place very little or no reliance.

<margin>Unstable, inconstant people.</margin>
When one recalls that the eel cannot well endure truly troubled water, and that fishermen—seeking to catch a fine batch of them—must stir the bottom and make the water muddy and turbid, one notices that this proverb is used to signify that when the State and the citizenry are in turmoil and the rabble is master, spoils are often made to the sorrow and damage of others; and that sometimes the lowliest sort of men attain status, offices, and positions of honor. *Franzius* in *On Animals* noted it thus on *page 580.*

<margin>Fishing well in troubled water: how this is to be understood proverbially regarding the rabble.</margin>
> In discord, even the worst man attains honor.
> <note>original Greek: "Ἐν δὲ διχοστασίῃ καὶ πάγκακος ἔμμορε τιμῆς." A common ancient Greek proverb regarding political instability.</note>
>
> [*The base rabble attains honor and status when the State is in turmoil.*]

To which end some well know how to make use of disturbances, misunderstandings, quarrels, divisions, and riots with this very goal, to the sorrow, damage, and shame of many. *Alciatus, Emblem 88.* <note>Andrea Alciato (1492–1550) was the author of the first "Emblem Book," which combined images and mottos to teach moral lessons.</note>

> *Whoever seeks to catch eels, if he sweeps clear*
> *Rivers, or dares to approach mudless lakes,*
> *Will be empty-handed and waste his effort. Let him therefore stir up*
> *Much chalk, and let his hand disturb the glassy waters,*
> *And he shall be rich. Thus a troubled Republic is a gain to those*
> *Who, restricted by laws in peace, go hungry.*
> <note>original Latin: "Anguillas quisquis captat..."</note>

-> That is: <-

> *He who wishes to catch eels, and fishes in clear water,*
> *Will soon find that he misses his mark.*
> *But if he chooses to stir the clear water with an oar,*
> *He shall carry away many fish according to his wish.*
> *Thus one sees that the State in unrest gives profit*
> *To those who would have lived in need during peace,*
> *When the laws kept their greed in check.*

Claudius Minoïs <note>Claude Mignault (1536–1606), a famous commentator on Alciatus's emblems.</note> in the notes on Alciatus, *page 339,* quoting Aristophanes: <note>From the play "The Knights," where a politician is compared to an eel-fisherman who only catches anything when he stirs up the mud.</note>

> For you are like those who hunt for eels.
> When the lake is still, they catch nothing.
> But if they stir the mud up and down,
> They take them; and so you take, when you disturb the city.
> <note>original Greek: "Ὅπερ γὰρ οἱ τὰς ἐγχέλεις θηρώμενοι πέπονθας..."</note>

<column-break/>

-> Which amounts to this: <-

> *You follow the example of the eel-catchers.*
> *When the water is still, there is nothing to catch. But as soon*
> *As the water is disturbed, it begins in the pools*
> *From all sides to swarm and teem.*
> *And the fisherman, once he has set out his gear,*
> *Finds a rich catch in his net.*
> *Thus you seek to disturb the whole State,*
> *To carry away great spoils in that unrest.*

Lucan, in *The Civil War, Book 1.*

> *Hence comes devouring usury, and time greedy for interest,*
> *And shattered credit, and war profitable to many.*
> <note>original Latin: "Hinc usura vorax, avidumque in fœnore tempus, Et concussa fides, & multis utile bellum."</note>

-> Which is as much as: <-

> *Here grows usury and greed of a base nature,*
> *Violated trust, and war, which brings profit to many.*

# FACE, <term>Panim</term> / <term>Prosopon</term> / <term>Facies</term>, <term>Vultus</term>, also <term>Opsis</term>.
<note>original: "פנים / πρόσωπον / facies, vultus, ook ὄψις." The author provides the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin terms for "face."</note>

**THE FACE** is the front part of the human head, which is the uppermost part of the body. <term>Panim</term> comes from <term>Panah</term> [meaning] he has beheld, looked somewhere, turned himself, or moved toward or away from something. <term>Prosopon</term> from *pros* and *ops*, [meaning] before or near the eye, as they say.

It is a wonder-work of the mighty and perfectly wise Craftsman <note>A common theological reference to God as the "Artifex" or Divine Architect.</note> that among so many hundreds of thousands of people, no two are found who are fully and in all things identical to one another; although there are examples of those who could hardly be distinguished from one another, of which I could bring forth countless examples from historical records. However, there must be some distinction for identification: so that Augustine, with right and reason, calls this a great wonder in his writings against the Pagans <note>Likely referring to *The City of God*, Book 18, Chapter 8.</note>, *Chapter 8.*

<margin>The Human Face, a masterpiece.</margin>
It bears a reflection of God’s image, face, and majesty. There is something exalted in it; Constantine, in the law <term>Si quis in Metall.</term> <note>Refers to a law in the Codex of Justinian (C. de poenis) regarding punishments.</note>, abolished branding on the face, giving as the reason: *so as not to disfigure the face, which is drawn after the likeness of divine beauty.* Micaiah suffered great indignity when blows were given to his jawbones by Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah. *1 Kings 22:24.* Job also had experience of this, *Chapter 16:10.* Furthermore, one reads more of it, such as *Psalm 3:8.* Spitting in the face is also taken very ill and as a great insult, *Job 30:10; Numbers 12:14.* This happened to the Messiah. *Isaiah 50:6; Matthew 27:30; Mark 15:19; Luke 18:32.* This crime, it is said, had to be atoned for among the Jews with two hundred drachmas or 30 guilders. *Bava Kama, Chapter 8.* <note>The Bava Kamma is a section of the Talmud dealing with civil matters and damages.</note>

<margin>Beauty not being taken away by branding, hitting, spitting, etc.</margin>
After Carolus Paschalius, in his book *On Crowns*, Chapter 51, Section 3, had spoken extensively of the excellence of the human head, *page 289, etc.,* in which human dignity chiefly shines forth, he proceeds to the consideration of the front part of the head, the face; and citing various writers, he expresses himself in this manner: *Who does not stand amazed at the other thing which is attributed to the face, which face is an image of the mind: for, because the forehead...*

<meta>This page transitions from the entry on the "Aal" (Eel), which concluded with reflections on social instability and unreliable characters, to a new, extensive entry on the "Aangezicht" (Face). It establishes the face as the mirror of the soul and the site of divine reflection.</meta>

# FACE.
A 2
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

The head is the upper lintel of man; therein are seated Dignity and Majesty. Shame, though hidden in the heart, leaks out through the eyes—eyes which nature has made remarkable for their softness, sharpness, and fire. Within the nose hides Ingenuity. And in the cheeks, the noble blush of modesty swells forth. From the tongue rolls the salt of wisdom: finally, in the <margin>* Atticus: an entire being is not just, as he says, an affection, that is, an Attic visage <note>Aristophanes, *The Clouds*; Erasmus, *Adages*, p. 305. The "Attic face" refers to a style of bold, unshrinking speech associated with Athens.</note>, an unabashed face <note>original: "bakhuis," a colloquial term for a face or "mug."</note> that boldly dares to say and blurt out everything, and knows nothing of flinching or blushing.</margin> Attic face, but also a divine one. Certainly, the face in a human is what a prow is to a ship, what the zodiac is in the heavens, and what the image is in a signet ring. There, the living and express likeness is found—that is, the whole person.

Therefore, it has been said that the face is the mirror of the soul. For however the mind may be inwardly disposed, it is very difficult for a person's face to conceal it.

-> *O, how difficult it is not to betray a crime by the face!* <note>original Latin: "O quam difficile est crimen non prodere vultu!"</note> <-

-> That is: <-

-> *How hard it is to hide a fault through the sight of the face!* <-

<margin>How the Face is sometimes understood.</margin> The Face of man is sometimes understood in a narrower sense as man’s most elevated, vivid, and excellent upper part. For God

-> *Gave to man an uplifted face.* <note>original Latin: "Os homini sublime dedit," from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.</note> <-

-> That is: <-

-> *Fashioned man with his face and eyes looking straight upward.* <-

Wherein one sees the eyes, eyebrows, nose, mouth, lips, cheeks, the chin, etc. Sometimes it is understood more broadly, as the principal part representing the whole—for the person themselves and their presence, as seen in *Acts 3:13* and *5:41*, *2 Corinthians 4:6*, etc.

<margin>Expressions concerning the face.</margin> Regarding the Face now, whether understood in narrower or broader senses, the following figures of speech may serve: *to cover the face*, or *that it be covered*, as an act of shame or indeed of disgrace. *To disfigure the face* through despondency and despair, gloom, or an over-studied humility, even feigned godliness. *To bow the face* as a sign of reverence and humility. *To turn the face toward someone*, or *to turn it away from someone*, a sign of affection and esteem, or of aversion, displeasure, and contempt, which is sometimes followed by anger and plagues. *To let the face be seen*, or *to hide it*, a proof of rejection and displeasure, or of favor and intimacy, etc., of which more shall be spoken in detail hereafter.

<margin>Face attributed to God, angels, and animals.</margin> One sees that a face is attributed in Holy Scripture to God, angels, and animals (in visions), and to the heaven and earth (as a surface or appearance), though often metaphorically and according to imagination.

One finds that the Jews, whether within or outside of Palestine, when praying and offering sacrifices, turned their faces toward the Sanctuary, and specifically toward the Holy of Holies, as the learned and diligent Professor Campegius Vitringa points out in *Archif. page 179 etc.*, citing Rabbenu Asher's *Commentary on Megillah Chapter 3: 36-38*. This rests on a common rule found among the ceremonies in the *Orach Chayim <note>A code of Jewish Law</note>, Chapter 94, 51*, because in the Holy of Holies was found the Ark of the Covenant, alongside the <term>Kipporet <note>Hebrew: כפורת, the Atonement Cover</note></term> or <term>hilasterion <note>Greek: ἱλαστήριον, the Mercy Seat</note></term>, the golden mercy seat. On this, the aforementioned Professor says: "For just as the entire Ark was a representation of Christ, so the mercy seat primarily represented <term>atonement <note>Greek: ἱλασμὸν (hilasmon)</note></term>, the reconciliation which we have in Christ, our intercessor and mediator with his Father. Paul, in his Letter to the Romans, even calls Christ the <term>mercy seat <note>Greek: ἱλαστήριον</note></term> or the atonement, *Romans 3:25*: 'Whom God set forth to be an atonement through faith in his blood.' Under the Old Testament, the <term>Kipporet / hilasterion</term> (the mercy seat) was covered with a certain precious veil, because the ransom by which atonement and redemption were to happen had not yet been paid; but in the New Testament, the veil is torn—that is, according to the Apostle, the flesh of Christ being broken on the cross—so the entire ark, along with the mercy seat of the ark and all things which were in this most holy place, are seen and set plainly open before everyone’s eyes. Compare this with *Revelation 11:19* and *1 John 2:2*." This holy covenant-chest with the mercy seat upon it was as much as God’s throne of grace; therefore, they had to turn their bodies and eyes toward it. But we, in the New Testament, turn toward Christ, who is in the heavens (*Matthew 6:9, Hebrews 6:16*) and has brought about the reconciliation. <margin>The turning of the face toward the East, and toward the Holy of Holies.</margin>

### The Face of God.
<margin>God's Face.</margin>

When one remembers that God is an infinite, absolutely perfect, and simple spirit, having no flesh and bones, and therefore cannot fall under the sight of our physical eyes (*John 4:24, 1 Timothy 6:16*), one can easily imagine that the term "face" cannot be applied to God literally. However, one must seek the ground for this application and attribution in the contemplation and observation of His essential virtues and perfect attributes, which are perceived in His works. <margin>Not to be understood literally or physically.</margin> <margin>Yet finds its basis in His virtues and works.</margin>

One learns to know and distinguish someone by the rays on their face and the reflection of light from their face. Each person has a distinct disposition and form of the face.

I, along with many scholars, prefer to understand the Face of God as God's essential virtues, attributes, and perfections, by which He is not only distinguished from the idols of the Heathens, but also has no one who is His equal. These attributes—primarily regarding righteous punishment and the gracious deliverance and salvation of sinners—shine forth as if from a mirror, with the depiction and mention of God's virtues and works with which Holy Scripture is filled.

God has shown these virtues and perfections in a singular and emphatic way in His Son, His express image, and the radiance of His glory—or glorious reflection—to which the following passages are usually applied: *Exodus 23:20, 21* and *33:14, 15*; *Isaiah 19:2* and *63:9*; *Matthew 3:2*. There He is called the Face, the Angel of the Face, and the Angel of the Covenant. See further "God's image" and "express image" in *Colossians 1:15* and *Hebrews 1:3*; that he who has seen Him has seen the Father (*John 14:9*). This Son is also <margin>The Son of God is, in an emphatic way, the reflection of His Father’s face and image.</margin>

...righteousness, and all true adornment of the Holy Spirit: people who swim along the ground, people who are of this earth, whose portion is in this life, who mind earthly things. *Psalm 17:14; Philippians 3:18, 19.*

<margin>Easily startled and terrified.</margin>
Of people who, lying with their hearts, senses, and thoughts in the world—and as if drowned in it—nevertheless cannot endure the troubled waters of necessity, disturbance, and adversity; they become despondent and are easily captured and mastered.

Of people who, though they live in the mire of sin and the filth of fleshly movements and lusts, and even wallow therein—*Isaiah 57:10*—nevertheless cannot or will not endure the thunder-speeches and lightnings of threats from the Law, or sharp rebukes—*Amos 5:10*—but run, flee, and can find no place of rest due to the constraints of their conscience. *Proverbs 28:1; Joshua 48:22 and 57:31; Romans 2:9.*

<margin>Enduring no rebuke or threat.</margin>
Of people who are not only seldom to be found or spoken to at home (which is why it is said: *He is as easy to catch as an eel by the tail*), but upon whose words, promises, nature, and such, one can place very little or no reliance.

<margin>Unstable, inconsistent people.</margin>
When one remembers that the eel cannot well endure troubled water, and that fishermen, seeking to catch a fine haul of them, stir the bottom and make the water muddy and troubled, one notices that this proverb is used to signify that when the State and the citizenry are disturbed, and the rabble is master, a catch is often made to another’s grief and damage, and that sometimes the lowliest sort of men attain statehood, offices, and positions of honor. Fransius <note>Wolfgang Franz (1564–1628), a Lutheran theologian known for his work on animals in the Bible.</note> noted this in his work *On Animals* <note>original: "de Animalibus"</note>, *page 580.*

### FACE, פנים, πρόσωπον, facies, vultus, also ὄψις.
<note>The entry provides the terms in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.</note>

THE FACE is the forward part of the human head, which is the highest part of the body. *Panim* <note>Hebrew: פנים</note> comes from *panah* <note>Hebrew: פנה</note>, meaning he has beheld, looked somewhere, turned himself, or moved toward or away from something. *Prosopon* <note>Greek: πρόσωπον</note> comes from *pros* (towards) and *ops* (the eye or face), as it were, "before the eyes."

<margin>The human face a work of wonder.</margin>
It is a wondrous work of the mighty and perfectly wise Master Craftsman that among so many hundreds of thousands of people, no two are found who are fully and in everything identical to one another; although there are instances of those who could hardly be distinguished from each other, of which I could bring forth countless examples from the histories of the times. Nevertheless, there must be some difference for recognition: so that Augustine, with right and reason, calls this a great wonder in his work against the heathens <note>likely referring to *The City of God*</note>, *Chapter 8.*

<margin>Beauty stripped away by branding, striking, spitting.</margin>
It bears a reflection of God’s image, face, and majesty. There lies something sublime within it; Constantine <note>Roman Emperor Constantine the Great.</note> in the law *si quis in Metall. C. de pœnis*, abolished branding on the face, giving as a reason that the face, which is drawn after the likeness of divine beauty, should not be defiled. Micaiah suffered great indignity when he was given blows to the jaw by Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah. *1 Kings 22:24.* Job also had experience of this, *Chapter 16:10.* Furthermore, one reads more of this in *Psalm 3:8.* Spitting in the face is also taken very poorly and as a great insult, *Job 30:10; Numbers 12:14;* it also befell the Messiah. *Isaiah 50:6; Matthew 27:30; Mark 15:19; Luke 18:32.* This crime, it is said, had to be atoned for among the Jews with two hundred drachmas or 30 guilders, *Bava Kama Chapter 8.* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning civil matters and damages.</note>

After Carlo Pasquale <note>original: "Carolus Paschalius," 1547–1625, an Italian diplomat and writer.</note> in his book *On Crowns* <note>original: "de Coronis"</note>, *Section 1, Chapter 3*, had spoken at length and breadth of the excellence of the human head, *page 289, etc.*, in which human dignity primarily shines forth, he proceeds to the consideration of the forward part of the head, the face, and citing various writers, expresses himself in this manner: *Who is not also stunned by that other quality which is attributed to the face, which face is an image of the mind: for, because the forehead...*

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the "Face," specifically focusing on how God’s character and presence are revealed through the "Face of the Son" (Christ) and various biblical idioms involving the face.</meta>

# FACE.

the Father in his virtues, and emphatic name and works, has shown and explained, *John 1:18 and 17:6–26 according to Ps. 22:23, 2 Cor. 3:18, and 4:4–6.*

<margin>Further explained.</margin>
Certainly, in the Son we see God’s Face; that is, how holy, righteous, wise, mighty, faithful, merciful, and gracious the Lord is; with what wisdom and propriety he decrees and governs all things, and with what power he sustains everything. From his Son radiates a light of wisdom and purity for knowledge and joy, as he is the way, the truth, and the life—the light in which one, beholding the light, is made joyful, *Ps. 36:10 and 89:16, 17.*

Which face or virtues God now no longer covers with clouds and curtains, or keeps hidden in the Holy of Holies, *Isa. 45:15, Ps. 104,* but lets be seen without the veil and clouds of old shadows and riddles, both in his Son and in the Gospel, in the year and the day of his good pleasure and salvation. *Isa. 40:5–9 and 49:8, 2 Cor. 3:18, Eph. 1:6, 7.*

<margin>Terms and expressions regarding the faces of God and men, explained.</margin>
After all this, we wish to mention and explain the particulars for understanding the scriptural terms and expressions concerning the face of God and of men more closely.

<margin>The face as the principal part, taken for the whole, the person themselves, and their presence.</margin>
1. The face, as the foremost, uppermost, and most visible and recognizable part, is often taken for the entire person. For since one has a person present when beholding their face, the face is taken for a person’s presence, whether a man or God himself: for their presence, appearance, or being in their sight. Of men, *Job 33:5, Ps. 23:5 and 34:1, Acts 3:13, Isa. 2:17.* Of God, *Gen. 17:1: Walk before my face and be upright. Gen. 32:30, Exod. 20:3, Prov. 8:30.* This signified as much as God’s extraordinary self-manifestation and revelation.

2. And since it sometimes differs greatly how someone behaves or appears when present—whether one has someone for or against them, as a friend or an enemy—it is noted that a person’s face is sometimes taken for their favor. Upon this depends service, help, and benevolence, especially when the face is pleasantly, lovely, and joyfully spread out, as if smiling upon one. Thus it is requested of God that his face might shine, *Ps. 4:7 and 31:17*; therefore it is taken for favor, and applied to men *Exod. 16:15* to draw some advantage from someone in their presence *1 Kings 10:24.*

3. And when, in a fierce, stern, and surly face, the eyes are deep-set, and the eyebrows and forehead are wrinkled and frowned, it is considered a sign of wrath or perceived displeasure; because one usually perceives someone’s inner emotions from the face, the eyes, and the nose <note>In Hebrew thought, the nose is often associated with anger, as "flaring nostrils" signify rage</note>. Especially when the face becomes inflamed or falls, etc., so one might think, upon finding such terms, whether they were intended to convey someone's wrath or anger. By this passion, when someone is inflamed in spirit, they are to be feared and avoided, *Jer. 1:8, Ps. 34:17, 1 Pet. 3:12.*

4. A stiff face *Deut. 28:50* <term>bold or hard of face</term> <note>original Hebrew: "עז פנים" (az panim)</note> signifies men who are bold, daring, without any fear, hard, brave, without compassion or mercy, sparing no one.

<column-break/>

<margin>Expressions derived from the faces of God and men are also various.</margin>
And as for the full-fledged expressions derived from the face of God and of men, these too are various and do not all convey the same meaning.

1. *To set one's face against someone* surely signifies no good, but rather being incensed with someone, and is the countenance with which God has sometimes caused his judgments to be announced. *Lev. 17:10 and 20:5 and 26:17, Ezek. 4:3 and 13:17, etc.*

2. *To lift up one's face, or not to lift it up, but to cast it down along with the eyes, or to cover it:* signifies either joy and boldness, or sadness, shame, or embarrassment, *Job 10:15, 16 and 11:15 and 22:16, Ezra 9:6, Luke 18:13.*

3. *To fall down on one's face* can be interpreted in various ways, depending on whether one wants to show great fear of someone, or to pray and supplicate with earnestness, being the greatest act of self-annihilation and humiliation. *Gen. 17:7, 1 Sam. 25:23, Dan. 2:46, Job 7:6, etc.*
It is also associated with humility and shame, *1 Sam. 20:41, 1 Chron. 21:16, 1 Cor. 14:35.*
This also happens when one is entirely listless, extremely distressed, defeated, embarrassed, amazed, or horrified, *Ezek. 1:18 and 11:13, Num. 16:45, Dan. 8:17, Matt. 26:38, Luke 5:8.*

4. *To stand before someone's face* concerns those bound to service, and what inferiors ought to do before their superiors: to keep an eye on the gestures of the throne or chair, and to show diligence in hearing and executing their commands. If someone gapes, looks about restlessly, far and wide, or turns the face away, it shows little esteem or awe, alongside a lack of desire to understand obedience, *Deut. 1:38 and 10:8, Esther 7:9, Dan. 7:10, see further Jer. 2:27 and 32:32.*

5. *To accept or take up someone's face and person* means to be a respecter of persons, a favor-seeker, or a seeker of profit in things where it is not appropriate, such that one twists the law and violates truth, justice, and love. See examples of this in *Lev. 19:15, Deut. 1:17, Job 13:8 and 32:21 and 34:19, Ps. 82:2, Prov. 18:5 and 24:23, Mal. 2:9, Luke 20:21.*

6. *To appear before God's face, Ps. 100:2, etc.*—that is, to come to where he wishes to dwell, where he places the signs of his favorable and powerful presence and the symbols of his Son the Messiah, desiring to be sought, served, honored, and glorified through prayers, thanksgivings, etc., as was known to happen in the Tabernacle and the Temple.

7. *To behold God's face*, especially when he lets it shine over someone. See also under BEHOLDING. This is when the Lord, in emphatic power and with the display of his virtues as a God of the covenant of grace, lets himself be seen, known, and enjoyed in the Messiah, through firm tokens of his favor, sufficiency, and powerful help, *Ps. 4:17 and 89:16, 17, etc.*

8. *God's*
