<meta>This page continues the discussion of "the Face," transitioning from the general theological definition of God's face to specific biblical instances, notably the radiant face of Moses and the metaphorical concept of "cleaving" or "clinging" to God.</meta>

# FACE.

8. *Seeking God's face*, Ps. XXVII. 8. etc. can signify an earnest investigation of God in the power of his virtues, in the glory and fame of his name and works, in order to intelligently—in faith and love—recognize, serve, boast of, and praise him; to delight in him, and to bless and boast in him, insofar as he has declared himself in his Son to be able, willing, and destined to be, and has effectively become a God to the sinner through the revelation of his virtues.

### The Face of Moses.

<margin>The Face of Moses was very radiant.</margin>
Regarding what happened to Moses—Israel’s Leader, Mediator, and Lawgiver—in his face, and what he did concerning it, one can read *Exod.* XXXIV. and 2 *Cor.* III. 6, etc. Namely, that Moses' face, by virtue of long and close interaction with God and the Angel of the Covenant <note>The "Bondengel" or Angel of the Covenant refers to a divine messenger often identified in Christian theology as the pre-incarnate Christ.</note> on the Mountain, was so radiant and beaming with rays that Israel could not look him firmly, steadily, or boldly in the face, nor did they dare to look at him without trembling. The people's eyes became as if dimmed; their sight failed and became blunt, faint, and dull. Some believe they have found so much justification in the word <term>קרן</term> <note>Hebrew: qaran</note>—meaning a horn, strength, power, or by extension a projected ray, from which <term>קרן</term> <note>qaran</note> means to shine, light, and to emit rays from oneself in the manner of protruding horns. *Exod.* XXXIV. 29, 30—that they have felt entitled to paint Moses with two horns protruding from his forehead. However, the actual reason for this was <term>כי קרן עור פניו</term> <note>Hebrew: ki qaran 'or panaw</note>, *that the skin of his faces, or his face, had sent forth rays or shone*, <note>original Latin: "quod promicuiffet, feu resplenduiffet cutis facierum fuarum, feu faciei fuæ"</note> that is: *because the outer skin of his face had shone*, *Exod.* XXXIV. 29, 30. Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic.</note> translates it: *that there was a great splendor of glory upon his face.* <note>original Latin: "quod multus effet fplendor gloriæ faciei fuæ"</note>

How long this glory remained with him, I cannot say, except that it eventually vanished.

Moses' face, or the appearance he made because of his high Offices among Israel—namely, his introduced laws and ministry—was quite precious, magnificent, and glorious; both because of the manner in which it was introduced, and because of everything external that belonged to the place of service and the performance of the service. This was very precious and magnificent due to the gold, silver, sculpture, and embroidery, though it all had to grow old and vanish.

By Moses covering his face as Lawgiver for Israel's sake, it is considered not inaptly portrayed how great a veil <note>The Dutch "deksel" literally means a lid or cover, here used for the veil Moses wore.</note> his ministry brought over the word of grace and the doctrine of the promise. It also foretold with what kind of veil—both of the sight and of the heart—Israel was to be covered, *Deut.* XXIX. 4. and XXXII. 28, 29. *Isa.* VI. 10. *Jer.* V. 21.

Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original Latin: "More Nebochim"</note>, Book 3, Chap. 9, says: *The Law was given on a cloudy day to express a veil that turns away a true vision; but that veil of the eyes and the heart, consisting of blindness, prejudice, and the Lord’s judgment, shall one day be taken away.*

Believers of the New Testament behold with unveiled faces the Lord's glory, as in a mirror, in him who is God’s image and the reflection of his glory; in his person, virtues, works, and the Evangelical word, which has been richly poured out, relieving man of the yoke, servitude, fear, death, and damnation: filling and adorning the understanding and the heart with knowledge, holiness, love, and joy, leading to an ever-increasing radiance and ornament of all kinds of virtues.

On this subject, studious seekers of knowledge may consult *Cocceius* on 2 *Cor.* III; *Witsius' Economy* pages 621, 622; and *Miscellanea* part 1, pages 1-17; *Vitringa's Sacred Observations* part 1, page 117; *Camero* page 204; and, if anyone desires, also my own *Expansions* on 1 *Cor.* XI and 2 *Cor.* III, as well as my *Miscellanies*, Volume I, on *Isa.* XI. 11, 12. etc. I shall say no more of it.

### CLINGING, CLEAVING,
### <term>דבק</term> <term>κολλᾶσθαι</term> <note>Hebrew: dabaq; Greek: kollasthai</note>, *to adhere, to glue together*. <note>original Latin: "adhærere, agglutinare"</note>

<margin>Clinging or cleaving is a word of singular power.</margin>
**T**his is a word of power and emphasis, and is used on various occasions to signify something that is firmly joined and united with something else. The Hebrews expressed this through the word <term>דבק</term> <note>dabaq</note> and the Greeks through <term>κολλᾶσθαι</term> <note>kollasthai</note> or <term>προσκολλᾶσθαι</term> <note>proskollasthai</note>. Similarly, the Latins use the word *agglutinare* or *adghuinare*, to join together, to glue firmly to one another—namely, things that were previously separate and individual: just as *gluten* and *glutinum* serve as words for glue.

<margin>The union of things as if glued together.</margin>
Now, it is well known how certain things are firmly attached by glue. In ancient times, glue or the gluey, slippery water of the Nile was used for paper. One also knows how mud and clumps of clay cling together.

<margin>It is used to depict the close unity and strong bond of husband and wife.</margin>
These words, being meaningful and powerful, are found used by God's Spirit to express and depict the closest communion and the firmest, most unbreakable union between husband and wife, who have rights to and power over each other and each other's bodies; so that while this bond and union stands, they may unite with no one else, *Gen.* II. 24. *Matt.* XIX. 5. *Mark* X. 7.

<margin>Used in a bad sense regarding a harlot.</margin>
To consort with a harlot, to unite with such a one according to the flesh as one would live with a wife, practicing base lust, is called *cleaving to a harlot*, 1 *Cor.* VI. 19.

<margin>Used for idolatry as a spiritual whoredom.</margin>
Because idolatry is spiritual whoredom, the act of practicing idolatry—coupling oneself to it—is called whoring, or even cleaving to it. Thus one reads of King Joram, son of Ahab, that he cleaved to the sins of Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, 2 *Kings* III. 3.

<margin>To cleave to the Lord and be one spirit with him.</margin>
Conversely, to serve the Lord purely according to his pleasure, to make much of him and his service, to subject oneself to him alone in soul and body, to expect all salvation and protection from him, and to be of the same thought and will with him—such that one lets nothing pull them away from the Lord or his service and confession—is called clinging to or cleaving to the Lord, *Deut.* IV. 4. and X. 20. and XIII. 4. and XXX. 20. *Isa.* XXII. 5. <note>The author likely means Joshua 22:5.</note> Just as it is written of David and Jonathan in 1 *Sam.* XVIII. 1. So Asaph says in *Ps.* LXXIII. that he clings to or cleaves to the Lord.

<margin>An emblem of steadfastness.</margin>
<margin>To have a part and portion in something.</margin>
Thus it is also taken to mean remaining steadfastly with someone, not deserting them, loving them intensely, being firmly set on something, making it one's special work, and as if uniting oneself with it, *Ruth* I. 14. *Prov.* XVIII. 24. *Jer.* XIII. 11. It is also taken for

<column-break/>

Himself

BEHOLDING.

To become liable for something, and to have fellowship in it *Joshua XXIII. 22 <note>Likely a reference to Joshua 23:12-13 regarding entanglements with other nations.</note>, Ps. XLI. 9.* as opposed to guarding oneself against something, or being wary of something, *Ps. CI. 3.* for lasting judgments *Deut. XXVIII. 60.* which are attached to us and united with us, as if inseparable.

# BEHOLDING, LOOKING UPON,
<margin>Beholding and looking upon, as applied to the soul while the physical eyes perform their function.</margin>
->שבה / פנה / נבט / חזה <note>Hebrew: to turn toward, to look, to behold, to see</note> βλέπειν, ἐμβλέπειν, ἐπιβλέπειν <note>Greek: to see, to look at, to gaze upon</note>, *intueri*, *aspicere* <note>Latin: to gaze, to behold</note>, &c.<-

BEHOLDING or LOOKING UPON, as we know, occurs through the physical eyes, by which one casts their eye upon someone or something, paying attention to the nature of that person or matter.

<margin>This signifies pursuing something with the spirit: observing, paying close attention to something in order to learn from it for imitation or avoidance, or to notice something specific in a person or matter.</margin>
1. And so it is natural and fitting that beholding a person, matter, or work with a steady gaze and a careful eye implies paying intentional attention to it. It means observing everything in and around the person to adapt oneself accordingly and make use of it—whether as a lesson and model to follow, or to strengthen and comfort oneself. This is done after one believes they have encountered something extraordinary in the matter or person, *Exod. II. 11, Ps. XXXVII. 37, and XLVI. 9.* It is done to trust in God during times of need, to glorify Him for deliverances, and to abstain from wicked deeds, *Ps. LXXIII. 3.* Beholding with an "envious eye" involves watching everything closely; or with a "wise eye," observing Abraham’s unexpected and supernatural multiplication of offspring, after whose example He would also establish an abundant seed for the Church among the barren Gentiles, *Isa. LI. 1, 2.* Since the Hebrews who had confessed the Christian faith were facing persecution, reproach, suffering, and the seizure of goods by false Apostles, brothers according to the flesh, and Gentiles (incited by the Jews), Paul encourages them to self-denial, taking up the cross, willingness, and perseverance. He does this through the example of Jesus, who preceded them in this, and whose departure was a glorious reward and change of state. To follow Him, they had to constantly observe Him—His example, conduct, and end—in the race track, the arena of struggle and wrestling. They had to vividly present Him to themselves to align themselves accurately with Him: for a disciple was not better than his master. He had left them an example; He had presented Himself as a model for learning *Matth. XI. 28. etc. Matth. XVI. 24, 1 Pet. II. 21.* They were members of Christ: Christ's suffering was linked to His joy and glory, *Luke XXIV. 26, Philip. II. 8, 9, Hebr. XII. 1.* There had to be a conformity between Him and His members, *Rom. VIII. 17, 18, 2 Cor. IV. 17, Rev. III. 21.*

And considering how He had gone before them in trust and willing suffering, with the utmost courage for them and in their cause, they were moved by love for Him and gratitude for what He had done and undergone. They were to strive not only to follow in that track but also with the prospect of trust that He, who had wrought faith in them and called them to this race and arena of struggle, would also lead them, support them, deliver them by bringing them to the end, and bestow upon them the glorious joy and heavenly crown. *Isa. XLI. 14, Ps. XXXIV. 20, 2 Cor. XII. 9, 10, 2 Tim. IV. 7, 8, Rev. II. 10, 1 Cor. XV. 58.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Looking out, looking to the Lord, etc., is an image of the soul going out toward the God of the Covenant and of salvation, in faith, trust, prayer, and expectation of His merciful grace and delivering help; it sometimes expresses true conversion and the practice of internal religion.</margin>
2. When the "looking" or "looking out" of a human—the act of beholding—is fixed upon and toward the Lord, and relates to the God of the Covenant, then it signifies the outlook of the soul toward the Lord, trust in Him, and the certain expectation of His help, grace, and deliverance. This is more than just the sight of the eyes, though both are often paired: the going out of the heart and the looking out of the eyes. *Isa. XVII. 7. In that day shall a man look to his Maker, and his eyes shall have respect to the Holy One of Israel.*

When we observe the contents of the first part of this chapter, we become aware of the impending emergencies to be brought upon Damascus, the Syrians, and Ephraim.

Now, if the Israelites had a heart to notice such things, they would convert; and to do so is their duty, and it would be most beneficial for them. There would also be those who, having seen that they were deceived by false prophets and that the idols had met the fate predicted by the prophets, would return in repentance to the God of their fathers and serve Him in true faith, renouncing the errors of former times. See the History in *2 Chron. XXXIV. 9.* When God is called their "Maker" here, although He is the Creator of all creatures (and we do not wish to exclude that), it specifically refers to the making of Jacob’s descendants into His own separate people and nation: the leading out of Egypt, the guidance in and through the wilderness, the giving of the law, and the blessings in the land, *Deut. XXXII. 6.* It can also be understood in an even more sublime sense *Ps. C. 3.* because what we are in the state of grace, we are such from and through Him in the Messiah, the Angel of the Covenant, *Isa. XIV. 22, etc. Eph. II. 10, 2 Cor. V. 17, 1 Pet. II. 9.* The conversion of man is beautifully presented as looking toward and beholding God. For the entire work of Religion lies in a prudent contemplation of God <note>original: νόησις (noēsis) - intellectual perception or contemplation</note> and in an acknowledgment of God <note>original: ἐπίγνωσις (epignōsis) - precise or experiential knowledge</note> in all the perfection of His being and truth, just as He has revealed Himself in His Church to His people, accompanied by an agreement and fitting affection toward the God of Israel. This is practiced in, from, and through faith, without which one cannot please God or participate in His grace, help, and blessings. See the learned Professor Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist known for his commentary on Isaiah.</note> on this chapter and verse. *Ps. CXXIII. 1-3, Micah VII. 7, Josh. VI. 40 <note>This may be a typo in the original for John 3 or a different reference</note>,* where much light is applied to the beholding of the copper Serpent, *Num. XXI. 9, John III. 14, 15.*

<margin>Beholding and looking is attributed to God, who is a spirit: thus His seeing and beholding, especially of the miserable, powerless, and needy human, is often taken for God's compassion, grace, and help toward deliverance.</margin>
Regarding God, the act of seeing and beholding is used—even though He is a spirit and has no physical eyes—in the sense of being drawn to someone’s person, state, misery, or danger. It means He takes it to heart so that He powerfully has mercy on people, helps them, delivers them, shows grace, restores them, and blesses and does them good in a singular way, *Ps. XI. 7 and XXV. 16.* to the end, *Ps. XIII. 3, 4, 5, LXIX. 17, and LXXIV. 20.* This is so that, through the faithful promises of the covenant with their fathers, He may be ignited with inner compassion and active grace, help, and deliverance toward these children. *Isa. LXIV. 9, Ps. LXXX. 15, and CXIX. 153. Behold my misery, and help me. Luke IX. 38.*

OFFENSE.

<margin>
Also used to depict the pleasure that God takes in something.
</margin>
Again, when God is said to look upon something or to behold it, it is sometimes taken to mean beholding with pleasure and favor, such that he approves of whatever his eye is fixed upon, and he applies and maintains his powerful and gracious hand toward it. Thus the Lord looked upon Abel and his offering, *Genesis 4:4, Hebrews 11:4,* undoubtedly through a visible sign of ignition <note>The author suggests God's favor was shown by fire consuming the sacrifice.</note>, as could be observed. So too he will have had pleasure in Mary's humility according to *Luke 1:48,* following the spirit of *Isaiah 57:15, James 4:6, 1 Peter 5:5, Psalm 113:6, 7,* and *138:6.*

<margin>
God’s turning away and not beholding is taken to mean having a dislike for something, not approving it, and also making such displeasure known through punishments and judgments.
</margin>
Conversely, God is said not to look at something, or not to behold it, but to turn himself away from someone or their work; this occurs when the person, deed, or matter displeases him, and he shows his dissatisfaction, which is usually followed by his judgments and judicial punishments, *Numbers 16:15. Then Moses became very angry, and he said to the Lord, do not look upon their offering. Job 35:13, Isaiah 58:3, Amos 5:22, Habakkuk 1:13.*

<margin>
Numbers 23:21 somewhat explained.
</margin>
Yet it sounds much more favorable in *Numbers 23:21: He does not behold iniquity in Jacob, nor does he see wickedness in Israel.* Burman <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> in his *Law and Testimony* page 733, understands *vanity* to mean idolatry and every false path of righteousness, and by *trouble* he understands all labor and counsel that leads to evil; just as those two things are joined together in *Psalm 10:7* and *55:11.* It is as if to say: God has a delight in that people, because no idolatry, godlessness, or unrighteousness is prevalent among them.

Unless it might also mean that God is and remains faithful nonetheless, even if Israel might be unfaithful—that he overlooks the evil, forgives it, and does not always wish to punish according to strictness in his Jacob and Israel, such that he would withhold his deliverances, blessings, and promises on that account. Furthermore, one can look into what Polus <note>Matthew Poole (1624–1679), author of the *Synopsis Criticorum*, a massive compilation of biblical commentary.</note> has brought together on this passage from many prominent scholars.

### OFFENSE, STUMBLING BLOCK,
### <note>Hebrew: מכשול, מכשלה / נגף</note> Stumbling block, obstacle / plague; <note>Greek: προσκοπὴ, προσκόμμα, σκάνδαλον</note> offense, stumbling block, snare; *to give or set an offense*, <note>Hebrew: נתן / שום מכשול</note> to give or set a stumbling block; <note>Greek: προσκοπὴν διδόναι, πρόσκομμα τιθέναι</note> to give an offense, to set a stumbling block; *to cause to stumble*, <note>Hebrew: הכשיל</note>; *to stumble, to be offended*, <note>Hebrew: כשל</note>; <note>Greek: προσκόπτειν, σκανδαλίζεσθαι</note> to stumble, to be scandalized; *stumbling*, <note>Hebrew: חתי</note>; <note>Latin: scandalum, offendiculum, scandalizare, dare scandalum, ponere, jacere, ut quis offendat & impingat, enz.</note> scandal, hindrance, to scandalize, to give offense, to place, to throw, so that one might offend and strike against, etc.

<margin>
The root words explained, and the foundation laid for further clarification.
</margin>
CONCERNING OFFENSE or GRIEVANCE, according to the power and meaning of the original languages: I have found, regarding the Hebrew, in Buxtorf, Schindler, Cocceius, Leigh, Avenarius, etc. <note>A list of prominent 16th and 17th-century Hebraists and lexicographers.</note> that they all signify something in the way, and in human dealings, which affects them so strongly that they could easily strike against it, fall, stumble, hurt themselves badly, sprain their feet, etc.

And when this is transferred to the mental concepts and moral conduct of man, it can be understood as something—posed and brought forth through words, teaching, conduct, and the customs of someone—which stops someone, strikes them, is a hindrance, and prevents them from accepting something, doing it, or

<column-break/>

going forward and persevering in that which, if it had not occurred to them, they would likely have done otherwise.

As for the Greek words, regarding these I find that they mostly agree in meaning, for *proskope* <note>original: προσκοπὴ</note> (offense) comes from *proskopto* <note>original: προσκόπτω</note>, "I strike against with the foot or feet," such that the striking can be so strong that actual foot injury, spraining, weakening of the foot, falling, and stumbling follow.

<margin>
*proskope*: a hindrance, a stumbling block.
</margin>
Offense or grievance (*proskope*) is therefore taken for that which possesses the power to strike someone, make them strike against something, and to offend them; which offense can be worked out with and through someone's words, customs, and deeds, regarding matters which are held to be either permitted or forbidden. By these, one could offend someone, stop them, push them back, make them hesitate, and, after a confession has been made, cause them to withdraw from the congregation of believers—at least for some time, causing them to fall into doubt, to stand still in their previous confession, not to come forward as openly as a believer, nor to join the assembly of believers as before. Thus they are hindered from using the necessary nourishment for the soul and the means for sharpening their soul and spiritual desires for the practice of, and progress in, all kinds of Christian duties of virtue.

<margin>
*proskomma*: a hindrance, a stumbling injury.
</margin>
So too *proskomma* <note>original: πρόσκομμα</note> is taken for a hindrance, a stone of offense, a stumbling block, a stone of hindrance, which one lays in the way so that someone strikes against it, falls over it, and injures themselves on the block.

And from this, the word *skandalon* <note>original: σκάνδαλον</note> (offense, grievance) does not deviate much, as is said of *skazo* <note>original: σκάζω</note>, "I limp, I go lame." Thus a *skandalon* is something against which—being hard, heavy, and not yielding to the striking and movement of the feet on the path—one can strike their feet in such a way that they stumble, plop down, injure their feet, become weak, sprain them, and go lame.

This having been brought forward for some light and preliminary information, I proceed to the symbolic use.

a. We read of something that is an offense, gives offense, of a stone of stumbling, a rock of offense, of an offense to sin and stumbling, etc.

I follow the Scripture passages, insofar as they provide me with an occasion for explanation.

<margin>
Matthew 16:23 explained.
</margin>
*Matthew 16:23. But turning around, he said to Peter, get behind me, Satan, you are a stumbling block to me.* <note>original Greek: σκάνδαλόν με εἶ. original Hebrew: למכשול.</note>

You are an offense to me as much as is in you, and regarding your speech and discouragement: for you would, through a fear of reproach, pain, and shame, try to lead me away from the duty of required obedience and submission to my Father; you want to stall the work of the salvation and deliverance of sinners, which I have taken upon myself, as much as is in you. In my way and course, you lay a hindrance, a striking and stumbling block, either to remain standing still or to turn back; you are then an adversary to me, and highly hindering; therefore, get away, go behind me, and be no longer a hindrance to me in my work and purpose, as much as is in you or concerns you.

<margin>
Romans 11:9 and Psalm 69:23 explained.
</margin>
*Romans 11:9. And David says: Let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling block, and a recompense for them.*

The Messiah, having been greatly persecuted, despised, and scorned by his enemies in *Psalm 69:23,* prays and wishes...

<meta>This page continues the lexicographical study of "Beholding" (Aanschouwen), moving from its use in contexts of judgment and shared guilt to its primary spiritual meaning: a focused, soulful gaze upon God and Christ’s example. It correlates physical sight with spiritual attention and repentance.</meta>

BEHOLDING.

To involve oneself in guilt, and to have fellowship in it, *Joshua 23:22, Psalm 41:9,* in contrast to guarding oneself against something or watching out for something, *Psalm 101:3.* It also refers to lasting judgments *Deuteronomy 28:60* which are, as it were, stuck onto us and united with us as being inseparable.

### BEHOLDING, LOOKING AT,
<margin>Beholding or looking at, as applied to the soul, while the eyes perform their physical function.</margin>
->To look, to turn toward, to behold, to gaze <note>original: שבט (shebet) / פנה (panah) / נבט (nabat) / חזה (chazah)</note>; to see, to look into, to look upon <note>original: βλέπειν (blepein), ἐμβλέπειν (emblepein), ἐπιβλέπειν (epiblepein)</note>; to gaze, to behold <note>original: intueri, aspicere, etc.</note><-

BEHOLDING or LOOKING AT, as we know, occurs through the physical eyes, by which a person, having cast their eye upon someone or something, pays attention to what the nature of that person or matter may be.

<margin>It signifies pursuing something with the spirit, observing, or paying close attention to something in order to learn from it for the purpose of imitation or avoidance, depending on what one can remark in a certain person or matter.</margin>
1. And so it is also natural and appropriate that to behold a person, thing, or work with a steady gaze and a careful eye signifies as much as paying intentional attention to it. It means observing everything in and around the person well, in order to conform oneself to it and make use of it—whether as a lesson and example, or to strengthen and comfort oneself—after one believes they have encountered something extraordinary in the matter or the person, *Exodus 2:11, Psalm 37:37, and 46:9.* This is done to trust in God during times of need, to glorify Him for His deliverances, and to restrain oneself from wicked deeds, *Psalm 73:3.* To behold with an envious eye involves watching everything closely; to look with a discerning eye means noticing Abraham's unexpected and supernatural procreation and multiplication, following the example of which God would also provide an abundant "seed" for the Church among the barren Gentiles, *Isaiah 51:1, 2.* Since the Hebrews who had confessed the Christian faith were facing imminent persecution, insult, suffering, and the seizure of goods by false apostles, brothers according to the flesh, and the Gentiles (incited by the Jews), Paul encourages them to self-denial, taking up the cross, willingness, and steadfastness. He does this through the example of Jesus, who had gone before them in this, and whose departure was a glorious reward and a change of state. To follow Him, they had to constantly observe Him—and His example, conduct, and end—within the "race-track" and the arena of struggle and wrestling. They had to vividly set Him before themselves to carefully conform to Him; for a disciple was not better than his master. He had left them an example; He had presented Himself as a model for learning *Matthew 11:28 etc., Matthew 16:24, 1 Peter 2:21.* They were members of Christ: Christ’s suffering was linked to His joy and glory, *Luke 24:26, Philippians 2:8, 9, Hebrews 12:1.* There had to be a conformity between Him and His members, *Romans 8:17, 18, 2 Corinthians 4:17, Revelation 3:21.*

And considering that—how He had gone before them in trust and willing suffering with the utmost courage for them and in their cause—they had to strive to follow on that path, not only out of love for Him and out of gratitude for what He had done and undergone, but also with the outlook of trust. They trusted that He, who had wrought faith in them and called them to this race and arena of struggle, would also lead them, support them, deliver them by bringing them to the end, and bestow upon them the glorious joy and heavenly crown. *Isaiah 41:14, Psalm 34:20, 2 Corinthians 12:9, 10, 2 Timothy 4:7, 8, Revelation 2:10, 1 Corinthians 15:58.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Looking out, looking to the Lord, etc., and the soul's outgoing for salvation toward the Lord, etc. Covenant-trust, in faith, with prayer, and expectation of His merciful grace and delivering help: and it sometimes expresses true conversion and the practice of internal religion.</margin>
2. When the seeing or looking out of a person—this beholding—is fixed upon, toward, and to the Lord, and relates to the God of the covenant, then it signifies the soul’s outlook toward the Lord, trust in Him, and the certain expectation of His help, grace, and deliverance, rather than just the outlook of the eyes. Although, not infrequently, the two go together: the outgoing of the heart and the looking out of the eyes. *Isaiah 17:7: In that day a man shall look to his Maker, and his eyes shall have respect to the Holy One of Israel.*

When we observe the contents of the first part of this chapter, we become aware of the imminent emergencies to be brought upon Damascus, the Syrians, and Ephraim.

Now, if the Israelites had a heart to notice such things, they would repent; and to do so is their duty, and it would be most beneficial for them. There would also be those who, having seen that they had been deceived by the false prophets and that the idols had met the fate foretold by the [true] prophets, would return out of repentance to the God of their fathers and serve Him in true faith, turning away from the errors of former times. See the history in *2 Chronicles 34:9.* When God is called their "Maker" here, although He is the Maker of all creatures (and He does not wish to exclude that), it emphatically refers to the making of the descendants of Jacob into His own set-apart people and nation—their leading out of Egypt, their guidance into and through the wilderness, the giving of the law, and the blessings in that land, *Deuteronomy 32:6.* Likewise, it can be understood in an even more sublime sense, *Psalm 100:3,* because what we are in the state of grace, we are such from and through Him in the Messiah, the Angel of the Covenant, *Isaiah 14:22 etc., Ephesians 2:10, 2 Corinthians 5:17, 1 Peter 2:9.* The conversion of man is aptly presented as looking toward and beholding God, for the entire work of religion is situated in a prudent contemplation of God <note>original Greek: νόησις (noēsis)</note> and in an acknowledgment of God <note>original Greek: ἐπίγνωσις (epignōsis)</note> in all the perfection of His being and of the truth, just as He has revealed Himself to His people in His Church, accompanied by a corresponding and seemly inclination toward the God of Israel. This is practiced in, from, and through faith, without which one cannot please God or become a partaker of His grace, help, and blessings. See the learned Professor Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note> on this chapter and verse; *Psalm 123:1-3, Micah 7:7, Joshua 6:40,* where much light is applied to the beholding of the bronze serpent, *Numbers 21:9, John 3:14, 15.*

<margin>Seeing and beholding as applied to God, who is a spirit: thus His seeing and beholding, especially of the miserable, powerless, and needy person, is often taken for God's compassion, grace, and help toward deliverance.</margin>
Regarding God, although He is a spirit and has no physical eyes, "seeing" and "beholding" are used in the sense of drawing someone’s person, state, misery, or danger to His heart. This means He powerfully takes pity on people, helps them, delivers them, shows grace, restores them, and singularly blesses and does them good, *Psalm 11:7 and 25:16 to the end, Psalm 13:3, 4, 5, 69:17, and 74:20.* This is so that, through the faithfulness and promises of the covenant with their fathers, He might be kindled toward these children with inner compassion and actual gracious help and deliverance. *Isaiah 64:9, Psalm 80:15, and 119:153. Behold my misery and help me. Luke 9:38.*

It emphasizes that true religion consists of contemplating and acknowledging God's nature through faith.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the discussion on "Beholding" as a sign of God's favor or judgment and begins a new entry on the concept of "Offense" or "Stumbling," exploring the linguistic roots in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin to explain how physical obstacles serve as metaphors for spiritual hindrance.</meta>

OFFENSE.

<margin>
It is also used to depict the pleasure that God takes in something.
</margin>

Furthermore, when God is *said* to look upon something and behold it, it is sometimes taken to mean beholding with pleasure and delight. In this sense, God approves of that upon which he keeps his eye fixed, and he applies and maintains his powerful and favorable hand there. Thus, the Lord looked upon Abel and his offering, *Genesis 4:4, Hebrews 11:4,* undoubtedly by a visible sign of fire, as could be observed. In the same way, he will have taken delight in Mary's humility according to *Luke 1:48,* as well as *Isaiah 57:15, James 4:6, 1 Peter 5:5, Psalm 113:6, 7,* and *138:6.*

<margin>
The turning away and not beholding by God is taken to mean having an aversion to something, not approving of it, and also demonstrating this through punishment and judgment.
</margin>

Conversely, God is said not to look upon something, or not to behold it, but rather to turn himself away from someone or their work. This occurs when the person, deed, or matter displeases him, and he shows his rejection, which is usually followed by his judgments and judicial punishments, *Numbers 16:15. Then Moses became very angry and said to the Lord, "Do not look upon their offering." Job 35:13, Isaiah 58:3, Amos 5:22, Habakkuk 1:13.*

<margin>
Numbers 23:21 somewhat explained.
</margin>

Yet it sounds much more advantageous in *Numbers 23:21: He has not beheld iniquity in Jacob, nor has he seen perverseness in Israel.* Burman, in his *Law and Testimony* page 733, understands *vanity* <note>original: "ydelheit"</note> to mean idolatry and every false way of righteousness, and *trouble* <note>original: "moeite"</note> to mean all labor and counsel that leads to evil; just as those two things are joined together in *Psalm 10:7* and *55:11.* It is as if to say: God has a delight in that people, because no idolatry, godlessness, or injustice prevails among them.

Unless it might also signify that God, regardless of this, is and remains faithful even if Israel should be unfaithful; that he overlooks the evil, forgives, and does not always wish to punish with severity in his Jacob and Israel, such that he would withhold his deliverances, blessings, and promises for that reason. Furthermore, one can consult what Poole <note>original: "Polus," referring to the theologian Matthew Poole</note> has brought together on this passage from many prominent scholars.

### OFFENSE, SCANDAL

<margin>
Offense <note>original: נגף (negeph) / מכشלה (miksholah) / מכשול (mikshol) / דחי (dechi) / προσκοπὴ (proskope), πρόσκομμα (proskomma), Σκάνδαλον (skandalon)</note>; to give or place an offense <note>original: נתן מכשול (natan mikshol) / προσκοπὴν διδόναι (proskopen didonai), πρόσκομμα τιθέναι (proskomma tithenai)</note>; to cause to stumble <note>original: הכשיל (hikshil)</note>; to be offended or stumble <note>original: כשל (kashal) / προσκόπτειν (proskoptein), σκανδαλίζεσθαι (skandalizesthai)</note>; offense or stumbling <note>original: דחי (dechi) / scandalum, offendiculum, scandalizare, dare scandalum, ponere, jacere, ut quis offendat & impingat, etc.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
The root words opened, and the foundation laid for further explanation.
</margin>

REGARDING OFFENSE or SCANDAL <note>original: "AANSTOOT of ERGERNISSE"</note> according to the power and meaning of the original languages: I have found in the works of Buxtorf, Schindler, Cocceius, Leigh, Avenarius, etc., regarding the Hebrew, that they all signify something in the way, or in human activities, which affects people so strongly that they might easily strike against it, fall, trip, severely hurt themselves, sprain their feet, etc.

And when this is transferred to the mental concepts and moral conduct of man, it can be understood as something—placed and brought forth through someone’s words, teaching, behavior, or customs—which stops, strikes, or hinders someone, preventing them from accepting or doing something, or from proceeding and persevering in that which they likely would have done otherwise, had they not encountered it.

As for the Greek words, I find that they mostly agree in meaning; for *stumbling* <note>original: προσκοπὴ</note> comes from *I strike against* <note>original: προσκόπτω</note> with the foot or feet, to the extent that the striking can be so strong that actual injury to the foot, a sprain, weakening of the foot, a fall, and tripping follows.

<margin>
stumbling <note>original: προσκοπὴ</note>
</margin>

Offense or scandal <note>original: προσκοπὴ</note> is therefore taken for that which possesses the power to make someone strike against something and to offend them. This offense can be worked out by and through a person's words, customs, or deeds regarding matters which are held to be either lawful or unlawful. By these, one could offend someone, stop them, push them back, make them hesitate, and cause them to withdraw from the assembly of believers after having made a confession—or at least cause them to fall into doubt for a time, to stand still in their previous confession, not to come forward as openly as a believer, nor to join the assembly of believers as before. In doing so, they are hindered from using the necessary nourishment for the soul and the means for sharpening their soul and spiritual desires for the practice of and progress in all kinds of Christian duties of virtue.

<margin>
a hindrance, a stumbling block, a block in the way <note>original: πρόσκομμα</note>.
</margin>

Thus *stumbling block* <note>original: πρόσκομμα</note> is also taken for a hindrance, a stone of offense, a stumbling block, or a hindering stone which one lays in the road so that someone might strike against it, fall over it, and hurt themselves.

And not far from this is the word *scandal* <note>original: Σκάνδαλον</note>, offense or scandal, which is said to come from *I limp* or *I go lame* <note>original: σκάζω</note>. Therefore *scandal* <note>original: Σκάνδαλον</note> is something against which one—since it is hard, heavy, and does not yield to the striking and movement of the feet on the road—can strike their feet in such a way that they trip, thud down, hurt their feet, become weakened, sprained, and go lame.

This having been brought forward for some light and preliminary information, I proceed to the symbolic use.

a. We read of something that is an offense, that gives offense, of a stone of offense, a rock of scandal, of an offense unto sin and stumbling, etc.

I follow the scriptural passages insofar as they provide me with a lead for opening the meaning.

<margin>
Matt. 16:23 opened.
</margin>

*Matthew 16:23. But turning around, he said to Peter, "Get behind me, Satan! You are an offense to me."* <note>original: Σκάνδαλόν μου εἶ / למכשول</note>

You are an offense to me as far as it lies within you and your speech and discouragement: for you would try to lead me away from the duty of owed obedience and submission to my Father through a fear of contempt, pain, and shame; you wish to obstruct the work of the salvation and redemption of sinners, which I have taken upon myself, as much as in you lies. In my path and course, you lay a hindrance, a striking- and stumbling block, either to make me stand still or to turn back; you are then an adversary to me, and highly hindering; therefore, get away, get behind me, and as far as it lies in you, be no longer a hindrance to me in my work and purpose.

<margin>
Rom. 11:9. Ps. 69:22 explained.
</margin>

*Romans 11:9. And David says: Let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling block, and a recompense for them.*

The Messiah, having been greatly persecuted, despised, and scorned by his enemies in *Psalm 69:22,* prays and wishes...

# OFFENSE.

<note>original: "Aanstoot"</note>

...wishes upon them from God the severest blindness, hardening, punishment, and judgment, as his defeated enemies. It was true that the temple, altar, etc., had been his house, table, fire, and hearth, just as it was the workshop of the Priests and Levites, and the altar was their table, from which service they were accustomed to live. Now that the Messiah, the antitype <note>The "antitype" is the New Testament fulfillment of an Old Testament "type" or symbol.</note>, had come, and the Jews asserted their own righteousness while showing aversion to and denial of Christ’s righteousness, they no longer sought God’s house, altar, and table. Thus, the wish is that their table might become a downfall, an offense, and a retribution to them. *Wittichius*, in his commentary on the letter to the Romans, page 518, writes: *Christ then curses the Jews here, and wishes that the entire Law of Ceremonies, and thus the altar and the temple, may serve as a snare and a trap for them. This happened first insofar as the Jews were fixed upon outward things, and being carried away and blinded by them, they neglected the internal meaning and the duties of godliness. Secondly, insofar as they were gathered in great numbers at Jerusalem for the Passover feast—by divine judgment and the occasion of the temple and the offering of sacrifices—and were thus rooted out and destroyed to the last man, as the history of the destruction of Jerusalem teaches.* And that proverb seems here to be aptly taken from the way in which wild animals are caught by a placed bait, so that the Jews were caught by that which they considered to be bait.

Regarding the words "an offense"; *An offense is that which gives occasion to limp, stumble, or fall, from a word which signifies going lame.* Thus they have stumbled and rejected Christ, not seeing that he was signified through the outward ceremonies. See also Van Peenen, and Professor Gerbrand van Leeuwen on this passage, where fine points appear. See further under the word TABLE.

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:22, 23 explained.</margin>
1 Corinthians 1:22, 23. In the context I read: *For since the Jews demand a sign, and the Greeks seek wisdom, we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block and to the Greeks foolishness.*

Regarding these words, I have explained myself in the opening of the first letter of Paul to the Corinthians, on pages 64 and 65, as follows.

Concerning the word *Skandalon* <note>Greek: Σκάνδαλον</note>, translated as "offense" or "stumbling block," the learned give their thoughts. They call it a stone of stumbling, a hurdle, an obstacle against which one knocks oneself on the road, getting hurt by the blow or stumbling, limping, or becoming lame. Some believe it comes from *Skazein* <note>Greek: Σκάζειν</note>, to go lame; others mean that it signifies: *A small beam in the instruments by which wolves, foxes, or mice are caught.* <note>original Latin: "Tigillum in instrumentis, quibus capiuntur lupi, vulpes, aut mures."</note> That is: *A small beam, bolt, and swinging trigger or tongue, upon which certain bait is placed, in order to catch wolves, foxes, and mice.*

The Messiah, about whom more will be said later, appears as a stone of stumbling in *Isaiah 8*, upon and over which the Jews would fall, verse 14; *Isaiah 28:16; Luke 2:34; Romans 9:33.*

It is certain and sure that the Jews sought a worldly Prince, a temporal redeemer; yet our Savior frequently set himself against that wrong opinion, *Luke 17:20, 21; John 18:36.* But the Pharisees and Scribes had thrown away the key of knowledge and lost it, *Luke 11:52.* See Professor Campegius Vitringa on this place, *Sacred Observations, part 1, page 115,* etc. They found their own righteousness; they were slaves of Pagan Sages and the moral teachers among them. It is said that the Pharisees followed Plato and the Stoics, the Sadducees the Epicureans, and the Essenes the Pythagoreans; so that Heathenism had taken God’s place in the temple. Furthermore, they took offense at the outward insignificance of Christ. For in his birth, person, status, following, or train and retinue, nothing seemed to show itself that suggested royal luster, state, pomp, or dignity; for in everything he appeared to them as humble, despised, and of no value, *Isaiah 53:2, 3.* Especially his ignominious and painful suffering, his worthless death on the cross, was in their way and a great obstacle, even though it was thus foretold of the Messiah, and they themselves had brought him to such an end, *Matthew 27:20, 21,* etc., *Acts 3:15.*

<column-break/>

<margin>1 Corinthians 8:9 explained.</margin>
1 Corinthians 8:9 states: *But take care that this liberty of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to those who are weak.* About which I have delivered my explanation. The word *proskomma* <note>Greek: πρόσκομμα</note> signifies a stumbling block, a stone that has been placed in someone's path as an offense, so that by knocking against it he might hurt himself, stumble, and fall. Be on your guard then, you who say you are made free from the Law of obligation by Christ, and have received the right and power to all food and drink without distinction: that you, strongly insisting on your freedom and eating of the idol-sacrifice, do not throw a hindrance and stone before your weak brother, who does not yet understand that piece of freedom—indeed, who thinks that doing such is not permitted—lest he leave the Christian company, return to Heathenism or Judaism, or be carried away by your deed to act against his conscience.

<margin>Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16. Luke 2:34. Romans 9:33. 1 Peter 2:7 clarified.</margin>
We read of the Messiah that, having appeared, he would be a stone of stumbling, a rock of offense, etc. *Isaiah 8:14* and *28:16; Luke 2:34; Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:7.* Regarding these places, one can consult Poole in general on *Romans 9:33*, Wittichius, Cocceius, Van Peenen, Gerbrand van Leeuwen, and others. I shall here make use of the thoughts and elaborations of Professor Campegius Vitringa on Isaiah for the benefit of my reader, as I intend.

After this learned gentleman had expressed his beautiful thoughts on the first part of Chapter 8, verse 14, his Reverence writes on page 219: *The second thing attributed to the Messiah, directly opposite and contrary to the first, is that which follows: "But for a stone of stumbling, and for a rock of offense to both the houses of Israel, for a trap and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem."*

The Hebrew words present no difficulty for a literal explanation. *Eben negef* <note>Hebrew: אבן נגף</note> is the same as what the writers of the New Testament call *skandalon*. It actually signifies a stone that is in the way, which [stone] not only stops the traveler and walker and is the cause of his fall, but also that he knocks himself against it and is hurt, and is struck with a certain edge, which is the actual meaning of the word *negef* <note>Hebrew: נגף</note>: *percutere*, to strike, *plaga afficere*, to inflict a wound, *talassein* <note>Greek: ταλάσσειν - to strike/shake</note>, to beat through, to hit in such a way that one creates a wound from which a painful edge comes; which has the same power in "a rock of offense," the other figure of speech: for since a rock is steep, hard, sharp, and immovable, no one can knock against it without significant injury. The sense is: that God would manifest himself among the Jews in such a way...

# OFFENSE.

...be made manifest, that he would provide to most the occasion for the gravest fall or punishment, injury, or damage; which cannot be well understood in any other way than that God, through his **singular providence**, would bring it about that among them a very visible event occurred, or a divine appearance—and indeed a most wonderful one, yet contrary to the common prejudices of this nation—concerning which appearance they would err in their judgment. This error would be of the greatest importance, regarding both their temporal and eternal state, so that they would fall into the gravest evils, calamities, or miseries. One may further examine this Author's hypothesis and the effects thereof. I will, since my purpose here is to prune some expansions, proceed with his Reverence's page 220, etc., and follow only the marginal notes to prevent great length. The linguistic Reader is requested by me to leaf through that learned and exquisite work, noting its spirit.

The premise of this Prophecy is the revelation of the Kingdom of the Messiah among the Jews, which was entirely contrary to their prejudices, and from that came the cause of the most significant error and sin, and of great misery.

The prejudices of the Jewish nation implied that he, as one originally from the royal house of David, would establish an external kingdom with much pomp and state, and having delivered the Jews from the domination of the Romans, would subject the peoples of the earth to the Jewish nation. But in this expectation regarding the Christ, they were sorely disappointed. For besides the fact that he appeared very insignificant and humble in outward appearance, he passed by the rulers and teachers who sat in the *seat of Moses* <note>A reference to the authority of the religious leaders in Jerusalem; see Matthew 23:2.</note>, and keeping himself little in Jerusalem, and spending most of his time in Galilee, he chose indeed honest but, according to the world, lowly people, which inspired little respect. For the rest, he shone above all others in wisdom, the divinity of his teaching, holiness of life, authority in speaking and instructing, pleasantness, and miracles; but for the rest, that was all he was. This way and manner of the revelation of God's kingdom in Israel had the appearance of a temptation and trial of the Jewish nation, through which the counsels, deliberations, and judgments concerning the way of salvation, the true nature of the Kingdom of Heaven, and their internal and hidden inclinations of mind toward God and his true Kingdom, were to be revealed.

They found in the revelation of the Kingdom of God that which greatly offended them, as it was entirely contrary to their prejudices and fleshly desires. Therefore they erred concerning the Messiah and his Kingdom, and stumbled against this stone—yes, I say, stumbled heavily—so that they fell with a great fall, and through grave crime made themselves guilty before divine justice to all kinds of evils and disasters. And especially his ignominious death and departure on the cross contributed to this offense, to which finally much was added by the doctrine and teaching of his Disciples and Apostles regarding the uselessness of Moses' Law under the household of Grace, etc. It would run too long if I wanted to cite everything that this Gentleman has intelligently brought forward and very learnedly worked out. Therefore I break off here, although much against my inclination, mean-

<column-break/>

while hoping that the remarks on Isaiah Chapter VIII, 14, will serve as a key for the Reader to unlock the other cited places. Indeed, I dare not express myself further, lest my work expand too far in my hands.

<margin>
b. Next, some passages occur to me in which mention is made of giving, placing, and putting forward an offense, or being an offense; and about such passages I will also say something in particular.
</margin>

<margin>
To give someone offense, to place it, or to be an offense.
</margin>

It is read in Leviticus XIX, 14: *You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the face of the blind.*
<margin>
Leviticus XIX, 14 explained.
</margin>

I wish first to take it literally and according to the letter. For a deaf person, not hearing, can neither excuse nor defend himself, and a blind person cannot see ahead to watch and guard himself. See concerning the struggle between Greed and Generosity, Prudentius <note>Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a Roman Christian poet (c. 348–413 AD).</note> in Dietericus in his Lexicon, page 172, letter 2, under the word <term>Σκάνδαλον</term> <note>original: "Σκάνδαλον" (Skandalon); the Greek root for "scandal," referring to the trigger of a trap or a stumbling block.</note>.

> He allows the blind to wander, and to go through many stumbling blocks.
> <note>original Latin: "Caecum errare finit, perque offensacula multa Ire."</note>

-> that is: <-

> He just lets the blind man roam about, and strike himself
> In walking.

And by the same author, concerning Concord and Discord:

> Never grieving when hurt, she forgives all stumbling blocks.
> <note>original Latin: "Nunquam laesa dolet, cuncta offensacula donat."</note>

-> that is: <-

> She never complains, no matter how one opposes her,
> She forgives the offense that one has given her.

But in a metaphorical and greater sense, I cannot consider it improper to say that it also implies that one ought not to speak ill of someone in secret, nor attempt anything that can be a snare and offense to the less clever and ingenious—for these are in a certain respect "deaf" and "blind." For certainly it is in no way fitting that one adds anything to someone’s plague and misfortune, making it heavier.

<margin>
1 Samuel XXV, 31 explained.
</margin>

One reads in 1 Samuel XXV, 31: *Then this shall not be a staggering nor an offense of heart to my Lord, namely, that you would have shed blood without cause, and when the Lord shall do well to my Lord, then you shall remember your handmaid.*

It seems David, being quite hasty and angry, had sworn an oath that he would cause Nabal and his male heirs to perish by the sword. To become enraged at a Nabal—a passionate, reckless fool—and for his sake to root out those who were not participants in the evil deed, would not have been a righteous action, and could have caused nothing but remorse and unrest in David's heart. And besides that, to have acted such a way regarding Nabal and his house could have been a hindrance to him in his high elevation of State, in further obtaining the favor and following of the people and the great ones; also it could have troubled him hereafter and placed a hindrance in his prosperous and peaceful reign. Both of these David understood, which he also showed in his speech of thanks and obligation to Abigail <note>Abigail intervened to stop David from slaughtering her household after her husband, Nabal, insulted David's men.</note> in the following words.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of "stumbling blocks" or "offenses" (Dutch: *aanstoot*), moving from the general concept discussed on the previous page to specific scriptural examples. It transitions from the Prophet Jeremiah's warnings to the apostolic instructions on Christian liberty and concludes with the historical-theological example of Balaam.</meta>

# OFFENSE.

> Jeremiah 6:21 <note>The source text says verse 31, but Jeremiah 6 only has 30 verses; the margin correctly identifies this as verse 21.</note>. *Therefore thus says the Lord: behold, I will lay stumbling blocks before this people, and the fathers and children together shall stumble against them; the neighbor and his companion shall perish.*

<margin>Jeremiah 6:21 briefly explained.</margin>Jeremiah seems to have delivered this prophecy to the wicked, evil, hardened, idolatrous, and ungrateful people of Israel before the exile to Babylon and Assyria. He appears to threaten them with the hostile and overwhelming power of the Chaldeans and Babylonians. Against this power—even if they were to join forces with all their might and draw friend, kinsman, and neighbor into their alliance—it would all be in vain, for an unavoidable downfall was ordained for them from on high.

<margin>Romans 14:13, 21 explained.</margin>We find in Romans 14:13: *Let us not judge one another anymore: but judge this rather, that you put no stumbling block or occasion to fall in your brother's way. Verse 21: It is good neither to eat meat, nor to drink wine, nor [anything] whereby your brother stumbles, or is offended, or [in which] he is weak.*

This exhortation refers to the "strong" believers—those more firmly assured of their Christian liberty. They had to ensure that they did not grieve, place a stumbling block before, or offend the "weaker" believers, who understood far less (or not at all) about the matter of Christian liberty. This was done so that some might not be frightened away from coming over to Christ and Christianity, and others, having already come over and given their names to Christ, might not turn back to the outside world. This risk occurred when they saw the eating and drinking of such things which they still judged to be unlawful. To act in such a way could not be reconciled with Christian love. Instead of grieving, weakening, and offending one's brother, one should instead strive to nourish and advance the seeds of the spirit and of faith. Beyond these foods and drinks, there were enough other nourishing, refreshing, and strengthening means in the world. Since true Christians should be focused on higher things than food and drink, the Apostle gives this reasoning for exhortation and instruction. Those desiring a broader report on this matter might read Wittichius, van Peenen, Gerbrand van Leeuwen, and the famous Coccejus <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology."</note> on the Epistle to the Romans.

<margin>2 Corinthians 6:3 explained.</margin>2 Corinthians 6:3 says: *We give no offense in anything, that the ministry be not blamed.*

My expansions on this second Letter of the Apostle Paul come down to this:

We—Paul, Timothy, and Sylvanus—guard ourselves very accurately against giving anyone offense in anything, whether by words, deeds, or customs. We take as close a care as is humanly possible that, in matters concerning doctrine and the use of created things, we undertake nothing by which we might offend someone, cause them to stumble, make them stand still, hesitate, or go backward in the course of godliness and the profession of Christian truth, etc. See my explanations of Paul’s second Letter to the Corinthians, pages 333, 334, etc.

<margin>1 Corinthians 10:32 explained.</margin>Therefore, Paul’s primary and general lesson was 1 Corinthians 10:32: *Give no offense, neither to the Jews, nor to the Greeks, nor to the Church of God.* And Philippians 1:10: *That you may approve things that differ <note>original: "τα διαφέροντα" (ta diapheronta), often translated as "things that are excellent."</note>, that you may be sincere and without offense until the day of Christ.*

The word "without offense" <note>original: "ἀπρόσκοποι" (aproskopoi)</note> sometimes signifies such persons who allow no offense to be received or who are not themselves offended; however, here it refers to everyone's 

<column-break/>

duty to ensure that one gives or places no stumbling block before another, lest he stumble and fall. The point here is: conduct yourselves in such a way that you give no one offense or scandal; walk wisely and cautiously, so that you give no offense to anyone among the Jews or Heathens, of whom the Church of God now consists, so that they might not think or speak ill of you. In matters of indifference <note>The author refers to *adiaphora*, or things not essential to salvation, like certain dietary customs.</note>, practice in love that which serves peace and edification. Do not stand too firmly on your own ground, nor press the point of your power and liberty to the extreme, but accommodate the weaker Jews and Greeks as much as your good conscience allows. Consider carefully whether you will most edify or cause offense by using your Christian liberty or by setting it aside for a time.

On Philippians 1:10, the great Coccejus expressed his <margin>Phil. 1:10.</margin> thoughts in this explanation: *It is the work of true and in no way flagging love to test the things that differ <note>original: "δοκιμάζειν τὰ διαφέροντα" (dokimazein ta diapheronta)</note>, that is; to fathom, investigate, and test not only which things differ from each other, but also what is more excellent, and to esteem and choose it above the rest as being joined with the greatest utility. This follows a double rule: 1. Romans 12:9, Abhor that which is evil, and cleave to that which is good. 2. 1 Corinthians 6:12, All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient.* Andocides against Alcibiades, page 31: <note>The author provides a Greek quote followed by a Dutch translation; I have provided the English translation here.</note> *It is a hard thing to be treated badly by people who understand neither justice nor equity; but it is much harder when someone knows what is useful and yet dares to transgress against it.*

*The fruit of the work of love is twofold: 1. That you are pure, simple, upright, without defect, without filth, and without stain in your thoughts, counsel, intentions, reasons, and actions. 2. That you are without offense, that is, that you have a good conscience and are not a scandal to others, so that the ruin of others cannot be laid to your account.*

The passage in Revelation 2:14 <margin>Revelation 2:14 explained.</margin> provides something remarkable; for which reason I shall bring something from learned and choice writers for its understanding and clarification.

The Lord had it against the people of Pergamum that they tolerated the Balaamites or the Nicolaitans in their fellowship. Balaam is described as the provider of counsel to Balak, because he was greedy for the pile of money <note>original: "op den geldklomp was vernikkerd" — an idiomatic Dutch expression for being obsessed with or "stuck" on money.</note>. Although he had not been able to curse Israel, whatever means he might have employed, he advised that one should entice and lure the Israelites to the religious services and feasts of the Midianites and Moabites. The primary part of these consisted of feasts, gluttonous drinking bouts, and lustful embraces. This was intended to lead Israel into idolatry with Baal-Peor and subsequently into fleshly lusts, causing them to fall under the righteous and severe divine judgment of wrath—for he had found no other way to destroy that people.

It seems indeed as if, when this wicked act occurred, Balaam and Balak had already departed from there, and to some extent this account had an old Jewish tradition as its basis. But it is not merely Jewish tradition, as it is noted that God's word in this matter by no means excludes Balaam or holds him innocent, but...

# OFFENSE.

B 2

but considers it against him, as seen in *Numbers 25:18* and *31:16*, *Micah 6:5*, and here in our text. I am inclined to think that Balaam—driven by a desire for reward and to please Balak—after so many failed attempts <note>original: "vergeeffiche pogingen," referring to his failed attempts to curse Israel directly</note>, must have given this counsel to the Midianites and Moabites; a counsel which, indeed, succeeded.

The primary force of this comparison (though in a certain sense we do not reject or exclude other interpretations) lies in this: just as Balaam the Prophet served as a counselor to the Moabites—advising them to lure the Israelites into practicing forbidden lusts and, through the works of the flesh, into idolatry, so that God’s heaviest judgments would descend upon them—so too did these false teachers. By granting believers the freedom to commit fleshly lusts in order to satisfy their own greed (following Balaam's example), they provoked God’s wrath upon the Church, resulting in the very heavy chastisements that usually accompany God’s anger.

Those who desire to read more on this may turn to Coccejus, Groenewegen, Marck, Vitringa on Revelation, Witsius, *Leiden Meditations page 488* <note>original Latin: "Meletem. Leidens."</note>, etc., and Campegius Vitringa, *Sacred Observations page 4, page 124* <note>original Latin: "Observ. sacr."</note>, etc.

*c.* From what has been discussed so far, one can easily and properly understand what is meant when the text speaks of an offense leading to sin and stumbling, as in *Psalm 91:12*, *119:165*, *Isaiah 3:6*, *57:14*, *Ezekiel 7:19*, *14:3, 4, 7*, *18:30*, *21:15*, and *44:12*. I shall occupy myself further with clarifying these passages, though as briefly and concisely as possible.

<margin>Psalm 91:12 briefly touched upon.</margin>
In *Psalm 91:12*, God’s singular care for those who trust in Him and fear no creature is expressed. It is described in such a way that all things come to the aid of the trusting person and work together for their good, even among the angels (*Hebrews 1:14*). Consequently, this path is unobstructed (*Romans 8:18*), and they do not harm themselves through any offense, fall, or scandal, because God makes their feet firm in His testimonies.

<margin>Psalm 119:165 also somewhat illuminated.</margin>
In *Psalm 119:165*, those who walk according to the standards of God’s Law—clinging closely to it and keeping it ever in their sight so that they may speak and act with truth, right, and justice—do not stumble. They have no restlessness or remorse of conscience, nor do they feel terror or fear. They do not wander in many detours; their eyes are not dimmed; they can always see ahead of them and find that the scandals and errors that cause others to stumble have been cleared from their path by the demonstration and power of the truth.

<margin>Isaiah 3:6 opened and the reader referred to a learned writer.</margin>
*Isaiah 3:6* is a discourse regarding the confused state of the Republic of the Jewish people. In this national emergency, there would be a great scarcity of prominent, robed statesmen <note>The author uses the term "getabbaarde," referring to officials wearing formal robes of office.</note> capable and willing to support the collapsing State during the time of Zedekiah and Jehoiachin. See Vitringa on Isaiah, *page 1, page 92*.

<margin>Isaiah 57:14 opened.</margin>
*Isaiah 57:14.* It seems there were quite a few things that could cause offense and hindrance: errors, scandals, prejudices, and false reports about the Messiah, His Kingdom, and the admission of the Gentiles (who were formerly excluded). It suggests the Church would not come to the inheritance of the world so readily unless these obstacles

<column-break/>

were cleared away and removed from their midst. Just as today, such obstacles are found not only among those who wish to be called Reformed Christians, but especially among those of the prominent and authoritative Roman Catholic Church community, who are a burden and a difficulty to the Jews, Turks <note>In this period, "Turks" was often used as a general term for Muslims.</note>, and Heathens, etc. See Poole <note>Matthew Poole, author of the "Synopsis Criticorum."</note>, and especially Vitringa.

<margin>Ezekiel 7:19.</margin>
*Ezekiel 7:19.* The abundance of gold, silver, and all desired things—through which God’s outward covenant people <note>The "outward covenant people" refers to the nation of Israel in their physical/legal relationship with God, as opposed to a spiritual one.</note> became pampered and wanton—led them to forget God and fall into idolatry, greed, and all manner of base dealings. This wealth will not only be unable to help them in the approaching disaster, but it will be the cause of their evil and downfall; therefore, like desperate men, they shall cast those things away from themselves.

<margin>Ezekiel 14:3, 4 receives some light.</margin>
In *Ezekiel 14:3, 4*, the text speaks of idolatry and the loathsome worship of images. Accompanied by a turning away from the living God, this wickedness must cause this people to fall into various follies, which finally cause them to collapse into divine disfavor and the weightiest judgments of vengeance.

<margin>Ezekiel 18:30 how it is opened by some.</margin>
In *Ezekiel 18:30*, the Lord very powerfully urges Israel’s conversion, demanding the loathing and rejection of their ways, dealings, and thoughts, so that they might not fall into the judicial hand and vengeance of the Lord their God because of their conduct. Thus they would avoid stumbling, falling, and failing to rise again, but instead perishing and passing away.

<margin>Ezekiel 21:15 how it is understood by some.</margin>
In *Ezekiel 21:15*, the hostile attacks and "stumbling blocks" leading to the destruction of Jerusalem are repeated three times: the first time, when Zedekiah was captured along with the greatest men and received a bitter portion; the second time, when the city was destroyed; and finally, when Nebuzaradan carried away the remnant. See *Jeremiah 52*.

Others note three very heavy judgments here, though to be brought upon the outward covenant people of the Lord at different times and by different powers:

> *a.* Brought upon Jerusalem by the Babylonians, verses 3 to 6.
> *b.* Befalling the Jews through Antiochus Epiphanes, verses 6 to 11.
> *c.* Brought home to the Jews by the Romans, verses 11 to 19.

How Gulichius understood this can be seen in his own work.

<margin>Ezekiel 44:12 opened.</margin>
*Ezekiel 44:12.* When one pays proper attention to the contents of this chapter, it is found that heavy crimes had been committed regarding both persons and things admitted into God’s house, which had nevertheless been rejected. It shows that people had served idols as well as the God of Israel in the Temple, which had been a stumbling block and offense to many, causing them to fall away from the purity of faith and service that should be offered only to the one true and living God.

*d.* Because man—due to his sinful weakness, lack of observation, and various forms of self-confidence (which is a form of audacity and spiritual pride)—possesses feet prone to stumbling, such that he frequently offends and falters, I shall provide a few more points regarding "stumbling" when opening certain texts. Then I shall take my leave of this symbolic "offending," etc. I shall follow the order of the Texts.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical exploration of the concept of "Offense" or "Stumbling," moving from general definitions to specific scriptural applications in the Psalms, Prophets, and the New Testament. It concludes the entry for "Offense" and begins the entry for "Ape."</meta>

# OFFENSE.

<margin>
Psalm 9:4
explained.
</margin>
Psalm 9:4. *When my enemies are turned back, they shall fall and perish at thy presence.*
Whether one applies this to David or to the Church—whose song of thanks this is for God’s deliverance and the exercise of vengeance upon the enemies of David, Christ, or the Church, such as the Jews, Heathens, the Antichrist, etc.—it at least signifies that the enemy is weakened by the fear of God, His judgments, and judicial punishments, as if they had become nothing; it shows that victory and relief have sprung from God's hand. See Cocceius, Gejerus, and van Til <note>These were prominent 17th-century theologians and biblical commentators.</note>.

<margin>
Psalm 27:
2 explained.
</margin>
Psalm 27:2. *When the wicked, even mine enemies and my foes, came upon me to eat up my flesh, they stumbled and fell.*
That which my mortal enemies sought to bring upon my person through cunning and violence to my destruction, has instead fallen upon their own heads. They struck their feet against the stone; the Lord entangled them in their own counsel, and the stone fell upon their own heads.

<margin>
Psalm 31:
11 clarified.
</margin>
Psalm 31:11 <note>Verse 10 in English Bibles</note> shows the effects that the cross <note>The "cross" here refers to personal suffering or trials.</note> and sorrow have on the soul and body when they are heavy and long-lasting. They take away life, courage, and strength: a metaphorical way of speaking, borrowed from such a state of weakening that one can hardly lift one's feet, but goes forward dragging, striking, and stumbling.

<margin>
Psalm 56:14
and 116:
8 explained.
</margin>
Psalm 56:13 <note>Verse 14 in Dutch</note> agrees with Psalm 116:8.
Because man is inclined through weakness and corruption to limp, trip, and stumble on the right path of God, he is all the more prone to it when errors, heresies, and offenses <note>original: "ergernisse en aanstoot"</note> arise. However, the Psalmist openly professes thanks to the Lord that He had cleared away offenses, errors, and heresies from his path and from before his feet, so that he, as a confessor of the truth, would not strike his foot, stumble, or fall.

<margin>
Psalm 93:
3 somewhat
explained.
</margin>
Psalm 93:3. The Hebrew word *Dokhi* <note>original: דכי</note> signifies the crashing, clattering, and striking of swollen waves and billows against the shores, rocks, and cliffs, by which they are broken. This is often used as a metaphor for the onslaughts of certain peoples and particular nations when they attack God's people and Church with great violence and stormy passion, whether with weapons or other means; just as the Greek word *proskoptein* <note>original: προσκόπτειν, meaning to strike against</note> is used in the symbolic clarification in Matthew 7:27.

<margin>
Psalm 105:37
explained.
</margin>
Psalm 105:37 seems to me to depict not only how the Egyptians, being weary of the plagues and disasters that befell them because of the God of Israel, even pushed the Israelites forward; and, in order to make them depart all the more quickly, willingly bestowed and loaded them with their gold, silver, vessels, etc. Thus Israel did not slink away or get chased off, but despite their long-lasting labor and heavy fatigues, they were not so weakened in body that the exodus was difficult for them. On the contrary, they were singularly encouraged and supported by their God.

<margin>
Psalm 107:
12 explained.
</margin>
Psalm 107:12 refers to humiliation, and various judgments and disasters, through which the holy and righteous God heavily chastises and visits distrust, ingratitude, and wicked deeds, so that a person's state is wonderfully weakened by it. This is a metaphorical way of speaking, borrowed from someone who, striking heavily against something on the road, sometimes hurts himself badly, such that a sprained foot, broken bone, or bruise may result, or he may fall down into the mire, a pit, or a hole, and sometimes pays for it with a severe illness or even death itself. See Cocceius, Gejerus, and van Til.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Isaiah 3:8
explained.
</margin>
In the words of Isaiah 3:8—*For Jerusalem is ruined, and Judah is fallen: because their tongue and their doings are against the Lord, to provoke the eyes of his glory*—it is shown what the condition of the aforementioned would be at the time of righteous judgment. Specifically, the approaching fall of the Republic of Israel is predicted: the "stumbling" occurred under Ahaz and Manasseh, leading to a wondrous weakening in strength and luster; the "fall" would come under Jehoiakim and Zedekiah. Also, the reason and cause are provided, namely the corrupt morals and lifestyle of the people, so that through words and works, they would bring upon themselves God’s wrath and disfavor, and God would tear away the pillars and foundations of the Republic and cause them to perish. See Polus, and especially Vitringa, part 1, page 92.

<margin>
Jeremiah 50:32
explained.
</margin>
Jeremiah 50:32 depicts for us proud Babylon fallen under the divine hand and judicial wrath, so punished, visited, and made small that there would be no lifting it up, serving as an example of what was to happen spiritually.

<margin>
Daniel 11:
19 explained.
</margin>
Daniel 11:19 shows us the unhappy end of Antiochus the Great. Having attempted to bring Egypt under his control and having set out against Ptolemy Epiphanes for that purpose, he was wonderfully halted, driven back, and crushed by Scipio Africanus, after Ptolemy Epiphanes had previously made a treaty with the Romans. This eventually took such a toll on Antiochus that he did not die kingly in the field in sight of his enemies, but met his end through a miserable death. See Junius, Gejerus on Daniel, *Epitome of the Histories* by Cluverius p. 178, and *Idea of Universal History* by Johann Bunon p. 58.

Concerning Matthew 4:6, see Psalm 91:11, 12 above.
In Matthew 7:27, the word *proskoptein* <note>original: προσκόπτειν</note> appears in the sense of a strong and violent striking, the strong and sudden falling down of winds and rain-showers. He stands firm, fixed, and immovable who, through the confession of faith from mouth and heart, builds upon the rock-stone Jesus, and demonstrates his rooted faith through works (Matthew 16:17, 1 Corinthians 3:11). But it is finished for him who yields to fleshly inclinations and strange doctrines that are pushed through with passion and strong following, nor resists offenses, and thus, leaving Jesus, chooses another foundation, etc. See Walaeus, Priceus, Grotius, Polus.

Regarding Romans 11:32, more can be seen under STONE OF STUMBLING above.
