# APE.
<sig>B 3</sig>

<margin>They mimic humans and make strange gestures.</margin>
To imitate, *to mimic*: because apes are not only very similar to humans in their hands, feet, parts of the face, and internal organs, but they also wonderfully mimic the actions, outward works, and manners of humans. Ennius <note>A celebrated early Roman poet.</note> says:

> *How similar the ape, that most foul beast, is to us!*
> <note>original: "Simia quam similis turpissima bestia nobis!"</note>

->That is:<-

> *An ape, an ugly beast, how much it resembles us!*

<margin>Described more closely.</margin>
They are animals with an ugly face, a flattened nose, unsightly wrinkles and facial folds, etc. Some have a tail, others do not. They are somewhat hairless on their hindquarters and, on the whole, are not of a pleasant or attractive appearance. But what makes up for this deformity is that they are wonderfully cunning in their kind and trained to mimic human actions and hand gestures.

<margin>Where they are found in abundance.</margin>
They dwell in forests and on mountains. Alvarez <note>Francisco Álvares, a Portuguese missionary who traveled to Ethiopia.</note> testifies that he saw them by the two and three hundreds together in Prester John’s Land <note>A legendary Christian kingdom in Africa, often associated with Ethiopia.</note>. Jonston <note>Jan Jonston, a 17th-century naturalist.</note> also states that there are very many of them between Egypt, Libya, and Ethiopia.

<margin>Their wit and teachability.</margin>
Rare things are told of them: that they learn to play the flute, and even to play on the chessboard and with dice, to throw, and to dance. They cook, roast, run errands, and interact with small children—though that is very risky; they ride on a little goat, carry a helmet and shield, and throw and ward off the enemy's arrows. Martial <note>A Roman poet known for his Epigrams.</note> says in his 14th book:

> *The clever ape who evades the thrown spears.*
> <note>original: "Callidus emissas eludere Simius hastas."</note>

->That is:<-

> *The Ape is clever at escaping the thrown weapon.*

Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet.</note> in his 5th Satire:

> *He who is covered by shield and helmet, and fearing the whip, learns to hurl the javelin from the shaggy goat.*
> <note>original: "Qui tegitur parma & galea, metuensque flagelli / Discit ab hirsuta jaculum torquere capella."</note>

->Which amounts to this:<-

> *He who carries a shield and storm-helmet, and fearing the rod, learns to swing the throwing-spear at the master's command.*

This animal performs very rare and wonderful things, and it behaves or conducts itself strangely by the sour pulling of its deformed face and by pointing with its upper hand-like paws. It grins or laughs, mocks and gnashes. It takes all kinds of food for itself—apples, nuts, etc. It also knows how to use the cat's paws to pull the chestnuts out of the ashes, and in almost everything, it mimics humans, by whom, nonetheless, it is most often caught.

It does not hear praise of itself unwillingly, just as it also likes to see people making a fuss over its young.

<margin>Pride, and love for their young. Lustful.</margin>
In its shameful ugliness, it is still possessed with a kind of pride. It likes to look at itself in a mirror and shows off its similar-looking young, which it coddles and squeezes so much that many a time one is choked to death. It is a foul, lustful, and wanton animal, which also sometimes lurks for and besets women.

However monstrous this animal may be, the Hea-

<column-break/>

thens hold it in greater value and honor. No one would gladly harm their hands on them or defile them with its blood, perhaps because of the similarity to humans it has in many parts, or because they falsely believe that human souls pass into that animal, must suffer much therein, and do penance for a time. At the very least, apes are held to be very clever animals and creatures of the great God; indeed, by some they are honored as gods, as one reads of an Ape Temple among wild peoples and a holy Monkey-tooth. When this tooth was taken from them by the Portuguese, they sought to get it back by an offer of seventy thousand ducats. It is well known that many make a great deal of apes, clothing and decorating them. Yet an ape remains an ape, and the ape always peeks out in one way or another, of which there is a proverb:

<margin>Honored as idols by the Heathens.</margin>

<margin>Highly valued by some.</margin>

> *An ape is an ape even if it wears golden insignia.*
> <note>original: "Simia est simia etiamsi aurea gestat insignia."</note>

->That is<-

> *An Ape remains an Ape, even if it were dressed with golden ornaments.*

The devil has been called "God’s ape" because he mimics Jehovah with an outward appearance; indeed, he seems to have brought many matters of the Jews' religion, customs, and ceremonies over to the Heathens as idolatry and superstition, which could be further demonstrated and elaborated upon.

<margin>Satan called God’s ape.</margin>

Those who mimic someone in everything, so that it is unseemly and they are recognized for it—sometimes being caught and trapped like the ape because of it and not coming off well regarding their reputation and esteem—are compared to apes. It is said, "He is the ape of this or that person." Thus, the Orator Tirianus was called the ape of his time because he had not very successfully mimicked the letter-writing style of Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero.</note>.

<margin>What it means to become the ape of someone.</margin>

One might compare to apes those people who have many deformities, both in respect to their body and spirit, and who are strangely obsessed with their own whims and fruits, with their children, etc., whom they coddle, gaze at, praise, and gladly put on display, wanting them to be wondered at and praised, even if quite a few flaws and deformities, etc., are among them—especially when they show foolish "monkey love" <note>A term for over-indulgent, blinding parental love.</note> toward their children, and rather coddle them than raise them properly.

<margin>Those who are obsessed with their "puppets" and are too foolishly fond of them are compared to apes.</margin>

Also those who want to reap the fruits of another's hazardous occurrences or painful labor—using another's service in matters they dare not undertake themselves, and meanwhile eating the chestnuts and cracking the nuts without the actual worker gaining anything from it—are compared to apes in their behavior. *Sambucus, Emblems, page 102.* <note>Johannes Sambucus was a 16th-century Hungarian humanist and emblem book author.</note>

> *In Bergen (a small town near the sea,*
> *From where the path lies to the fertile Zeelanders),*
> *A little ape recently gave a noteworthy*
> *Example, at once clever and humorous in its trickery.*
> *For when he had seen chestnuts buried in the hearth,*
> *He set about moving the ashes;*
> *But fearing the embers, he immediately*
> *Snatched them with the forced paw of a snoring puppy.*
> *The matter is worthy of recent belief.*
> *It is a virtue to be wary of another's misfortune.*
> <note>Translated from the original Latin: "Bergae (est oppidulum mari propinquum / Ad pingues patet unde iter Zelandos) / Nuper Simiola edidit notandum / Exemplum, simul, & dolo jocosum. / Nam cum castaneas foco sepultas / Vidisset, cinerem insistit movere: / Prunas sed metuens statim catelli / Stertentis pede surripit coacto. / Res est digna fide recentiori. / Laus est alterius malo cavere."</note>

# STUMBLING.

<margin>
Psalm 9:4
explained.
</margin>
*Psalm 9:4. Because my enemies turned back, fell, and perished from your presence.*

Whether one applies this to David or to the Church—whose song of thanks this is for God’s deliverance and the execution of vengeance upon the enemies of David, Christ, or the Church (Jews, Heathens, the Antichrist, etc.)—it at least signifies that the enemy is weakened, as if brought to nothing, by the fear of God, His judgments, and judicial punishments, and that victory and relief have sprung from God’s hand. See Cocceius, Gejerus, and van Til. <note>Johannes Cocceius, Martin Geier, and Salomon van Til were prominent 17th-century Protestant theologians and biblical commentators.</note>

<margin>
Psalm 27:
2 explained.
</margin>
*Psalm 27:2. When the wicked, my adversaries and my enemies against me, approached me to eat my flesh, they themselves stumbled and fell.*

That which my mortal enemies sought to bring upon my person through cunning and violence for my destruction has instead crashed down upon their own heads. They struck their feet against the stone; the Lord confused them in their counsels, and the stone fell upon their own heads.

<margin>
Psalm 31:
11 clarified.
</margin>
*Psalm 31:11. This shows what effects the cross <note>In this context, "the cross" refers to trials, suffering, or heavy burdens borne by a believer.</note> and sorrow have on soul and body when they are heavy and long-lasting. They take away air, courage, and strength; a metaphorical way of speaking, borrowed from such a weakening that one can hardly lift one’s feet and proceeds by dragging, bumping, and stumbling.*

<margin>
Psalm 56:14
and 116:
8 explained.
</margin>
*Psalm 56:14 corresponds with Psalm 116:8.*

Since man is inclined through weakness and corruption to limp, trip, and stumble on the right path of God, he is all the more prone to it when errors, heresies, offenses, and stumbling blocks arise. Yet the Psalmist openly confesses thanks to the Lord that He had cleared away offenses, errors, heresies, etc., from his path and from before his feet, so that he, as a confessor of the truth, would not strike his foot, trip, or fall.

<margin>
Psalm 93:
3 somewhat
explained.
</margin>
*Psalm 93:3. Doki <note>original Hebrew: דכי</note> signifies the striking, clattering, or beating of swollen billows and waves against the shores, rocks, and cliffs, by which they are broken. This is often used as a metaphor for the onslaughts of certain peoples and particular nations when they attack God’s people and Church with great violence and stormy passion, using weapons or other means; just as proskoptein <note>original Greek: προσκόπτειν, meaning to strike against or stumble</note> is used in the symbolic explanation of Matthew 7:27.*

<margin>
Psalm 105:17
explained.
</margin>
*Psalm 105:17 seems to me to depict not only how the Egyptians, being weary of the Israelites because of the plagues and disasters that befell them on account of the God of Israel, even pushed them forward themselves. To make them depart all the more quickly, they willingly gifted and burdened them with their gold, silver, vessels, etc., so that Israel did not depart by stealth or was chased away; rather, through long labor and heavy fatigue, they were not so weakened in body that the exodus became difficult for them, but on the contrary, they were singularly encouraged and supported by their God.*

<margin>
Psalm 107:
12 explained.
</margin>
*Psalm 107:12 occurs in the sense of scorn, and various judgments and disasters, through which the holy and righteous God heavily chastises and visits mistrust, ingratitude, and wicked deeds, so that a person’s state is wonderfully weakened. It is a metaphorical way of speaking, borrowed from someone who, stumbling hard on the road, sometimes injures himself severely, such that a sprained foot, broken bone, or bruise may result, and he falls down into the mire, a pit, or a hole,*

<column-break/>

*and even pays for it with a heavy illness, or indeed with death itself. See Cocceius, Gejerus, and van Til.*

<margin>
Isaiah 3:8
explained.
</margin>
*In the words of Isaiah 3:8: For Jerusalem has stumbled, and Judah has fallen, because their tongue and their actions are against the Lord, to provoke the eyes of His glory. This shows how it would be for the aforementioned people at the time of righteous judgment. Specifically, the approaching fall of Israel’s Republic is predicted: the stumbling would occur under Ahaz and Manasseh, causing a wondrous weakening in strength and luster; the fall would come under Jehoiakim and Zedekiah. Also, the reason and cause are provided, namely the corrupted morals and lifestyle of the people, so that by words and works, they would bring upon themselves and provoke God’s wrath and disfavor, and God would tear away and destroy the pillars and foundations of the Republic. See Polus, and especially Vitringa part 1, page 92.* <note>Matthew Poole and Campegius Vitringa were renowned 17th-century biblical commentators; Vitringa was particularly famous for his work on Isaiah.</note>

<margin>
Jeremiah 50:32
explained.
</margin>
*Jeremiah 50:32 portrays for us the proud Babylon fallen under the divine hand and judicial wrath, so punished, visited, and made small that there would be no rising again—as an example of what was to befall the spiritual Babylon.*

<margin>
Daniel 11:
19 explained.
</margin>
*Daniel 11:19 shows us the unhappy end of Antiochus the Great who, having sought to bring Egypt under his control and having set out against Ptolemy Epiphanes for that purpose, was wonderfully halted, driven back, and broken by Scipio the African <note>The Roman general Scipio Africanus, famous for defeating Hannibal.</note> after Ptolemy Epiphanes had previously made an alliance with the Romans. Antiochus eventually took this so much to heart that he did not die royally in the field in view of his enemies, but came to his end through a miserable death. See Junius, Gejerus on Daniel, Cluverius’s Epitome of Histories page 178, and Johannes Bunon’s Idea of Universal History page 58.*

> *See concerning Matthew 4:6 and Psalm 91:11, 12 above.*
> In *Matthew 7:27*, *proskoptein* <note>original Greek: προσκόπτειν</note> appears in the sense of a strong and violent striking, a strong and sudden falling down of winds and downpours. He stands firm, fixed and immovable, who builds upon the rock Jesus through the confession of faith from mouth and heart and proves his rooted faith with works (*Matthew 16:17; 1 Corinthians 3:11*); but it is over for him who yields to carnal inclinations and strange doctrines that are put forward with passion and strong following, nor resists offenses, and thus, abandoning Jesus, chooses another foundation, etc. See Walaeus, Price, Grotius, Polus.

### APE, קוף *koph*, Σιμία, *Simia*.

<margin>
Why apes
are called
Kophim and
Simia.
</margin>
I shall not "ape" the naturalists and historians to the extent of describing the various genera, distinctions, species, sub-characteristics, and natures of apes. One may consult ancient and modern writers on this matter.

In general, it is true that these animals are called *Kophim* <note>original Hebrew: קופים</note>, from *koph* <note>קוף</note> or *hakeph* <note>הקף</note>, meaning *to go around* or *to encompass* <note>original Latin: ambire, circumire</note>, as is said, because of their circling and manifold bodily contortions, with which they both exercise themselves and provide amusement to onlookers. They are also called *simia* <note>original Greek: σιμία</note>, as some believe, from *mimeisthai* <note>original Greek: μιμεῖσθαι</note>, meaning *to im-*

<meta>This page begins the entry for "Aap" (Ape/Monkey), following the conclusion of "Aanstoot" (Stumbling) on the previous page. It explores the natural history, symbolic meaning, and moral applications of the ape in 17th-century thought.</meta>

# A P E.
### B 3

<margin>They mimic humans and make strange gestures.</margin> To follow, to *mimic*: because apes are very similar to humans—not only in their hands, feet, parts of the face, and internal organs—but also in their actions, external works, and wonderful imitation of human customs. Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC) was a writer during the period of the Roman Republic, often called the father of Roman poetry.</note> says:

> *How like us is that most foul beast, the ape!* <note>original Latin: "Simia quam similis turpissima bestia nobis!"</note>

->That is:<-

->*An ape, an ugly beast, how much it resembles us!*<-

<margin>Described more closely.</margin> They are animals with an ugly mug, a flattened nose, unsightly wrinkles and facial folds, etc. Some have a tail, others do not. They are somewhat hairless on their hindquarters and, on the whole, do not present a pleasant or attractive sight. But what makes up for this deformity is that they are wonderfully cunning in their own way, and trained to mimic human actions and hand gestures.

They dwell in forests and on mountains. <margin>Where they are frequently found.</margin> Alvarez <note>Francisco Álvares was a Portuguese missionary and explorer who wrote about Ethiopia in the 16th century.</note> testifies that he saw them in groups of two or three hundred together in the land of Prester John <note>"Paapjansland" refers to the legendary kingdom of Prester John, often identified with Ethiopia in this period.</note>. Jonston <note>John Jonston was a 17th-century naturalist and physician of Scottish descent living in Poland.</note> also notes that there are very many of them between Egypt, Libya, and Ethiopia.

<margin>Their ingenuity and teachability.</margin> Rare things are told of them: that they learn to play the flute, and even play at the chessboard and with dice, throwing them and dancing. They can cook, roast, run errands, and interact with small children—though that is very dangerous; they ride on a goat, carry a helmet and shield, and throw or deflect the enemy's arrows. Martial <note>A Roman poet from Hispania best known for his Epigrams.</note> says in his 14th book:

> *The clever ape skilled at dodging thrown spears.* <note>original Latin: "Callidus emissas eludere Simius hastas."</note>

->That is:<-

->*The Ape is clever at escaping the throwing-weapon.*<-

Juvenal <note>A Roman poet active in the late 1st and early 2nd century AD, known for his Satires.</note> in his 5th Satire:

> *One who is covered by a shield and helmet, and fearing the whip, learns to hurl the javelin from a shaggy goat.* <note>original Latin: "Qui tegitur parma & galea, metuensque flagelli / Discit ab hirsuta jaculum torquere capella."</note>

->Which amounts to this:<-

->*He who wears a shield and storm-hat, and fearing the rod,*<-
->*Learns to wield the javelin at the master's command.*<-

This animal performs very rare and wonderful things, and it behaves or carries itself strangely by making faces with its deformed mug and pointing with its upper hand-like paws. It grins or laughs, mocks and gnashes its teeth. It takes all kinds of food for itself—apples, nuts, etc. It also knows how to use the cat's paws to pull chestnuts out of the ashes, and in almost everything it mimics humans, by whom it is nevertheless most often captured.

It does not dislike hearing its own praise, just as it likes to see people make a fuss over its young. <margin>Pride, and love for their young. Lustful.</margin> In its shameful ugliness, it is still possessed by a kind of pride. It loves to look at itself in a mirror and shows off its similar-looking young, which it fondles and squeezes so much that many times one is smothered to death. It is a filthy, lecherous, and wanton animal, which also sometimes spies on and waylays women.

However monstrous this animal may be, the Gen-

<column-break/>

tiles hold it in great value and honor. <margin>No one would willingly harm it or defile their hands with its blood, likely because of the resemblance to humans it has in many parts: or because they falsely imagine that human souls pass into that animal, must suffer much therein, and do penance for a time. At the very least, apes are considered very clever animals and creatures of the great God; indeed, by some they are honored as gods, as one reads of a temple of apes among savage peoples, and a sacred monkey tooth which, having been taken from them by the Portuguese, they sought to regain by an offer of seventy thousand ducats. It is well known that many make a great deal of apes, clothing and adorning them. Yet an ape remains an ape, and the ape always looks out from it in one way or another, of which the proverb is:</margin>

> *An ape is an ape even if it wears golden insignia.* <note>original Latin: "Simia est simia etiamfi aurea gestat insignia."</note>

->That is:<-

->*An Ape remains an Ape, even if it were dressed with golden ornaments of honor.*<-

<margin>Satan called God's ape.</margin> The devil has been called "God's ape" because he mimics Jehovah with an external appearance; indeed, he seems to have brought many matters of the Jews' religion, customs, and ceremonies over to the Gentiles as idolatry and superstition, which could be further demonstrated and elaborated upon.

<margin>What it means to be called someone's ape.</margin> Those who mimic someone in everything, so much so that it is unbecoming and they are recognized by it—and are sometimes caught and trapped like an ape because of it, not faring well in terms of their reputation and esteem—they are compared to apes. It is said, "He is the ape of so-and-so." Thus the orator Tirianus was called the ape of his time because he had unsuccessfully mimicked the letter-writing style of Marcus Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the famous Roman orator.</note>.

<margin>Those who are obsessed with their own "pretty dolls" and are foolish are compared to apes.</margin> One might compare to apes those people who have many deformities, both in terms of their body and spirit, and who are singularly obsessed with their "brain-puppets" <note>The author uses "herssenpoppen" (brain-puppets) to refer to delusions, idle fancies, or obsessive ideas.</note>, their works, their children, etc.—coddling, gazing at, praising, and gladly putting them on display, wanting them to be admired and praised, even if many flaws and monstrosities are found among them. This is especially true when they show foolish "ape-love" <note>The term "aapenliefde" refers to a blind, excessive, and ultimately harmful affection, like a mother monkey accidentally squeezing her baby to death.</note> toward their children, coddling them rather than raising them properly.

Also, those who wish to reap the fruits of another's hazardous circumstances or painful labor—using another's service in matters they dare not undertake themselves, and meanwhile eating the chestnuts and cracking the nuts without the actual worker gaining anything from it—are compared to apes in their conduct. *Sambucus Emblemata, page 102.* <note>Johannes Sambucus was a 16th-century Hungarian scholar and physician whose "Emblemata" was a popular book of moral illustrations.</note>

For the rest, all hypocrites or pretenders—those who appear to be something they are not, and whose "ape" occasionally peeks too roughly out of the sleeve <note>A Dutch idiom: "the ape comes out of the sleeve," meaning one's true, often negative, character is revealed.</note>, no matter how beautifully they adorn themselves with the vanished ornament of virtue—they may be placed alongside the apes. They appear to be what they are not, and behave differently than their inner nature dictates. And if one observes such people as poseurs, court jesters, mock-fools, stage actors, conjurers, and others who, acting strangely, make an "ape-face," one may rightly compare them to apes.

### EARTHQUAKE, *Ra’ash* <note>Hebrew: רעש</note> / *Seismos* <note>Greek: σεισμὸς</note>, *Terrae motus* <note>Latin: movement of the earth</note>.

<margin>The earth is subject to tremors and movements.</margin>
The Earth, however firm and immovable it may seem, is nonetheless subject to sometimes lesser and sometimes greater tremors and movements, called *earthquakes*. This trembling sometimes runs through larger, sometimes smaller parts of the earth. It is lighter or heavier, for a shorter or longer time, and less or more harmful in its effects.

<margin>Cause of the same.</margin>
These earthquakes arise from sulfurous and oily vapors and combustible materials, which have been found

<column-break/>

to be abundant beneath the earth. When these substances are prepared in sufficient quantity in the subterranean hollows, sewers, pipes, veins, and earth-channels, and are gathered together, they are ignited into flame by the inward spiraling of pressing winds, pressure, and impact, etc. This infinitely thins the nearby air and moves it with great power. These mixed and strongly moved particles, following their usual openings and vents and not finding a wide enough exit quickly enough, strike against sunken and tightly-clamped earth-matter when they resist the pressure. This causes the trembling, vibration, and shaking of the earth. This sometimes happens with rising repetitions, where new materials may come to light, making the expansion of the vapors greater and the impact against the upper crust of the earth more violent. It then happens that the earth tears, splits, and bursts open with violence, whereby some parts of the earth are thrown heaven-high into the air, and others sink downward; mountains, cities, and villages are devastated, sink down, and perish, while entire regions are filled with flowing streams of sulfur and oily substances. The after-effects are that harmful vapors, plague, as well as barren years and floods are born from it. Regarding this, one could consult Descartes <note>original: "Carteſius"</note>, De Mey's *Sacred Physiology*, Regius, Senguerdius, etc. <note>These are 17th-century natural philosophers and theologians who attempted to explain natural phenomena through mechanical and biblical lenses.</note> As for the further instances and effects of earthquakes, one can read of them in abundance in the *secular historians*.

<margin>Effect of the same.</margin>

<margin>Earthquake in general as a symbol in God's word.</margin>
*The earthquake*, God’s fearsome work in nature, to which God’s Spirit often makes allusions, is a symbol of strong stirrings and movements in the Civil and Church State, through which many matters and states are entirely confused and thrown into turmoil, with great and remarkable changes, or actual uprootings and turnings of the bottom to the top. This is particularly caused by disputes, quarrels, factions, pride, pomp, ambition, and self-interest; from which public uprisings, disturbances, internal and foreign wars, and such things are born.

<margin>From what, and in what, and how, shown with Scripture.</margin>
This foundation having been laid, I shall further demonstrate the symbolism of the Earthquake by clarifying some passages in God's word.

a. I establish in general that such works of God in nature, which do not occur daily, can serve as a sign of God’s unusual appearance, to make the impression of His formidable Majesty, all-working power, fearsome wrath, and punishing vengeance stronger upon the children of men. This is intended to make the human heart, having become small and submissive, tremble and shake before His judgments, and thus to prepare the heart for humility, the shunning of sin, and more diligent submission and obedience, so that they might seek the Lord their God with trembling. *Exodus 19:18; Psalm 18:7 <note>The text says 8, but modern numbering is often 7.</note>; Hebrews 1:5.*

<margin>God's primary purpose in the same.</margin>

<margin>Symbols of great changes in the civil and church state.</margin>
b. With specific application, I must note, according to my previous statement, that the earthquake serves as a symbol that here or there in the world, civil society, and the Church, such astonishing movements shall arise. These will work such great changes and upheavals, as a demonstration of divine justice and severity, that it shall be as if the heavens were falling.

# EARTHQUAKE. EARTH.

Something added from secular writers.

> *In flight, people by people, too reckless in their mockery,*
> *The heart in the body, from fear and humility, began to shrink;*
> *While he strikes the peaks of Athos, or Epirus' high mountains*
> *Or Rhodope, and all that defies the power of thunder,*
> *Throwing down the summits, and the heavy rains and their gusts*
> *He doubles, so that the woods and shores echo it,*
> *And showers of storm upon storm, and puddle upon puddle of rain.*

<margin>
Confirmed with general passages.
</margin>
Just as it appears previously in *Psalm 46:3* and *Isaiah 24:19*; that is, that such shakings and movements arose in the world that everything was turned upside down, so that even great kingdoms and mighty powers were overturned and destroyed.

<margin>
The proof in the kingdom of Babylon.
</margin>
Of which one finds a closer example in *Isaiah 13:13* regarding the once-dreaded dominion of Babylon; which Monarchy would be so shaken, shocked, and moved by a storm sent by God that it would be loosened and dismantled. One may consult Campegius Vitringa <note>A prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist (1659–1722).</note> on Isaiah, just as in *Isaiah 24:19* something similar appears, though it may portray something even more sublime; regarding which one may read the same author.

<margin>
And indicated by others.
</margin>
*Jeremiah 4:24, 25* portrays no better fate for Judah, and it is presented in almost the same way through symbolic language.

The final destruction of the Jewish land, city, temple, and religion—where formerly God's people and church found hiding and stability—is also portrayed in this manner in *Haggai 2:7, Hebrews 12:26,* and *Matthew 27:50-54.* One may read Coccejus, Strefo, Baunius, d'Outrein, etc., regarding the Epistle to the Hebrews.

As for further earthquakes, a symbol of similar divine judgments, punishments, and severities, of which we read in *Revelation 6:12, 14:17, 11:13-19,* and *16:8*; regarding those, one may consult Coccejus, Suicerus (*The Fates of the World and the Church, pages 254, 281, 404, etc.*), Professor Marck, Vitringa, Groenewegen, etc.

<column-break/>

### EARTH, <gloss>Hebrew: *Eretz*</gloss> <gloss>Greek: *gea, gē, gaia*</gloss> <gloss>Latin: *terra, orbis, tellus*</gloss>

<margin>
Earth, how it is understood.
</margin>
By the EARTH, although this term is sometimes taken quite broadly for the entire globe and sphere of the earth mixed with the waters, I shall understand the dry part, habitable for humans and cattle, made dry by the diversion of the waters into the depths (*Genesis 1:10, Job 38:4*).

<margin>
Formerly mixed with water, and covered by it.
</margin>
This is described as waste and empty, without light or ornament, buried under the waters, without foundation: <gloss>Hebrew: *tohou vabohou*</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: תהו ובהו; traditionally translated as "without form and void."</note>; not arranged, not ordered, everything still mixed together, unfashioned, <gloss>Greek: *akosmos*</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἄκοσμος; meaning "without order" or "unadorned."</note>, without neatness or ornament, not yet measured by the plumb line, irregular, not sunk down and built up according to the plumb line from above (*Isaiah 34:11*). Regarding this matter, one can see fine things in Coccejus (*Summ. Theol. page 216*), in Momma (*oecon. page 167*), Heidanus (*corp. theol. page 294*), Stillingfleet in his *Sacred Origins* (*page 365, etc.*), and also regarding the Heathen's "Chaos" or "Bajart" <note>"Bajart" likely refers to a confused mass or disorder.</note>, Grotius regarding the true Christian Religion (*pages 25, 26, 27, 28, 32, etc.*).

<margin>
How these could cease, and the creation be carried forward.
</margin>
On the second day, the Lord made a division between the earth and the waters, and caused the waters to sink down toward the basins and deep abysses. It is not at all improbable that this was carried out by divine order through a strong, pressing wind, or through powerful thunder accompanied by an earthquake (*Psalm 104:5-9*), whereby the earth, rising above the waters while its innermost fine substances were set in motion, was pushed outward, causing the uppermost crust of the earth to rip and split. With the upheaval of some parts and the sinking of others, mountains, hills, plains, fearsome depths and abysses, subterranean pipes, hollows, and watercourses were born. Indeed, it was later found that mountains, valleys, pools, rivers, and lakes came forth in this manner; though I by no means presume to say or determine that it happened exactly so at the first appearance.

<margin>
Opening of the name.
</margin>
As for the names, in Hebrew I see the earth called <term>*Eretz*<note>Hebrew: ארץ</note></term>, which some say comes from <term>*Ra'atz*<note>Hebrew: רעץ</note></term> meaning "to shake, tremble, or shudder"; either because the earth is subject to tremors and shakings by winds and subterranean fire, etc., or because it shakes and trembles when something strong and heavy falls upon it or is driven over it. Others derive the noun from <term>*Routz*<note>Hebrew: רוץ</note></term> meaning "to run" here and there, either because the heavens are moved around the earth, or because people and cattle move upon it, or because, according to the thoughts of some, the earth turns and is moved. <note>A subtle reference to the then-controversial Copernican heliocentric theory.</note>

The earth is called in Greek <gloss>*Gea, Gē, Gaia*</gloss>; from <term>*geino*</term>, "I beget or bring forth," or from <term>*geinomai*</term>, "I am begotten or brought forth": perhaps not only because it has its origin from the powerful and sufficient will and command of God, but also because it provided the material form for man's body and, like a fruitful mother, brings forth a thousand kinds of things from her womb for humans and cattle.

# EARTH.

<margin>Rotation or stillness of the earth, left undecided.</margin> I shall by no means involve myself in the thorny disputes regarding whether the sun stands still and the earth rotates; it is certain that there are opinions for and against this. Those who are seized by a desire for investigation may open the past and newer writings, whether by Cartesius <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher whose mechanical philosophy influenced early modern science.</note>, Regius, du Bois, Velthuizen, Valerius *Sacred Philosophy* pages 34, 151; Dougt in the New Testament page 216; de Mey *Hallelujah*, pages 81-84; Dieter. *Biblical Antiquities* page 53, etc.; Groenewegen *Catechism* page 151; Burman’s *Law and Testimony* page 21; Leenhof’s *Chain*, volume 1, page 35, etc.

<margin>What was judged about this in ancient times by the Pagans.</margin> The principal opinion of the Pagans amounted to this: that the earth, like a globe or ball hanging in the air, was supported and moved by it, as in *Ovid, Fasti book 6.* <note>A Latin poem by Ovid detailing the Roman calendar.</note>

> *The earth, like a ball, supported by no prop,*
> *Hangs as a heavy weight in the balanced air.* <note>original Latin: "Terra pile similis nullo fulcimine nixa, / Aëre librato, tam grave pendet onus."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Like a ball the earth hangs in the midst of the air,*
> *Where nothing supports her, however heavy she may be.*

->Lucretius, in the 2nd book:<- <note>Titus Lucretius Carus, Roman poet and philosopher, author of *On the Nature of Things*.</note>

> *This the ancient learned Greek poets sang,*
> *That she, sublime in a chariot, drives a yoke of lions,*
> *Teaching that the great earth hangs in the space of air,*
> *And that earth cannot stand upon earth.* <note>original Latin: "Hanc veteres Graium docti cecinere poëtae, / Sublimem curru bijugos agitare leones, / Aëris in spatio magnum pendere docentes / Tellurem, neque posse in terra sistere terram."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Greek poetry has taught us from of old,*
> *How she rules the lion-team on its axle:*
> *Showing us in elaborate and skillful songs*
> *How the whole globe of the earth is hung in the air,*
> *And that this globe can find no footing upon a globe.*

<margin>On the foundation of the earth.</margin> Some allow themselves to believe that the waters are the foundation and the supporting mechanism of the earth. One encounters some who send us to the center point or dot of the terrestrial globe, called by the Latins *punctum globi terrestris* <note>original Latin: "the point of the terrestrial globe"</note>; others recognize nothing in this but God’s commanding word and powerful will.

<margin>God's purpose in the creation of the earth.</margin> It has been noted that God made the earth dry and habitable for men and livestock, for the revelation of His sufficiency, wisdom, power, and goodness; to subsequently carry out His eternal decree and intention, in His Son, effectively, for the revelation of His wisdom, supremacy, justice, holiness, goodness, truth, mercy, severity, etc.; for which reason the earth shall remain until He has gathered His own from all the generations of the earth.

Having let this precede, I shall apply myself more closely to the opening of the Holy Scripture, and show how, and in what sense, one ought to understand the word Earth, and that which appears therein with further descriptions.

1. The *earth*, which carries and feeds men and livestock, is sometimes taken for that which she feeds and carries, *tanquàm continens pro contento* <note>original Latin: "as the container for the contained"</note>—the container for the thing contained, as the Rhetoricians say: that is, in general, for the people who are on the earth and dwell there, *Deuteronomy 32:1. Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth.* <note>The Dutch text cites verse 7, but the quote is verse 1.</note> One may look at this place in Burman’s *Law and Testimony*,

<column-break/>

page 911, etc., where one notices that his Reverence understands by heaven and earth everything that is in heaven and on earth.

By the heaven, one could also understand the literal one, which gave testimony of glory to our Speaker, God the Savior, at His birth *Matthew 2:2*; at His baptism *Matthew 3:16, 17*; in His suffering and death *Amos 8:9, Matthew 27:45*; in His ascension *1 Timothy 3:16*, etc. See the aforementioned writer. So also the earth, being taken literally, either as the Jews dwelling in Canaan, or the Church in a cultivated and fruitful world. *Isaiah 60:2*, which passage I have noted is applied to the later state of the Church in the New Testament; see Cocceius and Gulichius.

Also, the earth is sometimes taken as a part for the whole, for people who, having surrendered themselves to the beast, are seduced and corrupted by the same in confession, faith, and morals, though they still show some appearance of godliness and zeal. *Revelation 13:3, 8, 12* and *19:2.*

Furthermore, the earth and the people of this earth are taken for animalistic men who crawl in the dust, not having the spirit, who mind, seek, and practice earthly things, delighting themselves therein and seeking nothing higher, *Psalm 17:14, Philippians 3:19.* See Cocceius, Salomon van Til, and others on *Psalm 17*, etc.

2. It has subsequently been noted that when the earth is set against the sea and the islands, especially when the word <term>תבל</term> <note>Hebrew: *Tebel* - the inhabited world or fertile land.</note> is used, and <term>ὀικουμένη</term> <note>Greek: *Oikoumene* - the inhabited world.</note>, then by the earth and the land which is cultivated and sown through the preaching with the seed of the divine word, is understood the Church, which bears fruit in confession and faith: the land where the Church finds a dwelling and covering. By the sea and the islands are understood the restless, wild Heathens and far-off nations, *Psalm 46:3, Psalm 96:11, Psalm 97:1, Revelation 10:2 and 12:16 and 13:11.* One may consult Cocceius, Gulichius, van Til, and on Revelation, Cocceius and Vitringa; for I cannot expand upon everything.

3. I can also very easily concede that the earth sometimes emphatically signifies the Jewish land promised to Abraham and his seed: Palestine, the land of Immanuel, which earth the Lord would strike with the ban and the sword of His mouth; thus to be understood of the Jewish nation and their land, city, and sanctuary, *Isaiah 42:4, Matthew 12:20, Isaiah 8:8 and 11:4, Malachi 4:6.* In whose place the Messiah’s dominion was to extend to the whole earth, that is, all peoples and nations: why it is then said that the meek should inherit the earth. *Psalm 2:8, Psalm 8, 34, 72, 100, 117, and Psalm 37:29, Matthew 5:5.* See Glassius, Cocceius, van Til, etc.

4. When one reads of the earth, or of the land of the living, *Psalm 27:13: I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living. Psalm 52:5: Yea, He shall root thee out of the land of the living. Psalm 142:5: I cried unto thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my refuge and my portion in the land of the living.* Where everywhere <term>ארץ</term> <note>Hebrew: *Eretz* - earth or land.</note> "earth" appears. So one can partly consider to be expressed by this the state of life on earth among the living, set in opposition to the state of death and being among the dead in the grave or in hell.

<margin>Land of the living.</margin> It would also not be out of place to consider that by the "land of the living" one may understand the land alongside the ecclesiastical state of Israel. For although they were under the administration of darkness, wrath, and death (*2 Cor. 13*) in some respect, one can nevertheless say of them, their land, state, and dealings—because the true seed of Abraham, the Israel pure of heart, the tabernacle, temple, God’s fire and light, God’s words, laws, and institutions were found there—that it is the "land of the living," especially in contrast to the dead, hopeless Heathens lying in idolatry, superstition, and the darkness of ignorance (*Isa. 9:1; Matt. 4:15, 16; Isa. 60, etc.*).

<margin>Applied to the inheritance lands of the Church.</margin> I am also not at all averse to bringing this to an even greater emphasis, applying it to the inheritance land, or the inheritance lands belonging to the Church, in its head and king Jesus. In this "church-land" and these lands, there are many in whom Christ lives, who have been made alive by the spirit of his life (*Gal. 2:20; Eph. 2:1*); who live through faith in Christ, which breaks forth and shows itself in all good works and true and pure love (*Hab. 2:4; Rom. 1:19; Gal. 5:6; James 2:17*). This is in contrast to those who are natural men, unregenerate, dead in sins and trespasses, dead to God and unfruitful, not having the Spirit. It is also in contrast to those who show a semblance of life through outward mouth-confession and godliness without power or sincerity, who sometimes fall away from the acknowledged truth due to shifting winds and their own lusts, and whose buds and flowers falling off, they die a second death.

<margin>On the state in heaven.</margin> Yet in the absolute sense, one could cast one's eye upon the heavenly state: immediate fellowship with the living God, the Prince of Life, the life, and the tree of life, etc. See Coccejus, Glassius, and van Til on *Psalm 27:13* <note>Johannes Coccejus, Salomon Glassius, and Salomon van Til were prominent 17th-century theologians known for their linguistic and covenantal approach to the Bible.</note>, with whom Theodoretus <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393 – c. 458 AD), an influential theologian and bishop of the early Christian church.</note> agrees, saying and writing that the land of the living is: <gloss>the expected life, as being separated from death, and corruption, and sorrow and pain</gloss> <note>original Greek: "τὸν προσδοκώμενον βίον, ὡς τοῦ θανάτου κεχωρισμένον, καὶ φθορᾶς, καὶ λύπης καὶ ὀδύνης"</note>. And on *Psalm 116:9*, he remarked: *David by no means calls the present life the land of the living, in which one perceives tears, sighs, illnesses, sins, disasters, and death; but the life freed and stripped of all these things, wherein without any adversities the possession of virtue and the riches of righteousness are present without labor.*

<margin>Ends of the earth.</margin> 5. When one speaks of the "ends of the earth" or the "uttermost parts," one could, with respect to certain passages of Divine Scripture—as with an allusion to David’s and Solomon’s extensive reign, prototypes of the Prince and King Messiah—apply this in a fainter sense to Canaan, the land of Immanuel. In *Psalm 2:8*, the Heathens are distinguished from the ends of the earth; so too in *Psalm 22:28 and 98:3; Isaiah 52:10*. However, since the Messiah was to be King not only as far as David and Solomon, but over the whole earth, and not over a specific limited land, and was to swing his scepter everywhere, we can understand "the ends of the earth" in a more excellent sense. Although the earth, due to its roundness, has no actual ends, we understand not only the nations that were near Canaan and lived on the continents, but also the islanders and the most distant nations. For the understanding and confirmation of

this matter, read the following Oracles: *Ps. 2:8 and 8:6; Ps. 24:1 and 59:14; Ps. 67:8 and 72:8, 9; Ps. 98:3, 4; and Ps. 72:11, 17, 19; and 117:1; Isa. 45:22 and 49:6; Zech. 14:9; Rom. 10:18*, etc.

6. It is neither entirely strange nor ungraceful when one sees the human heart compared not merely to earth, but also to stony earth (*Matt. 13:5, 8, 25; Heb. 6:7*), which must be made fruitful by God and cleared of errors and prejudices. Regarding this, I shall make an extract from the learned work of the Lord Professor Campegius Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist at the University of Franeker.</note> on the Parables of the New Testament, page 23, §. 40, etc.

<margin>Stony earth.</margin> §. 40. The Lord Jesus compares this sort of listeners to a stony earth, which indeed receives the seed into itself, but in which it can strike no deep roots, but shooting up quickly, is dried up by the heat of the sun. In which comparison there is no less grace than in the preceding one.

§. 41. To notice this grace, one must suppose that a stony earth, as the name itself indicates, is an earth whose ground is stony, or rather a stony ground which is covered and as if clothed on top with a little earth, and which has no depth at all. This kind of land was abundant in Palestine (*Matt. 27:51; 1 Kings 19:11*) and such earth has that relationship to the seed, that it can receive it and make it grow, yet nonetheless produce no substantial, much less lasting fruit.

<margin>Stony land in Palestine.</margin>

<margin>Stone, a symbol of a hardened heart.</margin>
<margin>End of the world.</margin> <note>This marginal note refers to the ultimate judgment or the hardening of hearts before the end.</note> §. 42. A Stone appears in the Holy Scripture as a symbol of a mind that is so hardened in its evil prejudices that it cannot at all bow and adapt itself to the rule of its duty prescribed in God’s Law, or of the truth revealed by God. Thus it is spoken of as a "stony heart" (*Ezek. 11:19 and 36:26*); the earth, on the other hand, is a symbol of a mind that has such fundamental principles in it that it is suited to receive the truth. When these two conflicting things are nevertheless joined together, a "stony earth" must signify a mind whose internal fundamental principle or disposition is corrupted by false prejudices, but in which there nevertheless remain—or at least are found—some good and laudable qualities, through which the person might outwardly seem not unfit for the Kingdom of God.

§. 43. In most of the Jews, for example—whose nature and character the Lord Jesus Christ primarily portrays in the first place, as shall be further demonstrated—there were certain false and erring prejudices, or wrong fundamental principles, regarding God and His attributes, regarding the Messiah, His Kingdom, and its righteousness, in which they were strengthened and hardened. These prejudices constituted the internal ground of the soul, and to that extent, they were stony. Yet there were in some of them still some good and praiseworthy dispositions, such as, for instance, first: the common use and exercise of sound reason, which those contemporary believers show themselves still to have somewhat, while they paid attention to the teaching and miracles of Jesus Christ, and recogn—

recognized; in which they differed from those whom the Lord Jesus had compared to a completely hard and trodden earth, *verse 19*. Secondly, there were still some fundamental principles of a true judgment regarding spiritual things within them. As an example, they were convinced that the Jewish people were in a miserable state, that they needed a redeemer, and that such a redeemer had been promised to them in all the ancient oracles of God; that one must investigate the time when he was to come; indeed, that this time had already arrived. §. 44. And there is truly a very striking comparison in this subject, which the Lord himself has already explained in *verse 21*. Namely, the base of a stony earth is stone or rock, which is nevertheless externally covered by a certain good soil, capable of receiving seed into itself and making it grow; yet, this earth is not capable of allowing the sown seed to root deeply enough because of the stoniness of the ground, which does not allow the seed to shoot downward. For this reason, the growth and fruit cannot be powerful, and especially not lasting, because the seed lacks "depth of earth," and thus, as Luke says, lacks a sufficient influence of moisture and richness. But when the sun becomes hot, it withers, and all the sooner <margin>Emblem of the Temporary Believers.</margin> because it had shot up more quickly and higher. This is an excellent emblem of such listeners whom we are accustomed to calling **Temporary Believers**: <note>original: *Tydtgelovigen*; those whose faith is fleeting and lacks deep spiritual roots.</note> for 1. Their hearts are filled with prejudices concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, his Kingdom, and his righteousness. 2. These prejudices have shot deep roots or are deeply placed in their hearts. 3. Because these prejudices are many and firmly attached to one another, they constitute the entire ground of the soul and of judgment. 4. Because of these prejudices, they are not capable of receiving the truth of the Gospel as it is in Jesus Christ into themselves, just as little as a stone rock is capable of receiving seed into itself. 5. In whom, however, some literally good and praiseworthy dispositions are found, which are capable of working a certain faith in Jesus Christ within them; yet this faith usually shows itself suddenly, and indeed with a great outward appearance—that is, with joy and zeal. 6. Because these dispositions have this outward fruit or effect, it appears as if the entire ground, that is, the whole soul of such a person, were good earth; hence the difficulty of distinguishing a temporary believer from a true believer. 7. Just as the earth covering the stone rock cannot make the seed take root—since the stone, as is evident, resists and turns away the root—so the prejudices that constitute the ground of the soul in temporary believers are the cause that the truth of the Gospel, which is in Jesus Christ, is not most clearly understood by them, nor <margin>What "depth of earth" signifies.</margin> accepted with a heartfelt love and consent. For by "depth of earth," of which the Lord Jesus speaks, is understood a mind that is properly receptive

<column-break/>

of the truth. Now, the mind is receptive to the truth, on one hand, when there is a natural capacity or cleverness to understand and distinguish the truth, and on the other hand, when the mind is emptied of false prejudices, with which a person being filled has no "depth of earth," just like a stone rock. 8. However, since the essence, and especially the durability and permanence of the fruit, depends on the root, it cannot be that faith which is not grounded on this firm foundation, and has not shot deep roots into the soul, would bring forth essential, much less permanent, fruits; and this is for lack of "moisture" according to Luke, that is, of the Holy Spirit, who has not been poured out internally into the hearts of such people. 9. On <margin>Affliction compared to the heat of the sun.</margin> the contrary, when oppression comes, which is compared to the heat of the sun—just as in *Psalm 121:6* and *Isaiah 4:6*—which struggles against the prejudices through which one had promised oneself all prosperity and temporal well-being in Christianity, and against fleshly lusts: then one sees that this faith, and the temporary believer, becomes offended because of it, and very easily falls away from his faith.

This cleansing must occur through plowing and harrowing; furrows must be made in the earth to receive the seed that will be scattered; and finally, it must be watered and cultivated. Such earth is an excellent emblem of the mind of a person: 1. Which is by nature evil and empty, because of the misconceptions and lusts which are mixed into the soul—the soul itself being originally good—after the fall of our first ancestors; indeed, with which the soul of man is entirely filled. 2. From which errors, misconceptions, and evil lusts the mind must be freed if it is ever to give fruit. 3. And that through the word of the Gospel itself, insofar as it not only announces grace, but also pronounces God's judgments, by the meditation of which the mind is, as it were, cut through and pierced. *Acts 2:37.* 4. And thus being cut through, and cleansed of prejudices, and furrows having been made in the soul, it receives the word of grace, which is proclaimed in the Gospel, into and within itself.

*Page 10. §. 22.* By the earth that receives the seed, Jesus Christ teaches that one must understand the person, insofar as he is provided with a capacity and power to hear and understand God's word, *verse 19.* Whereby "hearing" is not merely intended to signify the outward hearing, through which he receives the sound of the proclamation in his ears—which man has somewhat in common with the beasts—but whereby he also receives it somewhat in his understanding or comprehension, without it however penetrating to his heart, that is, his will and affection. truth as something lovely and fitting for God through a modest judgment, accepts it, and approves it. Since these faculties in a person belong to their soul or mind: it thus appears that by the "earth" in this parable, what is especially understood is the soul or the mind of man.

7. One finds certain things, and their qualities and conditions, named after the earth—such as being "of the earth," "earthly," "earthly things," etc. This refers to that which is built up from dust, is brittle and perishable, and must decay and die because of the entry of sin, *1 Cor. XV. 40-47. 2 Cor. IV. 7.* **Earthen vessels**, <note>original: "Aarde vaaten"</note> that is, built up from earth, maintained by the earthly, wandering upon the earth in the performance of office and ministry, weak and powerless out of and through themselves, and also less glorious and esteemed in the eyes of the world. See my expansions on *2 Corinthians*, and also there on *2 Cor. V. 1. Earthly Tabernacle.*

In *Col. III. 1, 2.* and *Philip. III. 19.* we read of things that are above, and those that are below; and of people who "mind earthly things," meaning trivial and perishable things, and the pursuits of the world: grandeur, pleasure, governance, riches, status, and pomp *1 John II. 16.* One can also think of the Jewish land and its comforts, pleasures, advantages, the tabernacle, temple services, and physical rituals. In *Philip. III. 19.* I find that Coccejus <note>Johannes Coccejus (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for "Covenant Theology."</note> mainly applies this to the Roman clergy and their pursuits. One can consult Davenant, Aretius, Coccejus, Suicer, Knibbe, d'Outrein, etc., on this matter.

8. I have read *Jer. XVII. 13. O Lord, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you shall be ashamed, and those who depart from me shall be written in the earth; for they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living waters. Jer. II. 13.*

Just as that which is written in the earth is easily erased by rain, wind, or the grinding of feet, and falls into the book of oblivion; whereas <margin>What it means to "write something in the earth."</margin> when one wishes to offer something to eternal memory, one writes it in lead, rocks, or columns: since one lives by the contrast that names are "written in heaven," in the "book of life," or "of the lamb," *Rev. XXI. 27.* etc. This manner of speaking can mean that the name and memory of the godless, who would forsake Israel's rock and Savior, would be rooted out from the earth, that they would die and fall, and reach such contempt among those who wait upon the Lord, that they would be like the dust of the earth to be trodden upon, which they would shake off, despise, and have nothing to do with. One can consult Poole <note>referring to Matthew Poole's "Synopsis Criticorum," a famous 17th-century biblical commentary.</note> on this, to show that they were rejected by God and would not be counted among the people of God and the heirs of eternal life, regardless of what greatness, status, power, appearance, name, or esteem they might have had on earth. These things would perish along with them.

As for the passage in *John VI. 6-8* <note>The author likely means John VIII (8):6-8, the account of the woman caught in adultery, as Jesus does not write in the earth in John 6.</note> where it is recounted that Christ, having turned his face away from the Pharisees after they presented him with a trap-question, bowed down twice and wrote in the earth; concerning this I must say that, because the matter is very obscure and no reason is given to us for this writing in the earth, nor is the content of his writing mentioned, scholars have helped themselves with various guesses. Among others, these suggest: that Jesus wrote

<column-break/>

in the earth, whereas formerly the Law was written on tablets of stone, to show the distinction between the inscription of the Law and the Gospel prepared in hearts—which are like earth—made fruitful for God by the Holy Spirit. Others believe that Christ wrote in the earth to signify that men who cause conflict, accuse, and sometimes drag one another before a judge, are but earth, dust, and worthless ashes. Others again believe that Jesus, knowing the wicked plot of the hypocritical Pharisees and their pretended refinement, feigned zeal, and godliness—while they sought nothing but the praise of men and their wonder, along with the increase of temporary honor and goods—perhaps intended to signify by writing in the earth that their internal and external persons were not upright nor pleasing to God. Rather, they should only be recorded as having earthly wisdom, and not that which is from above; as seeking not God’s glory, but their own praise; not as those who had their birth from God, but from the earth. *Luke XVI. 15. Job VIII. 22, 23.* Some others make an allusion to the high order regarding the woman suspected of adultery, who had to drink the dust from the floor of the Tabernacle as a test, and suffered no harm if she was innocent. So too could these Pharisees, if they were innocent of the crime they attributed to the woman, drink that trial-cup without fear; for Christ said to the Pharisees: *He who is without sin among you, let him cast the first stone at her.* Aretius <note>Benedictus Aretius (1505–1574), a Swiss reformer and theologian.</note> remarked on this that <margin>The opinion of Aretius.</margin> Christ wishes to represent here that the law which, under the Old Testament, commanded the sin of adultery to be punished with death, was now already forgotten among the Jews, or at least fallen out of use: nevertheless, that adulterers and adulteresses will by no means escape God’s weighty judgment, and that missing His grace and heaven, they will be shut out, and thus forgotten by Him.

9. We read of the "old" and the "new heaven," and of the "old" and the "new earth" *Isa. LXV. 66 [LXVI:22]. 2 Pet. III. 12, 13.* especially *Rev. XXI. 1.* regarding which place and naming I shall make some remarks. <margin>On the passing away of the old and the coming of a new heaven and earth; the breaking loose, igniting, and burning by fire, etc.</margin>

*Ouranos* <note>original Greek: ἔρανὸς [sic: οὐρανὸς]</note>, the heaven, perhaps descends from *Or* <note>Hebrew: אור</note> light, or from the Chaldean word *Oren* <note>Hebrew/Chaldean: אורן</note> the day, according to the Doric dialect *ōranos*, essentially meaning fire and light, because the moon, stars, and the finest particles that create daylight would appear in the upper air.

The **Earth**, called *gea*, *gē*, or *gaia* <note>Greek: γέα, γῆ, γαῖα</note>, comes from *geō*, "I bear" or "bring forth," either because God brought the first man forth from the earth, or because the earth, as a universal mother, brings forth everything for the sustenance of the lives of men and cattle; or from *gay* <note>Hebrew: גיא</note> a valley; or from *gay* / *gi* <note>Hebrew: גיא / גי</note> a dale, low place, or valley, because the earth, in relation to the heaven, lies like a plain, low place, or valley—at the very least, the surface and crust of the earth is very uneven, occupied by hills, mountains, and valleys. <margin>This vision is not to be applied to the general Deluge in the time of Noah, though some things might be conceded.</margin>

I do not think, nor do I expect, that anyone will believe that John was looking back at what occurred at the time of Noah in the Deluge, when everything seemed a "Bajert" <note>A term for a chaotic, unformed mass or "the Deep."</note>. Regarding that extraordinary and very famous event, I remark:

*a.* That it appeared as though the waters above were poured downwards through a cloud and a break in the atmosphere.

*b.* That the seas and the depths, the water-hollows and the whirlpools, were as if burst open, and perhaps by the pressure of wind and air were driven above the highest mountain peaks.

*c.* That through this general flood, everything that had life outside the Ark perished; cities, villages, houses, etc., were overturned, uprooted, and washed away, and everything became entangled together, thus becoming a **Bajert** <note>original: "Bajert." This term refers to a state of total confusion or primeval chaos, similar to the "void" before creation.</note>.

*d.* After which—and still in Noah’s time—following the return of the waters to their lowlands and depths, the ceasing of the excessive downpour of rain, the drying of the earth’s upper crust, the repopulating of the earth, and the releasing of all kinds of animals and birds, it must have appeared to be a new world, a new heaven, and a new earth.

I note this only in passing regarding the Deluge, yet I expect no one to think that John (as I have warned) has that event in mind. For if one wished to understand this "new heaven and new earth" as the great change brought about by the Deluge in the time of Noah—already some thousands of years past—then it was not new at all. Thousands of people had already seen that before John and in his time. We still see it daily. It would no longer be anything uncommon enough to make such a great fuss over. Nor was it in any way necessary to obtain either an uncommon vision or to be carried away to a high mountain for this. Furthermore, in the account of the Deluge set down by Moses, I do not find any mention of an old or new, much less a **holy city** descending from God out of heaven. Also, the contents of *Chapter XIX* and *XX*, which precede this chapter, had no place in Noah’s time; and if one were to sift and winnow it a bit more closely, one could say in truth that in Noah’s time no "new heaven or earth" in the proper sense appeared; indeed, the sea as a sea existed and remained, and it was still there in John’s time.

Therefore, I still maintain that no one, whether from divine or worldly histories, is able to show me that what appeared to John in his vision has yet received its fulfillment in its most excellent power.

<margin>The Author does not seem to think it proper in all parts to apply this vision solely to the actual destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple, along with the dispersion of the Jews across the entire earth;</margin>

Setting aside the general Deluge, this vision could suffice if it were brought home literally only to the destruction of Jerusalem and the visible temple, along with the scattering of the Jews across the entire earth; although I am willing to grant some things. Namely, that Jehovah established his signs of powerful and favorable presence in a singular way among Israel in the wilderness, in Canaan, and in the tabernacle and temple; that the Lord established among that people the High Priest shining like a sun with divine ornaments—the breastplate, Urim, Thummim, gold plates with the Lord's holiness—the "moon" of the Jewish Sanhedrin <note>The Sanhedrin was the supreme judicial and religious council of the Jewish people.</note>, and the usual and unusual "stars," such as the Prophets, Priests, Levites, and Teachers.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, I am willing to admit that Jehovah took more pleasure in ancient times in the land of Canaan, and that the land and the people within it were plowed, harrowed, cleansed, fertilized, planted, and sown with the seed of the Lord’s word and blessings more than any Heathen <note>Non-Jewish or "Gentile" lands.</note> land, through the labor of the vinedressers and husbandmen, *Ps. 81:14, Isa. 5, Matt. 21, Rom. 3:9,* etc. Consequently, I admit that this exemplary and moving Kingdom—this "old heaven and old earth"—perished, disappeared, and was rolled up; that in, with, and through Christ, everything has become new, *2 Cor. 5:17.* That through the Evangelical calling of the Gentiles, a new generation has arisen; that a new and different service, way of teaching, privileges, and church customs have entered, *Jer. 31, Hag. 2, Heb. 12,* so that the old is abolished, *Col. 2.* 

Furthermore, I also admit that the Jewish Church and Civil State—like a burning mountain through the fire of internal divisions, domestic strife, and wars—burning and falling, was thrown into the sea of as-yet-ungraced Heathendom under Titus Vespasianus <note>Titus (39–81 AD) was the Roman Emperor who, while still a general, besieged and destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple in 70 AD.</note>, *Isa. 42:24, 25, Matt. 22:24, Rev. 8:8, 9.* Subsequently, I also understand that a new heaven and new earth have come in its place: an unshakeable kingdom of heaven, a new city and heavenly Jerusalem with its head placed in the heavens, *Eph. 2:6.* That the heavenly and earthly have been brought into one sum, *Eph. 1:10.* That all generations provide members of God's household, *Eph. 2:19, Gal. 3.* That they are heavenly in their citizenship, conduct, and contemplation, *Dan. 7, Phil. 3:20, Col. 3.* I also understand that one may call Jesus the Sun, that the Apostles, shepherds, and teachers are stars, and that one could even find planets and wandering stars here, even the twelve signs of the Zodiac, and so forth. I am also aware that some scholars believe it sufficient to apply this vision to the abolition of the Old Covenant and the introduction of the New Covenant, the abolition of the Old Covenant having been united with the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple, along with the exile and scattering of the Jews across the entire earth.

<margin>Although some things may be granted.</margin>

<margin>Opinion of the Author.</margin>

Yet for now, such an explanation cannot satisfy me in all parts, because I am of the opinion that this vision brings us to a much later time of the New Testament, which will be followed by the resurrection of the dead and the general and final judgment. The reasons moving me are:

1. With the change of the Jewish Church and Civil State, the seven Vials <note>Also known as the Seven Bowls of God's Wrath in the Book of Revelation.</note> had not yet been poured out.

<margin>Reasons and remarks.</margin>

2. The enemies mentioned in *Chapter XIX* and *XX* were not yet condemned, nor was their power taken away.

3. At that time, the "sea" (taken figuratively and in the power of imagination) still existed, namely:

*a.* A "sea" and multitude of fleshly and earthly-minded Jews, with monstrous misconceptions concerning the Messiah, the purpose of his coming, his kingdom, the justification of the sinner in the judicial court of God, etc.

*b.* A "sea" of the most fierce, wild Heathendom; barbaric peoples in the east, north, and south; the Roman Heathen empire; for the mountain was thrown into the sea, *Rev. 8:8, 9,* and later a beast rose up out of the sea. Also, the second Vial was later poured out upon the sea, etc.

# EARTH.

## C 3

One thing alongside the other seems to teach me clearly enough that, although the Jewish heaven and earth may have been granted to the Christians and the Christian Church, there has nevertheless remained a sea of Heathenism. Because of this, I believe I may lawfully conclude that this vision is not fully satisfied by simply applying it to the change of the Jewish state and the introduction of the Christian one.

<margin>At what time this vision stands.</margin>
In this regard, I hold firmly that this vision refers to the Messiah’s kingdom, the Kingdom of God, the immovable Kingdom descended from God out of heaven. However, I place the most excellent fulfillment and revelation of it in the later times, near the end of the world, when the Antichrist shall have been judged, the hostile powers overcome, and the Jews and Heathens enlightened through a powerful calling, converted, and gathered and joined into the Church community.

<margin>A few more things brought into consideration.</margin>
**a.** As far as the course of the Heaven of the first Apostolic Christian Church is concerned—which entered with the rolling up and disappearance of the old Mosaic one—I notice in it the Evangelists, Apostles, Prophets, Pastors, and Teachers as greater and smaller stars and lights. These stars are held in Jesus's hand, alongside the true, right, enlightening, refreshing, warming, healing, and fruit-bearing Sun: the light of the world, the glorious image and divine reflection. *Ps. XXXVI. 8, 9; 1 Cor. I. 30; 2 Cor. IV; Eph. III. 18; Hebr. I.*

**b.** Yet I also view this heaven and church-state as not being without planets or "wandering stars," bitter like wormwood, who later fell out of this heaven *Apoc. VI. 7, 8.* <note>The author uses "planets" in the ancient sense of wandering stars that do not follow a fixed path, symbolizing heretics.</note> Arius, along with his followers, drifted here, claiming there was a time when Jesus was not God, thus denying the true and eternal Divinity of the Son.

**c.** Subsequently, there fell from this heaven a very prominent star, a teacher, a presumed head and light, who set up a counter-heaven and counter-earth against the true heaven and earth. He established an exercise of ecclesiastical and civil power, usurping such authority for himself that he held all powers established by God under his control. He exercised all power in heaven and on earth, sitting in God’s house and temple as if he were God *Isa. XIV. 12, 13; 2 Thess. II.* Through this, the form, simplicity, and adornment of the church-heaven was wonderfully changed in appearance. One saw a mixture of Judaism, Heathenism, and Mohammedanism, alongside a clutter of priests and clerics of many orders, garments, rules, duties, and offerings of every kind, value, power, and effect; images, the invocation of Angels, and fabricated saints made from deceased men.

Indeed, one still remembers well how, during the reign of the Beast <note>A common Reformation-era term for the Papacy, referencing the Book of Revelation.</note>, this Papal form of heaven and earth—the light of the sun of Jesus, the Evangelists, Apostles, and the other first Church founders and Martyrs—was not a little obscured, extinguished, and changed as if into a dismal night. This happened through introduced ignorance, human traditions, decrees, superstitions, transubstantiation, the mass, purgatory, the service of angels and saints, and the five "tacked-on" Sacraments, meritorious works, etc. Did this look any longer like such a new heaven and earth descended from God, when one saw Jesus and the A-

<column-break/>

-postles kicked out like the sun and stars, and saw the Pope with his Cardinals coming in their place? Was it not a language of pride, blasphemous and provocative, to say: *the Pope is the sun, the Emperor the moon, the Cardinals and Bishops the stars*? And by legal consequence, that the Emperor, Kings, and Princes of the earth, like the moon before the sun and stars, must bow down before the Pope and Cardinals. Is it not an intolerable pride, and blasphemous, that the Pope allows himself to be respectfully greeted and kissed with the address: *Our Lord and God the Pope.*? <note>original: "Onze Heer en Godt de Paus." This refers to the Latin title "Dominus Deus noster Papa" sometimes found in medieval canon law commentaries.</note> Innocent III, in the Letter to the Emperor, in the Gregorian Decretals, book 1, title 33, chapter 6. <note>original: "Innocentius III. in Epist. ad Imperat. in Decret. Georgian. libr. 1. tit. 33. cap. 6." The text likely refers to the Decretals of Gregory IX.</note>

I believe and expect, therefore, that before the full revelation and display of what appeared to John in the vision, there will still occur the complete fall of the Papal heaven and earth—the kingdom of the Beast—and that the impotence of the Powers which have supported the Roman beast shall be sufficiently revealed. And to this matter I apply *Isa. XXIV. 23: Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously.* From which *Apoc. VI. 12, etc.* does not deviate far: *And I beheld when he had opened the sixth seal, and, lo, there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the moon became as blood; and the stars of heaven fell unto the earth.*

During this Papal heaven and earth, there has remained a "sea," both literal and figurative, for which see the word SEA. For even if it is so that under the superior power of the beast, some Kings and wild nations—such as the Lombards, Vandals, Poles, Hungarians, etc. of old—submitted themselves to the Pope, it came forth more from compulsion, superior force, and fear than from love and the persuasion of the conscience. And even now, there are those who have joined and united themselves neither with the Papal heaven and earth, nor with the true Church. Therefore, among them, the unadulterated seed of the living and eternally abiding Word of God is not sown; for which reason, saving faith, Christian love, hope, and holiness are not found among them.

<margin>A closer presentation of the Author’s sentiment.</margin>
Coming therefore to a closer explanation and a defining presentation of my concepts, I conceive the matter regarding this new heaven and earth thus: that John was shown in a vision, and given to understand, the future state, luster, and glory of the Church of Jesus Christ on earth, after the absolute fall and judgment brought upon the kingdom of the Antichristian Beast, with the conversion of the Jews and the gathering of the Heathen into the Church community and the true faith, near the resurrection and the judgment.

<margin>Some further opening of things to be expected.</margin>
Therefore, explaining myself somewhat more broadly in this, I say that I still expect that the Gospel of Christ and its preaching shall exercise such power upon the eyes, understandings, and hearts of Kings, Princes, Lords, and their subjects—the choice, the select of the nations—that they together shall notice that the Papal power and dignity is usurped and is nothing other than tyranny, ambition, and self-interest; that the Roman errors, idolatry, etc., touch the honor of the adorable God, and the honor and glory of Jesus the surety, mediator, high priest, only lord, head, king, and lawgiver, as if to the heart, and are a deadly poison in the soul.

I note this only in passing regarding the *Zundvloed* <note>The Great Deluge or the Flood of Noah</note>, yet I expect no one to think that John (as I have warned) has that event in mind. For if one wished to understand this "new heaven and new earth" as the great change brought about by the Flood in Noah’s time—already some thousands of years past—then it would not be new at all. Thousands of people had already seen that before John and in his own time. We still see it daily. It would no longer be anything uncommon enough to make such a great stir about. Furthermore, it was by no means necessary to receive an uncommon vision or to be carried away to a high mountain for such a purpose. In the account of the Flood set down by Moses, I do not find any mention of an old or new city, much less a holy city descending from God out of heaven. Also, the events mentioned in *Chapters XIX* and *XX*, which precede the contents of this chapter, had no place in the time of Noah; and if one were to sift and winnow it a bit more closely, one could say in truth that the sea remained as a sea, and that it was still there in John’s time.

Thus, I still maintain that no one, whether from divine or worldly histories, is able to show me that what appeared to John in his vision has yet received its fulfillment in its most excellent power.

Therefore, setting aside the general Flood that occurred in Noah's time, I say further that I cannot believe one can be satisfied by interpreting this vision solely in a literal sense as the destruction of Jerusalem and the visible temple, along with the scattering of the Jews across the entire earth. Furthermore, I concede that this exemplary and moving Kingdom—this old heaven and old earth—has passed away, vanished, and been rolled up; that in, with, and through Christ everything has become new (*2 Cor. 5:17*); that through the Evangelical calling, a new generation has arisen from the Heathens; and that a new and different service, way of teaching, privileges, and church customs have entered (*Jer. 31; Hag. 2; Heb. 12*), so that the old is abolished (*Col. 2*).
