Consequently, I also understand that a new heaven and new earth have come in its place: an immovable kingdom of heaven, a new city, and a heavenly Jerusalem with its head set in the heavens (*Eph. 2:6*); that the heavenly and earthly have been brought into one sum (*Eph. 1:10*); that all generations provide members of God's household (*Eph. 2:19; Gal. 3*); and that they are heavenly in their citizenship, conduct, and contemplation (*Dan. 7; Phil. 3:20; Col. 3*). I also understand that one may call Jesus the Sun, and the Apostles, shepherds, and teachers the stars, and that one could even find planets and wandering stars here, even the twelve signs of the Zodiac, and so forth. I am also aware that some scholars believe they can be satisfied by applying this vision to the abolition of the old and the introduction of the new covenant, the abolition of the old covenant having been joined with the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple, alongside the exile and scattering of the Jews over the whole earth.

*...the heavens are the work of your hands: they shall perish, but you shall remain; and they shall all grow old like a garment. You shall change them like a robe, and they shall be changed. But you are the same, and your years shall have no end.* <note>Quoting Psalm 102:25-27, often cited in the New Testament (Hebrews 1) to contrast the changing nature of the physical world with the eternal nature of God.</note> Following this, I have read that the earth remains God’s work and exists in eternity; also that the world’s fashion passes away, but not that the substances absolutely cease to be. This is presented to us by the Psalmist in the 148th Psalm, verse 6: *And he has established them forever and ever: he has given them a decree which none of them shall transgress.* Ecclesiastes 1:4: *One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever.* 1 Corinthians 7:31. <note>The author uses these verses to argue for the "persistence of matter"—the idea that the physical earth is permanent even if its outward appearance changes.</note>

*e.* And the passage in Romans 8:19, 20 comes to me with great emphasis: *For the earnest expectation of the creature <note>original: "schepzel." In 17th-century Dutch and English, this refers to all of created nature, not just animals.</note> waits for the manifestation of the children of God; for the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who has subjected the same in hope. Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.*

<margin>
Note for the strengthening of the Author’s opinion on Romans 8:19, 20.
</margin>

This last passage serves my purpose in so far as it does not speak of the destruction of the creatures, but of their deliverance. It seems to me contrary to the nature of all creatures to groan for their own total annihilation; however, it is natural for the creature to groan for its deliverance and liberation. Since Paul has linked and fastened the deliverance and liberation of the creature to the deliverance of the children of God, it does not seem strange to me at all that the groaning of the creatures is not for their destruction, but for their deliverance from vanity <note>In this context, "vanity" or "futility" refers to the frustration of nature's original purpose due to the Fall of Man.</note> and bondage.

<margin>
Further remarks on Romans 8:19, 20.
</margin>

Having brought forward Romans 8:19, 20, etc., I further express some of my concepts and thoughts upon them as follows.

I recall what Moses brought forward concerning the first forming of all creatures. *Genesis 1:2.*

Next, how matters stood with the first humans, when they were declared rulers over the universe.

I place before myself most vividly the use and the end of these creatures.

I am mindful that for the sake of sin, corruption entered in, and the earth was cursed; and subsequently, what kind of governance is held, and what use is made of God’s creatures by the ungraced <note>The "unbegenadigden"—those who have not received divine grace and thus live in a state of sin.</note>, and toward what end they usually direct everything, etc. Such things, I say, being properly meditated upon, this then comes to my mind:

*a.* For the sake of man’s sin, the earth and everything is cursed, to plague the sinner, to increase his sorrow and labor, producing many thorns and thistles, especially where he is most reluctant to find them.

*b.* That the air we breathe is often poisonous, vaporous, cold, heavy, full of tempests, thunder, lightning, hail, snow, instabilities, storms, etc., as experience teaches.

*c.* Sun, moon, and stars are sometimes so darkened and overcast by mists, smoke, and heavy vapors that they refuse to grant their rays and fertilizing influence.

*d.* Also, the heavens sometimes become like copper, and the earth like metal, so that the corn, foliage, and

<column-break/>

shoots of grass wither and scorch, and the earth refuses the hoped-for yield to cattle and men.

*e.* And however beautiful someone's gardens, fields, and sowings might look, one sometimes reaps and plucks little, because vermin, the borer-worm, caterpillar, beetle, blight, and other insects graze upon and gnaw everything away.

*f.* And regarding the sun, moon, and stars: they must grant their light to evil people as well as good, and endure that by their light and shine, the most foul abominations and impurity are committed, as well as virtuous deeds and general duties.

*g.* The earth, sea, air, winds, and further other creatures, bear, carry, feed, and are of service to both the evil and the good, the unpious and the pious.

*h.* And how lamentably are God's creatures often misused by the ungraced—through ignorance, for gluttony, pride, or otherwise?

*i.* Being even snatched by some out of their rank and dignity, made into gods and goddesses, honored and served. <note>A reference to idolatry, where elements of nature are worshipped instead of the Creator.</note>

*k.* How often are God's creatures misused against the law of love, to trouble, plague, pain, and grieve one another—yes, even to kill and poison?

Truly, if many creatures possessed understanding, judgment, and a voice, they would groan against the abuser, complain, and wish to be released from them all.

<margin>
Final points regarding the previous matter.
</margin>

Finally, it being established that heaven and earth shall not be annihilated, but that from the substances purified by fire, a new heaven and earth shall come forth, the question arises: for what purpose could these possibly serve?

Upon which we offer the following as some instruction to the reader:

1. When one binds oneself to the Divine Scripture, which speaks of places for the blessed and the damned, then we already have two primary uses in the created world.

2. And granted, I were to admit that after the resurrection, the earth will no longer provide sustenance to any cattle or man, and as before, will no longer be the fixed dwelling place of men, nor be cultivated or planted, etc.; that no trade shall be conducted there, the seas and waters no longer sailed or fished, etc.; what then? Could those great bodies have no other, more noble and higher use? Who, after all, has fathomed God's depths, or searched through the treasury of God's wisdom? What does dizzy man know, who cannot reach halfway along the Lord’s path?

3. And even taking this matter to its furthest and sharpest extreme, what would it matter if I declared outright that I do not know the future end and use of the renewed universe? Could God, for that reason, not have an end in mind and know the use of that All?

4. Suppose I said: God shall deliver the groaning creature from vanity and bondage, and bring it to its first, uncorrupted state, and then delight Himself in His creatures; what sound reason could be brought against this?

5. And if I went further to say that the Lord will do that so that angels and blessed men might rejoice and be glad in God and His liberated creatures, what, pray tell, could be said against this?

6. Was I also not free to think and believe...

Regarding the destruction of the earth, even the Heathens <note>The author refers to "Heidenen" (Heathens/Pagans), specifically the classical Roman poets, to show that the concept of a final conflagration was known even outside of Biblical revelation.</note> seem to have heard something of it. *Ovid* in the first book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> *It is also remembered in the fates that a time shall come, when the sea, the earth, and the seized palace of heaven shall burn, and the laborious mass of the world shall struggle.* <note>original Latin: "Esse quoque in fatis reminiscitur affore tempus, Quo mare, quo tellus, correptaque regia coeli Ardeat, & mundi moles operosa laboret."</note>

> *That heaven, earth, and sea must burn with bright flames,*
> *And the worldly structure fly apart.*

*Lucretius* in the fifth book:

Nor does it escape my mind how new and wonderful this seems to the soul: that there shall be a future destruction of heaven and earth.* <note>original Latin: "Una dies dabit exitium, multosque per annos Sustentata ruet moles, & machina mundi. Nec me animus fallit, quam res nova miraque menti Accidit, exitium coeli, terraeque futurum."</note>

->Which amounts to this:<-

> *The day shall come when the world shall perish,*
> *With all the wild structure that has stood so long.*
> *My heart bears witness, however strange it may seem,*
> *All that blooms on earth shall vanish in the end.*

What more shall I say, or could I say of this, while I acknowledge myself to be among those who as yet only know and prophesy in part?

### AARON, אהרן / Ἀαρὼν.

<margin>Allusion to the name AARON.</margin>
Dealing with AARON <note>Hebrew: *Aharon*; Greek: *Aarōn*.</note> as an example, I shall gather as briefly as possible what pertains to his name, descent, marriage, office, and deeds.

The word AARON means, according to common opinion, as much as *Mountain-man*, or *of the Mountain*. However, one finds that linguists do not derive this name from certain roots in the same way. For some will have it that this noun אהרן <note>Aharon</note> descends from הרר / הר / הרה <note>harar / har / harah</note> which signifies a mountain, or an exalted place above the common surface of the earth. It is noted that this name, or otherwise the word *mountain*, is derived from the Hebrew הרה <note>harah</note>, *to conceive, to be pregnant*, and in its time *to give birth*. During which time of pregnancy the belly expands and swells to a noticeable thickness and height. Thus a mountain is called *Har*, as much for its weight and swollen prominence above the common surface as because a mountain is "pregnant" with many substances and raises itself above the sea and waters. Others again have expanded their thoughts on this in different ways, namely that the name of AARON might well be composed of הר <note>har</note>, a mountain, and a verb רנן <note>ranan</note> which means *to skip, jump, or leap up*, and thus *Aaron* would mean a mountain of joy and leaping. But I do not know if

<column-break/>

it would not be better to derive this name from רנן <note>ranan</note> and רן <note>ran</note>, *to mutter, grumble, or make a wailing sound*; since one usually hears such sounds in the hollows of the mountains. But I do not wish to dwell on such interpretations, considering myself to have explained enough regarding this wordplay.

<margin>Aaron, the son of Amram.</margin>
AARON was the son of Amram, a name said to mean *exalted people*. Furthermore, he was the elder brother of Moses, and thus a son or firstborn of the exalted people, and a Levite. See *Exodus 2:1-2 and 6:19; Numbers 26:59.*

<margin>His marriage to Elizaba.</margin>
He took as his wife Elizaba <note>Elisheba</note>, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon, Prince of the house of Judah. Regarding these names, one finds these allusions: namely that *Elizaba* means *my strong God of the oath, of the dutiful, or of abundance*; from "seven" or a sevenfold part.

<margin>Aaron serves as Moses' mouth before Pharaoh.</margin>
When Moses showed himself unwilling to plead the case of the Israelites before the King of Egypt—which had to be done through the power of eloquent speech, and because he was too hindered in speech—he found such favor with God that Aaron was joined to him to speak the word according to his uncommon ability. He was certainly a man of state and standing in Israel, and thus appeared (as we said of his name) as an exalted mountain. In this way, in the holy pages, mountains and hills are also symbols of illustrious personages who have dominion over the lesser sort of men.

Having spoken of Aaron thus far, I would proceed to his high Church authority, were it not that I had another plan of matters in mind. Following this, it seems to me not entirely out of place if I show—so far as this discussion is concerned—that Aaron can be regarded in many parts and respects as a type of the Christ <note>Typology is a method of biblical interpretation where people or events in the Old Testament are seen as "types" or foreshadowings of Jesus Christ in the New Testament.</note>; which, however, finds its greatest emphasis in his consecration to and performance of his high priestly office, with all that pertains to it.

<margin>Comparison between Aaron and the Christ.</margin>
Regarding the name of AARON, I have already brought forward the wordplay of some concerning it, which can be repeated here.

In respect of this name, one could make this transition: that Christ is like a stone hewn out of the mountain (*Daniel 2:34-35*), from the midst of his brothers; and making up the mountain of Zion and Jerusalem, he was raised up by God according to the flesh (*Deuteronomy 18:15-18; Psalm 22:23; Romans 15; Hebrews 2:11-12*). He was also anointed by the Father over the Church-mountain (*Psalm 2:6*), destined to become highly exalted and very prominent in the world (*Isaiah 2:2-3*); which Church he himself established as a firm foundation and refuge, like a mountain and a rock (*Matthew 16:18; Proverbs 18:10*), etc. He was transformed in appearance upon a mountain (*Matthew 17:2*); he was raised from the Mount of Olives to the highest peak of his reward, majesty, power, honor, and glory, assuming the glory he had with the Father before the mountains were born and the fountains were heavy with water (*Proverbs 8:24-25; John 17:5*). He brings it to pass that in his fellowship, and through the nearest and closest connection to the sharing of his acquired goods and blessings, his members exult, trip, leap, and jump for joy, being unrestrained in the Lord (*Psalm 4:8; Isaiah 54:1; Romans 14:17; Philippians 4:4; Luke 1:46-47*), etc.

It is added that Aaron was Amram’s son, which has been translated as the *magnified and exalted people, the eldest son and firstborn among the others*, etc. See what we have [written] above...

# AARON.

<columns>
2
</columns>

...have said. Again, by way of allusion, one can truly say regarding Christ that he has his origin <note>Dutch: "sprong," literally "leap" or "spring," referring to his lineage.</note> according to the flesh from that people, and from that house and lineage, both in general and specifically from that of David, whom the Lord chose, set apart, made great, and raised to a Royal Priesthood—indeed, elevating David to King. He himself is also high and exalted, being God, the Son of God, Prophet, Priest, and King, the head of the people whom the Lord exalts, expands, and glorifies. At the same time, he is the firstborn of the mother's womb: the only-begotten, the firstborn, the own and beloved Son of God, the firstborn among many brothers.

And if one accepts the opinion of some that this word <note>The author is likely referring to the name "Aaron" or the concept of the "firstborn" mentioned previously.</note> means *the firstling of the fruits, a handful, that which is taken from the lump and dedicated to God for the sanctification of the whole lump*, then it is undoubtedly certain that Christ is the firstfruit (*1 Cor. 15:20*) who rose on the first day of the week (*Matt. 28:6*) to justify and sanctify the members of his body (*Rom. 4:25, Rom. 6*) and to assure them of their resurrection to life, immortality, incorruptibility, and glory (*1 Cor. 15:21, 22, 23, etc.; Phil. 3:21; 1 Thess. 4:14, 15, 17*). However, we shall speak of this more closely under the word FIRSTFRUIT.

That Aaron took as his wife Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon—meaning, as is testified, *my strong God, of the venerable, of the oath, of abundance, constituting a sevenfold part, lord of nations and commander* <note>The author provides an etymological breakdown of the Hebrew names: Elisheba (God is my oath) and her kin, linking them to Christ’s attributes.</note>, my willing people, and what is more—gives me occasion to be able and permitted to say according to the truth as far as Christ is concerned: that he has betrothed a wife to himself, and that she was given to him as a wife by the supreme Governor and Commander of the people, by the God of strength and of the taking of oaths, who has sworn him into his priesthood (*Ps. 110:4; Heb. 7*). And this wife is gathered from the Jews and Gentiles through the seven ages of the New Testament (*Hos. 2:18, 19; Isa. 54:3, 5, 6; Eph. 5:23, 24, etc.; Rev. 21*). This daughter, bride, and wife swears allegiance to him (*Isa. 44:5, 6*); she is the daughter of El Shaddai <note>term: El Shaddai (God Almighty)</note>, the wife of him in whom there is a fullness (*John 1:16; Isa. 12:3; Isa. 61:1, 2, 3*), a fullness of the Godhead, of wisdom and knowledge, indeed all fullness (*Col. 1:19 and 2:3–9*). She is the willing, zealous, and militant people (*Ps. 110:3; Tit. 2:14*) to whom a sevenfold part is granted, as well as the Spirit and the waters of grace and salvation, in streams, richly and abundantly (*Ps. 68:10–19; Isa. 35:6, 7 and 44:3, 4; Joel 2; John 4:14, 6:35, and 7:37, 38, 39*).

<margin>Aaron in his Church-office a pattern of Christ.</margin>
Since I have already said before that Aaron, especially in his High Priestly office and Church administration as the first and the head of all priests, was a prominent example <note>term: "voorbeeld" (example/type). In biblical studies, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note> of our Jesus, I shall—as briefly as possible (for in the following pages and in its proper place I am to speak of high and low Priests, of washing, anointing, Priestly clothes and ornaments, sacrifices of all kinds, and such)—mention a few things concerning Aaron’s Priesthood as a sketch. For this reason, the reader will bear with me that I touch upon some matters here without treating them exhaustively, but postpone them to a better opportunity according to my plan.

I shall primarily make use now of what appears in *Exod. 28:41*: *And you shall put them upon Aaron your brother, and his sons with him; and shall anoint them, and fill their hands, and

<column-break/>

sanctify them, that they may minister unto me in the priest's office.* Compare also *Exod. 29:1, 2*.

I do not say that the anointing was the first thing performed regarding Aaron’s inauguration; nor that putting him into his High Priestly garment was the first of the stately ceremonies. Far be it.

<margin>Aaron anointed.</margin>
Regarding Aaron’s anointing to the High Priestly office, I note briefly that he had to be anointed, sanctified, and have his hands filled <note>term: "hands filled" (handen vullen). A literal translation of a Hebrew idiom for "consecrating" or "ordaining" someone to a task.</note> so that he might serve in the Priestly office.

<margin>the Anointing.</margin>
The first thing in this presentation is the anointing, which was performed with pure olive oil and a mixture of very precious and fragrant spices, by whose power this oil gave off a very strong and exceedingly pleasant scent. See regarding the composition thereof *Exod. 30*. Further in this my work under the words OIL, ANOINTING, ANOINTING OIL, PRIESTLY ANOINTING.

Which anointing, performed at God’s command, was a public proof and sign that he, having been chosen for that office, was also rightly inaugurated into the same. And just as the holy anointing oil was a symbol of the Holy Spirit, so the anointing which God had commanded signified that God, by showering this person with the gifts of the Spirit, would make him capable of the proper performance of his office.

However, since *Exod. 28:41* presents us with the plural number in the phrasing, *You shall anoint them*, and not exclusively, *You shall anoint Aaron*, this has provided the learned with material for reflection and writing: whether the anointing belongs to all priests, or only to the High Priest, and thus to Aaron.

It is not my intention to bring up here everything that is argued for and against. I will only say that the observations of the learned primarily amount to this:

I. First, it is established that Aaron was anointed alongside his sons, who were to follow him in the highest Church office and administration. See *Lev. 6*.

II. It is also understood that he who, upon the death or incapacity of the High Priest, succeeded him in the high Church office, had to be anointed (*Exod. 30:30*), which did not happen when one [ordinary] priest succeeded another.

III. That by way of eminence, only the High Priest is named *the anointed priest* (*Lev. 4:3 and 21:10*).

IV. Furthermore, that in the inauguration of the High Priest, one reads of his anointing; but nowhere of the anointing of the common priests, nor of any divine command for it (*Exod. 29:7, 9; Lev. 8:12*).

V. That if one grants a kind of anointing to the common priests, it would be granted with the following stipulations: namely

a. With a scarcer measure of oil, that is, not as richly as was done to Aaron (*Exod. 30:22; Lev. 4:5, 8:12; Ps. 133*).

b. With oil mixed with the blood of sacrificial animals (*Exod. 29; Lev. 8*).

c. That Aaron received both anointings: the common one with the other priests, and the uncommon one as High Priest. For he had some garments in common with the other priests and had to perform most Church duties with them. Therefore, his right ear, thumb, and toe also had to be sprinkled.

VI. From these observations, according to the opinion of some, one would not understand the matter poorly if one posited...

# AARON.

<columns>
2
</columns>

...stated that the common priests, as sons and children—indeed, as the very garments of their head, the High Priest—were considered to be anointed through him.

<margin>Manner of the anointing.</margin>
Regarding the manner of this anointing, more details are recounted than, in my judgment, can be verified. In the matter of the High Priest's anointing, it is said that it took place upon his bare head. Others deny this, maintaining that it did not occur on his bare head, but over his mitre <note>Dutch: "muts," referring to the priestly turban or headdress.</note>, all over. Meanwhile, the matter is not so clear that it cannot be disputed. However, since the matter is such that the anointing and sprinkling of many holy objects served not for defilement or desecration, but for sanctification and purification, why should one keep the anointing away from the high-priestly mitre? But leaving that dispute undecided, it seems to us that no anointing oil was spared for the high-priestly anointing, since it descended from Aaron’s head into his beard, and even to the borders and hems of his garments, which were just as exemplary and holy as his mitre.

That Moses, having richly poured the holy oil over Aaron, and stroking it with his fingers from one eyebrow to the other, formed the shape of a Greek $\chi$ <note>The Greek letter "Chi," the first letter of *Christos* (Anointed One).</note>, or a Hebrew כ <note>The Hebrew letter "Kaph," the first letter of *Cohen* (Priest).</note>, signifying as much as *Christos* (Anointed) and *Cohen* (PRIEST), as if he wished to say thereby, "You are a priest," etc.—we consider this to consist more of a Jewish tradition than a Scriptural proof. Therefore, I do not dwell on such stories, but let them be worth as much as they are worth.

<margin>How long Aaron had to remain in the Tabernacle after the anointing.</margin>
We have clearer information regarding the time the anointed priest had to remain in the tabernacle. This consisted of seven days, which he had to spend for himself to offer sacrifices, and to sanctify and anoint the sanctuaries with sacred oil. See *Exodus 29:30; Leviticus 8:32, 35.*

Furthermore, his hands had to be filled—undoubtedly in the name of God and on behalf of the people—with a certain portion of the offering. For into his hands was given both what he would do for himself and what he would do for the people before God; and he was not to appear before God with empty, but with filled hands <note>The "filling of hands" is a literal translation of the Hebrew term for ordination, *millu'im*.</note>.

Concerning what Aaron, as the appointed High Priest, had to sacrifice, one can find a more extensive report in *Exodus 29.* As for me, I hold the view that the filling of Aaron's hands was as much as a public acknowledgment of the lawfulness of his calling and appointment, through which he solemnly accepted the administration of his office. See *Leviticus 6:20 and 8:33;* also *Hebrews 5:4.*

To this is added that he had to sanctify Aaron, which is called *washing* and *cleansing* in *Exodus 29:8*; namely, with water from the great copper Washing-vat <note>The Bronze Laver.</note>, which was tapped or led down through taps or pipes into the base, or arranged in small vessels for purification, so as not to defile the whole at once. See *Exodus 40; Leviticus 8; 2 Chronicles 4:6,* from which it appears that the priests, as far as the body was concerned, had to be entirely clean and pure before they put on the holy garments, were anointed, and performed any sacrificial work.

<margin>Priests placed before the tent of Meeting.</margin>
To the aforementioned solemn circumstances was added that they had to be placed before the tent of Meeting, under the open sky, between the altar of burnt offering and the Ark of the Covenant, being the divine dwelling place. See *Exodus 29:1, 2, 3, etc.*

For Aaron, being about to become a public person and to perform the affairs of the people before God, had to be recognized in his dignity by the Jewish body <note>The community of Israel.</note>.

<column-break/>

For this reason, he had to be presented openly to the people, and his hands filled immediately, in order to actually be able to serve the priestly office.

<margin>His garments.</margin>
He was dressed in the holy garments, which are spoken of in *Exodus 29,* and which are dealt with in this work under each specific name, to which we refer the reader. Among these garments were those he had in common with the other priests. Others, however, were special and unique to him alone. As a sign of his holy separation in this office and excellence above his brothers, he had a garment of ornament and glory, as being God’s first servant in the palace of His holiness. Without such garments, no work could be performed in God’s sanctuary.

<margin>Double offering.</margin>
Furthermore, he had to offer a double sacrifice to God, to de-sin <note>Purify from sin.</note> himself and the people, and to sanctify everything; being a more exalted person, and representing the people with confession of sins, which he laid upon the sacrificial animal. See *Exodus 29; Numbers 19; etc.*

With the sacrificial blood, his right earlobe, his right thumb, and his right toe had to be smeared. See *Exodus 29:20, 21.*

When all these solemnities regarding the High Priest were observed, it was believed that he was enabled to approach the Lord, to perform his own affairs and those of the people before Him, as mediator and intercessor.

Having touched upon these circumstances only in passing, I shall, following my plan, share with the reader my thoughts on the things I believe the observant High Priest could see and notice: namely, the High Priest, paying attention to his election from among his brothers, to his presentation and appointment, and so forth, could well understand:

a. That, since he had a sinful and flawed nature, just like his brothers—neither worthier, wiser, more capable, nor holier than they—it was an act of God’s free power and goodness to choose him above all others, and to deem him worthy of the high office of Mediator and Intercessor for his brothers before God.

b. And since his election and inauguration had their origin in the Divine pleasure and command, and his public consecration did not occur without presentation to the people, it appeared therefrom not only that God is a God of order, but also that no one may intrude into any holy ministry before he is lawfully called thereto. *Hebrews 5:4.*

c. Since everything came to him not because of or on account of anything that was within him, but solely and only from the outside—that is, from God and His ordinances—and all the aforementioned solemnities and garments put on him outwardly could work no inner and true change toward greater virtue before God and men (because he remained who he had been before), he could well understand that he was appointed by God to serve in the Church government and the dispensation of grace as an example of a certain High Priest, after the order of Melchizedek, whom He would cause to come forth from his midst due to His own inner capability, to become his soul-surety; whom He would raise up in the likeness of the flesh (to be able to have proper compassion) from the midst of His brothers. See *Deuteronomy 18:18, 19; Psalm 110:4; Jeremiah 30:21; Zechariah 6:12, 13; Hebrews 2:17, 18.*

<sig>D 2</sig>

Since, by the high command of God, before he dared to approach to perform the priestly service for the people, he had to wash himself from head to foot, he could—without straining his thoughts too much—understand:

**a.** That if he, through natural and physical uncleanness, could have no communion with the God of purity and holiness to stand as a surety for himself and his people, he could do so much less regarding the spiritual uncleanness clinging to him through sin and corruption. *Psalm 5 and 24.*

**b.** Seeing himself raised above others in the dignity of his office, yet placed alongside them under the necessity of having to wash and purify himself, he could lawfully make this conclusion: I, and those whom I serve, are all sinful, unclean, and deficient, and must therefore be inwardly washed and purified. See *Job 14:4; Psalm 51:7; Isaiah 64:6.*

**c.** He could also well conceive that the soul could not be affected by water, let alone be purified by it; and that although he and the others, being unclean according to the Law, washed themselves with outward water, they nevertheless remained inwardly before God as they had been before; and by lawful consequence,

1. That in his outward appearance he was an example of such a High Priest who, as the Holy One of God, would have no need of washing. *Psalm 16:10; Isaiah 53:11; Jeremiah 30:21; Hebrews 7.* <note>The author is contrasting Aaron's need for ritual washing with the inherent holiness of Christ.</note>
2. And thus, in his fellowship, in his blood sacrifice, and in his spirit, he would purge the sins of his people, purify them, and present them sanctified before God.
3. And while he himself, being an imperfect high priest, was nevertheless an example of the true and perfect High Priest, it behooved him—both for himself and for the relationship he had with the people—not to rest in outward washings, nor to teach or incite the people to rest in them. Instead, he was to seek the true purification, and teach the people to seek it in the Messiah, the High Priest, in His bloody obedience, and in the spirit of holiness. *Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36; Zechariah 3:9 and 13:1.*

When the High Priest, finding himself naked beforehand, observed how he was clothed by Moses at God’s high command with garments of distinction, holiness, ornament, and purity—even though in himself he remained the same person—and that he might not approach God or perform any holy work without these garments, but only in and with them; then he could indeed, having the Divine Scripture and experience at hand, very easily take up these thoughts:

**a.** Before God I am sinful and naked, without God’s image and glory, without the covering of my own righteousness, without the ornamental garment of holiness. For if I do not possess the outward garment of myself, much less the inward.
**b.** If no one may be a worldly and physical priest without these outward clothes, then no one can be a spiritual priest pleasing to God without inward clothes and ornament.
**c.** However, through all this outward display, I represent such a High Priest who, having been raised up, shall possess the inward reality in, from, and through Himself; who shall also clothe His people and members with righteousness, salvation, and holiness. *Psalm 132:9; Zechariah 3; Isaiah 61:10; Jeremiah 30:21, 22.*
**d.** The High Priest, having taken this properly into observation, learned from this: first, that he must put on his ornamental robes; second, to preserve them accurately; third, to behave himself purely and cleanly, so as to always portray and keep alive his "counter-image" <note>Dutch: "tegenbeelt," a theological term for the "Antitype" or the reality (Christ) prefigured by the "Type" (Aaron).</note> within himself and among the people; fourth, that he always had to set before his soul and the people, and deeply impress upon them, that they, along with him, were to seek the garments of salvation and ornament from the Priest of the divine oath; who, being Himself righteous and holy, would clothe His people with the garments of salvation and righteousness. *Psalm 45; 132:16; Isaiah 61:1, 2, 3; Zechariah 3:9.*

When the High Priest saw himself so richly doused with holy anointing oil above his companions—who were themselves anointed in, with, and through him—and was held to be glorified and prominent in this, then he could proceed to these emphases in his meditations: namely,

**a.** Just as he alone was chosen by and through God to this high-priestly dignity and preferred above others, so he, being by nature unworthy and incapable, had to obtain, and would obtain, his capability from the God of the Covenant.
**b.** That since he excelled above his companions in anointing and the richness of the anointing oil, he had to ensure that he also surpassed all others in virtues and priestly reflections.
**c.** When he recalled that he contributed nothing to his own fitness for that office, nor to the fitness of the other lesser priests, and yet these were held to be anointed in and with him; he had immediate cause to consider that he was an example of such a High Priest upon whom the Holy Spirit and His gifts would not only rest, being richly poured out *Psalm 45; Isaiah 11 and 61; Daniel 9:24*, but that He would also communicate from the abundance of His Spirit to His members, garments, and priests; who for this reason were also called "anointed ones" and "priests." *Psalm 45; Isaiah 35 and 44; Joel 2; Psalm 8.*

When Aaron’s hands were filled <note>Dutch: "handen gevult," a literal translation of the Hebrew term for "consecration" (*millu'im*).</note> so as to be able to offer, both for himself and for the people, with confession of sins, and he furthermore had to remain in the Holy Place for seven days to pray, sacrifice, and purify and sanctify everything according to the law of the carnal commandment <note>A reference to Hebrews 7:16, describing the old Levitical law.</note>, then he could well perceive:

**a.** That he was a sinner before and with God.
**b.** That he had and possessed nothing of himself to pay the debt of his sins or for true reconciliation with God.
**c.** And consequently, he could reconcile and pacify the people recommended to him with God just as little as he could himself. *Psalm 49:8, 9, 10.*
**d.** And that through the powerlessness of all his high-priestly performances, both he and the people needed a Mediator, High Priest, and sacrifice of a better nature, more excellent value, power, covenant, and effect; of whom he had the honor to be an example in his person, dignity, character, deeds, and effects; who would bear the iniquities of the people, end and seal the transgressions, the crimes...

...stated that the common priests, as sons and children—indeed, as the very garments of their head, the High Priest—were considered to be anointed through him.

<margin>The manner of anointing.</margin>
As for what follows regarding the manner of this anointing, more details are told than, in my judgment, can be proven. Regarding the High-Priestly anointing, it is said that it took place on his bare head. Others deny this and maintain that it did not happen on his bare head, but over his miter, everywhere. Meanwhile, the matter is not so clear that there cannot be a dispute over it. However, since the matter is such that the anointing and sprinkling of many holy things was done not for defilement or profanation, but for sanctification and purification, why would one keep the anointing away from the High-Priestly miter? But leaving that dispute undecided, it seems to us that no anointing oil was spared for the High-Priestly anointing, since it descended from Aaron’s head into his beard, and even to the borders and hems of his garments, which were just as exemplary and holy as his miter.

That Moses, having richly poured the holy oil over Aaron, stroked it with his fingers from one eyebrow to the other to form the shape of a Greek $\chi$ <note>The Greek letter Chi, the first letter of *Christos*.</note>, or a Hebrew כ <note>The Hebrew letter Kaf, the first letter of *Cohen*, meaning Priest.</note>—signifying as much as <term>Christos</term> <note>Anointed One</note> and <term>Cohen</term> <note>Priest</note>, as if he wished to say thereby, "You are a priest," etc.—we consider to be more a matter of Jewish tradition than of Scriptural proof. Therefore, I do not dwell on such stories but let them be worth as much as they are worth.

<margin>How long Aaron had to remain in the Tabernacle after the anointing.</margin>
We have clearer information regarding the time the anointed priest had to remain in the Tabernacle. This consisted of seven days, which he had to spend for himself to offer sacrifices and to sanctify and anoint the sanctuaries with holy oil. See *Exodus 29:30; Leviticus 8:32, 35.*

Furthermore, one had to "fill his hands"—doubtless in the name of God and on behalf of the people—with a certain portion of the offering. For there was placed into his hands both what he should do for himself and what he should do for the people before God; and he was not to appear before God with empty, but with filled hands. <note>The phrase "filling the hands" is a literal translation of the Hebrew term for ordination (*millu'im*).</note>

Concerning what Aaron, as the appointed High Priest, had to offer, one can find more extensive reports in *Exodus 29.* As for me, I remain with the view that the <term>hand-filling</term> of Aaron was as much as a public recognition of the lawfulness of his calling and appointment, through which he solemnly accepted the administration of his office. See *Leviticus 6:20 and 8:33; also Hebrews 5:4.*

To this is added that he had to sanctify Aaron; which in *Exodus 29:8* is called washing and cleansing, namely with water from the great copper wash-vat <note>Often referred to as the Bronze Laver.</note>, which was tapped or led down through taps or pipes into the base, or arranged into small vessels for purification, so as not to defile the whole amount at once. See *Exodus 40; Leviticus 8; 2 Chronicles 4:6,* from which it appears that the priests, as far as the body was concerned, had to be entirely clean and pure before they put on the holy garments, were anointed, and performed any sacrificial work.

<margin>Priests placed before the Tent of Meeting.</margin>
In addition to the aforementioned solemn circumstances, they had to be placed before the Tent of Meeting, under the open sky, between the altar of burnt offering and the Ark of the Covenant, which was the divine dwelling place. See *Exodus 29:1, 2, 3, etc.*

For Aaron, being about to become a public person and to perform the affairs of the people before God, had to be recognized in his dignity by the Jewish body [the congregation].

<column-break/>

For this reason, he had to be presented publicly to the people, and his hands filled immediately, in order to actually be able to serve the priestly office.

<margin>His garments.</margin>
They put the holy garments on him, which are spoken of in *Exodus 29,* and which are dealt with in this work under each specific name, to which we refer the reader. Among these garments were those he had in common with the other priests. Others, however, were particular and unique to him alone. As a sign of his holy separation in this office, and his excellence above his brothers, he had a garment of ornament and glory, as being God’s first servant in the palace of His holiness. Without such garments, no work could be performed in God’s sanctuary.

<margin>Double offering.</margin>
Furthermore, he had to offer a double sacrifice to God, to de-sin <note>To atone or purify from sin.</note> himself and the people, and to sanctify everything; being a more exalted person and representing the people with the confession of sins, which he laid upon the sacrificial animal. See *Exodus 29; Numbers 19; etc.*

With the sacrificial blood, his right earlobe, his right thumb, and his right toe had to be smeared. See *Exodus 29:20, 21.*

When all these ceremonies concerning the High Priest were observed, it was believed that he was made capable of approaching the Lord, to perform his own things and those of the people before Him, as a mediator and intercessor.

Having only touched upon these circumstances in passing, I shall follow my plan and share with the reader my thoughts on the things I believe the observant High Priest could see and notice: namely, the High Priest, paying attention to his election from the midst of his brothers, to his presentation and appointment, and so forth, could well understand:

**a.** That, because he had a sinful and deficient nature, just like his brothers—neither worthier, wiser, more capable, nor holier than they—it was an act of God’s free power and goodness to choose him above all others, and to deign him to the high office of Mediator and Intercessor for his brothers before God.

**b.** And since his election and inauguration had their origin in the Divine pleasure and command, and his public initiation did not occur without presentation to the people, it appeared from this not only that God is a God of order, but also that no one may intrude into any holy ministry before he is lawfully called to it. *Hebrews 5:4.*

**c.** Because everything came to him—not because of or on account of anything that was within him, but purely and only from the outside, that is, from God and His ordinances—and all the aforementioned ceremonies and garments put on him externally could work no inward and true change in him toward greater virtue before God and men (because he remained who he had been before), he could well understand that he was appointed by God to serve as an example in the Church government and the dispensation of grace of a certain High Priest after the order of Melchizedek. This Priest God would cause to come forth from the midst of him, due to His own inner capability, to become his soul’s surety; whom He would raise up in the likeness of the flesh (to be able to have proper compassion) from the midst of His brothers. See *Deuteronomy 18:18, 19; Psalm 110:4; Jeremiah 30:21; Zechariah 6:12, 13; Hebrews 2:17, 18.*

When his right ear or earlobe, his right thumb, and his right toe were sprinkled and smeared with the blood of the sacrificial animals, this gave him the opportunity to reflect:

> a. Far be it from me that I should wish to rest only upon what has been said. I wish to raise and spiritualize both my own and my reader's thoughts and contemplations higher, and thus show everyone how the essence, the substance, the pith and marrow of all these outward and symbolic matters concerning the old-fashioned High Priest is found in and through the counter-image <term>antitype: the reality or person that a symbol (type) points toward</term> Jesus, the Christ. To this end, I have maintained the following order and taken this path.

<margin>Aaron and Christ compared.</margin>
Aaron was chosen by God as High Priest, and made known and presented to the people of Israel in his order by Moses, so that they should recognize and accept him in this dignity, and go to God through him; Christ, the Son of God and of Mary, was appointed from eternity and sworn in as priest, *Psalm 2; 110:4; Proverbs 8; Zechariah 6:12, 13.* Compare with this *Acts 5; Hebrews 13; Revelation 13:8; 1 Peter 1:20.* He was previously proclaimed and announced by Moses and the Prophets, and symbolized by the High Priest of that time, *Job 33; Psalms 40 and 69; Isaiah 53; Psalm 110:4; Jeremiah 30; Daniel 9; Zechariah 3:6, 9.* Thus, Christ was able to appeal to their testimony, *John 5:39; Revelation 19:10,* for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

Christ, having entered the world and been sent by God, was publicly proclaimed for and as such for the aforementioned great end, and presented to the world to be recognized as such, and to go to God through Him; namely:

> a. By the Father in a heavenly manner, *Matthew 3:17 and 17:4, 5.*
>
> b. By the Angel at His approaching birth, *Matthew 1:21.*
>
> c. By John His precursor, *John 1:32.*

<column-break/>

> d. After the offering of Himself, after His death, resurrection, ascension, and entry with His blood into the Holy of Holies, He was proclaimed, declared, and proven—principally by the Apostle Paul—to be a faithful and capable High Priest of our confession, *Hebrews 3:1, 2, 3;* the great and eternal one, *Hebrews 5:6;* the sworn High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, *Hebrews 5 and 7;* having all required qualities for the execution of His office. *Hebrews 7:26, etc.*

If one now considers the precise washing of the High Priest, required for the exact purification of the flesh according to the law of the fleshly commandment, as a symbolic means of his impurity and weakness: it is certain that our High Priest Jesus had no need of such purification. One need only look at *Psalm 16*, at *Isaiah 53*, and *Jeremiah 30*, and compare them with *Matthew 1; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 7:26; 1 Peter 1:19.*

<margin>Jesus baptized.</margin>
Nevertheless, to preserve the solemnity and to fulfill all righteousness of the law, He was baptized by John His precursor in the Jordan when He was about to proceed with power in His high-priestly office. *Matthew 3.*

He sanctified Himself for His people as Priest, sacrifice, and altar. *John 17.*

In His resurrection, He was justified, sanctified, and declared free from the burden and curse of sins that had lain upon Him. *Romans 1:4, 5; 1 Timothy 3:16; Galatians 3:13; Hebrews 9:28.*

Washing His members and spiritual priests—His children in fellowship with Him—with His blood and Spirit, He seals and testifies to this through the Word, through the Sacraments, and through faith, both internally and externally. *Acts 2:39 and 9:22; 1 Corinthians 1:30 and 6:11; 1 John 1:7.*

If Aaron's nakedness had to be covered, and he thus paraded covered with divine ornamental robes; if he had to wear them when he performed his priestly work; our High Priest Jesus had no need of them at all. For He was the image of God: He bore God's image and glory in the most emphatic way, *Colossians 1; Hebrews 1.* His birth and conception were spotless, holy, and without blemish, as coming forth from the midst of God. *Jeremiah 30; Matthew 1.*

His whole life was exemplary, holy, without spots, and blameless. *Mark 1; John 8; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 7:26, 27; 1 Peter 1:19.*

With such garments of salvation, righteousness, and holiness—both underneath and above, both internally and externally—He gifts and clothes His priests and favored ones. *Psalm 45:13; Isaiah 61:10; Zechariah 3; 1 Corinthians 1:30; Revelation 7:15.*

If Aaron appears to us with a rich anointing of holy spiced oil, fragrant and refreshing, and descending from his head down into his beard and to the hems of his holy garments; our High Priest Jesus has been anointed from eternity, *Proverbs 8; 1 Peter 1;* not with outward or physical oil, but with the Holy Spirit and His gifts, symbolized by the oil, *Isaiah 11 and 61; Matthew 1; Luke 4;* and that far above the lesser fellow-priests. *Psalm 45; John 3; Hebrews 1:9.*

By which fragrance and scent of His anointing He is wonderfully pleasing to God and the saints. *Psalm 45; Song of Solomon 1; Luke 1 and 2; Ephesians 5:2.*

With, in, and through the High Priest Jesus, those who are His children, body, members, and in a certain sense also His garment, receive from His fullness and become spiritual Priests and Kings, especially in the N. <note>The text likely cuts off "N. Testament" (New Testament)</note>

...a generous measure of his anointing oil and anointing. *Psalms 8 and 69; Isaiah 35 and 44; Joel 2; Isaiah 11 and 54; John 7:37, 38, 39.*

Aaron's hands were filled <note>The "filling of hands" is a biblical idiom for ordination or consecration to the priesthood</note> so that he could offer for himself and for the people, with confession and the laying of sins upon the sacrificial animal; but to Jesus our high priest, a body was granted for an offering, so that he might be enabled to offer himself through the eternal spirit. *Psalm 40; Galatians 4:4; Hebrews 10.*

That body he also took upon himself from a mother’s womb for that very purpose. *John 1:14; Philippians 2; Hebrews 2:14.*

Yet he did not, like Aaron, offer himself first for himself and then for the sins of his people, but only for his people, as he himself was holy and without blemish. *2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 5:7.*

He offered no animal flesh and blood, as Aaron did, but himself, *Hebrews 9 and 10; Ephesians 5,* so that his spiritual priests, following his unique and perfect atoning sacrifice, might offer up to God in and through him the sacrifices of praise—their souls, bodies, tongues, gifts of love, etc. *Romans 12; Psalms 144, 149; Isaiah 43; 1 Peter 2:9; Hebrews 13*—after he carried their sins in his body upon the cross and brought us to God.

Imagine seeing Aaron smeared with blood on his right earlobe, right thumb, and big toe: and then turn toward Jesus, the High Priest of our confession. Observe him closely, and you will perceive from his engravings <note>The term 'graveerselen' refers to the wounds or 'marks' of Christ</note> and descriptions that he had no need for such outward smearing, being holy and sinless: having also pierced ears as God’s willing and obedient servant, possessing an internal desire and love—indeed, a burning zeal—to accomplish all that was pleasing to God. *Psalm 40, 69; John 4; Hebrews 10.*

Nevertheless, Jesus' head, ears, hands, and feet were truly sprinkled with his own sacrificial blood during his suffering and offering upon the Cross. *Psalms 22 and 40; Isaiah 53 and 63; Matthew 26 and 27.*

Aaron had to remain, as has been shown, for seven days in the Lord's sanctuary for the anointing and sanctification of all holy things: but this was entirely unnecessary regarding Jesus, the high priest of our confession. For on the cross-beam he cried out, *It is finished.* *John 19.* And through a single offering, he has perfected forever all those who are sanctified through him. *Hebrews 7 and 9.* And this sacrifice of his maintains its power through the seven ages of the New Testament. And during these periods, having hidden himself and been as if locked away in the heavenly sanctuary, he carries out his priestly work in that place for the sanctification of all holy persons and matters. *Romans 8; Hebrews 7; 1 John 2.*

And when he comes forth toward the last day and shows himself in public, he shall then completely sanctify and perfect all that is holy, presenting his own to the Father pure, perfect, and unblemished. *1 Corinthians 13 and 15; Philippians 3; Ephesians 5.*

If I wished to speak of the types of sacrifices with which Aaron was inaugurated into his high-priestly office, and transfer them to the High Priest Jesus and his sacrifice, and further pay close attention to them all, I would see no end to the allusions to be observed here. For which reason I will intentionally pass by many things untouched,

<column-break/>

in order to speak of them in a more convenient place. However, I wish to make my allusions to Aaron as the speaking mouth—both for God and for Moses before Pharaoh—for the lightening of the yoke of the burdened people, indeed for the preparation of the exodus from Egypt; as he was a man powerful in eloquence and gifted with a rich flow of speech, and transfer the same spiritually to Jesus, our advocate.

<margin>The great name of JESUS.</margin>
Jesus, as Prophet and supreme teacher, speaking in the name of his Father, has a very great name. *Deuteronomy 18:15; Joel 2:23; Matthew 13:17 and 17:4, 5; Hebrews 11.* He appears to us as elegant and wonderfully graceful in speech and reasoning *Psalm 45*; thus Supreme Wisdom praises her lips. *Proverbs 8:6, 7. The opening of my lips shall be sheer rightness: for my palate shall deliberately speak the truth, and wickedness is an abomination to my lips.*

These lips and mouth, wonderfully eloquent and pleasant, he opened on earth. See *Psalm 78:1, 2; Isaiah 40:5.* But after his departure into the heavenly sanctuary, he has touched, sanctified, and made the mouths and lips of some fit and graceful to speak in his name through his spirit. One may see the famous Mr. Adolf Lampe in his exercises on the 45th Psalm, where one will find learned, pleasant, and persuasive matters.

Jesus, this speaking mouth, approached those who oppressed the people through their Commandments, Ordinances, and burdens that increased from time to time. He set before their eyes the Lord's displeasure and the approaching wrath, *Matthew 5:15, 23.* He sought to save his people from those burdens and heavy yoke, and to lead them out of that pit to the freedom of God's children. *Zechariah 11; Matthew 11:28, etc.* But I restrain the further play of my thoughts, having something like an appendix to add to what has already been said about the person of Aaron in particular: namely, a treatise on two rare cases through which the Lord miraculously confirmed Aaron's authority; first in Egypt by the transformation of his Staff into a Dragon, *Exodus 7:10.* Thereafter in the wilderness, when his Priestly dignity was contested, by the blooming of the Almond rod, which was inscribed with his name. *Numbers 17:8.*

<margin>Miracle of Aaron's staff.</margin>
Before God confirmed Aaron in his Ecclesiastical office, he validated the authority and the mission of both him and Moses through a primary miracle in the court of Pharaoh, which is recounted in *Exodus 7:10. And Aaron cast down his staff before Pharaoh's face, and before the face of his servants; and it became a Dragon.*

Intending to explain the ten plagues in Egypt in the appropriate place in this my work, and more broadly elsewhere in a separate treatise, I will only briefly note here that the root word <term>תנין</term> <note>Hebrew: Tannin</note> translated as "Dragon," is not understood in this way by all commentators. For some take this word in the sense of a house-snake. Others generally in that of a serpent, without determining of what kind, nature, or size it was. Many again in the sense of a Crocodile, partly a land- but primarily a water-animal, very well known and esteemed by the Egyptians.

# AARON.

[One] finds *snake, whale, great serpent* etc. translated as *dragon*. For the latter, however, the learned Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a famous French Protestant scholar who wrote 'Hierozoïcon,' a massive study of animals in the Bible.</note> appeals to the Syrians, Arabs, and Hebrews, who generally take it to mean that, as seen in *Hierozoïcon III, 4.*

I, meanwhile, concerning myself little with this distinction and not defining the nature or size of this animal, am of the opinion that whatever name one wishes to give it, it must have been a quite large and frightful beast.

<margin>The Author's opinion on this.</margin>
Since God alone can perform true miracles, which we cannot fully fathom in any way—as appears from *Exodus 15:11, Psalm 72:19, and 77:16*—I am of the opinion that His hand, acting upon faith, upon obedience, and upon the casting down of the staff before the eyes of Pharaoh, wrought this miracle.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
To refute my opinion, one might bring against me that which is recounted in *Exodus 7:10, 11* concerning the Egyptian artists <note>In this context, "artists" refers to practitioners of the occult arts or magicians.</note> summoned by Pharaoh, who put their incantations to work in the same manner. *For* (so the words of Scripture report) *each one threw down his staff, and the staffs became dragons: but it simply comes down to whether these artists truly changed their staffs into natural snakes or dragons, or only in appearance.*

<margin>The names of these master-artists explained.</margin>
But before I proceed to the investigation of this matter, I shall say something regarding the names of the persons summoned. I have found that these titles are explained as follows.

The word חכמים <note>Chakamim</note>, translated as *wise men*, is intended to mean *masters in the secret and liberal arts, naturalists, and astronomers.*

The word מכشפים <note>Mechashepim</note> is said to mean *soothsayers, diviners, jugglers, or conjurers; people who, through clever sleight of hand and rapid movements of the hands, hinder the observation of the onlookers, so that one—unable to keep an eye on their actions—accepts the appearance for the truth, without truly getting behind the secret of their skill in these artistic maneuvers.*

By חרטמים <note>Chartummim</note> are understood clever people who, through their great knowledge of nature, know how to perform things at which one’s understanding must generally stand still. Of such people it is said: *They did likewise with their enchantments.* By the Hebrew word that means *enchantments*, we are to understand *mutterings, mumbles within the mouth, and well-practiced dexterities.*

The root word is derived by some from להט <note>Lahat</note>, *a flame, glint, or flickering of a sword, a polished blade, or a spear.* Others again derive it from לוט <note>Lat</note>, meaning *to cover and hide.*

<margin>The Author's opinion.</margin>
Regarding the latter, I consider that these men, when throwing their sticks or staffs to the ground, would have added some mutterings, commonly called incantations. For these sleights of hand do not reach their goal unless the onlookers are detained by certain circumstances and, as it were, led up the garden path: so that the artist, through his swift and sudden actions, is able to deceive the sight, which cannot follow his calculated bowing and movement of limbs so quickly.

However it may be, one of two things is true. Their staffs were changed into true dragons, or only in appearance. If the change truly happened, it must have been worked either by them, or by God, or by the devil: unless one comes to the conclusion that it is firmly

<column-break/>

established and believed that something occurred by which Pharaoh and his people imagined those dragons had come there, and yet there was something that was truly seen by them, without them noticing in what manner those dragons had appeared, which were then devoured and swallowed up by the dragon that came from Aaron’s staff. Since the substance of the matter depends on this, and the work turns upon this hinge, it seems to me that it is my task to pause a while on the investigation of this, and to weigh more closely what the following words contain: *The Egyptian sorcerers also did so by their enchantments and mutterings.*

<margin>The judgment of the Commentators and others on this.</margin>
The Commentators <note>The 'Kanttekenaars' refers to the authors of the marginal notes in the Dutch Authorized Version (Statenvertaling) of the Bible.</note> and other scholars, for whom I have high regard, view this work as a foul deception of the devil, holding that these hypocrites did everything either through dexterity or the meddling of the devil, merely in appearance; and that Pharaoh and his courtiers were led to believe they saw what they did not see, because it was not there.

On this occasion, I shall bring forward something concerning the Rod and incantations of Mercury, of which Virgil speaks in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*. The words of the poet are:

> *Then he takes his WAND: with this he calls forth pale spirits* <note>original: "Tum VIRGAM capit: hac animas ille evocat orco / Pallentes"</note>
> *from the underworld, others he sends down to grim Tartarus:* <note>original: "alias sub tristia tartara mittit:"</note>
> *He gives and takes away sleep, and unseals eyes in death.* <note>original: "Dat somnos adimitque, & lumina morte resignat."</note>

Which, according to Vondel’s translation <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) was the preeminent Dutch poet and playwright, often called the "Dutch Shakespeare."</note>, sounds like this:

> *He takes hereafter the ROD, which can stir souls,*
> *Even the pale ghosts he summons from Pluto’s throne,*
> *And other souls to the mournful pool of misery*
> *He sends through its power. Sleep comes creeping in,*
> *And flees before it: it closes the eyes of the dead.*

Concerning these mutterings, and the supposed power of such incantations, we also find something mentioned by Ovid in the fourteenth book of the *Metamorphoses*,

> *Three times nine times she murmurs a song with her magic mouth.* <note>original: "Ter novies magico carmen demurmurat ore."</note>

That is, according to the translation of the same:

> *She mumbles within her mouth a full three times nine times*
> *A dark magic verse.*

Valerius Flaccus, at the place where Jason must be encouraged, also speaks of it in the seventh book [of the *Argonautica*],

> *Now she rolls and fixes the charms through all the limbs* <note>original: "Carmina nunc totos volvit figitque per artus / Aesonidae"</note>
> *of Jason, and through the shield with a sevenfold murmur* <note>original: "septeno murmure fertur / Per clypeum"</note>
> *it is carried, and she made the spear heavier for the man.* <note>original: "atque viro graviorem reddidit hastam."</note>

That is:

> *Upon this she works immediately on Jason’s entire limbs,*
> *And rolls through his shield with her magic words*
> *Repeated up to seven times with grim muttering,*
> *And adds force and new strength to his spear.*

From which it can be inferred to some extent that these supposed masters, in throwing their staffs to the earth, would also have made use of some mutterings, mumbles, or incantations within the mouth, which according to their claims were of singular power and effect to the ignorance of the people. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the miracle performed before Pharaoh. # AARON.

[They] have unique grips and dexterity to deceive the onlookers.

<margin>Judgment of the Church Fathers.</margin>
Among the learned, one finds those who judge that the throwing down of these staves did not produce real snakes, but only bare forms, without life and movement, but that the devil or some spirit brought movement into them. Among these are to be counted Tertullian, Justin, Ambrose, Jerome, Rupert, Gregory of Nyssa, Prosper, and others. <note>These are early Christian theologians and writers from the 2nd to 5th centuries AD.</note>

<margin>Judgment of others.</margin>
Against this, others say that they were truly snakes or dragons, because the serpent that rose from Aaron's staff swallowed them; this indicates something substantial and physical. All the more so because in the account of Moses it is not denied that they were true dragons that were swallowed. Whether the change of the staves into dragons truly happened through the work of the devil, or whether these artists <note>Magicians or practitioners of the occult.</note> knew how to pick up the staves through inscrutable dexterity and, hiding them, smuggle snakes in their place, seems to have been left undecided and undetermined by some, as this seems to be noted by Philo, Origen, Theodoret, Augustine, and others.

Furthermore, I believe I have noticed that even if one assumes they were true snakes or dragons, one does not imagine they were of the largest kind. Nor is it strange to feel that quite some time would have passed between the actual performance by Aaron and that of the magicians summoned afterward. Neither is it beyond probability that these wicked guests would have had knowledge of their summons to court, through which opportunity may have been given to them to prepare themselves for the clever execution of their work. To this is added that some have remarked that it is not clearly stated whether these artists performed their work in the presence of Moses and Aaron.

Those who allow for true transformations cite a very rapid motion, through which the material parts of the staves were dissolved and so changed that dragons or snakes came forth from them. So that by this motion the particles were rearranged, and thus the outward form was changed. One may look this up in Thomas, Cajetan, Del-Rio, Rivet, Calovius, Doughty. *Anal. Sacr.* <note>original: "Analecta Sacra"</note> *de Mey Phys. Sacr. &c.* <note>The author is citing a variety of 17th-century Catholic and Protestant theologians and "sacred physicists" who tried to explain miracles through natural philosophy.</note>

One finds those who seem to lean toward an opinion by which they posit that it pleased God to also change the staves of these deceivers into dragons and snakes, though not to strengthen lies and superstition, but to test, blind, and harden the King, just as it says in *Deuteronomy 13:1, 2, 3.* But one may rightly doubt this, because it is not to be suspected that the Lord performed anything here against Himself, or favored these people with any appearance of approval, and thus wished to spoil such an unusual work, performed by Him, with another unusual work.

If one may posit (that which we touched upon above) that this work occurred in the absence of Moses and Aaron, one would almost lean toward the idea that these people brought forth some dragons and snakes that they had brought hidden with them, after they had cleverly hidden their staves. Toward which opinion one could be moved by the wonderful actions of our modern-day conjurers, who know how to mislead even the most discerning eye.

<column-break/>

But we determine nothing regarding this, giving the reader his freedom in letting his thoughts wander over this passage.

There is no lack of learned men who are of the opinion that Jannes and Jambres <note>Traditional names for the Egyptian magicians, mentioned in the New Testament but not the Old.</note> may well have been among these deceivers, as it is mentioned of them that they opposed Moses. See *2 Timothy 3:8,* of whom we shall perhaps speak more broadly at a later opportunity.

<margin>Jannes and Jambres.</margin>

Although nothing is heard in the divine history of what Moses and Aaron brought forth regarding this feat of skill, something quite strange and wonderful comes before us nonetheless. For it says: *But Aaron's staff swallowed their staves.* Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD), a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> mentions something of which not the slightest sign appears in the account left by Moses.

<margin>Thoughts of Philo the Jew.</margin>
He mentions that when each had thrown his staff to the ground, there immediately appeared a great multitude of dragons, which moved around Aaron's dragon. That thereupon Aaron's dragon, raising its upper body, opening its mouth wide, hissing terribly, and inhaling much air, drew all these dragons as if toward itself, and swallowed them one after another; and then returned to its previous form of a staff, and appeared in that state. But as we encounter nothing of this in the divine history, we shall leave the human account for what it is worth.

The word <term>בלע</term> <note>Hebrew: "Bala," meaning to swallow, engulf, or consume.</note> means *to swallow, to devour, to gulp down*, and that in such a way that nothing of it shows on the outside.

One has reason to think that these dragons were swallowed one after another; unless one wanted to suppose that Aaron's dragon was exceptionally large, and consequently had a large belly, and the other dragons were quite smaller. For otherwise, one would greatly multiply the miracles.

<margin>Aaron's dragon changed into a staff.</margin>
That the staff of Aaron was thereafter brought back to its previous nature and quality, no one will venture to deny who believes that which is mentioned in the fifteenth verse.

<margin>Story of Rabbi Simeon.</margin>
The Jewish masters note as something remarkable that the staff of Aaron, used in this miracle, was the same staff that later blossomed and bore almonds. Rabbi Simeon tells strange and wonderful things about it. Thus he speaks: *The Rod, with which Moses and Aaron performed wonders in Egypt, is the same that later grew green, blossomed, and sprouted buds in the wilderness. It is the tree that God pointed out to Moses in the wilderness to make the bitter water sweet. It was cut from the tree of life, which was planted in paradise by the hands of the Angels. It is that which they sent to Adam, when he had sent Seth to paradise, to obtain forgiveness for his sins through a humble prayer to God. Thereupon the Angels commanded Seth to plant this tree, with the promise that as soon as this planted tree should bear fruit, Divine mercy would descend, and at that very same moment the gates of heaven, which had been closed until then, would be opened. Thereupon Seth planted this branch in the wilderness, where it was found by Moses. He cut a branch from it, which since then has borne the name of God's rod. He adds that this rod is also the same tree on which Moses hung the Serpent, through which the Lord willed that the whole world should be saved, and determined that as soon as King Messiah should come, He would send His mercy downward from heaven upon Adam.*

The previous page discussed the nature of the "dragons" and the names of the Egyptian sorcerers; here, the author explores whether the magicians' feat was a genuine physical transformation or a demonic illusion, while also recounting legends concerning the origins of Aaron's rod.</meta>

<page-num>31</page-num>

# AARON.

...possessing special grips and sleights of hand to deceive the spectators.

<margin>Judgment of the Church Fathers.</margin>
Among the learned, some judge that the throwing down of these staves did not produce real snakes, but only bare forms without life or movement, into which the devil or some spirit introduced motion. Among these are to be counted Tertullian, Justin, Ambrose, Jerome, Rupert, Gregory of Nyssa, Prosper, and others. <note>These are prominent early Christian theologians and scholars, often referred to as the Church Fathers.</note>

<margin>Judgment of others.</margin>
Against this, others say that they were truly snakes or dragons, because the dragon that arose from Aaron's staff swallowed them; this indicates something substantial and physical. Furthermore, in the account by Moses, it is not denied that they were true dragons which were devoured. Whether the transformation of the staves into dragons truly happened through the working of the devil, or whether these craftsmen, through untraceable agility, managed to pick up the staves and, hiding them, sneakily substitute snakes in their place—this seems to be left undecided by some, as appears to be noted by Philo, Origen, Theodoret, Augustine, and others.

Furthermore, I believe I have noticed that even if one assumes they were true snakes or dragons, one should not imagine they were of the largest kind. There is also a suspicion that quite some time must have passed between the actual performance by Aaron and that of the craftsmen summoned afterward. Nor is it beyond doubt that these wicked guests would have had knowledge of their summons to court, which might have given them the opportunity to prepare themselves for a clever execution of their work. To this is added what some have remarked: that it is not clearly mentioned whether these craftsmen performed their work in the presence of Moses and Aaron.

Those who allow for true transformations suggest a very rapid movement, through which the material parts of the staves were dissolved and changed in such a way that dragons or snakes emerged from them. Thus, through this motion, the particles were rearranged, and so the external form was changed. See on this matter Thomas, Cajetan, Del-Rio, Rivet, Calovius, Doughty’s *Sacred Analysis*, de Mey’s *Sacred Physics*, etc. <note>These citations refer to a mix of Medieval Scholastics and 17th-century Protestant and Catholic theologians who attempted to explain miracles using the natural philosophy of their time.</note>

One finds those who seem to lean toward an opinion that God was pleased to change the staves of these deceivers into dragons and snakes as well—not to strengthen lies and superstition, but to tempt, blind, and harden the King, just as is written in *Deuteronomy 13:1, 2, 3.* But one may rightly doubt this, as it is not to be suspected that the Lord would perform anything here against Himself, or favor these people with any appearance of success, and thus wish to ruin such an unusual work performed by Him with another unusual work.

If one may suggest (which we touched upon above) that this work occurred in the absence of Moses and Aaron, one would almost lean toward the idea that these men brought forth some dragons and snakes which they had brought hidden with them, after they had cleverly concealed their staves. One could be moved toward this view by the wonderful actions of our modern-day conjurers, who know how to mislead even the most discerning eye.

<column-break/>

But we determine nothing here, giving the reader his freedom in letting his thoughts wander over this passage.

<margin>Jannes and Jambres.</margin>
There is no lack of learned men who are of the opinion that Jannes and Jambres <note>Traditional names for the Egyptian magicians, mentioned in the New Testament but not the Old.</note> may well have been among these deceivers, as it is mentioned of them that they withstood Moses. See *2 Timothy 3:8,* of whom we shall perhaps speak more broadly at a later opportunity.

Although nothing is heard in the divine history of what Moses and Aaron produced during this feat of skill, something quite strange and wonderful nevertheless comes before us. For it says: *But Aaron’s staff swallowed their staves.* Philo mentions something of which not the slightest sign appears in the account left by Moses.

<margin>Thoughts of Philo the Jew.</margin>
He mentions that when everyone had thrown their staff to the earth, there immediately appeared a great multitude of dragons, which moved around Aaron’s dragon. Upon this, Aaron’s dragon, raising its upper body, opening its mouth wide, hissing terribly, and inhaling much air, drew all these dragons toward itself as if by force, and swallowed them one after another; and then returned to its previous form of a staff, appearing in that state. But as we encounter nothing of this in the divine history, we shall leave the human account for what it is worth.

The word <term>bala (בלע)</term> <note>original: "בלע"</note> means *to gulp down, to swallow, to ingest*, and that in such a way that nothing of it shows on the outside.

There is reason to think that these dragons were swallowed one after another; unless one wished to suppose that Aaron’s dragon was exceptionally large, and consequently had a large belly, while the other dragons were quite small. For otherwise, one would greatly multiply the miracles.

<margin>Aaron’s dragon turned back into a staff.</margin>
That the staff of Aaron was thereafter brought back to its previous nature and quality, no one will venture to deny who places faith in what is mentioned in the fifteenth verse.

<margin>Account of Rabbi Simeon.</margin>
The Jewish masters note as something remarkable that the staff of Aaron used in this miracle was the same staff that later bloomed and bore almonds. Rabbi Simeon tells strange and wonderful things about it. Thus he speaks: *The Rod with which Moses and Aaron performed wonders in Egypt is the same one that later turned green, blossomed, and shot forth buds in the wilderness. It is the tree that God pointed out to Moses in the wilderness to make the bitter water sweet. It was cut from the Tree of Life, which was placed in Paradise by the hands of the Angels. It is the same rod they sent to Adam when he had sent Seth to Paradise to obtain forgiveness for his sins through a humble prayer to God. Thereupon the Angels commanded Seth to plant this tree, with the promise that as soon as this planted tree should bear fruit, Divine mercy would descend, and at that same moment the gates of heaven, which had been closed until then, would be opened. Thereupon Seth planted this branch in the wilderness, where it was found by Moses. He cut a branch from it, which since then has borne the name of God’s rod. He adds that this rod is also the same tree on which Moses hung the Serpent, through which the Lord willed that the whole world should be saved, and decreed that as soon as King Messiah should come, He would send His mercy downward from heaven upon Adam.*

->Behold<-

It also details an expansive Jewish legend tracing the origin of Aaron’s rod back to the Tree of Life in Paradise.</summary>
