# AARON.

If anyone takes this as current coin <note>The author uses a metaphor of "current coin" to mean "valuable or acceptable information."</note>, may he find it to his advantage. To me, such follies—which are found in great numbers among the Jews—are of no value. Therefore, I do not wish to occupy myself with such useless things, but rather proceed to weightier matters.

When we observe how the staff of Aaron took on the form of dragons or serpents, appearing poisonous in outward show while it swallowed and killed the others—not without a divine miracle and unusual providence—it seems to me that one could here be mindful of the unusual deed of God. Through this deed, He sent His son not only in the flesh, but in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, He condemned sin in the flesh (*Romans 8:3*). Likewise, He was regarded as being plagued and punished by God for His own misdeeds (*Isaiah 53:3, 4, 5*), even though the truth of the matter was that He was paying the debt for which He had remained the guarantor. (*Psalm 69:5; Romans 4:25; 2 Corinthians 5:21.*)

And thus, in His transformation through His death, Christ has swallowed up sin and death along with the tyrant of death—the serpent and the ancient dragon—with his poison. He has annihilated him, crushed his head, and caused his works and dominion to cease (*Hebrews 2:14, 15; 1 Corinthians 15:54, 55, 56, 57; 1 John 3:8*). Subsequently, He also caused the Jewish "serpents"—that brood of vipers and enchanting master-craftsmen who knew how to win over and bewitch the common people—to melt away and disappear through His judgments, as if He had swallowed them. These were the ones who contradicted His teaching and miracles, mocked Him, and openly slandered Him, as if He had made a secret conspiracy, and who, by imposing burdens on His people, did not desire that they should go out free and frank.

It shall be no different with the master-craftsmen in "spiritual Egypt" <note>A common biblical metaphor, often used in this period to refer to corrupt religious institutions or those who lead people away from the truth.</note>, who have performed quite large and many signs and lying wonders. For the Lord shall destroy them by the breath of His mouth, and the destructive judgments shall fall upon them and their supporters in such a way that their memory shall cease from the earth. (*Revelation 11.*)

After this first case, there now follows the other, no less noteworthy, which happened concerning him and his staff after he had already been anointed as High Priest.

<margin>The miracle of Aaron's Almond Rod.</margin>
This miracle, consisting of Aaron's staff turning green, budding, blooming, and bearing almonds in a single night, I shall treat more closely under the word **ALMONDS**, to which I refer the reader. Concerning the historical event and what pertains to it, one may consult *Numbers 17:17*.

Twelve rods or staves had to be taken, one for each tribe. Upon these, the names of the twelve distinct Tribes had to be written.

Whether the travel-staves or walking sticks of the twelve Tribal Chiefs were used for this, or their staves of authority, or such as each Tribal Chief saw fit, or otherwise almond rods—in order to have uniform sticks—I shall leave undecided for this time.

<margin>Tribal names written on the rods.</margin>
The Tribal names were written on the rods, but the name of **AARON** was written for the Tribe of **LEVI**.

Concerning how this writing of the names was carried out, there are various considerations. For it is uncertain whether they were written on strips of parchment and each strip attached to each distinct staff; or whether they were marked on the staves with some ink or paint; or whether the letters were written therein by engraving; also whether each head of a tribe wrote his own Tribal name himself to

<column-break/>

prevent all sinister suspicion. Leaving all this aside, I note that all these staves were laid before the Lord's face, and this transaction was accurately observed; it being probable that through posted sentries <note>The author suggests that guards were used to ensure no human tampering occurred during the night.</note> it was carefully watched whether anything occurred prematurely in or around God's sanctuary upon which one could legally ground any contradiction.

This having been performed so solemnly, the decision and outcome depended solely upon the Lord.

The Lord then—who had chosen His servant Aaron, called him, and confirmed him in his High-Priestly office through Moses—decided the matter over which there was dispute in favor of Levi and Aaron, acting as Supreme Judge. Namely, He caused Aaron's rod in one night to turn green, bud, bloom, and bear almonds. It could be that these leaves and fruits remained on the rod even when it was placed in the Ark, by God's high command, as a memorial of the miracle and confirmation of Levi's Priesthood and Aaron's highest Church government.

I by no means think that this singular event happened to Aaron without Divine guidance or any further outlook; rather, I believe He allowed this to happen to the <term>exemplary High Priest</term> <note>In this context, "exemplary" (voorbeeldig) means "serving as a type or foreshadowing."</note> because something similar was to occur among the Jews to His Son, the antitype of Aaron. Wishing to defend and confirm the dignity and everlasting Priesthood of this Son, He intended to perform something that would be miraculous, divine, and astonishing.

To me it is certain that Christ is not only called a *root, a twig, a rod*, and a *shoot* out of a dry earth (*Isaiah 11 and 53*—one may search for these titles in this work), but that He is also a miraculous and an immediately God-begotten *sprout* and rod, without manly assistance (*Isaiah 4 and 7; Jeremiah 31; Matthew 1; Luke 1*); a *shoot* and *sprout* who during His life showed Himself miraculously alive, active, and powerful in words and wonders.

This much is certain: if someone wished to deny that the later Jews—preoccupied with the idea of a Messiah as a temporal Savior and worldly King—disputed Jesus's High-Priestly office on the grounds that He sprang from Judah and not from Levi, he would thereby show that he had not read the writings of the Rabbis with proper attention and observation, and had very little understanding of the aim of Paul in *Hebrews 7*.

One may see concerning this the thoroughly learned work of the Reverend and famous Mr. Tako Hajo van den Honert <note>A prominent Dutch theologian (1666–1740) known for his works on biblical history and the relationship between the Old and New Testaments.</note>, Professor at Leiden, on *Psalm 110*, along with his Supplement in defense, pages 367, 373.

For among other things, this was also the reason for His being cut off from the land of the living. (*Isaiah 53; Daniel 1; Matthew 27.*)

This Jesus, like a dry staff and a cut-off rod, was laid in the grave before the Lord's face, and the grave was sealed, watched, and guarded (*Psalm 16; Isaiah 53; Hosea 6; Matthew 28; 1 Corinthians 15; Romans 1; 1 Timothy 3:16; 1 Peter 3*), whereby He was justified by Him who was near Him against His enemies (*Isaiah 49; Romans 1:4, 5 and 4:25*), having afterwards served His everlasting priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek (*Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7*), being in incorruptibility and immortality and continual activity as High Priest before the Lord's face,

The author argues that these Old Testament miracles were "types" or foreshadows intended to validate Christ's authority against those who would later dispute it.</summary>

<header>AARON. CARCASS. ABADDON.</header>

...and observing the affairs and interests of his people. *Rom. VIII. Hebr. VII. 10, 11.* preserving like a wondrous tree of life his buds, flowers, and fruits *Apoc. XXII. 2.* serving not only his priesthood according to Melchizedek's order <note>Melchizedek was a mysterious king-priest in Genesis; the author refers to the theological idea of Christ's eternal priesthood</note> in his immortal and glorified body, but also bringing it about that his members and sons—having been made living and fruitful in his fellowship *Rom. VI. 8. Joann. XV.* in and through him, and the constant inward working of his spirit—though in themselves dry, sapless, and fruitless rods and shoots, turn green, grow, and become fruitful in all good works, *Ps. I. and XCII. Joann. XV. Gal. II. Philipp. I. 4, 8.* and acquit and behave themselves as spiritual Priests and Levites *Matth. I. 1 Petr. II. 9. Apoc. I. 5.* He shall, after their bodies have been cut off by death and have lain in the earth for a time as dry and sapless, raise them up before the Lord’s face according to his example, make them green, and clothe them with new powers, activity, immortality, and glory *1 Kor. XV. Philipp. III. Job XIX. 1 Theſſ. IV.* when he shall place them forever near and with himself before God’s face.

<margin>Aaron confirmed in his dignity.</margin>
Aaron, thus inaugurated in his office, immediately aroused the envy of many. It seemed to be taken ill that Levi alone should be the priestly tribe, and that Aaron and his family should raise their heads above all Israel. For they held, or at least pretended, that Israel was holy and God’s beloved people; and thus they could not see why Levi and Aaron were more entitled to this ministry than others in Israel.

<margin>Conspiracy against him.</margin>
Upon this they conspired together. Some set themselves up as heads (see under KORE <note>Referring to the rebellion of Korah in Numbers 16</note>). They began to openly dispute the governance with Moses and Aaron, and reproached them, to all appearances, that they had cunningly drawn to themselves that highest power and dignity, both in civil and ecclesiastical matters, outside of divine order. And they considered this to be a smallness and an insult to themselves; something they could no longer tolerate.

This disturbance being at its most intense, the Lord came between them, punished the heads of the troublemakers, stilled the restless multitude, and confirmed Aaron in his office by an unusual work.

<margin>Conclusion of this chapter.</margin>
Quite many other matters I could have brought to this chapter: but I save many of them to treat them elsewhere more closely and extensively. Therefore I break off here, to begin with matter of an entirely different nature.

### CARCASS, a corpse, a dead body, etc.
### Corpse / Prey / Body, Cadaver. <note>original Hebrew/Greek: נבלה / טרף / σῶμα</note>

<margin>Hebrew and Greek meanings.</margin>
This is called in Hebrew *Terefah*, *Teref*, or *Nevelah* <note>original: טרפה ,טרף or נבלה</note>; in Greek *Soma* <note>original: σῶμα</note>, in Latin *Cadaver*, in Dutch a *lyk*. It is understood to mean worm-bait, a dead trunk, whether slain or torn, and specifically also livestock that was not slaughtered by man or killed in an ordinary way.

<margin>One was allowed neither to eat nor touch those animals.</margin>
The shadow-law <note>The "shadow-law" refers to Old Testament rituals that the author believes foreshadowed spiritual truths</note> regarding types of impurity dictated that one was forbidden not only from eating those animals, but also from touching those animals and people. Because of the first, one was unclean until evening and had to wash, and because of the last, one was unclean for seven days, etc. Concerning both, one reads *Exod. XXI. Levit. V. and XI. and XVII. and XXII. Deut. XIV. Ezech. XLI. and XLIV. Num. XIX.*

<column-break/>

I can well perceive that the Lord in all parts stood very strongly for purity, and that he primarily wanted to teach Israel to strive for inner purity of heart. Therefore, external impurity clearly depicted the inner impurity belonging to the soul, which must displease him above all things. I likewise believe it was meant to teach them not to mix too closely with those who were spiritually dead in sins, and to have no fellowship with dead works *Eph. V. Hebr. VI.* It also showed that the sting of sin’s death with its tyrant—indeed, death as a wage for sin—had not yet been taken away, overcome, and finished. This is why Israel was still under the ministry of death and condemnation, *2 Kor. III. 6, 7.* All of this was first to be taken away in the evening of the Old Testament and in the evening of the death of the believers, who groan because of the body of death. *Rom. VII. 23. 1 Kor. XV. Hebr. II. 14, 15. Joan. III. 5. Rom. VI. 23.* This was brought about by the Christ through his bloody merits, by which we are cleansed from dead works to serve the living God. The power of this is shown in the seven times of the New Testament.

<margin>How God hated sin, inner impurity, the dead, and crimes.</margin>
<margin>One had to guard against it.</margin>
<margin>Sin was not yet atoned for, and death not yet robbed of its sting.</margin>
<margin>Impurity to be removed in the evening of the O.T.</margin>

I also find mention of a dead carcass or body to which people would be gathered, *Matth. XXIV. 28.* <note>original: XXIV. 2, 7.</note> Regarding the sense and meaning of Christ, people do not agree with one another. I shall briefly say how it has been understood.

<margin>The dead body where the Eagles shall be.</margin>

Some understand the carcass or dead body to be Christ as killed and crucified, to whom the believers, like heaven-faring eagles, would turn through faith in love, to consume him as nourishment for their souls. This they would not seek in the desert, nor in the Roman Mass or ciboria <note>containers for the Eucharist</note>, but in and under the pure administration of the Word and the Holy Supper.

<margin>Various opinions. By Eagles, the believers are understood. Christ understood by the carcass.</margin>

Others interpret it as the coming of Christ for judgment and the gathering of the elect to him in the clouds of the air. Others again make stranger leaps, and understand by this carcass the elect from all nations; by the eagles, the gifts of the Spirit that were to be communicated to them for stirring and quickening.

By others, the eagles are understood as the predatory false apostles, belly-servers, and seductive spirits who, being out for prey and the misleading of others, would betake themselves not to the living, pure, and true confessors of faith, but to the dead.

<margin>False Apostles understood by the Eagles.</margin>

To attach the conclusion here: some understand by the carcass, or dead body, the Jews who were dead before God, the dying Church, and the civil state of Israel, to whom the Romans—carrying eagles on their standards—would come running to make them a prey. Of these views, the first and the last please me best.

<margin>Stubborn Jews destroyed by the Romans.</margin>

### ABADDON, APOLLYON,
### Destruction / Destroyer. <note>original: אבדון / Ἀβαδδών, ἀπολλύων</note>

<margin>Derived from various roots, and the meanings fashioned from them.</margin>
This word ABADDON is derived by some from *Ab* <note>original: אב</note>, a father of judgment, or from *Abaddon*, a father, and *Adon*, a lord; others from *Abad* in the *piel* form, *Ibbed* <note>original: אבד</note>, he has devastated, ruined. The word *Apollyon* comes from *apollyo* <note>original: ἀπολλύω</note>, I loosen, I undo, and *apolyon*, together meaning *destruction, devastation*.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the term "Abaddon," specifically its etymological roots and its prophetic application to the "King of the Locusts." It then transitions to a new entry for "Abel," exploring the meaning of his name and the nature of his sacrifice compared to his brother Cain.</meta>

<page-num>34</page-num>
<header>ABADDON. ABEL.</header>
<meta>catchword: be-</meta>

destruction, ruin, one who destroys, ruins, and loosens; one who is destroyed and ruined, who goes under, and is destined for a fall, as the Latins call him *pestis* <note>original: "pestis" — plague or pestilence</note>, and *scelus* <note>original: "scelus" — a wicked person or crime</note>, who is the most base and destructive.

Otherwise from the Hebrew *abaddon* <note>Hebrew: אבדון</note> meaning *ruin, destruction*, or from *abaddon* who perverts justice and destroys.

One sees the word applied to various things, namely to the grave, the lower parts of the earth, hell, the state of death, and of misfortune; read *Job 26:6 and 28:22 and 31:12, Deuteronomy 32, Proverbs 15, 17, and 27*. It is also applied to a person because of his work and activity in *Revelation 9*.

The grave and hell, *qeber* <note>Hebrew: קבר</note> and *sheol* <note>Hebrew: שאול</note> in *Job 28:22, Psalm 88:12, Proverbs 15:11*, are called destruction, devastation, and ruin because they bring these things about: so *Abaddon, Apollyon* <note>The Greek name meaning "The Destroyer"</note> is an worker of destruction and devastation. *Glassius, Sacred Grammar, Book 3, Tract 7: "among the Hebrews it is customary to use abstract terms more often for the sake of emphasis in place of concrete ones."* <note>Latin: "cum Hebraeis in more fit, abstracta saepius emphaséos causâ usurpare pro concretis." Salomon Glassius was a famous 17th-century theologian.</note> Because, he says, the Hebrews have the habit of using abstract concepts to give a more powerful meaning to combined things.

*Abaddon*, etc., a primary destroyer and devastator, who in the Greek is called *Apollyon*.

Thus a "piece of villainy" is used for a "villain," "deceit" for a "deceiver," and "greed" is taken for a "miser."

God is called *yeshuah* <note>Hebrew: ישע</note> or *teshuah* <note>Hebrew: תשוּעה</note>, the salvation of the saints who place their hope and trust in him. *Psalm 27:1*. That is, my preserver, savior: in contrast is *Abaddon*, ruin, devastation, or a devastator, destroyer. It is true, one can in a certain sense apply this to the devil, who has ruined everything and seeks to devastate, who is himself devastated, and whose kingdom and works are destroyed and broken by him who is the *soter* <note>Greek: σωτὴρ — savior or preserver</note>, or preserver and savior. Yet with singular emphasis it is applied to the King of the Locusts, the one called the "Steward of Christ" <note>The author likely refers to the Pope, a common Protestant identification of the Antichrist during this period</note>, who changes the times (*Daniel 7*), who presumes to have the key of hell, to be able to bind and loose, as father and lord in the Church and State, who loosens the laws, and poisons many souls with himself and drags them to destruction; who causes heavy destruction through wars and Inquisitions, who looses and releases subjects from their oath and loyalty, who himself goes to destruction and shall be undone as the "man of sin" and "son of perdition" (*2 Thessalonians 2, Revelation 17*), etc. He shall be mocked, judged, condemned, devastated, and undone by Him who alone is King, Judge, and Lawgiver: *Isaiah 33, James 4:12*.

---

### ABEL or HABEL, הבל / Ἄβελ.

I shall not set down everything that can be read extensively in learned writers concerning the sad and unnatural event recounted in *Genesis 4*; but only that which can provide me with the occasion for something else and matter for further reflection.

<margin>The name of ABEL.</margin>
I begin then with the name הבל ABEL, which some have derived from *abel* <note>Hebrew: אבל</note>, meaning *he was sorrowful, he wept, and is lamenting*; although not with the utmost accuracy if one pays attention to the spelling, it is just as well derived from *hebel* <note>Hebrew: הבל</note> which signifies: *vapor, vanity, that which has no stability or permanence.* For surely man walks in a shadow <note>literally "an image"</note>, and all is vanity. Yes, all is subject to vanity for the sake of sin.

<column-break/>

Moses, who is quite brief and abrupt in reporting most matters, intended among other things not only to record the lineages and family trees, but also to show right from the start in Adam’s house the great distinction between seed and seed <note>the righteous and the wicked</note>.

<margin>Abel and Cain differ.</margin>
Abel and Cain were two brothers from the same parents, but not exactly of one birth, although there is absolute impossibility involved in that claim regarding Cain <note>The author alludes to a theological debate over whether Cain and Abel were twins</note>.

As for their temporal calling, one tilled the earth, the other shepherded the livestock. *Tertullian on Genesis:*

> The care of this one fed the innocent sheep,
> But the other turned the earth with the curved plow.
<note>Latin: "Innocuas hujus pascebat cura bidentes, / Ast alius curvo terram vertebat aratro."</note>

-> Which is to say: <-

> *The care of one kept him busy with the livestock,*
> *And the other plowed the land.*

The type and work of their piety lay in their offering, which they both made; Cain of the fruits of the earth, Abel of the fat of the livestock, each from what he handled.

As for the offerings before the Law, whether they were of Divine institution, and furthermore regarding the time, persons, places, types of offerings, etc., that shall be dealt with in the future when I mention the offerings.

Furthermore, whatever may be of these investigations—whether Adam preceded his sons in offering and had taught and instilled it in them; or whether they brought theirs to their father and he, as father and eldest, offered in their place, etc.—to answer that on firm grounds is not in my power, due to the deep silence of Scripture.

Regarding Abel’s offering: he receives the testimony that he and his offering pleased God, indeed that he offered in faith, *Genesis 4, Hebrews 11*. It pleased the Lord to look graciously upon him and to be satisfied with his deed; and so he will have renounced his own righteousness and works, and expected all salvation and blessings in the seed of the woman <note>A reference to the first prophecy of the Messiah in Genesis 3:15</note>.

Therefore, I cannot find the greatest salvation precisely in the fact that he hurried and hastened himself in the offering or the performance of the sacrifice and did not hesitate, or that he specifically took from the fat of the beasts, or that he precisely did not have a disturbed and averse heart—as some want to claim without firm ground that Cain had toward his brother—but I find more ground and firmness in his faith and God’s good pleasure, who turned His face toward him and took pleasure in him and his offering.

<margin>Sign of the offering.</margin>
By what sign and divine mark Abel was notified of this, so that Cain noticed it and it could feed his wrath; I confess, it is not so clear and certain. -> That is: <-

-> *He, enraged, broke his neck with his hands.* <-

For my part, to apply this historical case to other matters, I know well that Adam is a type <term>type</term> <note>A "type" is a biblical person or event seen as a prophetic symbol or "foreshadowing" of a later person or event, usually Jesus Christ.</note> of Christ, and that Adam was the father of Abel; I also know well that Christ's blood is more excellent and powerful than that of Abel (*Hebrews 12*). I am aware that Abel’s blood cries out for vengeance, and that Christ’s blood brings about reconciliation and forgiveness: but for that reason, I see no particular difficulty that would prevent me from viewing father and son as living emblems and portraits of Christ and his experiences. And why any less than Aaron and his sons? And what absurdity lies in the matter and its application?

For my part, I am not at all opposed to the observation that the believers among the Jews, especially the Apostles—who had the signs of God's spirit and favor, like Abel—were hated, envied, slandered, persecuted, and killed by their brothers because of their faith and the reasonable offerings of the New Testament (*Psalm 44, Romans 8*); and that in place of these confessors and righteous offerers, others—like Seth in Abel's place—were appointed, placed, and established by God from among the Gentiles.

I can also certainly allow that Cain lives again in the Antichrist, and that the true Abels are killed by him, whose blood cries out for vengeance (*Revelation 6*), as will be further noted under the name CAIN. But it seems to me that the learned have not misunderstood it poorly when they bring to our minds, on the occasion of Abel’s experience, the person and the departure of the Christ.

If Abel means smoke, vapor, vanity, or inconstancy—certainly according to outward appearance—so was Christ, with all men, and for himself according to his state and the estimation of the erring people: fragile, brittle, perishable, a trivial thing, and regarded as such (*Psalm 62:10 and 144:4; Psalm 8: What is man?; Isaiah 53:2-3; Psalm 22: a worm and no man*, etc.), just like the rest of men.

Abel had Cain as a brother; Christ had the Jews, whom I shall bring into the discussion of CAIN (*Deuteronomy 18:15; Romans 1 and 9; Hebrews 1 and 10*).

If Abel had the testimony that he was righteous and pleased God (*Hebrews 11*, etc.; *Matthew 23*), with more reason did the Christ (*Isaiah 53:11; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 7; Matthew 3:17 and 17*).

If Abel sacrificed, and offered a more excellent sacrifice

than Cain? Christ offered himself through the eternal spirit as a sweet-smelling savor to God (*Ephesians 5:2; Hebrews 9:14*, etc.).

Was Abel’s sacrifice ignited by fire? Christ himself was (*Psalm 40 and 69; Hebrews 9:14*). <note>The author likely refers to the "fire" of God's judgment or the passion of Christ's sacrifice.</note>

And what happened to the Jews was the fate of Cain, which shall be spoken of in its proper place.

### ABRAHAM, אַבְרָהָם / Ἀβραάμ.

As for ABRAHAM, his birth, household, calling, faith, encounters, married state, deeds, etc., I will not express myself at great length regarding everything—partly to avoid mixing everything together, and partly because there will be further opportunity under the names of HAGAR, ISAAC, SARAH, etc., to bring his person into view and make some remarks; also to avoid being forced, in the treatment of the aforementioned names and persons, to either repeat the same thing or send the reader elsewhere. <header>ABADDON. ABEL.</header>
<meta>Catchword: be-</meta>

...struction, ruin, one who devastates, corrupts, and looses; *one who is devastated and corrupted, who goes down and is destined for a fall*, as the Romans call him *plague* and *wickedness* <note>original: "pestis, en scelus"</note>, for he is the most foul and destructive.

Otherwise from the Hebrew *Abaddon* <note>אבדון</note>, meaning destruction or ruin, or from *Abaddon* meaning one who perverts justice and corrupts.

One sees the word applied to various things, namely to the grave, the lower parts of the earth, hell, the state of death, and misfortune; read *Job 26:6; 28:22; 31:12; Deuteronomy 32; Proverbs 15, 17, and 27*; it is also applied to a person because of his work and activity in *Revelation 9*.

The grave and hell, *Sheol* <note>שאול</note> and *Abaddon* <note>אבדון</note> in *Job 28:22, Psalm 88:12, and Proverbs 15:11*, are called destruction, devastation, and ruin because they bring such things about: thus *Abaddon* or *Apollyon* <note>The Greek equivalent</note> is a worker of destruction and devastation. Glassius, in his *Sacred Grammar*, book 3, tract 7, notes: *Since it is customary for the Hebrews to more emphatically use abstract terms in place of concrete ones.* <note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656) was a Lutheran theologian known for his work on biblical philology. This note explains that "Destruction" is used as a title for a "Destroyer."</note> Because, he says, the Hebrews have the habit of using abstract things for a more powerful meaning in place of composite ones.

*Abaddon*, etc., a principal destroyer and devastator, who is called *Apollyon* <note>ἀπολλύων</note> in Greek.

Thus a "villainy" is used for a "villain," "deceit" for a "deceiver," and "avarice" is taken for a "miser."

God is called *Yeshua* or *Teshuah* <note>ישع or תשועה</note>, the salvation of the saints who place their hope and trust in him (*Psalm 27:1*); that is, *my preserver and savior*: in contrast stands *Abaddon*, destruction, devastation, or a devastator and destroyer.

It is true, one can in a certain sense apply this to the devil, who has corrupted everything and seeks to devastate; who himself is devastated, and whose kingdom and works are destroyed and broken by Him who is the *Soter* <note>Greek: σωτὴρ, meaning Savior</note>, or preserver and savior. Yet with singular emphasis it is applied to the King of the Locusts, the so-called Vicar of Christ <note>A common Protestant identification of the Pope as the figure of Abaddon from Revelation 9</note>, who changes the times (*Daniel 7*); who presumes to have the keys of hell, to be able to bind and loose, as father and lord in the Church and State; who looses the laws, and poisons many souls and drags them to destruction; who causes heavy destruction through wars and Inquisitions; who looses and releases subjects from their oath and loyalty; who himself goes to destruction and shall be undone, as the man of sin and son of perdition (*2 Thessalonians 2, Revelation 17*, etc.). He shall be mocked, judged, condemned, devastated, and undone by Him who alone is King, Judge, and Lawgiver (*Isaiah 33, James 4:12*).

### ABEL or HABEL, הבל, Abel.

I will not set down everything that can be read extensively in learned writers regarding the sad and unnatural event related in *Genesis 4*; but only that which can provide me with occasion for something else and a more substantial rendering.

<margin>The name of ABEL.</margin>
I begin then with the name ABEL <note>הבל</note>, which some have derived from *abal*, meaning he has been grieved, has wept, and is lamenting; although this is not with the utmost accuracy if one pays attention to the spelling, it is just as well derived from *Hebel* <note>הבל</note>, 

<column-break/>

which signifies: *vapor, vanity, that which has no stability or permanence.* For certainly man walks in a shadow, and all is vanity. Indeed, all is subject to vanity for the sake of sin.

Moses, who is quite brief and clipped in reporting most matters, intended among other things not only to note the lines and genealogies, but also to show immediately in Adam’s house the great distinction between seed and seed <note>Referring to the "godly seed" of Abel vs. the "ungodly seed" of Cain</note>.

<margin>Abel and Cain.</margin>
Abel and Cain were two brothers from the same parents, but not of the same birth, although there is no absolute impossibility involved in the matter.

As for their temporal calling, one farmed the earth, the other shepherded the cattle. Tertullian on *Genesis*:

> *One's care was for the innocent sheep,*
> *The other turned the earth with a curved plow.*

-> That is to say: <-

> *The care of the one kept him busy with the cattle,*
> *And the other plowed the land.*

The nature and work of their piety was found in this: that they both offered sacrifices; Cain from the fruits of the earth, Abel from the fat of the cattle, each from that which he handled.

As for the sacrifices before the Law <note>The Mosaic Law</note>, whether they were of Divine institution, and further regarding the time, persons, places, types of offerings, etc., that shall be dealt with in the future when I mention the offerings.

Furthermore, whatever may be of these investigations—whether Adam preceded his sons in sacrificing and taught and instilled it in them; or whether they brought theirs to their father and he, as father and eldest, sacrificed in their place, etc.—to answer these on firm foundations is not in my power, due to the deep silence of Scripture.

Regarding Abel’s offering: he carries away the testimony that he and his offering pleased God, indeed that he offered in faith (*Genesis 4, Hebrews 11*). It pleased the Lord to look upon him graciously and to let his deeds be acceptable; and thus he will have renounced his own righteousness and works, and expected all salvation and blessings in the seed of the woman <note>A reference to the promise in Genesis 3:15</note>.

Therefore, I cannot find the greatest salvation precisely in the fact that he hurried and hastened himself in sacrificing or performing the offering and did not hesitate; or that he specifically took from the fat of the beasts; or that he did not have a resentful and averse heart, as some wish to claim Cain had against his brother without firm ground. But I find more ground and stability in his faith and God's pleasure, who turned His face toward him and took delight in him and his offering.

By what sign and divine mark Abel was informed of this, so that Cain noticed it and could feed his wrath thereby, I confess is not so clear or certain. It is true that mention is made of an *empyrismo* <note>original: ἐμπυρισμὸς, meaning "kindling" or "ignition"</note>, a lighting of his offering by heaven's fire; also of the rising of the smoke of his offering, of a good angel sent to him, of an audible voice of God, or an inner divine assurance, etc. Although there is no impossibility or absurdity enclosed in one or the other, I am nevertheless of the opinion that one cannot precisely grasp it or prove it *apodictically* <note>meaning with absolute certainty</note>, that is, absolutely...

<margin>The lighting of the offering.</margin>

### ABRAHAM.

father; Haran and Nahor were, as is generally thought, his two older brothers.

He was called by God himself out of Ur of the Chaldeans, *Acts VII. 1, 2, 3. Joshua XXIV.* and, as the great Burman <note>Likely Frans Burman (1628–1679), a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian and professor at Utrecht.</note> rightly has it, five years before the death of his father Terah, in the year 2078 after the creation, 421 after the flood, 70 years after Abraham's birth, and 430 years before the departure of the children of Israel out of Egypt, *Exodus XII. 40. Galatians III. 17.*

<margin>Ur of the Chaldeans.</margin>
"Ur of the Chaldeans" is interpreted by some Jewish scholars in the sense of a **burning furnace**. <note>The Hebrew word 'Ur' can mean 'fire' or 'light,' leading to the legend that Abraham was literally delivered from a fire.</note> It is said that the King of the Chaldeans gave an order to throw Abraham into it, because he was said to have broken the idols of his father Terah and publicly mocked the idolatrous service of the Chaldeans and Persians; however, it is claimed the Lord brought him out of that burning furnace unharmed.

Regarding this story, although it contains no absolute impossibility, it nevertheless lacks sufficient proof to be believed,

1. Because I have found not the slightest mention of this in the Holy Writ.

2. Furthermore, I read in *Genesis XI. 31.* that several other persons departed from Ur of the Chaldeans with Abraham. Were these also in the burning furnace of Ur?

3. I have noted that in *Genesis XI. 31.* Ur is called the **land** of the Chaldeans, but not the furnace or burning oven.

4. The prominent Jewish scholars did not have a burning furnace in mind when they translated it: *from the valley, the mountain border, from Ur, a city or place of the Chaldeans.*

I shall therefore categorize it among the Jewish fables and follies, as long as further and sufficiently clear proof is lacking.

The Lord commanded Abraham to go out from his fatherland, his father’s house, and his kindred, toward a foreign and—to him—as yet unknown land, which He would show him. *Genesis XII. 1. Acts VII. 3. Hebrews XI. 8.*

The Lord intended to release him from the <term>idolatry</term> <note>The worship of created things rather than the Creator.</note> concerning the sun, moon, and stars—the first kind that was in vogue—and to instill in him His knowledge, fear, and service; to establish a covenant with him and the <term>seed</term> <note>Used here in the biblical sense of 'offspring' or 'descendants.'</note> which He was to give him; to bring his faith, obedience, and patience to the point of testing and practice; to set him as a father in nature and in faith; and to bring his seed to the inheritance of two kinds of goods, with which He would establish two kinds of covenants in different times, the Old and the New, which would be like two parts of His eternal Testament. With this abandonment and departure, He wished to teach that man's highest good and place of rest are not located in any fixed dwelling or earthly inheritance (*Hebrews XI and XII*) and to sketch out what would be promised and fall to the lot of Abraham's descendants in the course of time.

This was a burden and a trial for the flesh, and quite hard and heavy for a merely natural man: for to have to leave one’s fatherland, house, and kin, and that at such an advanced age, being uncertain where he would end up, and not knowing what he would encounter or how long the wandering, traveling, and roaming would last, is certainly not at all pleasant for someone who is well-to-do, firmly settled, and has many friends and relatives. Meanwhile, one notices that the most generous promiser and most faithful re-

<column-break/>

-warder of those who serve Him, made excellent promises to Abraham concerning temporal, spiritual, and eternal life, regarding him and his seed in two ways (*Genesis XII, XIII, XIV, and XV* etc.), renewed several times, and confirmed with proofs of divine faithfulness. As for the natural seed, which was to inherit Canaan after many persecutions, sorrowful states, and oppressions, it was to be the seed and people that would proceed from him by the until-then barren Sarah. As for his spiritual seed, which would follow him and be like him as a father in faith and works, these would be the believers, especially from among the <term>Gentiles</term>, <note>Non-Jewish people.</note> as he became the father of the world, and in the same manner as he would be justified and inherit his blessings. *Romans XI. Galatians III. 6, 8, 14, 29. and IV. John VIII. 39.* etc.

In the meantime, the Lord promised him a good of the eternal testament, beyond which no more perfect good can be imagined. Namely, Abraham was not to fear, for He would be his **shield**, and his **exceeding great reward**: which meant not only that He would cover, protect, and provide for him in such a way that no one could harm him; but also, preeminently, that He would be his God, his good, portion, salvation, and life, and would justify him, sanctify him, raise him from the dead, and make him live before His face—which, as is fitting for God, could only happen in the promised **seed of the woman** <note>A reference to the first prophecy of a Savior in Genesis 3:15.</note> *Gen. III. 15. Psalm XXXIII. 12. Hosea I. 7. Jeremiah XXIII. Psalm LXXIII. 25, 26. Matthew XXII. 1 Corinthians I. 30. Acts IV. 12. John XIV. 6. Galatians III.* etc. Both of these things Abraham understood and embraced through faith, before he even received the sign of circumcision in his flesh. *Romans IV. 11.*

Regarding this <term>Patriarch</term>, <note>A founding father of a family or religion; here referring to Abraham.</note> the example of those who were to be justified through faith without circumcision and the law, there would still be quite a lot to say:

<margin>Name of Abram changed to Abraham.</margin>
Such as how he saw his name changed from *Abram* to *Abraham* as a prophecy and a divine sign—becoming not only a great and exalted man and father, but also the father of many nations.

And that between him and the Lord, in a singular and highly solemn manner, a covenant was made, friendship established, and the promises confirmed, of which one can read in *Genesis XV.*

It seems characteristic of mankind, whose souls act upon and through the body as if bound to it, to desire something external.

Abraham's descendants desired signs. God then commanded our Patriarch, strong in faith, to take a heifer, a goat, a ram, a turtledove, and a young pigeon, all in their full vigor and strength. He followed the received command, dividing them into heaps, laying one part over against the other; however, he did not deal with the birds in such a manner.

I would almost believe that Abraham noticed the Lord wished to strike and confirm a covenant with him. Certainly, in and during the establishment of covenants, it was an ancient custom to cleave certain animals and lay the cloven parts against each other, and to pass through between them, as a sign that he who broke the covenant was worthy of being treated in such a manner, etc. However, I do not dwell on this antiquity here. Here were two very unequal parties, and changeable man had to deal with the unchangeable God.

-># A B R A H A M.<-

->E 3<-

Now when this division had been made by Abraham, the birds of prey descended upon that carrion, but they were driven away by Abraham, and blown away as it were; whether they were eagles, vultures, hawks, etc., which prey upon dead carcasses and swoop down.

One would certainly not be wrong to assume that Abraham regarded this phenomenon as an omen of evil significance.

Furthermore, it is recorded of him in *Genesis 15:17: And it came to pass, when the sun went down, that a deep sleep fell upon Abraham; and, lo, a horror of great darkness fell upon him.*

It is not without reason that one might guess that Abraham, being weary from staying awake the previous night and from his daytime activities—the slaughtering of the livestock, etc.—fell asleep; or that God induced the sleep in him, in which, because of the birds of prey he had encountered as a bad omen, heavy thoughts and dreams arose, not without terrors. Unless one understands that the Lord cast these upon him, at which opportunity He informed him how it would go with his seed and the inheritance of the promised Canaan. Wherein the Lord shows not only when the inheritance would be claimed, and who would accept it; but also what troubles, struggles, and persecutions, both in Egypt and in the wilderness, would precede it before they came to the ancestral possession. Just as the inheritance of the world <note>Likely referring to the spiritual inheritance of the Kingdom of Heaven by Christians.</note> would not be accepted and obtained without effort, persecution, wandering, and the exercise of patient meekness. However, it was also the case that the Lord would deliver his seed with a strong hand and punish the enemies in an exemplary manner; just as the "second Egypt" <note>A common Reformation-era metaphor for any oppressive power or the worldly system opposing the faithful.</note>, the measure of its iniquity being full, shall be miraculously punished before the inheritance of the entire world is taken into full possession and handed over.

That which subsequently appeared to Abraham, before the sun went down and it became fully dark, was what Moses relates: *And behold, there was a smoking oven and a burning torch that passed between the pieces.*

That which appeared to Abraham, as if passing through the split and divided pieces, seemed to him to be an oven that gives off smoky vapor, and a fiery and shining torch.

The oven filled with smoky vapor could be viewed, not without some foundation, as representing Abraham’s fleshly descendants consisting of the dust of the earth, who would have to labor at the oven in Egypt in bricks and stones; just as the fiery and shining torch could be a symbol of the Lord, who is a light in Himself and uniquely so to His own in Goshen <note>The region in Egypt where the Israelites lived, which remained light during the plague of darkness.</note>, while He is a consuming fire to the enemies. And so one can think that the Lord and Abraham, with his seed in him, like two parties confirming the covenant, passed through those parts placed apart and opposite each other, as immediately follows: *And on that same day the Lord made a covenant with Abraham, saying, etc.*

<margin>Significance of the sacrificial animals.</margin>
As to what is signified by that three-year-old heifer, ram, goat, turtledove, and young pigeon, and the treatment of them, it is not difficult to think that the Lord, just as He did later with Israel, wished to confirm His covenant here with Abraham in a solemn manner. And that these three animals, divided and in their prime, were symbols of the three generations, namely of Kohath, Amram, and Moses, and of their encounters and adversities, especially before they came to the peaceful possession of Canaan—of their oppression in Egypt, their status as strangers, and their wandering in the Wilderness, where the Lord was to them a light, a fire, and a pillar of cloud.

The turtledove and young pigeon, not split or divided, can bring to our mind the fourth generation of Israel, sighing because of the pressure, reproach, and insults done to them by the enemies; their innocence, guiltlessness, and patience, thereafter flying like a dove out of Egypt toward the Wilderness.

The birds of prey falling upon the carrion can be viewed as symbols of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, as well as the predatory and devouring kings and nations who attacked Israel in the Wilderness and before the full possession of Canaan. Nevertheless, by Abraham’s driving and blowing them away, it is symbolized how the Lord would drive away the enemies, blow upon them, and completely frustrate and put to shame their power, violence, and crafty designs; especially delivering them through Moses and bringing them into the inheritance through Joshua.

Abraham’s terror in his sleep can make us think of the terrors that would fall upon Israel toward the "setting" of Joseph, who had been a favorable sun to them, when another king arose who had not known Joseph.

The smoking oven, as has already been said, can represent the iron furnace (*Deuteronomy 4*) <note>Deuteronomy 4:20 refers to Egypt as the "iron furnace."</note>, the heaviest oppressions of Abraham’s race in Egypt, as well as their labor in preparing and baking bricks, along with other heavy torments.

The fiery and shining torch can depict the Lord's light of favor and comfort in all their heaviest torments: His wrath to punish the Egyptians and set them ablaze, and to scorch those in His anger who would break the covenant and commit profanities. Also how He would be a light to Israel in the howling Wilderness, surrounded by predatory harpies <note>In this context, "harpies" refers to rapacious or predatory enemies.</note>.

Unless one, climbing to something higher, would wish to view everything as a symbol or means of representing the incarnation, the suffering, death, and resurrection of the Son of God—the antitype <term>antitype: the New Testament fulfillment of an Old Testament "type" or symbol</term> of the sacrifices, with whose blood the better covenant and testament is confirmed.

<margin>Christ symbolized by the oven.</margin>
By the oven made of earth and smoking, one could imagine the Christ, insofar as He shared with His own the body and the lowly dust made of earthly and perishable parts (*Hebrews 2:21 and 4:15*); from which a smoky vapor would rise due to God’s burning wrath and fire of vengeance for the sins that had arisen, in His heavy suffering of soul and body, accompanied by the deepest humility and the obscuring of the rays of His divine brilliance and glory.

<margin>The Divine nature symbolized by the torch.</margin>
The fiery torch can then also represent His Divine nature, the fiery flames of His love by which He is consumed (*Psalm 69:10*), and has offered Himself blameless to God (*Hebrews 9:14*); just as by the same Spirit He also raised Himself, when He, in the likeness of the animals, was divided in His death, yet living

<column-break/>

-># ABRAHAM<-

and active according to his Divine nature, he walked between the dead and the living, swallowing up death in victory, and thus passing through death into life: living now in eternity, without the birds of prey—the Jews and Heathens—who attacked him, being able to prevent him from rising, even though they had sealed his grave well. Nor could they entirely crush him or weaken him so much that he would not live like the birds <note>Likely referring to the spiritual "birds" or "fowls of the air" mentioned earlier in the text as symbols of life or resurrection</note> and swallow up and overcome death.

<margin>Transition to other matters.</margin>
Let this suffice regarding this event and this encounter of Abraham. Other matters remain for me to contemplate and consider.

<margin>Abraham's marriage.</margin>
Abraham was married to Sarah, who remained barren until her old age; yet who, contrary to the course of nature, became pregnant and gave birth to Isaac.

While Sarah was barren, Abraham, on the advice of his wife, went in to Hagar the Egyptian, the handmaid, and fathered Ishmael.

<margin>His journey to Egypt.</margin>
Abraham traveled to Egypt because of the famine, and there he placed the chastity of his wife in great danger due to a kind of necessary withholding of the truth out of fear <note>Referring to Abraham identifying Sarah as his sister rather than his wife</note>, as he also did later with Abimelech.

<margin>Circumcision a sign of the Divine Covenant.</margin>
The Lord confirmed His covenant with Abraham and his seed through the sign of circumcision.

<margin>Rescue of Lot.</margin>
Abraham rescued his nephew Lot, who had set out with him.

<margin>Abraham's faith tested.</margin>
Abraham's faith and steadfastness were put to the test by the command to offer up his son Isaac.

<margin>Meeting with Melchizedek.</margin>
Melchizedek met him, presented him with bread and wine; Abraham gave him a tenth of everything and was blessed.

The significance of these persons, encounters, and events as symbols will be further demonstrated and extensively pointed out under the words **SARAH**, **HAGAR**, **ISHMAEL**, **ISAAC**, **MELCHIZEDEK**, etc.; therefore, I will by no means detain the reader here with them, as everything can be found under its own main heading.

<margin>Comparison between Abraham and Christ.</margin>
I can well see that one can make some comparison between Christ and Abraham, insofar as He left His heavenly fatherland and descended into a foreign land, where, although rich and heir to all things, He found Himself in a meager state (*Matthew 8:20; 2 Corinthians 8:9; Isaiah 53:2, 3; Zechariah 9:9; Philippians 2:6, 7, 8*). That He was always found as obedient to God, trusting, and steadfast as Abraham, being Abraham's seed. That He, like Abraham, was a Rabbi, Prophet, and a singularly great friend of God, from whom the Father kept nothing hidden (*Matthew 3:17 and 17:15; Deuteronomy 18:15; John 1*), etc. That He rescued His brothers from sin, death, and hell, just as Abraham rescued his brother <note>Lot is often referred to as Abraham's "brother" in the sense of a close kinsman</note> who had been captured and led away. That He also, like Abraham, prayed for the transgressors (*Isaiah 53:12; John 17; Matthew 27; Luke 23:34; Job 34; Romans 8*).

But it is also clear enough that the Lord intended to set Abraham as the father, patron, and example in his justification for the Gentiles in the New Testament, who, in the uncircumcision and without the Mosaic law of works, would be justified by faith alone, working through love (*Romans 4; John 8; Galatians 3 and 4*).

Thus they are Abraham's followers, seed, and children—not precisely those who are his physical seed or who carry the sign of circumcision in their flesh, but those who have Abraham's faith, 

<column-break/>

do his works, and are justified in the same manner as he. And with the language of Paul (*Romans 9:6, 7, 8*), the Jewish scholar Abrabanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century philosopher and statesman</note> in his work *The Inheritance of the Fathers* <note>original: "Nachalath Avôth"</note> agrees in many parts; as he writes, according to my translation, thus:

> Every person is recognized by their character, whose disciple they may be. He who walks in the ways of the Lord is among the disciples of Abraham, our father, since by accustoming himself to his character, he has also learned his works. But he who is corrupt in character, even if he be from the children of Israel, see, he is not of Abraham’s disciples, because he has not imitated the character of Abraham.

See Hulsius regarding *The Privileges of the Old Testament* <note>original: "De Voorrechten des O. T."</note>, the 10th discourse, page 361, and Vitringa in *Sacred Observations* <note>original: "Obs. Sacr."</note>, book 5, chapters 3 and 5; also Lampe in his exercises on the 45th Psalm, volume 2, pages 462, 463, etc., where his Reverence writes thus:

> The Jews even admit that Abraham is a general spiritual father of all believers. The primary reason for this fatherhood is the special covenant that God entered into with Abraham, through which he was appointed as a covenant head of all subsequent believers, so that he received general promises belonging to the universal Church until the end of the world, which, accepted by him through faith, gave a continuous right of reclaim until everything God promised him is fulfilled in his posterity: which right of reclaim he himself exercises in heaven, and his posterity here on earth. And for this reason, the bosom of Abraham (*Luke 16:22, 23*) is used as a symbol of the Church to express his fatherhood.

See him further on the 45th Psalm, pages 117, 118.

A forsaking in general of that which, in the state of corruption, is esteemed, sought, and meditated upon alongside and above the true and highest good: whether it be indeed shameful, like sins; or whether it has a semblance of good, like wealth, honorary office, pleasure, friendship, and this life itself, etc.

Consequently, I can see here in general that one must look to Abraham as a moral example, not fixing one's heart on any fatherland, kinship, or temporal goods, but looking forward to the future (*Hebrews 2:13, 14 and 13:14*). This was especially necessary in Christ’s time, when for His sake one had to leave father, mother, sister, brother, house, yard, indeed everything. To this the children of Abraham, the Apostles, were singularly constrained, as they had to go under divine guidance to a foreign land inhabited by wild and strange Heathens, to preach to all nations, and to endure and take possession of it, not without many oppressions and grievous encounters, in which their hearts were lifted up by Jesus’ promise that He would be with them, not leave them orphans, give His peace, etc. (*John 14:17, 18; Matthew 28:20*).

Yes, such was the experience of the Church (*Revelation 18*) when she received the command to go out from Ur of the Chaldeans, where Babylon also lies: the spiritual place where idolatry is found (*Revelation 18:4; 2 Corinthians 6:17*), about which more will be said under the words **BABYLON** and **EGYPT**, etc.

To present everything in this wide field not wordily, but many matters very concisely, one could show several correspondences between Abraham and Christ; Abraham and the Church and faithful church members, namely, between Abraham and Christ.

-># ABRAHAM. ABSALOM.<-

<page-num>39</page-num>

It was in accordance with God’s command and will that Abraham should go out from his fatherland, house, kindred, etc., into a foreign land, following the voice of the God who called him, to be His servant.

Christ, by Divine will and calling, in order to be the Father's servant, had to appear in the flesh, be sent forth, be placed under the law, and thus come to earth, thereby leaving His paternal home and heavenly dwelling. *Isaiah 42; John 14; Galatians 4:4, 5; 1 Timothy 3:16; John 3:13.*

Abraham was a friend and lover of the Lord. *Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23.* Christ preeminently *Proverbs 8:30; John 1:18; Matthew 3:17 and 17:4, 5*—and a lover of God, seeking His glory through righteousness and obedience. *Psalm 40; John 4:34 and 10; Psalm 18.*

God did not hide His purpose from Abraham *Genesis 16 <note>The author likely intends Genesis 18:17, where God asks, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am doing?"</note>*, much less the whole of His counsel from His Son, for the counsel was between the two of them *Zechariah 6:12, 13.* He had heard everything *John 1:18*; He would give an account of the decree *Psalm 2:7*; He and the Father were one. *John 5:26 and 10:30.*

In Abraham’s wanderings, Christ resembles him, if not surpasses him. Quite early He had to flee to Egypt. He was born in Bethlehem, raised in Nazareth, He stayed in Galilee, He traveled through the Jewish land preaching and performing wonders and signs; yet in a much more destitute state than Abraham. *Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 8:20; Philippians 2:7, 8; 2 Corinthians 8:9.*

Was Abraham a Prophet, Priest, Great Prince, and Prince or King? *Genesis 14, 17, and 18.* Christ is preeminently a great Prophet, unique High Priest, and eternal King.

Did Abraham rescue his captive nephew Lot? Christ [rescued] His brothers from under the power of Satan, sin, death, the law, and the curse thereof, etc. *Luke 1:74, 75; John 8; Luke 11; Isaiah 62; Psalm 63:20; Galatians 4:4, 5; Hebrews 2:14, 15; 1 Corinthians 15, etc.*

Is Abraham introduced as an example, even though he had sin, defilement, spiritual faintness, and weaknesses?

Christ is the sinless one preeminently. *Matthew 11:29 and 16:24; John 13:15; 1 Peter 2:21; Hebrews 12:2.*

Were great promises made to Abraham? Was he, in the first rays of his marriage, served and blessed with children? Did he grow greatly in number afterward? Was he heir of all things, etc.?

One and all are found in an exalted degree in Christ, for He is the heir of all things. *Hebrews 12; Psalm 8:6, 7, 8.* All promises and blessings are in Him. *2 Corinthians 1:20; Galatians 3:16; Ephesians 1:3, 4.* In the beginning His seed was small, but it grew most wonderfully after His soul's labor. One prominent part of it was previously in bondage, the other free.

Abraham was buried by his two sons: Christ by His two sons, the disciples of the wise. <note>This likely refers to Isaac and Ishmael burying Abraham, paralleled with Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus—often called "disciples"—burying Jesus.</note>

Abraham is an example of the righteousness of the Gentiles.

Again, he can be regarded as a model of the Church of the New Testament, since following his example, one is justified through faith alone, without circumcision or the works of the law. *Romans 4; Galatians 3 and 4.*

The Church is outside its fatherland, dwelling away from the Lord *2 Corinthians 5; Hebrews 11 and 12*, having been with Abraham in Egypt, then here, then there.

Just as in Abraham’s household there is an Eliezer, the chief, so there is Christ *Hebrews 3; Ephesians 1; Colossians 1; Psalm 8; Matthew 28*; under Him stand all servants. *Ephesians 4; 1 Corinthians 8.*

<margin>God makes His counsel known to the Church.</margin>
God makes His counsel and purpose known to the Church, also regarding the spiritual Sodom, through His word, Spirit, Christ, the Apostles, Prophets, etc. The members of the church are Prophets, Priests, and Kings. *1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1, etc.*

### ABSALOM. <note>original: אבשלום (Ab-shalom)</note>

<column-break/>

Absalom was one of the sons of David, whom he begot by Maacah his wife, the daughter of Talmai, King of Geshur. *2 Samuel 3:3.* Rabbi David Kimchi and other Jewish writers have left us in writing that he took this woman or daughter as his wife after he had overpowered her in war, because she was exceptionally beautiful.

<margin>Meaning of ABSALOM-</margin>
Absalom means: *a father of peace, of perfection, of retribution*, or *the father’s peace, perfection, retribution*. A son with a good and great name, but of very bad merits and qualities. Quite beautiful as far as the body was concerned, from the head to the sole of the foot, especially adorned with elegant and heavy head-hair, about which he carried himself with no small pride and haughtiness; which later became his noose, as one shall hear. *2 Samuel 14 and 18.* Yet he was of evil mental qualities, an unnatural son of a god-fearing father; as virtue is no inheritance.

Of him one reads that he had Amnon killed by his servants. Amnon, heated by passionate and lewd desire and love for his half-sister Tamar, had abused and raped her, and afterward cast her out. (Absalom, after he had kept Tamar in his house for some time and feigned his hidden hatred and resentment, arranged a feast at Baal-hazor, to which he had invited the other sons of the King, and struck when Amnon was heated by wine). And because he could well judge that it would displease his Lord father, he fled to his grandfather Talmai, King of Geshur. *2 Samuel 13.*

Meanwhile, as King David was moved with such strong longing for Absalom that it could be easily noticed by Joab, Joab—by setting up a cunning woman of Tekoa, who used a parable and applied it to David—brought it about that Absalom obtained the freedom to return from Geshur to Jerusalem, provided that he had to keep himself hidden in his dwelling for two full years.

When this greatly annoyed Absalom, who sought something else, he tried to get back into his father's favor through the influence of Joab, who had much power over David. For this same purpose, he summoned Joab to him twice; when Joab refused to come to him, he had his servants set Joab's fields of grain on fire.

It seems, however, that Joab, although displeased, yet fearing a worse outcome, dared to speak to King David on behalf of Absalom.

<meta>This page transitions from the life of Abraham to the history of Absalom, David’s son, focusing on his rebellion, his death, and the broader moral lessons regarding the use of "feigned piety" in political schemes.</meta>

-># ABSALOM.<-

<page-num>40</page-num>

...and brought it so far, that Absalom was admitted to the kiss of peace and reconciliation by his Lord father. *2 Samuel 14.*

But after the peace and reconciliation were achieved, Absalom’s hidden enmity truly began, until it burst forth in full force. Absalom, then longing for his father’s kingdom, sought to win over the common people with flattery and coaxing; and to carry out his design, he feigned religious devotion, misleading his Lord father with a vow which, though long overdue, he sought to fulfill at Hebron. Meanwhile, he had secretly arranged matters—while hoodwinking the people following him—so that at the sound of the trumpets, they would cry out loudly: *Absalom is King at Hebron.*

In the meantime, since he needed counsel and action for his undertaking, Ahithophel of Gilo was summoned, with whom he made a firm alliance.

When this came to the ears of his Lord father David, he saw fit to take flight with his followers. Departing from Jerusalem with several spiritual and civil persons, alongside the Ark (which he afterwards sent back), he crossed the Brook Kidron, praying that the Lord would turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness. At the same time, he did not neglect to make use of secret maneuvers and cunning in order to uncover Absalom's secrets and frustrate his plot. He then sent his confidant Hushai to Jerusalem, who was clever enough to manage his affairs so as to spy on everything that happened and report it to David through trusted messengers. *2 Samuel 15.*

Hushai, having gone to Jerusalem and joined himself to Absalom, was at first held in suspicion, but was afterwards accepted as Absalom’s confidant. David, meanwhile, having arrived at Bahurim, had to endure no small insult swallowed from Shimei <note>Shimei cursed David and threw stones at him as he fled.</note>.

Absalom, having arrived in Jerusalem after his father’s departure, sought to carry out his designs. Finding the counsel of Ahithophel pleasing, he publicly abused the concubines of his father David in Jerusalem. *2 Samuel 16.*

But because Absalom’s wicked intention could not be accomplished solely by sleeping with his father's concubines, Ahithophel gave Absalom this advice: he should gather twelve thousand men, pursue David, and try to take him by surprise. When this advice was shared by Absalom with Hushai, the latter opposed it, providing Absalom with entirely different counsel, while meanwhile neglecting not to inform David of both plans.

When the proud Ahithophel saw that his advice was rejected, he departed, set his house in order, and hanged himself. *2 Samuel 17.*

Meanwhile, after the armies had been mustered and David had crossed the Jordan—staying at Mahanaim to await the outcome of the battle—both armies advanced upon each other. In this main encounter (after David had commanded that they should deal gently with Absalom), Absalom’s army was defeated and thrown into total confusion. This resulted in Absalom taking flight on a mule through the thick oaks of the forest, where he became caught by the hair of his head in a tree,

<column-break/>

hanging there after his mule had run out from under him. When this was announced to Joab by someone, Joab pretended to be displeased that the man had not killed Absalom in that state. After this, Joab rode toward him at a full gallop, pierced his heart with three arrows, and then had his servants finish the task of taking his life. After Absalom was taken down from the tree, they threw him into a pit in the forest and covered him with a heap of stones; thus Absalom left nothing behind but a pillar he had built for himself in the King’s Valley, called *Absalom's Hand* <note>original: "Absaloms hand". The Hebrew word 'Yad' can mean both 'hand' and 'monument'.</note>.

This end of Absalom, when David was informed of it by Ahimaaz and Cushai, struck him so deeply that his heart was cut through with grief, causing his mouth to say: *O my son Absalom, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee! 2 Samuel 18, etc.*

This is, in brief, the essential history concerning Absalom’s person and deeds.

<margin>See Absalom’s hypocritical conduct based on the flattery of the people, while meanwhile seeking to outwit others with physical beauty and a good countenance, to undermine authority, and to seize the highest command for himself.</margin> It seems to me that in Absalom and his conduct, there live again all those who—with cunning, a semblance of godliness and religion, and flattery, supported by physical beauty and a good countenance—seek to outwit others, undermine authority, and seize the highest command for themselves. Many examples of this appear in divine and human histories, both of those who sought to set themselves up as Kings in place of the legitimate sole rulers to whom they were not related by blood, and of those who were related by blood, whether in the nearest degree or in a collateral line.

It seems that a religious pretext and a varnished godliness can achieve a great deal in such cases; indeed, it is the primary means by which one keeps their secret desires hidden while striving to reach and strike their target.

Lactantius <note>A 4th-century Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> says somewhere: *Some strengthen their path to power through feigned piety, doing many things that the pious do, and doing so all the more readily because they intend to deceive.*

Another also puts it well, writing in this manner: *The wicked Spirit once sired two daughters, one of whom is Hypocrisy, and the other Ambiguity. These he eventually betrothed to the statesmen, who feign themselves to be pious, acting as if they were inflamed by the love of God and neighbor and intended nothing other than the preservation and well-being of the entire Republic, while they are nonetheless inclined toward lies and deceit, etc.*

Barnabas Facius, in book 2 of *On the Doctrine of Princes*, chapter 5: *Outside of religion, a Prince has nothing more powerful or useful. If he wishes to wage war, he must pretend it is for religion, and thus he has no one who contradicts him. If he wishes to fill the exhausted treasury, emptied by useful services, he must pretend that the neighboring King or Prince is brewing a war over religion, etc.*

Thomas Campanella in *On the Spanish Monarchy*, book 1, chapter 5: *It is manifest that Philip of Macedon made himself Monarch of all Greece through cunning and religion. And in chapter 6: For the lust for power has taken up almost no other cloak but this.*

Spannochius says: *They have religion in their mouths, and they strive for command with their hearts. They coat the heart with flattery and soft words, while they violently extort money.*

Forstnerus, on book 1 of Tacitus: *Princes play with the cloak of religion, making it...*

# ABSALOM. AHAB.

*God sees all their dealings, though they hide their ambition under the title of religion and justice.*

And so Daniel Klaffenius says in *Political Religion*: *Thus is religion the cloak of the extreme godlessness, the cover of inhumanity, the veil of wonderful and barbaric cruelty.* <note>Daniel Klaffenius was a 17th-century author who wrote on the intersection of faith and statecraft.</note>

To stroke the people, to speak to their liking, to act compassionately and familiarly, and to flatter everyone marvelously, is the way to undermine someone's esteem, highness, and authority, and to reach the seat of power through the fickle commoners; a method of which Absalom made himself a master. Many similar examples are noted by Dieterich in *Biblical Antiquities, pages 354, 356, etc.*

Someone driven by such passions has a great advantage if, like Absalom, he is a handsome and exceptionally well-made man, upon whom people of old fixed their eyes and senses, as if the beauty of the body were proof of the inner abilities and virtues of the soul.

*Plato, in his Republic*, desired: *that the rulers and caretakers of the Republic should not only be steadfast and strong men, but, if it were possible, also the most beautiful.*

It is certain that stature and beauty contribute much to dignity, majesty, and awe. *Virgil says in the 5th book of the Aeneid:*

->Virtue is more pleasing when it comes in a beautiful body.<-
<note>original: "Gratior est pulchro veniens in corpore virtus."</note>

->That is:<-

<margin>The power of beauty.</margin>
*Virtue shines much more beautifully out of a beautiful body.*

*Curtius says in the 6th book, 7th chapter: Respect is born from the majesty of the body. They allow themselves to believe that no one is capable of great deeds except he who is gifted by nature with singular beauty.*

Following this general application, I am inclined to think and believe that one could find many great similarities between Absalom, with his counselor and followers and their deeds, and the Jewish civil and church leaders who—with smooth talk and a clever appearance of feigned godliness—undermined Christ's authority, kingdom, and dominion, attempting to take it for themselves.

<margin>The Antichrist.</margin>
But it seems to me that one must not overlook the Antichrist, the hairy crown <note>Psalm 68:21 refers to the "hairy crown" or "hairy scalp" of God's enemies.</note> *Psalm 68:22*, who, more than anyone else, through cunning and violence and under the guise of religious devotion and the power of wonders and signs, has placed and forced himself into Christ’s position, drawing the whole earth to himself; kidnapping Christ’s Bride <note>The Church</note>, fighting Christ in His Bride and the saints who alone pay Him homage and recognize Him as the lawful King and sole Ruler. *2 Thessalonians 2; Revelation 12, 15, and 17.* He shall also be cast into a pit and deep abyss, *Revelation 18 and 19*, whereby nothing shall be left of his memory but destruction and extreme misery, accompanied by a curse. Just as it happened with the Jews, and furthermore with all the enemies of Christ and His Church, who have kicked against the pricks <note>An idiom meaning to struggle uselessly against fate or divine will.</note> and found their downfall in their presumed highness and insane rage.

To speak of Ahithophel, Shimei, and the rest of Absalom’s supporters is by no means my aim, scope, or intent. What remains to be said or noted about them shall be found under their own names.

<column-break/>

### AHAB. אחאב

<margin>Ahab;</margin>
As for the life, character, and deeds of AHAB, I shall note the most important facts about him with extreme brevity.

<margin>the son of Omri.</margin>
He was the son of the godless Omri, King in Israel, which kingdom was distinguished from that of Judah by the split under Jeroboam and Rehoboam.

<margin>Becoming King in his father's place.</margin>
He became King in Israel in his father's place and reigned for twenty-two years.

<margin>His marriage.</margin>
He had taken as his wife Jezebel, the idolatrous daughter of Ethbaal, King of Sidon.

<margin>His life and conduct.</margin>
Regarding his life, character, and conduct: he far surpassed the previous kings in godlessness. He was abominable; he walked after the dung-gods <note>A derogatory biblical term for idols.</note> in the manner of the expelled Amorites. He continued the calf-worship and the sins of Jeroboam. He served Baal and bowed before him. To provoke God, he made a sacred grove. In the house he had built for Baal, he erected an altar, and Elijah was denounced by him as a "troubler of Israel."

<margin>Elijah accused by him.</margin>
Under him, idolatry reached its peak. He craved Naboth’s nearby vineyard to turn it into a kitchen garden. He promised Naboth a much more excellent vineyard in exchange, or a sum of money by which his inheritance would be amply paid for according to its value. When this proposal was refused because of the divine ordinance regarding ancestral inheritances, he showed himself to be heartily grieved and highly offended, etc.

<margin>Micaiah mistreated by him.</margin>
Under him, Micaiah—who could not agree with the counsel given to the King—was struck on the jaw and, by royal order, put on a diet of water and bread.

<margin>His humiliation and death.</margin>
After Elijah foretold God’s heavy judgments upon him, he humbled himself in sackcloth; and after the experience of the innocently stoned Naboth, he was mortally struck in battle by an arrow shot by a man in simplicity <note>meaning "at random" or "without specific aim"</note>, between the joints of his armor. Having been carried out of the camp in his chariot, he died; and his flowing blood, which had run into the floor of the chariot, was licked by dogs when the driver went to wash the chariot in the pool of Samaria. One reads of these various events in *1 Kings 17 to 22.*

As for the specific cases and events under his reign, they shall appear under the names ELIJAH, JEZEBEL, NABOTH, etc., so that everyone may receive what is specifically theirs, and I do not mix one thing with another.

If one wishes to see in the case and encounter of Naboth an image of what happened to the innocent Son of God and heir of all things—to whom the vineyard of the Church (consisting of Jews and Gentiles) belonged—it is especially notable: when He, being entitled to His property and the land of Canaan (called the land of Immanuel), wished to claim, nourish, and purify it (*Isaiah 5 and Matthew 21*), then we know how the Jews, seeking to seize the vineyard for an earthly kingdom and temporal fat revenues, bribed and set up two "men of Belial" <note>meaning "worthless" or "wicked" men</note> as false witnesses.
