# ABSALOM.

<meta>Catchword: a</meta>

... [Joab] brought it so far that Absalom was admitted to the kiss of peace and reconciliation by his Lord father. *2 Samuel 14.*

But after this peace and reconciliation was achieved, Absalom's hidden enmity truly began, continuing until it burst forth in full force. Absalom, then hungering for his father's kingdom, sought to win over the common people with flattery and caresses; and to carry out his intention, he feigned a religious spirit, misleading his Lord father with a vow which, though long overdue, he sought to fulfill at Hebron. Meanwhile, through secret dealings and by blinding the people following him, he had arranged things so that at the sounding of the trumpets, they would cry out loudly: *Absalom is King at Hebron.*

In the meantime, as he needed both counsel and action for his undertaking, Ahithophel of Gilo was summoned, with whom he made a firm alliance. <note>Ahithophel was David’s most trusted advisor who defected to Absalom; his name became synonymous with a brilliant but treacherous counselor.</note>

When this came to the ears of his Lord father David, he saw fit to take flight with his followers. Departing from Jerusalem with several spiritual and civil persons, alongside the Ark—which he later sent back—he crossed the Brook Kidron, praying that the Lord would turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness. At the same time, David did not neglect to employ secret maneuvers and cleverness so that he might discover Absalom's secrets and frustrate his designs. He then sent his confidant Hushai to Jerusalem, who was cunning enough to manage his affairs, spying on everything that happened and reporting it to David through trusted messengers. *2 Samuel 15.*

Hushai, having gone to Jerusalem and joined himself to Absalom, was at first held in suspicion, but was later accepted as Absalom's confidant. David, meanwhile, having arrived at Bahurim, had to endure a significant insult from Shimei. <note>Shimei was a relative of the former King Saul who cursed David and threw stones at him as he fled.</note>

Absalom, having arrived in Jerusalem after his father's departure, sought to carry out his intentions. Taking pleasure in the advice of Ahithophel, he publicly abused the concubines of his father David in Jerusalem. *2 Samuel 16.*

But because Absalom's wicked purpose could not be completed merely by sleeping with his father's concubines, Ahithophel gave Absalom this advice: he should gather twelve thousand men, pursue David, and attempt to overwhelm him. When this advice was shared by Absalom with Hushai, the latter opposed it, providing Absalom with entirely different counsel, while meanwhile not failing to report everything to David.

Now, when the proud Ahithophel saw that his advice was rejected, he departed, set his house in order, and hanged himself. *2 Samuel 17.*

In the meantime, after the armies had been mustered and David had crossed the Jordan, staying at Mahanaim to await the outcome of the battle, both armies advanced upon each other. In this major clash (after David had commanded that they should deal gently with Absalom), Absalom’s army was defeated and thrown into total confusion. This resulted in Absalom, taking flight on a mule through the thick oaks of the forest, becoming caught by the hair of his head in a tree, after his mule had run out from under him. When this was reported to Joab by someone, Joab pretended to be displeased that the man had not killed Absalom in that state. Thereupon, riding toward him at a full gallop, Joab pierced his heart with three arrows, and further had his servants finish him off. Afterward, Absalom was taken down from the tree and thrown into a pit in the forest, covered with a heap of stones. Thus, Absalom left nothing behind but a pillar he had built in the King’s Valley, called *Absalom’s Hand.* <note>The "Hand of Absalom" (Yad Avshalom) refers to a monument he built for himself because he had no son to carry on his name.</note>

When David was informed of this end of Absalom by Ahimaaz and Cushi, it struck him so deeply that his heart was cut through with sorrow, causing his mouth to say: *Absalom my son, Absalom my son, oh! that I had died for you, 2 Samuel 18, etc.*

This is, in brief, the essential part of the history concerning Absalom’s person and deeds.

<margin>See Absalom’s act of hypocrisy applied to the desires of the people.</margin>

It seems to me that in Absalom and his conduct, I see reborn all those who—through cunning, a show of godliness and religion, and flattery, supported by physical beauty and a good countenance—seek to deceive others, undermine authority, and seize the highest power for themselves. Many examples of this appear in both divine and human histories: both of those who sought to set themselves up as Kings in place of legitimate rulers to whom they were not related by blood, and of those who were related by blood, whether in the nearest degree or in a branching line.

It seems that a religious pretext and a varnished godliness have great power in this regard; indeed, it is the primary means by which one keeps one's "bosom-fruit" <note>An idiom for a secret plan or cherished ambition.</note> hidden while seeking to reach and hit the target.

> Lactantius says somewhere: *Some strengthen their path to power through feigned piety, doing many things that the pious usually do, and doing so all the more readily because they intend to deceive.* <note>Lactantius was a 4th-century Christian advisor to Constantine the Great.</note>

> Another also puts it well when he writes in this manner: *The evil Spirit once fathered two daughters, one of whom is Hypocrisy, the other Ambiguity; these he eventually married off to the people of the state, who feign piety, acting as if they were ignited by the love of God and neighbor and intended nothing other than the preservation and well-being of the entire Republic, while they are nevertheless inclined toward lies and deceit, etc.*

> Barnabas Facius, *On the Doctrine of Princes*, Book 2, Chapter 5: *Outside of religion, a Prince has nothing more powerful or useful. If he wishes to wage war, he must pretend it is for religion, and thus he has no one who speaks against him. If he wishes to refill the exhausted treasury, emptied by useful services, he must pretend that the neighboring King or Prince is brewing a war over religion, etc.* <note>Barnabas Facius (1400–1457) was an Italian humanist and historian.</note>

> Thomas Campanella, *On the Spanish Monarchy*, Book 1, Chapter 5: *It is public knowledge that Philip of Macedon made himself Monarch of all Greece through cunning and religion. And in Chapter 6: For ambition has taken up this cloak almost exclusively.* <note>Campanella was a 17th-century Dominican friar and philosopher known for his political theories.</note>

> Spannochius says: *They have religion in their mouths, and they strive for power in their hearts. They coat the heart with flattery and soft words, and they violently squeeze out the money.*

> Forstnerus, *On Book 1 of Tacitus*: *Princes play with the cloak of religion, making it into a...*

# ABSALOM. AHAB.

Many similar examples are noted by Dieterich in *Biblical Antiquities, pages 354, 356, etc.* <note>Conrad Dieterich (1575–1639) was a prominent theologian whose "Antiquitates Biblicae" provided historical context for scripture.</note>

Someone driven by such passions has a great advantage if, like Absalom, he is a handsome and exceptionally well-made man; upon such things, people of old fixed their eyes and senses, as if the beauty of the body were proof of the inner capabilities and virtues of the soul.

Plato, in *The Republic*, desired: *that the Rulers and caretakers of the Republic should not only be steadfast and strong men, but, if it were possible, the most beautiful.*

It is certain that stature and beauty contribute much to dignity, majesty, and respect. Virgil, in the 5th book of the *Aeneid*, says:

->*Virtue is more pleasing when it comes in a beautiful body.*<-
<note>Original Latin: "Gratior est pulchro veniens in corpore virtus."</note>

->That is:<-

<margin>The power of beauty.</margin>
*Virtue shines much more beautifully from a beautiful body.*

Curtius, in the 6th book, 7th chapter, says: *From the majesty of the body, respect is born. They believe that no one is capable of great deeds except he who is gifted by nature with singular beauty.* <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus was a Roman historian of Alexander the Great.</note>

Following this general application and transfer of meaning, I am inclined to think and believe that between Absalom, with his advisor and following, and the Jewish civil and church leaders—who with smooth talk and a varnished appearance of pretended godliness undermined Christ's authority, kingdom, and dominion, attempting to transfer it to themselves—one could find many and great similarities.

<margin>The Antichrist.</margin>
But it seems to me that one must not overlook the Antichrist, the hairy crown <note>Referring to Psalm 68:21, often interpreted as a sign of stubborn pride or unrepentant sin.</note> *Ps. LXVIII. 22.* who, surpassing all others in cunning and violence through feigned religious devotion and the power of wonders and signs, has thrust himself into Christ's place, drawing the whole earth to himself; kidnapping Christ's Bride [the Church], fighting Christ in His Bride and the saints who alone do Him homage and recognize Him as the lawful king and sole ruler. *2 Thess. II. Rev. XII. and XV. and XVII.* This figure shall also be cast into a pit and deep abyss *Rev. XVIII. and XIX.* whereby nothing of his memory shall be left but destruction and the utmost misery, along with a curse. Just as it happened with the Jews, and subsequently with all enemies of Christ and His Church, who kicked against the pricks <note>An idiom meaning to protest against a superior force or divine will, from Acts 9:5.</note> and found their downfall in their presumed highness and insane rage.

To speak of Ahithophel, Shimei, and the rest of Absalom's supporters is by no means my aim, scope, or intent. Whatever remains to be said or noted about them will be found under their own names.

### AHAB. אחאב <note>Hebrew: Ahab.</note>

<margin>Ahab;</margin>
Concerning the life, morals, and deeds of AHAB, I shall note the most important points with the utmost brevity.

<margin>the son of Omri.</margin>
He was the son of the godless Omri, King in Israel, which kingdom was distinct from that of Judah following the split under Jeroboam and Rehoboam.

<margin>Became King in his father's place.</margin>
He became King in Israel in his father's place and reigned for twenty-two years.

<margin>His marriage.</margin>
He had taken as his wife Jezebel, the idolatrous daughter of Ethbaal, King of Sidon.

<margin>His life and conduct.</margin>
Regarding his life, morals, and conduct: he far surpassed the previous Kings in godlessness. He was abominable; he walked after the "dung-gods" <note>A derogatory biblical term for idols.</note> in the manner of the displaced Amorites. He continued the calf-worship and the sins of Jeroboam. He served Baal and bowed before him. To provoke God, he made a sacred grove. In the house he had built for Baal, he erected an altar; and Elijah was denounced by him as a "troubler of Israel."

<margin>Elijah addressed by him.</margin>
Under him, idolatry reached its peak. He lusted after Naboth's nearby vineyard to turn it into a vegetable garden. He promised Naboth another vineyard in exchange that was far more excellent, or a sum of money through which his inheritance would be amply paid according to its value. When this proposal was rejected by Naboth because of the divine ordinance regarding ancestral estates, Ahab showed himself to be heartily grieved and highly offended, etc.

<margin>Micaiah mistreated by him.</margin>
Under him, Micaiah—who could not agree with the advice given to the King—was struck on the jaw and, by royal order, put on a diet of water and bread. <note>Specifically, the "bread of affliction and water of affliction" mentioned in 1 Kings 22:27.</note>

<margin>His humiliation and death.</margin>
After Elijah prophesied God's heavy judgments upon him, he humbled himself in sackcloth; and following the fate of the innocently stoned Naboth, he was mortally wounded in battle by an arrow shot by a man in "simplicity" <note>Meaning the archer shot at random, without specifically targeting the King.</note> between the buckles and his armor. He died after being carried from the army in his chariot; his flowing blood in the chariot-bed was licked up by dogs when the driver went to wash the chariot in the pool of Samaria. One may read of these various events in *1 Kings XVII to XXII.*

As for the specific incidents and deeds during his reign, these will appear under the names ELIJAH, JEZEBEL, NABOTH, etc., so that everyone may receive what is specifically theirs, and I do not mix one thing with another.

If one wishes to see in the case and encounter of Naboth a reflection of what happened to the innocent Son of God and heir of all things—to whom the vineyard of the Church (consisting of Jews and Gentiles) belonged—especially as He, being entitled to His property and the land of Canaan (called the Land of Immanuel), wished to plant, fatten, and purify it *Isa. V. and Matt. XXI.*; then one knows how the Jews, attempting to seize the vineyard for themselves while pursuing an earthly kingdom and the temporary fat revenues of that vineyard and field, bribed and set up two <term>men of Belial</term> <note>A biblical term meaning "worthless" or "wicked" men; in the trial of Naboth, two false witnesses were used to condemn him.</note>;

# AHAB. ACHAN.

<note>This opening section draws a typological parallel between Naboth—the innocent man whose vineyard King Ahab stole—and Jesus Christ.</note>
...had, declaring he had blasphemed God and the King—even the Emperor—and that he had set himself up as God’s son and the King of the Jews, and finally, under the pretense of legal proceedings, they put him to death, taking possession of his vineyard for a time. Yet, a just and remarkable vengeance descended upon their heads because of that innocent blood.

<margin>Micaiah represented by Christ's disciples.</margin>
I also clearly see that one finds the experiences of Micaiah <note>Micaiah was the prophet who alone told Ahab the truth about his impending defeat, while four hundred other prophets lied to please the king; see 1 Kings 22.</note> relived in the disciples of our Lord, who were struck on the jaw, scourged, despised, and imprisoned by the Jews; likewise in *Paul* and *Silas*, and many others in *Acts 5, 16, and 23*, etc., because they, like the others, would not prophesy [falsely], and were accused (as Elijah was) of troubling Israel and the crowds.

<margin>The fate of the reformers.</margin>
Just as such has been the common lot and experience of those who have freely rebuked sin, uncovered godlessness, and urged for reform, refusing to act like "dumb dogs" <note>A reference to Isaiah 56:10, often used by reformers to describe clergy who fail to speak out against corruption.</note> or to speak merely to please the faces of men.

I can also well perceive that in Ahab live all those kings and great men who, through promises and under the appearance of law, strive to seize and snatch up the property of their subjects.

And even that many great people, however idolatrous or ruined in their morals, can (like Ahab) be brought to a stinging of their conscience and an outward show of penance and humiliation by divine threats.

But if Jezebel provides a portrait of the Babylonian Whore <note>A common Protestant identification of the Roman Catholic Church with the "Whore of Babylon" from the Book of Revelation.</note>, then I can well imagine that the kings and great ones who commit adultery with that whore and are at one with her, are the "Ahabs" of this world. Never was whoredom and godlessness raised to a higher peak than in the Council of Trent <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) was the Catholic Church's formal response to the Protestant Reformation.</note>, and the greatest damage, insult, and persecution has been done to the pious and innocent "Naboths" by Emperors, Kings, and Princes, when they were seduced and incited by the Roman Jezebel. For what happened to Jan Hus, Jerome of Prague, etc., is portrayed to the life by Church history. The root of all evil is pride, insatiable greed, and avarice. But such people shall meet no better fate than Ahab. See *Revelation 18 and 19; Psalm 68:21, 22, 23.* <note>Original references: Apoc. XVIII. and XIX. Ps. LXVIII. 22, 23, 24.</note>

### ACHAN. עכן <note>Achan</note>

<margin>Achan.</margin>
**A**s for the history of ACHAN, son of Carmi; one reads of it in *Joshua 7*. His name is translated as "one who tramples" or "one who brings everything into confusion." He is also called Achar in *Joshua 22*, about which more will be said hereafter.

I shall draft the history briefly. The deeper thoughts and explanations can be sought from the commentators.

<margin>Divine command at the taking of Jericho.</margin>
Joshua, by divine order, had commanded that during the taking of Jericho—which was by a divine work without Israel’s intervention—nothing that had life, from humans to cattle, should be spared, except for Rahab and her friends, because she had sheltered the spies. He commanded that from the gold, silver, copper, and the iron vessels, nothing should be touched or claimed for private possession or use under threat of a curse, since the Lord desired these for Himself.

Notwithstanding this prohibition and the heaviest threats, Achan, the son of Carmi, stole from the cursed goods an elegant Babylonian garment, a tongue of gold <note>original: "goude tonge"; likely a "wedge" or "bar" of gold.</note>, alongside two hundred shekels of silver, hiding it all together beneath the earth in his tent.

<margin>Goods stolen by Achan.</margin>

Because of this, the Lord’s anger burned fiercely against Israel, so much so that they—emboldened by the taking of Jericho and thereafter regarding the small town of Ai and its inhabitants as nothing—sent only about three thousand men there to take it. However, the outcome was so poor that the people had to retreat in shame, leaving behind thirty-six men, and return to the main body of the army.

<margin>God's anger against Israel.</margin>

Because this made the enemy bold and courageous, and Israel, on the contrary, despondent, Joshua found himself greatly dismayed. Therefore, falling on his face and humbling himself very deeply before the Lord, he poured out a heavy and humble lamentation.

<margin>Dismay of Joshua.</margin>

On which occasion the Lord not only revealed the committed sacrilege to Joshua but also testified that Israel would be visited with subsequent defeats if the crime were not removed from Israel through the execution of punishment.

<margin>God's testimony regarding the committed sacrilege.</margin>

Hereupon, the Lord showed Joshua how the lot should be cast to determine the tribe, the head of the ancestral house, and the person who had committed the sacrilege. This being put into effect, Achan’s person was finally singled out by the lot. He, as is generally held, was led with his family to the Valley of Achor—perhaps named so because of this—and there stoned and burned.

<margin>Achan punished.</margin>

Truly a heavy and remarkable case, occurring at the conquest of Canaan and at such an early time. Similarly, in the beginning of the New Testament, when they stood ready to claim the inheritance of the world, a no less rare and singular case can be observed in the persons and experience of Ananias and Sapphira, husband and wife. *Acts 5.*

<margin>Ananias and Sapphira.</margin>

Certainly, the Jews, appearing to be enemies of idolatry after the captivity in Babylon, nevertheless robbed what was holy, not giving to God what they owed Him, or falsifying it, converting spiritual matters to their own possession and use (*Romans 2:22*), and robbing God of His due honor by establishing their own imagined righteousness, and thus failing to recognize God's righteousness by rejecting the lawful Lord and King, Christ, etc. See further *Matthew 1:7, 12, 13* and *3:9, 10*, which is why their land was struck with a curse, their city and temple destroyed and burned with fire, and they were brought to utter desolation.

<margin>Punishment of the Jews.</margin>

I am also inclined to believe that it will go very poorly for those who steal the goods dedicated to God and holy services—at the falling of the spiritual Jericho by the trumpet of the holy Gospel—and who transfer and alienate them for their own profit. Although, regarding these goods, strictly and singularly speaking, I do not see this ban expressly laid or pronounced. What I have further to remark on this will appear in the treatise on the VALLEY OF ACHOR, to which I refer the reader.

### ACHITOPHEL. <note>Hebrew: אחיתפל</note>

<margin>Achitophel.</margin>
In passing, I have already made some mention of Achitophel while discussing the life, deeds, and end of Absalom; I must now more closely sketch his own conduct and demise.

<margin>Meaning of the name.</margin>
As for the name ACHITOPHEL, depending on whether one derives it from *Ach* <note>original Hebrew: אח, meaning "brother"</note> and *Tophal* <note>original Hebrew: תפל, meaning "foolish" or "fatuous"</note>, or from *Naphal* <note>original Hebrew: נפל / אח, meaning to flow away, pour forth, fall, or attack</note>, it signifies: *my brother's fall or ruin, my brother's insanity, folly, or the one of insanity*.

<margin>A foolish act committed by him.</margin>
Although he was recorded as a man of great wit and a clever brain by David and Absalom <note>2 Samuel 16:23</note>, he committed a foolish and insane act, and his vain and foolish pride caused him to plunge headlong into ruin from the height of his status. *The Lord has brought his counsel to shame.*

He was a counselor to King David, but when it appeared to him that Absalom's light was rising and David’s was setting, he worshipped the rising sun. Being summoned from Giloh, he made a firm covenant with Absalom, while the people hurried toward Hebron, mostly out of curiosity and ignorant passion. What advice he whispered to Absalom has been told in the account of ABSALOM’S life and deeds. However, having perceived that Hushai’s advice had been approved and followed while his own was rejected—and seeing what the consequence of this would be for David, who would now easily overcome the matter—he <margin>He hangs himself.</margin> hanged himself out of heartache, despondency, and unbearable insult.

<margin>His faithlessness.</margin>
<margin>He hangs himself.</margin>
Here I see something in Achitophel that is noticed in almost all times and in many cases: that friends and counselors easily waver, fall away, and "adore the rising sun" <note>An idiom for supporting a new power while abandoning an old one.</note> upon a change of circumstances and times, as Tacitus testifies in the sixth book of his *Annals*. Thus, knowing someone's secrets, they defect to the enemy, either through bribery or personal interest.

<margin>Fickleness of friends.</margin>
So it is that Achitophel is to me an example of all those counselors and courtiers who join together and conspire against their lawful Kings, Princes, etc. From this perspective, he is also a symbol of those who join with the Roman Harlot <note>A common 17th-century Protestant reference to the Roman Catholic Church.</note> to offer counsel against the true King David—the Messiah—and his kingdom.

<margin>Achitophel an example of faithless courtiers.</margin>
Likewise, one may consider him an example of those who, having received the greatest benefits and the most prominent offices and services from someone, play the part of the ungrateful rogue, lifting their heels against their benefactors without having any reason other than the motivation of fickleness, self-interest, feared political changes, or the decline of their benefactor's state, power, and status.

<margin>And ungrateful people.</margin>
And although there is some difference between the office and status of Achitophel and Judas, between the motivation, insight, and end of their existence, and between the actions of Achitophel and Judas; and perhaps some difference between the manner of death of Achitophel and Judas, I nevertheless believe that one can notice several similarities between the two in certain respects.

<margin>Comparison between Achitophel and Judas.</margin>
It is known that Achitophel was very intimate with David—indeed, his counselor, upon whom the King relied heavily <note>2 Samuel 16:23</note>—and that he 

<column-break/>

also held a prominent office, and was thus a participant in all the court secrets and interests.

Judas was chosen as an Apostle by the true David <note>Jesus Christ</note>, to whom the secrets and keys of the Kingdom of Heaven were revealed and entrusted. He was intimate with Christ, his table-friend, and a participant in his secrets: to whom he had entrusted the purse <note>John 13:18, Psalm 41:10</note>.

Achitophel, driven by reasons of state, may have had self-interest, even though he was never offended but greatly exalted by David (the righteous King chosen by God), and had received nothing but benefits; yet he lifted his heel against him and conspired with the King's son against the King.

Judas—whatever insight he might have had beyond self-interest—made things quite as bad as Achitophel. For, most faithlessly falling away from the true and God-anointed King David over Zion (the mountain of God’s holiness), he addressed himself to those who sat on Moses’ seat as gods and children of God, offering his help to capture Jesus for a sum of money, once he noticed that they did not desire Jesus as King, and the cry went up: *we have no King but Caesar.*

Thus, he falls upon him with a kiss, to distinguish him from the others, pointing out the way and the means by which they could capture him.

And just as one cannot explicitly say that Achitophel had any long-standing hatred or specific grudge against David, outside of his own interest, personal advantage, and the imagined rise of Absalom's sun (by which he thought to make his fortune): so too I do not see that Judas was moved by a long-standing hatred and grudge against Jesus. Rather, his long-standing greed brought him to this, and he perhaps thought to himself that once Christ was captured, he would escape, either through his power and wisdom, or through the service of the people, or through clear evidence of his innocence—or that the Jews were not serious or intending to put him to death.

Achitophel, seeing that his counsel was rejected and had come to nothing, brought death upon himself by (as we read) hanging himself.

Judas, having noticed that things went with Jesus beyond and against his expectation, was brought to despondency and insanity by the stings of his striking conscience, and hanged himself.

<margin>Despair of Achitophel and Judas.</margin>
And so one perceives in both of them that *evil counsel is worst for the counselor* <note>original Latin: "quod malum consilium consultori sit pessimum"</note>: and that he who digs a pit of destruction for another, falls into it himself.

# ACHOR'S VALLEY. REARGUARD.

The Valley was specifically named the "Valley of Trouble" <note>Hebrew: *Achor* means "trouble" or "disturbance."</note> thereafter, because Achan, the troubler of Israel, received his punishment there.

It is a valley not far from Jericho, to the north, near Gilgal, where Israel's state became very troubled through idolatry. *Joshua 10:15 and 9:15. Amos 5:5.*

It appears to have been a fertile region full of beautiful pastures: for there, Israel enjoyed the spiritual grain of Canaan, *Joshua 5*, and by alluding to Achor, the Lord promises something good to the Church of the New Testament after preceding trouble, confusion, and sorrow. *Hosea 2:14. Isaiah 65:10.*

I can well believe that Achor's Valley—a valley of trouble, both through the malice of the inhabitants of Ai and Achan's wicked deed, through which some Jews perished—could well be regarded as a depiction of the torments, troubles, and persecutions that befall the godly, the people of God on earth, from false brothers both within and without; and that these same things are assigned to them by the Lord's providence as the hoped-for glory and entrance into the heavenly Canaan. *Romans 5:3, 4 and 8:35, 36 etc. Hebrews 12:11, 12. etc.*

Also, that God already grants His people here on earth the heavenly grain, the first fruits of the heavenly Canaan, as a firm and well-assured hope and pledge that the full satisfaction will be in the Canaan above.

But I am simultaneously convinced that God’s Spirit, when alluding to Achor's Valley and promising something excellent to the church, also meant and sketched something unique, which one will not imprudently suspect if one attentively considers the two aforementioned places, *Isaiah 65:10 and Hosea 2:14.*

One should then observe that upon the first entry into Canaan, the people of God were immediately troubled, disturbed, visited, and punished because of Achan’s participation in the "devoted thing" <note>original: *het verbannene*; referring to the items Achan stole which were under a divine ban or "herem," set apart for destruction</note>, which one was not allowed to touch, nor to covet or strike at. Israel was punished for Achan's wicked deed as if he were a fellow member of Israel’s citizenry. For a time, until the ban and crime were removed, they were prevented from being victorious over their enemies and from taking possession of the land of Canaan, even though they were already in it, had taken Jericho, and had tasted the grain of the land.

I also find quite a bit of similarity between this first event of Israel in the taking of Canaan—the inheritance of Abraham’s natural offspring—and the taking of the world, the inheritance of his believing seed, the good of the New Testament or Covenant, especially in the early times.

If ever anything should have been banned, it should have been communion with idol sacrifices, and making oneself conformable to idolaters in life and customs; yet it was perceived in the early times that people went wonderfully astray in this, *1 Corinthians 8 and 10.* Of this, Cyprian speaks in *On the Lapsed*, chapter 5, and Eusebius clearly enough when he says that because of this sin, Diocletian was sent by God's hand against the Christians.

And this had to stiffen and strengthen the heathens, and consequently brought a great hindrance to the course of the Gospel and the taking of the inheritance of the world.

Alongside this, regarding Achor’s Valley of confusion, trouble, and the halting of the course of the Gospel and the expansion of Jesus’ Kingdom es-

<column-break/>

pecially in Canaan, to follow Jesus and His teaching and kingdom, one can note that much evil, disturbance, and hindrance was brought by Canaan itself and the perception of it as the land of the Lord, promised to the fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, into which they had been led by God's hand: the temple, the holy city, along with all those ancient divine laws, rights, and institutions. From these they could hardly pull away their hearts and minds, *Isaiah 25:7. Psalm 45:11. Luke 14:18, 19, 20. Acts 21:20. Galatians 2.* To this especially helped the deception of the false Apostles, the mixing of the Law and the Gospel, along with the persecution by the Ishmaelites <note>A common historical metaphor for persecutors of the true church</note>. *Galatians 4:20. Acts 4. Song of Solomon 1:6.*

<margin>Expansion of Jesus' Kingdom among the Heathens.</margin>
As for the expansion of Jesus’ Kingdom among the heathens, when the church, the Israel of God, was already in the wilderness of the world, some resistance was found at first—an Achor's Valley—because some followed the Heathens too much and familiarized themselves with them. Worldly wisdom, imagined eloquence, trained masters of art, and wicked deceivers, the persecutions, heresies, and other things more, were an Achor’s Valley to the church.

But when the Lord struck that great hindrance of Jerusalem’s city and temple with the ban, let it be burned, and so openly departed from there; yet through the godliness, steadfastness, and confession of faith of many Martyrs, and the defense of both the Christian doctrine and the innocence of the Christians, the eyes of the tyrants and enemies of the truth were opened. When Constantine the Great performed such remarkable service for the Christians and the Christian church; when the kings and princes themselves began to embrace the Christian doctrine: then the door of hope was opened, and a wide entrance granted.

<margin>Door of hope opened.</margin>
But the same was afterwards stopped and closed in many parts by the subsequent Heretics and Heathens in the East, and the Antichrist in the West, who loves the Babylonian cloak <note>A reference to the specific item Achan stole; here used to symbolize the vanity and corruption of the Roman Church/Antichrist</note> and adorns himself with the banned things like a harlot, of which he will in time be robbed and stripped naked. And so we still look forward to the door of hope being opened and the access being paved to the enlightenment of Jews and Heathens in later days. For Jesus must indeed rule as King, until all kings and peoples shall be subject to Him.

<margin>Later closed.</margin>

### REARGUARD, REAR-MARCH, <note>original Hebrew: מאסף / אחרונה</note> by the LXX Translators <note>original Greek: *ὀπισθοφυλακῶντες, οἱ ἔσχατοι*</note>, the rear of the army <note>original Latin: *extremum agmen*</note>.

<margin>Rearguard.</margin>
<margin>from where derived.</margin>
**R**EARGUARD and REAR-MARCH is derived from the usual arrangement of armies that have set out. For a wise and prudent commander-in-chief takes care that the tail or the rear of his army is well covered, so that no enemy, placed in ambush, may attack it from behind and—before it can pivot and place itself in the required state—strike it or bring it into disorder. Likewise, it is useful to keep the front ranks in order and light, and to enclose the stragglers and those who would want to desert, forcing them to return to their ranks.

# REARGUARD.
<sig>F 3</sig>

<margin>Concerning the meaning and power of the words.</margin> The word **אחרונה** / **אחרון** <note>Hebrew: *Acharon* / *Acharonah*</note> is derived from **אחר** <note>Hebrew: *Achar*; Latin: *post*, *postea*, *postquam*</note>; meaning behind, after, thereafter, or after that. **אחרונה** / **אחרון** refers to that which comes after something else that preceded it, following at the very back: so that in an army it signifies the hindmost troops, well-armed, who close and cover the ranks.

The word **מאסף** <note>Hebrew: *Me’asseph*, "the gatherer"</note> comes from **אסף** <note>Hebrew: *Asaph*</note> meaning he has gathered, collected from behind, or drawn together that which was either scattered or spread out into a single main body, bringing it within a firm perimeter and enclosing it. <note>Greek: *ἐπισυναγωγή* (episynagoge), a gathering together.</note>

<margin>Places cited for the military account.</margin> After we have noted these things, the matter requires that a few passages be brought forward which show us this military usage.

Regarding the divine guide, moving forward through the pillar of cloud and fire and covering and enclosing Israel's army, this is applied in *Exodus 13:21.*

Regarding a human closing-band, rearguard, or rear-march, *Numbers 10:25* is cited: *Then the standard of the camp of the children of Dan set forward, which was the rearguard of all the camps throughout their hosts: and over his host was Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai.*

*Joshua 6:9, 13:* And the armed men went before the priests that blew with the trumpets, and the rearguard came after the ark, the priests going on, and blowing with the trumpets.

*And seven priests bearing seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the Lord went on continually, and blew with the trumpets: and the armed men went before them; but the rearguard came after the ark of the Lord, the priests going on, and blowing with the trumpets.*

*1 Samuel 29:2: And the lords of the Philistines passed on by hundreds, and by thousands: but David and his men passed on in the rearguard with Achish.* Burman <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a Dutch theologian.</note> noted on page 308 that this was to serve as a bodyguard for Achish, and to cover the advancing army from an enemy attack from behind.

However, it is spoken of metaphorically and with allusion—both to the hindmost protective troops in armies and with respect to the pillar of fire and cloud—principally by the Prophet Isaiah.

<margin>Used figuratively, with metaphor and allusion to military practice. Isaiah 52:12 explained.</margin> It will be well worth the effort for me to strive to bring some light to the passages I have in mind, the first of which is:

*Isaiah 52:12: For ye shall not go out with haste, nor go by flight: for the Lord will go before you; and the God of Israel will be your rearguard.*

I believe an allusion is being made to the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt, and to the divine guidance through the pillar of cloud and fire, going before the army and closing and covering the rear, so that the enemy army did not dare to attack them from the front or the back.

Whether in a literal sense Israel is urged to depart from the physical and actual Babylon, no longer tarrying there or lingering, and not mixing with the unclean heathens, under the promise that the Lord would march with them, guide them, cover them, and bring them to a safe dwelling place, alluding to what occurred during the exodus from Egypt and the guidance and protection in the Wilderness; or whether the "Israel of God"—the leaders, captains, and keepers, the Apostles, and the first-gathered army of Christ—are exhorted not to delay in the exodus and abandonment of Jerusalem, the temple with its fittings and its surroundings. For the Lord had already left this place, as it was profaned in many ways, and on the feast of Pentecost had exalted Himself and made Himself known before the peoples gathered there from all who are under heaven, through the Apostles and disciples of Christ, being ready to reveal Himself further through general preaching, with the promise that He would guide them and bring them to a secure dwelling.

Whether one also wishes to view it by prefiguration and spiritual transfer to that which was later to be heard by those enclosed in the spiritual Babylon and Egypt—those who practiced fellowship with the city that calls itself great and holy, yet is inwardly very defiled, harlot-like, and unclean—*2 Corinthians 6:17; Revelation 18:4.* And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, "Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues."

I shall close this section with another passage no less important.

<margin>Isaiah 58:8 explained.</margin> *Isaiah 58:8: Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the Lord shall be thy rearguard.*

Gulichius <note>Abraham Gulichius (1642–1679), a follower of the theologian Cocceius.</note>, the diligent compiler and concise presenter of the thoughts of the great Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a famous Dutch theologian known for federal theology.</note>, presented his opinion thus on page 308: If they had not neglected the preceding duties, the world would have perceived that they were truly reformed. They would also surely have achieved great and rapid progress and, like a Christian host, prosperous in their military campaigns, would have been invincible in their passage; all the more so when the righteousness of Christ, through which He obtained the inheritance of the world, marched before them, and the glory of God—that is, His singular blessing and the abundance of the Holy Spirit—formed the rearguard.

Adrianus Junius in his work *Analytico practico* <note>Practical Analysis</note>, page 90 etc., insofar as it belongs to my purpose here, I cannot and must not pass over, even though he is somewhat detailed. The protection and preservation of the Church is taught in this march and military band, the expectation of which

> a. Is not situated or consisting in strengths, wisdom, and other human and fleshly means in themselves. See *Psalm 33:16 etc.; Psalm 60:13.*
> b. But in God, to whom the first and last army is attributed. Compare and take note of the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt, and furthermore their other marches and armed warfare. The Ark of the Covenant, the pillar of fire moved before them, and from all sides their army was surrounded by a cloud. Something greater, therefore, is attributed to God, as He is indeed called a shield, horn, and rock.

The first military rank is attributed to the righteousness of the Church.

Your righteousness does not appear in just one way.
1. Christ Himself is "The Lord Our Righteousness," which our annotators also observe.

# GOD’S REARWARD. אֲחוֹרֵי יְהוָה. <note>original Hebrew: *Achorei Yehovah*</note>
### *The Back Parts of God*, τὰ ὀπίσω. <note>original Latin: *Posteriora Dei*; original Greek: *ta opiso*</note>

One lives by the Lord, as in *Isaiah 45:15: "Truly you are a God who hides himself,"* concerning which one may consult my *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Mengelstoffen," referring to a collection of various scholarly or theological essays</note> on *Acts 17:23*. God, being a simple <term>simple: in theology, this means "uncompounded" or not made of different parts; God is a single, unified essence</term>, infinite, and absolutely perfect spirit, cannot fall within the reach of our sight; one cannot see Him with the eyes of the body. Being immaterial and infinite in perfections, He cannot be encompassed by our finite and limited understanding, nor can He be represented or compared to anything. Thus, it was a mere fiction of the Heathens <note>The author uses "Heathens" to refer to the ancient Greeks and Romans</note> when they spoke of the appearance and the beholding of the Deity; and in this, we even have many Heathen writers who agree with us. So speaks Dion Cassius, dealing with the Jews: *“That God is unutterable and formless”* <note>original Greek: *ἄῤῥητον κ’ ἀειδῆ*</note>, *“who can neither be expressed by words, nor can be grasped by us.”* And so writes Orpheus: *“He is among them, yet no mortal sees Him, though He sees all.”* <note>original Greek: *ἐκ δ’ αὐτοῖς αὐτὸς περιγίγνεται οὐδέ τις αὐτὸν εἰσοράᾳ θνητῶν, αὐτὸς δέγε πάντας ὁρᾶται*</note>

Minutius Felix: (*He cannot be seen, for He is too pure for the sight; not be touched, for He is too holy for the touch; not be measured, for He exceeds the grasp of the senses: He is infinite, and unmeasured, and only to Himself is He as great as He is known.*)

And Euripides:
> Tell me, what God must I think of?
> The one who sees all and is himself unseen. <note>original Greek: *θεὸν δὲ ποιῶν εἴπεο μοι νοητέον; Τὸν πάνθ’ ὁρῶντα κ’ αὐτὸν οὐχ ὁρώμενον.*</note>

->that is:<-

> *What God would you have me reveal to myself?*
> *The one who sees all, yet remains hidden from every eye.*

To see the deity was judged not to be beneficial for man; indeed, if it happened without permission, it cost the man dearly, as Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> has noted from Pausanias and Callimachus regarding *Exodus 33:23*.

It is then clear enough to me that when "God's Rearward" and "seeing God's Rearward"—and not His front—is spoken of, such is not literally or strictly applicable to God. As a pure, simple, and infinite spirit, He possesses neither front nor back. Therefore, it must be understood and taken very figuratively, as something borrowed from physical things through the imagination, yet corresponding to the divine essence, suited somewhat to our understanding and experience.

The word "Back," in the plural, *The Back Parts* <note>original Hebrew: אֲחוֹרֵי (*achorei*); original Greek: τὰ ὀπίσω (*ta opiso*)</note>, is placed in opposition to the *Face* <note>original Hebrew: פנים (*panim*)</note>, the front parts, the countenance, or the forehead.

It is clear that one sees more clearly and distinctly from the front, by looking at someone's face, than from behind, when one can only behold their shape and part of their clothing, and everything only from a distance. To see and speak with someone mouth to mouth, face to face, implies great access, friendship, and familiarity. It is the work of friends to act so. One can believe that Moses walked much more familiarly with the Lord than other Prophets. I also hold that his visions and the addresses of matters—manifestations through symbols, outward signs, the inward understandings of occurring matters—would have been much clearer, more vivid, and more powerful, both outwardly to his senses and inwardly to his understanding, than those of the other Prophets. His access, conversation, and negotiation with the Lord were much more familiar, with less fear, bashfulness, dismay, and trembling. Indeed, he is spoken of with singular praise and emphasis in *Deuteronomy 34:10, 11, 12*. To see the Lord, and to have a singular movement from Him, along with actual proofs and visible or audible signs of His presence and singular activity, was something that moved and struck a man quite strongly. (*Judges 6:23 and 13:22.*)

<column-break/>

I could also well maintain this: that since God, appearing to the fathers, usually made Himself known to them through signs of His presence, and at the same time through special and emphatic names (as can be noted from *Genesis 15:7, 17:1, 26:24, 20:13, 31:13, etc.*), Moses also desired of God that the Lord would please, in this or that way—through singular names, signs, or the unlocking of His counsel and future dealings—to reveal Himself to him, so that if he were asked by Israel for one thing or another, he might have something singular to answer on the Lord's behalf.

Yet until now, I have not come to the closer definition of "God's Rearward," which Moses alone would be permitted to see as the Lord passed by, covering him with His hand as He went. Nor have I shown what this figurative and flowery way of speaking seems to mean.

It is obvious that not all theologians have behaved the same way in this matter. For learned writers tell us that Gregory of Nazianzus, and alongside him Theodoret, understood it as the <margin>Interpretation of Gregory of Nazianzus and Theodoret.</margin> divine dispensations <note>original: "huishoudingen," referring to God's management of the world</note> and powerful effects or works. Illyricus <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a Lutheran reformer</note> has his eye on the outcome—the ultimate end of the works of God—from which one learns to know the Lord's virtues and perfections. Thus, one sees and learns to know Him not *a priori* <note>reasoning from cause to effect (from God's essence to His works)</note>, but *a posteriori* <note>reasoning from effect to cause (from the works back to God)</note> (as they say in the schools): not from the front, but from the back, from the execution of His decree, counsel, and the purposes of His works, which He places outside Himself through His all-sufficient will. (*Romans 1:20, Acts 14:17, etc.*), with which many writers agree.

Gregory of Nyssa takes it as a way of speaking that imagines Moses would have the Lord as a guide; that he should not run ahead or come alongside Him, but follow from behind. For he requested that God's face might go with him. <margin>Of Gregory of Nyssa.</margin>

I also wish to hold it as an indisputable truth—according to my first premise, which is strengthened by the testimony of the Heathens—that no one in this life, being in a sinful and imperfect state, in the body of sin and death, can endure God's glory and comprehend Him proportionately. Also, a sinner as such cannot endure God's presence, as He is a consuming fire. He cannot rightly approach God with the hope of having received access and grace. The Lord...

# THE BACK PARTS OF GOD.
### The back of the LORD. <note>original Hebrew: אחורי יהוה</note>
### *The Rear Parts of God, the things behind.* <note>original Latin and Greek: Posteriora Dei, τὰ ὀπίσω</note>

One lives by Jehovah, *Isaiah 45:15, that he is a God who hides himself*, regarding which one may consult my Miscellanea <note>original: "Mengelstoffen"; likely a reference to the author's previous collected writings</note> on *Acts 17:23*. God, being a simple, infinite, and perfectly complete spirit, cannot fall within the reach of our sight; one cannot see him with physical eyes, and being immaterial and infinite in perfections, he cannot be grasped by our finite and limited understanding, nor can he be represented or compared to anything. Therefore, it was a mere fiction of the Heathens when they spoke of the appearance and the beholding of the Deity, and in this, we even find many Heathen writers in agreement with us. Thus speaks Dio Cassius, dealing with the Jews: *That God is unutterable and formless* <note>original Greek: ἄρρητον καὶ ἀειδῆ</note>, *who can neither be expressed by words, nor can be contained by us.* And so writes Orpheus: *He himself is among them, yet no mortal sees him, but he sees them all.* <note>original Greek: ἐκ δ' αὐτοῖς αὐτὸς περιγίγνεται οὐδέ τις αὐτὸν εἰσοράα θνητῶν, αὐτὸς δέγε πάντας ὁρᾶται.</note>

Minutius Felix: (*He cannot be seen, for he is too pure for the sight; not be touched, for he is too clean for the touch; not be estimated, for he surpasses the grasp of the senses: he is infinite, and unmeasured, and only to himself is he as great as he is known.*)

And Euripides:
> What kind of God do you want me to show myself?
> The one who sees all and is himself unseen. <note>original Greek: Θεὸν δὲ ποιὸν εἴπω μοι νοητέον; Τὸν πάνθ' ὁρῶντὰ κ' αὐτὸν οὐκ ὁρώμενον.</note>

-> that is: <-

> *What God do you wish that I should show to myself?*
> *Who sees everything, and remains hidden from everyone's eyes.*

Beholding the deity was judged to be not beneficial to man, as that occurring without permission cost man dearly, as Grotius has noted from Pausanias and Callimachus on *Exodus 33:23*.

It is then clear enough to me that when one speaks of God's Back Parts, and of seeing God's Back Parts and not his front, such is not applicable to God properly or literally. He, as a pure, simple, and infinite spirit, possesses neither front nor back. Therefore, it must be understood and taken very improperly as a metaphor, borrowed from something physical, yet in accordance with the divine essence, suited somewhat to our comprehension and experience.

Back <note>original Hebrew: אחור</note>, in the plural, Back Parts <note>original Hebrew: אחורי</note>, the things behind <note>original Greek: τὰ ὀπίσω</note>, are placed in opposition to the Face <note>original Hebrew: פנים</note>—the front parts, the countenance, the forehead.

It is clear that one sees more clearly and distinctly from the front, and from the sight of someone’s face, than from behind, when one can only behold their stature and a portion of their clothes, and everything only at a distance. To see someone and speak with them mouth to mouth, face to face, implies great access, friendship, and familiarity. It is the work of friends to act so. One can believe that Moses dealt much more familiarly with the Lord than other Prophets. I also hold that his visions and the addresses of matters—manifestations through symbols, outward signs, and the inner understanding of occurring matters—must have been much clearer, more vivid, and more powerful both outwardly to his senses and inwardly to his understanding than those of other Prophets. His access, speech, and dealings with the Lord were much more familiar, with less fear, bashfulness, *dismay*, and trembling: indeed, he is spoken of with singular praise and emphasis in *Deuteronomy 34:10, 11, 12*. To see the Lord and to have a singular impression of him, alongside actual proofs and visible or audible signs of his presence and singular activity, was something that affected and struck a man quite strongly. *Judges 6:23* and *13:22*.

I could also hold it to be the case that, since God appearing to the fathers usually made himself known to them through signs of his presence and simultaneously through unique and emphatic names—as can be noted from *Genesis 15:7, 17:1, 26:24, 20:13, 31:13* etc.—Moses also desired of God that the Lord would be pleased to discover himself to him in one way or another, through unique names, signs, and the disclosure of his counsel and future dealings, so that if he were asked anything singular on behalf of Israel, he might have something to answer from the Lord’s side.

But until now, I have not come to a closer definition of God’s Back Parts, which Moses alone was permitted to see as the Lord passed by and covered him, as if with a hand, in the passing. Nor have I shown what this improper and figurative way of speaking seems to mean.

It is manifest that not all theologians have expressed themselves in the same way on this. For learned writers tell us that Gregory of Nazianzus, and alongside him Theodoret, understood it as the <margin>Interpretation of Gregory of Nazianzus and Theodoret.</margin> *divine economies* <term>divine economies: the way God manages or governs the world and the salvation of humanity</term> and *powerful effects* or works. Illyricus focuses on the outcome, the furthest extent of God's works, from which one learns to know the Lord's virtues and perfections. Thus, one sees and learns to know him not *a priori* <term>a priori: knowing something from the cause before seeing the effect</term>, but *a posteriori* <term>a posteriori: knowing something by looking at the results or effects after they happen</term> (as they say in the schools)—not from the front, but from behind, from the execution of his decree, counsel, and the intentions of his works, which he places outside himself through his all-sufficient will, *Romans 1:20, Acts 14:17*, etc., with which many writers agree.

Gregory of Nyssa takes it as a way of speaking that imagines Moses would have the Lord as a leader, and that he must not run ahead of him or get in his way, but follow from behind. For he requested that God's face might go with him. <margin>From Gregory of Nyssa.</margin>

I also wish to hold it as an indisputable truth, according to my first premise which is strengthened by the testimony of the Heathens, that no one in this life, in a sinful and imperfect state, being in the body of sin and death, can endure God's glory and comprehend him proportionately. Also, a sinner as such cannot endure God's presence, as he is a consuming fire. He cannot rightly approach God with the hope of having received access and grace. The Lord

...called obedience, is the righteousness of the Church by imputation <note>To "impute" is a theological term meaning to attribute something—in this case, Christ's righteousness—to someone else's account.</note>.

3. The good which Christ has earned through his death, or rather the righteousness belonging to that good, is called righteousness; as it is granted, and thus explained by the marginal annotators. Compare *Isaiah 26:1.*

4. Even good works are called the righteousness of the Church, whose principle, perfection, fountain, and sum is faith and love.

# GOD'S BACK PARTS. <note>original Hebrew: יהוה אחורי "Jehovah's Back Parts"</note>
### The Rear of God <note>original Latin: Posteriora Dei; original Greek: τὰ ὀπίσω</note>

One reads of Jehovah in *Isaiah 45:15* that he is *a God who hides himself*, regarding which one may consult my Miscellany on *Acts 17:23.* God, being a simple, infinite, and absolutely perfect spirit, cannot fall within the reach of our sight; one cannot see him with the eyes of the body. Being immaterial and infinite in perfections, he cannot be encompassed by our finite and limited understanding, nor can he be represented or compared to anything. Thus, it was a mere fiction of the Heathens when they spoke of the appearance and the beholding of the Divinity, and in this, we even have many Heathen writers who agree with us. So speaks Dio Cassius, treating of the Jews, *that God is unutterable and formless* <note>original Greek: ἄῤῥητον καὶ ἀειδῆ</note>, *who can neither be expressed by words, nor can be grasped by us.* And so Orpheus writes: *He is indeed among them, yet no mortal beholds him, but he sees them all.* <note>original Greek: ἐκ δ' αὐτοῖς αὐτὸς περιγίγνεται οὐδέ τις αὐτὸν εἰσοράᾳ θνητῶν, αὐτὸς δέγε πάντας ὁρᾶται.</note>

Minutius Felix: (*He cannot be seen, for he is too bright for the sight; not be touched, for he is too pure for the touch; not be measured, for he surpasses the grasp of the senses: he is infinite, and unmeasured, and to himself alone is he as great as he is known.*)

And Euripides:
> *What kind of God do you wish for me to show you?*
> *The one who sees all, and himself remains unseen.*
<note>original Greek: Θεὸν δὲ ποιὸν εἴπεο μοι νοητέον; Τὸν πάνθ' ὁρῶντὰ κ' αὐτὸν οὐκ ὁρώμενον.</note>

To see the divinity was judged to be not beneficial to man, as that which happened without permission cost man dearly, as Grotius has noted from Pausanias and Callimachus on *Exodus 33:23.*

It is then clear enough to me that when one speaks of God's Back Parts, and of seeing God's Back Parts and not the front, such is not properly or literally applicable to God. As a pure, simple, and infinite spirit, he possesses neither a front nor a back. Therefore, it must be understood and taken very improperly as a figure of speech borrowed from something physical, yet in accordance with the divine essence, suited somewhat to our comprehension and experience.

The word *back* <note>original Hebrew: אחור</note>, in the plural *back parts* <note>original Hebrew: אחורי</note>, or *the rear parts* <note>original Greek: τὰ ὀπίσω</note>, is set in contrast to *the face* <note>original Hebrew: פנים</note>, the front parts, or the forehead.

It is clear that one sees more clearly and distinctly from the front, and from the sight of someone's face, than from behind, at which time one can only behold their stature and part of their clothing, and everything only in the distance. To see someone from mouth to mouth, or face to face, and to speak with them, signifies great access, friendship, and intimacy. It is the work of friends to act so. One can believe that Moses walked much more familiarly with the Lord than other Prophets. I also hold it to be true that his visions and the speeches concerning matters—revelations through symbols, outward signs, and the inner understanding of occurring things—would have been much clearer, more vivid, and more powerful both outwardly to his senses and inwardly to his understanding than those of the other Prophets. His access, speech, and dealings with the Lord were much more familiar, with less fear, bashfulness, *consternation*, and trembling: indeed, he is spoken of with singular praise and emphasis in *Deuteronomy 34:10, 11, 12.* To see the Lord, and to have a singular affection from him, along with actual proofs and visible or audible signs of his presence and singular activity, was something that affected and struck a man quite strongly. See *Judges 6:23* and *13:22.*

I could also well maintain that, because God appearing to the fathers usually made himself known to them through signs of his presence and at the same time through special and emphatic names (as can be noted from *Genesis 15:7, 17:1, 26:24, 20:13, 31:13* etc.), Moses also desired of God that the Lord might be pleased to discover himself to him in this or that manner, through special names or signs revealing his counsel and future dealings, so that he, being asked something special by Israel on the Lord's behalf, might have something to answer.

However, until now, I have not come to a closer definition of God’s Back Parts, which Moses alone was permitted to see as the Lord passed by, covering him as if with a hand while passing. Nor have I shown what this improper and figurative way of speaking seems to mean.

It is obvious that not all theologians have expressed themselves in the same way on this. For learned writers tell us that Gregory of Nazianzus, and alongside him Theodoret, understood it as the <margin>Interpretation of Gregory of Nazianzus and Theodoret.</margin> *divine economies* <term>divine economies: the way God manages or governs the world and human salvation</term> and *powerful workings* or effects. Illyricus has his eye on the outcome, the extremity of God's works, from which one learns to know the Lord's virtues and perfections; so that one sees and learns to know him not *a priori* <note>from cause to effect</note>, but *a posteriori* <note>from effect to cause</note> (as they say in the schools), not from the front but from behind—from the execution of his decree, counsel, and the intentions of his works, which he places outside himself through his all-sufficient will. See *Romans 1:20, Acts 14:17,* etc., with which many writers agree.

Gregory of Nyssa takes it as a figure of speech representing that Moses should have the Lord as a leader, and that he should not run ahead of him or come to his side, but follow from behind. For he requested that God's face might go with them. <margin>From Gregory of Nyssa.</margin>

I also wish to hold it as an indisputable truth—according to my first premise, which is strengthened by the testimony of the Heathens—that no one in this life, being in a sinful and imperfect state within the body of sin and death, can endure God's glory or comprehend him proportionately. Also, a sinner as such cannot endure God's presence, as he is a consuming fire. He cannot rightly approach God with the hope of having received access and grace. The Lord...

# KICKING BACK.

...turns his face away from him. *Exodus 4:6, 7; Jeremiah 30:21; Ezekiel 8:16, etc.*

I likewise hold it to be true that the beholding and enjoying of God here in this life, and hereafter in the state of blessed glory, differs quite as much as seeing him either from the front or from the back, *1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 Corinthians 15, etc.* I also believe that the fathers <note>The "fathers" refers to the Old Testament patriarchs and prophets.</note> had to be content with the promises, riddles, imaginings of things, figures, and shadows; but that the seeing and knowing of God in the beholding of the Son—the image of the Father—alongside the word of fulfillment, without figures and riddles, differs as much as seeing from the front or from the back. Now that one knows God's way, and contemplates with <note>original Greek: νοῦ καὶ ἀφελείᾳ / "mind and simplicity"</note> in God's face, letting it shine and having hallowed his name; he has bared his arm and the whole earth knows the way of the Lord, *Matthew 13; Luke 8; 2 Corinthians 1 and 3; Job 1 and 14; Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1, etc.; Psalm 8:1, 2.* although Moses saw the Lord from the back, and came to know him singularly through those names he gave himself, which he would gloriously clarify and confirm through the exercise of his virtues appearing before us, *Exodus 34.* These he would nonetheless only hear proclaimed in the distance, accompanied by recognizable signs of divine radiance and luster, yet only as if in passing.

### KICKING BACK, <note>Hebrew: בעט / Greek: λακτίζειν / Latin: recalcitrare</note>

<margin>Kicking back is characteristic of stubborn oxen.</margin>
Kicking back with the feet or legs is primarily characteristic of luxurious, stubborn, and rebellious oxen. Since it was customary to plow with these animals in ancient times, they were prodded by the driver or the husbandman when they were stubborn or sluggish with sharp, long reeds, arrows, or other tools tipped with points <note>These are "goads," sharp sticks used to guide livestock.</note>. Now, when the ox harnessed in the plow-rope kicked backward, he only bruised himself, and having gained nothing, he nevertheless had to remain walking in the plow-rope.

<margin>How it is understood metaphorically.</margin>
*Kicking back* is sometimes a metaphorical way of speaking, signifying that someone behaves with base ingratitude, rebellion, disobedience, and a wanton spirit despite having received blessings and benefits.

*Kicking back* against the pricks <note>original: "prikkels," referring to the sharp points of the goads.</note>, and thus wounding and hurting oneself, is a phrase borrowed from the oxen that pull the plow; it is applied to the senseless actions of those who, setting themselves against those more powerful than they are, greatly disadvantage themselves. This happens especially when man presumes to oppose the Lord.

I shall clarify this from several ancient writers:

->Pindarus in Pythian Ode 2 says:<-

> *One must not contend against God, but bear the yoke placed upon the neck lightly, for it helps. To kick against the goads is a slippery path.*
<note>original Greek: χρὴ ἦ πρὸς θεὸν οὐκ ἐρίζειν, Φέρειν δ' ἐλαφρῶς ἐπαυχένιον λαβόντα ζυγὸν ἀρήγει. ποτικέντρα λακτιζέμεν τελέθει ὀλισθηρὸς οἶμος.</note>

->That is:<-

*To strive with God is an unseemly thing.*
*One bears the yoke upon the shoulders much better.*

<column-break/>

*But it is a slippery way to kick*
*The heels against the pricks.*

In Terence's *Phormio*, Davus says to Geta the slave:

*These things came to my mind: for what ignorance it is, to kick against the goad.*
<note>original Latin: Venêre in mentem isthæc mihi: nam quæ inscitia est, Advorsum stimulum calces.</note>

[<gloss>I thought as much: for how else would that go? It is folly to kick one’s heels against the pricks.</gloss>]

He meant to say that it was a foolish undertaking to try to incite oneself against the son of his lord and master.

Pliny in the Panegyric:

*It is useless, it is vain, nay, it is harmful, to wish to kick against the goad.* <note>original Latin: Irritum est, vanum est, imo noxium est, adversus stimulum calcitrare velle.</note> That is: *It is in vain, it is idle, yes, harmful, to wish to strike the heels against the prick.*

Aeschylus in Agamemnon:

> *Do not kick against the goads, lest you strike them and suffer.*
<note>original Greek: πρὸς κέντρα μὴ λάκτιζε, μὴ πήσας μογῇς.</note>

[<gloss>Do not thrust against the pricks, if you do not wish to wound yourself severely.</gloss>]

The same in Prometheus:

> *You stretch a limb against the goads.*
<note>original Greek: πρὸς κέντρα κῶλον ἐκτενεῖς.</note>

[<gloss>You stretch a limb against the pricks.</gloss>]

Euripides in the Bacchae:

> *Being a mortal, I would rather sacrifice to God than, being angry, kick against the goads.*
<note>original Greek: πρὸς κέντρα λακτίζοιμι θνητὸς ὢν θεῷ θυμώμενος.</note>

[<gloss>Mankind, incited against God by wickedness, strikes against the pricks with heels that recoil.</gloss>]

The same in Peliades:

> *Do not kick against the goads of those who are stronger than you.*
<note>original Greek: πρὸς κέντρα μὴ λάκtiζε τοῖς κρατοῦσί σου.</note>

->That is:<-

*Yield to the one who is stronger than you,*
*For you would only strike against the pricks,*
*And miserably increase your own sorrow.*

Let this be enough; one may consult Glassius's *Sacred Rhetoric, book 3, tract 6, regarding prepositions, page 760*; Grotius on *Acts 26*; also the passage cited by Calov; *Dieteric's Antiquities of the New Testament, page 460; Kranfer's Phosphor, page 201.*

Using this kindled light, I proceed to further open and explain some texts.

<margin>Explanation of some passages.</margin>
Deuteronomy 32:15. *But when Jeshurun grew fat, he kicked backward*, etc.

The great Burman in his book, *The Law and the Testimony, page 917*, wrote the following about it:

The third part contains a reference to the base ingratitude of the Israelites. He calls Israel Jeshurun, which is as much as "the upright one," because he ought to be such; or rather, this word signifies "one who sees God," as the Israelites saw God, first in the sign in the wilderness, and thereafter in Christ; compare Zephaniah 3:1. Woe to those to whom it is given...

# KICKING BACK. STURGEON.
<note>original: ACHTERUIT SLAAN. ACCIPENSER.</note>

G

is to be seen, namely God in the flesh. He now sets forth three stages of blessing for her, and likewise of sin. *1. That he became fat, namely from being thin, as happened in the times of the Judges. 2. That he became thick, which happened under the Kings. 3. That he was covered with fat, which refers to the times following the Babylonian captivity, when he had greatly multiplied and become powerful.* <note>The author is interpreting Deuteronomy 32:15, where "Jeshurun" (Israel) grew fat and kicked.</note>

The three stages of sin are: *1. That he kicked back, a likeness of rebellious and wanton oxen, which, when they are goaded by the plowman to plow, kick back against the goad, from which that manner of speaking comes, Acts 9:5 and 26:14. So also Israel, having become fat and wanton, kicked back against the goads of the law, by which it was urged to its duty. compare 1 Samuel 2:29. This they did when they set up altars and images against the command of God; which began under the Judges, and was thereafter continued by Jeroboam and others. 2. He forsook God who had made him. Which they did when, abandoning the true worship, they introduced the service of false Gods; which particularly happened in the times of Ahab, and of others before and after him. 3. That he despised or acted treacherously toward the rock of his salvation. Which sin, exceeding the previous ones, was fulfilled against the Lord Christ himself, whom his people handled shamefully, even killing him. His suffering and death are expressed here in this way: since the word used here can also mean to make a dead body, which they indeed made of Christ's body.*

One may consult Pole <note>Matthew Poole (1624–1679), author of the *Synopsis Criticorum*.</note> and other interpreters.

<margin>1 Samuel 2:29 explained.</margin>
The passage 1 Samuel 2:29 is explained by Burman on page 21 thus: *The ingratitude was, that 1. he kicked back against God's slaughter-offerings and meat-offerings, having been well fattened thereby. 2. He honored his sons more than God, regarding them while despising the meat-offering of the Lord. 3. That they fattened themselves from the chief of all the meat-offerings of the people of Israel. Since Eli did not prevent this sin, but shared in the enjoyment of it—for he was also a Priest, and they could act in his name—it is therefore also attributed to him here.*

<margin>Psalm 41:10 opened.</margin>
I find Ahithophel compared to Judas in *John 13:18;* for where he should have served Jesus as his benefactor, lord, and master, loved him tenderly, and clung to him firmly, he instead shamefully sold him and craftily betrayed him, coming against him with an armed band. Thus his base ingratitude and ghastly treachery are portrayed by the behavior of some bold, malicious horse or beast that strikes, gores, and tramples its benefactor and master. See Gejerus, Cocceius, van Til, and others.

<margin>Acts 9:5 opened, with Acts 26:14.</margin>
*Acts 9:5. It is hard for thee to kick the heels against the pricks.* That which is called in Acts 5:39, *to fight against God.* Also Acts 23:9.

Quintilian VI. 5. cited by Priceus on this passage, says:

> *It is harmful to fight against those things which you cannot obtain; where it is necessary to be defeated, it is expedient to yield.* <note>original Latin: "Nocet pugnare iniis, quae obtinere non possis, ubi vinci necesse est, expedit cedere."</note>

<margin>Vain efforts of Paul against Christ.</margin>
The same appears in *Acts 26:14.* and seems to mean that Paul, wishing to continue blaspheming the name of Jesus and persecuting the truth and the congregation of Christ, as he had done until now, would undertake a vain work; and he would not only never be able to overcome the superior power of the Glorified One, but it would result in his own harm and pain, since he had to do with him who is God. And so Aretius says further on this passage: *thus are those who have fought against God miserably overthrown and rooted out: Pharaoh, Saul, Herod, the Pharisees, Caiaphas, Julian, Porphyry. Therefore let all men learn not to fight with God; not only those who openly oppose themselves against God, as the Ungodly do: but also those who, under a show of godliness, persecute the pious because they will not listen: It is hard for thee to kick the heels against the goad. Job 12. Who indeed shall break down, when the Lord builds up? The Lord who is in Heaven shall laugh at them.*

### STURGEON <note>original: ACCIPENSER, ACIPENSER, or ACIPENSIS</note>, taken by us for the Sturgeon.

<margin>Sturgeon, a very rare fish, also in price.</margin>
It is, if one wishes, a fish with reversed or inverted scales; that is, where other fishes have scales lying down or flatly extended toward the tail, this fish has the scales pointing toward its head. It is said that it swims against the current, is very rarely caught, and is held in great value, being a rare dish for great people, princes, kings, and emperors. Some call him *Elops, Rhodiginus Chapter 5* calls him *Penser*, others *Catulus*, etc.

<margin>A princely dish.</margin>

> *What mortal was ever affected by such great fortune,*

> *Whose side I shall return to the hiding places of my teeth and hands.*
> <note>original Latin: "Quis est mortalis tantâ fortunâ affectus umquam, / Quam ego nunc sum? cujus haec ventri portatur pompa, / Vel nunc qui mihi in mari Accipenser latuit antehac / Cujus ego latus in latebras reddam meis dentibus, & manibus."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Whose eyes are they, that ever saw anyone as lucky*
> *As I am now? What a great state my belly wishes to keep!*
> *The Sturgeon, which before this hid from me in the sea,*
> *I shall send inside with my hands and teeth alike.*

The palaces and tables of kings also rarely had the sight of it. Martial in the 13th book:

> *Send the Sturgeon to the Palatine tables.*
> *Let rare gifts adorn the ambrosial feasts.*

# KICKING BACK.
<note>original: ACHTERUITSLAAN.</note>

I likewise hold it to be true, that the beholding and enjoying of God here in this life, and hereafter in the state of blessed glory, differs as much as seeing Him either from the front or from the back, *1 Corinthians 13:12. 1 Corinthians 15. etc.* I also believe that the fathers <note>referring to the Old Testament Patriarchs</note> had to be content with the promises, riddles, imaginings of things, figures, and shadows; but that the seeing and knowing of God in the contemplation of the Son—the image of the Father—alongside the word of fulfillment, without figures and riddles, differs as much as seeing from the front or from the back. ### KICKING BACK, <term>ba’at <note>Hebrew: בעט</note></term> / <term>laktizein <note>Greek: λακτίζειν</note></term>, <term>recalcitrare <note>Latin</note></term>.

<margin>Kicking back is peculiar to stubborn oxen.</margin>
Kicking back with the feet or legs is primarily characteristic of luxurious, stubborn, and rebellious oxen. Since it was customary in ancient times to plow with these animals, they were goaded by the driver or the husbandman when they were stubborn or sluggish, using sharp, long reeds, arrows, or other tools tipped with points. Now, when the ox harnessed in the plow-trace kicked back, he only hurt himself; having gained nothing, he still had to remain walking in the harness.

<margin>How it is used metaphorically.</margin>
*Kicking back* is sometimes a metaphorical way of speaking, signifying that someone behaves with base ingratitude, rebellion, disobedience, and a wanton mind despite the blessings and benefits they have received.

*To kick against the goads*—and thus to wound and hurt oneself—is a phrase borrowed from the oxen that pull the plow; it is applied to the senseless actions of those who, setting themselves against those more powerful than they, greatly disadvantage themselves. This happens especially when man presumes to oppose the Lord.

I shall clarify this from some ancient writers:

->Pindar, Pythian Ode 2, says:<-

> <term>One must not strive against God, but bear the yoke placed on the neck lightly. To kick against the goads <note>original: ποτικέντρα λακτιζέμεν</note> is a slippery path.</term>

->That is:<-

> *To quarrel with God is an unseemly thing.*
> *One bears the yoke upon the shoulders much better.*
> *But it is a slippery path to strike one's heels*
> *Against the goads.*

In Terence, in *Phormio*, Davus says to Geta the slave:

> *These things came to my mind: for what ignorance it is to kick your heels against the goad.* <note>original: Advorsum stimulum calces.</note>

> [<insert>That is what I thought: for how else would that go? It is folly to strike one's heels against the goads.</insert>]

He meant to say that it was a foolish undertaking to try to set oneself against the son of one's lord and master.

Pliny in the *Panegyricus*:

> *It is fruitless, it is vain, indeed it is harmful, to wish to kick against the goad. That is: It is in vain, it is idle, yes harmful, to wish to strike the heels against the prickle.*

Aeschylus in *Agamemnon*:

> <term>Do not kick against the goads, lest you strike them and suffer.</term>

The same in *Prometheus*:

> <term>You stretch your limb against the goads.</term>

Euripides in the *Bacchae*:

> <term>Being a mortal, I would kick against the goads if I were angry with God.</term>

> [*Mankind, incited by malice against God, strikes against the goads with his heels so that it recoils.*]

The same in *Peleus*:

> <term>Do not kick against the goads of those who are stronger than you.</term>

->That is:<-

> *Yield to the one who is stronger than you,*
> *For you would only strike against goads,*
> *And miserably increase your own sorrow.*

Let this be enough; one may consult Glassius, *Sacred Rhetoric, book 3, treatise 6, on prepositions, page 760*; Grotius on *Acts 26*; also cited by Calovius on that passage; *Dieteric, Antiquities of the New Testament, page 460; Kranser, Phosphor, page 201.*

<margin>Explanation of some passages.</margin>
Making use of this kindled light, I proceed to further lay open and explain some texts.

*Deuteronomy 32:15. But when Jeshurun grew fat, he kicked back, etc.*

The great Burman, in his book *The Law and the Testimony, page 917*, wrote the following about it:

The third part contains a rebuke of the base ingratitude of the Israelites. He calls Israel "Jeshurun," which is as much as "the upright one," because he ought to have been such; or rather, this word signifies "the one who sees God," as the Israelites saw God in this way, first in the sign in the wilderness, and thereafter in Christ. Compare *Zephaniah 3:1.* Woe to him to whom it is given...

# KICKING BACK. STURGEON.
