He now establishes in her three stages of blessing, and likewise of sin. 1. *That he became fat, namely from being lean, as happened in the times of the Judges.* 2. *That he became thick, which happened under the Kings.* 3. *That he was covered with fat, which refers to the times following the Babylonian captivity, when he became greatly multiplied and powerful.*

The three stages of sin are: 1. *That he kicked back*, an image of rebellious and pampered oxen, which, when pricked by the husbandman to plow, kick back against the goad; from which that manner of speaking comes, *Acts 9:5 and 26:14.* So too *Israel*, having become fat and pampered, kicked back against the goads of the law, by which it was urged to its duty. compare *1 Samuel 2:29.* They did this when they set up altars and images against God's command; which began under the Judges, and was thereafter continued by *Jeroboam* and others. 2. *He abandoned the God who had made him.* Which they did when, forsaking true worship, they introduced the service of false gods. This occurred particularly in the times of *Ahab*, and of others before and after him. 3. *That he mocked or acted roguishly toward the rock of his salvation.* This sin, exceeding the previous ones, was fulfilled against the Lord *Christ* himself, whom his people treated shamefully, even killing him. His suffering and death are expressed here in this way. As the word used here can also mean *to make a dead body*, which they indeed made of Christ's body.

One may consult *Poole* <note>Matthew Poole, 1624–1679, English theologian</note> and other interpreters.

<margin>1 Samuel 2:29 explained.</margin>
The passage *1 Samuel 2:29* is explained by *Burman page 21* as follows: *The ingratitude was that 1. he kicked back against God’s slaughter-offerings and meat-offerings, being well-fattened thereby. 2. He honored his sons more than God, sparing them while despising the meat-offering of the Lord. 3. That they fattened themselves from the chief of all the meat-offerings of the people of Israel. Because Eli did not prevent this sin, but shared in the enjoyment of it—for he was also a Priest, and they could act in his name—it is therefore also attributed to him here.*

I find *Ahithophel* compared to *Judas*

Thus his foul ingratitude and gruesome treachery are portrayed by the behavior of some bold, malicious horse or beast that strikes, gores, and kicks its benefactor and master. See *Gejerus, Cocceius, van Til*, and others.

<margin>Acts 9:5 opened, with Acts 26:14.</margin>
*Acts 9:5.* It is *hard for you to kick your heels against the goads.* That which in *Acts 5:39* is called *to fight against God.* Also in *Acts 23:9.*

*Quintilian VI. 5.* cited by *Priceus* on this passage says:

<margin>Vain efforts of Paul against Christ.</margin>
The same appears in *Acts 26:14* and seems to mean that Paul, wishing to continue blaspheming the name of Jesus and persecuting the truth and congregation of Christ, as he had done until then, would be attempting a futile work; he would not only never be able to overcome the superior power of the Glorified One, but it would result in his own harm and pain, since he had to do with him who is God. Let all men therefore learn not to fight with God; not only those who openly oppose themselves to God, as the ungodly do: but also those who, under the appearance of godliness, persecute the pious because they will not listen: It is hard to kick the heels against the goad. Job 12: Who then shall break down, when the Lord builds up? The Lord who is in Heaven shall laugh at them.*

### ACCIPENSER, ACIPENSER, or ACIPENSIS, taken by us to be the Sturgeon.

<margin>Sturgeon, a very rare fish, also the scaled-animal in price.</margin>
**I**t is, as they say, a fish with reversed or inverted scales; that is, where other fishes have scales lying down or flatly extended toward the tail, this fish has its scales pointed toward its head. It is said that it swims against the current, is very rarely caught, and is of great value, being held as a rare dish for great people, princes, kings, and emperors. Some call it *Elops*; *Rhodiginus Chapter 5* calls it *Penser*, others *Catulus, etc.*

*Pliny's Natural History, Book 9, Chapter 17* speaks of it. *Stuckius, Cicero, Martial, Plautus, etc.* testify to the same: that it is seldom caught, and was formerly a delicacy for great personages, belonging to the tables of kings and great princes.

<margin>A royal dish.</margin>
It was customary to bring it to the tables of princes in garlanded dishes, accompanied by singing and the blowing of pipes and trumpets. It was a stealthy and rare snack if a common man were to set his teeth into it. *Plautus in Bacchides:*

> What mortal was ever affected by such great fortune,
> As I am now? For whose belly is this procession carried,
> Even now the Sturgeon, which until now lay hidden from me in the sea,
> Whose side I shall return to the hiding places with my teeth and hands.
> <note>Latin original: "Quis est mortalis tantâ fortunâ affectus umquam / Quam ego nunc sum? cujus haec ventri portatur pompa / Vel nunc qui mihi in mari Accipenser latuit antehac / Cujus ego latus in latebras reddam meis dentibus, & manibus."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Whose eyes are they, that ever beheld someone as lucky*
> *As I am now? What a great state my belly wishes to keep!*
> *The Sturgeon, which hid itself from me in the sea before this,*
> *I shall send inside with my hands and my teeth.*

The palaces and tables of kings also rarely had the sight of it. *Martial* in the *13th book:*

> Send the Sturgeon to the Palatine tables.
> Let rare gifts adorn the ambrosial feasts.
> <note>Latin original: "Ad Palatinas Accipensem mittite mensas. / Ambrosias ornent munera rara dapes."</note>

->Which amounts to this:<-

> *A Sturgeon, that beautiful fish, serves to be offered to princes;*
> *What is rare belongs at the tables of the gods.*

# STURGEON. ADAM.
<note>original: ACCIPENSER. ADAM.</note>

Whatever the truth may be regarding this fish, and the precise description of it, I have until now read no one who has given me a thorough account of it.

There are more rare fishes in the sea, and those which are seldom caught: there are also many that swim against the current, but whether there are many with reversed scales, I do not know.

<margin>Finned, scaled, edible fish, regarded as symbols of those among the heathens who have received grace.</margin>Since the sea in general signifies heathendom in God's Word, and the finned and scaled fish were clean and fit for food (*Leviticus 11, Deuteronomy 14*), so I can generally see represented by clean fish those among the heathens who are cleansed and sanctified, who restrain themselves within the sea of heathendom, and who have this in common with most of God's children: that in the sea of this world they must often swim against the current and are subject to much adversity, which is endured by them with willingness, patience, and much strengthening and comfort. However, I do not yet see what could be represented by these reversed scales, by the fact that they are seldom caught, and only appear on the tables of the great. Therefore, if one is to make any application or allusion here, one must not look so much at what this fish has in common with many others, but what it has that is particular and its own, by which it is distinguished from all others.

<margin>Reversed-scale fish.</margin>Let me this time think of something else, and let this Sturgeon—with its backward scales and long, protruding sharp snout—bring to my mind such persons who either have their senses crosswise, or who misuse reason, assuming perverse forms and shapes, swimming as it were against the current of sound reason, good morals, upright courtesy, and upbringing: court jesters, flatterers, buffoons, etc., whom no common man’s status allows one to keep, to whom a modest, godly, and earnest man will seldom lend his ear, but who are nevertheless sought after at most courts, highly esteemed, and dearly paid for. See an example of this in Martial, Book VIII, Epigram 13:

<margin>Sturgeon compared to court jesters, sycophants, and buffoons.</margin>> *He was called a fool; I bought him for twenty thousand.* <note>original Latin: "Morio dictus erat, viginti millibus emi."</note>
> *Give me back my money, Gargilianus; he is wise.* <note>original Latin: "Redde mihi nummos, Gargiliane, sapit."</note>

->That is:<-

> [*He passed for a fool: I bought him straightaway at a high price.*]
> [*Give me back my money: I find him all too wise.*]

And things proceed so extravagantly at some courts that court jesters and buffoons are valued even above truly noble, earnest, and shrewd statesmen and councilors, and such a fuss is made of them that one might well agree with *Guevarra* <note>Antonio de Guevara, c. 1481–1545, Spanish chronicler and moralist</note>, who was of the opinion *that wisdom must be perverse, or the world must have lost its taste for wisdom.*

What power do these men not often possess at court? One can sometimes win more from princes through them than through the prince's own councilors and noblemen. They are used for amusement and pastime, and even to uncourtly prick, comb down, and mock this or that person one is angry with, through their sharp and boorish mouths.

<column-break/>

### ADAM. <note>Hebrew: אדם (Adam), Greek: ἀδάμ (Adam), Latin: Adamus</note>

<margin>Adam created.</margin>**T**HE divine History gives us to understand that God created the first man ADAM on the sixth day of creation out of the dust of the earth, and breathed a breath of life into his nostrils, forming him after His image, adorning him with uprightness, introducing him into a Paradise and palace of all kinds of fullness and abundance, and setting him over the works of His hands.

<margin>Immortality prepared for him.</margin>And although he was built up from earthly dust and separable parts, so that it was possible for him to return to his primary elements, he would nevertheless—had he persisted in his uprightness—not have died.

Since the Lord wished to multiply mankind through procreation, and Adam found no one in the likeness of his nature while the other creatures found their mates, he was overcome by a very deep sleep, at which time the Lord formed a woman for him from one of his ribs, introducing the law of mingling for procreation, upon which He gave His blessing. So that one must regard Adam and Eve as the origin and root of mankind, and the head of the human race, the woman being from the man.

<margin>Origin of the human race.</margin>And although the Lord had provided everything for man, it pleased Him nevertheless to show him a Tree in the Garden which Adam was given to cultivate, from which he was to abstain under threat of death and His extreme displeasure.

<margin>His transgression.</margin>But Adam, through love, did not intellectually limit his will to the consideration of what God willed; rather, he followed the example of his wife, who was misled by the serpent, and ventured to eat of the fruit forbidden to him.

<margin>Imputed to descendants.</margin>This deed—as a deed of him who was the root of mankind, in whom the whole of nature, or humanity, was contained—God, as a free and sovereign Lord, has placed to the account of all his descendants, imputing to them his unrighteousness or crime, so that He can deliver them all unto death and destruction, just as all who are born from him after that fall are subject to sin, misery, and the punishment of death.

<margin>Remedy for this ailment.</margin>But the Lord did not allow man to come to that sin and to that destruction through his own fault without knowing a remedy for that ailment; even from eternity, He had resolved within and by Himself to use a powerful means against this, for the illumination of His virtues and perfections: just as all His works are known to God from eternity.

In order not to dwell too long on this matter, which has been extensively and powerfully worked out by the learned, we only have to note that Holy Scripture teaches us that, just as Adam's crime and unrighteousness becomes the property of all his descendants by imputation, and thus the guilt and obligation to punishment passes to all, so through the imputation of the righteousness of the second Adam, Christ, many are made righteous, released in Him from the punishment, defilement, and servitude of sin, and entitled to life. This work of grace and salvation is begun in this life through justification, sanctification, adoption as children, and sealing by the Holy Spirit, and is completed hereafter, of which Paul speaks clearly in *Romans 5, 1 Corinthians 15, 2 Corinthians 5, Colossians 3, Ephesians 4,* and in other places.

<margin>Adam's sin atoned for by Christ.</margin>And herein I believe that one singularly...

# ADAM. ADDER.
<note>original: "G 2" - printer's signature; "LIX." - catchword referencing the next section or Psalm.</note>

...one must seek the correspondence between the first and the second Adam, according to the purpose of Paul in *Romans 5:14* and *1 Corinthians 15*.

It is true that the second Adam, Christ, could not bring about a restoration until the first had disrupted and overturned everything through sin, and He could not carry out His counsel in this matter until man and sin existed. However, this in no way prevents us—when observing God's eternal order, arrangement, and predestination, as we now experience the matter through its outcome and divine revelation—from noting many things in Adam that were so disposed by God to be <term>symbols and portraits<note>original: "zinnebeelden en schilderyen"</note></term> of what is perceived in the second Adam and His works and experiences. This is much like how we notice that in the "re-creation," the original creation is alluded to, and in the renewal of the world through Christ, specific and clear modes of speech are borrowed from it. Although, I am indeed of the opinion that Paul in *Romans 5* primarily places the correspondence in the <term>imputation<note>The legal attribution of one person's actions to another.</note></term> of Adam’s transgression unto punishment, and in the imputation of Christ’s righteousness unto acquittal and life.

Holding this then as the most important point, and turning everything upon that pivot, I shall also note some things that may seem a bit more far-fetched, or which have a closer relationship to this matter.

<margin>Meaning of the word ADAM.</margin>
Adam in Hebrew means as much as "earth," or "taken from the earth"; which some claim is of a red-colored hue.

That such earth exists no one can deny, yet that Adam was composed from such earthy matter is not a proven thing. Christ appears to us <margin>Christ red-colored.</margin> as red and ruddy, not so much in Himself, but by the circumstance of His suffering and struggle. *Song of Solomon 5:10, Isaiah 63:2.*

<margin>Adam God’s son.</margin>
That Adam is called God’s son in *Luke 3* is clear, and that Christ is such by excellence, no one can reject. *Psalm 2:7, Matthew 3:17 and 17:4, 5, Romans 8:32, John 1:18, Hebrews 1:1.*

<margin>Comparison between Adam and Christ.</margin>
That Adam was prepared by God is evident from the history of Moses; that Christ was born in an unusual way, without male intervention, from a virgin, through the overshadowing of the Spirit and the power of God, is undeniable. *Isaiah 7:14, Jeremiah 31:22, Psalm 40:7, Hebrews 10:5, Luke 1:31.*

That Adam could die has been proven, although death entered the world through sin, which would not have happened had he persisted in his righteousness. So Christ became like him and all his descendants in this regard, because of the sins He took upon Himself, *Hebrews 2:14 and 4:15*; He died, yet as the head and firstfruits of those who shall be raised with Him to immortality, He rose again. *1 Corinthians 15:45, etc.*

Adam was upright and good, shining with God’s image, yet in such a state that he could fall away, as the outcome has shown. Christ was good and upright, and of an unwavering goodness and righteousness, and preeminently the image of the invisible God. *Colossians 1:25, Hebrews 1:3.*

Adam was set over the works of God’s hands. Christ, *Psalm 8:7, 8 and 2:6, 8, Matthew 28:18, Colossians 1:16, 17, 18, Ephesians 1:31, 32, Hebrews 1:2.*

Adam had to cultivate the garden. Christ the church. *Song of Solomon 4, Isaiah 35 and 44.*

And to wrap everything up briefly: Adam received a wife from his own flesh for close fellowship, during his sleep to procreate seed, etc.

<column-break/>

Christ received the church in the sleep of His death, which was pleasant to Him, *Jeremiah 31:26*, of one blood with Him, *Hebrews 2:14 and 4:15*, His only one, *Song of Solomon 6:9*, in whose womb He procreates children through the seed of the Word and the life-giving Spirit. *Hosea 2, Isaiah 8:28 and 54, Psalm 110:2, Isaiah 53:10, Ephesians 5, etc.*

Which wife He loves, maintains, protects, etc. *Ephesians 5.*

What more could subsequently be said, both in comparison and in the exaltation of Christ above the first Adam, I shall not occupy myself with here. Let this be enough regarding Adam for my purpose.

### ADDER, ADDER’S POISON,
-><note>original Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: "אפעה ; εχιδνα, Vipera"</note> Viper.<-

<margin>Adder counted among the snakes.</margin>
The Adder is counted among the venomous species of snakes.

<margin>Various names, places, types.</margin>
Regarding the Hebrew naming, various species, the size, the places where these animals are most commonly found and where they are most venomous, and furthermore that which has been told and written of them that is rather lies, I shall not record here.

<margin>Their appearance.</margin>
In general, this is the truth regarding Adders: they are not large. They are described to us as generally having flat and broadish heads, thin necks (though some are rather bloated and thick), and having stunted tails. Some also tend toward a yellow, white, or pale color.

<margin>Difference between the male and female regarding the teeth.</margin>
It is told that the male has one tooth in his mouth, above and below, but the female has more teeth, and therefore one can tell from the tooth-bites whether one has been bitten by a male or a female.

<margin>They bring forth living young.</margin>
They are called in Latin <term>Viviparae<note>Live-bearers; animals that give birth to living offspring rather than laying eggs.</note></term>, because they cast or bring forth living young and not eggs, although it may well be that they are bred from eggs internally.

<margin>Remedy from their flesh.</margin>
Their flesh being eaten, it is said, improves the sight and even cures <term>leprosy<note>original: "Lazerye"</note></term>.

<margin>They also consume balsam.</margin>
It is sold to us as truth that the Adder consumes balsam juices, notwithstanding that such is the antidote to its venom, and that it turns into venom within it and is changed into it.

<margin>Its deadly poison.</margin>
It is claimed that the land tortoise, if it can only get hold of <term>origanum<note>Wild marjoram or oregano, historically believed to be an antidote to snakebite.</note></term> or oregano, does not fear its bite.

<margin>Many things compared to Adders.</margin>
Furthermore, to summarize everything briefly: it is a very venomous animal, from whose poisonous bites one dies quickly, at least within three or seven days. One finds comparisons using it and its eggs in the holy scrolls.

<margin>Dan and Israel’s evil thoughts.</margin>
The Tribe of Dan appears under the comparison of a snake, an adder-snake, *Genesis 49:17.* Israel is compared to it, *Deuteronomy 32.* Evil thoughts brought into action are compared to the <term>basilisk<note>A mythical serpent; here used to denote a deadly poisonous snake.</note></term> and adder’s poison. *Isaiah 59:5.*

<margin>Pharisees and Scribes. Those who hate rebuke, and slander, lie, and scold.</margin>
Pharisees and Scribes are called a "brood of vipers." *Matthew 3:7 and 12:34 and 23:37, Luke 3:7.*

Those who do not wish to notice their evil teachings and customs, and give no place to persuasion and rebukes, are compared to an adder that stops its ears. Whoever stings with the tongue and seeks to strike someone most sensitively through lying and slandering must hear that he is an Adder, and performs the work of poisoning. *Psalm 58:5.*

# STURGEON. ADAM.
<meta>catchword: a</meta>

As to what may be said of this fish, and the precise description of the same, I have until now read no one who has given me a thorough account of it.

There are many rare fish in the sea, and those which are seldom caught: there are also many that swim against the current, but whether there are many with <term>reversed scales<note>original: "omgewende schubben." The author refers to the unique bony plates of the sturgeon, which he interprets as being "backward."</note></term>, I do not know.

<margin>Finned, scaled, edible fish, regarded as symbols of the favored among the heathens.</margin>Since the sea in general signifies heathendom in God’s word, and the finned and scaled fish were clean and fit for food (*Leviticus 11, Deuteronomy 14*), I can generally see represented by clean fish those among the heathens who are cleansed and sanctified. These are they who refrain from the "sea" of paganism, and who have this in common with most of God's children: that in the sea of this world they must frequently swim against the current and are subject to many adversities, which are endured by them with willingness, patience, and much strengthening and consolation. Yet even then, I do not yet see what could be represented by these reversed scales, by the fact they are seldom caught, and that they appear only on the tables of the great. Therefore, if one is to make any application or allusion here, one must not look so much at what this fish has in common with many others, but what it has that is particular and unique to itself, by which it is distinguished from all others.

<margin>Backward-scaled fish.</margin>Let me this time think of something else, and let this Sturgeon—with its reversed scales and long, protruding, sharp snout—bring to my mind such persons who either have their senses "crosswise," or who misuse reason by adopting perverse forms and guises. They swim against the current of sound reason, good morals, upright courtesy, and upbringing; I speak of court jesters, flatterers, <term>buffoons<note>original: "potzemakers"</note></term>, and the like. To maintain such people is not permitted by the status of a common man, and a modest, God-fearing, and earnest man will seldom lend them his ear; yet they are nevertheless sought after at most courts, highly esteemed, and dearly paid. See an example of this in Martial, in Book 8, Epigram 13:

<margin>The Sturgeon compared to court jesters, sycophants, and buffoons.</margin>> *He was called a fool; I bought him for twenty thousand sesterces.* <note>original: "Morio dictus erat, viginti millibus emi."</note>
> *Give me my money back, Gargilianus: he is wise.* <note>original: "Redde mihi nummos, Gargiliane, sapit."</note>

-> That is: <-

> [*He passed for a fool: I bought him at once for a high price.*]
> [*Give me my money back: I find him all too wise.*]

And things proceed so extravagantly at some courts that court jesters and buffoons are valued even above truly noble, earnest, and shrewd statesmen and councilors. So much is made of them that one might well agree with <term>Guevara<note>Antonio de Guevara (c. 1481–1545), a Spanish writer and courtier famous for his moralizing works.</note></term>, who was of the opinion *that wisdom must be turned upside down, or that the world must have lost its taste for wisdom.*

What power do these people not often wield at court? One knows how to win over princes through them more effectively at times than through the prince’s own councilors and noblemen. They are used for amusement and pastime, and even to uncourtly prick, comb down, and mock this or that person one is angry with, using their sharp and rude muzzles.

<column-break/>

# ADAM. <note>Hebrew: אדם (Man/Red); Greek: Ἀδὰμ; Latin: Adamus.</note>

<margin>Adam created.</margin>The Divine History gives us to understand that God created the first man, ADAM, on the sixth day of creation from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his nostrils a breath of life, forming him after His image, adorning him with uprightness, and introducing him into a Paradise and palace of all kinds of fullness and abundance, setting him over the works of His hands.

<margin>Immortality prepared for him.</margin>And although he was raised up from earthly dust and potential divisible parts—so that it was possible for him to return to his primary materials—he nevertheless would not have died had he persevered in his uprightness.

Since the Lord wished to multiply mankind through procreation, and Adam found no one in the likeness of his nature (while the other creatures found their mates), he was overcome by a very deep sleep. At that time, the Lord formed a woman for him from one of his ribs, introducing the law of union for procreation, over which He gave His blessing. Thus, one must regard Adam and Eve as the origin and root of mankind, and the head of the human race, the woman being of the same race from the man.

<margin>Origin of the human race.</margin>And although the Lord had provided everything for man, it nevertheless pleased Him to point out a Tree in the Garden which Adam was to cultivate, from which he was to abstain under threat of death and His extreme displeasure.

But Adam did not, through love, intellectually bound his will to the consideration of what God willed; rather, he followed the example of his wife, who was deceived by the serpent, and ventured to eat of the fruit forbidden to him.

<margin>His transgression.</margin>This deed—being the deed of him who was the root of mankind, in whom the whole of nature, or humanity, was contained—God, as a free and sovereign Lord, has placed to the account of all his descendants. He has imputed to them his unrighteousness or crime, so that He can deliver them all over to death and destruction, just as all who are born of him after that fall are subject to sin, misery, and the punishment of death.

<margin>Imputed to his descendants.</margin>Yet the Lord did not let man come to that sin and destruction through his own fault without knowing a remedy for that malady. Indeed, from eternity, in and by Himself, He had intended to use a powerful means against this, for the clarification of His virtues and perfections: for all His works are known to God from eternity.

<margin>Remedy against this malady.</margin>To avoid lingering on this subject, which has been elaborately and powerfully worked out by the learned, we have only to note that Holy Scripture teaches us that, just as Adam's crime and unrighteousness becomes his descendants' own by <term>imputation<note>The theological concept where the legal standing or actions of one person are credited to another.</note></term>, and thus the guilt and obligation to punishment passes to all; so too, through the imputation of the righteousness of the second Adam, Christ, many are made righteous. In Him, they are released from the punishment, defilement, and bondage of sin, and entitled to life. This work of grace and salvation is begun in this life through justification, sanctification, adoption as children, and sealing by the Holy Spirit, and is completed hereafter; of which Paul speaks clearly in *Romans 5, 1 Corinthians 15, 2 Corinthians 5, Colossians 3, Ephesians 4*, and other places.

<margin>Adam's sin atoned for by Christ.</margin>And herein I believe that one finds the singular...

# ADAM. ADDER.
G 2
<meta>catchword: LIX.</meta>

one must seek the agreement between the first and the second Adam, according to the purpose of Paul in *Romans 5:14* and *1 Corinthians 15.*

It is true that the second Adam, Christ, could not bring about a restoration until the first had disturbed and thrown everything into turmoil through sin, and He could not carry out His counsel in this matter until man and sin existed: but such a thing does not at all prevent one, when observing God's eternal order, arrangement, and predestination—just as we now experience the matter by its outcome and divine unfolding—from noting many things in Adam as having been so arranged by God that they would be <term>symbols and portraits<note>original: "zinnebeelden en schilderyen"</note></term> of what is perceived in the second Adam and His works and experiences. This is much like how one notices that in the "re-creation," the original creation is alluded to, and from the same creation, specific and clear expressions are borrowed for the renewal of the world through Christ. However, I am indeed of the opinion that Paul, in *Romans 5*, primarily places the agreement in the imputation of Adam's transgression unto punishment, and in the imputation of Christ's righteousness unto acquittal and life.

Holding this then as the most important point, and turning everything upon that pivot, I shall also note something that might seem to be sought further afield, or which has a closer relationship to this matter.

<margin>Meaning of the word ADAM.</margin>
Adam sounds in Hebrew as much as "earth," or "taken from the earth": which some will have to be of a red-colored hue.

That such earth exists no one can deny, yet that Adam was composed of such earthy material is not a proven matter. Christ appears to us <margin>Christ red-colored.</margin> as red and red-colored, not so much in Himself as by the occasion of His suffering and struggle. *Song of Solomon 5:10. Isaiah 63:2.*

<margin>Adam, God's son.</margin>
That Adam is called God's son in *Luke 3* is clear, and that Christ is such by excellence, no one can reject. *Psalm 2:7. Matthew 3:17 and 17:4, 5. Romans 8:32. John 1:18. Hebrews 1:1.*

<margin>Comparison between Adam and Christ.</margin>
That Adam was prepared by God is known from the history of Moses; that Christ was born in an unusual manner, without human intervention, from a virgin, through the overshadowing of the Spirit and the power of God, is undeniable. *Isaiah 7:14. Jeremiah 31:22. Psalm 40:7. Hebrews 10:5. Luke 1:31.*

That Adam could die has been proven, although death entered the world through sin, which would not have happened had he persisted in his uprightness. Thus, Christ became like him and all his descendants in this regard because of the sins He took upon Himself (*Hebrews 2:14 and 4:15*); He died, yet He rose as the head and firstfruits of those who shall be raised with Him to immortality. *1 Corinthians 15:45, etc.*

Adam was upright and good, shining with God's image, yet in such a state that he could fall away, as the outcome has shown. Christ was good and upright, and of an unswerving goodness and uprightness, and by excellence the image of the invisible God. *Colossians 1:25. Hebrews 1:3.*

Adam was set over the works of God's hands. Christ, *Psalm 8:7, 8 and 2:6, 8. Matthew 28:18. Colossians 1:16, 17, 18. Ephesians 1:31, 32. Hebrews 1:2.*

Adam had to cultivate the garden. Christ, the church. *Song of Solomon 4. Isaiah 35 and 44.*

And to wrap everything up briefly: Adam received a wife out of his flesh for close fellowship, during his sleep, to beget seed, etc.

<column-break/>

Christ [obtained] the church in the sleep of His death, which was sweet to Him (*Jeremiah 31:26*), of one blood with Him (*Hebrews 2:14 and 4:15*), His only one (*Song of Solomon 6:9*), in whose womb He begets children through the seed of the word and the fertilizing Spirit. *Hosea 2. Isaiah 8:18 and 54. Psalm 110:3. Isaiah 53:10. Ephesians 5, etc.*

Which woman He loves, maintains, protects, etc. *Ephesians 5.*

What more could subsequently be said, both regarding the comparison and the exaltation of Christ above the first Adam, I shall not occupy myself with. Let this be enough regarding Adam for my purpose.

### ADDER, ADDER'S VENOM,
->Viper <note>original: Hebrew *Aph'eh* (אפעה), Greek *Echidna* (ἐχίδna), Latin *Vipera*</note><-

<margin>Adder counted among the snakes.</margin>
The Adder is counted among the venomous species of snakes.

<margin>Various names, places, species.</margin>
Regarding the Hebrew naming, various species, the size, the places where these animals are most often found, and where they are most venomous, and furthermore that which is told and written of them quite untruthfully, I shall not record here.

<margin>Their appearance.</margin>
In general, it is true of Adders that they are not large. They are described to us as generally having a flat and broadish head, a thin neck (although some are quite bulbous and thickish), and having deficient tails. Some also lean toward a yellow, white, or pale color.

<margin>Distinction between the male and female regarding the teeth.</margin>
It is told that the male has one tooth in his mouth, above and below, but the female has more teeth; and consequently, that one can tell from the tooth-bites whether one has been bitten by a male or a female.

<margin>They bring forth living young.</margin>
They are called <term>Viviparae<note>Latin for "living-bearing"</note></term> in Latin, because they bring forth living young and not eggs, although it may well be that they are bred from eggs internally.

<margin>Medicine from their flesh.</margin>
Their flesh being eaten, it is said, stimulates the sight and even cures <term>leprosy<note>original: "Lazerye"</note></term>.

<margin>They also consume balsam.</margin>
It is sold to us as truth that the Adder consumes balsam juices, notwithstanding that such is the antidote to its venom, and that such becomes venom within it and is changed into it.

It is claimed that the land tortoise, if only it can obtain <term>oregano<note>original: "origanum" or "orego"</note></term>, does not fear its bite.

<margin>Its deadly venom.</margin>
Furthermore, to summarize everything briefly: it is a very venomous animal, from whose poisonous bites one dies <term>quickly<note>original: "ylinx"</note></term>, at least within three or seven days. One finds comparisons using it and its eggs in the Holy Scrolls.

<margin>Many things compared to Adders.</margin>
The tribe of Dan appears under the comparison of a snake, an adder-snake (*Genesis 49:17*). Israel is compared to it (*Deuteronomy 32*); evil thoughts brought into action are compared to the <term>Basilisk<note>A legendary serpent king whose look or breath could kill.</note></term> and adder's venom (*Isaiah 59:5*).

<margin>Dan and Israel's evil thoughts.</margin>
Pharisees and Scribes are called a "brood of vipers." *Matthew 3:7, 12:34, and 23:33. Luke 3:7.*

<margin>Pharisees and Scribes.</margin>
Those who do not wish to notice their evil teachings and customs, and give no place to persuasions and rebukes, are compared to an adder that stops its ears. Whoever stings with the tongue and seeks to strike someone most sensitively through lying and slandering must hear that he is an Adder, and performs the work of the poisoning one. *Psalm 58:5.*

<margin>Those who hate rebuke, and lie and scold.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical theological dictionary, moving from the entry on "Adam" to "Adder" (Viper). # ADDER.

<margin>A child over the Adder-hole etc.</margin> *Isaiah 59:8. Proverbs 23:32. Isaiah 14:29. Jeremiah 8:17.* One reads of a nursing child that shall play over the hole of an adder, *Isaiah 11:8.* See my *Sacred Miscellanies* <note>original: "heilige Mengelstoffen"</note> on *Isaiah 11:8* for an explanation regarding the Adder. What I have understood by children, infants, etc., can be seen in the first part of my *Sacred Miscellanies*, page 88 etc., and regarding this passage, I have explained my opinion in the same book on page 108 etc. There I stated that the literal text could allow for it to be translated as:
> a. A nursing child shall look out with pleasure and desire toward the den of an Adder.
> b. Or shall enjoy itself because of the den of an Adder.
> c. Or shall play over the den of an Adder with cheerfulness and boldness, without hesitation or fear of being harmed.

The great Cocceius, in his well-wrought Hebrew Dictionary, has defined <term>פתן<note>Hebrew: Pethen, a venomous serpent or adder.</note></term> as "Adder-snakes." There it is suggested that Satan shall be trodden under the feet of the church in such a manner that it will be a pleasure for a child to mock the poisonous tyrants.

The venerable Nicolaus Gürtlerus, in his prophetic and exemplary Dictionary, page 96, seems to have understood this matter thus: *The witnesses of Christ, sucking the milk of the divine word from the breasts of the reformers, delight in the contemplation of the assembly of the Antichrist and its leaders residing in the cloisters; and those established in the truth (the weaned ones) shall, without danger of being lost, associate with the followers of the Antichrist.*

<margin>The Author's Explanation.</margin> For my part, if the thread and the timeframe of this prophecy can allow this interpretation as the primary meaning, I shall not oppose it.
I formerly understood it in this way:
That by the Adder, one could aptly understand the devil, with his servants and his followers.
By the nursing child, I represented Constantine the Great, with the first tender Christians who had come over from paganism, who were joyful because they saw the Adder’s den—the temples, chapels, and other places once dedicated to his service, lies, and deceptive teachings—now dedicated to the service and teaching of the Lord. See further my first *Miscellanies*, page 113 etc.

If I may say so, it seems to me that I was somewhat strengthened in my judgment later while reading the well-wrought work of Professor Campegius Vitringa on Isaiah. This Gentleman writes about it as follows:
> Regarding the secret sense of this symbol, the thoughts of the learned differ quite a bit. Jerome and many who follow him think here of the possessed, who were to be set free from unclean spirits by Christ’s disciples, who would leap upon the devils in their dwellings, according to Luke 10:19 and Mark 16:17, 18.
> Others have simply understood by it the powerful ones, the princes of this world, of whom the church formerly had great cause to be afraid; which is somewhat closer and simpler.
> Cyril understood it to mean either the bands of unclean spirits, or the dens and hiding places of the heretics.

By the hole of the Adder and the pit of the Basilisk <note>a mythical serpent king said to kill with a glance</note>, there are understood in a secret sense the schools and lecture halls in which the Rhetoricians and Philosophers—once sworn enemies of the Christian

<column-break/>

doctrine, true children of the devil and instructed by this master of theirs—poured out their harmful and deadly teachings and instructions, dipped in sharp gall, with a flood and stream of flowing eloquence, in order to suppress the Christian Religion and strongly recommend the old pagan superstition.

*At the same time, they attacked the pious practitioners of the truth with poisonous bites of slanders, maliciously decorated and picked up. In such schools, nurseries, and lecture halls—yes, even in the schools which were formerly the dens and pits of serpents, into which almost no one dared to go before without fear—the disciples of Christ, the subjects of His kingdom, and even the tender newly-baptized, enrolled in the church registry and newly come to a firmer knowledge of the Christian Religion and doctrine, would now dwell without any fear etc. One may consult His Reverence further.*

Thus one already perceives of what the Adder with its poison is a symbol. This I could now apply to the Pharisees and Scribes who pressed upon Jesus’ footsteps, clothing it with various reasons for comparison: yes, applying it to that evil and wicked generation, the brood of Satan, who did the works of Satan *John 8:44* <note>The text incorrectly cites Isaiah 8:44; the context refers to John 8:44.</note> and imitated their evil forefathers, being even more cunning than them.

<margin>The Adder as a symbol of the Pharisees and scribes.</margin> > *Ætas parentum pejor avis* <note>Latin: "The age of our parents is worse than that of our grandparents."</note>: Our parents are not as good as their parents.
> *Mali corvi malum ovum* <note>Latin: "From a bad crow, a bad egg."</note>: A bad egg, a bad chick. *Matthew 11 and 13. Acts 5 and 28:26.*

<margin>Regarding the wicked heretics, who yet have the balsam of grace.</margin> Furthermore, I see here a symbol of all very wicked heretics, who although they consume the balsamic sap of the Word, nevertheless change it into poison, though they can be cured of their poison by nothing else. Just as he who has the balsam of the Word in his heart need not fear any poisonous person or wicked heretic. Just as a good conscience wards off all poison from itself, so that one is not dried up or consumed by the fiery bite. To tread upon that sort of poisonous animals *Psalm 91:13* is to trample, crush, and subdue them without harm.

<margin>Against the Adder bites an antidote: a good conscience, as the most excellent balsam.</margin> Although I have already touched upon some things, I still have quite a lot to bring forward from secular authors, which I thought well to add here upon proofreading. Namely, I shall first present a scriptural observation from Baumannus in *Selections*, page 931, in which he compared the heretics to Adders; His Reverence presented it in this manner: *a.* One does not see the teeth of the Adders; they lie covered and quite hidden. The heretics and hypocritical deceivers gloss over their teachings with the appearance of holiness, so that one might not notice their attempt to deceive.

<margin>In what respect the Pharisees and the Adders are shown by Baumannus.</margin> *b.* The poison of Adders is deadly. So too the opinion of the heretical masters is harmful to the soul and destructive. *2 Peter 2:2.*

<margin>Heretics compared to Adders.</margin> *c.* The Adder’s sting and wound is incurable. The heretics wound unto death, because they change truth into lies, righteousness into unrighteousness, God’s grace into lewdness, and cause the right life to be exchanged for spiritual death.

*d.* The heretics are the cause of the death of the mother church. Just as the young of the Adders, in their haste to come forth, pierce the belly of their mother—as it is told—that is, they bring deadly pain to the mother church.

# ADDER.

...the church, though it can never be uprooted or perish.

<margin>Beza in *Emblems*, page 126.</margin>
> *Just as viper offspring gnaw through the mother's entrails,* <note>original: "Viperei erodunt ceu matris viscera foetus"</note>
> *So the church of the saints is gnawed, alas, too much by many*
> *Whom she herself nursed as a foster child in her own bosom,*
> *But not with the same outcome or reason.*
> *For the unhappy viper dies so that they may be safe.*
> *This church, on the contrary, remains, not to perish even when they are extinguished.*

<margin>Beza’s emblem.</margin>
[*The young of the adder bore through the mother's entrails.*
*So the church, alas, is attacked by many*
*Whom she had cherished in her soft lap*
*And protected in danger, saved from all need.*
*But the outcome is not the same. The young causes death*
*To the old: but the church endures the heaviest blow,*
*Stands firm, and never finds herself deprived of heaven's help.*]

<margin>The same shown from Gerardus.</margin>
Indeed, I find the Pharisees and their brood—vile deceivers, liars, and slanderers—compared to snakes, adders, and vipers by Gerardus <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a Lutheran scholastic theologian</note> in his *Harmony of the Gospels*. *Matthew 3 and 23:33.*
1. Because of their inclination to cause harm, and to kill and destroy the soul, *Numbers 21.*
6. They travel across lands and cities to make others like themselves, and then they become children of hell.
2. The Pharisees are generally more cunning and trained to deceive and outwit, for they wear the cloak of hypocrisy and appear so simple that one would expect no evil from them, but would entrust them with everything. *Matthew 5, 15, and 23.*
3. They possess a poisonous and corrupting venom in their teaching. *Deuteronomy 32.*
4. They are prone to slander and sting with the tongue. *Psalm 40, Ecclesiastes 10.*
5. They stop their ears, *Psalm 58,* and give no place to warnings, rebukes, or convincing reasons.

See this presented more broadly by Baum. in *Select.* pages 931, 932, etc. But now also to the secular writers.

<margin>The female bites the head off the male in lust.</margin>
We are informed that when the male goes with the female, having put his head into the mouth of the female, the female, in the heated urge of mating, bites off his head. I have found this cited to represent both an unchaste woman and the fruit of vile fleshly lust and the defilement of the flesh. *The reward of pleasure* <note>original: "Voluptatis præmium"</note>, says Florentius van Schoonhoven in his *Emblems*, page 142, and he adds these verses:

> *When the viper mates and lies drunk with the sweet motion of Venus,*
> *The insidious female cuts off the male.* <note>original: "Vipera, contruncat insidiosa marem"</note>
> *All love has this: at first it pours out its joys,*
> *But afterward it drives the heart of the enjoyer with stings.*

<margin>Representing the fruit and effect of fleshly and vile lust.</margin>
[*As the adder, caught up in the play of Venus,*
*Feels the long-desired pleasure of amorous lust,*
*She kills her mate through cunning, while she moves wantonly.*
*Thus love is accustomed to release its desire and joy,*
*But the heart only feels the sharpness of the stings after the enjoyment.*]

Pliny in the 10th book, chapter 62, and Horus Apollo, etc., confirm this:

<column-break/>

The foolishness and destructiveness of easily vanishing lust was also meaningfully presented by Boethius, Book 3, Poem 7:

> *Every pleasure has this:* <note>original: "Habet omnis hoc voluptas"</note>
> *It drives those who enjoy it with stings,*
> *And like a swarm of flying bees,*
> *When it has poured out its pleasing honey,*
> *It flees, and with a too-tenacious bite*
> *It strikes the wounded hearts.*

Which was translated by François van Hoogstraten thus:
> *This is the nature of lust,*
> *It constrains with stings, harsh and sour.*
> *Whoever enjoys her sweetness,*
> *And where she pours out honey, she departs*
> *And flees, like a swarm of bees,*
> *And leaves the taster in lamentation,*
> *In the parting, where she bites and stings,*
> *And breaks the heart through long pains.*

Remorse, along with pain, generally follows thoughtless and wanton joy and lust. Homer, *Odyssey*, Book T.

> *Joy and sorrow seized his heart at once.* <note>original: Τὼ δ' ἄμα χάρμα καὶ ἄλγος ἕλε Φρένα.</note>

[*He is accompanied in joy*
*By sorrow that torments him.*]

Plautus in *Amphitryon*:

> *It is so arranged in the life of men,*
> *It is so pleasing to the gods, that sorrow follows as a companion to pleasure.*

[*Thus it is ordained for all men*
*By the arrangement of the Gods, that pain accompanies lust.*]

Seldom are there roses without thorny pricks, sweet without sour, honey without gall. The honeybee also has its stinger.

<margin>A whore compared to an Adder.</margin>
A wicked woman, who is lustful, gasps for her husband's death and brings him to his end, says Adrianus Junius in his emblems.

> *When she rushes into love, the Viper [Echidna] flatters her husband,*
> *Soon, being satisfied, she cuts off the inserted head with her mouth.* <note>original: "Mox satura insertum præscidit ore caput"</note>
> *The wicked wife is stroked, burning with lust,*
> *Immediately, panting, she demands the death of the man.*

He who mingles and stays with a wicked whore will be finished off by her in one way or another.

> *Just as the bitten viper dies through excessive love.* <note>original: "Per venerem ut nimiam vipera morsa perit"</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Adder" (Viper), moving from the general description of the animal to its allegorical and prophetic significance in Scripture and church history. It focuses specifically on the prophecy of the nursing child in Isaiah 11 and how the viper represents the enemies of the faith—from ancient philosophers to modern heretics.</meta>

# ADDER.

<margin>A child over the Adder's den, etc.</margin>LIX. 8. *Prov. XXIII. 32. Jes. XIV. 29. Jer. VIII. 17.* One reads of a nursing child that would play over the hole of an adder, *Isaiah 11:8.* See in my *Sacred Miscellanies* <note>The author's own theological work, *Heilige Mengelstoffen*</note> on *Isaiah 11:8* for an opening regarding the Adder. What I have understood by children, infants, etc., can be seen in my first part of the *Sacred Miscellanies*, page 88 etc., and as for this passage, I have explained my opinion in the same book, page 108 etc. There I said that the literal text could allow for it to be translated as:
> a. A nursing child shall look with delight and desire toward the hole of an Adder.
> b. Or shall delight themselves because of the hole of an Adder.
> c. Or shall play over the hole of an Adder with cheerfulness, boldness, and without timidity or fear of being harmed.

The great Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian</note> in his elaborate Hebrew Lexicon, has <term>Pethen</term> <note>Hebrew: פתן, a venomous snake or asp</note> Adder-snakes: There it is given to understand that Satan shall be trodden under the feet of the church in such a way that it will be a delight for a child to mock the poisonous tyrants.

The venerable Nicolaus Gürtlerus <note>A Swiss-Dutch theologian (1654–1711) known for his work on biblical prophecy</note>, in his prophetic and exemplary Lexicon, page 96, seems to have understood this matter thus: *The witnesses of Christ, sucking the milk of the divine word from the breasts of the reformers, delight in the sight of the assembly of the Antichrist and its leaders residing in the monasteries; and those established in the truth (the weaned) shall, without danger of being lost, associate with the followers of the Antichrist.*

<margin>The Author's Explanation.</margin>For myself, if the thread and the timeframe of this prophecy can allow this explanation as the primary meaning, I shall not be against it.
I previously understood it in this way:
That by the Adder, one could aptly understand the devil, with his servants and those who belong to him.
By the nursing child, I represented Constantine the Great <note>The first Roman Emperor to convert to Christianity</note>, with the first tender Christians who came over from paganism, who were joyful because they saw the Adder’s den—the temples, chapels, and other places dedicated to his service, lies, and deceptive teaching—consecrated to the Lord’s service and teaching. See further my first *Miscellanies* page 113, etc.

If I may say so, it seems to me that afterward, while reading the elaborate work of Professor Campegius Vitringa <note>A famous 17th-century commentator on Isaiah</note> on Isaiah, I was somewhat strengthened in my judgment. This gentleman writes about it thus:
> *Regarding the secret meaning of this imagery, the thoughts of the learned differ quite a bit. Jerome and many who follow him think here of the possessed, who were to be set free from unclean spirits by Christ’s disciples, who would leap upon the devils in their dwellings, according to Luke 10:19 and Mark 16:17, 18.*
> *Others have simply understood the powerful ones by it, the princes of this world, whom the church formerly had great cause to dread; which is closer and simpler.*
> *Cyril <note>Likely Cyril of Alexandria</note> understood it as either the bands of unclean spirits, or the dens and hiding places of the heretics.*

By the hole of the Adder and the pit of the Basilisk, are given to understand in a secret sense the schools and lecture halls, in which the Orators and Philosophers, formerly sworn enemies of the Christian

<column-break/>

doctrine, true children of the devil and taught by this master of theirs, poured out their harmful and deadly teachings and instructions, dipped in sharp gall, with a flood and stream of flowing rhetoric, to suppress the Christian Religion and strongly praise the old pagan superstition.

*Who at the same time maliciously bit the pious practitioners of truth with poisonous bites of slanders, maliciously devised and gathered up. In such schools, nurseries, lecture halls—yes, even in the schools which were formerly holes and pits of serpents, into which almost no one dared to venture before without fear—now the disciples of Christ, the subjects of His kingdom, even the tender newly baptized and those enrolled in the baptismal register of the church, and those recently come to a firmer knowledge of the Christian Religion and doctrine, would move about without any fear, etc. One may look further into his Reverence’s work.*

Thus one already perceives of what the Adder with its poison is an emblem. This I could now apply to the Pharisees and Scribes, treading in Jesus' footsteps, clothing it with various reasons of comparison: yes, applying it to the evil and wicked generation, the brood of Satan, to those who did the works of Satan, *John 8:44* <note>The original cites "Jes. VIII. 44," likely a slip for John 8:44: "You are of your father the devil."</note> and imitated their evil ancestors, being even more cunning than they.

<margin>The Adder as an emblem of the Pharisees and scribes.</margin>> *Ætas parentum pejor avis:* The age of our parents is worse than our grandfathers. <note>A quote from Horace, Odes 3.6, suggesting moral decline over generations.</note>
> *Mali corvi malum ovum:* From a bad crow, a bad egg. <note>A proverb meaning a bad father produces a bad son.</note> *Matth. XI. and XIII. Act. V. and XXVIII. 26.*

<margin>Of the wicked heretics, who have the balsam of the word of grace.</margin>Furthermore, I see here an emblem of all very wicked heretics, who, although they consume the balsamic sap of the Word, nevertheless turn it into poison, yet they can be cured of their poison by nothing else. Just as he who has the balsam of the Word in his heart need fear no poisonous person or wicked heretic. As a good conscience wards off all poison from itself, so that one is not dried up and consumed by the fiery bite. To tread upon those types of poisonous animals, *Psalm 91:13*, is to trample and crush and subdue them as if without harm.

<margin>Against the Adder's bites an antidote: a good conscience, as the most excellent balsam.</margin>Although I have already touched upon some things, I still have quite a bit to bring in from non-sacred writers, which I thought good to add here upon re-reading. Namely, first, I shall present a scriptural observation from Baumannus in *Select.* page 931, where he compared the heretics to Adders: His Reverence presented it in this manner. *a.* One does not see the Adder's teeth; they lie covered and quite hidden. The heretics and hypocritical deceivers gloss over their teachings with the appearance of holiness, so that one might not notice their attempt to deceive.

<margin>The Pharisees and the Heretics: what regard Baumannus showed.</margin>*b.* The poison of the Adder is deadly. So also the opinion of the master-heretics is harmful to the soul and destructive. *2 Peter 2:2.*

<margin>Heretics compared to Adders.</margin>*c.* The Adder's sting and wound is incurable. The heretics wound unto death, because they change the truth into a lie, righteousness into unrighteousness, God’s grace into lewdness, and cause the right life to be exchanged for spiritual death.

*d.* The heretics are the cause of the death of the mother church. Just as the young of the Adders, in their hasty coming forth, pierce the belly of their mother, as is told—that is, they bring deadly pain to the mother church...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Adder" or Viper. While the previous page examined biblical prophecy, this page explores the viper as a symbol for internal enemies of the Church and the moral dangers of worldly pleasure, drawing on both religious and classical authors.</meta>

# ADDER.

<sig>G 3</sig>

...attacks the church, though it can never be uprooted or perish.

<margin>Beza in Emblem, page 126.</margin>
> Just as the viper's offspring gnaw through their mother's entrails,
> So is the church of the saints gnawed at, alas, too much by many
> Whom she herself fostered as nurslings in her own bosom,
> But not with the same outcome or reason.
> For the unhappy viper perishes while her offspring survives;
> She, on the contrary, remains, not destined to perish though they are extinguished.
<note>original Latin: "Viperei erodunt ceu matris viscera fœtus, / Sic quos ipsa suo fovit alumna sinu / Roditur, heu, nimium sanctorum ecclesia multis, / At non eventu nec ratione pari. / Vipera nam salva infelix prole interit illis. / Hæc contra exstinctis non peritura manet."</note>

<margin>Beza’s emblem.</margin>
[*The young of the adder bores through the mother’s entrails.*
*So the church, alas, is attacked by many,*
*Whom she had cherished in her soft lap*
*And protected in danger, saved from all need.*
*But the outcome is not the same: the young causes death*
*To the old; but the church endures the heaviest blow,*
*Stands firm, and never finds itself deprived of heaven's help.*]

<margin>The same shown from Gerhard.</margin>
Indeed, I find that the Pharisees and their brood—vile deceivers, liars, and slanderers—are compared by Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a Lutheran scholastic theologian, in his *Harmonia Evangelica*</note> in his *Harmony of the Gospels* to snakes, adders, and vipers. *Matthew 3:7 and 23:33.*
1. Because of their inclination to harm, and to kill and destroy the soul, *Numbers 21:6.* They travel through lands and cities to make others like themselves, and then they become children of hell.
2. The Pharisees are generally more cunning and trained to deceive and outwit, for they wear the cloak of hypocrisy and appear so simple that one would expect no evil from them, but would entrust them with everything. *Matthew 5, 15, and 23.*
3. They possess a poisonous and corrupting venom in their teaching. *Deuteronomy 32.*
4. They are prone to slander and sting with their tongues. *Psalm 40, Ecclesiastes 10.*
5. They stop their ears, *Psalm 58,* and give no place to admonitions, rebukes, or convincing reasons.
See this presented more broadly by Baumgarten in *Selecta*, pages 931, 932, etc. But now let us turn to the secular writers.

<margin>The female bites off the male's head during pleasure.</margin>
We are informed that when the male mates with the female, having placed his head in the female's mouth, the female, in the heated urge of the union, bites off his head. I have found that this has been cited both to describe an unchaste woman and to illustrate the fruit of vile, fleshly lust and the defilement of the flesh. "The reward of pleasure," says Florentius van Schoonhoven in *Emblems*, page 142, and he adds these verses:

<margin>Representing the fruit and effect of fleshly and vile lust.</margin>
> When the viper mates and lies drunk with the sweet motion of Venus,
> The treacherous female cuts off the male.
> All love has this: first it pours out its joys,
> But afterward, it drives the heart of the one enjoying it with stings.
<note>original Latin: "Cum coit & dulci veneris jacet ebria motu, / Vipera, contruncat insidiosa marem. / Hoc venus omnis habet, primo sua gaudia fundit, / Postmodo sed stimulis corda fruentis agit."</note>

[*When the adder, enraptured in the game of Venus,*
*Feels the long-desired delight of romantic lust,*
*She kills her mate through cunning while she wantonly tosses.*
*Thus love is accustomed to shoot its lust and joy,*
*But the heart only feels the sharpness of the stings after the enjoyment.*]

Pliny in the 10th book, chapter 62, and Horapollo <note>An author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs, often cited in emblem books</note>, etc., confirm such things:

<column-break/>

The foolishness and destructiveness of fleeting pleasure was also ingeniously presented by Boethius <note>The Roman philosopher (c. 477–524 AD)</note> in Book 3, Meter 7:

> All pleasure has this:
> It drives those enjoying it with stings,
> And like a swarm of flying bees,
> When it has poured out its pleasant honey,
> It flees, and with a too-persistent
> Bite, it strikes the wounded hearts.
<note>original Latin: "Habet omnis hoc voluptas, / Stimulis agit fruentes, / Apiumque par volantum, / Ubi grata mella fudit, / Fugit, & nimis tenaci / Ferit icta corda morsu."</note>

Which was translated by François van Hoogstraten thus:
> *This is the nature of pleasure,*
> *It constrains with stings, harsh and sour.*
> *Whoever enjoys her sweetness,*
> *And wherever she pours out honey, she flees*
> *And escapes, like a swarm of bees,*
> *And leaves the taster in lamentation,*
> *In the parting, where she bites and stings,*
> *And breaks the heart through long pains.*

Regret, along with pain, usually follows thoughtless and wanton merriment and pleasure. Homer, *Odyssey*, Book T <note>Book 19</note>:

> Joy and grief seized her heart at the same time.
<note>original Greek: "Τὼ δ' ἄμα χάρμα καὶ ἄλγος ἕλε Φρέna." The Latin follows: "Lætitia huic mœrorque simul præcordia cepit."</note>

[*He is accompanied in joy*
*By sorrow that torments him.*]

Plautus in *Amphitruo*:

> It is so arranged in the life of men,
> So it pleased the gods, that sorrow follows pleasure as a companion.
<note>original Latin: "Ita comparatum est in ætate hominum / Ita diis placitum, voluptati ut mœror comes consequatur."</note>

[*Thus it is arranged for all people*
*By the decree of the Gods, that pain accompanies pleasure.*]

Seldom are there roses without thorny pricks, sweet without sour, honey without gall. The honeybee also has its stinger.

<margin>A harlot compared to an Adder.</margin>
A wicked woman who is lustful longs for her husband's death and brings him to his end, says Hadrianus Junius <note>A Dutch physician and humanist (1511–1575)</note> in his emblems.

> When she rushes into love, the Viper flatters her husband,
> Soon, satisfied, she cuts off the inserted head with her mouth.
> The wicked wife, glowing with lust, strokes him.
> Panting, she immediately demands the death of the man.
<note>original Latin: "Cum ruit in venerem, blanditur Echidna marito, / Mox satura insertum præscidit ore caput. / Improba palpatur, tentigine fervida conjux. / Continuo letum poscit anhela viri."</note>

[*When the adder is enraptured by the urge to mate,*
*She does not rest until she has moved her mate to it:*
*But when she is satisfied with playing, then she robs*
*The male, whom she had flattered, of his head.*
*So is a vile woman driven by lust,*
*Who, when she is satisfied, seeks the life of the man.*]

He who mingles and stays with a vile harlot will be finished off by her in one way or another.

Joachimus Camerarius speaks of unchaste love in his emblems and applies these verses to it:

> Thus may anyone perish who shamefully clings to a harlot,
> Just as the bitten viper perishes through excessive love.
<note>original Latin: "Sic pereat quisquis meretrici turpiter hæret, / Per venerem ut nimiam vipera morsa perit."</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Adder" or Viper. Following the previous page's focus on the viper as a symbol for internal enemies of the Church, this page shifts to moral allegories regarding lust, divine retribution, and the virtue of temperance.</meta>

# A D D E R.

[*He who follows, loves, and flatters harlots deserves to perish,*
*Just as an adder loses its life in the midst of its pleasure.*]

Harlots drain their lovers dry or infect them with something that causes them to waste away; indeed, once they are tired of them, they may even bring about their end. See also the *Emblems of Altdorf* <note>Referring to the *Emblemata Anniversaria Academiae Altorfinae* (1597), a collection of emblems from the University of Altdorf.</note> on page 28, a medal depicting two adders, with the inscription around the rim: WICKED VENUS IS THE DESTRUCTION OF THE MIND <note>original Latin: *MENTIS VENUS IMPROBA CLADES*</note>: that is:

->*Unchaste and wanton love*<-
->*Corrupts the virtuous mind.*<-

Furthermore, because the mother adder bites off the head of the male in the heat of mating, <margin>A symbol of how evil is rewarded with evil.</margin> she is also punished by her own young; being many in number and each trying to get out before the other, they pierce through her belly. This is presented as an emblem of righteous punishment. *Just punishment* <note>original Latin: *Justa ultio*</note>, says Schoonhoven <note>Florentius Schoonhoven (1594–1648), a Dutch poet and emblem writer.</note>, and he presents the matter thus:

> *The viper, who during mating had previously killed her husband,*
> *Suffers this same punishment from her offspring;*
> *Though slow Nemesis <note>The Greek goddess of divine retribution.</note> seems to delay the penalty,*
> *Yet from behind she shakes her harsh whips.*
<note>original Latin: "Vipera, quae coiens occiderat ante maritum, / A sobole hoc iisdem supplicium patitur; / Tarda licet Nemesis poenam differre videtur, / Attamen à tergo dura flagella quatit."</note>

[*The poisonous adder, who had caused her mate to die,*
*Must receive the same punishment from her young.*
*Though strict vengeance seems to delay the sentence,*
*She soon overtakes the sinner with whips as her prey.*]

Every deed meets its reward <note>original Dutch idiom: "Boontje krygt zyn loontje," literally "The little bean gets its little reward."</note>: the gods eventually take their fill of disgust and punish evil in its time; the evildoer rarely escapes entirely unpunished. As Horace says:

> *Rarely has punishment, though she has a limping foot,*
> *Failed to catch the wicked man who flees before her.*
<note>original Latin: "Raro antecedentem scelestum / Deseruit pede poena claudo." From Horace's *Odes*, III.2.</note>

[*Punishment, however limpingly she walks,*
*Does not abandon the rogues who have gone before her.*]

Both old and young suffer, and the old receive what they previously dared to do; thus, in doing evil, one receives his portion and punishment. Joachim Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a German physician and botanist famous for his emblem books.</note>, *Emblems* century 4, page 182: *Everyone is weighed down by their own example.* <note>original Latin: *Suo quisque premitur exempla.*</note>

> *Behold, how the viper pushes out its young through a ruptured womb;*
> *She took away the father, and her offspring took her away.*
<note>original Latin: "Ecce, ut rupta alvo protrudat vipera gnatos, / Sustulit illa patrem, sustulit hanc soboles."</note>

[*See how the young adder forcefully pierces the belly*
*Of the mother: she who had first murdered her own mate.*
*Now she suffers this punishment from her own young.*]

As the old led the way, so the young follow: <margin>A symbol of hereditary evil, and that like produces like.</margin> as the egg is, so is the chick; *a bad egg, bad chicks* <note>original Latin: *malum ovum, mali pulli*</note>. Worthy of evil seeds are the harvests <note>original Greek: τῶν πονηρῶν σπερμάτων ἄξια τὰ γεωργία</note>; evil seeds, evil fruits; as the tree is, so are the fruits, says Nicephorus Gregoras. In the works of Theophylactus Simocatta, Proclus writes to Archimedes: "You shall have children who are true images and likenesses of paternal vice; for so the offspring of the viper inherit maternal impiety, tearing open the womb that carried and nourished them." <note>original Greek: καὶ παῖδας ἔχεις παθικῆς κακίας εἰκόνας ἀληθῶς καὶ ἰνδάλματα, οὕτω γὰρ καὶ τὰ τῆς ἐχίδνης κυήματα μητρικὴν ἀνοσιότητά δωαδέχεται. τὴν κυοφόρον καὶ τίθηνυν γαστέρα διαῤῥηγνύονται.</note> You shall have a true and expressed image of the father's defects in the children. Thus the young adders imitate the godlessness of their mother, while they tear open the belly that carried and fed them.

<column-break/>

The saliva of a fasting human overcomes the <margin>The saliva of a fasting human is good against snakes.</margin> adder; which I find interpreted as an emblem of the sobriety of moderation, which restrains and subdues fleshly desires. Schoonhoven says on page 168, *lust is overcome by sobriety* <note>original Latin: *sobrietate superatur venus*</note>; and gives us this epigram:

> *The viper, sprinkled with the fasting saliva of men,*
> *Expires, if the physicians are to be believed:*
> *So the lustful flesh, if you treat it more harshly,*
> *Collapses, and will bow its neck under the yoke of the mind.*
<note>original Latin: "Vipera jejunis hominum consparsa salivis / Exspirat, medicis si fit habenda fides: / Sic lasciva caro, si tractes durius illam, / Concidit, & mentis sub juga colla dabit."</note>

[*By the fasting saliva of a human shall the adder die,* <margin>A symbol of abstinence and sobriety.</margin>
*If the physicians can gain any of our belief.*
*So it is with the flesh: if you attack it somewhat severely,*
*It will yield and the mind will stand ready to serve.*]

Witnesses to this are Pliny, Galen, Alexander of Aphrodisias, Pierius, and Lucretius in book 4 of *On the Nature of Things*:

> *It is certainly true that a serpent, touched by human saliva,*
> *Perishes, and consumes itself by biting.*
<note>original Latin: "Est utique ut serpens hominis contacta salivis / Disperit, ac sese mandendo conficit ipsa."</note>

[*A snake smeared with the saliva of a fasting human*
*Will die: indeed, it often bites itself to death.*]

The flesh and its impulses must be subdued—Colossians 3, Galatians 5, 1 Corinthians 9—or they will play the master and no longer listen to the bit and bridle of reason. Prudentius <note>Aurelius Prudentius Clemens (c. 348 – c. 413), a Roman Christian poet.</note> says:

> *Hearts unburdened by sparse diets*
> *Better receive the indwelling God.*
<note>original Latin: "Parcis victibus impedita corda / Infusum melius Deum receptant."</note>

[*A heart strengthened by sobriety*
*Is best prepared to receive God.*]

Moderation ensures a lasting state and condition. Intemperance, in whatever form it may be, is always harmful and dangerous. See the *Altdorf Emblems*, page 11. Joachim Camerarius, century 4, page 172, agrees with this in his *work of sobriety* <note>original Latin: *sobrietatis opus*</note>:

> *The snake dies when touched by human saliva:*
> *Alas for me, how great is the work of sobriety!*
<note>original Latin: "Emoritur serpens hominis contacta saliva: / Hei mihi quam magnum sobrietatis opus!"</note>

[*No snake can resist the saliva prepared for it.*
*O how full of power is the work of sobriety!*]

This moderation, called *sophrosyne* <note>original Greek: σωφροσύνη</note>, signifies <margin>This sobriety and moderation further presented.</margin> as much as "preserving the mind" <note>original Greek: σώζουσα τὴν φρόνησιν</note>, or keeping the understanding whole and healthy. Plato says of it that it is "the ornament and the restraint of certain pleasures and desires." <note>original Greek: κόσμος καὶ ἡδονῶν τινων καὶ ἐπιθυμιῶν ἐγκράτεια</note>. Xenophanes, in his letter to Lamprocles, says: "No evil grows in a man who has laid moderation and abstinence as the foundations of wisdom." <note>original Greek: κακὸν οὐδὲν φύεται ἐν ἀνδρὶ, θεμέλια θεμένω σοφίας, σωφροσύνη καὶ ἐγκράτειαν</note>.

And so Macarius <note>Likely Macarius of Egypt (c. 300–391), a Coptic Christian monk and hermit.</note> spoke very aptly regarding this emblem in Homily 16: "Therefore one must use moderation in all things, so that the goods which we seem to have may not be turned to our destruction." See also Johann Heinrich Ursinus in *Analecta*, part 1, page 249.

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion of the "Adder" or Viper (symbolizing internal enemies and moral corruption) to a new alphabetical entry: "Adel" or Nobility.
