# NOBILITY.

### NOBILITY, NOBLE STATUS, THE NOBLES;
-><note>original Hebrew: "Bnei Tuhma / Bnei Horin / Horin"</note> Children of a pure line / Children of freedom / Nobles; <note>original Greek: "eugeneis, endoxoi, episēmoi"</note> Well-born, renowned, distinguished; <note>original Latin: "nobiles, nobilitas"</note> nobles, nobility.<-

<margin>Nobility.</margin>
**N**OBILITY, NOBLE STATUS, NOBLES, is a designation of high, distinguished birth, deeds, virtues, sometimes riches, and esteem, and authority.

<margin>Roman Nobles.</margin>
Among the Romans, those were noble or aristocratic persons who had the power and right to set up statues, and who excelled above others, and who possessed the statues of their ancestors; not statues of wax to the size of the whole body, but from the shoulders upward. See Martinus’s *Etymological Lexicon* <note>Matthias Martinius (1572–1630), a German theologian and philologist.</note> and Goodwin’s *Roman Antiquities*.

<margin>New Nobles.</margin>
New Nobles <note>term: *Novi homines* | "New men" who were the first in their family to achieve high office.</note> were those who only had their own statues and not those of their ancestors, and therefore, although not from great elders, were nonetheless highly distinguished through their own deeds, virtues, and honorary offices, and were of the first nobility in their lineages. Among the Romans, these were the *Patricians, Curule Aediles, Praetors, Censors, Consuls:* though it is testified that not all of those had statues.

<margin>Statues of the ancestors.</margin>
People were wonderfully pleased with these statues; they placed them on their estates, lands, and in the gates of their houses: they adorned them with swords, shields, helmets, ship-beaks <note>The *rostra*, or prows of captured enemy ships, used as trophies.</note>, and everything that had been triumphantly seized from the enemy. The deeds were pressed into wax with letters, so that the observer could read them, and the descendants of the lineage would imitate them. Scipio, in Sallust’s *Jugurtha*: *quod si majorum suorum imagines contemplarentur, animos suos vehementer ad virtutem accendi sentirent.* That is: *If they would view the images of their ancestors, they would feel their hearts powerfully ignited to the pursuit of virtue.* See Kipping’s *Roman Antiquities*.

<margin>Athenian Nobles.</margin>
Among the Athenians, there were noble lineages and persons who were called <note>original Greek: "Eupatridai"</note> *Eupatridae* <note>Meaning "those of good fathers" or "well-born."</note>, who were descended from those ancient heroes whose names, eulogies, and deeds are to be found in the recognized writings: such as the *Praxiergidae, Etuobatadae, Alcmeonidae, Cynidae, Ceryces, etc.*

<margin>Helmets.</margin>
He who had acquitted himself laudably through acts of war in long-lasting conflicts received a closed helmet; he who, springing from this trunk, followed in the same footsteps, confirmed his nobility and wore an open helmet. See Paschalius. <note>Carlo Pasquale (1547–1625), author of *Coronæ*, a work on crowns and heraldry.</note>

From of old, those who could trace their descent from the Trojans were held to be of great nobility. See Servius’s commentary on the fifth book of Virgil's *Aeneid*.

Chrysostom, in his 4th Oration, relates that there was a *Spartan* family which, from of old and as if by nature, had a branded lance upon the body; and if anyone who claimed to be sprung from that house lacked that mark, he was rejected as illegitimate and a bastard.

Mention is made of a Nobleman's ring. See Livy, books 23 and 26; Kirchmann, chapter 16; Rubens, *On Clothing* <note>original Latin: "de re vestiaria"</note>, book 1, chapter 8; Goodwin, page 300, etc.

The Egyptians, as well as the Jews, all claim nobility for themselves.

<margin>Nobility of the Jews.</margin>
Of the Jews, one reads in *Bava Kama* <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with civil matters and damages.</note>, chapter 8. Rabbi Akiba says:
> <note>original Hebrew: "Afilu aniyim shebe-Yisrael ro'im otam k'ilu hem bnei horin"</note>

*Even the poor in Israel are regarded as Nobles, since they are children of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.*

<column-break/>

Among the Jews, one was considered to be of noble lineage if one was from a Royal or Priestly family.

The famous Jewish historian Flavius Josephus recorded this regarding his own descent in the description of his life, writing: *I am then from no obscure or low lineage, but one that is from the rank of Priests through a long successive sequence: and certainly, just as other peoples value other reasons for nobility, so among us the right to possess sacred things is proof of a distinguished descent.* But I am not only from the lineage of the Priests, but also from the first rank of the twenty-four orders established by David, between which there is no small distinction. Indeed, as far as my maternal descent is concerned, I belong to the lineage of Kings.

<margin>Nobility of Josephus.</margin>

<margin>Degrees of Nobility among the Jews.</margin>
Among the Jews, the degrees of nobility were higher and lower. To belong to David’s royal house and lineage was the highest nobility. Next to this was the lineage of the Hasmoneans, having held the supreme command in both church and state. Next to this was the lineage of the Priests, who were again valued according to their rank and order of service with their privileges.

No one was chosen for the great assemblies except nobles; for it was held: that God did not dwell except among the noble; which is explained as *strong, rich, wise men.* One may consult Maimonides's treatise *On the Sanhedrin*, chapter 11; Selden, *On the Succession of the High Priests*, book II, chapter 11; Abarbanel on Daniel; Vitringa, *Sacred Observations*, part 2, page 24, etc.

I would almost think that the most excellent nobility of emperors, kings, princes, dukes, counts, barons, etc., was derived from this in former times; however, not all can climb so high or trace their descent from there, especially in countries where one is not accustomed to having such heads.

As for what else pertains to the nobility of kings, princes, and lords, natural <note>gloss: illegitimate</note> sons and "play-children" <note>term: "speelkinderen" | An old Dutch term for children born out of wedlock.</note>, the distinctions in their coats of arms, the quarterings, primary and lesser nobility, and such things, I shall not dwell upon them.

<margin>Nobility of Jesus.</margin>
I observe in our Savior Jesus—howsoever lowly He may seem according to the outward state of this life (*Isaiah 53, Zechariah 9, Philippians 2*)—that He was of the very greatest Nobility among the Jews, being sprung from David’s house and lineage (*Matthew 1, Luke 3*); yes, higher than David, who called Him his Lord (*Psalm 110:1*), whose birth and descent is from heaven, by the Holy Spirit, from a virgin mother, who distinguished Himself and made Himself famous above all nobility through inward and outward virtues and heroic deeds, having obtained a name above all names, exalted above all Kings and Lords. (*Philippians 2, Revelation 17 and 19*).

All believers chosen in Christ are, in, through, and with Him, made into children, sons, daughters, priests, kings, heirs of God, and co-heirs of Christ, born of God (*John 1, Ephesians 3, Galatians 3 and 4, Revelation 1*), etc.

God has stamped His image upon them (*Colossians 3, Ephesians 4, Romans 8*).

And even if it is so that they are lowly and despised according to the world—the world knows them not, and God’s gracious choice is no respecter of persons (*1 Corinthians 1:26*)—nevertheless, in Holy Scripture, something is called noble that is precious, excellent, very desirable and costly, a distinction (*Job 30:15, Proverbs 26:8, Song of Solomon 4:13-16 and 7:13*), etc.

The tokens of their nobility are having wrestled free from the servitude of sin, serving God in righteousness...

# NOBILITY.

### [Continued]

to serve in holiness and truth <note>original: "righteousness and truth"</note> *Luke 1:74, 75; Romans 6; John 8* and not to let oneself be brought under any human yoke, but to stand fast in Christian freedom *Galatians 5*. They possess a ring of dignity, of freedom, of the pledge, and the seal of the Holy Spirit as a guarantee of the spiritual marriage. See d’Outrein's *Parables of the Prodigal Son* <note>Johannes d'Outrein (1662–1722) was a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian.</note>.

Certainly, the best nobility is not being a slave to sin, but rather to be well-known for all kinds of virtues, as Jerome says to Celantia, and Chrysostom in his commentary on Matthew.

<margin>Virtue is the best nobility.</margin> Caussinus <note>Nicolas Caussin (1583–1651), a Jesuit writer known for "The Holy Court."</note> understood it well when he said: *The Nobility must apply themselves to virtue; for if they possess nothing other than the virtues of their ancestors, they are like the Jackdaw, a target for mockery and scorn when its borrowed feathers are plucked away. And, he continues: Virtue makes a person noble, and not a vestibule or an entire room filled with the statues of illustrious ancestors; one must rely on virtue, and not solely on one's blood.*

<margin>Example of Lycurgus.</margin> Lycurgus, the lawgiver of the Spartans, taught his people through the example of two dogs born of one and the same mother. One dog was foul and base, while the other was noble-natured. He showed what training and upbringing could achieve; "You see, O Spartans," he said, "that the lineage of Hercules, from which you boast to be descended, cannot help you unless you add the pursuit of your own virtue to the praise of your ancestors."

And in this, he says no more than what the Heathens have taught and said through the light of reason, education, and experience.

->Juvenal in his 8th Satire:<-

> *Though ancient waxen masks decorate your halls on every side, virtue is the one and only nobility.*
> <note>original Latin: "Tota licet veteres exornent undique cerae / Atria, nobilitas sola est atque unica virtus."</note>

Which the Knight Jacob Westerbaan <note>Jacob Westerbaan (1588–1670) was a Dutch physician and poet who translated classical works into the Dutch vernacular.</note> has rendered thus:

> *Though your whole house hung full of ancient paintings,*
> *Though your great hall were adorned with many rows*
> *Of statues made of metal, wax, or marble stone,*
> *Yet virtue alone is what creates Nobility.*

->Ovid, Book 1 of *Letters from the Black Sea*:<-

> *If neither wealth nor the famous name of ancestors, but integrity and talent make one great.*
> <note>original Latin: "Si modo non census, nec clarum nomen avorum: / Sed probitas magnos, ingeniumque facit."</note>

[*So neither money nor the praise that touches our ancestors,*
*But godliness and wit alone make one exalted.*]

->Virgil in the 6th book of the *Aeneid*:<-

> — — — *But to extend one's fame by deeds, this is the work of virtue.*
> <note>original Latin: "Sed famam extendere factis / Hoc virtutis opus."</note>

[*To keep one's martial fame un-withered,*
*And spread it far and wide through brave deeds,*
*Is the task of noble virtue alone.*]

<margin>Memorable saying of Alfonso, King of Aragon.</margin> Alfonso, King of Aragon <note>Alfonso V (1396–1458), known as "the Magnanimous," King of Aragon, Sicily, and Naples.</note>, hearing himself praised by someone for being a King, the son of a King, the grandson of a King, and the brother of a King, let it be known that he held what the praiser so highly exalted in very low esteem. For that praise belonged not to him, but to his ancestors, who through justice, moderation, and the excellence of their other virtues had acquired the kingdom for themselves; the descendant deserved no praise for this, unless he held the possession through virtue rather than mere inheritance.

The goodness and nobility of one's relatives is of no use if one is personally deprived of virtue, says Chrysostom in his 5th Homily on Matthew.

And to this end all the sayings of the ancient Poets agree, as I shall show with these examples.

<column-break/>

->Lucan in his Panegyric to Calpurnius Piso:<-

> *For what help are halls propped up by images or ancestral triumphs? What use is a record-book full of many consuls? To him whose life falters, all honor of the race is lost; his only praise is in his origin.*
> <note>original Latin: "Nam quid imaginibus, quid avitis fulta triumphis / Atria, quid pleni numeroso consule fasti, / Profuerint? cui vita labat perit omnis in illo / Gentis honos, cujus laus est in origine sola."</note>

[*What help is it to go parading with images,*
*That show off under the vaults of wide halls,*
*And that one knows many mayors <note>term: "burgermeesters" | used here to translate "consuls," the highest elected officials in Rome.</note> in his lineage,*
*And heroes shining through triumphs without end?*
*All this glittering honor and luster is lost,*
*If your fame is born only from your lineage.*]

->Ausonius in the *Sayings of Solon*:<-

> *It is much more beautiful to become noble through effort than to be born noble.*
> <note>original Latin: "Pulchrius multò parari, quam creari nobilem."</note>

[*It is much better to ennoble oneself through virtue*
*Than through birth.*]

Certainly, what use is that which belongs to another, if one does not make oneself worthy of it and possess it oneself? Therefore Ovid rightly says:

> *For lineage and ancestors, and those things we did not do ourselves, I scarcely call our own.*
> <note>original Latin: "Nam genus & proavos, & quae non fecimus ipsi, / Vix ea nostra voco."</note>

[*For lineage, ancestors, and all that we in fact*
*Did not perform ourselves, I hardly call—with reason—*
*Our own.*]

->Seneca in *Hercules Furens*:<-

> — — — *He who boasts of his lineage praises what belongs to another.*
> <note>original Latin: "Qui genus jactat suum: / Aliena laudat."</note>

[*He who boasts of his race, praises that which is someone else's.*]

->Juvenal in his 8th Satire:<-

> *But I would not wish you, Ponticus, to be valued for the praise of your kin if you yourself do nothing for future praise; it is a wretched thing to lean on the fame of others.*
> <note>original Latin: "Sed te censeri laude tuorum / Pontice noluerim, si tu nihil ipse futurae / Laudis agas: miserum est, aliorum incumbere famae."</note>

Which the ingenious Mr. Jacob Westerbaan translates into Dutch as follows:

> *But I, Master Nobleman (to return to you again),*
> *Would gladly clear the misunderstanding from your thoughts,*
> *That you—because of your lineage (unless you saw it*
> *Most gloriously completed through your own virtues)—*
> *Should want to be esteemed alone, and stand upon the deeds*
> *Of your ancestors. He is not well-advised,*
> *Who wishes to build his own honor upon that of another.*

I am wonderfully pleased by the saying of the excellent orator Cicero in his Oration against Sallust: *When his non-noble lineage was thrown in his face, he said: "It is enough for me; I would rather flourish through my own deeds than enjoy the imagination of my lineage, and live in such a way that I am the beginning of Nobility and an example of virtue for my descendants."* Excellent indeed!

<margin>Nobility lies in good character.</margin>When Democritus was asked what nobility consisted of, he gave this answer: *The nobility of beasts or of cattle lies in a good, firm body; but that of men lies in the proper disposition of their character.*

### BREATH, <note>original Greek: πνοὴ, pnoe</note>, <note>original Hebrew: רוּחַ / נְשָׁמָה, Ruach / Neshamah</note>, *Breath* <note>original Latin: Halitus</note>.

BREATH, or BREATHING, is a continuous alternation of inhaling and exhaling the surrounding air, by means of the lungs and the windpipes, through the constant expansion and contraction of the chest.

*Breath* and *breathing* constitute the animal life <note>The "animal life" refers to the biological life of the "anima" or soul that animates a body, shared by humans and animals alike.</note>, and breathing is a sign of that life, upon which the circulation of the blood and the internal flow of vital fluids largely depends; it is common to both humans and beasts. When the breath is stifled or ceases, the animal life in the body also stops. Regarding this, one may consult Descartes, Regius, and others <note>René Descartes and Henricus Regius were influential 17th-century thinkers who wrote extensively on the mechanical nature of the body and circulation.</note>.

<margin>To what breath belongs.</margin> *Breath*, and *breathing*, or *taking breath* belongs properly to that which is embodied and possesses an animal life; and although the root words in God's word do not always and everywhere signify the same thing, I shall nevertheless first apply it to man and, following the Scriptural passages, show with what distinction it is used.

<margin>Common breath.</margin> In the first place, Genesis 2:7 comes to mind: *And the Lord God had formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. Thus man became a living soul.*

<margin>Genesis 2:7 explained.</margin> *God breathed into his nostrils a breath of life:* God awakened in Adam a beginning of animal life, which caused this blowing of breath in him. I admit, it is also applied to irrational and breathing animals in general in Genesis 7:15-22; and although Moses speaks here of the man Adam, and might seem to stop at the animal level, I can very well accept what Burman <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> and others have noted; namely: *That the action of God, by which He made man breathe, is called an "insufflation" or "in-breathing," just as if He had breathed the breath and life—indeed, the rational soul itself—into man through a lovely breeze or a whistling sound. This breathing was a sign of the quickening of man. So that with this breathing God created the soul, as He breathed it into man, not outside the body, but within it; whereby man became a living soul, that is, a living person; not a dead image, as he was before, but living, moving, and speaking.* This is why the Chaldean Translator <note>Referring to the Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translates these words as *a speaking spirit*, since the rational soul shows itself first of all in speech, which is therefore unique to man. For man has specifically three advantages and ornaments above all animals. *First, the intellect*, through which he can find and devise everything necessary for him. *Then speech*, to express his thoughts and to interact with other men. *Finally, the hands*, through which he can put into action everything the intellect commands to be made, just as he carries out everything especially through his hands and rules over the beasts.

<margin>Observation of some scholars.</margin> I say then, that Adam received at once that which makes him a man and a rational creature: intellect, judgment, will, passions, and an immaterial and immortal, thinking, judging, and willing spirit, with free power and inclination.

<column-break/>

<margin>Genesis 7:15-22 explained.</margin> In Genesis 7:15-22, I read of the animals that entered the ark, and furthermore of the rest of all that lives and draws breath and was outside the ark, which was suffocated by the waters of the Deluge; this must be applied not only to men, but also to irrational creatures.

<margin>Job 15:30 explained, applied partly to God and partly to the wicked.</margin> Job 15:30: *He shall not depart out of darkness; the flame shall dry up his branches, and by the breath of his mouth shall he go away.*
One can well notice from all the circumstances that this speaks of one who intends no good toward God, nor men, nor toward what is right and virtuous, but who is godless and unpious; his misfortune and punishment are described, saying that he shall fall, not rise again, but be rooted out and perish. However, there seems to be some ground for doubt here as to whom one should best apply the phrase *by the breath of his mouth*: for some have taken it for the mouth of God, others for the mouth of the wicked. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (Solomon van Isaac), the famous medieval Jewish commentator.</note> takes it as: *by, or because of the breath, the blowing of his mouth, through which he has spoken rebellion.* Mercerus <note>Jean Mercier, a 16th-century French Hebraist.</note> seems to have held with this. Others prefer that by the mouth, one understands the mouth of the Lord; for the flame also comes from the Lord, which causes the young tree-shoots or the lot to wither and dry up; and that the shoot of the wicked, which bulges like a tree-sprout from the mouth or opening of the earth, shall be so taken away and perish by the wind of Divine judgment, that the tree of the wicked with its sprouts shall wither, turn to dust, and blow away. See Coccejus, Sebastian Schmidt <note>Johannes Coccejus and Sebastian Schmidt were prominent 17th-century biblical commentators.</note>.

<margin>Job 27:3 explained.</margin> *As long as my breath is in me, and the breath of God is in my nostrils. Job 27:3.*
It is indeed true that everything that possesses life and breath is subject to mortality and corruption. However, I do not believe that such was meant here by this manner of speaking and expression, as if to depict the inner meaning of the earnest speaker and witness.
It is clear from the second verse that Job is making a kind of oath and a strong declaration: that even though the Lord might have dealt with him so harshly and severely, he would nevertheless guard himself very closely, as long as he had life and could speak, so as not to transgress against God, justice, or propriety. See Piscator, Mercerus, Coccejus, Sebastian Schmidt, etc.

<margin>Psalm 150:6 explained.</margin> *Psalm 150:6. Let everything that has breath praise the Lord. Hallelujah. Every <note>original Hebrew: נְשָׁמָה, neshama</note>, soul, every breath.* Although many creatures can be said to praise God in their own way, man, gifted with intellect, judgment, will, tongue, and mouth, is best suited for it. Everything that has breath and draws breath—all rational men, into whose nostrils a breath of life was breathed by God, from Jews and Heathens, who can learn of the Lord's virtues and works from the light of their conscience, the observation of the world's stage, from God's wise and almighty government, and primarily from the divine Scriptures—and can hereby be ignited to the knowledge of the Lord and the glory of His great name.
To which end one needs not only breath for utterance, but also a heavenly spirit, a soul-inspiring and quickening breath of the Almighty.

<margin>Isaiah 2:22 explained.</margin> *Isaiah 2:22. Cease you (then) from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for wherein is he to be esteemed?*

*If your fame is born only from your lineage.*]

Ausonius in *Sayings of Solon*: <note>Ausonius was a 4th-century Roman poet and teacher.</note>

> *It is much more beautiful to become noble than to be born noble.* <note>original Latin: "Pulchrius multò parari, quam creari nobilem."</note>

[*It is far better to ennoble oneself through virtue*
*Than through birth.*]

Certainly, what does one gain from that which belongs to another, if one does not make oneself worthy of it, and possess it oneself? Thus Ovid says rightly:

> *For race and ancestors, and those things which we ourselves have not done,* <note>original Latin: "Nam genus & proavos, & quae non fecimus ipsi,"</note>
> *I scarcely call our own.* <note>original Latin: "Vix ea nostra voco."</note>

[*For lineage, ancestors, and all that we indeed*
*Did not do ourselves, I hardly call that which exists*
*In reality, our own.*]

Seneca in *Mad Hercules*: <note>Seneca the Younger, Roman Stoic philosopher and playwright.</note>

> ——— *He who boasts of his lineage:* <note>original Latin: "Qui genus jactat suum:"</note>
> *Praises what belongs to another.* <note>original Latin: "Aliena laudat."</note>

[*He who boasts of his family, praises what is someone else's.*]

Juvenal in his 8th Satire:

> — *But I would not wish you, Ponticus, to be valued for the praise of your kin,* <note>original Latin: "Sed te censeri laude tuorum Pontice noluerim"</note>
> *If you yourself do nothing worthy of future praise:* <note>original Latin: "si tu nihil ipse futura Laudis agas:"</note>
> *It is a wretched thing to lean on the fame of others.* <note>original Latin: "miserum est, aliorum incumbere famae."</note>

Which the ingenious Mr. Jacob Westerbaan thus translates into Dutch:

> *But I, Lord Noble-born (to return to you again)*
> *Would gladly keep the misunderstanding from your thoughts,*
> *That you, for your lineage (so that you yourself never*
> *Saw it most gloriously completed through your own virtues)*
> *Would wish only to be esteemed, and stand upon the deeds*
> *Of your ancestors. He is not well advised,*
> *Who wishes to build his own honor upon that of another.*

I am wonderfully pleased by the saying of the excellent orator Cicero in his Oration against Sallust <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero was Rome's greatest orator; this refers to the "Invective against Sallust" often attributed to him.</note>: *When he was reproached for his non-noble family tree, he said: "It is enough for me; I would rather flourish through my own deeds than enjoy the imagination of my lineage, and live in such a way that I am the beginning of Nobility and an example of virtue to my descendants."* Excellent indeed!

->B R E A T H.<-
H

<margin><note>original: "Adel gelegen in goede zeden."</note> Nobility lies in good character.</margin>When Democritus was asked what nobility consisted of, he gave this answer: *The nobility of beasts or cattle lies in a good, firm body; but that of humans lies in the suitability of their character.*

### BREATH, <note>original Hebrew: נשמה / רוח (*neshamah / ruach*); Greek: πνοὴ (*pnoe*); Latin: *Halitus*</note>

BREATH, or BREATHING, is a continuous alternation of inhaling and exhaling the surrounding air, by means of the lungs and the bronchial tubes, through the constant expansion and contraction of the chest.

*Breath* and *breathing* constitute animal life, and the act of blowing is a sign of animal life, upon which the circulation of the blood, as well as the internal flow of vital fluids, depends in no small measure; this is common to both humans and beasts. When the breath is stifled or ceases, so too does animal life in the body cease. On this subject, one may consult Descartes, Regius, and others. <note>René Descartes (1596–1650) and Henricus Regius (1598–1679) were influential philosophers and physicians who wrote extensively on the mechanical nature of the body and circulation.</note>

<margin>To what breath pertains.</margin>Breath, and breathing, or the drawing of breath, properly pertains to that which is embodied and possesses animal life. Although the root words in God's Word do not always and everywhere signify the same thing, I shall nevertheless first apply it to man and, following the Scriptural passages, show with what distinctions it is used.

<margin>Breath applied to man.</margin>In the first place, Genesis 2:7 occurs to me: *And the Lord God had formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. Thus man became a living soul.*

<margin>Genesis 2:7 explained.</margin><note>The author uses "geopent" (opened) to mean a scriptural passage is being analyzed or "unpacked" for the reader.</note> *God breathed into his nostrils a breath of life:* God awakened in Adam a principle of animal life, which caused this blowing of breath in him. I admit, it is also applied to irrational and breathing animals in general in Genesis 7:15-22. And although Moses speaks of the man Adam, and may seem mostly to stop at the animal aspect, I can nevertheless very well accept what Burman <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> and others have noted, namely: *That the action of God, which in man is called this breath and an inspiration, is as if He had breathed breath and life—indeed, the rational soul itself—into man through a lovely breeze or a whistling; which blowing was a sign of the quickening of man. So that with that blowing, God created the soul when He blew it into man, not outside the body, but within it; whereby man became a living soul, that is, a living person; not a dead image, as he was before, but living, moving, and speaking.* This is why the Chaldean Translator <note>Referring to the Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translates these words as *a speaking spirit*, since the rational soul first manifests itself in speech, which is therefore unique to man. For man has specifically three advantages and ornaments above all animals. First, the intellect, by which he can find and devise everything necessary for him. Then, speech, to express his thoughts and to interact with other men. Finally, the hands, through which he can put into practice everything the intellect commands to be made, just as he carries out everything especially through his hands and rules over the beasts.

I say then, that Adam simultaneously received that which makes him a man and a rational creature: intellect, judgment, will, passions, and an immaterial and immortal, thinking, judging, and willing spirit, with free agency and consciousness.

<column-break/>

<margin>Genesis 7:15-22 explained.</margin>In Genesis 7:15-22, I read of the animals that entered the ark, and furthermore of the rest of all that lives and draws breath, which, being outside the ark, was suffocated by the waters of the flood; this must be applied not only to men, but also to irrational creatures.

<margin>Job 15:30 explained, partly applied to God, partly to the godless.</margin>Job 15:30: *He shall not depart out of darkness, the flame shall dry up his branches, and by the breath of his mouth shall he go away.*

One can well perceive from all circumstances that this speaks of one who intends no good toward God, men, or what is right and virtuous, but who is godless and impious; whose misfortune and punishment are described, saying that he shall fall, not rise again, but be rooted out and perish. However, there seems to be some ground for doubt here as to whom the phrase *by the breath of his mouth* best applies: for some have taken it for the mouth of God, others for the mouth of the godless. Rabbi Salomo <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> interprets it as: *by, or because of the breath, the blowing of his mouth, through which he has spoken rebellion.* Mercerus <note>Jean Mercier (1510–1570), a French Hebraist.</note> seems to have held with this. Others prefer to understand the mouth as the mouth of the Lord; for the flame also comes from the Lord, which causes the young tree-shoots or his lot to wither and dry up. And that the shoot of the godless, which bulges out like a tree-sprout from the mouth or opening of the earth, shall be so taken away and perish by the wind of Divine judgment, that the tree of the godless with its sprout shall wither, turn to dust, and blow away. See Cocceius and Sebastian Schmidt. <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) and Sebastian Schmidt (1617–1696) were prominent 17th-century biblical commentators.</note>

<margin>Job 27:3 explained.</margin>*As long as my breath is in me, and the breath of God is in my nostrils. Job 27:3.*

It is indeed true that everything possessing life and breath is subject to mortality and corruption. However, I do not believe that such was the intention of this manner of speaking and expression here, to portray the inner meaning of the earnest speaker and witness.

It is clear from the second verse that Job is making a kind of oath and strong declaration: that even though the Lord might have dealt with him so harshly and severely, he would nevertheless very carefully guard himself, as long as he had life and could speak, so that he did not transgress against God, justice, and propriety. See Piscator, Mercerus, Cocceius, Sebastian Schmidt, etc.

<margin>Psalm 150:6 explained.</margin>*Psalm 150:6. Let everything that has breath praise the Lord. Hallelujah. Every נשמה (neshamah), soul, every breath.* Although many creatures can be said to praise God in their own way, man—endowed with intellect, judgment, will, tongue, and mouth—is best suited for this. Everything that has breath and draws breath, all rational men, into whose nostrils a breath of life has been blown by God, from both Jews and Gentiles, who can learn of the Lord's virtues and works from the light of their conscience, the observation of the world's stage, from God's wise and sovereign governance, and especially from the Divine Scriptures; and by this be ignited to the acknowledgment of the Lord and to the glory of His great name.

For this, one requires not only breath for the utterance, but also a heavenly spirit—a soul-inspiring and life-giving breath of the Almighty.

<margin>Isaiah 2:22 explained.</margin>*Isaiah 2:22. Cease ye (then) from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for wherein is he to be esteemed?*

# B R E A T H .

I acknowledge that there appears here a description of the vanity, fragility, and transience of all people, who vanish so quickly that even greatness, power, and high social standing do not remove the reality and experience of general fragility and transience. Consequently, we are presented here with an admonishing and instructive discourse on true prudence: that one should not rely on man, however great and high in power, status, or reputation he may be, for he is easily choked and perishes. And what is there, after all, in and about man that one should make such a great matter of him, when God holds Himself back and withdraws His providence, influence, spirit, and grace from him? See *Psalm 146:3.* For those who desire more on this, see the learned Professor *Campegius Vitringa* on this passage. <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note>

<margin>Daniel 5:23 explained.</margin>
*Daniel 5:23. But the God in whose hand is your breath, and with whom are all your paths, you have not glorified.*

I recognize, as before, the vanity, fragility, and absolute dependence of all people—yes, even of kings and absolute rulers—and also that God, who gives the breath of life by blowing it in, can also withhold it. If the Lord were to do so, it would be the end of this magnificent, proud king's life, state, splendor, and glory. Consequently, the king could not think, will, or act without God, His influence, and His governance (*Proverbs 21:1, Jeremiah 10:23, Philippians 2:13*). Before His eyes, the King's internal and external matters lay bare; He knew them and would weigh and judge them. In consideration of all this, Daniel seeks to convince the King that he had gravely sinned against himself, because he had extinguished the general light within him. He had failed to confirm through his conduct that which was a matter of universal testimony—that the Divinity must be honored, acknowledged, and glorified infinitely above man—but instead had shamefully and culpably neglected it. See Gejerus and Junius. <note>Martin Geier (1614–1680) and Franciscus Junius (1545–1602) were prominent biblical commentators.</note>

<margin>Acts 17:25 explained.</margin>
*Acts 17:25. Nor is He served by human hands, as though He needed anything, since He Himself gives to all life and breath and all things.*

When one examines the text well and notes Paul's intention, one notices that he wishes to demonstrate and teach that man cannot place God under obligation, and that God does not need man; rather, man needs and requires God in all parts and respects. Man, being dependent on God and receiving everything from Him, is greatly indebted to God, his essential Lord and benefactor.

<margin>God needs nothing and receives nothing.</margin>
God needs nothing outside of Himself; He receives nothing from man. One performs no actual service or benefit for Him, such as diligent and faithful servants perform for and bring to their masters. For He is sufficient unto Himself; He gives, but receives nothing.

But let us hear and see what others have also said.

->Apuleius, following Plato:<-
> *Needing nothing himself, he himself bestows all things.* <note>original Latin: "Nihili indigens, ipse conferens cuncta."</note>
> [<gloss>He himself, needing nothing, grants everything.</gloss>]

->Lucretius on the Divine nature:<-
> *Powerful in its own resources, needing nothing of ours.* <note>original Latin: "Ipsa suis pollens opibus, nil indiga nostri."</note>
> [<gloss>He has His own power, and has no need of ours.</gloss>]

->Seneca, On Benefits, Chapter 4, 9:<-
> *He does not need what is contributed, nor can we contribute anything to him.* <note>original Latin: "Nec ille collato eget, nec nos ei quicquam conferre possumus."</note>
> [<gloss>He has no need of gifts, and we can bring Him nothing.</gloss>]

->Lactantius in the Dialogue of Hermes Trismegistus:<-
> *Nothing is lacking to him, who himself is everything.* <note>original Latin: "Nil deest ei, qui ipse est omnia."</note>
> [<gloss>Nothing is lacking to Him, who is Himself all things.</gloss>]

<margin>God grants life, breath, and all things.</margin>
And how can it be thought or said in truth that He should lack anything, or that we could contribute anything to Him? Since He grants to everyone life, breath, and everything.

By this, the Lord's all-sufficiency, power, goodness, influence, and governance—along with the absolute dependence and neediness of us all for life—is defined and expressed in the most powerful and emphatic way.

And so here we see both man's first formation and ensoulment, and God's maintenance, support, and blessings.

This point is also confirmed by sacred and secular writers, found in abundance in Priceus's commentary on this passage; therefore, from many examples, I give these few. One may apply these lines from Ovid here, from the 14th book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> *That I speak and breathe, and the heavens and the light of the sun*
> *I behold (can I be ungrateful and forgetful?)*
> *He himself gave.* <note>original Latin: "Quod loquor, & spiro, cælumque & lumina solis / Adspitio, (possumne ingratus, & immemor esse?) / Ipſe dedit."</note>

->Which Vondel translates thus:<-
> *For that I speak and live, and behold the heavenly light,*
> *An unforgettable virtue, I enjoy through His faithfulness,*
> *Who gave me life.* <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) was the preeminent poet of the Dutch Golden Age.</note>

->Aristides, Oration 1:<-
> Zeus is called so by us because he is the cause of life and being for everyone. <note>original Greek: Ζεὺς, ὅτι ζωῆς τε καὶ οὐσίας ἑκάστοις ἐστὶν αἴτιος, κέκληται ἡμῖν. The author references the Greek etymological connection between the name Zeus and the verb "to live" (zēn).</note>
> [<gloss>Jupiter is named by us as the cause of both life and being for all.</gloss>]

->Lactantius in his Instructions, Book 1, Chapter 11:<-
> *By whom we are formed, animated, and enlightened.* <note>original Latin: "A quo fingimur, animamur, illustramur."</note>
> [<gloss>By whom we are formed, inspired with soul, and enlightened.</gloss>]

->The same in Book 2, Chapter 12:<-
> *He himself fashioned the body; he himself infused the soul by which we breathe.* <note>original Latin: "Ipse corpus effinxit, ipse animam, quâ ſpiramus, infudit."</note>
> [<gloss>He Himself formed the body, He infused the soul through which we drew breath.</gloss>]

<margin>God and Divine matters.</margin>
Thus far I have occupied myself, and exercised my reader, with the contemplation of breath insofar as it belongs to man. Now it may be fruitful, and pertain to my purpose, that I proceed to speak of breath insofar as it relates to God, any divine person, work, or means with which the divine hand joins and unites itself. And again, I shall follow the list of the divine Books of the Bible.

# B R E A T H .

H 2

<margin>Job 4:9 explained.</margin> *Job 4:9. By the blast of God they perish, and by the breath of his nostrils are they consumed.*

This appears to me as a figurative representation of God’s wrath and vengeance; it is frequently portrayed through the nostrils—snorting, swelling, the inflaming of the nose, and sudden, heavy breathing—as is characteristic of those who are enraged. 

Those who appear to me to be the subject of this discourse are the godless, workers of unrighteousness, whom the Lord would punish here and hereafter. Rabbi Solomon <note>original: "Rabbi Salomo," referring to the medieval commentator Rashi.</note> understands this as God’s storm and wrath. The Chaldean <note>The "Chaldeër" refers to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> understands it as the Divine decree, His particular providence and wrath, through which the godless wither, dry up, and shrivel; they are rooted out and perish, just as grass or the fruits of the field and field-crops dry out, scorch, and perish by a violent, parching wind. See further Cocceius, Schultens, and Schmidt <note>Johannes Cocceius, Albert Schultens, and Sebastian Schmidt were prominent 17th-century biblical scholars and Hebraists.</note> on this passage.

<margin>Job 32:8 explained.</margin> *Job 32:8. But there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding.*

It is beyond dispute that, although knowledge and wisdom often come with years, observation, and diligence, wisdom does not always come with age, nor is it bound to advanced years. One finds young people who are wise, and old people who are foolish. The Spirit of God—which is a spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge—being within a person, enlightens the understanding, teaches and leads into all truth, governs the judgment, and gives the ability and boldness to speak the truth and true wisdom, which primarily falls to the lot of the humble. See Mercerus, Piscator, Cocceius, Schultens, and Schmidt. <note>Jean Mercier and Johannes Piscator were influential Protestant theologians known for their commentaries.</note>

<margin>Job 33:4 explained.</margin> *Job 33:4. The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life.*

It seems Elihu wishes to exhort Job to listen, showing himself to be humble and yielding alongside Job, as is seen subsequently. He attributes to God’s Spirit the first formation of the body and the giving of life in nature, by which one lives and breathes; perhaps also attributing to that Spirit here an almighty power and exercise of strength for enlightenment, recreation, and making one truly alive, wise, and active.

<margin>Job 37:10 explained.</margin> *Job 37:10. By the breath of God frost is given: and the broad waters are frozen.*

God awakens the frost through His spirit—and also through the cold easterly wind when it blows strongly—so that the surface of the waters stiffens, overflows, and is covered over with a ceiling of ice.

<margin>Psalm 18:16 explained.</margin> *Psalm 18:16. Then the channels of waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were discovered at thy rebuke, O Lord, at the blast of the breath of thy nostrils.*

I have noted that this lofty and symbolic description has been taken as a figurative representation of powerful thunder and strong earthquakes, by which the foundations of the earth and mountains are moved, the earth is torn open, and thereby pools, marshes, and floods are caused, in order to portray divine wrath, punishment, and devastation upon enemies, and so forth. However, the great Cocceius, whom one may consult, says that such things were seen in a historical manner during the leading out of God’s people from Egypt through the Red Sea, and later through the Jordan; that floods and rivers within a land can signify troops, armies, and powers—as worldly powers under the name of God’s people,

<column-break/>

and the sea outside and around the land can signify worldly power outside the boundaries and the name of the Church. Through this symbolic language, it is understood to mean the removal, emptying, and subduing of power, both inside and outside the Church, of those who seek the destruction of the Church. Such was the emptying of the Jewish people, as well as the Roman and heathen domains, and the destruction of other nations who were struck down and inflamed as enemies against the Church. And certainly, the Church was delivered from the Jewish and Heathen people by no less a miracle and hand than when God’s people were delivered of old from Egypt.

<margin>Isaiah 11:4 explained.</margin> *Isaiah 11:4. But with righteousness shall he judge the poor... and he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked.*

It is manifest from the entire administration of the New Testament that Christ the Lord, Head and King of His Church, teaches and judges her in such a way that He instructs His people and convinces them of what is true, according to the most perfect and equitable rule of the law and the teaching of the New Testament. However, if we pay proper attention to it, this part of the fourth verse presents us with a judicial judgment and punishment which He, in defending His church and people, shall execute upon the wicked and stubborn enemies—both His own and those of His people—when the affairs of His Church appear most dark, confused, and desperate. By these judgments and punishments, He shall bring the enemies to defeat and devastate them in righteousness.

However, the matter then depends on how one understands this proverb, and to what time and what persons it should be applied, since there is quite a variety of thoughts among the learned concerning this. I have declared myself on this in the first part of my *Holy Miscellanies* <note>original: "heilige Mengelstoffen," likely the author's previous publication.</note>, page 39, etc.; but since that little work has been sold out for several years, I shall express my thoughts on it more closely and bring the expressions, which are quite figurative and symbolic, under closer examination.

The word <term>שבט</term> <note>Hebrew: "shebet," meaning a rod, staff, or scepter.</note> translated as *rod*, signifies a rod of the scepter, a staff, or a switch, and is more properly applied to the hand than to the mouth; also, the smiting of the earth with a scepter is not exactly literal.

But <term>שבט</term> (*shebet*) in the power of the imagination signifies some means or something through which one punishes and disciplines, chastising those who are disobedient, licentious, spiteful, or rebellious, in order to bring them, if possible, to obedience, discipline, and good morals. *Proverbs 13:24 and 23:12; 2 Samuel 7:10.*

<margin>How it differs in meanings.</margin> <term>שבט</term> (*Shebet*), a scepter, rod, staff, or switch, portraying power and royal or judicial authority, can be used and applied to oppression as well as to prosperity. *Genesis 49:10; Psalm 45:7; Ezekiel 19:14; Amos 1:5.*

Since Jesus' Kingdom is spiritual and not of this world, His scepter is of the same nature and quality; therefore, the Word and the Law, along with the spirit and heart-changing grace, are well understood by it, as is the power through which He fells and subdues His enemies by His word. Thus, it is called a scepter of righteousness, but also an iron scepter. *Romans 5:16; 2 Corinthians 10:2-6; Psalm 45:7 and 29.* The Professor Taco Hajo van den Honert says on *Psalm 110, page 109*, etc., and Professor Adolf Lampe in *Psalm 45, part 1, page 434*, etc.—not without reason and very fittingly—we understand by this the scepter of the Messiah,

<margin>Figuratively applied to the mouth.</margin>

# B R E A T H .

<meta>Catchword: Job</meta>

I acknowledge that we find here a description of the vanity, fragility, and transience of all men, who vanish so quickly that even greatness, power, and high social standing do not remove the reality and experience of our universal frailty. Therefore, we are presented here with an admonition and a lesson in true prudence: that one should not place trust in man—no matter how great or high in power, status, or reputation he may be in this world—because his life depends on his breaths, which, whenever God wills, are easily withheld, and thus he suffocates and perishes. And what is there, after all, in or about man that one should make such a great matter of him, when God holds Himself back and withdraws His providence, influence, gifts, and grace? See *Psalm 146:3.* For those who desire more on this, see the learned Professor Campegius Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note> on this passage.

<margin>Daniel 5:23 explained.</margin>
*Daniel 5:23. But the God in whose hand your breath is, and whose are all your ways, you have not glorified.*

I recognize, as before, the vanity, fragility, and absolute dependence of all men—even of kings and monarchs—and that God, who gives the breath of life by breathing it in, can also withhold it. Should the Lord do so, then it would be over for this magnificent, proud king's life, state, splendor, and glory. Consequently, the king could not think, will, or carry out anything without God, His influence, and His governance (*Proverbs 21:1; Jeremiah 10:23; Philippians 2:13*). The King’s inner and outer affairs lay bare before His eyes; He knew them and would weigh and judge them. In consideration of all this, Daniel seeks to convince the King that he had grievously sinned against himself, because he had extinguished the general light within himself. He had failed to confirm through his conduct that which was common testimony—that the Divinity must be honored, acknowledged, and glorified infinitely above man—but had instead shamefully and blameworthily neglected it. See Gejerus <note>Martin Geier (1614–1680), a German Lutheran theologian.</note> and Junius <note>Francis Junius (1545–1602), a Huguenot theologian.</note>.

<margin>Acts 17:25 explained.</margin>
*Acts 17:25. Neither is worshipped with men’s hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things.*

When one examines the text well and notes Paul’s intent, one perceives that he wishes to show and teach that man cannot put God under obligation, and that God does not need man. Rather, man needs and requires God in all parts and respects; and man, being dependent on God and receiving everything from Him, is greatly indebted to God as his essential Lord and benefactor.

<margin>God needs nothing and receives nothing.</margin>
God needs nothing outside of Himself; He receives nothing from man. One does Him no actual service or benefit in the way that diligent and faithful servants do for their masters. For He is sufficient unto Himself; He gives, but receives nothing.

But let us hear and see what others have also said.

> Apuleius, quoting Plato:
> *Nihili indigens, ipse conferens cuncta.*
> <gloss>He himself needing nothing, bestows all things.</gloss>

> Lucretius on the Divine nature:
> *Ipsa suis pollens opibus, nil indiga nostri.*
> <gloss>He possesses his own power and has no need of ours.</gloss>

> Seneca, *On Benefits*, Chapter 4, 9:
> *Nec ille collato eget, nec nos ei quicquam conferre possumus.*
> <gloss>He has no need of anything given, nor can we contribute anything to him.</gloss>

> Lactantius, in the *Dialogue of Trismegistus*:
> *Nil deest ei, qui ipse est omnia.*
> <gloss>Nothing is lacking to him, who himself is all things.</gloss>

<margin>Life, breath, and all things are granted by God.</margin>
And how can it be thought or said in truth that He should lack anything, or that we could contribute anything to Him? Seeing as He grants to all life, breath, and everything.

By this, the Lord's all-sufficiency, power, goodness, influence, and governance—alongside our universal and absolute dependence and need for life—is certainly defined and expressed in the most powerful and emphatic way.

And so we see here both man’s first formation and ensoulment, and God’s preservation, support, and blessings.

This point is also confirmed by sacred and secular writers, found in abundance in Priceus <note>John Price (1602–1676), a scriptural critic who used classical literature to illustrate biblical texts.</note> on this passage; from the many examples, I provide these few. One may apply these lines from Ovid, from the 14th book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> *Quod loquor, & spiro, cælumque & lumina solis*
> *Adspitio, (possumne ingratus, & immemor esse?)*
> *Ipse dedit.*

> Which Vondel <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679), the preeminent Dutch poet and playwright.</note> translates thus:
> *For that I speak and live, and behold the heavenly light,*
> *An unforgettable virtue, I enjoy through his faithfulness,*
> *Who gave me life.*

> Aristides, *Oration I*:
> Ζεύς, ὅτι ζωῆς τε ἦ, καὶ οὐσίας ἑκάστοις ἐστὶν αἴτιος, κέκληται ἡμῖν.
> <gloss>Zeus is named by us as being the cause of both life and being to all.</gloss>

> Lactantius, in his *Divine Institutes*, Book 1, Chapter 11:
> *A quo fingimur, animamur, illustramur.*
> <gloss>By whom we are formed, animated, and enlightened.</gloss>

> The same in Book 2, Chapter 12:
> *Ipse corpus effinxit, ipse animam, qua spiramus, infudit.*
> <gloss>He himself formed the body; he infused the soul through which we breathe.</gloss>

<margin>God and Divine matters.</margin>
Thus far I have occupied myself and exercised my reader with the contemplation of breath, insofar as it pertains to man. Now it shall be fruitful, and part of my purpose, to speak further of breath insofar as it relates to God, any Divine person, work, or means with which the Divine hand joins and unites itself. And once again, I shall follow the list of the Divine books of the Bible.

# BREATH.

**H 2**

<margin>Job 4:9 explained.</margin> *Job 4:9. By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his nostrils are they consumed.*

This appears to me as a figurative means of describing God's wrath and vengeance; it is often depicted through the nose—snorting, swelling, and the igniting of the nostrils—as well as sudden and violent breathing, all of which serve as images of indignation.

Those who seem to me to be the subject of this conversation are the godless, the workers of iniquity, whom the Lord would punish both here and hereafter. Rabbi Salomo <note>The author refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki, 1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> understands this to mean God's storm and wrath. The Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum, the Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> understands it as the Divine decree, His particular providence and wrath, by which the godless wilt, wither, and dry up, being rooted out and perishing just as grass and the fruits of the field and field-crops dry up, scorch, and perish by a violent, parching wind. See further Cocceius, Schultens, and Schmidt <note>Johannes Cocceius, Albert Schultens, and Sebastian Schmidt were prominent 17th and 18th-century biblical scholars and Hebraists.</note> on this passage.

<margin>Job 32:8 explained.</margin> *Job 32:8. But there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding.*

It is beyond contradiction that, although knowledge and wisdom often come with years, observation, and industriousness, wisdom does not always come with age, nor is it bound to advanced years. One finds young people who are wise and old people who are foolish. The Spirit of God—which is a spirit of wisdom, understanding, and science—being within a person, enlightens the understanding, teaches and leads into all truth, governs the judgment, and gives the capability and boldness to speak the truth and true wisdom; this is something that falls chiefly to the humble. See Mercerus, Piscator, Cocceius, Schultens, and Schmidt.

<margin>Job 33:4 explained.</margin> *Job 33:4. The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life.*

It seems Elihu wishes to admonish Job to listen, showing himself to be humble and yielding alongside Job, as is seen subsequently. He attributes to God's Spirit the first formation of the body and the giving of life in nature, through which one lives and breathes; perhaps also attributing to that Spirit here an almighty power and an exercise of strength toward enlightenment, recreation, and a true making of life, wisdom, and activity.

<margin>Job 37:10 explained.</margin> *Job 37:10. By the breath of God frost is given: and the breadth of the waters is straitened.*

God produces frost through His spirit, and also indirectly through the cold eastern wind when it blows strongly, so that the surface of the waters becomes stiff, frozen over, and covered as if with a floor.

<margin>Ps. 18:15 explained.</margin> *Ps. 18:15. Then the channels of waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were discovered at thy rebuke, O LORD, at the blast of the breath of thy nostrils.*

I have noted that this exalted and symbolic description has been understood as a figurative means for powerful thunder and strong earthquakes, by which the foundations of the earth and mountains are moved, the earth cracks, and through which pools, marshes, and floods are caused. These are used to depict divine wrath, punishment, and devastation over enemies, and so forth. However, the great Cocceius, whom one may consult, says that such things were seen in a historical manner during the leading out of God's people from Egypt through the Red Sea, and later through the Jordan. He suggests that floods and rivers within a land can signify groups, armies, and powers—even worldly ones—under the name of God's people,

<column-break/>

and the sea outside and around the land can signify the worldly power outside the borders and name of the Church. Through this symbolic language, it is understood to mean the removal, emptying, and subduing of power, both within and outside the Church, of those who seek the destruction of the Church. Such was the emptying of the Jewish people, as well as the Roman and pagan domains, and the destruction of other nations who acted as struck and ignited enemies against the Church. And certainly, by no lesser miracle or hand was the Church delivered from the Jewish and Pagan people than God's people were delivered of old from Egypt.

<margin>Isa. 11:4 explained.</margin> *Isa. 11:4. But he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked.*

It is manifest from the entire administration of the New Testament that Christ—Lord, Head, and King of His Church—teaches and directs the same, such that He instructs His people and convinces them of the truth, according to the most perfect and equitable rule of the law and the doctrine of the New Testament. Yet, if we pay proper attention, a judicial judgment and punishment appears to us in this part of the fourth verse. This is a judgment He shall execute—while defending His church and people—over the evil and stubborn enemies of both Himself and His people, at a time when the affairs of His Church appear most dark, confused, and desperate. Through these judgments and punishments, He shall strike down and devastate the enemies in righteousness.

However, it subsequently comes down to how one understands this saying, and to what time and what persons it should be applied, since there is quite a diversity of thought among scholars regarding this. I have explained my views on this in the first part of my *Sacred Miscellany*, page 39, etc.; but since that little work has been sold out for several years now, I shall express my thoughts more closely here and subject these expressions, which are quite figurative and symbolic, to closer examination.

The word <term>Shebet <note>original Hebrew: שבט</note></term>, translated as *rod*, signifies <margin>Rod of the mouth.</margin> a scepter, rod, or twig, and is more properly applied to the hand than to the mouth; likewise, the "smiting of the earth with a scepter" is not strictly literal in that sense.

But <term>Shebet</term> in the power of imagery gives us to understand some means or something through which one punishes, disciplines, and chastises those who are disobedient, debauched, resentful, or rebellious, in order to bring them—if it were possible—to obedience, discipline, and good morals. *Prov. 13:24 and 23:12; 2 Sam. 7:10.*

<margin>How various in its meanings.</margin> <term>Shebet</term>—a scepter, rod, staff, twig, or power—depicting royal and judicial authority, can be used and applied for oppression as well as for prosperity. *Gen. 49:10; Ps. 45:6; Ezek. 19:14; Amos 1:5.*

Since Jesus' kingdom is spiritual and not of this world, His scepter is of the same nature and quality; therefore, word and law, along with the spirit and heart-transforming grace, are well understood by it. This also includes the power by which He fells and subdues His enemies through His word, and thus it is called a scepter of righteousness, but also an iron scepter. *Rom. 5:16; 2 Cor. 10:2-6; Ps. 45:6 and 2:9.* Professor Taco Haio van den Honert says on *Psalm 110, page 109,* etc., and Professor Adolf Lampe in *Psalm 45, part 1, page 434,* etc. <margin>Figuratively applied to the mouth.</margin> *not without reason, and very appropriately, we understand by this the scepter of the Messiah,*

It focuses on the symbolic use of the "rod of the mouth" as a metaphor for divine authority and the spiritual power of Christ's word.</summary>

# BREATH. ADVOCATE.

*...become that same word of truth, but animated by His spirit, of which we spoke in the preceding section.*

Next, we must consider how one should interpret the word <term>שבט</term> *Schebet* <note>The Hebrew word *shebet* can refer to a rod, a staff, or a royal scepter.</note>. I shall cite what I have written in my aforementioned book, page 39. Whether one takes the word *Schebet* in the first sense—as a rod of chastisement—or in the latter sense—as a scepter of kingly dominion and authority—it remains remarkable that this scepter is attributed not to the Messiah's hand, but to His mouth. This is quite unusual, considering that kings hold their scepter in their hand, not their mouth, as a sign of power and authority. This suggests to me that the Messiah will not require an outward sign, a scepter of power and capability, to punish the inhabitants of the earth as the wicked and violent; rather, He shall possess such power through His word and His mighty command and will. Or otherwise, just as kings touch something with a scepter and grant a firm sign with it—which is the same as <margin>A means of representation.</margin> confirming something or giving a command for prompt execution by their ministers of state—so too, at the word of command from the Messiah, instruments will immediately be at hand to execute the King’s decree and established will.

And so, the Lord Professor Adolf Lampe <note>Friedrich Adolf Lampe (1683–1729), a prominent German Pietist theologian and professor at Utrecht.</note>, in his learned exercises on the glory of the Prince Messiah in *Psalm 45*, part I, page 433, etc., <margin>Meaning of "Scepter" by transference.</margin> noted that a scepter is not only a sign of imperial governance, but is also used in a transferred or metaphorical sense for a word that inclines the senses and moves one to obedience.

See also the Reverend Eustathius <note>Eustathius of Thessalonica, a 12th-century scholar known for his commentaries on Homer.</note> on Homer’s *Iliad*, Book A: *and not without reason, he says, for what the King does with the scepter, an Orator also achieves and does with his words*, according to the saying of Virgil in the first book of the *Aeneid*:

> He rules their minds with words and soothes their breasts. <note>original Latin: "Ille regit dictis animos & pectora mulcet."</note>

> [He soothes the outbursts,
> And settles their wrath.]

Next, we encounter *the earth, and the smiting of the earth with this rod of his mouth.*

I shall not dwell on every detail; one may consult the learned Lord Professor Campegius Vitringa <note>A famous Dutch theologian (1659–1722) known for his commentary on Isaiah.</note> in his work on *Isaiah 11*, and my first volume of *Sacred Miscellanies* on that same chapter.

<margin>The Earth, and the godless. Who and what they signify to some.</margin> By "the earth" and "the godless," some have understood the Antichrist; others have understood carnal, animalistic, earthly-minded people, or very wicked and gross sinners. Some understand the <term>רשע</term> *rashang* <note>Hebrew for "the wicked one."</note> to be the Devil. It seems to me that by "the earth," one should primarily understand that territory and that vast, well-known, formidable region of the Roman domain, where the Messiah was to establish His <margin>What the author understands by this.</margin> glorified Kingdom. At that time, this also included the region of India. The former was, without contradiction, inhabited by worldly, carnal, seekers of worldly wisdom, superstitious, and idolatrous people who—armed with all the power of Satan and incited by him—used all manner of craftiness, persecution, slander, and open violence to halt the foundation and expansion of the Messiah’s Kingdom and to root it out. Joined with them were the wicked, godless Jews seeking their own righteousness, who killed the Messiah and slandered and persecuted His disciples, joining themselves to the aforementioned purpose with decrees, efforts, persecutions, and acts of violence among the Romans (*Psalm 2:22; Acts 4:27*).

But to pull everything together as briefly as possible: it is certain that we must understand these to be the public, well-known enemies of the Messiah, His people, and His Kingdom—those who held a name in the world but were stiff-necked. They would be brought under the Messiah's punishments in such a sensible and visible manner that it could be seen and noticed by everyone.

As for how some have chosen to apply this to the Messiah’s word and law for the sake of conviction and conversion, combined with the singular cooperation of the Holy Spirit, one may see my aforementioned *Sacred Miscellanies* p. 43, etc.; also Tako Hajo van den Honert in *Psalm 110*, page 109; and Lampe in the exercises on the 45th Psalm, part 1, page 435, etc. How I have understood it regarding God's judicial judgments, the announcement of wretched downfall, and the subsequent heavy punishments, devastation, and ruin of the Jews, along with the plagues upon the Roman domain, can be seen in my first *Miscellanies* pages 40, 41, 48, 49, 50. See especially the famous Lord Professor Vitringa in his learned work on Isaiah.

Let this be enough for now. On SCEPTER, ROD, etc., various matters will sufficiently arise.

### ADVOCATE, PLEADER, LEGAL COUNSEL
-> *παράκλητος, Advocatus, Patronus.* <-
<note>The author provides the Greek (*parakletos*) and Latin (*advocatus*, *patronus*) terms for a legal defender or advocate.</note>

<margin>The name of Advocates known since antiquity.</margin> THE name of ADVOCATE has been known since ancient times by ecclesiastical and secular writers, although in certain respects it differed from common usage among us today. There were Advocates and Patrons of kingdoms, provinces, cities, monasteries, churches, etc., under <margin>Though differing in status, rank, and benefit.</margin> whose administration, oversight, and defense many great and prominent matters were placed. And accordingly, depending on the diversity of the matters, the greater or lesser extent of their authority and providence also varied.

<margin>What kind of person is understood by this.</margin> However, as we are most accustomed to understanding it among ourselves, it signifies a legal counsel, a master of jurisprudence, a pleader who—as one entitled and called to the task—represents and defends someone's case through speech, writing, or good advice and action, according to the laws.

A person who is recognized as capable by the public Lecturers of Law, and is bolstered by their testimony, is admitted to the public roll after taking an oath, to lead the discourse there as a pleader.

<margin>Description of an Advocate.</margin> I see that Jacobus Menochius <note>Giacomo Menochio (1532–1607), a famous Italian jurist.</note> described the office of an excellent Advocate thus: *the office of an honorable Advocate is to aim and strive entirely toward this: that disputes be settled and reconciled, friendship among men be preserved, and the helping hand be offered to the party.*

<margin>Duties of an Advocate.</margin> To this belongs that a pleader comforts and gives courage to the one he serves—as much as is reasonably possible and based on good grounds—encouraging him, urging him to pursue his case, and providing him with counsel that is salu-

# ADVOCATE.
### H 3

...is beneficial, brings his case before the Judge and defends it, and speaks for him in all faithfulness and earnestness, pursuing his case with the closest circumspection and alertness, and omitting nothing of that which he—according to laws, customs, etc.—judges in good conscience to belong to the advantage of the one who has employed him and his good cause.

<margin>Rules for Advocates.</margin>
Furthermore, I have observed that these public persons, regarding their office of pleading and its practice, have certain instructions, ordinances, and rules, namely:

<margin>Not to accept bad cases.</margin>
a. That they may not accept cases to defend which they know beforehand to be unjust and evil.

<margin>Not to take an interest in the lawsuits.</margin>
b. That they may not have a share <note>Original: "aandeel." This refers to a "contingency fee" or a personal stake in the outcome of the litigation, which was often legally barred to ensure impartiality.</note> in the matters they shall bargain for and maintain.

c. That they may not work against the people who have accepted them as intercessors; they must be for, not against, the accepted cases, and in defending and pleading the taken-up case, they must guard against meeting their opponents with all manner of rudeness, unbridled words, scolding, slandering, etc.

<margin>Not to keep a case dragging on.</margin>
d. Seeking no delay or suspension and dragging-out of the case to anyone's disadvantage or torment, but continuing the plea as much as is possible and advisable.

<margin>To avoid repetitions.</margin>
e. Guarding oneself against repetition and fruitless extensions and unnecessary dawdling; drawing up the essence of the documents concisely, and organizing all documents under his letters a, b, c.

f. In drawing up the case, omitting or neglecting nothing concerning the facts and proofs, because judgment is passed according to these, and the judge in this regard in no way fulfills what has been bypassed by the <term>advocate</term> <note>Original: "pleitvoogt," literally a "pleading-guardian."</note>.

<margin>Necessity of this office.</margin>
How excellent and highly necessary this office is according to the constitution of this state, alongside the institutions and ordinances of the Sovereign, I shall not aim to describe; nor shall I presume to paint many pleaders and Advocates with a rough and uneven brush. It would be a lamentable state if there were no good, pious, and faithful advocates in the land among so many <term>extortionists</term> <note>Original: "bloedtegels," likely an archaic variant or OCR error for "bloedzuigers" (bloodsuckers/leeches).</note> and parasites, takers and supporters of evil causes: yet one always finds monstrosities and stains of shame among all human states and callings. These are faults of the persons and not of the office. The shameful use does not preclude the rightful use; the good and righteous must be held at a higher price, and the ill-reputed punished according to the merits and laws of the land. If this happened as it should, one would not so often see the right twisted into the crooked, and the crooked into the right.

<margin>The evil among the good.</margin>

<margin>The sinner has the highest need for an Advocate.</margin>
But let that be said enough regarding the office of Advocates or Pleaders. Furthermore, it remains for me to see and show to what persons one can aptly transfer this in a figurative sense, and in what manner it can be applied to their performance and treatment, according to the grievances, documents, and proofs that one can find in Holy Scripture, corresponding with divine law and the judicial process in the matter of sinners. Those who have many parties, accusers, complainers, and demanders of punishment shall have to fall in judgment if they stand on their own and have no defender, spokesperson, or Advocate to promote their case and lawsuit to their advantage and bring it to a happy end.

<margin>Such a one is mentioned by Divine Scripture.</margin>

<margin>All men have a law.</margin>
If one views man as a sinner, subject to the law according to which he has to direct his actions and omissions,

<column-break/>

then the law points to the will of the Supreme Lawgiver; it makes known that the deeds of man are illegal and contrary to the will of the Lawgiver: and because it is strengthened with the <term>curse</term> <note>Original: "vlockſpraak," referring to the formal pronouncement of divine condemnation found in the Law.</note> over the lawbreaker, the law and sin demand the execution of what was threatened concerning the guilty, and condemns the whole world lying in sin as worthy of death. *Gen. III. Deut. XXVII. Gal. III. Ezek. XVIII. Rom. II. and III. and VI. 23. 1 Cor. XV.*

<margin>This shows the duty and the punishment.</margin>

<margin>Condemns all flesh.</margin>
The certain knowledge of the law of the Lawgiver demands the sentence of damnation in case of law-breaking and transgression; and man, having a consciousness of his deviating and unrighteous deeds, has a capacity for his own self-condemnation and accusation, *Rom. I. and II. 1 John III.* while the devil plays the part of accuser and executioner. *Heb. II. Rev. XII.*

<margin>The conscience stops the mouth and consents to the judgment.</margin>
God, the judge of all the earth, *Gen. XVIII.* announces through His word and the conscience how He could deal with man as a sinner according to His right, and already sets up the <term>tribunal</term> <note>Original: "vierſchaar," the traditional term for a court of justice, literally referring to the four benches that enclosed the space where judges sat.</note> beforehand in the innermost part of his conscience. Meanwhile, man—who knows and acknowledges himself as sinful, and God as holy, righteous, and of irresistible power—has such a preconception of his approaching state that, fearing and foreseeing the inevitable judgment of destruction that will be pronounced over him, he fears, starts, trembles, and shakes, *Isa. XXXIII. Heb. XII. Ps. XC.* and whichever way he turns or twists, the hope of mercy and of a mediator, patron, and advocate is taken from him: for no angel or man can, upon the accusation and striking of his condemning conscience, provide or furnish him with any ground of comfort and hope of mercy in his misery against the accusation and charge.

<margin>God's word convicts the world of sin and judgment.</margin>

<margin>God Himself has appointed, promised, and described an Advocate.</margin>
However (O grace in the word of strong and eternal comfort!), he becomes aware in the promises, shadows, and prophecies of a Messiah, <term>Surety</term> <note>Original: "borg," one who takes legal responsibility for another's debt or obligation.</note>, Intercessor, and Advocate, who shall plead upon His right, righteousness, suffering, love, and perfect obedience, and shall present Himself for the Persons whose cause He has taken up, according to the covenant of eternity given to Him by the Father for redemption and salvation, *Job XXXIII. Ps. XL. Heb. X.* He sees Him in the word of fulfillment as having come, having suffered, and having obeyed. He sees Him killed, raised, ascended into heaven, crowned with honor and glory at His Father's right hand.

<margin>The excellence of Jesus' Advocacy.</margin>
Him he confesses to be the Savior of the world, and His righteousness he embraces through faith; upon His intercession, love, faithfulness, covering, and protection, he relies fully.

He who has come to the Christ is not refused or cast out, but Christ conducts Himself as the defender of his person and affairs. Also, He is Himself the Judge; and establishing Himself upon the eternal covenant, His suretyship, brought-forth righteousness, obedience, and the suffering of death, He denies the creditors and accusers their claim, because He has fulfilled the right of the law in their place, having done and suffered everything the law demanded or threatened; desiring for that reason not only that the one guilty in himself shall, for His sake, be free from punishment, but also be declared justified in, with, and for His sake unto the inheritance of eternal life, and be brought to where He is. And thus He appears many times, as I have said, in the holy rolls, *1 John II. 1, 2. Rom. VIII.* who prays for us, *Heb. VII. and V. John XVII.* so that, although there is something in the actually guilty...

# ADVOCATE. ABYSS.

...is what makes them worthy of damnation and, by their own nature, guilty of punishment; yet for them there is no condemnation, *Romans 8:1*. It is true that accusations and charges are brought against them, demanding punishment, death, and damnation, but everything is refuted and the demand is denied, so that they do not come into the judgment of condemnation, *Romans 8, John 5, Hebrews 5 and 7, Job 33 <note>The OCR reads LXIII, but Job 33:23 is the standard reference for an "interpreter" or advocate.</note>.* To ensure their security, it is even handled so that the legal "handwriting" of debt is torn up, <note>Original: "handschrift rects gescheurt." A reference to Colossians 2:14, where the list of a person's sins is described as a legal document canceled by Christ.</note> *Colossians 2*, and Christ, having been delivered up for the sins of His people, was raised for their justification. *Romans 4:25.*
