Christ is such a mediator and advocate, and He alone; He fully settles the legal case of His own people to their release and triumph. *Acts 4:12, John 14:6, 1 Timothy 2, Hebrews 5 and 7.*

<margin>He has His legal counsel, the Holy Spirit.</margin>
Furthermore, He sends down from the highest His Spirit, who also acts as an <term>Advocate <note>Greek: "paraklētos," often translated as Comforter or Counselor, but literally one called to stand alongside another in a legal setting.</note></term> and intercessor, insofar as He applies to the chosen and called saints that which is in Christ. Through the Word and under its ministry, He comforts them inwardly, teaching how believers can meet their Covenant God and Father with boldness; how they must and can defend themselves against the accusations of their conscience, the law, and Satan. He assures them that acquittal in the supreme judicial judgment, along with the inheritance of glory, will by no means escape them; while He and His indwelling, and His initial work toward holiness—with comfort of heart in all crosses and distress—must be viewed as a seal, a pledge, and a preceding portion of that state and that perfecting good which they shall possess hereafter and obtain in soul and body.

<margin>Whose services in this are described.</margin>
Having presented this with little elaboration, I could strengthen, distinguish, and work this out with a series of scriptural proofs if I deemed it necessary; however, I shall leave it to the discerning reader and only place a few texts belonging to this subject here together, such as *John 14, 15, and 16 <note>The OCR reads Job, but these chapters in John contain the primary teachings on the Holy Spirit as Advocate.</note>; Romans 8; Ephesians 1 and 4; 2 Corinthians 1; 1 John 3; 2 Corinthians 4:17, 18.*

<margin>Proven with Holy Scripture.</margin>
Thus one finds that Christ is an Advocate of excellence, working through and with His Spirit.

<margin>Jesus is an Advocate in the highest degree and power.</margin>
He is the only one; He is always so; He is always heard, *John 11 <note>Specifically John 11:42, "I knew that thou hearest me always."</note>*. He pleads based on His own obedience and right. This plea takes place before the court of heaven. Here there is no appeal; this concerns crimes against highly offended Majesty, the state of the soul and body, and eternal well-being or inheritance, against which nothing can be valued or weighed. He never loses a plea, and the verdict is carried out; He enjoys nothing for it but thanksgiving; the whole work springs from matchless love for God's glory in the salvation of sinners.

***

### ABYSS, DEPTH, <term>The Deep <note>Hebrew: "tehom"</note></term>
### <term>Abyss <note>Greek: "abyssos"</note></term>, <term>Depth <note>Greek: "bathos"</note></term>, <term>Hell <note>Latin: "infernum"</note></term>, <term>Bottom <note>Latin: "fundum"</note></term> etc.

<margin>Meaning.</margin>
This word occurs among the Hebrews and Greeks under the words <term>Deep <note>Hebrew: "tehom"</note></term>, <term>Abyss <note>Greek: "abyssos"</note></term>, and <term>Depth <note>Greek: "bathos"</note></term>, and it literally signifies the ABYSS: the unfathomable depth, the immeasurable whirlpools of water, not only of the sea but also under the earth, as can be proven from many texts.

<column-break/>

<margin>Figuratively, a manifold suffering.</margin>
A more improper and figurative use is seen when it is understood as the lowest parts of the earth, or the state and place of the wretched, *Luke 8:31*, where one finds the word <term>Abyss <note>Greek: "abyssos"</note></term>. *Revelation 9:1, 2.* The key of the pit of the abyss, the power over the dead, and the presumed power to banish and thrust into the abyss, or to deliver from purgatory.

<margin>Abyss as a symbol of affliction.</margin>
One reads in *Psalm 69:3, 5, 6* of bottomless mud, the depth of the waters, and a pit; which, being applied to the Messiah, can signify His extreme distress, scorn, pain, suffering of soul and body, alongside the state of His death, *Ephesians 4:9*, just as the abyss is a symbol of extreme distress, humiliation, pressure, and torment. *Psalm 42:8 and 71:20; Ezekiel 26:19.*

<margin>A pit and angel of the abyss.</margin>
One also reads in the Revelation of John, *Chapter 9:1, 2*, of a pit of the abyss, of a king and angel of the abyss, Abaddon and Apollyon; of a beast that rises out of the sea, a beast that rises out of the abyss, *Revelation 11 and 13*; which depicts the Roman hierarchy from hell, and a confluence of all kinds of peoples and heathens having its beginning there—by no means an angel or servant of God, or one who has received his beginning from heaven, no vicar of Christ, but the Antichrist.

<margin>Abysses of the earth.</margin>
One reads in *Psalm 71:20* of the abysses of the earth, from which the Lord would bring up the church after many distresses, making her alive: by which I can well believe is understood the deliverance of the church from many and heavy struggles, the departure from Babylon, the liberation from deception, and the rare life from the dead through the conversion of Jews and Gentiles, with and upon the downfall and fall of Babylon.

<margin>Abyss calls to abyss, an image of the distress and persecution that follow one another.</margin>
One hears David and the church testify: *Abyss calls to abyss at the noise of your waterspouts; all your waves and billows have gone over me.* It can signify that sea called to sea, one to the other, so that many adversities, like raised and roaring waves, went over the head of the church and seemed to swallow it up; which has been the turn and lot of the Christian church both under raging heathendom and under persecution-spewing papacy. *Revelation 12.*

<margin>Restoration from Bashan, the depth of the sea. Deliverance of the church from under the oppressors in the east and west, gathering of the troops from Jews and Gentiles.</margin>
The Lord promises in *Psalm 68:22* the deliverance of His church, the restoration from Bashan and from the depths of the sea, by which one may think it is told that the church would be raised up and brought back from under the power of her overlords who oppressed her violently, in the east or the west, or the gathering from Jews and Gentiles who still remain, *Isaiah 11*, through the preaching of the Gospel, as the "dry bones" would be stirred and moved, and the sea would give up her dead.

Thus the abyss appears to signify something that seems difficult, precarious, and as if impossible. *Deuteronomy 30:13, Romans 10:7.* Just as in olden times, when navigation was not yet known and the Israelites did not understand seafaring, it seemed precarious and very dangerous to cross the sea. Therefore, it was a worrisome work and a very bold thing to attempt and undertake such a thing.

<margin>Abyss an unsearchable thing.</margin>
Consequently, the abyss and the depth appear as a designation when something is introduced that is unsearchable or unfathomable; indeed, there appears an unfathomable ocean of converging virtues and perfections of the Most High God. *Psalm*

# RADIANCE, Radiance <note>Original Greek: ἀπαύγασμα (apaugasma), meaning a light shining out from a source.</note>,
->*Resplendence.* <note>Original Latin: Resplendescentia.</note><-

<margin>Christ a radiance of the glory of his father.</margin>
It is well known that the Apostle speaks of this in *Hebrews 1:3*, applying it to Him through whom the Father has spoken to us in these last days.

<margin>Application of the scholars.</margin>
Since I am compiling a dictionary, it will not be at all improper for me to present the thoughts of the most prominent scholars as briefly and concisely as possible, and as far as the weight of the matter allows, without my assuming mastery over anyone’s opinion.

The scholars, then, make various allusions, all with the aim of bringing to light the power, beauty, and emphasis of this Apostolic manner of speaking, if such a thing were possible.

It is clear enough from all circumstances and the most emphatic expressions used by the Apostle, that in "radiance" he certainly looked upon something that, through its concentrated light and rebounding rays, gives off a great brilliance and a distinguished reflection of itself. However, as to what exactly the Apostle may have had in view, there is not the greatest agreement among scholars; therefore, for the benefit of the reader, I will incorporate some of their views into this work.

<margin>Various opinions.</margin>
A. Some have been pleased by the allusion to the cloud of glory above the <term>Ark of the Covenant <note>Original: "bondtkist."</note></term> and the <term>Mercy Seat <note>Original: "zoendeksel."</note></term>, in which the Lord dwelt, and from which cloud He spoke to the High Priest who sought His counsel. This is then regarded by them as a shadow and a symbolic means of representing Him in whom the fullness of the Godhead would dwell—truly, properly, and substantially (that is, bodily, no longer merely symbolically)—in a much more excellent and emphatic way, and thus establishing Himself among His people to speak as if mouth to mouth and face to face. *Hebrews 26:11 <note>Likely a citation error in the original for Hebrews 1 or 8.</note>, Deuteronomy 18:18, 19, John 1:14, Colossians 2:9, 2 Corinthians 6:16, Revelation 1:3, Hebrews 1:1, etc.*

B. Others, judging that the Apostle's intent is to exalt Jesus, as the mediator of the better covenant, above Moses, the mediator of the <term>imperfect <note>Original: "berispelyken," meaning "faulty" or "blameworthy," referring to the Mosaic covenant's inability to save.</note></term> covenant—so that the Hebrews might step over from Moses to the Christ, from the old and imperfect to the new and better, from the less glorious to the more glorious—are of the opinion that Paul alluded to what is recounted regarding Moses' face in *Exodus 34:20 and 2 Corinthians 3:13*; namely, that the face of Moses shone brightly after having spent forty days with the Lord on the mountain. See under **FACE OF MOSES**. However, regarding that accidental shining of Moses' face, it is noted that: a. this radiance did not come from Moses' inner being; b. it came to him from without and was accidental, a borrowed light; c. it did not remain with him permanently, but at best lasted only until his death; d. it only

<column-break/>

came to him after many of his years had passed.

But He of whom Paul spoke was and remained the glorious radiance of the Father, out of and through Himself, etc., by virtue of His nature an eternal generation.

C. Furthermore, one encounters learned men who think Paul might have had his eye on *Ezekiel 1 and 10*, where mention is made of the four living creatures which gave off fiery rays of light, constituting the Lord’s glory, *verse 28*. See under **LIVING CREATURES OF EZEKIEL**. This serves as a symbolic means of representing the Son of God, and the gracious and distinguished servants in and of Him in that kingdom.

D. Other scholars prefer the view that the reference is to the **Urim and Thummim**, on the high priestly breastplate—Truth and Light, or shining perfection—a symbolic representation of Him who is in the bosom of the Father, through and from whom is grace and truth, the speaking mouth of the Father, the light of the world. See under **BREASTPLATE**, under **URIM**, and **THUMMIM**.

E. Some again find it fitting to remember the names under which the Messiah, the Son of the Father, appears, being named and described as God’s Face, the Angel of the Lord’s Face, in whose innermost being is the name Jehovah, the Angel of the Covenant, etc. *Exodus 23:21, 22, etc., and 33:14, 15. Isaiah 63:9. Malachi 3:1.*

F. And so as not to present everything in vast detail, I say that a large number of learned writers believe Paul here has his eye on the natural sun, its light, rays, and reflection, which illuminates, warms, cherishes, and fertilizes the world; for which reason He also sometimes appears under such descriptions. *Psalm 36:10 and 84:12 and 89:16. Malachi 4:2. John 1:8, 9. John 8:12. Job 9:5. etc.*

One also finds among the scholars those who do not split or separate all these observations from one another, but judge that, since they are all good and relevant to the matter, they could be kept and united together, to take from each that which can help set the "radiance of glory" in the greatest luster and emphasis. However, we leave the intelligent reader full freedom of choice, while we take closer notice of the manner of speaking and the words belonging to it.

"Who being" <note>Original Greek: ὃς ὢν (hos on).</note>, who thus is present, thus was, before He set Himself at the right hand of God, and was crowned by the Father with honor and glory as God’s wonderful Son, "the radiance of (his) glory" <note>Original Greek: ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης (apaugasma tēs doxēs).</note>. "His" is not in the Greek, but it is added by our translators because the Son of the Father is being spoken of: since He is called the express image of His substance, etc.

<margin>God's Glory.</margin>
Glory <note>Original Greek: Δόξα (Doxa); Original Hebrew: כבוד (Kavod).</note> in respect to God, Moses says, is to be allowed to see and thoroughly know, *Exodus 33:18, 19 and 34*; it is the same as His name, through which He is glorious over all the earth in *Psalm 8*. One can very appropriately understand by God’s glory God’s all-surpassing excellence and eminence, on account of His essential virtues, attributes, and perfections, which He displays most illustriously in the works of creation, general...

# RADIANCE.

providence, governance, and especially in the work of grace, recreation, and the redemption of death-deserving, damned, and powerless sinners, through the discovery of His wisdom, omnipotence, goodness, justice, holiness, truth, immutability, love, and mercy.

**Glory** <note>Original Greek: Δόξα (Doxa)</note> and **Glory** <note>Original Hebrew: כבוד (Kavod)</note> correspond very well and signify something that is weighty and significant, held in high esteem, and greatly valued—something that strongly affects the eye and carries much weight in a person's judgment and heart.

Thus it is spoken of in *Nehemiah 9:5: Let them praise your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.* One cannot form a high enough conception of it within oneself, nor devise words or expressions powerful and emphatic enough to somewhat approach or equal this glory. Similarly, **Glory** <note>Original Greek: Δόξα (Doxa)</note> also signifies radiance, luster, shimmering splendor, and rays of light, whether from the sun or any other highly luminous and radiant body that is pure light; all the more so here, because this glory is Divine and is attributed to the Father, of whom the Son is a **radiance** <note>Original Greek: ἀπαύγασμα (apaugasma), meaning a light shining out from a source</note>, a **radiance of glory** <note>Original Greek: ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης (apaugasma tēs doxēs)</note>. According to the Hebrew manner of speaking and writing, this is the same as a glorious, powerful, very excellent, and eminent radiance.

<margin>Derivation of this word.</margin>
Regarding the derivation of this word, learned men have noted its origin and composition: it first descends from **light** <note>Original Greek: αὐγή (augē)</note>, a light and shine like that of the sun, or the day produced by the sun. From this comes the word **to shine** <note>Original Greek: αὐγάζω (augazō), αὐγάζειν (augazein)</note>, to illuminate or give off light; and subsequently **to beam forth** <note>Original Greek: ἀπαυγέω (apaugeō), ἀπαυγάζω (apaugazō)</note>. I give off bright rays, I flash, I glitter, in Latin **to gleam** <note>Original Latin: corusco</note>.

And so some have thought it could be understood in this way: that the Son is called a **radiance of glory**, as the Son of the Father, having life in himself just as the Father has it in himself (*John 5:26*). In this, the Son is like a gathering of the rays of divine virtues through eternal generation, which caused these divine rays gathered in him to shine outward, beaming out and through his words and miracles, etc.

One can consider the person of whom Paul speaks—as they say in the schools—**essentially** <note>Original Greek: ἐσωδῶς (esōdōs), meaning according to the inner essence</note>, regarding his divine nature and the same essence which he possesses alongside the Father and the Holy Spirit, being of one essence with the Father, of the same nature, majesty, power, and glory. And in that regard, he is not, strictly speaking, the Father's radiance, but one with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Thus he is equal to God (*Philippians 2:6*), the glorious and invisible God himself (*1 Timothy 6:16*).

<margin>Observation.</margin>
However, what must be carefully observed here is that Paul, with singular skill and prudence, brings forward the person of whom he speaks under the concept and description of the Son, heir, and Lord of all, through whom he made the world, so that he might immediately come into his inheritance.

In him, as the Son, is a reflection and collection of everything divine, of that which is in the Father, as Father, and which manifests itself in the Son, as Son—a light born from light, **light of light** <note>Original Latin: lumen de lumine, a central phrase from the Nicene Creed</note>, as they spoke at the Council of Nicaea.

<column-break/>

And insofar as he is the Son of the Father from all eternity, possessing the same essence and life, so he is one with the Father (*John 10:30*). He who sees and knows him, sees the Father (*John 10:9, 10, 18* and *1:2*). Therefore, he has the same glory (*John 1:14*), which glory he also possessed as the firstborn before all things, before the world was (*Proverbs 8, Colossians 1:15, John 1:5*).

And regarded as God's <term>Wonder-Son</term> <note>Dutch: Wonderzoon; a term emphasizing Christ’s miraculous and unique nature beyond standard filial descriptions.</note>, he has divine glory, or the glory of the godhead, which is his own along with the Father. This glory, arising from a melting together of all virtues and perfections, allows itself to be seen transparently and most discernibly in him and his works, as mentioned above. See under **ALPHA** and **OMEGA**.

Yet, we must also consider him—who is God's Wonder-Son and of one essence with the Father—as God, Savior, <term>Surety</term> <note>Dutch: Borg; a theological term for one who takes legal responsibility for the debt or sins of another.</note>, Mediator, and executor of the Father's counsel. After he appeared in the flesh for the work of redemption, he gave a reflection of what is in the Father, and of what the Father gave him as his Son to have in himself through eternal generation (*Exodus 23:33, John 5:26, Isaiah 63, Malachi 1, John 1:14*), passages also cited above. To that extent, there is a reflection of the Father upon the Son, so that by seeing and knowing him, one sees and knows the Father in the power of his own emphatic name, glory, and essential virtues. Thus one must understand the following testimonies: "he who sees me, sees the Father who sent me" (*John 10:30* and *14:9, 10, 11*), just as one sees and learns to know the sun through its light and rays. Therefore it is said that he is the image of the invisible God (*Colossians 1:15*) through the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (*2 Corinthians 4:6*).

And thus the Father, in, from, and through his Son, **made flesh** <note>Original Greek: ἐναρκωθείς (ensarkōtheis)</note> and revealed in the flesh, has caused his essential glory, his essential virtues, and perfections to shine forth and through. He caused the fullness of the Godhead to dwell in him bodily—truly and substantially, not shadow-like or as a mere example, and not for a short time, but forever (*Colossians 2:9*)—enclosing in him all treasures of wisdom and knowledge (*Colossians 2:3*), and consequently the wisdom of God (*Proverbs 8*), having become wisdom from God, etc. (*1 Corinthians 1:30*). He caused his manifold spirit to rest upon him (*Isaiah 11:2* and *61:1*) and that without measure (*John 3:34*). This spirit manifested itself in him not only very early, but with such power that everyone was rightly astonished by him (*Luke 2:40, 46, 47, 50*). Indeed, in this Wonder-Son of God, a ray of God's emphatic name—of purity, justice, and holiness—has appeared, in which God's image and glory may certainly be sought and placed (*Exodus 34, Ephesians 4, Colossians 3*).

Consequently, he is described as the righteous servant of God (*Isaiah 53:11*), as the glorious one from the midst of them (*Jeremiah 30:21*), God's holy one and favored one (*Psalm 10:10*), prefigured by the pure priests, perfect and clean sacrificial animals, and, according to experience, described as the holy one born of Mary (*Luke 1:35*), as he who knew no sin (*2 Corinthians 5:21*), as holy, innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners (*Hebrews 7:26, 1 Peter 2:22*), who committed no sin, nor was any deceit found in his mouth (*1 Peter 3:18*), etc. From all of which, having been properly noted, one perceives the following saying to spring forth: *John 1:14. The Word became flesh,*

# RADIANCE. AGATE.

...and *dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.* <note>Original: "en heeft onder ons gewoont, en wy hebben zyn heerlykheit aanschout..." referencing John 1:14</note>

Furthermore, one can consider the Son as the *radiance of glory*, causally, effectively, and ministerially <note>Original Latin: "causaliter, effective, ministerialiter"</note> in that he, *is the Son of the heavenly Father* <note>Original Greek: "υἱὸς τῆς πατρὸς ἐπουρανίου ἐστὶ"</note>, the Son of God revealed in the flesh. In this state, he made known his father’s name, virtues, and glorious attributes as the great prophet—as seen in Deuteronomy 18:18—and as the teacher of righteousness <note>Joel 2:23, John 1:4–9</note>. As John 1:18 says: *No one has ever seen God; the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has explained (him to us).* Matthew 11:27 adds: *All things have been delivered to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him.* In John 17:6 and 26, he says: *I have revealed your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world... and I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known.* This was according to the promise in Psalm 22:22: *I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you,* and Psalm 40:10: *I do not hide your righteousness in the midst of my heart; I speak of your truth and your salvation; I do not conceal your lovingkindness and your faithfulness in a great congregation.*

Indeed, he is the radiance of glory in his Divine acts and great miracles, which belong only to a formidable Deity <note>Psalm 72:18</note> and are attributed to the Messiah in prophecy <note>Isaiah 35:5-6</note>.

In him, upon him, and from him has appeared and shone forth a glorious radiance of divine virtues, converging in him as the active High Priest and sacrifice for sins. This occurred when he offered himself blameless to God through the eternal spirit as a sweet-smelling aroma <note>Ephesians 5:2, Hebrews 9:14, according to Psalm 40:6 and Hebrews 10:5-6</note>, from which we perceive a great radiance of God’s glory and virtues. Romans 3:24–26 states: *And are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Whom God put forward as a propitiation <term>propitiation: a sacrifice that restores a relationship</term> through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins... so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.* See also Romans 8:3: *For what the law was powerless to do because it was weakened by the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh to be a sin offering, and so he condemned sin in the flesh.* He did so to reveal his essential virtues, grace, and love in him <note>Job 33:26, Ephesians 1:6–10, 1 John 4:9–10</note>.

Finally, as Mediator, after he had humbled himself and made his soul an offering for sin <note>Isaiah 53:10, Philippians 2</note>, he was made a partaker of his throne, majesty, honor, and glory, and the high governance over all things <note>Matthew 28:18, Ephesians 1, Philippians 2:8–9, Colossians 1, Hebrews 1:3</note>.

I could say more if I did not strive for brevity. One may consult the works of Cocceius, Schmidt, Hoeke, Braunius, d'Outrein, Kreygten, etc. See also the entry for **SUN**, as some make comparisons to it in this context.

### AGATE, or AGATE STONE,
-> Shebo / Achates / Achates <-
<note>Hebrew: שבו / Greek: ἀχάτης / Latin: Achates</note>

<margin>Naming of the Agate stone.</margin>
This stone is found named *Shebo* <note>Hebrew: שבו</note> from *shaba*, meaning *he has taken and held fast*, as it is considered worthy to be taken, held, and preserved. Or it may come from the Arabic word *shaba*, meaning *he has been equal or become similar*, because the Agate stone possesses many colors and forms, containing within it the lines and images of many things. The word *Achates* is thought to come from *Achad* <note>Hebrew: עקד</note> due to the many spots with which this stone is set, permeated, and streaked—from which *Achod*, *Akod*, or *Akud* is the Hebrew term for *variously colored, streaked, spotted, and striped*. This is why the Agate is also called *perileukos* <note>Greek: περίλευκος</note> because of its white circular stripes which run through it.

It is clear that Agate stones come in all sorts of colors and that one finds many rare stripes, colors, paintings, and images in them. I could bring forth sufficient proof of this from many learned and well-known writers; so much so that Orpheus—or whoever took his name—could truly say that the Agate has as many as a thousand colors.

> *Drink the many-formed Agate with unmixed wine,*
> *The noble Agate, which sows every kind of shape.*
> <note>Original Greek: Καὶ πολυιδέα πῖνε μετ' ἀκρήτου βρομιοιό / Μόρφην παντοíην σπείμενον ἐσθλὸν ἀχάτην.</note>
>
> *The noble Agate is drunk in wine, which imitates a thousand colors,*
> *And all the forms of things.*
> <note>Original Latin: Nobilis in vino bibitur, qui mille colores, / Atque omnes rerum formas imitatur Achates.</note>
>
> That is:
>
> *One drinks the noble Agate in noble wine,*
> *The noble Agate, which shows us a clear appearance*
> *Of a thousand colors and endless forms.*

One may consult Boetius, Scaliger, Dieteric, Pliny, Bochart, Phaleg, etc., regarding this.

There is also the Agate stone of Pyrrhus <note>Pyrrhus: a King of Epirus famous for his gems</note>, rare and very famous among these same writers and others. In this Agate, the nine Muses and Apollo with a harp in his fist were distinctly seen—and so naturally that the spots and stripes, arranged by nature itself, ran through the stone so that each of the nine Muses kept her own characteristic mark and token.

It is said that they grow to such a weight and body that one can fashion bowls and drinking glasses out of them.

Some say that it was one of the stones in the breastplate of the High Priest, and that upon it stood the name of the tribe of Gad; others say Asher, whose portion was said to be rich and royal <note>Genesis 49, Joshua 19:24, Deuteronomy 33:24</note>.

It is well known that in our times the Agate is not of great value, but formerly, being rare, it rose to a high price; Pliny serves as a witness to this.

These stones are found in Germany and Bohemia, but the best are in the Indies. One also speaks of beautiful Agates found in Sicily by the river Achates, of which Pliny, Solinus, Isidore, and Bochart tell us.

As for what concerns the power and virtues of the Agate, they differ according to the color and type,

# AGATE. HAGAR.

...according to the testimony of the writers, regarding which matter I shall note something further:

<margin>Property of the Agate.</margin> It is called the "healthy stone": it is said to be useful against the stings of snakes and scorpions; that it makes a person eloquent, and makes a man fall in love with his wife; that the red Agate strengthens the sight; that the Eagle lays an Agate stone in its nest so that its young might be sufficiently armed against venomous pests, and other such things, which I cannot exactly give too much credit to; although I do believe that there is power in it, and that it serves as a singular ornament.

Nicolas Caussin <note>Nicolas Caussin (1583–1651) was a French Jesuit and polymath, known for his works on symbols and rhetoric.</note> remarks that the Agate stone, with its various colors and manifold images, is a symbol of the pleasant variation and change in tempering one's speaking or writing style, in which orators compete against each other for the prize. Angelo Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a prominent Italian Renaissance humanist and poet.</note> expresses himself on this as follows:

> *Here, rich eloquence clothes itself in various countenances,*
> *And now is carried along like a rushing torrent,*
> *In the manner of a river; now it dries up in a parched bed,*
> *Now it relaxes itself, now restrains its wanderings.*
> *Now it suits a simple style, now it shines full of charming*
> *Flowers.*
> <note>Original Latin: "Hic varios sese in vultus facundia dives / Induit & vasto nunc torrens impete fertur, / Fluminis in morem, sicco nunc aret in alveo, / Nunc sese laxat, nunc exspatiata coercet. / Nunc inculta decet, nunc blaudis plena renidet, / Floribus."</note>

Which words contain this meaning:

*Eloquence here takes on various forms.*
*Now it flows like the rush of a river.*
*Now it creeps slower like waterless streams.*
*Now it loosens the reins much wider in speaking.*
*Now it is unadorned, which suits it gracefully,*
*Then it walks in flowery dress and unusual ornament.*

<margin>Agate of Pyrrhus.</margin> He notes the Agate stone of King Pyrrhus <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus (c. 319–272 BC). Natural history lore claimed his favorite agate featured a natural depiction of Apollo and the nine Muses.</note> as a symbol of a wise man who possesses many and varied sciences within one and the same bosom, through which he makes himself very elegant and pleasant; for which he presents the excellent person of Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great (c. 330–379), one of the Cappadocian Fathers.</note>, who was very highly praised and valued by Gregory the Great.

If the name Asher <note>The OCR reads "Afterstan," likely a transcription error for "Aser," the tribe of Asher.</note> was engraved upon it, then I would well believe that its beauty and richness <note>The Dutch "vettigheid" (fatness/richness) refers to the blessing of Asher in Genesis 49:20.</note> could be represented by it to some extent, *Genesis 49:20, Joshua 19, Deuteronomy 33:24.* And then, in turn, Asher would be a symbol of the happy church—surpassing previous eras and much endured misery—in the latter days, to which all the great and small shall flow, and the church will experience a happy time and extend itself far and wide, adorned with all kinds of beautiful colors and qualities.

If the twelve stones on the breastplate of the high priest represent the twelve tribes and the twelve Apostles—who would judge the church built on the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets—and the church of the New Testament in the latter days, especially that city from heaven, *Revelation 21*, then the Agate and the Beryl are as significant as they are; and the names of the Apostles stood on those foundations, each having laid the foundation; so I would well believe that through these twelve glorious stones and foundations, the glory, luster, and ornament of the Gospel truth, and thus of the New Testament church, is made known. But since this is the eighth stone in the order of the holy temple construction and counting, and Matthew appears to us as the eighth Apostle in rank and order, it seems to me that one might have some suspicion as to whether he might not, with some ground, be compared to this Agate stone or beryl; see William Cave <note>William Cave (1637–1713) was an English church historian whose works on the lives of the Apostles were widely read.</note> regarding the life and virtues of Matthew.

<column-break/>

### AGAR or HAGAR. הגر <note>Hebrew: Hagar</note> *Agag.* <note>The heading likely includes "Agag" as a secondary entry or variant spelling in the source.</note>

THAT which will allow us to regard HAGAR or AGAR as a prototype or symbol is enclosed in the historical narrative of Moses, *Genesis 16 and 21*, and grounded in the interpretation of Paul, *Galatians 4:22, 23, etc.*, without whose explanation we would never have discovered the secret. It will then, I judge, not be entirely useless for me to give the history and bring some light to it before I move on to the secret meaning of the representation.

The one who comes into consideration here is the maidservant of Sarah, who perhaps had others as well. She is named Hagar, and with distinction regarding her nationality, she is called "the Egyptian"; in Arabic her name means *petra*, or *rock*.

<margin>Position of the Jews regarding Hagar.</margin> The Jews wish to maintain that this Hagar was the daughter of King Pharaoh, who, being at his court, was appointed as a lady-in-waiting to Sarah, given to her, and departed with her from Egypt. And the Chaldean translator Jonathan <note>Refers to Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> on *Genesis 16* seems to be of this opinion. And Rabbi Shlomo <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> adds that this happened when Pharaoh had seen God's wonders for Sarah's sake. However, others claim that Hagar was the maidservant of the Queen Widow Chuzia, who ruled the kingdom in place of her minor son, and that she then gave her to Sarah. But it is mere guesswork; nevertheless, there seems to have been something in Hagar—being born of Ham's lineage—that she fared better than the other maidservants, so that Sarah's eye fell upon her, whether because of her beauty, politeness, fresh youthfulness, graceful stature, or other gifts.

It was past Sarah's time due to her high years. And since she had never given birth, she seemed to have lost hope entirely, the more so because she had been barren for ten years after God's promise was made and her arrival in Canaan. She then, considering the matter hopeless, or perhaps imagining to herself that Abraham's seed would indeed become as numerous as the stars, but not necessarily through her specifically with Abraham, gave her husband this advice, without waiting for further explanation or clarification: he should go in to Hagar the Egyptian, saying perhaps, "Maybe I shall be built up out of or through her," that is, receive children for the continuation of our lineage and the support of my house, so as to obtain the promised seed, the multitude of children, and the promised inheritance.

<margin>Strange advice from Sarah.</margin> A strange and rare piece of advice from a woman to her husband, both strengthened by an unusual appearance of God and a promise. I hardly believe that Sarah will be followed by other women. It was also not all too fitting; they might perhaps later complain about it with Sarah. Meanwhile, it also happens that men do not delay with Abraham in this matter until they are requested to do so by their Sarahs.

Abraham had that weakness, that he listened to his Sarah, whose proposal seemed quite earnest. For the text says: *and Abraham listened to the voice of Sarah.* He would, in my opinion, have done just as well if he had resisted his wife with reason in this matter and had in no way complied with her. In the meantime, I see that it would go...

# H A G A R.

I 2

...happened with the consent of his wife, and upon her advice; one can also well conclude that he was not weary of his Sarah, nor did he prefer a foreign woman, nor did lustful fleshly drives and impulses spur and prick him toward this. Rather, he consented to it both to give his wife satisfaction and because he perhaps thought that God would indeed give him a seed from his own loins, but precisely not out of and by his old Sarah.

<margin>Sarah’s Displeasure.</margin>
When Abraham, following the advice of his wife, had gone in to Hagar the handmaid, she conceived immediately and became pregnant. But take note: regret soon "impregnated" Sarah’s mind. For this Hagar, having become Abraham's concubine, once she was pregnant by her master, began to behave strangely and acted differently than before. She became bold because Abraham had gone in to her, that he showed her some affection, and had perhaps taken her as his concubine; she was proud that she had conceived immediately, while her mistress had remained childless for so long. She perhaps began to hope for the inheritance and to count on it. She may have let herself go quite a bit, showing herself to be haughty, speaking sharply and tartly to Sarah, and withdrawing her service with disdain. Perhaps also Sarah, becoming jealous, imagined that Abraham made quite a fuss over Hagar and exalted the handmaid above her, and so on.

Certainly, there must have been something in Sarah's thoughts that made her so disturbed, causing her to speak so sharply and earnestly against her husband, as one can read in the writings of Moses, so that the Lord Himself was chosen as judge over the matter.

It would indeed seem as if Hagar played the part of a Xantippe <note>Xantippe was the wife of the Greek philosopher Socrates, traditionally depicted as a shrewish and difficult woman.</note> and a total shrew in Abraham's absence, or that Abraham, because she was pregnant, allowed her a bit too much; at the very least, Sarah takes the matter in such a way that Abraham is implicated, as if he were largely to blame for that injustice, that spite, and that grief by supporting the handmaid.

It also appears that Abraham wished to yield quite a bit to his disturbed and disgruntled wife. He leaves Hagar—even though she was pregnant by him—to the treatment of his wife, so that it might be made manifest that he in no way exalted or loved the handmaid above his wife.

<margin>Hagar humbled by Sarah.</margin>
Sarah avails herself of this opportunity and humbles Hagar. Whether Sarah caused her to be despised, or no longer desired that she be recognized or known by Abraham and kept as his concubine, or whether she had her beaten by others and imposed upon her the duties of a handmaid of a lower rank, or something else; it must have been something quite insulting and painful. Since Hagar’s mind could not endure it, she took flight and departed toward Shur, where the Angel of the Lord found her at a fountain of water in the wilderness. This was a city, so it is said, situated diagonally across from Egypt, perhaps named Shur <note>The author suggests a connection between the name Shur and the "outcome" or "departure" (uitkomste) of her journey.</note> because of the event, since the Angel of the Lord, or the Lord the Angel of the Covenant, met her there. His question and the proposal of her duty to return and humble herself under Sarah’s hands—along with the added promise of a numerous seed, the naming of the son she was to bear, and his character, nature, and occupation—are noted more closely by Moses; as are Hagar’s observations regarding her situation, the promise of the Angel, and the fact that she bore Abraham a son.

In the meantime, Ishmael grew up, and a long

<column-break/>

time passed before Sarah became pregnant. According to what the continuation of the history shows, Hagar returned and remained with her Ishmael in the house of Abraham.

<margin>Isaac Born.</margin>
Finally, in accordance with the Divine promise, Sarah bears a son who is named Isaac. As he grows up, he is weaned, on which occasion Abraham had a great feast prepared. During this event, Ishmael mocked Isaac, perhaps through the instigation and doing of his mother Hagar. It must have been a painful insult and a dangerous business, for Paul explains it thus, and Sarah took it so seriously and took such offense that she demanded Hagar and her son be cast out, and by no means inherit together; a thing which Abraham could not entirely approve of. However, the revelation of the Lord made him follow the pleasure of his wife, being somewhat encouraged by the renewed promise that He would bless her seed and make it very numerous. Thereupon Abraham provides her with water and bread in a bottle; and with that she wandered on and came into the wilderness of Beersheba. When the supply of water was exhausted, she became despondent, placed her son under the bushes, withdrew from him a bowshot's distance, and cried in her distress to the Lord. He heard the boy's voice, spoke to Hagar with a renewal of the previous promise, and opened her eyes so that she saw a well of water, filled the bottle, and gave the boy a drink, etc.

This is given only in passing regarding the history and the singular event (for I shall speak of Sarah and Isaac hereafter, and here only in the distance and for the sake of the thread of history). We must now more closely weigh what this household of Abraham was an example of, and what considerations can be made regarding this occurrence on a Scriptural foundation, alongside the experience within the literal Jewish race.

<margin>The Author’s reflections on this.</margin>
In this regard, I must say beforehand that, although various considerations and remarks can be made about these events and encounters, one must nevertheless look at the most essential and principal parts. One acts most safely here by following Paul's framework and adhering strictly to his interpretation. I judged, therefore, that Hagar and Sarah represent two covenants: Hagar the Old Covenant of Sinai, bearing children (as Hagar did her son) into outward bondage; Sarah the New Testament or Covenant of Zion, bearing free sons by the power of the promise (*Jeremiah 31, Ezekiel 37:8*) and heirs of the promises of the covenant. Those who are and remain in bondage with Hagar and her son do not inherit these promises; they are therefore cast out, both the covenant and those covenant-members, along with the old nature of the covenant. But let us look at both a bit more closely.

It shows us, then, that Abraham would have two kinds of seed, but from two different women, whose fertility would appear at different times. One seed would be fruitful, yet one would be in bondage and the other free, according to their mothers; one would be an heir and remain in the house, the other would indeed have an inheritance, but distinct from the inheritance of the other, and would be cast out. That there would be a conflict between the two mothers and their children, followed by the rejection and casting out of the one.

<margin>Meaning of Hagar.</margin>
Hagar signifies in Arabic a rock, a stony mountain. Sinai is a stony mountain in rocky Arabia—sandy, high, barren, and dry—which is represented by her (*Galatians 4:24, Acts 7*), from which the Law...

# AGAR. AGUR.

...is proclaimed in herself, without the added promises of grace, possessing nothing to make one fruitful or lively, *2 Cor. 3*, and thus the Old Testament or covenant was proclaimed for servitude with flashes of thunder and lightning.

Hagar, who gives birth to the Old Testament or the covenant of servitude, precedes Sarah in the order of birth; Sarah represents the New Testament or the covenant that gives birth to freedom. *Isaiah 54.*

Between the two mothers and their children, a dispute arises, particularly at the weaning feast. When the banquet of the New Testament was prepared, and Sarah—representing the New Testament or the covenant among the Jews, and especially among the Gentiles—began to bear free children, *Isaiah 26, Matthew 22, Luke 18*, and the weaning time came to teach the free sons to unlearn the "ABC" <note>The author uses "a, b, c" to refer to the basic "elements of the world" or the elementary rituals of the Old Law.</note> of the world, or to accustom them to firmer and more perfect food, and to learn to stand in their freedom; then there was a violent dispute between the Jewish Synagogue, impregnated by the law, and the Apostolic Christian Church, already fruitful through the promises of the better covenant. People argued regarding the Law and the Gospel, freedom and servitude, faith and the works of Moses' law. They slandered, persecuted, and despised one another; the Jews disputed the Gentiles' adoption and exaltation, *Luke 18, Hosea 2, Psalm 50:20, Song of Solomon 5:6, Galatians 3, 4, and 5*, etc. Thereupon the Old Testament or covenant, along with its adherents who held to their mother—though their preservation and salvation were greatly desired, *Acts 13, Romans 9 and 11*—was cast out and rejected from the inheritance, insofar as the Apostles left them, *Acts 13*, turning to the Gentiles. Thereafter they were openly cast out when the city and temple were destroyed, and so that other "heaven and earth" <note>A metaphor for the Jewish religious and political world order.</note> being rolled up, passed away; and the Jewish land, the heritage of the Old Testament, was given over to the bow <insert>destruction</insert> and to the Gentiles for devastation. *John 8:35, Matthew 8:12, 21, and 24:15, Psalm 118, Daniel 9:27, Isaiah 11:4*, etc., *Hosea 2 and 3.*

They were taken up like a great mountain and cast into the sea of Heathendom, wandering everywhere as if in a wild and parched desert, now fainting from hunger and thirst, from the looking for and longing for the Messiah, now that the flask of their comfort, promise, and hope is quite empty due to the elapsed time. And although they are in a land (for the most part) where the fountain is—since the desert has become a garden of Eden, a fountain of waters—nevertheless, because their eyes are blinded so that a veil lies over them, *2 Cor. 3*, they do not see the opened fountain, the welling waters, or the streams of living water, *Psalm 36:10, John 7:37, 38, 39, Zechariah 13:1*. Yet the time approaches when their eyes shall be opened, when they shall return to Sion and see the opened springs, and turning to the Lord, they shall draw the healing waters with joy from the fountain of life. *Zechariah 12:10, 11, Isaiah 12:3, 2 Cor. 3:16, Romans 11:25, 26*, etc.

This now concerns Hagar. Regarding the discourses on ISMAEL, SARAH, and ISAAC, that which is somewhat connected to this material should be noted further; though I believe I have already clearly enough stated the essentials according to Paul's aim, and therefore I shall leave it at this and move on to something else, after I have added one more thing here; namely:

That some regard Agar or Hagar as portraying a personification of sinners who, having withdrawn themselves from submission to God and what is good and right, still wish to flee and hide from the Lord like Adam, Cain, and Jonah, to escape His punishment and rebuke, etc.—this I can well tolerate. It is certainly best to submit <note>The Dutch idiom "het hooft in den schoot te leggen" literally means 'to lay one's head in the lap,' signifying surrender or submission.</note> and return to the Lord in submission, with repentance and sorrow, to find and obtain grace and forgiveness; to which the angels of the congregation constantly pray, exhort, and advise sinful, rebellious, and straying mankind. *Isaiah 55:6, 2 Cor. 5:20, 1 Peter 3:11, 22, 25.*

However, I rightly disapprove of the fact that some make an Agar or Hagar out of "Right Reason" and a Sarah out of "Scripture," using these names to rail scornfully against their brothers; or that they mix together those two sciences which have distinct foundations; or that they speak so slightingly of the "natural light" from God, who is the fountain of both.

### AGUR, אגור, ἄγυρ.

<margin>Uncertainty of the name AGUR.</margin>
One lives by <note>original: "אגור", Agur</note> *Proverbs 30:1*, just as by some other names. Among both ancient and modern scholars, it is not fully agreed whether it is a proper given name or a surname.

<margin>What AGUR means.</margin>
It appears to us that Agur descends from <note>original: "אגר", agar</note> meaning "he has *collected*" or "*gathered* together," as one does with fruits, either in heaps or into bundles; and so Agur is understood to mean one who is *collected* or *gathered* anew, or one who has *gathered* or is *collected*. And it is said that "Jakeh" <note>original: "יקה", Jakeh</note> signifies one who is *obedient*. Some also believe that Solomon bears this name in remembrance and recollection that, having sinned grievously and wandered from God and the way of godliness, he was mercifully brought back, converted, and came to himself. Others say it is because he brought forth many proverbs and sublime matters from his heart with his mouth, and *gathered* them together for the general benefit.

That he was the son of Jakeh is true, insofar as the root word signifies such a person who is obedient and submissive; for he was a son of David, that man after God's own heart, who had the reputation of pleasing the Lord and walking in all His ways.

I have noticed that some are of the opinion that Agur, alongside the other names, is a proper name, not a by-name or surname taken to represent, sketch, or call to mind something—namely: the name of this or that prophet, a great, wise, earnest, and godly man, who either recorded these proverbs appearing in this chapter, or from whom Solomon took these proverbs contained in this chapter and wrote them down for the general benefit.

What one subsequently learns of Agur—as if he had no understanding—does not prejudice his singular and great wisdom; no more than when one applies it to any other prophet or great, learned, and famous man of that time. For one may think that he wishes to show how he was, in and of himself, by nature foolish and senseless in divine matters; and therefore, that he could not have such sublime things without divine discovery and illumination, as well as out of modesty. Certainly, no one notices his own ignorance...

### MAPLE, PLANE TREE, or SYCAMORE; called by some *Acer* or *Marrubium*; but preferably named *Platanus*, and by others the PLANE TREE.

<margin>Description of the Maple and Plane tree.</margin>
**M**APLE, or PLANE TREE, *Platanus*, in Greek πλάτανος, from πλάτος or πλατὺς, meaning *wide, broad, or long*; since it stretches itself out very far, not only in height but also in breadth. The *Acer* or Maple-wood tree has a great similarity to it, being distinguishable by its sharp-pointed leaves, though it is not as broadly extended as the *Platanus* or Plane tree, nor does it have such wide, spreading leaves. Some also call them "Oren" <note>An archaic Dutch term for certain broad-leafed trees.</note>; it is a wood with variegated veins and colors, not found in great abundance; a wood from which things were shaped, especially writing tablets; as Ovid speaks of it in his *Love Poems*:

> — *To Venus, Naso dedicates his faithful servants:*
> *Though recently, you were but cheap Maple wood.* <note>original: "Veneri, fidas sibi, Naso ministras / Dedicat: at nuper vile fuistis Acer." Ovid (Naso) is offering his writing tablets to the goddess.</note>

->That is:<-

> *This tablet, which has served him faithfully*
> *In his amours, Naso offers to Venus now.*
> *How poorly this maple-wood was regarded before.*

Propertius:

> *I was a maple stump, carved by a hurrying sickle.*
> *A poor God in a pleasing city, before Numa ruled.* <note>original: "Stipes acernus eram, properanti falce dolatus. / Ante Numam gratâ pauper in urbe Deus." Numa Pompilius was the legendary second king of Rome.</note>

->That is:<-

> *I was a lowly stick of maple wood long ago,*
> *But formed in haste and carved into an image,*
> *Of a penniless God, before Numa ruled the realm.*

But more on this in the future.

<margin>Where it is planted and found.</margin>
The *Platanus* or Plane tree has soft and tender leaves; it is quite large and broad, stretching itself far and wide, and creating a thick and grand shadow or canopy; for this reason, it is placed not only in gardens but also on streets, by fountains, and near houses, which I can confirm with many examples from antiquity.

Martial in the ninth book of his *Epigrams*:

> *In the middle of the house, embracing the entire household,*
> *Stands a plane tree, Caesar’s, with thick foliage.* <note>original: "Aedibus in mediis, totos amplexa penates, / Stat platanus, densis Caesariana comis."</note>

->That is:<-

> *A Plane tree is seen in the middle of the house,*
> *Which encompasses the whole building with its thick leaves.*
> *It was planted by Caesar, laden with triumphs.*

<column-break/>

Petronius:

> *A noble Plane tree had spread summer shadows.* <note>original: "Nobilis aestivas Platanus diffuderat umbras."</note>

->Which is to say:<-

> *The broad Plane tree provided shade in the season.*

<margin>It loves water and the waterside.</margin>
It especially loves moisture and gladly spreads its roots by fountains and waters. Ovid:

> *As much as the Plane tree delights in the stream, as much as the poplar in the wave,*
> *And as the marshy reed in the muddy ground.* <note>original: "Quam Platanus rivo gaudet, quam populus undâ, / Et quam limosâ canna palustris humo."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Just as the Plane tree prefers to grow by a brook,*
> *The poplar by the water, and the reed again in a place*
> *That is marshy.*

<margin>Dedicated to the Spirits.</margin>
It seems that this tree was dedicated to the *Genii*, or the spirits who appeared in the name of the Gods and were called Guardian Spirits. It was believed that every person had such a guardian spirit over them, to whom they also dedicated or prepared a table. These Guardian Spirits are mentioned in Greek verses:

> *To every man at birth, a spirit is given*
> *To be the guide of his entire life.* <note>original: "Ἅπαντι δαίμων ἀνδρὶ τῷ γενομένῳ / Ἅπαντος ἐστι μυσταγωγὸς τοῦ βίου."</note>

[*To everyone on earth a spirit is given,*
*Who protects him and watches over his life.*]

<margin>Performances are held under it on birthdays.</margin>
Special signs of honor were seen regarding this on birthdays. See Persius in his second satire, Tibullus in the second song of his second book, and also in the fourth of the sixth book. See also Kipping regarding the specific Gods of the nations, p. 71, etc. For this reason, the spirit is depicted in the form of a reasonably tall man, with a covering on his back, entwined with a wreath of the Plane tree: Kipping, *On the Statues of the Gods*, p. 155. This is why Ovid called it the *platanus genialis* (the genial or festive plane tree), in *Metamorphoses* book 10, fable 2.

<margin>People used to sacrifice under it.</margin>
It is recounted that people used to sacrifice under the thick branches and leaves of this tree. Homer in the second book of the *Iliad*:

> *We performed perfect hecatombs to the immortals*
> *Under a beautiful plane tree.* <note>original: "ἔρδομεν ἀθανάτοις τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας / καλῇ ὑπὸ πλατανίστῳ." A hecatomb was a great public sacrifice of 100 oxen.</note>

->That is:<-

> *We offered to the gods*
> *Our sacrifice of a hundred bulls*
> *In the shadow of the Plane tree.*

<margin>A shady tree for pleasure.</margin>
People ate there, drank there, and slept under it. It was a tree of pleasure and esteem.

Virgil in the fourth book of the *Georgics*:

> *And the plane tree providing shade for drinkers.* <note>original: "Atque ministrantem platanum potantibus umbram."</note>

Which Vondel <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679), the preeminent Dutch poet and playwright.</note> translates thus:

> *He planted the Plane tree there,*
> *The shade-giver for the feast.*

<margin>Long-lived and keeping its leaves.</margin>
It is judged that these trees reach many years of age, and it is said of some Maples that they retain their leaves even in winter, as Varro and Theophrastus...

<meta>This page continues the entry on the Maple and Plane tree (Ahorn/Platanus), following the initial description of its physical characteristics and name origins. It moves from historical anecdotes about King Xerxes to the medicinal properties described by classical authors, and finally to the symbolic interpretation of the tree in political and religious contexts.</meta>

# MAPLE.

...which Theophrastus, Pliny, Ursinus, and others have left to us.

<margin>The folly of King Xerxes regarding this tree.</margin>
It is told of King Xerxes that while he was in Lydia with his army, he let them rest for an entire day simply because of the sight of a Plane tree. With what folly and superstition! He hung it with golden chains and jewels, as if the tree became more excellent through this, or as if a greater holiness flowed within it than in other trees. He even stationed a guard over it and, upon finally departing, had a golden Plane tree made. See *Aelian, book 2, chapter 14.* <note>Claudius Aelianus was a 3rd-century Roman author; this story illustrates Xerxes' legendary eccentricity.</note>

It is said that it was found in the Peloponnese and Macedonia, and that the Romans transported it to their country from a far and foreign climate.

<margin>It was watered with wine.</margin>
The rumor goes that people used to water this tree with wine. See Pliny, Macrobius, Ursinus, etc., and *Martial, book 19, Epigram 68.* <note>Actually Book 9; Martial often praised the shade of the Plane tree.</note>

> *The shade grows more joyful when pure wine is poured.* <note>original: "Crescit ab affuso laetior umbra mero."</note>

->That is:<-

> [If you water the tree with noble wine,
> Its shade shall be all the more pleasant.]

<margin>The grapevine would not grow upon it.</margin>
It was considered sterile and "unmarried"—not because it bore no fruit, but because the grapevine would not grow upon it, or because its fruits were of no use. <note>In antiquity, elms were "married" to vines because they supported them; Plane trees, though beautiful, were not used for viticulture.</note>

> *Martial, Book 3, Epigram 57.*
>
> *Not arranged with idle myrtle-groves,*
> *Nor the widowed plane, nor the clipped boxwood.* <note>original: "Non otiosis ordinata myrtetis / Viduaque platano, tonsilique buxeto."</note>

->That is:<-

> Not at all planted with widowed Planes,
> Or Myrtles unfit for bearing fruit,
> Or Boxwood, which one shears.

> And *Horace, Book 2, Ode 15.*
>
> *And the celibate Plane shall surpass the elms.* <note>original: "Platanusque coelebs / Evincet ulmos."</note>

->That is:<-

> And the unmarried Plane
> Shall far surpass the elms.

However, whatever is grafted onto it bears fruit, according to the testimony of Pliny, Porta, etc.

> *Thus sterile planes have borne strong apples.* <note>original: "Sic steriles platani malos gessere valentes."</note>

->That is:<-

> The sterile Plane has brought forth apples.

It is held that it must also be counted among other trees mentioned in *Genesis 30:37, Ezekiel 31:8, and Ecclesiasticus 24:19.*

Dioscorides relates in Book 1, chapter 91, that its leaves and nuts (or the rough, uneven, and woolly pea-like seeds) are cooling and dry. He notes that when these are crushed and mixed with vinegar, they make a good plaster, and that its bark, boiled with vinegar and used as a mouthwash, is very healing for toothaches. <note>Dioscorides was a Greek physician and the father of pharmacology.</note>

<margin>Use of its bark, leaves, and seeds.</margin>
It is told that if the leaves are placed in a stork's nest, they protect the nest and eggs against the night-owl, and that swallows are shy of it. See *Aelian, Meursius, Matthiolus, Lemnius,* etc. It is also said that the dust from the "peas" harms the eyes, ears, and voice; but the tender leaves boiled in wine, when the liquid is rubbed on the eyelids, dry up humors and are good against inflammation and swelling. The "peas" boiled in wine are said to be beneficial against snake bites, according to Dioscorides, Durantius, etc. Read these verses:

> *The Plane loves rivers and springs; and watered with wine*
> *It rejoices, and by its nature draws in moisture and cold.*
> *The bark and seeds dry out, and heal foul*
> *Ulcers; likewise the leaf repels scabies and leprosy.* <note>original: "Flumina amat Platanus, fontesque; meroque rigata / Gaudet, & humorem naturâ, & frigora ducit. / Cortex, & pilulae exsiccant, & sordida sanant / Ulcera, tum scabiem folium, lepramque repellit."</note>

->That is:<-

> The Plane loves the stream and springs, and with wine
> For its coolness and moisture it shall be sustained.
> The bark and pit dry up and heal the rough sores,
> The leaf knows how to turn away evil scabs and itches.

<column-break/>

<margin>Some who hid under it in storm, heat, and tempest suffered harm from it afterward, of which this can be a symbol.</margin>
I have noted that Themistocles observed the experience of the Plane tree, under which many hide during storms, burning heat, and downpours, both to be covered and refreshed. Yet, when the weather is good, they rob it of its foliage and branches. He noted this as a symbol of those who have enjoyed singular services, benefits, and protection from various people—and indeed from prominent personages—in times of persecution or other misfortune; but when the storm is over and there is prosperity and calm, they not only forget the benefit but sometimes even attack their benefactor and protector, speaking ill of him, robbing him repeatedly, and seeking to injure and diminish his widespread power. For so we read in Cassinus and elsewhere:

> *He compared himself to Plane trees, under which they run*
> *when caught in a storm. But when fair weather comes, those*
> *passing by pluck at them and revile them.* <note>original: "Ταῖς πλατάνοις ἀπείκαζεν αὑτὸν, ἃις ὑποτρέχουσι, χειμαζόμενοι. γενομένης δ' εὐδίας τίλλουσι παρερχόμενοι καὶ λοιδοροῦσι."</note>

->That is:<-

> He compared himself to Plane trees, to which
> everyone takes refuge in bad weather: but when the
> storms are over, they jerk and pluck at it, and
> rail against it without respect.

<margin>How kings and princes can be compared to the Antichrist in this regard.</margin>
The kings and peoples who have hidden under the high Antichristian Plane tree, having eaten, drunk, and fornicated, shall themselves eventually rob him and clip his wide-spreading branches of dominion (*Revelation 17*) and make them desolate. Its fruits are not good for the soul's nourishment; one suffers hunger there. The leaves and all its parts, though measured out quite broadly and beautiful to the eye—having an appearance of godliness—nevertheless have no healing power and do not take away the inner ailments of the soul. There is only the shadow of virtue, no power of godliness, for sound doctrine is not found there.

<margin>Also sometimes hiding under it in storm, heat, and tempest, they suffered harm from it afterward, of which this can be a symbol.</margin> <note>This margin note repeats the theme of the previous column's symbolism.</note>
One finds great Plane trees—empires, states, kings, princes, the wealthy, the powerful, and the worldly-wise—but they provide only a shade and protection to the church and pious subjects against the heat of persecution. Yet, from these taken together, one generally perceives little lasting and good fruit. Only this do the church and the pious sometimes gain: that under their reign they may lead a quiet, still, godly, and honorable life...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical and medicinal discussion of the Maple or Plane tree (Ahorn), transitioning from classical history to its symbolic representation of the Jewish state and the Kingdom of Christ. It then begins a new alphabetical entry for "Field" (Akker), exploring its literal and spiritual meanings in the Bible.</meta>

# MAPLE. FIELD.

...be able. *Ezekiel 17 and 31; 1 Timothy 3:2.* <note>The author uses these citations to illustrate the growth and height of symbolic trees.</note>

2.
<margin>The Jewish civil state.</margin>
The Jewish civil and ecclesiastical state was a Maple, extending itself far and wide, of great name and luster in the world, and uniquely beautiful in form. Many "lovers" <note>original: "boelen"; refers to political or idolatrous allies as described in the prophets.</note> came running to it. But when this tree began to wither, becoming fruit-less and leafless, it was plucked and stripped by its lovers, and finally uprooted by the *Assyrians, Babylonians*, and *Romans*, according to the divine oracles and the ignited beacons of judgment. *Jeremiah 4; Ezekiel 33; Matthew 3:10 and 8:12.*

3.
<margin>Divine protection in the kingdom of the church.</margin>
One may also, in a certain respect, see the Plane tree as a symbol—as it uniquely spreads itself out to provide shade, creating a certain safety from heat, downpours, and winds, where one can be refreshed and covered—representing the protection and covering of the Almighty, and the vast extent of Jesus' kingdom of heaven and His overshadowing grace; this can be done quite aptly. *Psalms 8:1-2 and 72:7-8; Isaiah 43; Psalms 36:8 and 91:1; Isaiah 4:6; Song of Solomon 2; Matthew 4.*

But it is also true that many came to nest under the shadow of this tree, this kingdom of heaven, seeking only outward rest while contributing very little of use to the tree itself.

And certainly, even if it was so beautiful that the tree healed many Jews, as well as Jewish Christians, *Gnostics*, and others who called upon the name of Jesus and settled beneath its shelter, nevertheless, no one ever brought greater dishonor and damage to this tree than they did.

4.
<margin>Healing through and under the Maple tree, Jesus.</margin>
Just as the fruits and leaves of the Maple tree, when boiled in wine, have been good and healthful for the healing of many of the aforementioned ailments; so surely with the excellent tree, Christ, are His leaves and monthly fruits for the healing of soul-sicknesses—His blood, Spirit, Word, and Sacraments—with the wine of comforting and heart-strengthening grace, kindled by the fire of the Spirit and pure love. *Malachi 4:2; Revelation 22; Zechariah 12:1; 1 John 1:7; 1 Corinthians 6:11; Psalm 119:11, 50, 77, 93, 111.*

5.
<margin>The fertilizing power of Jesus.</margin>
This tree has the quality of making whatever is grafted into it fruitful. *Romans 11; John 15:5-6.* The natural branches, the Jews, gave no good fruit; the foreign Gentiles gave fruit according to their grafting. *Romans 11.* The Jewish branches did not allow the vineyard of the Apostolic Christian church to flourish; they oppressed them, and for this reason, this vine had to be brought to the wilderness and open places.

6.
<margin>The ignorant night-owls do not spend the night under Him.</margin>
The blind night-owls and bats—who, flying by night, belong to the night of sin, ignorance, and heresy—do not actually nest under this tree. *Revelation 21:8-27; 1 Corinthians 6:10; 2 Corinthians 6:14-16; Isaiah 34.* These, although they would most like to harm the pure and merciful storks, <note>In traditional European emblem books, the stork was a symbol of piety and gratitude.</note> are instead driven away before they can achieve their aim, *Psalm 105; Acts 8; Isaiah 2:18-20; Zechariah 13:2;* etc., or they are enlightened and converted like Saul. *Acts 9; 1 Timothy 1:13-16; Isaiah 2:3; Ephesians 5:8; Titus 3:3; 1 Corinthians 6:11.*

7.
<margin>A school of practice held under the Maple by the fountains.</margin>
Just as in Athens the academy or school of learning was held under the Plane tree, and the Maple of King Dionysius in Sicily provided a nursery school under its shade; and as it often stood by fountains and rustling waters—so surely under the Maple tree Jesus, in His far-reaching kingdom of grace and His overshadowing, is a fountain of life, *Psalm 36.* There are His brooks and streams of water, *Psalm 1 and 46;* there is the school of wisdom; there one is made wise unto salvation through the scriptures, *2 Timothy 3:16;* taught by God, *Isaiah 54:13;* receiving the anointing of the Holy Spirit, *1 John 2:20.* There are many teachers and fathers in Christ Jesus, *Ephesians 4:12;* a wisdom that is not known by the worldly-wise, *1 Corinthians 2;* at which the wise men in Athens were completely taken aback, *Acts 17.* And whatever wisdom might have been fetched from Sicily, it was but foolishness compared to this. *1 Corinthians 2:6, 7-13, 14.*

But let this be enough regarding this tree; I shall pass on to something else.

<column-break/>

<margin>This brought spiritually.</margin>

### FIELD, FIELD-WORKERS, FIELD-WORK, <note>original Hebrew: שדה (*sadeh*); Greek: *ἀγρὸς* (*agros*); Hebrew: אכר (*ikkar*); Greek: *γεωργὸς* (*georgos*)</note> etc. *Ager*, <note>Latin: Field</note>

<margin>What a "Field" signifies.</margin>
It is commonly known that by "Field" one can understand a piece of land, large or small, which is kept for sowing or planting, whether inside or outside the cities. Sometimes it is taken somewhat more broadly, and at other times more narrowly and specifically, for someone's property and inheritance, or for a prominent land that a reasonably numerous people cultivates and occupies. *1 Samuel 6:1; Joel 2:22; Hosea 10:4 and 12:12.*

<margin>Understood as larger or smaller.</margin>
In another way, more figuratively and by way of imagination, it is taken as a symbol of the world; and in the world in the New Testament for those places where the seed of the Word is cast into the earth, which, following Christ's command, had to be done everywhere. *Matthew 28* and *Mark 16.* When this is uniquely fruitful, it represents the state or condition of the productive church under the ministry of the Word and the Sacraments, and under the fertilizing influence and working of God's Spirit. *Isaiah 60, 44, and 35; Hosea 2; Amos 9; etc. Matthew 13 and 21; Mark 13; etc.*

<margin>Figuratively for the world, and places where God's Word is preached.</margin>
See Vitringa in his *Treatise on the Gospel Parables*, page 63, Paragraph 13. <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note> To this Son of Man, as a Lord of the house, a field is attributed, which is called *His* field. The Lord Jesus explains this as the world; though by "the world" we must not understand this entire structure of heaven and earth that we commonly call the world, nor even the entire earth which we inhabit (called in the Greek the *οἰκουμένη* <note>original: *oikoumene*; the "inhabited world"</note> by the holy writers), but those parts of the inhabited world where Jesus Christ has His kingdom and church. This is also evident because what is here called "the world" is subsequently explained as the "kingdom of Christ," *verse 41.* We must take note of this here because it will be of use and benefit in the following explanation. Now, the world or the earth which we inhabit is called a field for no other reason than that, in a certain sense particularly defined in this parable: 1. It is capable of receiving, nurturing, and preserving a certain seed within itself. 2. Specifically, that part of the world in which the church is found, which is worked and cultivated, above other lands inhabited by wild and barbaric peoples, which in the Holy Scripture are compared to the sea and the wilderness. Thus, under the same symbol, the globe is aptly distinguished into the dry land and the sea. *Haggai 2:7.*

# MAPLE.

<margin>The folly of King Xerxes regarding this tree.</margin>
...Theophrastus, Pliny, Ursinus, etc., have left to us.

It is told of King Xerxes that while he was in Lydia with his army, he let them rest for an entire day at the sight of a Maple tree, hanging it (with what folly and superstition!) with gold chains and jewels, as if the tree became more excellent through this, or as if a greater holiness flowed within it than in other trees. He even stationed a guard there, and upon finally departing, he had a golden Maple made. See *Ælian, book 2, chapter 14.* <note>Xerxes I, the Persian King, was famously captivated by a large Plane tree, an event often cited by ancient authors as an example of his eccentricities.</note>

It is said that it is found in the Peloponnese and Macedonia, and that the Romans transported it to their land from a distant and foreign climate.

<margin>They watered it with wine.</margin>
The saying goes that people used to water this tree with wine. See Pliny, Macrobius, Ursinus, etc., Martial book 19, Epigram 68. <note>The Roman practice of "watering" Plane trees with wine was a sign of extreme luxury and status.</note>

->*The shade grows more pleasant from the poured-out wine.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Crescit ab affuso laetior umbra mero."</note>

->That is:<-

> [If you water the tree with noble wine,
> Its shade shall be the more pleasant.]

<margin>The vine would not grow upon it.</margin>
It was considered sterile and "unmarried," not because it bore no fruit, but because the grapevine would not grow upon it, or because its fruits were of no use. <note>In Roman viticulture, trees like the Elm were "married" to vines to support them; the Plane tree was often called "unmarried" (coelebs) because it was used only for shade.</note>

->*Not arranged with idle myrtle-groves*<-

However, whatever is grafted onto it bears fruit, according to the testimony of Pliny, Porta, etc.

->*Thus sterile planes have borne strong apples.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Sic steriles platani malos gessere valentes."</note>

->That is:<-

> The sterile Plane has brought forth apples.

It is maintained that it must also be counted among other trees mentioned in *Genesis 30:37, Ezekiel 31:8, and Ecclesiasticus 24:19.* <note>The author equates the "Armon" tree of the Hebrew Bible with the Plane/Maple tree.</note>

<margin>Use of its bark, leaves, and seeds.</margin>
Dioscorides relates in book 1, chapter 91, that its leaves and nuts—or the rough, uneven, and woolly pea-like seeds—are cold and dry by nature. He states that when rubbed and mixed with vinegar, they make a good plaster, and that its bark, when boiled with vinegar and used as a mouthwash, is very healing against toothache.

It is said that if the leaves are placed in a stork's nest, they protect the nest and the eggs against the screech owl, and that swallows are shy of it. See Ælian, Meursius, Mathiolus, Lemnius, etc. It is also noted that the dust from the "beans" and "peas" <note>referring to the seed balls of the Plane tree</note> damages the eyes and ears; but that the tender leaves boiled in wine, when the liquid is rubbed on the eyelids, dry up the humors and are good against inflammation and swelling. The "peas" boiled in wine are said to be beneficial against snake bites, according to Dioscorides, Durantus, etc. One may read these verses:

*The Plane loves the streams and springs, and watered with wine*
*It rejoices, and by its nature draws moisture and cold.*
*The bark and the little pills dry up and heal foul*
*Ulcers, while the leaf repels the mange and leprosy.*

<margin>Some, having hidden under it in storm, heat, and tempest, later damage it, of which this can be an emblem.</margin>
I have noted that Themistocles observed the experience of the Maple <note>Themistocles was an Athenian politician; the story illustrates political ingratitude.</note>, under which many hide during storms, burning heat, and downpours, both to be covered and refreshed, yet whom they rob of its foliage and branches when the weather is good. He noted this as an emblem of those who, having enjoyed extraordinary services, benefits, and protections from various people—and indeed from prominent personages—in times of persecution and other misfortunes, not only forget the kindness when the storm has passed and prosperity and calm return, but sometimes even attack their benefactor and protector, speak ill of him, rob him repeatedly, and seek to injure and diminish his widespread power. <margin>How the kings and princes fare under the realm of the Antichrist.</margin>
The kings and nations who have hidden under the high Antichristian Maple—eating, drinking, and fornicating—shall eventually rob it themselves, and clip its wide-spreading branches of authority (*Revelation 17*) and make it desolate. <margin>The Jewish civil state.</margin>
The Jewish civil and ecclesiastical state was a Maple, extending itself far and wide, of great name and luster in the world, and remarkably beautiful in form. Many "lovers" <note>In a biblical context, "lovers" often refers to allied nations or false idols.</note> came running to it; but when this tree began to wither, becoming fruitless and leafless, it was plucked and stripped by its lovers, and finally uprooted by the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Romans, according to the divine oracles and the "kindled beacons" <note>A metaphor for prophetic warnings or divine signs of judgment.</note> of God. *Jeremiah 4; Ezekiel 33; Matthew 3:10 and 8:12.*

<margin>The Divine protection and overshadowing in the kingdom of the church.</margin>
If one also wishes to see the Plane tree <note>original: "Plaanboom"</note> as a symbol—since it spreads itself out remarkably to create a canopy of shade, providing safety from heat, downpours, and winds, and offering refreshment and cover—it can quite aptly represent the protection and covering of the Almighty. If ever the fruits and leaves of the Maple tree, boiled in wine, have been good and restorative for the healing of many of the aforementioned ailments, then certainly, in the preeminent tree that is Christ, His leaves and monthly fruits are for the healing of the soul’s sicknesses. <margin>The ignorant night-owls do not spend the night under Him.</margin>
The blind night-owls and bats—those who fly by night and belong to the night of sin, ignorance, and heresy—do not actually nest under this tree. *Revelation 21:8–27; 1 Corinthians 6:10; 2 Corinthians 6:14, 15, 16; Isaiah 34.* Though these creatures would love to harm the pure and merciful storks <note>The stork was often a symbol of piety or "pure" believers in emblem books of this period.</note>, they are driven away before they can achieve their aim, *Psalm 105; Acts 8; Isaiah 2:18, 19, 20; Zechariah 13:2;* etc., or they are enlightened and converted along with Saul. *Acts 9; 1 Timothy 1:13–16; Isaiah 2:3; Ephesians 5:8; Titus 3:3; 1 Corinthians 6:11.*

<margin>A school of practice held under the Maple by the fountains.</margin>
Just as Athens had its academy or school of learning under the Plane tree, and the Maple of King Dionysius in Sicily provided a nursery under its shade—and as it stood not infrequently by fountains and rustling waters—so certainly under the Maple tree of Jesus, in His far-reaching kingdom of grace and His overshadowing,
