### FIELD, HUSBANDMEN, FIELDWORK.
**Hebrew: *Sadeh* (שדה) / Greek: *Agros* (ἀγρὸς),**
**Hebrew: *Gev* (גב) / *Ikkar* (אכר) / Greek: *Georgos* (γεωργὸς) etc. Latin: *Ager*.**

<margin>What a Field signifies.</margin>
In general, it is known that by "Field" one can understand a piece of land, large or small, which is kept for sowing or planting, whether inside or outside of cities. Sometimes it is used somewhat more broadly, or again more narrowly and specifically, for someone’s property and inheritance, or for a prominent land that a reasonably numerous people cultivate and occupy. *1 Samuel 6:1; Joel 2:22; Hosea 10:4 and 12:12.*

<margin>Understood in larger or smaller terms.</margin>
Otherwise, more figuratively and by way of imagination, it is taken as a symbol of the world. In the New Testament, it represents those places where the seed of the Word is cast into the earth, which, following Christ’s command, had to be done everywhere. *Matthew 28* and *Mark 16.* When this field is remarkably fruitful, it represents the state or condition of the fruitful church under the ministry of the Word and the Sacraments, and under the fertilizing influence and working of God’s Spirit. *Isaiah 60, 44, and 35; Hosea 2; Amos 9; etc. Matthew 13 and 21; Mark 13; etc.*

<margin>Figuratively for the world, and specifically for the places where God’s Word is preached.</margin>
See Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note> in his *Treatise on the Evangelical Parables, page 63, Paragraph 13.* To this Son of Man, as a Master of the House, is attributed a field, which is called "His field." The Lord Jesus Christ explains this as "the world," though by "the world" we must not understand the entire constitution of heaven and earth that we commonly call the world; nor even the entire earth which we inhabit, called *oikoumene* <note>original Greek: οἰκουμένη, meaning the "inhabited world."</note> by the holy writers. Rather, it refers to those parts of the inhabited world where Jesus Christ has His kingdom and church. This is also evident because what is here called "the world" is subsequently explained as the "kingdom of Christ," *verse 41.* We must take note of this here, as it will be of use and utility in the following explanation. Now, the world or the earth which we inhabit is called a field for no other reason than that, in a certain sense (which is particularly defined in this parable): 1. It is capable of receiving, nurturing, and preserving a seed within itself. 2. Specifically, that part of the world where the church is, which is labored upon and cultivated, stands above other lands inhabited by wild and barbaric peoples, which in Holy Scripture are compared to the sea and the desert. Thus, under this same symbol, the globe is elegantly distinguished into the dry land and the sea. *Haggai 2:7.*

# MAPLE.

<margin>The folly of King Xerxes regarding this tree.</margin>
...phrastus, Pliny, Ursinus, etc., have left to us.

It is told of King Xerxes that while he was in Lydia with his army, he let them rest for an entire day simply to gaze upon a Plane tree <note>The Dutch "Ahorn" here refers to the Plane tree (Platanus), famously associated with Xerxes in classical accounts.</note>. With what folly and superstition he hung it with golden chains and jewels, as if the tree became more excellent by this, or as if a greater holiness flowed within it than in other trees! He even stationed a guard over it and, upon finally departing, had a golden Maple made. See *Aelian, book 2, chapter 14.*

It is said that it is found in the Peloponnese and Macedonia, and that the Romans transported it to their land from a distant and foreign climate.

<margin>It was watered with wine.</margin>
The saying goes that this tree was watered with wine. See Pliny, Macrobius, Ursinus, etc., *Martial, book 19, Epigram 68.*

->*The shade grows more pleasant from the pouring of pure wine.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Crescit ab affuso laetior umbra mero."</note>

->That is:<-

> [If you water the tree with noble wine,
> Its shade will be all the more pleasant.]

<margin>The grapevine would not grow upon it.</margin>
It was considered unfruitful and "unmarried," not because it bore no fruit, but because the grapevine would not grow upon it, or because its fruits were of no use.

->Martial, *Epigram 57, book 3.*<-

->*Not arranged with idle myrtle-groves, nor with the widowed plane tree, nor the clipped boxwood.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Non otiosis ordinata myrtetis / Viduaque platano, tonsilique buxeto."</note>

->That is:<-

> By no means planted with the widowed Plane,
> Or Myrtles unfit to bear fruit,
> Or the Box-tree, which one shears.

->And Horace, *Ode 15, book 2.*<-

->*And the bachelor Plane tree shall surpass the elms.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Platanusque coelebs Evincet ulmos."</note>

->That is:<-

> And the unmarried Plane
> Shall far surpass the elms.

However, that which is grafted onto it bears fruit, according to the testimony of Pliny, Porta, etc.

->*Thus sterile plane trees have borne strong apples.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Sic steriles platani malos gessere valentes."</note>

->That is:<-

> The unfruitful Plane has brought forth apples.

It is held that it must also be counted among other trees mentioned in *Genesis 30:37, Ezekiel 31:8, and Ecclesiasticus 24:19.*

<margin>Use of its bark, leaves, and seeds.</margin>
Dioscorides relates in book 1, chapter 91, that its leaves and nuts—or the rough, uneven, and woolly pea-like seeds—are cold and dry in nature. He states that when these are crushed and mixed with vinegar, they make a good plaster, and that its bark boiled with vinegar is very medicinal for toothaches when used as a mouthwash.

It is said that if the leaves are placed in a stork's nest, they protect the nest and the eggs against the night owl, and that swallows are shy of it. See *Aelian, Meursius, Matthiolus, Lem-*

<column-break/>

-nius, etc. It is noted that the dust from the beans and peas <note>referring to the seed pods</note> damages the eyes and ears; but the tender leaves boiled in wine, when the liquid is brushed onto the eyelids, dry up the humors and are good against inflammation and swelling. The "peas" sodden in wine are said to be beneficial against snake bites, according to Dioscorides, Durantus, etc. One may read these verses:

*The Plane tree loves rivers and springs, and rejoices when watered with wine; it draws moisture and cold by its nature. The bark and the small pods dry out and heal foul ulcers, while the leaf repels the itch and leprosy.*
<note>original Latin: "Flumina amat Platanus, fontesque, meroque rigata / Gaudet, & humorem naturâ, & frigora ducit. / Cortex, & pilulae exsiccant, & sordida sanant / Ulcers, tum scabiem folium, lepraque repellit."</note>

->That is:<-

> The Plane loves the stream and springs, and with wine
> It shall be sustained for its coolness and moisture.
> The bark and pit dry up, and heal the rough sores,
> The leaf knows how to turn away evil mange and itching.

<margin>Some who have hidden under it during storm, heat, and tempest damage it; of what this can be a symbol.</margin>
I have noted that Themistocles observed the experience of the Maple—under which many hide during storms, burning heat, and downpours to be covered and refreshed, yet whom they rob of its foliage and branches when the weather is good. He noted this as a symbol <term>zinnebeelt; an emblem or allegorical image</term> of those who, having enjoyed exceptional service, benefits, and protection from others (and indeed from prominent persons) in times of persecution or other misfortune, not only forget the kindness when the storm has passed and prosperity and calm return, but sometimes even attack their benefactor and protector, speaking ill of him, robbing him repeatedly, and seeking to injure and diminish his widespread power. For so we read in Cassinus and elsewhere:

->*He compared himself to Plane trees, to which people run for cover; but when the weather is fair, those passing by pluck at them and revile them.*<-
<note>original Greek: "Ταῖς πλατάνοις ἀπείκαζεν αὑτὸν, ἃις ὑποτρέχουσι, και μαζόμενοι. γενομένης δ' εὐδίας τίλλουσι παρερχόμενοι καὶ λοιδοροῦσι."</note>

->That is:<-

> He compared himself to Plane trees, to which
> everyone takes refuge during bad weather: but when the
> storms are over, they tug and pluck at it, and
> rail against it without respect.

<margin>How the kings and princes become under the kingdom of the Antichrist.</margin>
The kings and peoples who have hidden under the high Antichristian Maple, who have eaten, drunk, and committed "fornication" <note>In the biblical sense of spiritual unfaithfulness or political intrigue.</note>, shall eventually rob it themselves and "clip the wings" of its widely praised branches of authority, leaving it desolate. *Revelation 17.* Its fruits are not good for the soul’s nourishment—one suffers hunger there. Its leaves and all its parts, though spread out wide and beautiful to the eye, having a "form of godliness," nevertheless have no healing power and do not take away the internal ailments of the soul. There is only the shadow of virtue, not the power of godliness, for sound doctrine is not found there.

<margin>Also some other princes and kings.</margin>
One finds great Maple trees: empires, states, kings, princes—rich, powerful, and worldly-wise—but they offer only a shade and protection to the church and pious subjects against the heat of persecution. Yet from these together, one generally perceives little lasting or good fruit. Only this do the church and the pious sometimes gain from them: that under their reign, they may lead a quiet, still, godly, and honorable life...

# MAPLE. FIELD.
<meta>Catchword: §. 14.</meta>

...could. *Ezekiel 17 and 31; 1 Timothy 2:2?* <note>The original cites 1 Tim. 32, but as that book only has 6 chapters, it likely refers to 1 Timothy 2 or another passage.</note>

<margin>The Jewish civic state.</margin>
The Jewish civic and ecclesiastical state was a Plane tree, stretching itself far and wide, of great name and luster in the world, and of an exceptionally beautiful form: many lovers came running to it. But when this tree began to wither—fruitless and leafless—it was plucked and stripped by its lovers, and finally uprooted by the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Romans, according to the divine oracles and the kindled beacons of judgment. *Jeremiah 4; Ezekiel 33; Matthew 3:10 and 8:12.*

<margin>The Divine protection and overshadowing in the kingdom of the church.</margin>
If one also wishes to see the Plane tree in a certain respect as a representation—insofar as it uniquely spreads itself out and creates a shade where one can be safe from heat, downpours, and winds, being refreshed and covered—of the protection and covering of the Almighty, and the wide-reaching extent of Jesus’ kingdom of heaven, and His overshadowing; one can do so quite aptly. *Psalm 8:1, 2 and 72:7, 8; Isaiah 43; Psalm 36:8 and 91:1; Isaiah 4:6; Song of Solomon 2; Matthew 4.*

But at the same time, it must be noted that many came to nest under the shadow of this tree, this kingdom of heaven, seeking outward rest, yet brought little benefit to the tree itself.

And certainly, although it was such that the tree healed many Jews, and Jewish Christians, Gnostics, and others who called upon the name of Jesus gathered and took shelter beneath it, nonetheless, no one has ever brought greater dishonor or damage to this tree than they did.

<margin>Healing through the health-giving <note>original: "ongezonden," likely a typo for "gezonde" (healthy) or "gezonden" (sent).</note> hornbeam <note>original: "hornboom," here used as a synonym for the Ahorn/Plane tree.</note> Jesus.</margin>
If ever the fruits and leaves of the Maple/Plane tree, boiled in wine, were good and restorative for the healing of many of the aforementioned ailments: then certainly, in the case of the eminent tree, Christ, His leaves and monthly fruits are for the healing of the soul's ailments—His blood, Spirit, Word, and Sacraments, with the wine of comforting and heart-strengthening grace, kindled by the fire of the Spirit and of pure love. *Malachi 4:2; Revelation 22; Zechariah 12:1; 1 John 1:7; 1 Corinthians 6:11; Psalm 119:11, 50, 77, 93, 111.*

<margin>The fruit-bearing power of Jesus.</margin>
This tree has the quality that it makes fruitful whatever is grafted into it, *Romans 11; John 15:5, 6.* The natural branches, the Jews, gave no good fruit; the strange Gentiles gave fruit according to their grafting, *Romans 11.* The Jewish branches did not allow the vineyard of the Apostolic Christian church; they oppressed it, and for this reason, this vine had to be brought to the wilderness and open places.

<margin>The ignorant night owls do not spend the night under Him.</margin>
The blind night owls and bats—those who, flying in the night, belong to the night of sin, ignorance, and heresy—do not actually nest under this tree, *Revelation 21:8-27; 1 Corinthians 6:10; 2 Corinthians 6:14, 15, 16; Isaiah 34.* These, although they would dearly love to harm the pure and merciful storks <note>The stork was a traditional symbol of piety and gratitude.</note>, are instead driven away before they can achieve their aim, *Psalm 105; Acts 8; Isaiah 2:18, 19, 20; Zechariah 13:2.* etc., or they are enlightened and converted along with Saul. *Acts 9; 1 Timothy 1:13-16; Isaiah 2:3; Ephesians 5:8; Titus 3:3; 1 Corinthians 6:11.*

<margin>A school of exercise held under the Maple by the fountains.</margin>
If in Athens they had the academy or school of learning under the Plane tree, and if the Maple of King Dionysius in Sicily became a nursery under its shade—since it stood not infrequently by fountains and rushing waters—then certainly under the Maple tree, Jesus, in His wide and far-reaching kingdom of grace and His overshadowing, there is a fountain of life, *Psalm 36.* There are His little brooks and streams of water, *Psalm 1 and 46.* There is the school of wisdom; there one becomes wise unto salvation through the Scriptures; *2 Timothy 3:16.* Taught by God; *Isaiah 54:13.* Receiving the anointing of the Holy Spirit; *1 John 2:20.* There are many teachers and fathers in Christ Jesus, *Ephesians 4:12.* A wisdom that is not known by the worldly-wise; *1 Corinthians 2.* At which the wise men in Athens were utterly astonished; *Acts 17.* And whatever wisdom might have been fetched from Sicily, it was but foolishness compared to this. *1 Corinthians 2:6, 7-13, 14.*

<margin>This brought to a spiritual conclusion.</margin>
But let this be enough regarding this tree; I shall move on to something else.

# FIELD. ALABASTER.

<margin>The world-field of Christ.</margin>
§. 14. The world is called the field of Christ, or of the Son of Man, insofar as it was promised by God the Father to the Son: first, according to the <note>original: "vreeraat"</note> counsel of peace—that He would delight in the world and allow it to be governed and ruled by Him according to His good pleasure. Second, the world was also brought forth by the Son, *Proverbs 8:11, Job 10.* Therefore, the earth is the Lord’s and all its fullness, *Psalm 24:1,* specifically that Lord who, in the continuation of that Psalm, is called the King of Glory. See the application and transition on page 69.

Those who are now under this ministry of the Word, accompanying the seed of the Word with spiritual fruitfulness; who are plowed, mowed, bedewed, and sprinkled—having been cleansed of the weeds of destructive feelings, teachings, impulses, and the effects of the sinful flesh—and grow up in the knowledge and grace of Christ, are called <term>God’s husbandry</term> <note>original: "godtsakkerwerk," literally "God's field-work," a reference to 1 Corinthians 3:9</note> and building, shoots of His planting, His vineyard leaves, etc., in the Holy Scriptures.

Regarding this field and its cultivation, we can observe that the common field of the world, of which every person and congregation is a part, is by itself—in the eyes of God—barren of wholesome and saving good, and is occupied with the weeds, thorns, and thistles of foul sentiments, reprehensible morals, heresies, and damnable effects of the flesh and spirit. *Romans 3, Galatians 5:19, 2 Corinthians 3:5.*

In this field, the good seed of the Word must be cast, *1 Peter 1:23, Matthew 13.* It must be moistened so that one can build upon the first foundations, to teach, exhort, rebuke, comfort, promise, and threaten, *1 Corinthians 3:6, 7, 8.* And such tasks require diligent husbandmen, who otherwise perform fruitless labor and do no good. *Proverbs 12:11 and 13:4 and 28:19 and 24:27-30, 2 Timothy 2:6, James 5:7, Isaiah 53:1.*

To be lazy and idle, or to sow bad seed and the weeds of foul doctrines and sentiments, is the work of hostile, lazy, and false workers, *Matthew 13 and 21:33 to 42, Mark 12, Luke 20,* etc. The good workers are called by God, the Supreme Husbandman, made capable, and appointed by Christ, *John 15, Matthew 21:23, etc., Mark 12:1, Luke 20:9, Isaiah 61, Psalm 68:12, Ephesians 4:12.* However, whatever the performance and active busyness of the builders may be, everything ends in vain without divine testing and fruit-making. Therefore, the water of His Spirit and the warmth of grace and love must animate everything, making it live and be fruitful, *1 Corinthians 3 and 15, Isaiah 35 and 44 and 55.*

Heavy is God’s judgment when He takes away spiritual fruitfulness and the seed of the Word, along with the sowers, *Isaiah 32:10, etc., Jeremiah 17, Amos 8:11, Joel 1:8, 9, etc.*

Everyone must then take care not to neglect the means of grace or spend them in debauchery; likewise, the sowers and husbandmen must ensure they cast good seed into the earth and love no slumber. Rather, to avoid punishment, according to the Roman laws (see <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author</note> Gellius book 4, chapter 12; <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian</note> Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 2), they must cultivate the field of the Lord with all diligence and faithfulness, with patience, awaiting the fruits and a favorable reward for their labor, *2 Timothy 2:7 and 4:7, 8, 1 Corinthians 9:17, 18, James 5:7.*

This was a matter and a way of acting which, in the Parable of *Matthew 22:5,* etc., was taken very poorly, when it was said: *Come to the Wedding, but they, paying no mind, went away, one to his field, the other to his trade.*

<column-break/>

This description undoubtedly portrays in general how corrupt, vain, and worldly-minded the human heart usually is—pursuing worldly and temporal things and goods more than spiritual and heavenly ones, and being more strongly set on the flesh than on the spirit. But in particular, this Parable was suited to the disposition of most Jews in the time of Christ and the Apostles, who were so preoccupied with "fat" Canaan that they rejected the excellent truth and goods of the Kingdom of Heaven offered to them by Jesus. It is manifest from all their dealings that they had no, or very little, understanding of the spiritual and lasting salvific goods of the Messiah; for if they had possessed a right understanding of Abraham’s blessings and the Messiah’s goods, they would have cared more for the Messiah’s righteousness. But lacking that understanding and right vision, they were mostly concerned with worldly goods. *To have was to have, and to get was an art.* <note>A Dutch proverb implying greed or pragmatism over morality.</note> *See Hosea 12:8, 9, Isaiah 5:8, Amos 8:3-6, Micah 6:10-12.*

On this, see <note>Campegius Vitringa, a prominent Dutch theologian</note> Vitringa on the Parables of the New Testament, page 462, etc., along with the learned remarks of Mr. <note>Johannes d'Outrein, a Dutch preacher and scholar</note> d'Outrein.

### ALABASTER, <term>Ἀλάβαστρον</term> <note>original Greek: Alabastron</note>, *Alabastrum* <note>original Latin: Alabaster</note>.

ALABASTER is a type of stone that grows in Carmania <note>An ancient province of the Persian Empire</note>, Cappadocia, and elsewhere: reasonably hard, cold, and cool, which can be hollowed out to make vessels and flasks useful for various things; just as it is also used for ornament and support. Columns, floor tiles, and other things are shaped from it. They are of various colors—white, black, honey-colored, etc.—and also run through with various veins, stripes, and colors. This is too well known to us to waste time on.

<margin>Power of Alabaster.</margin>
It is recounted that when burnt and mixed with resin, it softens all kinds of hardness, and mixed with wax, it stills stomach pain, and taken with milk, it stops diarrhea.

That it was used of old to make vessels, jars, and flasks to enclose precious oil and fragrant ointment, so that the strength might not evaporate and the natural coldness might preserve the spiced oil and ointment, is clear from countless writers. However, it is also true that not all the vessels for storing precious ointment and oil, though called "Alabaster," were actually formed from alabaster stone. They were also made of certain wood, silver, gold, glass, etc., as one can read in *Pliny book 13, Pollux book 6, Herodotus in Thalia, Aelian book 12, Dioscorides book 5, Theocritus, the Author of the Etymologicum Magnum, Vossius's Oratorical Institutions book 4, chapter 8, Epiphanius, Dilherrus, Dietericus's Antiquities of the New Testament, Hofmann's Universal Lexicon, Heinsius's Exercises, Bynaeus's "Christ Crucified," etc.*

<margin>Interpretation of the alabaster vessels.</margin>
Let this be enough regarding the literal sense of Alabaster. One could consider it—used for jars, flasks, ointment, and oil vessels, run through with all kinds of colors—as a symbol of Abraham's children formed out of stones, in whom all kinds of colors of various virtues for spiritual beauty are placed, with the oil of grace, sweet comfort, and good gifts of grace, through which they spread a good scent from themselves.

### ALOE, אהלות <note>Hebrew: ahaloth</note> .ἀλοὴ <note>Greek: aloē</note>, Aloe.

<margin>Two distinct plants named Aloe.</margin>
The name ALOE is said to be given to two very different plants: namely, to the spicy tree *Aloa*, which grows in *India* and *Arabia*, called by some *Sandalum*, *Agallochum*, and other names. A very fragrant wood used for incense, perfumes, and scented ointments, which is likely referred to in *Psalm 45:9. Proverbs 7:17. Song of Solomon 4:14.*

<margin>Symbol of Christ's Cross.</margin>
In ancient times, people used to chew the wood or rinse the mouth with its sap to prevent bad breath and produce a pleasant breath, according to the testimony of Dioscorides and Paulus Aegineta; this has been interpreted by some as a symbol of Christ's Cross.

> *The holy teacher refreshes the heart with a vital scent:* <note>original Latin: "Cor recreat doctor vitali sanctus odore:"</note>
> *Who always turns the wood of the Cross in his mouth.* <note>original Latin: "Qui semper lignum versat in ore Crucis."</note>

-> That is: <-

> *The holy teacher strengthens the heart with lovely scents,*

# FIELD. ALABASTER.

<margin>The world as Christ's field.</margin>
§. 14. The world is called the field of Christ, or of the Son of Man, insofar as it was promised by God the Father to the Son according to the council of peace <note>original: "vreeraat"; this refers to the theological concept of the *Pactum Salutis*, an eternal covenant between the Father and the Son</note>, that He should delight in the world and allow it to be governed and ruled by Him according to His good pleasure. 2. The world was also brought forth by the Son, *Proverbs 8:31, Job 10*, therefore the earth is the Lord's, and all its fullness, *Psalm 24:1*, specifically that Lord who, in the continuation of that Psalm, is called the King of Glory. See the application and transfer on page 69.

Those who are under this ministry of the Word, accompanying the seed of the Word with spiritual fruitfulness; who are plowed, fertilized, dewed, watered, and cleared of the weeds of destructive feelings, doctrines, impulses, and effects of the sinful flesh; and who grow in the knowledge and grace of Christ, are called in Holy Scripture "God's field-work" <note>original: "godtsakkerwerk"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 3:9, "ye are God's husbandry"</note> and building, shoots of His planting, His vineyard foliage, etc.

Regarding this field and its cultivation, we may observe that the common field of the world, of which every person and congregation is a part, is of itself—in the sight of God—barren of wholesome and soul-saving good. It is overgrown with weeds, thorns, and thistles of foul sentiments, blameworthy morals, heresies, and damnable effects of flesh and spirit. *Romans 3, Galatians 5:19, 2 Corinthians 3:5.*

Into this, the good seed of the Word must be cast *1 Peter 1:23, Matthew 13.* It must be moistened to build upon the first foundations: to teach, admonish, rebuke, comfort, promise, and threaten *1 Corinthians 3:6, 7, 8.* And such a task requires diligent husbandmen, who otherwise perform fruitless labor and achieve no benefit. *Proverbs 12:11 and 13:4 and 28:19 and 24:27-30, 2 Timothy 2:6, James 5:7, Isaiah 53:1.*

To be lazy and idle, or to sow bad seed and weeds of foul doctrines and sentiments, is the work of hostile, lazy, and false workers *Matthew 13 and 21:33 to 42, Mark 12, Luke 20, etc.* The good workers are called by God, the Supreme Husbandman, made capable, and appointed by Christ *John 15, Matthew 21:33, etc., Mark 12:1, Luke 20:9, Isaiah 61, Psalm 68:12, Ephesians 4:12.* Yet, whatever may be said of the performance and active busy-ness of the builders, everything ends in vanity without divine watering and fructification. Therefore, the water of His Spirit and the warmth of grace and love must animate everything, making it live and be fruitful. *1 Corinthians 3 and 15, Isaiah 35 and 44 and 55.*

Heavy is God’s judgment when He takes away spiritual fruitfulness and the seed of the Word, along with the sowers. *Isaiah 32:10, etc., Jeremiah 17, Amos 8:11, Joel 1:8, 9, etc.*

Every person must then take care not to neglect the means of grace or spend them in dissolution; likewise the sowers and husbandmen must ensure they cast good seed into the earth, loving no slumber, but—to escape punishment according to the Roman laws (see Gellius *book 4, chapter 12;* Dionysius of Halicarnassus *book 2*)—cultivate the field of the Lord in all diligence and faithfulness, with patience, awaiting the fruits and the favorable reward of their labor. *2 Timothy 2:7 and 4:7, 8, 1 Corinthians 9:17, 18, James 5:7.*

It was a matter and a practice which was very poorly received in the Parable *Matthew 22:5, etc.*, when it was said: *Come to the Wedding*, but they, *not regarding it, went their way, one to his field, the other to his merchandise.*

<column-break/>

This description represents, without doubt, how generally corrupt, vain, and worldly-minded the human heart is, chasing after worldly and temporal things and goods more than spiritual and heavenly ones, and that one is more strongly set upon the flesh than upon the spirit. Specifically, however, this Parable was suited to the disposition of most Jews in the time of Christ and the Apostles, who were so preoccupied with the "fatness" of Canaan <note>referring to the physical land of Israel as a land of plenty</note> that they rejected the excellent truth and goods of the Kingdom of Heaven offered to them by Jesus. It is manifest from all their dealings that they had no, or very little, perception of the spiritual and lasting blessings of the Messiah; for if they had possessed a right understanding of Abraham's blessings and the Messiah's goods, they would have cared more for the Messiah's righteousness. But lacking that perception and right vision, they were mostly concerned with *worldly goods*. To have was to have, and to get was an art. See *Hosea 12:8, 9, Isaiah 5:8, Amos 8:3-6, Micah 6:10-12.*

On this, one may see Vitringa on the Parables of the New Testament, page 462, etc., along with the learned remarks of Mr. d'Outrein.

### ALABASTER, *Ἀλάβαστρον* <note>Greek: Alabastron</note>, *Alabastrum* <note>Latin: Alabastrum</note>.

<margin>Alabaster.</margin>
ALABASTER is a type of stone that grows in Carmania, Cappadocia, and elsewhere: reasonably hard, cold, and cool, which can be hollowed out to make vessels and bottles useful for various things; just as it is also used for ornament and support, being formed into columns, floor stones, and other things. They are of various colors: white, black, honey-colored, etc., also shot through with various veins, stripes, and colors. This is too well known to us to waste time upon it.

<margin>Power of Alabaster.</margin>
It is recounted that when burnt and mixed with resin, it softens all kinds of hardness, and mixed with wax, it stills stomach pain, and taken with milk, it stops diarrhea.

That it was used of old to make vessels, jars, and bottles to enclose precious oil and fragrant ointment, so that the potency might not evaporate and the natural coldness might preserve the spiced oil and ointment, is clear from countless writers. However, it is simultaneously true that all the vessels for the containment of precious ointment and oil, though called <term>Alabaster</term>, were not precisely formed from alabaster stone. They were sometimes made of certain wood, silver, gold, glass, etc., as one may read in Pliny *book 13*, Pollux *book 6*, Herodotus *in Thalia*, Aelian *book 12*, Dioscorides *book 5*, Theocritus, the author of the *Etymologicum Magnum*, Vossius *Institutes of Oratory book 4, chapter 8*, Epiphanius, Dilherrus, Dieterich's *Antiquities of the N.T.*, Hofmann's *Universal Lexicon*, Heinsius' *Exercises*, Bynaeus’ *The Crucified Christ*, etc.

<margin>Application of the alabaster vessels.</margin>
Let this suffice according to the letter regarding Alabaster. One could consider it, used for jars, bottles, and oil vessels and shot through with all kinds of colors, as a symbol of Abraham's children formed from stones, in whom all kinds of colors of various virtues are placed for spiritual beauty, with the oil of grace, sweet comfort, and good gifts of grace, through which they spread a good scent from themselves.

Otherwise, one may also understand here the bottle of lov—

### ALOE, <note>Hebrew: *Ahalot* (אהלות); Greek: *aloe* (ἀλοὴ)</note>, Aloe.

<margin>Two different plants named Aloe.</margin>The name ALOE is said to be given to two very different plants: namely, to the spicy tree *Aloa*, which grows in India and Arabia, called by some *Sandalum*, *Agallochum*, or other names. It is a very fragrant wood used for incense, perfumes, and scented ointments, which is likely what is referred to in *Psalm 45:9; Proverbs 7:17; Song of Solomon 4:14.*

<margin>Symbol of Christ's Cross.</margin>Since ancient times, people used to chew the wood or rinse the mouth with a decoction of it to ward off bad breath and produce a pleasant breath, according to the testimony of Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose work was the primary source for herbal medicine for 1,500 years.</note> and Paul of Aegina. This practice has been interpreted as a symbol of Christ’s Cross.

> The holy teacher refreshes the heart with a life-giving scent:
> Who always turns the wood of the Cross in his mouth.
> <note>original Latin: "Cor recreat doctor vitali sanctus odore: / Qui semper lignum versat in ore Crucis."</note>

-> That is: <-

> The holy teacher strengthens the heart with sweet fragrances,
> Who always chews the wood of the Cross in his mouth.

<margin>The Aloe plant.</margin>I could record a great deal regarding this Aloe-wood and its fragrant tree if the desire took me, but I shall pass over to the Aloe herb and the plant with its oozing and drained fluids. That which is commonly called Aloe is a dripping moisture from the Aloe plant; it is green in color and almost always growing and verdant, for which reason it is perhaps called *semper vivum* <note>Latin: "always living."</note>.

It has a stronger effect upon the taste than upon the smell. The idea that it would be pleasant and sweet of smell does not seem probable to me from experience. However, trial teaches us that it is very bitter and not at all sweet, yet healthful when used rightly. Although it spreads little scent itself, it preserves other spices and their fragrance and power through its bitterness. Indeed, because of its guarding and preserving power, it was customary of old to mix it with those substances intended for embalming bodies, as can be seen in *John 19:39.*

<margin>The power of Aloe.</margin>It is testified that it moderately, and without sharpness, cleanses blocked and phlegmatic parts, softens the belly, purges the intestines, removes and improves bad bile, and strengthens the stomach. When rubbed on the forehead and temples, it stills headaches and is useful against melancholy,

<column-break/>

the flow of blood, and suchlike, as may be searched for in Pliny <note>Roman naturalist and author of "Natural History."</note> *book 27, chapter 4*, Dioscorides, etc.

This has traditionally been applied to Christ’s cross, or the crucified Christ, and the teaching of Him who was crucified; it is capable not only of strengthening the heart but also of expelling the corruption within us and driving away the causes of many spiritual diseases and ailments. For this reason, Paul wished to know nothing else than Christ and Him crucified *1 Corinthians 2:2*, through which a rare change came upon him. *Galatians 2:20,* etc.

> The always-living Aloe, which puts forth leaves, flowers, and a healthful tear,
> Is to me, O Christ, Your Cross.

<header>ALOE. ALOSA. ALPHA.</header>

In the next chapter concerning herbs, he says: *Aloe is a herb that has very bitter sap.*

By the "aloe-tree," one understands the Agallochum tree or "Paradise-wood" of old, which today is known by the name of Xylaloe or aloe-wood. What is said regarding this can be found in abundance by the very learned Mr. Adolf Lampe, currently a Professor at Utrecht, in the aforementioned treatise.

<margin>Connection of Aloe with Myrrh.</margin>
The aloe herb grows in Syria, Coelesyria, Arabia, and especially in India: see Galen’s *On Simple Medicines*, book 6. Salmasius in *Plinian Exercises*, page 153. Heinsius’s *Aristarchus*, page 518. Ursinus in *Trees of the Bible*, in the spice garden. Bodeus à Stapel in his *Commentary on Theophrastus*, book 7, page 903. Munting in his herb-book, and Hofmann in his dictionary.

Aloe, particularly the aloe herb, has a great connection with myrrh, and they are joined together in *Psalm 45* and *Song of Solomon 4*.

Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037).</note> says: *the best Aloe is the Socotrine, whose moisture is like saffron, and its scent like that of myrrh; it is clear, easily crushed, and free from lime-like impurities.*

Munting says in his herb-book: *the Socotrine is the best, and so named because it is produced on the Island of Socotra in India.*

It was used in anointing oils; along with myrrh, it was also used in the embalming of the dead. It was used in pharmacy and medicine. It is very bitter in taste. Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and father of botany.</note>, in book 3, chapter 25, calls it *apogeuomeno pikrotatē* <note>original: "ἀπογευομένῳ πικροτάτη"</note>, *the bitterest thing one can taste.*

Regarding *Psalm 45:9*, I find that the garment of Christ has been understood to mean His majesty and glory; and it is then thought that the spices signify the permanence and incorruptibility of this His state and glory at the Father’s right hand.

Some understand Christ's three offices, being Prophet, Priest, and King. Others, if the Bride of the Church may be considered here, understand faith, love, and hope, or in general the various gifts of the Spirit and Christian virtues. *Galatians 5:22.*

On *Psalm 45* and *Song of Solomon 4:13-18*, some, such as Geesteranus, have noted that these represent spiritual gifts, very worthy and pleasant; see page 293 of his work.

Udemans, in his work on the *Song of Solomon*, regards saffron, myrrh, and aloe as purging and purifying agents, and understands them to represent rebukes, exhortations, and threats. *1 Thessalonians 4:14.*

Mollerus sees here the bitter cross-bearing of the Church, which is indeed hard, yet medicinal.

Others find here a symbol of Christian hope, which always lives and is never put to shame, practiced and growing under the Cross, preserving the soul from corruption. *Job 13:15; Romans 5:5; 1 Thessalonians 5:8.* Generally, it signifies Christ’s suffering on the cross. See Lampe’s *Exercises on Psalm 45*, part 1, page 553, etc.

### ALOSA, a Fish, called by us the Shad.

I have found that the fish ALOSA is named *Clupea* and *Trissa*; it is said to be not unlike the carp, except that it has smaller scales. I find it called *Jesen* and *Elzen*; it is found in the sea and swims up the rivers Nile and Elbe <note>original: "Albus"</note>, from whence it is said to flee back to the sea upon hearing thunder.

As we are told, it is caught in the Tiber, not far from Rome. The Italians imagine that God and nature have granted this delicacy to them alone. The Venetians, it is said, call it *Chiepa*, others *Clupea*. It is reported to be a small fish, yet Kallisthenes in book 13 of *Concerning Gaulish Affairs* <note>original: "περὶ τῶν γαλατικῶν"</note> and Plutarch in *On Rivers* contradict this, saying that viewed by itself it is a reasonably large fish, though small in comparison to the whale, the sheatfish, or the *Adano*, of which Pliny makes passing mention in book 9, chapter 15, informing us that the fish *Clupea*—if it is the same as the *Alosa*—is singularly greedy for a certain vein in the throat of the whale, by the seizing of which it is killed.

<column-break/>

Regarding this fish, we are informed by Aelian and Athenaeus <note>Ancient writers on natural history and food.</note> that it swims toward the sound of the cithara <note>An ancient stringed instrument similar to a lyre.</note> as if it were dancing; that it is enticed by small bells, by singing, and by the sound and rattling of earthen pots or baked stones; that the fishermen in their huts play musical instruments, sing, and dance, while the fish, imitating this with jumping and leaping, is caught through inattention in the cast and stretched nets. Furthermore, we are told that it, like many other fish, is full of a certain kind of small lice in its gills or jaws, by which it is sometimes killed. Nothing more concerning this fish occurs to me.

<margin>The catching of this fish.</margin>

It seems to me that through this fish—beset with worms, fleeing to the depths before the thunder, and being deceived and sinfully caught through song and merriment while leaping thoughtlessly—I can represent a person beset with a biting worm in the conscience. This worm gnaws at him lethally, and all the more strongly when he hears the crack of the thundering Law, the threats, rebukes, and curses, by which he is so distressed that he would gladly hide in the depths and conceal himself from the Lord. *Isaiah 29:15 and 33:14.* Therefore, to dull its stings, murmurings, bites, and remorses as much as possible, he amuses himself in worldly pleasure, music, and company—singing, dancing, and jumping—becoming in all things conformed to the world. In these snares, set for him by the destroyer of souls, he is finally carried away, ravished by luxury and thoughtlessness, and comes to a sudden end. *Psalm 73:18, 19, 20.*

<margin>Application to a human being.</margin>

### ALPHA and OMEGA. A & Ω.

He who sits upon the Throne describes Himself as being the ALPHA and OMEGA, A, Ω. *Revelation 1:8, 21:6, and 22:13.* Since theologians generally have not presented their thoughts with the same understanding and purpose, I consider it unnecessary and without any edifying utility to take upon myself the trouble of noting as much about it as currently comes to mind.

<margin>The Author's thoughts and expansion regarding Alpha and Omega.</margin>

a. Among the Hebrews, the alphabet consists of the Aleph and Tau, א / ת; among the Greeks, the Alpha and Omega, A, Ω—the first and the last letters.

It is said that Aleph or Alpha derives its origin from *eleph* <note>original: "אלף / אלף"</note> meaning the number one thousand; or from *alluph* <note>original: "אלוף"</note> a prince, prince, head, chief, or superior person, he being worth as much as a thousand of the common folk.

# ALPHA.

## K 2

<margin>Meaning of the A in Arithmetic.</margin>
A, in arithmetic, signifies one, and also a single or any certain thing which is unique or alone, of which there are no more.

<margin>Explanation of certain scholars.</margin>
Upon this, some scholars have built their interpretation when they took this description or circumscription, *I am the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end*, in this way: I am the first and the last letter of this book, which is to say: you, my servant John, know that it is I who sit upon the Throne, with whom you alone have to deal; I am the one who has made known to you, makes known now, and shall yet make known, that which you shall have to write; that it is I, and no one besides me, who appears in all that I have done, do, and shall do, and who shall provide the beginning, the progress, and the end. I, yes I alone, have commenced it, and shall also continue and complete it.

*b.* Others understand it in the following way: that it is given to be understood that he who sits upon the Throne is the only, eternal, unchangeable, all-sufficient, almighty, and true God. All other beings created by and through him have a specific moment of their origin, and they are in themselves changeable and perishable; they possess in and of themselves no inner strength, essential power, or sufficiency to endure and be active on their own. But this speaking person—he who sits upon the Throne—has his essence in himself, and remains before all things, enduring in and through himself without the slightest shadow of turning, having no beginning or end, sustaining all things through himself, or through his will and power, or his powerful will. To this end, the following are also cited: *Psalm 90:2 and 102:26, 27, 28; Isaiah 41:4.* "Who has wrought and done this, calling the generations from the beginning? I the Lord, who am the first, and at the same time the last, I am he." *Isaiah 43:10.* "That you may believe and understand that I am he, (that) before me no God was formed, and after me there shall be none." *Isaiah 44:8.* "And do not be startled, and do not fear; have I not declared it to you from of old, and proclaimed it? For you are my witnesses; is there also a God besides me? Indeed, there is no (other) rock, I know of none." *John 1:1, 2, 3; Colossians 1:16, 17; Hebrews 1:10, 11.*

To this could also be applied what is witnessed concerning the distressed and oppressed Christians in the time of the Arians <note>Followers of Arius who denied the full divinity of Jesus Christ.</note>; namely, since the Arians denied the eternal and true divinity of the Son of God, these Christians conversely had *Alpha* and *Omega* carved into their gravestones. By doing so, they signaled that even in death, they affirmed the honor and glory of the Son of God as the only, eternal, true God, of one essence with the Father, believing and expecting that he, rising over the dust on the last day, would make their dead bodies alive and reunite them with their souls, to make them partakers of his life and glory. *Job 19:25, 26, 27.* "For I know that my redeemer lives, and he shall stand last over the dust; and after they shall have gnawed through my skin, I shall behold God from my flesh, whom I shall behold for myself, and my eyes shall see, and not a stranger. My kidneys long greatly within my bosom."

*c.* And because the Alpha in the Greek Alphabet signifies "one" in counting and arithmetic, and consequently signifies something that is alone, single, and rare, and the Omega is the final closing letter, some have understood that neither before Christ, nor in his time, nor after him, was there, is there, or would there ever be such

<column-break/>

a Son of God or God-Savior; as being the eternally born, natural, proper, only-begotten, beloved Son, Lord, and universal Heir. *Psalm 2:7; Proverbs 8:24, 25, etc.; Micah 5:1; John 1:1, 2, 3 and 3:16-36; Romans 8:32; Colossians 1:17, 18; Hebrews 1:2.* While the elect, the called, and the saints are adopted as children and co-heirs in, with, and for his sake. *John 1:2; Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:5; Ephesians 1:5, etc.*

*d.* And since it has already been noted that the words *Aleph* and *Alpha* descend from *Alaph* or *Eleph*, meaning: a thousand, the pick, the finery, the most prominent and choice, a head, chief, or prince upon whom almost all things depend and turn, and who is worth as much as a thousand other persons, etc.; so for that same purpose further descriptions, titles of honor, and names have been sought out, which I shall not pass over, to clarify them somewhat for the reader's purpose and to emphasize them more strongly. Namely, one named such a person who held the primary management of affairs in hand, upon whose governance almost everything entirely depended: *prora atque puppis* <note>Latin: "the prow and the stern," meaning the beginning and the end, or the whole of a matter.</note>, the prow and the stern of the ship. Just as Orpheus, speaking of God, says:

> Zeus is the head, Zeus is the middle, from Zeus all things are made,
> Zeus is King, Zeus the beginning of all things, and the end.
<note>original Greek: "Ζεὺς κεφαλὴ, Ζεὺς μέσσα, Διὸς δ' ἐκ πάντα τέτυκται, / Ζεὺς Βασιλεὺς, Ζεὺς ἀρχὴ πάντων, ἠ δὲ τελευτή."</note>

-> That is: <-

> Jove is the middle and the head, through whom all
> Is brought forth that shows itself in the earthly vale.
> Jove is King and the beginning of all things.
> Jove completes it all.

When we apply these scholarly interpretations to our purpose, they portray the one sitting on the Throne as the most beautiful of all men, far above his companions. *Psalm 8:6, 7, etc.; Psalm 45:3-8; Song of Solomon 5:10; Philippians 2:9, 10, 11; Hebrews 1:4 to 10; Revelation 17:14 and 19:16.* He is the one whom it is all about, on whom everything stands and depends, who holds the management of everything in hand: the first, middle, and last letter, the substance of the shadows, the end and fulfiller of the Law, the spirit of the Prophecies, etc. *Genesis 3:15; Psalm 40:8; Luke 1:78 and 24:44; John 5:39; Revelation 19:10, etc.*

*e.* He is the *Alpha* and *Omega*, the first and the last letter, the highest and the lowest; that is, the first and highest as being of one essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, as God's Son, image, radiance, and universal heir, Lord of the house. He is the last and lowest because of his extreme and deepest humiliation, reproach, subjection, and suffering in soul and body, as God, man, surety, and mediator, in the course of his life and his most degrading death on the cross. Read *Psalm 22; Isaiah 53:2, 3; Matthew 8:30; and 20:28; Philippians 2:7, 8.* And after he had been the lowest, he became again the first, most prominent, and highest, because of the reward and fruit of his labor—the obtained honor, majesty, glory, and blessedness, and dominion and power over all things. *Psalm 8:6, 7, etc.; Psalm 110:1, 2; Isaiah 52:13 and 53:11, 12; Matthew 28:18; Luke 24:26; Philippians 2:9, 10, 11, etc.*

# ALPHA.

<margin>
The author’s expansion of thoughts regarding "the first and the last."
</margin>
...not only with respect to the work of creation and the bringing forth of all things, *Psalm 33:6; John 1:1, 2, 3; Revelation 1:5,* but very emphatically also by reason of the work of recreation <note>meaning: spiritual rebirth or regeneration</note>, redemption, and renewal, established for a humanity that had become sinful, damnable, and powerless, being the one who applies both the first and the last hand to this work. *Psalm 65:20 <note>likely referring to God as the God of salvation</note>; Isaiah 42:8, 43:11–15, 44:8, and 45:21, 22; Job 14:6; Acts 4:12; Colossians 3:11; 1 Timothy 2:5, 6; etc.*

However, since I still had something to say regarding this description or phrasing, *I am the first and the last*, which is understood by some as a further opening to explain what preceded it, I shall collect my thoughts and proceed to that point.

-> the beginning and the end <note>original Greek: ἡ ἀρχὴ καὶ τὸ τέλος, Dutch: het begin, en 't einde</note> <-

I have already pointed out to my reader that even those of the simplest understanding have viewed these words as a further opening and explanation of what came just before.

Yet, other scholars, not daring to suggest that the Holy Spirit would say the same thing twice in such a short span of words, are of the opinion that God’s Spirit intended to signify something distinct from the preceding. If one may assume this—since one ought to embrace the meaning in its full breadth and power unless there are weighty reasons to the contrary—then one might bring forward the following to understand this statement and declaration, the first and last $\aleph$ <note>the Hebrew letter Aleph, representing the beginning</note>.

<margin>
*a.*
</margin>
*a.* That this speaker, who was God from eternity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, whom God possessed in the beginning of His way, has, with the Father from all eternity, decided and firmly established what things He would give essence and existence to; how and in what manner He would establish a kingdom for Himself in the world, out of the world; and how He would make these, His subjects, partakers of His goods, glory, and blessedness. In such a way, the beginning of God’s way is by, from, and through Him, the Son. *Proverbs 8:22, 23: The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was.* Likewise, it is said in *Matthew 25:34: The kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world.* Therefore, mention is also made of an election and pre-ordination in, with, and through Christ. *Ephesians 1:1, 2, 3, 4, 5; 2 Timothy 1:9.*

<margin>
*b.*
</margin>
*b.* Furthermore, one does not view this declaration and description as if He—regarding His essence, being, existence, or endurance—knew or acknowledged anything or anyone that would have been before Him, or would have been above Him, or that He would have an end, etc.; far be it. But they understand these words, *I am the first and the last*, effectively or transitionally. In this sense, He who sits upon the throne is, in the first instance, the productive cause of all the beings that have been brought forth. It is He through whom the Father created and made all things. Just as it is written in *Psalm 33:6: By the word of the Lord were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth. John 1:3: All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made. Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:16 <note>likely Heb. 1:2</note>; Revelation 4:11; etc.* He is also the one who, regarding the work of the sin-

<column-break/>

ner’s recreation, redemption, and quickening <note>meaning: bringing to life</note>, was for that purpose previously ordained, promised, and foreshadowed, and was then sent into the world, delivered up, and raised. *John 1:16, 17: And of his fullness have all we received, and grace for grace. For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ. John 3:16–36; Acts 4:12; Romans 3:25, 26, and 4:25; 1 Corinthians 1:30; 1 Timothy 1:15: This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.*

<margin>
*c.*
</margin>
*c.* He who sits upon the throne is also the first, highest, and primary goal and end <note>telos</note> toward which everything is directed and in which everything must finish. And therefore it is said in *Proverbs 16:4: That he has wrought all things for himself. Romans 11:36: For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Colossians 1:16: That not only all things are from him and created by him, but also are unto him.*

Now, I shall present this somewhat more extensively and distinctly:

<margin>
Further presentation.
</margin>
1. It is known beyond all doubt that many very glorious virtues shine forth from the work of creation and the created things and beings: *Psalm 19:2, 3; Romans 1:19, 20.* His power, by way of command and calling, made all things receive their being and essence. What He spoke, was there; He commanded, and it stood fast; by the word of the Lord were the heavens made, *Psalm 33:6, 7, 8, 9.* He calls those things which be not as though they were, *Romans 4:17.* For thy pleasure they are and were created. *Revelation 4:11.*

And certainly, God displays, both in creating and in sustaining and governing, His wisdom, power, loving-kindness, and the further brilliance of His peerless virtues. *Psalm 104:24: O Lord, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches. Psalm 145:8, 9, 10 <note>original cites 45, likely 145</note>: The Lord is gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy. The Lord is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works. All thy works shall praise thee, O Lord; and thy saints shall bless thee.*

2. Which work of creation the Father shall have let the Son carry out, to the end that the Son, alongside and equally with the Father, might be acknowledged, sought, loved, served, honored, and glorified. *John 5:23: That all men should honor the Son, even as they honor the Father. You believe in God, believe also in me. John 8:50; Revelation 4:11: Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honor and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created.*

# ALPHA.

...recognized and proclaimed as such.

4. He is also [the Alpha] with respect to those who are bought and set free, whose goal and intention must be to boast and bless themselves in him, to believe in him, to trust him, to love him, to praise and glorify him, *Isaiah 43:21. Although I might have been able to suffice with what has been said, I will nevertheless add, with some shortening, what I have found in the works of excellent men.

<margin>Thoughts and explanation of Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a famous Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology" and his focus on biblical prophecy.</note>.</margin>
The honorable Cocceius, in his *Reflections on the Apocalypse*, on chapter 1:8, writes:

I distinguish the first saying, *I am the Alpha and Omega*, from the other; for it serves the fullness of the meaning when the general is joined to the particular, to understand the general from a distinct kind, sort, and form. I take *the Alpha*, according to the Greek proverb, in the sense of him who is the highest or supreme. Certainly, since the Greek idiom and their well-known usage imply that *Alpha* refers to that which is highest in its kind; it would be necessary that John had placed a stumbling block and spoken something untrue, if Christ were not the highest, or if Christ were the highest and John had failed to convey that. Therefore, the *Omega* signifies, by way of similar correspondence, the very lowest. For the Son was also lowered beneath all who are in the world, *Psalm 22:6. I am a worm and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people. Psalm 69 <note>The OCR text says 88, which may be a transcription error or a specific verse citation no longer in use; the context refers to Christ's suffering</note>; Ephesians 4:9. He, the Lord of glory, was crucified:* and because he was the lowest, it was fitting that he should be recognized as the highest. Compare *Isaiah 51 and 52:13, 14, 15.*

The second title of praise is, *beginning and end* <note>original Greek: ἀρχὴ & τέλος</note>, Aleph <note>the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, א</note> (meaning) from whom and for whom all things are: the prince or sovereign of life and salvation, whose is the glory, and whose glory the Father seeks, so that he might be glorified in him, the Son.

And on *Revelation 21:6*, the same Cocceius says: these are words of God, with which he gives it to be understood that everything was finished or accomplished which had to happen: and namely, that he, who is the highest, had become the lowest. That he, who is the beginning of everything, is also the end; and that he calls everything back to himself, to the end that he might be glorified in his own.

It seems to me that this is explained briefly, emphatically, meaningfully, and powerfully: and I cannot understand from what ground it has come that some have been neither able nor willing to join and unite themselves with these thoughts.

The very learned Professor Mark <note>Johannes van Marck (1656–1731), a student of Cocceius who became a highly influential Reformed theologian</note>, in his work on the Revelation, writes thus: *It is apparent to everyone that these letters α and ω are the first and last of the Greek Alphabet, in which language John wrote: thus the first and last are signified by them, not only in the matter of salvation, which nevertheless (I do not understand how such can stand with their suppositions and writings) the Socinians <note>A group that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ</note> attribute to Christ: also not only the first and last in the holy scriptures, of which he might thus be called the beginning and the conclusion, as many believe along with Rupertus. Finally, also not in respect to the highest dignity and deepest humiliation, or self-annihilation. Which explanation Cocceius drives with so much fire <note>meaning zeal or passion</note> that John would have placed a stumbling block and spoken something untrue if it were not understood that way. But absolutely, just as is read of God in Isaiah 41:4, 44:6, and 48:15, to signify his unity, eternity, and immutability.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Thoughts and explanations of Mark.</margin>
That it is said, "the beginning and end," must be taken as a further elaboration of the first part: or applied to the production of all things in nature and grace, and to the end of these, according to *Romans 11:36; 1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:10.*

Prudentius <note>A Roman Christian poet (c. 348–413 AD)</note> in his Hymn:

> *Alpha et Omega cognominatur, ipse fons, & clausula*
> *Omnium quae sunt, fuerunt, quaeque post futura sunt.*
> <note>original Latin: "He is named Alpha and Omega, the very source and conclusion of all things that are, were, and shall be hereafter."</note>

Which is to say:

*Through the first letter and the last is understood*
*The source and the conclusion of all that shall exist henceforth*
*Or is, or has been.*

Fulgentius <note>Likely Fulgentius of Ruspe (c. 462–533 AD), an African bishop and theologian</note> *Book 2.*

> *Principium Christus, quia ipse inchoavit perficienda:*
> *Finis Christus, quia ipse perfecit inchoata.*
> <note>original Latin: "Christ is the Beginning, because he himself began the things to be perfected: Christ is the End, because he himself perfected the things that were begun."</note>

That is:

*Christ is the beginning, because he himself has begun*
*that which had to be accomplished: Christ is the*
*end, because he himself has accomplished that which*
*was begun.*

And not ungracefully has Augustine said, in the 56th letter to Dioscorus: *Although the particular ends of created things are many and various, according to the diversity of matters, they are nevertheless by no means confused, for one is subordinate to the other: the primary one is one, and the less primary, the other (end): the supreme is one, the lower is the other: the supreme is one, to which the others are directed, and the order of all these is this: that from the very lowest, through the middle, the lower, and higher, the progression climbs to the supreme, whose end is the end of all ends, which encompasses all ends, above which, outside which, besides which, and beyond which there is no other end; but he is the α and ω: the α, as the beginning of all things, which have proceeded from him; the ω, as the end of all things, which have each directed their particular end toward him: and so they return and climb back to him, from whom they had descended and flowed forth, who is the blessed God from eternity to eternity.*

<margin>Thoughts and explanation of Campegius Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist known for his commentary on Isaiah and the Apocalypse.</note>.</margin>
I shall close this piece with the words and thoughts of the very honorable and very learned Professor Campegius Vitringa *on the Apocalypse*, who writes:

# ALPHA. WORMWOOD. ALTAR.

Page 22. "and" is very solemnly explained by the famous Mr. Cocceius <note>original: "Heer Coccejus"</note>, on *Revelation 1:8.*

Page 890. At the same time, in that juncture of time, it is shown that God is the beginning and the end: that He would finally show the promises made in the beginning of time in the end of the ages with full emphasis.

The Alphabet of the Divine name, sealed in the scriptures, would be read at that time, and could be learned in its entirety, when the church would compare the <term>Acherith</term> <note>Hebrew: אחרית; meaning the "latter things" or the "end"</note>, the last things, with the <term>reeschith</term> <note>Hebrew: ראשית; meaning the "first things" or the "beginning"</note>, the first things, and would find no less in the fulfillment than in the promises. *Isaiah 41:4 and 44:6.*

### WORMWOOD, <term>La'anah</term> / <term>apsinthos</term>, <term>pikria</term>, *Absynthium*.
<note>The author provides the name for wormwood in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.</note>

<margin>The unpleasantness of Wormwood.</margin>
Those who taste it are aware that WORMWOOD is not of the most fragrant or attractive taste, however healthy its use may be, and however good it is for the stomach and other parts of the body. Yet it is not known to me that this word is used as a symbol of something useful, wholesome, and tasty; rather, it appears in Holy Scripture as a symbol of that which is very sad, painful, and even unwholesome and harmful.

<margin>Wormwood as a symbol of sorrow.</margin>
And so I find that WORMWOOD, and that which is very bitter, appears as a symbol of grieving sorrow, very heavy adversities and torments, which are very much against the flesh, torment the soul, and are difficult to bear. Thus, the wicked flatteries and caresses of foreign women, and the outcomes of intimate association with them, are compared to the very bitter, *Proverbs 5:4. But her end is bitter as Wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword.*

The Lord threatens His unfaithful and rebellious people with painful adversities and judgments, and He makes these appear under the symbol of wormwood and gall, *Jeremiah 9:15. Behold, I will feed this people with wormwood: and I will give them water of gall to drink.* Almost the same is found in *Jeremiah 23:15.* The church has also tasted this in ample measure, for so she complains, *Lamentations 3:15. He hath filled me with bitterness, he hath made me drunken with wormwood.*

It is true that in the adversities which God sends to His favored ones, there lies a <term>sacred bitter</term> <note>Greek original: ἱερὸν πικρὸν (hieron pikron)</note>, a holy and wholesome bitterness, and the children of God also well know that adversities are useful to them, and turn out for the best according to God's purpose; which is why they are willing to taste that bitterness, *Romans 5 and 8; Hebrews 12:10, 11; Revelation 3:19; Psalm 119:71. It is good for me that I have been afflicted etc.; Isaiah 26; James 1.* And Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher</note> is not wrong when he says: *Prosperous fortune draws the straying away from the true good with its flatteries; adverse fortune usually leads them back to true goods, drawing them as if with a hook.* <note>original Latin: "Fortuna felix a vero bono devios trahit blanditiis, adverſa plerumque ad vera bona reducens unctrabit."</note>

<margin>Unjust Justice.</margin>
When the legal process is turned into violence, injustice, and oppression through gifts and partiality, it is quite as bad as if one poured gall and wormwood for the righteous, and nothing can seem more bitter or foul-tasting to him. *Amos 5:7 and 6:12.*

It was not of the best report or most pleasant after-

<column-break/>

echo, when one heard it said of Simon, *Acts 8:23. That he was a bitter gall, and a bond of iniquity.*

And when a bitter gall and wormwood are spoken of, *Deuteronomy 29:18*, it will surely also refer to the most wicked effects of sin, and the lack of required love turned into hatred.

When the star fallen from heaven, whose name was Wormwood, made the third part of the waters bitter, *Revelation 8:11*, it will surely signify this or that wicked arch-heretic, who by teaching and life established great destruction, and will have brought many to ruin, and thus polluted the Evangelical teaching of truth, drawing away and poisoning many. Nicolaus Gurtlerus in *Prophetic Vocabulary* <note>original: "Voc. Typico proph."</note>: After the blowing of the third trumpet, the false teacher corrupted the teaching of the Gospel, which is sweeter than honey, and gave his most bitter errors to a third part of men, distinguishing the false Christians from the Heathens and true witnesses of Christ. And if by this star Arius <note>A 4th-century priest whose teachings on the nature of Christ were declared heretical</note> is not specifically meant, he at least closely resembles it. Indeed, one reads of him:

> *Arius, the lethal poison of the human race,*
> *Born for the destruction of the law and the ruin of faith,*
> *Had polluted the nation and infected the whole world.*
<note>Original Latin: "Arrius humani generis lethale venenum, / Legis in excidium natus, fideique ruinam, / Polluerat gentem, totumque infecerat orbem."</note>

->That is:<-

<margin>Arius, a wicked heretic.</margin>
> *Arius, a plague for the human race,*
> *Came up from the abyss and brought about,*
> *Through wicked heresy, cunningly advanced,*
> *That land and teaching were entirely infected or crushed.*

From these small samples and applications, one will be able to sufficiently conclude what the symbol of Wormwood signifies; and on that basis, I will cease further investigation and move on to something else.

### ALTAR, <term>Mizbeach</term> / <term>Thysiasterion</term>, <term>Bomos</term>, *Altare*.
<note>The author provides the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin terms for Altar.</note>

<margin>One finds almost nothing of Altars before Noah's sacrifice.</margin>
Regarding ALTARS, although I consider some sort of Altar necessary for all sacrifices performed, one nevertheless reads nothing of them until Noah, having mercifully escaped the destruction of the floodwaters, built an Altar, and in faith and gratitude to God, sacrificed upon it, *Genesis 8.* Subsequently, I believe that the patriarchs followed one another in this, for so one reads of it in *Genesis 12, 13, 22, 26, 35,* etc. However, it does not occur to me that they had such an express divine command for it.

<margin>The first command comes in Exodus 20.</margin>
The first place where specific regulations are determined regarding the forming and erecting of Altars appears in: *Exodus 20:24, 25, 26. An altar of earth thou shalt make unto me, and shalt sacrifice thereon thy burnt offerings, and thy peace offerings, thy sheep, and thine oxen. In all places where I record my name I will come unto thee, and I will bless thee.*

*And if thou wilt make me an altar of stone, thou shalt not build it of hewn stone: for if thou lift up thy tool upon it, thou hast polluted it. Neither shalt thou go up by steps unto mine altar, that thy nakedness be not discovered thereon.*

I would almost conclude that a determination is made here, not regarding the Altar used for public...

# ALTAR.

belonged to the fixed, usual Levitical shadow-service <note>The "shadow-service" refers to Old Testament rituals viewed as "shadows" or symbolic precursors to the reality of Christ's ministry.</note>, and was solemnly introduced thereafter in *Exodus 27.* However, this also applied to personal and special cases—such as when someone, for a particular reason and a religious purpose, wished to offer a sacrifice to the Lord in the wilderness of the wanderings—that an Altar should then be erected either from green sods or rough clods and lumps of earth.

It also seems to me to approach the truth that Altars heaped up from earth, being unable to be moved, could easily be overturned; and that the Lord desired everything to be humble, so that the people’s senses might not be captivated by decoration and costly structures, and thus be carried away into superstition, idolatry, and other sins, or that the heathens might put such things to evil use.

And if they were inclined to build a stone Altar, they were required to make it of rough stones, without the art of stonemasons or engravers, and without carvings; without decorations and images, and by no means imitating the Heathens in this, or making it so that, remaining in existence after their departure, it might fall into the hands of the Heathens for idolatrous misuse; or that Israel, having more reverence for and expectation from such an Altar due to its greater decoration, antiquity, or otherwise, might not look away from the Altar of the Tabernacle or Temple and offer upon it, which was not permitted on any Altar once the Temple was built. Furthermore, the Lord did not want <margin>Steps to the altar forbidden.</margin> there to be steps to the Altar, for the reason *that nakedness might not be uncovered.* <note>Referencing Exodus 20:26.</note>

I cannot understand how one could reach the Altar or bring the sacrificial animal onto it, and perform everything properly and fittingly, if one wished to absolutely exclude all ascent or steps from it; and therefore one might wonder whether this did not refer only to those earthen or stone Altars which individuals might make, and by no means to the Altars of the Tabernacle and Temple. Indeed, one wonders whether it was only commanded, not as an eternal and fixed ordinance, but until further notice, or until the removal of the fear of the uncovering of nakedness, which shortly thereafter was sufficiently prevented by the command to use linen undergarments in the service. *Exodus 27.* <note>Exodus 28:42 actually specifies the linen breeches for the priests to cover their "nakedness."</note>

That all kinds of steps and ascents were not entirely forbidden was also the opinion of some who felt that the Lord had indeed forbidden making carved platform-steps, but not that one might use a rising ramp or something else for that purpose.

Meanwhile, it is also believed that attention was paid to the superstitious customs of the Heathens, which Israel was not to imitate; they particularly chose high places for the practice of sacrifice, for which they required high steps and elevated approaches. It was intended that the one offering sacrifice should not be exposed if, while taking wide strides, he met with the mishap of the wind playing under his low-hanging robe and lifting it, so that no similarity might be perceived between him and the servants of <term>Baal-peor</term> <note>A Moabite god whose worship was associated with licentiousness and exposure.</note>, who exposed their private parts; but that in the approach to God, shame, humility, reverence, modesty, and decency should be evident. *Hebrews 12:28.*

Having said and noted such things beforehand, the matter will require that I come somewhat closer and treat the Altars with some distinction.

One reads singularly of two in the holy scroll, namely the Altar of Burnt Offering and the Altar of Incense.

### ALTAR OF THE BURNT OFFERING, OR BURNT-ALTAR.
-> <term>Mizbeach Olah</term> <note>original Hebrew: מזבח עולה</note> / *Altar of Burnt Offering* <note>original Latin: *Altare Holocaufti*</note> <-

<margin>Bronze Burnt-Altar.</margin>
**T**HE BURNT-ALTAR was five cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note> long and wide, but only three cubits high, *Exodus 27.*
Solomon made it entirely of copper <note>Often translated as bronze in modern Bibles.</note>, twenty cubits in length, twenty in width, and ten cubits in height. *2 Chronicles 4.*

The internal material from which that Altar was constructed in its square was wood; the covering was of pure copper and sturdy copper plates, to protect the wood against the heat of the fire.

Inside it was hollow, to contain the ashes and to have air for fanning the flame. Some say it was to kindle and feed the wood therein, unless it lay rather on top of the copper grate.

Over the internal hollow, in the square inner space, lay a sufficiently heavy, latticed copper grate, through which the ashes fell downward.

Four rings overlaid with copper were attached to it; on the four corners were four projecting horns, all covered with copper. Furthermore, the coal pans, shovels, hooks, sprinkling basins, etc., belonged to this, all made of copper.

<margin>Place of the Burnt-Altar.</margin>
It stood in the court of the priests, on the east side of the Tabernacle, between the entrance of the Tabernacle and the entrance of the court in the open air, so that it could be beheld by Israel, so that the smoke-vapor might rise freely, and the interior of the Tabernacle would not be tarnished or fouled. *Exodus 27 and 40.*

Furthermore, it had to be sanctified and solemnly consecrated. *Exodus 29.*

<margin>Christ represented by the Altar.</margin>
I now hold with all the orthodox here, that Christ is represented by the Altar, priests, and sacrifice, who has offered Himself to God as a well-pleasing sacrifice for the sins of the elect, *Hebrews 7:27 and 9:14. Hebrews 13:10,* who is priest, Altar, and sacrifice.

It is certain to me that Christ’s cross, in its primary part and respect, cannot well be regarded as the altar, although there is some dispute among the learned over this. However, in a lower and lesser respect, one might also look upon His cross: the structure of the Altar bore the sacrificial animal; it elevated it and offered it as if to God; the Altar sanctified it.

It is certain in a sense that the wood of the cross bore Christ, and that He was exalted and elevated upon it, who offered and sacrificed Himself to God. *1 Peter 2:24.*

Upon which He was presented to God—not absolutely and in the most powerful sense, for that He did through His eternal spirit. *Hebrews 7 and 9:14 and 13. Psalm 40:7, 8, 9.*

It is true that His cross did not sanctify Him, as it is said of the Altar, *Matthew 23:19;* but it was also the case that the Altar did so with the fire upon it, which ignited the sacrifice: and that is a symbol of the Christ, the Son of God, and mediator of the covenant, who brought it about through His eternal spirit, as through a fire, that the offering was holy to God, *Ephesians 2. Hebrews 9:14.* A fire of zeal for the Father’s honor, a glow of love for the salvation of His people. *Psalm 69:10.* Although one can note yet another fire, with which the Lord ignited the sacrifice and ma- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "maken" (to make).</note>

# ALTAR.

making clear by *fire* <note>original Greek: *ἐμπυρισμὸν* (empyrismon), referring to the act of consuming by fire</note> that the sacrifice pleased him. *Ps. 69:10.*

Certainly, it was also his divine nature—he was God—that sanctified the human nature, preserved it as such, prepared it for suffering, and made it willing and ready. *Ps. 40:7, 8, 9, 10, 11; Heb. 10:5 to 10.*

It had to be an Altar not merely of wood, but covered with pure and durable copper, which resisted the power of the fire. Indeed, the Altar remained in existence and whole, while the sacrifice was consumed. Here I can imagine that, although the Divinity itself cannot properly suffer, it is nevertheless the suffering not only of him who is of the earth, *Isa. 4, 9, and 53,* but also of him who is God, whose arm supported him; so that, although his cross remained undamaged, he was nevertheless consumed as an offering by the fierce fire of God's wrath, with the bitterest pain of soul and body, and was struck in his heels unto death. *Gen. 3:15; Isa. 63:10; Matt. 26; Phil. 2; Ps. 22; etc.*

That the Altar in its squareness—in which the round circle of perfection is contained—appears to us as extended toward the four regions and winds of the world, and is presented with four copper-covered rings and two carrying poles; this brings fittingly to my mind how Christ is uniquely near to all nations in the New Testament, especially now that the word of the Gospel brings him through preaching to all regions of the world, without being bound to a single fixed place. *Ps. 68; Ps. 107:35; Matt. 28:19; Mark 16; etc.; Acts 9:15.*

<margin>The significance of the Horns of the Altar.</margin>
The horns sprouting on and out of that Altar remind me not only that there is strength in Christ's righteousness for those who embrace and acknowledge him as mediator through faith—so that they, though guilty of death in themselves, are nevertheless justified and declared free in, through, and for his sake, *Rom. 5:1, 2; Rom. 8:1; Rom. 3:24, 25; etc.; Isa. 27:5*—but also how he is entitled, by virtue of his sacrifice, to rule, to show power, to strike with horns <note>In biblical imagery, horns are a symbol of strength and kingly authority.</note>, to overcome his enemies and those of his people, to protect his kingdom with power, and to place his subjects in safety. *2 Sam. 22; Ps. 18; 1 Cor. 15; Heb. 2; Ps. 44; etc.* So too were those horns sprinkled with blood, so that one might think that his dominion and strength were in his blood, by which he was entitled and legalized to rule. *Isa. 53; Zech. 6:12, 13; Ps. 85:14; and 89:14, 15; Ps. 110; Luke 24.*

<margin>Altar placed in the open air.</margin>
That this Altar was placed in the open air, outside the Tabernacle and before the eyes of all the people, reminds me that the Lord, as a sacrifice for the sins of his people, as if he did not belong to the sanctuary, would die on the cross in the sight of the people, so that they might come to him as the sacrifice, Altar, and priest. *John 1:29; Rom. 3:25.*

When one sees that the Altar was sanctified, anointed, and set apart for its services, it shows me on one hand the vanity and powerlessness of the "shadows" <note>Referring again to Old Testament rituals as symbolic "shadows" of Christ.</note>; and therefore that the power consisted in the representation and sealing of the fact that someone would come who would sanctify himself to sanctify us, *John 17,* who was holy, innocent, and undefiled, *Heb. 7,* who would be singular, capable, and set apart. *2 Cor. 5:21; Isa. 53:11; etc.*
