### ALTAR OF INCENSE, OR INCENSE ALTAR, *mizbeach miktar / ketoret* <note>original Hebrew: מזבח מקטר / קטרת</note>,
### *Altar of burning, Altar of incense, Censer of incense.* <note>original Latin: *Altare suffimenti, suffitus Altare, Thymaterium suffitus.*</note>

REGARDING THE ALTAR OF INCENSE, which I undertake to treat, a detailed description can be read in *Exodus 30:1–10.*
I describe it briefly as follows:
The material was partly Shittim wood <note>Now commonly known as acacia wood.</note>, in the form of boards, subsequently overlaid with pure gold.
The shape and stature consisted of this:
The Altar of Incense was square, one cubit long and wide, and two cubits high, measured from the ground.
The elements that served for neatness and decoration were:
The four horns, protruding from the corners.
Covered on the top and sides with gold plates.
A crown and molding all around. *verses 1, 2, 3.*
And so that it would be transportable and portable, there were
Four rings for two carrying poles, overlaid with pure gold. *verses 4, 5.*
The place where it had to stand. *verse 6.*
Its use annually, besides the solemn sprinkling or atonement. *verse 10; Leviticus 16.*
The incense consisted of a mixture of finely ground *stacte* <note>the resinous sap of myrrh</note>, *onycha*, *galbanum*, and fine frankincense made into a lump or dough-ball.

Let this be enough regarding the historical letter: I shall proceed to further prospects and higher meanings, and first take note of some household insights and reasons for this order.

<margin>It did not flow from God's nature and essence to require such things.</margin>
When we remember that the God of Israel is a single and infinite spirit, *John 4:24,* then we can understand that he cannot be affected or refreshed by any material scents, and that God, being the Lord of heaven, earth, and everything—*Ps. 24:1; Ps. 50:9, 10, 11, 12, 13; Hag. 2:9* etc.—has no need to receive anything from human hands.

<margin>But from God's free will and power according to household and courtly reasons.</margin>
Yet it flowed from his free will and fixed command, having for this purpose reasons that were, as it were, household and courtly.
God served to be viewed as Israel's king, leader, and mighty protector, so that both God himself and the people of the Lord might be recognized and distinguished from other kings and peoples of the earth; and so that it might be public that his governance was a royal and divine supreme governance. He willed and desired it so, for the sake of both the inner and outer people, after the manner of Eastern kings and powers, to illustrate his greatness, glory, wealth, and power—even though he by no means needed such things for his own sake. The golden lampstand served for display, royal splendor, and light for the eyes, as he is a God of light.

<margin>Golden lampstand.</margin>
<margin>Gifts and incense lit for Gods and kings.</margin>
The golden table, with strengthening foods <note>The Showbread.</note>, served primarily for his courtiers and first servants.
Thus there were also incense-works of pleasant spices, for the nose and brain. For it is known that of old, people used to bring and burn gifts and incense not only to the so-called deities, but likewise to kings. *Tibullus, book 2, Elegy 2.*

*Let pious incense be burned on the hearths; let fragrances be burned.*

<margin>Because of the persistent smoke and vapor caused by the constant burning of offerings.</margin>Thus the Wise Men from the East brought gifts of gold, myrrh, and incense, *Matthew 2:11*, just as was prophesied in *Psalm 72:10: The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts. Isaiah 60:6, 7, 8, 9.*

And besides what has been noted, the Lord, as Israel's God and King, desired to have offerings cooked and roasted without fail every morning, evening, and many times throughout the day, year after year. This constant cooking, smoking, and roasting necessarily created a heavy smoke and a strong vapor, which would drift toward the Tabernacle and Temple. This made the nearby air thick and damp for the priests and Levites, consequently causing ill health, severe headaches, and chest tightness <note>The author provides a practical, "household" reason for the incense altar: it acted as a divine air freshener to protect the health of the workers.</note>. Therefore, the Lord, wishing to accommodate his household servants in this matter, gave the command to erect an Altar of Incense and to kindle a strong and pleasant fragrance.

<margin>Higher and more common reasons, and spiritual insights shown herein.</margin>Yet, beyond and above these domestic and courtly reasons, one ought to ascend to further views, higher ends, and more secret symbols. One should apply this to the only true and perfect High Priest, Jesus, who intercedes for his own on earth and especially in heaven. Likewise, it applies to his spiritual members—the ministers and priests of the New Testament—who, through his Spirit and the fire of zeal and earnestness, kindle their prayers and thanksgivings in Christ's name. They lay these upon him, the altar, to present them to the Father through his merits and intercession, making them pleasing.

However, this subject requires that I present it to the reader with more refinement and expansion. Giving my thoughts some room to play, I note these three things as a preface:

<margin>Some observations for the specific applications.</margin>
a. The Altar of Incense was not the same as the Altar of Burnt Offering. The latter stood in the open air and could be seen by the people, but the Altar of Incense was out of the people's sight, inside the Holy Place.
b. The Altar of Incense allowed nothing but incense.
c. Regarding certain requirements, it served not only the Holy Place but also the Holy of Holies.

<margin>And the transfer and application of these.</margin>When Christ was made under the law for his brothers to fulfill all righteousness, it was such that he prayed for his own on earth upon his offerings. But after he had offered himself blameless to God through the eternal Spirit, he entered into the heavenly Holy of Holies with his own blood. Having withdrawn himself bodily from his own through his ascension, he appears upon his offering with a hard-won right for his people before the Father, interceding for them. *Romans 8:35; Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1, 2.* And since no further sacrifice is necessary after his offering, there remains no other offering to lay upon him, the Altar, than that of praise and thanksgiving. *Psalm 50:13-23; Hebrews 13:15.*

<margin>The order maintained in this transfer.</margin>Yet it pleases me to come to specifics and to lay open the entire mystery of the Christian faith and worship more broadly and clearly. I shall do this by considering the Altar of Incense according to its primary materials, shape, decoration, attachments, and further use, as I described previously.

<margin>What the Altar's Shittim wood signified.</margin>A. The wood used as the base material for the Altar of Incense was hard and knotty Shittim wood <note>Shittim wood is Acacia, known for its durability and resistance to decay.</note>, which was afterwards covered and overlaid with gold.

Others before me have already noted that this wood, suited for this use, serves as a representation of the human nature of the Son of God, which he shared with his brothers. *Romans 8:3; Hebrews 2:11, 12-14-17.* He was a shoot and a tender plant, *Isaiah 11:1 and 53:2*, cut off and rooted out for the debt of sin he took upon himself, *Isaiah 53:8; Daniel 9:26*; yet in and through his resurrection, he became like incorruptible Shittim wood. *Psalm 16:10, 11; Isaiah 53:10; Revelation 1:18.*

<margin>The gold over it, what it signified.</margin>The Shittim wood was not merely gilded with thin gold leaf, but covered and overlaid with pure and thick gold plates, upon which the pleasant incense was placed and kindled. This has been noted as a representation of:

1. Christ’s glorious and precious virtues, gifts, and abilities, with which he showed himself to be adorned, filled, and covered during the course of his life. *Isaiah 11:2 and 61:1, 2; Luke 1:80 and 2:52; John 1:14 and 3:34.*
2. And especially as a representation of the honor, glory, and majesty he obtained after he had, in deep humility, offered himself blameless to God through the eternal Spirit. *Psalm 8:6, 7; Isaiah 52:13; Zechariah 6:12, 13; Philippians 2:8, 9; Luke 24:26.*

B. And regarding the form or figure of the Altar of Incense:

<margin>That the Altar was square, what that gave to understand.</margin>
a. 1. It was square, with its four corners extending toward the four parts of the world, and it was firm because of this shape. This serves as a symbol—as did the Altar of Burnt Offering—of how Jesus is equally near to everyone. *Galatians 3:28.*
2. And that he presents the incense of his intercession to the Father, always and perfectly for his own in the four corners of the world, *Romans 8:35; Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1, 2*, upon whom those living in all regions can also lay their prayers and thanksgivings. *Hebrews 13:15; Revelation 5:8 and 8.*

<margin>The horns of the altar.</margin>
b. This Altar of Incense had four golden horns protruding from the four corners. Horns in Holy Scripture are symbols of strength and abundance. To this extent, it seems to me that it can be applied to Christ in the following way: that through them are signified
1. Jesus's right and power, by virtue of his perfect high-priestly sacrifice, through which he satisfied God's justice and the demand of the divine law for his people, whom he bought and ransomed, leading to this counter-claim: that his enemies...

Isaiah 60:6, 7, 8, 9.*

And besides what has been noted, the Lord, as Israel’s God and King, desired to have offerings boiled and roasted without fail every morning, evening, and many times throughout the day, year in and year out. This continuous boiling, smoking, and roasting necessarily created a heavy smoke and a strong vapor that drifted toward the Tabernacle and Temple, making the nearby air thick and damp for the priests and Levites. Consequently, this caused ill health, severe headaches, and chest tightness <note>This refers to respiratory distress or asthma-like symptoms caused by poor ventilation</note>. Therefore, the Lord, wishing to accommodate his household servants in this matter, gave the command to erect an Altar of Incense and to ignite a strong and pleasant fragrance.

<margin>Higher and more common reasons, and spiritual insights shown in this.</margin>Yet, beyond and above these practical and courtly reasons, one ought to ascend to further perspectives, higher ends, and more secret symbols. One should apply this to the one, true, and perfect High Priest, Jesus—who intercedes for his own on earth and especially in heaven—as well as to his spiritual members, the ministers and priests of the New Testament. These, through his Spirit and the fire of zeal and earnestness, ignite their prayers and thanksgivings in Christ’s name, laying them upon him as the altar, to present them to the Father through his merits and intercession, making them pleasing to Him.

However, this subject requires that I present it to the reader with more refinement and expansion. Allowing my thoughts some room to play, I note these three things as an introduction:

<margin>Some remarks for the specific applications.</margin>
* a. The Altar of Incense was not the same as the Altar of Burnt Offering. The latter stood in the open air and could be seen by the people, but the Altar of Incense was kept out of the people's sight within the Holy Place.
* b. The Altar of Incense allowed nothing but the incense itself.
* c. And regarding certain rituals, it belonged not only to the Holy Place but also to the Most Holy Place.

<margin>And the application and transfer of these points.</margin>When Christ was made under the law for his brothers to fulfill all righteousness, he indeed prayed for his own on earth alongside his offerings. But after he had offered himself blameless to God through the eternal Spirit, he entered into the heavenly Holy of Holies with his own blood. Having withdrawn himself bodily from his people through his ascension, he appears upon his sacrifice, interceding for his people with a hard-won right before the Father. *Romans 8:34 <note>The original text cites 35, but 34 contains the intercession</note>, Hebrews 7:25, 1 John 2:1, 2.* And because no further sacrifice is necessary after his offering, there remains no other sacrifice to lay upon him, the Altar, than that of praise and thanksgiving. *Psalm 50:13-23, Hebrews 13:15.*

<margin>The order maintained in this application.</margin>Yet it pleases me to come to specifics and to lay open the entire mystery of the Christian faith and worship more broadly and clearly. I shall do this by examining the Altar of Incense just as I previously described it: in its primary materials, shape, decoration, accoutrements, and further use.

<margin>The Shittim wood of the Altar and what it signified.</margin>*A. The wood used as the base material to construct the Altar of Incense was hard and knotty Shittim wood <term>Shittim: Acacia wood, known for its durability and resistance to decay</term>, which was afterwards covered and overlaid with gold.*

Others before me have already noted that this wood, suited for this use, serves as a symbol of the human nature of the Son of God, which he held in common with his brothers, *Romans 8:3, Hebrews 2:11, 14, 17*. He was as a tender plant and a root out of dry ground, *Isaiah 11:1 and 53:2*, cut off and rooted out because of the guilt of sin he took upon himself, *Isaiah 53:8, Daniel 9:26*. Yet in and through his resurrection, he became like an incorruptible Shittim wood. *Psalm 16:10, 11, Isaiah 53:10, Revelation 1:18.*

<margin>The gold over it and what it signified.</margin>The Shittim wood was not merely gilded with a thin layer of gold leaf, but was covered and overlaid with pure, thick plates of gold, upon which the pleasant incense was placed and ignited. This has been noted as a symbol of:

1. Christ’s glorious and precious virtues, gifts, and abilities, with which he showed himself to be adorned, filled, and covered throughout the course of his life. *Isaiah 11:2 and 61:1, 2, Luke 1:80 and 2:52, John 1:14 and 3:34.*
2. And especially as a symbol of the honor, glory, and majesty he obtained after he had offered himself blameless to God in deep humility through the eternal Spirit. *Psalm 8:6, 7, Isaiah 52:13, Zechariah 6:12, 13, Philippians 2:8, 9, Luke 24:26.*

<margin>The squareness of the Altar and what that was meant to signify.</margin>*B. And regarding the form or figure of the Altar of Incense:*
* a. 1. It was square, with its four corners extending toward the four parts of the world, and was firm in this shape. This serves as a symbol—much like the Altar of Burnt Offering—of how Jesus is equally near to all. *Galatians 3:28.*
* 2. And that he presents the incense of his intercession to the Father always and perfectly for his people in the four corners of the world, *Romans 8:34, Hebrews 7:25, 1 John 2:1, 2*, upon which those who dwell in all regions can also lay their prayers and thanksgivings. *Hebrews 13:15, Revelation 5:8 and 8.*

<margin>The horns of the altar.</margin>*b. This Altar of Incense had four golden horns protruding from the four corners. Horns in Holy Scripture are symbols of strength and abundance; and so far, it seems to me that one can apply this to Christ in the following way: that through them can be signified:*
1. Jesus's right and power, by virtue of his perfect high-priestly sacrifice, through which he satisfied God's justice and the demands of divine law for his people who were to be bought and redeemed. By this, his enemies—

# ALTAR.

...may be subdued and destroyed, and that He may expand His kingdom to the four winds of the world—a right of demand that has been granted to Him, *Psalm 2:8.* Just as such an expanded kingdom has been promised to Him, *Psalm 72:8; Zechariah 6:12, 13,* which the Father has assigned to Him. *Psalm 110:2.*

2. With that purpose: that from the horn of His fullness and abundance, they might enjoy the waters of joy and salvation, perfect bliss, life, and glory. *Psalm 65:10 <note>Original citation Ps. LXV. 20 refers to the Dutch States Translation numbering</note>; Isaiah 12:3; Luke 1:69; John 1:16; John 17:24.*

3. With that result and power: that through His strength and intercession, He may strike, subdue, and bring down His and His people’s enemies as if with horns; and that His chosen ones may overcome their enemies in, with, and through Him.

<margin>The four golden rings and the two carrying poles.</margin>
**C.** Furthermore, when one observed in the entire Tabernacle, and likewise on the Altar of Incense, four rings overlaid with gold and two carrying poles overlaid with gold—by means of which the movable sanctuary and this Altar of Incense could be transported from one place to another as time and circumstances required—then it seems to me that this could have portrayed:

1. The movable and changeable nature of that old, <term>symbolic</term><note>The author uses the word "voorbeeldig," meaning it serves as a "type" or shadow of a future reality</note> and imperfect church governance.

2. And that, although the kingdom of heaven shall hereafter be immovable and unshakeable on earth regarding its form and government through the Word, Spirit, and Sacraments; nevertheless, the application of all these means is by no means permanently tied to any one country, place, time, or specific people. Instead, the <term>means of grace</term><note>The tools God uses to bring salvation to people, such as preaching and sacraments</note> can be moved. This has been seen in the churches of Asia Minor and other regions of the world where God’s throne and Altars once stood and the light of the Gospel shone, but where darkness, idolatry, ignorance, and the Ark and Altar of Dagon <note>A reference to the Philistine god, symbolizing paganism or false worship</note> have now taken place.

3. And by logical consequence, that one must make use of the favorable time, the day of hearing, and the means of salvation, *Psalm 95:7, 8; Isaiah 55:6; Hebrews 3:7, 8 and 4:7,* before it becomes too late. *Proverbs 1:24, 25; Isaiah 65:12, 13 and 66:4, etc.*

4. And that, just as the Altar of Incense (along with the other furnishings of the Tabernacle) did not remain bound to a single province: one could also remember that Christ, with His intercession based on His sacrifice—and the prayers and thanksgivings to be laid upon Him as the Altar of Incense so that He may make them acceptable to God—do not belong to any one specific people in one place, but are brought from everywhere. For Jesus had to have His own people throughout the world. From all regions, men were to seek Him and pray and give thanks in His name. *Psalm 72:11-17; Malachi 1:11; John 4:19, 20, etc.; 1 Timothy 2:8.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Why first the lampstand, then the showbread, and finally the Altar of Incense were seen.</margin>
**D.** Furthermore, it is worth considering that upon entering the Holy Place, one first saw the golden lampstand; after that, the golden table with the twelve loaves of showbread; and finally, the golden Altar of Incense.

It seems to me neither groundless nor absurd to judge that this mystery is contained therein:

1. At the first entrance into the sanctuary of God’s church, Jesus as **Prophet** must first be heard, and seen and known by the soul as the world’s light, savior, and the wisdom of the Father, leading to knowledge, acknowledgement, confession of the mouth, and faith of the heart. *Isaiah 53:11; John 17:3; Philippians 3:8.*

2. Once one knows and acknowledges Jesus, one then accepts Him as **Priest**. One approaches Him, in Him, and before Him, through the ministry of the Word and Sacraments—a food and a joyful drink which feed and strengthen the soul and make it <term>spiritually drunk</term><note>A common mystical expression meaning to be overwhelmed with divine joy or the Holy Spirit</note>. *Psalm 23:5; Psalm 36:8, 9, 10; John 1:16; John 6:51-58; Isaiah 25:6 and 55:1, 2, etc.*

3. Having taught as Prophet and sacrificed Himself as Priest, Jesus immediately stands before His own with His lovely and powerful incense of intercession with the Father. But also, those who have known Christ through the "lampstands" of the outward Word and the inner enlightenment of the Spirit, and who have received a taste and proof of God’s goodness in Him—these are the ones truly capable of approaching the Altar of Incense in faith and in the fellowship of Jesus’ fullness, goodness, and sufficiency, bringing to Him their incense of prayers and thanksgivings. *Psalm 36:6-10; Hebrews 13:15.*

<margin>Why it was seen in the Holy Place morning and evening, and in the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement.</margin>
**E.** It is true that the lighting and the burning of incense on this Altar occurred every morning and evening; however, it happened only once a year that the High Priest entered the inner sanctuary <note>The Holy of Holies</note> with the incense.

1. I know from divine report that the Priest Jesus, while on earth, prayed early and late. Indeed, as Mediator, by virtue of His pledge as surety and His future satisfaction and sin-offering, He stepped forward and interceded for His people. *Job 33:24; Isaiah 53:12; Luke 23:34; John 17, etc.*

<margin>Christ the antitype of the high priests.</margin>
2. But Christ, as the <term>antitype</term><note>The spiritual reality that fulfills the Old Testament "type" or shadow</note> of the high priests, on the great and true Day of Atonement—after He had offered Himself blameless to God through the eternal Spirit, had taken away the sins of the land in a single day, and had reconciled and sealed sins and iniquities, *Daniel 9; Zechariah 3*—entered into the heavenly Holy of Holies. There, by the power of His bloody obedience, He stands forever before the Father without ever leaving. *Hebrews 7:8, 9; 1 John 2:1, 2, etc.*

3. The liberated priests of the New Testament <note>meaning all Christian believers</note> must, from the morning of the New Testament until the evening—indeed, eternally and always, having entered the year of promises—continually...

# ALTAR.

<margin>What the incense signified in general.</margin>
**F.** When I behold the incense, composed of myrrh, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense, all crushed and finely ground, then it seems to me that I find my Savior trodden, stepped upon, as if crushed, annihilated, and made small in his own self-emptying, *Philippians 2; Psalm 22; Isaiah 53,* in and through the suffering of his soul and body, in the garden, on the cross, and him as if melting in tears. *Psalm 22; Matthew 26:27; Hebrews 5:7, etc.*

And I note all this also as an offering of sweet savor, which has pleased the Father, *Ephesians 5:2.* Not only that, but without this incense, God’s spiritual priests <note>The author refers to the "priesthood of all believers," a common Protestant concept</note> could neither be acceptable to the Lord, nor pray and give thanks acceptably.

**G.** And when I rightly observe how only the fire from the Altar of Burnt Offering could be used to kindle the incense—so that in the kindling and burning of the incense offering, both these Altars came together and were united—then

<margin>No incense kindled except by the fire of the Burnt Offering Altar.</margin>
It seems to me that I see that very same fire, which kindled and consumed him as a sacrifice and burnt offering—namely, the zeal for his Father’s honor and God’s house, *Psalm 69:10; John 2:17; Ephesians 5:2*—would also kindle him to step forward for the honor of his Father and for the full redemption of his own; which he also could not do except on the grounds of his atoning sacrifice. If he were not, in a certain respect, conformed to the Altar of Burnt Offering with its requirements, he would not be conformed to the Altar of Incense with its requirements. But because the Burnt Offering Altar and Incense Altar belong to his priesthood, just as they belonged in a symbolic way to the office of the Levitical priesthood, so in this matter the Burnt Offering Altar and Incense Altar come together and are as one.

Stepping over to the priests again, I say: outside of Jesus as the Burnt Offering Altar, the burnt offering, and the atoning sacrifice, we can have no spirit of grace to pray and give thanks, *Zechariah 12:10.* Through him *Hebrews 13:15* alone can this incense be offered up. He who does not pray and give thanks through that fire given in him by Jesus—working in, upon, and out of the power of the Son of God’s sacrifice—comes before the Lord with a "strange fire," <note>A reference to Nadab and Abihu in Leviticus 10, who were punished for using unauthorized fire</note> which shall smoke against his prayers.

<margin>No offerings to be brought except upon the Burnt Offering Altar. No offerings on the Incense Altar.</margin>
**H.** When I take into holy consideration how one had to bring the atoning sacrifice etc. to the Burnt Offering Altar, and had to sprinkle it upon the four horns on the Great Day of Atonement (See under BURNT OFFERING ALTAR), and might bring nothing other than incense to the Incense Altar, and had to kindle it on the Great Day of Atonement in the morning and evening; and the high priest spent that entire day with sacrificing and interceding, with which that great annual day was completed etc.; then it comes to my mind how Jesus our high priest, with one sacrifice, has completed that "year of God’s good pleasure," saying *John 19:30; Hebrews 10:14,* how he prayed upon this sacrifice as high priest in the evening of the Old Testament and in the dawn of the New Testament, and at noon

will still pray and persevere, since he always lives to pray for us, and will also pray in the evening of the world, at the general gathering. Then it occurs to me at the same time that the spiritual priests of the New Testament must not approach him, the Altar of Incense, to pray and give thanks without Jesus’ atoning sacrifice; for it would be an open denial of his sacrifice, and a scorning and trampling of the blood of the New Testament, which could not be avenged otherwise than with the utmost disfavor.

# ALTAR.

...always and without ceasing kindle our incense to God in Jesus' name, praising and thanking him. *Colossians 1:12, 13. etc. Colossians 3:16, 17. 1 Thessalonians 5:18. Ephesians 5:18, 19.*

But because both the Burnt Offering and Incense Altars belong to his priestly office—just as they belonged in a symbolic way to the office of the Levitical priesthood—so in this matter, the Altar of Burnt Offering and the Altar of Incense come together as one.

Stepping back again to the priests, I say: outside of Jesus as the Altar of Burnt Offering, the burnt offering, and the atonement sacrifice, we can have no spirit of grace to pray and give thanks, *Zechariah 12:10;* through him *Hebrews 13:15* alone can this incense be offered. He who does not pray and give thanks by the fire that God gives in him through Jesus—working in, upon, and out of the power of the Son of God's sacrifice—comes before the Lord with a strange fire <note>original: "vreemt vuur" — a reference to the biblical story of Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10), who were punished for using unauthorized fire in their sensors.</note>, which shall smoke against his prayers.

<margin>No sacrifices to be brought except on the Altar of Burnt Offering. No sacrifices but incense on the Altar of Incense.</margin>

<margin>The four gold rings and the two carrying poles.</margin>

1. The mobility and changeability of that old, symbolic, and imperfect system of church government.

2. And that, although the kingdom of heaven shall hereafter be immovable and unshakeable on earth regarding its form and governance through the Word, Spirit, and Sacraments, the application of all these means is nonetheless by no means permanently bound to any single land, place, time, or specific people. Instead, the "means of grace" can be moved, as has been seen in the churches of Asia Minor and other regions of the world. Where God’s throne and Altars once stood and the light of the Gospel shone, there is now darkness, idolatry, ignorance, and the place of Dagon’s Ark and Altar. <note>Dagon was a god of the Philistines; the author uses this to show how a land can lose its Christian heritage and return to "paganism."</note>

3. And by logical consequence, that one must make use of the favorable time, the "day of hearing," and the means of salvation, *Psalm 95:7, 8; Isaiah 55:6; Hebrews 3:7, 8; and 4:7,* before it becomes too late. *Proverbs 1:24, 25; Isaiah 65:12, 13; and 66:4, etc.*

Rather, they are brought from no fixed place, for Jesus had to have his own people throughout the world. From all regions, people were to seek him and pray and give thanks in his name. *Psalm 72:11-17; Malachi 1:11 <note>original: "Mal. ### THE ALTAR seen by Isaiah, Isaiah 6.

Before I express myself further on this, I want the reader to observe with me that this chapter, and the matters contained within it, are attached and linked to the preceding fifth chapter. There, the Lord of the Vineyard disputes with his vineyard, and reproaches his people for their ungratefulness and unfruitfulness, declaring how he intended to deal with his people regarding their destruction—yet in such a way that, in his severity and wrath, he would still be mindful of kindness and mercy, so that it might be revealed that he by no means breaks his promises.

After this, Isaiah appears in figure and imagination before a seat and throne of judgment, upon which is seated He with whom judgment rests, ready to pronounce and execute justice as a proof of his severity against that evil, perverse, unfruitful, and adulterous generation of Israel.

To announce this severe and weighty judgment, He prepares and dispatches one <note>The prophet Isaiah himself.</note>, whose announcement of this judgment would be accompanied by the people’s hardening and blinding, so that the judgment stood firmly decided, ready to burst forth into final desolation.

<column-break/>

Since the link of prophecy sends us to such a joint of time in which the ultimate desolation of the Jews is perceived, paired with blinding and hardening;

Since it is clearly said in *John 12:40-41* <note>The author likely means John 12 here, though the text cites Isaiah XII.</note> that Isaiah saw the Glory of Christ;

And the Father has given him all power and judgment, *Matthew 28; John 5,* I understand it in this way: namely, that one must apply the symbols and depictions in and through this vision to the judgment brought upon the Jews at the time of Christ’s glorification and his sitting at the Father’s right hand in the heavens.

It does not please me at present to unlock and run through the entire sixth chapter, but I do wish, on the occasion of having dealt with the altars, to give some account of the altar that appeared to Isaiah.

I am quite willing to believe that what Isaiah recounts regarding the altar, the Seraph's tongs, the burning coal, the touching of the lips, etc., appeared to him in a vision and strong mental imagery and contemplation; and all of this was as vivid, powerful, and with such sensitive emotion as if what came to him in the vision and strong soul-imagination had appeared to his outward senses, eyes, and ears.

It does not mean, therefore, that it should be understood and taken properly and according to the letter. However, it depicted and sketched something which would certainly happen, between which and what appeared in the vision there would be a great and close correspondence.

One does not notice that the altar is described, nor is anything mentioned of its building materials, its size, or its actual location, which makes me think that it should not only be taken imaginatively, but that perhaps this altar corresponded with the one which stood in the temple at that point in time.

And so, by transference and spiritual meaning, I hold that by this altar is symbolized the Christ, *Hebrews 13:10,* who offered himself blamelessly to God through the eternal spirit, *Hebrews 9:14; Ephesians 5:2,* and bore our sins in his body on the cross. *1 Peter 2.*

<margin>The fire on the altar.</margin>
By the fire on that altar, I understand that according to the Lord’s meaning, there should be understood the power of Christ’s merits, applied by the working spirit to justify, sanctify, and prepare his own for all kinds of reasonable and pleasing services to God. *Otherwise:* Christ’s spirit and his singular gifts, *Romans 8; Galatians 4; John 7:37, 38, 39,* with which he would baptize, *Matthew 3,* falling and resting upon the Apostles under the symbol of divided tongues as of fire, *Acts 2.* By him who takes these fiery coals with tongs from the altar, etc., I can well imagine the Holy Spirit, who takes everything that he communicates—under and through the ministry of the word—from Christ the altar. But I can also imagine through this all those swift Seraphim <note>The "Seraphs" or Seraphim are high-ranking celestial beings in Isaiah's vision.</note> whom the glorified King Jesus is pleased to dignify, call, and send forth to his church and kingdom services, *Matthew 28; Mark 16; Ephesians 4;* especially the Apostles, who had an immediate sending and preparation from the Christ; who, being full of the spirit themselves, *Matthew 10; Luke 3; John 16; Acts 18* (among whom Peter and Paul excel), in all haste,

### AMALEK, AMALEKITES: <note>original Hebrew: עמלק</note>

<margin>Meaning.</margin>
In Hebrew this word means (*a licker*), *a smiter*; or *smiting*, in mixed Hebrew and Syriac.

It is a name given to the king derived from the people, and used for both the people and their chief, *Exodus 17:8–13, Deuteronomy 25.*

AMALEK and the AMALEKITES are to be counted among the descendants of Esau, *Genesis 36:12–16.*

A people belonging among the Edomites <note>The original uses 'Idumeërs', a historical term for the descendants of Esau/Edom</note>, living in the south of Canaan: called sinners, *1 Samuel 15:18.*

Israel had not been wandering long before the Amalekites fell upon them without cause, suddenly and without a declaration of war—unforeseen, while they were tired and exhausted—attacking the rear of the army. Because of this, the Lord gave the command that this generation, wherever they might be found, should be subdued and entirely rooted out, *Exodus 17, Deuteronomy 25, 1 Samuel 15, Joshua 10, 1 Chronicles 4*, etc.

It is true that Saul and David did their part in this: but it is also true that they remained in existence for a long time, and joining with the surrounding enemies, they greatly tormented Israel, just as they are recorded among the enemies in *Psalm 83*. It is said that they were first entirely rooted out by the descendants of Simeon.

I am inclined to believe that in Amalek one can see prefigured the generation of carnal Jews in Ishmael: who without cause fell upon the true Israel of God during the taking of the world's inheritance, and that the church had a long struggle with them while they joined with the Romans and stirred up the Heathens against the Christians. They were the first in this hostile undertaking and attack: for which they are by no means excused, but as far as their city, temple, and state are concerned, they were entirely rooted out as a mirror and example to others.

I also think that Amalek can be viewed as a symbol of the church's enemies while she is here below in the wilderness of the world, both spiritual and physical enemies, against whom she will have to fight from generation to generation until she is in the Canaan above; these must be finished and subdued; sin, the world, and corruption overcome.

<margin>Enemies of the church.</margin>
And so there are enemies of the church who, like Amalek, cannot be conquered by Joshua except through constant fasting and prayer, with the awakening of faith: *Prayers and tears are the weapons of the church.* <note>original Latin: *Preces & lacrymæ sunt arma ecclesiæ*</note>

And so, early in the dawn of the New Testament, an Antichristian Amalek arose, linked with a series of enemies, who, licking and deceitfully flattering with the tongue while he leaves the

<column-break/>

souls behind, destroys, slaughters, and kills Christ's flock, making war against the saints—especially toward the West. He, like the king of the Amalekites with his subjects who do him homage and worship him, has warred against the Israel of God from time to time, as if from generation to generation. Although some of his horns have fallen off, he still stirs and persecutes the saints. Yet the time fast approaches that the true Simeon, who hears and answers the sighs and prayers of those under the altar, shall one day avenge their blood and entirely root out the Antichristian Amalek, the man of sin, the son of perdition, and destroy him from the earth; for which we have firm and assured hope based on divine prophecies and threats. Simply look to the visions and oracles of John <note>Referring to the Book of Revelation</note>.

Very likely there are still Amaleks even in the present day, who are no better in religion or trade, and who have treated and handled our "Dutch Israel" <note>The author compares the Dutch Republic to biblical Israel, a common theme in 17th-18th century Dutch theology</note> none too civilly; it is not strictly required that one names the foreign powers and kings by their clear names. One can make a quiet application and transfer of this to oneself.

עמלק *Amalek*, a name for the people, is descended from Amalek the son of Eliphaz, Esau's son, a grandson of Esau, born of the concubine Timna, *Genesis 36:12–16, 1 Chronicles 1.* Timna <note>original: Thamnar</note>, it is said, means one who is forbidden, unlawful to use, and whom it is by no means permitted or free to take and hold according to right and reason.

Whether there are not sometimes those who climb to the throne who have not come into the world in the most spotless manner, I shall leave in the middle.

Amalek was the name of the people, and their leader was called Agag, which means one who ponders, who is somber of spirit, and constantly gives commands and orders. Whether there are not even today those sitting on thrones, somber of spirit, constantly thinking, weighing, and commanding out of full power—"I will it"—I shall also leave that there.

Amalek, the name of the people, is taken for the head, ruler, and king of the people. Thus we say: the Frenchman, the Spaniard, the Savoyard, the Hollander, the Englishman, etc.

Amalek means a people that strikes and inflicts wounds, is warlike, and prone to fighting and quarreling. Whether such are not at least found now, the wars of recent years have clearly shown.

Amalek was to the east and south of Canaan; and who is in that region with respect to our "Dutch Israel," one can trace from the maps.

Amalek was an idolater: many around us are such.

Amalek's kingdom once flourished: as does the kingdom of those who are like him in these days.

Amalek was Israel's old enemy: so too are there now old enemies of the Netherlands.

Amalek attacked by surprise and without a declaration of war: this has also happened to our Netherlands.

Amalek's wars with Israel were sometimes very doubtful in outcome: carry that over to our situation.

Amalek gradually weakened: time will tell.

### ALTAR seen by Isaiah, Isaiah 6.

Before I express myself further on this, I wish for it to be noted along with me that this chapter, and the substance contained within it, is attached and linked to the preceding fifth Chapter. There, the Lord of the Vineyard disputes with his vineyard, and reproaches his people for their ingratitude as well as their unfruitfulness, declaring how he intended to deal with his people regarding their extermination. Yet, he would do so in such a way that in his severity and wrath, he would still be mindful of kindness and mercy, so that it might be revealed that he by no means breaks his promises.

After this, Isaiah appears in figure and imagination before a seat and throne of judgment, upon which is seated He with whom judgment rests, ready to pronounce and execute justice, as a proof of his severity against that evil, perverse, unfruitful, and adulterous generation of Israel.

To announce this severe and weighty judgment, he qualifies and despatches one whose announcement of this judgment would be accompanied by the people’s hardening and blinding, so that the judgment stood firmly decided, ready to burst forth into final desolation.

<column-break/>

Since the link of prophecy sends us to such a joint of time in which the utter desolation of the Jews is perceived, paired with blinding and hardening;

Since *John 12:40-41* <note>The text cites Isaiah 12, but the reference to Isaiah seeing Christ's glory is found in John 12</note> clearly says that Isaiah saw the Glory of Christ:

And the Father has given him all power and judgment, *Matthew 28. John 5.* Thus I understand it in this manner: namely, that one must apply the figures and sketches in and through this vision to the judgment brought upon the Jews at the time of Christ’s glorification and his sitting at the Father’s right hand in the heavens.

To unlock and move through the entire sixth chapter does not suit me at present, but I do wish, on the occasion of having dealt with the altars, to give some account of the altar that appeared to Isaiah.

I am quite willing to believe that what Isaiah recounts of the altar, Seraph’s tongs, burning coals, touching of the lips, etc., appeared to him in a vision and strong mental imagination and contemplation, and all of it as vividly, powerfully, and with such sensible emotion as if that which came to him in vision and strong mental imagination had appeared to his outward senses, eyes, and ears.

It does not mean, therefore, that it should be understood and taken properly and according to the letter. The imagery, however, sketched something that would surely happen, between which and what appeared in the vision there would be great and close correspondence.

One does not notice that the altar is described, or anything mentioned of its building materials, or size, or its actual location, which makes me think that it should not only be taken imaginatively, but that perhaps this altar corresponded with the one which stood in the temple at that point in time.

And so, by transference and spiritual meaning, I hold that by this altar is symbolized the Christ, *Hebrews 13:10,* who offered himself blameless to God through the eternal spirit, *Hebrews 9:14. Ephesians 5:2,* and bore our sins in his body on the cross. *1 Peter 2.*

<margin>The fire on the altar.</margin>
By the fire on that altar, I understand that according to the Lord’s meaning, it should be understood as the power of Christ’s merits applied through the working Spirit, to justify, sanctify, and qualify his own for all kinds of reasonable and well-pleasing services to God. *Otherwise Christ’s spirit, and its singular gifts Romans 8. Galatians 4. John 7:37, 38, 39,* with which he would baptize, *Matthew 3,* falling and resting upon the Apostles under the symbol of divided tongues of fire, *Acts 2.* By him who takes these fiery coals with a pair of tongs from the altar, etc., I can well imagine the Holy Spirit, who takes everything that he shares, under and through the ministry of the word, from Christ the altar. But I can also imagine through it all those swift Seraphs <note>Seraphs: highest order of angels, often associated with fire</note> whom the glorified King Jesus is pleased to dignify, call, and send forth for his church and royal services, *Matthew 28. Mark 16. Ephesians 4,* especially the Apostles, who had an immediate sending and qualification from the Christ; who were themselves full of the spirit, *Matthew 10. Luke 3. John 16. Acts 18* (among whom Peter and Paul excel), in all haste...

### AMALEK, AMALEKITES: Amalek <note>original Hebrew: עמלק</note>

<margin>Meaning.</margin>
In Hebrew this word means *a licker*, *a smiter*; or *striking*, in a mixture of Hebrew and Syriac.

It is a name given to the king derived from the name of the people, and used for both the people and their leader, *Exodus 17:8-13, Deuteronomy 25.*

AMALEK, AMALEKITES are to be counted among the descendants of Esau, *Genesis 36:12-16.*

A people belonging to the Idumeans <note>The Edomites, descendants of Esau/Edom</note>, living in the south of Canaan: called sinners, *1 Samuel 15:18.*

Israel had not wandered long before the Amalekites fell upon them without cause, suddenly and without a declaration of war—unexpectedly, when they were weary and exhausted—at the rear of the army. Therefore the Lord gave the command that this generation, wherever they might be encountered, should be subdued and completely rooted out, *Exodus 17, Deuteronomy 25, 1 Samuel 15, Joshua 10, 1 Chronicles 4,* etc.

It is true that Saul and David did their part in this: but it is also true that they remained in existence for a long time, and conspiring with the surrounding enemies, greatly tormented Israel, as they are listed among the enemies in *Psalm 83.* It is said that they were first completely rooted out by the descendants of Simeon.

I am inclined to believe that in Amalek one can somewhat see foreshadowed the generation of the fleshly Jews in Ishmael: who without cause fell upon the true Israel of God during the taking of the inheritance of the world, and that the church had a long-lasting struggle with them while they conspired with the Romans and stirred up the Heathens against the Christians. They were the first in this hostile undertaking and attack. They are by no means excused, but regarding their city, temple, and civil state, they were completely rooted out as a mirror and example to others.

I also think that Amalek can be regarded as a symbol of the enemies of the church while she is here below in the wilderness of the world, both spiritual and physical, against whom she shall have to struggle from generation to generation until she is in Canaan above. These must be slaughtered and subdued; sin, the world, and corruption overcome.

<margin>Enemies of the church.</margin>
And so there are enemies of the church who, like Amalek, cannot be conquered by Joshua except through constant fasting and prayer, with the awakening of faith: *Prayers and tears are the weapons of the church* <note>original Latin: "Preces & lacrymæ sunt arma ecclesiæ"</note>.

And so, early in the dawn of the New Testament, an antichristian Amalek has arisen, bound with a chain of enemies, who, licking and flatteringly deceiving with the tongue while he forsakes 

<column-break/>

He, as the king of the Amalekites with his subjects who pay him homage and worship him, has warred against the Israel of God from time to time, as if from generation to generation. # ALMOND TREE.

### ALMOND TREE, NUTS, ROD, <note>original Hebrew: שקד (shaked), Greek: ἀμυγδάλη (amygdalē), Latin: amygdalus</note>

<margin>Form of the Almond Tree.</margin>
It is a tree of reasonable height and girth, with a rough, uneven bark, whose leaves very closely resemble those of the peach; it is cultivated towards winter, blooms in the month of January, and gives its fruit in March, though not in all parts of the world. One may read of this in Pliny, Book 16, Chapter 26, pages 324-353, etc.

The Hebrew word *shaked* <note>original: שקד</note>, which appears in *Genesis 42:11, Numbers 17:8, Ecclesiastes 12:5, Jeremiah 1:11, Exodus 25, and 37:19, 20,* is seen to be derived from *shakad* <note>original: שקד</note>, meaning *He has hastened, hurried, been active, has watched, was early ripe and timely*; because the Almond tree, in its blooming and producing of fruit, precedes all other fruit trees.

It is said that Almonds have two outer coverings or coats, of which the outermost is bitter, and the second is hard and somewhat rough: and that towards the harvest time, the outermost bark rips and falls away.

<margin>Bitter and sweet Almonds.</margin>
Regarding the varieties of Almonds, one finds them distinguished into bitter and sweet.

One makes or presses oil from them, as the Naturalists teach us.

<margin>Power of Almonds.</margin>
As to what power these Nuts or Almonds possess, one may hear from the physicians: at the very least, I have read that the juice of sweet Almonds softens the throat and lungs, and causes the fluids to be cast up from the chest, preparing them for spitting out.

That the fluid of bitter Almonds causes the tough and hard phlegm to rise easily from the chest.

That some bitter Almonds, eaten on an empty stomach, are wonderfully useful against the gravel <note>kidney stones or urinary sediment</note>.

That oil of Almonds is good against ailments of the lungs, kidneys, and sharp bladder complaints.

That one must eat some bitter Almonds beforehand if one intends to drink, so as not to become intoxicated.

That the root of bitter Almonds, whether boiled or unboiled, pleasantly stretches the skin of the face, removes wrinkles, and makes the countenance cheerful.

That Almond nuts sharpen the appetite and induce sleep, discharge water, benefit the monthly periods <note>menstruation</note>, and such like, upon which I shall not dwell.

They must have already been well-known and judged to be of good use, since one already reads of them in *Genesis 43:11.*

One finds that the Lord gave a command that there should be some likeness and correspondence between the Almond nuts and the bowls in the branches or shafts of the golden candlestick. *Exodus 25:33, 34 and 37:19, 20.* This pictorial representation can be found by Professor Witsius in *Sacred Miscellany*, and Goeree’s *Republic of the Hebrews, second part, etc.*

By way of metaphor and through imagination, the Preacher <note>Solomon, in the book of Ecclesiastes</note> speaks in Chapter 12:5 of the blooming Almond tree; by which I can think that he signifies the white and gray locks of hair with which the heads of the elderly are sometimes suddenly—and beyond their desire or expectation—adorned, just like the crowns of the Almond trees, by which they make themselves recognized from afar.

<column-break/>

> — Unexpected old age, etc.
> Untimely gray hairs are spread upon the crown of the head. <note>original Latin: "Inopin senect, &c. Intempestivi funduntur vertice cani."</note>

->That is:<-

> *For unexpectedly comes old age,*
> *And the head is covered with gray hairs before its time.*

One reads in *Jeremiah 1:11* that Jeremiah saw an Almond rod.

The common translation has "a watching rod," or as Symmachus says, "the night-watch-keeping rod" <note>original Greek: virgam γρηγορᾶσαν (virgam grēgorousan)</note>.

Maldonatus wishes it to be so named *because it was the rod of God. Or, because it shoots up and gives fruit so suddenly.*

Viegas is of the opinion that it is so named *because it was dotted as if with eyes.*

Henricus Ursinus in *Biblical Trees* understands it to mean *a comet in the likeness of an Almond rod, tapering towards the end or its tail.*

Hugo Cardinalis seems to understand by it *a crooked wood or hook, or a tool of vagabonds and thieves, with which they, while the master of the house sleeps, pull his goods toward themselves through the window.*

It seems to have been a symbol that the Lord would quickly fulfill His word and hasten His judgments, bringing the fruit and effect of His word upon the Jews—especially His judgments—through the peoples of the north.

The rod or staff being a sign and symbol of His power and vengeance: and that it was an Almond rod, according to the nature of the tree, was a symbol of the hastening of His judgment, so that they would soon—alas! though justly—perceive the flowers and fruits, the preparations and effects.

What the matter was regarding Aaron’s rod, I have shown previously.

Whether these bowls on the seven shafts or branches of the golden candlestick, prepared in the manner of Almond nuts, signified the various ministries, gifts, and abilities in the church—especially that of the New Testament (*1 Corinthians 12 and 14, Ephesians 4:12,* etc.)—or faith with its pleasant flowers, fruits, and works, receiving the healing and grace-fruits or benefits of Christ’s bloody merits—upon that I shall not express myself at present. It will be appropriate when I give an account of the golden candlestick.

Furthermore, when one considers the Almond nuts, both externally and internally, having a bitter and rough outer bark and an uneven and hard one within, in which the kernel is hidden and difficult to crack—whose outer skin must first split and rend before one can timely and properly reach the fruit—so I can well call to mind the saying of Plautus:

> *He who wishes to have the kernel from the nut must break the nut.* <note>original Latin: "Qui ex nuce nucleum esse vult, nucem frangat oportet."</note>

->That is:<-

> *He who wants to eat the kernel must first crack the nut.*

Symbolizing that if one wishes to attain virtue, learning, etc., it previously costs effort and labor. The first and second attempts, the labor and the effort, are in themselves rough, bitter, and hard, but the inner fruit compensates for and sweetens everything again.

# ALMOND TREE. AMASA. AMBER.

To reach the kernel of grace, and the power and fruit of consolation, so that faith, love, and hope may be more clearly observed, it is often necessary that the outer garment of our body be opened, torn, and split through persecutions, blows, etc. *2 Corinthians 4:8, 9, 10.*

> *The almond, split without, gives sweet fruits within,*
> *So the godly man, though afflicted in body, is strong in mind.*
> <note>original Latin: "Scissa foris, dulces dant intus amygdala fructus, / Sic pius afflicto corpore mente valet."</note>

->That is:<-

> *One peels the Almonds first, if one would taste the fruit,*
> *So the godly man feels not the pain touch his soul.*

The Heathens <note>Non-Christian ancients, specifically Romans</note> regarded a well-blooming and fertile Almond tree as a portent of a good and fruitful year, according to *Virgil, Georgics, Book 1.*

> *Observe as well, when the almond tree in the woods*
> *Clothes itself in blossom, and bends its fragrant branches,*
> *If the fruit prevails, then the grain harvest will follow,*
> *And a great threshing will come with great heat.*
> <note>original Latin: "Contemplator item, cum se nux plurima sylvis / Induet in florem, & ramos curvabit olentes, / Si superant fœtus, pariter frumenta sequentur, / Magnaque cum magno veniet tritura calore."</note>

Joost van den Vondel <note>The most famous poet of the Dutch Golden Age</note> translates this in this manner:

> *Take heed that (if the Almond tree everywhere*
> *Blooms most gloriously, and stands more open with leaves*
> *Than blossom, and the branch hangs almost crooked and broken*
> *By fruit, and the harvest covers it too blessedly)*
> *A rich corn harvest waits upon the field,*
> *A joyful threshing-time with a row of hot days*
> *Will follow.*

<margin>Medes inclined toward Almonds.</margin>
Among the fruits of Canaan, beautiful Almonds are also counted, *Genesis 43:10.* It seems to me that the Medes <note>An ancient Iranian people</note> were especially fond of these fruits. Information regarding this can be found in *Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 3, Chapter 11.*

### A M A S A, עמשא <note>Hebrew: Amasa</note>

<margin>Meaning.</margin>
AMASA had as his mother Abigail, David's sister, a daughter of Jesse: his father was Jether the Ishmaelite. *1 Chronicles 2:14-17.*
AMASA, it is said, means "one who is the people's gift": or "one whom the people have carried and exalted": or otherwise, "a prince and leader of the people."

<margin>Amasa placed in Joab's stead.</margin>
Amasa was appointed by David as army commander in Joab's place, *2 Samuel 19.* David sent him out to gather Judah against Sheba; while he was busy in this duty, Joab met him, and making a false greeting of welcome, took him by the beard and struck him with his sword at the fifth rib, so that his entrails poured out and he died, *2 Samuel 20.* Yet he received his retribution among all others from the peaceful and righteous Solomon. *1 Kings 2:31, 32, 33, 34.*

<margin>Comparison between Christ and Amasa.</margin>
Quite many similarities could be found between Christ and his experiences and Amasa, if one were to examine everything very precisely.
Was Amasa of David's lineage? Christ was as well.
If Amasa signifies a gift of the people, Christ is the gift par excellence. *Isaiah 9:5, Job 3:16, John 3:16, 4:10, Romans 8:32.*
If it signifies a lord, prince, and leader, Christ is also this par excellence. *Psalms 2, 72, and 110, Isaiah 9:5, Micah 5, Revelation 17 and 19,* etc.

<column-break/>

If it signifies one whom the people have carried and exalted: It is the Son of God, the angel of the covenant. *Isaiah 63:9.*
If Amasa was made head of the army: It is Christ, the Son of God and of man, who is the Lord of Hosts, who is the head and leader above all powers and strengths, the true Michael over battle-ranks with banners, the King of the ages, the King of kings, the Prince of the Lord's host from Jews and Gentiles, to which many texts can be brought.
If Amasa was greeted by Joab with a false face and brought down through envy: It is Christ, who was kissed and embraced with the false flattery of Judas, soothed by the Jews with Hosannas, and thereafter, out of pure envy, captured and put to death. *Matthew 21 and 22, Mark 15,* etc.
If Amasa's death was avenged: The Lord has avenged Himself upon the Jews, with Jesus’ blood coming upon the heads of the Jews and their children, as the destruction of their city and temple clearly demonstrates.
Let this be enough regarding this matter; let us move on to something else.

### AMBER, *Ambra, Succinum, Carabe,* Amber and Incense-stone.

IT is held that these names belong to one and the same substance, which I shall treat.
Regarding the origin, appearance, and effects of amber, or ambergris, people are not exactly in full agreement; especially not regarding its origin.

<margin>Various opinions on Amber.</margin>
That it has been named *Succinum* arose from the belief that it was a dripping, gummy resin and moisture, dripping from the cracked and split trunks and branches of fir and pine trees; as one can read that this was the opinion of Perottus and others in Olaus Magnus’ description of the Northern Lands, Book 12, Chapter 8, page 360.
Others are of the opinion that amber is spongy earth, washed away from hidden sea islands, floating on the sea waves, and cast upon the shore by the sea winds.
Others believe it to be either the excrement or the seed of true sea whales; and for this, Gargias, Clusius, Monardus, Gesnerus, etc., seem to have cast their votes.
However, I have noticed that most people lean toward the idea that it is a thick, fatty, gummy moisture, welling up from subterranean cracks and gulfs in the sea, floating on top of the water, washed to the shores, and thrown up by the winds and sea waves, gradually made stone-hard by the air and sunbeams.

<margin>Color of Amber.</margin>
Amber is of various colors: white, yellow, greyish, brown, and black.
One sometimes finds small animals, wings, claws, etc., within it; and that can happen when that gummy, thick substance is still soft, so that this or that small animal sticks to it, which is then covered by newly added substance and later appears and shows itself within this petrified material.
Amber is found near Sofola, Comaro, Demgaxa, Mozambique, Florida, and elsewhere.
How Amber rose to a high price under Nero, because people dyed hair with it and invented all sorts of finery to imitate Sabina Poppaea, Nero's "Venus-creature"; and how they also used it for nets in...

# A M B E R. A M E N.

...used in the root-beds to prevent wild animals from jumping over them, can be read in Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (23–79 AD), author of *Natural History*. The text cites Book 38, though Pliny’s work only contains 37 books; it likely refers to Book 37 where amber is discussed.</note> *book 38, chapter 13,* as well as in Jan de Bruine the younger, in his *Whetstone page 545.* Young ladies wore beads of it around their necks and hands.

<margin>Oil of Amber.</margin>
One makes a volatile salt, oil, and essence from amber <note>original: "Barnsteen," a Dutch term for amber meaning "burning stone"</note>, as well as an extract, as can be seen in the writings of the physicians.

<margin>Power of Amber.</margin>
Regarding its power and virtues, one attributes quite a lot of power and effects to amber, ambergris, and succinite <note>original: "barn- of brantsteen," both synonyms for amber</note>.

It is clear that amber, when rubbed, attracts straws and other lighter materials to itself, just as the lodestone attracts iron.

It is evident that when it is rubbed, it spreads a pleasant scent.

Furthermore, it is testified that the essence and oil are particularly good for epilepsy <note>original: "vallende ziekte," or falling sickness</note>, stroke, melancholy, cramps, fainting, plague, heart palpitations, stones and gravelly grit, dizzy spells, shortness of breath, jaundice, difficulty in urinating, the "risings of women" <note>an early modern medical term for hysteria or respiratory distress thought to be caused by the womb</note>, etc.

To show that when applied externally or even when used as incense, it works upon the brain to refresh it, and likewise to strengthen the heart and stomach and dry up superfluous fluids, and such things, I shall leave to the recommendation of the physicians. I shall hold myself content if I can think of something which equals this amber in virtues, power, and effects as a spiritual amber for spiritual things.

<margin>Application of Amber to spiritual matters.</margin>
He who wishes to be considered a true scripturalist not only holds it to be so, but he has found through experience that man is beset with just as many ailments of the soul as of the body, and that he requires an ambergris—a spiritual amber—against them.

To what shall I more suitably compare it and apply it than to the universal medicine of divine love, grace, the working of the Holy Spirit, and the power of Christ’s bloody merits? Certainly, if one attributes something healing to amber in its natural workings, it is the aforementioned which exercises just as much power upon the soul and its ailments.

If it be that the heart has a certain exhaustion and faintness, Paul will tell us: *Hebrews 13:9. It is a good thing that the heart be established with grace; not with meats, etc.*

If one has spiritual heart palpitations or anxieties through a busy conscience that brings crimes to mind, one has the strengthening remedy of Christ’s bloody merits through the working Spirit, *1 John 3:19, 20, 21. Romans 5:1, 2, 3. Romans 8:31, 32, 33, 34.* If one is beset with a kind of stoniness and spiritual numbness, the amber of grace and the working of the Spirit performs the cure. *Jeremiah 32. Ezekiel 36. Psalm 51.*

Is there a dizziness? Is the heart anxious? Are the fluids and tears of sorrow abundant? The amber of grace and consolation is for the drying up and improvement thereof. *Isaiah 61:1, 2, 3.*

Does amber bring any strengthening and refreshing to the nerves, tendons, etc.? It is even so. *Psalm 51:10-14.*

Is amber good against the plague? Against the plague of sin and general corruption, grace and the blood of Christ help in a wonderful and powerful way. *Zechariah 13:1. 1 John 1:7. 1 Corinthians 16:11.*

<column-break/>

If amber smells strongest when it is rubbed vigorously, certainly the graced soul gives off not only a good scent, *2 Corinthians 2:15, 16,* but especially so when it is rubbed by adversities. *Hebrews 12:11.*

And if ever amber causes faintness and swooning to cease, it is the grace of Jesus Christ. *2 Corinthians 12:9, 10.*

->### A M E N, אָמֵן, *Amèn.*<-

<margin>AMEN, not the name of a person.</margin>
Although the word AMEN appears multiple times in the Divine Book, and is more than once joined and applied to a Divine Person, it is nonetheless not a name which is properly assigned to any person as a personal name; and the great Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a famous Dutch theologian</note> already noted this before me, writing on *Revelation 3:14.*

This is something special and rare: for the meaning of אָמֵן <note>original: "Amen"</note> occurs, as far as I know, nowhere in the form of a proper name. It does occur in *Isaiah 65:16,* so that, "He who blesseth himself in the earth shall bless himself," בֵּאלֹהֵי אָמֵן <note>original Hebrew: "In the God of truth"</note>. *In the God of truth: and he that sweareth in the earth shall swear by the God of truth,* etc. Yet there it does not appear in the form of someone’s proper name, as if it stood that they should bless themselves in God, who is called Amen: for then it would be read in Hebrew as בְּאֱלֹהִים אָמֵן <note>original Hebrew: "in God Amen," where God is the absolute noun</note> and not *in the construct form,* בֵּאלֹהֵי אָמֵן <note>original Hebrew: "in the God-of truth," where "God" is linked to "Truth/Amen"</note>.

AMEN is taken there for אֱמוּנָה <note>original: "Emunah," meaning faithfulness</note> or אֱמֶת <note>original: "Emet," meaning truth</note>, so that "God of Amen" is the same as "God of Faithfulness," as Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian</note> had already noted. Our translators also do not have "in God the Amen," but "in the God of truth."

*Amen*, and אָמֵן <note>Amen</note> / אָמֵן <note>Amen</note> is frequently taken with the power and meaning of true, certainly, in faithfulness, so be it, etc.

It is a strong testimony and confirmation, like an oath.

He who heard the proposed covenant, with its many threatened curses, had to say "amen" upon entering the covenant. *Deuteronomy 27.*

The woman suspected by the jealousy of her husband had to say with doubling, upon the adjuration of the priest, "Amen, amen." *Numbers 5.*

The summoned witnesses, sworn by the judge, had to say "amen" when the investigation subsequently remained with the judge, as I am about to show more closely.

<margin>The word Amen used after thanksgivings.</margin>
One was accustomed in the Jewish Synagogues, upon hearing the prayers and thanksgivings, to say "amen": see my explanations on *1 Corinthians 14:16.* Leo of Modena <note>A famous Venetian Rabbi (1571–1648)</note> *page 24.* Called Gafan: *Vitringa on the Synagogue page 1093,* etc.

It had to be done in faith, with hope of being heard and full reliance upon God, therefore called by Jacob a prayer of faith. *Buxtorf, Lexicon at אָמֵן / Jalkut on Psalm 31. C. Vitringa, archif. p. 1094.*

Yet it was not to be done with great haste, or with a loud and reckless shout, but slowly, deliberately, and with good understanding. *Orach Chaim <note>A section of the Shulchan Aruch, the code of Jewish law</note> book 100. Maimonides, Hilchot Berachot, chapter 1. Vitringa, archis. p. 1096,* etc. One perceives some evidence of this in *Psalm 41:14, 72:19, 89:53,* etc.

And to note something further on *1 Corinthians 14:16,*

# A M E N.
**M**

...ing, to do such a thing was also the custom in the early Christian church. See *Tertullian* <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD).</note> and *Justin Martyr, Apology II, page 98.* <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100 – c. 165 AD).</note>

<margin>A layman in the congregation.</margin>
Now, when there was someone in the congregation, or the congregation itself, who occupied the place of a layman or an unlearned person <note>original Hebrew: א (*Aleph*, used here as a marker)</note>, an illiterate person who did not understand the languages—see *Buxtorf, Rabbinic-Talmudic Lexicon* <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a celebrated Hebraist.</note> under the word *Makom* <note>original Hebrew: מקום, meaning "place" or "station"</note>; *Lightfoot pages 701, 773, 920*; *Dilher, Demonstrations page 313*; *Doughty on the New Testament pages 69, 73*—and you praised and thanked God through the spirit of grace, and prayed with understanding, zeal, and power in the congregation: but you did so in a language foreign and unknown to the congregation; how then can and shall he, who does not understand your language, and consequently does not know what you pray for or for what you express thanks, say *Amen* to your prayer or thanksgiving?

Regarding the aforementioned passage in *Isaiah 65:16*, Professor Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian.</note> says: in no other way do I interpret *Isaiah 65:16*, as it contains an excellent prophecy regarding what would happen in the days of the New Testament.

He is this *Elohei Amen* <note>original Hebrew: אלהי אמן</note>, the God of Truth, or Amen; not only He whom we—as He invites and adjures us to come into the covenant—ought to *confess* <note>original Greek: ὁμολογεῖν</note> and *agree with* <note>original Latin: adstipulari</note>, to accept His testimony and answer "Amen" (*Psalm 27:8*); but He is even He who would at some time appear in the flesh and then testify that everything was now made "Amen," and specifically so in Him. "Amen" is therefore He who publicly testifies that the divine promises are fulfilled.

In *2 Corinthians 1:20* it is read: *For all the promises of God in him are Yes, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us.* Regarding this, I have explained myself in my work on the second letter of Paul to the Corinthians, page 67, as follows.

The blessed Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for federal theology.</note> expresses this concisely: *The promises of God are "Nai" (Yes); they have happened because one must assent to them, that is: that they are fulfilled; they are "Amen" because they require thanksgiving and glorification.*

All the promises and pledges of God, containing within themselves grace for the sinner, as well as a demonstration of the most excellent love and directed toward the singular honor of God in the significance of His name and the revelation of His virtues, have been shown through our service to be "Yes" and "Amen" <note>original Hebrew: א (*Aleph*, a marker)</note>, firm and indubitable truth in the Christ, so that not one word has fallen unfulfilled to the earth. It is manifest: God is truthful and not a lie (*Deuteronomy 32:4; Numbers 23:19*), and everyone is obliged to assent to this demonstrated and evident truth, and thus to seal that God is true (*John 3:33; Noldius, Concordance page 177; Dieterich, Sacred Antiquities, etc.*).

It is indeed the truth that Paul and his fellow messengers and heralds <note>original Greek: κήρυκες</note>, strictly speaking, did not add credibility or internal power to the promises and pledges of God to force someone to assent; no, but they have made the truth's power and its fitness to God seen and noticed as moral, rational means and instruments of what lay within those promises.

<margin>Christ the "Yes" and the "Amen."</margin>
One might also, with good reason and on a firm foundation, think and say that by this "the Yes and the Amen" <note>original Greek: ὁ ναὶ καὶ ἀμὴν</note> can be understood the Christ, the Amen and faithful witness (*Revelation 3:14*).

<column-break/>

whom one testifies to be such as He had promised to be and become: namely the God, shield, and exceeding great reward of Abraham and his seed, both of Jews and Gentiles; the blessed and blessing, the holy and hallowing seed promised of old and now raised up, just as the Christ frequently testified by and through Himself.

And in truth, God’s purpose and decree of grace is in the Christ (*Ephesians 1:3, 4, 5; Ephesians 2*); the Son, according to the Father's will, said a required "Yes" (*Psalm 40:8, 9; Job 33:24; Zechariah 4:12, 13*); He fulfilled everything, making it "Yes" and "Amen" (*Job 19:20*); He testified in His life, and demonstrated after His resurrection, that He was the one who was to come, and therefore He Himself and the multitude could appeal to the testimony of Moses and the prophets (*Luke 24:25, 26, 27; John 5:39, etc.; Vitringa, Sacred Observations page 3, 5, etc.*).

<margin>Amen attributed to the Christ.</margin>
<margin>How to explain the word Amen.</margin>
"Amen" is frequently attributed to the Christ (*Revelation 1:5 and 3:14*). As for me, I dare say with the very learned Professor Campegius Vitringa, one must explain the word "Amen" in *Revelation 1:5 and 3:14* such that "Amen" can have the meaning of "witness," since it is immediately followed by "the faithful and true witness," that is to say: *Ed Ne'eman* <note>original Hebrew: עד נאמן</note>, the steadfast witness, who is well-grounded in His testimony. Christ is therefore called "Amen" because He testifies to men that God is such as He promised to be: not only in general, as others have also said, but He has said: "the promises are fulfilled in me; I demonstrate that God is *true* <note>original Greek: ἀληθινὸν</note> in all His promises" (*2 Corinthians 1:20*).

I say further, that the Christ is "Yes" and "Amen" in such power and emphasis—that is, a faithful and true witness—and that no one has ever been as great and credible as the Great Prophet (*Deuteronomy 18:18*), witness to the nations (*Isaiah 54:4*), and teacher of righteousness (*Joel 2:23*), because:

> a. He is a divine "Amen" and witness, therefore true and unchangeable, omniscient, almighty, having everything in His counsel, will, and hand (*Deuteronomy 34:4; Numbers 23:19*).
> b. From which it flows and follows that He is the "Amen," a steadfast, faithful, and true witness; since nothing was decided or established from eternity without Him, and since He is sufficiently wise and powerful for the execution thereof.
> c. Others might be "Yes" and "Amen" only insofar as what they testified was certain, and what was foretold later became truth without their involvement; yet what they foretold and testified, they did not know from themselves (*2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:19, 20, etc.*).
> But in such a manner, Christ is the faithful and true witness, the "Amen," because He willed and testified everything from and through Himself, having entered into and concluded the counsel with the Father, to execute and fulfill it in and through Himself (*Psalm 2:7; Zechariah 6:12, 13*).
> d. Others before and after Him might testify: "this has happened" or "this shall yet happen"; but no one ever went so far as to say, "it happened through me" or "it shall happen through me." But Christ can say in truth: "it happened through me," and "it shall happen through me" (*Luke 1:78; 2 Corinthians 1:20*).
