...being, that it would cost so little effort to tear them out of their state and stability, whether directly by Himself or indirectly through mighty enemies whom He was about to stir up against them; just as any fisherman, by means of his fishhook, is able to tear a fish out of the water.

<margin>Habakkuk 1:15.</margin>
In Habakkuk 1:15, one reads: *He lifts them all up with the hook, he catches them in his net, and gathers them in his dragnet: therefore he rejoices and is glad.* <note>The author refers to the Babylonian conquest described by the prophet.</note> Here it is considered that the destructive actions of the King of the Chaldeans are being described, who overran everything with his oppressive and overflowing power, and among others led the people of God out of Canaan into captivity, just as a fisherman does with his fishhook, dragnet, and net, in which he catches and encloses them.

To *put a hook in someone's mouth or nose* is an image borrowed from fishing, sea monsters, and wild animals, used to restrain them so that they cannot escape, nor perform what they would otherwise attempt to do according to their inner nature and power. This manner of speaking has been used more than once by God's holy writers, such as in *2 Kings 19:28* regarding Sennacherib, King of Assyria; *Isaiah 37:29* regarding Pharaoh, King of the Egyptians; *Ezekiel 29:4* and regarding Gog and Magog in *Ezekiel 38:4*. This serves as a metaphor for God’s incomparable highness, wisdom, and power, through which He can restrain the greatest, mightiest, and boldest among men, whether directly by Himself or through other powers that He makes formidable and successful, so that "one knife keeps the other in its sheath," or one makes the other blunt and weak.

Regarding the *spiritual fishermen, nets, hooks, etc. Matthew 4:19, 13:47, and 17:27; Ezekiel 47:10,* I would rather share with my readers the choice thoughts and words of a great scholar of the Scriptures than my own.

Professor Campegius Vitringa <note>A prominent 17th-century Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note>, in his work on the Evangelical parables, page 277, etc., explains it thus:

> Since fishermen primarily have two types of tools which the Holy Scripture alludes to in its style of speech—namely, a fishing rod and a net—both of these correspond very well with the word of the Gospel, *Ezekiel 47:8*. The fish that are caught with the fishing rod are enticed by the bait with which the hook of the rod is surrounded, and are thus taken captive by the cunning and skill of the fisherman. The bait is like a symbol of all the promises and gracious benefits, of which the fulfillment—hanging, so to speak, at the end of the fishing rod of the Gospel—is eternal life. The line of the rod shows us the commandments of the Gospel, which whoever observes can no longer remain in the fellowship of the world. The hook of the rod, which fastens the commandments and promises of the Gospel to one another, represents the bond that God has placed between the goods of the covenant of grace and the conditions that must be fulfilled by the covenant partners. So it is that no one can partake of the bait—that is, the goods of the Gospel—who is not at the same time enticed and entangled by the hook or sting of the Gospel; that is, who does not commit himself to following the commands that Jesus Christ has prescribed for His covenant partners. Among these commands is the forsaking of the world and worldly desires. They are caught, as if by cunning and skill, who are transferred by the Gospel from the fellowship of the world to the Kingdom of God; who are, as it were, compelled by the Gospel to do that which they otherwise would not want to do: those who see such power in the arguments of the Gospel, which power they would otherwise naturally not want to see, so that they might peacefully enjoy fleshly lusts.

In Revelation 9:10, one reads the following concerning the locusts from the smoke: *And they had tails like scorpions, and there were stings <note>original: "angels"</note> in their tails; and their power was to hurt men for five months.*

<margin>Application to false teachers.</margin>
I have found that quite many and prominent theologians have applied this to false teachers, *Isaiah 9:14*, and specifically to the spiritual orders of the Jesuits and Monks, who appeared in whole swarms after the Council of Trent, having made great embassies to China and Japan to recruit new people for their king Abaddon; what cunning inventions and tricks they possess, in order to—under the appearance of winning and saving souls—torment them and inflict a thousand deaths, etc.; just as Brightman <note>Thomas Brightman, an influential English clergyman and commentator on Revelation.</note> cites this verse from Aeneas Sylvius <note>The birth name of Pope Pius II.</note> regarding the Monks:

-> *Non audet stygius Pluto tentare quod audent* <-
-> *Effraenis monachus, plenaque fraudis anus.* <-
<note>Latin: "Stygian Pluto does not dare to attempt what an unbridled monk and an old woman full of deceit dare." Pluto was the Roman god of the underworld.</note>

-> That is: <-

-> *The hellish Pluto would not dare to undertake,* <-
-> *That which a Monk or old woman dares to start.* <-

See Suicer, *Orbis & Eccl. Fata page 247.* Marck on *Apocalypse page 324,* etc. Groenewegen *on Apocalypse*, and especially Cocceius. Hoffman in *Chronotaxi Apoc. page 236* writes as follows:

> Therefore it is indicated that from the Jesuits' erroneous teachings such consequences flow, by which, as if by poisonous stings, men are shamefully harmed; such as the doctrine that one must not keep faith with heretics; that sworn treaties may be freely broken if the interest of the Roman Church requires it, and that one may lead those of different opinions astray with doubtful, ambiguous words and phrases, etc.

However, the famous Professor Campegius Vitringa, writing on Revelation, does not seem to be at home with this view, as he thinks he has found a more suitable match in the Goths under Ataulphus and Alaric, who devastated Italy, page 389, etc., page 395; and in the Ostrogoths, who harmed the Romans more with the tail than with the head, namely through their last prince Totilas, who dealt the heaviest blows to Rome and all of Italy.

When I speak here of an ANCHOR, I say beforehand: I do not speak of the cross-irons which people are accustomed to place in houses and walls to support gables and ceiling beams...

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of the "hook" as a tool of restraint and judgment, transitioning into the symbolic and historical study of the "Anchor."</meta>

# ANCHOR.

<meta>Catchword at bottom right: being-</meta>

...to restrain and hold the great vessel fast; but here I shall speak of ship's Anchors.

One reads in the histories of the Old Testament of ships and seafaring, but very little of ship's tackle, and even less of the ANCHORS of ships: and yet they are needed to hold against the tide, as well as in storms and tempests, so as not to fall upon rocks, shallows, etc. And though one reads little or nothing of them, it is nevertheless very likely that the ancients knew of and had at hand certain tools and means which they would have used as necessity required. Otherwise, one would have to think that the vessels of the ancients were smaller and lighter; that they only sailed along the shores with poles and oars, until in time, becoming bolder and more intent on commerce, they built heavier ships and, having invented sails, ventured deeper into the sea and the depths. Indeed, as has been observed in many things, it may have happened here as well: that over time, something was added to what was already invented for greater convenience and certainty; *it is easy to add to what has been invented* <note>Latin: "inventis aliquid addere facile est"</note>. It may be that before the invention of anchors, ropes and lines with heavy stones and cobbles were used, which, being lowered to the bottom of the waters, somewhat checked the vessel's progress.

<margin>Inventors of anchors.</margin>
The invention of ship's anchors is attributed to the Tyrrhenians; though Strabo, in his 9th book, credits this to Anacharsis <note>Anacharsis was a Scythian philosopher who traveled to Athens in the 6th century BCE</note>.

<margin>The usefulness of the same.</margin>
Be that as it may; in Paul’s time they were known and in use, and in the present day they are of immense and useful service.

And because ship's anchors—whether in calm weather to hold against the tide, or in storms and tempests for fear of falling upon sands, shores, rocks, reefs, and shallows—can be wonderfully helpful and have their uses, etc., symbolic expressions have been derived from ship's anchors. In this regard, I have found that a ship's anchor has been depicted with a Dolphin entwined around it, to represent the motto of Caesar Augustus: <term>Hasten slowly <note>Greek: Σπευδε βραδεως (Speude bradeos)</note></term>. The Dolphin is a very swift water creature. A lowered, heavy ship's anchor stops the progress of the ship; thus the Dolphin is a symbol of haste, and the lowered anchor a symbol of delay, for <term>to tarry or stay <note>Hebrew: עגן (agan) and עגון (agun)</note></term> comes from the root meaning *to delay, to hold back, to cause to linger*. Erasmus, *Adagia* page 241. Pierio Valeriano, *Hieroglyphica* book XXVII, chapter 9. And Pliny, in book XVIII, relates of the Dolphin that, being a friend to man, whenever he notices a storm or tempest is imminent, he winds and twists himself around the anchor to press and fasten it deeper and more securely into the seabed, so that the ship and the crew might be saved.

Alciatus, in his *Emblems* page 150, applied this quite aptly to rulers, princes, and kings who seek to preserve the ship of state: <note>Andrea Alciati (1492–1550) was the author of the most famous "Emblem Book," which used images and poems to teach moral lessons.</note>

> *Whenever the Titan brothers disturb the seas,* <note>The "Titan brothers" refers to the winds.</note>
> *Then the cast anchor helps the wretched sailors:*
> *The Dolphin, pious toward men, embraces this,*
> *So that it may be fixed more safely in the deep shallows.*
> *How fitting it is for mindful kings to carry these insignia,*
> *Being to their people what the anchor is to sailors.*

<column-break/>

->That is:<-

> *When the winds upon the sea a storm do wake,*
> *The anchor shall for seafaring folk a rescue make.*
> *The dolphin, who loves man with faith and heart,*
> *Coils 'round it so it holds fast and does not part.*
> *This lesson-filled emblem must a king well suit;*
> *A skipper finds his help in the anchor's root.*
> *So may a people in need their help in their prince find.*

An anchor serves as a symbol of certainty and safety, as if one were in a safe harbor; see Erasmus, *Adagia page 627.*

Two anchors cast out, at the front and back of the ship, are regarded as a symbol of the most perfect certainty and safety.

A woman has been depicted with an anchor to represent security in times of need and difficulty, for which purpose one is accustomed to carry good and heavy anchors with strong cables. Pierio Valeriano, book XLV, chapter 12. Erasmus, *Adagia page 92.*

We have more examples where someone is called the "anchor of the citizenry," meaning the cause of salvation, rest, security, and prosperity. Thus Plutarch records from the life of Solon: *That the state is fastened by the Council as much as by an anchor.* And Euripides, in *Hecuba*, described Polydorus as being the anchor of his lineage and house. See Claude Mignault's *Commentary on Alciati's Emblems*, page 524.

To "have cast one's anchor" was a symbol that one had "his sheep on the dry land" <note>A Dutch idiom meaning to be in a secure financial or personal position</note>; that through God's goodness and mild blessing, having overcome difficulty, one was well, at rest, and in a praiseworthy state. Pierio Valeriano, book XLV. Pindar, in the 6th *Isthmian Ode*, applied it to happiness and a state of honor. See Claude Mignault on Alciati, page 524. We say: *He has brought his anchor well to the bottom; he has his little boat on the dry land,* etc.

<margin>Anchor of the soul.</margin>
I am aware that Paul, in Hebrews 6:19, speaks of an anchor of the soul, which is sure and steadfast.

Since Paul had just spoken of two things—of strong consolation and of the hope set before us—interpreters deliberate to which the anchor should be applied: to the strong consolation or to the hope. However, since the Apostle last mentioned hope, in which a strong consolation lies enclosed (it being described as *a blessed hope, a hope of salvation and of eternal life, in which one can stand, which is firm, and can glory in all tribulations and adversities*, Romans 5:3, 4, 5 and 8:24, etc.), it should be further noted how hope can be introduced and presented under the symbol of a soul-anchor that is steadfast.

One can sufficiently conclude from Paul’s previous reasoning that, speaking of persons who have fled for refuge to the strong consolation and have seized the hope set before them—not letting it slip away, but holding it fast—he made use of the known truth: how a sinner, on account of committed sins, accusations, curses, and punishments, in order to be covered, free, and bold, takes refuge in the Messiah’s righteousness as if in a sheet anchor <note>The "plegtanker" or sheet anchor was the largest and strongest anchor on a ship, used only in the direst emergencies.</note>; just as someone overtaken by hollow sea-waves and a strong storm takes his last refuge in his anchor and strong cables.

Certainly, such is the situation of a believing Christian in this world. He, in this hollow and desolate sea, tossed by many mishaps, threatened and overtaken by storms and high sea-waves—

<summary>This page explores the historical origins and rich symbolic meanings of the anchor, moving from its practical use in ancient navigation to its representation of political stability and religious hope.</summary>
<keywords>anchor, seafaring, Dolphin, Caesar Augustus, Alciatus, Paul, Hebrews 6:19, hope, consolation, security, symbolism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Anchor from the previous page, specifically focusing on its symbolic meaning in the Christian life. It concludes the entry for "Anchor" and begins a new entry for "Anthias," a type of fish.</meta>

...finding himself under the dark nights and brown clouds of disfavor, and the thunder and lightning bolts of the law; in persecutions and anxieties, he takes refuge in the throne of grace and Christ's merits and intercessions. His trusting faith and his firm hope—born of that faith and the promises of the living and unchangeable God—having been cast out just as one does a ship's anchor, he finds that his anchor has sunk down upon such a firm and immovable ground of God's unchangeable counsel and faithfulness, that no ship has ever obtained greater certainty and steadiness through its cast anchor than his soul obtains through that living and hopeful faith.

I do not see that Paul <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul, specifically the imagery in Hebrews 6:19: "We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure."</note> mentions any further ship's tackle other than an anchor: however, because he describes the anchor as being cast out, reaching even into the innermost sanctuary where it is fixed and makes the soul fast and steady, it seems to me that by naming only a part, he understands the whole through it. He includes an anchor with its necessary accessories: a strong and long cable fixed to the ship and anchor. For what good can an anchor do without a cable? What usefulness does a cable bring without an anchor? What advantage comes from too light or too weak an anchor, or from a cable too short and brittle? A strong and heavy anchor and a strong, long cable are of no use without being fixed to the ship.

So one can, in a certain respect, understand by the anchor cable—by which both ship and anchor are tied to each other—the faithful trust, the <margin>Application.</margin> hopeful faith, or the hope of faith, which holds fast to the promised salvation. And just as the anchor cable extends between the ship and the anchor, fastening both together, so in this case the matter appears to me thus: that although the promised salvation is laid away in the heavens, the soul nevertheless attaches and fixes itself to this salvation through faith and hope. It looks out for it and hopes for it with tough patience; noting that faith and hope by no means let go of salvation, and for that reason the soul is united with it through hopeful faith.

Suppose now that a ship, beset by storm and weather, is preserved by resting on its rope and anchor. So it shall also be with the soul hoping and believing, which holds fast to the promises of salvation even though it is tossed and beset by storms. It is fixed to salvation, which cannot escape it, knowing that all things shall work together for its good. Salvation cannot escape it (*Romans 5:3, 4; 8:35*), therefore the soul fears not (*Psalm 23:4; 27:1; and 46:3, 4*). For faith, from which the hope resting on the divine promises is born, <margin>The Extension of Faith.</margin> stretches itself out through the cable of patient expectation, even unto Christ in heaven, in whom all God's promises—being firm and certain—receive their fulfillment (*2 Corinthians 1:20*).

Suppose once again that, while at sea, one finds a wind and storm arising: one encounters cliffs, rocks, whirlpools, and eddies. One would surely suffer shipwreck upon them and go to the bottom if one were not provided with a good and strong anchor and cable.

Apply that to a Christian traveler on the wild sea of this billowy world. Suppose for a moment that it becomes calm and the wind of grace slackens a bit; then the sea of the world becomes turbulent, toiling and tossing. A storm and tempest of mockery, disdain, and persecution arises. The whirlpools of worldly comfort, profit, and honor also do their part. One runs the danger of being dragged to destruction by the common flood and current. It is then that hopeful faith, being fixed to the anchor of salvation, holds the soul so fast that it neither drifts back nor is moved from its steadiness by any thing.

For it is entirely different with hopeful faith and salvation in Christ than it is with ship's anchors, cables, and seabeds. A rope and anchor can break, a cable can be too short and weak, and an anchor can by accident fail to take hold or may slip. The ground for anchoring can be too soft or too hard and rocky.

But this anchor is firm, and therefore the soul acting in the hope of faith is fast and certain. For faith, hope, and strong consolation are an anchor and cable forged and placed in the heart by God's Spirit Himself. Everything has its steadiness and constancy in God's eternal and unchangeable counsel and will, and in Christ's merits and intercession. As if already in the heavens, believers are placed there with Christ as their Head (*Ephesians 5:6*). The Spirit is a pledge of the inheritance, and the believers are kept by God's power for the blessed inheritance (*1 Peter 1:5*).

Our soul takes no hold through its anchor in this lower world. A ship's anchor is thrown toward the deep, lower than the ship itself; but the soul's anchor and ground is above the soul, in heaven. Isidore of Seville <note>Isidorus Hispalensis (c. 560–636), a scholar and archbishop whose "Etymologies" served as a primary encyclopedia for the Middle Ages.</note> (*Etymologies, Book 1, Chapter 2*) <note>Original Latin citation: "Orig. libr. 1. cap. 2."</note> has noted that in ancient times, when speaking of divine and heavenly things, it was the custom to use an inverted anchor as a symbol, with the two side-arms pointing upward; but with the arms pointing downward when one spoke and wrote of common, earthly, and trivial matters. Our anchor, anchor cable, and anchor ground are above, where Jesus has entered.

<margin>An inverted symbol used.</margin>

They are therefore well-advised who never separate faith and hope from each other. They are mother and daughter, tree and fruit. Through faith one obtains the right of inheritance; through hope the soul stretches itself out with patience toward that inheritance.

<margin>Faith and Hope are inseparable. The Power of Faith and Hope.</margin>

Happy are they who are esteemed to seek no anchor ground in the unstable and passing world and the things of this life, but in God. Though everything in the world shows itself in the utmost confusion, God—His will, word, oath, and promises—remains immovable (*Psalm 9:10; 22:5; 37:10; Numbers 23:19; 2 Timothy 1:12; and 2:12, 13*).

Let this be said enough regarding the Anchor.

Its loyalty.
</margin>
It is recounted that these fish are singularly loyal to one another and helpful, especially when one is caught on a fishhook. Namely, the one snagged by the hook stretches out the fishing line, while the others rub this line with their sharp fins so that it might more readily break and snap apart, allowing their companion to escape the danger more easily. Whatever else there may be concerning this fish can be seen in the works of Pliny, Jonston, Franzius, etc. <note>Refers to Pliny the Elder, Jan Jonston, and Wolfgang Franz, famous natural historians</note>; I have already said enough about it.

<margin>
Symbol of unity.
</margin>
I see in this creature—according to the accounts of historians and naturalists—something that ought to spur us as rational human beings toward mutual harmony, peace, and assistance, whether in domestic, civil, or Christian society and interaction. Certainly, if such a state took hold, the "harpies" <note>Mythological bird-like creatures, used here to represent destructive or predatory people</note> and ruinous birds of prey would not seek us out so readily, nor be capable of disturbing our homes and rest. And the work of our hands, our going out and coming in, would be more prosperous.

If anyone among us were already caught on the hook of sin, running the risk of being gently reeled in by the "deceiver of souls," we could—if we were truly earnest—frequently rescue him who is captured by death and hell from the snares of the devil and destruction. For through admonitions, sharp reproofs, and threats, many escape danger, and the chain of temptation is broken. Through such merits, many might spit out the bait of temptation which they had greedily and thoughtlessly swallowed—especially when someone feels for themselves that they are caught and deceived, and begins to grow earnest about being rid of those snares, bonds, and hooks.

The gall and wormwood <note>Bitter substances representing suffering</note> that Christ tasted, brought to the heart of the sinner through and with the honey-sweet grace of the Holy Spirit, heals him of all the fiery pimples, lumps, and swellings of sin, making him whole and smooth, and the healing prosperous.

When the head is seized with pain and woe through the constant and anxious pondering of sins and adversities—whether the sharp fluid of sorrow causes stinging and pain, failing to flow through due to thickening and blockage, etc. (one should consult physicians regarding this)—for my part, to still and remove all sorrow, blockage, and soul-piercing pains and woes, and to cause the sharp fluid to subside: I know of no more curative remedy than the enjoyment of the "holy water from the stone with seven eyes" (*Zechariah 3:9*), which is to meditate upon the bitter suffering of the Christ. One shall also find singular benefit here through tears of repentance. The comforts flowing from this suffering miraculously relieve, refresh, and comfort the soul. That is the true "bundle of myrrh" <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 1:13, often interpreted as Christ</note>. If anyone uses that rightly, they shall be healed of all manner of ailments.

<column-break/>

### ANTICHRIST <note>original Greek: Ἀντίχριστος</note>

<margin>
Paul, 2 Thessalonians 2, to be sufficiently understood.
</margin>
If one intelligently observes what follows: one sees that his writing has often been quite mindlessly misinterpreted for the worse. His expressions were taken the wrong way, and people began to convince themselves that the General Judgment was close at hand, which threw fear and terror into many hearts. Others neglected their civil and domestic duties, not caring at all for temporal welfare (*2 Thessalonians 3:10, 11*). Paul desired that they should not let themselves be deceived, or led by the nose, or led away from the known path of the trodden truth <note>original Greek: ἐξαπατᾶν, meaning "to deceive thoroughly"</note>. For that General Judgment Day, this appearance, was not yet so near, or even at hand; many things would have to happen beforehand. For that day does not come, unless first the apostasy comes, and the "man of sin" is revealed, the "son of perdition," who exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshiped as God, so that he sits in the temple of God as a God, showing himself that he is God, etc.

<margin>
Apostasy.
</margin>
The Apostle gives us to understand that before Christ's coming for judgment, there shall be the apostasy <note>original Greek: ἀποστασία</note>. The root word is taken in the sense of a falling away that is great and remarkable: not so much a falling away in the state or from the Roman Empire, as from the known and accepted doctrine of truth, and thus from Christ and the God of truth, speaking and commanding in and through His Word. Some take the word *apostasia* as a "substitute of the abstract for the concrete" <note>original Latin: *abstractum pro concreto*</note>, just as one might use "wickedness" for "the wicked man" <note>original Latin: *scelus* pro *scelesto*</note>, referring to an *apostate*, *renegade*, or *defector* par excellence, who also misleads others and carries them into apostasy. And in this sense, they want the Antichrist to be understood. See Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, Theodoret, Augustine, Jerome, Bellarmine, Suarez, etc. <note>A list of prominent early Church Fathers and later Catholic theologians</note>.

Thus, a falling away is frequently mentioned. *1 Timothy 3 and 4; 2 Timothy 3; 1 Timothy 1:19.*

It is acceptable and clear to me that quite many in the early times fell away from the faith—that is, from the pure doctrine of faith and the upright confession of the doctrine of truth—of whom our Apostle has given an account in his letters.

I also hold it to be true that many so-called zealots by no means desired to stand and bow under the yoke and command of the Emperor, pretending to seek "freedom"; yet the pronouncements of the Apostle point us to a later day, and to a decay for which the foundations were already being laid in his time.

<margin>
To be found in the Roman church.
</margin>
I have noted that one must singularly seek and will find this apostasy in the Roman Church: a falling away and decay not only in life and morals, but also in the doctrines and foundations of the faith; a deviation from the sound and true doctrine set down in the scriptures of Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles, taught by Christ the head of the church, and handed down to his own.

And certainly, in the modern Roman Church, one perceives doctrines running directly and hostiley against Holy Scripture and Christ's authority, power, honor, and dignity, of which I shall only note a few in passing. For there they teach:

# ANTICHRIST.

<margin>Debauchery of the Popes and clergy.</margin>
...that matters had decayed and reached such a point that, in the end, the Church would not permit the use of fire or the scalpel—the final remedies for incurable ailments. And Stella <note>Erasmus Stella, a 16th-century historian</note>, writing of Pope Benedict the Fourth, says, *That he performed nothing praiseworthy, since at that time all virtue had vanished from the head as well as all the members.* Many Popes were apostates, practiced foul arts, and held secret understandings with the wicked. This bestial and unbridled life is observed among the so-called clergy, and what is more, it is described clearly enough by Platina <note>Bartolomeo Platina, a Renaissance humanist who wrote 'Lives of the Popes,' often criticizing their vices</note> himself.

<margin>Son of perdition.</margin>
Paul speaks of a *son of perdition*.
One who goes toward destruction, who is destined for it, who leads others to destruction and destroys them: a corrupt child. *Psalm 44 and Romans 8: We are accounted as sheep for the slaughter:* like slaughter-sheep, or destined for slaughter.
Worthy of destruction and ruin, like children of wrath. Thus is Judas named. *John 17: the son of perdition.*
The Antichrist is also called the son of perdition, because he would destroy many in soul and body, and is therefore the foulest and most corrupt of men: named <term>Abaddon<note>Hebrew: "Destruction"</note></term> and <term>Apollyon<note>Greek: "Destroyer"</note></term>, *the destroyer and exterminator* <note>original Latin: "perditor & exterminans"</note>. See *Glassius's Sacred Grammar page 133; Hackspan on the New Testament page 474; Fesselius on Sacred Usage part 2, page 353; Dietericus's Antiquities of the New Testament page 8, etc.*

<margin>Saints opposed by the Antichrist.</margin>
That the Antichrist has devastated many lands and cities, that through his followers he wages war against the saints, incites kings and peoples, being drunk with the blood of the saints: that he plagues and poisons souls and ruins morals, is such a well-known and clear truth that we, alongside the Roman writers, need only necessarily look at their doctrines, opinions, and manifold experiences.

This one had to be revealed, and his appearance precede that of the Christ; he had to raise his head, and his foul arts and cunning maneuvers had to be discovered. He was then still fresh in his birth; the foundations were being laid, but he did not yet show himself openly, as will appear from what follows.

<margin>Antichrist further described.</margin>
This man of sin, the son of perdition, is further described and identified by his tyrannical, high-minded, proud, and blasphemous nature, and his foul conduct and dealings.

Who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God, or that is worshiped as God, etc.

<margin>Adversary.</margin>
He is an <term>antikeimenos<note>Greek: "one who lies over against"</note></term> *adversary*, from <term>antikeisthai<note>Greek: "to oppose or withstand"</note></term> *to combat against, to stand against as a party*, who settles himself down opposite another, just as two hostile armies do.
The Antichrist sets himself against Christ, Christ's teachings, laws, and true servants: indeed, against everything high, exalted, and venerable, wishing to be <term>anomos<note>Greek: "lawless" or "above the law"</note></term> above all laws, bans, and compulsion: making laws according to his own whims, and imposing bonds under the heaviest threats.
How he sets himself against Christ and His glory, I believe has already been demonstrated clearly enough.
He is not only against Christ, but is also one who puts himself in Christ's place, saying he is His vicar and the successor of Peter; provided with the keys of the kingdom of heaven, exercising power in heaven, on earth, in hell, and in purgatory; being able to open, shut, forgive sins or retain them, to save or damn someone, to send one straight to heaven, or to make one stay a long or short time in purgatory, and so forth.
*Indeed, he exalts himself above that which is called God, and (as God) is worshiped.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Authorities called Gods.</margin>
The title of "Gods" was held by the authorities, and especially by those who sat in the seat of Moses, *Psalm 2: the Heathen*, though there is but one God, they nevertheless had many gods. *1 Corinthians 8.*
<term>Sebasma<note>Greek: "an object of worship or veneration"</note></term> refers to holy, venerable things: a service peculiar to God, the magistrate, altars, or images. <term>Sebastos<note>Greek equivalent of the Latin "Augustus"</note></term> is one who is worthy of esteem and honor: one whom people honor, respect, and stand in awe of, particularly Emperor Augustus, who was very widely and broadly famous and renowned, as we find in Pausanias, Stephanus, Dietericus, and Smetius.

<margin>Great honor shown to Augustus.</margin>
And not to dwell on this matter, he arrogates to himself the power, authority, majesty, and the say over and above princes, lords, kings, and emperors; indeed, everything that is venerable and holy, or regarded as such, while he prides himself with a varnished humility as the "servant of the servants."

<margin>Authority of the Roman Pope.</margin>
The Pope wears three crowns, shimmering with gold, pearls, and precious stones, as a King of Kings: he is adorned with purple shoes and a purple robe, as the emperors once were.

<margin>His splendor.</margin>
When a Pope is chosen, he is served by the emperor, kings, and princes if they are present in Rome, or otherwise by their ambassadors. Some have been found who had to hold his stirrup and escort him. He is carried by the great ambassadors in a costly litter, while the Host <note>The consecrated bread of the Eucharist</note> is carried about on a snow-white horse.

<margin>Honor shown to the chosen Pope.</margin>
It is imagined that the Pope is the Sun, and the emperor, princes, and worldly lords are the Moon, to whom the Pope grants his brilliance and light, and who have their light, power, radiance, and reflection through him.

<margin>The Pope as the Sun; princes as the Moon.</margin>
In former times, the Popes arrogated to themselves the right to depose and appoint emperors and kings. Thus Innocent III deposed Emperor Otto IV; Gregory IV, Conrad IV; Boniface VIII, Philip the Fair, King of France; Leo III chose and inaugurated Charlemagne as emperor; John XIII chose Otto; Clement chose Henry, calling him Augustus; Gregory VII deposed Henry and inaugurated Rudolf, saying:

<margin>Idolatry concerning the Pope.</margin>
...caretaker, manager, and as another God on earth. Stapleton <note>Thomas Stapleton (1535–1598), an English Catholic controversialist</note> calls the Pope, *the supreme god on earth*. Silvester Petra Sancta <note>A Jesuit writer known for his work on heraldry and theology</note> has brought a book to light in which he attempted to prove that the Pope is rightly and reasonably called "God." <margin>His proud behavior.</margin>
He also carries himself as if he were God, arranging everything according to his pleasure. He gives and breaks laws: whatever he speaks, commands, or forbids—even if it runs directly against the laws of Christ, or the commands and institutions of the Apostles—it must nevertheless be believed and obeyed. He rules and commands in heaven, hell, purgatory, in church, and state, in and over everything, as if he were God.

And to wrap everything up briefly and put it in order, I shall gather some testimonies. Thus writes the Jesuit Vasquez <note>Gabriel Vásquez (1549–1604), a prominent Spanish Jesuit theologian</note>, *chapter 3, observations 2 and 3, and on 2 Corinthians 11:11*: <margin>Although it is the command of the Apostles, the Pope can nevertheless abolish it for lawful reasons, for the power of the Apostles to make laws is no greater than that of the Church and the Pope.</margin> Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a cardinal and one of the most important figures in the Counter-Reformation</note>, in *The Roman Pontiff, book 4, chapter 5*, writes thus: *If the Pope should err by commanding vices and forbidding virtues, the Church would nonetheless be bound to believe that the vices are virtues and the virtues are vices, unless she wished to sin against her conscience.* And further, *And in a good sense Christ gave to Peter, and consequently to the Pope, the power to bring it about that sin is not sin.* Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a famous jurist</note> in his *book on sacrilege, chapter 5*: "No one may cast doubt on the power of the Pope or ask, 'Lord, what are you doing?' even if it were the case that he consigned heaps of human souls to hell." And in *book 1, chapter 7 of the ceremonies*, one reads: *That the Pope stands in the place of reason.*

And subsequently one reads: *The souls of men are in the hand of the Pope, and religion consists in his good pleasure.* In imitation of Christ, Pope Paschal came forth in his High Priestly robes, wearing a belt with seven seals and seven keys. Agostino Steuco called Pope Leo X *the lion of the tribe of Judah.* Indeed, Leo was awaited as a Savior. Simon Beguius <note>Simon Begnius, Bishop of Modruš, who gave a famous oration at the Fifth Lateran Council</note> in the *Lateran Council and the gloss on the proem of the decretals of Gregory IX*: "The Lord Pope is esteemed to be the same person as Him whose place he occupies."

From which testimonies it is not difficult to grasp what it means,

*That he shall sit as a God in God's temple, showing himself as a God.*

<column-break/>

שב ו והאש <gloss>and to sit [on a throne]</gloss> <note>The Hebrew "shev" (to sit) is linked here to the concept of ruling</note>, is as much as *to rule*, just as it is taken by the Apostle in *1 Corinthians 15:25*.

He would not stand or serve as a servant, even though he calls himself *servus servorum*, "servant of servants."

Christ's Church is called a temple and house of God. *1 Corinthians 6, Ephesians 3, 1 Peter 2.*

One must not dream here of the literal temple in Jerusalem, which has long been destroyed and never rebuilt.

Jerome, in his letter to Algasia, *question 12*, understands it to mean the Church of Christ; so also Augustine, Primasius, Chrysostom, and Theophylact—as if he, with his followers, were the temple itself, says Augustine in his book *The City of God, book 20, chapter 19*; just as they also imagine that Rome is the mother church, indeed, the head of all churches.

Paul, proposing that the Thessalonians, having received oral instruction from him, still held these matters in good memory, continues on that footing, saying: *And now you know what withholds him, so that he may be revealed in his own time.*

Although they did not yet see the Antichrist appear, he would nonetheless emerge, noting that he would have his boundaries and deceptive tricks. Everything would steadily prepare itself for his birth. His time was not yet there. He was, for the time being, withheld and prevented from raising his head and sitting in the house of God in the manner just described.

One knows that everything, according to divine predestination, has its time. *Ecclesiastes 3.*

It is known to me that in this regard many learned men have cast their eye upon the Apostles, the early Church Fathers, and the zeal of the early Christians, alongside the heat of the persecutions against the Christian Church by Jews and Heathens for centuries in a row.

They believe both these things withheld the rise and appearance of the Antichrist. But I would stand with those who are of the opinion that the strongest withholding of the Antichrist was <margin>The withholding of the Antichrist.</margin> the imperial supreme authority in Rome, where he was prevented from nesting as long as the city of Rome was the seat of the Empire. But when Constantine planted the imperial throne and seat in *Byzantium*—Constantinople, or the City of Constantine—an opportunity arose for the Roman Bishop to raise his head in time and to claim the supreme command for himself, as the sequel will clearly enough demonstrate.

In this understanding and judgment were Tertullian, *book 4 on the resurrection, chapter 24*; Chrysostom on *2 Thessalonians 2*; Augustine, *The City of God, book 20, chapter 16*; Jerome *to Algasia, question 11*; Cyril in his *catechesis*; and a whole throng of others in our own day.

*He would come or be revealed "in his own time."*

Καιρὸς <note>Greek: Kairos</note> signifies *time, or opportunity for something*. From this comes ευκαιρία <note>Greek: Eukairia</note>, *good or fair opportunity*. And so the Antichrist would watch for his time, and when he judged it advisable, seize his chance to achieve his aim.

For, while it was true that the beginnings were already there, it did not yet pierce through so perceptibly; at a later time, this matter would be seen more clearly.

<margin>Mysteries of the Roman Church.</margin>
In the Roman Church, the smallest things as well as the greatest find their mystery, their hidden allusion, and their secret meaning. <margin>Artifices of the Antichrist.</margin>
His clever tricks were to cover, hide, and twist the simple, clear, and naked words of Christ and the doctrines of the Apostles. He made the people believe that the Holy Scripture was incomplete without tradition, without the supreme and infallible declarations of the Fathers, and the interpretation of the Pope and the Roman Church—claiming it was dark, defective, imperfect, and in no way sufficient for salvation.

To this end, the foundations and principles were already being laid early on: the Jews had their ancestral traditions and unwritten law. Men already began to strive for mastery (Mark 9 and Luke 9). They began to handle the Scripture with bold arrogance and, through stubborn opposition, peddle their own wisdom, thus aiming for mastery and making an assault on the truth (1 Corinthians 1 and 2; 1 John 1:18; and 3 John 1:9). And so, century by century, a corruption of doctrine and a chain of superstitious ceremonies crept in imperceptibly, as I could demonstrate by running through every age.

Certainly, the Papal and Antichristian supremacy was not raised to its peak in a hurry.

It will not be unhelpful for me to briefly sketch how the Antichrist ascended to supreme authority through various steps and paths.

Although the Roman Bishops long possessed a desire for supremacy—being Bishops in the empire’s capital city—they nonetheless could not achieve their objective to their satisfaction.

It is well known that the Bishops of Rome quarreled with the Bishops of other capital cities, particularly with those of Constantinople, regarding mastery and supremacy.

<margin>Metropolitans.</margin>
It is no less known that the Bishops of Constantinople, Rome, Antioch, Alexandria, and Jerusalem were all called "Metropolitans."

From this, it arose in time that one had to obtain the confirmation of their office in Rome.

In this manner, the Bishop of Rome uprooted the rule of the Greek <note>Byzantine</note> Emperor, who had moved from Rome to Constantinople.

<margin>Italy overrun by the Lombards.</margin> But in great haste, the Roman bishop was seized by a mortal terror, for the Lombards, seeking to overtake the rebellious cities, fell upon Italy like a swarm, taking Ravenna along with other cities.

<margin>The Pope in a tight spot.</margin> Now the Pope was in a corner: therefore he petitioned Pepin <note>Pepin the Short</note>—otherwise known as Charlemagne <note>The author likely means the father of Charlemagne, or uses the name as a dynasty marker</note>—who had been made King of France by Pope Zachary, asking him to come to his aid and drive the Lombards out of Italy with his troops. When Pepin allowed himself to be found and used for this purpose, he drove out the Lombards, and having made himself master of Italy, he gifted several cities to the Pope, which were then attached to the See of Peter. However, since the inhabitants of these cities by no means consented to stand under the Pope, the Pope was forced to declare the Emperor as the Roman Emperor, reserving for himself the title of Protector and Advocate of the Roman Church.

When this became tiresome to the Popes,

The Antichrist is designated here by particular marks and characteristics, so that one might cast an eye upon him who shall be the object of divine vengeance, and not be blinded when one sees God's righteous wrath.

### ANTIPAS, <term>Antipas <note>Greek: Ἀντίπας; traditionally interpreted as a martyr of the early church mentioned in Revelation 2:13</note></term>.

<margin>Account of Antipas.</margin>
Regarding ANTIPAS, of whom one reads in the Revelations of John, some would gladly have us believe that he was the bishop or overseer of Pergamum, who openly taught and suffered for Christ and his doctrine there, and cast out evil spirits in Jesus' name: for which reason he was supposedly captured by the governor or deputy and, being thrown into a glowing copper Bull <note>The "Brazen Bull," a legendary ancient execution device</note>, faithfully and steadfastly underwent martyrdom etc. Now this has been recounted by various people, and one has taken it over from the other based on loose rumor and simple storytelling, without a shadow of proof, namely: Arethas, Metaphrastes, Cedrenus, Surius, Pererius, Baronius, à Lapide. They even go so far as to specify the time when Antipas was supposedly martyred, namely in the year of our Savior's birth 93, and the tenth year of the reign of Domitian.

It is certain that this name appears but once in Holy Scripture; that he is mentioned either rarely or not at all in ecclesiastical histories; that what is recounted of his office, conduct, and end is given without sufficient proof and is partly fabricated.

And although some things are told of ANTIPAS so groundlessly, some nevertheless believe that there must have been a person by that name known at Pergamum at that time, who must have struggled singularly for Jesus' name, honor, and doctrine, for which reason he was brought to a painful end by the enemies of the truth.

# ANTIPAS.

<margin>Antichrist, a name for many persons.</margin>
Yet others believe the name refers to a single person, but should be understood symbolically for a certain kind and class of people to whom the description of Antipas applies. We see this in how the name of Elijah is used by Malachi; it is not used to portray a person with that literal name, but one who would come with the spirit and power of Elijah. In the same way, "Antichrist" is not the name of one specific individual, but of many persons possessing certain qualities and behaviors. One encounters several such designations in Holy Scripture—and especially in the Revelation of John—which must be understood and explained symbolically rather than literally.

Among these latter interpretations, there is some disagreement as to how and in what sense one should perceive and grasp the meaning.

For my part, I can imagine that if there truly was a literal Antipas in Pergamum who, for the sake of Jesus’s cause, did not hesitate to trade his life for a martyr’s death in defense of the truth, honor, and teaching of the Christ, he was recorded as a model. His example serves to embolden and encourage others, should necessity and the cause of Christ require it; and indeed, He has had several who followed in his footsteps.

<margin>The meaning of Antipas interpreted as Greek.</margin>
Alternatively, one might think with Saskerides <note>Johannes Saskerides (1572–1636), a Danish theologian</note> that the name Antipas, according to the style of the Greek language, signifies "against all" <note>original: "ἀντί" (against) and "πᾶς" (all)</note>. In this view, the designation is intended to depict, under the name of one person, all those who with one heart and soul would unanimously set themselves against heretics and heresies, even at the cost of their lives.

<margin>A further definition.</margin>
Or, if one still wished to seek a more specific definition, the name *Antipas* could be taken as a shortened form of *Antipatros* <note>original: "ἀντίπατρος"</note>, standing for the Christ, who is equal to God, one with the Father, and of the same nature, power, and glory—being *consubstantial* <note>original: "ὁμοούσιος" (homoousios), meaning of the same substance</note>. Under this interpretation, "Antipas" would refer to those who defended the Christ against the wicked Arian error <note>The Arian controversy was a 4th-century dispute over whether Jesus was equal to God the Father or a created being</note> with their mouths, pens, property, and blood.

<margin>The opinion of Vitringa.</margin>
The learned Campegius Vitringa <note>A prominent Dutch theologian (1659–1722) known for his commentary on Revelation</note>, in his work on the Revelations, page 96, considers it a mere fabricated tale, cobbled together from a superstitious brain, that a so-called Antipas, Bishop of Pergamum, was thrown into a glowing oven by the governor and miserably consumed because of his steadfast faith. He argues this because true history knows nothing of it.

He places this event in the period from 320 AD until near the end of the seventh century, a time of intense conflict regarding the "one-being-ness" <note>consubstantiality</note> of the Son with the Father. Furthermore, his excellency believes that "Pergamum" here signifies Alexandria, which was the source of that fierce and long-lasting struggle over Christ's true divinity, and where the "throne of Satan" was also located (page 97). As for "Antipas the faithful witness" who was killed, he maintains that in the prophetic interpretation of this letter, the explanation must be made in a mystical sense. Therefore, under this assumption, Antipas is a mystical or hidden name; however, it is not so easy to say what it means. There are those who have tried to translate it as *Anti-pope* and *Anti-papists* <note>original: "Antipapa & Antipapistae"</note>, but that is truly ridiculous and devoid of all probability. At that time, the title of "Pope" <note>original: "Papa"</note> was not yet reserved solely for the Roman

<column-break/>

bishops, nor had the Papal authority been filed up to such a height that those who unsuccessfully opposed that authority would have been considered martyrs. Therefore, no more probable opinion has occurred to me than the thoughts of Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian famous for his "Covenant Theology"</note>, who holds that the word *Antipas* is derived from "being deprived of a limb," or stands for *Antipatros*, which can mean *equal to the father* <note>original: "ἰσόπατρον" (isopatron) or "ἴσον τῷ πατρὶ" (ison tō patri)</note>. In this case, the defenders of Christ's equality with the Father are called "Antipas," as they placed the second divine person on the same level of perfection and dignity as the first. Among these, it is obvious that Athanasius <note>Athanasius of Alexandria, the chief defender of Trinitarianism against Arianism</note> shone above all others. One may see there in what manner his excellency has defended and clarified the thoughts of the great Cocceius.

<margin>The thoughts of Cocceius.</margin>

The witnesses, says his excellency—and Athanasius among them—were "killed" in Alexandria, either in a prophetic or historical style. In the prophetic way, using a mystically significant style, a public teacher is said to be "killed" when his mouth is shut regarding the truth which he has hitherto openly taught and defended, preventing him from teaching and standing for it further, as will be seen in Chapter XI:7.

Athanasius, a remarkable witness in this very important and difficult matter, was forced under Constantine, Constantius, and also under Julian to leave the church of Alexandria for a long time and to wander here and there in exile. During this time, the Alexandrian flock, being shepherdless, was not a little disturbed and tormented by the wolves.

<margin>The church of Alexandria abandoned by Athanasius.</margin>

This was also fulfilled according to the historical style in the final years of the reign of Constantius, who raged violently against the *Homoousians* <note>term: Homoousians: those who defended the "sameness of substance" between the Father and the Son</note> who defended the equality of being. Also under Valens, in the first years of his rule, many excellent confessors of the truth became confirmers of the truth through their deaths, because they could not be turned away from the sound truth and faith by threats and torments.

<margin>Fulfillment according to the historical style.</margin>

Or otherwise, if one wished to descend to later times and follow the Greek sense and wordplay with some belief, one might consider whether the name *Antipas* for *Antipatros*—"against the father" <note>original: "πατὴρ" (pater), "πατρὸς" (patros), "παππας" (pappas), "παππα" (pappa), from which "papa" or "father" comes</note>—could not be applied to the Antichrist, who imagines himself to be the universal father. In this sense, Antipas would be those who set themselves against this "father," disputing his authority, honor, credibility, and the obligation to believe and submit to him. Certainly, such things occurred under the Papal rule, when Satan had singularly erected his throne among them and the Roman church had degenerated in both doctrine and morals. This happened particularly in the tenth century, as one can read in Hottinger, the Magdeburg Centuriators, Spanheim, and Baronius regarding the year 912 AD, etc. What was the appearance of the Roman church then? How hideous: when the most powerful and wicked harlots ruled in Rome? At whose pleasure the seats were changed, bishops appointed, and—what is terrifying to say—they were introduced into the Chair of Peter. These lustful paramours, false Popes...

### ANSWERS, *anah* / *apokrinesthai*. <note>original Hebrew: ענה / Greek: ἀποκρίνεσθαι</note>

<margin>The meaning of ANSWERS.</margin>
TO ANSWER, taken in the most emphatic sense, means to bring forward a well-ordered, fitting, and relevant reason that satisfies the proposed matter or question, and therefore presupposes a question, a questioner, or questioners, as in *Proverbs 24:26, Matthew 4:4 and 12:39, Luke 2:37, Job 1:48 and 2:19 and 3:5.*

Otherwise, answering is also taken for beginning to speak, commencing some discourse even if one was not asked, or seizing the opportunity to make use of it. *Proverbs 15:1:* "a soft answer," that is, a soft word and reason. See *Matthew 3:15 and 19:27 and 25:26. Gejerus on Proverbs, Lexicon Pasor on apokrinesthai.* <note>Refers to the works of Nicolaus Geier and Georg Pasor, noted 17th-century biblical scholars</note>

Sometimes Answering is taken for bringing something forward to obtain some relief, further opening, or explanation. *Matthew 12:38, Revelation 7:13.*

Having said this in general, I limit it either to (a) God, or so-called Gods, and those who pretend to do their work and give answers; and (b) subsequently to humans.

(a) When answering or not answering is attributed to God, it signifies several distinct things:
> 1. Answering with words or deeds: hearing, helping, giving the requested and desired thing, or even something more excellent. *Genesis 35:3, Psalm 34:5, Job 9:16, Psalm 3:5 and 118:5, Isaiah 30:19 and 58:9 and 65:24.*
> <margin>I read Psalm 45:5: "And your right hand shall teach you awesome things."</margin>
> Upon this, Fred. Adolf Lampe <note>Friedrich Adolph Lampe (1683–1729), a prominent German Pietist theologian and professor</note> says the following regarding *Psalm 45*, page 336: "But if the right hand of earthly heroes gives birth to astonishing slaughters and defeats, how much more awesome are the great deeds of the Messiah’s right hand? The root word *nooraooth* <note>original Hebrew: נוראות</note>, 'awesome' or 'terrible' things, expresses such deeds that, through their greatness and excellence, exceed all expectation and credibility, and instill high regard in all subjects and terror in all enemies. Very often it is used to express that chain of miracles that God performed when He delivered Israel and brought them into the land of promise. *Deuteronomy 10:21, 2 Samuel 7:23, 2 Chronicles 17:21, Psalm 106:22.* All of which, since it was a pattern for the inheritance of the Gentiles <note>The non-Jewish nations</note>, to which our royal Prophet tangibly alludes, he also rightly uses the same word in *Psalm 65:6*: 'awesome things in righteousness you shall answer us, O God of our salvation! O trust of all the ends of the earth, and of those far away upon the sea.' Where the word *nooraooth*, awesome things, is used regarding this same calling of the Gentiles. One can compare this with *Psalm 145:6 and Isaiah 64:3*; except only that the latter seems to refer primarily to the final campaign against the Gentiles, which shall also have its *nooraooth*, or awesome things and deeds. If anyone wishes to investigate these awesomenesses more closely, they must compare all the specific miracles—such as the preceding cloud, the parted waves of the Jordan, the falling walls of Jericho, the standing still of the sun and moon, the driving out of the Canaanite kings, and all the other mighty wonders—to all the circumstances of the New Testament in the ascent and military campaign toward the world’s inheritance, to which the Prophets continually allude. See, for example, *Psalm 18:30-46 and 68:13-18, Habakkuk 3:3-11*, which places receive their full light from our proposition. And who can call these deeds anything but awesome?
> For (1) they are so great and illustrious that they far exceed all human power and display visible signs of Divinity, *Isaiah 40:12-26 and 41:4.* (2) They arouse reverent awe for the King among His people. *Psalm 89:8, 9, 10.* (3) They strike the enemies with amazement and fear. *Psalm 48:6, 7 and 97:4-7.*

<column-break/>

2. Not to answer means not to hear, not to grant the request, and sometimes to send the opposite of what was prayed for. *2 Samuel 22:42, 1 Kings 18:26, Psalm 22:3, Proverbs 1:28.* Which sometimes happens:
> Because the request was not made in faith.

3. Answering through sensible punishments, judgments, and chastisements, where the Lord is regarded as Lawgiver and Judge. *Ruth 1, Psalm 88:8, 90:15, 94:5, Ezekiel 14:4, 7, 8.*

Answering and not answering transferred to humans, signifying:
1. Being willing, teachable, obedient, subjecting oneself to what is heard, and therefore not so much with speaking, but answering with the deed—

### A P I S.

<margin>Apis, the name of an Egyptian king.</margin>
APIS was, as is written, the name of an Egyptian king who lived and ruled in the sixth century before the arrival of the Israelites in Egypt. Some speak of him as a foreigner; others as an Egyptian and Egyptian king. He was in power before Abraham, as they say.

Memphis in Egypt, it is said, was founded and built by Minaeus, and rebuilt and improved by APIS, whom some identify with Osiris.

<margin>Apis, king of the Argives.</margin>
APIS, king of the Argives, so we are told, was a son of Jupiter, begotten by Niobe, the daughter of Phoroneus. See *Marsham's chronic canon pages 84, 85, 231. Josephus' Antiquities, Book 8, chapter 2. Hoffman's Universal Lexicon.*

As for this Apis or Osiris, it is recounted of him that he taught the unrefined and unskilled people to plow with yoked oxen; likewise how to prune trees and vines, and how to strip the green field of its grassy crown, and other such things; about which one can read in *Aventinus, Annals, Book 10.*

Tibullus once sang in his praise:

> *Primus aratra manu solerti fecit Osiris,*
> *Et teneram ferro sollicitavit humum.*
> *Primus inexperte commisit semina terræ,*
> *Pomaque non notis legit ab arboribus.*
> *Hic docuit teneram palis adjungere vitem,*
> *Hic viridem durâ cædere falce comam.*
<note>Latin: "Osiris was the first to make plows with a skillful hand, and with iron he stirred the tender earth. He was the first to entrust seeds to the untried ground, and gathered fruit from unknown trees. He taught how to join the tender vine to stakes, and to cut the green foliage with a sharp sickle."</note>

->That is:<-

> *The plow was first by Osiris designed,*
> *To break the earth’s crust with tools of its kind.*
> *'Twas he who cast the seed into the land,*
> *And gathered fruit from trees at his command.*
> *He bound the vineyard up, and pruned the leaf,*
> *To bring the harvest of the grape relief.*

<margin>Apis, an ox.</margin>
Apis was an ox, an image of an ox, or an ox-calf, not improbably made by Aaron and celebrated by Israel with a feast, dancing, and jumping, after the Egyptian manner. See Kircher in his *Oedipus*, Hammond, etc.

It is testified that Osiris was honored in Egypt in the form of a singular or rare ox named Apis. One reads of this in *Pliny, Book 8, chapter 46; Aelian, Book 4, chapter 8; Fuller's Miscellany, Book 2, chapter 7; Selden's On the Syrian Gods, Book 1, chapter 5; Kipping's Antiquities, page 133, etc.*

Apis, says Strabo in *Book 17*, is a sacred ox or cow which was held as a god and honored in Memphis, just as he was held as a god in Heliopolis; provided that Mnevis and Apis are not the same.

The eloquent orator Cicero, in his conversation with one of the Epicurean gang in *On the Nature of the Gods, Book 1*, asks: *What do you feel regarding Apis, the holy Egyptian ox? Does he not seem a God to the Egyptians?* This is reinforced <margin>Apis regarded as God.</margin> by Pliny with his testimony in *Book 8, chapter 46: The ox, which they call Apis in Egypt, is honored as a god.* And Mela sails quite a broad course when he writes: *Apis is the god of all nations.*

<margin>Description of Apis.</margin>
Of this Ox or Apis, one reads rare and unbelievable things. Note well the following: Mela, in Book 1, chapter 9, writes thus: *it is a black ox, known by certain spots, and distinguished from all others by its tail and tongue. It is born very rarely. It does not come from the mating of cattle, but is conceived from the deity by heavenly fire; and the day of its birth is unique and holy among the people.*

Ammianus Marcellinus, in Book 22, speaks of it thus: *Apis the ox is recognizable by various birthmarks or figures, especially standing out by the appearance of the luna cornuta <note>Latin: "horned moon"</note> or crescent moon on its right side; which, when it has died after being submerged in the holy fountain following its fixed lifespan, another is sought with public mourning*, etc.

Plutarch writes of him as follows: *he is of black color, having a square light on his forehead, showing himself in the shape of a horned moon.*

One reads of him in Bochart’s *Hieroz.*, Selden’s *On the Syrian Gods, & in the additions by Beyer*, Marsham’s *chronic canon*, Dilherr’s *Truth*, Witsius’s *Egyptiaca*, Goodwin’s *Moses & Aaron*, Seneca’s *Natural Questions 4*, Solinus *chapter 32, etc.*

Even more closely and broadly, one reads of him in Alexander ab Alexandro, *Genial Days, page 321.* In Egypt, according to all testimony, the oracle of Apis is praised. *It was an Ox, which was also called Serapis. His body was covered with a black color, having a white shining crown, and his back speckled with white spots. His tail was set with double hairs, and his tongue marked with a jar or pitcher. He was not permitted to exceed the speckled yearly cycle, or the limit of his lifespan. When he was submerged in the lake, his funeral was held very solemnly, both with torn clothes and hanging hair. And when they had found such an ox, they were joyfully merry.*

It is recounted of him, though one can give little credit to it, that he used to pour out oracles, though not at all in the old fashion; but that, when one was consulting him, and he took the fodder offered to him, it was a sign of luck, prosperity, and honor; but if he refused the fodder, it had to be taken as a sign of disaster, misfortune, humiliation, and shame, etc.

It is said that Apis, held for a god...

# APIS. APOPLEXIE.

He was judged to be very strong and mighty; for Aelianus speaks of him thus: *Apis is a very strong and mighty god of the Egyptians.* <note>Latin: *Apis est fortissimus et potentissimus Aegyptiorum Deus.*</note> Jeremiah 46:15: *Why are your strong ones taken away? They did not stand, because the Lord drove them away.*

The LXX <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translators have *Apis, your chosen ox*. <note>Greek: ἄπις, ὁ μόσχος ὁ ἐκλεκτός σου (*Apis, ho moschos ho eklektos sou*).</note>

It is told that the priests of Isis did not bring him water from the Nile, but from a particular well; yet they would <margin>Apis submerged in the Nile.</margin> submerge him in the Nile. See Alexander ab Alexandro, page 349.

That very many nations held the ox in great value and honor is sufficiently clear and well-known. Even if they did not form and serve a complete ox with ceremonies, it was at least an ox's head. That people made a special matter of this livestock, as being very useful and profitable, is known from antiquity. See Beyer's additions to Selden's *On the Syrian Gods* <note>Latin: *De diis Syris*.</note>, Herodotus *Book II, chapter 4*, Diodorus Siculus *Book I*, Saubert's *Palaestra*, Dilherr's *The Truth*, etc., also my own *Sacred Miscellanies*, part II.

This having been said regarding Apis, the question arises: what might the Egyptians have meant and represented by him?

<margin>Various things represented by him.</margin> Some have focused their eyes on their King Apis. Others on the river Nile. Some on the Sun. Some on the Moon. Yet others on Jupiter. Finally, Ruffinus, Jerome in *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, Grotius, Junius, etc., focus on Joseph in Egypt; and with this agrees Arnoldus Montanus in the description of the memorable embassies of the United Netherlands to Japan, holding it as credible that the <margin>Joseph represented by Apis.</margin> Egyptians, as compensation and in honor of Joseph—because of his services and foresight so that Egypt did not perish by famine—set up an ox-statue as his memorial, so that the following generation might know that Egypt had been protected by his foresight against the famine.

Vossius seems to me to belong here as well; however, he derives "Apis" from the Hebrew words *Ab* or *Abba* <note>Hebrew: אבא / אב</note> meaning "father," from which Apis was thus named Joseph because of his care and singular providence.

<margin>Also the Nile.</margin> Some, however, maintain that the river Nile must be understood by it, which flooded the land at least once a year and made it fertile with its silt: especially since the Nile water is a God to the Egyptians, and indeed a strong and mighty God, as one who extinguished the fire, the God of the Chaldeans.

<margin>Various origins of the name NILE.</margin> The name of the Nile has been derived in various ways: namely, from the Egyptian and Phoenician word *Neel* or *Nel*, and such from the Hebrew word *Nachal* <note>Hebrew: נחל</note> meaning "a river." Others from "bringing new silt," <note>Greek: νέϊ μίσω (*nei miso*) and ἀεὶ ἰκ (*aei ik*)</note> as if it were in the Saxon tongue, *Ni leem* ("new loam/clay"), because the Nile brings new loam or silt every year <note>Greek: Νεῖλος παρὰ τὸ νέαν, ἤτοι ἐνιαυσίαν ἄγειν ἰλὺν (*Neilos para to nean, ētoi eniausian agein ilun*)</note> and spreads it over the Egyptian fields.

But others, in my opinion, derive the word not ungracefully from the word for "black" or "dark brown": <note>Hebrew: שחور (*Shachor*)</note> the river Nile is called *Seiris* and *Siris*. See Selden and Beyer, and Fuller in *Miscellanea*, etc.

Yet for now, I can well lean toward those who believe Joseph to be symbolized by him: although I generally hold with Clement of Alexandria in *Stromata <note>Clement's work "Miscellanies," discussing hieroglyphics in Book V.</note>* that the ox is a symbol of agriculture, of the earth, and of necessary sustenance.

We also find him <note>Joseph</note> thus named or compared to an ox. Deuteronomy 33:17. He interpreted the dream of Joseph by the fat and lean cows. He made the whole land of Egypt into a <margin>Compared to an ox.</margin> granary against the famine. He held the greatest authority under the king in Egypt. Oxen are exceptionally useful and profitable, also fit for plowing and threshing, and were placed among the sacred animals by the Egyptians. For these and other reasons, it is not entirely improbable that one remembers Joseph through this Apis.

### APOPLEXIE, PALSY, STROKE.

<margin>Description of the Stroke.</margin> Although the treatment of this ailment would best suit the physicians, I shall nevertheless note something regarding this heavy ailment from the esteemed books of the doctors. Namely: they say it is an ailment through and in which the workings of the soul and motion, along with feeling, suddenly cease; the person falls suddenly to the earth, with the eyes dilated <note>Literally "whistling of the eyes," a historical term for a fixed, wide stare.</note>, loss of understanding, sight, and hearing, and not infrequently accompanied by a deep sleep, with heavy snoring and gasping; such that he gives no answer or proof of feeling upon calling, pulling, or bumping.

<margin>Cause of the same.</margin> It is caused by various things: namely, by general and heavy blockages, so that the "animal spirits" <note>Historically, "animal spirits" were believed to be fluids or essences that traveled through the nerves to produce movement and sensation.</note> cannot shine through, nor flow into the brain or the nerves. This is brought about by heavy phlegm and slimy fluids that fall upon the nerves from the head.

Also by the squeezed or burst blood from the arteries into the cavities of the brain, which remaining there, the most volatile spirits fly away, and the watery fluids flow off, such that the coarser blood parts that remained behind coagulate and clot, and can only be made fluid again with great difficulty through the power of medicines.

Added to this is another cause: the sensible injury and denting of the skull by hitting, bumping, falling, and other harm; strong and persistent cold; vapors from charcoal in a narrow and closed room; the excessive and careless handling of mercury, and such.

<margin>Heavy consequences.</margin> As for the cure, it is held to be difficult and impossible. At least, most people go the way of all flesh <note>A euphemism for dying.</note> because of it. See Hippocrates' *Aphorisms*, Book II, chapter 24, and VII, chapter 14. Thus I read in Beverwyck:

> If someone is wounded in the head,
> His brain is dazed in that same hour.
> He is soon quit of his head-sore,
> For he passes away in a short time.

However, one should not commit such persons to the earth too early, as there are examples of people who have recovered.

<margin>Remedies.</margin> Concerning the means of restoration, many agree; on some, there are contradictory opinions. However, while this

# APOPLEXY.

<margin>Remedy.</margin>
As for the differences [of opinion among doctors], I shall leave those to the physicians and merely note the remedies or methods of healing considered here and elsewhere.

Namely, one is instructed to rub the spine and the temples of the head with *aqua antiparalytica* <note>original Latin: "water against paralysis or lameness."</note>. Generally, rubbing is very highly regarded; and it is held that if any movement occurs, the body must be kept active and in motion.

It is added that one must strongly rub the hollow of the feet with salt and vinegar.

That cupping <note>A medical practice using glass cups to create suction on the skin to "draw out" ailments.</note> in the neck and on the head, alongside the application of a Spanish fly <note>A topical blister-inducing ointment made from the dried beetle *Lytta vesicatoria*, used as a counter-irritant.</note>, is very useful.

Bloodletting is both praised and rejected.

Sneezing powder <note>A "sternutatory" used to induce sneezing and clear the head.</note> is recommended and forbidden, as it may shake the brain too violently, causing the "sinning substances" <note>The perceived harmful humors or fluids thought to cause the disease.</note> of the arteries to pour into the cavities of the brain; yet there is less concern if one gets rid of the bad substances through the nose.

The administration of penetrating clysters <note>Enemas.</note> and pills, etc., is praised.

Smelling Rue, Castoreum <note>original: "Beverzwyn" — a medicinal secretion from beavers.</note>, and burnt amber.

Anointing the area under the nose with volatile salt of ammonia, hartshorn, soot <note>original Latin: *sal vol. ammon. corn. cervi, fuligin.*</note>, etc.

Prying open the sufferer's mouth and giving *Aqua vitæ Matthioli* <note>Matthioli’s "Water of Life," a famous herbal spirit used as a restorative.</note>, theriac water, etc.

The sufferer must be sat upright as much as possible; providing light, nourishing, and moderate food, and well-purified drink, for which various recipes can be found among physicians; excessive sleep, too much heat or cold, melancholy, fright, etc., should be avoided.

If this ailment occurs once and one recovers, the causes are rarely entirely removed; one often relapses, for the openings and pathways widened by the pressure of that blockage—or those remaining partially occupied and clogged—allow similar substances to enter more easily in the future.

This ailment—since one loses their understanding, sight, hearing, touch, smell, and taste, and possesses only a softer or stronger breath, thus appearing to have less [reason] than irrational but living creatures—is a visitation not of the least, but of the most dangerous kind, and healing is rare. Yet, because of findings that are not entirely hopeless or fatal, some hope remains for at least some restoration and healing, if not full.

Let this suffice; I leave the rest to be recommended by the doctors.

As for this APOPLEXY, or <term>POPLSY</term> <note>An archaic term for apoplexy or paralysis.</note>, in which one lies without feeling in a deep sleep, unable to see or hear due to general blockage and a lack of irradiation <note>The perceived flow of "animal spirits" through the nerves.</note>, standstill, and numbing of the spirits; an accident in which so many ailments and misfortunes converge that one does not know oneself and lies open to all harm and death—unless someone else cared for us, applied healing remedies, and God blessed them—these physical ailments can remind us of the natural state of the soul of every

<margin>Apoplexy compared with the corruption of the soul.</margin>
unconverted sinner, who through general corruption and the loss of God's grace, is so positioned toward God that he does not see, hear, or feel, but falls unconcerned, unfeeling, and like the blind into his final destruction.

<column-break/>

To demonstrate this, I need only God's word, which teaches us how it is regarding the spirit of deep sleep, which is aggravated in great part by:
a. Self-indulgence and the flattery of imagination. *Deuteronomy 29:19. Luke 12:19. Revelation 3:17.*
b. The dizzying and sleeping-potion of stroking and tickling joy, the prosperity of this world accompanied by rest. *Luke 2:19. Ezekiel 16.*
c. Lazy idleness and neglect of practice, even of civil virtues.
d. God's righteous judgment, after misused and despised means of salvation. *Isaiah 6 and 29. Job 12.*

This has as its companion and cause that one walks in darkness, that the eyes of understanding are closed, and one gropes and walks like the blind. *Isaiah 59:10.*

So are all natural men positioned. *1 Corinthians 2:14. Ephesians 2 and 4.*

This worsens and becomes more incurable:
> a. When, rejecting the light, one loves darkness more and closes one's eyes to external means. *Job 1:5 and 3:19. Matthew 8:18, etc.*
> b. When between our eyes and the truth and salvific goods come pleasures, the greatness of life, and riches, which are like sand in the eyes and spread such a thick mist and darkness that one cannot see through it all to recognize the lovely beauty and constancy of truth and virtue. *2 Timothy 3:8. 1 John 2:15, 16, 17.*
> c. Neglect in examining one's own corruption, impotence, defects, etc., so that one becomes a total stranger to one's own house <note>Metaphorically, one's own soul or internal state.</note>.
> d. Whereupon follows final abandonment to oneself and misuse of all kinds of means of light. *Romans 1. Isaiah 29. Romans 11. 2 Corinthians 3. Isaiah 6.*

Accompanied by deafness and insensitivity, so that one listens to no admonition, punishment, promise, or threat; and whatever visitations and blows strike and hit a person, they remain equally unfeeling; so that one delights in evil and spreads it without fear. *Jeremiah 6:10 and 7:27, 28 and 44:16, 17 and 2:20. Isaiah 1:5. Amos 5:12.*

To which much is contributed by:
> a. Sinning against God's mercy.
> b. The postponement of God's righteous punishments. *Romans 2:4, 5. Ecclesiastes 8:11. Isaiah 5 and 7.*
> c. The habit of sinning. *Isaiah 18 and 57:10. 2 Peter 10.*

Against this converging evil, the grace of God is necessary and powerful for healing. It works lovely and powerfully through the strength and merit of Jesus's sacrifices, which, being applied more and more by the indwelling Spirit, causes the sinner to awaken from the sleep of sin and carelessness. It awakens in him a vision of himself, of God's grace, the power and merit of Jesus's sacrifices, God's justice and holiness, his own impotence and worthiness of damnation, the necessity and usefulness of communion with Christ, and truth and virtue in their beauty, value, and utility; the feeling of his misery, concern for himself, desire for conversion and breakthrough sanctification, and more besides.

And to this end, as moral and external means, it is useful and necessary to strongly [call out] <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "roe-" suggests the Dutch "roepen," meaning to call or cry out.</note> to him who sleeps...
