This I have noted regarding Apoplexy or Stroke in a spiritual sense; an experienced Christian can examine it further, elaborate upon it, and everyone may make use of it.

### APOTHECARY, PHARMACIST.

*Merchant* <note>Hebrew: רכל Rochel</note>, *Perfumer or Compounder* <note>Hebrew: רקח Rokeach, Rokach</note>, a buyer, seller, a trader of herbs and spices; one who handles and prepares the same, an APOTHECARY, *A seller of drugs and dealer in pigments* <note>Latin: "Pharmacopola & pigmentarius"</note>.

<margin>Anointing oil.</margin>
One reads of holy anointing oil, made according to the art of the Apothecaries, *Exod. 30:25*, etc.; of daughters taken to be Apothecaries <note>often translated as "perfumers" in modern Bibles</note>, *1 Sam. 8:13*; of a trade of spice-merchants, *1 Kings 10:15*, and spiced wine, *Song of Sol. 8:2.*

One reads of balm in Gilead, *Jer. 8*; of ointment and oil of joy, *Ps. 45, Isa. 61*; and whatever else appears in the holy pages.

Naturalists testify that every animal has its own help and medicine: the swallow, the *Celandine*; the hart, *Dittany*; the pigeons, the laurel; the stork, the *oregano*. Unhappy is the man who, against his soul’s ailments, does not know his antidotes and medicines, nor the Apothecary where he shall go to fetch them; or if he knows both, yet like Babylon will not let himself be healed, *Jer. 51*, though she was plastered <note>meaning her wounds were treated with medicinal poultices</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>Ailments of the soul.</margin>
One must not imagine that the soul has fewer or lighter ailments and diseases than the body; they are quite as numerous and dangerous; *The diseases of the soul are endless desires* <note>Latin: "Morbi animi sunt immensae cupiditates"</note>, that is: the diseases of the soul, says someone, are infinite lusts. *The diseases of the soul are more destructive and more numerous than those of the body* <note>Latin: "Morbi perniciofiores pluresque sunt animi, quam corporis"</note>, so says Cicero (*De Finibus* 1.7 and *Tusculan Disputations* 3) and Seneca (*On Anger*, Book 2, chapter 9). In this state we are born, creatures subject to no fewer spiritual than physical ailments.

I do not care to list all the ailments of the soul, nor the various medicines or antidotes; there is spiritual blindness, deafness, leprosy, madness, insensitivity of the heart, lethargy, coldness, "gout of the feet and hands" <note>a metaphor for being unable to walk in God's ways or do good works</note>, many passions, self-love, sadness, brooding, despair, envy, wrath, revengefulness, pride, gluttony, and such like.

One has drinks of various kinds, heart-strengtheners <note>cordials</note>, pills and plasters, corrosives of various natures, power, and effect. One has *simples* <note>Latin: "simplicia" — single-ingredient herbal remedies</note>, compound and mixed medicines. General and *panaceas* <note>Latin: "Generatia & panacea"</note>, universal and all-powerful aids and medicines, such as:

> Faith in God and Jesus Christ, presented so as to partake in the enjoyment of divine grace in Christ.
>
> Pure and unfeigned love for God and neighbor; the practice of pure religion, both internal and external.
>
> Avoiding evil and sin in every possible way.

These healing medicines, however general and influential in the healing of all kinds of soul-ailments, nevertheless allow for specific medicines according to the symptoms and particular ailments, as will be shown elsewhere under the symbolic soul-ailments.

The Holy Scripture is the spiritual Apothecary, in which one finds the medicines of the soul, for teaching, reproof, correction, and instruction in righteousness, indeed, full healing and salvation. *2 Tim. 3:15, 16, 17.*

<margin>Christ the chief Perfumer.</margin>
The chief Apothecary and spice-merchant is Christ, with whom is the prepared holy anointing oil, *Ps. 45, Isa. 61, Dan. 9:24*, with which one is anointed, *2 Cor. 1:21, 1 John 2:20*, etc. With him is healing and medicinal water, *Zech. 13:1, John 1:7, 8*, fruits and leaves for healing, *Mal. 4, Rev. 22, 1 Cor. 6:11*, and in a word, everything is in and with him; and through his preparation in the Holy Scripture, the full shop, the richly stocked Apothecary, is to be found.

The Prophets, Apostles, Evangelists, Pastors, and Teachers stand under him, and offer those medicines, and strive to sell and apply them to souls according to the variety of their ailments, giving counsel and instruction on how to use these medicines rightly, having the skill and experience of master physicians. O woe to them, if they plaster over the soul-ailments lightly and make the wounds stink!

# APPLE, APPLE TREE, *Tappuah* <note>original Hebrew: תפוח</note>
# *melon*, *melea*, *Malus*, *malum* <note>original Greek: μήλον, μηλέα; original Latin: Malus, malum</note>.

<margin>Diversity of the trees and fruits.</margin>
Just as the trees differ, so too are the fruits of various sorts, sizes, colors, and flavors. The general term is an APPLE and APPLE TREE, and therefore I shall not delve into the various specific species or types.
When the Lord wishes to punish any people, He causes the trees to wither. *Joel 1:12.*
It is well known that the naming of a tree, whether in general or by a specific kind, appears as a symbol <note>original: "zinnebeelt"</note> for man, whether in the state of grace or of nature. However, I will not dwell on that here, but will focus with specificity on the Apple tree and its fruits, as they appear symbolically in the sacred scrolls.

<margin>Apple tree as a symbol of love.</margin>
It is said that among the heathens, an APPLE TREE was a symbol of love, and that love grows, flourishes, and is nurtured under the Apple tree; that lovers honored and sent one another apples, and played beneath the apple trees. But I shall clarify this somewhat.
That the apple tree was a means of representing love among the ancients, and that playful, greening, and growing love was depicted under the apple tree; that apples appear as dedicated to Venus, the goddess of love; that on some coins Venus is found depicted with an apple in her hand; that the love of two sweethearts was expressed by the kissing of an apple; that honoring or throwing an apple to one another was a sign of love, and that one wished to unite with such a person, etc.—I do not think anyone will attempt to dispute this with me; see *Pierius Valerius, Concerning the Fruit or Apple, book 54; Ursinus, Biblical Arboretum, pages 418, 420; Alciatus, Emblem 190; and Claudius Minois, Observations on Alciatus’s Emblems.*
Thus Galatea and Clearista throw apples to the youths in the works of Virgil and Theocritus, from which comes the phrase *meiobolein to eis aphrodisia deleazein* <note>original Greek: μηλοβολείν τὸ εἰς ἀφροδίσια δελεάζειν</note>, *Ursinus, page 418*, meaning "to throw apples to entice into love-making." To represent love and fertility in the married state, the bride held an apple, <term>a moon-sphere <note>The author uses "maanbol," likely referring to the round poppy head mentioned in the following Latin verse</note> in her hands.</term>

Which some wish to mean as much as: **she offers me her love.**

<margin>Bonds of the married state.</margin>
On one and the other, Claudius Minois has expressed his view thus, page 649, etc.: *There are two things which particularly suit those united by the bond of marriage, and which make that state firm and mutually binding, namely: fidelity and love.*

<margin>The hand a sign of fidelity.</margin>
Regarding fidelity, the dog serves as a sign, being the most faithful animal. Of love, an apple or an apple tree is a means of representation; the marriage bond, which occurs through the union of both bodies, is primarily nurtured and preserved by fidelity and constancy. The apples were dedicated to Venus, to whom also the golden Hesperian apple was assigned. Hippomenes defeated Atalanta by this means; Galatea also struck her suitor with an apple. The epigram of Plato Laertius refers to this:

<margin>Apple, symbol of love.</margin>
<margin>Apples dedicated to Venus.</margin>

> *I hit you with the apple; take it if you love me.* <note>original Greek and Latin: "Τῷ μήλῳ βάλλωσε; οὐ δ' εἴ μεν ἔχουσα φιλεῖς με, / Malo ego te ferio; cape, fi me diligis, illud."</note>

->That is:<-

*I throw an apple to you: take it if you love me.*

Atalanta, daughter of Schoeneus, set a footrace before her suitors on the condition that she would strike down those she defeated. Hippomenes, who was deeply in love with her, engaged in a race with the girl through the art of Venus, and threw a golden apple once, twice, and a third time at her as she ran past him. The girl, being charmed by the rarity of these apples and their extraordinary beauty, hesitated a while, and thus he outran the girl and defeated her. *Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 10.*
*Thus Galatea sought her man*, that is: *Galatea, a sea-nymph, was wonderfully loved by Polyphemus.* See Ovid in the 13th book of the *Metamorphoses*.

But in Virgil Maro, Eclogue 3, I would prefer to understand the following:

> *Galatea, a playful girl, hits me with an apple.*

->That is:<-

*The playful Galatea throws at me from the apple bushes*
*With apples at my head.*

...to mean rather that he complained about her because she threw a lot of insults and slanderous words at his body.
But the fact is that the Apple tree, <term>*tappuah* <note>Hebrew term for apple</note></term>,

is considered a fruit-bearing tree of a not-at-all pleasant shape, with thick branches, spreading far and wide with broad green leaves; providing a lovely and dense shade against the heat of the sun and the rain; bearing pleasant blossoms, dappled with white and red, and apples fragrant of scent and lovely of taste, being of exceptional use in the household, from which one also makes *cider* or apple-drink.

<margin>Application to Christ.</margin>
Among the wild trees of the human race—whether of high or low status, various callings, fruits, and effects, as all natural men are—Christ far surpasses the trees; He and His fruits are compared to them. *Song of Sol. II. 3-5.* One reads of this in *Song of Sol. VII. 8. and VIII. 5.*

I choose to believe that He is compared to an apple tree, both because of His fruits, gifts, and grace—which are just as abundant, fragrantly strengthening, and nourishing as those of the apple trees—which He provides not only earlier or later, like some apple trees, but monthly, *Revelation XXII.* <note>The author refers to the Tree of Life in the New Jerusalem which yields fruit every month.</note> His fruits and even leaves are for healing, for righteousness, and life, *1 Cor. I. 30. Mal. IV. 2.* Hiding under whose wings and shadow one finds gentle and sweet refreshment, strengthening, rest, and protection against the heat of God's wrath and persecution. *Ps. XXXVI, Ps. XXIII. Matt. XI. 28. etc.*

That His blossom is dappled, white and red, represents His pure white holiness, fair obedience, and love, dappled with the blood-red color of His endurance and bloody suffering; therefore He is called *dazzling and ruddy, Song of Sol. V. 10.* <note>original: "blank en root," a traditional Dutch translation of the description of the Beloved.</note>

One perceives the wish and prayer of the church, Christ's bride, *Song of Sol. II. 5.* that she may be sustained with apples. I would think that the church, in her state of languishing so as not to faint or succumb, desires teachers—who are the distributors of the mysteries of Christ—to most earnestly apply to her the promises and assurances of God in Christ through the ministry of the word of righteousness. This is so that she, tasting the power of divine grace in the merits of Christ, might be restored and strengthened, and thus be able to respond properly to the encounters and favors of the lover of her soul.

One reads of the church, Christ's bride: *Song of Sol. ch. VII. 8. And the fragrance of your nose like apples.* I will not insert here what various scholars have noted about this. I would think that whether Christ or one of His companions speaks of the church, the bride, one must view the church as inwardly sanctified and purified by Christ’s blood and Spirit, and filled and adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. She is beautiful and lovely of scent not only inwardly but also outwardly through Christian virtues and the word of teaching, *2 Cor. II. 16, 17.* It is a good fragrance of Christ for awakening and strengthening, like the scent of apples spreading far and wide, making it fragrant and pleasant to Christ and His sheep because of her right-mindedness and discernment in feeling and doctrine; just as the nose and smelling are symbols of pure contemplation, judgment, and observation. *Isa. XI. 30.*

*Ursinus, Biblical Trees, page 421.*

Just as they have received Christ, so they walk in Him. *Col. II. 6.* The heavenly apple-scent and grace ward off all foolish chatter and useless words from the mouth and tongue of a Christian sanctified to God.

Just as a stinking breath is a sign of how it is with the stomach and intestines; so stinking and rotten words indicate that the heart is corrupted and a cesspool full of evil desires. *Matt. XII. 34. and XV. 19.*

On the contrary, a wise and graced heart shows that one is healthy in understanding and judgment and acts quite differently. *Prov. VI. 23. Eccles. X. 12.*

# APPLE.

Not all words fit every place, time, and person. Timely words are in themselves useful, pleasant, full of radiance and elegance, and often possess great power.

<margin>Gospel teaching.</margin>One may consider as such words the Gospel teaching, received in a pure and faithful heart, which, being brought forth from the earthen vessel <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 4:7, suggesting that God's power is shown through human weakness.</note> by a pure mouth and stamped with a holy life, are of wonderful power and consequence. *2 Cor. IV. 7. 2 Cor. V. 10. 2 Cor. II. 14, 15, 16.*

<margin>Remarks on Song of Sol. VIII. 5.</margin>One also reads, *of being awakened under the apple tree, and born with the sorrow of the mother. Song of Sol. VIII. 5.* I know that various remarks and explanations occur regarding this passage, all of which I shall not include here; one should consult the commentators. Some apply this to the Church, formerly in a quite miserable state, as described in *Ezekiel XVI. 1-15*, as if born from Mother Eve, having sinned in the garden, but now coming out of Heathendom and out of that state with much confidence to the bridegroom, leaning on him, and finding all abundance in and by him—he who was born of his mother according to the word of the chief promise.

Others explain it thus: *I have known and called upon your name as my Savior, though you were not yet born; and the word of promise refreshed and sustained my soul, indeed was as heart-strengthening and refreshing to me as the scent and smell of apples; yet I did not cease to heartily wish for your coming and appearance in the flesh.*

However, those who wish to look a bit further believe that the Church in the later times of the world, as it runs toward the end, is introduced here as having formerly sat and rested under the apple tree Jesus in the heat of the persecution by the Jews and Heathens, awakening him through prayers and sighs, that he might avenge the blood of his servants; that she, being now again in distress, cries out to him that he would hasten to her aid and deliverance, so that it might appear that he was her savior and helper.

Those who do his will are called Christ's mother, sister, and brother, *Matt. XII.*, especially the first Apostolic Christian church, which with incomparable labor, patience, oppression, and love, brought forth Christ in the hearts of the elect, causing Christ to take shape in them. *Gal. IV. 2 Cor. VIII. 23.*

Christ is also from the church and the fathers according to the flesh, *Rom. IX.*; she conceived and brought him forth in hope and expectation. *Rev. XII. 2.*

One may further consult other writers on this.

I shall briefly bring together what is considered regarding the comparison between the apple tree and Jesus, and what is or can be said mostly in the explanations of the texts.

To which I first let precede Gargon’s <note>Matthew Gargon (1661–1728) was a Dutch Reformed minister known for his literary and theological works.</note> *Useful Pastime on the Song of Solomon*, pages 21, 22:

> Compared to the fruitless trees of the woods, you, my chosen one, are
> A greening apple tree that bears the fruits of life,
> And provides a cooling shade that drives away the sun’s violence.
> How sweet! how blessed it is! to dive into such a shadow,
> And under God's protection, to pluck the fruit of salvation!

Next follows what has been gathered from Durham, Udemans, Geesteranus, Groenewegen, Oldenburg, <note>A list of prominent 17th-century Reformed theologians and commentators.</note> and very many other writers on this:

a. An apple tree has in common with all other trees that the earth is its mother; yet the earth brings forth wild forest trees; the art and labor of the grafter and planter certainly do much here.
1. So is Jesus indeed from the earth, and born as his brothers. *Gal. IV. 4. Hebr. II. 14. Isa. LIII. 2.*
2. However, he is not like the trees of the forest and absolutely equal to others in everything, but is to us a mediator, tree of life, holy, etc. He is of the husbandman and grafter, who has grafted him into the human race. *Ps. XV. Jer. XXX. 21. Luke I. 35. Isa. IV. 2. etc.*

<column-break/>

b. It is, as it appears outwardly, indeed such that an apple tree does not reach the height, strength, and prestige of the cedars of Lebanon or the oaks of Bashan; yet it is more capable of providing useful nourishment.
The Christ, according to the outward appearance, was not to have anything about him that might smack of worldly pomp, splendor, luster, and the power of the flesh. *Ps. VIII. 22. Isa. LIII. Philip. II.*
Here one had to look at the internal and most useful qualities for the benefit, help, grace, and assistance of sinners, *John I. 14-16. Col. I. 19.* and so he is a true tree of life, *Rev. II. 7. and XXII. 2.* So says Theodoretes: <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD), an influential theologian of the early Church.</note> *He is more excellent not only as God's son, but also as the son of man, as sinless, and one must behold him in the excellence of his gifts. Ps. XLVI. 3.*

c. An apple tree spreads its branches wide; it is full of leaves and creates a heavy shade for hiding against the heat of the sun.
Jesus spreads himself through the whole man and takes him in, *Eph. III. 15.* especially in the New Testament, he spreads himself over the entire earth. *Dan. II. 35.*
Under his branches of grace—wings of protection—is a hiding place against the burning heat of God's wrath, and safety in the fire of persecutions. *Ps. XXXVI. 8. Ps. XCI. 1. Isa. IV. 4. Mal. IV. 2.*

d. The flowers of the apple tree are magnificent and lovely in beauty of form: <note>original: "Vario distincta colore"</note> *Distinguished by various colors*, of the apple <margin>blossoms.</margin> <note>original: "quae candida parte, parte rubent"</note> *which are white in part, and red in part*, that is: *Diverse in color, here white, and there again red; white, elegant red, lovely in scent.*
Jesus' white innocence, his unblemished <margin>Refer-ence to Jesus.</margin> holiness, his most perfect and whitest love and obedience, joined with the fiery purple-red of his burning love for his father’s honor and the deliverance of his people, his bloody suffering, his endurance, *Ps. LXIX. 10. Song of Sol. V. 10.* shows itself in the utmost grace, *Psalm XLV. 3*, to which the all-surpassing scent and fragrance helps not a little. *Song of Sol. I. 3. 2 Cor. II. 15, 16. Eph. V. 2.*

e. Naturalists say unanimously, and it is confirmed by experience, that apples in general, and especially lemons and citrons, strengthen the brain and the fainting heart. The apples themselves are good for food, so that their tree is very useful. The fruits of Christ the apple tree are many and manifold: reconciliation, *Rom. III. 25. 2 Cor. V. 19. 1 John II. 2.* true wisdom, *Eph. I. 17, 18. 1 Cor. I. 30.* righteousness and the right to life, *Rom. V. 21. Rom. V. 1, 2. Isa. LIII. 11.* holiness and fruitfulness, *John XV. 2. Col. I. 10.* he is an <note>original: "arbor & pomum amoris"</note> *tree and apple of love*, *Rom. V. 5. Gal. # APPLE. LABOR.

The suffering and endurance of the believers are food and drink, *John 6:55*. What do you think? Did the bride of the church—being sick, weakened, and indeed exhausted by strong longings of love for the most intimate communion with Jesus—not have reason to burst forth in such wishes and prayers? Thus speaks Gargon in his *Useful Pastime on the Song of Solomon*, p. 22.

<margin>Sighs of the church for Jesus.</margin>
> *Refresh me by the wine of Christ’s doctrine and comfort,*
> *And by the apple-scent of zeal for God’s offspring.*
> *I swoon, I swoon with love, my love! my treasure! my delight!*
> *Your strong left hand makes me rest in peace.*
<note>original: "flinkerhant" (left hand). This refers to Song of Solomon 2:6: "His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me."</note>

She had reason to pray that she might be strengthened, supported, and made alive by the promises in Christ, and the fruits of his suffering, obedience, and Holy Spirit, so that, being strengthened with grace and power, she might respond to Jesus' love and benefits.

<margin>Wearing wreaths of apples.</margin>
That in ancient times, in the month of August, people wore crowns and wreaths of woven and strung apples; and that especially the grafters and planters did so, is a fact known to the researcher and the student of antiquity.

->Horace, Epodes 2.<-

> *Or when Autumn has raised in the fields*
> *his head adorned with mellow fruit.*
<note>original: "Vel cum decorum mitibus pomis caput / Autumnus arvis extulit."</note>

->That is:<-

> *When Autumn lifts his head,*
> *Now richly overloaded with ripe apples.*

To which, as it is believed, Silius Italicus, book 14, has pointed as if with a finger:

> *He defiled the seasons of Autumn,*
> *blooming with widespread gifts.*
<note>original: "Temporaque Autumni latis florentia donis / Foedavit."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Defiled the time of Autumn, widely blooming in its gifts.*
> *And Propertius, speaking of Vertumnus <note>The Roman god of seasons, change, and plant growth.</note>, book 4:*

> *Here the grafter pays his vows with a crown of fruit,*
> *When the pear tree has borne apples on its reluctant trunk.*
<note>original: "Insitor hic solvit pomosa vota coronâ / Cum pyrus invito stipite mala tulit."</note>

->That is:<-

> *The diligent grafter now fulfills his promises,*
> *Now that the high pear trees bear apples despite themselves.*

See Paschal, *On Crowns*, book 1, chapter 13; book 4, chapter 1. Hofman, *Lexicon*, page 567.

### LABOR, WORKING, LABORER, <insert>פעל / פועל / עמל , πόνος, πονεῖν, μόχθος, κόπος, ἐργάτης.</insert>
<note>The original includes Hebrew (po'al, po'el, 'amal) and Greek (ponos, ponein, mochthos, kopos, ergates) terms for labor, toil, and a worker.</note>

<margin>Application of the word LABOR.</margin>
The designation of LABOR, appearing many times in the Holy Scroll <note>The Bible.</note>, is applied not only to cattle but also to the rational creature; and is taken not only for coarse and heavy Labor, which one does with the limbs of the body, but also for the strong and continuous activity and preoccupation of the human spirit, in that which one considers with purpose and intent, and desires with enduring patience, subjecting oneself through obedience to the will of God.

<column-break/>

Improperly speaking, one lives by God's LABOR and work, which costs God no effort, *Isaiah 40*, as it does for man, *Job 10, Psalm 138*. God's work is perfect, *Deuteronomy 32*, which is applied by some to Christ, in whose suffering and active obedience—for the righteousness and perfection of his own—nothing is lacking.

So it is spoken of the laboring of the Messiah, *Isaiah 49*, how he had in a certain sense labored in vain; and *Isaiah 53*, of the labor of his soul, by which one can understand all that he has done for the redemption of his people and the sanctification of his father’s name through righteousness.

<margin>Labor of the Messiah.</margin>
Every man is born to labor. This labor happens with the body and particularly with the hands, in order to eat one's own bread, which often does not happen without sweat, effort, and sorrow.

<margin>Man born to labor.</margin>
So there is a labor and working with the understanding, the tongue, the pen, etc., which the soul performs particularly with constant exertion. If it concerns the spiritual and eternal well-being of the whole man, it is called: *working out one's salvation with fear and trembling; laboring for the food that does not perish, but which remains unto eternal life; seeking the kingdom of God and his righteousness; not spending one’s labor for that which cannot satisfy, etc. Philippians 2:12, John 6, Matthew 6, Isaiah 53:1, 2.* This now must be the occupation of every person; on this he must constantly think, will this, and be intent upon this through the continuous use of the means, without slowing down.

The Lord is intent upon man's salvation and deliverance: and in this he has fellow-laborers, *1 Corinthians 3*, that is, such rational and moral instruments who, according to his command, calling, qualification, and sending, must seek the salvation of men from the heart, and for that purpose rightly divide the word of salvation, teaching, exhorting, rebuking, comforting, refuting, awakening, in season and out of season. These are they who labor in the word, who strive to bring about Christ's form in the listeners. Laborers in the vineyard and harvest, who in no way strive to labor in vain, have as their chief aim and goal the conversion of many people, the extension of Jesus' kingdom, the glorification of God in his saints; not their own glory and self-interest. There are wrong laborers, hirelings, unfaithful ones, who not only do wrong and forbidden work, seeking their own honor and interest, but also, perverting the word, draw the disciples away from after the Lord; those who put the word up for sale; lazy servants and belly-servers, and such like. Of these one can read with discernment and distinction in *Matthew 20, Job 10, 1 Corinthians 3, Galatians 4, 1 Thessalonians 5, 1 Timothy 4 and 5, 2 Timothy 2, Revelation 2, Philippians 3, 2 Peter 2, etc.*

And to give the reader a bonus, so that he may better use what has been said and distinguish one from the other more capably, I shall present the following.

a. Labor is presented with words which indicate that laboring is burdensome, and wears down and weakens the body and its powers not a little: <insert>μόχθος, κόπος, עמל.</insert> <note>mochthos, kopos, 'amal: Greek and Hebrew terms specifically emphasizing toil, weariness, and exhaustion.</note>

# LABOR.
<note>original: "ARBEID"</note>

## Q. AREND.

<margin>Ovid, book *Letters from the Black Sea*:</margin>
<note>original: "Ovidius libr. de Ponto"</note>

> *You see how in the hard fields (and what is stronger than an ox?) / the work breaks the powerful bodies of bulls.*
> *The soil which is never accustomed to rest in a fallow field / grows old and weary from constant fruit-bearing.*
> *The horse will perish if he always enters the contests / of the circus with uninterrupted runs.*
> *Though it may be strong, the ship will be broken in the sea / if it is never hauled out of the flowing waters to stay dry.*
> *An immense series of labors also weakens me: / and forces me to be an old man before my time.*
> *Leisure nourishes the body, and the mind is also fed by it. / On the contrary, immoderate labor consumes both.*
<note>original Latin: "Cernis ut in duris (& quid bove firmius?) arvis / Fortia taurorum corpora frangat opus..." etc.</note>

->That is:<-

*You see how the body of the bulls is broken*
*(What is harder than a bull?) by the work that weakens them.*
*The land, which always bears and is never allowed to lie fallow,*
*Will soon deny its fruits to the owner.*
*A horse, that would compete in the race-track without end,*
*Succumbs to all the burden, and falls completely.*
*A ship that endlessly continues to ply the wild sea,*
*Will not stay upright if it is not hauled up.*
*Thus I too am weakened, as all the labor wears me down,*
*And forces me to become old and gray before my time.*
*Rest must give nourishment to the soul and the body.*
*But labor without measure weakens and breaks life.*

<margin>Labor of Paul, Timothy, and Silvanus.</margin>
Paul testifies in *2 Thessalonians 3:8*: *Neither did we eat any man’s bread for nothing, but worked with labor and travail night and day, that we might not be burdensome to any of you.* If Paul, Timothy, and Silvanus had eaten no one’s bread for free among the Thessalonians, it was a clear and public proof that they had not preached for the sake of bread; they had not "stuck their feet under someone else's table" <note>A Dutch idiom for being a dependent guest or freeloading.</note> while loving the seats of honor; but each of the three occupied themselves on all occasions with teaching and instructing the congregation, and thought no effort or labor too bitter. In the remaining time, early in the morning and late at night, even into the deep of the night, they slaved away at their learned trade, in order to be allowed to eat their own bread. Gamaliel <note>A celebrated Pharisee and teacher of the law in the New Testament.</note> had advised his disciples that they should learn some art or trade besides their studies in order to be able to subsist. It seems people were noble-minded in the old days; science could fall into low esteem; gifts and presents sometimes arrive late, and appear very meagerly. Science <note>In this context, "science" or "wetenschap" refers to formal theological or academic learning.</note> sometimes runs for bread. See my explanations on *1 Corinthians 9* and *2 Corinthians 11* and *12*; consequently, that was a labor which could weaken soul and body.

b. Since temporal means are often obtained through labor, and since they cost care and anxiety in the keeping, and even more in the increasing, spending, and investing—for *it is easier to seek than to protect what has been acquired* <note>original Latin: "facilius est quaerere, quam parta tueri"</note>; because it is easier to gain something than to preserve what is won—it seems to me that temporal goods in this respect can be called labor and effort, *Genesis 31:42, Job 20:18, Psalm 105:44, Psalm 107:12.* See Cocceius, Sebastian Schmidt, Gejerus, and others on Job and the Psalms.

c. Otherwise, labor and effort also signify heavy grief, a cross, misery, and everything that, being distressing, falls heavier than labor—as it takes away a person’s sleep and rest and contentment, and makes the body grow thin, the eyes sink in, and sometimes causes a person to waste away and die. *Job 3:10* and *5:7, Psalm 90:10*, etc.

d. Sins provoke labor, *Isaiah 43:24*, since they are sometimes not only devised with intention and plot and worked out with effort; but they also fall heavy and distressing upon the Lord and the pious, and they cost the Messiah soul-labor, *Isaiah 53:11*, in his labor of suffering, death, etc. And though he may have received little reward or repayment from many for his preaching, wonders, and signs (for few believed, *Isaiah 53:1, Isaiah 49:4*), he nevertheless received from his Father the reward of his labor, namely glory, honor, dominion, joy, seed, people, and inheritance. *Psalm 110, Hebrews 12:1, Philippians 2:8, 9, 10, Isaiah 53:10.*

e. Someone’s labor is his handiwork: and it is sometimes also applied to God, and made relative to man, and that gives us footing to behold man as God’s handiwork, both in nature and in the reformation, *Job 3:10, Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9, 10, Psalm 100:3, Ephesians 2:10*, etc.

As for what further concerns labor and laborers, Lord Campegius Vitringa <note>A prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist (1659–1722).</note> says in his explanation of the Gospel parables, page 384, etc.

<margin>Labor spiritually applied.</margin>
A laborer is one who labors and works, and does everything that belongs to the cultivation of the vineyard: to clear the vineyard of stones, to manure it, to cut off the lush branches and useless vines; to gather the fruits of the vineyard, to bring them into the winepress; to press wine from the grapes, etc.

<margin>of God’s Word.</margin>
In a spiritual way, this signifies that the ministers of the Gospel have a special activity, and practice it regarding the church, observing all duties toward it, just as the vinedresser does toward the vineyard.

Laborers are the teachers and overseers of the church, because:

<margin>Teacher’s office a difficult work.</margin>
1. Their labor is no less difficult—indeed, one might say, in a certain respect more difficult—than the labor of those who cultivate fields or vineyards; for their duty is, with the greatest exertion of spirit and strength, to incessantly provide for the benefit of the flock of Christ: always to watch, to labor, and to undergo all difficulties, so that it may go well with the flock. Therefore, there is no more difficult work than the work of a spiritual shepherd, when one is to serve that office rightly.

2. They clear away stones, that is, prejudices, errors, and offenses.

They manure, by liberally sharing the nourishment of doctrine, through which the spiritual life is fed.

They cut off those who do not walk worthily according to the Gospel of Christ and bear no fruit in Christ, through the pruning knife of God’s Word, a part of which is the command to practice church discipline: which is as much as pruning away the lush and useless vines.

<summary>This page explores the concept of "Labor" through classical poetry, the apostolic example of Paul, and the spiritual metaphor of the vineyard. It argues that while excessive physical labor exhausts the body, spiritual labor—specifically the ministry of the Gospel—is a demanding but essential duty modeled on Christ's own "soul-labor."</summary>
<keywords>Labor, Ovid, Paul the Apostle, Timothy, Silvanus, Gamaliel, Messiah, Campegius Vitringa, vineyard metaphor, ministry, church discipline, 2 Thessalonians 3:8</keywords>

### EAGLE, <note>original Hebrew: נשר (nesher)</note> <note>original Greek: ἀετὸς (aetos), αἰετὸς (aietos)</note>.

<margin>Eagle, king of the birds.</margin>
THE EAGLE, named *nesher* <note>original: נשר</note>, as some wish from the Arabic word *Nasara*, meaning to tear with the crooked beak, is called by the Greeks *aetos* <note>original: ἀετὸς</note> and *aietos* <note>original: αἰετὸς</note>. It is a king among the birds, just as the lion is among the four-footed animals; called by Pindar the "king of birds" <note>original Greek: οἰωνῶν βασιλῆα</note> and in the Pythian Odes, "the eagle of Jupiter, the leader of birds" <note>original Greek: Διὸς αἰετὸν, ἀρχὸν οἰωνῶν</note>.
Horace, Book IV, Ode 4:

> *Like the winged servant of the lightning bolt,*
> *To whom the king of the Gods granted dominion over the wandering birds,*
> *Having found him faithful*
> *In the kidnapping of golden-haired Ganymede.*
<note>original Latin: "Qualem ministrum fulminis alitem, / Cui rex Deorum regnum in aves vagas / Permisit expertus fidelem / Jupiter in Ganymede flavo."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Just as the prince of birds goes striving illustriously,*
> *To whom the head of the gods has given high authority*
> *Over all the feathered creatures*
> *That swirl through the clouds;*
> *A favor well-bestowed upon him;*
> *Because in the abduction of the beautiful Ganymede*
> *He behaved so faithfully.*

See on this Alciati, Emblem 4, and Claude Mignault, page 83.
Kipping, *Roman Antiquities*, page 83, etc., calls him:

->THE EAGLE, QUEEN OF BIRDS, AND JUPITER'S SERVANT.<-
<note>original Latin: "AQUILA REGINA AVIUM, ET JOVIS MINISTRA."</note>

->That is:<-

->*The king of birds, and the servant of Jove.*<-

Because the Eagle is wonderfully fast in flight, he has been dedicated to Jupiter, and described as his weapon-bearer, depicted with the three-pronged lightning bolt in his claw. And because of this, the Eagle is taken both for Jupiter himself and for his sign. Theocritus:

> *Jupiter's auspicious bird, this is Jupiter's sign.*
<note>original Greek: Διὸς αἴσιος ὄρνις Ζηνὸς πετάδε σῆμα. / Latin: Jovis fausta avis, Jovis hoc signum.</note>

->That is:<-

->*Jupiter's lucky bird, Jupiter's sign.*<-

<margin>An unclean bird.</margin>
He is recorded among the unclean birds in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14. There are various species of eagles. According to the diversity of nations and languages, they bear different names. Their exact size cannot be precisely determined. The colors also vary. However, in general, those things are said of them which one can read more expansively in Pliny, Aelian, Bochart, Franz, and Johnston, etc.; namely, that the Eagle has a firm and upright stature.
<margin>Appearance of the eagle.</margin>
That his legs are sturdy and firm, yet contain little marrow. That his eyes are small, greenish-gray, hollow, and deep. His beak or neb is crooked, and in old age it curves entirely around so that he dies of hunger. He has wings stretched out straight, curved at the top. His claws are hard, curved, or hooked. He has a fierce and sharp sight, so

<column-break/>

that he can look directly into the sun without blinking, by which he also tests his young to see if they are legitimate or illegitimate.

Lucan, Book IX:

> *And when Jupiter's bird has brought forth from the warm egg*
> *Its featherless young, it turns them toward the rising sun.*
> *Those who could endure the rays, and with direct light*
> *Sustained the day, are preserved for the uses of heaven:*
> *Those who yield to Phoebus, lie rejected.*
<note>original Latin: "Atque Jovis volucer calido cum protulit ovo / Implumes natos, solis convertit in ortus. / Qui potuêre pati radios, & lumine recto / Sustinuêre diem, cæli servantur in usus: / Qui Phœbo cessêre, jacent."</note>

->That is:<-

> *When the young of the Eagle have now come*
> *Out of the eggs, she places them before the face of the sun.*
> *If she finds one there who could endure such light,*
> *She lets him enjoy himself through the expanse of heaven,*
> *The rest remain excluded from the use of the clouds.*

Silius Italicus in the 10th book:

> *Not otherwise does the weapon-bearer of great Jupiter*
> *Test his doubtful offspring by the lamp of Phoebus:*
<note>original Latin: "Armiger haud aliter magni Jovis / Explorat dubios Phœbea lampade natos:"</note>

->That is:<-

> *The weapon-bearer of the thunderer Jove*
> *Tests his young whether it shall be a match for the sun.*

Claudian:

> *He consults the burning rays, and with the light as teacher*
> *He proves the strength and character of his offspring.*
<note>original Latin: "Consulit ardentes radios, & luce magistrâ / Natorum vires, ingeniumque probat."</note>

->That is:<-

> *He tests the strength of his young by the light of the sun,*
> *Whether it could already endure the rays of that brilliance.*

He flies heaven-high, and makes his nest on the tops of mountains, in the most elevated rocky crags. He lives on the prey of animals, and feeds on pigeons, geese, swans, chickens, sheep, deer, hares, turtles, fish, snakes, crabs, and carrion. He is found on Mount Taurus, Caucasus, in the kingdom of Peru, Germany, Poland, Britain, Denmark, and wherever much prey falls.
It is testified of him that he protects his nest against poison by means of the *Aetites* <term>the "eagle stone," a hollow geode believed to have protective and medicinal properties</term> stone, and cleanses it with the herb *Callitrichum* <term>likely Starwort or Maidenhair fern, believed in folklore to have purifying qualities</term>.
It is said that he despises the crows and other birds that are envious and biased against him, flying much lower than he, out of magnanimity.

Regarding this, the proverb holds: *The Eagle*
*Does not catch flies.*
<note>original Latin: "Aquila / Non captat muscas."</note>

->That is:<-

->*The Eagle catches no flies.* also:<-

->*The Eagle looking at wood-worms.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Aquila Thripas aspiciens."</note>

->That is:<-

->*The eagle does not concern itself with small creatures.*<-

One may see on this Erasmus, *Adages*, pages 675, 315.

It means to say, *Great men and spirits do not occupy themselves with trifles: an elevated mind overlooks insignificant things.*
It is said that his gall, though bitter and sharp, when tempered and mixed with Attic honey, wonderfully [improves] the...

<meta>This page continues the entry for "Arent" (Eagle) from page 122. The previous page established the eagle's status as the "king of birds" and a symbol of Jupiter. This page explores the eagle's natural behaviors and their theological applications to God, Christ, and the faithful.</meta>

# EAGLE.
<note>Dutch: Arent</note>

...[he] brightens his sight, that he singularly struggles with dragons, carries his young on his wings and not between his feet like other birds, being heaven-bound in flight, and thus out of reach of other birds and arrows; that he is swift of flight and persistent in flying; that he lives a very long and vigorous life, and his strengths are as if renewed in old age; and that among all birds he has a very strong sense of smell, by which he scents carrion from afar, making the slain his prey, and with his young drinks the blood; and what is more is too long to describe or to prove with ancient and trustworthy writers. I have already said enough to translate it and apply it to various objects according to my aim and scope, with which, cutting away many unnecessary things, I shall occupy myself in what follows.

<margin>Application to God.</margin>
The Eagle of singular strength, faithfulness, and care regarding his young—carrying them, covering them, and coming to their aid, ensuring that their nest is firm and at an unapproachable height—can vividly sketch for me how God carries His own as on Eagle’s wings, places them in a high, firm, and unapproachable dwelling, being so near to them and such a help that no one can harm or damage them. See this regarding Israel, *Exodus 19:9 and 32; Deuteronomy 29:2 and 32; Isaiah 61:9; Psalm 56:5-12 and 91:1; Jeremiah 23:24; Romans 8* and His children. God stirred the children of Israel to the exodus from Egypt; He fed them, protected them, and carried them.

An Eagle because of his all-penetrating sight, before whom nothing is hidden or can be kept secret. *Psalm 139:1, 2, etc.; Hebrews 4:12, 13.*

Who has His dwelling in the heights, elevated above all the peaks of the mountains. *Isaiah 66:1; 1 Kings 8; Acts 7 and 17; Isaiah 40:22.*

No slaughter or prey makes the Eagle so great, but the Lord makes Him greater. See an example of it in *Isaiah 16:24.*

The Lord is above all kings, who are to Him as a mere nothing, a speck of dust on the scale, a drop in the bucket <note>original Dutch: 'emer' (bucket)</note>. *Isaiah 40:15.*

Again, the Son of God as the Angel of the Covenant, King and Savior of His people, <term>the God-man</term> <note>original Greek: θεάνθρωπος (theanthrōpos)</note>, the perfecter and cause of their salvation, may be compared to an Eagle, insofar as He has a swift sight, a deep judgment, indeed is a knower of hearts. *Job 2:25 and 21:17; Hebrews 4:12; Isaiah 11:2, 3.*

And if ever the Eagle becomes locked in battle with the Dragon, to finish him off and rob him of his violence and power? It is the Christ who, as the seed of the woman, had to crush the head of the Serpent, *Genesis 3:15*, overpowering him and his house, and wresting his vessels from him, *Isaiah 49:24, 25; Luke 11:21, 22*, who has brought him and his works to naught. *1 Corinthians 15:25, 26; Hebrews 2:14, 15; 1 John 3:8.*

And never did the Eagle fly so high, or spread his nest on so heaven-high a rock, but Christ ascended higher, and established His dwelling in the infinitely higher, *Psalm 47:6 and 68:19 and 110:1; Hebrews 1:3; Ephesians 4:8, 9, 10, etc.* bringing His seed and children onto a rocky stone. *Psalm 18; Matthew 16:18; Psalm 84:4; Proverbs 18:10.*

In ancient times it was held that the Eagle carried the souls of emperors, kings, and prominent princes to heaven or into the stars, as mentioned by Herodian, *Book IV*, and Artemidorus, *Book II, chapter 10.*

<column-break/>

And since it was the custom to burn the dead bodies on funeral pyres, an Eagle was placed on these pyres, which was released upon lighting the fire to carry the souls of the emperors and commanders upward.

<margin>Eagle released at the burning of corpses.</margin>
Upon which perhaps Lycophron had his eye, when he calls Achilles the Eagle, because he carried away the dead body of Hector with him on the chariot. See *Franciscus Rosseus, Archaeology, Book V, chapter 33; Hofmann, Universal Lexicon.*

Truly it is Jesus, who has not only ascended to heaven, but with, in, and through whom the believers, as in their head and in Him as the firstfruits, are seated in the heavens, *Ephesians 2:6*, their names are written in His book, *Revelation 21:27*, He shows them to the Father on His high priestly breastplate, and wills that they be where He is, *John 17:2-4*, He prepares their place and shall take them to Himself. *Job 14:2, 3; 1 Thessalonians 4:16, 17.*

Does the Eagle put his young to the test by making them look directly at the sun? Not only do the pious look directly toward Him, the Sun of Righteousness, but He makes them endure the burning rays and heat of the sun of tribulations. *Romans 5:4 and 8; Revelation 3:19; 1 Peter 1:7 and 4:12; Song of Solomon 1:6.*

If an Eagle renews his strengths, *Psalm 103*, and lives long; Christ has taken up an incorruptible life, and from weakness has become stronger. *1 Corinthians 15; Philippians 3; Isaiah 53:10, 11, etc.*

<margin>Eagle, king of the birds.</margin>
Is the Eagle king and most excellent of all birds? Christ is the most excellent and fairest of all men, *Psalm 45:3*, although being sinless, He is in many parts like us, *Hebrews 2 and 4*; He is the supreme captain above all, *Hebrews 12:1, 2*, the head of all and above all authority and power, *Ephesians 1:20, etc.; Colossians 1:18; Philippians 2:8, 9, 10*, having all power in heaven and on earth, *Matthew 28:18*, a King above all kings, a Lord above all Lords, *Revelation 17 and 19; Psalm 72 and 2; Daniel 7; Luke 1, etc.*

Likewise, one can compare the believers to heaven-bound Eagles in various respects, namely:

Because of the exceptional clarity and sharpness of their eyes, through which they see much further, higher, deeper, clearer, and more distinctly; that is, they know, discern, and acknowledge what is truth and virtue, also comprehending what God is, what divine truth and works are to the holiness of God's name and the salvation of His favored ones. Others are compared to them as blind, *Ephesians 4*, having eyes in front and behind, knowing the past, foreseeing and expecting with hope the future, *Ezekiel 1:10; Revelation 4:8*, eyes of circumspection to walk cautiously, to watch, and to be on their guard; enlightened and cleared eyes. *Ephesians 1:18, 19 and 3:9-18, 19; Isaiah 54:13; 1 John 2:20.*

If the Eagle flies high and only looks down for his prey, flying into and above the clouds, not bothering himself with trifles, as the proverb says, <term>the eagle does not catch flies</term> <note>original Latin: aquila non captat muscas</note>; making his nest in the rock, *Job 39:30, 31, 32, 33*; certainly the believers do not seek the things that are below, except for so much as they need to exist and be able to be active. They fly higher, *Colossians 3:1, 2; Philippians 3:20*, they have a hiding place, *Psalm 91:1; Proverbs 18:10*, a heavenly city. *Hebrews 11:15, 16; Revelation 21.*

Has an Eagle a swift, unwearied, persistent flight? So it is also with the believers, who with far-

# EAGLE
<note>Dutch: Arent</note>

...renewal of powers, becoming stronger and stronger through the practice of grace, *Psalm 48:8, Proverbs 4:18, Psalm 103:3, Isaiah 40:31, 1 Corinthians 15:58, 2 Peter 3:18,* and the full heavenly flight and activity without weariness or fainting shall follow hereafter. *1 Corinthians 15, Philippians 3:21, etc.*

The Eagle is said to renew its strength, appearance, and feathers.

We read of this in *Psalm 103:3,* rhymed by Dathenus <note>Petrus Dathenus (1531–1588) was a Dutch theologian known for his metrical translations of the Psalms</note> thus:

> Who fills your mouth with good and joy,
> And makes you young, and full of youth besides,
> Just as one sees the Eagle become young.

But this is better said by Vondel <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) is considered the most prominent Dutch poet and playwright of the 17th century</note>:

> He grants your heart all that your heart can wish.
> He stretches your youth beyond the limit of men,
> Rebirths you again,
> Not otherwise than the eagle.

Buchanan <note>George Buchanan (1506–1582) was a Scottish scholar who wrote a famous Latin paraphrase of the Psalms</note> has it thus in his Latin Psalms:

> *Who with a generous hand gives you more things* <note>original: "Qui manu larga tibi plura donat..."</note>
> *Than you can ask with your mouth, or hope for in your soul.*
> *He preserves your youth, green in its flower,*
> *In the manner of the eagle.*

Philips Marnix <note>Marnix van St. Aldegonde, a key figure in the Dutch Revolt and author of a Psalm translation</note> has,

> *Who satisfies your mouth with goods,*
> *So that your youth is renewed and unharmed*
> *Just as the youth of an Eagle becomes.*

The prominent and edifying poet Gargon, in his *Instructive Pastime*, has rhymed it thus:

> *Praise, praise the Lord, who has shown you grace,*
> *And mildly satisfies you always with holy food.*
> *And grants you a joyful Eagle's youth.*
> *He does not let His people be oppressed too much.*
> *But can, when it pinches, pluck them from their disasters,*
> *And overload them with prosperity, peace, and joy.*

Eagles do not renew the beak so much as the feathers, *Micah 1:16, Psalm 103:5.* In prose <note>original: "onrym"</note> it is written that the believers, through renewal, shall be like an Eagle in its youth and strength, a new creature, *2 Corinthians 5:17,* a new workmanship in Christ, *Ephesians 2:10,* by the putting off of the old man and the putting on of the new man. *Ephesians 4:22, 23, Isaiah 43:18, 19, Revelation 21:5, Isaiah 41:32.*

If the Eagle guards its nest and young against poison and impurity by a type of pearl <note>likely a reference to the 'eagle-stone' or aetites, believed to protect the nest</note> and a type of maidenhair fern: certainly, every person must purify and cleanse his heart. There all fruit is received, *Matthew 15, 2 Corinthians 7:1, 2.* The wicked must go, the heretics and heresies be gone; the pearl of the pure word must be the antidote. *Matthew 7, 1 Thessalonians 5, Titus 3, 1 Corinthians 5 and 6.*

Is the Eagle near the dead and the torn? Spiritual Eagles are presented thus, both in the Word and the Lord's Supper, *Matthew 24, Job 6,* unless one wishes to take it in another sense, as was said regarding the word CARRION.

One reads in *Revelation 12:14* that two eagle's wings, which were quite large, were given to the woman. I would understand by this that the church, having been for so long under the persecution of the Roman emperors, received two wings or two prominent parts of the empire in order to be fed and to hide there—namely Spain and France, to which England was formerly joined—under Constantius Chlorus, until the church afterwards under Constantine the Great received greater space in the wilderness of Heathendom. Others have other interpretations here which one can investigate.

<margin>The Eagle as a symbol of princes.</margin>
Furthermore, I can well observe that the Eagle is a symbol of great kings and princes, whether of Nebuchadnezzar, Pharaoh, and other kings, *Ezekiel 17:3-12,* proud and exalted ones, *Jeremiah 49,* Obadiah *verse 4,* who are cruel, plundering, and devastating, living according to their will and lust, swiftly flown in. *Hosea 8:1, Habakkuk 1:8, Jeremiah 48:40, Jeremiah 1:15.*

<margin>Coins struck at the inauguration of princes.</margin>
It was customary at the inauguration of emperors, kings, etc., to bring forth coins, showing the prince on one side and an Eagle on the other, or the prince sitting upon the Eagle. See Kipping, *Roman Antiquities, page 637,* and Hofmann, *page 141.*

Indeed, it is recounted that of old among the Persians no one was chosen as king or emperor unless he had an Eagle's nose—that is, a curved and hooked nose, currently still called an imperial nose. From this comes "Eagle nose" and "Eagle" being used for "Emperor." According to the testimony of Plato. *Plutarch* says Pyrrhus of the Epirotes was called the Chief Eagle. See Claude Mignault <note>original: "Claudius Minois"</note> in *Alciato's Emblems, page 202, etc.*

Otherwise, the Eagle can also represent commendable and virtuous intentions and princes who are sharp of sight and fine of judgment, far-seeing, swift to the aid of their subjects, who maintain right and justice without respect of persons, righteousness and faithfulness, tolerating no flatterers or men of injustice in their courts, *Psalm 101:4, 5,* taking care that their sons are not poisoned, poorly raised, or misled, so that they might not degenerate from princely magnanimity and make the saying true: *the children of heroes are a scandal* <note>original Latin: "heroum filii noxae"</note>—that is, *children of the great are often disgraces.*

Because the Eagle chose foul, dead, and stinking carrion for food, it is—as for other reasons—declared unclean. Those who have fellowship with dead works, who hold with foul, rotten, stinking speech, and associate with those who are spiritually dead before God and who stink, and love their company and trade, they are unclean before God. *Ephesians 5, 1 Corinthians 15, 2 Corinthians 6, etc.*

The fierce and harsh "Eagle's gall" of sharp and earnest rebuke, mixed with the "Attic honey" of pure and sweet love, friendliness, and politeness, has brought many to a sight of their evil and blameworthy life, and taught them to distinguish the good from the evil and base deed. *Psalm 141:3, 4, 5.*

The Eagle, as a strong, courageous, and undaunted bird, I find brought forward as a symbol of brave heroes, on whose tomb one may—with right and reason—place not an innocent and anxious dove, but an Eagle. See Alciato's Emblems 33, page 39. SIGNS OF THE BRAVE <note>original Latin: "SIGNA FORTIUM"</note>.

# EAGLE. ARIEL. ARK.
<note>original: "ARENT. ARIEL. ARKE."</note>

### HONORARY EMBLEMS OF THE BRAVE.

> *What cause moves you, bird of Saturn, that you sit* <note>The eagle was often associated with Jupiter/Saturn in classical mythology.</note>
> *High upon the tomb of great Aristomenes?*
> *I declare this: as much as I excel in strength among the birds,*
> *So much does Aristomenes excel among the demigods.*
> *Let timid doves sit upon the burial mounds of the timid;*
> *We eagles give favorable signs to the intrepid.*
<note>original Latin: "Quae te causa movet volucris Saturnia..."</note>

->That is:<-

*Why, O Eagle, are you placed upon the grave*
*Of Aristomenes, that undaunted hero?*
*Just as all feathered creatures must give way to me,*
*So must all who bore arms lower their flags to him.*
*A dove should be shown on the grave of the faint-hearted:*
*But the grave of the brave is crowned by an Eagle.*

See this also presented with variations by Claudius Minois <note>Claude Mignault (1536–1606), a French jurist and commentator on Alciato's Emblems</note> on pages 199-201.
However, as great and strong as the Eagle may be, the beetle <note>The text uses "paartsworm," a term for a beetle or gadfly, in the context of Aesop's fables.</note> coming into battle with him causes him enough harm; this is brought up as a fable to teach that one should not hold a smaller enemy in too low a regard. Alciati's Emblem 168, page 175: *One must also fear the smallest.* <note>original Latin: "A MINIMIS QUOQUE TIMENDUM"</note>

> *The beetle wages war and provokes the enemy of its own accord,*
> *And though inferior in strength, it overcomes through cunning.*
> *For it hides itself secretly and unrecognized in the eagle's feathers,*
> *To seek the hostile nest through the highest stars.*
> *And by piercing the eggs, it prevents the hope of offspring from growing:*
> *In this way, it departs having avenged the disgrace brought upon it.*
<note>original Latin: "Bella gerit scarabaeus & hostem provocat ultro..."</note>

->That is:<-

*The Beetle challenges the Eagle to a fight,*
*Though it seems he can accomplish nothing through his strength.*
*He cunningly hides himself in the bird’s broad feathers,*
*To thus reach the nest through the airy space.*
*There he attacks the eggs, and thus smothers the young.*
*Thus he avenges himself, for the wrongs he suffered from the other.*

Add to this the enlightening explanation of Claudius Minois at the same place.
Let this be enough regarding the Eagle; I shall bring the Sea-eagle to its own letter.

### ARIEL, אריאל, *Ariel*.

<margin>The name ARIEL applied to rational and irrational things.</margin>
**A**S for this name, it is given to persons as well as to living and inanimate things: *Numbers 26:17,* of Ariel the family of the Arielites; *Ezra 8:16,* one of the heads of the people who returned from Babylon.
Again, to the altar of burnt offering, or to its hearth, because of the constant heavenly fire that devoured and consumed the sacrifice: *Ezekiel’s* altar; and in a broader sense, Jerusalem and the temple in which the altar of burnt offering was, to destroy which the Lord would come up, *Isaiah 29:1, 2, 7,* like a strong and devouring lion, Ariel. *Ezekiel 43:15, 16.*
Otherwise, ARIEL signifies a fierce, strong lion, a lion of God, *Numbers 26:17, 1 Chronicles 11:22,* etc., or heroes.

<column-break/>

<margin>Derivation of the word.</margin>
As for the derivation of this word, it is not formed in one and the same way. For some derive it from *Ari-El* <note>Hebrew: ארה אל</note>, he has seen the strong God—the vision or beholding of the strong God. Others from *Har-El* <note>Hebrew: הר אל</note>, the mountain of God—a great, beautiful, high, and eminent mountain, as the Hebrews name eminent things after God. Some from *Ari* <note>Hebrew: ארי</note>, a *lion*, from *plundering, tearing, devouring*, from which *Mari* is also derived.

I judge that the word is composed of *Ari*, a *lion*, and *El*, the *strong God*, meaning a *lion of God*, a great, fierce, and strong lion.
Judah is compared to such a lion, *Genesis 49.* Preeminently, Christ is the Lion of Judah’s tribe, *Revelation 5:5,* who sprang from that tribe as one having authority, and who delivered so many commanders and lawmakers. He who snatched his own as a prey from the claws of the fiery and hellish dragon. *Isaiah 49, Luke 11, 1 Corinthians 15.* Of invincible strength and bravery, himself the strong God, *Isaiah 5* <note>Likely referring to the "Mighty God" in Isaiah 9:6</note>, mighty to deliver, marching in his great power, *Isaiah 63.* Who roared over his enemies and finished them. *Isaiah 11 and 63, Hosea 2, Psalm 45:4, 5, Psalm 110, Hebrews 14:15* <note>Likely a citation error in the original for Hebrews 7:14</note>; who destroyed the city and temple, and made the Ariel and altars with their belongings disappear as defiled, having, as the expected sacrifice, *Psalm 40, Hebrews 10,* offered himself blameless to God through the eternal spirit and the glow of love for God’s honor and the salvation of his people, as a sacrifice of a sweet-smelling savor. *Ephesians 5, Hebrews 5, 7, and 9, Psalm 69.* So that the sacrifices must be laid upon him. *Revelation 5 and 8, Hebrews 13.*

Since which time there are no more gods, lords, guardians, or authoritative princes from Judah. *Psalm 45 and 82, Colossians 2.* He is the only Lord. *1 Corinthians.* He is also the radiance and face of God. *John 1, Hebrews 1, Colossians 1.* He who has seen him has seen the Father. He is that mountain of God, that great mountain, that bedrock and rock <note>term: petra (Greek/Latin for rock)</note>. *Isaiah 2, Daniel 2, Matthew 16,* etc., which grinds the mountains, etc., a mountain exalted above all mountains and hills. *Isaiah 2.*
Who has plucked the fruits of the labor of his soul. *Isaiah 53.* Not having labored in vain. *Isaiah 49.*
But I will express more regarding these and similar matters under the word LION.

### ARK, NOAH’S ARK, תבה, *Kibotos*, *Arca*.
<note>Hebrew: Tebah; Greek: Kibotos; Latin: Arca</note>

<margin>The building of an ark commanded to Noah.</margin>
**O**Ne reads in the holy scroll not only of the divine command given to Noah to build an ark, but also of the inducing causes and reasons.
I shall briefly point out both so that I may more conveniently make the application and transition in what follows. One reads of it in *Genesis 6, 7, and 8.*
In *Genesis 6:1, 2,* one reads that mankind began to multiply on the earth: that daughters were born, that the sons of God looked upon the daughters of men, and some took them as wives.
Since the world had already stood for some time, and Adam’s lineage had multiplied, it is well...

# ARK.

It is well to think that daughters were also born there.

When it says האדם <note>original Hebrew: *ha-adam*; the man/mankind</note> *the man*; and our translators render it *men*, it must be understood in a collective sense; or as referring to the race of the Cainites <note>The descendants of Cain, often contrasted in theology with the "holy" line of Seth</note>, since the holy race had been spoken of previously, not merely as a naked human, simple flesh, without spirit, grace, and life before God.

The fact that daughters were now born to this race cannot well be understood to mean that there were none before, for as Cain's race continued itself, there must have been daughters. It refers then to the great multiplication: and they are mentioned by Moses to provide an opportunity to show how those two different races were mixed together; which was the cause of the great evil and corruption in doctrine, life, and morals, as well as the heavy punishment that followed.

<margin>Sons of God.</margin>
By the sons of God, some understand the *good angels, assigned to protect humanity*. See Josephus *Antiquities, Book 1, Chapter 4,* Philo *Book 1,* Athenagoras, Eusebius, Tertullian, Lactantius.

Others understand *the devils and evil spirits, as Rabbi Eliezer, etc.*

Others, *the sons of the powerful, giants, judges, gods.*

Others, *giants, strong and brave men.*

Finally—the view that pleases me best—*Seth's descendants, sprung from the holy line, in distinction from the race of Cain.*

<margin>Crime of Cain’s sons.</margin>
By taking the daughters of men—that is, of Cain and his sons—as wives upon seeing their beauty, they committed a transgression; not precisely because their eye loved beauty, but because they exalted outward beauty above the inward beauty of virtue.

That they bypassed the holy seed and lineage.

That they sought no holy offspring, and so out of fleshly lust coupled themselves with these, who were flesh.

That they took these with a kind of violence and the impulse of passions (as seen in *Matthew 24:38, 39*), and exposed themselves to seduction by pulling the yoke with the unbelievers (*2 Corinthians 6*).

<margin>Threat of God's judgment.</margin>
Upon this, the Lord declares how He would no longer endure them, and after 120 years would execute His judgment upon them (*verse 3*).

This is found explained in this way, namely: *My spirit shall not always be in man to strive and wrestle with the flesh and corruption; I shall cause him to perish.*

Others interpret it thus: *since they are but flesh, not having the spirit, and unwilling to listen to my spirit in my servants who have the spirit—Enoch, Noah, etc.—so I shall not deliberate long on what I shall do with them, for I shall punish them and destroy them from the earth.*

However, I shall still grant them 120 years for their reflection and improvement in my long-suffering; which one must not take as if this were merely a shortening of the human lifespan to that length and no longer, so that no one would henceforth reach higher years. For neither before nor after the flood did the number of 120 years remain a fixed rule; rather, it must be viewed as a specific period of time after which God’s heavy and righteous judgment was to follow (*Matthew 24:38, 39; 1 Peter 3:19*).

<margin>Various opinions.</margin>
In verse 4, it is said that *there were giants, etc.* Nephilim. Over this, people dispute and differ in thought. For some take it literally to mean very large and uncouth men, far exceeding the common height, who

<column-break/>

would have been among the Cainites; which is not yet so clear. That there were very tall and monstrous men, children of Anak, I will not deny; but that they were found only in Cain's race is doubtful.

That there were Nephilim and sons of Anak, I believe, and that they were named such not just and solely because of their physical stature, but especially because of their disposition, morals, and conduct, as being harsh, forceful, hard, cruel men, who attacked others with violence, making them dance to their pipes and laying down the law for everyone, so that people were terrified of them. These were those who lived in the city of Enoch <note>The text uses "Hanog," a variation of Enoch</note>, attacking the children of Seth, the brood of Lamech, Jabal, and Tubal-cain.

These bred their own kind: and of them Moses says, *these are mighty men, who of old were men of renown.* Those who had sprung from that mixed seed made themselves notorious, feared, and respected, as those who enforced their word and authority with violence and prescribed laws to everyone, without anyone having the heart to utter a peep against them. They brought everything under their power, committing malice, violence, and destruction, as the sequel sufficiently shows.

<margin>Increase of wickedness.</margin>
How wickedness had increased, the Lord shows in *verse 5.* Here is shown the original corruption as the root: the resulting evil in its effects; the magnitude of the corruption, everything being corrupt and evil, which then clearly revealed itself in power as they went grazing without fear; and God showed Himself as judge, that He knew it, with an intention to righteously punish the evil as an example to others.

The sight of this conduct of these pestilential people, which caused Him to testify His displeasure because of the evil, was accompanied by a firm intention to make a change in the state and the face of mankind on earth, and this the Lord makes understood in *verse 6*; for properly speaking, repentance does not befall an unchangeable, perfectly wise, and blessed Being at all. It must be understood <term>θεοπρεπῶς</term> <note>original Greek: "theoprepōs"; meaning: in a manner fitting for God</note> in a manner becoming to God, although spoken <term>ἀνθρωποπαθῶς</term> <note>original Greek: "anthrōpopathōs"; meaning: with human passions or in a human-like way</note> after the manner of men, showing His righteous displeasure, loathing, and intention to make them cease, and to change their state and punish them. Therefore, it is a change not in God's will, but in His work and creation. See the evidence of this in *verse 7,* when He wished to destroy everything from humans to cattle from the face of the earth.

<margin>God's displeasure over sins.</margin>

The irrational creatures had not sinned, but humans had sinned regarding the creatures, and for the sake of sin, the creature was subjected to vanity (*Romans 8*). God showed His highest and extreme displeasure. He is an almighty Lord; He can do with His own according to His pleasure.

However, how this destruction of everything—with the exception of the remnant of cattle and people He would preserve, which was as nothing—must be understood is clear from what was kept in the Ark.

<margin>Noah graced by God.</margin>
Noah (*verse 8*) found grace in the eyes of the Lord. His own He wished to deliver from the all-overflowing violence (*2 Peter 2:9*). The Lord wished to make him a partaker of the promises in the seed of the woman, and to provide a proof of His mercy in the day of His wrath: nor would He let the righteous perish with the unrighteous, as a proof of His justice, truth, and faithfulness.

-># ARK.<-

The holy seed was to be the foundation and support of the earth. From that lineage the seed of the woman <note>A theological reference to Genesis 3:15, traditionally interpreted as a prophecy of a future Savior born of a woman.</note> was to come.

One had to tell of God's wonder-working in the following generation.

The new world was not to be seeded and populated through a new creation, but through the procreation of the old.

<margin>Noah’s lineage.</margin>
Following this is his lineage, *verse 9*, which some understand thus: namely, these are the deeds and encounters of Noah, which Moses describes hereafter. Or, this is his lineage and descent. Or, these are they who derive their birth from him, through whom the new world was to be populated, *Genesis 5:32* and *6:10*: Ham, Japheth, and Shem, of whom more will be dealt with in the following.

<margin>His conduct.</margin>
How Noah lived is noted in *verse 10*: he walked with God. Through the fear of God, he was deterred from evil. He did not walk according to the flesh. He preached repentance, as seen in *2 Peter 2:5-10*, and threatened and exhorted those who, as Peter wrote, were in prison <note>A reference to the "spirits in prison" mentioned in 1 Peter 3:19, often debated by theologians as those who lived before the Flood.</note>. *1 Peter 3:19.* Through his life, teaching, the building of the ark, and his preservation, he condemned the world, *Hebrews 11:6*, etc., and foretold the approaching judgment with soul-torment because of sins.

And certainly, it was quite a great thing not to be swept away by such a powerful and general stream and flood of wickedness. It was a manifest proof of the grace and preserving power of God, so that evil had no hold on him; for *verses 11 and 12: the earth, and all flesh was corrupt, and had corrupted its way.* By which it is shown that those people, abusing the long-suffering and the kindness of God, had by no means come to repentance.

<margin>God’s grace over him.</margin>
That He had used all kinds of means, though in vain, for the preservation of the first world through Enoch, Noah, and others.

That the corruption was so great and general that Noah alone in his generation was found righteous and upright.

That the corruption was not only outward but also inward, and thus shone through, spreading from the heart to all members and deeds, manifesting itself in the heart, in religion, in life, in morals, against luxury, malice, disturbance, and violent and evil dealings.

That, although among men one can and must judge only from the external according to clear evidence; He <note>God</note> knew and searched the internal and external, and therefore, His judgment would be according to truth, in justice.

Since the Lord had purposed in His heart to destroy the wicked world.

Since He had given the world 120 years for deliberation and repentance.

Since He had justified His judgment.

Since He had testified that the righteous Noah had found grace in His eyes, so that He would spare him and deliver him from the general destruction, etc. The Lord then proceeds further: He discloses His counsel, and since He wished to preserve Noah and his family through a means, He points out to him what he shall have to do. He gives him the command for the building of an ark, *verse 14.* The holy scroll mentions two kinds of arks: namely, the Ark of the Covenant and this one of Noah, called <term>התבה</term> (*Hateva* <note>original Hebrew: *ha-tevah*; meaning a box, chest, or basket</note>) and <term>הארון</term> (*Haaron* <note>original Hebrew: *ha-aron*; meaning a chest or coffin, used for the Ark of the Covenant</note>); called by the 70 Translators <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> *Kibotos* (*Kibootos* <note>original Greek: *kibotos*; a wooden chest</note>), a chest or ark, both having the form or

<column-break/>

shape of a chest, and in some respects being similar to one another.

<margin>Shape of the Ark.</margin>
Noah’s ark, however, was an elongated square, without a rudder, rowing bench, oars, mast, bowsprit, main-ropes, sails, or anchors, floating solely upon divine grace and providence. The building material was Gopher wood, over which there is a dispute as to whether it was fir trees, beech trees, pine trees, or cypress wood. For my part, I shall not determine it.

The architectural form is shown thus: *You shall make it with rooms, an ark, chest, or ship of three decks; unless it means something else, with various stalls and partitioned spaces to place and stable the livestock separately.* And so that this structure might be watertight, both from below and from above, the Lord gives this command: *He shall pitch the ark within and without.* With pitch, bitumen <note>original: *Joodenlym*, literally "Jew's glue," a historical term for asphalt or bitumen from the Dead Sea</note>, or other tenacious joining material; it had to be watertight so that it might not perish through the intrusion and seeping in of water.

<margin>Size.</margin>
The height, breadth, depth, and length are determined in *verse 15.* If one calculates it accurately, it is more than a *morgen* of land <note>An old Dutch unit of area, roughly equivalent to two acres; enough land to be plowed in a morning.</note>, in which one can hide quite a lot; namely, when one calculates the length, depth, and breadth together: 300 cubits <note>original: *ellen*; an ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm</note> in length, 50 in breadth, and 30 in height.

What further was to be observed regarding it can be read in *verse 16.*

It is probable that there was more than one light or window in the ark; for if there were three stories in it, one window could not provide these three separate stories with proper light. And therefore, it is nearest to the truth that it must have been a loose window which one could open and close; with a sloping roof or overhang for drainage; and that the other light-givers would have been fixed and glazed windows or skylights.

There was a door for entry on the side; much light in the middle to be able to lead the species of livestock to the stalls and stables, both on the right and left sides.

Of the three stories or decks, the heaviest was at the bottom or in the middle; the lightest at the top; the lowest provided much light <note>perhaps referring to ventilation or access</note> arranged for receiving the animals' waste and uncleanness, etc.

Through these three decks or floorings, with the partitioned stalls, the ark structure gained more stiffness; and the required provisions found a sufficiently suitable place for concealment and storage.

And so that such a command might not seem strange to Noah, the Lord reveals His intention to him in *verse 17*: namely, since the flood of sin overflows mankind, He would stir up an all-overflowing flood of water, through which He would cause everything that breathes air in and out, of livestock and men, to perish.

<margin>God’s covenant with Noah.</margin>
However, it pleased the Lord to establish a covenant with Noah, and to preserve him, his wife, sons, and daughters-in-law by means of that ark; to which end He gives command to bring all kinds of livestock, with their required provisions, into the ark, of which it is noted that an account is given in *Genesis 7.*

The Lord then, having declared that He would spare Noah and his family, gives him command in *verse 2* <note>Referencing Genesis 7:2</note> to take with him into the ark a certain and fixed number of all kinds of livestock and birds: for after seven days He would cause it to rain for forty days consecutively—

-># ARK.<-
