each other, and therefore he must not waste time. *See verses 3, 4, 5.*

Where it appears that clean and unclean animals are spoken of.

This could make us wonder whether Noah had some divine prohibition against abstaining from certain foods?

Or whether "clean" and "unclean" only had regard to the sacrifices. <note>In the biblical context, "clean" animals were those permitted for sacrifice to God or later for consumption under Jewish law.</note>

Or whether they were only distinguished in this way because people at that time, regarding their use, made a voluntary distinction.

Or was it Moses, writing at a later time, who called them such, since by divine command in his time a distinction had to be made between clean and unclean food?

<margin>Number of the animals.</margin>
The exact number of each is given, namely of the clean he had to take 7 and 7; of the unclean, only male and female.

Whether this means 7 pairs and then a seventh, in order to be able to offer it as a sacrifice after the Flood, is a matter of consideration.

*Verse 6.* states that Noah reached 600 years of age when the Flood came.

*Verse 7.* with the beginning of the flood, Noah entered the ark.

*Verse 8, 9.* the various species of animals came to the ark, and Noah received them and brought them to their places.

<margin>Reflection on the animals.</margin>
Here the question arises as to how this took place: namely, whether Noah caught them in time, or did an angel of God lead them there?

Or did they, by God's command, come and fly to the ark themselves, as they once did to Adam when he gave all the animals their names; and how they came from all corners of the world to the ark. For myself, I accept that it happened, but I do not determine *how* it happened. The Lord knows, and nothing is impossible for Him.

*Verse 10, 11 etc.* mention is made of the year, month, and day, both of the Flood and of Noah's entry into the ark: and of the cattle and birds. And then it says, *all the fountains of the great deep were broken up, and the floodgates of heaven were opened.* <note>original: "zyn alle fonteinen des afgronts opgebroken, en de fluizen des hemels geopent."</note>

The earth is founded upon the waters. Under and in the heart of the earth are whirlpools and water-sluices. God pressed the waters, and so they burst forth from the ocean, seas, and earthly pits and pipes, and sprang upward with force. Alongside this, the Lord caused the floodgates of heaven, or the clouds, to tear, burst open, and pour water upon the earth for the duration of 40 days and nights. But before this, when Noah with his family, the cattle, the birds, and the necessary provisions were in the ark, God immediately, by His power or through an angel, etc., shut the door behind Noah, securing it well, *verse 16.*

<margin>Inundation of the world.</margin>
Through the opening of the depths and the continuous downpours, the ark floated, and the water grew in height to 15 cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters, based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note> above the highest mountain. And in doing so, the ark could float without striking anything or becoming grounded. Thus, neither the monstrous animals nor the giants could escape. Thus, everything that remained on the earth had to give up its breath; the more so because the waters stood upon the earth for 150 days.

As for what followed regarding the receding and drying of the earth, Noah's testing by the raven and the dove, his departure, and other things; one may read of them in *Genesis chapter 8.*

<column-break/>

Noah thought of the Lord, likely having thoughts that corresponded for the most part with the harper <note>King David</note>, in his 46th String-song <note>Psalm 46, which speaks of God as a refuge even when the earth changes and waters roar.</note>. The Lord, speaking after the manner of men, also thought of Noah, both to preserve him by means of the ark and to deliver him from it, providing a beautiful opportunity for a proper exit; and to this end, He raised *a wind over the earth*, a passing wind, and the waters became still, etc. Likely a wind that raised and separated the clouds: a drying wind: a pressing wind *Exodus 14.* driving the waters back to their depths, *Psalm 109:6, 7 and 147:18.* So that the waters no longer increased, seeing that the Lord made the water-givers and carriers stand still.

Just as the waters had 150 days for their rising height, so they also had 150 days for their retreat and receding. As the water receded and decreased, the ark rested on Ararat in the 7th month, on the 17th day, when Noah had been in the ark for 5 months, *verse 12, 14.*

It is maintained that Ararat is situated in Armenia, toward the region of Assyria; this is called the Gordyene mountains, crowned as high as heaven: some place it in Phrygia. It is called *Imalum*, also <margin>Ararat.</margin> *Karda*, where some pieces and lumps of it are still found, so we are told; but I do not dispute it.

The mountaintops were seen on the first of the tenth month of the year, when Noah made a test of how the earth was situated after a lapse of 40 days from when the mountaintops could be seen. He then opened the window in the roof, <margin>Raven sent out.</margin> and let out a raven, which flew to and fro until the earth was sufficiently dry.

It is a wild bird that loves the open air, and delights in the hanging mountains, and certainly does not choose the heights.

It seems that Noah did not get the correct report of the condition of the earth from the raven: and therefore, after a lapse of 7 days, he sent out a dove, which, having flown off each time, returned, *verse 8, 9.* After 7 days he sent another, and it returned again with an olive leaf, stalk, or sprout. And as the earth was still soft, and the upper silt not sufficiently dried out, he sent out another yet again.

The dove is a tame bird; she loves her young, is fairly loyal to her coop, and flies high and far.

Now, if Noah entered the ark in the 600th year of his birth, in the 2nd month of the year, on the 17th <margin>Noah’s stay in the ark.</margin> day: and if he departed from it in the six hundred and first year of his age, in the 2nd month, on the 27th day, then he was in the ark for one year and 10 days.

What Noah subsequently did out of gratitude to God; how God established and confirmed His covenant with him, and what more there is, will yet be discussed under the words NOAH and RAINBOW, etc.

I have presented this important, rare, and exemplary case at greater length so that in the following, the soundness of the application to various times, persons, and matters might be more distinctly noted. I shall then step over to the application.

I first hold that just as the ark was the means of Noah's preservation, one can <margin>Application.</margin> <note>The author is moving from the literal history to "typology," where Noah's Ark is seen as a symbol or "type" of Christ or the Church.</note> and should seek and find the counterpart of the ark in Him through whom the church and believers are saved from the...

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of Noah’s Ark, moving from the physical description of its occupants to a detailed "typological" comparison—where the Ark is seen as a historical foreshadowing of Jesus Christ and the Christian church.</meta>

->### ARK.<-

the future wrath, secured against all storms, torrential rains, and soul-destroying accidents, which might rightfully come upon them for their sins.

And to make but a few comparisons from many similarities, behold the following:

<margin>Comparisons.</margin>
a. The ark was not prepared without God’s counsel and command. Noah would not have thought of such a means; it is from the Lord.
That God’s Son has become an ark for his own people for their salvation, and for that purpose took on flesh and blood, is from the Lord, according to His counsel and the eternal covenant of peace, which no angel or man would ever have conceived. *Zechariah VI. 12, 13; Psalm XL; Hebrews X; Psalm CXVIII; Galatians IV. 4, 5.*

b. The ark was built in the most evil of times, when all flesh had corrupted its way. Christ took on the seed of Abraham (*Hebrews II*) and became man in the most wicked of times, when it was proven that the whole world was damnable before God, and everyone turned to his own way. *Isaiah LIII; Romans III and VIII; Psalm XIV.*

c. The ark consisted of the fruit of the earth, yet of firm and durable wood. Christ, although from the earth (*Isaiah XI and LIII*), like his brothers in all things except sin (*Hebrews II and IV*), was nevertheless to see no rot or corruption; though put to death in the flesh, he lives incorruptibly (*1 Corinthians XV; 1 Peter II*) and is thus a tree of life.

<margin>Three levels in the ark.</margin>
d. There was proportion between the length, width, and depth of the ark. These provided three chambers or three levels, in order to hide and preserve everything in its proper place.
Augustine <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD) was an influential early Christian theologian who often looked for mathematical and symbolic meanings in the Bible.</note> thought, regarding this proportion of the ark, that it might well have been built according to the proportions of a human being. For if one wants the ratio of a person's length to their width to match exactly, it is as 50 is to 300, which is 6 to 1. Thus, the width of a human body to its length is 6 to 1, being six times as long as it is wide. Just as 30 to 300 is 10, so too the thickness from the back to the chest against the length from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet is 10 to 1—that is, ten times as long as it is thick. Otherwise, and more preferably, one finds in Christ and his love and work of salvation a height, depth, and breadth (*Ephesians III*); in him there is space to shelter both Jews and Heathens <note>Original: "Heidenen," referring to Gentiles or non-Jewish nations.</note>. In him, as if in three levels, are preserved and enclosed the elect from three distinct times: before the Law, under the Law, and under the Gospel (*Hebrews XIII*). In him are three states: lower, middle, and upper—infants and sucklings, youths, and men and fathers—according to the various measures of grace from the working Spirit of Christ.

<margin>Application to Christ.</margin>
Therefore, some have understood the three kinds of animals symbolically:
a. The birds representing high-flying Christians who lift themselves up through extraordinary power of grace.
b. The cattle representing Christians who are slower of spirit and grace, holding to the first principles.
c. The creeping animals representing the Heathens.
Indeed, those more or less excelling in knowledge, faith, love, and hope have various symbolic representations in Holy Scripture. *Isaiah XI. 6–9; Isaiah XL. 30, 31; etc.*

<column-break/>

e. Clean and unclean cattle were in the ark. It is true that they are all unclean in themselves; however, regarding the judgment of the Jews, the Jews were compared to clean cattle and the Heathens to unclean cattle (*Isaiah XI; Acts X*). These two nations together are in Christ (*Acts X; Romans III and X; Galatians III; Colossians III; Luke II. 14–32; Isaiah XLIX*); every tribe and kind (*Revelation V*), for it is certain and sure that the Heathens also had to be brought in, and that savage peoples are compared to wild, unclean animals. *Psalm XXII. 17; Matthew VII. 6 and XV. 26; Isaiah XI. 65; etc.*
If the Lord intended to symbolize something through the ark, why not also through that which was kept in the ark by His order? He had no need for anything; why should He preserve one more than another?

f. The ark had a light and a window. Those who were in the ark were enlightened; that is Christ himself, and he brings it to pass (*Malachi IV; John I and VIII; Ephesians I and III*) through word and spirit (*Ephesians V; Matthew V; Luke II; Isaiah LXI*).

g. The ark had only one door. Christ is the door (*John X and XIV. 6*); there is no other access to salvation (*Acts IV. 12*) but through him, as if wounded in his flesh (*Hebrews X. 20*).

h. There was a time of seven days and no longer. There are seven periods of the New Testament; after that, there is no more time. *Matthew XXV.*

i. People mocked the building of the ark; they did not think it a necessary or suitable means of salvation, even though many outwardly helped to promote and advance this means.
Even though Pontius Pilate, with his auxiliary bands of Jews and Heathens, was instrumental in completing this "ark" according to God’s counsel (*Acts II and IV*); even though a great Jewish man cried out, "it is expedient that one man should die, so that the whole nation does not perish"; people mocked the Christ and his death on the cross. *1 Corinthians II; Isaiah LIII.*

k. In the ark was sufficient provision for all that had life. In Christ is everything for the spiritual life (*John I; Colossians I; Isaiah LV*): fullness, wine, milk, bread, food, manna. *John VI; Isaiah XXVI; John I.*

l. The ark was entirely in the water, from above and below, in storm and tempest. Christ, throughout his life, and especially at the end of his life, was in the depths, in miry waters, torrential rains, storms, and tempests, stirred up against him from above and below, by God and men. *Psalm II, XLIX, and LXIX; Psalm XVIII and CXVI; Matthew XXVI and XXVII; Psalm XXII; Isaiah LIII.*

m. The pitch sealed the joints. God, and no man, preserved the ark. Christ’s steadfastness was evident in His arm which sustained him (*Isaiah LXIII*); his zeal and love, and the trust in his God, kept his head above water so that he did not sink and was not swallowed by the waves (*Psalm LXIX and XXII. 9; Hebrews V*). Some have understood it such that by the pitch one could understand the Divine nature of Christ, which showed itself outwardly through his teaching, as a reward of works, which supported and preserved the human nature. *Psalm LXIX. 16; Psalm XVI. 10.*

n. Everything that was outside the ark perished, but what was inside was preserved. Outside of Christ there is no salvation; in him is salvation and life.

Where it appears that clean and unclean animals are spoken of.

This might lead us to wonder whether Noah then had some divine prohibition to abstain from certain foods?

Or whether "clean" and "unclean" only had regard to the sacrifices.

Or whether it was simply distinguished in this way because, at that time, people made a voluntary distinction regarding its use.

Or was it Moses, writing in a later time, who called them such, since by divine command in his time a distinction had to be made between clean and unclean food?

<margin>Number of the animals.</margin>
The exact number of each is given: namely, of the clean he was to take 7 and 7; of the unclean, only male and female.

Whether this means 7 pairs and then a seventh, to be offered after the Flood, is a matter of reflection.

*Verse 6* states that Noah reached 600 years when the Flood came.

*Verse 7.* With the beginning of the flood, Noah entered the ark.

*Verses 8, 9.* The different animal species came to the ark, and Noah received them and brought them to their places.

<margin>Reflection on the animals.</margin>
Here the question arises how this worked: namely, whether Noah caught them in time, or whether an angel of God brought them?

Or whether they came and flew to the ark themselves at God's command, as they did formerly to Adam when he gave all animals their names; and how they came from all corners of the world to the ark. For me, I accept that it happened, but how it happened, I do not determine. The Lord knows, and nothing is impossible for Him.

*Verses 10, 11, etc.* mention the year, month, and day, both of the Flood and of Noah's entry into the ark: and speaks of the cattle and birds. And then it says, *all the fountains of the great deep were broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened.*

The earth is established upon the waters. Beneath and in the heart of the earth are whirlpools and water-gates. God pressed the waters, and so they burst forth from the ocean, seas, and earthly whirlpools and pipes, springing upward with force. Alongside this, the Lord caused the floodgates of heaven, or the clouds, to tear, burst open, and pour water upon the earth for the duration of 40 days and nights. But before that, when Noah was in the ark with his own, with the cattle and birds and the necessary provisions, God immediately, by His power or through an angel, etc., shut the door behind Noah, securing it well, *verse 16.*

<margin>Flooding of the world.</margin>
Through the opening of the depths and the continuous downpours, the ark floated, and the water grew in height to 15 cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> above the highest mountain. In this way, the ark could float freely without bumping or running aground. Thus, neither the monstrous animals nor the giants could escape it. So everything that lived on the earth had to give up its breath; all the more because the waters remained on the earth for 150 days.

As for the subsequent receding and drying of the earth, Noah’s experiments with the raven and dove, his exit, and other matters; one can read of them in *Genesis chapter 8.*

<column-break/>

Noah thought of the Lord, likely having corresponding thoughts for the most part with the harper <note>A traditional reference to King David, the author of the Psalms.</note> in his 46th Psalm <note>original: "Snarenlied," literally 'song of strings' or psalm.</note>. The Lord, speaking in human terms, also thought of Noah, both to keep him safe by means of the ark and to release him from it, providing a beautiful opportunity for a suitable exit; and to this end He raised *a wind over the earth, a passing wind, and the waters became still, etc.* Likely a wind that drove away and separated the clouds: a drying wind: a driving wind *Exodus XIV* <note>A reference to the wind that parted the Red Sea.</note>, driving the waters back to their depths, *Psalm CIX. 6, 7* and *CXLVII. 18.* So that the waters no longer increased, seeing that the Lord made the water-givers and carriers stand still.

Just as the waters had 150 days to reach their highest surge, they also had 150 days for their withdrawal and receding. As the water withdrew and receded, the ark rested on Ararat in the 7th month, on the 17th day, when Noah had been in the ark for 5 months, *verses 12, 14.*

It is held that Ararat is located in Armenia, toward the region of Assyria; this is called the Gordyene mountains, crowned as high as heaven: some place it in Phrygia. It is called *Imaus* <note>A name used by ancient geographers for various high mountain ranges in Asia, including the Himalayas or the Hindu Kush.</note>, also <margin>Ararath.</margin> *Kardu*, where pieces and fragments of it are still found, so we are told; but I do not dispute it.

The mountain peaks were seen on the first of the tenth month of the year, when Noah made a test of how the earth was situated after a period of 40 days from when the mountain tops could be seen. He then opened the roof window, <margin>Raven let out.</margin> and let out a raven, which flew to and fro until the earth was sufficiently dry.

It is a wild bird that loves the open air and delights in hanging mountains, and certainly does not choose the high ground.

It seems Noah did not get the proper report on the condition of the earth from the raven: and therefore, after 7 days, he sent out a dove, which, having flown off each time, returned, *verses 8, 9.* After 7 days he sent another, and she returned with an olive leaf, stalk, or sprout. And as the earth was still soft and the top silt not sufficiently dried out, he sent yet another one.

The dove is a tame bird, she loves her young, is fairly faithful to her coop, and flies high and far.

If Noah entered the ark in the 600th year of his life, in the 2nd month of the year, on the 17th <margin>Noah's stay in the ark.</margin> day: and if he left it in the six hundred and eighth <note>Biblical accounts usually cite the 601st year; the text here reads "agtfte" (8th), which may be a printer's error or an alternate calculation.</note> year of his age, in the 2nd month, on the 27th day, then he was in the ark for one year and 10 days.

What Noah subsequently did in gratitude to God; how God established and confirmed His covenant with him, and so forth, will yet be discussed under the words NOAH and REGENBOOG <note>Rainbow</note>, etc.

I have presented this important, rare, and exemplary case at length, so that in what follows one might more distinctly notice the soundness of the application <term>application: the theological transfer of the literal story to a spiritual meaning</term> to various times, persons, and things. I shall then move on to the application.

the coming wrath, secured against all storms, torrential rains, and soul-destroying calamities that might justly befall them because of their sins.

And to make but a few comparisons from many similarities, behold the following:

<margin>Comparisons.</margin>
*a.* The ark was not prepared without God's counsel and command. Noah would not have thought of such a means; it is from the Lord.

That God's Son became an ark for His people for their salvation, and for that purpose took on flesh and blood, is from the Lord, according to His counsel and the eternal covenant of peace <note>The "eternal covenant of peace" refers to the theological concept of the *Pactum Salutis*, an agreement within the Trinity before time began.</note>, which no angel or man would ever have thought of. *Zechariah 6:12, 13; Psalm 40; Hebrews 10; Psalm 118; Galatians 4:4, 5.*

*b.* The ark was built in the most wicked of times, when all flesh had corrupted its way. Christ took on the seed of Abraham, *Hebrews 2*, and became man in the most wicked times, when it was proven that the whole world was damnable before God and everyone turned to his own way. *Isaiah 53; Romans 3 and 8; Psalm 14.*

*c.* The ark consisted of the fruit of the earth, yet was made of firm and durable wood. Christ, though from the earth <note>original: "uit de aarde", referring to his human lineage</note>, *Isaiah 11 and 53*, like His brothers in all things except sin, *Hebrews 2 and 4*, was nevertheless without corruption or decay to be seen; though put to death according to the flesh, He lives incorruptibly, *1 Corinthians 15; 1 Peter 2*, and is thus a tree of life.

*d.* There was proportionality between the length, width, and depth of the ark. They provided three compartments or three levels, to hide and preserve everything in its proper place.

<margin>Three levels in the ark.</margin>
Augustine thought, regarding this proportionality of the ark, that it might well have been built according to the proportions of a human being. For the ratio of a man's length to his width, if one wants it to correspond exactly, is as 50 is to 300, which is 6 to 1. Thus, the width of a man's body to his length is 6 to 1, being six times as long as he is wide. Just as 30 to 300 is 10, so also the thickness from the back to the chest against the length of the body from the head to the soles of the feet is 10 to 1—that is, ten times as long as it is thick. Otherwise, and preferably, one finds in Christ and His love and work of salvation a height, depth, and breadth, *Ephesians 3*; in Him there is a space to shelter both Jews and Gentiles. In Him, as in three levels, the elect of three distinct times are preserved and enclosed: before and under the Law, and under the Gospel, *Hebrews 13*. In Him are three states: lower, middle, and upper—infants and sucklings, youths, and men and fathers, according to the varying measure of the grace of the working Spirit of Christ.

<margin>Application to Christ.</margin>
Furthermore, some have understood the three types of animals symbolically:
*a.* The birds representing high-flying Christians who lift themselves up through extraordinary power of grace.
*b.* The cattle representing Christians of more enduring spirit and power of grace, holding to the first principles.
*c.* The creeping animals, the Gentiles.
Indeed, those more or less excelling in knowledge, faith, love, and hope have various symbolic representations in Holy Scripture. *Isaiah 11:6-9; Isaiah 40:30, 31, etc.*

<column-break/>

*e.* Clean and unclean cattle were in the ark. It is true that all are unclean in themselves; however, as far as the judgment of the Jews is concerned, the Jews were compared to clean cattle and the Gentiles to unclean cattle, *Isaiah 11; Acts 10*. These two nations are together in Christ, *Acts 10; Romans 3 and 10; Galatians 3; Colossians 3; Luke 2:14-32; Isaiah 49*; every tribe and kind, *Revelation 5*. For it is certain and sure that the Gentiles also had to be brought in, and that unruly nations are compared to wild, unclean animals. *Psalm 22:17; Matthew 7:6 and 15:26; Isaiah 11, 65, etc.*

If the Lord intended to represent something through the ark, why not also through that which was kept in the ark by His order? He had no need of anything; why preserve one thing more than another?

*f.* The ark had a light and a window. Those who were in the ark were enlightened; that is Christ Himself, and He brings it to pass, *Malachi 4; John 1 and 8; Ephesians 1 and 3*, through word and spirit, *Ephesians 5; Matthew 5; Luke 2; Isaiah 61.*

*g.* The ark had only one door. Christ is the door, *John 10 and 14:6*; there is no other access to salvation, *Acts 4:12*, through Him as if wounded in His flesh. *Hebrews 10:20.*

*h.* People had seven days of time and no longer. There are seven time-periods of the New Testament; after that, there is no more time. *Matthew 25.*

*i.* People mocked the building of the ark; they did not think it a necessary or suitable means of salvation, even though many externally helped to promote and advance this means.

Even if Pontius Pilate, with his helping bands of Jews and Gentiles, was instrumental in carrying out this "ark" according to God's counsel, *Acts 2 and 4*; even if a great Jewish leader <note>Referring to Caiaphas the High Priest</note> cried out, "it is expedient that one man should die, that the whole nation perish not"; yet they mocked the Christ and His death on the cross. *1 Corinthians 2; Isaiah 53.*

*k.* In the ark, there was sufficient provision for everything that had life. In Christ, there is everything for the spiritual life: *John 1; Colossians 1; Isaiah 55*; fullness, wine, milk, bread, food, manna. *John 6; Isaiah 26; John 1.*

*l.* The ark was entirely in the water, from above and below, in storm and tempest. Christ, throughout His life—and especially at the end of His life—was in the depths, in miry waters, torrential rains, storm, and tempest, stirred up against Him from above and below, by God and men. *Psalm 2 and 49 and 69; Psalm 18 and 116; Matthew 26 and 27; Psalm 22; Isaiah 53.*

*m.* The pitch sealed the joints. God, and no man, preserved the ark. Christ's steadfastness was proven by His arm which saved Him, *Isaiah 63*; His zeal and love, and the trust in His God, kept His head above water so that He did not sink down and was not swallowed by the waves. *Psalm 69 and 22:9; Hebrews 5.* Some have understood it such that by the pitch one could understand the Divine nature of Christ, which manifested itself outwardly through His teaching—as a reward of His works—which supported and preserved His human nature. *Psalm 69:16; Psalm 16:10.*

*n.* Everything outside the ark perished, but whatever was inside was saved. Outside of Christ there is no salvation; in Him is salvation and life.

o. However, few entered; most perished. Many run to destruction, *Matthew 7, Matthew 22,* but few are saved. *Luke 12:32.*

<margin>Comparisons of the Ark with Christ.</margin>
p. After enduring many torrential rains, whistling winds <note>original: "geffinger", an archaic term for the whistling or howling of wind</note>, and storms, the ark was placed upon one of the mountains of Ararat by means of the receding and subsiding waters. Christ’s suffering was His path to highness and rest, *Philippians 2; Psalm 110:7; Luke 24;* He is placed above the highest mountains at the right hand of God in the heavens. *Psalm 68 and 4; Ephesians 4; Acts 1; Hebrews 1.*

Regarding the dove sent out from the ark, returning first without anything, and later towards evening with an olive branch, etc.

<margin>Observations about the Dove of the Ark.</margin>
The thoughts of scholars on this matter vary; some view the dove as a symbol <term>verbeeltmiddel: a representational means or type</term> of the Holy Spirit; others as a symbol of the teachers of peace and reconciliation in the New Testament in a fitting and subordinate sense, since these could not and might not proclaim peace until they were chosen, set apart, made capable, and sent for that purpose. *Isaiah 52:7; Romans 10; 2 Corinthians 5:19, 20.*

For it is difficult for anyone to believe that this happened by chance without God’s special providence, or without Noah’s predetermination, especially when the dove had already found a resting place for the sole of her foot; that one returned without an olive branch, and this specific one returned just toward evening with an olive branch. Since the ark, along with its end and its effects, was entirely symbolic <note>The author uses the concept of "types" or "examples," where Old Testament events foreshadow New Testament truths.</note>, it would be hard to believe that this detail was not also symbolic.

Therefore, it has been judged that it would be neither unseemly nor contrary to the discovery of truth and the outcome of the matter—according to the diversity of the dispensation of the times—if one were to understand it in this way:

That the dove returning without an olive branch provided Noah with the occasion to think and conclude that, because the waters still covered the earth, God’s wrath kindled by sin was certainly not yet entirely stilled in its power, emphasis, and most apparent evidence.

This is a fitting symbol that all the times before the revelation of the true Noah <note>The name "Noah" means "rest" or "comfort"; the author identifies Jesus as the "true Noah" who brings ultimate rest.</note>, the bringer of rest and peace, were times, in a certain respect, of wrath, curse, and the "handwriting of ordinances" <note>A reference to Colossians 2:14, the legal debt of sin.</note>, and in another respect of divine tolerance, because He did not immediately reconcile, nor was His wrath yet stilled. *Romans 3 and 4:15; Ephesians 2:15; Colossians 2:14; 2 Corinthians 3:6-9, etc.*

But the dove returning toward evening with an olive branch could have been a symbol of how—toward the evening upon which the deep night of the destruction of the old heaven and earth followed—God’s wrath having been quenched and stilled in Jesus' blood, the Spirit of Christ was richly poured out, and the ambassadors of peace were sent everywhere to display the olive branch of peace and victory in Jesus' blood. *Psalm 72:1; Isaiah 52:7; Psalm 68:12; 2 Corinthians 5:19, 20, etc.*

<column-break/>

Again, one can view the ark in many respects as a magnificent and sweet symbol of the church on earth, according to its outward ministry.

<margin>The Ark a symbol of the church on earth.</margin>
a. The principal master builder according to divine command was Noah. He also had fellow laborers for that great structure in those evil and corrupt times; although God and Christ are the principal builders and craftsmen of the church. *1 Corinthians 3; Matthew 16:18; Zechariah 6:12.* However, He has fellow laborers for that principal work in evil times, *Psalm 3; Romans 1, 2, and 3; Matthew 3;* specifically the Evangelists and Apostles, and subsequent ministers of the New Testament. *1 Corinthians 3; Ephesians 4.*

b. Made of firm and durable wood, not only such in and through itself, but through the power of the indwelling Spirit, which preserves the believers from destruction and corruption in doctrine, life, and morals; having within themselves an ever-remaining and imperishable seed. *1 Peter 1:5-23.*

c. In the church there is great expansiveness, especially in the New Testament; many animals can be gathered therein, Jews and Gentiles from all sorts of generations: in the Father's house are many mansions, *John 14:2,* where people from all generations can sit at the table. *Matthew 8:11.* So ran the prophecy. *Isaiah 49.* So sounds the word of fulfillment. *Romans 3 and 10; Galatians 3; Colossians 3, etc.*

d. The three stories in one and the same ark, in which the animals were placed distinctly, composing the ark into one great body and structure: these bring to my mind the church in three principal and special times, yet one body. Namely: that of the patriarchs before the Law, that of the Jews under the ministry of the Law, and the highest and last under the Gospel.
There are higher and lower stages of the measure of grace, by which there are infants, children, youths, men, and fathers in Christ in the church, alongside higher and lower states and callings. *1 Corinthians 12 and 14; 1 John 2.*

e. And for all these, one finds in the ark of the church—under the administration of the Word of Grace and the Sacraments—a distinction of nourishment: milk and solid food. *1 Corinthians 3; Hebrews 5.*

f. The light and the window in the ark of the church is specifically Christ, *Malachi 4:2; John 1 and 8;* the Evangelical word of grace, *Psalm 19 and 109; 2 Corinthians 3; Isaiah 54;* and as crystalline glass windows: the Apostles, Evangelists, Pastors, and Teachers, who give light through doctrine and conduct. *Matthew 5.*

g. The only door is Christ, *John 10:9;* the outward beautiful opportunity that the Gospel of...

<margin>The transfer of the Ark to the church.</margin>
*h.* Into this ark come all sorts and kinds of animals, from both Jews and Gentiles. *Acts 10; Isaiah 11.* In the outward church, until it ceases to be the means of preservation on earth, one will find the clean and the unclean, the good and the evil, the chaff and the corn—everything mixed together outwardly until that great separation shall be made. *Matthew 25; Matthew 3.*

*i.* Many help Noah build, yet they are not all the rightful builders; each has his own insight and interest, *1 Corinthians 3; Matthew 25; Matthew 21; Philippians 1:15, 16, 17,* acting as hirelings and "belly-servants" <note>Those who serve their own physical desires or selfish interests rather than God.</note>. *John 10.*

*k.* That which keeps the ark of the church tight and firmly closed is not only the *copher* <term>copher: A Hebrew word for 'pitch' used to seal the ark, which theologians link to 'kaphar' meaning atonement or covering.</term> of Christ’s blood and spirit, but also the unity of the spirit through the bond of peace and love. *Colossians 3:14.*

*l.* The preaching of the Crucified One and the righteousness of faith is mocked and considered useless, just as the building of the ark was. *Isaiah 53; 1 Corinthians 12; Philippians 3:18.*

*m.* For the journey to the ark of the church—to be delivered from the overflowing destruction of sin and from God’s wrath—a delay is given for a time of seven days, or the passage of time in the New Testament. This is the "time of finding," *Isaiah 55:6,* the "today," *Psalm 95; Hebrews 4,* our day, *Luke 19;* after this, the door of grace is shut. *Matthew 25.*

*n.* Although many could enter and were called by the building of the ark, nevertheless few entered and were saved. Many are called, but few are chosen. *Matthew 20 and 22.* Many did not enter and hindered others from entering, as with the Jews. *1 Thessalonians 2.* It is a "little flock," *Luke 12:32.* Those who did not enter were swallowed up by the waters: there is no salvation outside of the outward and inward entrance into the church.

*o.* The Ark, in its tossing upon the waters, under the violence, howling, and swinging of the winds and the waters from above and below, yet under the protection of God so that it was not swallowed up, etc., brings to my mind how the church must wrestle with the waters and winds of persecution and heavy trials. In the world, she has tribulations, *John 14;* entering with much tribulation, and having entered, she is no less beset by storm-winds and downpours, so that the little ship of the church seems ready to sink to the depths, *Matthew 8; Psalm 44; Romans 8;* yet she is preserved and steered by God and His Anointed. *Psalm 46, 56, 124, 83, and 107; Matthew 16:18; Psalm 23, 27, and 3.*

*p.* Was there not sent out from the ark a dove, which brought back an olive branch, when the Lord’s grimness was at its peak and the waters of judgment were receding?
> Surely when God’s vengeance was satisfied through His Son and His anger was stilled—when the acceptable time and day of salvation and deliverance had come, *2 Corinthians 6; Isaiah 49*—one saw the Holy Spirit (who had previously revealed Himself under the symbol of a dove, *Matthew 3*) sent out from the true "bringer of rest," Christ, according to the promise. *Psalm 68; Isaiah 35 and 44; Joel 2; Acts 2; John 7:37, 38, 39; John 14 and 16.* Through the Gospel and the Apostles flying far and wide, this Spirit has everywhere proclaimed peace and reconciliation. *Isaiah 52; 2 Corinthians 5:19, etc.* The raven was a symbol of those who desert the faith and the church without returning, moving with many restless stirrings.

<column-break/>

*q.* Finally, the ark was lifted by the waters above the tops of the mountains and came to rest on Ararat, etc.
> The waters of persecution have carried the church everywhere through the cross and through wrestling upon the swollen waters. -># THE ARK.<-

*All this follows Peter’s proposition in 1 Peter 3:21 <note>The text cites 1 Pet. III. 2, but the context refers to verse 21 regarding baptism.</note>, that it is a corresponding type to our baptism, prefiguring the same thing that is now signified to us as already accomplished in and through baptism. For the ark is a prefiguration of Jesus, the true Ark, in whom alone there is safety against and in the midst of the deluge of God’s wrath. This is like an immersion into the waters of God’s indignation poured out upon Him, attacked by all those streams of Belial <note>A biblical expression for destructive or wicked forces.</note> and the temptations of Satan, as a demonstration of God’s justice for the condemnation and destruction of sin and Satan (Romans 8:3; Hebrews 4 <note>Original text says XIV; Hebrews has only 13 chapters.</note>). This was for the killing of the "old man" <note>A theological term for the unregenerate human nature.</note> as being killed and crucified together in and with Him (Romans 6:6-8). For by His dying to sin, all His people are also reckoned in Him, having died to sin together in and with Him. Through this, it is brought about that sin and its power certainly shall and must be destroyed; and it serves to turn away the curse which He bore, and the divine indignation which He carried out. Just as He also, through His divine power and without failing, overcame all of this in His resurrection, He thereby showed that, having swallowed up death, He had acquired life and immortality for His own. Just as immediately thereafter the Holy Spirit descended—like the antitype <note>The reality represented by a symbol.</note> of that dove with an olive branch of peace—as a proof of the acquired reconciliation and of the love of God (1 John 4:13). Thus, those who are His, having died, been buried, and raised with Him, have passed from death to life, and so become heirs of the acquired righteousness and of the new world.*

*Furthermore, that ark is also a prefiguration of Christ’s church, being built up in Him and in His fellowship, and well-joined together by the unity of the Spirit. It appears thus as that little ship tossing and bobbing in the midst of the waves of the world, yet raised above them by Christ’s power, safe beneath all the downpours of God’s judgments and Satan’s temptations, along with all those who are within it through a true faith—outside of which there is no escape, but only destruction (Joel 2). Its doors stand open for all the elect from among both Jews and Gentiles, gathered therein from the world by the power of the Spirit during the seven days or times of the New Testament, until it finally, once raised above all the violence of the waters in whose midst it still struggles, shall rest upon the heights of the earth (Isaiah 58:1; Revelation 21). After all of this, those who are within shall finally inherit the new heavens above.*

### ARK OF THE COVENANT,
### <note>original: "ארון / Κιβωτὸς, Arca foederis"</note> Ark of the Covenant.

<margin>Maker of the Ark of the Covenant.</margin>
**R**egarding the ARK, called <note>original: "ארון" (Aron)</note> *Aron*, Moses provides us with an account of it in Exodus 25 and 37. It signifies *a.* a coffin (Genesis 50:26), *b.* a treasure chest (2 Kings 12; 2 Chronicles 1:22), *c.* the covenant chest for enclosing the Law.

The maker was the famous artist Bezalel <note>original: "Bezalcel"</note>, who also prepared the most prominent works of art (Exodus 36 and 37).

<margin>Form of the Ark.</margin>
The shape of the Ark was a rectangular square, two and a half cubits long, and one and a half cubits wide and high (Exodus 25). Whether one should calculate the cubit as 5 or 6 hand-palms, I shall not determine; at the very least, it was of a fit size to hold the tables of the Law.

<margin>Made of Shittim wood.</margin>
The wood from which the ark was constructed was firm and durable Shittim wood <note>Acacia wood.</note>.

<column-break/>

The chest or ark was not merely gilded, but overlaid with gold plates; being perhaps the work of such a skillful master so that everything in the Lord’s cabinet would be artistic and magnificent, skillfully and elegantly prepared with pierced foliage-work.

How thick or heavy these plates or gold coverings were, I do not find specified. It was covered with gold plates on the inside and the outside, so that no wood could be seen or recognized, in order to prevent decay.

This ark was wrought all around its upper rectangular edge with a golden crown—a golden border or molding, raised and protruding above the top edge of the ark, perhaps made of translucent foliage or flower-work. Perhaps it had an outer border or rim, like the side parts of the ark, so that the Mercy Seat <note>The lid of the Ark.</note> lowered into it might fit and close tightly.

The covering that covers the top and closes the Ark of Atonement—the *kapporeth* or Mercy Seat—is represented to us as being not only of pure gold, but also provided with four gold rings, which the Cherubim take hold of with their hands, and thus hold the Mercy Seat fast.

<margin>Four rings with their carrying poles.</margin>
Four cast gold rings were attached to the ark, into which the two carrying poles were inserted and were to remain; both were made of Shittim wood and overlaid with gold (1 Kings 8; 1 Chronicles 13 and 15).

As to where the four rings were actually placed: it may be that the ark had a base, or something upon which it stood, and thus was not on the bare ground. But whether they were in this base or actually in the four extreme corners, from the middle of the top and bottom, I shall not argue with anyone; however, the latter seems most probable to me for the sake of the ornament, the balance, etc.

As for the hand-poles or carrying-poles, they were of a proper length, protruding sufficiently at all ends of the ark; they made a protrusion and a bulge outward against the veil (2 Chronicles 5:9).

The Levites, and among these, the children of Kohath <note>original: "Kaaths"</note>, had to carry them on their shoulders. What the Jews tell us in the Talmud, and some Rabbis following them, that they had to carry the ark—not two with their faces toward the ark and two with their backs to the ark, but all with their faces toward the ark—they have not yet readily proven; this being a nearly impossible way to carry it, and without any divine proof, it would be a slow progress full of danger.

<margin>Stone tablets.</margin>
Inside the ark were the stone tablets of Moses, made by divine command (Exodus 30:6; 31:18; 1 Kings 8:9).

Whether the broken stone tablets, the pieces and fragments, were now in the ark, as Rabbi Zakuth and Aben Ezra maintain; and whether the golden jar with the Manna, Moses’ budding staff, and the book of the law were in it; or whether such things were in a small chest separate by the ark; or whether one should take "in" to mean "before," "near," or "beside," as pertaining to the ark, etc.; the last of these pleases me best. However, I do not wish to don armor <note>i.e., to fight or argue fiercely.</note> against anyone over this.

God had indeed proclaimed the Law by word of mouth from Sinai, but had not yet inscribed it on stone tablets and handed them over until after the passing of 40 days, when Moses was to descend from the mountain. These Moses subsequently broke. It is not improbable that the stone tablets in the ark are...

...inserted. *Deuteronomy 10:1-5 and 1 Kings 8:9, etc.*

Regarding the claim that the golden jar containing the manna, along with the rod of Aaron, were placed inside it; *Paul, in Hebrews 9:4,* would seem to say so: though
> a. such a claim does not agree with *Exodus 25*, nor with *Exodus 16:33-34, Numbers 17:10, 1 Kings 8:9, and 2 Chronicles 5.*
> b. the phrase "in which" can be understood as referring to the Holy of Holies <note>The author argues that Paul might have meant these items were in the sacred room, rather than inside the Ark itself.</note>.

This instrument is called *the Ark and the Tables of the Covenant, and of the Testimony.*

I think the reason for this naming consists of the following: 1. Because upon these stone tablets were written the words of the covenant—that the Lord was the God of Israel and their Sanctifier. 2. And it was the sign that Israel was the Lord’s people, who had bound themselves to their God in faith, obedience, love, and good works. 3. To be able to bind and demand this of Israel by that sign in their midst: and by behaving according to its contents, to be able to claim the Lord's promises. *1 Kings 8:9.*

<margin>Shape of the Mercy Seat.</margin>
And as for the Mercy Seat <note>original: "Caphoret," a term derived from the Hebrew word for 'covering' or 'atonement'</note>, it followed the shape of the Ark, being an oblong rectangular piece of pure gold, let in to cover and close the hollow of the Ark within the gold molding.

Searching for the reason for the name Mercy Seat <note>original: "Capphoreth"</note>, I found that the root was thought to be found in how tightly it closed like a pot, just as if it were smeared with pitch; because it was annually sprinkled with the blood of the sacrificial animal, and was the seat and resting place of the Divine Majesty, who allowed Himself to be reconciled and appeased there in the aforementioned manner. And because that Mercy Seat was a figurative means of Christ and the blood of atonement, which He would one day pour out. *Romans 3:24, 25.*

The four rings served to let the Mercy Seat in, or so that the Cherubim could be lifted out together with the Mercy Seat.

<margin>Two Cherubim.</margin>
One reads of two Cherubim as belonging to the Ark and the Mercy Seat, *Exodus 25:18, 19, 20, 21,* both of gold.

Some maintain that they were either cast or beaten out of the same plate and lump of gold by the craftsman’s skill; others that they were formed separately, yet skillfully attached to the Mercy Seat so that it appeared to be a continuous work.

It is not likely that they stood with their feet on the common floor or base of the Ark; but rather that they were placed entirely on top of the Mercy Seat, kneeling with their feet, with their faces bent forward looking toward the Mercy Seat, overshadowing it with raised wings. *Hebrews 9:5.* Regarding their appearance elsewhere, see CHERUBIM.

As for the further outer covering or veil of the Ark, I do not see that it had anything unusual, except during the marches in the field or camp; when the Tabernacle was broken down, the Ark was carried before the army as a guide to designate the resting place: a

<column-break/>

sign of the divine presence and singular favor, for the comfort of His people in their trials and for the terror of their enemies. *Numbers 10.*

<margin>Smoke-vapor.</margin>
Above the Ark was a smoke-vapor or cloud in which the Lord appeared, and from which He gave answers. This presence of the Lord is called *Shekinah* <note>original: "schekina," a Hebrew term for the "dwelling" or "settling" of the divine presence</note>, God's dwelling-place. Regarding this, there might be a dispute as to whether the Lord created that cloud, or if it was the cloud that went before as Israel's camp-leader, or if it was created by the High Priest by lighting incense on the Great Day of Atonement, *Exodus 18 and 40, 2 Chronicles 5:27, Leviticus 16.* However, my intent here is not to trouble anyone by disputing over this.

The proper place for the Ark of the Covenant was in the Holy of Holies, separated by the veil.

Concerning the Ark with the Mercy Seat, its location, and its accessories, various names and expressions are used; so that the Cherubim with their wings are regarded as God's seat and sitting-place, and the Ark with the Mercy Seat—excluding the Ark itself—as the Lord’s footstool, and therefore the place of bowing before God's presence. *Exodus 25, Numbers 7, Psalm 80, 99, and 132, 1 Chronicles 28, 2 Samuel 7, Revelation 11 and 15.*

The Ark is called the ARK OF THE COVENANT and of the Testimony, serving as a testimony of the established and confirmed covenant of the Lord with His people. Within it lay the divine law, in which God testified how He wanted Israel's conduct to be, and on what conditions He would be their God in the most exceptional power. It was a proof of His presence, to whom they had to take refuge in faith and confidence: His peace and Mercy Seat <note>original: "ἱλαστήριον" (hilastērion), the Greek word for the place of propitiation</note>, *Hebrews 9:5,* upon which the Lord, sitting, spoke of forgiveness, reconciliation, and peace to the faithful Israel. *Daniel 9, Romans 3, Exodus 30 and 31, Hebrews 19:4, 5, etc.*

The Ark with the veil is called Israel's honor, *1 Samuel 6 and 4;* God's power, strength, and glory, *2 Chronicles 16, Psalm 78;* His throne for bowing down, *1 Chronicles 28, Psalm 99 and 132;* the speaking-place of His sanctuary, and His footstool, *1 Kings 6, Numbers 7, Psalm 99:5;* the house of the Mercy Seat, *1 Chronicles 28;* His dwelling, *2 Samuel 2;* and so forth.

<margin>Fates of the Ark.</margin>
The fates of the Ark have been various, and its travels and wanderings many; for it wandered a very long time in the wilderness, *Numbers 18, Acts 7;* it was carried by Joshua over the Jordan when the Lord dried it up and paved the way to the inheritance of Abraham, where a stir came in the Valley of Achor and the walls of Jericho tumbled down. Furthermore, it came to Shiloh. *Joshua 18, Judges 20, 1 Samuel 1 and 4.*

It was captured by the Philistines and taken into Dagon's house, where a great wonder was seen regarding Dagon; after which it was sent to Beth-shemesh, where the people of Beth-shemesh were struck by a heavy misfortune. From there it was taken to Kiriath-Jearim. *1 Samuel 7.* From there to Baale-Judah, as far as Nacon's threshing floor. *2 Samuel 6.* When Uzzah thoughtlessly supported it, death struck him as punishment. The house of Obed-Edom was remarkably blessed because of the presence of the Ark, which gave David some incentive to move the Ark to his city, *2 Samuel 6,* where it seems to have been until finally under ki... <note>The catchword 'ko-' indicates the text continues with 'Koning Salomo' (King Solomon) on the following page.</note>

# THE ARK.

King Solomon [gave it] a permanent place in the temple, until the time when, with the destruction of the temple, it met its ultimate disaster.

I believe that the Egyptians and many pagan nations also had their ark, case, or chest, in which they kept and carried around their so-called gods, holy relics, and sanctuaries, as one may observe from the following from

Tibullus, book 1. 8.

> *And the light chest privy to hidden sacred rites.* <note>original: "Et levis occultis conscia cista sacris."</note>

->That is:<-

> *The chest*
> *That carries knowledge of her hidden sanctuaries,*

in which people locked away the holy things to keep them secret.

Catullus,

> *A group zealously celebrated the hidden mysteries in hollow chests, mysteries which the profane desire in vain to hear.* <note>original: "Pars obscura cavis celebrabant orgia cistis, Orgia quæ frustra cupiunt audire profani."</note>

->That is:<-

> *A part zealously celebrates the hidden sanctuary*
> *Of the chests, shielded from the ears of the godless.*

Ovid in the second book of *The Art of Love*:

> *If the mysteries of Venus are not hidden in chests, and the hollow bronze does not ring with frenzied blows; yet they are in common use among us, but in such a way that you would wish them to remain hidden.* <note>original: "Condita si non sunt Veneris mysteria cistis, Nec cava vesanis ictibus æra sonant: Attamen inter nos medio versantur in usu, Sed sic, inter nos ut latuisse velis."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Though Venus’s sanctuary is hidden in no chests,*
> *And the humming metal gives no sound when struck,*
> *Yet the use thereof has not departed from us.*
> *But nevertheless it remains hidden from our sight.*

This was done, I say, to hide them and to inspire reverence.

Apuleius in *The Golden Ass*, book II.

> *A chest was brought back by another, containing secrets, completely concealing the works of magnificent religion.* <note>original: "Referebatur ab alio cista, secretorum capax, penitus celans opera magnifice religionis."</note> that is, *Another brought back a chest, containing the mysteries, but completely hiding the works of the grand religious service.*

Ovid in the second book of the *Metamorphoses*.

> *Pallas had enclosed Erichthonius, a child created without a mother, in a chest woven of Actaean wicker. She had given him to the three daughters born of double-shaped Cecrops to be guarded, but with the command that they should not look upon her secrets.* <note>original: "Pallas Erichthonium, prolem sine matre creatam, Clauserat Actæo textâ de vimine cištâ. Virginibusque tribus gemino de Cecrope natis Servandam dederat, sed enim inconfeſſa quid eſſet, Et legem dederat sua ne secreta viderent."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Minerva shut Erichthonius, a motherless one, quickly*
> *And quietly and secretly, before anyone would suspect it,*
> *In a basket, woven of tough Actaean wicker;*
> *She gave to the three daughters of Cecrops, lord of the land,*
> *This child, born of snake and man, and commanded that the basket* <note>The mythological Erichthonius was often depicted as being half-serpent or guarded by a serpent.</note>
> *Not be opened, but that it be kept quiet and concealed.*

<column-break/>

That the pagans' chest or case consisted of cedar wood and was wonderfully adorned and glittering with gold, gemstones, artistic carvings, wreaths, etc., can be seen from Minucius Felix, Pausanias, Euripides, Oppian, Caelius Rhodiginus, and Spencer.

However, a singular point of importance here is whether the Ark—like most things belonging to the outward religion of the Jews in Israel—was borrowed from the manners and customs of the Egyptians and pagans; or whether the pagans, through both the devil’s inspiration and mimicry, borrowed and adopted theirs from the Jewish people. For my part, I will not stand with Spencer and others for the first opinion, but content myself with that of great and learned men. Bochart in *Phaleg* part 1, book 1, chapter 18; Ritterhuys in his commentary on *Oppian*, book IV: *Thinking upon the whole matter, I judge thus: that the devil, as he is an imitator of all God's work, and an <term>empaiktēs</term> <note>original Greek: ἐμπαίκτης; meaning a mocker or scoffer</note> or mocker, likewise willed to set these chests or arks of his against the Ark of the Covenant of God's people, which was assembled by divine command. And so, in most religions of the deified, an ark or diabolical chest has been in use, such as those of Bacchus, Ceres, Isis, etc.*

Huetius in *Demonstratio*: *For the chests which were in the Greek and Egyptian feasts, especially in the Eleusinian mysteries <note>Ancient initiation ceremonies for the cult of Demeter and Persephone.</note>, in which were enclosed the trifles that Clement of Alexandria enumerates, were likenesses of the Ark of the Covenant, etc.*

And I do not see that what is assumed has been sufficiently proven: namely, that the antiquities and services of the Egyptians are of an older date than those given by God through Moses to Israel, which the great Stillingfleet has proven powerfully enough.

And although these various ceremonies and customs differ greatly from one another, I would rather hold with Dilherrus in *Demonstratio* and others, that the Egyptians and pagans borrowed theirs from the religion and customs of the Hebrews; for I cannot well reconcile how the Lord would not only have adopted the Egyptian idolatries and superstitions, but also ordained them for a service befitting and pleasing to Him; all the more so, because many things and ceremonies in the Egyptian and Israelite religions are directly opposed to one another.

Nor do I yet see how the Egyptian superstitions and idolatries were established by God—adapting Himself to the dullness and fleshly disposition of the Jewish people—as shadows and examples of the Messiah and the divine blessings in him. And this is even more so when I consider that the Jewish state was intended to be not a conformity or joining together, but to create and erect a separation and a "middle wall of partition" between the Jews and pagans. How then could it be consistent with this that the Jews were punished for mimicking the pagans? One may consult the great Witsius in his *Aegyptiaca* and *Miscellanea*.

For my part, I hold with the learned men of sounder mind and judgment in this: that Christ was the end of the law, making it disappear, but also the "body" of all the "shadows," and that one must seek the fulfillment in him, *Romans 10:4, John 1:17, Hebrews 10:1, and 8:5.*

# THE ARK.

5. *Hebrews 4:14-16; Revelation 11:19.* Without this mystery of faith, outward worship would necessarily devolve into a mere ceremony—nothing more than the crudest and most dull practice, which would be unbecoming to God, who is a spirit. It would have been intended merely to prevent Israel from longing for Egypt <note>The author suggests the complex rituals were a concession to keep the Israelites from returning to Egyptian paganism</note> and to preserve a people who were as superstitious, even as idolatrous and physical or "fleshly," as the Heathens themselves were.

One would not proceed on a poor footing if one observed that the God of heaven and earth—being in a singular way the God of the covenant, the king, and the lawgiver of Israel—wished to provide a somewhat visible display and representation of this for the joy, pride, and glory of His particular covenant people. *Exodus 4:22 and 19:5, 6; Psalm 47; Romans 3 and 9.*

1. Kings usually have their palace, throne, cabinet, retinue, and courtly household in the capital city of the kingdom.
The God of Israel, as King within Jerusalem, had the temple as His court and palace; the Holy of Holies was His innermost cabinet, and the Ark and the mercy seat were His throne, etc.

<margin>Comparison of earthly Kings with Christ.</margin>
2. Earthly emperors and kings have a magnificent throne of silver, gold, and ivory, with imagery and ornamental carvings of the sun, moon, humans, angels, and four-footed or winged animals, etc.; this is done to create an image of their wealth, power, glory, and awesomeness.
> Thus, the God and King of Israel, the Lord of Hosts, the King of Kings, the Lord of Lords—to whom the earth and all its fullness belongs (*Psalm 24:50; Haggai 2*)—was certainly entitled to establish such an outward sign of His greatness and awesomeness to depict His wealth and dominion over angels, humans, birds, and four-footed beasts.

3. Eastern emperors and kings rarely or never let their faces be seen openly; they hid their majesty behind a curtain. From behind it, they heard and spoke; those approaching the throne had to cover their faces out of respect, bowing down before the throne, etc. What wonder then, if the Lord wished to depict that awesome, that unbearable presence for man—who is dust, indeed sinful dust—in and around the approach to His throne. So it is, that:
*a.* It has pleased the invisible God, who dwells in an unapproachable light (*John 1; 1 Timothy 6:16*), to cover His majesty as if with a cloud. So I read in *Isaiah 45:15: Truly you are a God who hides himself, the God of Israel, the Savior.* And so I read in the verse by Joannes Six van Chandelier <note>A 17th-century Dutch poet known for his religious verses</note> on *Psalm 104:*

> *You sit clothed, from top to bottom,*
> *With majesty, awe, and glories.*
> *The Lord covers, from the world’s sight,*
> *As with a garment, Himself with visible light.*

And *Psalm 97:2: Clouds and darkness are round about him.* And in verse:

> *Always watchfully on heaven's bow,*
> *A fire-flame before His eye,*
> *And sets His adversaries*
> *Ablaze on every side.*
> *Along with Him, around the world's sphere,*
> *His lightning bolts shot forth,*
> *He enlightened the day,*
> *And the earth, seeing it,*
> *Fell into the distress of trembling.*

*b.* People bowed before it, they turned toward God's throne, and the Cherubim covered their faces. *Psalm 95, 99; Isaiah 6, etc.*

<column-break/>

4. Kings had their imperial and foundational laws engraved and written on durable materials; they had them locked away and carefully preserved as something of the utmost importance; they were kept close to the throne. They wanted to preserve them uncorrupted, and having been holily sworn to, they wanted them strictly followed in all things.
*a.* The God, King, and Lawgiver of Israel had His fundamental law engraved on stone tablets.
*b.* He desired that they should be carefully preserved in the <term>Ark of the Covenant</term> <note>original: "bondkiste"</note>.
*c.* He had provided a copy to Israel.
God’s seat and throne were founded upon grace, truth, and righteousness (*Psalm 89*). The God of the covenant and of oath-taking wished to fulfill His covenant and confirm it as the Faithful One. *Deuteronomy 32; Numbers 23:19; Isaiah 54:56.*
He could also rightfully demand of His people that they fulfill what they had so solemnly sworn.

5. We view the Cherubim as a representation of the Angels, as if carrying God upon their wings, covering their faces, keeping their eyes fixed upon the mercy seat, the Ark, etc. See under CHERUBIM.
*a.* They represent His heavenly servants. *Revelation 5; Daniel 7.*
*b.* They are witnesses to the solemn confirmation of the Lord’s covenant with Israel.
*c.* They are avengers of the violated laws.

6. The Lord, dwelling above the Ark in the cloud, moved ahead of His people so that they would follow Him as their leader in their journey.
*a.* For they were not yet in the land of Immanuel <note>The Promised Land/Palestine</note>, where He wished to establish His seat and throne; He moved ahead to take possession of it, and thus they, as His people, had to follow in His tracks.
*b.* This was so they might be encouraged by the sign of His presence (*Leviticus 26:12; Psalm 46; Jeremiah 8*) and to strike terror and amazement into the enemy. *Numbers 10.*

Now, when we wish to make the spiritual application and transfer to Jesus Christ, we must call to mind the administration of the kingdom of heaven, or the Church of the New Testament, through the glorified King—through whom the Father governs all things and carries out His covenant of grace, and who has been set forth by God the Father as a <term>Kaphoreth</term> <note>Hebrew term for the Mercy Seat or Atonement Cover; used here to link Christ to the Ark's lid</note>. *Romans 3:24, 25; 2 Corinthians 5:19, 20, 21; Hebrews 9; Revelation 11:19; Matthew 28; Ephesians 1; Colossians 1; Hebrews 1; Psalm 110.*

Let me then try to see how I can sequentially transfer what was noted in the Ark of the Covenant to Christ.
Thus comes into consideration the mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ.

# THE ARK.

<margin>Representation of Christ's human nature.</margin>
a. The Ark or chest of the covenant was overlaid with gold on the outside, but that which was covered with gold inside and out was knotty and thorny, yet incorruptible wood <note>original: "onverderffelyk hout," likely referring to Shittim or Acacia wood, known for its durability</note>. 
This is considered to represent the human nature of Christ: a shoot from the stem of Jesse, a root out of dry ground, *Isaiah 4; 11–53;* indeed, in Himself and by comparison, He is "green wood," *Luke 23,* yet He appeared—though without sin—in the likeness of sinful flesh. Because of the debt He took upon Himself as a guarantor, He was placed under the sin and curse of the law. He was fit, like the Ark, to receive the law into His innermost being and to carry out the covenant grounded upon that law. To fulfill this, He was cut off from the land of the living; yet, though He tasted death and destruction, He saw no decay, and was crowned before the Father's face with an immortal and incorruptible life. Various references to this are found in *Hebrews 2:4; Romans 8; Galatians 3:4; Daniel 9; Isaiah 53; Psalm 40; Hebrews 10; Psalm 16; Acts 13; etc.*

<margin>Concerning His Divine nature.</margin>
b. The Ark of the covenant was so thoroughly overlaid and clothed with pure gold, inside and out, that the wood could not be seen.
I have found that through the gold covering the Ark, people have seen a representation of the divine nature of our Jesus, which is more glorious, precious, and incorruptible than gold. Others have noted that the Ark appears here as if in the Holy of Holies—a pattern of heaven—and that many things belonging to the symbolic House of God were made of gold. Since Jesus' divine nature was not first united with His body in heaven, but already at His incarnation, and since gold is not everywhere a symbol for the Godhead, it is my view (and I believe not without foundation) that if we apply the wood of the Ark to Christ's human nature, we can appropriately see the gold as covering and making radiant Jesus’ once-humbled body. Now that He is in the heavenly sanctuary, the gold represents the honor, glory, and incorruptibility with which He has been overlaid, such that His humble form as a servant is no longer seen. *Psalm 8; Philippians 2; 2 Corinthians 3; 1 Corinthians 15; Hebrews 7 and 12.*

<margin>Application.</margin>
c. The golden rings and carrying poles, which were to remain attached so that one would not touch or carry the Ark directly—an act that went poorly for Uzza, *2 Samuel 6; etc.*—shall without doubt be applied to Christ in this manner:
1. When Christ had risen from the dead, having laid aside mortality and corruptibility and having completely overcome the necessity of suffering and death, He was barely willing to be touched; He withdrew Himself, left the world, and ascended to heaven, *John 20:17 <note>The original OCR reads "Job. XX. 17," but this is clearly a reference to John 20:17, where Jesus tells Mary Magdalene, "Do not touch me."</note>,* and He is no longer known according to the flesh. *2 Corinthians 3.*
2. And since the power of His bloody sacrifice must extend through the four corners of the world, *1 Timothy 2; 1 John 2; Revelation 1 and 5,* so must He and His 

<column-break/>

blood be carried to all peoples and nations through active preaching by the spiritual Levites <note>The author compares Christian ministers to the Levites who carried the Ark</note>. *Matthew 28; Romans 10; 1 Corinthians 15:5.*

d. The golden molding around the Ark, into which the mercy seat <term>mercy seat|The gold lid of the Ark, known as the 'verzoendeksel' in Dutch, where atonement was made</term> fit and which covered the inner hollow of the chest, being something magnificent and royal:
This is held to be a symbol of the kingly power which the glorified Jesus possesses—His honor and glory, *Philippians 2; Psalm 110; Hebrews 12; Psalm 8*—to display, demonstrate, and adorn His majesty, right, and glory, so that He may rule as King upon His sacrifice, *Psalm 2,* and bring His enemies into subjection. *Psalm 110; Psalm 45; Philippians 2; 1 Corinthians 15.*

e. The mercy seat of pure gold, covering the space within the Ark, serves to represent the actual or active and suffering obedience of the Church's guarantor, Jesus Christ. This is a price of infinite value and everlasting power, in which and upon which God's gracious purpose and covenant take their stand; it is the seat of peace and is supported by Him, covering the guarantor and His spiritual body in all parts. *Acts 20:28; 1 Corinthians 6:20; 1 Peter 1:18, 19; Daniel 9; Zechariah 3:9; Romans 3:24, 25; Romans 8:1; etc.*

f. Regarding the Cherubim on the mercy seat: See the entry under CHERUBIM.

g. Regarding the law on stone tablets, the manna in the golden jars, and Aaron's rod: see each item under its own name and title.
Thus, we note briefly and in passing that:
a. Christ is the manna, the heavenly bread, the food of the soul, who once descended from heaven, and after His ascension became a hidden manna. *See MANNA. John 5:6; 1 Corinthians 10; Revelation 2:17.*
b. Christ possesses an everlasting priesthood and was confirmed in it through His resurrection, ascension, and His sitting at the Father's right hand. *Psalm 110; Romans 8; Hebrews 4:5–7; 1 John 2.*
c. The law was inside the hollow of the Ark, with the mercy seat above and over it.
1. The law was within Jesus' innermost being. *Psalm 16:40; John 4; Hebrews 10.*
2. Jesus is the fulfiller of the law's demands. *Romans 3:5; Romans 8; John 19; Hebrews 9.*
3. Therefore, the ground for accusation was taken away from the law. *Romans 8.*
4. He is the fulfiller of the promise, writing the law into the hearts of His kingdom's subjects through His Holy Spirit, and thus making the covenant promise stand and hold firm. *Isaiah 54, 56; Jeremiah 31; Ezekiel 36; 2 Corinthians 3.*

h. And regarding the divine Shekinah <term>Shekinah|The visible presence or glory of God dwelling among His people</term>, the cloud, the indwelling, and the answers: see the entry under SHEKINAH. To be brief, it represents:
1. Him in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwells, *John 1; Colossians 2:9,* so that he who sees Him, sees the Father. *John 14.*
2. Him through whom the Father has spoken in these last days. *Deuteronomy 18:15–19; Matthew 3:17 and 18:4, 5; Hebrews.*
3. Him through whom one goes to the Father. *John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2; Hebrews 4:16 and 13.*

<meta>This page continues the typological study of the Ark of the Covenant. ### THE ARK.

<margin>Location of the Ark.</margin>
*i.* When we consider the actual location of the ark, it was in the Holy of Holies, the third and innermost chamber.

Jesus, having fulfilled all the duties of His priesthood insofar as they were to be observed on earth and in His sanctuary, has entered into the heavenly Holy of Holies with His own blood, *Hebrews 9.* Therefore, we must not seek Him on earth, but in heaven. *Colossians 3; Hebrews 4:16; and 10:19.*

*k.* Because in ancient times the true and certain perfecting atonement had not yet been brought, the annual sprinkling had to be repeated, *Hebrews 9.* But Jesus—being both the ark and the mercy seat <note>original: "verzoendekzel," the gold lid of the Ark where atonement was made</note>—having been sprinkled once with His own blood as a more excellent and powerful blood, requires no further sprinkling.

He has granted access to the heavenly realms through His role as guarantor <note>original: "borgtogt," a legal-theological term for Christ's "bail" or "surety" for humanity</note>, and has reconciled and sanctified that which was still on earth, *Hebrews 2:20 and 9:23.* Thus, through His blood and sprinkling, the way to the heavenly sanctuary has been opened in both right and power for free access. *Hebrews 9:8 and 10:19, 20.*

One could easily understand the weakness and imperfection of these symbolic things—which consisted largely of sacrifices, sprinklings, and washings—when one observed: *a.* that it all only affected man externally and regarded man's outward state, but did not penetrate to the inner being, the soul of man. *b.* That many things had to be repeated daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly. *c.* Had the Lord been able and willing to find satisfaction in something external and animalistic, He would undoubtedly not have pressed His people into such difficult and costly persistence and multiplication, but would have been satisfied with a single sacrifice and washing, alongside the confession of guilt and the plea for gracious forgiveness.

But the Lord takes no pleasure in these, *Psalm 40; Hebrews 10;* therefore, His decree was to sketch out the coming redemption of sinners in this symbolic way through a better sacrifice from the Messiah: namely, how He intended to exercise His grace and mercy toward the sinner through the revelation of His holiness and justice in and upon the guarantor.

Because Jehovah, according to that eternal decree, had already admitted many children to glory in former times based on the word and infallible satisfaction of the soul-guarantor, *Job 33; Romans 3; Hebrews 2;* so His decree required that He show, in a certain turning point of time, how this was accomplished by Him while preserving His justice and truth. To this end, in the fullness of time, He sent out His Son and placed Him under the Law. *Galatians 4:4, 5; Isaiah 53; Romans 3;* when the Lord, through the Gospel, publicly presented His sent Son to the world as a reconciliation or mercy seat, it became manifest upon what ground and condition He had previously led many into glory.

Having previously made some comparisons between the Ark of the Covenant and Christ, I shall next show how the church—Jesus' body, gathered from Jews and Gentiles and brought into one total sum with the heavenly beings—being

<column-break/>

partly in heaven and partly still on earth, covered by the righteousness and intercession of the great mediator, can be compared to the Ark of the Covenant in several respects.

*A. The covenant chest consisted of thistly, knotty, and durable wood.*
> The church as a body, consisting of many members, is—as far as the material and animal body is concerned—subject to corruption, misery, and destruction as a "bad tree" because of sin, the pronounced curse, and the hardships of this life. *Genesis 3; Psalm 89; Job 7; Psalm 90; Romans 5:6; Hebrews 9:27.*
> The members of the church are, in their union of faith with Jesus, died, buried, and raised with Christ, *Romans 5:6; Colossians 3; 2 Corinthians 5; Romans 7;* and justified from sins, having died. *Romans 6:7.*
> When the members of the church, as members of Christ, shall be raised and—following the example of the ark—led into the heavenly Holy of Holies, then their bodies shall be clothed with immortality and incorruptibility, in the likeness of Jesus, their head. *1 Corinthians 15; Philippians 3; 1 Thessalonians 4.*

*B. The gold on the outside and inside of that durable wood, making the chest decorative, precious, and shining.*
> Can represent to us how the bodies of the church members—initially prepared on earth for the immediate communion and presence of God—shall be clothed with immortality and incorruptibility, and further covered with gold. For the church above and below is indeed the same body, though some parts and members are more or less glorious and perfect.
> The church and its members are, outwardly and inwardly, as if clothed and covered with things more excellent than gold, namely:
> *a.* With Jesus' imputed righteousness, against which no gold can be weighed, *Acts 20:28; 1 Corinthians 6:20; Isaiah 61:10; 1 Peter 1:18, 19; Revelation 3.*
> *b.* The gold of noble faith, accepting and holding fast to Jesus, with the purchase and ransom price. *Isaiah 27; Job 1:12; 1 Peter 1:7.*
> *c.* The gold of true and heavenly wisdom and knowledge. *Job 28; Psalm 12:19; Proverbs 3; Ephesians 3; 1 John 2.*
> *d.* The gold of beautiful virtues and gifts. *Psalm 45; Isaiah 61; 2 Peter 1:5, 6, 7.*
> *e.* That which is transferred to the heavenly Holy of Holies in the church, taking place in the most excellent power, as bodies are adorned with immortality, lack of want, incorruptibility, and glory. *Psalm 16:17; Daniel 12; 1 Corinthians 15; Philippians 3; etc.*

*C. The golden molding and crown around the covenant chest.*
> Makes me cast my eye upon the wreath and crown of the dignities of the church, beginning on earth, and of those who are made and declared Prophets, Priests, and Kings. *Exodus 19; Psalm 105:232; Isaiah 62; 1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:5.*
> That which, by excellence in the heavenly state, takes place in the church, being united with the crown of victory, of life, of righteousness, and of glory. *2 Timothy 4:7, 8; 1 Peter 1; Revelation 2:3.*
