# A R K E.

<margin>Note on the rings and carrying poles.</margin>D. *Considering the golden rings and carrying poles on the Ark of the Covenant;*
I observe the Ark in two ways. 1. When it was in its wanderings, having as yet no fixed dwelling place. 2. When it was beyond wandering, having obtained a fixed dwelling place.
a. In the heavenly state, the means of bearing the Ark will not be necessary. There, deep rest is found, and the Lord shall be all and in all.
b. But in the struggling and wavering church on earth—since the Lord does not bind Himself to any one land or people, as happened in former times (*Revelation 2:3; Matthew 28; Mark 16; Revelation 5; etc.*)—so:
1. The means of carrying—the Word and Sacraments, the preaching and the ministry—are, through the rational "bearers," most precious and dear.
2. The bearers are those authorized for the Lord’s work and service, like the Children of Kohath <note>The Kohathites were the Levite clan specifically assigned to carry the Ark and sacred vessels during the Exodus</note>, called and sent out. *Psalm 63:12; Isaiah 52:7; Matthew 28; Mark 16; Ephesians 4; 2 Corinthians 5:19, 20; Hebrews 4; etc.*

E. *Inside the Ark, the Lord's Law was found; nearby, in its presence, and as if joined and united with the Ark and the Law, were the golden jar of manna, and Aaron’s staff or rod, etc.*
Applying this spiritually, I observe the Church; *a.* either on earth, yet brought to a single sum with the heavenly, differing only in degrees and stages of appropriation: *b.* or <term>exochēn</term> <note>original Greek: ἐξοχὴν, meaning "by excellence" or "preeminence"</note>, by preeminence, in heaven.
1. Through the fall into sin, the Law in man is broken and almost entirely devastated; there are only a few defective remnants of it left in man. *Romans 1:2.*
2. But the Lord writes upon the hearts of His people anew by the finger of His Spirit, making new tablets out of hearts of flesh. *Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 36; 2 Corinthians 3.*
3. They hide and lock up the Lord’s law, keeping it in their hearts with purpose and delight, in order to speak and walk according to it. *Deuteronomy 6:6; Psalm 109:11; Jeremiah 15; Psalm 1; Romans 7.*
4. The knowledge of the Lord’s Law and Word is found abundantly among them. *Isaiah 54; Psalm 109; 2 Corinthians 3; Ephesians 3; 1 John 2:20.*

<margin>The manna.</margin>To me, the manna is a symbol of the Son of God, the bread and the food of the soul, descended from and taken up into heaven; it is in various respects the manna and the "hidden manna." *Isaiah 5:6; 1 Corinthians 10; Revelation 2:17.* See the entry for MANNA. That is, it is constantly with and in the church, through the Word and Sacraments. The church also enjoys the fruit and power of His sacrifice and intercession—both below and above in heaven—through communion and proximity to Him whose priesthood never ends or passes to others. At the same time, this symbolizes the indisputable and eternal right, and the everlasting dignity, found within the church in communion with the High Priest Jesus, to hold and practice the royal priesthood. *Isaiah 62; 1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:5.*

F. *That the Covenant-chest and the stone tablets of the Law are called the Ark and the Law of the Covenant—I consider this to be the reason:*
Since the Lord had promised in the Covenant of Grace that He would write His law into the hearts of those in the covenant (*Jeremiah 31; Ezekiel 36; 2 Corinthians 3*), from which it would appear that He was their God and they were His people, so the aforementioned writing of the law in the heart is an irrefutable proof and hallmark that He has betrothed that people and has accepted them into His covenant of grace, righteousness, peace, and faithfulness. *Isaiah 54; Hosea 2:18, 19.* And such produces in them the "answer of a good conscience" <note>A reference to 1 Peter 3:21 regarding baptism and internal faith</note> in and through Christ. *1 Peter 3.*

<column-break/>

F. *The Mercy Seat, covering the Covenant-chest and the Law within: and the Lord resting above upon the Mercy Seat, etc.* This can represent, as noted above and already stated, the suffering and active righteousness of Jesus the "Soul-Guarantor." As the substitute surety, He has fulfilled the demands and justice in all parts, and has satisfied God the Judge. He brings it about that no accusation can be grounded, attached, or take hold against His own, who are perfectly covered by His righteousness and intercession against all accusations, wrath, and curses. *Isaiah 40:49; Job 33; Psalm 32; Isaiah 61:10; Daniel 9:24; Zechariah 3; Romans 3:25, 26; Romans 5:1, 2, 3, 8; Galatians 3:13; Galatians 4:4, 5; etc.*

H. *Regarding the golden Cherubim upon the Mercy Seat, their form and services, etc.* Regarding the spiritual application, whether to the angels, *b.* believers, *c.* or to the shepherds and teachers, one may look under the entry CHERUBIM.

I. *Regarding the divine Shekhinah, the cloud, the indwelling, the glory, the speaking, etc.* One should read what is noted under the entry SHEKHINAH.

K. *Regarding the annual sprinkling of the Ark with the blood of atonement, one may see what is said under* SPRINKLING: as well as what was said earlier in this piece. At the very least, it serves to depict the communion and the power of the church's communion in Jesus’ blood, through *a.* the answer of reconciliation (*2 Corinthians 5:19, 20*); *b.* through faith (*Acts 15*); *c.* through the Holy Spirit (*1 Corinthians 6:11; Psalm 51; Jeremiah 32; Ezekiel 36; 1 John 1:7; Hebrews 8, 9, 10*); *d.* and one's own diligence (*2 Corinthians 7:1, 2; Hebrews 12; Philippians 3; 1 Peter 1; Revelation 22*).

L. *The dwelling and resting place of the Ark was within Jerusalem, the upper city in the Holy of Holies.*
The true Solomon, Jesus, has gone before to prepare a place for the church. She is already in it, and seated with her Head (*Ephesians 2*). There she has her citizenship and conversation. *Philippians 3:20.* The heavenly and the earthly are made into one citizenship and one sum through Jesus. They are the "saints of the high places" (*Daniel 7*). Their names are inscribed in the citizen-roll of the inhabitants of heaven. *Luke 10:20.* Their hearts are already above. *1 Corinthians 5:1, 2; Colossians 3; Philippians 1; Psalm 84; etc.* Their final resting and most blessed dwelling place is above in the heavens. *Matthew 25; 2 Corinthians 5; Philippians 3; 1 Thessalonians 4; Hebrews 4:5.*

# ARK. ARM.

<margin>The Church compared to the Ark.</margin>Upon this unveiling of the innermost sanctuary, we have seen the Ark as a symbol of Christ. Now, I shall compare the Church of the New Testament—composed of Jews and Gentiles made into one body, covered and overshadowed by the *Caphoreth* <note>The Mercy Seat or the lid of the Ark</note> (*Hebrews 9*)—with the Ark of the Old Testament, and demonstrate the points of agreement I can identify between them. I begin the work thus:

Regarding the fates, struggles, and falls of the Ark: it is clear that it struggled and wandered for a very long time in the desert, particularly in the regions of Arabia. This brings to mind the shared struggles of the Jewish people before they reached the inheritance of Canaan, where even at the end, they did not find themselves in total peace.

I see at the same time how my Savior wandered for thirty-three years in a desert and wilderness of Judaism, teaching and performing miracles, not without opposition, pressure, and reproach, having no fixed resting place to lay His head. (*Matthew 8*)

I also know that the early Christian Church, because of the persecutions incited by Jews and heathens, was forced to wander.

Joshua, with his ark-bearers, brought the Ark through and across the Jordan; the Lord brought it through the same, while the drying of the waters paved a way for the passage.

The Apostolic Christian Church—under the chief guidance and leadership of the true Savior Joshua, namely Christ—moved toward the inheritance of the Gentiles through the Apostles who carried the "holy things." They carried the Ark of His Church, paving a level path through truth and righteousness, the stability of His throne (*Psalms 68, 85, and 89*). They caused the Jewish ecclesiastical and civil state to dry up like a Jordan through internal division, taxation, robbery, plundering, and final destruction. This was followed by the initial Jewish and Pagan rages and persecutions, like an overflowing Jordan-pool under Diocletian <note>A Roman Emperor known for the last and most severe persecution of Christians</note>, which nevertheless dried up and became crossable.

But hardly had that storm been overcome when the dragon, judging himself harmed and weakened by the Ark’s proximity, exerted all his power and strength. He pressed upon the Church through his servants (*Revelation 12*). Yet the Church, though troubled in the "Valley of Achor," received a "door of hope" under Constantius Chlorus and Constantine the Great, who gave her two wings and his empire as an inheritance and a place of refuge. However, the Church had barely 328 or 350 years of interval before something dangerous was seen to befall her.

The Ark fell into the hands of the Philistines while Israel, without having sought counsel from the Lord’s mouth, carried it into their camp against the enemy, leaning more on the Ark than on the Lord. (*1 Samuel 5 and 6; Psalm 78:61*)

I know well that the Jews, similar to the Philistines in many respects, captured Christ. He most strongly plagued both those who took Him captive and those who held Him, mocking them and bringing them to death; He subdued and triumphed over spiritual and physical enemies in His death and resurrection. (*Psalm 68; Colossians 2; Hebrews 2:14; 1 John 3:8; Genesis 3:15; 1 Corinthians 15*)

I also know that when the Church, like Israel, became unbelieving, deaf, hardened, and evil (*Isaiah 6 and 53:1; Acts 13*), she was carried away to the Gentiles. But it is also noteworthy that when Christianity became ungrateful, careless, and falsely confident, it was barely free for 328 or 350 years before it fell into the power of the "Philistine"—the Antichrist—in whose "House of Dagon" <note>Dagon was the god of the Philistines; here, the author uses it as a metaphor for the corruption of the Church</note> it was miserably mocked and tormented. It is true, he sought to pair his Dagon with Christ, placing light and darkness, righteousness and unrighteousness side by side (*2 Thessalonians 2*). This is, however, incompatible (*2 Corinthians 6*); just as Dagon fell prostrate before the Ark, so Belial could not hold his ground against Christ, nor unrighteousness against righteousness. God plagued them (*Revelation 16*); she fell, and they were forced—though not out of love for the truth, but with a varnished appearance—to let the Church go out, and to behave themselves with feigned submission. (*Revelation 14 and 3:9; Psalm 66:3, etc.*)

After this, the reckless curiosity and the improper conduct of the Beth-shemites and that of Uzzah received a deadly blow. One was not permitted to touch the Ark, nor to look into it; it was not to be carried on a wagon, but borne by the consecrated Levites. <note>References to 1 Samuel 6 and 2 Samuel 6, where individuals were punished for treating the Ark with insufficient reverence</note>

How restricted it was to come near; how the old ministry was filled with the fear of death (*Hebrews 2*). How heavy it shall fall upon those who irreverently and without right approach the holy things (*1 Corinthians 10 and 11*). Striking hands against Jesus, or the sanctuary, turns out badly for those who are not entitled to do so (*Psalm 2, 82, and 105; Acts 13*). "Saul, Saul," etc. One must approach the holy with fear, humility, and reverence. (*Psalm 2; Isaiah 6; Revelation 4*)

And to conclude: the Ark of Shiloh did not return to Shiloh, until it remained fixed under Solomon in the temple until the destruction of the city and temple. After Jesus was baptized in the Jordan, He had no rest; after He was in the hands of the Philistine-like Jews and was delivered from them, He was not in the [earthly] temple, but was taken up into the heavenly temple, into the Holy of Holies. There He remains until the final destruction and the restoration of all things (*Acts 1 and 3; Revelation 11*). Thus, the Church shall have no rest on earth until she rests in the Holy of Holies above.

### ARM, <note>original Hebrew: זרוע (zeroa)</note>, <note>original Greek: βραχίων (brachion)</note>, <note>original Latin: Brachium</note>. Pertaining to men and attributed to God.

<margin>The Arm taken symbolically.</margin>What part the ARM is to the human body, and of what strength, activity, and performance it is capable once positioned, is known through experience; therefore, it is not necessary for me to expand upon it at length.

However, the point is this: the word ARM, while properly belonging to the human body—which a person stretches out, bares, lets hang, or lifts up, etc.—is used improperly and symbolically in Holy Scripture and by secular writers.

The arm is thus a symbol of power, strength, authority, force, and dominion. Its meaning varies depending on the context of the expression: whether it is for someone's good or for their ill. Regarding man, his state, authority, power, elevation, lowering, help, or breaking, we find these borrowed and figurative expressions, namely: *to bare one's arm, one's arm...*

It then introduces the "Arm" as a symbol of power and authority in both human and divine contexts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical exploration of biblical symbols, moving from the conclusion of "Ark" on the previous page to a detailed entry on "Arm" as a representation of power, action, and the divine will.</meta>

# ARM.

<margin>Idioms explained.</margin>
To *stretch out* or *raise* the arm: though this is applied to God in *Isaiah 52:10, Psalm 136:12*, and elsewhere, it is nevertheless borrowed from the customs of men. Specifically, it refers to those who entered the wrestling ring or the battlefield against their enemies, stripping themselves as much as possible of all burdens and the hindrance of clothing, so as to be able to wield their weapons and attack their enemy without obstruction. For this purpose, wrestlers cast off the weight of their garments, as we are taught by Philostratus in *The Life of Apollonius, book vi*, Tacitus in *Annals, book xiv*, Chrysostom in *Homily 3 to the People of Antioch*, and Lydius in *Agonisticon*, etc.

Thus, men let their clothes hang upon their backs, sometimes tying them fast, in order to move the arm and hands with greater ease and freedom.

Plautus in his *The Braggart Soldier*, Act 4, Scene 4:

> ->*With your arm bared to the breast,* <note>original Latin: "Expapillato brachio"</note><-
> ->*Girded up, and pretend as if you were a ship's pilot.* <note>original Latin: "Praecinctus, atque affimulato quafi gubernator fies."</note><-

->That is:<-

> *You must bare your arm and gird yourself:*
> *And act as if you had become a sailor.*

Statius, *Thebaid, book i:*

> ->*Soon as their anger swelled enough from words thrown back and forth,* <note>original Latin: "Mox ut jactis fermonibus ira, / Intumuêre fatis"</note><-
> ->*then indeed both rose up and bared their shoulders.* <note>original Latin: "tum vero erectus uterque / Exertare humeros."</note><-

->That is:<-

> *As soon as wrath sets them going with words,*
> *They both rise and show their arms naked.*

And Silius Italicus, *book xii:*

> ->*She shall shake torches dipped in the whirlpool of Phlegethon,* <note>original Latin: "Accenfas quatiet Phlegetontis gurgite taedas." Phlegethon is a river of fire in the underworld.</note><-
> ->*Bare-armed, now ready for the greedy fight.* <note>original Latin: "Exertos avidae pugnae nudata lacertos."</note><-

->That is:<-

> *She shall swing the torch dipped in hellish water,*
> *And show, now ready for the struggle, her bare arms.*

In contrast to this stands *folding* the arm or tucking it into one's bosom, which was considered the work of cowards or lazy people, as alluded to in *Psalm 74:11 and Proverbs 19:24*. It is more heroic to "pluck the arm out of the bosom."

To *break* someone's arm, or to "eat the flesh of the arm" (*Job 31; Psalm 37:17; Jeremiah 48:25; Isaiah 9:10*), is as much as to say: to diminish someone in whatever way possible—whether through weapons, riots, exhaustion, mutual strife, etc.—and to take away their authority or power; to weaken and subdue their lineage and followers (*Psalm 10:15*). The same is meant by *cutting off* someone's arm, which signifies weakening and subduing someone to such an extent that they have no power to resist or offer rebellion (*1 Samuel 2:31*), whether by themselves or through their army and followers (*Daniel 11:15, 22, 26, 30; Ezekiel 30:24, 25*). In this way, an army is sometimes understood as having two "wings," like two extended arms.

The *fleshly arm* (*2 Chronicles 32:8*) stands for everything that man devises and puts into effect,

<column-break/>

by himself, or through and with others for his help, in which he firmly trusts and relies (*Jeremiah 17*), while turning away from God's grace and help.

*To be an arm to someone*, or to *strengthen someone's arm* (*Psalm 83:9; Isaiah 33:2; Ezekiel 30:24, 25*), must be understood as supporting, strengthening, showing help in counsel and deed, and shielding or protecting them.

As for what more specifically concerns the "arm" when applied to God, along with the idioms relating to it: one knows that God—an infinite and simple spirit—possesses no human limbs. Therefore, such terms must be understood very improperly, through imagination, and <term>Θεοπρεπῶς</term> <gloss>Gode betamelyk; in a manner becoming to God</gloss>. Consequently, by "God's arm" we must understand the all-sufficiency of God's will, through which everything exists irresistibly and is exactly as He wills it to be.

And so, the holy scrolls frequently speak of God’s *arm, mighty arm, uplifted arm, outstretched arm, eternal arm*, and the greatness of His arm—which descends, strikes, and rules, through which He delivers and carries out, subdues, and crushes, and which is seen and bared (*Exodus 15:16; Deuteronomy 33:27; Psalm 44:4, 71:18, 89:14, and 98:1; Isaiah 30:30 and 52:10; Deuteronomy 4 and 5; Exodus 6; Psalm 136; Jeremiah 48; Isaiah 40*).

These expressions, according to their distinct natures, signify the various effects of the all-sufficient, infinite, and eternal God and His will. When He, through His almighty command, acts outside of Himself for the good or ill of any person or nation—so that one can intellectually and clearly perceive it was not caused by man, as it exceeds human wisdom and limited power—then such a thing is testified of God. It is described in human terms, using the same idioms and images we use to depict human actions through the arm, power, governance, following, authority, and so forth.

And because the Lord does not always work immediately <note>directly</note> but also mediately <note>through means</note>, causing rare and unusual things to appear which must be attributed to a supreme cause in their execution (since the effects exceed purely natural and subordinate causes), I have noticed that scholars have interpreted the passage in *Isaiah 53:1*—"Who has believed our preaching, and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?"—in various ways. Some are of the opinion that the "preaching" and the "Lord's arm" are one and the same in this case, the latter being <term>ἐξηγητικὸν</term> <gloss>explanatory</gloss> of the former. This is because when God joins His power with preaching, it becomes a powerful means of salvation (*Romans 1:16*): the strong scepter, the Messiah's arrow and bow (*Psalm 45:4-6 and 110:2*), and spiritual weapons, mighty in God (*2 Corinthians 10:4-5; Hebrews 4:11-12*), though hidden to many (*2 Corinthians 4:3-4*).

Therefore, the Messiah and His ambassadors of the cross lament the fruitlessness of their labor among the fleshly, blind, and hardened Jews (*John 12:38*).

Others prefer to steer this toward both God and Christ: namely, that the Jews did not at all notice Christ's birth from a virgin as a work of God...

# ARM.

God's wonder-work: *Isaiah 7:14* and *9:5; Jeremiah 31:22; Matthew 1:23; Luke 1:35; 1 Timothy 3:16.* Christ’s miracles, and those of the Apostles in his name; the Lord’s wonders at Christ’s death and resurrection, seen in the sun, the earth, the graves, those who rose, the veil of the temple, etc. Yet some understand "the arm of the Lord" to mean the Messiah, of whom Isaiah treats throughout that entire chapter <note>Isaiah 53</note>, being of one essence with the Father, through whom the Father created all things, and who carries and governs all: *John 1; Colossians 1; Hebrews 1; Revelation 4.* He is especially seen in the work of the re-creation and the redemption of the sinner, through whom the Father executes and rules everything, defeats His enemies, supports His "seed" <note>His followers or offspring</note>, and provides victory over their enemies: *1 Corinthians 15:55, 56, 57; Romans 7:25,* etc. This is how Augustine, Bede, Rupert, and others have understood it; and not without elegance or foundation, since the previous expressions regarding Him—as Israel’s Lord, head, king, lawgiver, protector, etc.—fit and suit Him exceptionally well.

One also reads in the sacred pages of *taking into one's arms, embracing, carrying, and gathering: Genesis 33:4; 2 Kings 4:16; Isaiah 40:11 and 49:22; Hosea 11:3; Mark 9:36; Luke 2:28.* However one considers or takes it, the imagery is borrowed from loving people, tender-hearted mothers, and nurses; from faithful and discerning shepherds. Therefore, it portrays great and tender care, love, close guarding, and preservation. When this is applied to God and His Son, the "Angel of the Covenant" <note>A term for a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ</note>, Israel’s guide and guardian, it becomes a powerful metaphor for His close supervision, kind embrace, steadfast and supportive preservation, gentle caressing, soft treatment, and a proof of His loving knowledge and recognition of His own property.

And so says Jerome, cited by Johann Heinrich Ursinus on Hosea <note>Hosea 11:3</note>: *I, who was a father, became a nurse, and I carried my little child in my bosom or arms, so that it might not be harmed in the wilderness; and so that they might not be terrified or become skittish because of the great heat or the darkness; by day I was a cloud, by night a column of fire: so that I might enlighten with my light and heal those whom I had protected. Even when they had sinned and made themselves a calf’s head, I allowed room for repentance, etc.*

### ARM, ARMOEDE <note>Poor, Poverty</note>, דלל / אביון <note>Hebrew: *dalal* (to be low/impoverished) / *ebyon* (needy)</note>, *πένης, πτωχός, πενία, πτωχεία, ἔνδεια, ἀπορία* <note>Greek: types of poverty ranging from working poor to complete destitution and lack of resources</note>, Pauper, egenus, paupertas, egestas <note>Latin: Poor, needy, poverty, want</note>.

**T**o be **P**OOR, and to suffer POVERTY and want, signifies a definite absence of the necessary things of this life which a person needs for their existence, residence, and activity, such as food, drink, and clothing <note>literally "cover"</note>.

<margin>Levels of poverty.</margin>
To be POOR and in POVERTY allows for various degrees; the extreme is when one lacks everything and must receive food and clothing from others. Otherwise, one is called poor according to external status if they barely, and in a meager and restricted manner, obtain what is necessary through the labor of their hands or other lawful means.

<margin>Causes of poverty.</margin>
To be poor, or to fall into poverty, has quite many and varied causes: being born to poor parents, the plundering of one's goods, a natural inability to earn one's own bread, fire, flood, disasters at sea, failing trade, laziness, squandering, and such things.

The rich and the poor meet one another, *Proverbs 22*; the Lord makes rich, and He makes poor. *1 Samuel 2.*

To be poor and to suffer poverty is a heavy burden. Where poverty is, everything is lacking. Menander used to say:

> *Οὐδὲν πενίας βαρύτερον Φόρτιον.* <note>original Greek: Nothing is a heavier burden than poverty.</note>

->That is:<-

*No heavier burden than poverty is found.*

It is indeed true that it would not be useful for human society if everyone were equally wealthy. Mercy and service must take place among one another; and no one would stoop to the humblest services or lowly—and yet highly necessary—arts and endeavors.

Experience, the Lord’s lament, and the description of the state of some teach that many are kept down, crushed, worn out, and emaciated—דלל דלים <note>Hebrew: *dalal dalim*, "to languish" or "the poorest of the poor"</note>—through stinginess, greed, oppression, exploitation, and other circumstances. *Psalm 41:2; Job 34:19; Psalm 113:7; Psalm 72; Proverbs 22; Isaiah 10; Ezekiel 16; Amos 4, 5, and 8; James 2; etc.*

That poverty prompts one to schemes and the invention of both skills and devices is clear, from which comes the saying: "poverty seeks cunning" <note>Latin: *paupertas quaeritat artes*</note>, which can be interpreted and turn out both for good and for ill.

*Horace, Book II, to Florus:*

> *Et laris, & fundi paupertas impulit audax*
> *Ut versus facerem.* <note>original Latin: Poverty, bold in its need, drove me—lacking home and farm—to write verses.</note>

->That is:<-

*Because I was not rich in house or farm, to making verses*
*I was driven by necessity in many matters.*

*Plautus in Stichus:*

> *Jam illa omnes artes perdocet, ubi quem attigit.* <note>original Latin: Now she (poverty) thoroughly teaches all arts wherever she touches someone.</note>

->That is:<-

*When she visits someone, she teaches him all the arts.*

*Martial, Epigram II:*

> *— ô Quantum cogit egestas!* <note>original Latin: Oh, how much want compels!</note>

->That is:<-

*To what does poverty not drive us!*

People considered themselves unhappy because of poverty, all the more because the poor are little respected and seldom uproot themselves from their lowly state; at least, so spoke the Heathens.

*Juvenal in his third Satire:*

> *Nil habet infelix paupertas durius in se,*
> *Than that it makes men ridiculous.* <note>original Latin: *Quam quod ridiculos homines facit.*</note>

These expressions, according to their different natures, signify the various effects of the all-sufficient, infinite, and eternal God and His will. When He exercises His almighty command—whether for the good or ill of any person or people—such that one can clearly perceive it was not caused by man (surpassing human wisdom and limited power), it is attributed to God. It is described in human terms using idioms and images that we use in depicting human actions through the arm, power, governance, following, and authority.

And since the Lord does not always work immediately <note>directly</note> but also mediately <note>through means</note>, causing rare and unusual things to appear which must be attributed to a supreme cause, as the effects surpass purely natural and subordinate causes, I have observed that scholars have interpreted the passage in *Isaiah 53:1 ("Who has believed our report? # POVERTY.

->That is:<-

*Wretched poverty has nothing harder to lament,*
*Than that it must endure the mockery of everyone.*

Plautus in *Stichus*:

> From the time I was a tiny boy, I have been a laughingstock;
> Because poverty caused it, I became a figure of fun.
> <note>original: "Jam inde à pauxillo puero ridiculus fui; Eo quod paupertas fecit, ridiculus forem."</note>

->That is:<-

*From the time I was a small boy, I have stood as a target of mockery.*
*And it was poverty alone that did this to me.*

Juvenal in his third Satire:

> They do not easily rise up, those whose virtues are obstructed 
> by narrow circumstances at home.
> <note>original: "Haud facile emergunt, quorum virtutibus obstat Res angusta domi."</note>

->That is:<-

*He shall hardly raise himself from the dust to honor,*
*Whose noble drive and virtue are met by poverty and grief.*

<margin>Christians slandered.</margin> It was cast in the teeth of the Christians that—due to the poverty brought upon them through persecution, robbery, and other mistreatments—they were burdens to the state, useless people, and pests, bringing no benefit to humanity. This was a claim blurted out with ignorance, passion, and lies, contrary to love and experience, as Tertullian defended the Christians against this base slander in *Apology, chapter 42.* <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note>

How this can be, while we live among you, I ask: *while we use the same food, clothing, and manner of life. We are no Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmannen"</note> or Indian Gymnosophists <note>A group of ancient Indian philosophers who lived in solitude and practiced asceticism, often without clothing.</note> who live in the forests and sequester themselves from human or civic social life. We know very well what we owe to our great Creator, and therefore we despise none of His creatures; though we also take care to use them moderately and soberly. For this reason, we do not live in the world without making use of your marketplaces, courts, baths, meat markets, shops, stables, and other places of your commerce. We go to sea and to war alongside you; we till and farm the land; we engage in trade and crafts among you, and offer what we have produced for your use. How we, living accordingly among you and with you, seem to be useless, I cannot see.*

Salomon, for good reason, prayed to be spared from poverty as a matter of necessity, *Proverbs 15.* <note>The author likely refers to the spirit of Proverbs 30:8, as Proverbs 15:16-17 deals with the "better is a little" theme.</note> However, innocent poverty is better than unjust riches.

->It is better to be poor with honor than to be rich with evil.<-
<note>original Greek: "Καλῶς πένεσθαι μᾶλλον, ἢ κακῶς πλουτεῖν."</note>

In the midst of poverty, one can be rich if one has a contented heart in one’s state. There are "poor rich men" who never have enough. *A wealthy man is needy who does not have enough: it is not he who has little, but he who desires more, who is poor. Seneca, Epistle 10.* <note>Seneca the Younger was a Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> That is: *A poor rich man is he who does not have enough: he is not poor who has little, but he who desires more.*

So speaks Octavius in Minutius Felix's work, regarding the charges of Caecilius: *That most of us are accused of poverty is no shame, but our honor; for the mind, just as it is weakened by abundance and luxury, is strengthened by frugality and necessity. And yet, how can he be poor who lacks nothing? Who does not desire*

<column-break/>

*that which another possesses? Who is rich toward God? Much more is he poor who, though he has much, yet desires more, etc.* Bias, according to Ausonius, had as a motto: *Not he who has little, but he who desires more, is poor.* Who is rich? He who desires nothing. Who is poor? A miser. Cicero says in his sixth Paradox: *To be contented with what one has is the greatest and surest wealth.*

And Diodorus Siculus: *He considered self-sufficiency to be the greatest wealth.* <note>original Greek: "Ὑπελάμβανε τὴν αὐταρκείαν μέγιστον πλοῦτον ὑπάρχειν." Diodorus was a Greek historian.</note>

And so, in a certain respect, a poor man is elevated above one who is rich, *Proverbs 19, Ecclesiastes 10.*

To the poor, one must show love and charity, *Leviticus 15:11.* <note>Likely referring to Deuteronomy 15:11, regarding the poor always being in the land.</note> To conduct oneself wisely regarding the wretched is wisdom, *Psalm 41.* Mercy and sharing must not be forgotten, *Hebrews 13.* Love must reveal itself through testing, *1 John 3.* It is strongly recommended. The merciful shall be graciously rewarded; a heavy judgment shall fall upon the unmerciful and the oppressors, *Proverbs 19 and 28; Mark 10; Matthew 25; Galatians 6; Isaiah 32; Ezekiel 16; Proverbs 21; James 2; etc.*

He who gives quickly, gives twice, with a cheerful and inclined heart, according to and sometimes beyond his means, *1 Corinthians 16; 2 Corinthians 8 and 9.* It must not be done with grudging and stinginess, as if one cannot bear to part with it.

However, it is not to be praised that one should suffer want oneself by giving to others; love begins with oneself. *I will give to the needy, but so that I myself do not become needy: I help him who is perishing, but so that I myself do not perish, says Seneca.* That is: *I shall give to the destitute, but in such a way that I do not become destitute myself: I offer my hand to him who is lost, but so that I am not lost myself. One may give and continue to give.*

<margin>Generosity of Paula.</margin> I cannot praise the actions of a certain woman named Paula, who borrowed money and took it at interest to give to the poor, saying: *I wish, in order to help others, to die poor myself, and to lie in my coffin in a begged shirt.* <note>Saint Paula of Rome (347–404 AD) was a wealthy widow and disciple of St. Jerome who gave away her entire fortune.</note>

The ill-reputed Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman Emperor.</note> said this in praise of the Christians, regarding their generosity and care for the poor, travelers, and strangers of all religions: *It is a shame that while the Jews let none of their own beg, and the godless "Galileans" <note>Julian's derogatory term for Christians.</note> come to the aid not only of their own, but also of our enemies, we alone should be negligent in such a necessary duty.*

If mercy and Christian compassion receive any spur or provocation, it is from the powerful and soul-stirring discourse of Lactantius, *Epitome chapter 7,* cited by Cave in his *Primitive Christianity*, page 567, etc.: *Since human nature is weaker than that of the other creatures that come into the world armed with the power to defend themselves and harm others: so our wise Creator has given us a tender, compassionate affection, so that we might place the safety of our lives in mutual help for one another; for being all created by one God and descended from one common father, we ought to regard ourselves as each other's kin, and are obliged to love all people: and so that our innocence and integrity may be perfect, not only not to do any wrong to another, but not to avenge ourselves when someone does us wrong; for which reason it is even commanded to pray for our enemies. We ought—*

<header>ARM. ARMAGEDDON.</header>

[We] are therefore [encouraged] to be kind, courteous, and sociable, so that we might help and stand by one another; for, being ourselves subject to miseries, we can—in the event that we need help—expect the same with greater comfort from others when we have not refused it to others.

Certainly Seneca highly praised this virtue, and Cicero speaks of it quite laudably in *On Duties, Book 1, etc.* <margin>Praise of generosity.</margin> He says that humans come closest to the Divinity through giving. Nothing can be more honorable or more dignified than to despise money, or if you possess it, to apply it to beneficence and generosity.

The Jews called the gifts and alms given to the poor *Tzedakah* <note>original Hebrew: צדקה</note>, meaning **righteousness**, because it is rightfully fitting that one comes to the aid of the needy, although they spoke very broadly of this as something meritorious. Regarding this, one may consult Lightfoot in *Hebrew and Talmudic Hours on Matthew VI*, Witsius in the *Preface to the works of Cave & in the dissertation on Justice*, Buxtorf and Cocceius in their *Lexicons at the word Tzedakah*, Vitringa in *The Ancient Synagogue, page 783*, and my book on *2 Corinthians IX, etc., page 528, etc.*

For this collection and distribution of what was gathered, they had from of old chosen men called *Gabbaim* <note>original Hebrew: גבאים; these were charity collectors or treasurers</note>, while the supreme authority remained with the *Beth Din* <note>original Hebrew: בית דין</note>, the ecclesiastical Council, or the Chief Teacher in the city who had oversight of the Synagogue. See Selden, *On the Sanhedrin, book I, chapter 14, and book II, chapter 7*; Vitringa in *The Ancient Synagogue, pages 811, 814, 821, 827*; Leo of Modena; Buxtorf’s *The Jewish Synagogue, etc.*

<margin>Spiritual poverty.</margin> Physical poverty represents spiritual poverty, and the state and condition of the sinner as powerless and damnable before God; in which he, seeing in himself nothing but sin, powerlessness, damnability, and unworthiness with convincing clarity, and having a low opinion of himself as miserable, worthy of doom, and strengthless, applies everything toward justification, sanctification, adoption, sealing, and full salvation from God, out of pure grace for Christ’s sake, presenting himself fully as an object of mercy; and acknowledging that what he has—which is good and pleasing to God—is received from God, without whom he can do nothing. Such poverty is spoken of in *Psalms 9 and 21, 67 and 72; Isaiah 11:4, 14, 41, and 66; Matthew 5; and elsewhere.* And these poor are happy, because they are not sent away empty, but are endowed with spiritual blessings and riches from God in Christ; upon which I shall not dwell further.

### ARMAGEDDON Ἁρμαγεδδών, הר מגדו, Mount Megiddo.

The thoughts of the learned—both regarding the origin and composition of this place-name, and regarding the event to which it may refer—as well as its application and interpretation to show its fulfillment, vary so widely from one another that it will be difficult for me to present everything in a proper order. And since Professor Campegius Vitringa, whose learning is well-known and celebrated, has explained himself regarding this name and the prophetic proposition in *Apocalypse [Revelation] Chapter XVI:16*, I shall inform the reader of this learned man’s thoughts. On *page 729, etc.*, he writes as follows:

<margin>Thoughts of Vitringa.</margin> *Chapter XVI:16: And they gathered them together into a place called in Hebrew ARMAGEDDON. These words must be translated in this way, as others before us have also cautioned, for the Greek 'synēgage' [they gathered]* <note>original: τὸ συνήγαγε</note> *clearly connects with the subject being discussed in this prophecy, namely, 'unclean spirits' [pneumata akatharta]* <note>original: πνεύματα ἀκάθαρτα</note>*, which our Dutch translators have also rightly noted. The intervening words of awakening and warning in verse 15 caused Beza’s eyes to be drawn away from the 14th verse, so that he incorrectly translated it as 'and he gathered' [et congregavit], attributing it to God.* <margin>Error of Beza.</margin> <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a major Protestant reformer and scholar; Vitringa argues he misidentified the subject of the verb.</note>

*They would finally, through their shameless and persistent croaking, bring about that which they so greatly sought. They would breathe counsel into the princes of the earth. The disputes over Religion had to be decided and ended by war, in which all parties would then involve themselves. They themselves would be the war-trumpets and torches, and the spokesmen regarding the alliances between the princes of the factions which would be concluded. They would, with counsel and deed in the negotiations, help to advance that undertaking and the execution of so great a work. In which respect the kings of the earth are said to be gathered in a place which in Hebrew is called Armageddon. By which secret name is undoubtedly meant a certain large field in Europe, in which battlefield the parties shall come to blows, of which the prophet has warned us in Chapter XIV:20, regarding the treading of the wine-harvest and press outside the city; which wine-harvest whoever undertakes to determine before the outcome of events, displays the vanity of his intellect. All this seems to appear from Chapter XIV:20, that it must be sought in a hostile region. The vat of the winepress of God's wrath, which would be trodden, is said at that time to be outside the city, by which city in that place Jerusalem must undoubtedly be understood, a symbol of the church. In the prophecies it is marked out and made known by two secret names. Which place of strife Joel Chapter III:4 calls the 'valley of God’s judgment' [vallem judicii Dei]* <note>original Hebrew: עמק יהושפט - Emek Yehoshaphat</note>*. The Spirit here says Armageddon, at the same time teaching that it is a Hebrew name.*

*Regarding this name, the guesses of the interpreters are many and various, and one might even add "trifling," which I shall not list. Armageddon is written in Hebrew as 'Har Megiddo' [the mountain of Megiddo]* <note>original Hebrew: הר מגדו</note>*, to which words this composite name returns when dismantled, and by no means to 'cherem nidchon' [the destruction of their host], which is the invention of Drusius; which could be admitted if our common translation were not much easier. And with this name, there is an allusion to the name of the Valley of Megiddo in Zechariah XII:11, 'Bik’at Megiddo'* <note>original Hebrew: בקעת מגדו</note>*, by which is meant that very great valley or plain between the mountains of Galilee, or rather Gilboa, which had fallen as a portion to the half-tribe of Manasseh, in which Valley Josiah unfortunately came to blows with Pharaoh Necho, the Egyptian king (2 Chronicles XV:22). But before that time, Barak and Deborah fought a much more successful battle against Sisera, the general of the Phoenicians; to which latter event Grotius believes that this...*

->That is:<-

*Wretched poverty has nothing more painful to lament,*
*Than having to endure the mockery of every person.*

Plautus in *Stichus*:

> <note>original Latin: "Jam inde à pauxillo puero ridiculus fui; Eo quod paupertas fecit, ridiculus forem."</note> Since I was a tiny boy, I have been a laughingstock; because poverty made me so, I would be a laughingstock.

->That is:<-

*And it was poverty alone that did this to me.*

Juvenal in his third Satire:

> <note>original Latin: "Haud facile emergunt, quorum virtutibus obstat Res angusta domi."</note> Those whose virtues are obstructed by narrow circumstances at home do not easily rise.

->That is:<-

*He shall hardly raise himself from the dust to honor,*
*Whose noble drive and virtue are struck by poverty and grief.*

<margin>Christians slandered.</margin>
The Christians were accused of being burdens to the state, useless people, and pests, due to the poverty brought upon them by persecution, robbery, and other mistreatments. It was claimed they brought no benefit to humanity—an accusation blustered out through ignorance, passion, and lies, contrary to love and experience, as Tertullian defended the Christians against this foul slander in *Apology, chapter 42.*

How can this be, I ask, while we live among you: *while we use the same food, clothing, and manner of life? We are no Brahmans or Indian Gymnosophists <note>A group of ancient Indian philosophers who lived in solitude and practiced asceticism, often without clothing.</note> who dwell in the forests and sequester themselves from human or civil social life. We know very well what we owe to our great Creator, and therefore we despise none of His creatures; although we also take care to use them moderately and soberly. Therefore, we do not live in the world without making use of your marketplaces, courts, baths, meat markets, shops, stables, and other places of your commerce. We go to sea and to war alongside you; we till and cultivate the land; we engage in trade and crafts among you, and offer what we have produced for your use. How we can be seen as useless while living among and with you in such a manner, I cannot see.*

Solomon, with good reason, prayed for relief from poverty as a driving necessity, in *Proverbs 30:8 <note>The source cites XV, but the famous prayer "give me neither poverty nor riches" is in Proverbs 30.</note>*; yet innocent poverty is better than unjust riches.

<note>original Greek: Καλῶς πένεσθαι μᾶλλον, ἢ κακῶς πλουτεῖν.</note> It is better to be honorably poor than evilly rich.

In the midst of poverty, one can be rich if one has a contented heart in one's state. There are "poor rich men" who never have enough. *Seneca, Epistle 10:* <note>original Latin: "Dives egenus est, qui non habet satis: non qui parum habet, sed qui plus cupit pauper est."</note> *A poor rich man is he who does not have enough: he is not poor who has little, but he who desires more.*

So speaks Octavius in the work of Minucius Felix, responding to the arguments of Caecilius: *That most of us are accused of poverty is no shame, but our honor; for the mind, just as it is weakened by abundance and luxury, is strengthened by frugality and necessity; and yet how can he be poor who lacks nothing? Who does not desire that*

<column-break/>

*which another possesses? Who is rich toward God? He is much more poor who, though he has much, yet desires more, etc.* Bias, in Ausonius, had as a motto: *Not he who has little, but he who desires more, is poor.* Who is rich? He who desires nothing. Who is poor? A miser. Cicero, in his sixth paradox, says: *To be content with one’s own is the greatest and surest wealth.*

And Diodorus Siculus: <note>original Greek: Ὑπελάμβανε τῶν αὐταρκείαν μέγιστον πλοῦτον ὑπάρχειν.</note> *Hold it for certain: That self-sufficiency is the greatest wealth.*

And so, in a certain respect, a poor man is exalted above one who is rich, *Proverbs 19:1; Ecclesiastes 10.*

One must show love and charity to the poor, *Leviticus 25:35 <note>Source cites XV. 11.</note>*; to behave wisely toward the miserable is wisdom, *Psalm 41*; mercy and sharing must not be forgotten, *Hebrews 13*; love must reveal itself through deeds, *1 John 3*; it is strongly recommended. He who gives quickly, gives twice with a cheerful and inclined heart, according to and sometimes beyond his means, *1 Corinthians 16; 2 Corinthians 8 and 9*; it must not be done with grudging and stinginess, as if one cannot bear to part with it.

However, it is not to be praised that by giving to others, one should suffer want oneself; love begins with oneself. *I shall give to the needy, but so that I myself do not become needy: I help the perishing, but so that I myself do not perish,* says Seneca: <note>original Latin: "Egenti dabo, sed ut ipse non egeam: fuccurro pereunti, sed ut ipse non peream"</note> *One may give and continue giving.*

### ARMAGEDDON <note>Greek: *Armageddon*; Hebrew: *Har Megiddo*; "Mount Megiddo"</note>

The thoughts of the learned—both regarding the origin and composition of this place-name and the event it may refer to, as well as its application and figurative meaning to demonstrate its fulfillment—diverge so widely that it will be difficult for me to present everything in a proper order. And since Professor Campegius Vitringa <note>A prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist (1659–1722)</note>, whose learning is well-known and celebrated, has explained himself regarding this name and the prophetic proposal in *Revelation chapter 16:16*, I shall inform the reader of this learned man’s thoughts. On page 729, etc., he writes as follows:

<margin>Thoughts of Vitringa.</margin> *Chapter 16:16: And they gathered them together into a place called in Hebrew ARMAGEDDON. In this way, these words*

<column-break/>

*must be translated, as others before us have also advised; for the phrase "they gathered" <note>Greek: *to synegage*</note> clearly connects with the subject being discussed in this prophecy, namely, "unclean spirits" <note>Greek: *pnevmata akatharta*</note>, which our Dutch translators have also correctly noted. The interjected words of awakening and warning in verse 15 caused the eyes of Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a major Reformation scholar</note> to be diverted from the 14th verse; therefore, he translated it poorly as "and He gathered," <margin>Error by Beza.</margin> attributing the gathering to God. For, as is evident to everyone, this passage describes the result of the efforts and preparations of these unclean spirits, or spiritual frogs.*

*Through their shameless and persistent croaking, they would finally bring about what they so greatly sought. They would breathe counsel into the princes of the earth. Disputes over religion would have to be decided and ended by war, in which all parties would then involve themselves. They themselves would be the war-trumpets and torches, and the spokesmen regarding the alliances to be struck between the princes of the various factions. They would help advance the start and execution of so great a work with counsel and deed in these negotiations. In this respect, the kings of the earth are said to be gathered in a place which in Hebrew is called Armageddon. By which secret name is undoubtedly meant a certain large field in Europe, in which battlefield the parties shall come to blows; of which the prophet has already warned us in Chapter 14:20, regarding the vintage and the treading of the winepress outside the city. Whoever undertakes to determine this vintage before the outcome of events demonstrates the vanity of his intellect. All this seems to appear from Chapter 14:20, indicating it must be sought in a hostile region. The vat of the winepress of God’s wrath, which was to be trodden, is said at that time to be "outside the city," by which city in that place Jerusalem must undoubtedly be understood—a symbol of the Church. In the prophecies, it is designated and made known by two secret names. Which place of strife Joel in Chapter 3:4 calls the "Valley of Jehoshaphat" <note>Hebrew: *Emek Yehoshafat*</note>, a valley of God’s judgment. The Spirit here says "Armageddon," at the same time teaching that it is a Hebrew name.*

Regarding this name, the conjectures of the interpreters are many and varied—and one might well add, trivial—which I shall not list. Armageddon is written in Hebrew as *Har Megiddo*, the Mountain of Megiddo; to which words this composite name returns when dismantled. It by no means refers to "the destruction of their army" <note>Hebrew: *Cherem Gedon*</note>, which is the invention of Drusius, and which could be allowed if our common translation were not much easier. With this name, an allusion is made to the name of the Valley of Megiddo, *Zechariah 12:11*, by which is meant that very large valley or plain between the mountains of Galilee, or rather Gilboa, which had fallen as a portion to the half-tribe of Manasseh. In that valley, Josiah unfortunately came to blows with Pharaoh Necho, the Egyptian king (*2 Chronicles 35:22*); but before that time, Barak and Deborah fought a much more fortunate battle there against Sisera, the general of the Phoenicians. It is to this latter event that Grotius believes...

### ARMAGEDDON.

...this must be brought to [the account of] John; which could be granted if it were stated in the history of Barak with so many words that this battle had occurred in the valley of Megiddo. I do not deny that it can be concluded from history, and that Deborah also remembers this place in her song. However, that seems more obscure than that a reader of this prophecy would recall that event, and would not rather think of an event much more famous than that. For this reason, other interpreters of this prophecy have judged that it refers to the earlier and much more famous case, namely the battle between King Josiah <note>original: "Isaias" – likely a scribal error for Josias (Josiah), the king killed at Megiddo</note> and Pharaoh Necho, the Egyptian king, in which the pious king was unhappily slain. They have inclined their thoughts so that they are focused on a case similar to this one recorded in the history of the past century, <margin>Death of Gustavus Adolphus.</margin> namely the excellent Gustavus Adolphus, King of Sweden, a protector of the Protestant cause, who fell in the famous battle against his adversaries to the great sorrow of the church; a view that the famous Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian</note> does not find strange. Yet it appears, firstly, that these cases—though there is some similarity between them—are by no means identical in everything. For this outstanding prince, although falling to the remarkable loss of the church, nevertheless carried away the victory, which happened quite differently in the battle between Josiah and Pharaoh Necho. Furthermore, this cannot be easily reconciled with the aim of this vision; for here, the discussion is clearly about the most significant plague to be brought upon the enemies of the church, and indeed a universal one, which would bring with it the greatest changes in affairs and the destruction of the adversary's territory and power, as is most clearly evident from what follows in the prophecy.

The outcome of this hand-to-hand combat would therefore be happy for the church and bring her the greatest comforts. Therefore, nothing remains but to say that the Spirit, in forming this name, only intends its secret meaning—which he does elsewhere, as we have indicated previously and demonstrated regarding *Chapter XIII:18*—the spiritual <margin>Spiritual meaning.</margin> meaning of which is not far to seek: גדד, <term>Gedad</term> <note>Hebrew: "to cut" or "to gather in troops"</note> means to the Hebrews a "mountain of cutting off," for among the Chaldeans and also the Hebrews—as is clear from the derivatives in *Jeremiah 48:37* and *41:5*—גדד means *to cut off* or *to cut into*, which name is singularly appropriate in this place, where the enemies would be struck with as great a slaughter as ever. But the Spirit, with this name, has alluded to a similar one from Joel, who had called this field the *Valley of Jehoshaphat*. Since this place contains the idea of a mountain, the Spirit thought it good here to call it the *Mountain of Destruction or Cutting Off*. These things are smooth and easy, if I am not mistaken, and consequently leave no further difficulty.

Therefore, there is nothing more to report here except what deserves the greatest observation: that no history concerning Christendom has shown the fulfillment of this prophecy. Thus, Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> and the Bishop of Meaux <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704), a French bishop and theologian</note> are as much "run aground" here as anywhere, since they explain the plagues brought upon the Beast as the calamities which the Lord had destined for Pagan Rome. The Bishop, who interprets the Beast as the reign of Diocletian, brings this prophecy home to the battle of Emperor Valerian against the Persians, in which Valerian, being defeated by the Persians, was captured and later put to death by them. When he himself was not satisfied with this, and knew well enough that his readers would not be satisfied, he falls back upon Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD)</note> who, after a long interval, was mortally wounded in battle by the same Persians. Between these cases and those of the Old Testament history of Ahaziah, King of Judah, and Josiah (*2 Kings 9:29*) who perished in the valley of Megiddo, he seeks some similarities or harmonies. Even if such an interpretation is not only false but also absurd, one must not attribute it to a lack of understanding or learning (which happens often enough otherwise), but to the presupposition which this learned man helps to defend. For this church leader could not have been unaware: **a.** That according to the better historical accounts, Valerian was captured by Sapor <note>Shapur I, King of the Sassanid Empire</note>, King of the Persians, through deceit and not in battle, as he writes; this is evident not only from Zosimus (*History, book 1, chapter 36*) but also from letters sent to Sapor regarding that event by Trebellius Pollio (*In Valeriano, chapter 4*). **b.** The case of Valerian has no connection at all with that of Julian; an entire century passes between the two events, while Julian also died as a victor. **c.** There is also no similarity between Ahaziah, struck down by King Jehu, and Josiah by Pharaoh Necho, and between Valerian and Julian struck down by the Persians. **d.** It is also quite absurd to suggest that in the capture of Valerian, the heaviest plague was brought upon the Beast, while the Bishop maintains that the Beast is the reign of Diocletian; thus the Beast would have perished before it was even born. **e.** And what is most important: there is nothing in the aforementioned things that serves the purpose of the prophecy, which makes this war universal—involving all the kings of the Roman territory who would make war on the church, upon whom God would openly take vengeance as persecutors of His church—of which war Joel prophesied that after its end, great changes for the comfort and salvation of the church would follow. All these marks, along with many others indicated previously, are missing here.

It is therefore a proof of blind affection to want to maintain one's presupposition despite the light of truth. Therefore, why did he not rather follow Grotius, who mentions here the battle of Constantine with Maxentius? Namely, because he clearly saw that the same marks were missing here, and that nothing appeared in this battle that corresponds with the matter and the aim of this symbolic imagery. We therefore still await with trembling the fulfillment of this prophecy, praying to God that He may be favorable to His church against all outcomes or events, and be pleased to remember her for good; for it will be times of heavy oppression, which the exhortation and awakening speech between verses 14 and 16 sufficiently demonstrates.

### ARMAGEDDON.

->T<-

...interpretation of the Prophecies, *page* 189, etc., which seems to state broadly regarding his own progress in the Prophetic [arts]: he desires that Armageddon signifies the Roman See <note>The "See" refers to the jurisdiction or throne of the Pope.</note> or the Vatican, from whence the lightnings of excommunication and cursing proceed: whose lightnings have many times swallowed up and destroyed entire lands: in which place and through which place all kings devoted to the Papacy shall be gathered, collected, and united: and he knows how to explain Armageddon and the three outgoing spirits, etc., in a wonderful way. Armageddon is for him "extermination through a curse-excommunication" in Hebrew and Syriac: the three outgoing spirits are words, laws, and false oracles of the Papacy, which are strengthened by the ban of excommunication; which are presented as a trio to represent perfection; to represent the three sources and the three parts of the Canon Law; and to represent the three main vices that rule there: *pride, greed, and shamelessness*, etc.

About which the Reverend and very learned Professor Johan Mark <note>Johannes Marckius (1656–1731), a prominent Dutch theologian.</note>, in his work on the Revelations, *page* 737, has noted this. Yet in this entire interpretation, I can in no way perceive that certainty which this learned man asserts. If sometimes the *mouth*, the *spirit*, the *spirit of the mouth*, signify the word, do they also signify it here? If the spirit is also the word, can the mouth, from which the spirit goes, easily be the same thing? If Armageddon is the added curse or excommunication, and at the same time coming out of the mouth, why is there a deep silence about this, and why is it called the place of the described and destroyed army? If the triple spirit is the three parts of the Canon Law, where then will the words and all the false oracles of the Papacy remain? And how great a distinction is there between performing signs and happening to strengthen something? Finally, do the Papal bulls sent to the kings not differ quite a lot from his Divine doctrines and from the books of Canon Law? And *certainly, I maintain*, says his Reverence, *that one should not easily come to such personal imaginings without necessity, and the learned man shows us none. And subsequently regarding the joint of time: how it is brought there to the drying up of the Euphrates, we have to see; also this does not agree with the proper calculation of time, since the oracles of the Papacy were born long before the year 1390, and after the year 1526; and that he himself derives the first part of the Canon Laws from the year 1200 and the third part from the year 1320.*

In which then the name of spirits is also drawn to the naming of Spiritual fathers. By others again, the name of spirits is brought to the quick agility and readiness.*

The going out of these spirits, from the first and the second beast, signifies that they serve the Antichrist's kingdom and the following of the Monks and are their subjects, belonging to that kingdom or this Monastic state. And it is no wonder that the Dragon is added there, since he is favorable to the Beast and moves him, and reveals himself all the more powerfully through these ambassadors. Indeed, they go out of the puffed-up and terrible mouth of the hellish society, insofar as they obey their chief leaders at the nod and signal of command. When they are said to be like Frogs, then this expresses the impurity of the doctrine and the morals, the puffed-up heart and the unbridled chattering, shamelessness, etc. With right and reason they are also called spirits of devils, since they are pushed forward by these and reach out their doctrine and service, *1 Timothy 4:1*, by whose power they easily perform one thing or another, and devise more other monstrous things by which they deceive. If any seek the favor of princes, they force themselves through the whole world, whether they like it or not, and rule them by force or by deceit; and these are in truth the emissaries of the Beast. Thither they direct all their counsels and efforts, so that they unite the minds of the princes by a similar hatred against the true church and its advocates and defenders, due to unlawful oppression, to the point that they draw their bands together for war. And that all the more strongly and eagerly, as they notice from the gathered peoples and from many revenues that they are in very great danger, and so strongly fear their downfall from the almighty God. And to say it in a word, here is the wicked activity of the beast, to provide itself as much as possible with the favor and help of the worldly greats through the emissaries against the day of evil.

# ARMAGEDDON. BRACELETS.

[Rome] would be led away, so that—in the ancient manner of strengthening it—they would no longer flow together, which would provide an excellent opportunity for enemies, even the most distant ones. Seeing this to her own detriment, the Antichristian church would exert her powers, finally moving the great and the rest of the inhabitants of the earth to her aid and support, and to the oppression of her enemies. Yet the Lord, on the other hand, would warn His own people so that they would not let themselves be led astray either by force or by deceit. These Antichristian movements would succeed to the extent that she would catch a great multitude in her snare to assist her; yet nevertheless, her end would be utter destruction, etc.

I shall bring forward one or two more passages on the occasion of this name and the similarity of the matter.

In *Joel 3:1–2* we read: *For behold, in those days and at that time, when I shall restore the captives of Judah and Jerusalem, I will also gather all nations and bring them down into the Valley of Jehoshaphat <note>The name Jehoshaphat means "The LORD judges."</note>, and I will enter into judgment with them there on behalf of My people and My heritage Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations and divided My land.*

This is understood to mean that a day of the Lord's judgment is presented here—"Jehoshaphat"—taking its name from the place where this figure of speech is derived, *2 Chronicles 20*, etc.

The Lord, through His influence and wonderful governance, would bring it about that the nations, having come to one mind, understanding, and alliance, would flow together as defeated enemies of His church and people—just as the Moabites, Ammonites, and the children of Mount Seir did long ago—and would penetrate even into the borders of the church-land. But when that blood-alliance <note>original: *vlockverwantschap*, likely referring to a cursed or sworn confederacy.</note> was thus gathered for something hostile against the church, then the Lord would contend and judge there. It would be His day of judgment, such that He would throw them into mutual confusion, making them fight one another and consume and break each other's strength: so that not Israel, but the Lord, to the glory of His name, would perform this work.

We do not dispute with anyone here whether *2 Chronicles 20* or a later event is intended. At the very least, the name "the Valley of Jehoshaphat"—a valley of divine judgment—indicates to me, in its later fulfillment, the divine judgment upon the enemies of the church rather than a specific physical place where such a thing must be carried out.

<margin>Translation <note>This refers to the application or "transfer" of the prophecy's meaning to a new context.</note></margin>
Next, the passage *Zechariah 12:10, 11, 12* through the end of that chapter comes into consideration. Regarding this prominent passage of prophecy, I have found that the most and purest theologians, with an allusion to the sad case of King Josiah in the Valley of Megiddo <note>King Josiah was a reforming king of Judah who died in battle at Megiddo; his death was a cause of great national mourning.</note>, have attributed this prophecy to God's Spirit and His heart-changing grace. This was poured out early upon the Apostles and the firstfruits of the Jews and Gentiles, leading to faith, conversion, and a godly sorrow for their sins and iniquities. They mourned because they had brought Jesus—God's holy child, the first-born and only-begotten—to a shameful death on the cross, and by their sins had given reason for Him to be wounded and crushed for their transgressions (*Isaiah 53:5*). This outpouring shall also take place in later days to work the same effect.

<column-break/>

I have noted that some have subsequently thought verses 12, 13, and 14 speak of a particular judgment of God upon those who would not weep over Jesus, as mentioned in verses 10 and 11: namely, that everyone, for his own particular interest and detriment during the destruction of the city, temple, and state of the Jewish power, would perform mourning, as can be further seen in Gulichius <note>Abraham van Gulich (1642–1679), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note>, etc.

I can well understand that those who remained unbelieving could have performed great mourning because of their loss, disasters, and woes which were approaching them (*Matthew 27:25; Luke 23:28*, etc.). To view this in itself may have some ground; yet I doubt that this is what is meant by God's Spirit. For in the words of this prophecy, I do not see a single word mentioned of that loss, of that damage, or of any sorrow and wailing due to the downfall of Jerusalem, the temple, and the republic. On the contrary, I see one and the same reason given for all—for great and small, of whatever state they may be: the Messiah and His piercing (*Isaiah 53*). The person of King Josiah was a type <term>Type: a historical person or event that foreshadows a future reality (the "antitype"), such as Jesus.</term> of the Messiah. For him, they once performed great mourning, and for nothing else. The transfer and application then also lead us to the Messiah, and not to a matter of an entirely different nature and a cause of an entirely different sort. The promise of the Spirit and its healing effects is too broad and wide for me to dare deny it to these houses and tribes (*Isaiah 35; Joel 2:28, 29*, etc.).

<margin>Josiah a type of Messiah.</margin>

Therefore, what satisfies me most for further conviction is that I understand it in this manner, namely:

> The House of David shall mourn because it helped bring about the death of the Messiah through its judicial high authority.
>
> The House of Nathan shall mourn because, having had the school of instruction, it cast away the key of knowledge <note>A reference to Luke 11:52, accusing the teachers of the law of hindering others from the truth.</note> and shamefully misused it to condemn and brand Jesus and His teaching as heresy. The tribe of Levi shall mourn because it clung to, and helped others cling to, the worthless and powerless sacrifices, with loathing and denial of the High Priest sworn by God, and His true, single, and perfect propitiatory sacrifice. The House of Simeon, etc., shall mourn because it lent its tongue and hand to the cursed conspiracy against the holy child of God. And furthermore, the rest of the people shall mourn because they let themselves be so shamefully misled and stirred up against the Christ, and because they cried out as ignorantly as they did passionately, *crucify him, etc.*

# BRACELETS. ASBESTOS.

...and feminine ornament: formerly worn by women as well as men; about which I shall not be wordy.

<margin>The best ornament.</margin>
Whatever may be the case with all this, I hold the best ornament to be: *A gentle, humble, and quiet spirit.* (1 Peter 3) and I say with Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD).</note> concerning the finery of women: *Step forward now, decked out in the cosmetics and decorations of the Apostles. Take from simplicity your whiteness, from chastity your blush and modesty; paint your eyes with humble reverence, hanging in your ears the word of God, hanging on your neck the yoke of Christ; submit your head to your husbands, and you shall be sufficiently adorned. Occupy your hands with good deeds, keep your feet at home, and they shall possess more pleasure than if they were set with gold. Dress yourselves with the silk of piety, with the fine twisted linen of brilliant white holiness, with the purple of chastity. Adorned in such a fashion, you shall have God as a lover.*

->Alcimus Avitus to his Sister<- <note>Avitus of Vienne (c. 450 – 518 AD) was a bishop and poet.</note>

> *And what does it benefit to deck a face that must perish,* <note>original: "Et quid enim prodest periturum comere vultum,"</note>
> *Or to burden decaying bodies with various gems,* <note>original: "Putria vel variis onerari corpora gemmis,"</note>
> *While the inner man is filthy, and defiles himself with crime?* <note>original: "Interior dum fordet homo, ac se crimine faedat?"</note>

->That is:<-

*What use is it to paint your face and appearance,*
*Or to add luster to the body with many stones,*
*If you are stained within by foul defect?*

One reads in the works of the forefather Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a French abbot and influential mystic.</note> the following: *A vain heart leaves an impression of its vanity on the body. Likewise, outward abundance is a mark of inward frivolity. Soft clothing testifies to a weak mind: for they would not labor so for the ornament of the body, unless they had first neglected and loosened the mind, which is unadorned in virtues.*

<margin>Upon this the Knight Jacob Cats <note>Jacob Cats (1577–1660) was a famous Dutch poet and statesman known for his moralistic emblems.</note> says:</margin>

*Let your good gifts shine instead of a flawless stone;*
*Pure discipline for pearls, and modesty for rubies:*
*Let that white, that noble red, adorn you above all,*
*For from there the soul shall shine for eternity.*

### ASBESTOS, non-combustible.

<margin>The stone ASBESTOS.</margin>
Regarding ASBESTOS, if it is the same as Amiantus <note>A fibrous silicate mineral; the name comes from the Greek for "unpolluted" because it could be cleaned in fire.</note>, one may look at what I have said regarding that word.

That some call it a certain herb in Taniu, in Tartary <note>A historical region in North and Central Asia.</note>, which grows around and upon a stone—not too long, yet shaggy-locked—and is purified by fire and not consumed, has been said by some and rejected by others.

Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit scholar and polymath who wrote on the "subterranean world."</note> and others call it a stone that, in the manner of alum, can be cut into threads; consisting of elongated fibers mixed with a fatty and tough moisture, so firmly joined by nature that it is not consumed by fire, nor can it be diminished or loosened by any vapors. Napkins, tablecloths, clothing, paper, and wicks for oil lamps are made from it, etc. However, although the wicks are never consumed, just as the other materials withstand the fire and are purified by it, it is nevertheless true that the 

<column-break/>

wick-material goes out for lack of oil. Furthermore, it is told of it that once it has caught flame, it is not extinguished by air, wind, or rain.

So says Dionysius Afer <note>A Greek geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> in the description of Arcadia:

> *Thus is born a linen that, once lit by fire,* <note>original: "Sic nasci linum, qui tacto accensus ab igne"</note>
> *Cannot be extinguished, which the Greeks by its true name* <note>original: "Extingui nequiit, quem Graii nomine vero"</note>
> *Call Asbeston; it shines with the color of iron.* <note>original: "Asbeston memorant, ferri nitet ille colore."</note>

->That is:<-

*Here grows a linen that, once set alight by fire,*
*Is never extinguished, and is named by the Greeks*
*Unquenchable, being furthermore colored like iron.*

See Kircher in *China Illustrated* page 251; in *Mundus Subterraneus*. Hofmann in *Lexicon Universale* under the word *Linum*. De Mey, *Hallelujah*. Isidore, Pliny, Solinus Chapter 7, etc.

Braun <note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708), a Dutch theologian who wrote on the clothing of Hebrew priests.</note> in *The Clothing of the Hebrews*, Book 1, Chapter 6, page 135, cites the testimony of Hierocles: *They use a linen garment made from stones. The threads are soft skins <note>original Greek: "Χρωνται δὲ ἐσθῆτι λινῇ τῇ ἐκ πετρῶν. Τὰ μηρύματα μαλακὰ δὲ δέρματα..."</note>, as they happen to be, from which fabrics are made, neither burned by fire nor cleaned by water; but when they are filled with dirt and stains, being thrown into the flame, they become white and transparent.* This writer is speaking of the Brahmans in India.

I shall say no more of this stone; one should consider AMIANTUS, along with the various applications found there.

<margin>Application <note>In the sense of a spiritual or metaphorical interpretation.</note>.</margin>
I find the virtues and properties of this stone applied to the unquenchable fire of hell; yet how such a neat application can be sustained, except merely in the name, I do not see: for this stone is not meant for burning and agonizing, but for giving light, and for durable and remarkable service. However, if one wishes to reflect on hell, one could think of the inhabitants of hell, insofar as they shall never be consumed by the unquenchable hellfire, just as their plague-fire shall never be extinguished; which, however, shall not serve for their purification.

<margin>Emblem of Faith.</margin>
But I would rather consider Asbestos as an emblem of faith, hope, and Christian love, which never perish, are never consumed, nor extinguished by winds, downpours, the fire of afflictions, or trials, but rather become stronger and are cleansed and purified of filth and the stains of sin, as long as there is sufficient oil of grace in the soul. *Psalm 44:12 to 21. Romans 8. Song of Solomon 8:7. Romans 5. 1 Peter 1:7. Psalm 66:10. 1 John 5:4. etc. Psalm 46.*
