# ARMAGEDDON. BRACELETS.

...Rome would divert, adding that they, according to the ancient manner of strengthening it, would no longer flow together, so that a fine opportunity would be given to the enemies, even the most distant ones; and that the Antichristian church, having noticed this to her detriment, would exert her powers, finally moving the great ones and the rest of the inhabitants of the earth to her aid and support, and the oppression of her enemies. Yet, that the Lord on the contrary would warn His own, that they should let themselves be seduced neither by violence nor by deceit. And that the Antichristian movements would succeed to such an extent that she would get a great multitude into her cord for her assistance, yet nonetheless her end would be extreme destruction, etc.

I shall bring forward one or two more places on the occasion of this name, and the similarity in the matter.

In *Joel 3:1, 2* we read, *For behold, in those days and at that time, when I shall turn back the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, I will also gather all Gentiles, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat <note>The name Jehoshaphat means "The Lord judges," making it a symbolic site for divine justice.</note>, and I will plead with them there for my people and for my heritage Israel, whom they have scattered among the Gentiles, and divided my land.*

It is understood thus: that here occurs a day of the Lord's judgment, Jehoshaphat, and such is the place from which this manner of speaking is borrowed, *2 Chronicles 20, etc.*

The Lord would, through His influence and wonderful governance, bring it about that the nations, having come to one mind, understanding, and alliance, would flow together as defeated enemies of His church and people, as formerly the Moabites, Ammonites, and children of Mount Seir did, and would penetrate into the borders of the church-land; but when that alliance of the cursed was thus gathered for something hostile against the church, then the Lord would contend and judge there. It would be His day of judgment, such that He would confuse them among themselves, make them fight one another, and mutually consume and break each other's powers: so that not Israel, but the Lord to the glory of His name, would perform this work.

We dispute here with no one whether *2 Chronicles 20* or a later event is being looked upon. At the least the name, the valley of Jehoshaphat, a valley and vale of divine judgment and justice, indicates to me in the later fulfillment more the divine judgment upon the enemies of the church than precisely the location where such is to be carried out.

Next comes into consideration the passage *Zechariah 12:10, 11, 12 <note>The original text mistakenly cites Zechariah 20 (XX), which does not exist; the context clearly refers to Chapter 12.</note>* until the end of that chapter.

<margin>Application.</margin> Regarding which prominent place and prophecy I have found: that the most and purest theologians, with allusion to the sad case of King Josiah in the valley of Megiddo <note>King Josiah was a reforming King of Judah who died in battle at Megiddo, leading to national mourning.</note>, have brought this prophecy home to God's spirit and His heart-changing grace—already early upon the Apostles, the firstfruits of the Jews and Gentiles—poured out toward faith, conversion, and godly sorrow on account of their sins, iniquities, and vileness, for having brought Jesus, God's holy child, the first- and only-begotten, to the ignominious death of the cross; and having given reason through their sins that He, for the sins and transgressions, was wounded and bruised, *Isaiah 53:5*, and that also in later days, to work out such things, an outpouring shall occur.

<column-break/>

I have been able to notice that people subsequently thought verses 12, 13, and 14 spoke of a particular judgment of God over those who would not weep over Jesus, as mentioned in verses 10 and 11: namely, that each would mourn for his particular interest and disadvantage at the destruction of the city, temple, and state of the Jewish Power, as such can be further learned from Gulichius <note>Abraham Gulichius (1642–1679) was a Dutch theologian known for his work on the prophets.</note>, etc.

I can well understand that those who remained unbelieving could have engaged in heavy mourning because of their loss, disasters, and woes which were approaching them, *Matthew 27:25, Luke 23:28, etc.* To want to consider such a thing in itself may have a basis: but that such is intended by God's spirit, of that I doubt; for I do not see in the words of this prophecy a single word mentioned of that loss, of this damage, and of any sorrow and wailing because of the downfall of Jerusalem, temple, and republic; but on the contrary, I see one and the same reason, among all, among great and small, of whatever state he may be, brought forward: the Messiah and His piercing, *Isaiah 53*. The person of King Josiah was an example of the Messiah. For him they formerly engaged in great mourning, not for something else. The transfer and application then also brings us to the Messiah, and not to a matter of an entirely different nature and a cause of an entirely different kind. The promise of the spirit and its healthful effects lies too wide and broad for me to dare to deny it to these houses and tribes in this matter. *Isaiah 35, Joel 2:28, 29, etc.*

<margin>Josiah an example of Messiah.</margin>

Therefore, what can most satisfy me for further conviction is that I understand it in this manner, namely:

> *The house of David shall mourn*, because it helped to promote the death of the Messiah through its judicial high authority.
> *The house of Nathan shall mourn*, because having had the school of instruction, it cast away the key of knowledge and harmfully abused it to vilely condemn and brand Jesus and His teaching as heretical. *The tribe of Levi shall mourn*, because it even clung to and helped others cling to the lowly and powerless sacrifices, with loathing and denial of the High Priest sworn by God, and His true, single, and perfect propitiatory sacrifice. *The house of Simeon, etc. shall mourn*, because it lent tongue and hand to the cursed conspiracy against the holy child of God. And furthermore, the rest of the people shall mourn, since they let themselves be so shamefully misled and stirred up against the Christ, and that they, as ignorant as they were delirious, cried out, *crucify him, etc.*

# BRACELETS. ASBESTOS.

...and feminine ornament: formerly worn by both women and men; about which I shall not be wordy.

<margin>The best ornament.</margin>
Whatever may be said of all this, I hold the best ornament to be: *A meek, humble, and quiet spirit.* 1 Peter 3. And I say with Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author who often wrote on modesty and moral conduct.</note> regarding the finery of women: *Come forth now, dressed in the cosmetics and ornaments of the Apostles. Take from simplicity your whiteness, from chastity your blush and shame; paint your eyes with humble reverence, hanging in your ears the word of God, hanging about your neck the yoke of Christ; submit your heads to your husbands, and you shall be sufficiently adorned. Keep your hands busy with good will, stay your feet at home, and they shall possess more pleasure than if they were set with gold. Clothe yourselves with the silk of piety, with the fine twisted linen of snowy holiness, with the purple of chastity. Dressed in such a fashion, you shall have God as a lover.*

->Alcimus Avitus to his Sister<-
<note>Alcimus Avitus (c. 450 – 518 AD) was a Bishop of Vienne and a Latin poet.</note>

> *And what does it profit to adorn a face that will perish,*
> *Or to burden decaying bodies with various gems,*
> *While the inner man is filthy and stains himself with crime?*
> <note>Original Latin: "Et quid enim prodest periturum comere vultum, / Putria vel variis onerari corpora gemmis, / Interior dum sordet homo, ac se crimine foedat?"</note>

->That is:<-

> *What does it help to paint your face and appearance,*
> *Or to add great luster to the body with gemstones,*
> *If you are stained within by foul defect?*

One reads in the works of the forefather Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a French abbot and primary builder of the Cistercian order.</note> the following: *A vain heart leaves an impression of its vanity upon the body. So too is external abundance a sign of internal levity. Soft clothes testify to a weak mind: for they would not labor so for the finery of the body, unless they had first neglected and loosened the mind, which is unadorned in virtues.*

Upon this says the Knight Jakob Kats <note>Jacob Cats (1577–1660), a famous Dutch poet and statesman known for his moralistic emblems.</note>:

> *Let your good gifts shine like a precious stone;*
> *Pure desire for pearls, and shame for rubies:*
> *Let that white, that noble red, adorn you above all;*
> *From there it is that the soul shall shine for eternity.*

### ASBESTOS, unburnable.

<margin>The stone ASBESTOS.</margin>
As for the ASBESTOS, if it is the same as the Amianth <note>Amianthus is a form of asbestos known for its flexible, silky fibers.</note>, one may look up what I have said under that word.

That some call it a certain herb in Taniu, in Tartary, which grows around and upon a stone—not too long, but shaggy-locked—and is purified by fire and not consumed, has been said by some and rejected by others.

Kircherus <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit polymath who wrote on everything from medicine to vulcanology.</note> and others call it a stone that can be cut into threads in the manner of alum; consisting of elongated threads mixed with fatty and tough moisture, so firmly attached by nature that it is not consumed by fire, nor diminished or loosened by any vapors. One makes from it napkins, tablecloths, clothes, paper, wicks in oil lamps, etc.; however, although the wicks are never consumed, just as the other materials withstand the fire and are purified by it, the wick-material nevertheless goes out for lack of oil. Furthermore, it is told of it that once having caught fire, it is not extinguished by air, wind, or rain.

So says Dionysius Afer <note>Dionysius Periegetes, a Greek geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> in the description of Arcadia:

> *Thus is born the linen which, once set ablaze by fire,*
> *Cannot be extinguished; which the Greeks by its true name*
> *Call Unquenchable [Asbeston]; it shines with the heat of iron.*
> <note>Original Latin: "Sic nasci linum, qui tacto accensus ab igne / Extingui nequiit, quem Graii nomine vero / Asbeston memorant, ferri nitet ille calore."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Here grows a linen that, once lit by fire,*
> *Is never extinguished, and is named by the Greeks*
> *Unquenchable; being furthermore colored with the tint of iron.*

See Kircher in *China Illustrated* page 251, and in *The Subterranean World*. Hofmann in *Universal Lexicon* at the word *Linum* [Linen], De Mey’s *Hallelujah*, Isidore, Pliny, Solinus Chapter 7, etc.

Braunius <note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708), a theologian who wrote extensively on the clothing of Hebrew priests.</note> in *On the Clothing of the Hebrews*, Book 1, Chapter 6, page 135, brings forward the testimony of Hierocles: *They use a linen garment made from stones. The threads are soft like skins, which they happen to weave, and from which fabrics are made that are neither burned by fire nor cleaned by water; but when they are filled with filth and stains, being thrown into the flame, they become white and translucent.* <note>Original Greek: "Χρῶνται ἐσθῆτι λινῇ τῇ ἐκ πετρῶν. Τὰ μηρύματα μαλακὰ ἢ δέρματα, ὃ δὴ συμβαίνουσιν, ἐξ ὧν ὑφάσματα γίγνεται, μήτε πυρὶ καιόμενα, μήτε ὕδατι καθαιρόμενα ἀλλ’ ἐπειδὰν ῥύπῳ καὶ κηλίδος ἐμπληθῇ ἐμβληθέντα εἰς Φλόγα, λευκὰ καὶ διαφανῆ γίνεται."</note> This writer speaks of the Brahmins in the Indies.

Of this stone I shall say no more; let one consider AMIANTH, along with the various interpretations there.

I find the virtues and properties of this stone applied to the unquenchable fire of hell; yet how such a neat comparison can be sustained, except merely in the name, I do not see: for this stone is not for burning and torturing, but for giving light, and for durable and remarkable services. However, if one wishes to allude to hell, one could think of the denizens of hell, insofar as they shall never be consumed by the unquenchable hellfire, just as their plague-fire shall never be extinguished; which, however, shall not serve for their purification.

<margin>Comparison of Faith.</margin>
But I would rather regard the Asbestos as a symbol of faith, hope, and Christian love, which never perish, are never consumed, nor extinguished by winds, downpours, the fire of oppression or trial, but rather become stronger and are cleaned and purified of filth and the stains of sin, as long as there is sufficient oil of grace in the soul. *Ps. 44:12 to 21. Rom. 8. Song of Sol. 8:7. Rom. 5. 1 Pet. 1:7. Ps. 66:10. 1 John 5:4. etc. Ps. 46.*

# ASPIS.

### ASPIS, or the Serpent of that name, <margin>pethen / akshub / shachal</margin> <note>These are Hebrew terms for various venomous snakes often translated as asp or adder.</note> also translated as Dragon, Adder, or Viper.

Regarding the ADDER, VIPER, and the Viper’s venom, I have given a report of this in the preceding section; so far as a distinction is made between them here, I shall treat it briefly, noting what the famously renowned writers of old have left behind concerning this matter.

<margin>Derivation of ASPIS.</margin> It is thought that the ASPIS is named from *aspergendo*, "sprinkling," because this snake sprinkles its venom upon humans by biting or spitting; or from *asperitas*, the "roughness" of its skin; or from *aspiciendo*, from its "sharp sight" and intense gaze. This last point does not find much favor with some, since it is described as having weak sight and sharp hearing, so that it wakes at the slightest rustle.

<term>Nicander</term> <note>Nicander of Colophon (2nd century BC), a Greek poet and physician who wrote "Theriaca," a poem about venomous creatures.</note> in *Theriaca, verse 162.*

> Burdened by sleep,
> It seems to blink continuously with heavy eyes.
> But when it perceives even a murmur, or with a ready ear
> some voice, it casts off sluggish sleep from its body.
<note>original: "Somnoque gravatis / Torpida continue nictare videtur ocellis. / Ast ubi vel murmur, facili vel percipit aure / Vocem aliquam, segnes reiicit de corpore somnos."</note>

->That is:<-

*The serpent seems overcome and burdened by drowsiness,*
*But if it hears a sound, it drives according to its nature*
*The sluggish sleepiness away.*

<term>Mercurialis</term> <note>Girolamo Mercuriali (1530–1606), an Italian physician who wrote on the history of medicine and poisons.</note> states: *to all asps these things are common; weak sight, slow gait, sharp hearing.*
<note>original: "omnibus aspidibus haec communia sunt; visus imbecillus, incessus tardus, auditus subtilis."</note>

->That is:<-

*In all serpents called Asps, these things are common: they have weak sight, a slow gait, and a fine and quick hearing.*

<margin>shachal</margin> <term>Bochart</term> <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant scholar who wrote a famous study on the animals of the Bible.</note> wishes this serpent to be named *Sachal* because of its brown and black color, as <term>Pausanias</term> <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> in *Attica*, and <term>Aelian</term> <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175 – c. 235 AD), a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric known for his works on animal behavior.</note> in the 6th book of his histories, testify.

And <margin>akshub</margin> *Psalm 140:4* comes from the Arabic word *Achasa*, to turn, to weave and bend in circles, to turn oneself in coils and bends, which these are said to do when, being angry, they set themselves in a posture for battle.

Nicander in *Theriaca, verse 166.*

> It describes sinuous coils in a smooth stretch,
> And thus raises its dreadful head from the middle of the circle.
<note>original: "Describit tereti sinuosa volumina tractu, / Horrendumque caput medio sic tollit ab orbe."</note>

->That is:<-

*It coils itself up with a round sweep,*
*And shows its hideous head from the middle of the turn.*

And it is testified that it takes its sleep having composed itself into many coils; from which the round shields, *aspides* <note>original: "ἀσπίδες"</note> were named, according to the testimony of the Commentators on <term>Aristophanes</term> <note>The famous Greek comic playwright (c. 446 – c. 386 BC).</note>.

<column-break/>

One finds three kinds: the Land-asp, the Spitting-asp (*ptyas*), and the Swallow-asp.

These serpents are found mostly in warm regions, in Spain, Africa, Egypt, and by the River Nile. <term>Olaus Magnus</term> <note>A Swedish writer and ecclesiastic (1490–1557) known for his "History of the Northern Peoples."</note> informs us that they are also found in the northern climate, with rough skin, of a greyish color, with glistening eyes, three, four, and five cubits long.

I believe that they are not of the same color everywhere. <term>Belluafensis</term> <note>Vincent of Beauvais (c. 1184–1264), a Dominican friar who compiled a massive medieval encyclopedia.</note> mentions *Aspides* of a blue color.

One attributes to them two upper teeth, one on each side of the jaw, standing outward like those of wild boars; with a continuous hollowness in which the poison is enclosed: I rather believe in little bladders on or near the teeth. See Aelian, <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the famous "Natural History."</note>, Belluafensis, <term>Jonston</term> <note>John Jonston (1603–1675), a Polish physician and naturalist of Scottish descent.</note>, etc.

Their eggs are described as being *small, round, bluish, poisonous, slimy, stinking, and sticking together.*

I find the Asp depicted thus by Nicander, and put into verse by Jonston in *Serpents, page 17.*

*This Asp stretches out in length like two arms,*
*As thick as a spear, with which one can protect*
*Oneself against lion and bull. Its color is often pale,*
*Now mixed green and grey, then as if it resembled fire.*
*It keeps itself in the earth of scorched Egypt,*
*Where the flood of the Nile hatched it in the black mud.*
*Its fierce forehead has two horns like a wart.*
*Its eye is like fire, spattered with bloody red:*
*Its neck melts with venom, and the beast starts to burn.*
*Thus it surely threatens death with its four sharp teeth:*
*In which it holds its poison, that brews a thousand torments,*
*Secretly hidden with cunning under the membrane.*

<margin>Bite of this serpent.</margin> As for its bite, it is as if invisible and very fine. At the wound, a swelling arises; after the bite, drowsiness follows; the eyes become dizzy; the face turns pale; the forehead cold; the victim yawns constantly; convulsions follow: and, as many believe, inevitable death. For the bite is held to be incurable, *Aelian book 1, chapter 54 and book 6, chapter 38. Bochart Hieroz. page 381.*

<term>Phile</term> <note>Manuel Philes (c. 1275 – c. 1345), a Byzantine poet who wrote on the characteristics of animals.</note> *chapter 59.*

> The bite of the asp is a bite unto death;
> No, no, Galen, do not even pour out your medicine.
<note>original: "Τῆς ἀσπίδος τὸ δῆγμα δητμ' ἔτι θανάτε, / Μὴ, μὴ Γαληνὲ, μηδὲ Φαρμακον χέῃς."</note>

->That is:<-

*The bite of the snake, which is called Asp,*
*Is deadly, unless the doctors know*
*A means for warding off the venom.*

However, one finds those who have presumed to be able to prevent this deadly evil. Pliny *book 8, chapter 23* and others speak of immediately cutting off the wounded part; others of green Oregano crushed, boiled in wine and drunk; some of garlic in beer, or of Apium <note>A genus of plants including celery and parsley.</note> in wine; some of the gall of a weasel; of the stomach of a stork; even of boiling and eating an Asp. See <term>Kircher</term> <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit scholar known for his wide-ranging interests, including his book "Mundus Subterraneus."</note> in his *Underground World.*

It is told that one [can charm] this Asp with its kin...

# ASPIS.

### T 3

[one can] charm similar creatures and make them stay still, so that they cause no harm: namely, by singing and playing, by which they are wonderfully soothed, tickled, and subdued. On good faith, I shall allow this to flow in here.

> Tibullus *Elegies, Book I, 9.* <note>Albius Tibullus was a Roman poet of the 1st century BC.</note>
> *Song restrains the path of the angry snake.* <note>original: "Cantus & iratae detinet anguis iter."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Singing halts the snake, however greatly it is enraged.*

Virgil: <note>From the "Aeneid," Book VII, describing the healer Umbro.</note>

> *To the viperous race, and heavily breathing hydras,*
> *He was wont to spread sleep with both song and hand,*
> *Soothed their rages, and relieved their bites by his art.*
<note>original: "Vipereo generi, & graviter spirantibus hydris, / Spargere qui somnos cantuque manuque solebat, / Mulcebatque iras, & morsus arte levabat."</note>

->That is, according to Vondel’s translation:<- <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) was the preeminent Dutch poet and playwright of the Golden Age.</note>

> *One who with gesture of hand and song, the adder’s nest*
> *And Hydras, a brood as stinking as the pest,*
> *Knew how to lull to sleep, their wrath to soothe,*
> *And heal their bites through his cunning art.*

Silius [Italicus] concerning the Marmaridae or *Psylli, Book III.* <note>The Psylli were an ancient North African tribe famed for their immunity to snake venom and their skills as charmers.</note>

> *At whose song the horned vipers lay mild.* <note>original: "Ad quorum cantum mites jacuêre cerastae."</note>

->That is:<-

> *At whose song the snake held itself still with its horns.*

The same:

> *At whose song the serpent forgot its venom.* <note>original: "Ad quorum cantus ferpens oblita veneni."</note>

->That is:<-

> *At whose song the snake forgot all its poison.*

<margin>Charming of Snakes.</margin>
Regarding the charming and conjuring of the Asp, whether with verses, the movement of sticks or hands, or by administering substances, etc., one reads more of it than I am inclined to believe. One reads several proofs of this in Bochart, <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a French Protestant scholar who wrote "Hierozoicon," a massive work on the animals of the Bible.</note> from which the proverb in *Psalm 58:5, 6* seems derived: that of stopping one's ears like an Asp or Adder, refusing to listen to the charmers, and so forth.

<margin>Symbolic application.</margin>
Whether one truly undertakes to charm this snake, or whether it stops one ear with dust and the other with its tail <note>A common medieval folk belief was that the "deaf adder" would press one ear to the ground and plug the other with its tail to avoid hearing the charmer's song.</note>, I would think that it serves as a symbol of those upon whom so little can be gained—as with an Asp—regardless of what means one might use or apply; and furthermore, that their venom and wound are deadly.

<margin>Symbol of hospitality.</margin>
I have read that the Egyptians made the Asp, as well as other snakes, tame and raised them in their houses, allowing them to come to their tables, and that the Asp is introduced as a symbol of hospitality, which must not be violated. See Causinus, page 427. <note>Nicolas Caussin (1583–1651), a Jesuit who wrote on Egyptian symbols.</note> I have also noted in his work, and in Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author of "On the Nature of Animals."</note> and others, that the Asp was the ornament of kings, just as the Basilisk was of the Gods, as a symbol of preeminent holiness: and that no injurious or violent hands might be laid upon it, lest Divine vengeance and just punishment follow such a person in all haste.

<column-break/>

I also read in *Isaiah 11:8: That a sucking child shall delight itself over the hole of an Asp or Adder.*

שעשע <note>Hebrew: sha'asha'</note> means *to play, to be joyful*, with great delight and soul-pleasure, to look about with pleasure and familiarity, and to amuse oneself, playing cheerfully and without bashfulness, without fear of being harmed. See Cocceius, Schindler, Pagninus. <note>References to famous 17th-century lexicographers and Hebraists.</note>

It signifies, says the first [Cocceius]: *That Satan would be so trodden under the feet of the church, that it would be a child's delight to play with the poisonous tyrants.* <margin>Interpretation.</margin>

One might likewise think here of those who are yet small in knowledge and weak in faith, who are fed and maintained with milk and not the solid food of weightier mysteries, *1 Corinthians 3:1; Hebrews 5:12-14; Psalm 8; Matthew 21; Isaiah 40:11.* And of the weaned ones, who consume more solid food and have progressed further, *Psalm 131:2; Isaiah 28:9.* And furthermore of the tender and weak, and indeed also more established Christians, being joyful under and with Constantine the Great, because they saw the places of the Heathens and of the devils dedicated to God and His Holy Spirit; and were able, without danger, to discover, handle, and deal with Arius and his heresy; <note>Arius (c. 256–336) was a priest whose teachings regarding the nature of Christ led to the Arian controversy.</note> whose followers carried a foul poison within them, presented as their sanctities, depths, and cunning, as though grown firm in faith and grounded in the knowledge of the truth that sanctifies and makes free. See my *Sacred Miscellany*, part 1, page 107, on *Isaiah 11:8.*

Subsequently, one may look up what has been said regarding the ADDER, ADDER-SNAKE, and ADDER’S VENOM.

For my part, when I see the Asp, I can imagine the crooked, devious serpent, the devil, who turns himself into all sorts of bends and appears in various colors and forms, *2 Corinthians 11.* He is provided, under Divine providence and permission, with power and skill to sink his poisonous teeth into man, to poison him through pride, despair, carelessness, promises, fear, threats, torments, and terrors, etc. Just as he has made man full of wounds and festering boils through the poison of seduction and sin: seized with a spirit of deep sleep and of insensitive and careless tranquility, spiritual blindness, the coldness of love, and occupied and filled both inwardly and outwardly with the irregular passions and movements of the body, so that his poison of sin and seduction is deadly, against which no charm avails. God’s power and providence can bridle him. With prayer, being sober, and watching, one must guard oneself against his fiery bite. The already discharged venom of sin and corruption, spread through soul and body, bringing about death and misery, cannot be overcome except by the power of Christ’s death and life, His blood and indwelling Spirit. Thus this Asp loses its power in our death and resurrection from the dust, *1 Corinthians 15; Romans 16; Hebrews 2:14, 15; 1 John 3:8,* when one is justified from sin; the last enemy destroyed; death swallowed up in full victory, for this is his heaviest and ultimate power. This is indeed commenced on earth but completed at the resurrection, in the incorruptible life, when there shall be a full satiation with God’s image in or upon the awakening.

Other applications to hypocrites, heretics, and similar men I shall not make, but set myself to something else.

### ASH, DUST, שחוק / אבק / אפר / עפר,
### *Cinis, Pulvis*, χὸς, κόνις, σποδὸς, τέφρα.
<note>The heading includes terms for ash and dust in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek, reflecting the scholarly nature of the original text.</note>

<margin>Use of the ash.</margin>
ASH is a foul and lowly thing, through which nothingness is signified, *Gen. XVIII.* <note>Genesis 18:27, where Abraham says, "I who am but dust and ashes."</note> Man, specifically, consists of dust and ash and shall return to that state. It was used by Jews and Pagans in times of humiliation and penance, when one suffered distress due to general or specific evils and misfortunes: with which one sprinkled one's head and clothes, or scattered it beneath oneself, and wallowed in it: and even ate it mixed with other food in extreme grief. This was done both to humble oneself and to depict one's nothingness and unworthiness, as well as to show one's weakened and oppressed state; likewise to move God or someone else to compassion and mercy. See *Job XXX. Isa. LXI. Jer. XXV. 2 Sam. XIII. Esther IV. Jer. VI. Ezek. XXVII. Job II. Ps. CII. Isa. XLIV. Joshua VII. 2 Sam. XII. Isa. XXVII. Lam. II. and III.* etc.

<margin>Penance of the first Christians.</margin>
That such was also the practice and penance of the first Christians has been shown to us in abundance by *Tertullian, Apol. ch. 40. and De Poenit. book 1. ch. 9. Cyprian, Epist. 47. Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. book v. Gejerus and Dilherr, Elect.* <note>These are citations to Early Church Fathers and 17th-century theologians like Martin Geier.</note>

<margin>Of the Jews and Pagans.</margin>
What the penitential use of this was among the Jews and Pagans can be learned thoroughly from *Gejerus, De luctu Hebraeor.* <note>On the Mourning of the Hebrews</note>, *Kirchmann, De Funer.* <note>On Funerals</note>, *Pfeiffer, Antiq. Hebr.*, *Dieterich, Antiq. V. T.*, *Doughty in Analect.* etc.

And so as not to insert everything belonging to this matter here, I shall merely provide a few examples from grey antiquity as proof, namely:

Homer, Odyssey 8. <note>Though cited as Odyssey 8, these lines are famous from the mourning of Laertes in Book 24, or Achilles in the Iliad.</note>

> Ἀμφοτέρῃσι δὲ χερσὶν ἑλὼν κόνιν αἰθαλόεσσαν
> Χεύατο κὰκ κεφαλῆς, πολιῆς ἀνιδὼν στεναχίζων.
<note>original Greek: "With both hands he took the soot-colored dust and poured it over his grey head, groaning heavily."</note>

->That is:<-

*He scattered, while sighing, with both hands*
*Upon his grey crown much ash, hot from the fire.*

Furthermore:

> Ἀμφοτέρῃσι δὲ χερσὶν ἑλὼν κόνιν αἰθαλόεσσαν
> Χεύατο κὰκ κεφαλῆς, χαρίεν δ' ᾔσχυνε πρόσωπον.
> Νεκταρέῳ δὲ χιτῶνι μέλαιν' ἀμφίζανε τέφρη,
> Αὐτὸς δ' ἐν κονίῃσι μέγας μεγαλωστὶ τανυσθείς.
<note>original Greek: "With both hands he took the soot-colored dust and poured it over his head, and defiled his fair face. The black ash settled on his fragrant tunic, and he himself lay mighty in his mightiness, stretched out in the dust." (Iliad 18.23-26)</note>

->That is:<-

*He scattered glowing dust on his head with both hands,*
*And smeared his fair face: it bore dust black from burning,*
*Clinging fast to his robe, however costly: and he lay*
*As great as he was, stretched out on the earth all day.*

Virgil, Aeneid 10.

> Canitiem immundo deformat pulvere, & ambas
> Ad caelum tendit palmas, & corpore inhaeret.
<note>original Latin: "He defiles his grey hair with foul dust, and stretches both palms to heaven, and clings to the body." (Aeneid 10.844-845, describing Mezentius mourning his son.)</note>

->That is:<-

*He scatters through his grey hair impure dust, and stretches*
*Two hands out, and hangs over the body stretched out.*

<column-break/>

And Aeneid 12.

> ————— It scissa veste Latinus,
> Conjugis attonitus fatis, urbisque ruina,
> Canitiem immundo perfusam pulvere turpans.
<note>original Latin: "Latinus goes with torn garment, stunned by the fate of his wife and the ruin of the city, defiling his grey hair sprinkled with foul dust." (Aeneid 12.609-611)</note>

->That is:<-

> ————— Latinus, thus terrified
*By the end of his spouse, the ruin of the city, sobs*
*And sighs, and tears his clothes, and scatters his grey locks*
*Full of filth and full of dust.*

Hecuba, in Seneca's tragedy *The Trojan Women*,

> Solvite crinem. per colla fluant
> Moesta capilli tepido Troiae
> Pulvere turpes.
<note>original Latin: "Loosen your hair; let the mournful locks flow along your necks, foul with the warm dust of Troy." (Seneca, Troades 83-85)</note>

->That is:<-

*Untie your hair, let it flow*
*Along your neck, sprinkled with ash*
*From Troy's ruins, still hot from the glow.*

And shortly thereafter:

> Solvimus omnes
> Lacerum multo funere crinem
> Coma demissa est libera nodo,
> Spargitque cinis fervidus ora.
<note>original Latin: "We have all loosened our hair, torn by many a death; the hair is let down, free from its knot, and the burning ash sprinkles our faces."</note>

->That is:<-

*Our hair is untied,*
*Which we defiled for so many corpses.*
*Our hair hangs loose and free.*
*The glowing ash covers our faces herewith.*

Catullus,

> — Primum multas expromam mente querelas,
> Canitiem terra atque infuso pulvere turpans.
<note>original Latin: "First I shall pour out many complaints from my mind, defiling my grey hair with earth and poured-on dust." (Catullus 64.223-224)</note>

->That is:<-

*I shall utter complaints for the sorrow I have suffered,*
*And scatter ash and dust in my grey hair.*

That which pertains to this, such as dust, sackcloth, etc., shall be touched upon at a more convenient time. Meanwhile, one may make use of the present, and greet the mentioned authors closely; also my *Miscellanies* [Mengelstoffen], Volume II.

As a supplement, also for further distinction regarding what has been said, let the reader make use of the following:

1. To scatter dust and ash on one's head can be considered to represent not only uncommon grief: but at the same time one's own frailty, nothingness, and worthlessness, as we—in consideration of our nothingness and impotence compared to God—pray for grace, forgiveness, and help. *Josh. VII. 6. 2 Sam. XXIII. 19. Job X. 9. Ps. CIII. 13. Isa. LXI. 1. Matt. XI. 21.* etc.
2. Man is called "dust" following the entry of sin and misery into the world, since his body is built up from dust; he walks upon the dust; he has as food that which comes forth from the earth's dust; he generally seeks, loves, and clings to dust and material things; and finally must return to dust.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical entry for "Asse" (Ash) and "Stof" (Dust) before transitioning to a major entry on "Assur" (Assyria). It moves from the symbolic meaning of dust to the historical and prophetic significance of the Assyrian Empire.</meta>

# ASH. ASSYRIA.

<margin>Dust as a symbol for vain people.</margin>
3. Furthermore, dust is a symbolic representation of base, vain, worldly-minded people who do not possess the Spirit, and whose portion is in this life. *Genesis 3:17, Isaiah 65:25, Psalm 17:14, Philippians 3:19, Jude verse 19, etc.*

4. Dust and ash, being nothing, having little permanence, easily vanishing, flying away, or being scattered, etc., can—according to the nature and power of the imagination—be regarded as representing something which in itself is of little value, which one counts for very little, and which is without permanence or durability. *Job 13:12, Isaiah 40:15, and 44:20, etc.*

5. To press someone down into dust and ash differs remarkably from raising them up out of the dust. *Lamentations 3:16, 1 Samuel 2:8, 1 Kings 16:2, Psalm 113:7.* <note>The author contrasts the imagery of humiliation with the imagery of exaltation.</note> Just as the first borrowed figure of speech intends to represent making someone very small, humbling them, and causing heavy grief and pain to overcome them; so, by way of contrast, the latter figure of speech will be a symbol that matter for joy, deliverance, and exaltation is being granted to someone.

---

### ASSUR, ASSYRIA. אשור <note>original: "Ashur"</note>

<margin>The location of Assyria.</margin>
ASSYRIA is a province or region, situated not far from Chaldea in the east by the river Tigris, whose capital is Nineveh; it is said to be located between two rivers, the Diaba (also called the Lycus) and the Adiava; it is named Kurdistan or Diarbech <note>modern Diyarbakır</note>, whose capital is Mosul. It was not built (as some believe) by Nimrod, by whom Babel was built, but was built and its primary foundations laid by Assur, son of Shem. Seeing the stirrings of Nimrod (from the lineage of Ham) and being dissatisfied, Assur went from there to the land that was named after him. *Genesis 10.*

I am well aware that some wish to rely on *Genesis 10* and *Micah 5:5*, but I find the land of Assur and the land of Nimrod to be distinct, even though they are grouped together. That they are joined there happens only because the people, who once constituted a civil body and state, were led away captive partly to Assyria and partly to Babylonia; and it is very likely that Babel was in the power of Assyria when Micah delivered this prophecy. For the rest, Nimrod founded Babel, and Assur founded Assyria.

Regarding the names Assyrians, Syrians, Syren, or Syreërs, and their lesser or greater extent, one can consult other writers, especially Bochart's *Phaleg* and Selden’s *On the Syrian Gods*. <note>original: "de diis Syris." Samuel Bochart and John Selden were prominent 17th-century scholars of biblical geography and mythology.</note>

<margin>Nineveh built by Ninus.</margin>
It is said that Ninus, the son of Assur, built Nineveh.

The idea that Assur, as well as Nimrod, was called Belus or Bel, does not carry as much difficulty as some imagine. It is a common name from בעל <note>original: "Baal"</note> meaning "Lord," and was very likely taken for God: which name was sometimes used. See Selden’s *On the Syrian Gods, etc.*

As for the world's chronology, in which the first and primary foundations of the Assyrian power (rightly held to be the first and greatest) were laid, I believe it cannot be so easily determined. Some speak of the year 1717 after the creation, others of 1843, etc. And

<column-break/>

that this absolute, sovereign, sole rule lasted 500 years; others say 1070; others 1300; some 1673, 1677, 1693; and thus, opinions differ significantly depending on whether one counts the intervening periods or not, and whether the empire fell to others or was joined with other kingdoms.

Hornius <note>Georgius Hornius, a 17th-century historian</note> calculates that of thirty-eight kings, Belus (or Assur, in my opinion) was the first, and Sardanapalus was the last, from whom Arbaces or Arbactus, leader of the Medes, took the empire. He states that the Babylonians and Assyrians again came into control of the empire after it had been in the power of the Medes for three hundred and fifty years.

<margin>Shalmaneser and Sennacherib.</margin>
Among the Assyrian kings particularly known in the Holy Scroll <note>The Bible</note>, one finds Shalmaneser and Sennacherib, by whom Jerusalem was besieged and Israel was led away captive beyond Damascus.

Among the Babylonians, Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar. After these were finished off by King Darius, the Assyrian empire fell into the hands of the Persians, at which time *Isaiah 10* and *Daniel 2* reached their end.

This is sufficient as far as it serves my purpose; I shall move on to something else.

<margin>Application of the names of kings and peoples.</margin>
I notice that God's Spirit, while retaining the proper names of kings and ancient peoples, applies them:
1. Either to peoples and states that inhabit that land and region.
2. Or to peoples similar in life, customs, and religion.
3. Or to peoples who stand fairly equal to the former in judgments and actions.
4. I notice that Babel, Sodom, and Egypt are often taken not literally, but must be taken spiritually and figuratively.
5. I find things that cannot properly be applied to Assur specifically, just as they cannot be applied to Babel. I believe, however,
6. That God's Spirit has determined the matter and the time, just as God makes everything beautiful in its time. I will therefore maintain that, if I cannot find the fulfillment regarding the ancient Assyrian empire itself, I may seek it in those who are similar to Assur and Assyria, or who inhabit the land of Assur and Assyria. Since I cannot find everything the Prophets foretold concerning Assur and Assyria in the old Assyria—any more than all other things can be found in Egypt, Babel, Sodom, etc., except as in a deficient history and imperfect sketch—it seems to me, especially as the thread of prophecy leads me there, that I must seek it in the descendants, or in those who inhabit the regions of these ancient peoples. This is especially true when there is a sufficiently close and neat correspondence between the old and the new, matching the speaker's purpose and the nature of what was delivered.

I shall then proceed on this footing, not to demonstrate, but—presupposing the service and wise labor of another man—say that when I hear the Divine Secret Scroll speak of Assur and Assyria, I shall understand it in some places to mean the Saracens, Turks, Mohammedans, and furthermore all peoples and kings, alongside the significant powers of the East, who occupy the province of Assyria and have acquired other lands besides. And so as not to make long elaborations,

### EVENING, LORD'S SUPPER, EVENING OFFERING, EVENING SHADOW, EVENING WOLF.

<margin>In which there is night and day. *Genesis 1.*</margin>
The word EVENING can be understood in a broader or narrower sense. Thus, "evening and morning" is taken for a full day or 24 hours.

When taken with more specific limits, however, it has a greater or lesser span of time: and so it is used for the time itself after the midday sun begins to decline, before whose setting several hours still pass.

Otherwise, it is taken more strictly for the time when the sun pants toward its setting <note>The Dutch "hygt" (panting/straining) suggests the sun's effort to reach the horizon.</note> or is already below our horizon, or when the light is twilight, dusky, and already dark.

<margin>Evening wolves.</margin>
Thus one reads of EVENING WOLVES, *Habakkuk 1, Zephaniah 3, Jeremiah 5,* which run in the evening, seeking their prey and bait. But that this is spoken of in an allegorical manner is not difficult to understand; and by these wolves one can understand not only the Jewish Pharisees and Scribes, but all those in the civil and ecclesiastical state who make use of the evening and darkness, and the twilight of ignorance and misery in the state of the people or the church, to serve the booty and robbery of the soul or the body, of temporal goods, etc.

<margin>Compared with the Pharisees.</margin>
I am inclined to believe that one can view the evening as a symbol of the Jewish civil and ecclesiastical state near the bleak night of its downfall, destruction, deepest ignorance, and extreme misery. To this refers *Genesis 49:27,* "in the evening he shall divide the spoil," which I see applied quite aptly to Paul—who was originally of the tribe of Benjamin—by Alting, Sigonius, Gürtler, etc. <note>These are 17th-century theologians: Jacob Alting, Carolus Sigonius, and Nicolaus Gürtler.</note> Paul, in the "evening" of the Jewish state, snatched away noble spoil from the Jews and Gentiles out of the hands of Satan. It also refers to the cycle of the world, before its final decline, as well as for man's time and state, which the night of his death precedes.

But it is also used generally as a symbol of judgments upon states and peoples, accidents, darkness, and gloom of soul or body—whether present, or firmly foreseen, threatened, and approaching—as in *Proverbs 7:9, Jeremiah 6:4, Ezekiel 12:4-7, Zephaniah 2:7,* etc. In these cases, evening and morning are introduced to signify a very hasty and sudden extermination and heavy judgments upon the enemies of God and His church, as in *Isaiah 17:14;* compare *Isaiah 37, 2 Kings 19.*

<margin>Evening and Morning signify weeping and joy.</margin>
Or that by evening and morning, weeping and joy are signified; to let it be understood how God's loving-kindness, mercy, and rescue are near His people, so that His loving-kindness and mercy exceed the exercise of His severity: and His severity is changed into loving-kindness and mercy; so that commonly wrath, severity, and judgments go before, paving the way to release, freedom, and assistance for compensation and soothing, *Psalm 30:6 <note>Note: Original cites Psalm 35:6, likely meaning 30:6: "weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning."</note> and 37:37, and 97:10. Isaiah 54:7, 8. Lamentations 3:22, 23-31. Job 16:20. 2 Corinthians 4:17.*

It is said in *Zechariah 14:7* that in the evening it would be neither day nor night, yet still light.

I am inclined to believe that in the evening of the Old Testament, in the time of Christ and His Apostles before the full night of the Jewish judgment of extreme blindness, hardening, and desolation, it was neither day nor night; light and darkness, a mixture of shadows and the body, law and Gospel, not without clouds and heavy mists: a state mingled with good and evil, prosperity and adversity, sadness and joy; and that in later times of the evening of the world and the church it will be just so; for one seldom finds a clear day, or one thing or another is lacking, which will be especially noticed in later times, whether one interprets it as the true church of Christ or the Antichristian one, when the supposed sun and moon shall begin to faint, and the stars be moved and fall from heaven.

Regarding what concerns the LORD'S SUPPER and EVENING OFFERING, I must still mention something.

<column-break/>

The word *Supper* <note>original: "Coena"</note>, *Supper* <note>original: "Δεῖπνον" (Deipnon)</note>, *Meal, Evening meal, the Lord's Supper* <note>original: "Δεῖπνον κυριακὸν" (Deipnon kyriakon)</note>, is known in the Holy Scriptures and by worldly writers.

<margin>Evening meal.</margin>
One finds it held by some that *Supper* <note>original: "Coena"</note> is the same as *common* <note>original: "κοινὴ" (koinē)</note>, since of old people began to eat separately. "Evening meal" comes from the time of the evening, formerly held at the 9th hour by the Romans <note>3:00 PM</note>, but on feast days at the 5th and 6th hours <note>11:00 AM or 12:00 PM</note>. Menzie Hoffman. *Universal Lexicon.*

<margin>The Lord's Supper.</margin>
The Holy Supper of the Lord is known from the Holy Scripture and appears under various names among the Church Fathers, namely: *The Lord's Supper* <note>original: "Δεῖπνον κυριακὸν"</note>; *blessing* <note>original: "εὐλογία" (eulogia)</note>, *thanksgiving* <note>original: "εὐχαριστία" (eucharistia)</note>, *the Lord's table* <note>original: "τράπεζα κυρία" (trapeza kyria)</note>, *breaking of bread* <note>original: "κλάσις ἄρτου" (klasis artou)</note>, *communion* <note>original: "κοινωνία" (koinōnia)</note>, *the Lord's Supper, blessing, thanksgiving, the table of the Lord, breaking of the bread, fellowship. 1 Corinthians 10 and 11.* *Sacrifice* <note>original: "Θυσία" (Thysia)</note>, *holy sacrifice* <note>original: "ἁγία θυσία" (agia thysia)</note>, *Mass, love feast*, and so forth; upon which I shall not dwell, nor give the reasons for these names.

*Revelation 3:20.* The Lord wishes to come in and keep Supper. Of the Supper, the wedding, the feast of the Lamb, one reads repeatedly in the holy scroll, beginning here on earth, and perfectly completed in heaven; and I believe that contained under this name, and depicted and sketched thereby, is the most inward, closest, sweetest, and most familiar exercise of fellowship between Christ and the church, and every believing soul for the enjoyment of Christ and His acquired grace and benefits, while the church and believing soul strive to give pleasure to Jesus with her pure love and fruits of love.

It is true that Christ in heaven, being in a state of full glory, *1 Corinthians 15,* needs nothing; yet He enters into the church and the humble souls of believers and holds Supper there—not exactly that one bakes unleavened cakes for Him, as happened for the angel or God's messenger in *Genesis 19;* no, properly speaking, Jesus consumes no food or drink, but the church and the believing soul treat Him to the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, *1 Corinthians 5:7, 8,* to pure love, the unleavened lump of an upright and undeceptive heart, *Proverbs 23:26,* "Son, give me your heart." Jesus's food is hearty with the sauce of humility, a small opinion of oneself, regret and

### THE LORD'S SUPPER

and humiliation because of sins; a humbled heart, *Psalm 51, Isaiah 57, Matthew 5.*

In *Revelation 3:20*, it is said that Christ *holds the Supper* with us when He receives with satisfaction the fruits of faith, hope, love, and all kinds of Christian virtues—which we produce through the grace of the Holy Spirit—and rests in them as if with a kind of delight and pleasantness.

We are said to hold the Supper with Christ when we enjoy the goods of grace and glory, which He earned for us through His obedience, with the greatest joy, gladness, and contentment—partially in this life, and fully after this life. For this communion is mutual and reciprocal; if we receive Christ as a guest in our souls, Christ will receive us as guests in heaven. The sign of our love is <note>original Hebrew: אהלי (Oheli)</note> *O my God!*; of Christ’s love <note>original Hebrew: עדי אתה (Adi Atah)</note> *you are my people*. This mutual affection creates mutual sufficiency and rest.

The goods of the believers are shared with Christ, and the benefits of Christ are shared with the believers in return.

<margin>See Vitringa on Revelation, page 159.</margin>
An allusion is made here to *Song of Solomon 4:16*, where there is mutual invitation, fruit, goodness, and hospitality.

The wine and drink poured for the lover of the soul are the tears of repentance, which He gathers in a bottle; the pure and hearty love for Jesus, more excellent than wine, *Song of Solomon 4:10: How beautiful is your excellent love, O sister, O bride? How much better is your excellent love than wine!*

Furthermore, the preparations are found described in *Song of Solomon 4:16: O that my beloved would come to his garden and eat his noble fruits; Song of Solomon 5:1: I have come into my garden, O my sister, O bride, I have plucked my myrrh with my spices, I have eaten my honeycombs with my honey, I have drunk my wine along with my milk.*

It is all through metaphor and imagination: and what shall one more readily understand by it than the inner beauty of the soul—piety, faith, love, hope, humility, gentleness, patience, temperance—all brought to the most excellent practice?

And why should I not set forth as an excellent dish the holy meditations, prayers, sighs, and words of the mouth, *Psalm 19:15 and 141:2, Romans 8*, etc.? Why should I disdain all works of love and charity as sacrifices in Jesus' name? *Matthew 25, Hebrews 13.*

Certainly, when Jesus possesses the hearts of men, and may possess the beautiful inheritance from Jews and Gentiles, that is His pleasure, delight, and satisfaction. *Isaiah 53, Psalm 16:3–6, Isaiah 60 and 62.*

<margin>Idle thoughts of the Jews.</margin>
But let us take more to heart and observe how and with what Jesus receives and entertains the church and every believing soul: namely, not with a banquet like Ahasuerus, *Esther 2*; not with a banquet as the Jews falsely claim, consisting of the largest animals and the noblest wine from Adam’s paradise cellar—not upon the outrageously large Behemoth and Leviathan <note>Behemoth and Leviathan are legendary biblical beasts; the author dismisses Jewish folkloric traditions about eating them in the afterlife as "idle thoughts."</note>, foolish thoughts, and dreams of coarse and sluggish brains.

<margin>Application of the Pelican to Jesus.</margin>
It is told of the Pelican bird that it feeds and gives drink to its young with its own breast-blood: Jesus feeds and refreshes His own with His flesh and blood, *John 5 and 6*; He Himself is the heavenly bread and manna, at

<column-break/>

once a fountain and a rock-stone. *Psalm 36:10, 1 Corinthians 10.*

Seneca and Ovid relate of a fountain in Ethiopia or the land of the Moors, from which water drunk either makes one mad or induces a deep sleep. But this fountain water makes the soul healthy, joyful, and active; it is living water, *Jeremiah 2*; it springs up unto eternity and quenches thirst, *John 4 and 7*; it is a full cup, *Psalm 23*. Here is fullness of merit, for all kinds of benefits, enjoyment, with joy, comfort, and contentment, *John 1:16, Psalm 23:1, Proverbs 13:25, Psalm 36:9, Jeremiah 31:25, Isaiah 25:6*. A Supper far more excellent than those of old, yet not yet brought to its perfection. *Revelation 21, Psalm 16 and 17.*

However, no one leaves it hungry or thirsty, *Song of Solomon 5:1.*

It is not a banquet used to trick or ambush someone under the appearance of friendship, *1 Kings 16, 2 Samuel 13*, and to strike them dead; but one of joy, peace, and love, to make the soul live in joy, *John 6:53, 54, Isaiah 61: I am joyful, etc., Romans 14:16, 17, Job 16:22.*

A continual banquet. That of Ahasuerus lasted 180 days, *Esther 1*; this one begins here in grace and is perfected in eternal joy and glory, *Psalm 16, Matthew 25*. Here it is merely a small taste and a preliminary breakfast, so as not to grow faint, but to sharpen the desire. *Psalm 42 and 63, Philippians 1, Romans 8.*

I also read of a great Supper of the Lord, *Revelation 19:17*, etc., but that is of an entirely different nature. And I believe that it specifically refers to the judgment of the enemies of the church—among whom one may specifically understand the Antichrist and those who have conspired with the Beast—who shall be plagued and crushed by other birds and animals, specifically the barbarians, etc. One may consult Cocceius <note>original: Koccejus</note>, Groenewegen, and others on this.

That which stands in *Revelation 19:17, 18*, etc., I have said contains a Supper of a different nature.

I have noticed that some have wanted to regard the angel standing in the midst of the sun as a sign and symbol of the extraordinary enlightenment regarding the knowledge of the Gospel, and of the Sun of Righteousness: by which first the Apostles and the Apostolic church, and thereafter the church at the Reformation, was enlightened and favored, gradually filling the earth.

By what appears there, I perceive that in a broader sense—namely, by the birds of heaven—one would understand the wild and barbaric peoples whom God has, as it were, called and invited to invade the Roman territory and everywhere the outward church had its seat, such as Italy, Spain, France, Syria, Africa, and elsewhere, *Ezekiel 39:17 and 56:8, 9*. This is then encompassed within no small span of time: primarily, one also understands by the birds the Turks and Saracens, merged into one.

See also *Isaiah 25:6* applied here: because God, through His righteous judgment, has given the riches, glory, and luxuries—which the Great Whore had unrighteously and greedily swallowed—as prey to the Heathens, inviting them as if to a banquet to feast upon them and fatten themselves. See Gulichius, Groenewegen, and other writers.

This figurative device is perfectly theatrical, where various persons flow in, and it serves the completion of the performance: wherein certain victory is promised to Christ, the supreme captain, and the troops who follow him; transferred there, as the commentators have shown, from *Ezekiel 39:17*, although the imagery of this discourse has also been in use in other divine oracles, such as *verse 6; Jeremiah 7:33 and 12:9; 1 Samuel 17:4-6*, which places Grotius has diligently noted. The artistic metaphor, if taken most simply, means that in the war or struggle in which Christ shall take vengeance on the enemies of His church, He shall carry out very terrible judgments, and inflict great—indeed, greater than expected—slaughters among the enemies. Because of the multitude, their fallen and slain bodies could not be buried and shall be left to the birds of heaven to prepare, by way of a metaphorical figure of speech, a supper from them: for such is the fate of unburied corpses, as Tzetzes somewhere recounts regarding *Petefaca* killed by Amytis, the daughter of Astyages, *Chil. 1. 1. verse 100.*

However, there is no doubt that a mystery lies enclosed herein. This angel can very aptly represent here the ministers of the Gospel, gifted with the light of truth—that is, with the knowledge of the word of grace, which is the word of the righteousness of Christ—abundantly clarified at the time of the <term>Reformation</term><note>The 16th-century religious movement that led to the establishment of Protestant churches.</note>: intending to show clearly from the prophecies of the Old Testament and also from the prophecy of this book, that the great day of judgment and of the Lord’s vengeance to be taken upon the enemies on this earth is at hand; it being the divine intent to severely avenge the innocent blood of His servants and the wrong done to His people. *Deuteronomy 32:42, etc.*

<column-break/>

Now it remains for me to speak of the two evenings, and the evening sacrifice, which, since it had much in common with the other burnt offerings, will not be treated by me at great length; there was also an uncleanness until the evening.

Whatever dispute one may make regarding the two evenings, for my part, I do not wish to argue over them, but merely say that I shall understand by them, along with many learned men, the time between the first afternoon descent of the sun and its setting. The first evening was shortly after noon when the sun descended; the second, when it already panted toward its setting, which among the Greeks was called the early evening and the after- or late evening, <note>original Greek: δείλην πρωΐαν καὶ ὀψίαν (deilēn prōian kai opsian)</note>: One may read Josephus, Masius, Bochart, Casaubon, Scaliger, Hofmann’s Lexicon, Goodwin, Bynaeus, etc.

<margin>Time of the eating of the Passover lamb.</margin>
Now between the two evenings, between 3 and 5 o'clock in the afternoon, the Passover lamb had to be slaughtered, thereafter roasted, and eaten before midnight; *Exodus 12; see Josephus Antiquities book 16, chapter 10; Bellarmine book 7, chapter 17; Maimonides on the Passover chapter 1, § 4.* Christ was crucified earlier, yet only died at three o'clock in the afternoon, and after hanging for a little while, was taken down by Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus.

Until which early evening and approaching after- or late evening Israel remained unclean, occupied with outstanding guilt of sin, a written bond, reproach, and remembrance of sins, having as yet nothing that could take away the conscience of sins, or bring about the true and proper <term>reconciliation</term><note>Atonement or making amends for sin.</note>, which is why all sacrifices and means of purification were so many times renewed and repeated.

One also reads of a daily evening sacrifice, as well as a morning sacrifice, consisting in the evening and morning of a year-old lamb as a burnt offering, no older than a year; however, earlier it was pure. *Exodus 22 and 29; Numbers 28, etc.*

The evening sacrifice was offered to God at three o'clock in the afternoon. On the Sabbath, another offering followed, *Exodus 29*, and when Passover fell on a Sabbath, it is said that they began the work earlier.

<margin>Grain and drink offering.</margin>
To this was added a grain offering of fine flour and oil, and a drink offering of wine. *Exodus 39, etc.*

This offering was consumed by fire.

I maintain that this offering also looked toward the true Lamb of God, *John 1:29*, who was consumed by the fire of zeal, *Psalm 69*, and offered Himself blameless to God through the eternal Spirit. *Isaiah 53:4, 5-12; 1 Peter 2.*

Who, although He suffered in the early morning of His life and in the evening of His life, early and late, like the morning and evening sacrifice, *Revelation 13:8; Hebrews 13:8*, yet suffered already early in the morning, was thereafter hung up, and at the time of the evening sacrifice gave up the spirit, *Mark 15:25-34*, thus making an end of all the sacrifices. *Daniel 9:21, 24, 26.*

At the same time, He is the grain offering of our souls, as He who feeds and refreshes us with the most excellent fine flour of the merits of His ground body, the oil of the poured-out Spirit, and the wine of grace, strengthening, and comfort.

I also believe that His members, overflowed with the Spirit, strengthened and gladdened by the wine of the grace and love of God poured out in their hearts in and through Christ, allow themselves to be ground like flour, whereby they do not shrink from filling up the remnants of Christ's sufferings. *Colossians 1:24; 2 Timothy 4:6; Philippians 2:17, etc.*

A constant feast. That of Ahasuerus lasted 180 days, *Esther 1*; this one begins here in grace and is perfected in eternal joy and glory, *Psalm 16, Matthew 25*. Here it is merely a small taste and a pre-breakfast, so as not to faint, but to sharpen the desire. *Psalm 42 and 63, Philippians 1, Romans 8.*

I also read of a great supper of the Lord, *Revelation 19:17,* etc., but that is of an entirely different nature. And I believe that it specifically refers to the judgment of the enemies of the church, among whom one may specifically understand the Antichrist and those who have joined with the beast, who shall be plagued and crushed by other birds and animals—specifically the barbarians, etc. One may consult Cocceius, Groenewegen, and others on this.

Regarding what stands in *Revelation 19:17, 18,* etc., I have said that it contains a Supper of a different nature.

I have noticed that some have wished to regard the angel standing in the midst of the sun as a sign and symbol of the extraordinary enlightenment toward the knowledge of the Gospel and of the sun of righteousness: with which first the Apostles and the Apostolic church, and later the church at the Reformation, were enlightened and blessed, gradually filling the earth.

From what appears there, I notice that in a broader sense—namely, by the birds of heaven—one would understand the wild and barbaric peoples whom God has, as it were, called and invited to invade the Roman territory and everywhere where the outward church had its seat, such as Italy, Spain, France, Syria, Africa, and elsewhere, *Ezekiel 39:17 and 56:8, 9.* This is not confined to a small span of time; primarily, one also understands the birds to be the Turks and Saracens, merged into one.

See also *Isaiah 25:6* applied here: because God, through His righteous judgment, has given the riches, glory, and luxuries—which the Great Whore <note>A common Reformation-era term for the corrupt Roman Church.</note> had unrighteously and greedily swallowed down—as plunder to the Heathen, inviting them as if to a feast to graze and fatten themselves therein. See Gulich, Groenewegen, and other writers.

This imagery is perfectly suited to its setting, where various persons enter in, and it serves to complete the presentation: wherein certain victory is promised to Christ, the **chief commander**, and the troops who follow Him. This angel can very aptly represent the **ministers of the Gospel**, gifted with the light of truth—that is, with the knowledge of the word of grace, which is the word of Christ’s righteousness—abundantly illuminated at the time of the **Reformation**. They shall clearly demonstrate from the prophecies of the Old Testament and also from the prophecy of this book that the great day of judgment and of the Lord’s vengeance upon the enemies on this earth is at hand; it being the divine purpose to severely avenge the innocent blood of His servants and the wrong done to His people. *Deuteronomy 32:42, etc.*

<column-break/>

Now it remains for me to speak of the **two evenings**, and the evening sacrifice, which, since it had much in common with the other burnt offerings, will not be treated by me at great length; there was also an uncleanness "until the evening."

Whatever dispute may be made over the "two evenings," for my part, I do not wish to quarrel over them, but merely say that I shall understand by them, along with many learned men, the time between the first afternoon-descending of the sun and its setting. The **first evening** was shortly after midday when the sun declined; the **second** was when it already panted toward its setting, which the Greeks called the early evening and the late or tardy evening, <note>original Greek: δείλην πρωΐαν καὶ ὀψίαν (deilēn prōian kai opsian)</note>. One may read Josephus, Masius, Bochart, Casaubon, Scaliger, Hoffmann’s Lexicon, Goodwin, Bynaeus, etc. <note>These are prominent 16th and 17th-century biblical scholars and philologists.</note>

<margin>Time of the eating of the Paschal lamb.</margin>
Now between the two evenings, between 3 and 5 o'clock in the afternoon, the **Paschal lamb** had to be slaughtered, thereafter roasted, and eaten before midnight; *Exodus 12. See Josephus, Antiquities book 16, chapter 10; Bellarmine book 7, chapter 17; Maimonides on the Passover, chapter 5, section 4.* Christ was crucified earlier, yet died only at three o'clock in the afternoon, and after hanging for a little while, was taken down by Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus.

Until which early evening and approaching late evening Israel was **unclean**, occupied with outstanding guilt of sin, a written bond, reproach, and a remembrance of sins, having as yet had nothing that could take away the consciousness of sins or bring about the true and proper atonement—which is why all sacrifices and means of purification were so often renewed and repeated.

One also reads of a **daily evening sacrifice**, as well as a morning sacrifice, consisting in the evening and the morning of a year-old lamb as a burnt offering, no older than a year, though earlier it was pure. *Exodus 22 and 29, Numbers 28, etc.*

The evening sacrifice was offered to God at three o'clock in the afternoon. On the Sabbath, another offering followed, *Exodus 29*, and if Passover fell on a Sabbath, it is said that they began the work earlier.

<margin>Grain and drink offering.</margin>
To this was added a grain offering of fine flour and oil, and a drink offering of wine. *Exodus 39, etc.*

This offering was consumed by fire.

I maintain that this offering also looked toward the **true Lamb of God**, *John 1:29*, who was consumed by the fire of zeal, *Psalm 69*, and offered Himself without blemish to God through the eternal Spirit. *Isaiah 53:4, 5-12, 1 Peter 2.*

Who, although He suffered in the early morning of His life and in the evening of His life—early and late, like the morning and evening sacrifice, *Revelation 13:8, Hebrews 13:8*—yet He had already suffered early in the morning, was thereafter hung up, and at the time of the evening sacrifice gave up His spirit, *Mark 15:25-34*, thus making an end of all the sacrifices. *Daniel 9:21-24-26.*

At the same time, He is the grain offering of our souls, as He who feeds and refreshes us with the excellent fine flour of the merits of His **ground body**, the oil of the poured-out Spirit, and the wine of grace, strengthening, and consolation.

I also believe that His members, drenched with the Spirit, strengthened and gladdened by the wine of the grace and love of God shed abroad in their hearts in and through Christ, allow themselves to be **ground like flour**, whereby they do not shrink from filling up the remains of the sufferings of Christ. *Colossians 1:24, 2 Timothy 4:6, Philippians 2:17, etc.*

It is a truth to me that on the Sabbath of the New Testament, one ought to bring a double offering to God: of prayers, thanksgivings, and the dedication of oneself in soul and body, on account of our redemption, freedom from sins, the yoke, and the fear of death leading to servitude. *Ezekiel 46:13, 14, 15. etc.*

<margin>Christ's sacrifice does not need to be repeated.</margin>
Since Christ's sacrifice lacks the imperfection that accompanied these ancient offerings, it does not need to be repeated. *Daniel 9; Isaiah 66; Hebrews 10.*

That these offerings—morning, evening, and throughout the entire day—were either accompanied by prayers and thanksgivings, or took their place upon the destruction of the City and Temple, or were already in practice, they could have in some measure sketched out the unceasing prayers and thanksgivings. And that prayers and thanksgivings are no less than morning and evening sacrifices, *Psalm 141* <note>The source text says Psalm 161 (CLXI), but as the Psalms only go to 150, this is likely a reference to Psalm 141:2, which mentions the evening sacrifice.</note> I also believe that the established hours of prayer and thanksgiving were in use quite early, *Acts 3 and 10 and 2:15.* However, to scrutinize this or to argue it extensively does not please me; nevertheless, to make a very brief overview of it in passing will not be useless.

### AZAZEL. עזאזל <note>original: "Azazel"</note>

<margin>Difference of opinions regarding Azazel.</margin>
One reads of AZAZEL in *Leviticus 16,* where it is found in our translation as *the goat that goes away* <note>The "Scapegoat."</note>, set in contrast to the goat for the Lord, which was offered for atonement. All the circumstances, being of deep insight and secret meaning, may well be read with attention. It is also certain that the Jews are so wrapped up in a secret regarding this, that one only makes guesses at the matter, without being certain whether one hits the mark or not: and of this mind were Maimonides <note>The Great Jewish philosopher, also known as Rambam.</note> *More Nebochim*, Jonathan, Samarita, Arama and others.

AZAZEL (עזאזל), which has been translated by imitation as the *outgoing goat*, is found to be hidden in such darkness, and wrapped in so deep a secret, that one only makes guesses at the matter, without being certain whether one hits the mark or not: and of this mind were Maimonides *More Nebochim*, Jonathan, Samarita, Arama and others.

However, many have ventured to maintain that AZAZEL (עזאזל) signifies a rough and high mountain, not far from Sinai, called *Tzokin* (עזוקין) by the Jews. One reads of this in the Babylonian Gemara *Joma fol. 66; Babyl. Bava Mezia fol. 36; in the book Siphre;* by Rabbi Kimchi in the book *Radic.* and Aben Ezra. This translation is listened to by Oleaster, Vatablus, Pareus, Morinus and others. They claim that the goat which was released and led away to this mountain by a certain man had a red-colored small patch of cloth, cut in the shape of a tongue: that the red patch was attached with one end to the goat’s head or horns, and the other end being fastened to the rocky mountain, the goat was pushed down, which, before it was halfway down, was already divided into a thousand shreds and pieces.

<margin>Trifling story.</margin>
Now if this red patch remained red, it was a sign from the God of the covenant, who remained angry; but, if it turned white, it was a sign of reconciliation, *Isaiah 1:18.* which then, with a trumpet from there, and in great haste at the sound of the first, was echoed throughout all of Palestine. See Freismuth *De Birco Emissario, Opus Theol. Germanor. pag. 215 and 216 etc.* Certainly a heap of trifles, for the invention of which one finds no ground in the Holy Scroll.

The opinion of understanding it as a mountain has long been shown to be idle and groundless, from these observations:

<margin>Observations.</margin>
*a.* One does not read in the original language *Azazel*, but *for*, or *to Azazel*.
*b.* One does not find that a mountain is set against the Lord as a person, but a person against a person.
*c.* Where is any mountain known by the name of Azazel?
*d.* Which of the travelers has ever seen or described it? And if it is a mountain, why does Moses not say, "the mountain Azazel"? Thus he speaks of Mount Sinai, Nebo, etc.
*e.* And is it believable, that at the annual feast, all the way to Sinai, so many miles away, through the waste and desert, over mountain and dale, a goat would have been led away?
*f.* It has also been noted that it should not then stand as עזאזל, but as עזאזל. <note>The author is likely making a grammatical or vowel-point distinction in the Hebrew.</note>
*g.* For the rest, one seems not so much on...

# AZAZEL.

<meta>catchword: turn</meta>

to have [a connection] with this supposed mountain, when one speaks of it as merely an hour's journey back and forth, or roughly three miles outside of Jerusalem, at the moment when one guesses that the goat would have reached the entrance of the wilderness. Thus, in a word, these seem to me to be old opinions and propositions without foundation—indeed, without even the appearance of a valid entry point.

There are those who do not understand it to be a mountain, but a desert, a wilderness, a place far from the common road, or somewhere where no one goes, out of the way; a place that is desolate and lonely. Thus, they derive it from the Arabic word *azala*, to remove or separate: <note>original: "azala"</note> *a goat that departs*, intended to be led into a desolate place, which goes away and is carried off. It is as if the text did not state afterward that it had to be carried away; as if it were the name of the goat itself and the place, and the goat was named after the place and its removal. It is as if the text did not set "for the Lord" and "for Azazel" against one another as opposites—as if Jehovah were not a person, and thus Azazel should also be understood as a person by contrast, but rather as if a person and a place were merely being set against each other.

I know that people—though with differing and various insights—derive or translate it as עז אשר אזל <note>original Hebrew: "ez asher azal"</note> *a goat that has departed*, from עז (*ez*), a goat, and אזλ (*azal*), to go away: or by the Greek term *apopompaios*, a free and released animal that is without a master or keeper. <note>original Greek: "ἀποπομπαῖος" (apopompaios), meaning 'one who wards off evil' or 'sent away.'</note>

Similarly, I recall that some equate the word with *apopompaios*, *diestelmenos eis aphesin*, *aperchomenos*, *apolelymenos*: *one who goes away, released, sent forth*. <note>original Greek terms: "διεστελμένος εἰς ἄφεσιν" (appointed for dismissal), "ἀπερχόμενος" (departing), "ἀπολελυμένος" (set free).</note> But I am also aware that this was not understood in the same sense or meaning by everyone, for people spoke of gods who warded off evil: and also of offerings made to turn away and appease some evil, or one or more evil spirits, or to the gods who had the power to ward off evil. See *Marsham, Canon Chronicus, page 205, etc. Witsius, Aegyptiaca, 120, etc.*

And although the Jews did not want this to be an offering strictly for the devil (for the animal remained alive; at least, it was not sacrificed), some nevertheless believe it was done to throw him a morsel, so that he would not disturb or disrupt the feast of atonement and the sacrificial rites, or accuse them before God—as if they wished to blind his eyes with this gift. *Witsius, Aegyptiaca, page 111; Rabbi Eliezer; Buxtorf, Synagoga, etc. Freism.* <note>The author suggests this idea of "bribing" the devil was actually forbidden by the Lord in Leviticus 17.</note>

We have now noted that Azazel has been understood as: the goat itself; the place to which it was led, whether a mountain or wilderness; a released, departing, sent-away goat; and—if the latter holds—for or to the devil, though not as a sacrifice or atonement.

<margin>Opinion of Le Moyne.</margin>
But before I come closer to the last-mentioned point, I must insert here a particular opinion of the learned Le Moyne, in his *Observations on the Epistle of Barnabas, volume 2.* He is of the mind that by Azazel one must understand *the All-Sufficient and Strong God*, implying that these two goats were for the Lord: the first for Jehovah, as Israel's Covenant God for atonement; the second for the All-Sufficient and Almighty God, who in time would become the God of the Gen-

<column-break/>

tiles. However, as learned as this invention and thought of my old, esteemed master may be, it cannot carry my consent. For if it truly must be understood this way, why then this doubling and division in the defining reason? Why not simply say, *both for the Lord?* To what end are these two names necessary? Indeed, if it were for one and the same God, why this strange determination by lot as to which of these goats would be for Jehovah and which for Azazel? Where does the Lord distinguish Himself as the God of the Jews and of the Gentiles through these two distinct names? Where is the Lord ever named Azazel in Holy Scripture or ancient Jewish writings? I do find in Jewish writings that Sammael (the devil) appears among them under this name, but never God. I notice that Jehovah and Azazel—the goat for Jehovah and the goat for Azazel—are distinguished and set against each other, and that the treatment of these two differs greatly, but by no means that they are taken as one and the same. For this reason, I shall for now refrain from this opinion.

<margin>Objection of the author.</margin>
What then? To come closer to my interrupted subject, I say that no simpletons <note>The author means "no small thinkers" or "learned men."</note> understand Azazel to be the devil, the head of the fallen evil spirits.

And if one pays close attention to the matter by way of allusion and application, one will perceive all the power, ingenuity, sweetness, and meaningfulness in it, for:

It is noted that an ancient Christian poet, writing about *Marcus* <note>Likely referring to Marcus the Gnostic.</note>, makes the devil appear under this name, when he sings:

They had eighteen prayers or formulas; the nineteenth was added against the heretics, among whom the Christians were particularly counted. <note>The author refers to the *Birkat ha-Minim*, a blessing added to the *Amidah* prayer</note> See Lightfoot, *On Acts, page 729; in his Hours 250; in the Four Evangelists 519; Chronology of the Temple, page 74.* Vitringa, *The Ancient Synagogue, pages 1033-1039, 1047.* And although they did not necessarily recite those formulas word for word every day, some were used at set times, specifically appointed prayers.
