<margin>Morning and evening prayers.</margin>
Thus, they had morning and evening prayers. Vitringa, *The Ancient Synagogue, 1055. etc.* Lightfoot, *On the Ministry of the Temple, page 720. etc.*

One had to pray, if not aloud at the time of the daily sacrifice, then at least by whispering quietly. Lightfoot, *in his Hours, page 490.*

The prayers were called offerings, and were just as necessary: *Sine stationibus non subsisteret mundus*, that is, *without the standing watches, the world would perish.* <note>The "stations" or *ma'amadot* were groups of laypeople who stood by during Temple sacrifices</note> See *Hebrews 13:15, 16; Kol Bo chapter 65; Maimonides chapters 1, 5, & 8; Selden, On Natural and Gentilic Law, Book III, chapter 3.* Vitringa, *The Ancient Synagogue, page 41.*

And it has been held from of old that with the sacrifices intended to take away the guilt of sin, a prayer and confession of guilt had to be included. Isaac Abrabanel <note>a famous Portuguese Jewish statesman and theologian</note> demonstrates this from the book *Zebachim* <note>a volume of the Talmud concerning animal sacrifices</note>, when he says: *The wise men have taught that with all sacrifices for sins, the confession of guilt must necessarily come.* See Cunæus, *The Hebrew Republic, Book III, pages 339. etc. 439.*

<column-break/>

### AZAZEL. עזאזל

<margin>Difference of opinions regarding Azazel.</margin>
Regarding AZAZEL, we read in *Leviticus 16*, where it is found in our translation as *the departing goat* <note>the scapegoat</note>, set in contrast to the goat for the Lord, which was sacrificed for atonement. All the circumstances, being of deep insight and secret significance, should be read with careful attention. It is also certain that the Jews consider a secret to be involved here, such that one only makes guesses at the matter without being certain whether they hit the mark or not; and of this understanding have been Maimonides in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "more Nebochim"</note>, Jonathan, the Samaritans, Arama, and others.

עזאזל *Azazel*, which has been translated as "the departing goat" by imitation, is found to be hidden in such darkness and involved in such a deep mystery, that one only makes guesses at the matter without being certain whether they hit the mark or not; and of this understanding have been Maimonides in *The Guide for the Perplexed*, Jonathan, the Samaritans, Arama, and others.

However, many have dared to maintain that עזאזל *Azazel* signifies a rough and high mountain, not far from Sinai, called צוק *Tzokin* <note>meaning "cliffs" or "crags"</note> by the Jews. We read of this in the Babylonian Gemara, *Yoma folio 66; Babylonian Bava Metzia folio 36; in the book Sifre:* by Rabbi Kimchi in the book *Roots*; Aben Ezra. This translation is listened to by Oleaster, Vatablus, Pareus, Morinus, and others. They claim that the goat which was released and led away to this mountain by a certain man had a red-colored piece of cloth, cut in the shape of a tongue: that the red cloth was fastened with one end to the goat’s head or horns, and the other end was tied to the rocky mountain; then the goat was pushed down, and before it was halfway down, it was already divided into a thousand shreds and pieces. Now, if this red cloth remained red, it was a sign from the God of the covenant, who remained angry; but if it became white, it was a sign of atonement, *Isaiah 1:18* <note>original: "Jes. III. 18." – the author refers to "though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool"</note>, which was then announced from there with a trumpet, and in all haste at the sound of the first, echoed through all of Palestine. See Freismuth, *On the Scapegoat, Theological Works of the Germans, pages 215 and 216. etc.* Certainly a heap of trifles, for the invention of which one finds no basis in the Holy Scroll.

<margin>Trifles.</margin>
The opinion that a mountain is meant by it has long been shown to be vain and groundless, from these observations:

<margin>Observations.</margin>
*a.* In the original language, one does not read *Azazel*, but *for* Azazel.
*b.* One does not find a mountain being set as an opposite to the Lord as a person, but rather a person against a person.
*c.* Where is there any mountain known by the name of Azazel?
*d.* Which of the travelers has ever seen or described it? And if it is a mountain, why does Moses not say "the mountain Azazel"? Thus he speaks of Mount Sinai, Nebo, etc.
*e.* And is it believable that on the annual feast, all the way to Sinai—so many miles away, through the desolate and dry, over mountain and valley—a goat would be led away?
*f.* It has also been noted that it should not then be written עזאזל, but עזאזל. <note>likely referring to a grammatical or orthographic distinction in the Hebrew</note>
*g.* For the rest, people do not seem to [rely] so much on...

### AZAZEL.

...to have anything to do with this imagined mountain, as some speak only of a journey of an hour here or there, merely about three miles outside of Jerusalem, when they guess that the goat will have reached the entrance of the wilderness. In a word, these seem to me to be old views and propositions without foundation, or even a semblance of logic.

There are those who do not understand it as a mountain, but as a desert, a wilderness, a place away from the common road, or where precisely no one goes, out of the way; a place that is desolate and lonely. This is derived from the Arabic word <term>azala</term> <note>meaning to remove or separate</note>, suggesting a goat intended to depart and be led into the desolate place, one that goes forth and is carried away. It is as if the text did not state afterward that it had to be carried away; as if it were the name of the one goat and the place, the goat of the place and the carrying-away being so named. It is as if the text did not set "for the Lord" and "for Azazel" in opposition and over against one another; as if Jehovah were not a person, and thus by contrast Azazel should also be understood as a person, but rather a person and a place were simply set against each other.

I know that some, though with different and varying insights, derive or translate the term as <term>ez azal othan</term> <note>Hebrew: עז אשל אותן</note>, *a goat that has departed*, from <term>ez</term> <note>Hebrew: עז, a goat</note> and <term>azal</term> <note>Hebrew: אזל, to go away</note>: or by the Greek term <term>apopompaios</term> <note>Greek: ἀποπομπαῖος</note>, a free and released animal that is without master or keeper.

Likewise, I recall that the word is equated with <term>sent away</term>, <term>separated for dismissal</term>, <term>departing</term>, or <term>released</term> <note>Original Greek: ἀποπομπαῖος, διεστελμένος εἰς ἄφεσιν, ἀπερχόμενος, ἀπολελυμένος</note>; but I am also aware that these were not taken in the same respect or meaning, for people spoke of Gods who warded off evil, and also of sacrifices to turn away and appease some evil, or one or more evil spirits: or to the Gods who could turn away evil. See *Marsham Canon Chron. p. 205. etc. Witsius Egypt. 120. etc.*

And although the Jews did not want this to be an offering strictly for the devil (for the animal remained alive; at least, it was not sacrificed), some nevertheless believe it was done to throw him a morsel, so that he would not disturb or disrupt the feast of atonement and the sacrificial rites, or accuse them before God, as if they wished to blind his eyes with this gift. *Witsius Egyptiaca p. 111. R. Eliezer in capite, Buxtorf. Synagog. etc. Freism.* Yet the Lord had clearly forbidden such things. *Lev. XVII.*

It has now been noted that Azazel has been understood as the goat itself; the place to which it was to be led, whether a mountain or desert; a released, departing, sent-away goat; and if the latter holds, to or for the devil, though not as a sacrifice or atonement.

But before I come closer to the last-mentioned point, I must interpose here a particular view of the learned Le Moine, in *Observat. ad epist. Barnabae, vol. 2.* He is of the opinion that by Azazel one must understand the all-sufficient and strong God, suggesting that these two goats were for the Lord: the first for Jehovah, as Israel's Covenant God for atonement; the second for the all-sufficient and almighty God, who in time would become the God of the Gentiles.

<margin>View of le Moyne.</margin>

<column-break/>

But however learned this invention and thought of my old esteemed master may be, it cannot win my consent. For if it must actually be understood in this way, why then this doubling and sifting in the defining reason, and why not simply say, *both for the Lord?* Why were these two names necessary? Indeed, if it were for one and the same God, why this singular determination by lot, as to which of these goats should be for Jehovah and which for Azazel? Where does the Lord characterize Himself as the God of the Jews and of the Gentiles through these two distinct names? Where is the Lord ever called Azazel in Holy Scripture or old Jewish writings? I find in Jewish writings that Sammael the devil appears among them under this name, but never God. I notice that Jehovah and Azazel—the goat for Jehovah and for Azazel—are distinguished and set against each other, also that the treatment of these two differs greatly from one another, but by no means that they are taken as one and the same: and for this reason, I shall for now refrain from this view.

<margin>The author's objection.</margin>

What then? To come closer to my interrupted subject, I say that no simpletons understand Azazel as the devil, the head of the fallen evil spirits.

And certainly, that view is not from today or yesterday; it has no small number of approvers, and it is not easily rejected. See *Lipmanni Nizzachon, R. Eliezer in Capit. R. Abraham. Origen on Levit. XVI and against Celsus, book VI. Mercerus in Preface to Genesis. Buxtorf in Synag. Hebraeor. Cocceius in Lexico, Witsius in Egypt. p. 121. and Oecon. p. 508, 509.* who has nothing against it; nor *Spencerus, Momma, Zwart, Leenhof, etc.*

And if one pays close attention to the matter by allusion and application, one will perceive all the power, ingenuity, sweetness, and richness in it, for,

It is noted that an ancient Christian poet, speaking of the heretic *Marcus*, makes the devil appear under this name, as he sings:

<note>Original Greek: Ἅσοι χορηγεῖ σὸς πατὴρ Σατὰν ἀεὶ, Δι' ἀγγελikῆς δυνάμεως ἀζαζὴλ ποιεῖν.</note>
> What your father Satan always provides for you,
> To do Azazel's work through angelic power.

Rendered into Latin,

<note>Original Latin: Haec tu illa, Satanae fretus auxilio patris, Azazelique, mira designas ope.</note>
> These things you perform, relying on the help of your father Satan,
> And with the marvelous power of Azazel.

In Dutch,

<note>Original Dutch: Uw vader Satan werkt voor u altoos met minnen, Door kragt van Azazel begoochelt gy de zinnen.</note>
> Your father Satan always works for you with love,
> Through the power of Azazel, he bewitches the senses.

If one derives the word Azazel from a strong one who departs, who is fleeing or swift: a departed or retreating goat; who can deny that Satan is called a prince, a mighty one, *Isa. XLIX. Luke XI.*? Called by the Phoenicians <term>azilos</term> <note>Greek: ἄζιλος</note> *alossa, alussa*, one who is strong and powerful: indeed, that he did not keep his first estate, *Jude verse 6.* A goat with whom God has no part or fellowship, *2 Cor. ### AZAZEL.

...certain and dark land, where one lives and wanders outside of God and His fellowship, which is why <term>shedim</term> <note>Hebrew: שדים, meaning demons or spirits</note> are called "solitary," as seen in *Job 2, Matthew 12:43, James 4, etc.* and described by Nachman <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, a medieval Jewish scholar</note> as the <note>original Hebrew: שרה מושל במקומות החרבן</note> "prince who rules in the desolate places."

<margin>Note from Selden.</margin>
Concerning this, Seldenus <note>John Selden, a 17th-century English polymath</note> has noted the following from Rambam <note>Maimonides</note> in his *Prolegomena*: *The Egyptians, serving demons, believed that they appeared in the form of goats, for which reason they called them <term>se’irim</term> <note>Hebrew: שעירים, meaning "hairy ones" or "goats"</note>. This imagination being widespread even in the time of Moses, the eating of goats was forbidden to this people.*

He is a stinking goat who, having turned away from God, not only misleads men into lust, wantonness, and foul sins—driving them forward—but also pushes them into their own destruction. He is like a stinking goat who delights himself in evil, and because of his foul stench of unrighteousness, he may no longer dwell with God nor the pious.

Now, for Azazel, that one goat was determined by lot.

It is recounted of these two goats that they had to be of the same color, age, size, price, and time of selection; however, if there were some small difference, they were not to be rejected solely on that ground: *Maimonides, Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim, chapters 5 and 6.*

Regarding the lots and the casting of lots, etc.: the names **Jehovah** and **Azazel** were written on wood, silver, or some mineral, parchment, or thick paper. These were placed in a jar, wooden box, or vessel and stirred together. When the two goats were placed directly across from the Priest, one to his right and one to his left, he would draw the lots with both hands—one lot in each hand. The lot in the right hand was for the goat standing opposite it, and likewise for the left hand. *Tractate Yoma, chapters 3 and 4; Babylonian Gemara, Yoma 4; Freismuth on the scapegoat, etc.*

<margin>Hands laid upon the goat.</margin>
It is a well-known matter that hands were laid upon the goat, by which one stepped away from his rights and ownership, praying that the sin and God's wrath, along with the curse, might come upon its head.

<margin>Difference among the Jewish masters.</margin>
Whether it had to be led away and sent by a man who was ready at hand, or chosen, capable, and fit—whether a Jew, a Gentile, or a proselyte; a Priest or a Levite—is a matter of some dispute among the Jewish masters.

This having been said briefly regarding the two goats, it should be further noted that the goat for Azazel was not sent away until the goat for atonement and purification was slaughtered, and every ceremony regarding it was completed according to the Law of Moses. See *Leviticus 16*.

<margin>Significance of the first goat.</margin>
It is held here that the first goat signified Christ, and that which He—as the true, only, and perfect High Priest—brought about for His people through His sacrifice and blood, having offered Himself blameless to God through the eternal spirit. I will not dispute this with anyone, but will later demonstrate it more closely in the treatise on the Day of Atonement and the goats. Here, we speak only of the goat for Azazel.

Some have believed that through the goat

<column-break/>

which was slaughtered, alongside the goat that went away laden with sins, it was merely shown that sins are carried and taken away. This suggests that sin must be avoided and escaped, and penance performed for it; the carrying and taking away of sin is such that God and Israel think of it no more, as if it were behind His back, never to arise before Him again. *Socinus, De Servatore, chapter 10; Grotius on Leviticus 16; B. Schem-Tob; Hales; Spencer, De Legibus Hebraeorum.*

<margin>Various opinions.</margin>
Some think of Christ and the Antichrist. Others understand the goat for the Lord to be the believers, the elect, or the repentant thief, or Christ Himself.

By the goat for Azazel, they understand the fallen angels, the rejected unbelievers, the unrepentant thief, or Barabbas.

Finally, others hold that these two goats sketched out Christ in different respects.

Namely, the goat that was killed would represent Christ according to His body—crucified and killed; the goat that remained alive and was led away represents Christ led outside Jerusalem with the burden of sins. His immortal soul is represented by him being both dead and alive through these two goats, as previously seen with the two birds <note>referring to the cleansing of the leper in Leviticus 14</note>. His Divine nature, which does not suffer, is like the second goat, which indeed bears the sin but also carries it away.

He was delivered to God as judge to be slaughtered, and to the devil to be tempted, tormented, and plagued, *Matthew 4; Luke 2:53.* As the goat was led away by Judas, Herod, Caiaphas, Pilate, and the Jews—and whatever more reflections and applications can be found in *Witsius in Oeconomia Foederum, Bierman, Bauman in Analecta, etc.*—too many to write out here.

Whatever may be said of this opinion, held as it is by many great masters, there is this to consider: not only are there many of a different judgment, but there are also quite a few significant difficulties that can challenge the acceptance of this view, namely:

One must carefully note that two distinct goats appear: two distinct and very different persons for whom they are intended; two very different treatments and outcomes of those treatments; and two singular timings and turns in which each receives its due. Indeed, the goat for Azazel has its turn at the very end, after all the solemn duties with the first goat have been performed—after the slaughter and the sprinkling of blood, as well as the atonement, have been completed. From this, one might conclude that one and the same person, Christ—though viewed according to different natures or states—cannot be represented by these two goats. Certainly, if one observes what concerns the first goat—the ceremony the Priest performed with it and its blood, as well as the work of atonement—one will find it all in Christ, as represented by the first goat (the sacrifice) and represented by the High Priest (offering Himself to God as a sacrifice for atonement and cleansing). To what purpose, then, is the second, since everything is contained in the first?

Also, the applications of the second goat borrowed and applied to Christ do not seem to flow well for various reasons: namely, after the first goat had borne the sins and the atonement and cleansing had already occurred through its death and sprinkling, the second goat still remained with the sins...

### AZAZEL.

...burdened: he still had to go to the wilderness and distant lands. Anyone who touched or transported him remained unclean and had to wash himself; atonement still had to be made over or for that goat, and so on. However, Christ could not be represented by him after his death and resurrection, because by his resurrection he was justified, and the believers with him. At that time, he was not unclean; his touch and fellowship did not defile so that one had to wash and be cleansed. In what respect has he—as the <term>antitype</term> <note>A biblical fulfillment of an Old Testament "type" or symbol</note> of the second goat—carried the sins into distant lands, into the wilderness, after he was killed as the antitype of the first? Must atonement still be made over him once he was slaughtered? That goat had to go to the wilderness when the first was slaughtered. Christ was indeed tempted in the wilderness before his death, but not after his death and resurrection. The wilderness is not a symbol of heaven, to which Christ ascended after his death and resurrection to enter the heavenly Holy of Holies with his blood. Thus, he was first tempted and tormented, and thereafter died; he was not tempted last and died first. Christ was not brought far outside Jerusalem, but the goat was brought to the wilderness. After the first goat's death, this goat remained alive and, as they say, was tormented by the devil; but the devil did not only torment Jesus, but also struck him in the heel, as the one holding the power of death. *Genesis 3; 1 Corinthians 15.* And who was it, truly, who led Christ into the wilderness after he was slaughtered as the antitype of the first goat? Neither Judas, nor Herod, nor Pilate, nor the Jews with their ecclesiastical or secular leaders.

<margin>Another opinion.</margin>
For these and other reasons and considerations, which carry quite some weight, one might easily lean toward another thought and opinion, which I shall set down here preferably in the exact words of learned men, namely:

> That the goat which fell by lot for Jehovah was an illustrious symbol of the Lord Jesus, his entire person, and his perfect sacrifice of atonement, through which he perfectly sanctifies all who shall be sanctified for eternity. And the other goat, for Azazel, was a symbol of the earthly High Priests and their subordinate band, as well as all the rebellious mass of that nation that set itself against Christ. Secondly, that the Lord Christ carried away the honor of coming upon the altar of God, and like the goat that was sacrificed and whose blood was brought into the Holy of Holies, so he also rightly appeared as the true Ark of the Covenant. But the goat for Azazel signified the High Priest with his band and the entire mass of the Jews, and that they were rejected by Jehovah, and thus had to wander over the face of the entire world, being handed over to the devil and the hardening of their hearts, bearing the guilt of all that righteous blood which was shed by them and their fathers, from Abel down to Christ. And that Jehovah, as if by lot—that is, by divine decree, both in his word and through deeds and outcomes—declared that he had chosen King Jesus as the only true High Priest, not after the order of Aaron, but after the order of Melchizedek. And that the single sacrifice of his Son, when he offered himself as a sacrifice of a sweet-smelling savor to God his heavenly Father, alone pleased him and gave him delight; but the sacrifices of the Levitical Priests displeased him, as they did not enter the Holy of Holies nor take away sin—

<column-break/>

—and therefore they would no longer serve a temple, sanctuary, or Holy of Holies, but would be scattered and sent away among the Heathens. And fourthly, that all this happened on the great Day of Atonement of Christ’s death, resurrection, ascension, sitting at the right hand of God, and the pouring out of his Holy Spirit, following the anointing of the true Holy of Holies. See Zwart’s *Dispensation of the Times*, page 517; Momma, van der Wayen, Cocceius, etc. <note>These are prominent 17th-century Reformed theologians, often associated with "Covenant Theology."</note>

Whether anything can be forcefully brought against this opinion that cannot be resolved is doubted by many. However, to share the objections of the learned with the reader, and not leave the work half-finished but give everyone reasonable satisfaction, one should observe the following well and intelligently. Namely, one might bring against this opinion:

*That we have one and the same description of these two goats, as both being intended for a sin offering; therefore, they both refer to Christ.* However, it has been noted that regarding these two goats, one has anything but the same description: not one, but two goats; not for one, but for two persons; not one and the same treatment. For how could it be a sin offering where the goat remained alive, was not sacrificed, and where no shedding of blood occurred (*Hebrews 9*)? Rather, one of the two was to be a sin offering, and not both, which the historical definition shows, since the one was not sacrificed, nor was its blood poured out, without which no forgiveness happens.

It is also said: *that atonement occurred through both, and that the lot was not cast over Christ and the rebellious members of the priesthood and the Jews, etc.*

But here too, it is noted that the misunderstanding of these men seems to have arisen from an insufficiently deep understanding regarding the preposition <term>לַעֲזָאזֵל</term> <note>Hebrew: "la-Azazel," usually translated "for Azazel"</note>, which, in such circumstances and figures of speech where sacrifices are mentioned, should not be taken as *for*, but as *over which*. Thus, it does not signify a sacrifice *through* which, but a person or thing *for* which and *over* which atonement shall happen. *Leviticus 16:18, 21, 33* and *4:20*, etc. See Cocceius, Freisimuth, van der Wayen, Momma, Leenhof, Zwart, etc. And certainly, this follows logically, for although the Jews are rejected and driven outwards—no longer standing as of old before the face of the Lord that manifested itself in Jerusalem and in the worldly sanctuary, which is now over the whole earth (*Psalm 8*)—they nevertheless still stand before God's face waiting for atonement, which shall come to them in the end of days, when they shall return from their rejection and exile. *Isaiah 59; Hosea 2 and 3; Psalm 85; 2 Corinthians 3; Romans 11*, etc.

It is true that, according to the literal letter, no lot was drawn over the Christ and the rebellious Jews to decide who would be killed and who would be sent away into the wilderness of heathendom, in separation from God and his covenant people. But also, by a literal lot, it was not determined between Christ as the slaughtered goat and the goat remaining alive (if one wishes to understand it that way) what would happen to him. However, insofar as Christ was foreordained by God, who determines the lot, he was pre-determined for such a sacrifice and priesthood—not after the order of Levi, but Melchizedek's order. His death, suffering, time, place, under whom and by whom, to what end, and with what effects and fruit, were specifically appointed—

# AZAZEL. VINEGAR.

cast out, demarcated, approved, and so on. Thus it is predestined, determined, and signified who are his seed and what is their inheritance: those who are the seed of the devil, who are unbelieving, hardened, deaf, and blind; why, when, and how they would be judged and cast out; and how, finally, grace would come to them and atonement would be made for them. What can one have against this?

The following difficulty is then raised, namely: *The goat bore the sins, and for that purpose hands were laid upon him; if this goat is a symbol of the rebellious Jews and their rejection and sending away, then they must also have borne the sins—that is, the punishment of the unbelieving and rebellious, etc.*

But what difficulty lies herein will not be seen by anyone who has an understanding of the Divine threat in *Exodus 20:5* <note>original: "Exod. XX. 5." This verse refers to God visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children.</note> and understands the saying of our Savior in *Matthew 25:35* and *Luke 11:50*, through which no forgiveness or atonement occurred; for even Christ’s blood remained upon them and their children, according to *Matthew 27*. Under this they remained like the goat, and remained with it in their exile and destruction, until such time as atonement shall be made for them.

As to the claim: *that it has not been seen that on a great Day of Atonement a sign would be given as an image of extermination, or of a very heavy and terrible judgment, etc.* If one observes the old dispensation <note>original: "huishoudinge," referring to the Mosaic Law or "Old Covenant"</note>, it was a ministry of death and condemnation, according to *2 Corinthians 3*. It wrought wrath; everything was bound with the curse. One had to sign a "handwriting of debt" <note>A legal metaphor for the Law's requirements</note> even as grace—though veiled—was perceived. So too were wrath, curse, fear of death, and extermination from the people; because God willed to work both wrath and grace. For He knew beforehand to whom He would show grace and toward whom He would exercise severity; who the true and the false Israel was; who would accept Christ and His sacrifice of the Son, and who would reject Him, take offense at Him, and stumble and fall, etc. What wonder is it that at one and the same time, grace and severity were depicted through two distinct goats? The feasts were for the joy of the believers, but not for the unbelievers. In the day of the greatest grace, the heaviest wrath was perceived, yet only over the unbelieving and disobedient (*Hebrews 3:18-19*; *Hebrews 2:3* <note>original: "Hebr. III. 36. Hebr. II. 3." The citation of 3:36 is likely a printer's error for 3:18-19</note>), and such a terrifying and righteous judgment lay in this ministry when they did not take refuge through faith in Him who was depicted by the sacrificial goat of atonement. That Israel did not understand it as such—at least not the great majority—I believe; however, this in no way diminishes the Lord's intent, goal, and purpose in this; for they had almost no or very little understanding of Moses' dispensation; for otherwise they would not have rejected the Rock of Salvation.

If it is brought up *that it would seem to follow from these men’s position as if Israel had to offer to the devil:* to this the answer is ready that even the Jews do not feel that it was an actual offering for the devil; much less the Christians or their theologians. It is true that God rejected the Jewish sacrifice and allowed that of Christ to prevail for Himself (*Psalm 40*). It is true that, according to divine determination, God and Satan each have their own. It is true that the unbelieving and rebellious people remained burdened with their sins. It is true that the fleshly, unbelieving, and rebellious Jews were handed over to Satan for blinding and hardening for a time, and sent away to Heathen lands, alienated from the church and the fellowship of the spiritual Israel of God—even though they were previously, according to the outward appearance, God’s people. But they were not "sacrificed" to the devil, any more than that goat was, which remained alive and wandered about.

If one wishes to say that the High Priest *and these two goats could not well have had reference to different persons, namely as drawing the lot for the Lord and for the devil, etc.* what difficulty lies in this? That they, outwardly drawing the lot, determined by God’s governance which animal should be for Him, the Lord, and which for Azazel; and that one observes here, as if climbing higher, a sketch of what determination the Lord, as sovereign, has made in, by, and through Himself regarding the lot of His Son and those given to Him; and also regarding the lot and the state of the rebellious priests and fleshly Israelites. The governance of both and their outcomes are from the Lord. They only performed the outward ritual; they could have had these two perspectives and handled these two distinct goats, even if they did not understand it in their own persons. Indeed, if they had understood and believed the word of the prophets, they would have taught Israel—yes, announced by this casting of lots and determination—what would happen to the Messiah, the only, true, and perfect sacrifice of atonement for His people: and how His blood and their misdeed would come upon the heads of those who would send Him away, with the abolition of the vain and powerless sacrifices, and the sending into the wilderness of those who would trample that blood and hold it in low esteem. But their blindness and unbelief, alas, caused them to pass it by.

*And as for the saying: that this goat and its treatment and experience belong to the time of the feast of atonement;* one still cannot notice from that what is intended or what can be achieved: for 1. meanwhile it clearly appears that everything concerning the atonement and sacrifice of the first goat was already finished. 2. That the experience of the second goat is recounted last. 3. And therefore the cleansing and symbolic atonement had already occurred. 4. Thus, what happened to the second goat did indeed take place on the day and the feast of atonement, but it was nonetheless not a means of atonement, as that had already happened. 5. But rather, it was as one for whom atonement was yet to happen; which is also what occurred to the Jews according to the flesh—the unbelieving and rebellious—in the year and on the day of the redeemed, when the time of God’s vengeance came; so that distinguishing well leads to good understanding and teaching.

<column-break/>

### VINEGAR, *Acetum* <note>Latin: vinegar</note>, חומץ <note>Hebrew: chomets, vinegar</note>, ὄξος <note>Greek: oxos, sour wine/vinegar</note>.

VINEGAR is prepared from sour, tart, and sharp wine that is not fit to be drunk. Also from beer and other substances. It is testified that, when drunk, it is healthy against the bite of the Asp and against poison (*Celsus, Book V, chapter 2*; *Dioscorides*, etc.). Also against the infection of the plague; that one must rinse the mouth with it to purify the teeth and the gums, and to wipe away the rotten phlegm; however, although many things are prepared with it—

--- Page 251 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on dietary and medicinal properties, transitioning from the previous page's warning about acidity into a detailed exploration of vinegar—both as a physical substance used by Roman soldiers and as a potent theological symbol in the accounts of the Crucifixion.</meta>

# VINEGAR.

[...one] makes and preserves, one must guard against too much acid, as it causes excessive irritation, fermentation, drying out, and emaciation, in addition to damage and hindrance to the brain.

<margin>The use of vinegar.</margin> VINEGAR is used for refreshment, staunching blood, contraction, the cleansing of wounds, etc. Pliny writes in Book XXXI, Chapter 11: <note>original: "Imponuntur spongiae ipsis epiphoris ex posca... usus earum est ad abstergenda, fovenda, operienda à fotu, dum aliud imponitur."</note> "Sponges soaked in *posca* <note>A mixture of water and vinegar, the standard ration for Roman soldiers.</note> are applied to eye inflammations; warm vinegar is used for headaches. Furthermore, fresh vinegar causes swellings to disappear, softens, and soothes; old vinegar binds wounds. Their use is to wipe, to bathe, and to cover after bathing until something else is applied."

One reads in the divine history that our blessed Savior was given sour wine or vinegar to drink, in fulfillment of the prophecy in *Psalm 69, Matthew 27, Mark 15, and John 19.* Maimonides, Casaubon, Heinsius, and others judge that this, along with other preparations, was brought by friends or merciful Jews according to ancient custom for refreshment during fainting, and for the soothing and cleansing of wounds.

Be that as it may, whether a soldier gave it as a drink to our Savior against the intention of those who brought it or not; it seems quite as likely to me that it was the drink of the common people and the soldiers, known of old by the Romans under the name of *posca*, water mixed with vinegar. I shall express myself somewhat further on this, as it belonged to the provisions of the soldiers; for which purpose cheese, bread, bacon, and vinegar mixed with water were provided. Furthermore, the outposts and border towns were provided with barley and straw or chaff, along with salt, for a year. See *Capitolinus in Gordianis* and *Vegetius, On Military Matters, Book III, Chapter 3.* Care must be taken that one never has a shortage of grain, wine, vinegar, and salt. And in Book IV, Chapter 7: *In order not to suffer want while being besieged and be forced to surrender, one must take care to be sufficiently provided with wine, vinegar, fruit, and apples.*

*Spartianus, in his life of Pescennius:* "He did not want anyone on the expedition to take wine, but that they should all be satisfied with drinking vinegar." See *Stukk. Conviv. cap. 21 Lydii flor sparsio.*

And so I think that the soldiers, not knowing when they would be relieved from their post, provided themselves, or were provided, with a vessel of *posca*—a common drink, the soldier's drink, used especially in great heat and thirst. Thus, a soldier gave the crying Christ, who said "I thirst," some of his *posca* or vinegar-water to suck. So says Juvencus <note>A 4th-century Christian poet who rewrote the Gospels in Latin verse.</note> regarding the prophecy of *Psalm 69* and its fulfillment in *Matthew 27, Mark 15, Luke 23, and John 19:*

> With a sponge tied to a lowly reed, he forced him
> To drink the sharp-tasting liquid pressed to his lips.
<note>original Latin: "Cogebat spongo turpi calamoque revincto, / Impressum labiis acidum potare saporem."</note>

->That is:<-

*He forced him with a sponge, tied to a reed,*
*To drink the vinegar he brought to his mouth.*

<column-break/>

On this incident of the vinegar, reached with the sponge to Christ while he was nailed to the cross, Jeremias de Dekker <note>A celebrated 17th-century Dutch poet known for his religious and moral verses.</note>—considered by Vondel and other connoisseurs as one of the most meaningful wits—expresses himself in his *Good Friday* poem in this manner:

> Your parched lungs thirsted, while we like swine
> ->Until we are sick with wine<-
> ->Burden both stomach and spirit.<-
> God here suffocates from lack, man from excess.
> He who is so ready, so ample, so generous with his gifts,
> ->To refresh all that lives<-
> ->With milk and sweet wine,<-
> Is refreshed while dying with wormwood and vinegar!

But whether this happened precisely to hasten Christ's death; or to refresh him so that he might feel the pain of his wounds more keenly, and thus see what might become of Elias; or whether it should be considered simple cruelty, I leave for others to judge rather than setting it down as certain. However, I would have the least objection if one viewed it as an instrument of mockery. For one reads this clearly enough in the Evangelists: that they mocked him with it because, according to the inscription, he was a King of the Jews, yet had to make do with the commonest drink instead of noble wine, and was thus equal to the slave and the soldier. Indeed, he had come in the form of a servant to suffer and to fight against his and our spiritual enemies.

<margin>Vinegar a symbol of bitterness.</margin> I believe that vinegar, because of its acidity, sharpness, and tartness, is a symbol of that which is unripe, unpleasant, and sharp; and in this respect, it is to be disapproved of and is harmful, just as Solomon compared a sluggard to vinegar and smoke in *Proverbs 10:26* and the untimely actions of someone to vinegar on nitre <note>Usually translated as "vinegar on soda" or "vinegar on a wound."</note> in *Proverbs 25:20.*

I also agree with Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his preaching.</note> in his *84th Homily on John*, that the "Jewish fruits" had become sour, tart, and sharp, distasteful to God and his Anointed (*Deuteronomy 32, Isaiah 5* and elsewhere). I also transcribe the following from him, with which Augustine on *John* agrees: "But the Jews were themselves vinegar, degenerating from the wine of the Patriarchs and Prophets; and as if filled from a full vessel with the iniquity of this world, having a heart like a sponge, deceitful through somewhat hollowed and twisted hiding places."

Therefore God has cast them out and rejected them, not wishing to taste them, as being worthy of spitting out. So sings Sedulius: <note>Coelius Sedulius, a 5th-century Christian poet.</note>

> --- For just as sweet wines
> When they are turned into dreadful vinegar,
> Lie cast out from the tables; so in former times
> A people accepted by God is now a hated race.

->That is:<-

> Just as the sweet wine
> Is banned from the table when into vinegar
> It has turned; so the Jewish people, formerly
> Loved and valued by the Deity, are persecuted by everyone.

<margin>Sin compared to vinegar.</margin> I have further noticed that the ancients compared the sour, sharp, and tart wine or vinegar tasted by Christ to the sour, bit-

# VINEGAR.

the tart and unsavory [nature] of our sin and corruption. This is how Hilary, Ambrose, and others understood it. *Thus Christ, in the Gospel of John, after he had tasted the vinegar, said, "It is finished," because he had drunk all the evil of human corruption.* And Athanasius writes: *The vinegar and the gall that were reached up to him, in which was the bitterness of the wrath caused by the violated Law, Christ drank and took away, so that in place of vinegar, he might pour out for us the wine which Wisdom has mixed, and in place of gall, the teachings which are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; so that for that which he tasted, he might say: "Taste and see, for the Lord is sweet."* <note>Athanasius of Alexandria was a 4th-century Church Father known for defending the doctrine of the Trinity.</note>

And from the harsh and sharp drink of vinegar given to Jesus, his disciples—who must follow him and take up their cross—can see what fate they should expect from the world, which lies in wickedness; they should not be discouraged by this, but rather be well-comforted. For Christ foretold, *In the world you shall have tribulation.* <margin>Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 26.</margin> <note>original: "Aceti potus & fellis cibus, acerbitates & amaritudines in hac vita sectatoribus veritatis pollicebatur. Illiusmodi potus & cibus in os doctoris nostri veniens, pressurarum nobis ac laborum & miseriarum praebebat exemplum. Quae omnia tolerare & perpeti necesse est eos, qui veritatem sequuntur: quoniam veritas acerba est, & invisa omnibus, qui virtutis expertes, vitam suam mortiferis voluptatibus dedunt."</note> That is: *The drink of vinegar and the food of gall promised sharpness and bitterness in this life to those who cling to the truth. Such a drink and food coming into the mouth of our Teacher provided us an example of tribulations, difficulties, and calamities. All of which things those who follow the truth must necessarily bear and endure: because the truth is sharp and hated by all those who, devoid of virtue, surrender their lives to deadly pleasures.*

<column-break/>

This vinegar, when drunk in, works strongly against the poison of sin and corruption, restraining the lusts of the flesh, <margin>Hebrews 12, Romans 5 and 8, etc.</margin> and in some respects one can compare <margin>Admonitions and rebukes compared to vinegar.</margin> biting, stinging, and purifying vinegar to the earnest and sharp admonitions and rebukes, through which many are preserved from destruction, and purified and healed of sins and errors, even though these initially struck them sensitively and appeared unsavory and painful.

# B A A L, <term>Baal <note>Hebrew: בעל, Greek: Βααλ</note></term>. Page 1

<image-desc>A large copperplate engraving depicting various scenes of idolatrous worship associated with Baal. In the foreground, figures are seen prostrating themselves before an altar and a statue on a pedestal. In the background, a classical temple structure is visible with the inscription "D. O. M." (To the Best and Greatest God) and "IUPITER". Various sacrificial vessels and a small altar with the words "MAN. SACRUM" (Sacred Offering) are shown to the right. The scene is populated by figures in ancient or orientalist attire.</image-desc>

<margin>What Baal, Bel, etc., signify.</margin>
**BAAL**, Beel, or shortened to Bel; Baalim, Belim, and so forth, signifies a lord, lords, or prince. It appears to be the same as Moloch, Milcom, or "king." It is used to refer to a god or an idol: one who has authority, command, and ownership over something, under whose power, dominion, and oversight people have placed themselves.

<margin>It is very probable that, in antiquity, the Sun was understood by this name.</margin>
And it is very probable that one should understand this to mean the Sun, that preeminent heavenly light, which seems to have been the first to be honored and worshipped. This same deity was likely worshipped as Moloch (the "king") by the Moabites and Ammonites, and as Baal, Beel, or Bel in other services and contexts. *1 Kings 19, Jeremiah 19 and 32.*

Sometimes it is found in a feminine representation as <term>Malkah <note>Hebrew: מלכה, meaning "Queen"</note></term>, *Jeremiah 7 and 44*, since the Moon, having dominion over the night, was also honored from ancient times.

<margin>Though one reads of various Baals, they were sometimes the planets—the Sun above all.</margin>
Thus one reads of <term>Baal-Samen <note>or Beel Samaim</note></term>, from <term>Shamaim <note>Hebrew: שמים, meaning "Heavens"</note></term>, the Lord or God of heaven, the Sun and Moon: <term>Jupiter Olympius <note>The chief Greek god associated with the sky</note></term>, or Jupiter the god of heaven. Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note> writes in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book I: <note>original: "μόνος οὐρανῷ Θεὸς"</note> "The only God in heaven," meaning the Sun. Augustine, in his *Questions on Judges*, notes that the Bels and Baalim are called <term>Joves <note>Latin plural for Jupiter</note></term>. See Ouwens’ *Theology*, page 347.

One reads in Friedrich Adolf Lampe’s <note>A prominent 18th-century German theologian</note> *12 Exercises on Psalm 45*, part 2, page 207, etc., of Baal-Sohemen.

Furthermore, one finds that Tyre was an idolatrous city. For they served Hercules, Venus, Astarte, Apollo, and Silenus—a fact we shall not prove further as it is well known. It is enough that one can see these mentioned idols of the Tyrians on the coins we have cited from Vaillant <note>Jean-Foy Vaillant, a famous 17th-century numismatist</note>; anyone who wishes can find more in the second volume of *Imperial Coins* and in Selden’s <note>John Selden, a 17th-century polymath</note> *On the Syrian Gods*, etc.

Strabo <note>An ancient Greek geographer</note>, in his 16th Book, adds Jupiter Olympius to this, which is likely why the eagle appears on the 6th coin. And undoubtedly this is the same as Belus, whom Josephus <note>The famous 1st-century Jewish historian</note>, in the 8th book, 7th chapter of his *Antiquities of the Jews*, calls the god of the Tyrians. This is the same as <term>Baal Scheemen <note>Lord of Heaven</note></term>, mentioned by Sanchuniathon <note>A legendary Phoenician author</note>, and by Augustine in *Questions*, Book 7, question 16, etc.

<column-break/>

<margin>How they are distinguished.</margin>
It is true that one reads in the Holy Scriptures of many "Baals" or "lords" (*1 Corinthians 8*). They were distinguished either by the place where they were honored and served, by their deeds and supposed benefits, or by the different rituals performed for them. The name was also given to deceased and deified humans. However, since the planets were often used interchangeably and the Sun was the most preeminent of the heavenly lights, the Sun is usually what is represented by the name everywhere. See Selden, Book II, Chapter 2; Dieterich, *Antiquities*, V. 7, page 552; Ross’s *Religions of the World*; Ouwens’ *Theological Works*, p. 342; etc. Also Burman’s *Law and Testimony*; Goodwin’s *Moses and Aaron*; Schedius’s *On the Syrian Gods*; Kipping’s *Roman Antiquities*; etc. Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Virgil</note> says: <note>original: "Affirios Saturnum, quem & solem dicunt, Junonemque coluisse, constat."</note> "It is established that the Assyrians worshipped Saturn—whom they also call the Sun—and Juno."

<margin>What honors were shown to Baal, the Sun.</margin>
Whatever one understands by the Baals, they were honored not only inwardly but also outwardly: by kissing [the hand] and "throwing the hand" toward the Sun; by building temples and chapels; by planting or choosing sacred groves; by carving images and bowing down before them; by offering sacrifices and praying to them, and so on. It was no common or daily task to sacrifice one’s children to Moloch, to make them pass through the fire, or to cut and pierce oneself with knives and lancets. *1 Kings 18, Jeremiah 19 and 32*, etc.

<margin>Baal-peor: who he was, what kind of god, and how he was honored.</margin>
To briefly report on the variety of Baals, one reads of <term>Baal-peor <note>Greek: Βεελ-φεγωρ</note></term>. *Numbers 23 and 31; Deuteronomy 3; Joshua 22; Psalm 106; 1 Corinthians 10; 2 Peter 2*, etc.

Whatever may be the case regarding this idol, his service, and why he was so named, I admit that scholars do not agree among themselves on this matter. I understand from Maimonides’ <note>The preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> *On Idolatry*, from Dionysius Vossius...

<margin>Baal, Bel, etc. what it means.</margin>
BAAL, Beel, or shortened to Bel, Baalim, Belim, etc., means a lord, lords, or prince. It appears to be the same as Moloch, Milcom, or "king." It is used for a god or an idol: one who has the authority to speak, command, and own property somewhere, under whose power, dominion, and oversight people have placed themselves.

<margin>It is very probable that in ancient times the Sun was understood by this.</margin>
And it is very probable that one should understand this to mean the *Sun*, that eminent heavenly light, which seems to have been the first honored and worshipped. It is likely the same as Moloch—an idol of the Moabites and Ammonites, a king—and the same as Baal, Beel, or Bel in service and other respects: *1 Kings 19, Jeremiah 19 and 32.*

Sometimes it is encountered in a feminine representation as <term>Malkah</term> <note>Hebrew: מלכה, meaning 'Queen'</note> in *Jeremiah 7 and 44*, because the Moon, having dominion over the night, was also honored in ancient times.

<margin>Although one reads of various Baals: they were sometimes the planets: the Sun preeminently.</margin>
Thus one reads of Baal-Samen, or Beel Samaim, for <term>Shamaim</term> <note>Hebrew: שמים, meaning 'Heavens'</note>, the lord and God of heaven, the Sun and Moon: Jupiter Olympius: Jupiter the god of heaven. *Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book 1:* "the only God of heaven," <note>original Greek: μόνος ὀρανῦ Θεὸς (monos ouranou Theos)</note> referring to the Sun. *Augustine, in Questions on Judges:* the Bels and Baalim are called *Joves*, or Jupiters. See *Ouwens' Theology, page 347.*

One reads in Friedrich Adolf Lampe, *12 Exercises on Psalm 45, part 2, page 207*, etc., regarding Baal-Sohemen.

Furthermore, one finds that Tyre was an idolatrous city. For she served Hercules, Venus, Astarte, Apollo, and Silenus, which we shall not prove further as it is well known. Let it suffice that one can see the mentioned idols of the Tyrians on the coins, which we have brought from Vaillant; anyone who wishes can find more in the second volume, the *Imperial Coins*, and in Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, etc.

Strabo, in his 16th Book, adds Jupiter Olympius to this, which is likely why the eagle stands on the 6th coin. And undoubtedly this is the same as Belus, whom Josephus, in the 8th book,

<column-break/>

in the 7th Chapter of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, calls the god of the Tyrians. This is the same as Baal Scheemen, whom Sanchuniathon mentions, and Augustine in *Questions*, book 7, the 16th question, etc.

<margin>How they are distinguished.</margin>
It is true that one reads in the holy pages of many "Baals" or lords (*1 Corinthians 8*). They were distinguished either by the place where they were honored and served, by their deeds, performances, and supposed benefits, or by the different types of service rendered. The name was also given to deceased and deified humans. However, because the planets were often used interchangeably, and the Sun was the most eminent of the heavenly lights, the Sun is mostly represented everywhere through this name. See *Selden, Book 2, Chapter 2; Dieter, Antiquities V. 7. page 552; Ross’s Religions of the World; Ouwens, Theological Works, p. 342, etc.; Burman, Law and Testimony; Goodwin, Moses and Aaron; Schedius, On the Syrian Gods; Kipping, Roman Antiquities, etc.* Servius says: *It is well known that the Assyrians worshipped Saturn, whom they also call the Sun, and Juno.* <note>original Latin: "Assyrios Saturnum, quem & solem dicunt, Junonemque coluisse, constat."</note>

<margin>What honor was shown to Baal, the Sun.</margin>
Whatever one understands by the Baals, they were honored not only inwardly but also outwardly: by kissing, and by "throwing the hand" toward the Sun <note>A gesture of blowing a kiss in adoration</note>. People built temples and chapels, they planted or chose sacred groves, they fashioned images and bowed down before them, they sacrificed, and they prayed to them, etc. It was no common or daily task to offer one's children to Moloch, or to make them pass through the fire, or to beat, prick, and stab oneself, etc. *1 Kings 18, Jeremiah 19 and 32, etc.*

<margin>Baal-peor, who he was, what kind of god, and how he was honored.</margin>
And to briefly account for the variety of Baals, one reads of Baal-peor <note>Greek: Βεελ-φέγωρ</note>. *Numbers 23 and 31, Deuteronomy 3, Joshua 22, Psalm 106, 1 Corinthians 10, 2 Peter 2, etc.*

Regarding this idol, its service, and why it was so named: I confess that the learned do not agree among themselves on this point. I understand from Maimonides *On Idolatry*, and from Dionysius Vossius,

# BAAL.

<margin>
Why he is named Peor.
</margin>
Fagius and many others—as can be seen and read in Selden, Beyer in his *Additions*, Goodwyn, etc.—state that he was placed as a <term>Priapus</term> <note>A Greek god of fertility, often depicted with a large phallus, guarding gardens.</note> of the gardens: naked, with his male member exposed, and so on; and that he was served by persons who were naked, or had their buttocks and other parts uncovered. This statue—naked and with the male rod exposed—was honored most by the female sex, who united themselves with him as if according to the flesh, and thus divested themselves of their virginity. See Beyer in his *Additions* from *Augustine, page 249; Selden, page 84, etc.; Dieterich’s Antiquities, page 368, etc.; Owen’s Theology, page 340, etc.*

<margin>
Various thoughts.
</margin>
It is true that I do not hold the heathens in such high regard as to think them above this, and their <term>Eleusinia</term> <note>The Eleusinian Mysteries, secret religious rites of ancient Greece.</note> cannot be entirely cleared of such things. However, I find that some have considered whether Baal-Peor might not be so named from the Hebrew *Baal Pa’ar* <note>original: פער</note>, meaning "to open," "to gape," or "to disclose." This might be because he stands with the opening and baring of certain body parts—namely the buttocks—or with the opening of the portal vein, or with an open mouth from which (according to the imagination) he used to bring forth oracles and speak through the power of Baal. *1 Kings 18, Jeremiah 2 and 23.*

<margin>
By conjecture so named from Mount Peor, where he stood and was honored with offerings to the dead.
</margin>
Finally, looking more at spiritual impurity and idolatry than the beastly, filthy impurity of the body (which accompanied it in certain cases, *1 Corinthians 10*), one might not be entirely mistaken or wander from the truth if one held that Baal is surnamed "Peor" because he is described by Mount Peor, upon which stood an idol’s house where he was honored. *Numbers 23:28, Deuteronomy 3:29, Joshua 22.* To whom "offerings to the dead" were made, *Psalm 106*; that is, just as sacrifices were offered to the subterranean gods <term>Jupiter Stygius</term> <note>original: "Jupiter Stygius", another name for Pluto, god of the Underworld.</note> and Pluto, the god of the dead. See *Burmann’s Law and Testimony, Selden on the Syrian Gods, etc.*

<margin>
Baal-Zephon, viewed by some as an idol statue intended to turn back and terrify those who wished to flee Egypt.
</margin>
One finds mention made of Baal-Zephon; but whether much stock should be placed in the Jewish stories regarding this, I would strongly doubt. It is said that this idol statue was made by Egyptian Sages or Sorcerers and placed in the wilderness to restrain the Israelites who sought to escape; from *Tzapha* <note>original: צפה</note>, to keep watch, to observe, or to watch the road and see who passes through. He is the <term>Baal Speculator</term> <note>Latin: "Lord Watchman".</note>. Rabbi Solomon <note>Refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki), a medieval commentator.</note> makes him out to be a copper dog, made by Egyptian sorcerers according to the face of heaven and the course of the stars and planets, and placed in the wilderness to terrify the Jews with his hideous and terrifying barking and howling, and to keep them from fleeing.

<margin>
Very likely named after the place: and perhaps placed to secure the road, and to be honored on the road.
</margin>
However, leaving this to the Jews, he was very likely so named from the place where he stood (*Numbers 33*) and was perhaps placed there either to secure the road or to be honored and served by the passer-by.

<margin>
Baal-Berith. Lord and master of the covenant, [Israel] having become unfaithful, bound themselves to Baal. 2. Or the covenant of Shechem and Abimelech. 3. Or certain goddesses.
</margin>
What this may be regarding Jewish circumcision will be discussed later in the discourse on Circumcision. Here it appears in another sense and respect: Baal-Berith, Lord or Lady of the Covenant; a god or idol of treaties and negotiations, who brings someone into a covenant and accepts them to stand under him as their God. We read of it in *Judges 8 and 9:1.* Because Israel, having become unfaithful to God, bound themselves to Baal. 2. Or the covenant of Shechem and Abimelech. 3. Or certain goddesses.

<column-break/>

and *Chapter 9.* Would it also be suggested here that Israel, having become unfaithful to their Covenant-God and Lord, entered into a covenant with Baal so that he might be their God or Lord? Or is it to be understood as the covenant of Shechem and Abimelech? Or must one understand by it *Berith*, or *Berythus*, honored as a goddess? For my part, I cannot give much certain account of it.

<margin>
Baal-Zebub, and Zebul. The god of flies: the dung-god. Fly-swarming. Honored in the form of a fly. As powerless as a fly. At least the name of the gods, idols, etc.
</margin>
As for the naming of Baal-Zebub—in the New Testament *Baal-Zebul*—the idol of the Ekronites, called the "god of flies," the "muck-god," and the "dung-god": this was either because he was served in the form of a fly, or because he drove away the very harmful flies (or failed to do so), or because he was depicted with a bare backside and dung, or because the devil flies and swarms around us (*1 Peter 5*) and is as powerless as a fly (without God's permission). Or is he <term>Jupiter Apomyios</term> <note>Greek: "The Fly-Averter," a title given to Zeus at Olympia.</note>, the driver-away of flies? I shall not dwell on it. See *Owen’s Theology, on the Syrian gods, and also my Miscellany, second part, page 492, etc.*

For the rest, I leave the idolatrous Baals behind. For although the heathens had many gods and lords—*Baalim*—they were <term>Elilim</term> <note>Hebrew term for idols, literally meaning "nothings" or "vanities."</note>, nonentities; there is only one God and Lord. *1 Corinthians 8.*

One notes from all this that "Baal" means a lord, master, god, or a divine or holy image, so named according to the variety of place, function, and honor. Now the practices regarding these named deities—gods, saints, deified and deceased men, their images, temples, groves, chapels, sacrifices, adorations, and such—were a spiritual harlotry and idolatry, accompanied by much fleshly impurity, and for that reason strictly forbidden by the one true God.

<margin>
Shown more closely regarding the idolatrous New-Roman Church.
</margin>
Baalim and Baals—lords and ladies, commanders, patrons, guardians and guardianesses, gods and goddesses—those of the New-Roman Church <note>A common Protestant term for the Roman Catholic Church after the Council of Trent.</note> have in the heathen manner in great number. These are set over cities, villages, and kingdoms to have oversight and protection against sickness and ailments, for the giving of benefits, and so forth. If I wished to prove this extensively, I would have much paper to fill. Their gods are multiplied according to the number of their cities (*Jeremiah 2:28*): Saint Nicholas, Hubert, James, Paul, Peter, George, Mark, John, Crispin, Severin, Ursula, Francis, Mary, Gabriel, Our Dear Lady of Halle, Scherpenheuvel, Loretto, etc. Mary is Queen of Heaven, to whom one commends oneself entirely, who has command over Jesus her son, and whatever else belongs to that treasury.

# B A A L.

*Christians venerate gods and goddesses no differently than God: nor do I see in many what the difference is between their opinion of the saints, and that which the heathens thought of their gods.* <note>Original Latin: "Christiani divos divasque non aliter venerantur, quam Deum: nec video in multis, quid sit discrimen inter eorum opinionem de sanctis, & id quod gentiles de divis suis putabant."</note> That is: *Many Christians show no other honor to the gods and goddesses than to God: and in many I do not see what difference there might be between the imagination they have of the saints, and that which the heathens thought of their gods.*

<margin>The Roman Lieutenant, devoutly a heathen Baal.</margin>
That one may regard the Roman Lieutenant <note>Dutch: "Steedehouder," referring here to the Pope as the "Vicar of Christ."</note>—Christ’s supposed Vicar on earth—as a <term>Baal</term> <note>Meaning "Lord" or "Master" in Hebrew.</note>, lord, prince, and king, whom people used to honor and serve under this name (namely, the Sun), requires no proof. One need only recall that he calls himself the Sun, and names the Emperor, kings, and princes the Moon. Also, when one remembers that he allows himself to be called Lord, God, the Pope, the Divine Majesty, and more besides. See under the word ANTICHRIST. Like God, he sits in God's house; he is worshipped; he claims to exercise power over God's laws, over the conscience, in heaven, on earth, in hell, in purgatory, and over the dead and the living.

<margin>His service and teaching is a service of the old Baalites.</margin>
One finds under him and in his kingdom the <term>Baalim</term> <note>The plural form of Baal, referring to various local manifestations of the deity.</note> and the service of Baal, as mentioned in *1 Kings 18, Jeremiah 19 and 32.* People cry and shout, howl and fast; they scourge and strike themselves; they stretch themselves out upon the earth, and prick and torment the flesh, and so forth—all to make the Baals hear and help.

<margin>There are Baal-Zephons along the roads, in little houses.</margin>
There are <term>Baal-Zephons</term> <note>Literally "Lord of the North," but interpreted here as protective roadside deities.</note> in the deserts, on the plains, on mountain and valley; every little deity stands in its holy little chapel or shrine along the roads, so that people might offer something to it or kneel before it, likely to keep the roads safe.

<margin>There are Baal-Beriths, masters of the orders and of the covenant.</margin>
One finds there <term>Baal-Beriths</term> <note>Hebrew for "Lord of the Covenant."</note>, orders of many kinds: those married to the Church, <term>kloppen</term> <note>Uncloistered devout women in the Netherlands.</note>, <term>kweezels</term> <note>A derogatory term for overly pious or hypocritical women.</note>, <term>beguines</term>, nuns, and abbesses. Each binds themselves to their patron and submits to the covenant.

<margin>There are dead offerings, and means for driving out Beelzebub.</margin>
There are offerings for the dead, unbloody masses, prayers, and offerings for the living and the dead who lie under the earth or are in purgatory—who can present everything in such a short space? There is holy consecrated water, the brush, and the aspergillum, with a thousand mutterings and exorcisms to drive away <term>Beelzebub</term> <note>Literally "Lord of the Flies."</note>; and all of it helps as much as a handful of flies. They are all together nothing but <term>drek-goden</term> <note>Literally "dung-gods," a common Reformist insult for idols.</note>, <term>elilim</term> <note>Hebrew for "nothings" or "idols."</note>, vanities; they have eyes and see not, feet and walk not, hands and feel not, noses and smell not, ears and hear not. In a word, it is all filth, stench, and foul slime in the eyes and nostrils of the Most High—a robbery of God's honor and a wicked contempt for Him who has received all power in heaven and on earth. Therefore, I shall not occupy myself further with these dung-gods and <term>Bagnalim</term> <note>A variant spelling of Baalim.</note>, but step over to something else.

<margin>Vanities and dung-gods, a handful of flies, a stinking and abominable idolatry.</margin>

### B A A L  H A M O N  בעל המון

<margin>Baal Hamon Song of Sol. 8:11.</margin>
Since the subject of Baal and Baalim has been spoken of, I shall also give an account of Baal Hamon, of whom one reads in *Song of Solomon 8:11.* Baal means lord, master, guardian, prince, commander, etc., as was said previously. Hamon is derived from *hamah* <note>original: המה</note> or *haman* <note>original: המן</note>, meaning to increase, to make grow, to multiply; to stir up a rustling, a noise, or a bustle, or to endure with noise. Thus *Hamon* would signify a multitude, abundance, a great quantity, whether of people or of money and goods, etc.; or a bustle, noise, or movement caused by many people, streams of water, etc. Consult Bythner in *Lyra Davidis*, Cocceius, Pagninus, Schindler, Robert’s *Hebrew Lexicon*, etc. Drusius cites an old interpreter: "a multitude in choice" <note>original Greek: ἐν ἐκλογῇ πλῆθος</note> or "in the restraint of the multitude" <note>original Greek: ἐν κατοχῇ σχολῇ — likely meaning a place where the crowd is gathered or held.</note>, or of the throng.

<column-break/>

<margin>A valley, a place where there is noise because of the multitude.</margin>
It is understood as a valley and a place of the multitude. A person, or a place of noise that has a multitude, where there is noise and a crowd, where there is a bustle.

<margin>Solomon represents Jesus, the King of Peace.</margin>
Regarding Solomon, appearing throughout this chapter, no one will have much difficulty understanding him to represent the King of Peace, the Beloved of God, the Christ; for many reasons he is named Solomon and represented by him, as is said and proven in its proper place.

<margin>The vineyard represents the church.</margin>
By the Vineyard, one understands the Church to be represented, for reasons of comparison to be further expressed under the word itself. *Isaiah 5 and 27, Jeremiah 21, Song of Solomon 7, etc.*

<margin>This is over the whole world: uniquely in Rome.</margin>
Christ's church is noted as being over the whole earth, *Matthew 13:18*, and uniquely in Rome, where formerly the authority over the whole earth resided; from whence the sound of the Gospel came, and faith was heard everywhere. *Romans 1.*

<margin>The keepers and teachers, the shepherds and students, the servants of Jesus Christ.</margin>
By the keepers and vineyard-dressers, watchmen, etc., are understood Apostles, Evangelists, and Teachers, who must do the work of the Lord in His vineyard—not as lords and for their own advantage, but as faithful servants, *1 Corinthians 3, 1 Peter 5*, for the use and glory of their Lord, *Matthew 20 and 21, Ephesians 9, Isaiah 62, Acts 20:28.*

<margin>The silver pieces represent the spiritual services and fruitfulness.</margin>
The silver pieces represent the interest, honor, and glory of the work of salvation, the fruit of the received gifts of the preaching service, and the income of the church and church members. Christ the Lord and heir must receive the honor, glory, and majesty of salvation and blessedness entirely. *Isaiah 49 and 53:12, Revelation 5:12, Psalm 68:20.* Meanwhile, the Teachers, as faithful servants, draw a fifth part as a spiritual and physical reward—here and hereafter—of proper honor, love, esteem, and obedience, to live from the service of the altar, etc. *Revelation 2:10, Daniel 12, 1 Corinthians 15:18, etc.* It is a sad and poor state when, like the Jewish vineyard-dressers, men kill the Lord of the vineyard, mock the sent messengers, cast them into prison, stone, and slay them, seeking to draw the inheritance to themselves and keep it. This happens when men strive for mastery, keep the advantages for themselves, and let the rightful Lord merely look on, etc.

<margin>The fifth part is the honor, love, and esteem: to live from the altar: the following reward.</margin>

<margin>What Solomon may have intended here.</margin>
Now, regarding what may have been intended here by Solomon and God's Spirit, various views occur. I have spoken in general. In particular, among the learned, one arrives at this: *Christ had a church, in the multitude of the heathens, given to Abraham as an inheritance, under the appointment of the Apostles, shepherds, and teachers. Now when the Apostles and Evangelists were dead, those who corrupted it brought the fruits thereof—the 1000 silver pieces—over as foul gain for themselves; as lords, they subjected the vineyard to themselves (verse 11), while in verse 12 all dominion (of men) is brought to naught, nothing remaining but the care of...*

<margin>The opinion of Adrianus Junius.</margin>

# P A T H.

From being kept and being servants, so the profit, the honor, and the glory come to Christ. See Junius, *Consolations of the Scriptures*, page 382.

<margin>The opinion of Henrik Groenewegen.</margin> Another view: that in the last days, Christ would have his church spread far and wide in the world, amidst the noise of the nations, differing in customs, languages, and religion: yet retaining the name and form of Christ’s vineyard, from which one would expect something good. But the keepers—who are not meant to rule, but to keep (Daniel 12; Ephesians 4; 1 Corinthians 9; and Galatians 6)—would, in this great noise and bustle of people fleeing to the church (Matthew 13:38), do everything for filthy lucre. Each brought in and seized power, not for the Lord, but for themselves; for verses 11 and 12 are set in opposition, and in verse 12 the Lord finally receives what is His. With quiet rebuke, they receive a fifth part of Christ's abundance, of His honor and glory, as ministers and instruments. But in verse 12, the church, no longer willing to endure that compulsion and domination, and having removed it from her midst, gives to Christ the honor and glory for everything. Isaiah 49:4 and 53:12; Revelation 5:12. Groenewegen in *Song of Solomon* 8:11, 12, and in his *Hieroglyphic Dictionary*.

<margin>The obscure clarified, and Song of Solomon 8:11 explained.</margin> It is true that those who have understanding can certainly perceive what these learned men intended to say. Yet, it also contains its own obscurities, and one does not find it brought over to its fixed time, nor clearly stated to whom it is specifically intended to be applied, etc. I shall proceed upon that assumption and attempt to make it appear somewhat clearer, brighter, and more demonstrated to the reader. It is true that Christ is the only Lord and heir of all things; the vineyard of the church belongs to Him. However, although He holds the ownership and the right to it and governs everything, He has nonetheless, as it were, departed; He has left the world, having commended His church and vineyard on earth to the Apostles, Evangelists, pastors, and teachers. His order is established once and for all (Acts 20:28; Ephesians 4:11, 12). In the beginning, Christ's servants behaved faithfully. The church, like a vine, began to spread its branches far and wide, entering the field of the world (Matthew 13). The Roman territory was also added to the Lord's inheritance (Romans 1). Christ’s church there was renowned. In Rome was the seat of the Roman Empire; but with the departure of the Emperor to Byzantium or Constantinople, his authority weakened in the West, and the primary obstacle being removed, there gradually appeared a <term>Man</term> <note>Hebrew: "Ish"; Greek: "Anēr" or "Anthrōpos"</note>, a son of perdition (2 Thessalonians 2). He exalted himself above all; like a God, he went to sit in God’s house and church, under the humble appearance of a "servant of servants," while behaving as a "Lord of lords." Through cunning, violence, and greed, he gained a massive following; everything was put up for sale by him. With him is the noise of the people, as of many waters; his hallmark is the multitude of followers; the world follows him, and the kings of the earth commit fornication with him.

This man has now drawn to himself everything that belongs to Christ—honor, glory, power, riches, etc.—and he and his followers (Cardinals, Bishops, Abbots, Prelates) pull all honor and profit to themselves, while the lesser ones bring everything into his lap from all over. Nothing is done or left undone without self-interest; everything has its price in money, while Jesus’s honor, authority, dignity, and the power of His obedience, bloody merits, and intercession are recorded as a dead entry in the ledger.

But in the Reformation, this peddling and the robbery of Christ’s honor took a completely different turn: the church went out of Babylon. She wished to show honor, love, and faithfulness to the faithful ministers, acknowledging that they were servants of Christ (2 Corinthians 4; 1 Corinthians 3), but not lords, guardians, or masters. To Christ alone, she understood she must give all honor and the title that He was her husband, head, lord, savior, and the cause of the acquisition and application of salvation (Psalm 68:20; Revelation 5; Joshua 14:6; Acts 4:12, etc.).

And such shall be even more preeminent in the last days, when Babylon shall go to its destruction and Jesus's kingdom and vineyard shall be extended everywhere (Revelation 19), when His honor shall not be stolen from Him (Isaiah 42). But let this be enough said regarding this matter for the future.

->PATH, BEATEN WAY, TO PREPARE THE WAY, etc. <term>Path</term> <note>Hebrew: "Salal", "Maslul", "Mesillah"</note>, to heap up or fortify a way <note>original Latin: "exaggerare munire viam"</note>, a way heaped up or fortified <note>original Latin: "via exaggerata, munita"</note>. The Seventy Translators: to prepare a way <note>original Greek: "ὁδοποιεῖν"</note>.<-

<margin>To what the Lord's Spirit refers when mentioning Path, Level, and High Path.</margin> Regarding this matter, which can be categorized under WAY and WALKING—as will also be spoken of in those places—I wish to note something here in passing.

I can easily concede that the Lord's Spirit does not only look at what is customary among men but also uses it for a higher purpose. Thus, I can imagine that it was sometimes the custom of old that when emperors, kings, and great princes were to travel somewhere with their household, retinue, and especially with their bodyguards or army, it was customary to level the roads, fill in the uneven places, and clear away all significant obstacles. At the very least, one reads of such instances in Flavius Josephus's *The Jewish Wars*, Book III, Chapter 5, and Book VI, Chapter 6. It could also be that reference was made to the customs of the Jews, who had to keep the roads to the Cities of Refuge smooth and level, as they also did before the annual main feasts to make the journey to Jerusalem easier and faster.

<margin>A general application of this.</margin> Assuming this—as can be seen in my *Miscellanies* regarding the Cities of Refuge in Israel—I proceed to matters of higher contemplation and further outlook. In this regard, I set as a fundamental rule of my contemplation and holy application that when I speak of the divinity of a "way" or "path" (whatever further description it may rightly receive), I must necessarily arrive at the path of the Divine commandments. Depending on what the church, the age, and the treatment brings and requires, this refers generally to the way of God’s commandments, laws, and ordinances; and specifically to the way of grace, faith, and loving-kindness, with the revelation of Divine virtues in His Son as the fulfiller of promises and pledges. And on this footing, it seems to me that I shall be able to give some light to many passages; at the very least, I shall...
