<header>W A V E.</header>
<sig>A 3</sig>

...I will apply my utmost brevity, for the reason already stated, that "WAY" and "WALKING" must be addressed more closely later.

<margin>Psalm 26:12 explained.</margin>
One reads in Psalm 26:12: *My foot stands on an even path; I will praise the Lord in the congregations.*

Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian who emphasized a "covenantal" or historical-redemptive reading of the Bible rather than just rigid dogma.</note> has noted that here the fruit of boldness and trust is made known, with respect to David and the Church. Previously, the church had been on slippery, steep, entirely rough and uneven ground; but now that her state was changed, she was, through God’s powerful and favorable action, brought out of distress and pressure into a firm, constant, and assured state; therefore she would praise the Lord in the assemblies, to which the congregation would now go up and flow without hindrance.

<margin>Psalm 68:5 explained.</margin>
One reads in Psalm 68:5 <note>In English Bibles, this is usually Psalm 68:4.</note>: *Sing to God, sing praises to His name, prepare the ways for Him who rides in the desert plains, etc.*

Georg Sohnius <note>A 16th-century German Reformed professor.</note> writes as follows: *He says this regarding the Ark of the Covenant, which until now had wandered about in the wilderness: for the Hebrew word "Araba" <note>original: ערבה</note> sometimes means the wilderness, as in Isaiah 40:3. Regarding this Ark, he says: prepare, pave the way—that is: clear it, make the way level, remove all obstacles, so that the passage may be lighter and easier.* And after his Reverence had brought forward some other interpretations, he proceeds to the metaphorical and higher spiritual meaning, writing: *How these things may now be applied to the Messiah is not obscure: for just as at that time the transporting of the Ark of the Covenant—through which the kingdom was confirmed to David and his descendants, and the love and favor of God was to be boasted and reported—was commanded to the pious: so now all believers with thankful hearts and the highest expressions of praise, now that the Messiah is revealed, must praise and proclaim His illustrious ascension, through which His kingdom is established and confirmed, and His constant presence and favor in the governance of the church. And just as at that time the way had to be cleaned and prepared before the Ark, so now for the Messiah, or for the Christ (prefigured by the Ark), the hearts must be prepared and He must be received: for our hearts are by nature rough, tangled, and overgrown with thornbushes and other things—that is to say, with the cares of this life and with other evil passions and inclinations, especially with the imagination and trust in one’s own righteousness. This preparation occurs when the heart turns to Christ through true and earnest repentance, and the defects are removed from the soul, and the obstacles which delay His coming to us are cleared out of the way: for Christ does not dwell in a defiled and unclean mind.* Thus John and other servants were sent ahead, so that they might prepare the way before His face. Malachi 3:1; Isaiah 40:3; Mark 1:2, 3; Luke 3:4. One can subsequently consult Pejerus, Cocceius, and van Til <note>Salomon van Til (1643–1713), a prominent Dutch professor known for his work on prophecy and the Psalms.</note> on this.

<margin>Psalm 84:6 explained.</margin>
In Psalm 84:6 one reads: *Blessed is the man in whose heart are the highways.* It seems to me that one could understand this as the safe, good, and proven way of life—of grace and salvation, of truth and godliness—which was walked long ago in faith and firm trust, with the denial of one’s own righteousness and hope in God the Savior, by the forefathers. *Hebrews 11.*

<margin>Psalm 143:10.</margin>
In Psalm 143:10, a prayer and soul-sighing comes before us: *Your good spirit lead me in an even land.* In and upon an even, paved, straight, and safe way, full of the demonstration and light of grace and truth where one can see ahead: your simple word, and godliness in power, free from errors, heresies, cunning deceptions, offenses, Satanic and Antichristian people, and the loose tricks used to mislead and outwit simple souls.

<margin>Proverbs 15:19 explained.</margin>
In Proverbs 15:19 one reads: *The way of the sluggard is as a hedge of thorns: but the path of the upright is well paved.* Lavaterus and Cartwright <note>Ludwig Lavater and Thomas Cartwright, 16th-century Protestant commentators.</note> agree here that the meaning is that a lazy person, finding everything to be against him, is reluctant to take on any matter of effort or importance; he finds and makes a thousand excuses and difficulties. In contrast, a noble-minded man acquits himself willingly and zealously in the calling in which God has placed him, so that what is a millstone to the first is but a feather to the latter: therefore one can expect nothing but shame and disgrace from the first, but from the latter, utility and honor for the state, the household, and the Church of God, etc.

<margin>Isaiah 11:16 cited.</margin>
Isaiah 11:16. *There shall be a highway: so that the holy and chosen seed may come flying to the windows of the church like doves.* See Cocceius, Vitringa, and the first part of my *Holy Miscellanies*: all obstacles shall there be removed.

<margin>Isaiah 33:8.</margin>
Isaiah 33:8. *Points to a great destruction, insecurity, and hindrances to the public and free religion, etc.*

<margin>Isaiah 35:8.</margin>
Isaiah 35:8. *The elevated path can mean that truth and power will be perceived with complete conviction, so that Christ is the only, true, and perfect God-Savior. God's grace, faith, and conversion alone are necessary. So that errors, heresies, darkening, and falsification of divine truth would pose no hindrance.*

<margin>Isaiah 40:3.</margin>
Isaiah 40:3. See above; and it can refer to John the Baptist preaching the Messiah, the approach of the kingdom of heaven, faith, and repentance, and the embracing of the Messiah.

<margin>Isaiah 49:11.</margin>
Isaiah 49:11. It can signify an unobstructed passage for the church and the Gospel, and a state of safety, like one who, going on a high and well-paved road, can see far and wide around him.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical entries for biblical and theological symbols. It concludes the previous entry (likely "Baan" or "Way") and begins a lengthy entry for "Baar" (Wave or Billow), focusing on its symbolic meaning as distress, worldly turmoil, and heretical pride.</meta>

# WAVE.

<margin>
Symbols of disasters and adversities: both light and heavy.
</margin>
...sink down into the cellars of the abyss. But more on this later in the comparisons.

Regarding the Waves and Billows, which now rise as high as heaven and then plumb the depths, causing the seafarers to tumble through the tossed ship-vessel and stagger like a drunken man (*Psalm 107*), breaking the strongest sea-castles, striking against the rocks and stony cliffs, covering the shores with foam, and making the water murky and turbid—by these things one can judge, as a symbol, lighter or heavier oppressions, persecutions, and God's judgments. This is true whether they strike a person, a family, or the church and state, and whether they are sent and inflicted upon us by God immediately or through intermediaries. One can read of these in the Holy Pages: *Psalm 42:8, Psalm 65:8, Jeremiah 5:22, and 51:55, Zechariah 10,* etc. Through these, one can also understand heathen nations and powers, which make everything tremble and shake, and seem ready to overflow and throw everything into chaos.

<margin>
Heathen powers, overflowing nations.
</margin>

<margin>
* Philotheus in Christian Symbols, page 182.
</margin>

> *The North Wind fell upon the sea, and the South Wind, thick with storms, and their wrath stirs up the swelling deep.*
> *No anchor cast here saves the shattered ship or breaks your fury, O cruel Aeolus!* <note>In Greek mythology, Aeolus was the keeper of the winds.</note>
> *Alas, struck by the shallows and dashed against the rocks, it breaks apart, and the torn, shipwrecked limbs of the vessel stir.*
> *Lift up your hands. From here, seek prosperous sails for the hulls; from here, seek light; from here, seek help for afflicted affairs.* <note>original Latin: "Incubuere mari Boreas, creberque procellis / Africus, & tumidum concitat ira fretum. / Non hic quassatam servat jacta anchora navim / Et frangit furias, Aeole saeve, tuas. / Heu inflicta vadis, scopulisque allisa fatiscit, / Et lacerata movet naufraga membra ratis. / Sursum tende manus. hinc prospera vela carinis, / Hinc jubar, afflictis hinc pete rebus opem."</note>

-> That is: <-

> *The winds pour down upon the sea, which, stirred up,*
> *Moves the depths and tosses the waves upward.*
> *Here the weak ship can no longer find help in an anchor,*
> *Now that the wind-god has let himself go in madness.*
> *Alas, the ship succumbs in the midst of the waves.*
> *The storm rages just as strongly, and knows no calming.*
> *The weak vessel barely moves its limbs.*
> *Lift your hands on high and pour out prayers.*
> *From there alone must you expect your rescue in distress.*

<margin>
Devastating pillaging, and war bands, etc.
</margin>
The sea with its waves can represent to us the sea of nations, and a world in turmoil, full of wars and disturbances, without the order of regulated rest and movement. This especially pinches and affects the Church, as when the Dragon spews entire rivers after the Woman (*Revelation 12*); when the rudder of prudent guidance according to the course of God’s law and right reason, and the anchor of hope, sometimes produce and bring little outward fruit. When one, with all the ship's rigging, can make little progress because of the troubled ocean and the pitch-black night of ignorance, heresy, and persecution—when storm follows storm—one must surrender their case and its outcome to the Supreme Pilot and Steersman, being ballasted with faith, hope, love, and all kinds of Christian virtues. Certainly, the sea of the world and the state of the Church is not always quiet and peaceful, even when the Church shines wonderfully with a light of knowledge and grace (*Revelation 11:2*). It most often happens that it is tempestuous, angry, and troubled.

<margin>
Wicked people, restless, and of a distressed mind, Isaiah 57.
</margin>
The wicked, the restless and uneasy sinners, with a distressed conscience and passionate impulses and movements, are compared to such Waves and Billows by *Isaiah, Chapter 57:20–21*: *But the wicked are like a driven sea, for it cannot rest, and its waters cast up mire and mud. There is no peace, says my God, for the wicked.*

<column-break/>

And from this, the Epistle of Jude, verse 13, seems to have borrowed its words and parable: <margin>Jude verse 13.</margin> <margin>Heretical people, restless, struggling.</margin> *when he compares some to wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame.*

The Waves of the sea and waters are a part of the sea and rivers, though they go as high as heaven and as deep as hell, striking against mountain, cliff, and shore, causing ships to rise, toss, and fall. They plunge back into the sea and return to their origin.

Certainly, heretical people—only Christians in appearance and name, poisonous teachers—are they not from, of, and for the world? They may seem to be united with the little ship of the church, but they do not belong to it; they return to their origin (*John 17; 1 John 2*) and love the world with their hearts (*2 Timothy 4:10*). <margin>Jude verse 13 explained and applied to the heretics and their windy nature.</margin>

Such heretical people, set in motion by the "wind of doctrine" and struggling in many lusts and impulses, have no rest in their inner being (*Job 20:20*). The evil one does not rest until he has done evil, brought grief to the pious, and made them stumble (*Proverbs 4; Psalm 5; Romans 3:12,* etc.). Now they are subtle, then coarse; here they strain at a gnat, there they swallow a camel. One finds them double-hearted and unsteady. In their ways, they are carried about and moved by every wind of doctrine—unstable people (*Ephesians 4:14; 2 Peter 3:16*). Indeed, the description of the comparison sounds like: wild, savage sea-billows, tempestuous, roaring, as if barking; just as Virgil speaks of <term>barking waves</term> <note>original: "undae latrantes," Aeneid 7.</note>.

These raise themselves as high as heaven, appearing to top the clouds (*Psalm 107:25–27; Psalm 65; Luke 17*) and to overleap the peaks of the mountains. They are symbols of people and "windy" Gnostics, who seemed to hold wisdom as an inheritance, speaking of high and great things, exalting themselves above all other teachers, who were to them merely "idiots" <term>Gnostics</term> <note>original Greek: γνωστικοὶ</note>, <term>as if deemed worthy of knowledge</term> <note>original Latin: "quasi Καταξιωθέντες τῆς γνώσεως"</note>, as if specially trained, surpassing others in the most subtle and penetrating knowledge, while they ate things sacrificed to idols, denied Christ, and practiced fleshly impurity—behaving as their interest and goal dictated. One can read of these people in *Cave, Hammond, Grotius, Pomarius, Spanheim's Church History, Stillingfleet*, etc. They imagined they could fathom God's wisdom and hold it as an inheritance (*Job 11*). Their imagined and windy wisdom made them rave and snarl at others along with Diotrephes (*3 John* <term>Epistle</term>). They were wise in their own eyes (*Proverbs 3 and 5*), speaking of things, secrets, outcomes, and mixtures that they themselves did not understand, and which were the fruits of windy and raving tongues and brains, about which one can read in the aforementioned writers.

One sees that the roaring Billows disturb the sea, trouble it, turn the bottom upward, toss and torture the ships, and sometimes cause them to sink, so that heaven, earth, and all elements seem mixed together, and everything is overrun with foam and a salty, roaring spray—just as *Virgil, Aeneid 3*, expresses this:

> *Thrice the cliffs gave a roar among the hollow rocks,*
> *Thrice we saw the foam dashed up and the stars dripping.* <note>original Latin: "Ter scopuli clamorem inter cava saxa dedere, / Ter spumam elisam, & rorantia vidimus astra."</note>

# WAVE.

->This is according to Vondel’s translation:<- <note>Joost van den Vondel was a famous Dutch poet and playwright, often called the "Dutch Shakespeare."</note>

> *Thrice clattered in the ears of all*
> *The sound of hollow rocks; thrice was seen*
> *The heavens sprinkled wet with foam, blow upon blow.*

<margin>Storms and waves of turmoil, persecutions, and troubles endured by the first Christians.</margin>
In those early times, one found men who stirred up the greatest movements and hurricanes against the Christian Church within the sea of paganism. At first, the unbelieving and hardened Jews played their part. Saul, before he became Paul, also did his utmost. The fleshly Israel <note>A reference to the descendants of Abraham through Hagar (Ishmael), often used by period theologians to represent those who persecute the "true" spiritual heirs.</note> was by no means lacking in this, following Ishmael's example. The pagan Philosophers had their share in it as well. The false brothers stoked the fire of rebellion, strife, and division not a little; for their wisdom was not from above. *Galatians 5; James 3:16, etc.*

<margin>Glassius.</margin>
*Salomo Glassius* in his *Sacred Rhetoric* says of this place: *the restless, untamed, wandering, and madly-driven men, possessed by a driving spirit, disturb the church with their godless lives and cause offenses.*

<margin>Bede.</margin>
And Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk and scholar.</note> makes himself heard in this manner: *the wild waves and tempestuous sea-billows are the perverse teachers, who are themselves always restlessly swollen, dark, and bitter, never ceasing to attack the whirlpools of peace, and the strength and stability of the church.*

<margin>Waves stirred up by the Jesuits.</margin>
And to come closer to home, one may see represented here the Roman Clergy, and among them the Jesuits. If ever anyone has set the world and the church in uproar, and moved and incited the worldly powers against the congregation of Christ, they above all have caused such unrest; of which the histories are so full that no proof is needed.

<margin>The rebellious rabble compared to wild, savage waves.</margin>
The passionate and rushing rabble, the very scum of a rebellious people, is like the tempestuous Waves, stirring up wondrous and rare movements in the civil state. When the populace is on the move, the good steersmen and Pilots of the little ship of state have a very difficult time. However, one sees these heaven-high Waves break upon the solid rocks of mutual unity and the good understanding between the authorities and good patriots: on which occasion the mutineers let their predatory and plundering nature shine through too clearly, under false pretenses of wanting to rescue the country's violated liberty. But let this be enough; we shall soon speak of another kind of Wave.

BEARD, *to let it grow, to shave, to pluck out, to take hold of, and to stroke, and such like.* זָקָן <note>Hebrew: *zaqan*</note>, πώγων <note>Greek: *pōgōn*</note>, *barba* <note>Latin: *barba*</note>.

<margin>From of old, much was made of the Beard, as it served as a sign of dignity and the mark of a Philosopher and a learned man.</margin>
That from of old, among almost all peoples, much was made of hair in general, and particularly of the BEARD as a masculine fashion, an ornament, and a hallmark of a good Sage <note>The original uses *Wyzeling*, a term for a philosopher or wise man.</note>, I would easily believe from the reports that learned men have left us. *See Balthasar Bonifacius, Ludicra History page 370; Alexander ab Alexandro page 290; Hofmann, Universal Lexicon.*

From whence comes the ancient designation, "bearded masters," in *Persius Satire 4* and *Juvenal Satire 4*. Prudentius calls Plato *Barbatus*, that is, bearded. *Horace, Book 2, Satire 3:*

->*Jussit sapientem pascere barbam.*<-
-><note>Latin: "He commanded the wise man to grow a beard."</note><-

<column-break/>

->That is:<-

> *He commanded us to let the wise beard grow.*

It was held to be something masculine; a sign of dignity, stateliness, and a hallmark of a Philosopher and a learned man. The Stoics laughed at this, and cared very little for being bearded.

Antiquity did not lack public mockers of the imagination that the beard either granted learning or was a mark of wisdom. It was said that if the Beard contributed anything to it, then the He-Goat would have a great advantage.

->*Reddere si valeat sapientem barba profunda,*<-
->*Esse potes doctus, barbiger birce, Plato.*<-
-><note>Latin: "If a long beard were able to make one wise, then you, O bearded goat, could be a learned Plato."</note><-

->That is:<-

> *If a long beard can give a man wisdom,*
> *Then you, O goat, can surpass all in wit.*

<margin>To cut off someone's Beard was intended as punishment and disgrace.</margin>
To shave, shear, trim, cut into, or pluck out not only someone's head-hair but also their Beard was not taken very well in ancient times; it was a great enough insult and shame. Indeed, not only for thieves but also for other criminals, the Beard was done away with as a disgrace and punishment. *See Rhodiginus page 110; Pancirollus title 44; Schedius, On the German Gods page 460; Dietericus, Antiquities of the Old Testament part 2, page 82; Geier, On Mourning page 205;* the more so because hair, and the nurturing of it, was held as a hallmark of liberty, by virtue of which it was by no means permitted for slaves to wear it. *Dempster page 1704–1707, etc.; Alexander ab Alexandro page 290, etc.*

<margin>In Isaiah 7:20, it signifies great diminishment, sorrow, and great destruction.</margin>
Thus, it was considered an insult if the Beard was entirely or halfway cut into, shaved off, or plucked out. How poorly David took this may be read in *2 Samuel 10*. This insult would also be done to the Messiah. *Isaiah 50:6*. It signified nothing good when the shaving of the hair and the Beard was reported in the holy scrolls, *Isaiah 7:20*, representing both a very great loss and heavy judgment, as well as heartfelt sorrow and lamentation. *Isaiah 15:2 [sic, 20]; Rhodiginus page 364, etc.*

<margin>The hair shaven in deep sorrow and mourning. Reconciliation sought thereby.</margin>
However, many famous writers tell us that in times of sorrow and great mourning, people not only shaved the head-hair but also the long Beard, and even tore and plucked it out. Also, that they shaved the head-hair along with the Beard and threw it by the funeral urn and the dead corpse, etc., to reconcile the gods of the underworld; traces of which one can find in Homer, *Iliad 23 [sic, 7] verse 141; in Odyssey 4 verse 197; Ovid, Heroides Epistle 11.*

> *Non mihi te licuit lacrymis perfundere justis,*
> *In tua nec tonsas ferre sepulchra comas.*
> <note>Latin: "I was not permitted to bathe you with rightful tears, nor to bring shorn locks to your tomb."</note>

->That is:<-

> *I have not wept for you while you lay upon the bier,*
> *Nor scattered my shorn hair upon your grave.*

One may look further into this in *Spencer page 11 [sic, 2], page 213, etc.; Paschalius, On Crowns page 96; Hofmann, Universal Lexicon page 239; Rhodiginus 366, etc.; Alexander ab Alexandro; Pierius in Hieroglyphics; Kirchmann, On Funerals.* The...

# BEARD.

<margin>In times of sorrow, men also let their beards and hair grow. Men swore by the beard.</margin>
This should not be understood too generally, as it is said that not only the Jews, but also the Romans and other nations, let their head-hair and beards grow in times of mourning. See *Rhodiginus page 366, etc.* <note>Lodovicus Caelius Rhodiginus was a 15th-century Italian scholar known for his massive encyclopedia of ancient customs.</note>

To call upon, testify, promise, or swear by one's beard used to be common practice, according to the account of *Rhodiginus page 363, etc. Iliad Book 10, verse 4551, and Euripides in Hecuba, in Medea, and in Andromeda.* Men swore by their beards, just as the Turks still do today. *Lydius on Military Matters, Chapter XXXIX. 11.*

<margin>To take hold of, stroke, and caress someone’s beard.</margin>
To take hold of, stroke, caress, and gently comb someone's beard was sometimes taken very poorly; yet sometimes it was interpreted positively and done to earn favor and mercy. *Rhodiginus page 111—362, etc.* It seems that men did this when they wished to kiss, welcome, and please someone. *2 Samuel 20. Pliny Book II, Chapter 45. Ursinus on the Passion page 8. Novarinus Schediasmata Book XI, Chapter 18. Homer’s Iliad A, Iliad X, Odyssey T. Lydii Flor. Sparsion. page 32, 33.*

> Tell the father 
> To calm the great flood; clasp his chin 
> While praying. 
<note>original Greek: εἴπατε πατρὶ / Κοιμῖσαι μέγα χεῦμα, περιπλέξεσθε γενύῳ / Δεσσόμεναι.</note>

> Tell the father
> That he may stay the rapid floods; touch his beard
> While pleading.
<note>original Latin: Dicite patri / Ut rapidos sistat fluctus, appendite barbam / Orantes.</note>

-> That is: <-

> Tell the Father, while grabbing him by the beard,
> That he should still the waves.

<margin>Men promised their hair or beard in case of mortal danger, as a pledge for a safe return.</margin>
Dedicating the first beard—the downy chin hair—to some deity also had its place. And to promise one’s beard and shave it off when in extreme danger, especially the danger of suffering shipwreck, was formerly the practice of the superstitious. *Valerius Flaccus, Argonautica Book I. See Spencer part 2, page 68, etc.*

> Eurytion is protected, and his neck hair saved, 
> Which his father will shave at the Aeonian altars upon his return.
<note>original Latin: Tectus & Eurytion servato colla capillo, / Quem pater Aeonias reducem tondebit ad aras.</note>

-> That is: <-

> Eurytion was also preserved with his beard,
> Which, having returned, he shall offer upon the altars.

See *Lucian in The Syrian Goddess. Dio and Xiphilinus on Nero, by Doughty in Analecta V. T. page 97. Alexander ab Alexandro page 184.* The promise was made on the condition that if one returned safely from the journey, it might even be offered to a river. *Ibid. and in N. T. page 97. Hofman’s Universal Lexicon page 239.*

<margin>Baldness, incision, etc., forbidden by God.</margin>
To make baldness upon the head, and to shave the beard smooth, or to make a round bald spot on the forehead with corners and incisions after the manner of the heathens and dedicate it to some deity, was forbidden. *Leviticus 14 and 16. Numbers 6, etc. Leviticus 19. Kunaeus, Republic of the Hebrews Chapter XVIII. Heinsius on Aristotle Chapter IV. Gejerus on Hebrew Mourning pages 217, 218, etc. Rhodiginus page 109. Spencer 215, page 1.*

<margin>It is doubted who first introduced the clean-shaven beard.</margin>
As to who first introduced the shaving of the beard—whether entirely smooth or with mustaches where something is preserved on the upper lip—I see that not everyone’s judgment and testimony agree.

<column-break/>

<margin>The youths in Rome were shaven.</margin>
As far as Rome is concerned, *Alexander ab Alexandro* in *Genial Days page 290* testifies that until the year 454, it was the custom that both old and young men remained unshaven. But when Publius Ticinius brought barbers with him from Sicily, it then became a custom for the youths to shave their heads and scrape their beards until their fortieth year. The first who shaved his beard daily is considered to have been Scipio Africanus, and after him, Augustus.

<margin>Among the Greeks.</margin>
From ancient times among the Romans, the beard was shaved off until the time of Emperor Hadrian, who was the first to let the beard grow. That the shaving of the beard also came into use among the Greeks in the time of Alexander is testified by Chrysippus, as Rhodiginus relates on page 109. The Egyptians, especially their priests, shaved their bodies entirely bald every third day. See *Rhodiginus page 366; also Dempster, and from him Gejerus on the Mourning of the Greeks page 200,* who says that Alexander first introduced this among the Greeks. See further *Hofman’s Lexicon page 269.*

<margin>Nazirites.</margin>
The Nazirites <note>A Nazirite was a person who took a vow of separation to God, which included not cutting their hair.</note> were not permitted to shave until the years of their Naziriteship were ended. Then their hair was shaved and thrown into the sacrificial fire. *See Numbers 6.*

<margin>Hair-cutting, a sign of reconciliation.</margin>
To cut someone's hair and to lay down one's hair before someone was quite remarkable. In such a way, a person was as if reconciled and appointed as an heir and successor. Thus *Alexander ab Alexandro* relates of the Lombards that to lay down one's beard for someone to keep served as a sign and pledge of firm friendship; he with whom the first beard had been placed was most closely bound to maintain that friendship. Among that same people, it was the custom that he whose hair was cut or trimmed was appointed as an heir, as we have just mentioned. I have this from Paul the Deacon and Rhodiginus. *See the latter, page 363.*

<margin>Aaron’s head.</margin>
In the 133rd Psalm, one reads of the anointing oil flowing down from Aaron’s head into his beard, and from there to the edges of his priestly garments. I have no desire to argue with anyone whether hair grows through nourishment or through protrusion and expulsion, or whether it is a part of the human body or a mere excrement. This stands firm: that it serves as an ornament and has its usefulness. But also that the beard grows around the mouth, comes forth from the skin, is rooted there, finds growth-material, and is increased and lengthened.

<margin>The believers.</margin>
All this makes me think of the Apostles and the first believers, who sprout from Christ, are rooted in Him, grow through Him to the full length of maturity, and are taught by Him, according as they partake more or less of His oil and are under the influence of His Spirit, which was poured out upon them early on. From other speculations, I shall refrain for the present and proceed to speak of:

# TO BEAR.
<sig>B</sig>

<margin>Brought to the Son of God, to be begotten of the Father, etc.</margin>...brought to the Son of God as being born, begotten of the Father, and thus named God’s **only begotten Son: his own, beloved John 1. Rom. 8. Matt. 3:17 and 17. the Son of his love Col. 1.** Not simply because of creation and being formed in his image, or boasting in the same, or because of excellence in power or glory—as the first man, the Angels, or the so-called gods are described <note>original: "Luc. III. Ps. LXXXII. 1 Cor. VIII."</note>—but in such a way as was never said to the Angels. <note>Hebrews 1:5</note>

<margin>How to understand this.</margin>From this birth and eternal presentation—through which the Son has life in himself, possessing the same essence with the Father, and being one with the Father—it follows that he is the Son.

<margin>Opinion of the Socinians and Remonstrants.</margin>We do not hold this sonship as the Socinians <note>A group that denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ.</note> and the Socinian-leaning Remonstrants <note>A Dutch theological movement; here accused of downplaying Christ's eternal divinity.</note> do, who deny that he is the actual Son of God from eternity, being of the same nature, power, and glory. They claim he did not exist before he was born of Mary, except by way of an eternal pre-determination to become such in time. They do not place his sonship in his eternal nature, but rather: **a.** In his supernatural, unusual birth. **b.** In his miraculous raising from the dead. **c.** In God's singular love for him. **d.** In his immortality. **e.** In his appointment to the office of <term>mediator</term> <note>One who acts as a bridge between God and humanity.</note>. **f.** In his holy nature, in which he came close to God. **g.** In the will of God that he should be called the Son of God and be worshiped and honored as God, gifted with singular glory and power. He appears in *Colossians 1* as the **firstborn of all creatures**: not as the first-created, but as the one who created and made everything. And in relation to the creatures, he is the one who, as the firstborn, has the right and power over all that belongs to the Father and comes from his hand, as the lord and heir of all. <note>Hebrews 1</note>

Concerning this birth, the ancients spoke with much reverence. Athanasius <note>A 4th-century bishop and defender of the Trinity.</note> said: *We have known him inexpressibly and incomprehensibly.* <note>original Greek: "Ἔγνωμεν δὲ ἀνεκφράсως καὶ ἀπερινοήτως"</note> And further: *that he is born of the Father without beginning and from eternity.* <note>original Greek: "υἱὸν ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀνάρχως καὶ ἀϊδίως γεγεννημένον"</note> Furthermore, these words were used: *timelessly* <note>ἀχρόνως</note> meaning from eternity; *inseparably* <note>ἀχωρίсως</note> meaning not apart from or outside the Divine essence, for the Son is in the Father, and they are one; *impassibly* <note>Ἀπάθως</note> meaning without actual suffering or any change in the Father or Son. And Fulgentius <note>A 6th-century North African bishop.</note> expresses himself thus: *Born of God, the Son of the Father: another in person, not another in nature; always with the Father, with whom he has natural immensity; always with the Father, with whom he has one natural eternity; always from the Father, from whom he has natural eternal birth; always in the Father, with whom he possesses the same equal divinity.* <note>original Latin: "Natus de Deo Patris Filius, alter in personâ, non alius naturâ: semper apud Patrem, cum quo illi est naturalis immensitas: semper cum Patre, cum quo illi est una naturalis æternitas: semper de Patre, de quo illi est naturliter æternitativitas: semper in Patre, cum quo illi una est æqualis divinitas."</note> Epiphanius, in his work *Against Heresies*, writes: *The Father is always Father, and there was never a time in which the Father was not.* <note>original Greek: "Πατὴρ ἀιεὶ πατὴρ, καὶ ἐκ ἦν καιρὸς ἐν ᾧ ἐκ ἦν ὁ πατὴρ."</note>

He is not called the Son merely because of his resurrection from the dead, as if David <note>Psalm 2:7</note> were looking only at that, or as if Peter <note>Acts 13:32, 33</note> meant only the resurrection. No, because:

<column-break/>

<margin>Reasoning of the Psalmist.</margin> **a.** It sounds very harsh, and it is not proven, that "being God's Son" and "being raised from the dead" must be taken as one and the same thing, or that he would be God's Son solely on that ground.
**b.** The Psalmist gives another reason: *today I have brought you forth,* <note>or "begotten you"</note> taking "today" in a manner becoming to God.
**c.** It is clear that he is called God's Son by excellence. <note>Rom. 8:32, John 1, Col. 1, Heb. 11:5</note> What advantage would he have if others were also raised before him, through him, with him, and after him?
**d.** Would he then be the cause of his own Sonship? For he raised himself. <note>Rom. 1, 1 Pet. 3, John 2:19 and 10:18</note>
**e.** It is one thing to be *demonstrated* to be the Son of God <note>Rom. 1:3, 4</note> and another thing for the resurrection to be the *root cause* of his Sonship and eternal birth.
**f.** Paul in *Acts 13:32, 33* speaks of his appointment and arrangement as mediator and lord, following the promise made; and then in verse 34, he speaks of the resurrection from the dead, clarifying the words of *Psalm 16:10*.

However, since there is no equal "Bearing" or begetting and sonship within nature or among men, I must be satisfied with what has been said and move on, for I know of no other comparisons to make.

<margin>Attributed to the woman.</margin> More properly, according to the nature and laws of birth and the union for the purpose of procreation, the act of "Bearing" is attributed less properly to the man and more properly to the woman, who conceives, carries, and bears or brings forth from the opening of the womb.

<margin>Bearing as stirring up or causing something, etc.</margin> Thus one sees the word **TO BEAR** used for causing something or bringing it about, as if from one's womb or hidden corners, through its causes or primary materials <note>Job 38:28, 29</note>. This can be understood in a natural or moral way, when human actions seem to make certain things follow inevitably. The fruit of desire is sin; the fruit of sin is death. <note>James 1:15</note> Just as we use the word **TO BEAR** to mean to cause or bring about <note>2 Tim. 2:23</note>, such as: *bearing trouble, strife, fighting,* etc. To bear, that is: to bring about.

<margin>To obtain something with singular desire, deliberation, or hope; to bring forth something held hidden in one's bosom.</margin> When someone—with a singular purpose, full thoughts, and strong, persistent desires locked in their soul—directs all their outward words, works, and activities to reach their goal, they are "pregnant" with their plan. When their inner will and longing eventually burst forth and become known, either achieving their goal or resulting in something unexpected, they are said to **Bear** something. This is because they bring forth what they had kept hidden and nurtured in their bosom for a time, and which they believed they had brought to full growth and ripeness. See *Psalm 7:15, Isaiah 26:17, 18 and 59:4, 5 and 33:11, Revelation 12, Isaiah 54, Galatians 4,* etc.

<margin>How Sinai or Hagar [bore] the old covenant law.</margin> One reads in *Galatians 4:24* that the covenant of Sinai, after the example of Hagar, bore children unto bondage. The Jews, as those bound to the law...

From this comes: *All that opens the WOMB, or what comes forth from it, shall be holy to God.*

The Lord opens or closes this, insofar as He makes one fertile or infertile, for a time or forever. If one has properly noted the scriptural ways of speaking, "one sees *a part taken for the whole*" <note>original: "pars pro toto"</note>. *Luke XXIII. 29.* explained further in *Matt. XXIV. 19.*

And because the Womb is hidden, being almost the innermost and middle part of the body, wherein one can scarcely comprehend the formation <margin>Abysses compared to the Womb.</margin>of life, the abysses of the sea and the depths and hollows of the earth are compared to it, *Job I. and XXXVIII.* as being the fertile and matter-providing main parts of the whole universe. Thus, the "Womb" is asked after as the master-worker and cause of the rain, dew-drops, ice, and the frost of heaven, *Job XXXVIII. 28, 29.* both in respect to their formation and their place and actual bringing forth, etc.

Thus, we encounter a remarkable passage mentioning the Womb in *Ps. CX. 3. Out of the Womb of the morning [dawn] shall be the dew of your youth.*

The 70 Translators <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> read this verse as follows: *With you is the beginning in the day of your power, in the splendors of your saints, from the womb before the morning star I have begotten you* <note>original Greek: "Μετὰ σοῦ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τῆς δυνάμεώς σοῦ, ἐν ταῖς λαμπρότησι τῶν ἁγίων σοῦ, ἐκ γαστρὸς πρὸ ἑωσφόρου ἐγέννησά σε"</note>, which was followed precisely by the common translation <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note>. *With you is the principle in the day of your strength, in the brightness of your saints: from the womb before the daystar I have begotten you.* <note>original Latin: "Tecum principium in die virtutis tue, in splendoribus sanctorum tuorum: ab utero ante luciferum genui te."</note>

I will not speak of the various readings, punctuations, and interpretations, especially those of the Church Fathers, and among them the Greek Fathers. One may consult the commentators. See *Glassius in Christologia Davidica, p. 117-127.* etc.

Now, while some have wished to apply this to the eternal and incomprehensible begetting of the Son of God—as being born already before the Sun and the first light of day—I do not see on what ground such a view would rest here. "Out of, or from the dawn," some interpret in the sense of: *Very diligently, industriously, with all earnestness, caution, and neatness*, as in *Job VIII. 5. Ps. LXVIII. 34. Prov. VII. 15.* etc.

I am very willing to believe that this refers to the people—the spiritual and faithful army of Prince Messiah—who would come to him as volunteers from Jews and Gentiles, especially in the early times of the New Testament through the preaching of the Gospel. I.* etc.), being the first-called by the Gospel, in distinction from those called in the full day when Jesus' kingdom had broken through everywhere (*Isa. II. Micah IV. Ps. II. Isa. XLIX and LX.*).

In the meantime, I would also say that I understand it in this way: namely, by the "dawn" which is in the east, from where the light comes to us and where the day is born <margin>what to understand.</margin>to us, I find it not absurd to understand the eastern part of the world, from where the light of truth and knowledge broke through to the western parts. Thus, the Gospel of the kingdom would shine like lightning in the east and shine through into the west. Just as the primary promises were first made there, so were they also first initially fulfilled there. <margin>The thought of Professor van den Honert.</margin>
It is an altogether charming idea conceived by the learned Mr. Tako Haio van den Honert, currently a famous Professor at Leiden, in his learned work on *Psalm 110*, where one sees "holy ornaments" translated as *armor of God’s sanctuary*, in which heroes are accustomed to appear, making themselves not a little awesome in the eyes of the beholder and their enemies. *Ezek. 23:6, 12, 13; and Ezek. 27:10.*

<margin>Armor of the Sanctuary.</margin>

But when we consider that armor in all well-ordered kingdoms is kept in armories or *Arsenals* to be ready for the day of the expedition, then it comes to mind whether <term>קודש</term> <note>Hebrew: *Kodesch*, meaning holiness or a holy place/sanctuary.</note> does not reveal here the Armory in which the weapons of the Lord's people are kept and brought out for the expedition—namely, the heavenly sanctuary.

### LABOR PAINS AND WOE.

Certainly, it is clear enough from experience that this distress is agonizing, very painful, oppressive, and sometimes fatal; indeed, it often falls upon women suddenly when they least expect it.

How a pregnant woman recoils against this, with how strong a desire and longing she is moved just to be delivered of a healthy and well-formed fruit, and to find herself released from her bonds and burden, is known to those who have bound themselves in a fruitful marriage.

<margin>When "Labor Pains" is used.</margin>
Who is now so ignorant that they would not know the figure of speech—that Labor Pains and Woe are brought up when the heaviest, most pressing, dangerous, unexpected, and unavoidable dangers, pains, and calamities threaten someone? Or when someone sighs under their misery and intensely pants for their release and liberation? Out of very many, I will insert only a few places here: *Ps. 55; Isa. 13, 21, and 54; Jer. 6, 49, and 50; Hos. 13; 1 Thess. 5,* etc.

Among other places, *Romans 8:22* is very remarkable in this regard: "for we know that the whole creation groans together, and [as it were] travails in labor pains together." Let me briefly set down something about these important words, alongside the views of others.

By the "whole creation groaning under vanity," etc., I by no means understand the evil spirits, nor the good and established ones, because they are in no way subjected to vanity; because I also read nowhere that they are called God’s creature <term>Κτίσις</term> <note>Greek: *Ktisis*, meaning creation or creature.</note> or <term>πᾶσα κτίσις</term> <note>Greek: *pasa ktisis*, meaning "all creation" or "every creature."</note> "the whole creation"; because they are not sent out and made subservient against their mind and will for the salvation of God's children.

The most common and simplest view then, before I raise anything else, is that by "the whole creation" one must understand the visible created world, made good by God to be subject in many parts to the service of men in its right state, before the curse was pronounced over it because of sin.

That *creation waits for the revealing of the children of God*. Properly speaking, this does not apply to the inanimate and irrational creation. It is a figurative, improper way of speaking, most common and peculiar to Orators and Poets. One finds it more often like this: *Deut. 32:1; Isa. 55:12; Ps. 19:2-7;* and with emphasis, *it waits with lifted head*. It is a manner of speaking transferred from man to the irrational creation. Someone who expects another, or looks forward to something from elsewhere, longs greatly; the long delay falls upon him...

*The revelation of the children of God.* It is true that those sealed by God are assured of their childhood <note>Meaning their status as adopted children of God.</note>, but it has not yet been revealed what they shall be. *1 John 3:2.* It is also certain that all those chosen for childhood from among the Jews and Gentiles have not yet appeared, been recognized, or become manifest. It is sure that not all are considered children of God, but only those who truly are; not all are children who are wrongly regarded as such or wish to be passed off as such.

<margin>Children of God.</margin>
The most certain mark of all shall be the separation of the sheep and the goats on the general Day of Judgment. By these words of the Apostle, it is said to be understood through a figure of speech <note>The author uses "Spraakverbeeldinge," referring to personification or prosopopoeia.</note> in an improper and metaphorical way, *that if the world, and all creatures in the world, had sufficient understanding, judgment, and observation, they would grasp how their present state—with the cursed birth brought by the fall and the coming of sin into the world—does not correspond at all to their state before the fall: and if they clearly and distinctly understood that at the revelation of the children of God they were to be released from their vanity and bondage, they would look forward as if with a lifting of the head and strong desire to see if that time were not approaching.*

The creature appears subject to vanity <note>original: "ydelheit," often translated in bibles as "futility."</note>, yet not willingly, but because of him who subjected it. *Vanity of vanities, all is vanity, Eccl. 1:2–8.* Nothing lasts forever. The heaven becomes heavily clouded and goes into deep mourning; vapors, mist, and blight are harmful to men, cattle, and trees. Sun, Moon, and Stars seem to have sunk into a dismal abyss. The heaven becomes like metal, the earth like copper. The air is pestilential, the winds become wrathful. The sea and rivers exceed their boundaries with terrible devastation and flooding. Beetles, locusts, caterpillars, worms, snails, and base vermin plague cattle and men.

<margin>Miseries of the world.</margin>
<margin>Abuse of the creature.</margin>
The creature is abused and wasted in all sorts of ways. The creature, made for God, is abused for God’s dishonor and robbery, and for man's ultimate destruction.

Such a state is now far removed from the first creation and the purpose of the creature in its use and subjection. If creatures had understanding and judgment, would they not strive to release themselves from this vanity and violation, and desire to be set free from it?

Because of, and by way of man’s transgression, for a curse and punishment upon man, God has subjected it to this vanity for a time; He allows man to abuse the creature.

However, the creature's liberation from bondage is tied to the freedom of the glory of the children of God. Improperly, hope is attributed to that irrational creature. Yet it is shown that there is hope because of God's counsel and promise, that a change will one day be made in this, and the creature brought back to its original state; when the children of God come into full glory, and the godless have been condemned to the abyss of hell, they will no longer be able to abuse the creature. Toward this change, toward this state, the Apostle says, *the creature groans, and is as if in labor pains.*

<column-break/>

It appears that the Apostle regards the whole universe as a great body and structure, consisting of many parts and members. Movement is considered the soul, the Sun the heart, the Moon the liver—which provides the entire body with necessary fluids, etc.

That entire creation groans alongside the children of God. It is an exaggerating way of speaking, by personification. Groaning—being a mournful breathing and pushing out of swallowed air from the hollow of the chest, caused by some present, expected, or foreseen evil, or a desire for some good that seems to be withheld from us—properly has no place in an irrational or lifeless creature. But if the creature knew its misfortune and state, and understood its approaching liberation, it would groan over it and long for it.

<margin>Meaning of groaning.</margin>
And now closer to our word, for which this was brought forward: the Apostle says *that the creature is as if in labor pains.* <note>The Dutch "baarens noot" refers to the distress of childbirth.</note> Groenewegen <note>Henricus Groenewegen (1640–1692), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> says in *Hieroglyphics*: *All movements and inclinations of the creatures, in that order in which they were placed by God, are so arranged that they might not always groan under vanity. And in the Psalms he says, citing this passage and Revelation 12: All the various changes and successions of things, states in the world, commotions of nations, and distresses of the church: are mere precursors of the dawning of the great day of glory, with which the entire creation is pregnant.*

<margin>Opinion of Groenewegen.</margin>
It does not say there "as if in labor pains," but "in labor pains." The little word (as) is inserted there to express that it is with the creature as it is with a woman who has the labor upon her body. Groaning improperly and figuratively under that labor and bondage, running as if toward the end, with so many and certain precursors of the approaching deliverance and change, that one would almost think the day of the Lord were at hand. And that began just after sin and has lasted until this time: so that from the whole of God’s dealings—the unfolding of His Testament, *Genesis 3:15;* the preservation of Noah and his family in the Ark and the destruction of the first world; the preservation of Lot in Sodom; the devastation of those godless cities; the establishment of the covenant with Abraham and Israel; the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple, etc.—one may conclude that the groaning of the creature and His children is not in vain, but a precursor of the fruit of deliverance and glory, which is to follow such groaning, sighing, and labor pains.

<margin>Groaning a precursor of deliverance.</margin>
But before I depart from this, I shall give the intelligent and studious reader another short sketch of a different opinion, which, if it can hold place and be judged to be consistent with the common meaning of the words, is quite shrewdly and ingeniously devised.

<margin>Gentiles under vanity.</margin>
It is beyond dispute that the Gentiles have been under vanity, serving the *Elilim* <note>original: "Elilim," a Hebrew term for worthless or "nothing" idols</note>, those futile and powerless idols and their images. *1 Cor. 8; Ps. 115; etc.* They worshipped the Sun, Moon, Stars, Leeks, Onions, etc. *Acts 14; Rom. 1:21*, walking in the vanity of their hearts and ruminations. *Eph. 4:4; etc.*

It is true that they served vanity, sin, and evil desires willingly and with delight; yet, they did not do so under the absolute perception of it being evil. No one loves sin as sin, evil as evil, or punishment and curse as such; rather, they love it under the perception of some supposed good, through God's righteous judgment of blindness and delusion. *Rom. 1, 2, and 3.* He shut

They wished to be with Plato, Socrates, Aristotle, Lycurgus, and others, of whom they had the delusion that they were truly happy.

<margin>Explanation of Mr. Lampe.</margin>
It pleases us to investigate the passage of Paul somewhat more closely and accurately, so that it may be more evident how much light is shed by our proposition. We divide the entire discourse into two parts: for therein comes:

I. The presentation, in which the hope of the entire church, regarding the greater glory of the believers after suffering and struggle, is depicted (verse 19). And

A. The subject of that presentation is the *expectation of the creature*. In which one must note the idiomatic way of speaking of the Hebrews, whereby a noun is taken for an adverb <note>original Latin: *substantivum regens pro adjectivo*, a "governing noun for an adjective."</note>, as the learned Johannes Vorstius has extensively pointed out in his *Sacred Philology on the Hebraisms of the N.T., Chapter 10*. To whose cited examples we could also add this passage. For it is as much as if the Holy Apostle had wanted to say: *the creature that expects with head held high*. *Ktisis* <note>Greek for "creation" or "creature."</note> or "creature" signifies here the church of all times. And *pasa*, "all" or "whole," means all believers of the universal church of all times: in such a way that what is called in another respect *kainè ktisis*, a *new creature* (*2 Cor. 5:17; Gal. 6:15*), is here also fittingly called *pasa ktisis*, the whole creature. As also in *Col. 1:15*, *the firstborn of all creatures*: where the fundamental reason for this first-birth directs us to the thought that we understand by "creature" nothing other than the Church. For He is the Firstborn of those whose brother He is, and whom He sanctifies: which is characteristic of the true members of the church (in relation to Christ). And thus the birthright of the Savior is revealed by the Apostle in its secret sense, as clear as noon, *Heb. 12:11* and also in our *8th Chapter, verse 29*. The ground of this naming must be drawn from the spiritual creation, which is symbolized by the world’s creation: whereby the whole church is a new heaven and a new earth, and every believer can be regarded as God's handiwork created in Christ Jesus, *Eph. 2:10*. In which sense this corresponds with *gnolaam* <note>A Dutch rendering of the Hebrew *Olam*, meaning world or eternity.</note>, eternal, *aiōn*, *kosmos*, "world." Which words, through their own power, express the totality and the universality of the world and men: and for that reason are frequently applied to the universality of the church. *See Rev. 5:13.*

<margin>Expectation with head held high.</margin>
*APOKARADOKIA*, *expectation with a raised head* <note>Greek term for eager, neck-stretching anticipation.</note>; is a particular quality of the church, and not of the inanimate world, which is not subject to passions, nor indeed of all men in general, who—

of which the greatest part of the hope of the believers is excluded. And this *lifting up of the head* is a symbol of **Hope**, which is often represented on Roman coins in the form of a woman standing with an upright head. The lifting up of the head signifies: 1. A fully certain expectation of the hoped-for good. 2. A very heartfelt longing. 3. A peaceful imagination that the thing hoped for will come to us from above through God's help, etc. Under the same symbol, the Savior also exhorts his disciples to a living hope. *Luke 21:28.* <note>The original cites Luke 2:28, but the context of "lifting up heads" refers to Luke 21:28.</note> Compare with this a similar way of speaking in *Psalm 133:1, etc.*

B. Of this creature it is said, *that it waits for the revelation of the children of God.*

<margin>Revelation of God's children.</margin>
1. There one sees the expected object, *the revelation of the children of God.* "Children of God" are not placed here in opposition to "the creature," as some object to us—because "the creature" signifies a universality of the whole Universe—but rather, they are understood to be included within "the creature." Here, "the creature" signifies the universal entire Church, acting as that mother (whose symbol we explained above) who recognizes all believers as her sons, especially those who will yet be brought in during the coming ages. This is as clear as day from the **Birth-pangs** attributed to this creature in *Romans 8:22*, proving that, in respect to the children who have God as their Father through the spiritual marriage, she is their mother.

<margin>REVELATION <note>Greek: ΑΠΟΚΑΛΥΨΙΣ (Apokalypsis)</note></margin>
**REVELATION** <note>Greek: *Apokalypsis*</note>, *the revealing of these children*, can refer to the opening of the Covenant of Grace, in which someone is adopted and recorded as an heir, and consequently admitted to the inheritance. Certainly, the word **REVELATION** is not only used for mysteries and hidden truths, but also for people and things themselves that appear at certain appointed times, as in *2 Thessalonians 2:6-8.* So one must also understand such a revelation here, through which the children of God—who are generally unknown to the world, and whose salvation-goods and heavenly privileges are promised and thus far veiled—are placed into full daylight by the outcome. Such a revelation was seen at the beginning of the New Testament, when the bride of Christ no longer wished to be as one who veils herself <note>original: *Song of Solomon 1:6*</note>, and all believers beheld the glory of the Lord with an unveiled face: *2 Corinthians 3:18*, which was accompanied by the enlightenment of the Gentiles. *Luke 2:32.* We expect a closer revelation in that time *when the Lord of hosts will swallow up the covering of the face with which all peoples are wrapped, and the veil with which all nations are covered. Isaiah 25:7.* But that revelation of salvation and inheritance will be most perfect in the last time, of which Peter speaks in *1 Peter 1:5*—unless one would rather understand by that "last time" the entire administration of the New Testament, in which salvation is revealed by degrees and will subsequently be revealed more closely.

2. That which they do is **EXPECTATION** <note>Greek: ΑΠΕΚΔΕΧΕΣΘΑΙ (*Apekdechesthai*)</note>. The creature *expects* that revelation. This act is unique only to the children of God, and this word is never used except in reference to them. They are those who expect the revelation of our Lord, *1 Corinthians 1:7; Hebrews 9:28*, compared with *Galatians 5:5; Philippians 3:20.* There are various degrees of expectation, variously depicted in *Psalm 130:5, 6; James 5:7, 8.*

<column-break/>

II. The confirmation of the proposition is urged by two lines of reasoning.

A. From the nature of the increase of God’s church, which the Apostle expresses in verses 20 and 21, wherein three things are to be well distinguished and have particular emphasis to confirm the Apostle’s proposition.

1. The humiliation itself, which is painted by two phrases, namely: *a. the subjection to vanity; b. the bondage of corruption* (verse 21).

This can contain four different subjects here, which must be joined together:

*a.* The constant fluctuations of life, especially sinful occurrences, by which our peace is disturbed. *Psalm 39:6; Ecclesiastes 1:2-14 and 2:1, etc.*

*b.* Judaism, and their vain walk and human institutions. *Psalm 4:3 and 31:3.*

*c.* Heathen idolatry and corrupt foundations. *Ephesians 4:17; Acts 14:15; Romans 1:22.* And idols are called "vanity." *Jeremiah 11:5; Jonah 2:9.* <term>Nothings <gloss>original Hebrew: *Elilim*, meaning powerless or non-existent gods</gloss></term>, *Zechariah 9:17.*

*d.* Antichristendom, and its followers. *Psalm 144:8; Psalm 127:1, 2.*

**SUBJECTION** <note>Greek: ΥΠΟΤΑΞΙΣ (*Hypotaxis*)</note>: by which cannot be understood an active subjection, as when someone is forced to obey another's command because it is against his will and yet imposed by God; this fits nothing but a passive subordination, as the word is taken in *Luke 10:16; Hebrews 12:9.* Thus are the believers subject to sin and its law: wherefore their life is also full of miseries. *Romans 7:17, etc.; Hebrews 12:1.* They are also subject to Judaism, Heathenism, and Antichristendom, because they have had to suffer much from them, and must yet suffer.

<margin>Hard life of the Believers.</margin>
**CORRUPTION** <note>Greek: ΦΘΟΡΑ (*Phthora*)</note> means the same thing that Paul had called *vanity*: but it expresses it somewhat more em-

# THE WOMB.

expounds further upon their misery and has both an active and a passive meaning: for it can express that which is subject to corruption, or that which brings corruption to others—everything included under the name of "vanity." That is, it is even subject to corruption because it ends in eternal death and, in a sense, brings death to believers by manifesting so many calamities and even temporal death. Examples include: Sins (*2 Peter 1:4*); the shadow-rites <note>The "shadow-rites" refer to the Jewish ceremonial laws which, according to early Christian theology, were mere "shadows" of the reality found in Christ.</note> of the Jews (*Colossians 2:22*). Heathenism has destroyed almost the entire church, yet it shall itself go entirely to ruin; and what is the Antichristian system other than a pit of perdition, where *Apollyon* <note>original: ἀπολλύων, meaning "The Destroyer," a name for the king of the bottomless pit in Revelation 9:11.</note>, the son of perdition, reigns over those who are lost? The Lord shall also destroy him by the Spirit of His mouth (*2 Thessalonians 2*), and the destruction of his precursors points toward this (*2 Peter 2:12*).

*BONDAGE* <note>original: ΔΟΥΛΕΙΑ (Douleia)</note> aggravates the terrifying image of misery. Do not understand "active bondage" here, which only fits the godless and the enemies of the church (*2 Peter 2:19*), although it is true that one can attribute a bondage of corruption to believers in a passive sense of subjection (*Romans 7:23-25*).

<margin>
Bondage burdens the image of misery.
</margin>

*Thus, believers also groan under the bondage of corruption*, because the remnants of sin still cling to them, and because they must struggle through many oppressions from the Jews, the Heathen, and the followers of the Antichrist (*Psalm 125:3; Joel 3:11, 12*).

<margin>
Believers under the bondage of corruption.
</margin>

2. The origin of this humiliation is presented in both an affirmative and a negative way: *not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same.*

*NOT WILLINGLY* <note>original: ’ΟΥΚ ΕΚΟΥΣΑ (Ouk ekousa)</note>, or *by constraint* <note>original: ἀναγκασῶς (Anagkastōs)</note> (*1 Peter 5:1*); for "willingly" <note>original: ἑκουσίως</note> is used by the Seventy Translators <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> for <term>with free-will <note>Hebrew: בנדבה (Bi-nedavah)</note></term> (*Psalm 54:8*) and <term>whose heart moves him <note>Hebrew: אשר נשאו לבו (Asher nesao libbo)</note></term> (*Exodus 36:2*). Namely: the creature does not lift up its heart to vanity; rather, the sign of the New Testament believers is that they do not lift up their souls to vanity (*Psalm 24:4*) and they sigh: *turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity.* They shrink from it, not only because vanity is defiled with sin—since they no longer sin willfully (*Hebrews 10:26*)—but also because it burdens the believers and causes many calamities to be suffered. It is certainly proper to submit oneself patiently to Divine Providence, but no one in their right mind will willingly embrace calamities (*Ephesians 5:29; Matthew 26:39; Psalm 120:5*).

*HE WHO SUBJECTED IT* <note>original: ΥΠΟΤΑΞΑΣ (Hypotaxas)</note>.
1. It is God Himself, according to His counsel and purpose (*Psalm 83:24*). 2. According to what was established immediately after the Fall (*Genesis 3:16-19*). 3. According to the covenant with Noah (*Genesis 8:4*). 4. According to the Prophets, who foretold the suffering of the church. 5. According to God’s active providence (*Psalm 44:13; Hebrews 12:9*).

3. The outcome of the humiliation consists in the promised deliverance: *in hope that the creature itself also shall be delivered into the liberty of the glory of the children of God.*

*In hope.* Thus Paul shows that when God subjected the creature to vanity, He also gave promises that He would lift it up again.

*That also the same.* This insertion indicates a contrast between those already introduced into glory and the "children" who formerly received only a "shadow-redemption."

*Shall be delivered.* Just as "bondage" signifies various calamities, so "deliverance" extends to all of these: from the old economy; from tyranny and violence in the last days; at death from the remnants of sin; at the resurrection of the flesh, etc. (*Job 8:32*).

<margin>
Bondage signifies calamities.
</margin>

*Into the liberty.* primarily belonging to the will. It is specifically characteristic of the New Testament, but it is not brought about all at once. As long as anything remains that causes hindrance and prevents believers from doing everything they wish and are obligated to do for God's honor, so long is the liberty not perfect. The liberty and the glory of the church go hand in hand: and as she proceeds from glory to glory, so she also proceeds from liberty to liberty (*2 Corinthians 3:18*).

Now, since such great hope is granted to this creature subjected to vanity, what is more reasonable than to cling to God's promises with constant expectation, and to persevere therein until they are fulfilled?

<margin>
To cling to God's promises.
</margin>

<column-break/>

B. The closer proof is from the example of the church, which has been in the world until now, *for we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now.* As long as God's creature has been on earth, so long has the anxious expectation for the coming deliverance been extended. For, although they first longed for the coming of the Savior, they nonetheless also desire at the same time that all other promises might be fulfilled: the application of the salvation brought forth, and the perfect enjoyment of the promised glory. Therefore, two passions are presented here: *groaning together* and *travailing in pain together.*

*Groaning together.* Philo, in *Allegories of the Law, Book 2, p. 100, etc.* <note>Philo of Alexandria was a Jewish philosopher who used allegorical methods to explain the Torah; the author here uses him to define the depth of human suffering.</note> Groaning is an inward and heartfelt sorrow; often we mourn without groaning, but as often as we sigh/groan, we are painfully overwhelmed and burdened with sorrow. And in his book *That the Worse is Wont to Attack the Better, p. 117*, he uses the same language. See examples: *Genesis 3:23, 24; Genesis 4:2.*

<margin>
What groaning is.
</margin>

*Genesis 5:29 and 15:2. Genesis 49:18. Job 19:27.*

Also in *birth-pangs* <note>The Dutch "Baarensnoot" refers to the labor pains or travail of childbirth.</note>. This signifies the time when the birth is near, and it can be fearlessly applied to the Church of the Old Testament. To this belonged (pertaining to the great work of redemption) the entire yoke of the Law, all the Jewish judgments, and the Assyrian and Babylonian captivities.

Union of all members of the Church.

### THE WOMB OF THE DAWN.

<margin>
How the "Womb of the dawn" is to be understood.
</margin>
This must be understood not, *a.* in an active sense, as a womb from which the dawn produces something. But *b.* in a passive sense, as that from which the dawn itself is brought forth.

The clouds are the literal womb of the dawn, providing a faint or shimmering light to the inhabitants of the earth through the reflected rays of the rising Sun, serving as a herald of the approaching day. Yet, since everything in this Psalm <note>This likely refers to Psalm 110:3, "from the womb of the morning: thou hast the dew of thy youth."</note> must be understood in a spiritual manner, we see clearly that we must understand this dawn, and the womb from which that dawn was to be born and appear, in a spiritual sense here.

<margin>
To be understood in a spiritual sense.
</margin>
This dawn—that is, the first light of the Gospel, which was to be a herald of the approaching day of salvation—also had its womb, where it stood ready, as it were, to be born and to come forth.

<margin>
The Holy Spirit as the womb of the spiritual dawn.
</margin>
And what else can the womb of this spiritual dawn be but the Holy Spirit himself? For if the dawn comes, properly speaking, out of and through the clouds when they are shone upon by the rising Sun and become "pregnant" with light; who does not see that this spiritual dawn—this first light of the Gospel, which was to be a certain herald of the day of salvation—had to come forth out of and through the Holy Spirit? This occurs when the rays of the newly rising Sun of Righteousness—that is, when the merits of the Messiah—should begin to break through Him at the beginning (*John 16:13, 14, 15*), to enlighten the church, first with a pleasant shimmering light, then with a continuing increase, and so shining until the full midday (*Hosea 6:2, 3; 2 Samuel 23:4; Matthew 4:2; Isaiah 21:13; Proverbs 4:18*).

Since this spiritual dawn had to emerge from the Holy Spirit, just as the natural dawn is born from the clouds, we see here a new reason why the

<column-break/>

Holy Spirit appears in God’s word under the symbol <note>The author uses the term "zinnebeelt," referring to an emblem or symbolic representation.</note> of the clouds (*Isaiah 4:5 and 5:6; Nehemiah 9:12; Isaiah 63:10-14; etc.*).

<margin>
How the clouds are used as a symbol.
</margin>
Now, from that same womb from which this dawn emerges, these armaments <note>Refers to the "holy garments" or "spiritual weapons" mentioned in the context of the Messiah's people.</note> would come forth—that is, from the Holy Spirit: for when the enemy comes against the Messiah’s people like a flood, then the Spirit of the Lord shall lift up a banner against him (*Isaiah 59:19*). It is also from this that the willingness, which was to be awakened in the Messiah’s people through these armaments of the sanctuary, is not obscurely attributed to the Holy Spirit as the cause of this willingness (*Psalm 51:14; Psalm 68:10-12; and Joel 2:28, 29*).

I shall satisfy myself with what has been said and step over to something else.

->BABEL, with its first foundation, city, tower, master builder, and confusion of tongues. The kingdom of Babel and that which belongs to it, and what is said of it in the holy scroll: to what it is applied, along with its mutual correspondences, and so forth. <note>original: בבל (Hebrew), Βαβυλ, Βαβυλὼν (Greek) — all meaning Babel or Babylon.</note><-

<margin>
The author's opinion on BABEL.
</margin>
Regarding BABEL, which was honestly so named in its first foundations due to the confusion of tongues, I shall set down my opinion here with much modesty.

I hold that after the general Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note>, mankind, keeping together and having multiplied remarkably, could not for long sustain themselves with their livestock on the slopes of the mountains and in very narrow places. Consequently, they must have collectively looked out for a more spacious and fertile region. Thus they came to the plain and expanse of Shinar, a very precious, rich, and fertile land in the east—the very best of the whole east, according to the accounts of Herodotus (*Book I*), Strabo (*Book XVI*), Pliny (*Book I, Chapter 26*), etc. There they came to a mutual agreement to build a city and a tower, under the chief leadership of Nimrod, and not of the Assyrians as Marsham maintains in *Can. Chron. p. 507*, arguing that one ought to shift it to the lifetime of Nabonassar. For the Divine history in *Genesis 10* tells us clearly. And one must make a distinction between the city of Babel and the kingdom of Babel, for Babel is distinguished from it as a beginning. It is not said of Nimrod that he captured or seized it, but that he *built* it. That he would have abandoned it because of the flooding of the Euphrates is not found in the text. One also reads later of the kings of Shinar (*Genesis 14*), a proof that it was not abandoned.

<margin>
The city and Kingdom of Babel distinguished.
</margin>
Regarding the fact that the great Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a famous French Protestant biblical scholar.</note> maintains in his *Phaleg* that *Nimrod was not yet born at the time of the building of Babel’s tower and the city's foundation, or at least was still very young, and therefore not the founder, and that he otherwise would have been scattered; and thus that he arrived with a troop of Cushites after the dispersion to resume the halted and unfinished work; and also that he and Junius, Vatablus, etc. maintain that Nimrod went from Babel to Assyria and there built Nineveh, etc.*—upon that I remark that one does not read in the holy history what Bochart wishes to suppose. It is true that in *Micah 5:5* one reads of Assyria and the land of Nimrod, but one cannot conclude from that with Bochart, *a.* That Nimrod was the founder of Assyria.

<margin>
Observation on Bochart and others.
</margin>

# BABEL.

Syria. *b.* Whether Asshur <note>The Hebrew name 'Asshur' is often used both for the person and the land of Assyria.</note> and the land of Nimrod are one and the same. *c.* And that Nimrod would not have built Babel: for Asshur and Nimrod's land are distinguished there, although they are also joined together there, because Judah was led captive to Babel and Israel to Assyria: and that, when Micah wrote, Babylon had fallen into the hand and power of the Assyrians.

<margin>Nimrod, founder of Babel. Asshur of Assyria.</margin>
Otherwise, I hold it that Nimrod should be considered the founder of the kingdom of Babel, and Asshur the founder of the kingdom of Assyria, with the kingdom of Babel preceding that of Assyria: and not Nimrod of Assyria and Nineveh, as Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> and others have judged. I understand through *Genesis 10:11, "and out of that land went forth Asshur,"* etc., not Nimrod going from Babel to Assyria and building Nineveh there. But I take Asshur as a man’s name, the son of Shem: and in doing so, I do not need to invent any *ellipsis* <note>A grammatical omission where words are understood but not stated.</note> or word-reference, such as "into Asshur (or Assyria) Nimrod went." And so the land, afterwards called Assyria, was occupied by Asshur.

If one wishes to say that Asshur’s life and deeds are then recounted before he was even born? I answer: what difficulty is there in this, that there be a preliminary account? In this same chapter, *Genesis 10:22*, his birth is recorded. It was a matter of convenience that Nimrod and the beginnings of Babel's kingdom had been spoken of. There are more such preliminary accounts, as in *Genesis 11:12*, where in the middle of a break and as if in a glimpse, something more is inserted and told. See also *1 Kings 10:11, 12, 13, etc.*

Holding myself strictly then to the historical account of Moses in *Genesis 10*, I hold it that Nimrod, the son of Cush and grandson of Ham, laid the foundations of the Babylonian Monarchy: not actually Semiramis, Ninus, or anyone else, as has been thought from Ctesias, Diodorus, Theocritus, Strabo, Ovid, Trogus, Mela, Solinus, etc., while Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian</note> leaves it undecided whether one should consider Semiramis or Belus (Nimrod)—honored and known by those names among his people and nation—to be the first founder or establisher of Babel.

While I mention Bel or Belus here, one should imagine no other person than Nimrod. For he whom the pagans call Bel and Belus, Moses calls Nimrod, and he was honored with many reverences and ceremonies as their head and kingdom-founder, as can be read in *Alexander ab Alexandro, Books III and VII.* Bel and Belus is Baal: lord, god, or head, just as there have been so many and various Bels and Beluses. See *Selden, Syntagma II, Chapter I, etc.*

Nimrod from <term>מרד</term> <note>original: "מרד" (m-r-d); the Hebrew root for 'rebel'.</note> means he rebelled, or offered insurrection—a rebel—if one wishes merely to ascribe the name to the deed. For it is held that the old father Noah, as by a last will, divided the entire earth among his three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and pointed out to each his inheritance, but that Nimrod, of Ham's lineage, by no means kept to this arrangement. See *Eusebius's Chronicle (Greek), 10; Philastrius of Brescia, On Heresies, 118, etc.* To which I say, that such a thing is supposed and said, but by no means proven, and that in the Holy Scriptures there are no divine traces of this.

As for the city which Nimrod, with the rest of humanity, occupied and built so soon after the

<column-break/>

Deluge <note>original: "Zundvloet"</note>: I am quite willing to believe that Semiramis, Nebuchadnezzar, and Nitocris (the wife of Evil-merodach) contributed singularly much to the enlargement, adornment, and strength of that city, and indeed of the kingdom of Babel: and that very much could be said of that city, the city walls, the perimeters, the tower, the temple, and the idol-image, if I were to succeed in describing it. But regarding this, one should look to Bochart's *Phaleg*, Marsham's *Canon Chronicus*, Dieteric's *Antiquities of the Old Testament*, Goeree's *Biblical Antiquities*, and *The Republic of the Jews*, part one, etc. In what follows, something of this appears in the distance. And that this city, like others, was small at first and was thereafter extended, enlarged, and strengthened as the capital city of the kingdom of Babel and the place of the kings' court, is very probable, according to the gathered testimonies of the ancient writers.

Thucydides, in his first book, speaks of un-walled cities that were inhabited like villages. These were nothing more than hamlets. So too Herodotus says that the heroes of Taphi and Teleboa lived in villages. See further Festus on the word <term>COMISSATIO</term> <note>original: "COMISSATIO"; a Latin term for a village revelry or procession.</note>, and Perizonius in his treatises on *Babylonian Origins*.

Of Nimrod it is written in *Genesis 10:8, 9, 10* that he began to be a mighty one on earth: *that he was a mighty hunter before the face of the Lord:* and that a proverb is derived from him. I have noted that a "strong and mighty hunter before the face of the Lord" is understood in this sense: *that he was a hunter, persecutor, and oppressor of men, who sought to bring everything under himself and his governance by force, and thus strove with his following for the highest authority and rule, and for defense built a city, and a tower within the city.*

For my part, I profess to have singular great respect for the learned and their well-sifted thoughts: however, it seems to me that there is no reason to depart so suddenly from the simple letter and history, and to make of him merely a tyrant, persecutor, and oppressor of men, bypassing the proper and literal meaning of the words: for I find neither tittle nor iota in the Holy Scriptures suggesting that Nimrod was such an attacker and persecutor, let alone a destroyer of the Holy Seed <note>The lineage of the faithful leading to the Messiah.</note>.

I would then most closely think that he was a very bold, brave, and courageous hunter before the face of the Lord: not precisely against the Lord or his Holy Seed; as if "before the Lord" or "before His Face" should merely be understood as "against the Lord and the Holy Seed." Rather, that in hunting he went to work so boldly and keenly as if, having Divine protection to his advantage, nothing could harm him. See *Genesis 22, Psalm 51, and Psalm 72.*

In the land of the East—Canaan, Babylonia, etc.—there were many wild and ravenous beasts, as is confirmed by the holy writers in *Exodus 23, Judges 14, 1 Samuel 17, 2 Kings 17,* etc., and also by secular writers such as *Pausanias in Attica, Herodotus, Valerius, Bochart (Hieroz. p. 1. Lib. III. Kap. 4), Perizonius (Dissert. de Orig. Babyl. 7. part. 6.), etc.*

Consequently, I would think that those who had killed and destroyed lions, bears, tigers, etc., and thus given proof of their strength and bravery, received not only the people's applause—

> In former times, hunting was a training for war among the Persians. <note>original: "Olim venatio tyrocinium militiæ apud Persas." Xenophon, Cyropaedia, Book I; Florus on Viriatus, Book XI. 27.</note> That is: *Among the Persians, hunting was once a practice-exercise for war.*
