Hinc robore corporibus, animisque sumpto, jam non circa feras tantum subsistere, sed in latrones præda onustos impetus facere."</note>

<margin>Romulus and Remus.</margin>
That is: *Thus born and thus raised, as soon as they began to grow up, they did not stay hanging about the stables or the cattle, but they went to the hunt and crisscrossed the woods. Having become stronger in body and increased in courage, they did not leave it at pursuing wild game, but attacked the robbers laden with booty.*

However, it could be that Nimrod later perhaps turned his power and authority into a harsh tyranny; it could be, I say, yet the matter is not so clear or proven that one could or should rely upon it.

But before I speak of the Empire of Babel, remaining with its first origins, it will not be ill-advised, according to the opinion of many learned men, to state and expose the actual design of Nimrod, with his followers, from all of humanity gathered there and still living together, in building the city and tower.

<margin>Design of Nimrod.</margin>
<margin>Opinion of some.</margin>
That some have believed that Ham's <note>Ham was the son of Noah whose descendants were traditionally associated with the peoples of Africa and parts of Asia; in some interpretations, his line is viewed as rebellious.</note> lineage had formed a conspiracy to disturb the children of Seth <note>Seth was the third son of Adam, often representing the "godly" line in contrast to the line of Cain or the rebellious descendants of Ham.</note> through heavy wars, and thus—with one tongue and lip—to strengthen themselves against them and, if possible, to frustrate Noah's prophecy of *not becoming a servant of servants*, etc. It does not, it seems to me, proceed so easily in all respects. For it assumes, contrary to the text, that the nations were already separated from each other and staying in different and remote places. In doing so, one seems to believe that these nations had already withdrawn from Noah’s fellowship and obedience during his lifetime. It assumes an unproven thing: that the Hamites already wanted to disturb and make war upon the Sethites.

Yet the common opinion of many contemporary theologians <note>The author refers to 17th-century Reformed scholars like Coccejus and Heidegger.</note> amounts to this: *That this city and that tower were built with the intention that the Council and assembly of those who would hold the supreme command and authority over Religion might be attached and fixed to that city and tower; so that in matters of Faith, one might turn there as to the mother and capital city; so that the same tongue and speech—that is, the faith and confession concerning Jehovah, whose name alone was then known—might be preserved, and all wrong opinions and sects might be kept away; so that all might remain linked together by laws, peace, and harmony in the matter of doctrine and religion, etc.*

Now this, being a counsel taken apart from the Lord; being a worldly arm; being a design to rule under a religious pretext, against God’s counsel to have them inhabit and populate the earth everywhere; against the separation of the holy line; and against the decree of Divine election and rejection; so the Lord broke their design, confused them in their tongue and speech, caused them to be of different thoughts and opinions, both regarding supreme power and the matter of religion, not feeling and speaking one and the same thing, from which mutual division and the splitting and separation of peoples followed. Read on this: Coccejus, Momma, Heidegger, Groenewegen, Leenhof, Huisinga, Fabritius, etc. <note>These were influential Dutch and German Reformed theologians of the 17th and early 18th centuries.</note>

Some have understood it in this way, which comes very close to the first: *that Nimrod and his followers, having banished all fear and religion from his heart, being strong, violent, and having a very large following, vied for supreme command, and to establish his power, began to build a city and tower, so as to establish a kingdom. For Scripture says: this was the beginning of his kingdom.* See Spencer, Dietericus, Musculus, etc.

Some take it as: *in order not to be scattered, and to make a name; to leave a monument to the following generation.* And thus, it is considered a matter of pride and a thirst for fame.

Since the one and the other have been briefly stated by me and shared with the reader, I cannot let it pass without drafting my remarks upon it.

<margin>The Author's Remarks.</margin>
As for the opinion of the theologians who believe that the entire design was to establish a council there to keep the received doctrine of Noah and religion pure, etc., I must testify that I would readily embrace these thoughts if Moses <note>Moses is traditionally regarded as the author of Genesis.</note> had so declared it to us or put it in our mouths; but I find neither word nor response of it in his history. I also find no traces that they were all of one mind in matters of faith, religion, or in this design. And if they had this design, to preserve purity in doctrine and religion, then their goal was good, though perhaps something could be said about the means to their end: at least this, that they did not need such a large city or tower-structure for this purpose; for what could these external buildings contribute to actual harmony? And why does Moses not mention it even with a single word? Did God then want those who intended good to become divided in the matter of religion, and was He Himself the cause of it? And where in the holy scroll does "a name" signify a place of authority, a Council, and its gathering place? And on what grounds does one depart from the simplicity of the literal text and history?

As for the opinion of the scholars and our Translators, who interpret the word <term>שם</term> <note>The Hebrew word "Shem," which means "name" or "renown."</note> as a "name," just as if in that time one sought glory, splendor, and an immortal memory for posterity; and this is thus to be regarded as a work of pride and haughtiness, etc., this too requires its own reflection: namely, **a.** It seems to assume either that they were already scattered, or knew that they were about to be scattered from there; and yet their entire design was *not* to be scattered. **b.** Had they no other design than merely to make a name? God’s Spirit does not say that; but rather, *not to be scattered from one another*. Would they perform such a costly, heavy, and difficult work merely for a name...

# BABEL.

<margin>Thoughts on this obsession with names.</margin>
...commenced their work? It is supposed that those people were so "name-sick" <note>Dutch: "naamziek"; meaning obsessed with reputation or fame.</note>. From whom did they seek this name? Their goal was to stay where they were. Why seek it from other people, when they had no assurance that any people would ever live there after them? A name is most effectively gained through descendants. They could have preserved a name by erecting a pillar, or some statue, or a lighter monument, or through singular deeds. <term>C.</term> Yet what did a name contribute to their design of not being separated from one another? And even assuming they sought a name from posterity, they would at least have had to keep some record of it: carving it into some stone or facade; for otherwise, how would anyone know who had built this city and the tower?

<margin>The goal of the Tower-builders.</margin>
To say then what the truth of the matter is, I shall derive it from the objective of the city and Tower-builders. Their design was not to be scattered from one another, but to stay together. To this end, the building of the city, and especially of that heaven-high tower, was well-suited: for the word **Shem** <note>original Hebrew: **שם** (Shem)</note> signified, besides "a name," a clear sign, an open token, a beacon, and an elevated landmark. <note>See 1 Samuel 15:12, 2 Samuel 18:18, 2 Samuel 8:13, Isaiah 56:5.</note> A "name" being a characteristic—*nomen*, as if it were *novimen* <note>Latin: "a means of knowing."</note>—that is: for the identification of some person or thing, etc. See the Professor Perizonius in his *Dissertation on the Babylonian Origins*. Thus, that city and tower were a suitable sign of their dwelling and general gathering place, being visible from very far away across the trackless, undivided, and un-beaconed paths, seen far and wide by the shepherds and farmers, so they could head straight for the tower.

<margin>Contradicting God's counsel.</margin>
Insofar as this design did not agree with God’s counsel—as He willed that they should populate and cultivate the earth—He confused and scattered them. What subsequently concerns the confusion of tongues, the multitude and diversity of languages, inflections, and pronunciations, along with what pertains to that, can be found in my first volume of *Sacred Miscellany*.

<margin>The Battle of the Giants.</margin>
It may be that from this arose the fable concerning the Battle of the Giants and the piling up of the mountains Pelion, Ossa, and Olympus to thrust Jupiter out of his Kingdom; of which one may read in Josephus, Ovid’s *Fasti* (Book 15), Homer’s *Odyssey* (Book 11), Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* (Book 1), Bochart, Grotius, Bonfrère, Dansius, Peucer, and Dieterich's *Antiquities of the Old Testament*, and Perizonius in *Babylonian Origins*.

<margin>The Author's Opinion.</margin>
I am inclined to believe that the first founding of Babel’s city and tower was brought in by God's Spirit as a symbol <note>Dutch "zinnebeelt"; an emblem or type</note> of another Babel; however, I maintain that one may just as strongly fix one's eye on the Empire and the formidable power that arose from those beginnings over time. And so, rather than speaking at length about that power, I will briefly handle everything in which we can regard the Kingdom of Babel as a portrait of a second Babel, setting it out concisely and completely in its proper frame. It will not be unhelpful for me to apply every statement and proof to the spiritual Babel.

A. I shall then posit that Nimrod was the founder of Babel, and that Babel was the beginning, the capital of the Empire on the *Euphrates*, the city of the kings' court. Nimrod was a mighty hunter; and the word signifies a rebel, who

<column-break/>

openly offers resistance, strives against, and opposes. He built several other cities. <note>Genesis 10.</note>

<margin>Rome as the capital of the spiritual Babel.</margin>
Rome is the See and capital of the spiritual Babel, the seat of Nimrod, by the river or *Euphrates* of many peoples, which shall be dried up. <note>Revelation 17:1-15.</note> As an inheritance from Saint Peter, he possesses several other cities; but in Rome, he sits as king. The Pope is Nimrod who rebels and offers resistance to Christ, and is therefore the Antichrist, or Opponent of Christ, the *anomos* <note>Greek: ἄνομος; the lawless one</note>, without law, bond, or yoke, exalting himself above all <note>2 Thessalonians 2</note> and subjecting everything to himself, either by force, by craft, or through spiritual power and the appearance of religion. <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, *The Ungrateful*.</note>

<margin>Description of the Roman Pope.</margin>
B. The heaven-high tower is a beacon in the sea, an open sign to head toward, so as not to wander, and to be kept together; and when lions, bears, wolves, tigers, etc., appeared, to run toward it and find safety and protection there, as a people of one language and speech. To prevent all separation, it can serve us as a symbol not only of the heaven-high exaltation of the city of Rome, but also of Saint Peter’s See there, and of him who sits upon it, exalted above kings and emperors, speaking as if from on high <note>Psalm 73, 2 Thessalonians 2</note>, who usurps all power in heaven and on earth to open and shut heaven and the abyss, to make and break laws, to forgive sins, and to save. His luster, indeed his divinity, is armed with an infallibility. He is the Universal Bishop, Christ’s Vicar, and Peter’s successor. He maintains the one kind of language and speech; one must listen to him. Rome is the name and the watchword in the world: toward that church and this See everything must turn and betake itself, especially when lions, wolves, heretics, persecutors, and schismatics arise. Indeed, thus do the donkeys scratch one another, and thus sounds Babel’s harlot-song.

Thus says Boniface VII:
*That there should be only one name in the world: that only the name of the Pope should be recited in the churches: that no one should dare to oppose the Bishops or Rome, namely that Metropolis: that no one should be considered Catholic who does not agree with the Roman Church.* <note>original Latin: "Quod unicum sit nomen in mundo: quod solius Papæ nomen in ecclesiis recitetur: quod nemo audeat episcopos Romam, metropolim scilicet illam, appellantes: quod catholicus non habeatur, qui Romanæ ecclesiæ non concordat."</note> That is: *There must be one single name in the world: the name of the Pope alone must be mentioned in the churches: that no one should dare to set himself against the Bishops, or Rome, which is called the Mother City: that no one may be held as Catho-*

...to be held, *which does not agree with the Roman Church.*

The Bull of Boniface VIII also says: *Furthermore, we declare, define, and pronounce that it is absolutely necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff.* <note>original: "Porro subesse Romano Pontifici omnes humanæ creaturæ declaramus, definimus, pronuntiamus omnino esse de necessitate salutis." Kosterus in his *Handbook of Controversies regarding the Church* says: *All Catholics throughout the world, under one head, the Roman Pontiff, whom all obey—both princes and kings—as the Vicar of Christ, constantly retain the same faith, say the same thing, feel the same thing, believe the same thing in all matters, and do not differ in even the smallest article of religion.* <note>original Latin: "Catholici omnes ubique terrarum sub uno capite Romano Pontifice, cui omnes parent, & princes, & reges, ut Christi Vicario, eandem fidem constanter retinent..." Franciscus Costerus (1532–1619) was a prominent Jesuit theologian.</note> That is: *All Catholics throughout the whole world say the same, feel the same, and believe the same under a single head, the Roman Pope, whom all princes and kings obey in everything as the deputy of Christ, without differing in the slightest member of the Religion.*

And in order not to be devoured by heretics—as if by lions, bears, and wolves—and become their prey, what is said to be the best course of action? To believe what the Roman church believes, even if one does not know what it believes? Then one is just as well-secured against all heretics as if one sat in Babel itself, or upon Babel's tower.

<margin>The Growth of Babel.</margin>
C. Babel’s origins, though small and weak at first, have nevertheless grown and developed greatly into a very mighty city, indeed into a large and very formidable Empire, upon which it has greatly exalted itself, as could be demonstrated and illustrated at length from worldly histories. But look only to *Isaiah 14 and 47, Daniel 4, Jeremiah 50 and 51.*

That Rome has become great, and its Empire strong and mighty, one needs only the Divine testimonies. *Revelation 16:19 and 17:5 and 18:16-18-20.*

D. Babel’s harlotry, splendor, fleshly lust, idolatry, incantations, and wicked masters of craft are detailed and clearly given in the holy scroll: *Isaiah 47, Jeremiah 50 and 51, Daniel 1 and 3 and 6, Jeremiah 23.* I will add another sample of this from antiquity.

Such a feast is likely what the Babylonian women would have held, when they once stood ready for their lives <note>The Dutch "te kip stonden" suggests standing in wait or prostituting oneself.</note> before the temple of Venus, and well-garlanded at that, so that they might defile themselves according to the flesh with strangers.* See further De Mei in *Physiological Commentaries* p. 3. pag. 255. and Rhodiginus, Plutarch, Xenophon: Dieter. in *Antiquities of the Old Testament* pag. 641. Heidegger, *Mystery of Babylon* pag. 144.

How now the one and the other fits the spiritual Babel: spiritual and fleshly harlotry—the latter partly flowing from the prohibition given to the clergy against being allowed to marry, a doctrine of devils <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 4:1-3.</note>: what spiritual idolatry is committed with the Angels, Mary, and innumerable saints and their images: what splendor, finery, and pomp there is in Rome in their churches and chapels, etc.: what wantonness, foul lust, "dumb sins" <note>A historical euphemism for sodomy.</note>, incest, what incantations to drive out the devil: what jugglery to make a "mass-god" <note>A derogatory term for the consecrated Host in the Eucharist.</note> and set it out for worship, through which one openly blasphemes God and robs Christ of His honor: who would dare to demonstrate this exhaustively in a work where one gives only a sample of everything? Just turn to *Revelation 17:1-3, 13:14, 15 and 18:3, 7-10* and read the Commentators on these places, and further *Moulin, Aldegonde, Kabbeljauw, Mornay's "Mystery of Iniquity,"* etc.

<margin>The way prepared for Judah.</margin>
G. However unwillingly Babylon saw Judah depart, God nevertheless prepared the way (see *Jeremiah 50 and 51*). Likewise, people have departed from Rome at God's warning voice after a long captivity (see *Revelation 18*).

H. If there was confusion in Babylon—indeed, the city was named BABEL because of the confusion of languages—certainly one may rightly call Rome and that spiritual Empire BABEL. Even if the Jesuit Costerus <note>Franciscus Costerus, a prominent Jesuit theologian previously mentioned on page 20.</note> boasts so grandly: who does not know what confusion has arisen between the Eastern and Western churches? God has confused their language (*Psalm 55:9*), and how "harmonious" they are in that spiritual church-state is clearly shown by the clashing and contradictory Papal Decrees and Bulls, the Councils, the conflicting points of doctrine, and the various orders and opinions of the Thomists, Scotists, Franciscans, and Jesuits. <note>These represent different schools of Catholic philosophy and religious orders that often debated one another.</note> They are like Samson’s foxes: their tails are tied together, but their heads face away from one another. <note>A reference to Judges 15:4; the author suggests they are united only in their capacity for destruction, while their ideas are at odds.</note>

<margin>Differences among the Roman clergy.</margin>
I. Babylon’s fall and destruction did not happen suddenly; something still remained. (See *Marsham, Canon. Chron. pages 629, 630*). <note>Sir John Marsham was an English writer on history and chronology.</note> It received a great crack, but after that, it pulled its head under entirely. It is true that the spiritual Babylon received a "great crack" through the occurrence of the Reformation and through the breaking away of lands and kingdoms. And one still sees daily that the modern Roman kings and princes trim the power, authority, and income of this Nimrod. <note>Nimrod, the biblical hunter and king, was traditionally associated with the construction of the Tower of Babel.</note> And although, as with the Babylon of old, it is cried out that she sits as a queen and shall see no sorrow or grief, she shall nonetheless be suddenly broken—whether through the desertion of the great ones who have committed fornication with Babylon, or through the enlightenment of many and the power of truth, or through the victorious arms of foreign nations, or through a heavy and righteous judgment from God as an example to others. Time will reveal it. In the meantime, read *Revelation 14, 16, 17, and 18*, and await God's judgment with faithful trust, possessing your soul with patience. For He who is to come shall come, and shall by no means tarry. Look toward NIMROD.

### JEWEL <term>נזם</term>, <note>Original: "Bagge." A Dutch term for a piece of jewelry, trinket, or pendant.</note> *necklace, treasure, locket, etc.*

I find the word JEWEL only once in the Old Testament, namely in *Proverbs 11:22*. Our translation reads: *A beautiful woman who turns away from reason is like a golden jewel in a pig's snout.*

That women of old were uniquely fond of finery and ornament is well known. That they had all kinds of adornments—arm, neck, ear, and head ornaments, rings and bands—is read in both divine and worldly writers. <term>נזם זהב</term> <note>Hebrew: "Nezem zahav," meaning a ring or jewel of gold.</note> a golden Jewel; exactly what this was, the learned do not entirely agree: whether it was a golden chain hanging from the forehead to the nose and mouth; or a golden ornament in a half-moon shape over the forehead, extending to the ears, with a dangling gem or stone in the middle reaching the nose and mouth; or properly a precious stone attached to a golden ring or link, hanging from the pierced nose and ears; that I shall not currently undertake to dispute. See *Observations of Drusius, Book 7, Chapter 46; Luther; Villalpandus; del Rio, etc.* <note>These are various 16th and 17th-century biblical commentators and scholars.</note>

Solomon subsequently mentions female beauty, which undoubtedly lies in the good shape of the body, in the color, and the well-proportioned features of the face.
<margin>Female beauty.</margin>

# B A K K E N.
<note>Dutch: "Bakken" refers to cisterns, troughs, or basins.</note>

<margin>Vanity of beauty.</margin> Christian virtues do not include worldly and civil interactions; if a woman does not know how to please her husband through her good inner gifts; if she further knows nothing of this or that; <note>The original Dutch idiom "van tuiten nog blaazen" literally means "of horns nor blowing," meaning she is completely ignorant or unskilled.</note> what she must do or leave be in the household; what, where, and indeed how she should speak, keep silent, or behave toward her husband, children, friends, and neighbors; and if she is without discernment, observation, and understanding, and distinct judgment; then the man has little to gain, for her beauty costs him dearly enough. What else is to be expected than that, due to her beauty, being foolish or simple, she stands to be sufficiently outwitted and misled by those who like to aim for the lap of strange women? For she does not have enough sense to preserve that treasure of beauty: and so the husband must look about with Argus eyes. <note>In Greek mythology, Argus was a giant with a hundred eyes; here it means the husband must be hyper-vigilant.</note> She must consequently defile and sully her physical beauty with the ugliness of monstrous morals, foolish tricks, lax, tasteless, and untimely words, and in all parts blameworthy deeds, just as the sow with the gold jewel in its snout does not fail, according to its nature, to root in the mud and filth. And even if the beauty is such that a sow is adorned with something excellent, she remains a sow, and her heart always and in everything looks out sufferingly, and one judges that this jewel does not suit the sow well, as it is too precious to be so lightly regarded and so unworthily handled; which everyone will also judge of an unintelligent woman who is gifted with outward beauty. For she disfigures herself in that beauty through tarnishing vices, deeds, words, and gestures.

And such must fall all the more heavily upon her husband, seeing that they both are one, and the evil remains under his roof. *Internal ailments are the heaviest; the pains are all the more sharp as they are inward,* says *Augustine* regarding *Psalm 45.* <note>original: "Mala inteſtina graviſſima; dolores eo acerbiores, quo interiores"</note>

I can then notice nothing else but that Solomon, through this comparison, intends to give it to be understood that it is foolishness, solely and primarily when one seeks a wife, to look at physical beauty: that it is better to choose the beauty of the virtues and gifts of an intelligent woman. Although, yes, if one can have both, one need not spoil or despise the finest of nature. Beautiful outside and inside, if it may so happen to us, should not be rejected. Then the beauty becomes even fairer.

*Virgil* says well:

> Virtue is more pleasing when it comes from a beautiful body.
<note>original: "Gratior eſt pulchro veniens de corpore virtus."</note>

-> That is: <-

> --- The virtue that radiates from the beautiful body / Is more pleasant. ---

But if one must choose one of the two, beautiful and foolish, or she who has no discernment, who can neither perceive nor knows how to make proper distinctions: or not beautiful, yet an intelligent woman; then he is best advised who chooses the latter.

<column-break/>

BAK, in the plural, BAKKEN, *water cistern, and well. To hew out cisterns. Winepress vat,* <note>original Hebrew: באר (Be'er), בור (Bor), באר (Be'er); original Greek: φρέαρ (Phrear); original Latin: puteus, fovea, ciſterna (well, pit, cistern). Greek: λάκκος (Lakkos), meaning a pit or pond.</note>

<margin>Metaphorical Proverbs 5:15, 16.</margin> **O**ne reads something by comparison and allusion in *Proverbs 5:15, 16. Drink water out of your own Cistern, and the floods from the midst of your own well. Let your Fountains be dispersed abroad, the water brooks in the streets.*

It is true, one finds among the learned those who apply this to the word of the living God, from which one must drink and seek to satisfy one's holy thirst for knowledge; yet in such a way that one must not keep these streams of life to oneself, but spread them from within, and share them with others, perfecting, teaching, exhorting, and comforting one another, and letting one's light shine, as one is not infrequently encouraged to do in the holy scrolls.

<margin>The application.</margin> This finding and thought is edifying and good in itself; yet whether it agrees with the thread of the reasoning and with the context, that is doubted with logical grounds by the most and most prominent [scholars]: and therefore others have understood it in this way, namely: *That one must live cheerfully and moderately with his wife and children upon his blessings and received benefits from God: by no means neglecting, squandering, or uselessly spending the same: nor through a narrowness and stingy greed saving them or keeping them only for oneself; no, but from our means and abundance, let the streams and brooks flow to others for refreshment through benevolence and generosity.*

<margin>Generosity, a glorious virtue.</margin> A glorious virtue and quite necessary, indeed a healthy lesson, often heard, given, and impressed in the holy pages; however, for the previous reason, it is judged not to be specifically intended by Solomon here.

What then? I can very well unite or join myself in this with Chrysostom, Jerome, Jansenius, Bede, Hugo, and many modern theologians, who have understood it in this way, *That Solomon, through this flowery and figurative way of speaking, gives it to be understood that if one is of a marriageable age and finds oneself affected with a mixed thirst or desire: or is already bound to a spouse through marriage, he shall keep himself content and satisfied with his better half: blunting and satisfying his lusts: by no means aiming for the lap of a strange woman, 1 Corinthians 7, to the end that thus, through and from a legal marriage, honest, legitimate, and well-natured children may spring forth, who run outside in the streets, and may increase and adorn the citizenry and the church. Proverbs 23:27, Psalm 113:9, and 127 and 128. Isaiah 51:1, 2.*

Subsequently, one reads in *Jeremiah 2:13* about *hewing out broken cisterns.* That one hollowed them out and dug them into the ground to catch water, or to have water through boring, is sufficiently known. That here there is a contrast of the Lord, the fountain of living waters, against Israel’s broken Water-cisterns, which have or can keep no water, being broken and torn, everyone notices.

It gives it to be understood that God's outward Israel, having become unintelligent and unfaithful, had [lost] the only and true means of their salvation, help, and comfort in the knowledge of God—

# B A S I N S.
<note>Dutch: "Bakken." In this context, the author refers to cisterns or collecting basins.</note>

fellowship, favor, and help in the Messiah—having forsaken and being forsaken, being intent on the help of heathen kings: they have taken refuge in the law and its works, and the righteousness derived from the works of the law, through which no flesh shall or could be justified before God. *Romans 3, Galatians 2 and 3.* This is as useless as a broken or cracked basin that holds no water, or cannot retain it. In a word, *broken basins* can be symbols of everything that, at first and outward glance, seems able to provide joy and comfort, but which fails in its effect: such as wealth, honor, status, prestige, *the favor and help of men, etc.* All is unstable; it flows away and through. *Psalm 62:11, Proverbs 23:4, 5, Ecclesiastes 1:2, etc.*

<margin>Winepress-basin of God’s wrath.</margin> Furthermore, one reads of a winepress-basin of the Lord's anger and grimness, *Isaiah 63, Revelation 14 and 19,* where allusions are made to wine vats and grape presses in which, particularly during the vintage, people trod the grapes and crushed them to pieces with their feet, so that the blood of the grapes splashed onto their clothing. It is clear that this is also taken figuratively to represent how Christ, through His obedience in suffering unto death, slaughtered and overcame spiritual enemies, to the extent that neither Satan, the Law, nor sin holds power over His spiritual members any longer. And so He continues to tread them as the kingdom of darkness is increasingly broken down and shattered. When one further observes that He would shepherd the heathens with an iron scepter, and that He would crush His enemies in the day of His hot anger, *Psalm 2,* indeed, that He would fill the land with dead bodies, *Psalm 110,* and that all vengeance and judgment rests with Him, *Job 5 and 8, Matthew 28,* and that He comes to judge the nations without respect of persons, *Isaiah 11, Psalm 98,* etc., then it is not difficult to understand that one can relate to Him through these symbols: the singular and very heavy judgments which He executes by way of wine-pressing upon the rebellious Jews, the resisting Heathens who persecute Him in His congregation and members, the Antichrist, etc., of which the Jews have had a certain and felt taste of vengeance. See my first *Sacred Miscellany* page 287, etc., page 281, etc., constituting a clear, great, and terrible day. *Isaiah 13:13-19, Joel 2, Acts 2:19.* But more on this later under the words WINEPRESS, WINEPRESS-BASIN. ### BAKING, BAKE-OVEN, IRON OVEN, LIME KILN, KNEADING TROUGH, FIERY OVEN, or BURNING OVEN. <note>Hebrew: *Tannur* (oven); Greek: *Klibanos* (baking pot); Latin: *fornax* (furnace/oven). Hebrew: *Aphah* (to bake); Greek: *Sitopoios* (bread-maker); Latin: *pistor* (baker).</note>

I shall take these various things together here and, so as not to "mow the grass from under my own feet" <note>An idiom meaning to preempt oneself or exhaust a topic too early.</note> in what follows, I will treat them briefly.

<margin>Baking.</margin> The words BAKING, BAKE-OVEN, and KNEADING TROUGH appear several times in Holy Scripture. If applied to bread and other food dishes, it is taken quite broadly, referring to the Baker and the art of baking, which prepares many kinds of things in various ways to bring them to readiness.

<margin>Grain ground with hand-mills.</margin> Just as it was not customary to grind grain with windmills but with hand-mills—after it had been dried and, as it were, parched by the fire—so too was little or nothing known of the type of bake-ovens used today. Whether one baked leavened or unleavened cakes and breads, they were made to rise under hot ashes, baked on glowing stones, or under a stone or iron ring prepared for that purpose, heated or surrounded with glowing coals, as if smothered under loose ash. Because of this, they often burned on one side while being barely half-baked on the other, of which *Hosea* seems to speak in *Chapter 7.* Thus *Seneca* speaks of this: *Panes primum cinis calidus, ac fervens testa percoxit.* That is: <note>original Latin: "Panes primum cinis calidus, ac fervens testa percoxit."</note> *Bread is first baked under warm ash, and thereafter under hot tiles.*
*Ovid, Fasti Book 6:*

> Suppositum cineri panem focus ipse parabat,
> Strataque erat tepido tegula quassa solo.

Which *Arnold Hoogvliet* <note>A 17th-century Dutch poet known for his biblical epics.</note> translates thus:

> *But in olden times, the bread was baked within the house,*
> *In the ash upon each hearth, floored with stone tiles.*

What kind of Baking, Baker, and Bake-oven one should understand in *Hosea 7* is considered in verses 4, 5, 6, and 7; at the very least, it is spoken of by way of parable and imagery. I cannot understand it as anything other than the Jews of the two tribes <note>Refers to the Southern Kingdom of Judah.</note>—while the half or the rest had been carried away to Assyria—being represented as burning like a hotly stoked oven, through the heat of physical and spiritual adultery, and foul desire, and the lust of the flesh for all kinds of misdeeds, whereby Jerusalem had Samaria as a sister, which is described.

<margin>Jerusalem and Samaria.</margin> There, plots for the destruction of God's people were forged in the heart. The trouble and labor of pondering kneaded the lump of dough. He who played a part in it, and had "brewed it on the yeast," <note>A Dutch idiom meaning to hatch a plan or cause trouble.</note> waited firmly for the dough to rise. Strife was stoked among them like a fire; discord and foul desire fanned the flames; they waited for the morning light until the most suitable opportunity arose to oppress and carry away God's people, having deliberated so that they thought they could be calm and quiet about it, expecting a good outcome.

The internal stoker, who heated and fanned the hearts of the Jews, was Satan and the fleshly desire for idolatry and carnal luxury.

...adulteries of idolatry, and since lust and wantonness follow the service of evil spirits, it was a consequence that they served them, wallowing like fattened swine in the mire of lusts.

It was especially so when they observed the season of the established calf-worship or celebrated the birthday of King Jeroboam. See *Cyril, Jerome, etc.* <note>The author refers to the Church Fathers Cyril of Alexandria and Jerome, who often wrote on the idolatry of the Northern Kingdom of Israel.</note>

Certainly, when Jeroboam saw that he was flattered and that people sought to please him by following him, he could be at ease; they would not return to Jerusalem or reject him and his calf-worship. *So says Jerome: He, after he had cast the fire into the oven of their hearts, and saw that they were firmly raving, and there was no one who resisted his pleasure, was at ease.* But then punishment was near at hand, for the early morning of God's judgment day arrived, which carried them away by the Syrians to Assyria. All the while, the king remained quite at ease, and the people—for certain reasons—followed him in almost everything, breaking out into all kinds of wickedness and foul dealings.

<margin>Egypt's iron furnace.</margin>
In *Deuteronomy 4:20* one reads of Egypt's IRON FURNACE, as also in *1 Kings 8:51* and *Jeremiah 11:4*. It seems clear enough to me that this must be understood figuratively and metaphorically. For Egypt, and the state of the people there, was immeasurably hard and hot—that is, dangerous and heavy. It is compared to an Iron Furnace, which glows with intense heat and is difficult to stoke, wherein solid materials are dissolved.

<margin>Lime kiln.</margin>
One reads of a LIME KILN, and the burning into lime, in *Isaiah 33:12* and *Amos 2:1.* This is a grave matter and a metaphor for when one is reduced to nothing and dust by the fire of war, strife, or by literal fire, just as the material intended for lime is prepared, reduced, or crushed by the fire.

<margin>Burning furnace.</margin>
Mention is made of a burning FIERY FURNACE in *Psalm 21:10, Malachi 4:1,* and *Matthew 13:42.* This is again figurative and used by way of comparison, by which one can understand the heat of persecution, heavy judgments, wars, trials, and the Lord’s burning and blazing wrath as a punishment for His evil enemies, whether in this life or the next: against which heat and glow no flesh can endure.

And so one can take it as an emblem of the world, and of specific regions of the world, now here, then there, where the pious are made to feel it most hot and anxious through all kinds of crosses, scorn, and means of persecution, even death itself.

And does the Lord have a furnace and fire for Baking, roasting, and burning? *Isaiah 31:9.* This can be understood metaphorically: not only that God has His fire and hearth in Zion and Jerusalem—where He is honored and served by His people, and which He will therefore not forsake or leave—but that He will protect the city and its inhabitants against the Assyrian and all other enemies. He will stop and punish the enemies, coming there (to speak in human terms) to forge deadly weapons against the foe. This signifies that means were at His hand to stop, punish, and subdue the mighty enemy. *Psalm 7:12, 13, 14.*

I take another example from the memorable prophecy found in *Isaiah 22:15, 16*, compared with *2 Kings 18:18*, concerning Shebna and Eliakim. ### CHEEK-TEETH [MOLARS], <term>molars</term> <note>original Hebrew: מלתעות (milt'ot)</note>, <term>mill-teeth</term> <note>original Greek: μύλαι (mylai)</note>, *molar teeth* <note>original Latin: dentes molares</note>.

IT is well known concerning the TEETH and CHEEK-TEETH, and what one does and achieves with them according to the course of nature—how one gnashes with them, shows one's teeth, and tears and grinds with them: how remarkably Cheek-teeth are attributed to Lions, Bears, and wild boars. They are also applied to man, though then it represents little good.

<margin>Teeth applied to man.</margin>
Since these Cheek-teeth are uniquely characteristic of ravenous beasts—with which they seize their prey, carry it away, tear it apart, and grind it—one finds them applied to men; namely, cruel, degenerate, spiteful, greedy, unjust oppressors, bloodsuckers, and tormentors who make use of violence or cunning under the appearance of law; especially to men who are possessed and armed with power, malice, and predatory greed.

One lives by them, according to *Proverbs 30:14* and *Joel 1:6*. Job had broken them: *Chapter 29:17*. David and the Church prayed in *Psalm 58:6* <note>The text cites verse 7, which corresponds to verse 6 in many English translations.</note> that God would break the Cheek-teeth.

<margin>Cheek-teeth, a symbol of cruelty.</margin>
I would think that the Cheek-teeth attributed to the godless, cruel, predatory, and greedy—yes, even the unjust—represent their anger and grimness, severity, cruelty, and lust for prey. These, being strengthened by cunning and power, fall upon the innocent and weak without fear, oppressing them with craft and violence, sucking them dry, and bringing them to nothing. If open attack and hostility are then added, they are even sacrificed to their revenge and fury. And so the Cheek-teeth, through war, plunder, fire, and destruction, leave nothing behind.

To break these, then, was to halt their power, to resist and uncover their violence and cunning, and to render them incapable of further damage and devouring—just as it is with devouring and destructive bears and wild boars when their Cheek-teeth are broken out. This is, in my judgment, the most proper and meaningful thing one could say of it. I shall then let it rest and take another matter in hand.

BALAAM, or BILEAM, son of Beor, appears to us several times in Holy Scripture: *Numbers 22, 23, 24, and 31; Joshua 13; 2 Peter 2; Jude verse 11; Revelation 2, etc.*

<margin>Balaam.</margin>
<margin>His descent.</margin>
He was from Pethor, in Syria or Mesopotamia, situated between two rivers. *Numbers 22.* He is called a <term>soothsayer</term> <note>original Hebrew: קוסם (kosem)</note> in *Joshua 13*; one who helped himself by predicting future things from signs in the heavens, the flight and cries of birds. <margin>Profession.</margin>
At the very least, he was held to be one who knew more than the average man. Without doubt, he was a trained and base deceiver, as that sort of people usually are—cunning and sly, in order to drive the money out of someone’s purse and lead them by the nose. A craft forbidden by God. *Deuteronomy 18; 1 Samuel 15.*

<margin>His name.</margin>
His name signifies, along with <term>Nicholas</term> <note>original Greek: νικόλαος (Nikolaos), meaning "conqueror of the people"</note>, a lord, master, and guardian of the people, who fares well by them and lords over them. That he is called a seer and a prophet is sufficiently known. *2 Peter 2.*

To be a Prophet <margin>Saul a Prophet.</margin> is said even of those who are false. *Deuteronomy 13, 1 Kings 18, Matthew 24.* One reads of Prophets and Prophesying in *Matthew 7 and Joshua 11.* Judas was also an Apostle, and Caiaphas prophesied as well on one occasion. Nevertheless, it remains true that he was a soothsayer, a villain, and a seeker of filthy lucre, as the revelation was neither confirmed nor sanctified in him. In his heart, he by no means intended God's glory or the well-being of God's people, but it was a forced performance. He was an example of proud imagination, self-exaltation, wicked greed, and detestable malice, punished and presented as a mirror to others.

That he was a great boaster, conceited, and audacious, is clear enough to perceive from all his actions: even the greatest Prophets are not accustomed to speak much, as humility dwells within them: but he calls himself <term>שם העין</term> <note>original: "Shetum Ha-ayin," usually translated as "the man whose eye is closed" or "opened," interpreted here as "far-seeing"</note> a penetrating and far-seeing man, who sees further than the length of his nose; who knows more than what is right in front of him. He is a <term>גלוּי עינים</term> <note>original: "Gelui Enayim," meaning "having the eyes open"</note> one who sees with his eyes, to whom many things are revealed and shown: a <term>נפל</term> <note>original: "Nofel," meaning "one who falls down"</note>, who is sometimes in trances of the senses, and elevations and raptures of the soul, when he has Divine revelation. *Numbers 24.* This man speaks of such things. Who then would not think something grand of him? But how is <margin>Balaam unmasked.</margin> he better known? The Divine and historical account of Moses shows us that. I shall wind it up briefly and design it in a sketch.

Balak, king of the Moabites, waging war <margin>Balak’s undertaking.</margin> against Israel and rising up against them to halt the victorious and breakthrough weapons of this people by power and force of arms and men, found himself unable to carry this out. Since it had come to his ears that Balaam knew and could do more through his art of cursing and conjuring, he summoned him and requested that he put his art to work, so that with his incantations and curses he might halt Israel's progress and further frustrate and shame the intention of that people, under the offer of the most substantial reward.

Balaam, noticing that great things were expected of him, boasts purely and talks big, and meanwhile he is (as is characteristic of that sort of people) very greedy for payment.

He then advised that one must first offer sacrifices and <margin>Balaam's advice to Balak.</margin> seek to please the Divinity. He behaved as if he had great respect for Israel's God, and that He forbade him to curse Israel, and on the contrary commanded him to bless them, and therefore, that he was not master of himself nor of his art in this case and request of the king: however, he wanted to put it to the test to see if he might succeed. He did so and performed sacrifices. But the work turned out again contrary to his aim and desire. He sacrificed anew in the wilderness, he went to the height of Peor to see if it would be permitted to him to curse Israel. But there was also then no sorcery or incantation against Jacob and Israel. Therefore, he blessed the people and brought one of the most excellent prophecies to light; after which he finally gave the advice to Balak that one should adorn the Moabitish youth elegantly and lustfully and send them to Israel's camp, well-inclined toward embracing and the work of the flesh: but when Israel was heated and lustful, they should draw them to their land, and by no means consent to carnal mingling unless they went over to their religions, which, if it happened, would make God angry and curse them Himself, and then he would achieve his aim. His godless advice partially succeeded, but he missed the expected reward and was finally killed with the sword along with a numerous multitude of the people. <margin>Balaam's death.</margin> *Numbers 31.*

I can and will believe that God had this history described for a singular purpose, since one finds this remarkable case cited more than once in the holy scroll; and also hold that it served not only as a mirror but also as an example, sketching out how in the course of time people would also arise who, carried away by greed, would seek to introduce wicked destruction and fornication, but were to have no better fate or outcome than Balaam once met. So it is spoken of him in *Micah 6, 2 Peter 2, Jude verse 11, Revelation 2.*

As for me, I want to hold with many scholars that one saw Balaam live again when that physical and spiritual <margin>Balaam represented through fornications.</margin> fornication and wicked lust were seen to be practiced.

Unless one wants to apply it generally to those who wanted to place a stumbling block and offense before the congregation, and under the pretext of Christian liberty, sought to drag them away to godlessness and carnal lust, teaching them to go into the idol houses with the heathens and to eat of the idol sacrifices. *Acts 15, 1 Corinthians 8 and 10.*

It can also fit those who mixed the wickedest heresies with the true doctrine, the Gospel with the law, Christ with Moses, freedom with bondage. Also those who expressly gave themselves over to carnal lustfulness, teaching that it was thus permitted, while meanwhile they boasted of hidden wisdom and Divine revelations, and I know not what elevated boasting, like Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Menander, Basilides, the Gnostics, and the rest of that swarm.

### B A L A K, בלק, *Balak*

<margin>Derivation of the word BALAK.</margin>
בלק <note>Hebrew: Balak</note> *is said to come from* בלק <note>The root B-L-Q</note> *meaning: He has emptied and made bare; he has scattered; he has destroyed. It signifies laying bare that which is strong and very firmly secured and closed, robbing it of its stability, and paving the way for scorn and oppression: it means pulling out the roots, leading to devastation and withering. Some have translated it as one who entangles, devastates, and breaks someone down; or as one who licks or laps up.*

<margin>Balak’s behavior.</margin>
AT LEAST BALAK, the king of the Moabites, was such a person. And so, in order to weaken Israel—like an open city stripped of all strength and fortifications—and subsequently to uproot them, he seduced this people through the flattery and caresses of his Moabite daughters into physical and spiritual fornication. The marriages and fleshly minglings with the Moabite women served as a snare. *Hosea 6:5.*

Now, among other things, the Balsam must have fallen here, since one reads of the "Balsam of Gilead." *Jeremiah 8 and 46; Genesis 37 and 43.* It must have thrived well in the land of Canaan, and people traded in it, *Ezekiel 27:17*; that it occurred in Judea and thrived there, we are taught by *Pliny, Book XII, Chapter 25; Isidore, Dioscorides*, and others.

It is held to be a small tree, sprout, shrub, or bush, the most excellent of the woody plants, whose drops and seeping tears are very bright, clear, and strong-smelling—

# BALSAM.

Called <note>original: "בעל שמן" (Ba'al shemen)</note> "the lord of the oil," *Amos 6:6.*

Scholars dispute with one another whether the liquid or the small tree itself is called Balsam or *opobalsamum* <note>The pure juice or sap of the balsam tree.</note>. *Pliny, Book 12, Chapter 15,* seems to favor the former; but *Servius*, in his commentary on *Virgil’s Georgics*, is of the opposite opinion, maintaining that BALSAM is the name of the tree itself, named after its collected moisture, <note>original: "ὀπὸς" (opos)</note> "sap."

*Isidore, Pliny, Theophrastus,* and *Dioscorides* all testify that the leaves are similar to those of the rue plant. However, they are whiter than the wild violet, growing to a height of three cubits <note>About 4.5 feet or 1.4 meters.</note>. Yet when it is only a foot high, it spreads out into many slender and thin twigs or shoots. It must be pruned annually like a grapevine, according to the testimony of *Belonius, Observations Book 2, Chapter 39*; it is always green.

One must make incisions in it, from which the moisture then drips and seeps. See *Veslingius in Defense of Opobalsamum*.

It is noted that the rough root is entirely useless and sterile if one does not open it, or insert a stone within the cleft or opening made.

<margin>Virtue of the Balsam herb.</margin>
It is testified of this herb that it cleanses and heals very many defects; it is uniquely beneficial for ailments of the eyes: and it is a preservative against decay and rot. It smells exceptionally strong and lovely; and it strips poison of its power and very harmful effects.

<margin>Balsam in a broader sense.</margin>
I can easily believe that meanwhile the word BALSAM, EMBALMING, or BALSAM OIL is sometimes taken more broadly for a mixture of various spices, namely: *Myrrh, Frankincense, Aloe, Spikenard*, etc. In ancient times, people used these not only to drip upon and anoint the head, hair, hands, and feet, but among the Egyptians and Hebrews, they were also used to embalm dead bodies so that decay and rot might be prevented. Among the Jews, this was not only a sign of status and distinction among people of rank, but also a hallmark of their faith, hoping for the resurrection of the dead, according to the accounts of *Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Minutius Felix,* and *Prudentius*.

<margin>Difference between the embalming of the Jews and Egyptians.</margin>
However, there is this difference in the embalming of the Egyptians and the Jews: the Egyptians anointed the internal body, removing the intestines from the body and the brain through the nostrils. But the Jews anointed the body from the outside, with the intestines enclosed, because of which they required a greater quantity of spices.

Of the types of Balsam, mixed preparations, anointing oil, the act of anointing, etc., I shall not speak until each comes up in its proper place under its own letter. Only then, as it is presented here, will it cause me to reflect on something else and provide the opportunity to seek out the "Balm of Gilead" and offer it to everyone.

If I wished to treat Balsam scripturally, I would have a very broad and spacious field here. For I could apply it to God’s grace and ever-greening mercy: to Christ as Savior, and to the Gospel. But since God is gracious and merciful to wounded souls in His Son—and Scripture speaks of no grace, comfort, salvation, healing, or life except in and from the merits of Jesus Christ, through the working and application of the Spirit of the Father and the Son—I will include it here in its general sense. I shall arrange it according to the Father in its actual acquisition, to the Son in its procurement, and to the Holy Spirit in its appropriation, mediated through the Word for its preaching, and the sealing through the holy signs and seals of the covenant. And so let the reader understand it in the following application.

<column-break/>

<margin>Balsam in a spiritual sense.</margin>
a. By the Balsam, a low-growing tree growing in Canaan, I envision Christ, who sprouted there—lowly and small according to His outward appearance and status in the world, though He is the noblest Branch and of royal house and lineage. *Isaiah 4:2 and 12; Isaiah 53; Psalm 22:7.*

b. Just as this little tree lets a Balsam oil or liquid drip down of the strongest scent and most healing and pleasant fragrance, certainly Jesus is of no use to anyone except as one who came under the law, was beaten, wounded, and opened in His side, hands, and feet; therefore the fruits of His death and bloody suffering are brought into the holy record, *Isaiah 53:4, 5; 1 Peter 2.* This is why Paul wished to know and preach nothing else among the Corinthians but Christ, and Him crucified. *1 Corinthians 2:2; Philippians 3.*

c. That little tree is always green. Christ lives and works for eternity. He is a tree of life, the green wood; He lives forever to pray for us. *Romans 8; 1 John 2; Hebrews 7.* His righteousness is of everlasting power and value. *Daniel 9:24.*

d. And this is the nature of His power, and of the working of the oil of His Spirit—the Balsam of His most powerful and praiseworthy merits—that those who are rooted in Him partake of His Balsam-sap and His power of grace. They are always green through confession and the fruits of righteousness, of faith, and of pure love toward God and their neighbor. *Psalm 1:3; Jeremiah 17:19; John 15; Galatians 2:20,* which they also demonstrate. *Matthew 5; 1 Peter 2:12.*

e. Just as Balsam preserves against rot and decay: it is certainly the power of Christ’s merits, and in Him the Divine grace poured into the heart through the Holy Spirit, under and with the ministry of the healthy and pure doctrine of the Gospel, whereby all useless, unfruitful, and dead works are cut away. *Ephesians 5.* The members on earth are put to death. *Ephesians 4; Colossians 3; Galatians 5:24.* One is purified more and more from the decay and rot that sin and contamination bring about. *Romans 6; Romans 8; 1 Corinthians 6:11; Zechariah 13:1; 1 John 1:7.* The body of sin shall never fall so far that it would not be raised much more gloriously from the dust. *Isaiah 26:19 and 66; Job 19:25, 26, 27; 1 Corinthians 15:51, 52, 53, etc.*

f. And in case the Balsam is a healing medicine for defects of the eyes—whether they be inflamed, or tearing, or dim—in Jesus, within the Word, accompanied by the working Spirit and grace of God, there is the most precious and powerful Balsam, indeed an eye-salve, to become seeing toward God and the soul. *Revelation 3; Ephesians 1:17, 18 and 3.*

<margin>g.</margin> *III. 9-18. Psalm 19 and 119:105.* And so, just as the Balsam of Gilead <note>A rare perfume used medicinally, mentioned in the Bible as a symbol of healing.</note> heals and softens ailments and cleanses wounds, the grace of God in Christ—Christ with his attained treasures of salvation, offered through the word of comfort, embraced by faith, and applied by the Spirit of Jesus Christ—heals man when he is sick, leprous, powerless, and even dead in sins and transgressions. *Psalm 6:3 and 51:14. Isaiah 53. 1 Peter 2. 1 Corinthians 6:11. Luke 10:34. Romans 8:2. 1 Corinthians 1:30. Zechariah 13:1. 1 John 1:7.*

<margin>Scent of the balsam.</margin> <margin>h.</margin> Balsam is known for its lovely odor and powerful fragrance; one who is anointed and perfumed with it, or even just carries it, smells pleasant for that reason.
What is more pleasant, more heart-strengthening, more uplifting and refreshing to a distressed and dejected heart than the sight and experience of God’s grace? What is more comforting than Jesus and His merits? He who has grace in his heart—the Balsam of Evangelical comfort in his mouth—who walks according to that teaching and displays all kinds of Christian virtues, does he not smell precious? Does he not spread a beautiful and lovely fragrance *2 Corinthians 2:10-15. Ephesians 5:2.* by which he pleases God and men? *Titus 2:14. Philippians 4:8. Colossians 4:5, 6. Philippians 1:11.*

### BONDS, FETTERS, CHAINS, ROPES, etc.

Bonds are of various sorts and kinds, according to their material, shape, use, and purpose.
In general, they are used to bind something, to make it fast, or to fasten things together.

<margin>What bonds are taken for.</margin> BONDS and FETTERS are often understood as judicial instruments with which one secures criminals, or those held as such; so that after being heard regarding the accusation and crime, and after investigation, they may be released as innocent or punished according to the nature of the committed crime.

<margin>Bonds, the lot of the first Christians.</margin> To wear such things, to be cramped and locked up in them without guilt for the sake of Jesus, was the shameful part and painful lot of the Apostles, of Paul, and of the first Christians. It is true, it was hard for the flesh, but the intended glory of God, the love of the truth, their clear conscience, the sought-after strengthening of the believers, the assured help of God, and the heavenly reward made them carry these Bonds with willingness and view them as their ornaments. *Eusebius, Eccl. Hist. Book 5, Chap. 1. Cave, Primitive Christianity, page 473.* For this reason, the Martyr Babylas <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Antioch who died in prison; he famously requested to be buried with his chains as a symbol of his victory.</note> wanted to be buried with the Chains and Bonds he had worn in the prison. *Chrysostom on Babylas, Vol. 1. Acts 5 and 20. Ephesians 4. Philemon verse 13. Acts 9. 1 Corinthians 4. 2 Corinthians 11 and 12.*

<margin>Meaning of Bonds.</margin> BONDS and FETTERS then signify all that is painful and shameful, pressing someone under another’s violence, rage, and power. These are

<column-break/>

burdened by certain descriptions and diminishments, as well as by their duration.

Thus I read of the Bonds of Death *Psalm 18 and 116.* I am inclined to believe that death here refers to the pains of Christ, in soul and body, and the state of death from which the Lord rescued him. *Acts 2.* Deadly sorrow and pains with which he was entirely overwhelmed and beset. So the Church has had to endure the remnants of Christ's suffering, Fetters, and Bonds for nearly three hundred years. *Psalm 44. Romans 8. We are being killed all day long, etc.*

<margin>Of sins, etc.</margin> One reads of the Bonds of Sins with which the wicked man is tied fast. *Proverbs 5:22.* I would almost think that the wicked person is so much under the power of corruption as if he lay in Bonds and Fetters, such that he cannot release himself from sin: and that one must view the crime as fastening him to God as Judge; to Satan as the executioner of his punishment; to the Law, to thunder its bolts against him; and to death and hell as his place of punishment and torment.

<margin>The bond of the loins, Ps. 66:11.</margin> There also appears to me a Bond of the loins: a Bond placed around the loins. *Daniel 5:6.*

The loins are the location of the kidneys, in whose health a man’s strength is largely situated. By one who is "weak of loins," one understands a powerless and weak person: hence the name "weak-loined."

When someone’s loins become weak, it is the same as becoming very feeble, such that one can hardly keep the upper body upright or in balance; which can be brought about by striking someone stiffly in the loins, so that he winces and can neither straighten up nor stand, *Deuteronomy 33:11.* With and through weakness, the loins stagger, *Psalm 69:24.* Unless one prefers that through inner anxiety and the squeezing of the spirit, the king was forced to loosen the bond or the belt of his clothes to give the entrails a bit more room and play.

Placing a tight Bond around someone's loins undoubtedly means making someone distressed and anxious, and through torment, sadness, and servitude, bringing them so far that they do not know where to turn: also being without one's own freedom, under another's restraint and power.

Just as the Bond was placed tightly enough around the loins of the Israelites in Egypt for servitude and slavish treatment and oppression when they had to stand at the brick kilns. In Babylon and Assyria, spiritual Egypt and Babylon have their allurements to catch and entangle people in their snares and nets, after which the bond around their loins is placed tightly and securely enough when their freedom of conscience is taken away, making them so subject to the authority of men that they may neither believe nor teach against Papal Decrees, patristic teachings, and the decrees of the Councils; in such a way that it is not free for them to walk in the law and ways of their God. Thus one hitches them to a donkey's cart and cinches the harness strap around their loins to burden them with a donkey's load of command upon command, rule upon rule.

<margin>Eternal bonds.</margin> One reads in Jude, in his Letter, of Bonds and eternal bonds. Because there the [fallen angels]...

# BONDS.

When the fallen state and punishment of angels are discussed, and since angels are spiritual beings, the nature of the matter dictates that this is spoken figuratively, through imagery, or metaphorically. Something firm, certain, and irrevocable is intended—namely, that God did not wish to release them or loosen them from the obligation of the heaviest and everlasting punishment. Instead, He left them to lie in sin, lies, darkness, and destruction, so that they cannot release themselves from their hatred against God and men, nor from their love and desire for lies and injustice, in which they take the greatest pleasure. At the same time, it refers to the power and activity of an angered God, by which they are firmly kept for the great judgment and the most sensible eternal punishment, from which they will never be able to rid themselves—hardly less than someone who lies locked forever in heavy iron shackles under the eye of the Judge. And as the great Calvin <note>Jean Calvin (1509–1564), a central figure in the Protestant Reformation.</note> says of it: *They are entirely steeped in lies: they persist in wickedness and stubborn sinning: and are bridled by God’s power, so that they cannot perform all the evil they desire: being preserved as hopeless ones for heavier and eternal punishment.*

<margin>Bond of Kings.</margin>
So speaks the man of God, *Job Chapter XII:18*, of the bond of kings, which the Lord loosens: and says that He binds the belt to their loins.

Majesty, power, prudence, experience, good laws, and discipline are like the bonds of a realm; they provide the stability for the firm union of the kingdom and the authority of the king in times of peace and war. In the latter, he must be strengthened by a mighty army and have strong local fortifications as bonds around the realm.

<margin>Bond of the Realm.</margin>
In Ecclesiastes *Chapter VII:26*, the hands of a harlot <note>In the context of 18th-century biblical commentary, "harlot" or "loose woman" often serves as a metaphor for spiritual infidelity or the distractions of worldly vice.</note> and wicked woman are described as Bonds. I would think from the entire description that the Preacher <note>Traditionally King Solomon, the narrator of Ecclesiastes.</note> intends to sketch and imagine, through the symbols of nets, snares, and bonds, the practiced artifice, the state and finery, the flattery, words, glances, hand gestures, and further everything a harlot uses to draw someone in and make him her lover. One who is entangled in this is as if he were enchanted and wrapped in such bonds that he cannot rid himself of her, *Proverbs V:3-6 and VII and XXIII:26, 27. etc. Judges XVI.* and thus he is inevitably bound and tied to destruction by her.

<margin>Bonds of harlots.</margin>
->Plautus in Truculentus: 2, 7, 19.<-
<note>Titus Maccius Plautus was a Roman playwright (c. 254–184 BC) known for his comedies.</note>

> A harlot has brought my wretched master into poverty with her flatteries; she has deprived him of his goods, his light, his honor, and his friends.
> <note>original Latin: "Meretrix meum herum miserum sua blanditia intulit in pauperiem, privavit bonis, luce, honore, atque amicis."</note>

->That is:<-

> *A harlot has made my master poor through her seductive tricks.*
> *Now he finds himself stripped of wealth, stature, honor, and friends.*

<margin>Harlots compared to poison.</margin>
Diogenes Laertius <note>A biographer of Greek philosophers, likely writing in the 3rd century AD.</note> recounts of Socrates that *he compared beautiful harlots to a drink mixed with deadly poison. That at first they provide a sparkling joy; but that in the end, an everlasting pain follows.*

When one deals with those people, neither money nor goods can help. *Plautus in Truculentus 2, 7, 16.*

<column-break/>

> I think a harlot is just like the sea: it devours what you give it, and is never full. Give to her as much as you wish; it is seen nowhere, neither by the giver nor the receiver.
> <note>original Latin: "Meretricem ego item esse reor, mare ut est, quod des devorat, nec unquam abundat. Huic des quantum vis, nusquam apparet, neque datori neque acceptrici."</note>

->That is:<-

> *A harlot is to me as much as a sea. She devours all that you have given her.*
> *And give as much as you will: she never has too much in her life.*
> *It is gone instantly; neither giver nor receiver gains anything from it.*

She has endless means to feed the wantonness and titillation of the flesh—hooks to catch with her bait, and golden chains and bonds of beauty and embracing flattery, through which she overpowers the strong and cradles the weak in her lap.

Claudian <note>Claudius Claudianus (c. 370–404 AD), a Latin poet associated with the court of the Emperor Honorius.</note> in the 2nd Book on Stilicho.

> Luxury, an alluring evil, which is always inclined to arrange itself as the lust of the body dictates, numbs the senses with a thick darkness. She is indeed charming of face, but none is more foul within; with painted cheeks and draped in deceitful allurements, she binds her fierce serpents with red gold. She has entangled many with the hooks of pleasure.
> <note>original Latin: "Luxuries prædulce malum, quæ dedita ſemper Corporis arbitriis, bebetat caligine ſenſus, Blanda quidem vultu, ſed qua non tetrior ulla Interius, fucata genas, & amicta doloſis Illecebris, torvos auro circumligat hydros. Illa voluptatum multos innexuit hamis."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Luxury, an enticing evil, which is always inclined*
> *To arrange itself as the lust of the body is situated,*
> *Dulls the senses with a thick darkness,*
> *And causes more damage than is in Circe’s herbs.*
> *She weakens the limbs. And however lovely of being*
> *She appears, she is to be feared for the inner evil.*
> *The makeup colors the cheek, which keeps everyone enchanted.*
> *Out of cunning, she winds her snakes with red gold,*
> *And catches many people with the hooks of delight.*

One lives by Bonds, and to break and tear them, *Psalm II:3. Jeremiah V:5.* then again of the Bond of the covenant, *Ezekiel XX:3.* of a Bond of the yoke. Of the bound who hoped, being in a pit without water. *Isaiah LVIII:6 and LXI. Zechariah IX.*

<margin>Bond of the Covenant, of the Yoke.</margin>
It is certain that everything in the time of Christ and the Apostles was conspired and strained together, with all cunning, power, and violence, to prevent Jesus from becoming king, being recognized as the Messiah, and His teaching from being accepted and breaking through: so that men would not cast off the yoke of the Law and the dominion of those who sat on the seat of Moses, and take Jesus's yoke upon themselves. They did not want to believe in Jesus, embrace His teaching, or endure His rebuke. They preferred to remain under the Law and its curse. They made a covenant with death and hell. They preferred to side with Herod, Pontius Pilate, and the Roman Emperor. Everything was devised only to get Jesus out of the way, to root out His disciples, and to suppress His teaching through contempt, slander, persecution, etc. And when fleshly weapons did not prevail, they sought to split and break the Bonds of unity, love, and peace through incited men who spied on liberty, created factions, introduced and taught false doctrines, and advised—as something praiseworthy—the adapting to the times...

# B O N D S.

<note>original: E 2 (signature mark)</note>
<note>The text begins mid-sentence, following the catchword "the" from the previous page: "...to take [the sword] in hand, if only one could cause a disruption beneath it. Thus Christ’s teaching and followers would soon come to an end."</note>

<margin>Bond of the Covenant.</margin>
The Bond of the Covenant is the oath of adjuration, and the obligation toward the obedient observance of the conditions of the covenant, without which a covenant cannot well be confirmed; nor can a covenant remain standing, unless both sides sincerely fulfill the same for mutual peace and satisfaction. *Ezekiel 20:37.*

<margin>Bond of the yoke.</margin>
The Bond of the yoke—*Isaiah 58 and 61, Zechariah 9, Psalm 107:10-14*—I would think, depicts and outlines for us (not always and everywhere, or absolutely) those bound by sin to hellish punishment: those sold and enslaved to sins: the dominion of Satan. No, not all texts and circumstances allow for that: but here, and often more so, it refers to the Jews bound to the Law in solemn shadows <note>The "Shadow Law" or *Schaduwwet* refers to the Old Testament rituals which were seen by early modern theologians as "shadows" or precursors to the "light" of Christ.</note>, a heavy yoke, *Acts 15*, with the added burdens of the Jewish guardians, *Matthew 5, 15, and 23*. It refers to the crushing of the poor by not redeeming a brother who had become impoverished and sold into servitude, even though one was able and was the nearest kin: instead, they let him serve out his time, or forced him to bind himself until the Year of Jubilee <note>The Jubilee was a year of liberation every fifty years in ancient Israel, where debts were forgiven and slaves freed; see Leviticus 25.</note>. *Leviticus 25.* These Bonds are broken by the Law of Christ’s freedom, and by the abolition of Moses’s Shadow-law, the weakening and death of the so-called gods, alongside the destruction of the city and Temple. *Romans 7:1-6, John 8:36, Galatians 3 and 5, Colossians 2, etc., 1 Corinthians 8, Psalm 82.* After which time, the free Christian Church had to endure Bonds and Shackles, all kinds of miseries, distress, scorn, and persecution, especially under ten Roman Emperors, for over three hundred years. *Psalm 22, 44, and 107, Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 4, 2 Corinthians 4, etc.*

<margin>Bonds of the Christian Church.</margin>
Something still remains to be mentioned regarding the Bond, but in a tone that is much softer and more lovely. One reads in the scrolls of the New Testament, *Ephesians 4 and Colossians 3*, of a Bond of peace and of love. Love is considered a Bond of perfection.

<margin>Bond of peace.</margin>
<margin>Definition of love.</margin>
Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note>, when asked what love was, answered: *It is as a certain life binding two things together, or striving to do so.* Perfection, in a certain respect regarding the church made up of Jews and Gentiles, lies in true union and communion with Christ as the head, for the enjoyment of all His holy blessings through the working of the Spirit. The mutual union of the members of the body has love and peace as the perfect bond of joining, through which one wills and speaks the same, conversing for each other’s joy and perfection, teaching, exhorting, encouraging, and rebuking one another without any bitterness or sharpness; bearing with one another in weaknesses, forgiving crimes, not being embittered, not lightly suspecting one’s neighbor or speaking ill of him: but contributing everything that serves unity, friendliness, mutual joy, and perfection.

<margin>Definition of peace.</margin>
And to wrap it up briefly with Augustine in the *Words of the Lord* <note>original: *Ver. Dom.*, referring to Augustine's *Sermones de Verbis Domini*.</note>: Peace is the clarity of the spirit, the stillness or tranquility of the soul, the simplicity of the heart, the bond of love, the company of love. Peace is that which removes divisions, stills wars, restrains angers, treads the proud underfoot, loves the humble, brings the discordant to calm, and reconciles enemies. It is pleasant to everyone; it knows nothing of being exalted or puffed up, etc.

->Silius Italicus, Book 11, Punic War<-

> Peace is the best of all things
> Given to man to know: peace alone is better
> Than countless triumphs: peace is able to guard safety,
> And make citizens equal.
<note>original Latin: *Pax optima rerum / Quas homini novisse datum est: pax una triumphis / Innumeris potior: pax custodire salutem, / Et cives aequare potens.*</note>

->That is:<-

->That is:<-

> Become rich in small means through harmony.

Love contributes greatly to friendliness, mutual joy, and perfection.

->Horace, Odes Book 1, 13<-

> Are those whom an unbroken bond holds: nor, torn asunder
> By evil complaints,
> Will love dissolve them sooner than their final day.
<note>original Latin: *Felices ter, & amplius, / Quos irrupta tenet copula: nec malis / Divulsus querimoniis / Suprema citius solvet amor die.*</note>

->That is:<-

> O Thrice blessed are those who, entered into a firm covenant,
> Bind themselves fast to one another.
> Whose love, never disturbed by bitter quarrels,
> Is never seen to be divided
> By disaster or hardship,
> Before death separates them.

Bonding and binding sometimes stand in contrast to setting at liberty, unbinding, granting space, release, or acquittal; letting out from Bonds and Shackles, *Psalm 105:20, Acts 20:7*, or weighing the anchors, loosening the ship's ropes to sail into the deep. It is well known how Paul wished to be "unbound" <note>Usually translated as "to depart" or "to be dissolved."</note>, *Philippians 1:23.* It is not quite possible for me to include everything that could be noted and said regarding this. The body has been regarded in relation to the soul as a kind of prison, or at least as a hospital, even as a workshop.

Scindurus <note>Possibly a reference to a lexicographer or scholar of Hebrew/Greek roots.</note> notes in his *Lexicon* that **release, deliverance, or death** <note>original Hebrew: **פְּטִירָה** (*petirah*)</note> was the name given to it. When troops were sent home, it was called letting go, or letting depart: <note>original Greek: ἀναλύειν (*analyein*), ἀπολύειν (*apolyein*)</note>. "They released them to their home," <note>original Greek: ἀπέλυσαν εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν (*apelysan eis tēn oikian*)</note> says Polybius; "He released the Spartans homeward," <note>original Greek: τὰς Σπαρτιάτας ἀπέλυσεν οἴκαδε (*tas Spartiatas apelysen oikade*)</note> says Xenophon in *Agesilaus*.

<margin>To bind and to loose.</margin>
Here also applies *Matthew 16:19* <note>The source text cites Matt. 16:12, but the context of "binding and loosing" refers to verse 19.</note>, the binding and the loosing: declaring what is permitted and what is forbidden—what must be done and what must be left undone.
