See *Lightfoot in Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae; Spanheim’s Biblical Defenses Book I, Ch. 2; Matthew 22:13; John 20:23,* etc. Regarding this, the Jewish Masters, Teachers, and Scribes often went to work quite incautiously, incorrectly, and partially—forbidding what was free, commanding and permitting what should have been forbidden, keeping people under punishment and constraint, or releasing them, etc., where one ought to have acted quite differently. *Matthew 5:22 and 15:5, 6,* etc. One can consult Spanheim on this.

->BANNER, <note>original Hebrew: נס (Nees), דגל (Degel); original Greek: σημεῖον (semeion), σπλήγιον (splēgion); original Latin: vexillum</note><-

The word BANNER is well enough known in Holy Scripture, and many expressions are found therein regarding common military usage, applied to the people of God and the state of the Old Church, and especially the New Testament.

<margin>Meaning of the word BANNER.</margin>
The word *Nees* <note>Hebrew: נס</note> signifies a Flag, Standard, Banner, or Field-sign, which one plants or raises on high: under which one takes service or enlists for war; which one must follow; that which makes the troops and regiments recognizable from others, even the enemy’s; and that to which one retreats when scattered or put to flight.

<margin>Diversity of Banners.</margin>
These are found in all armies, though the form, materials, signs, colors, and so forth, sometimes differ greatly.

<margin>Captains for the tribes.</margin>
We read in *Numbers 1 and 2* that every tribe had to have a captain from his father’s house, and everyone served under his Banner, bearing the sign of his father's tribal house, into which Israel's army was divided.

<margin>Four Banners of Israel’s army.</margin>
It is said that Israel’s army marched forth in four columns or wings, having four Banners and primary field-signs: namely, that Judah’s field-sign was a lion; that of Ephraim, an ox or calf; that of Dan, an Eagle with a snake between its claws; and that of Reuben, a man holding the Mandrake plant <note>original: Dudaims</note> in his hand.

<margin>Field-signs of the Persians, Thebans, Athenians, and Romans.</margin>
Furthermore, it is recounted that the Persians had as a field-sign the image of the Sun; the Thebans, the Sphinx; the Athenians, the owl; the Romans thereafter, the Eagle. See *Alessandro Alessandri, Genial Days Book IV, Ch. 2; Lydius's Sacred Treatise on Military Affairs; Hofmann’s Universal Lexicon; Witsius's Aegyptiaca; Goeree,* etc. From here, we have very distinct expressions in the holy pages, borrowed from military usage, such as, namely, to set up a Banner for or over someone:

<column-break/>

<margin>Usage borrowed from [military].</margin>
...which I believe signifies: *to come to someone’s aid, to provide help for protection, in order to be crowned with victory, Song of Solomon 2, etc.*

To lift up the Banner, to raise it, to plant it somewhere—especially on high, upon someone’s ramparts or walls—I judge that this can signify: to rejoice, to be glorious, to be triumphant; to triumph in someone, through someone, or over someone, as in *Psalm 20:6.* This initially and as an example occurred in King David, and pre-eminently and in power has its truth in the triumphant King Christ, through His death, resurrection, and truth, whereby He is ruling in the midst of His enemies. *Psalm 110:2; Psalm 45. See Psalm 60:6; Isaiah 62:10, 11, 12; Jeremiah 51:12.*

<margin>Triumph of David and Christ.</margin>
To plant the Banner and raise it against someone generally means to prepare for war, to march out against someone to attack them hostilely. *Isaiah 13:2, etc. and 18:3; Jeremiah 4:6 and 51:27,* etc.

When he who carries the ensign or the sign faints <note>original: "verfmelt" - literally melts away, meaning to lose heart or collapse</note>, does not raise it on high, tears the Banner, hides it, throws it from his hands, or lets it fall, then things are in a bad state; then the soldiers' courage fails, and they easily fall into disorder, since there is no captain, leader, or encourager. *Isaiah 10:18.* <note>The source cites Isaiah 10:8, but the imagery of a standard-bearer fainting is from 10:18.</note>

<margin>God called the Banner.</margin>
When God is called the BANNER in *Exodus 17:15* <note>The name Jehovah-Nissi: "The Lord is my Banner."</note>, it is not spoken quite literally, but figuratively. Namely, He is the one we cling to, follow, under whom we serve, through whom we wish to triumph and overcome in the Lord, the righteousness of His people, who would sanctify and exalt His own through righteousness: He namely, who is the altar, and would destroy and subdue all enemies.

When it says of the Messiah: *Song of Solomon 2:4, "His love carried the Banner over me," and Song of Solomon 5:10 <note>The source cites 7:10, but the description of being "chief among ten thousand" is found in 5:10.</note>, "That he carries the Banner over ten thousand":* and the Holy Spirit is called His ensign-bearer, who carries and raises the Banner, *Isaiah 59:19*, I would most closely think that it shows He is that love—who is given out of love, who pours out love through the Holy Spirit into the hearts of those in the covenant, and makes the love of God and Christ urge them on and strongly go out in reciprocal love, *Romans 8; Song of Solomon 8; 2 Timothy 1.* He is the supreme Captain, *Hebrews 12:2*, whom the church follows, under whom she fights, through whose love she is led to the spiritual battle, through whose love she is powerful, safe, and victorious, *1 Corinthians 15; Romans 8; 1 John 4 and 5; Song of Solomon 8; Romans 5:5,* etc.

<margin>Field-signs of the spiritual troops.</margin>
That He has a mighty and numerous army, mentioned simply as ten thousands. *Daniel 7:10; Psalm 68:17; Revelation 5,* etc. These spiritual troops have as their field-signs Christ, the Truth, Love, Faith, Hope, Trust, and are therefore very terrible to their enemies. *Song of Solomon 6:4-10; 2 Corinthians 10:4, 5.*

When it says in *Isaiah 11:10, 11, 12,* that He who is the Root of Jesse shall stand as a Banner for the peoples, and the Gentiles shall seek Him; and subsequently, that He shall set up the Banner among the Gentiles; I would think that one must take it figuratively and imaginatively: namely, that Christ, as if raised on the pole of the cross, having triumphed over all His and our enemies, would be exalted among the Jews and Gentiles through the preaching of the Holy Gospel, as the true Messiah, supreme Captain, and Savior.

## BASAN <note>Bashan</note>, בשן, Βάσαν.

<margin>Location of Bashan.</margin>
BASAN was a land—a kingdom—located not over, but on the other side of the land <note>referring to the Transjordan region</note>, across the Jordan, situated at the eastern end of Canaan.

It was a kingdom with many cities and villages. One reads of Og, the King of Bashan.

It was a very beautiful, fertile, and famous region. It possessed tall oaks, grassy pastures, cows, bulls, calves, and sheep—stout, fat, strong, and luxuriant. One reads of it in *Deuteronomy 32; Job 13; Psalm 22* and *68; Isaiah 2; Zechariah 11; Micah 7;* and elsewhere.

It is held that Og the King and the inhabitants of that land were descended from the race of Giants, mighty men of renown. *Numbers 13; Deuteronomy 3; Joshua 12.*

<margin>Og, king of Bashan.</margin>
It was Og, king of Bashan, who with his subjects and dependents offered resistance to Israel early on during the conquest of Canaan: but he was brought down by God’s people, and his land was divided among the tribes of Reuben, Dan, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. *Numbers 13 and 32; Deuteronomy 3; Joshua 12 and 13.*

<column-break/>

It is indisputable that Bashan—its pastures, cows, bulls, oaks, and so forth—is frequently mentioned in the holy scroll, whether one takes and understands it literally and according to the letter, or figuratively, by imagination, allusion, and transference. I shall briefly illustrate the principal texts and, as the requirements of this work demand, concisely explain them according to my purpose. And thus they appear to me in rank and order, namely:

<margin>*Psalm 22:12* explained. <note>The Dutch text cites verse 16, but refers to the content of verse 12 in modern numbering.</note></margin>
Psalm 22:12. *Strong bulls of Bashan have surrounded me.* It is not difficult to understand that Bashan’s fat pastures and hilly mountains would have produced fat, beautiful, strong, and luxuriant cows, bulls, and oxen, which are to be feared and avoided when they thrust with their horns or kick out.

It is known that Israel’s people, church, and civil state were planted and placed upon a fertile hill, and that they became well-blessed, thick, and fat. *Deuteronomy 32:15; Hosea 13:6; Isaiah 1:2, 3, 4.* But they kicked back, repaying God's blessings and benefits with the most vile ingratitude, setting themselves against the Rock of Israel, the spring of their salvation, the Messiah.
<margin>The vile ingratitude of Israel.</margin>

It seems to me that our learned Annotators <note>Referring to the marginal notes of the Dutch *Statenvertaling* Bible.</note> on *Amos 4* have hit the mark when they understand the "cows of Bashan" to be the strong and powerful: the proud and godless Judges, who fatten themselves with the gifts of the rich while they oppress the poor people brought before them in judgment.
<margin>What is understood by the Cows of Bashan is explained.</margin>

On this basis, I would understand the "strong bulls" that surrounded the Messiah here to be not the common Jewish people—for they were sufficiently exhausted by the regents in state and church—but those who sat in the seat of Moses, who held the governance of the civil state and religion: the High Council, Priests, Scribes, elders of the people, and judges, who like fat, powerful, luxurious, and licentious ones, opposed the Christ with cunning and open violence, and gored him with horns, *Ezekiel 39; Acts 2* and *4; Psalm 2,* etc., as is known from the Evangelical histories and the acts of the Apostles.
<margin>Bulls of Bashan understood.</margin>

But it is quite as difficult to understand what appears in *Psalm 68:15, 22.* The words read thus:
> *The mountain of Bashan is a mountain of God; the mountain of Bashan is a mountain of many peaks. The Lord has said; I will bring back from Bashan: I will bring back from the depths of the sea.*

It is maintained that God’s Spirit is accustomed, when He wishes to exalt something as exceptionally high, fertile, beautiful, great, etc., and thus outstanding, to name it after God: such as mountains of God, cedars of God, city of God, man of God, etc. Thus, Bashan was certainly a mountain of God—a high mountain, a fertile land, a mighty kingdom, and its people were formidable and very powerful. However, that kingdom, and likewise the Assyrian and Egyptian powers, ought not to have been proud and haughty or looked upon God’s mountain, Zion, and Israel’s kingdom with contempt because of its smallness, nor set themselves hostiley against His kingdom. For even if Israel’s kingdom was not so large and extensive, it was nonetheless a fertile, beautiful, and ornate land. God had chosen that land and people and endowed them with many privileges. There He dwelt and wished to remain dwelling, and therefore He would not forsake His heritage; rather, just as He had rescued and delivered His people from Bashan, bringing that people down and under...
<margin>Israel’s kingdom.</margin>

Others take it literally so that not Bashan <note>original: "Basan"</note> is the subject, but the predicate of God's mountain, or Zion; namely, that *Zion, God’s mountain, is Bashan, or like Bashan: that is, a people and church-state, mighty, great with fat pastures, full of sheep, lambs, oxen, calves, melted together from twelve hills or mountains, the world-famous twelve tribes of Israel.*

And since Zion, God’s mountain, as well as Israel, portrays the kingdom of heaven, or the Church of the New Testament, so after the time of Christ’s ascension and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, the Zion and Israel of God has extended itself everywhere far and wide in the East and West, finding beautiful lands, very fat pastures, many mountains and hills—that is, peoples and powers bowing under Jesus, becoming God's mountain, exalted above the peaks and mountains (*Isaiah 2; Micah 4*) and thus containing the sheep of Christ scattered everywhere, possessing a very beautiful land and grassy pastures (*Psalm 23*).

But those lands which the Church possessed in the East, where the Greek Church was and partly still is; and in the West where the Latin Church was located; which fat lands and pastures, having been taken from her by the Eastern lords, Turks, Persians, and Ottomans, just as in the West by the Antichrist <note>Likely referring to the Papacy from a Protestant perspective</note>, having grazed away the fat pastures and oppressed Christ’s sheep, they shall again have to surrender the people of God. God shall gather His own from Bashan (the East) and the depths of the sea (Heathendom or Antichristendom) to bring them into a fat and abundant inheritance.

<margin>Comparison between Bashan and the Jews.</margin>
One also finds a kind of comparison between Bashan and the Jews, just as between Edom, Bozrah <note>original: "Botsra"</note>, Judaism, and Jerusalem; which, being in the eastern part of the world's inheritance, in respect to the depths of the sea, the islands, and the nations of the sea (*Genesis 10; Zephaniah 2; Isaiah 11 and 24*), would prevent as much as possible the taking of the world's inheritance. By colluding with the Roman Emperor, they plagued the Apostles and Christians with violence, bloody edicts <note>original: "plakkaten" - formal proclamations or laws</note>, and cruel persecutions. But the Lord would later surrender them to the Romans, as prey for their teeth, destroying them while they bathed in their own blood. Having sat for a long time without a king or priest, etc., God would at the end of days again lay His hand upon them, and gather and convert them (*Isaiah 11; Romans 11; 2 Corinthians 3; etc.*).

And as for the passages in *Psalm 135 and 136*, it seems to me that the benefits which God showed to His ancient Israel are recounted as proof that He is true and faithful in the conquest of Canaan, to come to the full possession of the inheritance from time to time. This is a sketch showing that God, who singularly displays His virtues and perfection in Christ and in the expansion of His kingdom, will thus bring His people to the full possession of the world, when He shall powerfully deliver them from Egypt, and...

<column-break/>

...subdue that king of Babylon <note>original: "Babel"</note> and the eastern enemies, destroying and putting to shame the idols and their images, when one shall serve Him with a single shoulder <note>An idiom meaning "unanimously" or "with one accord"</note> in spirit and truth as spiritual and true priests and servants of God. When the Jews shall be converted, and all believers—the true Israel of God—shall inherit the world, then the kings of the earth shall belong to our Lord and His Christ. This still awaits the fall of the Antichrist, the ending of the Eastern powers, the conversion of the Jews, and the gathering of the elect from the four winds of the earth by the angels of God (or of the congregations).

Furthermore, *Isaiah 2:13* speaks of the *oaks of Bashan*, just as of the high cedars of Lebanon; of elevated, haughty mountains and hills, high towers, and strong walls, etc.

If one examines this chapter closely, it speaks not only of the exaltation of God’s kingdom and the expansion of His name and virtues, linked with the righteous downfall of the Jewish civil and ecclesiastical state, but also of future times, when idols would be destroyed and the nations opposing God’s kingdom would be subdued. But since the Lord would begin His judgments at His house, and subsequently speaks specifically of the sins and punishments of the Jews—and the places mentioned here belonged to the Jews, and they placed their security and strength in them, etc.—I find, in the first place, not the least reason for difficulty in believing or thinking that the Lord would threaten their highest strongholds and strengths through the Romans, to have them cut down and devastated, thus stripping them and giving them as prey to enemies. Similarly, the Jewish Princes and priests, who held the power and authority and made everyone dance to their tune <note>original: "naar hunne pypen deden danssen"</note>, exalting themselves in their authority, wisdom, prudence, and holiness, would be humbled and brought under the power of the Romans or rooted out, as happened before, during, and after Christ. Furthermore, one can understand by this the high, glorious, and strong things of the world that withdraw themselves from Christ’s kingdom and teaching, though supported by worldly or spiritual power; such as the rule of the Pope, Cardinals, or Bishops, Prelates, etc.

As for *Isaiah 33:9, etc.*, I see and find that it is taken properly and according to the letter as the Jewish land, comprising all those parts, regions, and mountain areas which, because of their sins and iniquities, were specifically distressed and attacked by the Assyrians, the forests being cut down, the most fertile meadows and lands devastated, and furthermore Jerusalem besieged and brought to the utmost distress. On which occasion God would arise and exalt Himself through the deliverance of His people and vengeance upon the Assyrian. So then Lebanon, Sharon, Bashan, etc., as parts of the Jewish land or inheritance, would be understood literally.

<margin>Prophecy of Jeremiah.</margin> Regarding the prophecy of *Jeremiah Chapter 22:20* etc., one can take it literally and according to the letter as foretelling the calamities of God's people, to be carried away captive to Babylon. And so, to "howl from Bashan" <note>original: "op Basan te blaazen"</note> signifies trouble and a call to arms.

*Jeremiah 50.* It seems to me that regarding Lebanon, Bashan, etc., and the restoration to such mountains and fruitful regions as a benefit for the Lord's people, it can be very easily understood first and according to the literal letter as the destruction and subjugation of the kingdom of Babylon (where the Jews had been held captive) by the Medes and Persians; this was accompanied by the deliverance and exodus of the Lord’s people from Babylon to their own land. Exemplarily, one can apply it for various reasons and similarities to the Reformation and the exodus of our ancestors from [the spiritual] Babylon, which was followed by the Reformers' initial fall of Babylon, foretelling the complete fall of the New-Roman Babylon. *Jeremiah 51.*

The passage in *Ezekiel 27*, as also appears from the preceding, sketches for us to the life the rise, pride, commerce, and riches of Tyre, etc., alongside its destruction by the Babylonians, or Chaldeans. All of this can be understood according to the letter, and as such, BASHAN is mentioned there. That one should also consider the spiritual Tyre and its "harlot’s song"—the spiritual merchandising of the Word, Sacraments, heaven, God's gifts, God Himself, and everything that is holy, alongside its downfall (even though it says it shall see no sorrow and sits as a queen)—is, I think, fitting in every respect. Read with

with attention the 28th chapter. But more on this later under its own letter, in the description of TYRE.

Also in *Ezekiel 39:18*, the "fatlings of Bashan" are spoken of. While one sees the report of the downfall of Gog and Magog, it will undoubtedly signify, according to the imagery: the powerful, rich, and luxurious. It is enough for the present to have said how one must take the "fatlings of Bashan" by way of imagery.

In *Amos*, in the fourth chapter, the <margin>Cows of Bashan.</margin> "cows of Bashan" are spoken of, by which one sees that the great ones in Israel (in the divided, torn, and idolatrous kingdom, distinct from Judah, having Samaria as the royal capital and seat) are meant; just as it is spoken there and further described how they oppressed the people, what cruelty, violence, and licentiousness they practiced, and how after committing these things they were subdued and punished by God. So that Bashan’s pastures and fat beasts are alluded to, and specifically in this sense: that one should not understand them as literal fat beasts of Bashan, but rather as men; these fat beasts of Bashan being in many ways similar to godless and proud rulers who oppress, exhaust, and overpower others, etc.

Regarding *Micah* in the seventh chapter, verse 14, Bashan is not taken there according to the letter, but figuratively, with an allusion to the ancient Bashan and the division of the land of Canaan; and the content of this chapter is applied to the Church of Christ in later times, and that with distinct considerations: namely, that one either views the Church as praying for the conversion of the Jews, who formerly possessed Bashan; or of the Turks and peoples who currently inhabit it; or that the Reformed Church—which alongside the church and church-state of the Papacy, has had such fat pastures as Bashan in Germany, Bohemia, the Palatinate and elsewhere, yet was driven out of them—prays that she may occupy these places again and be restored therein.

In the Prophet *Nahum*, in the first chapter from verse 1 to 12, one reads of Bashan and <margin>Bashan and Carmel.</margin> Carmel. I would most closely believe that one must understand it first through the Jewish land and people (to whom this land had partly become an inherited possession) according to the letter and history, wondrously infested, plagued, and punished by God through the Assyrian, who thereafter also had his own lot and turn.

Also in *Zechariah, Chapter 11:2*, one reads of the "oaks of Bashan," of fallen "cedars of Lebanon," of a "strong forest" that has fallen down, etc. It appears to me most closely that here, under various symbols, are included the Jewish great ones—the high, proud, and violent, both in state and church—whom the Lord has felled.

Others take it literally in this way: that Bashan is not the subject, but the description of God's mountain, or Zion; namely, *that Zion, God's mountain, is Bashan, or like Bashan: that is, a people and a church-state, mighty, great with fat pastures, full of sheep, lambs, oxen, and calves, merged together from twelve hills or mountains, the world-renowned twelve tribes of Israel.*

And because Zion, God’s mountain, as well as Israel, depicts the kingdom of heaven or the Church of the New Testament, so after the time of Christ's ascension and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, the Zion and Israel of God have extended far and wide in the East and West. They found beautiful lands and very fat pastures, many mountains and hills—that is, nations and powers bowing under Jesus—becoming God's mountain, exalted above the peaks and mountains (*Isaiah 2; Micah 4*), and thus containing the sheep of Christ scattered everywhere, possessing a very beautiful land and green pastures (*Psalm 23*).

Yet those lands which the Church possessed in the East, where the Greek Church was and partly still is, and in the West where the Latin Church was found—which fat lands and pastures were taken from her by the Eastern lords, the Turks, Persians, and Ottomans <note>The author refers to the Ottoman Empire's expansion into previously Christian territories</note>, just as in the West by the Antichrist <note>In the context of 17th-century Dutch theology, "the Antichrist" almost always refers to the Papacy</note>, who grazed upon the fat pastures and oppressed Christ's sheep—these shall again have to surrender the people of God. And God shall gather His own from Bashan in the East and from the depths of the sea—the Heathendom or the realm of the Antichrist—to bring them into a fat and abundant inheritance.

<margin>Comparison between Bashan and the Jews.</margin>
One also finds a kind of comparison between Bashan and the Jews, just as between Edom, Bozrah, Judaism, and Jerusalem. These, being in the eastern part of the world's inheritance, would, in respect to the depths of the sea, the islands, and the nations of the sea (*Genesis 10; Zephaniah 2; Isaiah 11 and 24*), prevent as much as possible the world's inheritance from being claimed. Colluding with the Roman Emperor, they plagued the Apostles and Christians with violence, bloody decrees, and cruel persecutions. But the Lord would later surrender them to the Romans, as prey to their teeth, to destroy them while they bathed in their own blood. And having sat for a long time without king or priest, etc., God would at the end of days again lay His hand upon them, and gather and convert them (*Isaiah 11; Romans 11; 2 Corinthians 3, etc.*).

And concerning the passages in *Psalm 135 and 136*, it seems to me that they recount the benefits which God proved from time to time to His ancient Israel as a sign that He is true and faithful, during the conquest of Canaan to reach full possession of the inheritance. This is a sketch showing that God—who singularly displays His virtues and perfection in Christ and in the expansion of His kingdom—will likewise bring His people to the full possession of the world, when He shall powerfully deliver them from Egypt and

bring down that king of Babel and the eastern enemies, destroying and shaming the idols and their images. Furthermore, *Isaiah 2:13* speaks of the oaks of Bashan, just as it speaks of the high cedars of Lebanon; of exalted, proud mountains and hills, high towers, and strong walls, etc.

If one considers this chapter carefully, it speaks not only of the exaltation of God's kingdom and the expansion of His name and virtues, linked with the righteous downfall of the Jewish civil and ecclesiastical state, but also of future times when idols would be annihilated and the nations opposing God's kingdom would be brought low. Yet because the Lord would begin His judgments at His own house, and subsequently speaks specifically of the sins and punishments of the Jews, and because the places named here belonged to the Jews and they placed their security and strength in them, I find in the first place not the slightest reason for difficulty in believing that the Lord would threaten their highest strongholds and strengths with being cut down and devastated by the Romans, thus exposing them and giving them over as prey to enemies. Likewise, the Jewish princes and priests, who held the governance and authority and made everyone dance to their pipes, exalting themselves in their authority, wisdom, prudence, and holiness, would be humbled and brought under the power of the Romans, or rooted out, as happened before, during, and after Christ. Furthermore, one can understand this as the high, glorious, and strong things of the world that withdraw themselves from Christ's kingdom and teaching, though supported by a worldly or spiritual power, such as the rule of the Pope, Cardinals, or Bishops, Prelates, etc.

Regarding *Isaiah 33:9, etc.*: I see and find that it is taken literally as the Jewish land, comprising all those parts, regions, and mountain districts, which were particularly distressed and attacked by the Assyrians because of their sins and iniquities. The forests were cut down, the most fruitful meadows and lands devastated, and subsequently Jerusalem was besieged and brought to the utmost distress. On which occasion God would arise and exalt Himself through the deliverance of His people and vengeance upon the Assyrian. So then Lebanon, Sharon, Bashan, etc., as parts of the Jewish land or inheritance, would be understood literally.

### BASILISKUS, <note>Hebrew: *Tsepha* or *Tsephoni* (צפע ,צפעוני)</note>, <note>Greek: *Basiliskos* (Βασιλίσκος)</note>.

Whether one counts the BASILISK among the wingless and footless dragons, or among the species of snakes, it is called *Tsepha* or *Tsephoni*: by the Chaldeans <note>Aramaic speakers of the ancient Near East.</note>, *Hurman* (חורמן): by the Arabs, *Harmene*: by the Egyptians of old, *oubaios* (ουβαιος).

<margin>The Basilisk, king of snakes.</margin> It is held to be the little king among the snakes or dragons, either because it wears a kind of crown upon its head, or because with its sight or its hissing sound it strikes terror into all animals, drives away snakes and dragons, and snatches away and eats their hunted prey.

<margin>Size of the Basilisk.</margin> Its size is taken as three fingers in length, or twelve in breadth, according to *Pliny Book II, Chapter 21, and Grevinus quoting Nicander.*

I find it testified of him that he tends toward yellow, having three points on the head: in Galen <note>A famous Greek physician (c. 129–216 AD).</note> and in Avicenna <note>Written here as "Abenfina," referring to the Persian polymath Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037).</note> he is described thus: leaning toward yellow and black, with a head ending quite sharply, and with red eyes. <margin>Its appearance.</margin> Pliny describes it in his 8th Book, Chapter 21, as being no longer than twelve fingers, with a white spot on the head as if it wore a crown. And Grevinus presents it as three fingers long, having a yellow-colored body with three protrusions on the top of the head.

Some also make mention of small wings, which, however, are of little use to it.

As for its movement, it is told that it walks upright with the upper body from the belly up, and creeps with the hindquarters, without twisting itself into various coils.

Its origin is quite uncertain: for some speak of the eggs of the Ibis <note>A sacred bird in Egypt.</note>: others of an aged rooster's egg, buried in the mud or hatched by a toad or a snake. Some say that it is born and comes forth from a Ray <note>A type of fish.</note>, etc.

And, as is told, these animals are found in Cyrenaica, in Africa, etc., according to Pliny and Aelian: likewise in Ceylon <note>Modern Sri Lanka.</note>, Jaffna <note>Written as "Jafnapatan," a city in Sri Lanka.</note>, and more other parts of the world. Some say they are named *Cobras de Capelo* <note>Portuguese for "snakes with hoods," i.e., Cobras.</note>.

Furthermore, it is said that the Basilisk carries out an enmity with the weasel, whose scent it cannot endure at all, and for that reason it must die if one throws a weasel into its hole. <margin>Particulars of this animal.</margin> Also that the crowing of a rooster terrifies it unto death and causes it to die: that it is driven away if one travels with a rooster in the lands where it stays. That it dies by the power of its own reflecting poison if it beholds itself in a mirror.

It is very distraught and terrified when it beholds

<column-break/>

itself in a mirror. When a proud man views himself properly for once in the mirror of God’s Law, and has learned to know himself in his true form, *Seipsum territus horret* <note>Latin: "Terrified, he shudders at himself."</note>; then he must be terrified of himself. Thus writes Philotheus in *Christian Symbols, page 31*:

> *The Basilisk is terrified by the image of its own form,*
> *If it sees its members in a mirror held before it.*
> *Then, its eyes turned back upon itself with fatal light,*
> *It mourns, and trembles at its own sight.*
> *If a sinful man examines his own crimes,*
> *Placing the Holy Bible before his eyes.*
> *Then he shudders at himself in the mirror of the divine book,*
> *And trembles, terrified by his own appearance.*
> *Lo, mortal man, here is a cause fit for your grieving!*
> *Your foul crimes are as foul to you as they are to God.*

<margin>Comparison of the Basilisk to a proud man.</margin>

->That is:<-

> *The Basilisk takes fright when before its eyes*
> *In a mirror it sees its own body arise.*
> *When it views itself with its fiery eye,*
> *Then it mourns and it shudders with a sorrowful cry.*
> *When man sees himself with his sins heavy laden,*
> *And casts his eyes upon the God-hallowed pages,*
> *Then the mirror of God’s book makes him quite afraid,*
> *When therein he sees God’s law and commands displayed.*
> *Here you have, O mortal man, now ample cause to wail.*
> *The evil that displeases you, God’s displeasure shall not fail.*

Horus and others tell us that golden Basilisks were woven around the heads of kings (as a symbol of invincibility): as also around the heads of the statues of gods, as signs of their immortality and power over life and death. Likewise, that in Egypt they had golden Basilisks whose eyes were manufactured by art in such a way that they could be opened and closed. The open eyes being a symbol of the gods' mercy, benevolence, and providence. The closed eyes a sign of the gods' indignation, wrath, and threatening judgments and dangers, for which reason one then offered sacrifices, prayed for forgiveness, humbled oneself, etc.

It is thought that it was called *Hurman* (חורמן) by the Chaldeans because it devastates and brings down everything. It is a king of dragons and snakes, as it chases and drives them all away, so that they cannot stand before it, nor endure its venom, hissing, and scent, or sight, as Lucan writes in his 9th Book:

> *And pouring forth hisses that terrify all pests,*
> *Harmful before his poisons [reach], he drives away*
> *The common crowd far from himself, and the Basilisk reigns in the empty sands.*

->That is:<-

> *The Basilisk, when he hisses from his beak,*
> *Fills all with terror, wherever he may appear.*
> *Whatever is monstrous must immediately vanish before him.*
> *All vermin flee. He alone holds the field.*

It is testified that with its poison and pestilential breath it infects everything, scorches, dries out, ignites the air, and kills and contaminates through its sight; just as by looking at bleary eyes, one indeed gets bad and inflamed eyes, according to the account of Ovid, *Book II of The Remedies of Love.*

> When eyes look upon the wounded, they themselves are wounded,

Anyone desiring a more detailed account of the Basilisk may read Pliny, Aelian, Solinus, Aetius, Nicander, Bochart, etc. I have composed and condensed the most important points concisely.

As for the Basilisk, one finds that it is also mentioned in the Holy Scrolls, as will be seen in the following places: *Isaiah 11:8, 14:29, 30:6, 59:5, and Jeremiah 8:17*, under the words <note>Hebrew: *Tsephoni* (צפעוני - basilisk/viper), *Ephe* (אפע - viper), and *Pethen* (פתן - cobra/asp).</note>.

Regarding what more is said of the Basilisk in *Isaiah*, chapter 11, verse 8: I have stated in the first part of my *Sacred Miscellanies* <note>The author refers to his own previous scholarly work, likely titled *Heilige Mengelstoffen*.</note> regarding that prominent chapter, that I understood the Basilisk to preeminently signify the wicked arch-heretic Arius, and the nursing child to signify Constantine the Great, etc.
<margin>Arius compared to the Basilisk.</margin>

In that passage, I compare the heretic Arius to the Basilisk; he who, with the vapor and poisonous venom of his teaching, had infected and inflamed almost the entire world. He was "crowned" with a Bishop’s Miter, streaked with the white stripes and spots of hypocrisy, and possessed the "hiding holes" of deceptive expressions. He thrust into the hand of the world a <term>homoiousios</term> <note>Greek: ὁμοιούσιος, meaning "of a similar substance." Arius used this to argue that Jesus was not fully God.</note> (similar in being) instead of a <term>homoousios</term> <note>Greek: ὁμοούσιος, meaning "of the same substance." This was the orthodox position established at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</note> (self-existent, or of the same essence). He did not swear by the established and weighty point of truth fixed in the Council, but by his own falsely composed article of doctrine, which he kept hidden in his pocket.

Constantine, now weaned from Paganism alongside early Christianity, has—under the ecclesiastical authority of Athanasius, Eusebius, and other faithful Teachers—thrust his hand into the den, the hiding places, and the depths of the arch-heretic Arius. When Arius and his poisonous doctrine were condemned, he fell from the church-heaven like a star, more bitter than wormwood. *Revelation 8.* For this, one may consult *Spanheim's Ecclesiastical History*, *Georgius Hornius*, and *Zuërius Hornius' Universal History*, *Laetus*, etc.
<margin>Constantine infected by Arius.</margin>

As for the prophecy of *Isaiah* in chapter 14, verse 19: I have noted that the symbols of fiery and poisonous beasts mentioned there are viewed not according to their inner nature, but in respect to their effects in harming others. It is believed that Uzziah and Hezekiah are symbolized there as the rod and scourge of the Philistines (*2 Chronicles 26*, etc.).

<column-break/>

Yet other theologians have understood it in this manner: that by the rod and the serpent one may understand the Babylonians, who had as neighbors, followers, and subjects the Medes and Persians, by whom the house of Judah was disciplined and broken. From that tail and root came forth the empire of the Medes and Persians, which fell far more heavily and destructively upon the people of God. Because of the greater durability and permanence of that empire, it is compared to a Basilisk. Its successor, like a "flying dragon" overflowing everything, would be the Macedonian empire under Alexander the Great; under him, the "root" of Palestine—its prominent merchant city, Tyre—would be starved out, captured, and devastated.
<margin>Medes and Persians compared to the Basilisk.</margin>

*Isaiah 14:29.* BASILISK. Regarding this, the thoughts of the learned have been brought together at great length by the Professor Campegius Vitringa in his *Learned Commentaries on Isaiah*. His Honor himself writes thus: God informs the Philistines that they should not be joyful or abandoned in their prosperity when King Ahaz died and Hezekiah came in his place. For the successor of Ahaz, namely Hezekiah, would surely and severely avenge the insults, the damage, and the grief brought upon the Jewish nation by them; he, in turn, would certainly repay and restrain their practiced pride and cruelty.

Thus, Hezekiah would appear and reveal himself under the symbol of a Basilisk and a water-snake (though he was already reigning at that time), even though up to that point he had not yet brought any damage to the Philistines.
<margin>Hezekiah compared to the Basilisk.</margin>

The symbol of a Basilisk and a flying dragon fits King Hezekiah very well in this case: for a Basilisk is one of the harmful snakes that kills other animals not by biting, but by hissing and blowing. This is transferred to Hezekiah in a beautiful manner, as he conquered his enemies not only by hand and weapons, but by the "hissing and blowing" of his mouth—that is, by the very hot prayers poured out to God. In this same matter, as in many others concerning him, he serves as a symbol of the true Christ, the King of the Church, who would destroy the godless by the breath of His mouth. *Isaiah 11:4.*
<margin>His victorious conquest.</margin>

The imagery of a "flying dragon" must be attributed to his extreme speed; for he, unlooked for and yet ignited by righteous wrath and a desire for vengeance, would fall suddenly upon the Philistines and bite them mortally. This is characteristic of the fiery and flying serpents known from Divine History (*Numbers 21:6*). Hezekiah would bite more sharply and severely than his forefather Uzziah, and would not merely traverse a part of Palestine, but the whole of it, disturbing and troubling it, taking a sensible revenge upon it. He would not even spare Gaza, located in the furthest southern corner—a city against which Uzziah seems to have undertaken nothing (*2 Kings 18:8*). See further the Honorable Mr. Vitringa.

Regarding the prophecy of God in *Isaiah* chapter 30, verse 6: I find that great men there fix their eyes upon the Church of the New Testament in later times, when the image of the Antichrist was erected, and people had somewhat separated themselves from the New-Roman Church...

<margin>Simple explanation.</margin>
*Isaiah 59:5.* "They hatch basilisk eggs." It is clear that the eggs of snakes, adders, and the Basilisk cannot be eaten without harm; one must break the eggs and smother the young in the shell if one wishes to prevent the approaching danger.

It appears that this is spoken of in a metaphorical and figurative way, as God weighs the sin of the people and points out the hindrance by which the Reformation made no progress.

To hatch Basilisk eggs, which must not be eaten, perhaps shows us how dangerous thoughts and feelings, wicked and destructive tricks and counsels, and devilish practices are nourished in the heart and brought forth with the mouth. Furthermore, those things deliberated and put into action for execution are carnal, naughty, destructive, godless, blasphemous, and heretical—clashing with the healthy words of God, poisoning the soul, and furthermore being unwholesome and harmful to the Church of God and spiritual society. When anyone consents to and clings to these, they are the cause of their soul plunging into extreme danger.

Regarding *Jeremiah 8:17*, one should hold that God threatens his wicked and ungrateful people with destroying and devastating enemies—whether Assyrians or Babylonians—compared here to poisonous and destructive animals, against whom the people of God could not stand by their own power and wisdom, nor by promises or covenants, etc., whatever they might attempt. <margin>Thoughts on the Basilisk.</margin>
It is known, according to the testimony of Horus <note>Referring to Horapollo, an author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, that when the Egyptians wished to represent a person who has been deeply hurt and offended in their name and reputation by the foul and slanderous tongue of their neighbor, they drew a Basilisk, which strikes whatever comes near it unto death with its poisonous breath.

<margin>The Basilisk dies by its own poison.</margin>
If it is true that a Basilisk perishes by its own poison when it beholds itself in a mirror, then certainly one may hold that a person who prepares the poison of destruction for others with their counsels, slanders, and lies—and being inflamed by poisonous envy, begrudges their neighbor's happiness—will feel the backlash of their own trade, the fruits of their efforts, and the effects of their envy, often plunging suddenly into unavoidable ruin. Indeed, as Jerome writes, this is not seldom found in the outcome. *Like an arrow,* he says, *when it is flung against a hard substance, it now and then rebounds upon the thrower and inflicts a wound upon the wonderer: so it goes with a slanderer when he sees the face of the listener grow melancholy and overcast. For with his ears ringing, but closing them so that he does not hear the blood, he immediately falls silent. His face turns pale, his lips grow weak, his saliva dries up.*

# BASTARD.

<margin>Two kinds of bastards.</margin> From two persons who are both unmarried: whether it be that the mother is not a public and common harlot, or whether she is a public and common harlot, in which case the true and actual father cannot be known with certainty; for this reason, the illegitimate offspring is called SPURIUS <note>original: "SPURIUS," a Latin legal term for a child born of a woman who cohabited with multiple men</note>. Thus Plutarch says in *Problem 103* <note>referring to Plutarch's *Roman Questions*</note>: why is *Spurius* written as *s. p.*? and he answers, *s.* signifies *sine* (without) and *p. pater* (father), because he is born without a known father. NOTHUS <note>original: "NOTHUS," from the Greek *nothos*, typically referring to a child of a citizen father and a non-citizen mother</note> is what they called one who was a bastard born of adultery or incest.

Regarding the first kind, the jurists teach us that he might not bear the name of his father; that he or she, as a bastard of their father or relatives, might not inherit unless it was granted to them by a final will. These can be legitimized through marriage and gain inheritance rights, but only if there are no children already from a lawful marriage.

However, the second kind, born of adultery or incest, cannot inherit at all, unless something is granted to them merely for their necessary livelihood.

Caristius <note>a Greek historian cited in the *Deipnosophistae*</note> in the third book, and others, tell us that among the Athenians, one was called a BASTARD who was born of someone who was not an Athenian woman and citizen, whether from a harlot or a stranger; such a person could not count any blood relation or inherit, nor be admitted to a civil or ecclesiastical office, as these people had their separate places of worship.

Regarding bastards, one reads in *Deuteronomy 23:2*: *No bastard shall enter the assembly of the Lord.*

It does not seem to me that such a person was strictly and absolutely excluded from the Tabernacle, Temple, and the holy things, alongside the pledge of the covenant, *Leviticus 22:18, Numbers 9:14*, etc.; rather, I would most readily believe that this restrictive law applies to civil and ecclesiastical offices or ministries in Israel, so that one might not diminish or bring shame upon their authority and the dignity of the offices and service by accusing the ministers of the stain of illegitimate birth.

One reads in the Book of Wisdom, Chapter 4, verse 6, as follows: *For children born of unlawful beds are witnesses of wickedness against their parents, when they are examined.* Read further in Chapter 3, verse 16.

I judge that this positive command belongs to the civil and ecclesiastical state of Israel. But that such children, having come of age and having washed away the stain through an honorable life, and possessing extraordinary gifts and abilities, should not be promoted—I do not see what equity that would consist of.

I read in Zechariah, Chapter 9:6: *and the bastard shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.* I confess that the diversity of thoughts makes this text difficult and obscure.

Ashdod was a city in the land of the Philistines, in the land of Canaan. The land of the Philistines bordered partly on the sea; for this reason, it was called the Philistine Sea, divided into five lordships, mostly standing under one head and king. This was a mighty people, idolatrous and of wicked morals, serving Dagon <note>the chief deity of the Philistines, often depicted as half-man, half-fish</note>. A people who caused the people of God many difficulties and great trouble; sometimes the Philistines were struck and conquered, brought to peace and obedience, yet they broke loose again, mocking and persecuting the people of God: with whose women, against the prohibition, the people of God defiled themselves through marriage. *Nehemiah 13:23, 24.*

Ashdod was besieged and taken by the Assyrian. *Isaiah 20.* Alexander the Great—the actual son, not of Philip, but of Nectanebo the Great <note>refers to a popular legend from the *Alexander Romance* claiming Alexander was the son of an Egyptian sorcerer-king</note>—and Jonathan the Maccabee, brought that city and the land of the Philistines into subjection. Especially after the Jews' return from Babylon, the Philistines had to endure according to the divine threat. *Jeremiah 25, Zephaniah 2, Zechariah 9.*

If one does not wish to understand "the bastard" specifically as Alexander the Great or the Maccabee, then one can take the word *Mamzeer* <note>Hebrew: *mamzer*, meaning a person born of an illicit or incestuous union</note> in the sense of a stranger who would dwell there and hold authority, the land being robbed of its own inhabitants, as I notice it is understood by many theologians.

Also, the Apostle Paul in *Hebrews 12:8* uses the word BASTARDS in this sense: that if one wished to withdraw from the rod of God's discipline, to which almost all children of God have been subject—living as if without yoke, bond, or correction—one would then be removed from the roll of the names of God's children, and thus must be held and regarded as a bastard, illegitimate, entitled neither to the name of God's people nor to be an heir; just as bastards live outside all authority, oversight, chastisement, care, and hope of a paternal inheritance.

> But if you are without chastisement, of which all children have become partakers, then you are bastards and not sons.

*Nothoi estè* <note>original Greek: *νόθοι ἐστέ*, meaning "you are bastards"</note>—you are bastards. Not right and true children of God, even though you might have thought so and given yourselves out as such. The Lord then by no means recognizes you as His children and heirs: for the Lord chastises all His children. The children of God endure divine chastisement <margin>The true children.</margin> with willingness, patience, and submission: and if He does not chastise you at all, if He lets you run wild, if He does not concern Himself with you, and if you withdraw yourself from God's hand and rod, not desiring to be disciplined and improved, it is a clear proof that the Lord does not hold you for His sons, and you do not have the childlike nature within you.

Here a consideration arises regarding the certainty of the chastisement of all God's children: namely, that one indeed often sees it happen that some children of God are subject to no chastisements. But to this, one could give as an answer:

1. That they are not all recorded by God as pious and as His children, who appear such to us according to the outward appearance. Appearance often deceives.
2. Paul does not define the exact time when or how often He chastises His children, doing it to one earlier and to another later.
3. Also, all chastisements are not of equal weight, nor of the same nature.

*Further consideration is given to how it is possible to claim that chastisements could be proof that one is a child of God, given that the Lord also chastises the godless and bastards. Psalm 94:10, etc. To which one can give as a reply:*

1. That the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul in the book of Hebrews.</note> by no means intends to deny that the Lord sometimes sends plagues and rods of punishment to the godless to strike them with fear and terror; to keep them in check; to restrain them, so that violence does not gain the upper hand, and civil peace and rest are not too greatly disturbed and overturned.

2. Paul also does not say that being chastised by God is the only or the most important mark of a child of God.

3. But he says this: that God’s children are rarely or never throughout their entire lives without any chastisement: and that God, as a Father, chastises them out of love and for their own good.

4. Paul also places the primary mark in the quality of the conduct and the disposition of the one who suffers and is under the rod of chastisement: and in the fruit and effect of the divine chastisement. The [bastard] does not want to be chastised; he resists it, he grumbles and murmurs: he shows himself rebellious: nothing less than willingness and docility is heard from him: he rarely becomes better for it, but usually worse. It is entirely different with a true child of God.

And those who are born of this mother in her womb, not from the seed of the everlasting word of God, but through the spirit of lies and deception, are all those kings, princes, and peoples who most blindly embrace the teachings of this unfaithful and adulterous mother, and are thus born from the false and deceptive word of impure doctrine: who in turn commit adultery with their mother, binding themselves firmly—

### TRUMPET, <term>Shofar</term> <note>original: "שׁוֹפָר," Hebrew for a ram's horn trumpet</note>, <term>Salpinx</term> <note>original: "Σάλπιγξ," Greek for a trumpet</note>.
->See SOUNDING, TRUMPETS, etc.<-

TRUMPETS and HORNS, it is known, are commonly used in war, although they are also suited for various other matters and uses.

Insofar as they are used for military service, it is to sound the advance, the retreat, and the call to arms. *Judges 7, 1 Samuel 2, etc.*

One reads in *Numbers 10* of silver Trumpets, used both for gathering the people and for the military march.

We are told that if two were blown with a uniform sound, the people would gather and appear before the door of the tabernacle of meeting. *Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book 2, Chapter 2.* And if one Trumpet were blown with a uniform sound, then the leaders of the people would gather.

# BASTARD.

<margin>Two types of bastards.</margin> Of two persons who are both illegitimate: whether the mother is not an open and common prostitute, or whether she is an open and common prostitute, in which case the right and proper father cannot be known with certainty, and for that reason the illegitimate fruit is called *SPURIUS* <note>original: "SPURIUS" — a Latin legal term for a child born out of wedlock with an unknown father.</note>. Thus *Plutarch* says in *Problem 103*: why is *Spurius* written as *f. p.*? and he answers, *f.* signifies *sine* (without) and *p. pater* (father), because he is born without a known father. *NOTHUS* <note>original: "NOTHUS" — a Greek-derived term often used for a bastard born of a known father but a non-citizen or lower-status mother.</note> is what they called one who was a bastard born of adultery or incest.

Regarding the first type, the Jurists <note>legal scholars</note> teach us that he was not permitted to bear the name of his father: that he or she, being a bastard, could not inherit from their father or their paternal kin, unless it was granted to them by a last will and testament. These can be legitimized through marriage and gain inheritance rights, yet only if there are no children already born from a legal marriage.

But the second type, born of adultery or incest, cannot inherit at all, unless something is granted to them merely for the necessary maintenance of life.

Caristius in the third book, and others, tell us that among the Athenians, one was called a BASTARD who was born of someone who was not an Athenian woman and citizen, whether from a prostitute or a foreigner: such a person could neither count blood-kinship nor inherit: nor were they admitted to any civil or ecclesiastical office, as these people had their own separate places of worship.

As for what concerns bastards, we read in *Deuteronomy 23:2*: *A bastard shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord.*

It does not seem to me that such a person was absolutely barred from the Tabernacle, the Temple, and the holy things, alongside the pledge of the covenant, *Leviticus 22:18, Numbers 9:14,* etc. But I would most nearly believe that this restrictive law refers to civil and ecclesiastical offices or ministries in Israel, so that one might not diminish or bring shame to their authority and the dignity of the offices and service by attaching the stain of illegitimate birth to the ministers.

One reads in the book of Wisdom, the fourth chapter, verse 6: *For children born of unlawful beds are witnesses of wickedness against their parents, when they are examined.* Read further the third chapter, verse 16.

I judge that this firm command belongs to the civil and ecclesiastical state of Israel. But that such children, having come to years of maturity and having wiped away the blemish through an honest life, and possessing singular gifts and abilities, should not be promoted—I do not see upon what equity such a thing would stand.

I read in *Zechariah*, Chapter 9:6: *And the bastard shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.* I confess that the variety of thoughts on this makes the text difficult and obscure.

Ashdod was a city in the land of the Philistines, in the land of Canaan. The land of the Philistines bordered partly on the sea: for this reason it was called the Philistine Sea, divided into five governorships, mostly standing under one head and king. This was a mighty people, idolatrous and of wicked customs, serving Dagon. A people who caused the people of God much trouble and great difficulty; sometimes the Philistines were beaten and conquered, brought to peace and obedience, yet they broke out of their bounds, mocking and persecuting the people of God: with whose women, against the prohibition, the people of God defiled themselves through marriages. *Nehemiah 13:23, 24.*

Ashdod was besieged and taken by the Assyrian. *Isaiah 20.* Alexander the Great—properly the son, not of Philip, but of Nectabanus the Great—and Jonathan the Maccabee, brought that city and the land of the Philistines into subjection. Especially after the Jews' return from Babylon, the Philistines had to endure according to the divine threat. *Jeremiah 25, Zephaniah 2, Zechariah 9.*

If one does not wish to understand "the bastard" specifically as Alexander the Great or the Maccabee; then one can take the word *Mamzeer* <note>original: "Mamzeer" — Hebrew term for a child of a forbidden union, often translated as bastard.</note> in the sense of a stranger, who would dwell there and hold authority, the land being robbed of its own inhabitants, as I notice it is understood by many theologians.

The Apostle Paul also uses the word BASTARDS in *Hebrews 12:8* in this sense: that if one wished to withdraw from the rod of God’s discipline, to which almost all children of God were subject, and live as if without yoke, bond, or discipline, one then excluded oneself from the roll of the names of God's children. Consequently, one would have to be held and regarded as a bastard, illegitimate, entitled neither to the name of God’s people nor to be an heir; just as bastards live outside all authority, oversight, chastisement, care, and hope of a paternal inheritance.

> But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons.

*Nothoi ese* <note>original: "Nothoi ese" — Greek for "you are bastards."</note> you are bastards. Not right, legitimate children of God, even though you might have thought so and presented yourselves as such. The Lord then by no means recognizes you as His children and heirs: for the Lord chastises all His children. The children of God endure divine chastisement with willingness, patience, and submission: and if He does not chastise you at all, if He lets you run wild, if He does not concern Himself with you, and if you withdraw yourself from God’s hand and rod—desiring not to be disciplined and corrected—it is a clear proof that the Lord does not hold you as His sons, and you do not have a child-like nature within you.

<margin>the true children.</margin> Here a reflection arises regarding the certainty of the chastisement of all God's children: namely, that one indeed often sees it happen that some children of God are subject to no chastisements. Yet to this, one could give as an answer:

1. That in God's eyes, not all are recorded as pious and as His children who appear so to us according to outward appearances. Appearances often deceive.
2. Paul does not define the exact time when or how often He chastises His children, doing it to one earlier and to another later.
3. Also, all chastisements are not equally weighty, nor of the same nature.

*Further consideration is given to how it is possible to claim that chastisements could be a proof of being a child of God, given that the Lord also chastises the godless and "Bastards." Psalm 94:10, etc. To which one can give as an answer:*

1. That the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul, likely in Hebrews 12:8.</note> in no way intends to deny by this reasoning that the Lord sometimes sends plagues and rods of punishment to the godless to strike them with fear and terror; to keep them in check; to restrain them, so that violence does not gain the upper hand, and civil peace and rest are not too greatly disturbed and turned upside down.

2. Paul also does not say that being chastised by God is the only and primary mark of a child of God.

4. The "bastard" does not wish to be chastised; he sets himself against it, he grumbles and murmurs: he shows himself rebellious: nothing less than willingness and docility is observed in him: he rarely becomes better for it, but usually worse. It is entirely different with a true child of God.

When I think of a Bastard, there comes to my mind a mother who is a whore, and who breeds illegitimate children with one or many paramours, who cannot be called by the name of the legal husband, nor inherit from him.

<margin>Spiritual Tyre.</margin>

And those who are born of this mother in her womb—not from the seed of the everlasting Word of God, but through the spirit of lies and deception—are all kings, princes, and peoples who most blindly embrace the teachings of this unfaithful and adulterous mother, and thus are born from the false and deceptive word of unclean doctrine: who in turn commit adultery with their mother, binding themselves firmly—

# TRUMPET.

the army had to set itself in order, and break camp in an orderly fashion.

But if one had to charge at the enemy, then the sound was not only broken, but also fast and hurried. And if there was trouble, fear, or danger, even if it were not within the camp itself, one had to blow the Trumpet or Clarion. *Isaiah 4 and 6; Ezekiel 33; Amos 3; Zephaniah 1; etc.*

Certainly, the public signal must be known. For who would advance or retreat, and prepare themselves for battle [if the signal were unclear]? The entire army would fall into confusion, and the enemy would gain the greatest advantage. *1 Corinthians 14:8.*

It is well known that the people were called to the monthly and yearly feasts, to mourning, and to joy, by the sound of the Trumpets. *Psalm 47, 81, 98, 118, and 150; Hosea 5; Joel 2; etc.*

One blew upon the Trumpet in the practice fields of the ancients <note>The author refers to the athletic games of classical antiquity, such as the Greek Olympics or Roman contests.</note>, whenever one was to set upon their opponent, or run and race for the laurel wreath, etc. *See Lydius, Sacred Contests, page 80; Paschalius, On Crowns, page 377.* <note>original Latin titles: "Lydii Agonist. Sac." and "Paschal. de Coron."</note>

Not everywhere that one reads of Trumpets or Clarions in the scrolls of the Old and New Testament must one imagine actual instruments as they are now; rather, such must be understood and grasped improperly, figuratively, and by imagination, as can be sufficiently gathered from the passages themselves and the circumstances. To cite just a few examples and proofs from many:

One reads in *Psalm 47*, *That the Lord ascends with the sound of the Trumpet.* Who will apply that in the most perfect, literal, and full sense to an actual blowing of Trumpets? And not rather think that the blowing of Trumpets refers to the time of the procession of the Ark? Or to the shouting that a victorious army, or a gladdened people, makes because of victory; and that this represents how the ascending and triumphing Jesus is echoed by the heavenly host, *Revelation 5*, and how Jesus leads His enemies (among whom was Saul) in triumph, *Psalm 68; Ephesians 4*; being proclaimed as victor everywhere in the world by His ambassadors, the Apostles and believers, whose ministry—blessed and empowered by the conquering hero with the gifts of the Holy Spirit—is followed by signs and wonders, rare and sudden conversions, and victory over great opposition.

<margin>Scripture passages explained.</margin>
It is also said in *Isaiah 27* that *a great Trumpet shall be blown*; who shall not think that this signifies the proclaimed freedom of the Jews, under and by the command of King Cyrus, to depart from their captivity, *Ezra 1; 2 Chronicles 36*; or as others preferred according to the thread of Prophecy, that through the sound and power of the Gospel—made uniquely powerful and piercing by the Lord—in the last days, under the Turk <note>A common 17th-century term for the Ottoman Empire.</note>, the Eastern kings, and the Antichrist, as if from a second Egypt, or from Egypt itself, the Jews and all people shall be gathered in power, as belonging to the measuring line of Jesus' inheritance.

Again, when it is said in *Zechariah 9:14*, *The Lord shall blow the trumpet, and shall go forth with whirlwinds of the south*, etc. who will—given the thread and link of Prophecy—

<column-break/>

speaking of Israel's deliverance by King Jesus, and their liberation from the yoke and the ceremonial shadow-law, servitude, sin, fear of death, etc.—not conclude that this speaks not of a literal deliverance from Babylon, or a literal blowing of the Trumpet, but that something else is meant spiritually and figuratively? Namely, in general, that the Lord, and the glorified King Messiah, shall work such deeds of His almighty will that, being seen and heard by everyone, all shall have to confess that it is the Lord who has done it, and thereby acknowledge that He is God and the only Lord.

In particular, there is no matter better known or more undisputed from the Gospel histories than how the exalted Lord, through those from Judah and Ephraim—His Apostles—has trumpeted and led and advanced the storm in the South. Particularly in Greece, when the light of the Gospel shot through like lightning; Paul, preaching the Gospel with unbelievable success from Jerusalem even unto Illyricum, also performing many wonders and signs, and being provided with many gifts, whereby the wisdom of the wise perished, eloquence was muted, the power of human reasoning was destroyed, and every high thing was cast down: and through Divine strengthening, all violence, the cruelest torments, and the rages of Satan and the wicked were overcome. *2 Corinthians 10.*

One reads in *1 Corinthians 15:52* and *1 Thessalonians 4* of the last Trumpet which shall sound: also of the Archangel, and the voice of the Archangel.

It is indeed true that some here think of a created Angel, yet a prominent chief of the Angels, perhaps Gabriel or Michael; some think of a literal Trumpet or Clarion and its blowing; others of thunder and lightning and a great storm; others of a very great voice and piercing sound to awaken the dead and summons those who remain alive. But I do not perceive in any way how a literally taken wind-instrument would be capable of making the dead hear, of gathering their scattered dust together, and of bringing all people, spread over the entire globe, together.

I would then prefer to understand it improperly, figuratively, and symbolically: that by the <term>Archangel</term> <note>Meaning "Chief Angel."</note>, the highest head and commander of the Angels, is understood Christ the Son of God, as glorified, whom all the Angels of God must worship. *1 Colossians 1; Hebrews 1; 1 Peter 3.* The Angel of the Covenant. *Malachi 3.* And by the Trumpet, and the voice of the Archangel, the working of Christ as a working of Omnipotence, through which the dead shall be raised, and those remaining alive shall be changed in a moment of time and summoned before His Judgment Seat.

As for *Matthew 24*, where Angels with Trumpets are spoken of: one has reason to suspect that this does not literally refer to the preparation for the general Day of Judgment; but to the sending out of the Angels of the congregations—the Apostles primarily—with the Trumpet of the Gospel, to call together the people of Christ from under the four winds and to separate them from the unbelievers.

<margin>Seven Trumpets in John's writings.</margin>
In this manner, the man of God, John, speaks in his Revelation of seven Trumpets—not strictly as literal instruments or a literal blowing of Trumpets, but improperly, figuratively, and through symbolic imagination.

I have no objection to one seeing an allusion to the Trumpets that were sounded at the capture of Jericho. It appears that in the New Testament, one sees seven great and prominent periods of worldly events which are heard with the opening or unlocking of each of the seven seals. These Trumpets, especially the first six, announce many misfortunes, God's weighty judgments, and miseries. So it is that after the opening of each seal and the sounding of each blast, the state of the church in the world appears in a changed form. It is as if several Trumpets preceded His coming and appearance, crying out to us: "The Lord is near, the Lord comes."

They are God's illustrious work in church and state, calling for attention and observation of what the Lord works at various points in time to fulfill His purpose and prophecies. God's judgments are carried out as if on an open Theater of the church and the world, ringing in everyone's ears, alongside the omens and illustrious preparations for the public and tangible outcomes of what the Lord has purposed and foretold.

And so as not to repeat what has been said about the Trumpets, their blowing, the timing, and the purpose, let us freely believe that the Jericho of this world will only be fully captured with the sounding of the seventh Trumpet, when the last seal is opened. Thus, I compare the Gospel to the silver Trumpets <note>Psalm 12</note> upon which Christ and the Apostles blew, or proclaimed the Gospel of the kingdom. ### BDELLIUM (BEDOLAG)
->*Genesis II. 12. Exodus XVI. Numbers XI.*<-

<margin>Bdellium.</margin>
Regarding this BDELLIUM, or BEDOLAG <note>The Hebrew term is *bedolach*</note> mentioned in the aforementioned passages, scholars are by no means in agreement. Whether we shall easily come to a full agreement, I doubt very much, since Bdellium or Bedolag is mentioned barely two or three times in Holy Scripture, and described even less.

<margin>Judgment of the Scholars.</margin>
However, to achieve my aim in this work, I will briefly provide the judgment of learned men, both ancient and modern.

Some claim that Bdellium, Bedolag, or as Marcellus Empiricus and Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar</note> have it, BEDELLA, is an Arabian tree, or a small tree—a blackish-brown little tree, about the size of an olive tree with a strong leaf. Pliny <note>Natural History, Book 12, Chapter 9</note> says its oozing gum is called *Brocham* by some, *Malchram* by others, and *Maldacon* by still others. This gum has a strong scent, approaching Myrrh in essence and quality, according to Dioscorides <note>Book 1, Chapter 69</note>; the Arabs, says Delacampius, call it MOLACHIL or MOLACHAL. And Chytreus, commenting on Genesis 2:12, says: <note>original Latin: "Bdellium est arbor, ex qua lachryma fluit, seu gummi pellucidum odore, gustu amarum, Myrrhae affine."</note> *Bdellium is a tree from which a tear flows, or a transparent gum of scent, bitter in essence and quality, related to Myrrh.*

<margin>Power of the Bdellium.</margin>
Regarding the virtue and power of this gum, Ursinus, de Mei, and Coquius cite Dioscorides and Fernelius, stating that it warms, softens, and consumes, and drives away ruptures of the stomach area <term>hernia: "gescheurtheit des gemagts"</term> prone to oozing, when mixed and softened with fasting saliva. It brings space and air to the womb through fumigation and poultices, and expels the fetus and fluids. When mixed in a drink, it reduces stones, drives off water, and is usefully given to those coughing or bitten by snakes. Furthermore, it is very useful against ruptures and bursts, against side-pain, and irregular movements of the animal spirits <note>In early medicine, "animal spirits" were fluids thought to carry sensory and motor information through the nerves.</note>. Sprinkled on warming plasters, it is said to be useful against lumps and hardness in the nerves, etc. It is softened with water or wine.

Others maintain that Bdellium was by no means a type of spicy tree, but a precious stone or pearl, grouped with the stones to which manna is also compared because of its white clarity. Some take it for Crystal, others for Carbuncle, and others for a Diamond. Bochart <note>Hieroz. p. Post.</note> brings forward thoughts from Arabic translations and paraphrases supporting the meaning of a pearl. Vatablus, Eugebinus, Burmannus, and others can be consulted on this. The Talmudists in *Yoma, Chapter 8*, say, *the Manna was round as Coriander, and white as a Pearl.* And so the Jews say that the Bedolag was a type of white pearl or precious stone.

Leaving aside what the Bdellium or Bedolag exactly was (for I still hold that one cannot say much about it with certainty), and assuming it must fall into one of the two aforementioned categories, it seems to me that just as I find a tree of life in Paradise, I also find a Bdellium or Bedolag—not a literal tree-growth with its Myrrh-like gum, but Him who serves the church and the bride as a bundle of Myrrh, resting between her breasts <note>Song of Solomon 1:13</note>. I mean the Son of God and Savior of the world. For assuming the Bdellium has the aforementioned powers and effects, it is beyond all contradiction that Christ, through the power of His obedience in suffering unto death and His indwelling Spirit, heals His people, His beloved...

One blew upon the Trumpet in the ancient arenas when one was to either set upon an opponent, or to run and race for the laurel wreath, etc. *See Lydius, Sacred Contests, page 80; Paschalius, On Crowns, page 377.* <note>Original titles: "Lydii Agonist. Sac." and "Paschal. de Coron."</note>

Not everywhere that one reads of Trumpets in the scrolls of the Old and New Testaments should one imagine actual physical instruments as they exist now; rather, such things must be understood improperly, figuratively, and by symbolic imagination, as can be sufficiently gathered from the passages themselves and the circumstances. To cite only a few examples and proofs from many:

One reads in *Psalm 47*, *That the Lord ascends with the sound of the Trumpet.* Who would apply that in the most perfect, literal, and fullest sense to a literal blowing of Trumpets? Should one not rather think that it alludes to the blowing of Trumpets at the time of the procession of the Ark? Or to the shouting that a victorious army or a gladdened people makes because of victory? And that this represents how the ascending and triumphing Jesus is hailed by the heavenly host, *Revelation 5*, and how Jesus leads his enemies (among whom was Saul) in triumph, *Psalm 68; Ephesians 4*; being proclaimed as victor everywhere in the world by his ambassadors—the Apostles and believers—whose ministry, blessed and empowered by the victorious hero with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, is followed by signs and wonders, rare and sudden conversions, and victory over great opposition.

<margin>Scripture passages explained.</margin>
It is also said in *Isaiah 27* that *a great Trumpet shall be blown;* who will not think that this signifies the proclaimed freedom of the Jews, under and by the command of King Cyrus, to go out from their captivity, *Ezra 1; 2 Chronicles 36*? Or, as others preferred according to the thread of prophecy, that by the sound and power of the Gospel—made singularly powerful and piercing by the Lord in the last days—the Jews and all people shall be gathered in power from under the Turk <note>a common 18th-century term for the Ottoman Empire</note>, the Eastern kings, and the Antichrist (as if from a second Egypt, or from Egypt itself), as belonging to the measuring line of Jesus' inheritance.

Again, when it is said in *Zechariah 9:14*, *The Lord shall blow the trumpet, and he shall go forth with storms from the South,* etc. who, following the thread and link of prophecy, men-

<column-break/>

tioning Israel’s deliverance by King Jesus and their liberation from the yoke and the ceremonial shadow-law <note>the "shadow-law" refers to Old Testament rituals viewed as precursors to Christian truths</note>, bondage, sin, and the fear of death, etc., would not conclude that this does not speak of a literal deliverance from Babylon or a literal blowing of the Trumpet? Rather, something else is signified spiritually and figuratively: namely, in general, that the Lord and the glorified King Messiah shall work such deeds of His almighty will that, being seen and heard by everyone, all shall be forced to confess that it is the Lord who has done it, and thus acknowledge that He is God and the only Lord.

In particular, there is no matter better known or more undisputed from the Gospel histories than how the exalted Lord, through those from Judah and Ephraim—His Apostles—sounded the trumpet and led and advanced the storm in the South. Especially in Greece, when the light of the Gospel flashed through like lightning; Paul, preaching the Gospel with unbelievable success from Jerusalem even unto Illyricum, also performing many signs and wonders and being provided with many gifts, caused the wisdom of the wise to perish, the eloquence to be struck dumb, the power of human reasoning to be destroyed, and every high thing to be cast down: and through Divine strengthening, all violence, the cruelest torments, and the rages of Satan and the wicked were overcome. *2 Corinthians 10.*

One reads in *1 Corinthians 15:52* and *1 Thessalonians 4* of the last Trumpet which shall sound: also of the Archangel and the voice of the Archangel.

It is true that some here think of a created Angel, yet a prominent chief of the Angels, perhaps Gabriel or Michael: some think of a literal Trumpet and blowing: others of thunder and lightning and a great storm: others of a very great voice and piercing sound, to awaken the dead and summon those who remain alive. But I do not perceive how a literally taken wind instrument would be capable of making the dead hear, of gathering their scattered dust together, and of bringing all men, spread over the entire face of the earth, together.

I would then prefer to understand it improperly, figuratively, and symbolically thus: that by the Archangel—the head and commander of the Angels—is understood Christ the Son of God as glorified, followed by His sheep, and whom all the Angels of God must worship. *1 Colossians 1; Hebrews 1; 1 Peter 3.* The Angel of the Covenant. *Malachi 3.* And by the Trumpet, and the voice of the Archangel, the working of Christ as an operation of Omnipotence, through which the dead shall be raised, and those remaining alive shall be changed in a moment of time and summoned before His Judgment Seat.

As for *Matthew 24*, where Angels with Trumpets are spoken of: one has reason to suspect that this does not literally look toward the preparation for the general Day of Judgment, but toward the sending out of the Angels of the churches—the Apostles primarily—with the Trumpet of the Gospel, to call together the people of Christ from under the four winds and to separate them from the unbelievers.
