# BDELLIUM.

It is well known that trumpets are often used as a sign of God's approaching judgments, heavy wars, and hard but just chastisements, even if no literal Trumpets are actually present. The sign is named because it is fundamentally recognized as representing the thing it signifies.

<margin>Seven Trumpets by John.</margin> And in this manner, the man of God, John, speaks in his Revelations of seven Trumpets—not literally, or of an actual blowing upon Trumpets, but improperly, figuratively, and through symbolic imagination.

I have no objection to the idea that this alludes to the Trumpets sounded at the capture of Jericho: and that in the New Testament, one sees those seven great and prominent periods of worldly affairs which are heard at the opening or unlocking of each of the seven seals. These Trumpets, especially the first six, announce many misfortunes, the weighty judgments of God, and miseries. Thus, after the opening of each seal and the sounding of each trumpet, the state of the church in the world appears in a changed form; God works out what was established in His eternal counsel in such a way that every intelligent and observant person, noting the signs of the times, can perceive the outcome and appearance of things as clearly and distinctly as if several Trumpets preceded the Lord's coming and appearance, calling out to us: "The Lord is near, the Lord comes."

They are God’s illustrious work in church and state, calling for attention and observation of what the Lord works at various moments in time to fulfill His purpose and prophecies: God’s judgments carried out as if upon an open Theater <note>original: "Schouburg," referring to a public playhouse or stage</note> of church and world, ringing in everyone’s ears; alongside the phenomena and illustrious preparations for the public and tangible outcomes of what the Lord has intended and foretold.

And so as not to repeat what has been said regarding the Trumpets—their sounding, the timing, and the purpose—one may freely believe that the Jericho of the world shall only be fully captured with the sounding of the seventh Trumpet, when the last seal is opened. Thus, I compare the Gospel to the silver Trumpets *Psalm 12* upon which Christ and the Apostles blew, or proclaimed the Gospel of the kingdom, just as all faithful Teachers, or Angels of the congregation, announce the year of the redeemed, of freedom and joy, *Isaiah 61 and 63; Psalm 118; 2 Corinthians 6,* to be joyful and to shout. *Psalm 47; Zechariah 9; Matthew 21; Philippians 4; Romans 14.* This is to wake us from the sleep of sin and carelessness, *Romans 13; Ephesians 5; 1 Thessalonians 5,* to call us to the spiritual struggle and race, *1 Corinthians 9; 2 Timothy 2; 1 Timothy 1:18,* and to make us sober and watchful for the coming of the Lord.

### BDELLIUM BEDOLAG,
->*Genesis 2:12; Exodus 16; Numbers 11.*<-

<margin>Bdellium.</margin> Regarding this BDELLIUM, or BEDOLAG mentioned in the aforementioned places, scholars are by no means in agreement; and whether they will easily reach a full consensus, I doubt very much, seeing as Bdellium or Bedolag is mentioned barely two or three times in Holy Scripture, and described even less.

<margin>Opinion of the Learned.</margin> However, to achieve my objective in this work, I will briefly present the opinions of learned men, both ancient and modern.

Some claim that Bdellium, Bedolag, or as Marcellus Empiricus and Isidore have it, BEDELLA, is an Arabian tree, or a small tree—a blackish-brown small tree, about the size of an olive tree, with a sturdy leaf. Pliny says in *Book 12, Chapter 9*, that some call its seeping gum *Brocham*, others *Malchram*, and others *Maldacon*. This gum has a strong scent, approaching Myrrh in essence and quality, says Dioscorides in *Book 1, Chapter 69*. The Arabs, says Delacampius, call it *MOLACHIL* or *MOLACHAL*. And Chytreus, commenting on *Genesis 2:12*, says: <note>original Latin: "Bdellium est arbor, ex qua lachryma manat, ofte een doorzigtige gomme van reuk, bitter in wezen en hoedanigheit, verwantfchapt aan de Myrrhe."</note> *Bdellium is a tree from which a tear flows, or a transparent gum of scent, bitter in essence and quality, related to Myrrh.*

<margin>Power of the Bdellium.</margin> Regarding the virtue and power of this gum, Ursinus, de Mei, and Coquius cite from Dioscorides and Fernelius that it warms, softens, and digests. It dispels ruptures of the stomach <note>likely referring to hernias or internal tears</note> subject to seeping, when mixed and softened with fasting saliva. It brings space and air to the womb through fumigation and poultice; it discharges the fruit <note>the fetus or menses</note> and fluids. When mixed in a drink, it diminishes stones, drives out water, and is usefully given to those coughing or those bitten by snakes. Furthermore, it is very useful against ruptures and bursts, as well as against side-aches and irregular movements of the animal spirits. Sprinkled on warming plasters, it is said to be useful against lumps, hardness in the nerves, etc.; it is softened with water or wine.

Others maintain that Bdellium was by no means a type of aromatic tree, but a precious stone or pearl, grouped with the stones to which manna is also compared due to its white clarity. Some take it for Crystal, others for Carbuncle, others for a Diamond stone. Bochart in *Hierozoicon* brings forth thoughts from Arabic translations and paraphrases supporting the meaning of a pearl. Vatablus, Eugebinus, Burmannus, and others can be consulted on this. The Talmudists in *Joma, Chapter 8,* say, *The Manna was round like coriander, and white like a Pearl.* And so the Jews say that the Bedolag was a type of white pearl or gemstone.

Leaving aside what the Bdellium or Bedolag actually was (for I still maintain that one cannot say much with certainty about it), and assuming it must fall into one of the two aforementioned extremes, it seems to me that just as I find a tree of life in Paradise, I also find a Bdellium or Bedolag there. Not as a literal tree-growth with its gum like Myrrh, but Him who serves the church and the bride as a bundle of Myrrh, resting between her breasts. *Song of Solomon 1:13.* I mean the Son of God, and Savior of the world. For assuming that the Bdellium has the aforementioned powers and effects, it is beyond all contradiction that Christ, through the power of His obedience in suffering unto death, and His indwelling Spirit, [works upon] His people, His beloved...

### BED, BEDSTEAD
->Lying place, Couch, Bed <note>original Hebrew: מִשְׁכָּב ,עֶרֶשׂ ,מִטָּה (miškāv, ‘ereś, miṭṭāh)</note>, Bed, Couch <note>original Greek: Κλίνη, λέχτρον (Klīnē, lektron)</note>, Bed <note>original Latin: lectus</note>.<-

**W**hat one must properly understand by a BED and BEDSTEAD is sufficiently known through common household use and experience. They are places prepared, arranged, and set apart, especially for night’s rest and the refreshment of the body. It is also where husband and wife most intimately interact in love and according to their mutual marriage obligations, for sweet delight and the continuation of the human race in their offspring, striving to raise a holy seed for God while rendering the affection they owe to one another (*1 Cor. 7*).

That figures of speech are derived from the Bed and Bedstead—which one should not always understand literally or take too narrowly—will become sufficiently plain from what follows.

<column-break/>

<margin>To climb someone's Bed.</margin>
For who would take *climbing someone's Bed* (*Gen. 49*) only in the narrow sense of lying down on someone's bed to go to sleep? Would they not rather think it signifies sleeping with someone's wife, and thus defiling his bed? An act of lust and mingling, as mentioned by <insert>Hesiod in "The Shield of Hercules" regarding Mars and Venus, etc.</insert>

When God says *that their bedstead shall be too short* (*Isa. 28:20*), etc., who would understand this to mean only literally short and cramped bedsteads (which they could easily make longer with little effort or cost)? Should we not rather think that the Lord would bring a great fall upon the proud, wanton, and lustful Israelites, who were accustomed to stretching out on wide and very magnificent bedsteads (*Amos 6*)? He would distress them through the Romans (principally within Jerusalem), gathered there by the hundreds of thousands, in such a way that they would not know which way to turn or move.

When we read that God *throws someone into a bed* (*Rev. 2*) and elsewhere, it will undoubtedly signify something more than that simple physical act. And what is closest to the meaning? *Nothing other than inflicting very sensitive pain, grief, and torment upon someone, by whatever means it may be.*

That the Bed or Bedstead, and lying upon it, resting, etc., does not always need to be taken literally also appears from such passages where the literal meaning would be too dry and meager, and something higher seems to be sketched and imagined. For *suppose one reads (Ps. 3:6), I lay down and slept; I awoke, for the Lord sustained me. And (Ps. 4:5), Be agitated and sin not, speak in your heart upon your bed, and be still, Selah.* Who will not consider (without me explaining these two places in great detail or applying them specifically to David, Christ, or the Church) that it can be imagined here how the covenant-members and children of God, occupied with intense reflections and clothed in firm trust in God, being under the eye, oversight, and protection of God, can and may be at rest in all their encounters and experiences?

When the Holy Scripture speaks of lying on ivory bedsteads and such in a discourse of rebuke and threat, one may freely believe that this signifies pomp, show, pride, reckless rest, blameworthy indifference, and luxury—especially of the great men in Israel. These men concerned themselves little with the difficulties and calamities of the Church of God (*Amos 6*). Regarding this pomp, show, and splendor, one can read *Hofman in his Universal Lexicon* <note>Johann Jacob Hofmann’s *Lexicon Universale* was a famous 17th-century encyclopedia.</note>.

When one finds the Bride on her bed seeking Christ and not finding Him (*Song of Sol. 3:1-4*), might we not think that the Church, in times of adversity, pressure, and persecution—through Jewish and Roman wars and persecutions after the death and departure of most of the Apostles—began to slumber? Thus, a deadness, a slackness in zeal, and a lack of spiritual activity arrived, without rightly going out to Jesus, loving rest and peace (*1 Cor. 4:8*), without watching, praying, and standing in spiritual armor to fight and suffer for Jesus' name, even striving for the crown through martyrdom (*Rev. 2:10*). Certainly, at that time, one was not to seek Jesus on the bed. It was no...

# TO COVER.
G
<meta>catchword: to</meta>

no time for resting and ruling, but for being sober, fighting, watching, and praying; therefore one should not be guilty of laziness, carelessness, or unconcerned bed-rest, nor think that Jesus' Bed is not yet disturbed, His outward church not displaced, His confessors not moved, persecuted, or driven away, and thus Jesus must be sought elsewhere.

The Bed, the Bedstead of Jesus the Bridegroom, husband and lover of the soul and the church His Bride and Wife, I would not only take for the heart of all believers (*Eph. 3, Isa. 57:15, John 14*) but understand with others as the holy, universal, Christian church. There He dwells and rests (*Ps. 32, Isa. 66*); there one finds the place and means for the closest, innermost, most comforting spiritual union with Christ, the practice and awakening of the purest, most clinging, mutual pure love, under the ministry of the word, the Holy Sacraments, prayers, and thanksgivings. Here one learns growth in knowledge, Faith, Love, and all kinds of virtues (*Phil. 1 and 4, 1 Pet. 3, Ps. 92, Prov. 4*). Here one receives all kinds of pleasures from our Lover of the soul (*John 1:16* <note>The original OCR cites Job 1:16, but the context of "grace for grace" suggests John 1:16.</note>). Here one converts their neighbor, and children are born to God through the seed of the word and the service of Shepherds and Teachers (*Isa. 54, Joshua 8, Ps. 110:4, Gal. 4, 1 Pet. 1, Jas. 1, 1 Cor. 4*).

He who now leaves the church of Christ, and the place and means for the true, spiritual, and inner exercise of fellowship, stepping away from the Bed of Jesus and climbing onto the Bed of Jezebel <note>A biblical reference to spiritual unfaithfulness or following false teachings.</note>, pulls his heart away from Jesus or splits and divides his love, whether he falls into overt idolatry or spiritual [idolatry], smoking to another God (*Ps. 16*), choosing other saviors, mediators, and intercessors, setting up another head, or doing homage and acknowledging [another], he commits adultery and spiritual whoredom (*1 Cor. 6, Isa. 28, Ezek. 16, Hos. 1 and 7, Ezek. 23*), for Christ is the Husband (*Isa. 54, Hos. 2*). Concerning Garden beds, we shall speak under GARDEN and ORCHARDS. Having said this regarding the Bed, I proceed to something that was traditionally associated with the Bed and going to Bed.

### TO COVER, COVERED, COVERING.
->To cover, to hide, to wrap, to screen, to veil. <note>original Hebrew: טָלַל ,כָּסָה ,כָּרְבַּל ,סָכัךְ ,עָטָה</note><-
->*to cover, to shield, to veil, etc.* <note>original Latin: tegere, obtegere, velare, &c.</note><-

**W**hat these words actually signify according to the usage of our Dutch language is known to everyone.

It is true that "To Cover" is sometimes taken literally, sometimes figuratively, more broadly, or more narrowly, but the literal sense of the word is always alluded to. However, not lingering on the word as a word, I shall move on to scriptural modes of speech, alongside ancient customs, ceremonies, and their meanings.

As for the Heathens, when they turned to the gods, performed sacrifices, prayed, etc., it happened with a wrapped head, a covered face. Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman historian and philosopher.</note> in his *Roman Questions*, asking *Why did they pray to the gods with covered heads?* gave as an answer, *to signify thereby the dejection of the mind.* Lucretius <note>A Roman poet and philosopher.</note> in the fifth book must have had this in view:

> *Nor is it any piety to be seen often with a veiled head,* <note>original Latin: Nec pietas ulla est, velatum fæpe videri</note>
> *Turning toward a stone, and approaching all the altars,* <note>original Latin: Vertier ad lapidem, atque omnes accedere ad aras</note>
> *Nor to lie prostrate on the ground, and to spread one's palms* <note>original Latin: Nec procumbere humi proftratum, & pandere palmas</note>
> *Before the shrines of the God.* <note>original Latin: Ante Deum delubra.</note>

->That is:<-

> *It gives also a false appearance of godliness*
> *To be frequently covered with great ceremony,*
> *And to turn oneself to the images of the gods*
> *With honors, humbly offered to them,*
> *To go to the altars, to pour out one's prayer*
> *While lying on the ground according to the old law,*
> *To lift one's arms on high before the churches*
> *Of the gods.* — — —

So Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, credited with many religious institutions.</note> in sacrificing is introduced covered by Ovid in his *Fasti*:

> *He stood and, his head veiled with a snow-white garment,* <note>original Latin: Conftitit atque caput niveo velatus amictu</note>
> *He lifted his hands, already well-known to the gods.* <note>original Latin: Jam bene diis notas fuftulit ille manus.</note>

->That is:<-

> *Then the king rose up, who with the white cap*
> *Was adorned on his head, like the Priesthood;*
> *And stretched out his hands, already known to all the gods,*
> *Upward toward the high heaven.* — — —

Virgil in the third book of the *Aeneid*:

> *And before the altars we veil our heads with a Phrygian garment.* <note>original Latin: Et caput ante aras Phrygio velamur amictu.</note>

->That is:<-

> *Then we pray to the gods*
> *And cover before the altar with Phrygian silk*
> *Our head.*

Certainly, reverence and deep fear in submission caused the holy ones and children of God to cover their faces (*Exod. 3:6, 1 Kings 19:13, Isa. 6:2, 3*).

<margin>Exod. 28:40. Levit. 16.</margin>
The priests had to cover the head. The Jews pray with covered heads. (*Maimonides in Mishneh Torah, Vol. 1, Book 12, Ch. 5. Paul (*1 Cor. 11*) did not want the man to pray with a covered head. ### COVERING.

...the head in the Jewish Synagogues <note>It was traditional for Jewish men to cover their heads with a tallit or kippah during prayer to show awe before God.</note> was understood to be inconsistent with that confidence, freedom, and boldness to which the believers of the New Testament are called.

Next, I shall speak of covering the head and the face, and it will then become clear—*Song of Solomon 1*—that the New Testament church must not do so in the same respect or for the same reasons as people did in ancient times.

<margin>
Pagan women cover themselves.
</margin>
It is recounted and proven that pagan women appeared and walked the streets with their faces covered and their heads veiled. *On this subject, see Stuckius, De Conviviis, Book II, Chapter 28; Kirchmann, De Funeribus, Book II, Chapter 16; Dieterich, Antiquitates Veteris Testamenti, page 763; Fessel, Adversaria Sacra, page 11, Book II, Chapter 17, paragraph 4; Hoffmann, Lexicon Universale; d'Outrein in Parabolae, page 182, etc.; Geier, De Luctu, page 248, etc.*

Rebekah (*Genesis 24*) covered herself; (*1 Corinthians 11*) the woman must cover herself, having "power" <note>original: "magt"; likely referring to the "authority" or "veil" mentioned in 1 Cor 11:10</note> upon her head.

Some take it as a proof of shame. Others as a proof of submission to the husband.

> *To cover.*

> *Flammea sollicitum prævelatura pudorem.*
> <note>original Latin: "The bridal veil that will cover anxious shame."</note>

> *Lutea demissos velarunt flammea vultus.*

->That is:<-

> *The blue veil casts out all immodesty,*

For my part, I would believe that Paul wants to teach women that they must stand under the husband, and as those standing under someone else, they should be quiet, humble, and downcast. See what I have noted on *1 Corinthians 11*, and then also, if it pleases you, *Primatius, Carthusianus, Gothofredus, Salmasius, Camerarius, Selden's Uxor Hebraica, Buxtorf's Synagoga, Lightfoot, page 907; Salden's Otia, pages 85-90; Heinsius, d'Outrein, etc.; Ursinus' Analecta.*

One reads in *Pausanias, Book III, Laconica*, that *Penelope*, betrothed to *Ulysses* <note>Odysseus</note> by her father *Icarius*, when the latter asked her whether she wished to return with him to Lacedaemon or follow Ulysses in marriage, did not answer, but covered her face with her veil. This was not only out of shame but out of readiness to follow Ulysses, to marry, to submit herself to him, and to await protection from him.

Also the harlots.
</margin>
That even harlots and "light-o'-loves" <note>original: "ligte kooien"; an old Dutch term for prostitutes</note> used to cover and veil themselves is evident from

The heads and faces of those worthy of death and condemned to die were covered, as if they were unworthy of the light and of human sight and interaction; of which there are many examples.

<margin>
Also those guilty of death.
</margin>
*Livy in the 1st Book: Lictor, colliga manus, caput obnubito, infelice arbore suspendito*, that is: *Go hence, Executioner, bind his hands, cover his head, and hang him from an ill-fated tree.*

In the book of *Esther*, such a thing happened to Haman <note>The antagonist of the story, whose face was covered as he was led to his downfall (Esther 7:8).</note>. In *Chrysostom, Homily 5 on 2 Timothy*, we read: Ο' λησαὶ ἐν μὲν τοις δεσμωτηρίῳ ζῶντες, ἀδεῶς ζῶσιν, ὅταν δὲ παρὰ τὸ πέλασμα ἀγαγὼν τις ξίσῃ ἀυτὸς, διαλύονται τῳ φόβῳ. <note>original Greek: "Robbers, while they live in the prisons, live without fear; but when someone brings them out to the veil [to be executed], they dissolve with fear."</note> That is: *The highwaymen, as long as they sit locked in the dungeon, live peacefully; but when they are brought out to the covering, they melt and shrink away through fear, being now brought closer to death. </margin>
They covered the faces of the deceased, And the disfigured <note>The Dutch text seems to break here between the margin and the main text regarding the dead.</note>, whose faces were often uglier due to hunger. *Liber Minhagim, last Chapter*: he shall not look the dead in the face. *Schickard, page 157*, says this is so as not to hinder the memory of the survivors, since the sight of this is so harmful to the brain. *Rather, to forget him all the more readily. Geier, De Luctu, page 69.*

The fearful and the oppressed covered their heads and faces, as did cowards. *Exodus 3:6. Plautus in Mostellaria, Act II, Scene I: Capite obvelato, ut fugiat cum summo metu.* That is: *So that he may cover his head and run away in great fear. Shame and disgrace, insult, and distress are signified by covering the head and face, so that one did not dare to look up or look someone steadily in the eye; like downcast and ashamed children. From this comes the expression "to be covered with shame and disgrace." *Isaiah 44:16 and 69:8 and 89:46. Psalm 40. Isaiah 22 and 25:7, 8. Jeremiah 14:3, 4. Obadiah verse 10, etc.*

<margin>
Covering the head in mourning.
</margin>
When one wished to show mourning or sadness, to raise a deep and humble lamentation and wailing, one covered one's head and face, as if hiding them. We read of David in *2 Samuel 15*.

### COVERING.

*XV. 30.* concerning Absalom, *2 Sam. 19:4.* concerning Haman, *Esther 6:12.*

Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian</note> relates of Darius that he mourned the death of his wife for a long time with a covered head.

Seneca in *The Mad Hercules*:

> *For she herself, being sad, had her head*
> *veiled by the covering of her garment.*
> <note>original Latin: "Namque ipsa tristis, vestis obtectu caput Velata."</note>

->That is:<-

->*She was sorrowful, and with a veil she covered*<-
->*Her head.*<-

One may consult Gejerus on *Mourning* <note>original: "de Luctu"</note>, pages 254, 261, 263.

<margin>Everything covered in the Tabernacle.</margin>
If one casts an eye upon all that was in the Tabernacle <note>The portable sanctuary used by the Israelites</note>, everything was covered; every object had its covering cloth. The Ark of the Covenant also had its cover—not only the *Kapphoreth* <note>The Mercy Seat or Atonement Cover</note> but also its cloth. *Exodus 40, Numbers 4 and 22.* Moses also had a covering over his face, *2 Corinthians 3.* The Priests were covered with miters <note>head coverings</note>, hanging partly over their eyes.

<margin>Everything revealed in Christ.</margin>
This symbolized how that ministry was obscure and covered, and how everything lay wrapped in riddles, promises, shadows, or symbols. But now one sees clearly, without hindrance, the word of fulfillment lying open, and everything demonstrated and become truth in the Christ. *2 Corinthians 1 and 3.* One may look at what I have noted regarding this matter in *2 Corinthians 3.*

The Church in *Song of Solomon 1:8* had no need to be like one who covers herself by the flocks of your companions. The 70 translators <note>The Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament</note> have it thus: *lest I be as one who is covered by the flocks of your friends.* Some translate the word <term>ke'otyah</term> <note>original Hebrew: כעטיה</note> as "one who turns aside." Kimchi <note>A medieval Jewish rabbi and scholar</note> has it as "one who turns away and turns back." As one who wanders and straying, plays the harlot. See Bochart and Schindler in the *Lexicon*.

The Church, after many heavy persecutions among the Jews, not yet entirely separated from them—as if weary of pressure, slander, and persecution, and having no fixed and peaceful dwelling place—wishes to hear from her lover Jesus where she shall settle down to have rest. Noldius, in his *notes on the Concordance*, expressed it thus: *Make known to me the place where you shall graze, where I, being hidden from the Sun at noon when the heat is fiercest, may come to you; so that I am not seen as a harlot while I am covered because of the heat, and thus wander through the flocks of your companions.*

<margin>Description by De Bruine.</margin>
Jan de Bruine <note>A Dutch poet and writer</note> has this description: *and why should I not go around? and should I hypocritically cover myself by the flocks of other shepherds, your companions? no, certainly, I want to carry my heart on my tongue, and openly confess that I seek you, and wish to be where you are.*

That there were many hypocritical brothers is certain; that there were many who, out of fear and other reasons, did not speak freely is well known; that many conformed to the times and sought to make a mixture of Law and Gospel is discovered in Paul's letters.

That the first Christian Church under the Jews had a difficult time is taught by the Acts of the Apostles and the Apostolic letters.

That the Apostolic Christian Church endeavored more and more to separate itself, as far as the practice of

<column-break/>

external religion goes, rejecting Jesus and his righteousness, and seeking and setting up its own righteousness, needs no proof. She was no harlot to cover herself for that reason; she was no longer bound to the husband, the law, *Romans 7*, but was married to her maker and husband, the Lord of Hosts, *Isaiah 54, Hosea 2*—namely, Jesus. She wanted to love and cling to him purely, steadfastly, and alone, to serve him, and to be sheltered, protected, and cared for by him. And therefore, being "black" <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 1:5, often interpreted as being darkened by suffering</note> because of oppression and weary of misery, she wishes to understand where he will pitch his tent, so that she may come to him and practice the most intimate love with him.

It is true, they held her to be worthy of death, *Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 4*, for the sake of crimes. But this crime was taken away, the guilt dismissed, the sin covered. And as for her life and morals, she committed no offense according to the flesh, neither against divine nor against human laws; so that she had no need to cover herself as one guilty of death.

Regarding her state, it was true that she had a husband, namely Jesus, but for that reason she did not need to cover herself as before, when she was married to the law. *Romans 7.* She had to love and serve him, not with a slavish servitude and subjection, as in *Galatians 3 and 4*, but in freedom, *Galatians 5:1*; yes, with boldness, without fear and timidity, *Ephesians 3:12, Hebrews 4 and 10, Isaiah 54, Romans 14:17, Luke 1:74, 75, Hebrews 2:14, 15, 2 Corinthians 3.* Beside the sorrow, servitude, and fear, the shame and reproach were taken away. *Isaiah 54, 2 Corinthians 3:9, 10, 2 Peter 1:3, Romans 8:21–25, 2 Timothy 1:8, 1 Peter 4:16, Isaiah 29:22, Romans 1:16, and 5:3, 4, 5.*

One speaks of covering someone with shadows of death, etc. *Job 22, Psalm 140:10, Lamentations 2 and 3.* I would believe that it signifies visiting and disciplining someone so heavily with severe and manifold torments and judgments that he sees no way out or through, as if overcast with a heavy and black cloud, so that he cannot see away from himself, being occupied with such a weight that he cannot rid himself of it.

Thus one speaks in *Jeremiah 51:42: That the sea has risen over Babylon, and that she is covered with the waves.*

I would think that one must first look at the literal Babylon, taken by the troops of Cyrus, and flooded by the waves of his troops, and overrun as if by a sea to destruction. And then one can think of the spiritual Babylon, which has suffered much from the sea of Heathendom and the overflowing waves of the devastating nations, and will yet suffer much unto destruction and being washed away. And therefore, a heavy judgment of extreme destruction by foreign nations is signified here, so that one would see Babylon no more; just as the sea, with its roaring and overflowing waves, often leaves hardly a piece or stone for remembrance.

To cover someone's eyes, that is, to make it so that a person seeing does not see; and therefore in a <margin>Judgmental covering.</margin> spiritual sense, being transferred to the soul, understanding, and judgment of man, it signifies the judgment of man's blindness, *Isaiah 29.*

When one wishes in *Hosea 10:8: That the mountains...*

<header>BEGGAR.</header>

*...fall upon us, and the hills cover us, etc.* <note>referring to Luke 23:30</note> can generally be understood to mean that the people, rather than enduring such sorrows, insults, and pains any longer, wished that the mountains and hills would fall upon them to put an end to their grief, or to end their days beneath them in solitude and sadness. *Isaiah 2:19-21; Revelation 6:16; Hosea 10:8; Luke 23.*

Unless one should specifically understand it as the Harlot of Babylon <note>A figure from the Book of Revelation representing worldly corruption</note> being in distress and—being attacked by strong and overflowing foreign powers and troops—calling upon the mountains and hills (meaning greater and lesser kingdoms, states, and powers) for help, to be protected and covered by them.

At the very least, the Lord is said to cover someone when He shows them help and places them in a state of security. *Psalm 140:10; Isaiah 49 and 51.* In this way, the word has many uses, as has already been seen.

The expression also appears in *Psalms 32 and 35, etc.* regarding *those whose sins are covered*.

The Mercy Seat <note>The gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant, also called the Atonement Cover</note> covered the Ark alongside the Law which was inside it. The Law seemed not to be heard; its demands were not perceived. The Law of God was within the innermost parts of the Messiah to fulfill it. *Psalm 40.* Believers, united with Jesus, put Him on like a garment. Although they are soiled and occupied and infected with sins, Jesus' righteousness is there as if spread over them. *Psalm 132; Isaiah 61:10; Galatians 3. So that they, being in the light of God's Countenance because His Priests are clothed with righteousness and salvation, do not arise as guilty.*

<margin>
Sin destroyed through Christ.
</margin>
Sin, as a debt, is crossed out in God’s book of remembrance, as if deleted, and is no longer visible or legible through the full payment of Christ. After this, no debt remains to be settled, nor does anything stay open. This has its truth in the most powerful, literal, and comforting sense within the Church of the New Testament, after sin is atoned for, eternal righteousness is brought in, and the memory of the debt, along with the legal handwriting <note>original: "handschrift," referring to the record of debt in Colossians 2:14</note>, is deleted and abolished.

Let this be enough as a small sample of the word, and a sketch of its improper and figurative use. I shall now prepare to discuss something else.

### BEGGAR, BEGGING.
### <unclear>שאל</unclear> <note>Hebrew: Sha'al - to ask/beg</note>, ἐπαιτέω <note>Greek: epaiteō - to beg</note>, πτωχεύω <note>Greek: ptōcheuō - to be a beggar</note>, <unclear>אביון</unclear> <note>Hebrew: Evyon - a needy person</note>, πτωχὸς <note>Greek: ptōchos - a destitute person</note>, προσαίτης <note>Greek: prosaitēs - a beggar</note>, mendicus <note>Latin: beggar</note>, egenus <note>Latin: needy</note>, petens stipem <note>Latin: seeking alms</note>, etc.

<margin>
Beggars, a despised class of people.
</margin>
**A** BEGGAR is a despised creature. Begging is strangely attractive through laziness; hence the proverb, *it tastes as sweet as the beggar's bag*.

If someone has but a drop of noble blood and can subsist in any way through lawful means, even if he must manage poorly, he will not support himself with the fruits of another's sweat or painful labor. Instead, he would rather eat his bread by working with his hands, *1 Timothy 5:8-13*, or set himself to this or that occupation to survive. Horace <note>A famous Roman poet, 65–8 BC</note> was spurred to poetry by poverty. See him in the 2nd Book of his letters:

> *Poverty, bold through lack of hearth and land,*
> *impelled me to compose my verses.*
> <note>original Latin: "Et laris, & fundi paupertas impulit audax, Ut versus facerem."</note>

<column-break/>

-> That is: <-

> *Because I possessed neither gardens nor estates,*
> *That encouraged me to the making of poems.*

Plautus <note>A Roman playwright, c. 254–184 BC</note> turned the baker’s mill; another carried water to moisten the gardens. Furthermore, it is said, *paupertas quærit artes*, that is: *poverty seeks cunning*. Poverty is a visitation, and sometimes a plague from God. *Psalms 61 and 109; 1 Samuel 2; Lamentations 1:11-19 and 5, etc.*

It is true that one can fall into the deepest poverty through various paths, often through no fault or neglect of one's own: sometimes by unforeseen accidents, or by being born to poor and very deficient parents.

Not all poor people are Beggars, even if they are supported by wealthy and merciful people, or from alms and resources, in whole or in part. By Beggars, I mean those who go along the houses and roads, demanding bread or the maintenance of life, without working or taking up any lawful means to survive.

Divine History teaches us that there were many such people even in Israel, *Matthew 20 and 26; Luke 16 and 18; John 9; Acts 3*, and alas, experience teaches us that they exist to this day and everywhere; hence the proverb, *pauper ubique jacet*. That is: *He who is poor is everywhere pushed aside.*

Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot, 1602–1675, an English Hebraist</note> notes in *Hebrew Hours, page 640*, what types of appeals and motives beggars were accustomed to use of old, namely, *Zakki bi* <note>original Hebrew: זכי בי</note>: *grant me merit: or earn merit in or regarding me*. For they presented their own righteousness, merit, and inner worth before God through the giving of alms. Or they said, *A man says to his companion, grant me merit, or my master, grant me merit; or according to Rabbi Chaggi, look at me, pay attention to me, see who I was, and see who I am now.* <note>This refers to the *Vajikra Rabba*, a Jewish midrashic text, page 204-3.</note>

I am of the opinion that it would not be wrong at all if one wished to keep beggars out of the country and compel them to work, or—according to the condition of their bodies—support them through good means or employ them in certain matters. And the children of Beggars, who are otherwise raised to the same trade, should be compelled to take up some work, art, or craft.

*Pinto <note>Fernão Mendes Pinto, c. 1509–1583, a Portuguese explorer</note> relates in his travel logs that the King of the Chinese must take an oath that he will care for the poor and keep them at work. And that in Peking <note>original: "Pequien"</note> there are well over 500 schools for the poor and foundlings, in which they are taught to earn their living. Those who cannot learn a trade must set their hands to something else: the blind must turn mills; the crippled learn to knit and braid; those who have lame hands carry packs; those who are crippled and lame are taught to pray for the people. No one may set up a trade unless he agrees to teach and support two or three poor children; the mutes live from the fines collected from women who bicker with one another.*

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius, 1500–1574, a German humanist</note> was of that same opinion regarding lazy beggars and vagabonds, *part 2, chapter 74 in Horis Succisivis; Book 1, chapter 16; Justinian's Novels 8; de Quaestore 9, chapter 5, etc.; Plato, Book 2 of the Republic.* That there should be no beggar in our commonwealth.

Love—as glorious and useful as it is reasonable and Christian—ought to be tenderly practiced toward pitiful and needy people, as members of the common citizenry, or of the house and congregation of God. This is to prevent general vagrancy and the contemptible life of the "beggar's bag" <note>A term for the wandering life of a professional beggar.</note>; which usually brings with it public lawlessness, a release from all religion, and the extorting of alms to the detriment of honest and "shamefaced" <term>shamefaced poor</term> <note>Those who are poor but too ashamed to ask for help, often considered the most deserving of charity.</note> poor people.

If someone should reach the absolute limit and fall into deep poverty, being in every way unfit to earn a living in any degree, should such a person not rather beg than die of hunger? What then? I would think that the Lord clearly shows there that it is His good pleasure that the Jewish Magistrate, along with the overseers of the Jewish churches and all those blessed by God, shall take necessary care of the poor and needy according to their state and ability, so that through their sluggishness, lack of love, and blameworthy neglect, no one falls into the beggar's bag out of necessity: assuring them at the same time that, if they lived according to His laws and commands, doing for the impoverished what had been recommended to them, He would bless them, and they would by no means regret behaving themselves in such a manner.

<margin>c.</margin> The state of a sinner before God is even more needy and miserable than that of a common beggar, *Ezekiel 16, Revelation 3.* However, no one will easily resolve to beg except through the feeling and conviction of their own poverty. If someone does not feel and see their extreme poverty, sins, guilt, flaws, and helplessness, they will not seek help from or make demands of another. Therefore, spiritual and believing beggars appear as those possessed by a sensible conviction of their soul's state before God. *Psalm 22 and 51, Romans 7:24, etc.*

<margin>d.</margin> One beggar does not seek alms or necessary and generous support from another beggar. Two naked people cannot cover each other; they are both needy. Instead, one addresses the rich and the generous.
Regarding the soul, no one can help us but God, who is great and rich in mercy through His Son. None but Christ, the wealthy and merciful. *Acts 4:12, John 14:6, Isaiah 42 and 43, John 16, Revelation 3.*

<margin>e.</margin> A supplicating beggar presents his poverty and extreme embarrassment with heart-moving words and persistent entreaties, showing that he is in earnest.
No less so a believing and repentant sinner. *Psalm 32, 38, and 51; Romans 7:24; Psalm 119; 1 John 1:8, 9; Luke 17:16, etc.*

<margin>f.</margin> He does not demand it as an obligation or merit; he accepts what is given, which he had prayed for for the sake of God and Christ, thanking and blessing his benefactor.
A believing and repentant sinner seeks godliness, salvation, and Christ’s righteousness for life—as far as he is concerned—out of grace for Christ’s sake, to the glory of God’s mercy. He awaits divine grace with persistent entreaties and a humble state of mind. And he receives it through faith, with expressions of thanksgiving. *Psalm 132:2, Luke 18:13, John 1:12, Isaiah 27, Psalm 32, 51, 103, and 116, Ephesians 1:1-4.*

### B R O O K, W A T E R-B R O O K.
-><note>original Hebrew:</note> נחל <note>Nachal</note>, פלג <note>Peleg</note>, <note>original Greek:</note> χείμαῤῥος <note>Cheimarrhos</note>, πόταμος <note>Potamos</note>, <note>original Latin:</note> torrens, rivus, fluvius, flumen.<-

<margin>Description of a Brook.</margin> A BROOK is a flow of water in the manner of a stream, actually originating from rainwater and melted mountain snow, which plunges down from the mountain peaks into the valleys and flows along. Sometimes, because of the abundance and force of the falling and pressing water, it carries away pieces and boulders from the mountains, sand, and marshy clay, swelling strongly until it overflows its banks and the nearby lands. It is often planted with trees, so that one may shelter under them from the midday heat and breathe refreshingly. These brooks dry up quickly for lack of following mountain water; which is why they are distinguished from rivers and streams, which possess larger and more enduring waters, etc. One can read about both in the Latin poets, Virgil and Ovid.

<column-break/>

->Ovid in the Third Book of his *Amores* (Loves):<-

> *Nomen habes nullum, nivibus collecte caducis,*
> *Fontis habes inftar, pluviafque nivefque caducas,*
> *Quas tibi divitias pigra miniftrat hiems.*
> *Aut lutulentus agis brumali tempore curfus,*
> *Aut premis arentem pulverulentus humum.*
<note>original Latin: "You have no name, gathered from fallen snows; you have the appearance of a spring, from fallen rain and snow, which riches the sluggish winter supplies to you. Either you lead a muddy course in the winter time, or you press the parched ground, covered in dust."</note>

->That is:<-

> *You have no name, gathered only from the snow,*
> *You have no fixed dwelling place, nor a spring's flow.*
> *Your snow and rain puddles represent a fountain to us.*
> *This is all that the winter could give you.*
> *In winter one sees you move along full of mud*
> *And flow along the ground, looking nothing like a brook.*

->Again in the same Book:<-

> *Et turpi craffas gurgite volvis aquas.*
<note>original Latin: "I remember you were small, nor did I shrink from crossing you; your highest edge scarcely touched my ankles. Now you rush headlong from the melted snow of the nearby mountain, and you roll thick waters in a foul whirlpool."</note>

->That is:<-

->Virgil in the second Book of the *Aeneid*:<-

<note>original Latin: "A rapid torrent from a mountain stream flattens the fields, flattens the happy crops and the labors of oxen, and drags the forests headlong."</note>

->That is:<-

> *When one hears the rustling of a swift brook,*
> *Plunged down the rocky cliff, knowing neither bank nor path,*
> *And roars over fields and lush crops;*
> *Striking down the sweat of the plowman with its splashing,*
> *And dragging forests with it, and driving trees with the current.*

Now it is known and undeniable that, <margin>The brook taken figuratively.</margin> while the word BROOK must often be taken literally, one must likewise note its improper, figurative, and allusive use. This represents either refreshing, comforting matters, states, and encounters, or harmful, painful, anxious, and devastating misfortunes.

To give a few examples of both, I shall let the joyful, refreshing nature of grace and comfort for salvation in communion with Christ, through the Holy Spirit, go first, and then let the sad, painful, death-bringing, terrifying, and devastating follow.

<margin>a.</margin> I take the Brook as an image of God’s flowing gifts of grace, with the comfort of the Holy Spirit, for the refreshing, thirst-quenching, or filling of longing souls, leading to greater and more breakthrough fruitfulness in faith and the works of sanctification, or pure love, under the ministry of grace, especially in the days of the New Testament.

Thus I read of Streams of Water, *Psalm 1,* of Brooks of God's delights, *Psalm 36:9,* of Brooks—

# BROOK.

Brooks of the Rivers, *Psalm 46*, of an overflowing Brook, *Isaiah 66:12*, etc. being the Spirit with His gifts and operations, leading to knowledge, faith, justification, peace, and joy, which was promised in *Isaiah 35 and 44, Psalm 48, Joel 2, John 7:37, 38, 39, Acts 2, Ephesians 4, Romans 14:17, and John 1:16.*

This Brook had to increase and reach a great height, and at its peak, bring life and fruitfulness to both Jews and Gentiles, *Ezekiel 47*, of which we still look forward to the most excellent height and swelling.

One reads in *Proverbs 18:4* that the *wellspring of wisdom is a flowing brook.* This portrays to us how a truly pious and wise man is singularly useful to his neighbors, bringing forth words of sound understanding—words in their proper season: instructive and edifying words or reasons, because from the abundance of his heart comes the truth, which he neither wants to nor can withhold; the truth which he judges can and will make his neighbor wiser, more virtuous, and more prudent.

<margin>Worldly inconstancy compared to a brook.</margin>That one compares worldly and human inconstancy and changeability to a Brook—now empty, now full, now here, now there taking its course in the valley—does not lack a basis for application and transfer: for unstable "fair-weather friends" change easily and abandon someone, especially when the heat of adversity arises and their friend needs the most comfort and good counsel. But a good and faithful friend is a steady and abundant Brook that never fails or deviates.

<column-break/>

Meanwhile, I must not forget to note:

<margin>by idolatrous Israel. Brook taken for disasters.</margin>b. That the word BROOK, though with some description or a powerful addition of other meaningful words, is taken for great difficulties, miseries, distresses, anxieties, slanders, scorn, punishment, temptations—whether of body or soul, internal and external—inflicted by God as Judge, and provoked by sins, for a long or short time; yet sometimes so strong and violent that they seem to overpower the sufferer and cause him to perish through lack of physical strength or soul's capacity: or through Satan, the power of darkness, and wicked and gruesome men, to oppress the pious, to hinder their labor and zeal, to oppose their work with violence, or to break it down: as in *Psalm 18:5, Isaiah 48, Jeremiah 47, Psalm 124.*

Thus one reads of the Messiah, *that he would drink from the Brook on the way. Psalm 110:7.* Which Munsterus <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a German cartographer and Hebrew scholar.</note> understands thus: *he shall slay so many enemies, and shed so much enemy blood, that he could drink from it: that is, he shall achieve full victory and triumph over his enemies.*

Yet Vatablus, Tremellius, Junius, <note>Refers to François Vatable, Immanuel Tremellius, and Franciscus Junius, influential 16th-century biblical scholars and translators.</note> etc. have noted, *that Christ, marching forth with his army and having fought for victory over his enemies, pursues the victory with all zeal without neglecting it; not set on his mouth, not wanting to rest, nor amusing himself with wine or exquisite, beautiful, clear, and tasty liquid, but as if in passing, and like a brave hero, merely drinking from a running Brook, which is sometimes low or murky.*

Yet others apply it generally to all the suffering, grief, scorn, and pain of the Savior Jesus in His life, but especially to His manifold and most painful soul and body sufferings at the end of His life, *Matthew 26 and 27, Psalm 22, Isaiah 53, Psalm 69, 88, and 116.* Just as He also afterwards on the way, in the expanding and continuing of His kingdom among the Jews and Gentiles, suffered not a little in His members or congregation, *Acts 8 and 9,* which, in conformity with its Head, shall be oppressed, humbled, and drink from the Brook of wrath, grimness, persecution, slander, scorn, etc., *Revelation 12,* before it, following the example of Christ, shall lift its head high unto deliverance, honor, and glory.

*Psalm 110.* The drinking from the Brook on the way, says Mr. Tako Haio van den Honert <note>A Dutch Reformed theologian (1666–1740) known for his work "Messias verheerlykt" (The Messiah Glorified).</note> in *Messias verheerlykt* p. 35, etc., nowhere means, nor can it mean, to capture a bath that is reinforced by waters and Rivers. For although Sennacherib <note>King of Assyria (r. 705–681 BC) who besieged Jerusalem.</note> boasts in *Isaiah 37:25* <note>The text incorrectly cites Isaiah 32:15.</note> that he has dug and drunk waters, and with the soles of his feet made all the Rivers of the besieged places dry: yet his way of speaking differs too greatly from this one, which we find here in *Psalm 110:* for Sennacherib does not say, *I have drunk from the Brook on the way:* but he says, *I have made the Rivers of the besieged places dry,* and thus as if drunk them.

The Brooks on the road give no strength to any city or place: but the manner of speaking suggests that a traveler on the road contents himself with that Brook-water: or that he is forced to drink it because he has no other drink at hand for his refreshment

# CUP.

one can make use of. *page 221.* His Reverence <note>The author likely refers to a specific commentator mentioned in the previous pages.</note> writes: There are interpreters who believe that the person spoken of here is the Messiah. This interpretation rests solely on the ground that they believe *drinking from the brook on the way* is a symbol here of heavy suffering. Thus, they wish to show that this is the basis of the Messiah’s humiliation, etc.

But if we may say what seems less than satisfactory to us in this interpretation, it is:
1. That a narrative of the Messiah’s suffering, after such an excellent discourse on his glory, seems quite out of place.
2. And that until now *no one has proven* that in God's word, *drinking from a brook* is a symbol of suffering and difficulty.
I know well that rivers and streams, when they swell and threaten someone with flooding, are symbols of suffering and difficulties. But nowhere do I find that drinking from the rivers and streams is a symbol of suffering and difficulties, *Psalm 18:5 and 69:2, 3 and 93:3, 4. Psalm 124:4, 5. Isaiah 8:7, 8.*

Drinking from a cup is sometimes a symbol of suffering and difficulty, *Psalm 11:6 and 75:9. Jeremiah 25:15-17. Matthew 20:22 and 26:42. John 18:11.* as it is also a symbol of enjoying good things. *Psalm 16:5 and 23:5.*

Since it is not said here, *he shall drink from the cup*: but *he shall drink from the brook on the way*; and this way of speaking is nowhere in God's word a symbol of suffering and difficulty: so then this way of speaking must signify something other than suffering and the undergoing of pain.

And thus we find not the slightest difficulty here in applying this drinking from the brook on the way to God the Father, regarded as a warrior in verses 5 and 6, of whom verse 7 is spoken here by the Holy Spirit to the Son. The Holy Spirit would then say of the Father to the Son, *he shall drink from the brook on the way*.

This saying can be understood in two ways, for:
<margin>Twofold meaning.</margin>
1. It can mean that the Father, as a vigorous warrior <note>original: "Exod. XV. 3, 4."</note> in the hunting and pursuing of His Son’s enemies, would be so zealous that He would allow Himself no time to provide Himself with any other drink in His thirst, other than what the brook on or by the way—on which He hunted and pursued His Son’s enemies—provided and supplied to His hand. This was so that He might not be delayed in any way by seeking or waiting for a more palatable drink on the way, and thereby give the Gentiles an opportunity to escape by flight. This is all the more notable because heroes of war on the day of battle are more accustomed to sufficing themselves with water in their thirst. *Judges 7:5. 1 Samuel 14:24 and 26:11, 12. 2 Kings 19:24. 2 Samuel 11:11.* etc.
2. It can also mean that God the Father was set to contend and struggle with His Son’s enemies such that brooks of blood were to be shed on and along the way, *Psalm 68:24. Ezekiel 32:6.* with which the Father would be, as it were, filled and satisfied. *Numbers 23:24. Ezekiel 32:6 and 39:17-20. Deuteronomy 32:42. Isaiah 34:3-5. Jeremiah 46:10. Psalm 68:24.* One may consult His Reverence on this.

### CUP, <note>Hebrew: כוס (kos), Greek: κύλιξ (kylix), Latin: calix, Greek: ποτήριον (poterion), Latin: poculum.</note>

A CUP is any vessel in which a drink is offered for drinking.

It is said that especially at the Feast of the Passover, one drank four cups; the first with which one, as it were, consecrated and began the Feast, using these or similar words, *blessed be our God, King of the world, Creator of the vine,* which cup went around.

<margin>Four cups in the Passover Feast.</margin>
Why exactly four cups in the Passover feast? On this, all the wise men among the Jewish masters do not agree; for some allude to the fourfold redemptions and fourfold manners of speaking in the deliverance of Israel from Egypt; others to the four Monarchies of the world; some to the four cups which the Lord would pour out for Israel. *Psalm 23 and 16:5 and 116:13.* Others to the fourfold cups with which the Lord would present the Gentiles in His judgment, *Jeremiah 25:15 and 51:7. Psalm 11:6 and 57:8.* Some to the fourfold repeated cup. *Genesis 40:11.* One can consult on this: *Lightfoot in Horae p. 380. Saubert, Palaestra p. 84.* etc.

<margin>Passover table.</margin>
They set the table and place upon it the unleavened bread, bitter herbs, and the dipping sauce, alongside the roasted Passover lamb: they eat of the salad, dipped in vinegar to stir the appetite. The master of the meal takes one of the middle cakes and breaks it into two pieces. One piece he lays between the two whole cakes, the other he lays beside himself and covers it with a cloth. The bread on the table-plate is called the bread of poverty and misery, and everyone is invited to eat it. They pour the second cup full: they take away the roasted Passover lamb, and by so doing the children get the opportunity to ask why one eats unleavened bread and the Passover lamb with bitter herbs, and receives only a piece of bread—yes, even holding the meal at night, etc. *Buxtorf, School of the Jews, page 328.* etc. *Massekhet Pesachim, Chapter 10. Babylonian Talmud, page 116. Maimonides in Chametz U-Matzah Chapter 8. Lightfoot in Horae page 378.* etc. And after drinking the second cup, they strike up the songs of thanks, *Psalms 113 and 114.* *Lightfoot in Horae page 379.* etc.

After this, they set to feasting, eating, and drinking. At midnight, half of the hidden cake <note>The Afikoman.</note> comes forth: he gives everyone a piece; each washes his hands and sits down, and they pour the third cup. Everyone standing up, and having that piece of bread, and having eaten of the Passover, the third cup is taken, and with it one makes an end of the meal by drinking, thanking, and blessing. <note>Hebrew: כוס הברכה (Kos HaBerakhah)</note> *the cup of thanksgiving, Luke 22. 1 Corinthians 10:16. Lightfoot in Horae page 380. Saubert in Palaestra* maintains that Jesus used, blessed, and hallowed this cup as a part of the Sacrament of the New Testament.

The fourth and last cup after the meal is called the cup of praise, when they struck up and sang *Psalms 115 through 118*: <note>Hebrew: כוס הלל (Kos Hallel) and ברכת השיר (Birkat HaShir)</note> *the blessing of the song.* This was drunk off when they finished drinking. *Lightfoot in Horae page 381. Bynaeus, The Crucified Christ page 209.*

It is held that Christ ordained this last Cup to be a Sacrament of the New Testament, Matthew 26:30, Mark 14:26. Which last Cup—as Buxtorf teaches in *The School of the Jews* <note>original: "Schoole der Jooden," referring to Johannes Buxtorf's *Synagoga Judaica*</note> page 331—was followed by prayers and wishes for destruction and judgments upon enemies, taken from Psalm 69 and 79, and Lamentations 3.

<margin>Cup of Thanksgiving.</margin>
Account is also made of eating and drinking with the Levites and Priests in the peace offerings, or thank offerings for benefits received; at which time they sang loudly and lifted the cup of deliverance or salvation on high; otherwise called the cup of thanksgiving. 1 Samuel 1; 1 Kings 13; Numbers 28; 1 Corinthians 10.

<margin>Sabbath Cup.</margin>
Furthermore, mention is made of a Sabbath Cup, with two rounds of bread. Buxtorf, *Synagoga* <note>original: "Syn."</note> pages 256–280, etc. ends the Sabbath with a Cup, or shows with it that the Sabbath has ended. Leo de Modena page 79. Lightfoot in *Horae* <note>referring to *Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae*</note> page 298. Indeed, this occurred on every day and at every meal, with wine and beer: Leo de Modena, Buxtorf, etc.

<margin>Cup of Consolation.</margin>
I read further of a cup of consolation and strengthening, which was given to those who were greatly distressed and heavy of heart, to displace and soften their overwhelming sorrow. Proverbs 31:6, 7; Jeremiah 16:7.

From this, some believe that the wicked custom arose of giving strong drink to those condemned to death, even filling them up so that they would lose the use of their reason and senses. Maimonides, *Sanhedrin* Chapter 13. Galatinus Book VIII. Fagius on Exodus 22, etc. Hieronymus Pardus on Ezekiel 23. Dilherr, *Demoniacus* pages 9, 10, 11.

It is well known that Paul in 1 Corinthians 10 speaks of the Cup and table of devils, or Demons.

Certainly, there were appointed meals from which not only the so-called pagan deities (both good and evil) received their portion, but men also drank to the honor of the Deity for whom the feast was established, extolling their deeds and virtues. Sometimes they drank three glasses to various gods at a single meal: three Cups in honor of the Graces; and they ended the meal with a Cup. They also drank in honor of kings, great men, friends, etc.
<margin>Cup of Honor.</margin>

The author of *Apollonius* teaches that at meals they drank three Cups: the first in honor of Jupiter the Preserver; the second in honor of Good Fortune, or the Good Spirit; the third in honor of Mercury, to whom the oversight of dreams pertained. *Dissertationes Selectae* page 583.

Doughty <note>original: "Dougtæus"</note> in his notes on the New Testament records that before the meal, or at the beginning, they drank to the honor of <note>original: "θεῷ ἀγαθῷ"</note> the good God; or <note>original: "Διὸς σωτῆρος"</note> Jupiter the Savior. At the end of the meal, they drank and extolled the virtues and deeds of the gods with song, page 155, etc. Sometimes nine Cups were drunk because of the nine Muses. Horace, Book III, *Odes* 19. Apuleius, Book II, *The Golden Ass* <note>original: "Milesiar."</note> page 128.

They drank in honor of the gods, princes, and friends, and indeed as many Cups as there were letters found in their names. Martial, Book I, Epigram 62; Book VIII, Epigram 51; Book XI, Epigrams 37–95. Kipping, *Antiquities* page 518.

It is well enough known that one names the Cup and understands by it that which is in the Cup—*continens pro contento*: the container for the contained <note>A common rhetorical figure where the vessel represents the liquid inside</note>. # CUP.

For my part, I do not take it here in the sense of sorrow, torment, anxiety, and persecution; for the Church now finds herself in a contented state, in which—regarding the soul—she lacked no means of grace, but found herself so situated that she possessed the inward anointing, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the administration of the Word and the Sacraments. This is a cup of joy and salvation, once taken from her, now given in compensation and softening of her past suffering and grief, pain, persecution, and oppression—even under the Antichrist, <note>In the 17th-century context, "Antichrist" often referred to the Papacy or any power perceived to be suppressing the "true" Gospel and withholding the sacramental cup from the laity.</note> when the Cup was taken away from her.

What I have thus briefly presented regarding *Psalm 23:5* <note>The original text cites Psalm 21:5, but the context clearly refers to the "cup runs over" passage of Psalm 23.</note>—where I could have dealt more broadly with a Cup full of:

<margin>a. Judgments, punishments, plagues, and scorn. *Isaiah 60, Isaiah 51, Ezekiel 22, Revelation 14.*</margin>
<margin>b. Christ’s weighty suffering of body and soul. *Matthew 20:22, 23; Mark 10:38, 39; John 18:11.*</margin>
<margin>c. The Cup of Consolation, to somewhat moderate and displace sorrow. *Job 42, Proverbs 31, Jeremiah 16:7.*</margin>
<margin>d. The Cup of Salvation, deliverance, and thanksgiving. *Exodus 19, Psalm 116, Jeremiah 35, Matthew 26, 1 Corinthians 10 and 11, etc.*</margin>

Regarding this, I further note that the Seventy Translators <note>original: "70. Overzetters," referring to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, Augustine, and Euthymius, read *potērion* <note>original: "ποτηριον"</note>, *Your Cup*, not *potērion mou* <note>original: "ποτηριον μου"</note> *My Cup*, bringing the Cup to God or the Shepherd. However, this makes little change in the meaning; for even if it were poured by the Shepherd, it was nonetheless placed in the hand of the Church to drink.

<margin>The common reading and translation is *My cup is overflowing* <note>original Latin: "Calix meus inebriatus"; the author cites Psalm 16, but this refers to Psalm 23:5.</note>: my Cup is drenched, full, or intoxicating.</margin>

As for me, I give proper attention to the following things, namely:

1. That *Psalm 23* was originally spoken regarding the Messiah's scorn, adversities, and suffering on the cross—and the fruits of salvation springing from all this for the pious and upright.
2. That the scholars who have placed a brief summary of the contents above each Psalm have applied this Psalm to the subjects of the Messiah in the New Testament.
3. That David, being not the least among the Prophets, surely served us alongside the others. *1 Peter 1:10–12.*
4. That the Messiah is from David, is prefigured by David, is called David—and indeed is David's Lord.
5. That no one can be, or be named, a Shepherd with such emphatic power as the Messiah.
6. That the Messiah’s Kingdom and spiritual goods belong mostly to the state of the soul, both here and hereafter. *Luke 17, John 19, Romans 14:17.*
7. However, for better understanding, these are presented through physical things—which are necessary, useful, refreshing, and pleasant—as if in symbolic language. *Proverbs 8:19–21; Isaiah 25:6 and 55:1, 2; Song of Solomon 5:1; Matthew 22:1, 2; John 6:51, 53–56; etc.*

<column-break/>

I do not think for a moment that David—such an enlightened man, great prophet, favorite of God, and man after God's heart—would have occupied himself, or God's church and people, with a description of the great change in his domestic state, his royal table, choice foods and delicacies, or fine and pleasant drinks, which he held in common with heathen and idolatrous kings, princes, and lords. He would not, as a Prophet, compose a Psalm for posterity about his external state, pomp, and physical abundance, to be set aside and preserved among the stringed and singing songs, to be sung and played in its turn upon the temple heights. No, certainly; I trust much more that this heavenly Prophet described in the spirit the spiritual abundance of the Church under the Shepherd Messiah: in knowledge, faith, love, hope, grace, strengthening, comfort, and joy, through the working spirit of the Messiah, the Gospel of fulfillment, and the sealing pledges of love. 

Perhaps it will also not be poorly understood by us that David saw, in emphatic power and grand application, the deliverance and goods of salvation toward the last days—when the Church, having overcome and wrestled free from the greatest difficulties and temptations under the power of the Antichrist, will be able to say with the greatest strength and unhindered boldness: (verse 6) *Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the Lord forever.*

At the very least, it must be that David, applying the great change and elevation of his own state and temporal goods and the abundance of his "fatness," intended to sketch in a more sublime manner the spiritual nature of the Messiah's kingdom of grace and peace, and the abundance of all desirable things under His high governance. *Psalm 36:8, 9; Proverbs 8:19–21; Isaiah 25:6 and 55:2; Isaiah 35:25; John 1:16; etc. See Gejerus, Coccejus, van Til, and others.* <note>Martin Geier, Johannes Cocceius, and Salomon van Til were prominent 17th-century Reformed theologians and commentators.</note>

I read in *Psalm 116* <note>The text says "Pſ. CVI" (106), but the "Cup of Salvation" is in Psalm 116.</note> of the Cup of Salvation and deliverance: a Cup regarding which I would think there is an allusion to the cups of thanksgiving used with peace offerings or offerings made after a vow for benefits received. David and the Church wished to take this up and drink it with the Priests and Levites, singing and praising God. Alternatively, one may think of the Church of the New Testament, delivered from the dangers of death and distinguished adversities, which wishes to offer thanks and praise to God, *Psalm 50; Romans 12:1, 2; Hebrews 13:15.* And if this should not please someone, let them consider that David and the Church have been in more than one deathly agony; and that the death of God's favored ones is spoken of immediately thereafter; and therefore, that David and the Church behave as if comforted, drinking God's cup. If He wishes to chasten her heart, even unto death, she is satisfied. Precious death and the final exit will sweeten and compensate for everything. But if He does not wish to bring her to death, but to chasten her heavily, she is hardened to bear it; it will not harm but help, *Romans 9; Psalm 119; Hebrews 12; Revelation 3;* and she will boast in her tribulation, and when it comes, count it all joy, *Romans 5,* with which there is great fellowship, as I read of a following Cup of Thanksgiving in the...

The Holy Supper <note>The Eucharist or Communion.</note> *1 Corinthians 10 and 11, Matthew 26,* which is alluded to and derived from what has been said regarding the Passover cups, can be sufficiently concluded from the aforementioned.

It is a Cup which brings to our minds Jesus' extreme sadness and bitter soul-suffering, *Psalm 18 and 22, Matthew 26, Psalm 69 and 88.*

<margin>Cup of Consolation.</margin>
Yet, at the same time, it is a cup of consolation, for it assures us that the Christ has drunk the cup of the cross for us, *Isaiah 53, Galatians 3:13, Galatians 4:4, Matthew 26.*

And therefore it is a cup of salvation and deliverance, as a memorial and pledge that <margin>Cup of Salvation.</margin> Christ has borne God’s wrath, fulfilled the requirement of the law, and has delivered and set us free: and thus it is not a cup of fury, but of joyful remembrance and of thanksgiving. *1 Corinthians 10, Romans 7:24, Psalm 116.*

<margin>Cup of Zeal.</margin>
It is a *cup of zeal*, which Christ drank in zeal, *Psalm 69,* and when the Lord was zealous for the honor of His righteousness, *Romans 3, Isaiah 49 and 63.*

It is not a Cup of fornication and seduction, but of the purest, strongest, and most steadfast love of the Christ, who poured out His soul for us unto death, *Isaiah 53, Romans 5.* In that Cup is better wine than (as the Jews would have it) the red wine at the Passover feast: it is the red and precious blood of the blameless Lamb of God, *Matthew 26.* A wine of grace, comfort, and salvation, *Isaiah 25,* which quenches the thirst and fulfills the desires of the soul, *John 4:17,* to strengthen the heart with grace, to make it joyful and eloquent, *Isaiah 61:10, Psalm 4, Zechariah 9:17, 1 Peter 2:9.*

Making the soul drunk, *Psalm 36, Jeremiah 31:25, Song of Solomon 5,* because of the abundance of the Spirit and of grace in the New Testament, against the thirst and scarcity of the Old Testament, *John 7:37, 38, 39, Isaiah 44 and 35, Psalm 8, Joel 2,* through which the heart is entirely pierced and struck with love, such that it cannot fully comprehend its state, nor the height, depth, breadth, or length of God’s grace and love, etc.

No wine from Israel’s old vine, not fetched from afar from promises, shadows, and riddles, but from the word of fulfillment, from Him who is the true vine, *John 15.* Such wine of grace and consolation was never drunk so unmixed, or clear, strong, noble, lovely, and abundant under the administration of the Law: not old, but new wine.

Of an entirely different nature is the Cup and wine of God's wrath, fury, and staggering <note>original: "zwymelinge," referring to a state of being dazed or faint.</note>, heavy judgments, and weighty miseries, which stupefy the understanding, cause the soul to waste away through mourning, and die a thousand deaths: of which the Church may drink the top, but the enemies of Jesus and His Church drink the bottom, sucking out the dregs and the sediment: of such a cup, under various expressions, one can read in various places, *Psalm 60:5 and 11 and 75, Isaiah 51, Jeremiah 25 and 51, Lamentations 4,* etc.

This Cup shall the Roman harlot <note>A common Reformation-era term for the Roman Catholic Church, referencing the Whore of Babylon.</note> drink dry; she who has poured her abominations into a golden Cup for the purpose of seduction, *Revelation 17:5.* See regarding the Cup of jealousy, CUP OF ZEAL.

It is a beautiful title which the Man of Sin <note>A biblical title often applied to the Papacy by Protestant commentators of this period.</note> arrogates to himself: *a father of fathers, a*

<column-break/>

*shepherd of shepherds, the most holy father, the most blessed, the Vicar of Christ, the head of the church, the successor of Peter, the bride and the foundation of the church, the Prince of Priests, the Apostolic Bishop, the universal one in place of God, etc.*

*Revelation 17:4.* The conduct and the appearance of this woman are more clearly indicated. She had in her hand a golden Cup through which this harlot poured a love-potion for her paramours to ignite them with lust. See how it is named in *Revelation 15:8.* This drink signifies, metaphorically and figuratively, the false religious doctrine which commends idolatry and loathsome superstition to men, which is represented in a prophetic style by the word <term>שקוצים</term> <note>Hebrew: *shikutsim*, meaning "detestable things" or "abominations."</note> that is, <term>Βδελυγμάτων</term> <note>Greek: *bdelygmatōn*, meaning "of abominations."</note> *Isaiah 66:3, Ezekiel 5:11.* These <term>Βδελυγμάλα</term> <note>abominations</note> are <term>τὰ ἀκάθαρλα τῆς πορνείας</term> <note>the impurities of her fornication</note>, because they cause impure stirrings to arise in the mind, by which it is heated; they not only entangle the unwary in the fellowship of carnal religion but also ignite them such that they burn and blaze with love for the false religion, and pay for this fellowship, sometimes with the loss of their lives and temporal means: which, in a spiritual sense, means to become drunk from this drink.

The golden or gilded Cup is a <margin>Golden cup.</margin> symbolic means of every kind of method and tool by which the teaching of this religion is presented to men: such as the sermons of false teachers, the decrees and so-called Traditions of the Roman Church, wonderfully and finely swaddled <note>original: "bezwagtelt," suggesting something obscured or dressed up in fancy wrappings.</note> with the words of the Teachers of the ancient church, the Lateran Synods, and others of the same sort, in which the Papal authority has had the upper hand: the whole body of Canon and Papal law, openly read in the Academies: the sought-after subtleties of the Scholastic Teachers, specifically cobbled together to support the doctrine of the Roman religion, concerning the Bulls and letters of Indulgences: and furthermore all other things that are similar to the rest. Through this gilded Cup, Rome commends idolatrous superstitions to the people and ignites men in the lust of this spiritual fornication. A part of this love-potion consists of the doctrine of Indulgences, and no doctrine more pleasant than this can ever happen or appear to the flesh. Also, there is no piece which so powerfully favors all wicked defects and villainies, etc.

See this further presented and elaborated by the Reverend and learned Professor Campegius Vitringa, on *Revelation, page 759,* etc.

Antiquity, holiness, Catholic, universal, prosperity, luster, numerousness, the Prophetic light, power of wonders and signs, succession, etc. See there: the gold that glitters. But the interior of this Cup is full of fornication and deadly soul-poison; godlessness, impious, poisonous, soul-harming doctrines, blasphemy, apostasy from God, His grace, the Christ, grace, righteousness; idolatry, love of the world, invocation of creatures, beastly impurity, wicked lust, etc. See Cocceius, Heidegger, Vitringa.
