# IMAGE.

...preparing myself to move on to the treatment of something else.

### IMAGE, <term>pesel <note>Hebrew: a carved image or idol</note></term>, <term>temunah <note>Hebrew: likeness or form</note></term>, <term>tselem <note>Hebrew: image or shadow</note></term>, <term>eikon <note>Greek: image or likeness</note></term>, <term>imago <note>Latin: image or statue</note></term>.

<margin>Images and image-worship.</margin>
As for what specifically concerns IMAGES and IMAGE-WORSHIP, and the idolatry practiced with them—their origin and progress into gross, tangible, and ridiculous excesses—I have dealt with that in the second part of my *Sacred Miscellanies*, regarding "Kissing" <note>Referring to the practice of kissing icons or statues as an act of veneration.</note>. And under the word IDOLATRY, one will be able to satisfy their curiosity further.

It is well known that the word IMAGE is sometimes used in its literal sense, regarding something visible and material, as a means of representation—whether for reverence, awe, worship, honor, submission, etc. Whether one is moved to such things by certain figures, engravings, letters, likenesses, inscriptions, characters, or other signs: such likenesses, or the imitation of them, and bringing about any change, falsification, clipping <note>Likely referring to the "clipping" of coins bearing an image.</note>, or anything else to the material of the statue, is considered a very high and serious offense. Indeed, even to offer any insult or slight to the statues themselves is found to be taken seriously and punished very severely. Thus Suetonius relates in the *Life of Tiberius* that it meant death if one struck his servant near the Image of Augustus, changed clothes there, or, having his face stamped upon a coin, presumed to enter a secret place or a brothel with it. Philostratus, in the *Life of Apollonius*, relates <italic>that someone was condemned for impiety because he had struck one of his disciples who was carrying a silver coin on which the image of Tiberius was stamped.</italic> See Jan de Bruine the Younger in his *Touchstone of Wits, pages 42, 43.* Thus Tiberius wished that his statue should be as sacred and inviolable as himself. See Seneca’s *On Benefits*; Marquardus Freherus’ *On the Census Coin*; and Hofmann’s *Universal Lexicon, page 904.*

Think then how highly and heavily the King of all kings can and will take it, when one violates or kills His rational creature, formed after His image, or offers His saints scorn and evil. <margin>Gen. IX. Ps. CV.</margin>

Since I have made mention of the Image of God in man, I do not take the word "Image" or "likeness" to mean something material or visible, for God is a pure and simple Spirit; and therefore it does not pertain to his body. I also do not understand it strictly in respect to the essence of his soul—thinking and willing—in which God’s Image resides. Gold, silver, copper, etc., are not strictly the Emperor’s Image; but they are presupposed and required as a material, so that by artistic lines, strokes, or solid colors, his likeness may be imprinted or applied upon them. So it is with man’s soul, or his thinking and willing being. However, knowing, loving, and clinging to the truth makes us like God; assuming a disposition and capacity to be able to understand, judge, and will clearly and distinctly, and the ability and will to direct one’s deeds and life with rational delight, according to the known truth, to the glory of God. Otherwise put: in a love for God and the known truth, or the correspondence of our understanding and will with those of God; that, knowing God, one wills Him as our highest good, and all things to His glory—that is, to acknowledge Him and cling to Him as He is worthy. Put more distinctly: it is located in the right knowledge of the truth which is in God, and which is expressed in the creature to His praise; in a firm attachment or settled state of our will, with delight in and upon that known truth; in a representative and steadfast arrangement of all our deeds according to that known truth; in a governance of all creatures and things subject to our power or belonging to us, to the glory of God according to the known truth; from which inevitably arises an awareness of the goodness and uprightness of our deeds, and consequently a state of blessedness, contentment, and joy.

<column-break/>

Now this is a created image, imprinted upon man in time. That image could fall away and be erased from him, as has been shown. But in a far more excellent sense, with greater power than anyone else, the Christ, the Son of God, is called the Image of the invisible God, *Colossians 1*; the radiance of God’s glory, and the express Image of His substance, *Hebrews 1, 2 Corinthians 4:4*, who is the Image of God.

He is exactly like the Father, *Philippians 2.* God’s Name is within Him, *Exodus 23:21.* He who sees Him sees the Father, for He is exactly like the Father, and one with Him. *John 14:9, 10, John 5, and 10.* <margin>God’s Son equal with the Father.</margin>

He is so named, not as Crellius and Schlichting <note>Socinian theologians who denied the full divinity of Christ.</note> would have it, <italic>because He revealed God’s will and virtues to us through the Gospel.</italic> For Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles did that as well. No one who makes known the will of a king, describes his life, deeds, or virtues, and displays them, is called his Image for that reason. Rather, there is a greater correspondence between the king and his attendants in this respect than between the sketching of his will and the outlining of his planned deeds and virtues through the closest expressions and the clearest, most powerful, and liveliest representations and words. It is not according to the base opinion of the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Christ was a created being, not of the same substance as the Father.</note>, <italic>that Christ was indeed of a similar nature and essence, but not of the same.</italic> And to use a language familiar to the learned in this matter, we say that the Christ appears in this designation because He has His essence from and of the Father: because he who sees Him sees the Father: since through an eternal and incomprehensible generation, He is of one essence with the Father, of the same nature, power, and glory. See Cocceius, Crocius, and Davenant on *Colossians 1:15.* In Him one saw, as it were, the invisible God revealed in the flesh. *1 Timothy 3:16.* One saw all Divine virtues shining through Him.

And in this manner our learned Annotators <note>Referring to the *Kanttekeningen* of the Dutch States Bible.</note> write on *Colossians 1:15: Christ is called the Image of God, not only in respect to His Divine nature, being the eternal Word and the wisdom of the Father, but also in respect that He is God revealed in the flesh, through whom God’s glory, righteousness, grace, wisdom, and power are expressed to us in the Gospel, as in a mirror.* See also Calvin, Melanchthon, Balduinus, Crocius, etc.

Also insofar as He is God and Man: but not in respect to His body. God is a Spirit, *John 4:24, Acts 17:19 <note>Original citation likely intended Acts 17:29</note>, Romans 1:23.* Therefore He who is the Image of God must necessarily be a Spirit, or have a Spirit within Him, for the Image is spiritual, and God is a Spirit. Nevertheless, insofar as He is man, having a rational soul, understanding, and will, so He has...

<meta>This page continues the theological and historical exploration of "The Image," transitioning from the physical representation of monarchs on coins and statues to the spiritual "Image of God" in man, the "Image of the Beast" in the Papacy, and the relationship between the Law as a "shadow" and the Gospel as the true "image" or substance.</meta>

God has communicated some of his virtues to man, or impressions of his attributes: wisdom, righteousness, holiness. However, I will not dwell on this here.

An Image, when considered in terms of something material and visible, presupposes some solid substance as a subject, in which—through the art of engraving, carving, drawing, or painting—one captures a person’s form and essence as closely as possible. This may be done on a large or small scale, in or on gold, silver, copper, or marble; in rings, on medals, and so forth, to resemble someone. Because of this, people are accustomed to saying, *this is he, or that one; my father, my mother, the king, the emperor, etc.*

That such images of kings and emperors, and indeed their likenesses, have been found—whether in statues, in rings, or on coins—and that they have been honored, that sacrifices have been made to them and they have been worshipped, and placed upon and near altars in temples and sacred places, would take too long to demonstrate here. *See Kipping, Roman Antiquities, pages 631-775, etc.; Ursinus, Analecta, Vol. I, Chapter 56; Hoffman, Lexicon Universale, page 904.* <note>These are standard 17th-century references to classical history and archaeology.</note>

And that there were minted materials featuring the Image of the emperor for the payment of tribute, as a proof of submission, seems clear to me from the question and answer of Jesus: *whose Image is this, etc.* <note>Referring to Matthew 22:20, regarding the "tribute penny."</note> One may consult the discourse of Marquardus Freherus regarding the Tribute Penny.

No one may stamp or possess an Image other than that of God, as the Monarch. If Satan stamps any Image in or upon man; if the Antichrist possesses or sets up a particular Image, it is a theft of God’s honor, a false Image. When fallen man brought forth people after his own image and likeness, then God’s Image and stamp were erased. God by no means recognized it as His own.

Yet one lives by an Image of the beast, making it come alive and worshipping it; which, because it is not of God and contests the high and supreme authority of the only Lord, ends very poorly for those who honor it. *Revelation XIII, XIV, XV, XIX, and XX.*

I am thinking here not only and primarily of a literal and stated Image, or Images in the Roman Church and Roman state or body (the beast); nor of the Image of the Pope; but specifically of an Image in the minds of the Beast—those who make up the Antichristian body and kingdom. This is that internal "imagination" they have of the Pope’s supremacy, infallibility, and power, through which he is supposedly infallible by the constant help of the Holy Spirit, master over the faith, capable of giving laws, and able to bind the conscience to faith and obedience. By his command, one must accept and hand over everything without him giving a reason, simply because it pleases him through his full power. Thus, he, with his Consistory, decides and determines everything. He is the head, the master, the soul of all Councils, Cardinals, and Bishops; in such a way that nothing is valid except what is stamped with his Image and likeness: and everything must proceed in this way. On this, the monks and other clergy insist strongly, in order to maintain the unity of the church, the spirit, and the faith. In earlier times, men struggled fiercely for this, but until now they could by no means reach it, so long as they asserted and pursued the fallibility of the Pope, the superior

<column-break/>

distinction of the Councils above the Pope, the freedom to convene Councils for the Bishops without the Roman Bishop, and his supreme and determining power. They judged outright that he who sought to overrule his fellow Bishops and usurped supreme authority in the church was the Antichrist.

One reads in *Hebrews X:1 that the Law had a shadow of the good things to come, and not the Image of the things themselves:* where the Image is contrasted against the shadow.

Paul gives the reason why the Aaronic High Priest had to repeat and renew the annual sacrifices, and why Christ has perfected all with one sacrifice, without the necessity of repeating his offering.

<margin>The word Law taken broadly.</margin>
If one takes the word *Law* in its broadest sense, and understands by it the entire word of the promises and shadows concerning the future goods of the New Testament—initially and then perfectly enjoyed in the state of glory—I have no objection to that. I also find it acceptable if one thinks that Paul had in mind the practice of painters and artists, who make a rough sketch, an imperfect drawing with chalk or charcoal, before they finish the roughly outlined subject with solid and vivid colors. This rough sketch and imperfect drawing disappears more and more, and finally entirely, when the vivid colors, with highlights and depths, are laid over it.

<margin>Parable of the painters.</margin>
Thus, I view the Law in its execution as a rough sketch, an imperfect, dark underpainting <note>original: "doodverwinge," a technical art term for the first layer of paint that defines shapes before the final colors are added.</note> or drawing of that which would be clearly distinguished and perfectly seen and experienced in Christ and the word of fulfillment. Because of this, the shadow would yield and thereby be nullified. *The Syriac Translator says: the shadow is never the substance of things. Therefore, the Image is the substance of the things sketched and underpainted.*

The shadow implies that there is a body, although the body itself is sometimes not yet seen.

The shadow points us to the body.

<margin>Shadow and body.</margin>
The shadow does not have perfection like the body, but is a rough and imperfect drawing of the body.

The shadow and the body are two distinct things: though they have some similarities with one another and correspond to each other, the shadow nonetheless indicates that the body is not where the shadow is. One may consult Poole, Cocceius, Gerhard, Sebastian Schmidt, Schmidius, Hoecke, d'Outrein, and others on this matter.

Regarding this matter—as it will provide understanding in a case of exemplary and necessary Religion: the service under Moses and the service under Christ and the Gospel, under bondage and freedom, under the letter and under the spirit—I shall, with the reader's permission, reveal my thoughts on this piece somewhat more plainly for better comprehension.

<margin>Further explanation.</margin>
Under the rough and imperfect sketch and pre-drawing of old, it was such that in the imperfect design one could nearly see and guess what the Artist and Painter intended. In almost this same manner, the old and exemplary Religion is spoken of. *Galatians III:1: O you foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you...*

*...that you should not obey the truth: before whose eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified among you.* <note>original: "voor de oogen te vooren is geschildert geweest." This refers to Galatians 3:1.</note> and *Colossians 2:17. Which are shadows of things to come, but the body is Christ. And Hebrews 8:5. who serve as a copy and shadow of heavenly things.*

If my reader does not yet understand it in this way, I wish to speak more plainly, and say then: Through the *Tabernacle, the Temple, the rooms of both, the furniture and house-ornaments: the Priests, their work and practices regarding the livestock, etc.* the Lord drew a rough sketch: showing that his Son, as mediator, <term>surety</term><note>A legal term for someone who takes responsibility for another's debt; here, Christ paying the debt of sin.</note>, High Priest, and for the people, would bring about redemption through his deeds and suffering.

And if this saying of mine is still not understood by some, then I wish to speak even more clearly and say:

<margin>A closer explanation.</margin>
a. If the Lord dwelt in the Tabernacle and Temple through any sign, it provided a sketch of how the fullness of the Godhead would truly, substantially, and bodily dwell in the flesh to be assumed: and truly with his abiding Spirit, grace, help, comfort, and word in the church.

b. If there was in the Tabernacle and the Temple a light from the golden candlestick, to be able to see oneself, not to stumble, and to be able to work carefully; that artistic and manufactured light was an image and rough preview of how the light of the manifold Spirit would give a much more excellent light in Jesus unto fulfillment, etc. This was so that one might know what they, as God’s servants in his sanctuary, standing and walking, must observe to be pleasing to him, for God’s honor and the edification of the neighbor, in faith, in love, with joy and willingness.

c. If a table with Showbread was prepared there for the nourishment of the priesthood; it was an image of how he would provide for his spiritual priests and ministers under the new administration, not only with physical things for their necessary existence while they served the spiritual: but also the bread and food, not of meat and drink, but of word, spirit, grace, and earned treasures of salvation, through the Holy Spirit, in communion with him, who has become the bread of life and the drink of the soul. *John 5:6. Romans 14:17.*

d. If an altar of incense with its accessories was found there, where the continual burnings and ignitions were performed; it portrayed and gave to understand how in the church of the New Testament the spiritual Priests would pray, thank, and praise God in the Spirit in the name of the glorified Messiah.

e. If one saw and found there an altar of burnt offering: priests sacrificing, washing, sprinkling, and observing purity, etc. it portrayed the Messiah as mediator, Priest, altar, and offering, whose Spirit, working in the power and value of his obedience, would de-sin and cleanse the sinners: and how the spiritual Priests would strive to cleanse themselves and their neighbors from the contamination of flesh and spirit. *1 Corinthians 6:11. 2 Corinthians 7:1, 2. Hebrews 10:24, 25.*

<column-break/>

See, the Law gave a rough sketch and a pre-figuration of that through its practice by the Priesthood, both in the Tabernacle and in the Temple. But the Apostle, proceeding with his discourse, says further, *not the Image of the things themselves.*

the representation of someone is not the person himself, whose image it is. Never is the first sketch and the rough design as perfect as the piece itself when it is worked out, finished, and completed. The shadow is not the body. The Tabernacle, the Temple with its furniture, and all the ceremonies therein, being exemplary, were not that which they portrayed in some measure and in the rough.

One reads in *Psalm 39:7. that man walks as in an image.* <note>Often translated in English Bibles as "man walketh in a vain shew" or "shadow."</note> Certainly the life of a man is a shadow and a defective image of the true life: a performance on the <term>theatre of this world</term><note>A common 17th-century metaphor (Theatrum Mundi) suggesting that earthly life is a temporary stage play compared to eternity.</note>: a sight in a mirror: a ghost and a dream, a thought which quickly passes away. *Psalms 73 and 144. Isaiah 29. Job 14. Psalm 90.*

All the good and the joy of this life is not the true good, life, and joy, but merely an image and quite defective, of the life, happiness, good, and joy of heaven; which goods are prepared, hidden, and locked away for the children of God, who walk by faith and not by sight. *2 Corinthians 4 and 13. 1 John 3:2.*

They then, who are governed only by the outward senses and passions, without saving enlightenment and knowledge of the things which one does not see, they strive for the things that are seen. They have of their life, status, riches, honorary offices, worldly contentment, and joy, that imagination that their happiness and salvation lies solely and only herein. And from this head springs that bustling, rooting, toiling, the anxious concern, and the deliberation, the proud splendor, the idle elevation and imagination, while it is all unsteady, fickle, passing, and these people are often suddenly and unexpectedly cut off from this life, without hope of an eternal life, salvation, and good.

<margin>Image broadly taken.</margin>
The word Image is sometimes taken quite broadly, and gives to understand something in which one is in some measure like someone, and that which one has and possesses after someone else, etc.

So says Paul, *2 Corinthians 11:7. that the man is the image and the glory of God: but the woman the glory of the man.*

Woman and man both bear God’s image, insofar as it lies in knowledge, righteousness, and holiness. Beside this, the man has dominion over the woman.

The man was created first and directly after God’s image: after that the woman, after God’s image, previously placed within the man.

The man is the image of Christ, whose honor and glory may not be covered, but must radiate and shine through powerfully and clearly.

That the woman covers herself before the man, is subject, and obedient, as created out of him and for his sake, serves him for honor and glory. See my explanations of that passage.

The same Apostle in *2 Corinthians 3:18.* speaks of the image, and being changed into that image.

...composition could thus be interpreted: *we all without a veil, or with unveiled face, beholding the glory of God, the same image, the same form of the Lord, as in a mirror, etc.* <note>A paraphrase of 2 Corinthians 3:18.</note>

The glory, the same image of God, or form, the Christ, the Angel of God’s presence, God’s Presence, God’s Image; for he who sees him, beholds the Father, *Malachi 3, Exodus 33, John 14, Colossians 1:15, Hebrews 1:2* in his person, qualities, deeds, and teaching, etc.

The root word *metamorphōmetha* <note>original Greek: $\mu\epsilon\tau\alpha\mu o\rho\phi\acute{\omega}\mu\epsilon\theta\alpha$</note>, *we are changed*, means, *laying aside one's form and appearance, to take on another: to change in shape.*

Moses, by beholding the glorious Lord, changed in countenance or form, for his face shone and sparkled. The Apostles, the ministers of the New Testament, together with all the true members of Jesus Christ, are—by the beholding of Christ (the Lord’s Presence), the consideration of the demonstrated truths, and the shining virtues of God—made glorious, enlightened, shining, and changed. This happens not only inwardly through the irradiation of the soul, enlightenment, and the reformation according to the Lord’s Image, but they also give forth a radiance and light from themselves. This radiance and glow is seen both through the confession of the mouth and the holiness of their conduct. *Psalm 84, Proverbs 4, Matthew 5, 2 Peter 3:18.* They walk as children of light and of the day, and along the path of truth and holiness, they prepare themselves for the most perfect glory. *Ephesians 2:10 and 5, Psalm 17.* And all such things occur through the Spirit of Christ, according to and in following the style of the new covenant. *Jeremiah 31, Ezekiel 36, John 3, Ephesians 1 and 4.*

To this I shall add the expression of Mr. Hermannus Witsius <note>Hermann Witsius (1636–1708) was a prominent Dutch theologian and professor at Leiden University.</note>, Professor at Leiden, in *On the Apostles' Creed* <note>original: "in Symbolo"</note>, page (in my copy) 73. That which once happened to Moses *Exodus 34:29, 30* also occurs in a spiritual manner to those who behold God through the light of faith, earnestly and with perseverance. The rays of the heavenly spirit, proceeding abundantly from the Father of lights and received through faith, penetrate into the innermost part of the soul and clothe her with a new radiance of heavenly holiness. The more a believer beholds him in the spirit, the more clearly he observes his perfections, whose ornament is holiness. The more clearly he observes or knows them, the more he loves them with a more fervent love. The more strongly he loves them, the more passionately he desires to become conformed to the same, etc.

Grand and emphatic indeed!

It was certainly something great and grand in the days of old—indeed Israel’s boast and glory—to have "put on" Moses, and to have been baptized into his name, *1 Corinthians 10,* and in so doing, to step over into his teaching and ministry; but now the Apostles, the believers, and the Ministers of the New Testament have put on Christ. *Galatians 3.*

Formerly they were disciples of Moses, *John 9:28,* but now of Christ, *Matthew 16 and 28, Mark 16.* And therefore they safely lay aside Moses, his teaching, and his ministry, although it had been in glory, and they took on Jesus' yoke, teaching, and ministry. Herein they suffered no loss at all, for through the enlightenment and gracious working of Jesus' Spirit, they passed from a less glorious to a much more glorious ministry: from the servant to the Son and Lord: from the covering

<column-break/>

to the discovery <note>In the sense of "unveiling" or revelation.</note>, from servitude to freedom, from fear to the freedom and joy of the children of God: from the letter to the spirit, from the ministry of death and condemnation to the ministry of the spirit, of righteousness, and of life: from the ministry that passes away to the ministry which remains, from a movable to an immovable kingdom: from the law on tablets of stone to the law on fleshy tablets of the heart.

And so as not to skip what must be noted and highlighted in this matter, let one observe the language of the great Apostle, *1 Corinthians 15:49. And as we have borne the image of the earthly, so shall we also bear the image of the heavenly.*

By nature we are from the first Adam, the father of us all, just as his image is in us. He who sees us, sees him live again: we are like him in nature, qualities, and the punitive consequences of sin, through which the general nature in him suffered shipwreck. We are like him: sinful, mortal, leaning toward evil, powerless to do saving good, worthy of damnation before God.

The children of the second Adam, Christ—his seed, people, and generation—still have quite a bit remaining from the first Adam, yet that grows old and passes away by degrees through diligent, holy, personal practice, though not without struggle and resistance in this life. They bear Christ’s image and become partly and incipiently conformed to him. Nevertheless, as concerns the soul as well as the body, these shall partake of a greater conformity with him, both as to the soul in the body's crumbling into dust, and as to soul and body on the day of resurrection regarding knowledge, holiness, immortality, and glory.

The Apostle speaks further of the image of God’s Son, to whose conformity those whom he knew beforehand are ordained. *Romans 8:29.*

This image, in respect to which there must be a conformity according to his arrangement in those known beforehand by God, must be considered closely.

That God from eternity, out of fallen mankind, has appointed some in Christ to grace and glory, to the praise of his mercy and the boast of his supremacy, is an undeniable truth.

But because God is an all-wise God, a God of order, not denying himself in any of his works but clarifying his virtues, it should be taken into consideration how and in what manner the Lord, in time, carries out his eternal decree, counsel, and purpose in this. Such is shown to us more closely by Paul when he says that God has appointed them to be conformed to the image of his Son.

*Eikōn* <note>original Greek: $\epsilon\acute{\iota}\kappa\acute{\omega}\nu$</note> means an image, likeness, or model. Now, to be conformed to Christ’s image signifies that what is found in Christ should also be found in his members, so that there would be conformity between the members and the head.

It is true that Christ did not come to glory without oppression, suffering, insult, slander, and death. *Luke 24, Philippians 2, Hebrews 12:2.* Likewise, Christ’s disciple must take up his cross and follow his Lord and Master. *Matthew 16.* One suffers with him, to... <meta>catchword: "also" (met)</meta>

*...[prevented] you, that you should not obey the truth: before whose eyes Jesus Christ has been clearly portrayed, as crucified among you.* <note>Galatians 3:1</note> *And Colossians 2:17: Which are shadows of things to come, but the body is Christ’s. And Hebrews 8:5: who serve as the copy and shadow of heavenly things.*

If my reader does not yet understand it in this way, I wish to speak more plainly and say: Through the *Tabernacle, the Temple, both their chambers, the furnishings and house-ornaments; the Priests, their work and practices regarding the livestock, etc.*, the Lord sketched out in the rough: that His Son—as mediator, <term>surety</term><note>A legal term for someone who takes responsibility for another's debt; here, Christ taking on the "debt" of sin.</note>, High Priest, and for the people—would bring about redemption through his deeds and suffering.

<margin>A closer explanation.</margin>
And if these words of mine are still not understood by some, then I wish to speak even more openly and say:

**a.** Just as the Lord dwelt in the Tabernacle and Temple through some sign, it provided a sketch of how the fullness of the Godhead would truly, substantially, and bodily dwell in the flesh to be assumed; and truly with His abiding Spirit, grace, help, comfort, and word in the church.

**b.** Just as there was in the Tabernacle and the Temple a light from the golden candlestick, so that one could see, not stumble, and work with foresight; that artistic and manufactured light was an image and rough pre-showing of how the light of the manifold Spirit would give a much more excellent light in Jesus unto fulfillment, etc. This was so that one might know what we, as God’s servants in His sanctuary, standing and walking, ought to observe as pleasing to Him, for God’s glory and the edification of our neighbor, in faith, in love, with joy and willingness.

**c.** Just as a table with Showbread <note>The twelve loaves of bread placed weekly in the Temple, also called the "Bread of the Presence."</note> was prepared there for the nourishment of the priesthood; it was an image showing that He would not only provide His spiritual priests and ministers under the new administration with the physical needs for existence while they served the spiritual: but also the bread and nourishment—not of food and drink, but of word, spirit, grace, and attained goods of salvation—through the Holy Spirit, in communion with Him who has become the bread of life and the drink of the soul. *John 6:35, 51; Romans 14:17.*

**d.** Just as an altar of incense with its accessories was found there, upon which the continual burnings and ignitions were made; it imaged and gave to understand how in the church of the New Testament the spiritual Priests, in the name of the glorified Messiah, would pray to, thank, and praise God in the Spirit.

**e.** Just as one saw and found there an altar of burnt offering: with Priests sacrificing, washing, sprinkling, and observing purity, etc. It imaged the Messiah—as mediator, Priest, altar, and sacrifice—whose Spirit, working in the power and worth of His obedience, would de-sin and cleanse the sinners: and how the spiritual Priests should strive to cleanse themselves and their neighbors from the defilement of flesh and spirit. *1 Corinthians 6:11; 2 Corinthians 7:1, 2; Hebrews 10:24, 25.*

<column-break/>

See, the Law gave a rough sketch and a pre-figuration of those things through the practices of the Priesthood, both in the Tabernacle and in the Temple. But the Apostle, continuing with his reasoning, says further: *not the Image of the things themselves.* <note>Hebrews 10:1</note>

The depiction of someone is not the person himself whose image it is. Never is the first sketch and the rough design as perfect as the piece itself when it is worked out, finished, and completed. The shadow is not the body. The Tabernacle, the Temple with the furnishings, and all the ceremonies therein—being exemplary—were not that which they imaged to some extent and in the rough.

One reads in *Psalm 39:7, that man walks as in an image.* <note>Often translated in English Bibles as walking "in a vain show" or "like a phantom."</note> Certainly, the life of a human is a shadow and a defective likeness of the true life: a performance on the <term>Theater of this world</term><note>A common 17th-century metaphor (Theatrum Mundi) suggesting that earthly life is a temporary play or stage-show.</note>; a vision in a mirror; a ghost and a dream, a thought which quickly passes away. *Psalms 73 and 144; Isaiah 29; Job 14; Psalm 90.*

All the good and the joy of this life is not the true good, life, and joy, but merely an image—and a quite defective one—of the life, happiness, good, and joy of heaven; which goods are prepared, hidden, and locked away for the children of God, who walk by faith and not by sight. *2 Corinthians 4 and 13; 1 John 3:2.*

They, then, who are governed only by the outward senses and passions, without saving enlightenment and knowledge of the things which one does not see, they strive after the things that one does see. They hold an image of their life, status, riches, honorable offices, worldly contentment, and joy—believing that their happiness and salvation lie solely and uniquely in these. And from this source springs that bustling, rooting, toiling, the anxious worry, and the deliberation, the proud splendor, the idle elevation and imagination; while all of it is unsteady, fickle, passing away, and these people are often suddenly and unexpectedly cast down from this life without hope of an eternal life, salvation, and good.

<margin>The word "Image" taken broadly.</margin>
The word Image is sometimes taken quite broadly, and gives to understand something in which one is to some extent like someone else, and that which one has and possesses following someone else, etc.

Thus Paul says, *1 Corinthians 11:7 <note>The original text mistakenly cites 2 Cor 11:7.</note> that the man is the image and the glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man.*

Woman and man both bear God's image, insofar as it lies in knowledge, righteousness, and holiness. Alongside this, the man has dominion over the woman.

The man was created first, and immediately according to God’s image: thereafter the woman, according to God’s image, previously placed within the man.

The man is the image of Christ, whose honor and glory may not be covered, but must radiate and shine through powerfully and clearly.

See, of these things the Law gave a rough sketch and a preview through its practice by the Priesthood, both in the Tabernacle and in the Temple. But the Apostle, proceeding with his discourse, says further, *not the Image of the things themselves.*

The representation of someone is not the person himself, whose image it is. Never is the first sketch and rough design as perfect as the piece itself when it is worked out, finished, and completed. The shadow is not the body. The Tabernacle, the Temple with the furniture, and all the ceremonies therein, being exemplary, were not the thing which they portrayed to some extent and in the rough.

One lives *Psalm 39:7. that man walks as in an image.* <note>Often translated as "man walks in a vain shadow."</note> Certainly the life of a man is a shadow and a defective image of the true life: a performance on the Theater of this world: a sight in a mirror: a ghost and dream, a thought, which quickly passes away. *Psalms 73 and 144; Isaiah 29; Job 14; Psalm 90.*

All the good and the joy of this life is not the true good, life, and joy, but merely an image—and a quite defective one—of the life, happiness, good, and joy of heaven; which goods are prepared, hidden, and locked away for the children of God, who walk by faith and not by sight. *2 Corinthians 4 and 13; 1 John 3:2.*

They then, who are governed only by the outward senses and passions, without saving enlightenment and knowledge of the things which one does not see, they strive after the things that one sees. They have of their life, state, riches, honorary offices, worldly contentment, and joy, the imagination that their happiness and salvation lies solely and only in this. And from this source springs that tossing, rooting, toiling, the anxious care, and the deliberation, the proud splendor, the vain elevation, and imagination, while it is all unsteady, fickle, passing, and these people are often suddenly and unexpectedly cut off from this life, without hope of an eternal life, salvation, and good.

<margin>Image taken broadly.</margin>
The word Image is sometimes taken quite broadly, and gives to understand something in which one is to some extent like someone, and that which one has and possesses after someone else, etc.

So Paul says, *2 Corinthians 11:7. <note>likely 1 Corinthians 11:7</note> that the man is the image and the glory of God: but the woman the glory of the man.*

Woman and man both bear God’s image, insofar as it lies in knowledge, righteousness, and holiness. Besides this, the man has dominion over the woman.

The man was created first, and immediately after God’s image: after that the woman, after God’s image, previously placed in the man.

The man is the image of Christ, whose honor and glory may not be covered, but must radiate and shine through powerfully and clearly.

That the woman covers herself before the man, is subject, and obedient, as being created from him and for his sake, serves as his honor and glory. See my explanations on that place.

The same Apostle in *2 Corinthians 3:18* speaks of the image, and of being changed into the image.

One should consider the words of Paul in their context—

<meta>This page continues the exploration of "Image" (Beelt), specifically focusing on the transformation of the believer through the "image of God" as revealed in Christ, contrasting the temporary glory of Moses with the eternal glory of the New Testament.</meta>

# IMAGE

We can interpret the composition thus: *we all, without a veil, or with unveiled face, beholding the glory of God, the same image, the same form of the Lord, as in a mirror, etc.* <note>The author is paraphrasing 2 Corinthians 3:18, a central text for this discussion.</note>

The glory, the very image of God, or form, is Christ, the Angel of God’s presence, God’s Face, God’s Image; for he who sees him, beholds the Father, as seen in *Malachi 3; Exodus 33; John 14; Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:2* in his person, qualities, deeds, and teaching, etc.

The root word <note>original Greek: "metamorphōmetha"</note>, *we are changed*, means *laying aside one's form and appearance and taking on another: to change in shape.*

Through beholding the glorious Lord, Moses changed in countenance or form, for his face shone and sparkled. The Apostles, the ministers of the New Testament, along with all the true members of Jesus Christ, are—by beholding Christ, the Face of the Lord, and by contemplating the demonstrated truths and the shining virtues of God—made glorious, enlightened, radiant, and changed. This happens not only inwardly through the illumination of the soul, enlightenment, and reformation into the Lord's Image, but they also give off a glow and light themselves. This is a brilliance and radiance seen both through the confession of the mouth and the holiness of their conduct. *Psalm 84; Proverbs 4; Matthew 5; 2 Peter 3:18.* They walk as children of the light and of the day, and along the path of truth and holiness, they prepare themselves for the most perfect glory. *Ephesians 2:10 and 5; Psalm 17.* and all this through the Spirit of Christ, according to and following the manner of the new covenant. *Jeremiah 31; Ezekiel 36; John 3; Ephesians 1 and 4.*

On this point, I shall follow with the expression of Mr. Hermannus Witsius, Professor at Leiden, in his work *On the Creed*, page 73 of my edition: <note>Hermannus Witsius (1636–1708) was a famous Dutch theologian; "In Symbolo" refers to his commentary on the Apostles' Creed.</note> "That which happened to Moses long ago in *Exodus 34:29, 30*, also befalls in a spiritual manner those who behold God earnestly and with perseverance through the light of faith. The rays of the heavenly spirit, proceeding abundantly from the Father of lights and received through faith, penetrate into the innermost part of the soul and set her with a new brilliance of heavenly holiness. The more a believer beholds Him in the spirit, the more clearly he notices His perfections, whose ornament is holiness. The more clearly he notices or knows these, the more he loves them with a more fiery love. The more strongly he loves them, the more ardently he desires to become conformed to the same, etc."

Stately and emphatic indeed!

It was certainly something great and advantageous in the old days—indeed, Israel’s boast and glory—to have 'put on' Moses and to have been baptized into his name, *1 Corinthians 10*, and in doing so, to step over into his teaching and ministry; but now the Apostles, the believers, and the Ministers of the New Testament have 'put on' Christ. *Galatians 3.*

Formerly they were disciples of Moses, *John 9:28*, but now they are disciples of Christ, *Matthew 16 and 28; Mark 16.* and therefore they safely set aside Moses, his teaching, and his ministry—even though it had been in glory—and they took up Jesus's yoke, teaching, and ministry. In this, they suffered no loss whatsoever, for through the enlightenment and gracious working of Jesus's Spirit, they passed over from a less glorious ministry to a much more glorious one: from the servant to the Son and Lord: from the veil to the

<column-break/>

unveiling, from bondage to freedom, from fear to the freedom and joy of the children of God: from the letter to the spirit, from the ministry of death and condemnation to the ministry of the spirit, of righteousness, and of life: from the ministry that fades away to the ministry which remains, from a movable to an immovable kingdom: from the law on tablets of stone to the law on tablets of flesh in the heart.

And so as not to skip over what is necessary to be noted and illustrated in this matter, let one observe the language of the great Apostle, *1 Corinthians 15:49: And as we have borne the image of the earthly, so shall we also bear the image of the heavenly.*

By nature, we are of the first Adam, the father of us all, and his image is in us. He who sees us, sees him live again: we are like him in nature, qualities, and the punitive consequences of sin, through which the common nature in him suffered shipwreck. We are like him: sinful, mortal, leaning toward evil, powerless toward saving good, and worthy of condemnation before God.

The children of the second Adam, Christ—his seed, people, and generation—still have much remaining from the first Adam, but that grows old and passes away little by little through diligent, holy, personal practice, though not without struggle and resistance in this life. They bear Christ’s image and are made, in part and initially, conformed to him. However, regarding what concerns the soul as well as the body, these shall partake in a greater conformity with him—both regarding the soul in the body's crumbling into dust, and regarding soul and body on the day of resurrection—in terms of knowledge, holiness, immortality, and glory.

The Apostle further speaks of the image of God’s Son, to whose conformity those whom he knew beforehand are ordained. *Romans 8:29.*

This image, in respect to which there must be a conformity according to his arrangement in those known beforehand by God, must be viewed from up close.

That God from eternity, out of fallen humanity, has arranged some in Christ for grace and glory—to the praise of his mercy and the boast of his supremacy—is an undeniable truth.

But since God is an all-wise God, a God of order, never denying himself in any of his works but rather making his virtues clear, one must take into consideration how and in what manner the Lord carries out his eternal decree, counsel, and purpose in time. This is shown to us more closely by Paul when he says *that God has arranged them to be conformed to the image of his Son.*

<note>original Greek: "eikōn"</note> means an image, likeness, or model: now, to be conformed to Christ’s image signifies that what is found in Christ should also be found in his members, so that there might be true conformity between the members and the head.

It is true that Christ did not come to glory without oppression, suffering, insult, slander, and death. *Luke 24; Philippians 2; Hebrews 12:2.* Likewise, Christ’s disciple must take up his cross and follow his Lord and Master. *Matthew 16.* One suffers with him, in order to [be glorified] with [him].

<meta>This page continues the discussion on being transformed into the "Image" (Beelt) of Christ, specifically moving from the internal transformation of the believer to the historical and prophetic examples of "images" found in Scripture, such as Nebuchadnezzar’s statue and the idols of Israel.</meta>

# IMAGE

to be glorified with him. *Romans 8:17; 2 Timothy 3:12; Revelation 3.*

I believe that the Apostle certainly had this in mind here among other things; yet, I do not at all maintain that this would be the only and primary meaning, as the Remonstrants <note>A group of Dutch Protestants who diverged from strict Calvinism, often emphasizing human choice and the possibility of falling from grace.</note> and others have thought. Rather, I understand the matter such that the Apostle speaks of an arrangement and a calling to faith, love, holiness, and thus to glory. For otherwise, many God-forgotten heathens, non-Christians, and nominal Christians would be conformed to Christ’s image; for it is certain that they, just as much as believers, and often through no fault of their own, are mocked, slandered, persecuted, oppressed, and killed. If this were the case, what advantage or priority would the children of God have according to Paul’s design and purpose?

If becoming conformed to Christ’s image meant only enduring humility, suffering, persecution, an unworthy death, scorn, and slander as the established means to be glorified with and alongside Him, then many of the children of God would find their calculations incorrect—specifically those to whom such a state and such a shameful and painful lot is not ordained or does not happen.

<margin>Cross and reproach do not inherently contain happiness.</margin>
The cross, reproach, and suffering do not in themselves contain or bring about happiness <note>The author uses "geluk" here in the sense of "blessedness" or "spiritual well-being."</note>; to suffer these things and to be saved are not bound together in an unbreakable chain with salvation. It is by chance and God’s providence that those things work for the good of God's children. Otherwise, those who were most heavily oppressed, most sensitively insulted, and who suffered the most infamous and painful deaths would have to be the most assured of blessedness.

Paul’s purpose seems to me to be to show that one is conformed to His Son in this life through faith, love, holiness, and all kinds of acts of charity and tender piety, in which He is to be imitated; and that after this life—beginning in the soul and thereafter in the resurrection—they shall resemble Him in soul and body, being conformed to Him who is the Head. On this account, their salvation is firm and certain.

<margin>Conformity with Christ’s image.</margin>
Certainly, Christ is not the firstborn among many brothers solely because of the cross and suffering. Consequently, becoming conformed to the image of Christ consists not only, or even primarily, in suffering scorn, reproach, and the cross; but in a humble state of mind, self-denial, gentleness, patience, loving one another, being holy, and being faithful unto death, which is followed by blessedness and glory. *Matthew 11 and 16; Hebrews 13; Romans 6:8, 9-11; Philippians 3:21; Revelation 2:10, etc.*

<margin>The Image shown to Nebuchadnezzar.</margin>
Thus one reads in *Daniel 2* of an Image, or vision, which appeared to Nebuchadnezzar in his night-dream; yet, upon waking, it escaped him. This was a physical representation or likeness in the form of a Statue, made up of a head of gold, a chest of silver, a belly and thighs of copper, legs of iron, and toes partly of iron and partly of miry clay. This represented such states and successive kingdoms and regimes in terms of glory, luster, strength, durability, instability, etc., corresponding to the nature and value of the aforementioned metals, minerals, and earthly materials. Because of this, some judge

<column-break/>

the Babylonian empire to be represented first in rank and order of time, followed by the Persian, the Greek, and the Roman under Heathendom. By the mixed feet, they see the kingdom under the Antichrist, consisting of a worldly and ecclesiastical authority, with ten toes, or kings; regarding which one may leaf through the writings of learned authors.

<margin>The image of jealousy.</margin>
One reads in *Ezekiel 9:3* <note>The author likely refers to Ezekiel 8:3, which describes the "image of jealousy" (afgodsbeeld van ijver) at the entrance to the Temple.</note> of an image of jealousy, placed by Israel toward the North, in jealousy, or by the gate of the altar.

I do not think that this consisted solely in a false service by Israel—that they served God and approached Him apart from the Messiah, the Christ, who was to appear in the flesh, whose glory the Prophet saw. If they sought Him and served Him only outwardly, apart from the Messiah, they would have served nothing more than a vain, bare image or form—a mere nothing and a phantom that is nowhere, just as the Heathens served their Idols, *Elilim* <note>A Hebrew term often used for "worthless idols" or "non-gods."</note>, etc.

But I would rather think that it should be taken properly and literally as a history of what happened: that an Image was found erected in the house of the Lord, whether by Ahaz, or by Manasseh, though overthrown and destroyed by Josiah and Hezekiah, yet erected anew by the following kings. *2 Kings 16:10, 11:14; 2 Kings 21 and 23; 2 Chronicles 33, 34, and 36.*

These were not only broken by Josiah and Hezekiah through an awakened holy zeal for God; but they also provoked God, stirring Him to jealousy for His honor and spurring Him to righteous vengeance against His wicked, ungrateful, and idolatrous Israel. *Deuteronomy 32:21, etc.*

That they did this according to the manner of the idolatrous nations, especially the Egyptians among whom they had lived—seeking their favor, service, and help against the Babylonians, being inclined to return to Egypt—and that they mistrusted the Lord, conforming themselves to this nation against the Divine prohibition, is beyond dispute for me.

Meanwhile, that Israel served Baal and busied themselves with something that was a ghost, indeed a worthless thing, as they viewed God’s sanctuary, altars, and offerings merely as outward forms; that they did not observe the service of the Lord in faith; that they sought their own righteousness from the works of the law; and that they denied the righteousness of the Messiah—this is in itself truth and a clear matter. This was a whoring away from the Lord, a robbery of His glory and honor (*Isaiah 42, 43, 44, 48*), and therefore, it must stir Him to jealousy. *Psalm 16; 2 Timothy 2, etc.*

One reads of an express Image in *Hebrews 1:3*: "the express image of His person" <note>original Greek: "charaktēr hypostaseōs autou"</note>. This is the express, naked, clear, perfect, and abiding image.

Regarding this, a great deal could be said, if only we were able to fathom the Divine.

I know and confess that God is infinitely above me. I am by no means capable of encompassing God and the Divine with my understanding. Unless God spoke of Himself, and testified of Himself to be a Triune God, I would know nothing of that adorable mystery of my own accord...

<meta>This page continues the entry for "IMAGE" (Beeldt), specifically examining the Greek and theological terminology used to describe Christ as the "Image of the Father" in Hebrews 1:3, transitioning from the believer's experience to the nature of the Trinity.</meta>

# IMAGE

...to know: it feels quite daunting to a mortal to be active with his spirit in such heights and depths; yet with deep reverence and childlike stammering, I dare to say and write something about it in this my Dictionary <note>Original: "Woortboek." The author refers to his work as a lexicon or dictionary of biblical and theological terms.</note>, regarding what has appeared to me in other writers.

<margin>The Syrian [Syriac version] has: the image, the likeness of his being.</margin>
And the express Image of *his substance* <note>Original: "zelfstandigheit." This refers to Hebrews 1:3, "the express image of his person" or "substance."</note>.

The word *hypostasis* <note>Original: "ὑπόστασις." A central term in Trinitarian theology referring to the individual "person" or "subsistence" of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit.</note> (substance, or self-existence) is taken by some not in the sense of the Father’s essence, but in the sense of the Father’s person and existence, the Father being a distinct person or existence from the Son and the Holy Spirit, while all three persons possess one and the same essence. And so the learned Annotators say, *the person of the Father exists in and of himself, and is as the origin of the Son through an eternal and incomprehensible generation* <note>Referring to the "eternal generation of the Son," the doctrine that the Son is eternally produced by the Father without beginning or end.</note>. And so—

<margin>How to understand "Substance" [Self-existence].</margin>
—say Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a prominent Lutheran scholastic theologian.</note> and my Reverend Master in the order of the ministry, David Knibbe <note>David Knibbe (1639–1701), a Dutch Reformed theologian and minister.</note>: the Son is not the imprint of God’s essence, for he himself is God and has the same divine nature as the Father, communicated to him by the Father through eternal generation; but he is the imprint of his person and existence. For if he were the imprint of the essence, he would possess a "likeness of essence" <note>Greek: "homoiousia."</note> but not the same nature and essence with the Father. Therefore, he is an imprint of the person of the Father, as existing in himself like the Father, and therefore also a distinct person from the Father.

*Character* <note>Original: "χαρακτὴρ." Often translated as "express image."</note> (expressed Image): from *charasso* or *charatto* <note>Original: "χαράσσω, χαράττω."</note>, meaning *I press into, off, or out; I carve, I engrave*. It signifies *a form, image, or likeness impressed into something else*. And someone else has said that *character* is not an image or likeness by way of a reflection—such as when the reflection of light rays portrays the essence or form of this or that man on the surface of a mirror, which form is not impressed into the mirror so that it remains there, but vanishes as soon as the person moves away from the mirror. Instead, *character of the substance* [hypostasis] means as much as an *inherent substance* <note>Original Greek: "χαρακτῆρα ἐνυπόστατον."</note>, *an expressed, substantial, subsisting, permanent expression and image* <note>Original Latin: "expressam, substantialem subsistentem, permanentem expressionem, & imaginem."</note>. Athanasius <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian who defended the deity of Christ.</note>, *Diatribe on the Trinity*, Vol. II, page 240: *a self-existent and remaining image, imprint, and impression*. This has led some theologians, wishing to express their concepts regarding this divine height and depth as clearly and comprehensibly as possible, to explain themselves in this way: they have used a seal and a signet ring as a metaphor [symbol]. They imagine for us wax, or another material capable of receiving the impression of what is on the seal or signet ring; the impression or imprint that appears in the lump of wax displays what is engraved in the signet ring. When one compares the imprint with the stamp on the signet ring, they correspond in all parts so perfectly that someone knowing the person's seal or signet ring and seeing the imprint immediately says: "it is that seal, that coat of arms, etc.," of that person, and so forth. And those who have tried to illustrate it for us in this way have further unfolded this likeness as follows:

<column-break/>

*a.* A signet ring and the imprint in the wax, lacquer, etc., correspond with each other in the representation of what is engraved. He who examines the signet ring and the imprint, and compares them, finds that they match. In an even more perfect way, the Father and the Son match: for they match in the same essence, which is why it is said that Christ was in the form of God (Philippians 2:6; *John 5:10*) and in the possession of the same nature and the same essence—something not found in the relationship between a signet ring of copper, silver, or gold and the wax or lacquer.

<margin>Correspondence of the Father with the Son.</margin>

*b.* Yet one should further note this: that although the impressing seal and the impression in the wax have a neat and very close uniformity and correspondence, they are nonetheless so distinct that the seal does not have its impression from the wax, but the wax from the seal. Thus it is said: although God the Father and the Son are equal in nature, glory, majesty, power, honor, and splendor, they are nonetheless distinct persons. The Father does not have his existence from the Son, as the impression does, but the Father has given to his Son—as if by an impression of eternal generation—his existence, the equality in existence, and the possession of life in himself. (*John 5:26; John 10:30-38; Colossians 1:15; 1 John 4:9*, etc.)

*c.* And therefore, just as the seal or signet ring is not one and the same as the wax and the imprint in the wax—and the seal has its own existence separate from the wax—so too the Father and the Son are two distinct existences [hypostases]. Thus, the Father is not the Son, nor is the Son the Father (*John 5:32*). However, just as the impressing signet ring with its engraving corresponds exactly with the imprint in the wax, so also the Son, being most perfectly conformed to the Father, represents and displays the Father by virtue of possessing the same essence and the equality of nature. (*Philippians 2:6; John 10:14-19; Colossians 1:15.*)

*d.* A reflection of someone's image and face on the surface of a mirror does not remain there, and is thus not permanent. Anything imprinted in wax or other materials can wear away and perish over time through age, frequent use, or accident. But the Son of God is such an imprint of the personal existence of the Father that he is and shall remain an eternal and unchangeable image of the Father.

Let this be enough regarding the word IMAGE. I turn to the following subject, lest I be too long-winded.

# I M A G E .

to be glorified with him. *Romans 8:17; 2 Timothy 3:12; Revelation 3.*

I believe that the Apostle certainly had this in mind among other things; however, I do not at all support the idea that this would be the only and primary meaning, as the Remonstrants <note>The Remonstrants were a Dutch theological movement following the teachings of Jacobus Arminius; they often emphasized the role of human will and the shared experience of suffering in the Christian life.</note> and others have thought. Rather, I understand the matter such that the Apostle speaks of an arrangement and a calling to faith, love, sanctification, and thus to glory. For otherwise, many God-forsaken heathens, non-Christians, and nominal Christians would be conformed to the image of Christ, because it is certain that they—just as much as believers, and often through no fault of their own—are mocked, slandered, persecuted, oppressed, and killed. If becoming conformed to Christ's image consisted solely of enduring humility, suffering, persecution, an unworthy death, insult, and slander as the established means to be able to be glorified with and alongside Him, then many of God’s children would find their calculations incorrect—those to whom such a state or such a shameful and painful lot is not ordained or does not occur.

<margin>Cross and reproach include no happiness.</margin>
The cross, reproach, and suffering do not, in themselves, include or bring about happiness or blessing. To suffer these things and to be saved do not exist in a necessary bond or unbreakable link with salvation; it is by chance and God’s providence that these things work for the good of God’s children. Otherwise, those who were most heavily oppressed, most sensitively offended, and who suffered the most infamous and painful deaths would have to be the most certain of blessedness.

Paul's purpose seems to me to be to show that one must be conformed to His Son in this life in faith, love, holiness, and all kinds of acts of charity and tender godliness, in which He is to be followed; and that after this life—beginning in the soul and thereafter in the resurrection—they shall resemble Him in soul and body, being conformed to Him who is the Head. Because of this, their salvation is firm and certain.

<margin>Conformity with Christ's image.</margin>
Certainly, Christ is the firstborn among many brothers, but not solely because of the cross and suffering. Therefore, becoming conformed to the image of Christ is not only, or primarily, located in suffering insult, reproach, and the cross; but rather in a humble state of mind, self-denial, gentleness, patience, in loving one another, being holy, and being faithful unto death, which is followed by happiness and glory. *Matthew 11 and 16; Hebrews 13; Romans 6:8, 9-11; Philippians 3:21; Revelation 2:10; etc.*

<margin>Image shown to Nebuchadnezzar.</margin>
Thus one reads in *Daniel 2* of an Image, or vision, which appeared to Nebuchadnezzar in his night-dream; though upon waking, it escaped him. It was a physical representation or depiction through a Statue, made of a head of gold, a chest of silver, a belly and thighs of copper, legs of iron, and toes partly of iron and partly of miry clay. This depicted various states and successive kingdoms and governments in terms of glory, luster, strength, durability, instability, etc., corresponding to the nature and value of the aforementioned metals, minerals, and earth-stuffs. From this, some judge

<column-break/>

the following to be represented in rank and order of time: the Babylonian Empire; the Persian; the Greek; the Roman under Paganism; and through the mixed feet, the empire under the Antichrist, consisting of a worldly and ecclesiastical authority with ten toes, or kings. Concerning this, one may leaf through the writings of learned authors.

<margin>Image of jealousy.</margin>
One reads in *Ezekiel 8:3* <note>The text says Ezekiel 9:3, but the "image of jealousy" is described in Ezekiel 8:3.</note> of an image of jealousy, placed by Israel toward the North, in the gate of the altar.

I do not think that this would have consisted solely of a false service by Israel—that they served God and approached Him apart from the Messiah, the Christ, who was to appear in the flesh, whose glory the Prophet saw. In this way, by seeking Him and serving Him outwardly apart from the Messiah, they would have served nothing more than a vain, bare image, a form, a mere nothing and a phantom that exists nowhere, just as the Heathens served their Idols, *Elilim* <note>Original: "Elilun." Referring to the Hebrew *elilim*, a term for idols meaning "worthless" or "nothings."</note>, etc.

Rather, I would think that one ought to take it properly and literally as a history of what happened: namely, that an Image was found erected in the house of the Lord—whether by Ahaz, or by Manasseh—which was overturned and destroyed by Josiah and Hezekiah, yet was erected anew by the following kings. *2 Kings 16:10, 11:14, 2 Kings 21 and 23; 2 Chronicles 33, 34, and 36.*

It was not only broken by Josiah and Hezekiah out of a stirred-up holy zeal for God, but it also provoked God and stirred Him to jealousy for His honor, spurring Him to righteous vengeance against His wicked, ungrateful, and idolatrous Israel. *Deuteronomy 32:21, etc.*

That they did this after the manner of the idolatrous nations, especially the Egyptians among whom they had lived, seeking their favor, service, and help against the Babylonians—being inclined to return to Egypt, distrusting the Lord, and aligning themselves with this nation against the Divine prohibition—admits no doubt in my mind.

Meanwhile, that Israel served Baal and occupied themselves with something that was a ghost, even a trivial thing, as they regarded God’s sanctuary, altars, sacrifices, etc., as mere externalities; that they did not observe the service of the Lord in faith; that they sought their own righteousness from the works of the law; and that they denied the righteousness of the Messiah—this is in itself the truth and a clear matter. Since this was a whoring away from the Lord and a robbery of His glory and honor (*Isaiah 42, 43, 44, 48*), it must therefore provoke Him to jealousy. *Psalm 16; 2 Timothy 2; etc.*

One reads of an express Image in *Hebrews 1:3*: <term>the radiance of His glory and the exact representation of His being</term> <note>Original Greek: "χαρακτὴρ ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ" (charaktēr hypostaseōs autou). The author translates this as the "express, naked, clear, perfect, and remaining image" of God's substance.</note>.

Quite a lot could be said regarding this, if only we were able to fathom the Divine.

I know and confess that God is infinitely above me: I am by no means capable of encompassing God and the Divine with my understanding. Unless God spoke of Himself and testified of Himself to be a Triune God, I would know nothing of that adorable mystery by myself...

# IMAGE.

to know: it feels somewhat daunting for a mortal to be active with their spirit in such heights and depths: yet with deep reverence and childish stammering, I venture to say and write something about it in this my Dictionary, which has occurred to me from other writers.

And the expressed Image of his substance. *The Syrian <note>Referring to the Syriac Peshitta translation of the Bible.</note> has: the image, the likeness of his being.*

The word *hypostasis* <note>original: ὑπόστασις</note>—substance or self-existence—is taken by some not in the sense of the Father's essence, but in the sense of the Father's person and subsistence; the Father being a distinct person or subsistence from the Son and the Holy Spirit, while all these three persons possess one and the same essence. And so the learned annotators say, *the person of the Father exists in and of himself, and is the origin of the Son through an eternal and incomprehensible generation.* And so

<margin>How "substance" should be understood.</margin>

Gerhardus <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a prominent Lutheran scholastic theologian.</note> and my Reverend Master in the preaching order, David Knibbe <note>David Knibbe (1639–1701) was a Dutch Reformed minister and author of a well-known manual on divinity.</note>, say: the Son is not the impression of God's essence, for he himself is God and has the same divine nature as the Father, communicated to him from the Father through eternal generation; rather, he is the impression of his person and subsistence. For if he were the impression of the essence, he would possess a likeness of being, but not the same nature or the same essence as the Father. Therefore, he is an impression of the person of the Father as existing in himself, like the Father, and therefore also a distinct person from the Father.

*Character* <note>original: χαρακτὴρ</note>, expressed Image: from *charasso* <note>original: χαράσσω or χαράττω</note>, "I press in, off, or out; I carve, I engrave": it signifies a form, image, or likeness impressed into something else. And someone else has said, *character* is not an image or likeness by way of a reflection—like when the reflection of light rays represents the essence and form of this or that person on the surface of a mirror—which form is not pressed into the mirror in such a way that it remains there, since it vanishes as soon as the person moves away from the mirror. Instead, *the character of his substance* <note>original: χαρακτὴρ ὑποστάσεως</note> means as much as *a substantial, subsisting, and permanent expression and image* <note>original: χαρακτῆρα ἐνυπόστατον, ἐκφαυλὰμ, subsistantialem subsistentem, permanentem expressionem, & imaginem</note>: Athanasius, *Dialogues on the Trinity*, Volume II, page 240. A *self-existing and remaining image, and impression.* This has led some theologians, wishing to express their concepts regarding this divine height and depth as clearly and understandably as possible, to explain themselves in this manner: they have used a seal and a signet ring as an emblem or statue. They represent to us wax, or another material capable of receiving the impression of what is in and on the seal or the signet ring; the impression or print that appears in the lump of wax shows what is engraved in the signet ring. When one compares the impression or the printed thing with the stamp on and in the signet ring, they correspond with each other in all parts so perfectly that someone knowing the seal or signet ring of a person and seeing the impression says at once: it is

<column-break/>

that seal, those arms, etc., belonging to him, and so forth. And those who have tried to represent it to us in that way have subsequently unfolded this likeness more closely:

a. A signet ring and the out-print or impression in the wax, lacquer, etc., correspond with each other in the rendering of what is engraved. He who observes the signet ring and the impression and compares them with each other finds that they correspond. In an even more perfect way, the Father and the Son correspond: for they correspond in the same essence, which is why it is said that Christ was in the form of God (Philippians 2:6; John 5:10) and in the possession of the same nature and the same essence, which is not found to be the case with a seal or signet ring made of copper, silver, or gold and the wax or lacquer.

<margin>Agreement of the Father with the Son.</margin>

b. However, one then notes this: that although the impressing seal and the impressed wax have a neat and very close uniformity and correspondence with each other, they are nevertheless so distinct from each other that the seal does not have its impression from the wax, but the wax from the seal. Likewise, it is said that although God the Father and the Son are equal to each other in nature, glory, majesty, power, honor, and splendor, they are nevertheless distinct persons; and that the Father does not have his subsistence from the Son, but that the Father has given to his Son—as if by an impression of eternal generation—his subsistence, the equality in subsistence, and the having of life in himself. *John 5:26; John 10:30-38; Colossians 1:15; 1 John 4:9, etc.*

c. And therefore, just as the seal or the signet ring is not one and the same as the wax or the thing printed in the wax—and the seal possesses a self-subsistence apart from the wax—so also the Father and the Son are two distinct subsistences: so that the Father is not the Son, nor the Son the Father (John 5:32). Nevertheless, just as the impressing signet ring with its engraving corresponds exactly with the print in the wax, so too the Son, being perfectly conformed to the Father, represents and shows the Father because of the possession of the same essence and the equality of nature. *Philippians 2:6; John 10:14-9; Colossians 1:15.*

d. A reflection of someone's image and face on the surface of a mirror does not stay there, and thus it is not permanent. Anything impressed in wax or other materials can wear away or perish over time through age, frequent use, or accident: but the Son of God is such an impression of the personal subsistence of the Father that he is and shall remain an eternal and unchangeable image of the Father.

Let this be enough on the word IMAGE. I turn to the following matter, so as not to be too long-winded.

<meta>This page transitions from the entry on "Image" (referencing the divine image) to a new alphabetical entry for "Bones" (Beenen), shifting from the theological concept of Christ's personhood to the physical and metaphorical nature of the human skeleton.</meta>

# BONES.

### BONES, SKELETAL REMAINS, MORTAL REMAINS.
-><gloss>Hebrew: Bone, Bones</gloss>, *bones*<note>original: עצם, עצמות, *ossa*</note><-

<margin>Bones, the strongest parts of the body.</margin>
THE Bones are the very firmest parts of the human body, upon which the entire body rests, around which it grows and closes, giving the proper stability, and the primary strength and posture to the whole body.

When these are maimed, broken, weakened, twisted, decayed, or wasted away, etc., people must lie down, sit, or crawl, depending on whether the affliction is great, heavy, long-lasting, or brief.

Because the BONES and SKELETAL REMAINS are indeed the most powerful part of the body—the pillars and supports of that structure—it is no wonder that they are sometimes mentioned to represent the entire person. This is especially true since the most visible weakening is observed in that state when the human limbs sink and collapse, and a person can no longer stand nor move from one place to another due to the weakness, trembling, and staggering of the legs <note>The Dutch word 'beenen' refers to both 'bones' and 'legs'.</note>.

Now, it is certain from experience what sorrow and torment arising from many causes can bring about, leading to the ruin of the frame, the wasting of strength, and the total weakening of the person. For this reason, in the Holy Scrolls, when the strongest sorrow or greatest torment—which consumes the flesh, the marrow, the nerves, the strength, indeed everything—turns a person into a skeleton and makes them "die in their shoes," this misery is expressed by saying that the bones are terrified, or that the evil has penetrated even to the skeletal structure, from which this weakening and trembling comes. In *Psalm 6:2*, we find that they weaken and grow old, as if drying out (*Psalm 32:3; Proverbs 17*). When external violence and cruel torture are added, such as Christ endured when stretched out on the cross, one can easily count the bones (*Psalm 22:17*).

If a person, after preceding oppression, grief, scorn, and persecution, is permitted to see good days and enjoy God's goodness—so that the following joy surpasses the previous cause for sorrow, making it depart from the heart and be forgotten—one enters, as it were, into another life: one thrives and sleeps well. Good fluids are prepared and spread through the body. The strength penetrates powerfully, even to the bone; the change is externally very great and remarkable. This is conveyed in *Isaiah 58* and *66* by "making the bones strong" and "making them flourish like grass." It is also said that the bones that were broken and weakened, as if by crushing and wasting, rejoice (*Psalm 51*), for a person in such a case cannot feign it. Their face and behavior, along with the movement of their body, demonstrate it sufficiently.

And along this figurative tack, many texts in God’s Word must be turned and explained according to this manner of speaking.

To those knowledgeable in antiquity and well-read in the words of God, it is a known thing that remaining unburied, or digging up someone's bones from the grave to scatter them and turn them to dust and filth, exposing them to all kinds of indignities, was held by both Jews and Pagans to be a great scorn, judgment, and heavy punishment. It was not a proof of love, but of hatred; not of respect, but of contempt; not of friendship, but of open enmity, when one saw someone's remains meet such a fate.

<column-break/>

Ovid, in his poem against Ibis <note>A curse poem by the Roman poet Ovid.</note>:

> *May your bones rest no more happily than those of Pyrrhus,*
> *Which lay scattered across the Ambracian roads.*
<note>original Latin: *Nec tua quam Pyrrhi felicius ossa quiescant, Sparsa per Ambracias quæ jacuere vias.*</note>

->That is:<-

> *And your remains must not rest with more blessing*
> *Than those of Pyrrhus, which lay scattered along the ways.*

And see whether the same judgment of God is not threatened in *Jeremiah 8:1, 2* and perhaps also *Ezekiel 6*.

Horace in his Odes:

> *Alas, the barbarian victor will stand upon the ashes,*
> *And the horseman will strike the city with sounding hoof:*
> *The bones of Romulus, which lack wind and sun,*
> *Will he insolently scatter—a horror to behold.*
<note>original Latin: *Barbarus heu cineres insistet victor...* referring to the feared destruction of Rome.</note>

->That is:<-

> *The enemy shall stand upon the ashes of doleful Rome,*
> *And gallop through the city's bounds with his clattering hooves.*
> *The remains of Romulus, which lay safely buried*
> (*Who sees it without a sigh, who without tears?*)
> *Shall he scatter out of untamable arrogance.*

<margin>Care of the ancients for the remains.</margin>
Certainly, from of old, singular care has been taken for the bones of the dead; and although it was the custom to burn the corpses on woodpiles, if not the ashes, at least the remnants of the bones were carefully gathered and enclosed in jars of gold, silver, copper, baked earth, or even glass, according to each person's status or means.

<margin>The Collection.</margin>
This was called *Ossilegium* <note>From Latin: *os* (bone) + *legere* (to gather).</note>, which means the gathering of bones.

The vessels and the boxes were called *vasa* (vessels) and *urna* (urn).

They had a general box in which the specific family jars were enclosed, which they called *ossuaria* (ossuaries). I do not care to show with what circumstances, ceremonies, state, remarkable expense, or even waste of money this sometimes took place, but rather the essential facts just mentioned. Propertius, *Book II, Elegy 10*:

> *Let a tiny vessel receive my departed spirit.*
<note>original Latin: *Accipiat manes parvula testa meos.*</note>

->That is:<-

> *A small funeral urn must in the end encompass my ashes.*

Virgil in the 6th book of the *Aeneid*:

> *The gathered bones Chorineus covered in a bronze jar.*
<note>original Latin: *Ossaque lecta cado texit Chorineus aheno.*</note>

->That is:<-

> *The remains, then gathered together, were poured*
> *By Chorineus into a copper box or vessel.*
