# BONES.

I 2
<meta>catchword: us:</meta>

->*Tibullus Book III. Elegy 2.*<-

> *Let her, clad in a black garment, gather my white bones, the only part of my body that will remain.* <note>original: "Pars quæ sola mei superabit corporis, ossa, Incinctæ nigra candida veste legent."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Let her in deep mourning gather my white bones,*
> *The only part of my body that will remain.*

*See Balthasar Bonifacius, Ludicra History page 61. Kipping, Roman Antiquities. Kirchmann, On Funerals. Hofmann, Lexicon, etc.*

<margin>Transport of the bones.</margin> That one reads of transporting someone's bones to be buried elsewhere—particularly those of Joseph, taken to Canaan according to his request and command in *Exodus 13, Joshua 24, 2 Samuel 21,* etc.—may have had a specific purpose. *Hebrews 11:22* compare *Genesis 50:24, 25.* For he desired to be buried in the promised land, as he foreknew that his people would dwell there; he wanted to demonstrate that he believed and was certain that the Lord would give the land of Canaan to his brothers as an inheritance, in accordance with His many repeated promises. Also, it was so that upon the rise of a foreign or different king, his bones would not be treated with contempt or used for a type of idolatry.

Truly, the practice of digging up bones, shaking the graves, and throwing the skeletal remains—ostensibly for show—into a charnel house <note>A 'knekelhuis' or charnel house was a building where bones were stored when old graves were dug up to make room for new ones.</note> to demonstrate common mortality and frailty, does not seem to me to be a matter that deserves full approval. For the bones demand the earth just as much as the rest of the human body; and why should one part be covered with earth more than the other? Especially since they have already been covered with earth and buried. One can (if one properly observes the examples of the dying and those being brought to the earth) notice common mortality enough; and one does not necessarily need to gain space through this practice, for the bones of the buried are already lying there. One can find enough space if one seeks it.

And since it is observed most of the time that the bones of the wealthy are collected and placed in chests, why should the bones of the poor be disturbed, dug up, and publicly displayed in bone-houses in a manner of disregard, exposed to weather, wind, vermin, and other discomforts? Certainly, however educational this sight may be, the view of it is terrifying and hideous. One grows accustomed to it, however, and the emotional impact lessens over time. Such a sight is not always useful. Experience has taught how, on such occasions, people have taken up "holy remains"—the bones of this or that supposed saint—publicly displayed them, knelt before them, kissed them, performed masses and prayers for the deceased, and attributed strange power and dignity to the dead bones, and more of the like.

One reads by way of prophecy in *1 Kings 13:2, 3* that Josiah would burn the priests and smoke their bones upon the altar at Bethel, which was built for idolatry; and the fulfillment is recorded in *2 Kings 23:15, 16, 17* and *2 Chronicles 34:5.* This was done to defile that place and to show how seriously God took the matter, and to make understood the holy zeal of the counter-prophesying Prophet 

<column-break/>

who had zealously prophesied against the abominations, public idolatry, and inhuman cruelty of the children of Israel. Otherwise, among the Jews, one knows of no burning of someone's bones, but rather of burying them. *See Josephus, Antiquities Book XVIII, Chapter 23.*

<margin>Bones buried among the Jews.</margin> When one reads the phrase *bone of my bone, flesh of my flesh, my flesh, my bone* in *Genesis 2, 2 Samuel 19, Judges 9, Ephesians 5,* I hold that it signifies the closest and nearest blood relationship, kinship, and love. This is now applied in *Ephesians 5* to the communion that believers have with Christ: according to the flesh, as our brother (*Hebrews 2 and 4*), and according to the spirit, through faith, by which we cling to him in love, he being the head and we the members, being inspired, mastered, and governed by him (*1 Corinthians 12 and 14, 1 Corinthians 6*). He takes his church as his bride and wife, becoming as one with him (*Hosea 2:18, 19, 2 Corinthians 11, Song of Solomon 2:16, 1 Corinthians 6:15, Romans 8:9*), which the Apostle calls a mystery, wherefore it is also to be understood spiritually.

It serves as a parable and allusion when Christ compares the hypocritical Scribes and Pharisees to whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful on the outside but are full of dead men’s bones and all kinds of uncleanness within. *Matthew 23:27.*

Some parables and phrases derived from burial places are found in *Priceus* <note>John Price (1600–1676), a Welsh scholar known for his commentaries on the New Testament.</note> on this passage.

->Laberius:<-

> *Resembling a grave, I retain nothing of myself but the name.* <note>original: "Sepulchri similis, nil nisi nomen retineo."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Resembling a grave, I have nothing of it but the name.*

->Ovid:<-

->That is:<-

How truly the Jews plastered and whitewashed the graves to identify the unclean places and to guard against them, so as not to be defiled, can be read in Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Rabbinical scholar.</note> on this passage.

<margin>Hypocrites compared to painted, marked burial places.</margin> I have noted that the Jews themselves compared hypocrites to such whitened and plastered burial places. In the *Babylonian Sotah, page 22,* the hypocrites are called *dyed* or *marked ones.* <note>Hebrew: צבוعيן (*tzavuim*), meaning colored or painted, implying someone who puts on a false front.</note> And it is told of King Yannaeus <note>Alexander Jannaeus, a Hasmonean King of Judea.</note> that on his deathbed he warned his wife to beware of "painted people" who pretend to be Pharisees, whose works are like those of Zimri <note>Zimri was a prince of Israel who committed public immorality and was killed by Phinehas (Numbers 25).</note>, but who yet expect the reward of Phinehas. us: These "painted people" are those whose outward appearance does not match their nature; they are painted on the outside, but their exterior is not like their interior. Their works are evil, like those of Zimri <note>Zimri was a king of Israel who gained the throne through murder and reigned only seven days; he became a byword for a traitorous or wicked person.</note>; yet they demand the reward of Phinehas <note>Phinehas was a priest in the Old Testament rewarded by God for his zeal in executing wrongdoers.</note> and demand that people honor them as they would Phinehas.

Thus have they forgotten the maxim established of old among them, *Babylonian Talmud, Yoma, page 72, 2: A disciple of the wise, who is not the same on the inside as he is on the outside, is no disciple of the wise.*

Such people appear beautiful but are wicked within, varnishing their vice with a lovely appearance.

->Persius in his fifth satire:<- <note>original: "Pelliculam veterem retinens, & fronte politus / Astutam vapido servas sub pectore vulpem."</note>

> *Retaining your old skin, and polished on your brow,*
> *You keep a wily fox beneath your spoiled heart.*

->That is:<-

> *When you present yourself as a lamb upon your brow,*
> *And let a cunning fox within your breast reside.*

Bernard <note>Likely St. Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century abbot known for his influential writings on spirituality and morality.</note> captured this sort of person quite true to life, if one pays proper attention to his description.

<margin>Hypocrites described.</margin>
Hypocrites want to be humble without being belittled; poor without any lack; well-clothed without any worry. They are possessors of a pleasant rest without labor. Some smear honey around the mouth and flatter, while others extort. They are snappy like dogs, intent on clever deceit like foxes, and proud like lions; yet inside they are ravening wolves. They stand like bears reaching for empty glory and hidden lust. They want to be judges without authority, and witnesses without having seen anything; finally, they are false accusers, bereft of all truth.

That which one reads in *Ezekiel 24* concerning that pot with pieces of meat and bones, with fire stoked beneath it and a pyre of bones to cook it thoroughly—without the rust of the pot or the kettle being removed thereby—cannot well be understood except as a parable, in figure and imagination. it depicts the calamity and the weighty, righteous judgment that would befall the bloody city of Jerusalem through the Babylonians during their lengthy siege, the capture, the destruction of the city and temple, and the killing of great and small. This was to happen without them being purified or reconciled for the shed blood of so many prophets and pious men, whose bones buried beneath her cry out for vengeance and would heavy their judgment—alongside that extreme godlessness practiced upon young children when they were sacrificed to Moloch.

Again, one reads in *Ezekiel 37* that there were bones in the valley, as if on a flat field, through which the wind blew, and in time they moved and became alive, etc., until the end of that chapter. I take this up not in the sense that it speaks literally of the actual resurrection of the dead on the Last Day; no, but primarily of the remarkable change in the civil and ecclesiastical state of Israel. They were as if civilly dead while the Israelites were in the captivity of Babylon and scattered among that nation, but would receive freedom through Cyrus, etc., to depart freely from his lands, to rebuild the city and temple, and so forth.

After which time the previously divided tribes were melted into one and became a single kingdom, and in time showed themselves more lively, powerful, and active. Yet, although they were prosperous and as if overloaded with all kinds of external blessings, they only initially received the spirit of life—becoming like dead and lost sheep of the house of Israel—at the time of Christ and his exaltation, when he poured out his spirit upon all flesh. This spirit was not yet present in *John 7, Isaiah 35 and 44, Acts 2, Ephesians 4.* This occurrence among the first-fruits of these dead bones was a depiction of how the Lord would, in the latter days, lay his hand a second time upon the Jews and make them alive (*Isaiah 11, Romans 11, 2 Corinthians 13*), which would be paired with the gathering of the Gentiles to the great feast.

One further reads of the Divine command in *Exodus 12 and Numbers 9* regarding the Passover lamb, that no bone of it was to be broken. David says in *Psalm 34:21: He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken.* In *John 19:33* it is written *that the soldiers did not break the bones of the Christ, for he was already dead;* and in verse 36, he appeals to the Divine scripture.

<margin>Christ the lamb of God.</margin>
It is certain that Christ is the slaughtered lamb of God, our beneficial Passover (*1 Corinthians 5:7, 1 Peter 1:19, 20*). It was fixed in God's counsel that no bone of his should be broken, as he had to rise strong, fresh, and unmaimed in the members of his body—he who had healed so many cripples and made them leap. His servile death on the cross was enough, without adding a second servile punishment out of fury.

That this refers to the Passover lamb, I agree; however, I cannot pass over the testimony of the harper [David] in *Psalm 34:20, 21*, where I can understand "the righteous one" par excellence to be God’s righteous servant, who has become our righteousness (*Isaiah 53, 1 Corinthians 1:30, 2 Corinthians 5:21, Romans 5, etc.*). Rabbi Cabana says that one must interpret this as the Passover lamb of the body of the Messiah, which was not to be divided (*Galatinus book 10, Chapter 6; Ursinus, Meditations on the Passover Lamb, page 346*).

I can also well agree that one may have an eye toward the care God takes for his own, without whose will not a hair falls from their heads (*Matthew 10*), so that He sometimes miraculously and very suddenly changes and rescues their confused affairs and oppressed state.

Regarding "bone-breaking" (*crurifragium*), it was a punishment inflicted upon male and female slaves (*Suetonius in Augustus Chapter 67, in Tiberius Chapter 44*). See *Lipsius on the Cross, etc.; Lydius, Scattered Flowers page 267; Hofmann, Universal Lexicon; Kipping, Roman Antiquities, etc.*

<margin>Bone-breaking as an exceptional punishment.</margin>
It was not strictly that crucifixion and bone-breaking were tied together and belonged as one; no, it was a separate punishment. It seems to have been practiced with an iron sledgehammer, after the condemned had been stretched out on some anvil—partially corresponding to the modern practice of breaking on the wheel <note>The 'radbraken' or breaking on the wheel was a common form of execution in the author's time, where a criminal's limbs were shattered with a heavy wheel or hammer.</note>—but in this...

### BEAR, SHE-BEAR
### דב, *arktos, ursus, ursa.* <note>Hebrew: *Dob*; Greek: *arktos*; Latin: *ursus* (male), *ursa* (female).</note>

<margin>The derivation of this word is uncertain.</margin>
Regarding the name of this animal, *Dob*, linguists are not in full agreement as to its derivation. Some believe it should be derived from *dobeb*, meaning "shaggy" or "rough," having long, bristly hair and being by no means pleasant to look upon. Others prefer to see it derived from *daba*, meaning "to walk very slowly" or "sluggish," being heavy and slow due to its clumsy body and dull limbs. Yet others choose to derive it from *dobeb*, meaning "to growl" or "to grumble."

One may consult the dictionaries and works of scholars regarding this, such as *Bochart* in *Hierosol.* page 806, *Schindler, Pagninus, Cocceius, Forsterus,* and *Majus.* <note>These were prominent 16th and 17th-century scholars of biblical animals and languages.</note>

As for the animal itself, I will not describe it from head to foot. One can look it up in *Pliny, Bochart, Majus, Franzius,* etc.

It is a large, clumsy, rough-haired animal, very wild and cruel by nature, often placed alongside lions in scripture, as in *1 Sam. 17:34, Prov. 17:12* and *28:15, 2 Sam. 19:8, Job 13,* and *Amos 5*; especially the she-bear robbed of her cubs.

Its breath is strong and healthy to no one; they do not wish to have their snout touched, or they flare up in great anger and are not easily calmed;

> *Rabido nec perditus ore*
> *Fumantem nasum vivi tentaveris ursi.*
> <note>Latin: "Do not, out of your mind with a mad mouth, try to touch the smoking nose of a living bear."</note>

-> That is: <-

> *Mad you are, and have lost your mind,*
> *If you wish to touch the snout of a bear.*

It is said that bears have weak heads and are much troubled by weakness of the eyes. Because of the weakness of their heads, they cover them with their paws and roll downward from steep cliffs. They seem to be quite restless. It is said they are quite greedy, and for this reason they sometimes fast; they are also quite lustful, so much so that they sometimes do not spare women: for which reason the females give birth so early and suddenly.

It is said, though not proven, and therefore rightly denied based on reason and experience;

<column-break/>

that they would give birth to only a rough and unformed lump of flesh, and fashion it and set it right by brooding over it and licking it. <note>This was a common medieval myth—that "licked into shape" comes from bears literally licking their unformed cubs into the shape of animals.</note>

<margin>Food of the Bears.</margin>
Their food is said to be almost anything, though more specifically: a type of blackberry, wood sorrel, or sour clover; cuckoo-pint; tree fruits, pods, roots, meat (even if it were tainted and half-rotten), and honeycombs, which sometimes turns out very badly for them, as I shall mention hereafter.

It is said that in the evening and morning they lurk around pens and herds, tracking their prey. *Horace, Epode 16*, writing of the Elysian or "Happy Fields":

> *Nec vespertinus circumgemit ursus ovile.*
> <note>Latin: "Nor does the evening bear growl around the sheepfold."</note>

-> That is: <-

> *No Bears sniff there in the evening around the stable.*

<margin>Expressions derived from this.</margin>
As for this animal, the fact that one finds expressions and comparisons derived from the Bear and the wise She-bear in both sacred and secular writings is an indisputable truth and a certain finding.

<margin>Unrefined people are a symbol of Bears.</margin>
*Horus* <note>Referring to Horapollo, an author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> relates *that the Egyptians, wishing to depict a person who in his youth, due to his clumsiness in life and manners, had much to improve and polish, used for this purpose the symbol of a She-bear, cherishing her rough and unformed offspring, and incessantly shaping and licking it.*

And just as it is told of the Bear *that at a certain time, abstaining from food, he sucks his paw without seeking food from elsewhere:* so I would almost think that from this originates our well-known expression, *he sucks it out of his paw* <note>A Dutch idiom meaning "to make something up" or "to fabricate a story."</note>; as if inventing it from himself, without having it from elsewhere.

Again, *Gesnerus* <note>Conrad Gessner, a 16th-century Swiss naturalist.</note> testifies that the *Germans, when they wanted to politely mock someone's greed and stinginess, would say, "he sucks his paw like a Bear."*

If one wanted to sketch the folly of someone who, for a tingling joy and short pleasure, put his life in danger—an undertaking that turned out very poorly for him—*Cauffinus* tells us that a Bear was shown seeking honeycombs in the hollow of a tree (page 367). For he relates from *Olaus Magnus* <note>A Swedish ecclesiastic and writer known for his history of the Northern peoples.</note> in Book 18, Chapter 14, that since in Russia the bees mostly store their honey in hollow trees, and the Bears are crazed for it, the peasants fasten a wooden block with iron spikes to a branch of the tree. This block, hanging over the hole where the bees fly in and out, wounds the madly driven Bear as he seeks the bait, hitting his weak head, often so severely that he must die of it.

In the German work boasting the title, *Five Books of the Widely Renowned Naturalist Pliny the Second*, one reads in Book 2, Chapter 36, this account from *Gesnerus*: *In Norway and Poland, the Bears climb trees to eat honey. Therefore, the hunters go and build large holes in some trees. There they hang large, heavy wooden clubs studded with sharp nails. They smear these all around with honey, and then the bees fly all around them. When the Bears notice this, they climb the trees, and when they try to lift those prepared hanging clubs, they strike back*

Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century French abbot and mystic.</note> captured this sort of person quite true to life, if one pays proper attention to his description.

<margin>Hypocrites described.</margin>
Hypocrites want to be humble without being belittled; poor without any lack; well-dressed without worry; possessors of a delicious rest without labor. Some smear honey around their mouths and flatter, while others extort. They are biting like dogs; intent on cunning deceit like foxes; proud as lions; yet inside they are ravenous wolves. They stand like bears seeking vain glory and hidden pleasure. They wish to be judges without authority, witnesses without having seen; ultimately, they are false accusers, stripped of all truth.

That which one reads in *Ezekiel 24* regarding the pot with pieces of meat and bones, with fire stoked beneath it and a pile of bones for fuel, until it is sufficiently cooked—yet without the rust of the pot or the kettle being removed—can hardly be understood except as a parable, in figure and imagination. It sketches the misfortune and the weighty and righteous judgment which would befall the blood-stained city of Jerusalem by the Babylonians during their long siege, capture, and the destruction of the city and temple, and the killing of great and small. This happened without them being cleansed or reconciled for the shed blood of so many Prophets and pious men, whose bones buried beneath her cry out for vengeance and would weigh down their judgment, alongside the extreme godlessness committed against young children when they were sacrificed to Moloch.

Again, one reads in *Ezekiel 37* that there were bones in the valley, as if on an open field, through which the wind blew; in time they stirred and became living, etc., until the end of that chapter. I take this to mean not in the literal sense of the actual resurrection of the dead on the last day; no, but primarily of the remarkable change in the civil and ecclesiastical state of Israel. They were as if "civilly dead" while the Israelites were in the captivity of Babylon and scattered among those nations, but they would receive freedom through Cy-

<column-break/>

rus, etc., to depart freely from his lands, to rebuild the city and temple, etc.

After which time the previously divided tribes were melted into one and became one kingdom, and in time showed themselves more lively, powerful, and active. Yet, although they grew fat and were as if overloaded with all kinds of external blessings, they nevertheless only initially received the spirit of life—having been like dead and lost sheep of the house of Israel—at the time of Christ and his exaltation, when he poured out his spirit upon all flesh. This spirit was not yet present in *John 7, Isaiah 35 and 44, Acts 2, Ephesians 4.* This occurrence among the "firstfruits" of these dead bones was a sketch of how the Lord would, in the latter days, lay his hand a second time upon the Jews and make them living, *Isaiah 11, Romans 11, 2 Corinthians 13,* which would be paired with the gathering of the Gentiles to the great feast.

One further reads of the Divine command in *Exodus 12 and Numbers 9* regarding the Passover lamb, that no bone of it was to be broken. David says in *Psalm 34:21, "He protects all his bones; not one of them is broken."* In *John 19:33* it is written *that the soldiers did not break any bone of the Christ, for he was already dead;* and in verse 36, the author appeals to the Divine scripture.

<margin>Christ the Lamb of God.</margin>
It is certain that Christ is the slaughtered Lamb of God, our precious Passover, *1 Corinthians 5:7, 1 Peter 1:19, 20.* It was God's fixed counsel that no bone of his should be broken, as he had to rise strong and fresh, unmaimed in the members of his body—he who had healed so many cripples and made them leap. His shameful death on the cross was enough, without adding a second slave’s punishment out of rage.

However, while I agree that the Passover lamb is being referenced, I cannot pass over the testimony of the harper <note>A reference to King David as the author of the Psalms.</note> in *Psalm 34:20, 21.* There, by "the righteous one" par excellence, I can understand God’s righteous servant, who has become our righteousness, *Isaiah 53, 1 Corinthians 1:30, 2 Corinthians 5:21, Romans 5,* etc. *Rabbi Cabana says that this must be taken as referring to the Passover lamb of the body of the Messiah, which must not be divided. Galatinus book 10, Chapter 6; Ursinus, Meditations on the Passover Lamb, page 346.*

I can also well allow that one may have an eye on the care which God carries for his own, without whose will not a hair falls from their heads, *Matthew 10,* so that he sometimes changes and rescues their confused affairs and distressed state quite wondrously and very suddenly.

Regarding the "Breaking of Bones" <note>This refers to the Roman practice of *crurifragium* or *fractura crurum*.</note>, it was a punishment inflicted upon male and female slaves, *Suetonius in Augustus, Chapter 67; in Tiberius, Chapter 44. See Lipsius on the Cross, etc.; Lydius, Florum Sparsio page 267; Hofmann, Universal Lexicon; Kipping, Roman Antiquities, etc.*

<margin>Bone-breaking a special punishment.</margin>
It was not actually that crucifixion and bone-breaking were inherently tied together as one; no, it was a separate punishment. It seems to have been practiced with an iron sledgehammer, as if the condemned had been stretched out on an anvil. It corresponds in part to the modern-day "breaking on the wheel" <term>rabraaken: a form of execution where a criminal's limbs were shattered with a heavy wheel or hammer</term>; but in this—

*Isaiah 24:17, 18; Jeremiah 48; Revelation 9 and 11.* One woe has barely passed before another arrives anew: one enemy has hardly retreated before another, no less mighty, cruel, and evil, arrives to distress and devastate.

<margin>Wicked Princes compared to bears.</margin>
That wicked kings and princes, and those who hold a poor or weak people under their knee, are compared to lions and bears (*Proverbs 28:15*), as they restlessly abuse their power for extortion, oppression, robbery, persecution, etc., does not seem strange to me at all. I encounter them under this name and likeness, described elsewhere to the life. *Ezekiel 19, 22, and 38; Zechariah 11; Zephaniah 3; Matthew 23.*

When Jehovah punishes a people justly and very sensibly, making His judgments penetrate deeply—bringing it about that they are greatly displaced and melted away through wars, internal unrest, and fruitless undertakings—He provides public evidence of His wrath and His intention to openly punish and devastate a people; thus, He is sometimes represented as a lion or a bear. *Hosea 13:8.* And see then the Lord's wrath and work (*Amos 9:4, 5; Psalm 90; Hebrews 12; Psalm 18 and 78*), who then lurks like a lion or bear and shows that He knows the opportunity and has the means at hand to discipline, punish, and even uproot a people. *Lamentations 3:10.*

<margin>Comparison of Satan with a Bear.</margin>
If anyone should desire to make some comparisons between Satan and a bear—which roars when it is deprived of its young (*Isaiah 49; Luke 11*), and which is evil, lurking, and devastating or tearing apart everything that comes under its hand, and is therefore called *Abaddon* or *Apollyon* <note>The "Destroyer" in Hebrew and Greek respectively; see Revelation 9:11.</note> (*Revelation 9; 1 Peter 5:8*)—he will find them easily.

Among the animals appearing in Daniel, one also finds the bear mentioned. *Daniel 7.*

It is generally held that the Medo-Persian Empire is represented by the bear, and reasons for this similarity are given, for:

a. Just as bears are playful and so fond of sweets that they are obsessed with honey and honeycombs—which sometimes costs them dearly and ends badly—certainly those belonging to the Medo-Persian Empire bear the testimony of being very much inclined toward lusts, delicacies, luxury, and splendor; and that they, among other things, weakened their vision through excessive luxury and playfulness.

b. And just as one might consider the weakness of the head and eyes said to be in the bear to understand the condition of the heads and eyes of the subjects of the Medo-Persian Empire, one will find they are described as weak of head and eyes: not very skilled in war or endowed with great military science, being much broken by luxury and playfulness.

c. And as bears are gluttonous in both eating and drinking, and not at all well-behaved, the same is testified of the aforementioned people.

d. If bears are shaggy-haired, so were these people, being very long-haired.

e. If bears are coarse, clumsy, unrefined, and ill-fashioned, that people has been described to us in such a manner.

f. Are they growling, grumbling, and restless? Such traits are also attributed to this people.

A people who were nonetheless strong and cruel, and under King Cyrus and others made quite large conquests, having overcome the Assyrians, Arabs, Cappadociers, Phrygians, Lydians, Phoenicians, Bactrians, etc.

Yet, because some judge Constantine the Great and the first empire of the Christians to be sketched by the lion, it must follow in order that by the bear they understand not just any untamed, wild nations and enemies of Christianity, but more specifically the empire of the Goths (devoted to the Arian heresy), the Vandals, and the Lombards. These had, as it were, three ribs: *Italy, France, and Spain.* <note>Referring to the "three ribs in its mouth" of the bear in Daniel 7:5.</note>

The statement in *Isaiah 11:7* that the cow and the bear shall graze and lie down together—having been made tame and living peacefully, consuming the nourishment of the soul, the word of grace, and the doctrine of righteousness—can signify not only the enlightenment and conversion of coarse and wild peoples and enemies of Christ's church in general, but specifically of the Medo-Persians with their provinces and conquered nations. See what I have published concerning Isaiah chapter 11 in my *Holy Miscellany*, Part I, page 101, etc. *Witsius, Miscellanea, Part I; Bochart, Hierozoicon; Geier on Daniel, etc.* and after me Vitringa on *Isaiah 11:7* regarding the bear, page 332.

<margin>Enemies of the Church compared to Bears.</margin>
Bears, taken distinctly from lions, can signify enemies of the church: barbaric people, cruel, inhuman, endowed with power, staying in their caves, and raging against the church. The emblem, if understood as distinct from the emblem of the lions, leads us there. The Scythians, Goths, Bulgarians, Tartars, and Turks are of that sort.

Otherwise, it is a common symbol for the cruelty of rulers and tyrants raging against those lower ones who are subject to them, as it is used in *Proverbs 28:15.*

# BEER-WELL.

Jews and some Christians have reasonably observed that while other water-wells or fountains were provided to the people after they had murmured, this one was freely pointed out and provided to the people of God. Regarding this state of affairs, <margin>The Beer-well pointed out by God.</margin> it is written that in the presence of the people, and as if through the service of the great leaders, the well was dug and bored through with their staffs and rods. One also reads of this well—unlike the others—that a song was sung for it. This well was dug toward <margin>A song was sung.</margin> the end of Israel’s travels and wanderings, not far from the time when Israel was to enter and take possession of the land of Palestine as their inheritance.

When it is said that the Princes, Nobles, etc., dug this well with their staffs, it is not difficult to understand that it did not cost them much labor. Perhaps the ground was soft and sandy; perhaps by boring with their staffs, they struck water veins, or used them to hollow out the earth to form a sort of basin to receive the rising water. From there, being near Canaan, the water likely flowed toward the camp, following the wish of Israel and the alternating refrain of the song: *spring up, O well*—that is, make your waters swell and come forth abundantly. Meanwhile, the Lord himself performed the work and brought the water forth, for he said: *gather the people, and I will give them water.*

It is easy to believe that Moses, in all outward observances, went before the leaders and the people, and that he and the leaders of the people sang the song in good harmony, taking turns in parts. That one should think here of a well from which one had to draw water manually is not very likely; otherwise, one would have needed an innumerable number of wells, or the bulk of the army would have had to stay very close to it. It likely functioned as a springing well, letting its water follow through channels or gullies like flowing brooks, providing sufficient abundance for Israel’s numerous army in the desert. How long this well remained in existence I do not know, though it is still mentioned in *Isaiah 15:8*.

I have found that some have understood this well in a hidden and secret sense to mean Holy Scripture; Origen understood the "princes" to be the Prophets, and the "kings" to be the Apostles.

For my part—as I relate almost everything from the old state of the Jewish people to Christ and his congregation—just as the "rock that followed them" signified Christ (*1 Corinthians 10*), who is a "well of the gardens" (*Song of Solomon 4*), the "fountain of life" (*Psalm 36:10*), and the "opened fountain" (*Zechariah 13:1*); so would I also propose here that one may judge this Well to be a symbolic sketch of the Messiah, <margin>Christ symbolized by the Well.</margin> the Christ, along with the healing waters of his spirit and grace. (*John 4:14* and *7:37, 38, 39*).

I also believe that this well is dug and opened through the opening of the Scriptures and the ministry of Christ himself, the Apostles, the Pastors, and Teachers. This began early, when the church was ready to accept its inheritance from among Jews and Gentiles—not only among the Jews, but also in the desert of Heathendom (*Isaiah 35 and 44, Joel 2*). However, it shall be opened anew and abundantly during the final journeys toward the full inheritance of the world, through the assistance and efforts of kings and princes, as well as Pastors and Teachers, at their wish and prayer. At that time, a song of thanks shall be raised, singing by turns to God and the exalted King. See *Isaiah 12:3-6, Song of Solomon 8, Revelation 22, etc., Isaiah 41, Joel 3.*

<column-break/>

### BEAST, BEASTS OF REVELATION; <note>Hebrew: Behema (בהמה), Chayah (חיה); Greek: Therion (θηρίον)</note>

AS FOR THE BEASTS or animals—large, small, and of middling sorts—formerly split into clean and unclean, I shall not deal with them here at great length, as the specific animal species will be handled under their own names. I maintain that *Chayah* <note>Hebrew: חיה</note> means a "living creature," something that has life in it, and in that sense, man is also a living creature.

Likewise, *Behema* <note>Hebrew: בהמה</note> denotes a large, wild, or sturdy beast, as do the Greek *Therion* <note>Greek: θηρίον</note> and the Hebrew *Ba’ar* <note>Hebrew: בער</note>: especially *Chayah* and *Chayat*, which refer to a wild, cruel, and devouring beast.

I can imagine that a sort of dietary distinction existed before the Law among the believing Patriarchs, the Egyptians, and some other peoples; however, I do not read that the Lord had made a firm and certain determination at that time. Since one nevertheless reads of "clean" and "unclean" [in the story of Noah], one might wonder if Moses describes it this way in a retrospective narrative, distinguishing the animals according to the classifications of his own time.

Certainly, among the Jews, there was no foundational knowledge of "clean" or "unclean" except as a result of Divine determination.

That one found clean or unclean categories among other nations did not happen through Divine legal appointment, but rather through voluntary command, superstition, and false opinion: one ate this, while another abstained from it.

It is well enough known that the word "Beast" or "Beasts" must not always be taken literally, but often by comparison, in imagery, or figuratively.

And so as not to detain the reader too long with this, one reads of it in *Job, Chapter 18:3: Why are we counted as beasts?*

Some apply this question to Job and his supporters, who held to his side and his reasons. Others apply it to Bildad and his faction, who complains that the debate with Job was not broken off sooner, since Job showed in all his speeches how little he listened to them, regarding them as beasts and "know-nothings" who had little or no understanding of spiritual things or God’s dealings and ways with His children. Job thus reduced the matter to merely scolding, despising, and belittling them—an insult which Bildad judged they could or should no longer endure.

In *Psalm 49:13-21*, the outward state and end of the great, the proud, and those full of self-imagination—who seek and chase status, name, and glory in the world—is compared to the end of the beasts...

# BEAST.

Comparing people to beasts demonstrates vanity and folly, and is grounded in a shared external persistence and perishability regarding the visible part of their bodies and their temporal lives. We also see Asaph comparing himself to an irrational and great beast in *Psalm* 73:22: *I was so foolish and ignorant; I was like a beast before you.* There is a reason for this, for anyone who behaves without understanding and does not pay attention to the works of the Lord to investigate them (*Psalm* 92:7), but follows their own bare natural reasonings, urges, inclinations, and prejudices—judging God's ways by their own guiding star without looking higher or acknowledging, worshipping, and justifying the mystery of God's ways, but measuring them instead by the narrow yardstick <note>The original Dutch uses "elle" (ell), a traditional unit of length often used metaphorically for a standard of measurement.</note> of their clouded judgment while remaining attached to <margin>The ignorant compared to beasts.</margin> and entangled in outward things—such a person is irrational and like a great beast before the Lord. As long as they remain as they were, they are unfit to be taught or to become truly wise.

That humans are also compared to beasts because of their unfitness in life and morals should not seem strange to anyone, considering that we use such names among ourselves, and we see it recorded as such in the Holy Writ, *Titus* 1:12: *Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons;* 2 *Peter* 2:12, etc. See the commentators on these passages.

### HANGING, <note>Hebrew: "קלעים" (Qelaim)</note>, *Exod. XXVII and XXXV and XXXVIII. Curtain, tapestries, isia.*

<margin>Size of the Hanging.</margin>
THE outer Hanging, being like an enclosure and palisade around the Tabernacle, was 300 cubits. The courtyard of the outer or forecourt of the Tabernacle was an elongated square, having a length of 100 and a width of 50 cubits, and therefore the hung cloth for the length to the South and North was 100 cubits on each side; for the Eastern and Western parts, 50 cubits each, and therefore in total 300 cubits.

Now on the Eastern part, where one had the front and entrance gate, the cloth extended 15 cubits at the Northern and Southern corners, from the outer corner toward the middle, and in the middle. Between the Southern and Northern corners hung a special cloth of 20 cubits, which together with the two aforementioned corners made up 50 cubits.

<margin>Material of the hanging.</margin>
The hanging was entirely and generally of fine linen, translucent with small holes, not very densely woven or struck: perhaps interwoven with foliage and flowers. One could to some extent peek through it as through gauze and thin cloth, and see what was happening on the outer courtyard: the Priests, Levites, sac-

<column-break/>

rificial animals, the wash-basin, the copper altar, etc.

<margin>Height of the Hanging.</margin>
This hanging was 5 cubits high, half as high as the Tabernacle, so that one could see over it from the outside. For stiffness and stabilization, there were in total 60 pillars: 20 on the South, 20 on the North, 10 on the West, and 10 on the Eastern part.

On the Eastern part, there were 4 pillars for the entrance of the gate to fasten the 20-cubit cloth; the other 6 were three for the Northeast and three for the Southeast corner, and that cloth which came around those corners from the South and North for 15 cubits in length.

On the 4 pillars, bands and cords, or hooks, silver was found, along with the ground pegs: on the remaining 56, copper.

The hanging for the door, or gate of the forecourt, consisted of sky-blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, embroidered work. For the rest, the forecourt—in whose Southern and Northern middle-width the Tabernacle stood—was open from above, as if under the blue sky.

It is well known to me how Flavius Josephus, regarding *Jewish Antiquities* in Book 3, Chapter 8, and in Book 6, Chapter 6; and Philo the Jew in *The Life of Moses*, Book 3, have wonderfully exerted themselves to devise what the structure of the Tabernacle, the priestly garments, the hangings, and various colors might have been images or paintings of. This has also been briefly left to us by the learned Professors Witsius in his *Sacred Miscellanies*, Braunius in his two books concerning priestly garments, Bierman, and others.

> Josephus maintains *that the Lord divided the Tabernacle into three parts, of which, having given two to the priests, He kept the third for Himself. The first two depicted the earth and the sea, as an unholy place which is trodden by all men without distinction. The third place signifies heaven, which is inaccessible to the children of men. The twelve loaves set in order represent the twelve months of the year; the seven lamps, the seven planets; the cloths and hangings with their various colors, the various elements and primary substances, namely the linen, the earth from which that material springs; the purple color, the sea; the sky-blue color, the air; the red burning color (in Latin, Puniceus), the fire.*

> Philo the Jew maintains *that the small bells represented the thunder; the glittering gold pomegranates, lightning, etc.*

I cannot well bring myself to agree with Spencer <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian who argued that Jewish rites were "accommodated" from Egyptian customs.</note> when he is of the opinion that the lack of sophistication of the ancient age, and the religion confirmed by the long-standing use of the Pagans, would have provided the first origins for this Tabernacle of God. For (he says) since it was in use among the Egyptians and other peoples to place the images or monuments of the gods on a litter, or wagon-houses, or huts to be carried—either so they could show them special honor, or so they would have them constantly with them as traveling companions on their journeys and expeditions, as participants in the travels and dangers—and one could not easily abolish this custom, God was pleased to somewhat conform and adapt Himself to the manner and custom, and therefore to dwell in the Tabernacle and allow Himself to be led around and carried by His servants. > *They shall make the house and the vessels as a sanctuary of the king, as a royal house: and I shall dwell in the midst of them, as in the house and on the throne of glory, which they shall make for me there.*

The Rabbi, Shem Tob, in his commentary on the *Guide for the Perplexed, part 3, Chapter 45*, <note>Shem Tov ibn Shem Tov, a 15th-century commentator on Maimonides.</note> expresses himself thus: *God, whom they honor, has allowed such a house to be built for Himself as a royal house is wont to be. In a royal house, these things are required or found: some are there who guard the palace; some who perform the services and duties belonging to the royal dignity; those who prepare and set out the meals, and perform other services for the king. Others who daily sing and play on musical instruments. In a royal house, there is a fixed place for preparing the food: there is also a place where one burns spices for him: there is a table, also a chamber uniquely the king's own, to which cabinet no one has access except he who is closest to him, or whom he counts among his most special friends and confidants. Thus the Lord willed that all these things should be found in His house: so that He might not yield to earthly kings in anything. For He is the great King, who has absolutely no need of these things; yet from this, the reason and cause easily arises why the ordinary food was provided for the Priests and Levites. All these things were directed toward the end that the common mass of the Jewish people should understand that the King, the Lord of Hosts, had dwelt among them: for He is a great King, and terrible to all nations.*

It is true that Menasseh <note>Menasseh ben Israel (1604–1657), a famous Amsterdam rabbi and diplomat.</note> with his followers wishes to make us believe that the common open outer courtyard, lying exposed to weather and wind, heat, cold, and downpours, was a representation of the sublunary world <note>The earthly realm beneath the moon, subject to change and decay.</note> in which good and evil, holy and godless people dwell. The Holy Place, in turn, represents the starry sky, which shines because of the brilliance of the stars and the light of the Sun, planets, and constellations: and that for this reason, seven lamps were found in the sanctuary. And that by the Holy of Holies was represented the third heaven, the throne of God between the Cherubim, or the angels, etc. See Leydekker’s *Republic of the Jews*, page 511, etc. <note>Melchior Leydekker (1642–1721), a Dutch theologian.</note>

And who will take pleasure in recording at length the loose, groundless, and insipid reflections and interpretations of the Jews? For me, what has been said is enough. Paul, an enlightened and well-trained Jew, gives us a closer and better report concerning this, saying that all the old things of Moses' Law and household were shadowy. *Hebrews 10, etc.*

I confess, one must not go to work loosely and thoughtlessly in this matter, offering the world merely one's own inventions and thoughts for sale; however, one must not prune his labor and diligence too much through excessive scrupulousness, but try to follow the trail of the Apostle Paul, who has left quite a lot for us to consider. Mean-

<column-break/>

while, the language of the ancient and more recent learned men pleases us in many parts. Thus says Nazianzenus <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390), one of the Cappadocian Fathers.</note> in his *Oration on Easter*: *It falls very difficult, if someone should wish to reach the finest and most tender point, and to track down all observations from every shadow: as for example, that which is said of the Tabernacle, of the measurements, and the materials.*

And so writes Saldenus <note>Willem Saldenus (1627–1694), a Dutch Reformed minister.</note> in his work *Leisure Hours*, page 267, etc.: *Certainly the Tabernacle of the Old Testament had a special arrangement and decoration of materials and ornaments: sky-blue, purple, crimson, fine twisted linen, goat's hair, stones for setting, tassels and cords, etc. and what aids or tools did one not have to add in the building and completion of the altar, according to God's prescription, of which Moses makes a broad enumeration in Exodus 25:26, 27, 28. Through all of these, God undoubtedly wished to exemplify something. However, we shall undoubtedly act all the more cautiously if we—piously and respectfully—admit we do not know this or that detail, perhaps intended by the same but not yet revealed to us as such, rather than spending many good hours wishing to explain and interpret everything to a hair and precisely, etc.*

Calvin on the *Epistle to the Hebrews 9:5*: *Some things are not obscure, and are fit for the building up of faith: but one must make a distinction, and use moderation, to the end that we do not seek to be wise beyond what the Lord has pleased to reveal.*

Finally, I add to this the opinion of Moses Amyraldus <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), an influential French Protestant theologian.</note> in his preface to the explanation of the Psalms of David: *What the Apostles have done in general is like an example, according to whose direction all other theologians must arrange their thoughts and considerations in this study. In observing this matter, one serves to use this caution: that, just as the Apostles were sparing in this, we should try to avoid excess; just as they treated the most important principal things and overlooked the trifles, since they did not wish to display the fineness of their intellect, but pursued that which was useful for the building and strengthening of the church and truth. So let us skip over the things that are too thin, and cling to the body of weighty matters. Finally, just as they have proved the truth of their interpretations in no other way than from the clarity of the resemblance that runs between them and the things from which the allusions are drawn: so let us likewise draw the proofs of our explanations from those. Otherwise, the symbolic material is slippery and doubtful, wherein if man's wit indulges itself a bit too much, it breaks out into various heights, in which he seems rather to play than to act seriously and piously.*

<margin>
The author's opinion.
</margin>
For my part, I am willing to believe that the forecourt of the tabernacle, the curtain, and the fine twisted linen cloth—five cubits high and three hundred cubits long, as if from a single piece, transparent, with flowers and foliage—the cloth of 20 cubits for covering the gate and entrance, the 60 pillars with the copper feet, silver bands, and hooks, etc., were as a forecourt of the house of the King of Heaven, for ornament and fencing, from where one went into the house of the King: so that one might prepare and make everything ready there safely and orderly, without crowding or hindrance: but I also hold that one need not rest in this general explanation, but that one may quite...

# CURTAIN.

K 2

...could make sweet and edifying applications in this regard. When one finds such a cloth stretched all around the courtyard, and hanging before the gate or entrance to the East, through which one—as if through a cloud, mist, or thin veil—could see the bronze altar of burnt offering, the large wash-basin, the slaughtering, the pouring of blood and its collection, how the priests washed themselves, and so forth: to which closer sight the sacrificer might proceed onto the Priests' court, but could not penetrate or go further, while a Gentile man had to remain standing outside; so I would think that this stretched cloth could bring to our minds how even the Gentiles were separated from God and the fellowship of His sanctuary and His people by this hanging cloth (there being no "middle wall of partition" yet <note>A reference to Ephesians 2:14, where the "middle wall" between Jews and Gentiles is broken down by Christ.</note>): yes, even that the Jews could not approach God closely, but standing afar off, had to perform their services through God-consecrated Priests and Levites. This seeing through a cloud, a thin veil, and small openings, as if with a glimmering eye, sufficiently displayed the obscurity and darkness of the legal ministry <note>Referring to the Mosaic Law.</note>, however outwardly magnificent and glorious this "ministry of death and condemnation" might be, *2 Corinthians 3*.

Since the Jews could outwardly see the altar of burnt offering, the bronze wash-basin, the washing and cleansing, the slaughtering of the sacrificial animals, the receiving of the blood, etc., yet only barely, imperfectly, and as if with difficulty—because the curtain prevented them from beholding everything freely and without hindrance—they indeed saw the example to some extent, but did not clearly distinguish the "body" and antitype <term>antitype: the New Testament reality prefigured by an Old Testament "type" or symbol</term> of the matter, because everything was obscure, and the reality itself was still absent.

And although Israel saw the outward form and partook of the symbolic portion, without all of them enjoying the signified reality through faith, so one sees and enjoys—as if in the courtyard of the external church—in a Sacramental manner, the sign and seal of Jesus' sacrifice and blood for the forgiveness of sins and the cleansing of the conscience, ordained by Jesus in the New Testament. Yet nevertheless, they do not all, head for head, see, enjoy, and experience that which is signified and sealed thereby.

I find, according to the testimony of the Jews, flowers and foliage in the cloth, but no true, actual, and nourishing ripe fruits—only the hope thereof. I am willing to believe that in the outward appearance of the Jewish shadow-service, one indeed perceived the hope of the coming fruits, but not the fruits and goods themselves, as long as the Christ had not yet sprouted and bloomed, which lay indeed in the hope and promise, but was not yet present, *Isaiah 11, 53, and 27:6*.

<margin>Application of these ornaments to the state of the New Testament.</margin>
And if it pleased me to further apply the outer court with its curtain to the external church state of the New Testament, I could perhaps make quite many applications; namely:

The courtyard enclosed and surrounded with curtains, as if from one piece, made of many threads of twisted linen, fastened to the 60 pillars by which the Tabernacle was enclosed, would indeed seem to represent the external state of the Christian church, insofar as there are many members, yet they must be counted as one body consisting of Jews and Gentiles, and bound to one another, united, and tightly closed by order, discipline, peace, love, the same confession, and doctrine of truth: attached and made fast to the Apostles, Evangelists, shepherds, teachers, elders, and overseers—pillars in the house of God, which is the congregation: one body, one spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, etc., *Ephesians 2 and 4, Colossians 2, 1 Corinthians 12*.

That one found the entrance and gate—the cloth on four pillars—to the East: shall perhaps make us believe that the opening and access to the Tabernacle of God, descended from Heaven, was first perceived in the eastern parts of the world, where Jesus was preached as the door, the way, the truth, and the life, *John 14:6 and 10*; He who opens and shuts, *Revelation 3:7*, according to the Gospel and the description of Jesus' life and death, set forth by the four pillars, the four Evangelists.

That the curtain before the gate or entrance to the East, alongside the entire hanging, was of white, fine linen, will perhaps give us footing and ground to think of the snow-white, pure, and spotless Jesus, although He was for us—who are of the earth—like us in everything except sin, and was a root out of a dry ground, *Hebrews 2, 4, and 7; 2 Corinthians 5:21*; which is also required in those who enclose the church and are a linen curtain or hanging through a pure confession of truth and holiness of life: being clothed in white, with the righteousness of the saints, *Revelation 3:4-5 and 15*, etc., as it was especially situated in such a manner with the first Christian church.

The sky-blue color in that cloth for the entrance and door could bring to our minds Jesus, bruised and "beaten blue" <note>A play on the Dutch word for "bruised" and the color "blue," referencing the stripes of Christ.</note> for our sins, *Isaiah 53*; Him who has His birth from Heaven, even though He is fairly born of a mother’s womb: along with heavenly-mindedness, the seeking of things above, and the pursuit of the glory of Him who dwells in Heaven, *1 Corinthians 10, Colossians 3, Philippians 3:20, John 4*.

The purple color, a royal color, joined with that of scarlet, a red blood-color, may perhaps bring to mind Jesus, who through His blood and bloody suffering has the right to rule, honor, and glory, *Luke 24*; who through His blood makes our sins—though as red as blood and crimson dye—pure and white, *Isaiah 1, 1 John 1:7, 1 Peter 2*; who is red and white <note>Referring to the description of the Beloved in Song of Solomon 5:10.</note>, *Song of Solomon 5*; the church in Jesus' blood, reddish, *Song of Solomon 7:1, Revelation 1 and 7:14*; through whom we are kings, and must struggle even unto blood and death, *Revelation 2:20*. Purple death <note>original: "Θάνατος πορφύρεος"</note>: purple souls, according to Homer and Virgil <note>A literary reference to the ancient idea that the soul or life-force resides in the red blood.</note>.

For it is certain that in such a way Christ is the gate, entrance, and door. He must be viewed as such, and so He is depicted in the holy scroll. He who enters through Him must be such, and must envision such a state for himself.

If ever by this hanging, fastened to the pillars, through this door and gate, a separation was made from the other regions and parts of the world: certainly, he who does not enter through this door, Jesus, and does not penetrate to the forecourt, but remains outside this curtain of the church,

### B E H E M O T H, <note>Hebrew: בהמות, *Behemoth*</note>, *Psalm 50. Job 40.*

<margin>Meaning of the word BEHEMOTH.</margin>
BEHEMOTH signifies a very large animal, quite ugly, very strong; taken by some to be the Elephant, by others the Rhinoceros, and by others the Egyptian Nile-horse <note>The Hippopotamus</note>, also called the Sea-ox, Sea-pig, or Sea-elephant.

<margin>Various descriptions.</margin>
This person describes him thus, the other so. Some say he is two-sided, others four-sided: he resembles an ox from the front and a pig from behind: he has large, white, and hard teeth, like the elephant: a head like a cow, ears like a bear—short, thick, and rounded: his mouth is stretched wider than that of a lion: wide nostrils: curled lips: blunt horse-teeth, large eyes, a short neck, and a pig's tail: as fat as a sow, with short legs, cleft like those of pigs. So says *Bellonius, Book of Aquatic Creatures* <note>original: "Bellonius libr. aquat." Pierre Belon was a 16th-century French naturalist.</note>.

*Aelian, Book 2, Chapter 44* relates that it grows to the height of 5 cubits, that it has ox-claws, and three far-protruding teeth on each side of its mouth: in its ears, voice, and tail, it is like the horse, but with the rest of its body, it is like the elephant. *Aristotle* says that it has a mane like a horse, claws like an ox: a snout which is curled, protruding teeth, a tail like a wild boar: a voice like a horse.

<column-break/>

The entire description by Fabius Columna can be learned from Jonston's *On Animals*.

*Pliny* says: *In the River Nile there grows a yet larger animal than the Crocodile, which is called the Sea-horse. This has split claws, like an ox; a back, mane, and face like a horse; an upturned high snout: a short, curled tail; curved but very damaging teeth, like the wild boar: a hard, thick hide, from which they used to make shields and helmets, which could neither be hewn nor pierced through, unless they were soaked by long-lasting rain or moisture.*

Some, as I have already said, understand this to be the Rhinoceros, the horned-snout animal: others the elephant: some the sea-horse, or Nile-horse.

I shall briefly present the reasons of each.

Groenewegen, in his *Treasury of Emblems and Examples*, is of the opinion and judgment that, following the description found in *Job 40*, one must understand that animal to be the Rhinoceros—an animal with a horn on its nose—and not the Elephant: and he describes it as very large, coming next to the elephant: yet much fiercer than the Elephant, provided with a sharp horn with which it rips open the belly as if with a sword: for it is not the belly of the Rhinoceros, but that of the Elephant that is soft and weak: it has very firm plates on its sides, riveted and closed fast under the belly: it is more powerful of belly and bone than an Elephant: its scaly hide deflects all arrows and musket balls: its powerful and strong sword is its nose-horn.

It is quicker and more agile at climbing the heights than the Elephant, which prefers to be on the plains or in the thickets.

Yet many learned men, both ancient and modern, stand up for the Elephant, and believe that one must seek and find him in Job, and that the entire description is applicable to him: however, for various reasons, many have understood it to be the Sea-horse or Nile-horse, described somewhat previously.

And without saying beforehand who is right or wrong, I shall treat Job's words and present the feelings and reasons of both sides, whereupon it shall become manifest for which opinion one may most safely stand.

See now, *Behemoth, which I made along with you.*

This *along with* is taken by some as if it meant to imply, alongside man, created not on the fifth but on the sixth day.

Others understand *along with you* to mean an animal that dwells upon the earth, like man.

Again, some who take it for an Elephant understand *along with you* to mean that which easily becomes mild, meek, and tame.

However, those who understand it to be the Sea-horse or Nile-horse interpret it differently: *along with you*, that is, not far from you, in the Nile, in Arabia, in which region Job resided: and furthermore, so that God's power might be openly revealed, He wished to bring a wondrously large animal, the Behemoth, into view, not far from Job, so that He might not seem to be speaking of a workmanship unknown to him.

*He eats grass like an ox.*

Those who apply this to the Elephant say that it is wonderful that this animal does not devour or live on prey, or bait on the torn-apart, but is content with grass, hay, and herbs.

When one applies it to the sea-horse or Nile-horse...

<margin>Conclusion of this chapter.</margin>
But, to leave something for others to consider, and merely to form a sketch of everything for further guidance and the cultivation of Christian thoughts and holy allegories and reflections, I shall break off here and direct my thoughts to something else.

### B E H E M O T H, בהמות, *Psalm 50; Job 40*

<margin>Meaning of the word BEHEMOTH.</margin>
BEHEMOTH signifies a very large animal, quite ugly and very strong; taken by some to be the Elephant, by others the Rhinoceros, and by others the Egyptian Nile-horse <note>original: "Nylpaart" - the Hippopotamus</note>, also called the Sea-ox, Sea-pig, or Sea-elephant.

<margin>Different descriptions.</margin>
One describes him this way, another that way. Some say he is two-sided, others four-sided: he resembles an ox in the front and a pig in the back: he has large, white, and hard teeth like the elephant: a head like a cow, ears like a bear—short, thick, and rounded: his maw is gaped wider than that of a lion: wide nostrils: curled lips: blunt horse-teeth, large eyes, a short neck, and a pig’s tail: as fat as a sow, with short legs, cleft like those of pigs. Thus says *Bellonius, Book of Aquatic Animals.*

*Aelian, Book 2, Chapter 44,* recounts that he grows to the height of 5 cubits, that he has ox-claws, and in his mouth on both sides three far-protruding teeth: in the ears, voice, and tail, he is like the horse, but with the rest of the body, like the elephant. *Aristotle* says that he has a mane like a horse, claws like an ox: a snout which is curled, protruding teeth, a tail like a wild boar: and a voice like a horse.

<column-break/>

The entire description by Fabius Columna can be learned from Jonston’s *Of the Animals.*

*Pliny* says, *In the River Nile there grows yet a larger animal than the Crocodile, which is called the Sea-horse. This has split claws like an ox, a back, mane, and face like a horse, a high upturned snout: a short curled tail, and curved teeth as damaging as those of the wild boar: a hard, thick hide, from which shields and helmets used to be made, which could neither be hewn nor pierced through, unless they were soaked by long-lasting rain or moisture.*

Some, as I have already said, understand it to be the Rhinoceros, the horned-snout animal: others the elephant: some the sea-horse or Nile-horse.

I shall briefly present the reasons of each.

Groenewegen, in his *Treasury of Emblems and Examples*, is of the opinion and judgment that, following the description found in *Job 40*, one must understand that animal to be the Rhinoceros—an animal with a horn on its nose—and not the Elephant: and he describes it as very large, coming closest to the elephant: yet much more cruel than the Elephant, provided with a sharp horn with which it rips open the belly as if with a sword: for it is not the belly of the Rhinoceros, but that of the Elephant which is soft and weak: it has very firm plates on its sides, fastened and closed under the belly: it is more powerful of belly and bone than an Elephant: its scaly hide deflects all arrows and musket balls: its sword, powerful and strong, is its nose-horn.

It is quicker and more agile in climbing steep places than the Elephant, which prefers to be on the plains or in the thickets.

Yet many learned men, both ancient and modern, advocate for the Elephant, and believe that one must seek and find him in Job, and that the entire description is applicable to him: however, for various reasons, many have understood it to be the Sea-horse or Nile-horse, described somewhat previously.

And without saying beforehand who is right or wrong, I shall treat Job's words and present the views and reasons of both, after which it shall become clear which view one may most safely support.

"Behold now, *Behemoth, which I made with thee.*"

This *with thee* is taken by some as if it meant to imply "alongside man," created not on the fifth, but on the sixth day.

Others understand "with thee" to mean an animal that stays upon the earth, like man.

Again, some who take it for an Elephant understand "with thee" to mean that which becomes easily manageable, meek, and tame.

But those who understand it as the Sea-horse or Nile-horse interpret it differently: "with thee" means "not far from you," in the Nile, in Arabia, in which region Job stayed: and therefore, so that God's power might be openly manifest, He wished to bring a wonderfully large animal, the Behemoth, into view, not far from Job, so that He would not seem to be speaking of a work unknown to him.

"*He eateth grass like an ox.*"

Those who apply this to the Elephant say it is wonderful that this animal does not devour or hunt for prey, nor feed on torn flesh, but is satisfied with grass, hay, and herbs.

When one applies it to the sea-horse or Nile-horse...

# BEHEMOTH.

Others say it is quite more wonderful, for it is understandable that a land animal would act so, but that this animal comes out of the water onto the land and there eats hay, herbs, and grass is quite a bit rarer: furthermore, they say, there is something in the comparison to an ox <note>The original Dutch uses "runt," referring to a head of cattle or an ox</note>, not only because it eats hay as an ox does, but also that it is in some measure like an ox with respect to the size of its body, the shape of the head, and the posture of the legs.

*Behold now, his strength is in his loins, and his power is in the navel of his belly.*

Now it is clear that the Elephant has a soft belly, and is at its weakest and most tender there. For this reason, the Rhinoceros seeks to strike him there with his horn: and so there are more small animals which often cause his death there. So as not to occupy the Reader further with this, he may look this up in *Pliny, Solinus, Aelian, and Bochart's Sacred Zoology* <note>original: "Bocharti Hierof." referring to Samuel Bochart's Hierozoicon</note>.

But the Hippopotamus <note>original: "zee- ofte Nylpaart," literally sea- or Nile-horse</note> is itself so firm and thick of hide on its belly that one cannot pierce it with an arrow or a lance. Read *Bochart's Sacred Zoology, Book V, Chapter 14, page 757.*

*When he pleases, his tail is like a cedar.*

Those who apply this to the Elephant say the tail is short, and he has little help or protection from it against flies: yet he holds it straight up, stiffly upwards, when he wishes. Others believe one must understand this through metaphor: his shaft, or masculinity, which is short and small in proportion to his large and uncouth body: his testicles lie internally close to his kidneys and the spermatic vessels, like spread and manifold branches, carrying the seed to him from there.

Those who attribute it to the Hippopotamus say: why resort to improper explanations and not stay with the tail? It is true that the Hippopotamus has a short and curled tail; yet he can curl, raise, swing, and move it, according to the testimony of Achilles Tatius, Ammianus, and Belon. Meanwhile, it is also compared to a cedar because of its roundness, smoothness, stiffness, and strength.

*His bones are strong as brass; his bones are like bars of iron.*

That could perhaps also be applied to the Elephant. Especially to the Hippopotamus, which has no cartilage like most sea fish and animals, but the bones are very stiff and hard. Its teeth are considered firmer and harder than those of the Elephant; it whets them at times, striking them against the mountains. If one strikes them with iron, sparks of fire fly out.

Its nerves, muscles, and tendons around its hips are heavy, thick, densely woven, and strong.

*He is the chief of the ways of God.*

He is a singularly great monster-animal, a masterpiece of the fingers of God, say those who attribute it to the Elephant. But those who stand for the Hippopotamus say that in the Hippopotamus strange things coincide: namely, unusual size, extraordinary power and strength, an impenetrable hide, a very large and wide mouth, great greed in eating, white and uncommonly hard teeth; it lives on the land and in the water; it exits backwards toward the water so as not to be watched or surprised; being too fat, it performs bloodletting on itself <note>A common historical myth that hippos would press against sharp reeds to bleed themselves to maintain health</note>, whether by rubbing itself against something or falling on some sharp edge, etc. Read *Pliny in Book 8, Chapter 26 and Book 28, Chapter 8; Pliny Abridged, page 182; Bochart’s Sacred Zoology, etc.*

<column-break/>

*He that made him has girt him with his sword.*

Those who understand the Elephant by this do not agree with one another on how this should be understood; and to present their various thoughts briefly: some believe that the Elephant is such an animal that man cannot tame or handle it, but only God who created it; yet this runs contrary to all experience, and therefore does not hold up.

Others say, *God constrains him so that he does not draw or extend his sword;* but what does that mean? What and which is his sword? How does he draw it? Does he indeed extend it? How and in what is he constrained by his maker?

Others translate: *God his maker causes, or makes, the elephant to meet him, to be subject to him, to be obedient to his commands, and though wild, large, coarse, and strong, yet to lie down as if tame, to eat hay, and not go on the hunt and devour, like other predatory animals.*

Others understand by the Elephant’s sword, girded to him, his large and strong trunk <note>original: "snuit"</note> with which he takes up fodder and breathes air, which he can blow out to a distance of 10 cubits, with which he shows his strength as if with a sword. But how much more easily do we apply this to the Hippopotamus and its long and sharp teeth, its curved teeth, sharp and bent like a scythe, a curved saber, or a pruning knife—a "hooked sword," a "curved blade," <note>original: "ensis falcatus, gladius, curvus"</note> otherwise called a "Harpe" <note>An ancient Greek term for a curved sword or sickle</note> by the ancients? See *Bochart’s Sacred Zoology, pages 761, 762.*

*Because the mountains bring him forth food, therefore all the beasts of the field play there.*

I find precisely not much more in this than that he eats green grass, hay, and earthly herbs, and also stays on the land and on the mountains, not robbing, seeking booty or prey like the large and wild beasts, but using grass and hay like the smaller and tame cattle.

*Under the shady trees he lies down: in a covert of the reed, and the mud.*

It is true, it is said that he seeks and loves the pools, the marshy land, the thickets and trees by the rivers and pools, etc., staying there and entering the water up to his snout, which he keeps just above; see *Bochart, Cocceius on Job, de Mei, etc.*

But it is sufficiently known that the Elephant enters the water very reluctantly; that he does not sleep and rest lying down, but standing; and stays mostly and preferably in forests and flat fields. For what he does out of necessity is one thing; what is characteristic and natural to him is another.

Therefore, one might again suspect that one should think of the Hippopotamus, which stays in the reeds, in the mud, in marshes, on the bank, under the trees; as Marcellinus in the 22nd Book, Belon, Gesner, and Bochart have abundantly shown us, and which I shall therefore by no means further demonstrate.

*Behold, he does violence to the rivers, and is not alarmed; he trusts that he could draw the Jordan into his mouth.*

I would not think that this refers to the greedy drinking of the Elephant, which is said to guzzle down nine Macedonian measures at once—commonly six or seven—at a single...

For my part, I would more readily think that the Hippopotamus <note>original: "Nylpaart," literally Nile-horse</note> was intended, for this does not fit the Elephant, but rather the "Sea-horse," which enters rivers without fear; it is in no way terrified by the waters, whether the waters go over its head or not. *Shall one catch him before his eyes? Shall one pierce his nose with snares?*

That Mercerus, following Jewish grievances and applying this to the Elephant, thinks this refers to its gluttony—as if it positioned itself through its greedy drinking as if it would guzzle the entire river empty—seems flimsy to me, and neither serving the matter nor consistent with the mode of speech. Others attribute it to the great difficulty of catching it. Others to the ease of its capture.

Others attribute it to God, the Creator, that He, by His will and nod, governs, rules, and restrains the large and boorish Elephant just as if He restrained and guided him with His eyes and with cords through his nose, leading him wherever He wills.

Yet I do not see why one should not remain with the Behemoth and consider God to be the subject of the conversation. I would then prefer to understand it in this way: that the Hippopotamus <note>original: "Nyl- ofte Zeepaart"</note> is not easily caught or killed, except by craft and deceit, and not by force. <note>original: "Zie Bocharh Hierof. pag. 768."</note>

As for what the Jewish masters of trifles <note>original: "beuzelmeesters"</note> have left in their writings concerning the Behemoth, although it seems to carry little weight and is mostly fabricated, I will nonetheless record it in passing, though I certainly do not believe it should be understood according to the literal letter, but perhaps in figure and imagination. But let us look closer at the Jewish traditions.

<margin>Jewish views on the Kingdom of the Messiah.</margin>As for the trifling Jews, they have a worldly understanding of the Messiah's kingdom: they hold that at the time of His coming, they shall all gather together in the Holy Land from all corners of the world, and then the feasting shall truly begin. Indeed, one should not imagine a dry or meager meal; for they shall drink old wine, grown in Paradise, and preserved for that purpose in Adam's cellar. Imagine how old it must be, having become "pitted and measled" <note>An idiom meaning well-aged or seasoned</note> with age. Imagine what strong hoops must surround that vat, and how large the vat itself must be. A banquet not for one day, week, month, or year, but it shall always be a pot of fat, a day of feasting, and a banquet, up to the ears in fat and grease. The Great Christians, kings, and princes shall merely be their servants to pour the wine, till the land, tend the cattle, etc.; but they, the Jews, shall alone be God's servants and priests—indeed, they shall have dominion over all peoples. They shall greatly lengthen their lives, for they shall live in a very healthy climate. The corn shall grow luxuriantly, like

<column-break/>

the branches and the foliage of trees. Foreigners will indeed bring it into the Jews' barns, but they shall not eat of it. People will marry and make good cheer; there will be no war, rumors of war, or weapons of war, but a deep peace shall prevail, and peace, joy, and gladness shall have no end.

Friends, do you not wish to believe it too hastily? Yet do not doubt it, for the circumcised swear by it that it shall be so. For understand me, they say, *if this or that be not true, if I do not do this or that, then may I not eat of the great ox of the field, etc.* Now it must surely be the truth; all the more because Menasseh ben Israel asserts it with the high authority of Rabbi Saadia Gaon, Rabbi Moses Maimonides, and Abrabanel. See further Rabbi Solomon Jarchi, Rabbi Venaki, etc.

That which they shall then eat is the Leviathan and the Behemoth; never was there a greater ox than this, for they tell us that he grazes upon a thousand mountains in a single day, yet during the night the grass and foliage grow back again. <note>original: "Ps. L. 10." Psalm 50:10</note>

One should take note that, just as God created all creatures in pairs, male and female, to multiply, He also placed a male and female here. But since they (if they multiplied) would be too destructive and would graze everything bare, leading to the ruin of the world: God killed the female and laid her in salt <note>A humorous aside: "zoo zal 't vleesch vry zout zyn!" — "so the meat will be quite salty!"</note> for that great banquet of the pious, and castrated the male. And thus it becomes entirely fat.

Now one should know that the King Messiah will amuse himself with the battle between Behemoth and Leviathan, and those two shall set upon one another. <note>Citing Job 40:15, Psalm 104:21, and Job 41:6</note> Yet the Leviathan shall be defeated. <note>Citing Job 50 and Psalm 74:13</note> This will undoubtedly provide a fine spectacle.

It is true that many Jewish masters (if one were to take it literally) are ashamed of this, and would prefer it to be understood in a secret and allegorical way, such as Rabbi Simon bar Abraham in the *Book of Zohar*, Rabbi Gabay, and Menasseh in *Book 11 of the Resurrection, Chapter 19*. <note>Citing Huet against the Jews and Hoornbeeck against the Jews</note> However, that it was understood non-literally and in imagination from ancient times is not yet clearly proven.

According to what I have been able to discern from reading H. Groenewegen in his *Fore-shadows and Emblems*, his Reverence believes that, just as animals and statues are often taken for human states and powers in Holy Scripture, and this animal is a very large and strong beast—one that stays on land and in water simultaneously—one might think it symbolizes the outward state of the Church. This refers to the time after she had outwardly accepted Christianity under Constantine, and Satan was forced to leave Heathenism when the earth rose above the water. Therefore, the power and the great kingdom are called the Beast of John—namely, those beastly men who do not have the Spirit of God; upon which beast the harlot sits and which she rules and governs, while it destroys and wastes everything; yet eating like the clean cattle, hay, and the food of clean oxen.

Others apply it to Satan: but accompanied by his powers, vassals, servants, and tools.

The creature Behemoth is very large, and according to how it is described, it has great similarity to a horse, ox, bear, swine, and elephant, as much in its head, mane or hair, tail, ears, divided feet, and claws, as in its wide or distended mouth and large, white, hard teeth.
