If one does not wish to understand the monks and Jesuits by its tail, one might perhaps think of their cunning and very deceptive tricks, and paternal institutions, traditions, foundations, and inventions of state, supported with much-claimed antiquity and authority, exalted to the heavens and maintained, *Jeremiah 9:14.* Certainly, the monks and Jesuits, being of the ecclesiastical order, have bloody ordinances, intolerable laws, stiff and bold fundamental rules, varnished with a religious appearance of devotion and of Roman Catholic church interest: namely, that one must keep neither faith nor word with heretics; that one may employ ambiguities and holy deception if the interests of the church require it. Agreements, promises, and covenants entered into with heretics must be kept only as long as it is advisable, and no longer, etc. See *Cocceius, Groeneweegen, Hoffman on the Revelations, Chapter 9.*

They hide themselves and are covered by the trees, etc.; that is, cunning inventions, base grips and tricks, and ambiguities serve as their hiding place and aid. They do not come out openly; they hide from the truth and powerful confessors and proponents. They lay snares and ruses for them in secret to entangle them. The trees and high-ranking persons of state are their shade and concealment.

The creatures wish to be and graze near that beast, for with it are hay and grass, income, riches, and estates; for the beast gives power to buy and to sell; it is formidable, and almost no one dares oppose it.

It does violence to the rivers; that is, the streams and brooks of the clear waters of God’s Word and Sacraments, making them turbulent and mixing them with the slime and mud of traditions, superstition, and falsehoods.

The ministry of grace, truth, and Sacraments among the true sheep of Christ, it disturbs and troubles wherever it can, through violence, war, and cunning.

It would swallow up the Jordan; that is, some understand by the Jordan the stream of Evangelical truth and the ministry of the Word and Sacraments under the working of God’s Spirit, which refresh the sanctuary, *Psalm 23 and 46.* It behaves as if it would dry them up, swallow them down, or cause them to cease.

Otherwise, it intends to reach the crossing of the Jordan and, with Joshua, to overcome all hindrance and difficulty to lead its Israel...

# BELIAL.

...leading Israel into the ancestral possession of the Holy Land (think of the Crusades and the journey to the Holy Land), and even into the inheritance of the whole world. To this end, it has long sought to rule over the Eastern Church and to "drink in" the East, represented by the river Euphrates. As Virgil wrote in his *Georgics*:

Unless one believes that the Euphrates here could represent the Roman Empire, which the Pope has poisoned and has long sought to make completely subject to himself. For he can never come to full dominion unless all the great ones of the earth worship him and receive laws in both church and state from him, *Revelation 13 and 17.* Read Van Giffen, and with him Lyranus, etc., on *Ezekiel 66, page 104.*

<margin>Strength of the monster-beast.</margin>

->BELIAL, BROOKS OF BELIAL, DAUGHTER OF BELIAL, WITNESS OF BELIAL, CHILDREN OF BELIAL, MEN, COUNSEL, DEED, WORD, SONS. *2 Samuel 22; 1 Samuel 16; Psalm 18 and 101; Judges 19; Proverbs 16; Deuteronomy 15; Proverbs 19; Psalm 41; Nahum 1; etc.* Belial <note>Hebrew: בליעל; Greek: Βελίαλ.</note><-

<margin>Explanation of the word BELIAL.</margin>
The word BELIAL serves to be explained and illuminated from its origins, whereby one will easily notice what all the various names signify.

Some believe the word BELIAL is composed of *Beli* <note>meaning "without"</note> and *Ol* <note>an ancient word meaning "he has worked" or "he has been busy"</note>. In this sense, Belial would mean one who is lazy and idle, *without service or usefulness.* And since lazy idleness—the resting bench of the flesh—is the devil’s pillow, and doing nothing teaches one to think of evil, it is taken to mean a *good-for-nothing or a villain who is useful to no one.* Others derive it from *Beli* <note>"without"</note> and *Ya’al* <note>"to ascend, increase, progress, or profit"</note>; it then refers to a person who is not useful, who does not ascend or reach toward better thoughts—a rogue for whom there is no cure, a piece of rotten wood. Others derive it from *Beli* <note>"without"</note> and *Ol* <note>"yoke, discipline, or bond"</note>. The Talmudists call the *sons of Belial* <note>Sanhedrin fol. III</note> "those who have cast the yoke of Heaven from their necks." <note>original Hebrew: שפרקו על שמים מצואריהם</note>

And so, Belial signifies one who is without a yoke, who has cast off the yoke of labor, godliness, and the Law of God;

<column-break/>

an unjust person, a villain, a thorough rogue. On this, one may consult *Buxtorf's Lexicon, Mercerus, Cocceius, Robertson, Leigh, Drusius' Observations Book I Chapter 7, Bythner's Lyre of David, Glassius' Rhetorical Grammar, and Pfeiffer's Dubia Vexata Scripturae.* See further my notes on *2 Corinthians 6:15.*

From what has been said, it is now easy to understand, without much labor or effort, what the aforementioned titles mean. To call someone a Belial, a man of Belial, or children of Belial; to speak a word of Belial or commit an act of Belial, is the same as calling him a scoundrel, a rogue, a villain, or a good-for-nothing who turns right into wrong, speaks and acts falsely and godlessly to the scorn, slander, oppression, and injustice of his neighbor. Such a person asks after neither God nor His commandment, but living as a profligate, rejects all discipline, banishes all fear, and is therefore useful to neither God nor man. Instead, he is a dishonor to God and highly detrimental, vexatious, and destructive to his neighbor in word, counsel, and deed.

<margin>Brooks of Belial.</margin>
And so the "Brooks of Belial" <note>Psalm 18:4, often translated as "floods of ungodliness"</note> are rushing troops and bands of the godless and hellish powers who set themselves loose upon Christ, persecuting, scorning, reviling, slandering, mocking, and lying about Him. These are they who have cast off every yoke, every fear of God, and every true love for truth, right, and justice, banishing God and their fellow man from their hearts.

From this, one can deduce the meaning of a "witness of Belial," a "word," "act," or "counselor of Belial"—namely, one who seeks nothing through counsel, deed, or testimony other than the grief, torment, scorn, damage, shame, and downfall of the innocent and righteous, and does so with evil intent and premeditated malice.

If one turns things in this direction, one has the key in hand to unlock all expressions and titles of this nature.

<margin>Satan a Belial.</margin>
Paul teaches us in *2 Corinthians 6:15* that Satan is a Belial: an *evil one* <note>Greek: πονηρὸς</note>, a wicked being of the highest degree who has cast off the yoke of the Lord; an inventor of lies, injustice, slander, torment, and grief; a counselor of foul and evil deeds, and so forth.

But to remain with the children, men, counselors, sons, and daughters of Belial among the children of men: I am convinced that through these titles one sees clearly and vividly portrayed the "lawless one," the "man of sin," the "son of perdition," the Antichrist—the Roman Pope, the imagined Vicar of Christ on earth—along with his daughters, sons, and children: the priests, monks, Jesuits, lay-sisters <note>kloppen</note>, beguines, bigots <note>quezels</note>, and that entire swarm of useless locusts, that swarm and scum of useless begging monks, and those cloistered and "Cellite-brother" ballasts and useless tools.

<margin>The Antichrist portrayed.</margin>
And to expand on this a little, consider with me *2 Thessalonians 2: the man of sin, the son of perdition,* etc., and review what was said under the word ANTICHRIST. For what else does he do but violate God's Law and commandments? He introduces and forces his own commands, orders, and teachings—which are devilishly foul and soul-destroying—in their place, under the promise of salvation and the threat of punishment, excommunication, and calamity. Toward what do his decrees and counsels strive, if not to destroy the saints through fire and sword...

-> BELLEN [Bells], פעמון, מצלות, κώδων, κύμβαλον, tintinnabulum. <-
<note>original languages: Hebrew *pa'amon* and *metzillot*; Greek *kōdōn* and *kymbalon*; Latin *tintinnabulum*.</note>

I shall take this word somewhat narrowly to mean ear-ornaments, though also, in the distance, for bells or little tinklers which produce sound; however, I shall reserve the broader meaning for the word SCHELLEN [Small Bells/Chimes]. For what appears here will be only in passing, and insofar as one finds the word BELLEN in our Dutch translation: all the more because in the following sections on ornaments and golden bells, more must be said.

-> BELLEN. See under SCHELLEN: פעמון, מצלות, κώδων, κύμβαλον, tintinnabulum. <-

<margin>Shape of the Bells.</margin>
BELLEN, otherwise also called chimes, are fabrications of all kinds of metal and resonant materials, with an internal hanging clapper which, when stirred and moved and striking against the inner curve, creates a sound, more or less shrill and strong. Sometimes they are also filled with a round iron, tin, or lead pellet or small ball within a closed round cavity, to create a sound through an up-and-down, jumping motion; for which purpose, besides being an ornament, they are also hung around horses so they can be heard from afar, and as some believe, to give the horses courage.

Regarding the chime-wearing of Priests as an ornament and to make their presence known, perhaps also for other ends, one may look under the word SCHELLEN.

The knowledge of languages, without prudent use in love, and without being joined by translation for those who do not know the language, is nothing but a beating of the air without any fruit or edification, *1 Corinthians 13:7*. See under SCHELLE.

<margin>Meaning of Bells.</margin>
By bells, one understands at first glance head- and ear-ornaments, attached to the ears, hanging from and in the pierced earlobes, or otherwise fastened near the ears.

<column-break/>

Of these bells, *Isidore* recounts in *Etymologies, book 19, chapter 31*: The ear-ornaments or earrings are named in this manner from the pierced ears, from which very precious stones were hung. The use of these was in Greece: the girls wore them in both ears, the servant boys in the right ear.

> *Juvenal, in his satires:*
>
> The soft windows in the ear
> Have proven it. <note>original Latin: "Molles quod in aure fenestræ / Arguerint." This refers to pierced ears as a sign of being a foreigner or a slave.</note>

-> That is: <-

> *That which the holes in my ears*
> *Prove.*

One reads of this luxury in *Isaiah 3:20, 21* and *Ezekiel 16:12*; and it must have been quite magnificent and coarse, such that Paul rebuked this finery in *1 Timothy 2*.

<margin>Magnificent ear-ornaments.</margin>
*Jerome, writing to Demetrias*, gives us well enough to understand that it went quite far, when he says: *so that I may remain silent regarding the costliness or value of the ear-ornaments, of the bright color of the pearls, as giving testimony of the depths of the Red Sea, of the green color of the Emeralds, of the shimmering rays and flames of the white Ceraunians (a stone said to fall with thunder and lightning), of the sea-color of the hyacinths, for which the inclinations of young ladies burn, and toward which their mad efforts singularly extend. Upon these they set their senses every day; this is their chief concern, that they hang their paternal inheritance from their ears.* *Seneca* speaks of this excess and magnificence somewhere:

> Two and three inheritances hang from each individual ear. <note>original Latin: "Bina ac terna patrimonia fingulis auribus pendent."</note>

-> That is: <-

> *As they walk stiff with pearls,*
> *Two estates upon their ears they load.*

> *Plautus, The Menaechmi, Act 3, Scene 3:*
>
> Give me some earrings
> To be made, drop-pendants weighing two nummi. <note>original Latin: "Inaureis da mihi / Faciundas pondo duum numum stalagmia."</note>

-> That is: <-

> *Let me have a pair of heavy ear-ornaments made.*

*Stalagmia* is an ear-ornament having the form of a hanging water drop, as the commentators on this passage say. This magnificence and foolish finery was, through a strange infatuation and esteem which one had for mute beasts and even for fish, transferred to them. Thus one reads of the bells of the heart dedicated to Diana and the Nymphs; of the elephant named Ajax belonging to Alexander; of the Moray eel of *Drusus* and *Crassus*. See *Philostratus* in the *Life of Apollonius, Book 2*; *Pliny, Book 6, Chapters 1 and 32, Chapter 2*; *Aelian, Book 12, Chapter 30*; *Hofmann's Lexicon, page 909*, etc.; also on oxen. See *Columella, Book 6, Chapter 1*.

These ornaments and bells were not only fashioned from gold and gemstones, but also from copper, wood, flowers, and roses.

> *Ovid in the 10th book of the Metamorphoses:*
>
> And from twin ears shone pearls
> Of equal bronze, around the hollow temples. <note>original Latin: "Parilique ex ære nitebant / Auribus in geminis, circum cava tempora bacæ."</note>

# B E L L S.

->That is:<-

<margin>Weight of the ear-ornaments.</margin> And these, by their weight, caused the earlobes to sink and hang down almost to the shoulders, upon which no small "interest" <note>The author uses a pun on "rente" (interest/rent), implying the cost of the jewelry was a heavy financial burden as well as a physical one.</note> hung.

Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet active in the late 1st and early 2nd century AD.</note> in his 6th Satire:

> *Whose ear is hung with diamond and stones,*

What Seneca <note>A Roman Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero.</note> says in *Book VII of On Benefits*, I shall set down in rhyme:

> *One could feast for an entire year*
> *On the costly folly of her ribbon and her feathers;*
> *From her ruffled collar one could stretch out two shirts,*
> *Four cloaks from her skirt, three pairs of breeches from her sleeve:*
> *From the ear-weight of her stretched lobes*
> *One could count out three rents, one purchase, and four hires.*

<margin>Bells of the beasts.</margin> Subsequently, one reads of little bells and large bells which were placed on cattle, mules, horses, etc. See Apollinaris <note>Likely referring to Sidonius Apollinaris, a 5th-century Gallo-Roman poet.</note> *Book II, Letter II.* Phaedrus <note>A Roman fabulist who translated Aesop into Latin verse.</note> in the seventh Fable of the second book:

> *Two mules went burdened with packs,*
> *One rich with a load, walking with its neck held high,*

> <note>original Latin: "Muli gravati sarcinis ibant duo, / Ille onere dives, celsa cervice eminens, / Clarumque collo jactans tintinnabulum."</note>

Which Mr. David van Hoogstraten <note>A Dutch physician and poet (1658–1724) known for his translations of Phaedrus.</note> has thus translated:

> *Two Mules go with packs, heavy to carry.*
> *The first beast, upon which the treasures lay,*
> *Went bravely forward, and rang with his bell,*
> *Hanging from his neck.*

Among the great, bells were hung around the necks of horses, as Euripides <note>A great Athenian playwright of the 5th century BC.</note> says in *Rhesus*:

> *And Medusa, as if on the shield of the goddess,*
> *Of bronze, fastened to the horses' foreheads,*
> *Rings out fear with many bells.*
> <note>original Greek: "Γοργὼ δ' ὡς ἐπ' Αἰγίδος θεᾶς / Χαλκὴ μετώποις ἱππικοῖσι πρόσδετος, / Πολλοῖσι σὺν κώδωσιν ἐκλύπει φόβον."</note>

->That is:<-

> *The head of Medusa, as on Minerva’s <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena.</note> shield,*
> *Adorned the head of the horses in their gallop,*
> *Where they gave a sound with their bells.*

The same in the 3rd act:

> *See the gold-bound strength of the body,*
> *Hear the boastful clanging of the bells*
> *Ringing by the shield-straps.*
> <note>original Greek: "Ἴδε χρυσόδετον σώματος ἀλκὴν, / Κλύε κόμπας κωδωνοκρότους. / Παρὰ πορπάκων κελαδέντας."</note>

<column-break/>

->That is:<-

> *But note how magnificently they are attired,*
> *And the sound of the bells, which ring out firmly.*

Likewise, among the magnificent Persians, one found this horse-adornment. See Apuleius, *The Golden Ass, Book X*; also Joannes Pontanus <note>An Italian humanist poet (1426–1503).</note> in *As.*

Among the Greeks, a bell-sign was hung around the neck of a criminal, so that no one, by touching him unawares, might be defiled. See Plautus in *Pseudolus Act I, Scene III.*

A single place occurs to me in the Old Testament where I read of the bells of horses, namely: *Zechariah 14:20. In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD.*

The passage *Zechariah 14:20*, where Bells are spoken of, is intended to mean something else. Ridderus <note>Franciscus Ridderus (1620–1683), a Dutch Reformed theologian known for his polemical and devotional writings.</note>, who made it his business to always cross his Brethren’s path <note>A Dutch idiom meaning to challenge or contradict his colleagues.</note>, presented their view in this way: the meaning is, say the brethren, that those who have been "horses"—that is, those upon whom the Bishops have sat, and whom they have brought under their servitude—shall have free access to God in Christ, just as the High Priest who wore this title on his forehead had free access above other priests. <margin>The sharpness of Ridderus.</margin>

Furthermore, his Reverence says: The answer is, it may be that Papal Bishops are being looked at, although we do not believe it; 2. thus it must have been seen at the beginning of the Reformation; but the brethren wanted to bring us to the end of the world, by Jerusalem in Jesus' new kingdom.

I do not see in all parts that Gulichius <note>Abraham Gulichius (1642–1679), a German-Dutch theologian who wrote on the "Economy of the Covenants."</note> restricted it to such an extreme time, but rather to the servitude under the yoke of the ceremonies of the Old Testament and under the all-forcing guardians, gods, and superiors: representing that the service of the New Testament would be free from the law of ceremonies, and from all compulsion and domination.

It is indeed so that some have assigned a rather meager meaning to these prophetic words: by transferring them to the actual finery and adornment of horses used by some nations, who, being conquered, would have their horses dedicated to the actual service in God’s sanctuary.

Unless there is not much more shown here of how the church and the believers—pliant and willing under the Lord's hand, powerful in the Lord and in the strength of His might, equipped like heroes for battle, like armor from God’s sanctuary, armed with the Gospel of Peace—were to give a ringing sound of the Gospel, a beautiful and penetrating confession of the truth, accompanied by the power of godliness and holiness of life and conduct, to the glory of God and the fame of the Savior, their chief captain. See further under CHIMES [SCHELLEN].

I understand here by the "horses," pre-eminently the Evangelists and the Apostles, and the noble-minded confessors in the first Christian church, who were free from the Jewish confessors who led them into legalistic servitude: and over- <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing the thought on the next page.</note>

# BELLS.

...those whom the Roman prelates <note>The text refers to the "Roomse kerkvoogden," or Roman church-guardians, likely meaning the Catholic hierarchy.</note> sat upon in fear, should serve God in spirit and truth, zealously and willingly, as Priests of the New Testament, and approach Him boldly, as those possessing the Lord's holiness, without having need of [earthly] Priests or a shadowy high priest. These were to be adorned with the bells of the Gospel, so that through the ringing sound of the preached word—the holiness, the commands of God, holy, refined, and pure—the mystery of redemption might be made known throughout the whole world as if with a raised voice. This was so that just as sin and destruction entered the world through hearing [the serpent], so too sin might be driven out by hearing the Gospel, and faith and holiness might be awakened in the hearts of the listeners. *Ps. 19; Rom. 10:17, 18; Luke 10; Matt. 28; Mark 16.* When the Lord gave the word, and the company of those who brought good tidings was a great host: *Ps. 68.* When one must not remain silent, *Isa. 56 and 58; 2 Tim. 4:2,* and one must call out to these listeners: *Isa. 52:7.* How lovely upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good tidings, who publishes peace; who brings good tidings of good, who publishes salvation; who says to Zion, your God is King! Whereby I then metaphorically understand by "the bells" the word of the Gospel, of peace, and of righteousness.

<margin>Bells understood metaphorically.</margin>
And since I previously mentioned something of neat finery and bells—which evil pride the Apostles in their letters (*1 Tim. 2; 1 Pet. 3*) and the Fathers and godly men have urged us to cast off and avoid—I feel inclined to briefly recount how God's daughters ought to be decorated.

No one wants (says Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note>) women to be slovenly dressed; nor certainly with a peasant-like getup; but with such conduct that expresses a well-composed mind. Thus says the Knight Jacob Kats <note>Jacob Cats (1577–1660), a famous Dutch poet known for his moralizing emblems and verses.</note>:

> Stay then within this measure, and regarding your dress
> Be not all too slovenly dirty, nor all too mightily wide.

Not too showily adorned, but stately, dignified, well-ordered: fit to cover the limbs, not too thin and transparent despite the biting cold—just like the Coan clothing <note>Refers to "Coae vestes," a type of ancient Greek silk from the island of Cos, famous for being so thin it was transparent.</note> of thin and transparent silk fabrics, through which one could see the muscles and moving parts. It was called by Petronius *ventum textilem* <note>original: "ventum textilem," meaning "woven wind."</note>, a woven wind; and *nebulam lineam* <note>original: "nebulam lineam," meaning "a linen mist."</note>, a linen fog. By Seneca, *non tegentem vestem* <note>original: "non tegentem vestem," meaning "a garment that does not cover."</note>, a garment that does not cover; by Nazianzenus <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople.</note>, *togam vitream* <note>original: "togam vitream," meaning "a glass gown."</note>, a glassy gown. Of which Lucius Seneca gives an account in *On Benefits, Book VII, Chapter 9*: *I see silk clothes—if they may indeed be called clothes—through which neither the body nor shame can be protected; which having been put on, the woman can hardly deny upon oath that she is naked.*

<margin>Transparent clothing.</margin>
Jerome, in his 21st Sermon, makes himself heard: *Do you women of Antioch wish to decorate your faces? Do it by no means with pearls, but with modesty and honorableness, and thus you shall be a pleasing sight to your husbands.*

Away with foreign fashions. Well says Master Constantijn Huygens <note>A celebrated Dutch Golden Age poet and diplomat.</note>:

> O Holland, old fame of simple dignity,
> Where do we find a shield for your righteousness
> In the painful pursuit of overseas finery?

Plutarch, in his lessons concerning marriage, says *that the Egyptian women were formerly kept unshod, so that they might better stay at home; and if one took away from women the embroidered shoes, the strings of pearls, the precious stones, and costly ornamental robes, they certainly would not be so prone to wandering and staying out of the house.*

<margin>Egyptian wives unshod.</margin>
Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD).</note>, on the adornment of women, writes thus: *Come forth, equipped with the ornaments and finery of the Apostles, taking up the white of simplicity, the red of chastity, painting your eyes with shame and your spirit with silence, hanging from your ears—behold there the bells—the word of God, and binding to your neck the yoke of Christ.*

To this, Kats again applies this:

> Let your good gifts shine instead of a gifted stone,
> For pearls, pure discipline; and shame, for rubies:
> Let that white, that noble red, decorate you above all;
> From there it is that the soul shall shine for eternity.

The word of life and righteousness must always hang as if from the ears. In order to observe the will of God after hearing it, our ears must be "pierced" <note>A reference to Psalm 40:6, often interpreted as a sign of a willing servant whose ear is bored to the doorpost.</note>. *Ps. 40.* No pearl so beautiful, no ear-ornament so famous, as the gold, silver, and precious stones of the surpassing word of wisdom, truth, and the righteousness of life.

More on all of this in its proper place.

### BELONE, ACUS, RAPHIS, GEEPE, NEEDLEFISH. <term>Belone</term> <note>original Greek: Βελόνη (Belonē), meaning "needle."</note>

This is a certain sort of fish, which is said to stay in Hungary, in the River Tibiscus <note>The Tisza River.</note>. The figure, form, or appearance is said to be quite distinct. One may see the image or drawing of it by Johnston <note>Jan Jonston (1603–1675), a Polish physician and naturalist of Scottish descent.</note> in his work on Animals and Fishes.

It is said to be named "Needlefish" or *Belone*, as it is reasonably long, thin, and pointed. I find it called a *Storlein* <note>Possibly a diminutive of "sturgeon" (Steur), though applied here to the needlefish.</note>, somewhat inclining toward yellow, with a small head, a hard mouth, tapering to a point and long. The horny upper lip is turned up and set somewhat above, in the manner of a trumpet. It is an elbow long <note>Approx. 18-22 inches.</note> and a finger thick. It has eyes as small as a grain of barley. In its mouth on both sides are four gills. The anus is in the middle of its body. If it has fins on its body, they are very small.

<margin>Appearance of this fish.</margin>
It is said that it gives birth in the winter with a gaping belly. Its womb is quite small, its eggs not numerous but large. It is told that its offspring makes a tear and wide opening in the lower belly for a readier and easier exit, and this quite early and as if untimely, which slit afterwards closes and heals by itself.

Oppian <note>A Greco-Roman poet who wrote the Halieutica, a poem on fishing.</note> recounts that when it has escaped the snares and nets of the fishermen, it turns itself around and, with its sharp teeth and mouth, tries to break the fishing net; and by striking its teeth into the fishing line, it remains hanging there, and in that manner is caught by the fishermen.

<margin>Manner of catching it.</margin>

But if anyone should happen to find pleasure, upon the occasion of the description of this fish, in thinking of those people who are blinded by passion, and of small judgment and little understanding—and who therefore have very small "eyes of the mind"—slender and thin due to wasting envy, appearing yellowish due to the overflowing bile of anger, resentment, and thirst for revenge, spawning in the wintertime of cold love: bringing forth eggs and fruits of harmful thoughts and effects with outbursts and too-hasty a lack of sufficient judgment and deliberation; who, having escaped the traps and snares, foolishly and madly seek to soften themselves, whereby they cause themselves to plunge into ruin and into the power of their enemy and waylayer: in a word: those who, having barely escaped danger, plunge themselves into ruin through their own fault, resentment, and untimely revenge—as for me, I shall not have much against it, and thus I take my leave of the fish *Belone* <note>The Belone is the needlefish or garfish. ### BENJAMIN <note>Hebrew: בנימין, "Son of the Right Hand"</note>

BENJAMIN was the twelfth son of Jacob. Rachel was his mother, who, because of the painful labor—the sorrowful and death-inducing birth—named him *Benoni*, or the son of my sorrow; for as she brought him into the world, she gave her last gasp. But the old father Jacob, with a turn and a small change, called him Benjamin—son of the right hand—greatly beloved, valued, the son of his strength in his great old age (*Gen. 35* and *44*), or a memorial of so dear a wife. His last and smallest child.

<margin>Benjamin's birth.</margin>
It was Benjamin without whose intervention, presence, and face his brothers would not see Joseph's face; the cup hidden <note>The text says "de geſtooken," referring to the silver cup Joseph had hidden in Benjamin's sack to test the brothers.</note> (*Gen. 44:2*), though they enjoyed favor there (*Gen. 43:5* and *44:23*).

<margin>Joseph seen by his brothers through him.</margin>
It was Benjamin at whose presence, following the hostage-taking and guarantee, Simeon was released from his confinement (*Gen. 42:24* and *43:23*).

<margin>Simeon released through him.</margin>
And although something was demanded of him following the outward treatment which he had in no way stolen or carried away from Joseph—namely, Joseph’s silver cup, which had come into his sack by Joseph’s secret hand—Benjamin’s portion and share, or gift, was indeed five times larger than that of his brothers (*Gen. 43:34* and *45:22*).

<margin>Benjamin's portion.</margin>
Having briefly presented this concerning Benjamin, Jacob’s youngest son by mother Rachel, I have noticed that people have sought to find some similarities between him and the Son of God and Mary: which, if I were to present them, would undoubtedly come down to this, namely:

<margin>Correspondence between him, Jesus, and Mary.</margin>
> a. The church of the faithful Fathers and Prophets, which outwardly according to the flesh was in bondage, yet according to the spirit was free: received Christ in promise, and in faith, with much trial and sorrow, carried and gave birth to Him, who was made under the Law (*Gal. 4:4*), a minister of the circumcision (*Rom. 15:8*) from the fathers as concerns the flesh (*Rom. 9:5*), the brother of the Jews—sin excepted, like us in all things (*Heb. 2* and *4*). After His birth, long desired, believed, and hoped for, the mother—the Synagogue, bound to the husband, the Law—died (*Rom. 7*).

<column-break/>

> b. This Jesus being the Messiah, although a son of sorrow <note>Original: *Benoni*</note>, is declared by the Heavenly Father to be His Benjamin, His beloved Son, the Son of the Everlasting One, or the Ancient of Days (*Isa. 5* and *42; Matt. 3:17* and *17*); placed by Him at the right hand of His power and glory in the heavens (*Heb. 1; Ps. 110:1*), the beloved of His people (*Song of Sol. 1:13, 2, 5, 7, 8,* etc.).

> c. No one can see God, truly know Him through experience, enjoy the light of His countenance, His favor and saving fellowship, or approach Him with boldness and confidence, except in, through, and with Him (*John 14:6; Rom. 5:2; Eph. 2:18* and *3:18; Heb. 10:19*).

> d. Just as Benjamin, by and with his coming, can be said to have delivered his troubled, bound, and locked-up brother Simeon; it is certain that the Benjamin Jesus, through His appearance, did the same—both regarding the restraint under the law, as the Jews were placed as if in custody (*Zech. 9; Isa. 61; Gal. 3:23*), and regarding the shackles and bonds of sin (*Luke 1:74, 75; Heb. 2:14, 15; 1 Cor. 15* and *1 Cor. 1:30,* etc.), just as He shall one day appear for the full deliverance of His brothers (*Ps. 68:20; 1 Cor. 1:30*).

> e. From Benjamin was demanded that which he had not stolen or secretly carried away, namely Joseph’s cup; it is true that Jesus, as a sovereign and voluntary surety <note>The term "borg" refers to a legal guarantor or someone who takes on another's debt.</note>, knew what He had taken upon Himself (*Ps. 40; Job 33*) and what the Lord would cause to fall upon Him (*Isa. 53*). Yet it was no personal crime of His. What He had not robbed, He had to pay (*Ps. 69:5*); He knew no sin (*2 Cor. 5:21*) nor did He do any (*1 Pet. 2* and *3*). Haimo <note>Haimo of Halberstadt, a 9th-century monk and scholar.</note> on *Ps. 69:5*: *Tunc in illa tribulatione exsolvebam: poenas solvebam pro his, quae non rapui sc. pro peccatis, quae non perpetravi.* <note>Latin note: "Then in that tribulation I paid: I paid the penalties for those things which I did not snatch; namely for the sins which I did not commit."</note> That is: *Then I suffered in that sorrow, that is, I paid the penalty for the things I had not robbed; namely for the sins I had not committed.* He had committed no robbery of God’s honor (*Phil. 2; John 5* and *10*) nor any crime.

What then shall we judge of our Benjamin, Jesus, *Psalm 45 and 16*, who possesses a fullness? *John 1:16 <note>The original text cites Job 1:16, but the context of "fullness" and the accompanying citations suggest John 1:16 is intended.</note>, Isaiah 11, John 3:34, Philippians 2, Colossians 2:3.*

<margin>Comparison between Benjamin and Paul.</margin>
Alongside this, it has pleased some to suggest in passing that they have found several similarities between Benjamin and Paul.

It is certain that he is a "Benjaminite." *Philippians 3.* It is also true that while he was still Saul, he must be regarded as belonging to his mother, the Jewish Synagogue, raised at the feet of the great Gamaliel: once converted as Paul, he became an Apostle, a son of the Apostolic mother church.

<margin>The church tormented by Paul.</margin>
It is well known what grief, pain, and torment he caused his mother, the Apostolic Christian Church, *Acts 8 and 9, 1 Corinthians 15, 1 Timothy 1,* etc., and how many tears he cost her.

He was also a "Benoni" <note>Benoni means "Son of my Sorrow."</note> to the Jewish Mother-Synagogue. No one contended more strongly with his mother than he: exposing her shame, demonstrating her weakness, and causing her to languish and die. *See his letters to the Romans, Galatians, Colossians, and Hebrews.*

It is also certain that he is the last son, and an Apostle *1 Corinthians 15*, brought forth in haste, born unexpectedly at a time when he was least expected. More on this later. He was the youngest and last of the Apostles, conceived and brought forth in the womb of the church when no more Apostles were expected and Jesus was already glorified.

<margin>Paul the youngest Apostle.</margin>
It is also certain that this Benoni, according to God's arrangement and naming, was a "Benjamin" <note>Benjamin means "Son of the Right Hand."</note>, a blessed and powerful instrument in the Lord’s right hand among the Jews and Gentiles, *Acts 9*. His measured portion in gifts, abilities, the boundary line <term>meetfnoer: a measuring line or the scope of one's assigned ministry</term> of his Apostleship, his labor and zeal, was an extraordinary portion.

<margin>His extraordinary portion.</margin>
If anyone was blessed by God with gifts, abilities, and talents, and if anyone's boundary line stretched far and wide, Paul certainly deserves to be seen as blessed above all others, so that in both respects he did not need to yield even to the most eminent of the Apostles. *2 Corinthians 11.*

And if ever anyone was a deadly pain and grief to his mother—the Jewish Synagogue—after his birth from God and calling to the Apostleship, it was certainly he. For it was he who called and brought his brothers according to the flesh to freedom, and made the temple structure, with Moses' religion and shadow-laws, to totter, *Isaiah 6 <note>The author likely refers to the spiritual shaking of the old order.</note>*, insisting on the freedom through which the mother-synagogue began to gasp for breath and huff her final sigh. Read more on *Psalm 68:27 <note>The original cites 68:2, likely a typo for 68:27-28 which mentions Benjamin.</note>*.

The Lord Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian known for Federal Theology and typological interpretations of Scripture.</note> applies the final words—*dividing the spoil in the evening*—to the evening hour or the end of the Jewish commonwealth, when the night drew near that would cloud it with final destruction. By "spoil" he understands those people who had to be delivered from the power of the devil and handed over to Christ and his congregation; this meaning of the sun-symbol is powerfully proven from *Isaiah 53:12*. Now, it is clear that no one among the descendants of this tribe is 

<column-break/>

known to have done anything similar at the end of the Republic <note>Refers to the Jewish state/commonwealth before the destruction of Jerusalem.</note> except Paul alone, who converted so many lands and peoples, so many slaves of the devil, to the faith of Christ; he therefore calls the successful outcome of his work his "joy," after he had fought bravely. *2 Corinthians 2:1 etc.* See Salomon van Til <note>Salomon van Til (1643–1713), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> in his *Antidote*, page 200.

From this Benjamin, son of Jacob, fathered by Rachel, and from these symbolic contemplations and applications, I pass over to the descendants of this Benjamin, appearing hereafter under the name of:

<margin>Transition of the writer.</margin>

### BENJAMINS STAM.

<margin>The departure of Benjamin’s tribe.</margin>
From Benjamin, the son of Jacob and Rachel (a free woman), born in Canaan, a very large and numerous lineage sprang, numbering 35,400 heads at Sinai: and at the entrance into Canaan, 45,600 men of war. This tribe, according to the testimony of *Rabboth Bemidbar* <note>Numbers Rabbah, a Jewish exegetical text on the Book of Numbers.</note>, is said to have had a wolf on a multi-colored field as its banner and field sign. Its inheritance was not very large, but rich and good, lying between Judah, Ephraim, and Dan, and extending from the Jordan toward the Great Sea, ending above Ramah in a narrow corner. This later had the name of the House and Tribe of Benjamin among the heads and tribes of Israel.

<margin>David’s house, Jerusalem and Benjamin’s tribe.</margin>
This tribe, along with that of Judah, remained loyal to the House of David when the other ten fell away, *1 Kings 12.* Jerusalem, formerly called Jebus, was in Benjamin’s tribe and was its capital. Thus the city and the temple stood on Benjamin’s ground, though as some believe, the sanctuary itself was excluded <note>The border between Benjamin and Judah was famously said to run through the Temple courts.</note>, *Joshua 18 and Psalm 78:68, 69.*

<margin>The bravery of Benjamin’s tribe.</margin>
This tribe was very populous and bold in warring, and on one occasion fought against the other tribes, being victorious in two battles, though thereafter it was almost entirely destroyed by ruse and force of arms, *Judges 20 and 21*, but later it flourished again and became numerous. From this tribe sprang Saul, the first king, who did quite great things and won victories; it is also judged that Mordecai, Esther, etc., sprang from Benjamin. It is said that this tribe is represented by the Jasper stone. See JASPER.

As far as the Tribe of Benjamin is concerned, we find in the Scroll of the Book a paternal blessing and a prophetic prediction, *Genesis 49:27 and Deuteronomy 33:12, Psalm 68:27* etc., which are doubly worthy of being viewed closely and treated with the proper reflections of "cooked thoughts" <note>A metaphor for well-deliberated or "digested" meditations.</note>.

One reads of Benjamin, predicted in the spirit by the old Jacob, *Genesis 49:27: Benjamin shall raven as a wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey, and at night he shall divide the spoil.*

<margin>Seducers represented by beasts.</margin>
I know that in the holy pages all kinds of beasts—lions, bears, leopards, and also wolves and evening wolves—are spoken of *Jeremiah 5, Zephaniah 3, Habakkuk*, and that harmful and deceitful seducers are found represented by them, *Matthew 7 and 10, Acts 20:29.*

It is also noted that there are distinct types of wolves, since they do not all run together in heaps or parties and take common spoil, which is thereafter divided. For...

# BENJAMIN’S TRIBE.

for one also finds *lone robbers* <note>original Greek: *μονόπειραι*, referring to solitary pirates or plunderers</note>, who are solitary thieves and takers of spoil.

It is indisputable that this is spoken figuratively and by way of illustration.

And I am of the opinion that one should not take this comparison in a negative sense, as in *Jeremiah 5, Zephaniah 3:3, Habakkuk 1, Matthew 7 and 10, or Acts 20:29*, but in many respects in a positive sense, as a prophecy and a fatherly blessing. For it is one thing for someone to be compared to a lion, bear, leopard, or something else *in a certain respect* <note>original Greek: *κατά τι*</note>, and another to be compared *in all respects* <note>original Greek: *κατά πάντα*</note>, absolutely and without limit. One finds in those types of animals good natural virtues and strengths, as well as harmful effects.

Not all taking of spoil or robbery is to be called evil in an absolute and unlimited sense; one must ensure that one hits upon the root of the comparison and does not go beyond its purpose, without carrying over everything that can be observed in the illustrative animal. Otherwise, one will commit many improprieties. For even God, <margin>Prudence to be observed in comparisons.</margin> Christ, and the believers are compared to animals and things, all of which must not be carried over to them absolutely or without limit. For the Lord is called, in a certain respect, a lion, fire, light, etc. Christ a lion, fountain, sun, etc. Similarly, Satan is compared to a lion in *1 Peter 5:8* <note>The original cites 1 Peter 3:9, but the famous "roaring lion" passage is 5:8.</note> because of his wicked persecutions leading to the destruction of men's souls. Again, Christ is compared to a lion because of his heroic power and courage in fighting and subduing his enemies in *Revelation 5*. The chosen, called saints are compared to palm trees, cedars, etc., because of their excellence and fruitfulness, and so it is with other images of comparison. One must then be careful in the application, not to carry over everything, and to pay proper attention to the purpose and the circumstances.

Having said this as a preliminary word, I wish to share with the reader what antiquity thought on this matter, and what the learned of our time have proposed regarding it.

The Jewish interpreters handle this comparison in a strange way. It mainly comes down to this: *that one should know that Jerusalem, the temple, and the site of the altar of burnt offering stood on Benjamin's ground. That portion where the altar of burnt offering stood, and where the Priests and Levites were, and the sacrifices were slaughtered, skinned, divided, and burned—from which the Lord, the Priests, and the Levites had their share—they called* the portion of the predator <note>original Hebrew: *חלקו של טורף* (chelko shel toreph), meaning the portion of the one who tears or plunders</note> or the tearer. *Targum, Onkelos, Chaldean, Jonathan, Jerusalem [Targum], and the Talmud in the tractate* Sacrifices <note>original Hebrew: *זבחים* (Zevachim), a tractate of the Mishnah/Talmud dealing with animal sacrifices</note> *Chapter 5, folio 53. See Heidegger’s History of the Patriarchs, Jacob Laurentius, etc.*

But who does not notice that this is too forced and too meager?

For where else is God’s altar called a ravenous wolf, an altar established by Divine order for His service?

Here the text speaks of Benjamin, and not of his jurisdiction or the altar built on his ground; otherwise, it would have to refer to the altar itself.

Why does he divide spoil or rob more in the evening than in the morning, or more in the morning than in the evening? Sacrifices were offered at both times.

And even assuming the altar of burnt offering stood on Benjamin’s ground, Benjamin himself did not devour anything; nor did he divide spoil. That altar belonged to Levi’s tribe, and the Priests lived from the altar.

<column-break/>

Thus, it would have been more fitting if such a thing had been said of the tribe of Levi.

Barradius <note>Sebastiano Barradas (1543–1615), a Portuguese Jesuit known as the "Apostle of Lisbon," famous for his commentaries on the Gospels.</note> has a peculiar judgment here. He believes *that since Jerusalem stood on Benjamin’s ground, one may think here of its inhabitants; and he says the Jews ate the prey in the morning when they brought Christ to Pilate to be crucified; and in the evening they divided the spoil when the soldiers cast lots over Jesus' clothes.* <margin>Barradius contradicted.</margin> My judgment is that this view is neither acceptable nor sufficient, for I find no reason why I should apply Benjamin’s saying to Judaism in general more than the blessings of the other tribes; it is a particular blessing. If it had to be understood this way, why was it not applied to Judah and Levi, the primary causes of Christ’s suffering? How do the soldiers fit in here? They do not belong to Benjamin.

Furthermore, I have noticed that this prophecy of father Jacob is specifically applied to the entire tribe of Benjamin, and that the naming of the wolf, the dividing of spoil, and the tearing, etc., must be regarded as a metaphor for the strength, bravery, experience in war, and the valiant courage of those of Benjamin’s tribe. It is for this reason that this animal is dedicated to Mars, the god of war, and is itself called *Martius, Martialis*, etc. <note>Latin: "Of Mars" or "Warlike."</note>

Yet since Paul was not very old, and he was converted immediately on his journey against the Christians, there seems to be no "morning" and "evening" between them <note>The author is debating whether Paul's life fits the "morning and evening" structure of the prophecy in Genesis 49:27, since his conversion happened relatively early.</note>. We find, besides the aforementioned place, another <margin>Remarkable passage from Moses.</margin> description flowed from the pen of Moses, well worthy of notice; it appears to us in *Deuteronomy 33:12: And of Benjamin he said, the beloved of the Lord shall surely dwell by him, he shall cover him all the day long, and he shall dwell between his shoulders.*

I have noticed that some take it as a figure, a wish, and a prophecy. If I have understood their meaning correctly, they understand it in this way: *That the Lord truly will and shall hold the Tribe of Benjamin dear and precious, just as father Jacob made a singular point of Benjamin: that He may love him, and cover him with His wings of protection, doing him well and nurturing him: and graciously bring it about that even if the ten tribes should fall away from David's house, yet Judah and Benjamin may remain faithful and united together in that royal house, so that the Lord, dwelling in the Temple—which stood on Benjamin's ground—might overshadow and favor them together.*

Indeed, as Benjamin's territory is described, the city, the temple, and the altar stood at least for a major part on Benjamin's ground, *Joshua 18, Psalm 78:68, 69.* They bordered each other and seemed as if melted into one: outwardly, overshadowed by the Lord dwelling in the temple, as one saw the depicted Cherubim with their outstretched wings above the Ark of the Covenant.

However, if I have properly examined and understood the opinion of other eminent men, they believe that the "beloved of the Lord" must be distinguished from Benjamin, as promised to him: and that by this "beloved" one should preeminently understand the Messiah, the Son of God, His dearly beloved, *Isaiah 5, John 10, Matthew 3:17 and 17,* who would make His tabernacle among His brothers while Judah and Benjamin were still united in Jerusa-

lem, and inhabit the temple, as it were, and glorify it with His teaching, signs, miracles, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. *Haggai 2, Malachi 3, Joel 2, Psalm 68, Acts 2, Ephesians 4.*

Indeed, they believe that one may go further, and in the united Judah and Benjamin observe the united Jewish and Gentile people, or the church from Jews and Gentiles, which He would always be with, covering and overshadowing with His grace, power, and majesty—terrible to His and her enemies—so that He would dwell between the shoulders of these two securely, steadfastly, and undisturbed.

Another notable passage should be taken <margin>Another remarkable passage.</margin> here, namely, *Psalm 68:27: There is little Benjamin, who ruled over them, the princes of Judah (with) their council: the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.*

Four tribes of Israel appear in this text, in the general progress, the gathering and shouting because of the Messiah's ascension and victory, as all Christians will allow. It is something strange that Benjamin's Tribe was nearly destroyed, yet before and after was very brave and warlike, having stood in favor of the succession of Saul's sons to the throne against the house and kingdom of David, and being the one tribe among all others that marched out hostilely with its following against Judah and David; yet afterward, it was found among its brothers in escorting the Ark, and so steadfastly adhered to King David and his house after Saul's death. *2 Samuel 3, 4, and 5.*

It was indeed something wondrous and unexpected that Saul, afterward also called Paul, from Benjamin's tribe, *Philippians 3,* who had turned himself so partially and hostilely against Christ, His own, and His kingdom, was so suddenly <margin>Paul's conversion.</margin> turned around and found among Christ's servants, followers, among the Christians, even the Apostles: a public and clear proof of the triumphing Christ and His church. No wonder then that the Holy Spirit and the church of Christ are introduced here as being greatly amazed and cheering for the victor Christ, *Acts 9:26, Galatians 1:23.*

Certainly, just as Benjamin was born long after Joseph and his other brothers, quite some time passed between the calling of the Apostles and the conversion, calling, and preparation of Paul for the Apostleship. Was Benjamin the youngest? Paul was also the youngest of the Apostles, *1 Corinthians 15, Galatians 1:17, etc.*

Was Benjamin born as if in haste, and as an untimely fruit? Paul was born at a time when one could least expect it. Therefore he called himself an <term>ἔκτρωμα <note>original Greek: *ektroma*, referring to an untimely birth, miscarriage, or "one born out of due time" (1 Cor 15:8)</note></term>, a fruit that appears untimely and unexpectedly, and thus not without sensible pain. On this *Osiander* says: *Just as a fruit coming from a miscarriage has no life, so Paul was not from the number of God's children: and he would have perished in that blindness, as also in his godliness, unless the Lord had taken pity on him.* Balduinus lets himself be heard thus: *Just as the untimely fruits of the womb do not come into the world without the extreme pain of the mother, so Paul was not accepted among the children of God without the greatest preceding pains and torments of the congregation, which she had to endure in his persecutions.* Cluverius in his *Apostolic Division*: *Paul calls himself a miscarriage, or untimely born, because...*

that he was like a miscarriage <note>original: "misdragt". This refers to 1 Corinthians 15:8, where Paul describes himself as "one born out of due time," often translated from the Greek *ektroma* (miscarriage or untimely birth).</note>. Surrounded by darkness, *he wounded the mother church, and was as if deadly to her while she gave birth to him.*

Others, as I find it, take it in this sense: namely, that the Apostle compares himself to a miscarriage because he was very unexpectedly and suddenly converted, enlightened, chosen, and appointed as an Apostle; while in himself, due to his hostile persecution, he was worthy to be buried in the earth like a miscarriage, and to be considered as nothing. Professor Campegius Vitringa <note>Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note> in his <margin>Thoughts of Vitringa.</margin> *Sacred Observations, volume 3, page 48* has noted this. Namely, *Paul calls himself one untimely born, that is, an imperfect fruit, which comes forth at an unexpected time due to a lack of strength and age.*

The Apostle calls himself such because he was so suddenly converted by Christ and chosen for the Apostolic dignity at a juncture of time when one had no expectation that more Apostles were to be called. He seemed least suited for this if one looks at his former conduct. And that he is called נער <note>Hebrew: *Na'ar*, meaning "youth" or "servant."</note>, *Neoteros* <note>Greek: "the younger."</note>, the small, or young, or younger, happens because he is "the last of all the apostles" <note>original: "πάντων ἀποσόλων ἔσχατος"</note>: although one can also attribute it to the low and small opinion he had of himself, and thus to his humility. *Galatians 1:17, Ephesians 3:8.*

It also seems to me that he was <margin>Paul the youngest Apostle.</margin> "the younger," not only the last of all the Apostles called, but also the youngest in years, though clever enough above others and beyond his years. *Acts 7:58, Galatians 1:17.*

It is evident that Paul, while still Saul, seemed born for the sorrow, torment, and downfall of the Apostolic Christian church, and for that reason was a "Benoni" <note>Hebrew: "Son of my sorrow," the name Rachel gave Benjamin as she died.</note>: but the heavenly Joseph turned the matter so suddenly and wonderfully that from Benoni he became Benjamin <note>Hebrew: "Son of the right hand."</note>. He also became the primary cause of the death and downfall of the mother of Sinai, bearing children into bondage. *Galatians 4.*

However, although he speaks of himself with humility, he was nevertheless through Divine <margin>Yet the most excellent.</margin> assistance and grace the most excellent of the Apostles, both in zeal and in gifts, abilities, and holy church services. *1 Corinthians 15, 1 Corinthians 11, 2 Corinthians 11. See Romans 15.*

It is then no wonder that he here leads the way as one who rules, who teaches, chastises, and guides, provided with power, authority, and the Apostolic rod; yet not to tear down, but to build up. *1 Corinthians 4:15, Galatians 4:19, 1 Corinthians 15:10, 2 Corinthians 11, etc.*

Now it is noteworthy that, although there were twelve tribes, only four are named. Whether the other tribes were to be replaced specifically by these four—or whether the ones closest to and furthest from the temple were named to signify their unity in religion, while Dan and Asher were further removed from the Tabernacle—I do not yet see how that can be sustained.

For now, I would hold that these four tribes are picked out because the Apostles of our Lord were <margin>Four tribes selected.</margin> chosen from them: namely, from Benjamin, Paul. From Judah, those who are called our Lord's brothers, such as James the Less, *Galatians 1:19, Mark 15:40, Joshua 19:2.* Jude, the brother of James; James the Great and John, the children of Zebedee, *Matthew, Mark 15:40.* Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot. From Zebulun, located in Galilee: Peter, Andrew, Philip, *Joshua 1:45, 46, etc.* Bartholomew, whom some believe to be Nathanael, *Joshua 1:46, Matthew 3, Joshua 21:2.* From Naphtali: Matthew and Thomas, *Matthew 9.*

Now, if anyone should wish to consult many learned men of this same opinion on this matter, he may turn to Jerome, Theodoret, Lyra, Pellicanus, Sognius, *Alting in Shilo & in Additions; Burman on the Synagogues; Cave’s Apostolic Antiquities; Witsius’ Miscellanea & Meletemata; Gerbrand van Leeuwen on Romans; Vitringa in Sacred Observations volume 3 and On the Synagogue page 1048, etc.* If one asks to what church, church era, and state of the church Jacob's blessing and Moses' prophecy can be applied in later times? However, this in no way prevents something similar and more excellent from occurring in the evening of the world and the morning of the glorious kingdom: for as of yet, I do not perceive the fulfillment in its most excellent power. Here, I am by no means looking at the thousand-year reign of the Chiliasts <note>Chiliasts were those who believed in a literal 1,000-year earthly reign of Christ (Millennialism).</note>, nor the prior resurrection of the martyrs, nor a physical appearance or government of Christ on earth. I expect that the church will one day reach such a height that she shall dwell "between the shoulders": that the envy and strife between Ephraim and Judah <note>The author interprets the biblical tribes of Ephraim and Judah as symbols for the Reformed and Lutheran churches.</note>—Reformed and Lutherans, brothers and brothers—shall give way, when they shall attack the "Western Philistine" <note>Likely a reference to the Papacy or other enemies of the Protestant Reformation.</note> with one accord. That zeal shall awaken to also act with power upon the Easterners and the Jews scattered there. That one shall lay hands on Edom and Moab—the Saracens and Turks, blinded by the deceptions of Muhammad—and strike them through the sharpness of the sword of the Gospel. Meanwhile, the inlet of the sea shall be struck, either by external powers or by internal disturbances (*Isaiah 19*) or the conversion of kings. And that the conversion of the Jews is set to be worked out, so that following the firstfruits, the full harvest may be gathered. *Isaiah 11, Romans 11, 2 Corinthians 3, etc.*

### BOARD, BOARDS of the TABERNACLE, קרש, table, plank.

FOR the structure, enclosure, and walls of the Tabernacle, the Lord ordained certain building materials. The Boards had to be made of Shittim wood. *Exodus 26:15 and 36:20.* <margin>Shittim wood.</margin>

These were, some believe, the firmest and densest cedars which grew on Lebanon: or one must believe that they grew in the desert of Shittim, and thus the wood from or out of Shittim was called Shittim wood <note>Shittim wood is generally identified as Acacia.</note>.

"Standing shittim wood," *Exodus 36:20*, is taken by some to mean straight trees—not crooked, slanted, or bowed, but upright-growing trees. Others take it for Shittim trees from which planks shall be sawn into Boards, to stand upright like a wall or a palisade, as a part of the structure of the external, visible Tabernacle. <margin>Shittim wood.</margin>

# BOARDS.
M 2
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

...made by the height of the Tabernacle, each Board had to have a length of ten cubits.

Regarding the cubit as the unit of measurement in the architecture of the Tabernacle, I note that Lightfoot in *Gleanings in Exodus, page 179* <note>original: "Ligtfoot in Spicil. in Exod." refers to John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Hebraist.</note> and Goeree, in the second part of *The Republic of the Hebrews, page 58*, etc. <note>Willem Goeree (1635–1711) was a Dutch author who wrote extensively on Jewish history and biblical antiquities.</note> set that cubit at one and a half feet, and not three feet per cubit: *Exodus 36:21-26.* <note>The source text uses "Hand.", likely an abbreviation for the "Acts/Deeds" of Moses in Exodus.</note>

<margin>Width of the boards.</margin>
And as for the width of the Boards, they were one and a half cubits wide, *Exodus 26:16.* Lightfoot in *Gleanings, page 179* calculates the width at 27 inches. And Goeree, in the second part of the *Republic, page 58*, at 36 inches, with the cubit being calculated at 24 inches.

<margin>Thickness of the same.</margin>
As for the thickness of the Boards, it is not specified by Moses: therefore, one must make a guess. Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> says they were one cubit thick. 9 inches, says Lightfoot in *Gleanings, page 179*; but Josephus speaks of four inches. Josephus likely assumes that the bars, or wooden ribs and crossbars, were not pushed through the hollowed-out Boards across their width—at least, without doubt, the middle one; Lightfoot in *Gleanings, page 180.* Be that as it may, Josephus seems to come closest. For if they were of that [Rabbinic] thickness, and one calculates the length, width, and thickness together, they would have been beams rather than planks or Boards. And who could have carried them?

<margin>Number of the boards.</margin>
As for the number of the Boards, there had to be 20, each of one and a half cubits, for the South side: 20 on the North side, *Exodus 26:18-20* and *36:23*, making the length of the Tabernacle thirty cubits. Six Boards on the West side: and two Boards on both [corner] sides to close the work and give it sturdiness and stability, *Exodus 26* and *36.*

<margin>The decoration of the same.</margin>
All of these were overlaid with gold, *Exodus 26:29* and *36:34*; not simply gilded, but probably covered with gold plates, perhaps with all kinds of foliage such as palm trees, pomegranates, and other elegant imagery.

<margin>Silver pins.</margin>
Mention is also made of two silver pins <note>Often translated as "tenons" in English Bibles.</note> for each Board, at the bottom of the Boards, *Exodus 26:17.*

<margin>Silver bases.</margin>
Also of two silver bases <note>original: "voeten", often called "sockets" in biblical translations.</note> for each Board, one base for each pin, into whose hollows the silver pins undoubtedly slid deeply and locked tight, thus allowing the Boards to rest or sink down upon the bases.

Now, so that these upright Boards might be and remain firm and closed, and stand perfectly straight as a solid, compressed, and fastened body, the Lord commanded that Moses should make five bars on each side, serving as wooden ribs, bolts, or crossbars.

How thick and how long each had to be is not specified: but it is noted that they were overlaid with gold.

The third [bar] had to be in the middle. Whether it went through the width of the Boards via a drilled-out hollow, or whether it was pushed through gold rings or staples alongside the other four, I cannot determine, although the latter seems not improbable to me.

It then consists of seven points of stability: two pins and five bars.

Here you see, then, briefly, the external

appearance of the Tabernacle.

<margin>nal form of the Tabernacle.</margin>
What may be depicted through this remains to be examined more closely.

I can certainly concede that everything was so beautiful and precious, as befits a house and dwelling of the Heavenly King, intended to arouse awe and reverence.

But that nothing else should be hidden beneath it, or enclosed within it, I cannot accept—the more so since the Apostle Paul has told us more than once that these were shadows and images of other things. I will say, then, how I, alongside the learned, would like to have it understood: namely, that one understands the Tabernacle as a figure and image of Christ, and the dwelling of his divine nature in his human nature. Through this, his human nature was showered and covered with wondrous, even elegant gifts and beauties, even though his body, like the <term>Shittim wood<note>Acacia wood, which was highly durable and resistant to decay.</note></term>, was a fruit of the earth in which he was like us in all things, sin excepted; so that those two natures remained inseparably united even in his death and dismantling. Compare the following texts from the *Old and New Testaments* <note>original: "O. en N. Rolle" (Old and New Scrolls).</note>, namely *Isaiah 4* and *53:1*, *Hebrews 2* and *4*, *Isaiah 14*, *John 1:14* and *2:19*, *Colossians 2:8, 9*, *John 3*, *Isaiah 11:3*, *Isaiah 61:1*, etc.

<margin>Tabernacle, an image of Christ.</margin>
But I must also think of the church of Jesus Christ and its living members as living and elegant stones, raised up into a solid building: although in themselves they are not imposing, they who even dwell as if in a Tabernacle, *2 Corinthians 5:1-4*, *2 Peter 1:13, 14.* They constitute and build up the Lord's tabernacle and temple, his house and dwelling—namely the congregation—just as he dwells in each person's body as in a temple. See *1 Timothy 3:15*, *Ephesians 2:22*, *Revelation 13:6*, *1 Corinthians 3:16* and *2 Corinthians 6:16*, *Revelation 21:3*, *Hebrews 3.*

They are the living stones, *1 Peter 2:5*, and a wall, *Song of Solomon 8:8, 9.* They are as if overlaid with gold, glorious within, and decorated with all kinds of gifts and virtues, and adorned with Jesus's bloody righteousness, far more precious than gold or silver, *1 Peter 1:18, 19*, *1 Corinthians 6:20*, *Psalm 45:14*, *Zechariah 12:10*, *Revelation 12.*

These, gathered from Jews and Gentiles, are like two side-walls and walls with their corner-closers and joiners, which, through Jesus's righteousness and intercession, having sunk down upon him, remain firmly joined and united, *Psalm 119:22* <note>Likely a reference to the cornerstone; Psalm 118:22 is more common for this.</note>, *Ephesians 2.*

By the silver bases, in which the silver [pins] of the Boards stand and upon which they rest with their pins, one understands faith working through love, by which all members cling to Jesus and become one spirit with him, *1 Corinthians 6:17.* While they are united with him and rest upon him as the foundation, *1 Corinthians 3*, they stand immovably firm in Jesus's fellowship, divine love, and grace: while they also grow more and more and are rooted in the silver-bright and precious Word and the knowledge thereof, *Psalm 12*, *Psalm 119:205, 113*, *1 Peter 3*, etc.

Furthermore, they are firm and attached, as if by 5 or 7 joints, as one body, spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, God, and father of all, *Ephesians 4.*

### MOUNTAIN, MOUNTAINS,
### Mountain. <note>original: "הר [Har], ὄρος [Oros], mons"</note>

<margin>The variety of mountains.</margin>
Mountains are very high-protruding and sometimes heaven-high clods and crusts of earth, which cleave the clouds of heaven with their high and very sharp peaks.

These differ from one another tremendously in height, breadth, length, ridges, sharpness, shape, and materials.

One finds them provided with all kinds of minerals: gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, etc. One finds coal, chalk, and stone mountains whose peaks are covered with thick snow. There are also those provided with trees, plants, herbs, and a multitude of animals and birds: sending out brooks, causing fountains to spring forth: having within them hollows and waters, well-stocked with fish, sending out streams of sulfur, etc., and whatever else there may be; about which one can receive enough light and information from the writers of natural history.

Through Mountains, lands and kingdoms are sometimes distinguished from one another: in times of need and distress, one often safely takes refuge in them: one can hide oneself in the clefts and caves. They are sometimes inaccessible: firm and immovable. How mountains are born: how Mountains come from plains, and dales and valleys—even pools and bottomless pits and lakes—come from Mountains, is not my purpose to demonstrate here scientifically; but rather how God's Spirit many times makes use of the naming and likeness of Mountains to sketch out for us what can be observed both in God's ways and in human and ecclesiastical states and occurrences.

<margin>God's counsel compared to Mountains.</margin>
For example, one finds heaven-high mountains of singular size, whose roots and foundations are of an unfathomable depth, so that if one wished to trace them, one would have to descend as if into the abyss. Since God's ways and thoughts are now infinitely higher and deeper than the ways and thoughts of men, *Job 11; Isaiah 55,* and in God's counsel and work of salvation regarding eternal election and reprobation, along with the execution of His purpose, there is a height, depth, length, breadth, and a deep abyss, is it any wonder then that such is also compared to a Mountain, and Mountains? *Psalm 36:6, 7; Romans 11; Ephesians 3:10; etc.*

And since the mountains are sunk down upon impenetrable, broad, and firm roots and foundations, by virtue of which they stand as if immovable: although they are spoken of improperly and in

<column-break/>

imagination as melting before God's face, being moved, and appearing with a possibility of being moved, *Job 9; Psalm 46 and 97,* yet God's unchangeable promise, His steadfastness and faithfulness in fulfilling His given word, is exalted above this stability. *Psalm 46; Isaiah 54.*

And since one would judge that he who lives on a mountain has a firm and eternal dwelling: that he who has taken his hiding place in the inaccessible clefts and caves of the Mountains is safe against enemy power, cunning, and persecution, *1 Samuel 23; Psalm 11 and 104; etc.,* so it happens that God's protection and hiding causes a firm and well-assured state: and perhaps from this comes the manner of speaking about "establishing someone's mountain" or "being a high retreat and hiding place for someone." *Psalm 18 and 20 and 30; Proverbs 18; Psalm 111; etc.*

Since the kingdoms, <term>Monarchies</term><note>The author uses 'Monarchies' to refer to the great world empires like those of the Babylonians or Romans.</note>, and human states in this present world stand out quite high above others, appearing quite firm and as if immovable—due to good laws, wise kings and regents, numerousness and vastness, advantageous location, and the "sinews of war"—under which states and governments one can live, grow, and flourish well and securely: and mountains and hills allow for a remarkable distinction in height and greatness; so I maintain that by this naming of mountains and hills in the Holy Scroll are represented monarchies, kingdoms, and greater and smaller states in the world, *Isaiah 2; Micah 4; Isaiah 41 and 42; Jeremiah 5; etc.*

<margin>Powers represented by Mountains.</margin>
When the worldly kingdoms and powers practice nothing other than murder, resentment, violence, and robbery, as was the custom with the God-forgetting Heathens, what are they then other than mountains of prey, Mountains of leopards? Especially when they are further stained by evil sentiments, base customs, and ways of life: which are nonetheless forced to subject themselves to the church of Christ, even if it were only hypocritically, *Psalm 76; Psalm 68; Song of Solomon 4:8; Deuteronomy 33; etc.*

Now, when the kingdoms and great or mighty states descend upon someone else: are melted into another empire: when the name and form of government changes and passes away, so that they are as if no longer seen; just as it happened with those of the Babylonians, Assyrians, Persians and Medes, the empire of the Greeks and Romans, yes, even with the prominent Mountain of the Jewish civil and ecclesiastical state, which was cast into the sea of Heathendom and has no more being or form; when at the Apostles' wish and prayer, yes, faith and hope, resting on the Divine promise and power, such a Mountain or state perishes (for faith is indeed the victory), when one overcomes insurmountable opposition, the height and depth of adversities appearing to hinder the doors of the Gospel and the expansion of Jesus' kingdom, does one not then move a Mountain, indeed Mountains? *Isaiah 40:4 and 49:11; Matthew 17 and 21; 1 John 5.*

<margin>The moving of the mountains.</margin>
When one reads of the *moving* of the Mountains out of their places, *Revelation 6 and 16,* can one not judge them to represent how one power is marched out hostiley against another, being

And when one reads that the Mountains are no longer found (*Daniel 2; Revelation 16*), does this not represent that prominent kingdoms cease to be? Or that they exist as if they were not—that is, they can no longer oppose Christ's kingdom as before, or cannot immediately resist with power and good effect?

<margin>The kingdom of the Messiah compared to a mountain.</margin> Indeed, is there anything in the holy scrolls better known and clearer than that the dominion, the kingdom of Prince Messiah, is compared to a Mountain—a very high Mountain, Mount Zion—towering above all Mountains, to be established and to triumph over all Mountains and hills, or kingdoms and states, as something high, eminent, immovably firm, and fruitful? *Psalm 2 and 125; Isaiah 2:2; Micah 4; Daniel 2:35-44, 45; Hebrews 12; Psalm 68; Matthew 16; etc.*

And so as not to pass by the remarkable passage of *Zechariah 6:1, 2, 3, etc.*, I am inclined to note something upon it, though only in passing.

<margin>Diversity of opinions regarding this vision.</margin> Learned writers, both ancient and modern, are by no means in agreement regarding this vision: for, by the four chariots, some understand four kingdoms or Monarchies; others, four orders of Angels (*2 Kings 2 and 6; Psalm 68:18*), and so the Lord says, *these are the four spirits of heaven.* Others understand them as troops of war and military bands. *Luther* and others [understand them as] the preaching of the Holy Gospel in the New Testament to the four winds or regions of the world.

By the two bronze <note>original: "kopere", which can mean copper, brass, or bronze; in Biblical contexts, usually bronze</note> Mountains, as symbols of firm and lasting governments, etc., *Grotius* desires that one understand *the gates and heavy, difficult paths and passes of Cilicia, over and through the mountains, through which the Babylonians, Persians, and Alexander with his Captains and Generals marched into Syria, Judea, and Egypt.* Others wish to understand by them Mount Zion and Mount Moriah, upon which Mount Zion David had his royal house. And that through this imagery it is suggested that the Lord would preserve the Jewish State and the Priesthood against all violence and enemy attacks until the coming of the promised Branch.

<margin>The understanding of Coccejus.</margin> The great *Coccejus*, it seems to me, understood it in this manner: *In the Prophet Zechariah, in the sixth Chapter, is described the state and condition of the world and the church up to the coming of the Christ and the establishment of his kingdom.*

<margin>The two bronze mountains.</margin> *Regarding what is depicted by the four chariots (See Haggai 2:21, 22, 23; the symbols in verses 2 and 3), the two bronze Mountains are the kingdom of Judah and Israel, or the kingdom of David and the kingdom of the Messiah.*

<margin>Multi-colored horses.</margin> *The horses of various colors and forms are partly bloody and shed blood in Judah; partly they fall heavily and burdensomely upon the people and cause sorrow; partly they are gentle and kind; partly bloody and cruel.*

<margin>The four chariots.</margin> *Meanwhile, the four chariots, or kingdoms with their military troops, shall remain so upon the neck of the holy land until the fourth one is present, under which the kingdom of the Messiah shall be established.*

<margin>Black horses.</margin> *Verses 6, 7: the black horses in the land toward the North are the Medes and Persians, who fell upon the Jews heavily and with difficulty, but not very bloodily; toward which North—Babylon and Assyria—Israel and Judah were carried away captive.*

<margin>White horses.</margin> *The white horses after or behind these black horses, which went toward the same region and the land of the North so that they might take that land and bring the people under them—who meanwhile were easy and not disadvantageous to Israel—are the Greeks under Alexander.*

<margin>Hail-spotted horses.</margin> *The hail-spotted ones pulling toward the South, after the Persian empire was brought down under Alexander, and especially the generals of Alexander, and among these Ptolemy, the son of Lagus (from whom Daniel 11:5), against whom the efforts and counsels of the Seleucids were perceived (Daniel 11:8, 9). Then also Euergetes came into Asia and mastered the castles and strongholds of the empire: though because of rebellion he had to return again to his kingdom (Daniel 11:8, 9, etc.).*

<margin>Red horses.</margin> *The red and bloody horses that went out, etc. (verse 7). The Romans intentionally wanted to have Judea in their power: and they were permitted to have power over Judea. These were the red horses. Mark these things well. Pompey took Jerusalem and wrested the kingdom from Hyrcanus. Gabinius, Crassus, Bibulus, etc., have possessed the same. The census <note>original: "De beſchryving", referring to the Roman taxation and enrollment</note> took place. The Jews were esteemed as subjects of the Roman empire. There were constant governors. Archelaus was banished. Judea was made into a province. Under Nero, the city and state were destroyed.*

<margin>Opinion of Hulfius.</margin> Henricus Hulfius, a currently famous Professor, does not agree with the foregoing and writes thus in his book *The Valleys of the Prophets* <note>original: "de Vallibus Prophetarum"</note>, which I shall present with some shortening: *One is accustomed to explain this as the Medes and Persians sent into the Northern end; of the Seleucids in Egypt and Ptolemais; and of the Romans destroying the land of the Jews.*

*But in my opinion, the order and chain of the Prophecies which the Writer has kept conflicts with this. And there is too great a similarity with the seven spirits standing before Christ's throne (Revelation 4). And one must particularly observe that the works of these run counter to this, for they are said to have brought and placed the Spirit of God in all lands, which must be understood powerfully and in a spiritual manner.*

*The four chariots through the four winds, or the spirits that stand before the Throne, are the various effects of the Holy Spirit.*

*The Angels made into winds are the Apostles, the politicians, and all those who, from the four corners of the world standing before God's Throne, having received Divine commands, carry them out very hastily.*

*These come forth from between two bronze Mountains. From the ecclesiastical government of Judea—Zion—and the imperial government, very heavy to the church: or from Judea and Zion (Psalm 50:2, Psalm 110:2, Isaiah 2:3, Hosea 1:11), Sinai and Zion: the Jews lived between the kingdom of Israel and Judah: between Mount Gerizim and Zion.*

*The color of the horses arises from the naming and the explanation of their effects or works.*

*Because the Dragon, in the Revelations, was about to carry out persecutions, he is made as red.*

*Because Christ was to bring peace, he goes out on a white horse toward heathendom.*

*When one sees here black horses, and thereafter white ones following behind, bringing the Spirit of God into the North and causing it to rest there: so by this is given to understand the conversion of the*
