# MOUNTAIN.

...unto repentance and the embrace of white peace, or reconciliation in Christ, in Assyria and Babylon.

The hail-spotted and round-spotted horses <note>Referring to the "grizzled" or "dappled" horses in Zechariah 6:3</note> moved toward the South—meaning Edom and Egypt—and brought in various sorts of Idumeans and Jews, who were quite "spotted" or varied in their doctrine.

Certainly, more than once Christ Himself during His life sent out messengers to preach everywhere, namely the seventy disciples mentioned in Luke 9 and 10. They were also sent further out to the districts and exits toward the parts of Babylon, and to the scattered of the house of Israel (Luke 14:23). If the Jews withdrew themselves, it was in Babylon, Assyria, and Egypt, as well as in Antioch and Seleucia. The law of the Lord had to go out from Zion (Psalm 110). The disciples and Apostles also went to Samaria (Acts 8). But when the Jews made themselves unworthy of eternal life, killed Stephen, and slandered and martyred the Apostles—who became "red," <note>Likely a reference to the red horse of martyrdom or the "redness" of blood</note> namely Peter and James—it became time that they, though staying in those parts for a while, turned for a major part to the Gentiles. They preached to all creatures, and among these the scattered Jews living in Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt, for these seemed to have some prior claim (Acts 13:46; Psalm 45:11, 12; Song of Solomon 1:7, 8, 9; Matthew 28:18, 19, 20; Revelation 6:2; Psalm 110:2; Psalm 50:2; Isaiah 2:3; Hosea 1:11; etc.).

<margin>Mountains as a symbol of difficult matters.</margin>
Those who desire a broader account should consult the aforementioned book. Very high mountains, mountains of difficulty—as in "looking up against a mountain"—represent a matter that is almost insurmountable. To stand upon a mountain is a symbolic means of being above the difficulty, etc.

<margin>Symbol of a goat on a mountain.</margin>
Philotheus <note>Likely referring to the author of an emblem book, such as *Philothei Symbola Christiana*</note> presents to us a rock goat or chamois standing on the peak of the mountains, as a symbol of certainty and tranquility in all things (in *Ged.* page 51, etc.).

> Now the goat sits unafraid on the heavenly mountain,
> And lifts its head above the clouds to the stars.
> Below, the untamed East winds hiss, and the South wind
> Pours forth many dark waters from the shaken clouds.
> Now, secure, it has escaped the rabid force of dogs
> And the clever, stretched nets that the right hand draws.
> It fears nothing. Nor shall you dread greater things
> When you, my soul, cross the threshold of the earth.
> Why do you cling to the earth, my mind? You shall sit secure
> If you seek to be closer to the great God.
> <note>Original Latin: "Jam sedet æthereo non territa caprea monte, / Et nubes supra tollit ad astra caput..."</note>

-> This amounts to the following: <-

> Now the goat is at rest, beyond fear and trembling,
> Finding herself on a mountain, raised heaven-high.
> Below her, the wind drives its storms hard,
> And it rains torrent upon torrent, as if all would perish.
> Now she is in safety and rest, outgrown the raging barking
> Of the dogs, and the tension of snare and net.
> She fears no danger. Be you also not afraid,
> My soul, when you have risen above the earth.
> Why do you cling to the earth, O soul? You shall dwell happily,
> If you wish to present yourself closer to the Creator.

<margin>Representation of a heavenly mind.</margin>
See him further regarding a mind that floats in the heavenly realms and treads the earthly underfoot (page 106).

> A horrid storm harasses the middle of the mountain,
> And a great gale presses against its lower side.
> But its exalted head it lifts far above the heavens,
> and this part of it always acts in serenity.
> Why do I linger in these lands? If only the heights give me rest,
> I shall despise the lower fates with their evils.
> The lower parts forever boil, agitated by tumult:
> True rest is given above, and it shall not perish.
> Thunderbolts are not generated above the highest clouds,
> But keep their three-pronged weapons for humble places.
> The mind that loves piety hears all the more tranquilly,
> The closer it is to God, who rules the stars.

> Nothing in this world can disturb the serene mind,
> Which is always well-joined to the eternal God.

<column-break/>

-> That is: <-

> The middle of the mountain is battered by the storm.
> The lowest side is constantly crumpled by the tempest.
> But he keeps his head always raised to Heaven.
> No storm cloud can move him or make him tremble.
> What does the earth matter to me, if I may be at rest on high?
> I shall despise her: she bears nothing but grief and pain.
> Below, everything is constantly moved by disturbances.
> One finds rest only at the high arches of heaven.
> That which is highly exalted braves the lightning bolt.
> Only the low stands exposed to that scorching light.
> The closer a soul shall bind itself to God,
> The more safety, the more rest she shall find.
> If the body suffers through pain, and collapses,
> The soul flies heavenward, where she is protected.
> He who unites himself with the Creator of all things,
> Feels himself surrounded by no danger or calamity.

One reads of people hiding themselves in the mountains, caves, and rocks; and of a melancholy cry: "Mountains fall on us, and hills cover us," etc. (Isaiah 2:19; Hosea 10:8; Luke 23; Revelation 6; etc.).

I can well believe that such a thing springs from great fear and distress, in order, if it were possible, to escape the danger.

But I cannot quite see that it is an absolute wish merely to be dead, and specifically to be crushed by the mountains; rather, if it cannot be understood that way, it refers to taking refuge in kings, lands, and peoples to escape the foreseen and approaching judgment. It is at least the language, the wish, and the stunned and desperate cry of those who, despairing of their own strength, nevertheless try to escape the feared and insurmountable danger—through a numbing of the intellect and the pressures of conscience—by fruitless means.

### BERYL, BERYLLUS, Βήρυλλος.

<margin>Beryl the eighth foundation stone.</margin>
BERYLLUS is a noble stone, the eighth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem, the holy city of God descending out of Heaven (Revelation 21:20).

What kind of stone should be understood by this in Hebrew, as a stone in the High-Priestly Breastplate, is somewhat uncertain to determine because of the diversity of opinions among scholars. For if I have noted it correctly, some turn to the Turquoise, or Chrysolite, or to the Sardonyx, or Carbuncle, or Agate, or the Amethyst; but that the thoughts of the learned are so different from one another, will much...

# BERYL.

...perhaps originated from the fact that this stone has much in common and a great similarity with the other aforementioned stones.

Since this stone is the eighth in the counting of the foundation stones, and <term>Shebo</term><note>The Hebrew word *shebo* (שְׁבוֹ) refers to a specific gemstone in the High Priest's breastplate, often identified as agate or beryl.</note> is the eighth in the row of the breastplate stones, it has been thought that *Shebo* might indeed be the Beryl.

<margin>Appearance of the Beryl.</margin>
Regarding the color and "water" <note>A jeweler's term for the clarity and luster of a gem.</note> of this stone, it is described as belonging among the pure and very bright stones: tending quite a bit toward green, specifically sea-green, yet somewhat pale, a grayish-green like the color of the sea, or a brine-like green as the sea appears when it is still and calm. However, they are found in various colors and lusters. *Epiphanius* writes of it: <note>original Greek: "γλαυκίζων ἐστὶ, θαλασσοβαφὴς, ἔχων εἶδος καὶ τῆς ὑδεραέρας γλαυκίτιδος"</note> that it possesses the color of the sea and represents the softer appearance of the Hyacinth <note>In historical texts, "Hyacinth" often refers to a blue sapphire or a similar blue-toned stone.</note>. *Dionysius* tells of the Indian Beryl:

> *Others track, upon the outcropping of torrents,*
> *The bluish stone of beryl; or diamond.*

->That is:<-

->*One seeks the blue stone Beryl, or diamond.*<-

And regarding the Assyrian Beryl:

> *Indeed, it brings from the sea a stone even more precious than gold,*
> *The bluish stone of the moist beryl, the stone that remains*
> *And grows on the rocks, like the serpent-stones.* <note>original Greek: "ὄφιήτιδος πέτρης" (ophietidos petres), likely referring to ophite or serpentine rock.</note>

->That is:<-

->*He brings from the sea a stone even more precious than gold,*<-
->*The blue stone Beryl, the stone that stays hidden*<-
->*And grows on the rocks, like the serpent-stones.*<-

It is a sort of green such as is perceived in the eyes of cats. From the common Beryls, people used to make green goblets or drinking glasses—or at least attach the stones to them.

*Juvenal* in his fifth satire:

> *— And Virro holds bowls*
> *Uneven with Beryl. — — — —* <note>original Latin: "Et inaequales Beryllo Virro tenet Phialas." This refers to a wealthy host using cups encrusted with large, uncut gems.</note>

->That is:<-

->*Where Virro’s cups are set with Beryls.*<-

There were some of a lesser sort, less greenish with a certain golden shimmer; even poorer ones that tend toward the Hyacinth; and of still less value are those that tend toward a deep copper-green.

Consequently, one might find them sea-green or Hyacinth-colored; with a golden luster; and having a thick "skin." They must be cut into a hexagonal shape (six-sided), for it is said this stone has a thick crust or outer skin. Even if it were polished, it would remain somewhat dull; therefore, it serves best to be cut with six facets or surfaces, so that the rays from six sides might give off stronger reflections and lusters to one another.

<margin>Its origin from India and Germany.</margin>
Regarding the birthplace of the Beryl stone, it is generally recounted that India supplies it, as does the root of Mount Taurus on the banks of the Euphrates. Beryls of lesser value and looser colors are supplied by Germany and Bohemia.

<column-break/>

Regarding its healing powers and further capacities for effect, I have not encountered much among the writers; what they do recount, I shall leave to the reader for the price at which I received it <note>A Dutch idiom meaning "I tell it as I heard it, without vouching for its truth."</note>.

It is told that Beryl powder, mixed with a certain liquid, is good for sharp "sinkings" <note>A historical term for "fluxes" or discharges of fluid, often referring here to eye infections or cataracts.</note> falling down upon the eyes. When mixed with oil or rosewater and taken internally, it is wonderfully useful for weak stomachs. That Beryl powder with rose oil is good against bruised and inflamed eyes; and that someone who carries a Beryl stone upon themselves feels that they become more stout-hearted, and more of such things are told. *One may look this up in Pliny, Book 37, Chapter 5; Solinus, Book 52; Jonston, page 42; Dietericus's Biblical Antiquities of the New Testament, page 198; de Mei's Physical Commentary, page 116; Hofmann's Lexicon under "Beryllus"; Braun's On the Clothing of the Hebrews, etc.*

<margin>Power of the Beryl.</margin>

Regarding the stones mentioned in *Revelation 21*, I shall share with my reader what *Calvin* briefly noted from other writers, without saying that I accept it for myself as "good coin and current money" <note>Another idiom meaning he does not necessarily endorse these interpretations as absolute truth.</note>. *In general, it is believed that the virtues of the Apostles are expressed through them, though to transfer and define these specifically for each Apostle would be very difficult, for they differ in rank and numbering order. Matthew 10:2, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:14.*

<margin>Peter's faith represented by the Jasper. The walk of James represented by the Sapphire. John by the Chalcedony. Andrew by the Emerald. Philip by the Sardonyx. Bartholomew by the Sardius. Thomas by the Beryl. Matthew by the Chrysolite. James son of Alphaeus by the Topaz. Jude by the Chrysoprase. Simon the Canaanite by the Hyacinth. James brother of John by the Amethyst.</margin>

Through the **Jasper**, it is held that the unyielding faith of **Peter** is represented.

Through the **Sapphire** of heavenly color, sparkling with golden specks, it is thought that the heavenly walk of **James** is represented: his departure and brilliance due to his precious martyr’s blood.

Through the **Chalcedony**, which resists cutting and engraving, the Apostle **John** is represented, who could not be killed by violent hands.

Through the **Emerald**, it is thought that **Andrew** is represented, who "greened" <note>Meaning he flourished or prospered spiritually.</note> before all others (*Joshua 1:41*).

Through the **Sardonyx**, the bloody martyrdom of **Philip**.

Through the **Sardius**, **Bartholomew**, from whom the skin was stripped.

Through the clear **Beryl**, **Thomas**, who had "clear eyes" after the resurrection of Christ.

Through the **Chrysolite** of India or Ethiopia, **Matthew**, representing his birthplace and apostleship.

Through the **Topaz**, **James son of Alphaeus**, the brother of the Lord, who in his being, appearance, and further qualities resembled our Savior very well.

Through the **Chrysoprase**, **Jude**, and his golden confession of faith among the Edessenes.

Through the **Hyacinth**, **Simon the Canaanite**, because of his imitation of Heaven.

Through the **Amethyst**, **James the brother of John**, because of his burning love.

For my part, I leave each to their own concepts and retain mine. If it be truth that the Beryl is the *Shebo*, which *Shebo* was the eighth stone in the High Priest’s breastplate representing Joseph’s tribe, then I ought to bring forward something regarding Joseph, though there will be much more to say about Joseph later.

# BERYL.

by his wife Rachel, *Gen. 30:24.* And Rachel called his name *Joseph*, saying: *the Lord add to me.*

Joseph was wonderful, friendly, good-natured, and lovely, easily forgiving and forgetting the suffering he endured, repaying his hostile brothers good for evil.

<margin>Meaning of Joseph.</margin>
*Joseph* means, so they say, *increase*, *a prince*, *a ruler*, or *one who has and possesses more than others*. This certainly proved true for Joseph: for although he was sold by his brothers as a servant and slave, he became a free man—indeed a Prince, Count, and a great Regent. In place of shackles and bonds, a golden chain was hung around him, and a royal ring was placed upon his hand. He increased and flourished wonderfully in his lineage, and his descendants formed two tribes among the twelve, each with a distinct inheritance in Canaan.

*Gen. 49:26* calls him "one separate from his brothers," upon whose head blessings would rest: a <term>Nazirite</term><note>The Hebrew word *nazir* (נָזִיר) means "consecrated" or "separated." While later associated with ascetic vows, here it refers to Joseph being set apart from his kin by his trials and eventual status.</note>. This cannot be strictly understood according to the later laws of the Nazirite vow, as those had not yet been introduced or established. However, Joseph was a person hated by and cast out from his brothers: he was a rare example of steadfastness and chastity, a model of beauty and grace, especially regarding the inner beauty of virtue. He was the pearl and crown of Jacob’s house: the most exceptional pillar, benefactor, and sustainer of Jacob’s family in Egypt. He was the only one of Jacob’s family who, through his virtues and merits, was raised to such high state governance at Pharaoh’s court in Egypt. Consequently, he is named with right and reason—according to the character and emphasis of the Hebrew language—*one separated from his brothers*.

When I then further consider that Beryl and <term>Shebo</term><note>The eighth stone of the High Priest's breastplate, often identified as Agate or Beryl.</note> stood upon the High Priestly Breastplate and on the foundation of the New Jerusalem, and that Joseph was represented by the *Shebo*, and that I must hold Christ as the first and most prominent foundation stone of the church and the church-state; then it seems to me that I shall not do poorly by demonstrating some similarities between Christ and Joseph.

<margin>Similarity between Christ and Joseph.</margin>
Was Joseph "one separated from his Brothers," which *Nazirite* signifies? So too was Christ a chosen, anointed, and "separated" one for the high offices he would hold, as can be read in *Ps. 2, Prov. 8, Eph. 1,* etc., and this from all eternity.

Certainly, in his inner nature, origin, birth, and way of life, he was singularly distinct from his brothers. *Jer. 30:21, Isa. 53:11, 2 Cor. 5:21, Heb. 7:26,* etc. He was wonderfully and strongly hated by his brothers, persecuted, an outcast, and sold.

Was Joseph a servant? Christ was also; for this his ears were pierced <note>A reference to the law in Exodus 21 where a servant's ear is pierced to signify life-long service; typologically applied to Christ's obedience.</note>, *Ps. 40, Heb. 10,* and he is repeatedly called God’s servant. *Isa. 42 and 53:11, Phil. 2.*

Was Joseph a handsome man, full of charm and beautiful gifts? Christ was also, *Ps. 45:3, Song of Sol. 2 and 5:10,* etc., *Luke 2:52, Isa. 11:1.*

Was Joseph raised from a very low state to honor, glory, riches, and high office?

No less so Christ; the passages serving

<column-break/>

this purpose are many: *Ps. 2:6 and Ps. 45:7, 8, Ps. 72, Ps. 110:1, 2, Isa. 52:13, 14, Eph. 2:9, 10,* <note>The text cites Luke 14:26, but the context of exaltation suggests the author may have intended Philippians 2:9-10.</note> etc.

Did Joseph not repay his hostile brothers for their disdain, cruelty, and wickedness, but instead repaid good for evil? Who is so unskilled in the Divine letters that he would not know that Christ prayed for the transgressors, *Isa. 53:12, Luke 23:34, 1 Pet. 2:23*? Indeed, in spiritual famine and thirst, he feeds, refreshes, strengthens, and satisfies the hungry and thirsty souls with himself, and with his holy wine and spirit-water. *Ps. 23:1, 2, 3-5, 6, Ps. 36:8, 9, 10, Isa. 55:1, 2, John 6:35, John 1:16,* etc.

But, let this only be said in passing, since I had to deal with the *Shebo*, or Beryl, on the High Priestly breastplate as a symbol of Joseph and his tribe.

<margin>The Beryl, a foundation stone of the New Jerusalem.</margin>
Now I should speak concerning the Beryl as a foundation stone of the New, holy, and Heavenly Jerusalem, descending out of Heaven from God.

To reach my objective, I briefly repeat what I previously noted regarding Beryls, namely:

1. The first and most prominent color and luster is a pleasant and bright sea-green.
2. It also tends somewhat toward sky-blue.
3. It sometimes sparkles with golden lusters and reflections.
4. When one looks at the "skin" or outermost crust, the rays are somewhat dull and obstructed; however, when stripped of its crust and ground into a six-sided shape (hexagon), it then gives off a wonderfully beautiful and brilliant light from the collection of rays from these six sides.

Everywhere, in the transfer and spiritual interpretation of the 12 stones, I establish as a firm truth beforehand that Christ is the foundation of the church and the church-city—the choice stone—as will be discussed under the words FOUNDATION and STONE elsewhere. Therefore, I shall first attempt to apply this to Christ as the foundation, upon which work I now begin.

<margin>Application of the Beryl to Christ.</margin>
A. When I, having observed a pleasant and eye-strengthening sea-green in the Beryl, pass over to Jesus, then I find in him everything that can refresh, lift up, and strengthen the eye and heart: the "green" of grace, love, kindness, friendliness, and meekness. Pure grace, love, and mercy were the source of his coming, and of him as a gift and Divine present. *John 3:16, Gen. 49:10, Luke 1:71, Rom. 5:8, and 8:32, 2 Cor. 5:14.*

To practice love, mercy, and inner compassion was part of his assumed office, and for that purpose he took on human nature. *Heb. 2:17, 18 and 4:15, 16.*

He showed it effectively in his mercies and inner compassion: moved with tears, healing many who were sick and those who were beset with all kinds of evils...

# BERYL.

...brought *Matt. 4:23, 24; Luke 8 and 19:41, 42* with the greatest kindness toward him, inviting them to the blessings of salvation, *Isa. 45:22 and 55:1, 2, 3; Matt. 11:28,* etc., in his friendly and lovely dealings. *Isa. 40:11; Isa. 42:3; Matt. 11:29, 30.*

**B.** If I see and behold in any Beryl a certain color which tends and draws toward the color and form of heaven: it seems to me that I perceive in my Jesus something which is even more excellent—namely, everything that is heavenly and divine: such as his heavenly origin, birth, nature, and descent. *Jer. 30:21; Matt. 1; Luke 1; John 1:1, 2-14 and 3:13; 1 Cor. 2:8.* The Lord of glory. *1 Cor. 15:47.* The Lord from heaven. His heavenly-mindedness, and intimate familiarity and conversation with his heavenly Father, always being occupied with inner desire and contentment in the work of his heavenly Father, *Ps. 40:9; Luke 1:49; John 4:34; John 17:4.* After his work was finished, he was most intimately and closely joined and united with heaven, the Father, and the Father’s glory, being taken up, glorified, and going to sit at the Father’s right hand. *Acts 1:9; Eph. 4:8; Heb. 1:3-13; Ps. 110:1, 2; Heb. 12:2.*

**C.** If I find in the Beryl golden specks, reflections, like golden ripples? I encounter in my foundation stone of Zion and Jerusalem everything that is divine, precious, and incomparably brilliant, through a divine luster, image, and reflection. See under **IMAGE** and **REFLECTION**. I see in him God and Man, everything that is precious, and with which no gold can be compared regarding his inner beauty, gifts, and virtues. *Ps. 45:3; Isa. 11:2; Song of Sol. 5:10,* etc. *Col. 1:19; Col. 2:3-9.* I notice in and by my precious foundation stone of Zion, proudly and firmly laid, *Isa. 28:16,* everything that is dear and precious to buy and redeem sinners, and to place them in the freedom and dignity of the children of God. *Acts 20:28; 1 Cor. 6:20; 1 Pet. 1:19; Rev. 1, 5, and 3:8.*

**D.** He who knows the noble Beryl knows very well that it appears with a rough skin and bark <note>Dutch: *schorsse*, referring to the unpolished exterior or matrix of the gemstone.</note>: yet he knows at the same time what is hidden under this rough external bark, so he does not take offense at it. Nor will it, for this reason, be worth a cent less to him.

To him who casts an eye upon Jesus’ external appearance—his form, his physical presence—I know and confess, it offers little to the imagination: the exterior brings forth the form of humility, insignificance, weakness, etc. *Ps. 22:7; Isa. 53:1, 2, 3; Phil. 2:7, 8.* Yet those who knew and understood him, and what the actual reason for this was, noticed it as an engraving of the Messiah, *Zech. 9:9,* did not take offense at it, and felt and spoke of him no differently. *Ps. 45:3; Josh. 1:14,* etc.

**E.** If I see that the Beryl, being cut with six sides <note>This refers to the natural hexagonal crystal system of beryl (emeralds, aquamarines, etc.).</note>, delivers a collection of beautiful and shining rays, etc., I behold in my Jesus—when I lift the aforementioned bark from him with my thoughts—six wonderful, rare, and divine rays, as God’s wonderful Son; *Isa. 9:5;* namely: 1. The government is upon his shoulder. 2. His name is Wonderful. 3. He is Counselor. 4. He is Mighty God. 5. He is Everlasting Father. 6. He is Prince of Peace.

If I contemplate my Foundation Stone Jesus, I see six Divine rays reflecting from him. For upon him rests: 1. the Spirit of wisdom. 2. Of understanding. 3. Of counsel. 4. Of might. 5. Of knowledge. 6. Of the fear of the Lord.

If I look upon him in the execution of his accepted offices as God the Savior, I find again in and with him: 1. The Divinity. 2. The Humanity. 3. In which nature he is mediator between God and men. 4. The great Prophet. 5. The only and perfect High Priest. 6. The eternal King.

**F.** Let it be a truth that a suitable remedy for the eyes is prepared from the Beryl stone: that it is good for the heart, to take away faintness and faint-heartedness, and therefore useful to carry with oneself, etc. Jesus works such things through himself in such a way as one could never expect from any Beryl stone, being observed in the fruits and powers of his three offices, namely:

1. As **Prophet**, through himself, through word and spirit, enlightening and strengthening the eyes of the soul. *Luke 24:31-45; Rev. 3:18.*

2. As **Priest**, taking away sin, guilt, and impurity, reconciling God and making peace with the sinner, acquiring right and boldness, and access to God, interceding for us. *Rom. 5:1, 2, 3; Rom. 8; 1 John 2:1, 2.*

3. As **King**, protecting, shielding, and disposing the mind, *2 Cor. 12:9; Josh. 14:27.*

<column-break/>

More similarities between the Beryl and the Christ I shall not bring forward at this time: but in a lower and fainter sense, in a subordinate sense, I turn to Matthew the Apostle, joined and united in, through, and with the Beryl Jesus, and clothed with Christ's Spirit, the eighth Apostle: whose life and conduct I shall describe very briefly.

<margin>Calling of Matthew.</margin>
Matthew, the son of Alphaeus, is also called Levi. *Matt. 9:9; Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27, 28, 29.*

Regarding his worldly profession, he seems to have been a Tax Collector <note>Dutch: *Tollenaar*. In the biblical context, these were often locals contracted by the Roman Empire to collect taxes, frequently viewed as traitors or extortionists.</note>, perhaps a type of Tax Farmer <note>Dutch: *Pagter*, one who pays a fixed sum for the right to collect taxes and keeps the surplus.</note>, having his custom house at Capernaum, on the shore of the Galilean sea, perhaps to collect transit money, or something similar from persons crossing over, and for incoming and outgoing goods on behalf of the Emperor. *Matt. 17:27 and 22:21; Luke 3:21;* etc.

<margin>Tax Collectors disregarded.</margin>
Now as for the office of Tax Collector, which I have dealt with elsewhere in my *Sacred Miscellany*, it is true that some prominent persons among the Romans held that office; however, I do not think it was done for the sake of respect, but out of a kind of domestic decay <note>Possibly implying financial ruin or loss of family status.</note>, and thus for the sake of profit; but be that as it may—

# BERYL.

However it may be, it does not occur to me that anyone, besides a certain Sabinus among the Roman tax farmers and collectors, has ever earned a good reputation or name: from which I would easily conclude that those (who held that office from time to time) must have possessed little virtue: or that the office must have added a sense of contempt and common hatred even to those who were otherwise virtuous enough. And the latter seems not entirely groundless, though I would not wish to dismiss the former either: for as I see it, there seems to have been something to it. For the Jewish maxim and rule of thumb dictated: *Do not marry a son or daughter from a family where there is a tax farmer or collector; for all tax farmers are birds of prey, harpies, and rogue sinners.* <note>The "tax farmers" or publicans were locals contracted by Rome to collect taxes; they often overcharged to keep the surplus for themselves.</note> It would be a sad and poor state of affairs if the office made a person so; nevertheless, there must have been a reason in ancient times that in the Divine Book, one finds tax collectors and sinners placed side by side, *Matthew 9 and 18.* Upon investigating this, I found these probable reasons brought forward, namely:

<margin>Tax collectors a hated people.</margin>

<margin>Reasons for this.</margin>

1. That this service must have been generally hateful by its very nature to the Jews, because it was a visible symbol of their being a people dominated by a foreign power, and therefore not free: a point upon which they stood strongly and felt pressed.
2. To which may be added that the tax farmers and collectors were usually quite hard and sharp in their demands, having the "to have and to hold" mentality in their message.
3. Among other reasons, it can be considered that the collectors, having to deal not only with Jews but also with Gentiles, were necessarily defiled by the latter according to the Law of Purity and Impurity; these Gentiles were recorded by the Hebrews as being no higher than dogs, swine, and the unclean.
4. To which may be added that the morals and lifestyle of these collectors were perhaps quite rough and scandalous. Be that as it may, Matthew was also a tax farmer or collector. What his previous life and morals were like, I confess I cannot say; but this I know: he was a Disciple and an Apostle of Jesus Christ.

It is not unlikely that Matthew, being at the tax house in Capernaum—where Jesus stayed for some time with his disciples, preaching and performing miracles and signs, *Matthew 11:23, 24. etc.*—would have had the opportunity to see and hear Jesus; and perhaps he also witnessed Jesus' miracles.

When Jesus called this collector to him and ate with him, and Matthew had heard Jesus' reasoning, Jesus requested that he follow him. The history does not say that Matthew took any time for deliberation, or excused himself under the pretext of his profession and interest in his earthly calling: but it would seem that he was ready at once. Perhaps he also gave a

<column-break/>

friendly feast to his fellow officials to take an honorable leave, and perhaps also to provide them with the opportunity—by hearing and seeing Jesus' teachings and miracles—to also come over to his teaching and follow him. But however it may have been, this was the fact: Matthew listened, followed, and became first a Disciple and thereafter an Apostle of Jesus Christ, and seems to have remained among or with the Jews until the death of Jesus. *Matthew 12, Mark 3, Luke 8.*

It is related that Matthew departed for foreign regions: though first, he left behind his Gospel writing, described by him in Hebrew, to the Jews as a testament or memorial. But I do not express myself further on that matter. <note>original: "Hebreeuws" — Early church traditions suggested Matthew wrote an initial Gospel in Hebrew or Aramaic before the Greek version.</note>

Regarding his subsequent travels and Apostolic deeds, with what pertains to them, I have found it written that the Apostle is said to have traveled to Persia, and having preached there, moved on to Asia and India: from there to Africa, or the Land of the Moors <note>The "Morenlant" refers to Ethiopia in historical contexts.</note>, and that among many others, he also converted King Aegippus; but that the following King, Hyrtacus, finding him teaching in the temple, placed him in custody and had him beheaded in the capital city of Naddavar.

<margin>The deeds of Matthew.</margin>

When we consider Matthew in himself, as a believer, then we should place him among the "ornamental stones," *Isaiah 54:11, 1 Peter 2:4, 5.* But when we view him as an Apostle, as a writer of his Gospel, as an untiring preacher, and as a blood-witness <note>A martyr.</note>, then we may with right and reason regard him as a foundation stone, to whom one could very easily apply what has been said of the Beryl. Unless, of course, I should assume that the intelligent reader, by making the transition themselves, would gladly release me from this elaboration; and would rather hear how every living church member, considered as a stone, can and must strive to become like the Beryl, and to portray it within themselves and their practices. This I wish to unfold and lay open more closely, yet briefly.

> a. The pleasant sea-green reveals itself when one has laid aside all hatred, envy, wrath, and greed for revenge: and thus displays a calm sea, in the green of love, humility, gentleness, long-suffering, etc. *Colossians 3, Ephesians 4.*
>
> <margin>Church members compared to the Beryl.</margin>
>
> Thus one must be green and fruitful in faith, love, confession, and all good works: as fruits of the spirit and of love, which never grows cold, withers, or becomes unfruitful. *Psalm 1:3, Psalm 92:13, 14, 15, Jeremiah 17:8, Philippians 4:8.*
>
> b. The heaven-colored <note>Sky-blue or azure.</note> hue and uniform appearance must be shown in the disposition of the heart before God: and through one's walk before men.
>
> For which it is wonderfully healing and useful, above all, to seek the kingdom of God, *Matthew 6:33,* not to be conformed to this world, *Romans 12:2,* and not to love it, *1 John 2:15,* as a lover of the earth...

# BERYL.

<sig>N 2</sig>

<margin>Two scales.</margin>
They cannot be heavenly-minded, *Psalm 13:4, Philippians 3:18, 19,* and since overcoming such [worldly] things sometimes involves a great deal of work, everyone is advised to weigh things as if in two scales against each other.
1. In one scale, place the world with everything that is in it: and then he shall find that everything is, for the most part, material, soulless, lifeless, irrational, and corruptible—capable of being stolen from us by fire, water, theft, etc. It all remains outside of us. One is not inwardly improved by it, nor made more virtuous; it breeds trouble and anxiety, and helps nothing in sickness and pain; when we die, we must leave it all here.
2. In the other scale, above, is God, and heaven, etc. It is all permanent; it makes a person happy through its possession; it satisfies the heart, *Psalm 16:11, Psalm 17:15, Psalm 31:20, 1 Corinthians 2:9, and Romans 8:18, 2 Corinthians 4:17.*
The latter is capable of completely winning over the soul, and igniting it with a sigh for the heavenly, and toward a walk on high, *Psalm 42:1, 2, Psalm 63, 2 Corinthians 5:2, 3, Philippians 1,* etc.

c. The specks of gold, and the golden reflection in the Beryl, represent the "church stones" <note>This refers to believers, who are often described as "living stones" making up the spiritual temple of the church.</note> in the possessing and revealing of:
1. Heavenly knowledge, wisdom, and the confession of Divine truth, which surpasses all gold, silver, and precious stones, *Job 28:12, 13,* etc., *Psalm 19:10.*
2. In noble faith, *1 Peter 1:7,* laying hold of the gold of Jesus' obedience, *Revelation 3:18,* the incorruptible gold of a noble mind, and precious character and virtues, *2 Peter 1:5, 6, 7.*

d. The rough Beryl-skin, covering the inner precious beauty: yet that must be increasingly stripped away; it is called a "foreskin," flesh and sin, corruption, etc. This happens through what is called conversion, renewal, the dying off of the "old man," and the resurrection of the "new man," the crucifying of the flesh, etc.

e. A believer must give various types of reflections: read *Colossians 3:12-14 and 2 Peter 1:5, 6,* and you will find these virtuous reflections in that number.

f. What the Beryl does and works regarding the improvement and strengthening of the sight and the heart: believers, as Beryls, can bring this about regarding themselves and their neighbors—toward the eyes of the soul and the heart, according to the inner person of the heart—by teaching, exhorting, instructing, rebuking, comforting, etc. *Ephesians 4, Colossians 3:3, 1 Thessalonians 5, Hebrews 5 and 10:24, 25.*

<margin>Believers represented by Beryls.</margin>

### BERSEBA, or BEERSEBA באר שבע.
<note>Hebrew: "Well of the Seven" or "Well of the Oath."</note>

<margin>Location of Beersheba.</margin>
**B**EERSHEBA is the name of the Desert, a region, and a city in Judah or Simeon, at the southern borders of the land of Canaan, in which Hagar and Ishmael lived as outcasts, with only a bottle of water and some bread—that is, very meagerly and 

<column-break/>

scantily provided, etc. One may look this up in *Genesis 21.*

Abraham had a tabernacle and a well there, which, having been taken from him, was thereafter restored by a solemn agreement. Isaac lived there and had various encounters, *Genesis 21 and 26.* Just as Beersheba lay at one extreme, so Dan lay at the other; hence the expression, "from Dan to Beersheba." <note>A common biblical idiom used to describe the entire extent of the land of Israel, from north to south.</note> Samuel’s sons, Joel and Abijah, the judges of Israel at Beersheba, did not behave very well, *1 Samuel 8:2.* It seems that there and elsewhere, great corruption in the service of the Lord, idolatry, image-worship, and high places had been introduced and established. To prevent the contamination and fellowship with those unfruitful and dead works, one had to stay away from there, *2 Kings 23:8, Amos 5:5, and 8:14.*

<margin>Allusion to the Historical events.</margin>
If there is anything more to note, it will follow hereafter; in the meantime, it pleases me to note something by way of allusion to the historical events, *Genesis 21 and 26.*

<margin>Hagar and Ishmael.</margin>
It is a Desert and region famous because the maidservant Hagar, with her son Ishmael, fathered by Abraham, struggled, sighed, and lamented there on account of her son, whom she thought would perish of thirst; for she had received a meager supply, a bottle with water and some bread or provisions, which was quickly emptied in that barren, dry, and hot land. Meanwhile, she saw no chance of obtaining water. She did not see the well or the fountain, etc. This brings to my mind how the Jewish and "servant" mother-church, with her sons, true Ishmaels—after they persecuted and despised the free mother-church and the free son—is cast out, *Galatians 4.* They are left with only the water-bottle and some bread from the Old Testament, from which they had to fetch water and bread, soul-food and drink, having the words entrusted to them of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms. But that same church has been made mostly powerless through the traditions, declarations, and explanations of the elders, and their scholars—the Pharisees and Scribes, *Matthew 5, 15, and 23.* The Law, which had Jesus as its end, being situated in promises and shadows, could not last long, nor bear fruit anymore, once the essence and body of the matters had arrived.

<margin>Application to the Jewish church.</margin>

Since the Jews did not recognize or accept the Messiah, yet looked out for Him with strong desires, they had to find themselves faint, in a parched land and without water, once the time and the signs of His coming had passed, *Psalm 42 and 113, Zechariah 9.* <note>The author uses "waterless pits" as a metaphor for a religious system without the "living water" of Christ.</note> For what could the cracked and waterless cistern of righteousness from the works of the Law truly avail? Meanwhile, although the water-well—indeed, the fountain of life, Israel’s spring, Jesus—was near, as if opened and accessible, *Zechariah 13:7, John 4 and 7, Psalm 36:10,* they lacked, like Hagar, the sight of veiled eyes, *2 Corinthians 3, Isaiah 6.* And such shall not improve until they become truly seeing, when they shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of salvation, *Isaiah 12, Zechariah 13, 2 Corinthians 3,* etc., and quench their soul’s thirst with those seven springs of water, *John 4, Revelation 21, Zechariah 3,* etc.

Here Abraham and Isaac lived, or had their tabernacle. They [disputed] concerning the water-well

# BEERSHEBA.

<note>original: "Berseba"</note>

[Isaac] had many quarrels, and had to suffer injustice and insults from Abimelech’s shepherds and servants. Whatever wells were subsequently dug became a "bone of contention"; they were filled in with all kinds of filth until a solemn covenant was made, and then solemnly renewed and confirmed—indeed, strengthened with an oath and a gift of seven ewe lambs. See *Genesis 21 and 26*, from which comes באר־שבע <note>transliteration: Be'er Sheva</note>—a "well of the seven," or "of the swearing of an oath."

On this occasion, it occurs to me that the state of the church and of God’s children on earth is a second Gerar: a place of exile and foreign residence where the streams and storms of hatred, envy, persecution, and oppression rush swiftly and strongly, threatening to overflow the pious. They live in a valley and a howling wilderness—barren, parched, hot, and dry. And if they did not find there wells of water and waters of consolation, they would waste away from sadness and perish, faint with thirst.

<margin>The state of the church on earth.</margin>
Surely Isaac’s true offspring would have long ago perished from thirst and lack of comforting holy water, had things gone according to the desire, passion, and efforts of the "Jewish Philistines." <note>The author uses "Philistines" as an allegory for those he considers enemies of true faith—here specifically referring to the legalism of the Pharisees and later the Catholic Church.</note> For they had used their glosses <note>interpretive comments</note>, soulless traditions, and wrong explanations to enervate, weaken, dry up, and stop the wells of the Prophetic promises, shadows, and examples of the Law. *Matthew 5, 15, and 22.*

My father the king Abimelech with his triple crown—I mean the Pope—along with his Philistine servants and officials, have stopped the water-wells of the Old and New Testaments. Yes, even the seven water-springs from the Rock, Jesus (*Zechariah 3 and 13:1*, etc.), they have blocked with hay, straw, and stubble—indeed, with the rubble and foul dung of traditions, decrees of councils, lessons of the fathers, self-righteousness, invocation of saints, the Mass, and so on.

And if these had not been opened and cleansed of the dung, one would have had to perish for lack of true salvation and the water of comfort.

But just as Christ and his Apostles opened and purified these same wells (*Matthew 5, 15, and 23*), and among the Apostles especially Paul; so too have our Reformers acquitted themselves in this task. For long enough one had to hear, in the Jewish fashion, that the traditions and declarations of the church fathers, the decrees of councils, and the interpretations and definitions of the Pope were the "key" to Holy Scripture. Everyone had to listen to these and believe in them under threat of banishment, fine, and the forfeiture of salvation. The Scripture was held to be a "mute, dead, and deaf judge," and without the Roman interpreter, it was just like a bell without a clapper. The vanity, arrogance, and lawlessness of such a view has been shown and pointed out by the Reformers, so that one should turn little, or not at all, to fabricated and unfounded traditions, soulless interpretations, reckless decrees, and spiritless councils—those "waterless cisterns" and wells of meritorious and superfluous works, intercessors, imagined saints, masses, icons, and so forth. Thus it has been proven to the point of silencing [opponents] that Jesus was a perfect Savior, and that to seek and find His salvation elsewhere is a denial of the single and perfect sacrifice of Jesus Christ—and consequently, the Mass is a cursed idolatry.

<column-break/>

Indeed, when Isaac’s servants dug wells to draw water, people made sport of them. They claimed it was on the Philistines' ground and that Isaac had no right or power there; it was not up to Isaac or his people. No one was allowed to dig except the Philistines and those sent and authorized by them. And who had granted Isaac’s people the right and power? Consequently, when they did dig, the wells were taken from them by force and violence. There was scolding and slandering; the right and power to dig the ground for wells was disputed and denied. On this occasion, the wells were named *Esek* and *Sitna*—meaning "Violence" and "Slander."

<margin>Esek and Sitna. Application to Jesus and the Apostles.</margin>
Did it not happen in almost the same way with Jesus and His Apostles? Was there not a very long dispute over the legality of their mission, and by what power they spoke and did these things? Did the Pharisees and the Scribes not have the official "bulls" <note>official papal or religious edicts</note> to be allowed to teach? Must the rest not keep silent? Did they not say, "The crowd that does not know the law is cursed"? Did they not dispute the power and mission of Christ and His Apostolic men to "dig" in the Word to seek out the holy waters and treasures of heavenly wisdom?

<margin>Also applied to the Reformers.</margin>
Was it not the same with the existence of the Reformers? Over what has there been dispute, if it was not over the legality of their mission? Did they not say, "You are ours? We are the Catholic Church? The Apostolic teaching, antiquity, and succession are with us"? Did they not take away from the laity the ground to dig—the writings of the Old and New Testaments? Did they not persecute and slander them, dragging them before the court of King Abimelech, the Pope? How and where was "digging" allowed to them? They certainly did not wish to tolerate it on their own ground.

Therefore, Isaac and his household had to move further away and withdraw from the court and from Abimelech. And then they dug a well and named it *Rehoboth* <note>meaning "broad places" or "room"</note>. Then they had more rest and space.

When Christ’s "cross-bearers" <note>believers or missionaries</note> had moved a bit further from the court at Jerusalem and had entered the soil of the Gentiles—the land of Immanuel, the inheritance of the Lord, and the furthest outposts of Canaan—they had some space and breathing room (*Acts 8*). Yet even there they were not fully safe until they had entirely left the ground of the Jewish Philistines and arrived at Beersheba—the land sworn to by the King Messiah (*Psalm 2 and 72; Isaiah 49*), the inheritance of Abraham.

<margin>Hardship endured by the first Reformers.</margin>
The first Reformers, though they withdrew somewhat from Rome, might have had some breathing room here and elsewhere in the territories of princes and under their protection, but it was only for a time. One had to move from there as well, when one journeyed toward the "Beersheba" of the Netherlands.

It is true, things were quite bad here; people tried to dispute our land and our freedom through heavy and bloody wars—this "well" was contested by the Spanish Inquisition. But thanks be to the Lord, who has given us *Rehoboth* (room) and an open door, through which we have wrestled out of the violent yoke and been declared free Netherlanders.

And since then, that well has been opened more and more, and cleansed of Roman filth and superstition.

<header>CIRCUMCISE.</header>
<sig>N 3</sig>

<margin>
Healing waters transported everywhere.
</margin>
The wells of the East, West, South, and North have been dug by our keels and fleets, and the opened sea-well gives wealth like streams of water, through which the healing waters of the comforting truth are transported—without the dregs of idolatry—to the most distant peoples as something healing and life-giving.

Indeed, we had hardly found "Rehoboth" <note>meaning "room" or "space," referring to Genesis 26:22</note> and space, or our enemies and persecutors sought us out for peace. They persisted like Abimelech <note>the Philistine king who made a treaty with Isaac</note> for covenants, confessing that the Lord was with us: and so these regions have become like seven [wells], yet a single well—a well of health, fullness, and the abundance of desired things.

Would to God that in this Beersheba there were not sometimes found Judges and Regents like Joel and Abiah <note>referring to 1 Samuel 8:2-3</note>, who do not do what is right, inclining their hearts toward greed, taking gifts, perverting justice, and not walking in the footsteps of the previous Samuels.

Yes, would to God that no idolatrous high places or idolatrous images were found there <note>referring to Amos 5 and 8; 2 Kings 23</note>, but that they were barred from our midst.

Having noted these things regarding Beersheba—though I could give free rein to my thoughts on other applications—I shall, in order not to be too long-winded, content myself with what has been said and prepare myself for something else.

### CIRCUMCISE, CIRCUMCISION,
### <note>Hebrew:</note> Circumcision, To circumcise; <note>Greek:</note> I circumcise, circumcision; <note>Latin:</note> I circumcise, circumcision.

As far as CIRCUMCISION is concerned, if anyone has read even a little, it is known to them that not only father Abraham in his person, house, and lineage, but also many (if not all) peoples have practiced Circumcision. However, that is not the only point; there is also a dispute among scholars whether the Heathens received Circumcision from the Jews, or whether the Jews, through Divine institution, received it from the Egyptians, etc.

<margin>
Circumcision common to many nations.
</margin>
That the Egyptians, Colchians <note>people from the eastern coast of the Black Sea</note>, Arabs, as well as some other nations, had Circumcision quite early is easy to prove. But it is by no means so easy to prove that the Jews had it later, or that they received it from the Egyptians.

It is true that Herodotus <note>a Greek historian known as the "Father of History"</note> says in Book 2, Chapter 104, *that only the Colchians, Egyptians, and Ethiopians have circumcised the foreskin from the beginning: and that the Phoenicians, or Syrians, who lived in Palestine (namely the Jews), admit that they received this custom from the Egyptians.*

Diodorus Siculus <note>a Greek historian</note> in his 2nd Book, Celsus, Origen, and Julian appear to agree with this. See further proofs of this in Spencer <note>referring to John Spencer’s "De Legibus Hebraeorum"</note>, pages 1 and 27, etc. For me, this is answered and cleared out of the way by the Lord Professor Hermannus Witsius <note>a famous Dutch theologian, 1636–1708</note>; therefore, I will only say this in passing:

1. They spoke and wrote this way because they knew no better, and did not have sufficient reports of the scriptural and patriarchal antiquity.
2. What was held in high regard among the Heathens if it was not "powdered with grey antiquity"? Thus, they had to stamp all their opinions and customs with a series of passing centuries.
3. Where do Josephus <note>a 1st-century Jewish historian</note> or true Jews say that the Heathens not only had Circumcision before them, but also that they [the Jews] received, adopted, or learned it from the Egyptians? *See the Aruch Lexicon, the Appendix of Drusius, Preterita, Book 6, etc. There the opposite is said: namely, that they (the Jews) were the first to be circumcised, and for that reason, to distinguish them, the Heathens were called the uncircumcised.*
4. And even assuming that neither Josephus nor even some Church Fathers had gently let this opinion of Herodotus and others slide, or had consented to it with silence, was it therefore the truth? Or was such a thing enough to set oneself against the simple Holy Scripture?
5. Christ says that Circumcision is "from the fathers" <note>referring to John 7:22</note>, and before the Lord gave the command to Abraham to circumcise himself and those of his house <note>Genesis 17</note>, I do not read that Circumcision was in use. And by "the Fathers," I do not know that one should understand the Egyptians or other peoples, but rather Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, etc.

<column-break/>

I am willing to believe, then, that the Egyptians, Arabs, Colchians, and others also had Circumcision among them quite early, but by no means as early as Abraham. Much less do I believe that the Jewish people received Circumcision from God in imitation of certain ancient things. But what seems very probable to me is this: since not only father Abraham but also Ishmael was circumcised in his thirteenth year, and very many nations sprang from his physical seed (distinct from the seed of the promise), and Ishmael's lineage extended far and wide—and seeing that Joseph in Egypt had the highest authority in everything next to the king <note>Psalm 105:21, 22</note>—I would prefer to believe that Circumcision passed from them to the Egyptians as well as to other nations. Although I am willing to grant that, regarding the time, manner, circumstances, end, and purpose, they [the other nations] added much of their own and likely made quite large changes. And regarding what has been said, I am willing to go along somewhat with the reports of some scholars when they describe to us the imagined utility of the snipping off of the foreskin of the flesh, namely:

<margin>
Report of the scholars.
</margin>
a. That Circumcision was observed so greedily to prevent a certain evil, danger, or destruction with the cutting off of the foreskin during the passing of water—especially when it was hot and sharp, which could easily cause inflammation if the male member remained covered with the foreskin. *Philo <note>a Jewish philosopher from Alexandria</note> on Circumcision says: "There are many reasons why it is not advisable to depart from this ancient custom: for with this, one seeks to prevent a kind of evil that is difficult to cure, namely the Carbuncle <note>a severe cluster of boils or skin infection</note>, which easily grows on the uncircumcised."*

It then makes me wonder why the Jews in the wilderness did not get Carbuncles; that one...

# CIRCUMCISION.

...whether one knew of this before or after the Circumcision: and I would almost think that Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note> had a carbuncle <note>An inflamed swelling or boil; here used metaphorically to suggest a feverish or delusional conceit.</note> in his own wisdom-swollen and sharp brains when he wrote this.

<margin>b.</margin> It is also claimed that circumcision can contribute much to natural fertility and procreation; for Philo adds, *circumcision was highly necessary for the sake of fertility, and the broad propagation of one's kind: for it has been found that the circumcised are very fertile, surpassing other nations in this.* Whatever the truth of this may be, I believe that circumcision does not actually contribute to procreation, nor does it make anyone fertile or more fertile. That the Jews have been very fertile since ancient times is well known, but nowhere do I read that the trimming of the foreskin is the cause of this.

<margin>c.</margin> And while I am willing to believe that people imagined circumcision caused a kind of cleanliness: I shall never in all eternity believe that the Jews, for that reason, were or are cleaner and more chaste. It is one thing what one ought to be and was obliged to be, and another what actually happened: one thing the obligation, and another that such a thing would flow from circumcision as such. And for such a purpose, the aged father Abraham would not have found it necessary.

Whether it was practiced among the Egyptians so that they might achieve purification and become holier and more fit for astronomy, land-surveying, and further arts, can be seen in Herodotus in *Euterpe*; Josephus *Against Apion*, book 2; Ambrose volume 4, etc.

It was all of their own making, and of no power or value. Certainly, one does not read that the Lord gave the Sacrament and sign of circumcision to anyone outside of Abraham and his lineage. If the Heathens had it, it was through adoption and not because of Divine institution. They—at least few of them—maintained the time appointed and determined by God. For some circumcised on the eighth day, others in the thirteenth or fourteenth year: not only those of the male, but also of the female sex, and so forth. And as I have already said before, I hold that circumcision passed from Abraham to the Jews and then to other peoples. Thus writes Justin Martyr: *Abraham was the first to receive circumcision according to the flesh.* <note>original Greek: Ἀβραὰμ ὁ πρῶτος τὴν κατὰ σάρκα περιτομὴν λαβών</note> Origen, in *Against Celsus*, book 1: *Celsus, not finding that circumcision was used by the Jews [first], and thinking they borrowed it from the Egyptians, preferred to believe the Egyptians rather than Moses, who relates that Abraham was the first of all men to be circumcised.* Theodoret, in *Questions on Exodus, 3*: *it appears that the Egyptians in those times were not yet circumcised, but afterwards they adopted the law of circumcision, following the Hebrews with a blind zeal.* The ceremony of circumcision, says Bochart in *Phaleg* book 4, chapter 30: *passed from Abraham to the Arabs, and from them to the Egyptians.*

I note that learned men have sought to give the world the impression that God commanded the trimming of the foreskin to Abraham and subsequently to his people Israel to teach them that they must guard against fleshly lust and wicked mingling with those too closely related by blood, which was very common among the Heathen nations: as Spencer <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian and Hebraist.</note> on *Circumcision*, page 25, noted from Photius's *Epistle 205*, etc. Some have also taught that God gave the command to cut the foreskin from the flesh so that He might deter Israel from the wickedness which was common among the Egyptians and other nations regarding the male organ, etc. See Spencer, alongside the writers he cites.

This presupposes that the circumcision of the Jews is of a later time—which I deny—and furthermore, that the Lord had this specific and express purpose in mind, which one should not merely state but must prove more closely if it is to be accepted and find favor.

<column-break/>

<margin>Abraham circumcised.</margin> But not to dwell on these and similar things, God commanded circumcision to be given to Abraham (Genesis 17) when he had reached 99 years: it is said to be in the year 2107 after the creation of the world, 406 years before the departure from Egypt.

That Abraham and the Jews of old would have observed circumcision with as many ceremonies and circumstances as the later Jews does not have enough weight of reason or importance to make us agree and believe it so easily. Certainly, the circumstances among modern-day circumcised people are so many that there is no end to be found to them. To provide merely a skeletal overview, I note the following regarding the manner and ceremonies of circumcision.

<margin>Ceremonies of Circumcision.</margin> Concerning the child who was to be circumcised: they washed him beforehand with clean water and wrapped him in pure linen; and if he should happen to soil himself before the circumcision, he was cleansed anew and wrapped in pure linen, so that the circumcision would not be defiled.

<margin>Day of Preparation.</margin> The day preceding the circumcision was called the Day of Preparation, on which the child was closely watched: they did not go to rest that night; friends and kinsmen came to the house of the father and mother, and a kind of open feast was held there.

When the eighth day had arrived, two chairs were placed in the house of the father, or in the Jewish Synagogue, close to the chest of the Ark: or a seat on which two could sit: or three—one for the circumciser, one for the godfather, and one for the Prophet Elijah, who is said to attend the circumcision as one very zealous for Divine honor and obedience (1 Kings 19:20, Matthew 3:1).

The *Mohel* <note>The ritual circumciser.</note> or circumciser was recognized by his long and sharply filed thumbnails: often a master of circumcision and very experienced in that art.

The witness or godfather is called the *Sandah*, or *Baal Berit* <note>original Hebrew: בעal ברית</note>, meaning Master or Lord of the Covenant.

These chairs being set, the *Sandah* (godfather) and the *Mohel* (master of circumcision) enter: and, as reported, twelve youths, each with a burning light, to represent the twelve patriarchs. Two youths follow with cups full of red wine: one with the circumcision knife: one with a vessel containing sand.

# CIRCUMCISION.

Some come with rose oil, soft linen, dragon's blood <note>A bright red resin obtained from various plants, used historically in medicine to stop bleeding.</note>, coral dust, and compresses with rose oil.

Others come with heart-strengthening items, such as malmsey wine, cloves, nutmeg, and cinnamon, to provide some relief to the parents, godfathers, etc., should they become faint or anxious.

When everything is prepared as has been described, the *Mohel* <note>The ritual circumciser.</note>, or master of circumcision, goes to sit opposite the godfather, the *Sandah*, or *Baal Berith* <note>The 'Master of the Covenant,' who holds the child during the ceremony.</note>, and begins to chant the song that the children of Israel sang when they crossed the Red Sea. At this sound, a woman comes as a godmother, and having taken the child from the mother, brings it to the door of the room where the child will be circumcised, at which point they all stand together. But the *Sandah*, the *Baal Berith* or godfather, takes the child from there and cries out: *Baruch habba* <note>original: "Baruch habba" – Hebrew for "Blessed is he who comes."</note>, welcome, or blessed be he who comes on the eighth day.

Hereupon the godfather, being seated, places the child on his lap, with the face or front of the body toward the circumciser, who sits opposite him. Then the circumciser loosens the swaddling clothes and exposes the lower parts; after which he rubs the foreskin numb and calls for the circumcision knife, made of stone, steel, glass, etc., suitably prepared: sometimes set with precious pearls and stones. He then cuts off the foremost skin, the thick upper skin: and tearing the thin under-skin with his long and sharp nails, he pulls it upward and thus exposes the tip of the male member; and while he is busy with this, he cries out: *Blessed be Thou, O God our Lord, and King of the world, who hast sanctified us with Thy commandments, and hast given us the covenant of circumcision.*

After this, he throws the severed foreskin into the sand, as proof of their hope that their seed shall be as the sand on the seashore, *Gen. XX.* and *XXVIII.*, because Balaam, seeing the foreskins, could not curse Israel, *Num. XXIII.*, and to feed the serpent therewith. *Isa. LXV.* <note>This refers to a traditional Jewish interpretation (Midrash) where the dust/sand relates to the serpent's food and the humility of Israel.</note>

After this, he takes a mouthful of the red wine and spits it upon the child’s member: he sucks the wound three times, spitting what is sucked out into the sand: he anoints the circumcised part with oil, wraps it with soaked compresses, sprinkles dragon's blood and coral dust upon it to staunch the bleeding, and wraps his member with soft bandages and cloths.

After all this, the child is swaddled, while the child's own father begins to cry: *Blessed be God, the King of the world, who has sanctified us with His covenant and commanded that we shall enter into the covenant of our father Abraham.* Hereupon all the bystanders cry: *As he has entered into the covenant of Abraham, so may he enter into the Law of Moses, into marriage, and into good works.*

After all these ceremonies, the godfather stands straight up facing the Circumcision Master, and having taken the cup with red wine, then pronounces many blessings over the child as well as its parents: he cleanses his mouth and hands, after which the child is brought to the mother: and after all this, among wealthy people, they keep good cheer for several days, and the circumciser must remain ready for several days and ensure that no harm comes to the child.

That among the Jews the Sacrament of cir-

<column-break/>

-cumcision is very highly valued, and much is attributed to it, can be perceived from their writings. For it is considered the greatest sin to despise and abhor circumcision, *Hilcoth part 2* <note>Referring to the *Hilkhot* or laws in the Mishneh Torah.</note>; indeed, none but those who are circumcised shall ascend to God. *Deut. XXX. 12.* in the *Kabbala* <note>The Jewish mystical tradition.</note>. Circumcision delivers from the judgment of hell: *Baal Hatturim* <note>A commentary on the Torah by Jacob ben Asher.</note>, etc.

But let this be enough to make only a short sketch. I now stand ready to proceed to matters of greater importance and weight, and to note the end and purpose of the Divine institution.

<margin>Purpose of the Divine institution.</margin>
To come now to the matter, one must know that God had promised father Abraham, after the first main promise in *Gen. III. 15.*, that this blessed seed would come from him and his lineage. He had also promised him a numerous seed, not only according to the flesh, but also according to the promise—namely Isaac—and from and through him, a great and mighty people. He promised him Canaan as a hereditary possession, after a period of some years, not for his fleshly seed in general, but for Isaac's descendants: and tells him that in the future, from that seed, the promised "seed of the woman" would spring, in whom not only the seed sprung from him and Isaac, etc., would be blessed and graced, but also the other nations, who would have sprung from him by his handmaids, and from these again in the course of time, and become very numerous. *Gen. XII.* and *XVII.* and *XVIII.* and *XXII. Gal. III. etc.*

<margin>God's promises to Abraham.</margin>
Now all this Abraham believed and agreed to, although he was old and mother Sarah very weakened, and the womb being as if incapable of fertile procreation; and so he received and underwent the sign and seal of God's covenant and promises when he had reached 99 years; and for what else than for a sign and seal of God's covenant and Testament? *Gen. XVII. Rom. IV.* For the remembrance of that covenant with Abraham, for the entry into the same, in firm hope that God would fulfill His word in both respects, I would think and believe that it pleased God to have Abraham's descendants enter into Abraham's covenant through the clipping away of the foreskin.

Certainly, the Jews are not so wrong when one hears them say, in the *Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Berachot*: *Blessed be He who has sanctified His beloved from the womb, and placed a sign in his flesh, and sealed his sons with the sign of His holy covenant.* Moses of Coucy <note>A 13th-century French rabbi and author of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol.</note> in the *Treatise on Circumcision* says that the father, when the child was circumcised, used these words: *Blessed be the Lord our God, who has sanctified us with His commandments, and commanded us that we shall make this child enter into the covenant of Abraham—the covenant of which circumcision was a sign and seal.* Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397), an influential Bishop of Milan.</note> in the *4th chapter to the Romans*: Circumcision has nothing excellent in itself, but it is only a sign: which sign the descendants of Abraham received for this purpose, that it might be known that they were Abraham's children, who, giving faith to God, had received that sign: so that they might emulate Abraham's faith and believe in Christ, who was promised to Abraham.

But let this be enough to make only a short sketch. I am now about to proceed to matters of greater scope and weight, and to consider the end and purpose of the Divine institution.

<margin>Purpose of the Divine institution.</margin>
To come to the matter now, one must know that God had promised to father Abraham, after the first primary promise (*Gen. 3:15*), that this blessed seed would come from him and his lineage. He had also promised him a numerous seed, not only according to the flesh but also according to the promise—Isaac namely—and through him, a great and mighty people. He promised him Canaan as a heritage after the passage of some years—not for his fleshy seed in general, but for Isaac’s descendants—and promised him that in the future, from that seed, the promised "seed of the woman" <note>A Christian theological term for the Messiah, based on Genesis 3:15.</note> would sprout, in whom not only the seed sprouted from him and Isaac, etc., would be blessed and graced, but also the other nations, who would have sprouted from him by his handmaidens, and from these again in the course of time, and become very numerous. (*Gen. 12, 17, 18, and 22; Gal. 3, etc.*)

<margin>God’s promises to Abraham.</margin>
Now, Abraham believed and agreed to all of this, although he was old and mother Sarah was very weakened, her womb being as if unable to fertilely procreate; and so he received and underwent the sign and seal of God’s covenant and promises when he had reached ninety-nine years. And for what purpose other than as a sign and seal of God’s covenant and Testament? (*Gen. 17, Rom. 4*) For the remembrance of that covenant with Abraham, and for entry into the same—in firm hope that God would keep His word in both one and the other—I would think and believe that it pleased God to make Abraham’s descendants enter into Abraham’s covenant through the trimming of the foreskin.

Certainly, the Jews do not have it so wrongly when one hears them saying, in the *Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Berachot* <note>original: "Talm. Hierof. Tract. Berachet"</note>: *"Blessed be He who has sanctified His beloved from the womb, and placed a sign in his flesh, and sealed his sons with the sign of His holy covenant."* Moses of Coucy <note>original: "Mozes Kottenfis"; a 13th-century French rabbi and author of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol.</note> in the *Tractate on Circumcision* says that the father, when the child was circumcised, used these words: *"Blessed be the Lord our God, who has sanctified us with His commandments, and commanded us that we shall make this child enter into the covenant of Abraham"*—the covenant of which circumcision was a sign and seal. Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397 CE), Bishop of Milan.</note> in the *4th chapter on Romans*: "Circumcision has nothing excellent in itself, but it is only a sign: which sign the descendants of Abraham received for this purpose, that it might be known they were Abraham’s children, who, giving faith to God, had received that sign: so that they might emulate Abraham’s faith and believe in Christ who was promised to Abraham."

And so the Lord promised to do such on His part, to confirm that He would strictly keep or fulfill His promises: and Abra-

# CIRCUMCISION.

...to obligate Abraham and all Israel to faith, obedience, and full submission to him, their Covenant-God. Both the one and the other flow and follow naturally when one observes them wisely. *See Genesis 17:10, Romans 4:11, etc.*

Furthermore, I can imagine that the Lord wished to press his stamp and mark into the flesh of Abraham and his seed, so that just as they were separated by the later "middle wall of partition," <note>A reference to Ephesians 2:14, symbolizing the barrier between Jews and Gentiles.</note> they might also be distinguished from the Heathens <term>Gentiles</term> by this cutting away, as the people of the Lord, holy or set apart for him. For thus speaks *Irenaeus, Book IV, Chapter 30*: God did not give circumcision to his people as a perfecter of righteousness, but so that Abraham’s lineage might be recognizable and remain so. *Tacitus* <note>A Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD) known for his descriptions of Jewish customs.</note> also had this in mind when he wrote in *Book V*: they ordered the reproductive organ to be circumcised to be recognized thereby. And *Jerome, on Galatians 3*, writes thus: because Christ would come from the seed of Abraham, and many centuries would pass from Abraham to Christ, God—taking care that the seed of Abraham, his beloved, would not be mixed with other nations, or that his family might in time become uncertain—stamped the assembly of Israel's flock as if with the brand-mark of circumcision. Now the Heathens, as the uncircumcised, were kept away, *Ephesians 2.*

Indeed, I believe that the Lord commanded circumcision to Abraham, and subsequently to his seed, as a sign and seal that he was their God and they were his people (*Genesis 17, Romans 4*), and furthermore as a sign and seal of the righteousness of faith—that he would forgive their sins and iniquities and remove the certainty of sin; for otherwise, how can God call himself the God of anyone, or any man be judged able to approach God boldly, or call God *his* God? *Colossians 2:11, 12, 13, 14.*

And I firmly believe that it was a sign and seal that the God of the covenant would sanctify him and them: indeed, that whatever man has by nature, what is born with him, and the tainted manner of his procreation—the old and evil nature—is of no value before the Lord and must be cut off, cast aside, crucified, and killed; that he must be born again, as one having the foreskin on the heart, ears, hands, etc. Compare, meanwhile, these passages: *Ezekiel 16, Job 14, Psalm 51, Romans 2:28, John 1 and 3:5, Leviticus 41, Deuteronomy 30, Ezekiel 36, Romans 6, Colossians 2:13, 14, etc.* Thus *Athanasius* says that the cutting off of the foreskin signified nothing other than "the stripping away of birth" <note>original: "ἢ τῶ γενέσεως ἀπέκδυσιν"</note>. And elsewhere: circumcision was a figure and example of "the stripping away that occurs through baptism" <note>original: "τῆς διὰ τῶ βαπτίσματος ἀπεκδύσεως"</note>.

And the Jew *Philo, in On Circumcision*: The circumcision of that member was an image of the cutting away of the passions that delude the soul; and since among the allurements of pleasures, those that affect and tickle that member have the primary influence, the legislators for that reason commanded that one should, as it were, mutilate that member, to signify thereby that one must cut off the remaining pleasures.

And that circumcision occurred on a hidden, despised member and part, so that through a cutting—painful and bloody—the entire body

<column-break/>

might be made holy and preserved, brings several things to my mind, which I shall present somewhat more distinctly for the clearer sorting and guidance of thoughts: namely, that it was not merely located in the fact that one publicly passed for a Jew and presented oneself as circumcised and stamped by the Lord, crying "Lord, Lord," and thinking that for this reason one held a superior advantage over a Heathen; no, that outward appearance, according to the letter of the law, could also be found in some Heathens. Or even if one had the advantage of the "cut flesh" over a Heathen, one could stand equal to him due to the wickedness and impurity of the heart. One had to have circumcision in the hidden place, in the heart, to serve God in the spirit, if one were to be a true Jew: for otherwise the power of the Lord was righteous, *Jeremiah 9:26, 27:* all the Heathens have the foreskin, but the entire house of Israel has the foreskin of the heart. And therefore the Lord could take no pleasure in them, even though they had the outward covenant sign in their flesh; without faith and the works of Abraham, they were like the children of the Moors <note>The author uses "Moors" here to refer to distant, non-covenant peoples, following the imagery in Amos 9:7.</note>, *Ezekiel 64, Amos 9.* See then *Romans 2:28, 29, Colossians 2:10-14.*

<margin>Circumcision.</margin>
Circumcision was painful and bloody. Certainly, corruption and sin must bring about soul-ache, sadness, pain, killing, and the crucifying of the self, *Psalm 51, Matthew 5 and 11, Acts 2:37, Galatians 5:24, Colossians 3:4, 5, Acts 2, Colossians 8.*

And when one saw a small, humble part of the body cut off—not without pain and bloodshed—for the preservation and sanctification of the whole body, whereby one initially cast off the corruption in the "old man": so one could, seeing the smallness or imperfection of the shadow, and the weakness of the letter and the outward sign, and noting God's covenant and its proper divine effect according to the outlines of the Prophets in their writings, become aware that someone—related to them as their own flesh, though in the eyes of the flesh and through wrong judgment, naught, small, and despised—would be cut off for the preservation of the entire body, since it would not be for himself, *Psalm 22, Isaiah 53, Daniel 9,* which would not happen without the shedding of blood, *Hebrews 9:22, 23, 24.* <note>The author is interpreting circumcision as a "type" or foreshadowing of the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.</note>

<margin>Transition.</margin>
To this was added in the course of time that, although circumcision from the fathers was a seal of the righteousness of faith (accounted even while still in the "foreskin" <note>Meaning, while Abraham was still uncircumcised.</note>, *Romans 4, Genesis 17*), it was nevertheless later brought under Moses to the keeping of the entire law; as when at circumcision and faith, to demonstrate one's faith, one had to strictly observe the laws of Moses, *Galatians 5:3, 4, Acts 15:1-5.* He who then allowed himself to be circumcised testified that he took up and accepted Moses' yoke and teaching, having this firm intention: that in the keeping of such things his happiness, salvation, and life consisted, and he could please God.

<margin>Circumcision a sign of accepting the Law.</margin>
Now, that the Lord commanded that the child should first be circumcised on the eighth day, I believe, was to signify that the Lord wished to show a kind of mercy toward the tender child, exhausted by birth, and let it come to breath and some strength before he wished to have the circumcision performed...

It emphasizes that the physical act serves as a metaphor for the "circumcision of the heart" and foreshadows spiritual rebirth and the sacrifice of Christ.</summary>
