<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of circumcision, shifting from its role as a communal marker to its spiritual significance for the individual believer and its fulfillment in the life of Christ. It addresses why Christ, though sinless, underwent the rite and how the "circumcision of the heart" replaces the physical ritual in the New Testament.</meta>

# CIRCUMCISION.

...to undergo [the rite]: and to show that He, as the free master-worker of His grace, is not bound to the outward means and Sacrament; all the more because Abraham was already justified before circumcision, while still uncircumcised, *Romans 4*. However, the Lord accepts His own into His covenant early and wishes to obligate parents to hallow their children to Him, and not to Moloch <note>An ancient Near Eastern deity associated with child sacrifice, here used as a metaphor for worldly or pagan influences.</note>, the world, or otherwise.

<margin>Children circumcised after the passing of a Sabbath.</margin>
If circumcision was to occur according to Divine institution, it is certain that under Moses' solemn shadow-law <note>The "shadow-law" refers to Old Testament rituals viewed by Christians as foreshadowing New Testament truths.</note>, a Sabbath passed before the child was circumcised.

Regarding the Sabbath of Abraham and the fathers, I leave that aside; I do not find it instituted or restricted to the seventh day.

And concerning impurity, as under the law of Moses—regarding mothers and children, sheep, lambs, etc.—such was not fixed in Abraham's time: but certainly in Moses' time, with the solemn law and the "shadowy" Sabbath as a sign of sanctification and rest from every yoke and sin. *Rabbi Simeon, the son of Jarchus in the Pesikta* <note>The Pesikta is a collection of homiletic rabbinic interpretations. "Son of Jarchus" likely refers to the famous commentator Rashi.</note> asks: *why did the law determine circumcision for the eighth day? Circumcision is postponed until the woman in childbirth passes from her impurity to purity.*

In addition to this, Cyprian <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage.</note>, with his assembly of 66 Bishops, was of the opinion that this circumcision on the eighth day prefigured the resurrection of Christ on the eighth day <note>The "eighth day" refers to Sunday, the day after the seventh-day Sabbath, symbolizing a new beginning.</note>, in which the true circumcision and our salvation are perfected. And in this, Cyprian is followed by many in these days. At the very least, it remains that Christ lay in the grave on the Jewish Sabbath and had not yet been openly justified after He had offered Himself for the sake of sins, *Hebrews 9.* But after the Sabbath, on the 7th day, He was seen without sins and justified, *Romans 1 and 4:25*; indeed, He was raised for our justification, and thus the believers are crucified, died, buried, and risen from the dead with Him. Since neither law nor circumcision affects one who has risen anymore, neither law nor the obligation of circumcision affects a "new creature" in Christ anymore. The old has passed away, *Romans 6, 7, and 8, and 2 Corinthians 5*; it is a new life *Romans 6, Colossians 2, Ephesians 2, Romans 8.*

That Christ—who was in Himself without sin and without the "foreskin of the heart"—was circumcised can be understood from various perspectives if one considers that Abraham's seed had to be circumcised. Now the Messiah, the hallowed, hallowing, and blessing seed, was promised to Abraham and had to spring from his loins and his seed; moreover, because the Jews would not have recognized Him as such if He were not circumcised, He was circumcised. *Romans 1 and 9.*

<margin>Why Christ was circumcised.</margin>
Certainly, He had to be our brother and be like us in everything (sin excepted). *Hebrews 2 and 4, Job 19.* What could be more fitting than to undergo the same fate and receive the same stamp and mark in His flesh?

Should He be a minister of circumcision, *Romans 15:8*, and the promise made to the fathers be firm in Him: He would subject Himself to the law in servitude for the redemption and liberation of His people, *Galatians 4:4, 5*, for which He had pledged His soul and offered Himself for service, *Job 33, Psalm 40, Isaiah 42.*

<column-break/>

and *Isaiah 53, Hebrews 10.* Thus He had to be circumcised and so become a debtor to keep the whole law, *Galatians 5*, and precisely observe that which was impossible for the flesh, it being powerless. *Romans 8.* Thus He wished to fulfill all righteousness, *Matthew 5, John 6.* Thus He came as a servant, *Matthew 20:28*, and became a servant of those who ruled, *Philippians 2:7, 8, Psalm 40:7, 8.* And so He who previously stood as a servant to serve and obey, would afterward sit and rest, to also make His members free from the servitude and accusation of sin—the stern drivers of death. *Romans 6, 7, and 8, Galatians 4 and 5, etc.*

He who, out of contempt, was not circumcised, or who pulled the foreskin back over or through artificial means <note>This refers to "epispasm," a surgical procedure used in antiquity by some Jews to hide their circumcision and assimilate into Hellenistic culture.</note>, was not counted among the people of God: he had no freedom or right to the Divine approach, no legal inheritance in Canaan.

<margin>Circumcision of the heart necessary for salvation.</margin>
Without faith, the circumcision of the heart, and sanctification, no one could see God or appear on His mountain. *Psalm 15 and 25, Hebrews 12.* And whoever considers the blood of the New Testament unclean and tramples it underfoot shall meet no lighter fate. *Hebrews 10:28, 29.*

Briefly, and to pull it all together, I note regarding the circumcision of the heart, which happens without hands, etc.

<margin>Observation on this.</margin>
Whereas the circumcision which occurred on the foreskin of the flesh—with hands and a circumcising knife—was painful, bloody, and only external, taking something away from the sufferer and actually contributing nothing: the circumcision that has come in place of the first occurs internally at the heart, without a knife or human hand, under the Gospel, through the spirit of adoption; it takes away the external distinction between those in circumcision and those in the foreskin, viewed externally and distinguished according to the covenant-manner of old.

Though this internal circumcision of the heart occurs in full power at death, it is nonetheless true that such a person—in whom the spirit of sonship, by the power of Christ's circumcision and obedience according to every demand of the law, puts its power to work—is brought to a convicting sight and judgment of his sins, his worthiness of damnation, and his powerlessness. Thus he rejects his own righteousness from the works of the law, throwing it away like a "polluted garment" <note>original: "maanstondig kleet"; literally a menstrual cloth, used biblically as a metaphor for ritual impurity or worthless righteousness (Isaiah 64:6).</note>, *Isaiah 64, Romans 3, Philippians 4, Revelation 3:17.* And he puts off the "foreskin of corruption" which is born in him and belongs to him from the flesh and with the flesh, *Job 14, Psalm 51, Job 3.* Through daily restraint, resistance, and weaning, he kills, crucifies, puts off, and pulls it away, *Romans 6:6-12, 17, 18, Romans 7, 1 Corinthians 9, Colossians 3, Galatians 3.* Which one can observe to happen:

a. Either through the bodily circumcision performed on Jesus on the eighth day, by which He, as the true seed of Abraham, bound Himself for the sake of the brothers to the fulfillment of every demand and righteousness of the law, and brought about the circumcision of our hearts as the deserving cause: as a sign and seal of our spiritual circumcision. *Matthew 3:15, Romans 15:8, Galatians 4:4, 5.*

b. Or through Christ effectively as that God who circumcises the heart, reconciling us with God not only through the fulfillment of every demand and righteousness of the law,

->WAGES, ὀψώνιον <note>original Greek: opsōnion</note>, *provisions* <note>original Latin: obsonium</note>.<-

<margin>Uncertain derivation of this word.</margin>
Regarding the word ὀψώνιον <note>original: opsōnion</note> WAGES, it is a military term, as most agree: yet from whence it is derived, there is some disagreement among the learned. For I notice that some derive it from ὀψάριον <note>original: opsarion</note> *something to eat with or in addition to bread*. Others from ὀψέ-ὤνιον <note>original: opse-ōnion</note> *I roast*. Others from ὀψέ <note>original: opse</note> *late*, being a type of food that one bought late for the midday or evening meal. Others from ὠνέομαι <note>original: ōneomai</note>, *I buy*, and ὄψον <note>original: opson</note> *everything that is eaten with bread*.

Some take it for the soldier's pay, which was paid to the soldiers after a period of six months: yet some take it much more broadly, and among these Wages, bread was not the least part.

*Glassius in Sacred Rhetoric, page 411* <note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656) was a German theologian famous for his work on biblical interpretation.</note> expresses it thus: *Wages signify provisions, adornments, and delicacies, by which the hired soldiers, who made much of their belly and gut, were enticed to put their lives in the balance.*

*Dilherrus in Truth, page 210* <note>Johannes Michael Dilherr (1604–1669) was a noted German polymath and theologian.</note> says that ὀψώνιον <note>original: opsōnion</note> wages (*besides bread and drink*) is taken for everything that is roasted and prepared. And he cites *Athenaeus, Book VII*.

*Martyr, Aretius, Pareus, Wittichius, etc.* <note>A list of prominent Protestant reformers and theologians.</note> tell us *that these were military laws, or the reward of the soldiers, consisting not only in copper or silver money paid every six months, but also in all kinds of foodstuffs—bread, cheese, fish—and clothing.* And it is taken very broadly, says *Glassius*, for the entire military reward, and even that which was given to the paid soldier as a punishment.

This word appears in the New Testament four times: *Luke 3:14, Romans 6:23, 1 Corinthians 9:7, 8,* and *2 Corinthians 11:8.* And in all places it refers to a certain military service and reward.

<margin>Lesson for the Soldiers.</margin>
Christ wished to make use of the lessons of John His forerunner, of whom He relates among other things that *in Luke 3:14* he gave this lesson to the soldiers: they should be satisfied with their wages, and by no means rob, plunder, or forage, nor here or elsewhere deprive the citizen or farmer of anything through craft, violence, or threats—as frequently happened, however strict the military discipline might be.

Paul in *2 Corinthians 9:8, 9,* <note>The author likely intended 1 Corinthians 9 here, as noted in his next citation.</note> armed from head to toe in spiritual armor, being in the service of the supreme captain Jesus, had received no wages from anyone, not even from the Corinthians, nor extorted anything from them by craft or violence; indeed, he had not even desired such, although no one serves in the war for nothing, and a laborer is worthy of his hire, *1 Corinthians 9:7, 8.*

Sin and Satan—after corruption entered the world through the first Adam, *Romans 5*—appear to us under the symbol of a king or tyrant who rules in and over the children of disobedience. This tyrant has very many hired soldiers who, being as it were sold into doing evil, offer their members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness, *Romans 6.*

<column-break/>

Now they must also enjoy a reward for their unfruitful and dead works of darkness, for which they are covered with eternal shame. Now the Apostle tells us in *Romans 6:23* that the service of sin has death as its wages: death of both soul and body; both spiritual and physical, for now and eternity, so that they are always dying while living, and living while dying, and seeking death, which flees from them, *Revelation 9,* with an ever-gnawing conscience and the certainty of eternal misery in the hellish pool.

<margin>Misery of the sinners.</margin>
A miserable reward for services rendered to a tyrant, a wretched end after so many tireless services! But what better shall he give, whose portion is in the abyss, and who is called a liar and a murderer of men? See *John 8.*

Behold there how, and in what respect, wages are taken metaphorically.

->SPRINKLING, THE ACT OF SPRINKLING, with a brush of cedar wood, hyssop, and red thread, with water, blood, the ashes of the red heifer, with the blood of the Passover lamb and the sacrifices, upon all holy things, the defiled, the lepers, etc.<-

<margin>Meaning of the sprinkling.</margin>
THAT the SPRINKLING, the ACT OF SPRINKLING with blood, water, the ashes of the red heifer, etc., under Moses' shadowy dispensation <note>The "shadowy dispensation" refers to the Old Testament period, viewed as a "shadow" or precursor to the "reality" of Christ.</note> signified the sanctification, separation, and purification of the flesh and the spirit in a literal and spiritual sense, is a matter too well known for anyone to reasonably attempt to deny it.

The tool with which the sprinkling was performed—whether on the lintel, both doorposts, persons, altars, etc.—would have been most closely a brush or sprinkler made from a cedar handle, three hyssop twigs with their sprigs, fastened with a red thread wound around the cedar handle.

Regarding the sprinkling with the blood of the Passover lamb on the lintel and doorposts, one reads of this in *Exodus 12.*

<margin>Blood of the covenant.</margin>
One finds mention made of the blood of the covenant, with which the people, the book of the law, and the altar were sprinkled. *Exodus 24.*

One reads of the sprinkling of the burnt-offering altar and sometimes the incense altar and the veil, *Leviticus 4.*

Of the sprinkling of the tabernacle and the ministers of the earthly and movable sanctuary at the time of the dedication. *Leviticus 8.*

Also of the sprinkling on the Great Day of Atonement, *Leviticus 16.* Of the sprinkling of the leper on the third and the seventh day: furthermore, of the sprinkling of the unclean. *Leviticus 14.*

One and the other are to be spoken of more extensively in the treatise on Israel's feasts, the Passover, the red heifer, lepers, the unclean, etc., and thus I shall not put my sickle into the corn too early, or mow the grass before me: however, on the occasion of "sprinkling," something must be said as a side-note and supplementary work.

It is common knowledge that even the Heathens <note>Referring to the Greco-Roman and other non-Jewish ancient peoples.</note> for the most part had similar practices to the Jews, such as temples, altars, priests, sacrificial animals, washings, purifications, and sprinklings with the blood of sacrificial animals, ashes, pure—

## S P R I N K L I N G.

That the Heathens sprinkled almost everything with fountain, river, and sea water—holy objects, altars, and persons on various occasions—is made clear from the following. *To be sprinkled.*

That is, according to the translation of Arnold Hoogvliet: <note>Arnold Hoogvliet (1687–1763) was a popular Dutch poet known for his biblical and classical translations.</note>

*Turn yourself toward the east, pray this prayer thrice,*
*And wash your hands in the living water-bed.*

That the altars were sprinkled with the blood of sacrificial animals, received in sprinkling basins, is well known,

Virgil in the 6th Book of the Aeneid:

*Others apply the knives, and catch the warm blood in bowls.* <note>original Latin: Supponunt alii cultros, tepidumque cruorem / Excipiunt pateris.</note>

->That is, according to Vondel’s translation:<-

*Another throats the cattle, receives the lukewarm blood*
*In sacrificial cups.*

<column-break/>

In the third Book:

*We bring in foaming bowls of warm milk, and cups of sacred blood, etc.* <note>original Latin: Inferimus tepido spumantia cymbia lacte, / Sanguinis & sacri pateras, &c.</note>

That is, according to the words of the same Translator:

->One sets down sacrificial jars<-
*With lukewarm milk that foams, and brings the offering-men*
*Many cups of sacrificial blood.*

Virgil in the first Pastoral Song <note>Referring to the *Eclogues*.</note>:

> ——— A tender lamb from our folds
> Shall often stain his altar. <note>original Latin: Illius aram / Sæpe tener nostris ab ovilibus imbuet agnus.</note>

->That is:<-

*I shall often bring a lamb to the altar for him*
*From our pen, and sprinkle his table with that blood.*

The sprinkling tool, the whisk, or sprinkling brush, is held to have consisted of "fortunate" olive wood, an olive or laurel branch, called a *Thallus*. <note>original Greek: θάλλος</note>

Some argue for the olive branch, such as Porphyry in *The Cave of the Nymphs*: *In litanies and supplications they hold out the branches of the olive.* <note>original Greek: ἐν τοῖς λιτανίαις καὶ ἱκετηρίαις τὰς τῆς ἐλαίας θάλλος προτείνουσιν.</note> See

Virgil in *Ciris*,

*Sprinkling the altars with a branch.* <note>original Latin: Spargens altaria Thallo.</note>

->That is:<-

*Sprinkling the altars with a branch.*

See further Virgil, 6th Aeneid; Theocritus, Idyll 12.

However, Servius and Ovid in the 5th Book of the Festivals argue for a whisk of laurel.

*Hither comes the merchant, his tunic girded, and pure*
*He draws water from the fountain to carry in his urn.*
*From this let the laurel be wet; with the wet laurel are sprinkled*
*All things that are to have new masters.*
*He himself sprinkles his own hair with the dripping laurel,*
*And begins to speak prayers in his accustomed voice.* <note>original Latin: Huc venit incinctus tunica mercator, & urna / Purus suffusa, quam ferat, haurit aquam. / Uda sit hinc laurus, lauro sparguntur ab uda / Omnia, quæ dominos sunt habitura novos. / Spargit & ipse suos lauro rorante capillos, / Incipit & solita dicere voce preces.</note>

Mr. Hoogvliet translates this as follows:

*There comes the merchant with his garment girded round the body,*
*And draws a bucket full, after cleansing and bathing,*
*And carries it along, and dips therein the laurel leaves,*
*And hallows the merchandise, which he hawks to everyone.*
*The laurel branch sprinkles his own head in the end,*
*When he thus mutters the common prayer before the deception.*

But it by no means stopped at sprinkling with water for purification: for they also used sulfur and burning torches extinguished in the water, alongside the water, of which I shall again show some examples.

Virgil, *Ciris*:

*Three times he purifies the old man with flame, three times with water, three times with sulfur.* <note>original Latin: Terque senem flamma, ter aqua, ter sulphure lustrat.</note>

<meta>The previous page established that ancient cultures, specifically the "Heathens" (Greeks and Romans), used water and branches for ritual purification. This page continues that exploration by discussing the use of sulfur, torches, and sacrificial ashes in these rites, before contrasting these pagan "sprinklings" with the divinely ordained rituals of the Israelites.</meta>

## S P R I N K L I N G.

That is:

> *She cleanses the old man three times with water, fire, and sulfur.*

Juvenal, in his second satire:

> ——— *He would wish to be purified, if sulfur with torches were provided, and if there were a wet laurel branch.* <note>original Latin: "Cuperet luſtrari, ſi qua darentur Sulphura cum tædis, & ſi foret humida laurus."</note>

That is:

> *Each of them immediately sought—if there were a sulfur torch or a wet laurel branch—to purify himself.* ———

Virgil, *Ciris*:

> *But the nurse, arranging sulfur in a wide earthen vessel, burns narcissus, cassia, and fragrant herbs.* <note>original Latin: "At nutrix patula componens ſulfura teſta Narciſſum, caſiamque, herbas incendit olentes."</note>

That is:

> *Meanwhile, the nurse mixes sulfur in a jar, setting fire to cassia, narcissus, and fragrant herbs.*

Tibullus, *Elegies*, Book II:

> *And she purified me with torches.* <note>original Latin: "Et me luſtravit tædis."</note>

That is:

> *She also purified me with torches.*

<margin>Ashes of the sacrificial animal used in the sprinklings.</margin>
That the Heathens also used the ashes of the burnt sacrificial animal for scattering, sprinkling, and as a means of purification, no one need deny.

Ovid, *Fasti*, Book 4:

> *The blood of a horse shall be the incense, and the ashes of a calf.* <note>original Latin: "Sanguis equi ſuffimen erit, vitulique favilla."</note>

That is:

> *The horse’s blood and the ash of calves shall serve you as incense.*

And further:

> *He burns the calves with fire, so that the ash may cleanse.* <note>original Latin: "Igne cremat vitulos, purget ut ille cinis."</note>

That is:

> *He burns the calf, so that he may purify with ash.*

And after that:

> *I have indeed often brought the ash of a calf and bean-stalks—toasted purifications—with full hands, to show my piety at your feast.* <note>original Latin: "Certe ego de vitulo cinerem, ſtipulamque fabalem. Sæpe tuli plena februa toſta manu."</note>

That is:

> *I have ever often brought the ash of calves and bean-stalks, a purification offering, to show my godliness, with full hands to your feast.*

For my part, I can well imagine that when the Lord commanded all these sprinklings and purifications, it could awaken a deep impression in the heart of Israel regarding

<column-break/>

God's majesty and holiness, leading to a singular reverence. Indeed, it might also make one think that the Lord could not be much concerned with the external act alone. Therefore, by exercising their senses in this way, He intended to lead them toward something higher and more hidden, indicating that he who would keep Him must be holy and pure. It showed that sin and the stains of sin bar man from intimate communion with God; consequently, there must be something—outside of man himself—that clears the way, works the purification, and brings about friendship.

<margin>The purpose of the sprinklings.</margin>
I believe, indeed, that many Jews, as well as countless Heathens, convinced themselves that once this purification through sprinkling had occurred, they were then pure before God. They believed that through the intervention of the established offerings, they were reconciled with God—as I could show, if necessary, from the writings of both the Jews and the Heathens.

<margin>Distinction between the ceremonies of the Jews and the Heathens.</margin>
Furthermore, from what has been said, I can well observe that however great a similarity there might seem to have been between the sprinkling and purification of the Jews and the Heathens, there is nonetheless a very great and remarkable difference in many respects. This is true not only in the end and purpose, but also in many additional ceremonies—matters that run counter to and conflict with one another.

The idea that the ceremonies of the Heathens were of an older time—that God partially borrowed the ceremonies from the Egyptians, etc., and gave them to the Jews with various changes and contradictions merely to keep that "hard, wild, and ignorant" people occupied with external activities, to habituate them specifically to Him and His service, and to draw and keep them away from the idolatry of the Heathens seen in Egypt—does not yet sit well with me. <note>This refers to the "Egyptian Hypothesis" debated by 17th-century scholars like John Spencer, who argued that Jewish law was an adaptation of Egyptian customs.</note>

I would rather align myself with those scholars who are of the opinion that the Heathens—those who had dealings with the Jews and their prominent teachers and who investigated the religion, customs, and laws of Israel—partially adopted and put them into use (albeit with many and great changes). I have been brought to this understanding by the highly enlightened Apostle Paul in his letter to the *Hebrews, Chapters IX, X, and XI*, etc.: that all these things were of a more sublime sense, imagery, and significance. And since the learned gentlemen <term>Stillingfleet<note>Edward Stellingfleet (1635–1699), an English theologian who defended the uniqueness of Christian and Jewish revelation.</note></term> and <term>Witsius<note>Herman Witsius (1636–1708), a Dutch theologian known for his work on the covenants.</note></term> have relieved me of the effort of refuting Spencer, Marsham, and others, I shall follow in the footsteps of Paul to weigh these ceremonial sprinklings more closely. I will serve the studious reader with my own observations as well as the thoughts and feelings of scholars from both older and more recent times.

<margin>Further investigation of these ceremonies.</margin>
As for the sprinkling-whisk <term>aspergillum<note>A bundle or brush used for ritual sprinkling.</note></term>, if one may rely entirely on the report of <term>Buxtorf<note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a leading Hebraist who detailed Jewish customs in his 'Synagoga Judaica'.</note></term> and other learned men, the bundle of <term>hyssop<note>A plant used in biblical purification rituals; its exact identification is a subject of historical botanical debate.</note></term> would have consisted of a cedarwood handle and three stems of hyssop, from each of which at least three other twigs branched out, tied firmly with a red thread. See *Buxtorf in Talmud, Ursinus' Passion & Herbal*, and several others. This whisk is believed to have been used in nearly all sprinklings.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on ritual purification, moving from the pagan practices of the Greeks and Romans described on the previous page to the symbolic theological meanings behind the specific materials used in the Israelite "sprinkle-brush" (aspergillum). It focuses on the interpretations of various Reformed theologians regarding the spiritual significance of the cedar, hyssop, and scarlet thread.</meta>

### S P R I N K L I N G.

<margin>
Disagreement among scholars regarding the sprinkle-brush.
Thoughts on the Trinity.
</margin>
What was signified by this bundle, or <term>sprinkle-brush</term> <note>original: "quispel," a tool used for ritual sprinkling, usually made of branches</note>, is quite difficult to determine, for the reason that scholars differ so markedly from one another on this point.

If I recall correctly, the learned Fagius <note>Paul Fagius (1504–1549), a German Renaissance scholar of Hebrew</note> believed that one could see in it the Divine Trinity, in whose name we are baptized, or sprinkled for the cleansing of sins. And perhaps the great Witsius <note>Herman Witsius (1636–1708), a prominent Dutch theologian</note> in his work *Egyptiaca* <note>original: "Egypt. pag. 118-119."</note> had this in mind, when his Reverence is heard to say:

*There are learned men who believe that the double substance of which the sprinkle-brush consisted—namely, cedar wood, hyssop, and the red or purple thread—sketches out how the merits and death of Jesus are communicated by the will of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, for the sake of righteousness and life.*

<margin>
Observation by Witsius.
</margin>
The Cedar tree, growing on the high mountains and the peak of Lebanon—tall, durable, and long-lived—can, they say, signify the Father. The Hyssop, a low-growing sprout found in the cracks and joints of walls (1 Kings 4:33), can signify Christ, the Son of Man, humble and despised. The purple and blood-red color is a symbol of His blood, indeed the blood itself. Blood is the vehicle of the Spirit: what prevents us, therefore, through holy imagination, from seeing here the Holy Spirit, who is colored scarlet-red through the fire of love—the love of God and of all that is good? Yet if one should judge that this is "spun from too fine a thread" <note>an idiom meaning over-analyzed or far-fetched</note>, or sought from too far away: one may think that Christ is represented by the entire sprinkle-brush. In this view, the cedar wood, because of its hardness, longevity, and high growth, sketches the eternity of the Divine nature in Christ and His excellence; and its scent and penetrating fragrance represent the demonstration and radiance of the Spirit in words and obedient submission. The Hyssop represents Jesus's lowly human nature; the red thread represents the imputation of sins alongside His bloody suffering. The Psalmist makes mention only of Hyssop in Psalm 51, understanding the rest to be included therein, since the rest, alongside Jesus's human nature, runs together toward the same powerful effect, and because the certainty of all grace depends upon His incarnation. Thus far that learned man, my most Reverend Master: to whom Professor Salomon van Til also appeals. In his work *The Sign of the Adder against Joncourt* <note>original: "Adderteken van Joncourt"</note> page 135, his Reverence replied that what Joncourt noted as a contradiction in Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian</note> is truly no contradiction at all, but only a different manner of understanding. He argues that the Lord Cocceius makes no such distinction in meanings that they cannot be subordinate to one another, if one simply views the matters from different perspectives: that the cedar twig, which served as the handle for the sprinkle-brush, represents the Father, who commands and orders our cleansing to be applied. Let the hyssop signify that Christ, despised on the cross and rejected by the Jews, thereby earned the cleansing power. Let the band that binds the hyssop to that cedar handle be the Holy Spirit, whose will cooperates in the work of our cleansing. Let that mystery in the application of salvation show the Father, Christ, and the Holy Spirit as working together in the operation of grace in and around the elect sinner. In that same representation, one can observe that the cedar wood has added a pleasant scent to that same brush, which revealed itself in

<column-break/>

the Son’s words and works, when He supported Him in and through the indwelling Divinity. Let the Holy Spirit, as if colored or dyed with the scarlet color, be considered as helping to effect this work of grace by virtue of the blood of cleansing, and thus also effecting the application of Christ’s blood in the consciences and hearts of believers, whom He cleanses through the gift of faith.

Partly agreeing with this, and partly deviating from it, are the ideas devised by others, such as Theodoret, Gregory the Roman, Augustine, Ursinus, etc. These can be traced in Ursinus’s *Treatise on the Passover and the Red Heifer* <note>original: "Tract. de Pasch. de Vacca Rubra"</note>, pages 300-370. See also Burman, Bierman, and others.

<margin>
The assembly of the sprinkle-brush applied to Christ.
</margin>
Some (as has already been heard from Witsius) apply the entire assembly of the sprinkle-brush to Christ, such that the cedar handle would signify Christ’s powerful and incorruptible death for sin.

The hyssop signifies Christ’s humiliation—His despised, yet powerful and active state.

The red thread signifies Christ’s blood: or Holy Baptism, or the ministry of the Holy Spirit, which applies the power of Christ’s cross to us and sprinkles us with it.

Others believe that the cedar wood handle represents, on the side of God and Christ, either Christ’s Divine nature or His cross and its preaching—the foundation of preaching (1 Corinthians 1:23 and 2:2, Philippians 3). On our side, it represents hope, which must dwell securely and steadfastly on high.

Through the Hyssop would be known—with respect to the adorable Trinity—Christ as God-man, Christ as a fruit of the earth, low, humble, and lowly esteemed (Isaiah 4 and 11 and 53, Philippians 2); or the ministry of the Holy Spirit, through and with the Word, despised, humble, bitter, and yet restorative, through which the earned blessings of Christ are applied for justification and sanctification (Psalm 51, Isaiah 52:12, etc.), alongside the sweet scent and warmth of the Holy Spirit when He, applying those blessings, sprinkles the soul and cleanses it from spiritual leprosy. On the side of the covenant-member, it signifies faith—though small and low, yet rooted in the rock, cleansing the heart and making one see the invisible (2 Corinthians 4, Hebrews 11, Acts 15:9).

By the purple or red thread of binding, some understand Christ—though white and pure in Himself, yet purple-red because of the sins He took upon Himself (Isaiah 1:18) and His bloody suffering for the sake of sin (Acts 5, Isaiah 53 and 63, 2 Corinthians 5:21); or Christ’s body and soul united together; or the Sacraments, in which His bloody suffering is shown to us. Or, on the side of the covenant-member, love, which reveals itself as through glowing coals (Song of Solomon 8, 2 Corinthians 5).

This is, to my knowledge, the principal and essential points to which the thoughts of the learned can be brought.

One knows that Israel had to sprinkle the lintel and both side posts with the blood of the Passover lamb using hyssop, while they ate the Passover indoors.

Which was the sign upon which the Lord assured them He would pass over their houses and persons during His passage and spare them. By this, they signaled that they relied on God’s faithfulness, while they endeavored to use what the Lord had commanded as a sacrament and visible pledge, and...

<summary>This page explores various theological interpretations of the "sprinkle-brush" (aspergillum) used in biblical purification rituals, specifically how the cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet thread symbolize the Trinity, Christ's dual nature, and the application of grace.</summary>

### SPRINKLING.

O 3
<meta>Catchword: op-</meta>

<margin>Differences among scholars regarding the sprinkling brush. Thoughts on the Trinity.</margin>What was signified by this bundle, or sprinkling brush, is quite difficult to determine, because scholars differ so remarkably from one another on this point.

And perhaps the great Witsius in *Aegyptiaca* <note>original: "Egypt. pag. 118-119." referring to Herman Witsius’s work on Egyptian and Jewish rites.</note> has this in view, when his Reverence is heard to say:

> There are learned men who believe that the double substance of which the sprinkling brush consisted—namely, cedar wood, hyssop, and the red or purple thread—sketches out how, through the will of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the merits and death of Jesus are communicated for righteousness and life.

Yet, if one should judge that this is "too fine a thread" <note>An idiom meaning a point too subtly argued or over-analyzed.</note> or perhaps a bit far-fetched: one may think that Christ is represented by the entire sprinkling brush, so that the cedar wood, because of its hardness, longevity, and high growth, sketches the eternity of the Divine nature in Christ and his excellence; and its scent and penetrating fragrance, the demonstration and radiance of the Spirit in words and obedient submission. Thus far that learned man, my much-revered Master: to whom Professor Salomon van Til <note>A Dutch theologian (1643–1713) known for his work on the tabernacle and music.</note> also appeals, when his Reverence, in his *Adder-Stings of Joncourt* <note>original: "Addersteken van Joncourt," a polemical work against Pierre de Joncourt.</note> page 135, <margin>From Salomon van Til.</margin> etc., answered thus: *that what Joncourt noted as a contradiction in Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), founder of Federal Theology.</note> is truly no contradiction, but only a different way of understanding, and no contradiction of itself; and that Mr. Cocceius makes no such difference in meanings that they cannot very well be subordinated to one another, if one only considers the matters in their various aspects: that the cedar twig, which served as the handle for the sprinkling brush, represents the Father, who commands and orders our cleansing to be brought about. Let the hyssop signify that Christ, despised on the cross and rejected by the Jews, earned the cleansing power through that very act. Let the band that binds the hyssop to that cedar handle be the Holy Spirit, whose will cooperates in the work of our cleansing: let that mystery in the application of salvation represent the Father, Christ, and the Holy Spirit as working together in the operation of grace, in and around the chosen sinner. In that same representation, one can observe that the cedar wood has added a pleasant scent to that same brush, which revealed itself in the Son's words and works, when the indwelling Divinity supported him. Let the Holy Spirit, as if colored or dyed with the scarlet hue, be considered as helping to work this work of grace, by virtue of the blood of cleansing, and thus also working the application of Christ’s blood in the consciences and hearts of the believers, whom he cleanses through the gift of faith.*

Partly agreeing with this, and partly departing from it, is what others have devised, such as Theodoret, Gregory of Rome, Augustine, Ursinus, etc. To be searched for in Ursinus in his *Treatise on the Passover and the Red Heifer* <note>original: "Tract. de Pasch. de Vacca Rubra."</note>, pages 300-370, etc. See also Burman, Bierman, and others.

<margin>The composition of the brush applied to Christ.</margin>Some (as has already been heard from Witsius) apply the entire composition of the sprinkling brush to Christ, in such a way that the cedar handle would signify *Christ's powerful and incorruptible death on the cross.*

*The hyssop, Christ's humiliation, his despised, yet powerful and active state.*

*The red thread, Christ's blood: or Holy Baptism, or the ministry of the Holy Spirit, which applies the power of Christ's cross to us and sprinkles us with it.*

Others believe the handle of cedar wood represents, on the side of God and Christ, *either Christ's Divine nature: or his cross and the preaching of it, the foundation of preaching* (1 Corinthians 1:23 and 2:2; Philippians 3); and on our side *hope, which must dwell securely and be steadfast in the heights.*

Through the Hyssop, there would be recognized—with respect to the adorable Trinity, or Christ as God-man—*Christ as a fruit of the earth, low, humble, considered of little account* (Isaiah 4, 11, and 53; Philippians 2); *or the ministry of the Holy Spirit, through and with the Word—despised, humble, bitter, and yet restorative—through which the acquired blessings of Christ are applied for justification and sanctification* (Psalm 51; Isaiah 52:12, etc.), *alongside the sweet scent and warmth of the Holy Spirit, when he, applying those blessings, sprinkles the soul and cleanses it from spiritual leprosy. On the side of the covenant-member: faith, though small and low, yet rooted in the Rock, cleansing the heart and making one see the invisible* (2 Corinthians 4; Hebrews 11; Acts 15:9).

By the purple or red thread used for binding, some understand *Christ, who is indeed white and pure in himself, yet purple-red because of the sins taken upon him* (Isaiah 1:18) *and his bloody suffering for the sake of sin* (Acts 5; Isaiah 53 and 63; 2 Corinthians 5:21); *or Christ's body and soul united together; or the Sacraments, in which his bloody suffering is shown to us. Or, on the side of the covenant-member: love, which shows itself as through glowing coals* (Song of Solomon 8; 2 Corinthians 5).

This is, to my knowledge, the principal and essential matter to which the thoughts of the scholars can be brought.

One knows that Israel had to sprinkle the lintel and both side posts with the blood of the Passover lamb using hyssop, while they ate the Passover indoors.

Which was the sign by which the Lord assured them he would pass over their houses and persons during his passing through, and spare them. By this, they signaled that they relied on God's faithfulness, while they endeavored to use what the Lord had commanded as a Sacrament and visible pledge, and their...

### SPRINKLING.

ordained *Exod. XII. 13. Hebr. XI. 28.*

<margin>Representation.</margin> It represented how the Lord, in His avenging justice, would spare those (and their children) whose consciences were sprinkled with Jesus’ blood, *Isa. LII. 15. Hebr. XII. 14. Col. I. 13, 14-20. I Pet. I. 2.*

Now the Lord sprinkles the conscience with Jesus’ blood to cleanse us from an evil conscience and from the consciousness of sins, *Hebr. X. 2--22.*, when He applies to His covenant-partners the power of Jesus’ obedience in His blood for justification and sanctification, granting His Spirit for that purpose.

As for an evil conscience and the consciousness of sins, we are aware that we are by nature dead in sins and trespasses, children of wrath, enslaved to sin, and daily—even frequently—stumbling. See *Eph. II. James III.* regarding a conscience of sins.

For although from of old there was an awareness that God passed over sins and, as it were, looked through His fingers <note>A Dutch idiom meaning to "overlook" or "turn a blind eye to" something.</note>, not punishing them in the guarantor or the guilty party, there was nonetheless an internal awareness that the misdeed demanded punishment, and the debt was not yet actually settled. For the law kept sin and the memory of it alive, not without <term>reproach <note>original Greek: ὀνειδισμός (oneidismos), meaning shame or disgrace</note></term>, *Hebr. X.*

We sprinkle ourselves with the brush of hyssop, with the blood of the Passover, *Christ, 1 Cor. V. 7. John. I. 29.*, when we, through faith, embrace the teaching of Christ’s cross and apply to ourselves the power of His bloody merits for justification, sanctification, and life for the sake of righteousness, *Rom. V. 1. Acts XV. 9. and XVI. 31.*

Just as the posts of our doors are accessible to us, and the entrance is ready and nearest to us, so it is with our [door]posts and hearts in respect to God and the glorious King. These must not be closed to the corruption of sin and the destroyer, but opened to the Lord, *Ps. XXIV. 7. Rev. III. 20.*

While the Passover lamb was eaten inside the house, on the outside, not just one post but both side-posts, and not the threshold but the upper lintel had to be sprinkled. Thus, the blood was not trodden upon. Thus, one could remember the benefit when going out and coming in; thus, one saw the distinction between the Jews and their dwellings and those of the Egyptians.

Certainly, the blood of the Covenant and of the New Testament must not be trampled underfoot, *Hebr. X. 29.* One must not only practice fellowship with Christ the Passover internally through faith, but also confess and display it outwardly with mouth and works, *Rom. X. 10. 2 Tim. II. 20.*, going in and out in Jesus’ name, and always being mindful of His death, *1 Cor. XI.* etc.

And since one lives by the sprinkling of the blood of sacrificial animals—such as on the right earlobe, the right thumb, and the great toe, etc., *Exod. XXIX.*—I shall, for the sake of brevity, say this along with a learned man: *that when God bores through the ear for obedience and prepares the hands to take hold of their portion, the ears and hands are cleansed by Jesus’ shed blood. In a word, when Christ’s obedience and the power of His suffering are transferred to the soul and the body and all its members, they then become instruments of righteousness, Rom. VI. and XII., and the obedience of those who hear, love, and observe His word is then pleasing to Him.*

<column-break/>

If we see the priests and the altar sprinkled with the blood of sacrificial animals and thereby sanctified, *Exod. XXIX.*, I observe Christ sprinkled, *Isa. LXIII.*, and sanctified in and through His own blood, *Hebr. X. 29.* Indeed, all who have embraced Christ through faith and approach God with boldness in Him and His blood are consecrated into a spiritual priesthood, made capable by the oil of the Spirit to lay upon the altar—which is Christ—their persons, their lives, prayers, thanksgivings, alms, etc., *Rom. XII. 1 Pet. II. 9. Hebr. XIII. Rev. VIII. and I. and V.*

One finds that along with the red heifer, cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool had to be thrown into the flame to be consumed together into dust and ashes, collected, and kept in a clean place outside the camp. *Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> in Paras Cap. III. says: They gathered nothing of her ashes to place them in the court, but they divided all the ashes into three parts. One part they placed in Chiel—the castle or border place—and another part on the Mount of Olives, and a third part was divided among all the watches of the Levites. With what was distributed to the watches, the priests purified themselves; with what was placed on the Mount of Olives, the Israelites sprinkled; and that which was stored was kept and preserved, as it is written: "and it shall be for a keeping for the congregation."*

With this—that is, with these ashes—living water had to be mixed. A clean man had to perform the sprinkling with the brush. He himself became unclean and had to wash his clothes. One had to sprinkle seven times; on the third and seventh day, in the evening, one was clean. It had to happen opposite the tent of meeting. He who was not cleansed was cut off and could not appear in the Lord’s sanctuary.

Let him <note>The author referring to himself or the reader.</note> also note something here.
What the cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet <margin>The author’s observation.</margin> are doing here with the red heifer in the fire has its own considerations. It will be more appropriate when I deal with the Red Heifer and its burning. The Jews say that this was given to understand that Israel’s sins were burned at the same time. If the cedar wood, the hyssop, and the scarlet are not symbols of Christ—as has been heard and seen above—they might perhaps signify the believers, crucified and dead with Christ, prepared to die with and for Him, having fellowship in His suffering and death as if united with Him, and having to fulfill the remnants of His suffering; however, I do not insist upon this.

At the very least, from this material arose a sharp lye for sprinkling, though mixed with living and pure water. Certainly, the covenant-partners necessarily require the biting power of Christ’s death and suffering, alongside the pure water of Holy Baptism and the Holy Spirit, to become clean and to wipe out the stains of sin, *Jer. II. and XXXI. Ezek. XXXVI. Acts II. Col. III. 5. Gal. V. 24. Ps. LI. 1 Cor. I. 30. 1 Cor. VI. 11.*

The preservation of those ashes in a clean place outside the camp can bring to mind the enduring power of Jesus’ death. How He was kept in a clean and new grave outside Jerusalem; how He is in heaven, not in Jerusalem or under the Law, to...

# SPRINKLING.

to suffer: how the memory of Christ’s suffering and death must be preserved in a purified heart, leading to daily renewal and a more pervasive holiness. The fact that these stinging ashes <note>A reference to the ashes of the Red Heifer used in purification rituals (Numbers 19).</note> had to be mixed with pure water can show us that the stinging power—which awakens sorrow in the soul and sensible pain because of sin, as a "sorrow according to God" *2 Cor. 7* <note>original: "droefheit naar Godt," often translated as "godly sorrow."</note> for the removal of sin—is not produced unless the water of God’s Spirit and grace is added to it. *John 3:5, Ps. 51, Ezek. 36.*

The fact that this sprinkling took place directly across from the tent of meeting <note>The Tabernacle</note>, to clear the way for entrance into the sanctuary, perhaps shows us how Jesus underwent His soul’s bitter suffering in Gethsemane, in the garden and on the Mount of Olives, directly opposite the temple and the city; without which no one truly is in the tent of meeting, or may appear there. But being sprinkled with it, one may appear and dwell in the tent of the Lord and upon the mountain of His holiness. *Ps. 15, Ps. 100.*

<margin>Sevenfold sprinkling.</margin>
That this sprinkling happened exactly *seven times* could perhaps signify either the sevenfold operation of Christ’s Spirit, *Rev. 1*, perfectly applying the power of Christ’s obedience and suffering unto death; or how Jesus’ blood and Spirit would cleanse in all seven time periods of the New Testament, and had to be sprinkled upon both Jews and Gentiles for purification. Or perhaps it shows how we still need the sprinkling every day, from the first day of our rebirth until the day of our rest, Sabbath, or full redemption. *Rom. 6, Heb. 4, 2 Cor. 7:1-2, Heb. 12, Phil. 3.*

And if one wishes to look more closely and dwell longer on the cleansing on the third and seventh day toward evening: I find it said that this refers to the cleansing in the first and last times; to the cleansing of some earlier and others later; to our early, initial, and full cleansing in the evening of our life; to the cleansing in the middle and at the end of the week, when the slaughter-offering and grain-offering were abolished and the Gentiles were sprinkled, and at the end of the week everything was destroyed; or to the singular sprinkling in the third period, when the dragon had to vacate his place, *Rev. 12:7, 8-17* and *6:5* and *8:10*; and in the last time, when the beast and the false prophet shall be cast into the lake of fire and the dead shall rise, *Rev. 19* and *20* and *20:12* and *8:1* and *11:15.*

The fact that the sprinkling had to be performed by *a clean man*, who himself then became unclean and had to wash his clothes, perhaps portrays that the pure Jesus, who cleanses and sprinkles others, was treated as unclean because of His fellowship with our sins and punishment, yet was declared pure and holy in the resurrection from the dead.

That those who perform the service of sprinkling must be blameless; *1 Tim. 3* and *4, 1 Pet. 5*; although by interacting with the unclean and sinful, they also stain their garments and have need of cleansing.

Staying no longer on this, I will further illuminate a few places which seem to have some connection with what has already been discussed, and display the symbolism within them.

<column-break/>

*Song of Solomon 5:2* states that the hair is sprinkled with *night-drops*. This is applied to those who cling to Christ, the confessors of the Gospel, who are tormented by many disasters in the night of adversities, etc.

*Isaiah 52* says of the Messiah that He shall sprinkle the Gentiles. Here there seems to be an allusion to the ancient sprinklings, giving it to be understood that He would make them partakers of the power of His blood for justification and sanctification, alongside the sign and seal of the baptism of sprinkling for the forgiveness of sins and the holiness of the covenant in Jesus’ blood.

*Isaiah 63:1* presents the Prince Messiah as sprinkled on His attire and garments, like one who has trodden the winepress and has marched forth in His strength, while He found the enemy’s strength upon His garment.

Now this seems to me to portray how Christ, in His struggle against physical and spiritual powers, is depicted not only as a conqueror—taking vengeance on His wicked enemies (specifically the Jews, Edom, and Bozrah), *Ps. 110*, having carried out a heavy and great slaughter—appearing as if with sprinkled clothes; but also in His suffering and on His cross, when He was bloodied and sprinkled on His head, face, hands, side, and feet. And even though it appeared that the law, the "old man," and Satan’s instruments—Christ’s enemies—had so much power that they scourged Him and nailed Him to the cross, He nevertheless triumphed in that garment, in this form. *Col. 2:15, 1 Cor. 15, Acts 20:28.*

<margin>Triumph of Christ.</margin>
However, there are those who have understood it differently, applying it to the Messiah gathering His enemies in the last days and treading them as if in a press.

Because after Jesus’ suffering, one hears of a great Jubilee feast. *Isa. 61, Luke 4:17-20.*

Because one hears of the rebuilding of desolate places by foreign plowmen and vinedressers.

Because the church is already clothed with the Messiah’s salvation, verses 10, 11.

Because here the Jews seem to pray for calling and conversion in their rejection, verse 7, etc.

Furthermore, the Messiah does not appear in a passive, suffering sense, but in an active, working sense: not sprinkled with His own blood, but with the blood of enemies; the pressing occurs not in the spring but in the autumn, therefore it is not to be applied to the early, but to the late New Testament church period, etc. See *Gen. 49:11*, especially *Rev. 19:11-16.*

And nothing was more offensive to Jews and Gentiles than that He rode forth victoriously on the white horse, conquering so that He might overcome. Therefore, Jesus’ members and garments—the Apostles and Teachers—had to fulfill the remnants of Jesus’ suffering and bear the marks of the Lord. *Gal. 6, 1 Cor. 4, Rom. 8*, etc.

Let this be enough regarding this. It will appear more elsewhere.

<header>BETHEL.</header>

<margin>
Bethel named Bethaven.

This place seems certainly to be distinguished from Bethel, although Bethel was also changed and, because of wicked idolatry and calf-worship, named Bethaven, as will be shown hereafter.

<margin>
Meaning of Bethaven.
</margin>
Bethaven means a house of vanity, lies, idolatry, godlessness, falsehood, and torment: a place not far from Ai, where Israel suffered defeat.

That they had a calf-image and high places there, and practiced idolatry under Jeroboam and other kings, the letter of the text teaches us. *1 Kings 12. Hosea 4, 8, and 10.*

That Bethel seems to have received the surname Bethaven because of heavy idolatry and image-worship, vanity, nothingness, God's grief, and pain, I believe can be denied by no one.

<margin>
The house of the Antichrist lives again in Bethaven.
</margin>
And so I note in passing that in Bethaven one sees the house of the Antichrist revived, where idolatrous image-worship, the invocation of saints, and the raised image of <term>Mauzim</term> <note>Mauzim refers to the "god of fortresses" mentioned in Daniel 11:38, often used by Reformation-era writers to describe what they saw as the idolatrous protection of saints or worldly power in the Church.</note> is on display; where the man of sin, the son of perdition, sits and is honored as if in a *house of God*, as if he were God, *2 Thess. 2.* being there established the image of the beast and human authority.

But more on this under the word BETHEL.

### BETHEL, <note>Hebrew: בית אל, "House of God"</note>

<margin>
Old naming of Bethel.
</margin>
**A**s for BETHEL, this city was formerly called Luz, or Luzza, as will be noted hereafter: but it was named Bethel by Jacob because of the singular appearance of God, although it is already called such by way of anticipation in earlier stories. *Gen. 12, 28, and 35, etc.*

<margin>
Location of the city.
</margin>
It was located in the tribal inheritance of Benjamin. *Joshua 18:22.*

It appears that schools, or at least "sons" or disciples of the Prophets, were found there. *2 Kings 2:2.*

I say, Bethel, called a House of God, a gate of heaven because of the Divine appearance and Jacob’s ladder, which must be dealt with in the following, under the appropriate letter.

<margin>
Reason for the naming.
</margin>
However, now something concerning the reason for the naming of Bethel. It was a house of God, a gate of heaven. When Jacob awoke from sleep and his dream, he knew not only that he had dreamed, but also what had appeared to him in the dream: indeed, he had a good and vivid memory of his dream, as something unusual and divine, with appropriate emotions, awakening in him reverence and awe. For one hears him cry out, *Surely the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.*

Which one must not understand as if Jacob were ignorant that the Lord is omnipresent, working in all things, sustaining and governing all, *1 Kings 8, Jer. 23.* no, but Jacob did not know that it would please the Lord, beyond His general working and governing, to show Himself to him, Jacob, in such a manner: to bind Himself to him through such great promises and blessings. That he did not know; nor could he know it at all before the experience.

This experience now brought it about that one

<column-break/>

hears him cry out, *How dreadful is this place! this is none other than a house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.*

Whatever there may be of the fear of the godless, of that I say nothing. But this fear, with which Jacob’s heart was struck and seized, was a fear of awe, reverence, high and great esteem, as he noticed his unworthiness, his nothingness. It produced in him appropriate love and esteem for God, as He is worthy: making him, in comparison of himself with the Lord, see, acknowledge, and testify to his nothingness: making him praise and highly esteem everything that comes from God: making him consider God's ways and dealings with reverence: making him acknowledge and testify to his very strongest obligation and commitment to the Lord; from all of which flows a possession and circumspection, so as not to sin against the Lord. *Ps. 2:12. Philip. 2:12, 13. Jerem. 10. Rev. 14.*

<margin>
Effect of Jacob’s fear.
</margin>

Otherwise, one knows that since the interaction of men with the Lord and His heavenly messengers is little after sin, man—because of weakness, the contamination of sin, and the rarity of Divine or heavenly messenger appearances—is immediately quite moved and violently affected; of which the holy scroll gives various proofs, as in Moses, Daniel, Manoah, Zacharias, the shepherds, women, etc. *Heb. 12. Dan. 10. Judges 13. Luke 1 and 2, etc.*

<margin>
Commotion by the Divine appearance.
</margin>

*That place was dreadful:* venerable, awesome, fearful, to be dreaded: <term>nora</term> <note>original Hebrew: נורא</note> from <term>yare</term> <note>original Hebrew: ירא</note>, meaning he feared, respected, or was afraid.

The places in which it was claimed of old among the Heathens that the Deity appeared, or which were held to be suitable for the service of this or that Deity, were held as awesome and venerable.

<margin>
Reverence of the Chinese for their Emperor.
</margin>
It is told of the Chinese that upon seeing the imperial throne, they cast themselves down to the earth three times and prostrate themselves.

The palaces and courts of Emperors, Kings, Princes, and Sovereigns are awesome.

<margin>
Of the Turks for their churches.
</margin>
It is told of the Turks that they will not enter their Mosques with their shoes; just as Moses also had to take off his shoes. *Exod. 3.*

<margin>
Reverence regarding the Ark of the Covenant.
</margin>
The Ark of the Covenant <note>original: "Bondkiste"</note>, God’s mercy seat, could only be seen in passing, and well-covered, once a year by the High Priest.

<margin>
Concerning the Tabernacle and Temple.
</margin>
Israel only came into the forecourt of the tabernacle and temple. For God’s sake, the place was awesome and venerable. Even in public places of justice, there lies an awesomeness.

If the Lord had not appeared there to Jacob with a heavenly choir and procession, nor favored him with His speech and magnificent promise, what awesomeness would there have been in that place more than in any other, where he had previously lain down so peacefully?

*He calls that place Bethel, a house of God, a gate of Heaven.* One has no reason to think or believe that this place was named Bethel, a house of God, by Jacob as if he had a revelation through the Spirit that this was Moriah, upon which Solomon built a beautiful temple: no, those two places lay too far from each other. This is just like the <term>Jewish triflers</term> <note>original: "Joodsche beuzelmeesters." # BETHEL.

<sig>P</sig>

...that the stone upon which Jacob rested his head was taken to cover the mouth of the pit of the abyss; or that it was laid down as a cornerstone for the temple structure; or that Solomon had the name JEHOVAH <note>Original: "JEHOVAH"</note> carved upon this stone, enclosing it as a singular sanctuary within the temple, and other such stories.

It has already been said that, because of God’s appearance and his active heavenly messengers, it was a house of God and a gate of Heaven—or a beautiful, excellent heavenly gate.

How high, wide, or long it appeared to him, he does not say; it must also be understood in naming, metaphor, and figure, perhaps considering that he saw the Lord sitting in the gate, as the kings or judges of old did. He saw the ladder reaching into heaven with its top end, yet with its bottom end on earth, as if uniting heaven and earth, along which the heavenly messengers went out and in, climbing up and descending down to hear the King’s pleasure—in which gate the Lord spoke and made known his counsel, arrangement, and pleasure.

It is certain that it does not necessarily have to be exactly Luz or Luzza. If one is to find a Bethel, or house of God, Luz in itself had nothing over other places. Everywhere in the New Testament is a house of God, if one only seeks him there in spirit and truth, with lifted holy hands, without anger or quarreling, *John 4; 1 Tim. 2* <note>The original text cites "Job. IV" and "1 Tim. XXXII," likely printer errors for John 4 and 1 Timothy 2.</note>, even if one is out in the field or on the land; He is with all those who call upon Him in spirit and truth.

Our houses and dwellings must be Bethels, not Bethavens <note>Hebrew: "House of Vanity" or "House of Lies"</note> or houses of lies, vanity, and injustice. It goes poorly when people only meet there to eat, drink, gamble, and play, to slander their neighbor and sting them with the tongue. No, in our houses, as Bethels, we must guard against works of vanity, flippancy, falsehood, and lies; one must make oneself familiar with the Lord there, calling upon him openly with one's household, and going to sleep there upon the pillow of Divine providence, upon the stone of Jesus.

Certainly, our souls and bodies must be Bethels, or houses of God—dwellings of God in the Holy Spirit, *1 Cor. 3 and 6; 2 Cor. 6*—in which must be found faith, hope, love, humility, and purity. Not at all the spirit of the world, *1 Cor. 2* <note>Original: "1 Kor. XXI," likely a typo for 1 Cor 2</note>, thoughts of lies and falsehood, or vanity, pride, and lust, *Rom. 12:1-2 and 6.* A Bethel, in an even more excellent power, is Heaven—for the Lord’s sake, for the holy Angels, and the entire choir of blessed heavenly beings, *Isaiah 63.* Christ, in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily, *Col. 2*, as he tabernacled among his own, *John 1*, and when God was revealed in the flesh, *1 Tim. 3:16.*

The tabernacle and the temple were like a Bethel, or house of God, *1 Kings 8; Ps. 132.*

But in no less power is the church of the New Testament, alongside the public places where the festive Christian multitude gathers, a Bethel or house of God, *1 Cor. 3:16; 2 Cor. 6:17, 18; 1 Tim. 3:15; 1 Pet. 2:5; Matt. 18.* There the Lord wishes to appear and dwell,

<column-break/>

and to speak to the soul through his word with many promises of grace for comfort. There one finds the Angels of God, the "angels" <note>The author refers to the "angels" or overseers/ministers of the congregations.</note> and overseers of the congregations. There Christ, the ladder, is set up, so that we may climb from earth to heaven with our hearts and prayers, with much boldness and confidence. Here is the door and gate, Jesus, to enter into heaven through him, *John 14:6 and 10.* The rungs are faith, love, hope, knowledge, prayers, and sighs, *Ps. 84; Prov. 4; Ps. 42 and 63; Phil. 1; Rev. 22, etc.* Here is also a door of beautiful advantage and opportunity, which must not be neglected, lest in seeking it, one finds it cut off or closed, *Ps. 95; Isaiah 55:6; Prov. 1; Amos 8; Luke 19; Heb. 4 and 5.*

To enter through this gate into the house of God, one must go before and encourage one another, *Isaiah 2; Micah 4; Ps. 95 and 24 and 100, etc.* But since this is a Bethel, or house of God, no idolatry, lies, vanity, falsehood, or injustice may be perceived there; the place is too venerable, holy, and awesome for that. God wants to be sanctified by those who approach him, *Lev. 10* <note>Original cites "Levit. XV," likely referring to the sanctification required in Lev. 10 or 15.</note>, *Ps. 5 and 15.*

There, humility, attention, and reverence are required, *James 4* <note>Original cites "Jakob VI," perhaps meaning James 4.</note>, *1 Pet. 1:15-17*, holiness and purity of hands, *Ps. 24* <note>Original cites "Ps. CXCI," likely a typo for Ps. 24 or 15.</note>, *1 Tim. 2.* But as far as Bethel is concerned, even though it was so beautiful that Jacob called it a house of God, in the time of Jeroboam it was changed into a Bethaven. A calf, high places, and altars were found there, *1 Kings 12; 1 Sam. 13; Jer. 48; Hosea 4, 8, and 10; Amos 3.* One was forbidden to go there; the Lord would consume it, and the Lord forbade prophesying there, *Amos 5:5 and 7:13.*

<margin>Bethel changed into Bethaven.</margin>

See, thus the holy and venerable places become abominable because of public godlessness, vanity, and idolatry. It was like the king’s house, to which he had attached and fastened his apostate service.

Dear God, what changes and reversals are the houses of God, external churches, and congregations of God often subject to! Bethel, a house of God, has become a Bethaven—a house of vanity, lies, idolatry, and superstition; yes, a dwelling and den of murderers and public trade. For how does it stand with the congregations of Asia Minor, Corinth, Galatia, Ephesus, Thessalonica, etc.? Is the vile arch-deceiver not seated there? And how is Rome, once the mother city of Christendom, deformed and fallen! Does not the Antichrist, the man of sin, the son of perdition, sit there in God’s Bethel, *2 Thess. 2*? Where are the Bethels in France, Bohemia, Hungary, Moravia and Silesia, the Palatinate, etc.? Has not cursed idolatry taken place there? Does not the bread-god <note>A derogatory term for the Eucharist wafer used in polemical Protestant writing.</note>, the "strength," the <term>Mauzzim</term> <note>Original: "Maussim." Refers to the "god of fortresses" from Daniel 11:38, interpreted by Reformers as the worship of saints or worldly power.</note>, stand in the holy place? Does one not find there images of the saints, invocations of the deceased, and such things? Have we not received a divine command to depart from there, and not to preach or prophesy, since Babylon <note>Refers to the corrupted Church.</note> does not want to be healed, *Rev. 18*? And what else can we expect, according to the divine and revealed patterns, but that the Lord shall consume it and overturn it in his wrath?

# BETHESDA.

### BETHESDA, <term>House of Mercy</term> <note>original Hebrew: בית חסדא (Beit Chasda)</note>.

<margin>Bethesda, a water-bath.</margin>
BETHESDA is a water-bath, *John 5*, mentioned in the Holy Scriptures and by Jewish writers, which I am about to discuss here.

This water-bath appears outside the city of Jerusalem, yet within its surrounding territory and jurisdiction, situated at or near the Sheep Gate, called BETHESDA in Hebrew, having five porches, says John. The word GATE is omitted by ellipsis <note>An ellipsis is a grammatical term where a word is left out because it is understood from the context.</note>.

<margin>Naming of the sheep gate.</margin>
As for the reason why the Sheep Gate was so named, there is no complete agreement. It is thought that it was perhaps named such because of the sheep which were brought through this gate, as it was close to the temple, to the priests and Levites; or that near that gate there was something like a small market for small livestock, where one could easily find what was needed if they desired any small animal for a sacrifice; or because there was a bath there to wash and cleanse the livestock before they were slaughtered; or because there was a sheepfold there for the animals that were to be sacrificed. Whatever the case may be, both points may perhaps deserve the attention of scholars.

Bethesda lay nearby.

Scholars tell us that in the time of our Savior, the Hebrew language was hardly spoken, but that the language in use was a mixture and composition of Chaldean and Syriac. For this reason, one finds quite some variation and distinction in both the spelling and the derivation of the word; for some read <term>House of Mercy</term> <note>original: בית חסדא</note> as <term>House of Snaring/Fishing</term> <note>original: בית צידא</note>; others read Bethsaida; yet in the most numerous and accurate copies, one reads Bethesda.

<margin>Origin of the word Bethesda.</margin>
Regarding where one should derive the origin of the word, I have found that linguistic writers are by no means in full agreement; for some derive it from <term>House of Effusion</term> <note>original: בית שיד</note>, *a house of poverty and misery*; others from <term>House of the Poor</term> <note>original: בית עניא</note>, *a house or dwelling of the goats*; others from <term>House of the Outpouring</term> <note>original: בית אשд</note>, being the same as <term>House of the Shedding</term> <note>original: בית השדא</note>; others from <term>House of Mercy</term> <note>original: בית חסדא</note>, *a house of mercy, benevolence, and kindness*.

From what source this water-bath took its origin, I do not know if anyone can say with full certainty. However, people guess, and provide this explanation by way of conjecture: namely, some claim that King Hezekiah hollowed out Mount Accaza and diverted the water of Gihon there through subterranean caves; and if one may believe Flavius Josephus, *Book 5, Chapter 15* of the Jewish Wars, Solomon would have dug this fish-pond or water-bath.

Others claim that the water was brought there from the fountain of Siloah through subterranean caves or conduits. Some have their eye on the temple water, particularly on the "Great Sea" or the bronze washbasin, which was to a large extent mixed with the blood of sacrificial animals and with the filth of the temple, and was thus red-colored and murky, as some have described it; or caused by the water that, through rain or otherwise, flowed together and was collected there. Whether it was called a house of mercy and benevolence because

<column-break/>

it was a hospital for misery, or for miserable, poor people, where they were well-received and treated; where the charitable gathered to support and refresh these needy and miserable people; or because the Lord showed exceptional mercy and benevolence to various people there; certainly, many factors may have coincided.

<margin>Five porches.</margin>
For convenience, comfort, and proximity, there were five porches there, says John, or a building with five halls or rooms. The Syriac translator has "galleries," covered walkways where one was sufficiently protected from the heat and the rain.

Some have thought that the Stoic sect is derived from the word <term>porch</term> <note>original Greek: στοὰ (stoa)</note>, because these people were found in such halls, rooms, or walkways in Athens to enjoy the teaching of Zeno.

Be that as it may, they were undoubtedly galleries, halls, chambers, and rooms where one could walk, lie, sit, and see the water-bath, as well as the stirring of the same. It must have been a busy place, and one must have succeeded there, since a multitude of all kinds of persons, afflicted with various ailments, was to be found there, such as the sick, blind, lame, and withered, waiting for the stirring or agitation of the bathwater, in the hope of being healed.

The word <term>to stir up</term> <note>original Greek: ταράσσειן (tarassein)</note> seems to me to imply *a strong agitation or movement, through which everything is mixed together and the clear water becomes murky and troubled*.

<margin>Stirring of the water.</margin>
This stirring of the water is attributed to an Angel of the Lord who descended.

Whether an Angel of the Lord showed himself visibly and brought about this stirring by immersion or by stirring with some tool—who can tell us?

Unless one suggests with Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a famous Dutch jurist and theologian who often sought natural or cultural explanations for biblical events.</note>, *That the Jews, whenever something rare occurred, immediately attributed it to an angel of God*; or thinks that upon the intervention of the will and desire of an angel, the Lord performing the work, the water was thus stirred. At the very least, it is certain that without human help or service, such a stirring was perceived, and therefore, the finger of the Lord was present. Now one reads subsequently that he who first stepped into it was healed.

<margin>Healing in that bath.</margin>
That this healing occurred upon entering and being the first to descend into that bathwater, I judge by no means to have come from the fact that Isaiah is buried there, or because the blood along with the offal of the sacrificial animals was poured out there, as some seem to have thought; for then it would have helped at all times. Then this stirring would not have been specifically required, and the first to descend would have had no advantage over the second, third, and last. Where does one find a water-bath that is so generally beneficial against all kinds of ailments? I must then conclude that this was a miracle of the Most High, by no means brought about by the common nature and power of the water itself.

Whether this water-bath was stirred once or several times a year, or whether (regarding the stirring) a fixed time was observed, and whatever else it may be; for my part, I cannot determine it; nor whether that water-bath with these ex-
