Nor is it known how long it lasted after Christ's ascension. *Tertullian, in Chapter 3 of his work Against the Jews, writes that because of the Jews' unbelief, stubbornness, and ingratitude, it ceased to have these effects not long after Christ.* <note>original: "Tertullianus Kapittel 3. tegen de Jooden... Adversus Judaeos"</note> Therefore, since no report is made of this water-bath either before or after Christ's time, it would indeed seem that the Lord appointed this effect during Christ's time to symbolize that He would raise up and open another bath-water and fountain against the ailments of souls.

<margin>Use of the bath-water.</margin>
It is related that water was drawn from that bath-water during the great Feast of Booths, or Tabernacles. It is said that with this water was mixed the dust, or the ashes, for the purification and sprinkling of the unclean in Israel: it is related that this water ran and flowed very gently, and that it was looked upon with respect. *Isaiah 8:6. Read Otthon. Lex. Rabbin. Lightfoot in Centur. Chronol. page 190. & in Disquis. Chorograph. page 588. etc.* <note>The author cites John Lightfoot and Johann Ottho, famous 17th-century scholars of Hebrew and biblical geography.</note>

<margin>Miracle of Jesus regarding this bath.</margin>
Christ may have had this in view. *John 7:37, 38, 39.* What kind of miracle the Lord performed there can be read in John.

I hold it for certain that Christ, through this, as with all His miracles, intended to demonstrate His lawful mission, His oneness with the Father, and that He was the true Messiah: the more so because the hallmark of the Messiah required such things, *Isaiah 35:5, 6. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be opened: then shall the lame man leap as a hart, and the tongue of the dumb shall sing, etc.*

The Jews in their own writings confess that the Messiah shall perform wonders, *Talmud in Berakhot, Midrash Kohelet Chapter 1. R. Levi Ben Gerson, Buxtorf in the School of the Jews, etc.*

Even the Jews must confess that Christ performed many and very great miracles, yet (O blasphemous mouths!) they say it was through the dark arts, the help of the prince of devils, or the "uttered name" of Jehovah. <note>The "uttered name" or Shem HaMephorash refers to a Jewish folkloric tradition claiming Jesus performed miracles by stealing the secret, unpronounceable name of God from the Temple.</note> This is the old slander *Matthew 12:24. John 7:31. and 11:47. Matthew 11:2-6. John 2:23. John 5:36.* From this it appeared clearly and undeniably that He was no mere man, but truly God; for God alone can do wonders. Now, whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. *John 5:36.*

The physical ailments and the healings of ailments ought to have led Israel to a vision of the plagues of the heart, and the healing by the Lord, *Hosea 1:7. Isaiah 53:4. Matthew 9:12. 1 Peter 1:2-4.* namely the Messiah. Upon both the one and the other, I am pleased to offer some allegorical reflections and to make my observations.

<margin>Author’s observations.</margin>
Toward the feast, Jesus came to Jerusalem: toward the great feast of the New Testament, before that glorious banquet *Isaiah 26* began, to which the lame and blind on the outskirts would be invited, because the self-important and healthy invited guests did not wish to come, *Matthew 22.* When the year of redemption and of God’s good pleasure had come, *Isaiah 40 and 63. 2 Corinthians 6.* Christ came. He established for His sheep a bath and spiritual healing water, not from Gihon or from Siloah, but from Himself, the true <term>Shiloh</term> <note>meaning "the one sent"</note> or the Sent One *Isaiah 61*, from Him the fountain flowing forth for the healing of all kinds of soul-ailments *Zechariah 13:1. Matthew 4. Psalm 36. Job 1.* If this bath-water belonged to King Solomon, at the very least this healing water belongs to the true Solomon, the King of Peace and of Righteousness. And as it flows out of the excavations, hollows, and water-conduits of Accara: this healing water of the soul flows forth from the struck Rock, from the welling waters of Christ's inflicted wounds, bloody merits, and stripes *Isaiah 53* through which there is healing. The channels of Evangelical preaching upon the mountains, the Sacraments of the New Testament, carry the same to our souls: yet the angels, shepherds, and teachers, as rational and moral instruments, are wonderfully relevant here.

If the water might have sprung from the Temple, or been caused by the winter showers and rain-pools, or in part by the cleansing water and the blood of sacrificial animals; certainly, the cleansing and healing water of the soul flows down to us and toward us from the temple of Jesus's Divinity, and is caused by the grim and heavy downpours of God's hot wrath that fell upon Him, flowing out from Him to the outskirts of Jerusalem, toward the East side, etc., even to the healing of the Gentiles, *Zechariah 14.*

<margin>Correspondence of the church with Bethesda.</margin>
The church, meanwhile, is a house with various rooms: indeed a Bethesda, a house of mercy and benevolence: there one must come if one wishes to find the good opportunity to be healed: there is the bath-water of Holy Baptism, and the Word, and Christ's blood and spirit.

In this external house of the church, one has the blind, who do not see or know the way of truth and virtue, *Revelation 3.* This was especially the case with the Jews and Gentiles in the early times *Isaiah 6:6-9. John 8:29: 40, 41. Ephesians 2. Acts 14 and 17.*

There were the lame, and those very deficient in their gait and walk according to the rule of truth, in knowledge, faith, love, hope, and all kinds of exercises of virtue.

There are the withered, the marrowless, sapless, and spiritless people, having no life or power of godliness: like dry, parched, lifeless dead bones, for which—in order to turn green and increase—the water of grace and of the Holy Spirit was highly necessary, *Isaiah 35 and 44. Ezekiel 37.*

The external water had to be moved if it was to have power, and made murky, as it were, and strongly stirred.

The conscience must be troubled and unsettled, *2 Corinthians 8*, through the service of the "Angels" of the congregation <note>In this context, "Angels" likely refers to the ministers or messengers of the church.</note>.

If one did not descend into the water, merely seeing it did not grant healing. The external does no good. So also preaching and Sacraments, even the bath of baptismal water, do nothing if one does not descend into the same through faith and practice close communion with Christ's death, resurrection, and life.

<margin>The many years.</margin>
One was found there who had been beset with this sickness for 38 years. He was and remained in a poor state: certainly there is a sickness and ailment which has stayed with mankind for more than 38 centuries, ever since Adam's time, *Romans 5:12. etc.* and how many a man remains with his sinful ailments longer than 38 years...

Certainly, not everyone is cured of the plagues of the heart in their youth; however, just as we see that an old, thirty-eight-year-long ailment <note>This refers to the paralyzed man healed by Jesus at the Pool of Bethesda in John 5.</note> was cured, so experience teaches us that old, and already long-standing, often years-old soul-ailments are cured. This provides us with hope that the long-standing ailment of the Jews shall finally be cured. It is never beyond hope: the Lord comes when it pleases Him.

Here, the afflicted man found no help until Christ took pity on him and healed him; likewise, no Priest or Levite could help us. One brother could not redeem the other, *Psalm 49 and 69.* For the true healing to occur, Jesus had to be there, *Psalm 40, Hebrews 7, 9, and 10.* He alone was mighty to redeem, *Acts 4:12, John 4:6, 1 Timothy 2, Isaiah 63 and 43.* He helped us, the powerless, *Ezekiel 16.* We could not stir or move, *Ephesians 2,* being dead in sins and trespasses, etc., without powerful help and service, *Ezekiel 16, Isaiah 63.*

In the meantime, it is our duty to take heed, to stay by the water-bath, to wait for the movement, and, alongside prayers for healing (*Psalm 51, Ezekiel 36*), to utilize the ministry and help of men. If many sick and afflicted people go before us in conversion, our wish must be to be cleansed more and more of our ailments, without, however, wishing to limit the Lord to a specific time, or to certain means and instruments.

### BETHLEHEM, House of Bread, <note>Hebrew: בית לחם (Beit Lechem)</note> Bethlehem. <note>Greek: Βηθλεὲμ</note>

<margin>The location of Bethlehem.</margin>
Of BETHLEHEM I have very little to say; I will not speak of its greatness or its smallness. This Bethlehem, which I am considering, lay in the inheritance of Judah, *Micah 5,* to distinguish it from the Bethlehem in the tribe of Zebulun, *Joshua 19.*

It is a very fertile region, perhaps named Ephrata for that reason <note>"Ephrata" is often associated with fruitfulness.</note>: a city of David, as he was born there, *1 Samuel 16 and 18.* Otherwise, according to the character of the language, it signifies a *house of bread*.

It appears that there was a fine well at Bethlehem’s gate. David, heated from the battle, was desirous to drink water from it; but when it was drawn by three heroes at the risk of their lives and brought to him, he desired not to drink it, as if it were the blood of the heroes, *2 Samuel 23.* So much did he love his people. In doing so, he wished to set an example and be in the same condition as both the great and the small.

I note that scholars cite from Eusebius, Baronius, and Jerome to Paulinus (*See Lightfoot in Centuria Chorographica, page 208*) that from Emperor Hadrian until Constantine the Great, an image of Adonis was allegedly erected in Bethlehem. It is said that Emperor Hadrian, seeking to root out the Christian faith there, established and erected an image of an ox, a statue of Adonis, and a chapel.

<column-break/>

Whether such a story deserves belief, I doubt, seeing as Hadrian was not so much concerned with the Scriptures, but with the rebellious and insurgent Jews; and it is noted that the Jews of Bethlehem seem to have made little of it.

<margin>The privilege of Bethlehem.</margin>
Bethlehem has a special portion here: that David, who ruled in Israel, was born there as king, and that it is called his city, *1 Samuel 16 and 18.* But the greater privilege above all other cities is that the true David, promised to David—David’s offspring, the Beloved of the Father—was to be born there, and indeed was born there, *Micah 5, Matthew 2, Luke 2, 1 Samuel 7, Isaiah 4 and 11, Isaiah 55, Ezekiel 34, Hosea 3:17, and 17.*

Then the Bread from Heaven was found there—the heavenly bread which feeds the soul and takes away hunger, *John 5 and 6.* Then He was therein, or under Bethlehem’s gate, He who is a well and a fountain of living water, capable of satisfying both hungry and thirsty souls, from which one would draw water with joy, *Isaiah 12, John 6 and 7.*

Our David, in the battle against the Philistines—His enemies and ours—did indeed cry out because of the dryness in His throat, *I thirst, Psalm 22, John 19, and Luke 23*; but so that we should not perish from thirst, He would not drink upon the wood of the cross.

<margin>Transfer/Application.</margin>
The church, the City of God, is like Bethlehem; there are the green pastures, *Psalm 23.* There is the bread, Christ; the bread of the Word, and of the Holy Supper. There is the living water-well, that well which never runs dry, whose waters wondrously refresh and strengthen the soul until thirst and faintness completely pass away, *John 4, 5, and 6.* Those who hunger and thirst for that bread and this water of Jesus, with His righteousness and the grace of God through the Holy Spirit (*Matthew 5 and 6, Isaiah 55:1, 2, John 7*), are very fortunate. They may safely drink of this water of grace and salvation, which cost the hero Jesus His blood and life in the battle against the Jewish and hellish Philistines.

And in our spiritual battle, one must pierce through the enemy's battle lines; it may be necessary to fight even unto blood, but there is no need to fear if only one can obtain the saving water of Jesus’ bloody merits, grace, and the working of His Spirit. One shall live, even if one were dead.

And certainly, one does not reach the Heavenly House of Bread, or Bethlehem’s wellspring, without a blow or a push. One must fight and fear no danger. Hunger and thirst must be endured beforehand.

### BEECH TREE, <note>Hebrew: Tidhar, תדהר</note> Fagus, <note>Latin: Beech</note> phēgos. <note>Greek: φηγὸς</note>

Regarding the BEECH TREE, since mention is also found of it in *Isaiah 41 and 60,* it will not be entirely useless for me to note something about it from the writings of learned men.

<margin>Description of the Beech Tree.</margin>
This tree grows high, spreads itself far and wide, and provides a decent shade. For this reason, one finds in Virgil, in his first Pastoral Song: <note>The author refers to the famous opening of Virgil's Eclogues: "Tityre, tu patulae recubans sub tegmine fagi" (Tityrus, you reclining under the canopy of a spreading beech).</note>

# B E E C H   T R E E.
P 3
<meta>Catchword: That</meta>

> *Lying beneath the cover of a spreading beech.* <note>original: "Patulæ recubans sub tegmine fagi." — A famous opening line from Virgil's Eclogues.</note>

->That is:<-

> *Lying in the shadow of the broad Beech tree.*

The leaf is not as coarse or heavy as that of the Oak tree, but thinner and finer, so that the wind catches it more easily. It stands for many years. Because of this, Persius, in his fifth satire, compares an old man who is weakened and exhausted by gout to an old Beech tree. Thus he says:

> *Whom stony gout of the hand*
> *Has broken the joints, like the dry branches of an old beech.* <note>original: "Cui lapidosa chiragra / Fregerit articulos, veteris ramalia fagi." — Persius, Satires 5.109.</note>

->That is:<-

> *When the hand-gout bruises his weak limbs,*
> *Like a Beech tree abandoned by its youth.*

<margin>Derivation of its name. Its fruit.</margin>Among the Latins it is called *fagus*, and by the Greeks *phegos* <note>original: "$\phi\eta\gamma\grave{o}\varsigma$"</note>, named after the word *phagein* <note>original: "$\phi\acute{\alpha}\gamma\epsilon\iota\nu$"</note>, to eat or consume, because the nut thereof is eaten. The fruit is not oblong and round like the acorns of the Oak tree, but rather resembles the Chestnut. It is enclosed in a triangular husk, rough and prickly on the outside like a hedgehog; furthermore, it is sweet in taste, so that rats, mice, pigs, and bears are also fond of them. Pigs fed on these provide good bacon. See Pliny in Book XVI, Chapters 5 and 6; Ursinus in *Arboretum Biblicum* <note>A 17th-century botanical-theological work by Johann Heinrich Ursinus.</note> p. 138. In ancient times, it is claimed, this was the food of men, who also ate acorns. Evidence of this is found in Ovid, *Fasti* Book IV:

> *Bread for the first mortals was green herbs,*
> *Which the earth gave with no one tilling.*
> *Afterward the acorn was born. It was well once the acorn was found,*
> *And the hard oak held magnificent riches.*
> *Ceres first, having called man to better nourishment,*
> *Exchanged acorns for a more useful food.* <note>original: "Panis erat primis virides mortalibus herbæ... Mutavit glandes utiliore cibo."</note>

Mr. Arnold Hoogvliet <note>A Dutch poet (1687–1763) known for his biblical and classical translations.</note> translates this in this manner:

> *The ancients lived on herbs, greens, and leaves,*
> *Which the earth brought forth from the unsown ground.*
> *Now they plucked the grass and clover into the mouth,*

> *But Ceres has given to man, whom she had called*
> *To better food, bread instead of acorns.*

# BEECH TREE.

->That is:<-

> *The merchant who desires to sail the sea with his wares*
> *In spite of the storm and the winds,*
> *Diligently prepares beech and alder wood,*
> *And fells the forest from which he builds his ships.*

<margin>Application.</margin>
If one were to apply the figure presented in Isaiah, chapters 41 and 60, under the name of the Beech tree, I can easily imagine that the general meaning would suffice: namely, that by means of the Gospel and the grace which God would bestow upon the wild Gentiles—whom He had left as a desert and a wilderness from the beginning of the New Testament and for a certain time thereafter, until the end of days when the fullness of the Gentiles should enter and all Israel be saved—these still unrefined and wild people would be brought to Eden, the Lord’s garden, watered, enlightened, converted, and would behave like tall, thick, dense, and sturdy trees. Thus, the professing Christian Church might find shade, refreshment, rest, and peace under their canopy.

<margin>Further application.</margin>
I wish to make some further applications here and give free rein to my thoughts.
The Gentiles, before their conversion, produced nothing but acorns <note>The Dutch "ekels" likely refers to beech mast or acorns—the meager "pig-food" of the unconverted state.</note>, a meager fare. The most prominent trees—that is, the Philosophers, Moralists, and Orators—came forward with that which was sought and greedily accepted by pigs and bears, meaning the common people who lacked foresight. That multitude

->*He lived on husks and second-rate bread,*<-
<note>original: "Vivebat siliquis & pane secundo" — Horace, Epistles 2.1.123.</note>

lived, as Horace says,

->*On pigs' food and coarsely baked bread.*<-

<margin>Explanation by Cyril.</margin>
Hear here Cyril of Alexandria on the 15th chapter of Luke. *Others*, he says, *once deprived of true gentleness, moderation, and love, have fallen into the extreme want of good things, and have taken for food the fables of the Greeks, which are understood as swill or husks; in which there is indeed some sweetness, but little nourishment, and on the contrary, much dryness. For the devil fed them with fables, and with a false sweetness of eloquence. For their teachings contain nothing but fictions and old wives' tales, presented with fine words, wherein lies the wisdom of the world, which because of its beautiful sound is called a clanging cymbal and sounding brass.* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:1.</note> See further d'Outrein in *Parables* page 42, etc.

<margin>From Stellingfleet.</margin>
One may add here Stellingfleet in his *Origines Sacrae* <note>original: "oorsprongelyke Outheden." Edward Stellingfleet (1635–1699) was a prominent English theologian.</note> p. 501, where he uses this language: *But above all other discoveries of Divine goodness, the sending of His Son into the world to die for sinners is the matter which the Scripture presents with the greatest life and eloquence. By eloquence I do not mean a skillful composition of words, but a dignity, weightiness, and persuasive power of the matters contained therein. And what is more powerful to melt our frozen hearts into a running stream of grateful obedience toward God than the strong reflection of the rays of God's love through Jesus Christ upon us? How dry and sapless are those long*

<column-break/>

*reasonings of the Philosophers, compared to this science! How feverish and how little satisfying are all those discoveries they had of God and His Divinity in comparison to those we have in the Gospel of Christ!* See my Notes on 1 *Corinthians* I.

<margin>Appearance of the Jews.</margin>
Was it any better among many of the Jews? They sought a worldly prince, a temporal redeemer (*Luke* XVII and *John* XVIII). They had rejected the true Catechism. Their own righteousness was raised upon the throne. For the most part, they were slaves to Heathen wisdom. It is testified that the Pharisees followed Plato and the Stoics, that the Sadducees held with the Epicureans, and the Essenes with the Pythagoreans. In this way, Heathenism found a seat in God's temple and in the minds of the people.

<margin>The Gentiles' origin from the Hebrews.</margin>
And if Plato, Socrates, and others had anything good, it certainly came to them from the Hebrews. Thus the Jewish lamp shone in the darkest night of Heathen ignorance: so that even the wise men had to confess that they owed the principal part of their wisdom to the "barbarians," that is, the Hebrews, as can be seen in Josephus in his two books against Apion; by Alexander ab Alexandro *Genialium dierum lib. VI. Cap. 5*; Justin Martyr in *Exhortation to the Greeks*; Clement of Alexandria *Stromata Lib. I*; Eusebius *Lib. IX* & *Demonstratio X*; Juvenal in his 10th Satire; Pico della Mirandola in *Prooemium Heptaplus*. See also my Notes on 1 *Corinthians* I:22, and Stellingfleet's *Origines Sacrae* p. 25, etc.

One can well understand that this wisdom of the wise shall perish, and the true wisdom, which is from above, shall by the trial of the spirit have another wisdom breathed into them, causing them to bear different fruits through God's guidance, who has kept His hand upon it. The bearing of these fruits continues even into old age.

<margin>Observation on the Beech Tree.</margin>
If this tree provides a shade under which shepherds rest with their livestock and take breath, it makes me think of the tall Beech trees—that is, the great kings and princes whose territory and power extend far and wide, under whose shade and protection the shepherds and teachers with their flocks, which is the congregation of God, would sit. See *Isaiah* XLIX:7-23.

<margin>Concerning the fruit.</margin>
If these trees give sweet nuts, one may say that, viewed morally, they also contribute their part in natural and civil life. See *Psalm* LXXII:10-16, *Isaiah* LXI:6, etc.

<margin>Concerning the bark.</margin>
If one wrote the marks of love and the names of loved ones upon the bark of this tree, consider the "new name" in *Revelation* II; being named after the Lover, *Jeremiah* XIV, *Acts* XI; God's name and that of the Lamb, *Revelation* VII, XIV, and XXII. They themselves would write that they were a tree of God, of the Lord, *Isaiah* XLIV. They have become "Paul's Letter," 2 *Corinthians* III:1, 1 *Thessalonians* II:19. They also went so far through weakness that they called themselves "of Paul," that is, they sided with Paul. See 1 *Corinthians* III.

<margin>Concerning the construction.</margin>
If ships or vessels were prepared from this timber, consider that from these trees would be prepared the little ships of the individual churches and congregations, just as they appear so distinctly in the letters of Paul and the Revelations of John. I have nothing more to say about this.

# WAVE and HEAVE OFFERING.

### WAVE and HEAVE OFFERING, <note>Hebrew: *Terumah*, *Tenupha*</note>.

<margin>Reason for the names of the WAVE OFFERING.</margin>
This offering is so named for its movement and lifting up before the face of the Lord. I shall not speak of these offerings in themselves, but only of the movement and lifting: one reads of the Wave-breast and the Heave-shoulder; of a golden Wave-offering; of Wave-bread; of the waving of the Wave-offering, and so forth in *Exodus 29 and 39, Numbers 6, 8, and 18, Leviticus 8, 9, and 23,* etc. One may consult the Concordances regarding this.

<margin>Difference of opinions on the Hebrew words.</margin>
Regarding the Hebrew root words used on this occasion, not all writers—among both Jews and Christians—share the same thoughts and expressions.
The word *Tenupha* <note>Hebrew: תנופה</note> is derived from *Nuf* <note>Hebrew: נוף</note>, *to shake, move, or to pass over something as if with the hand*: and as some believe, to bring and present it to God (*Exodus 35*), though not always by moving the hands toward all corners and regions of the world.

Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a prominent medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian.</note> distinguishes between *Terumah* <note>תרומה</note> and *Tenupha* <note>תנופה</note> in that *Tenupha* consists *in moving to and fro*, or that it is <note>Hebrew: תנועה אילך ואילך</note> *a movement here and elsewhere*.

But that *Terumah* is largely <note>Hebrew: הגבהה למעלה</note> *an elevation toward the heights*: and that he who makes this elevation says <note>Hebrew: מעלה ומוריд</note> <note>The text likely intended מוריד (morid), meaning to bring down.</note> that he first raises it, and thereafter lets it sink down, or descend.

Or that *Terumah* signifies *an elevation upward* and *Tenupha* *a movement to and fro, to the right and left sides*. By this, some Jews wish it to be understood that God fills all in all; therefore, it was reasonable to reach out and offer the sacrifice to Him, to whom everything far and wide belonged.

Thus R. Bechai <note>Bahya ben Asher (13th century), a Spanish rabbi and scholar.</note> writes on *Leviticus 8*: <note>Hebrew: מוליך ומביא למי שארבע רוחות העולם שלו מעלה ומוריד למי שהשמים וארץ שלו</note> *he moves it to and fro, toward Him to whom the four quarters of the earth belong. He reaches it up to Him above, and down below, who is the Lord of Heaven and Earth.*

And R. Levi ben Gerson <note>Also known as Gersonides (1288–1344), a philosopher and talmudist.</note> adds this observation: that the movement served <note>Hebrew: להורות על השם יתעלה השגוח בעליונים ובתחתונים ועל בכל פנות שרם בו</note> *so that one might notice that God's providence extends over everything, whether things are above or below.*

<margin>Observation.</margin>
For my part, I shall have little objection if one wishes to see in this waving and elevation a public demonstration of Divine righteousness, as Christ was presented as an atonement for our sins in His blood and raised upon the wood of the cross: being "moved" through the ministry of the Apostles, spiritual Priests, and Levites into all parts of the world (*Matthew 28, Mark 16, 2 Corinthians 5,* etc.) so that he, who is the propitiatory sacrifice, might be eaten through faith. This was something that ancient Israel was not permitted to do before the atonement and peace were struck (*Matthew 26:26, Hebrews 13,* etc.); even the Priest was not permitted to consume that which was offered for him. Let this suffice as a brief observation and application for now, as the different types of offerings must be dealt with in the following sections.

<column-break/>

### MUFFLING <note>The Dutch *bewimpelen* refers to the ritual covering of the lip or face.</note>.

The muffling of the face was formerly required of the leper (*Leviticus 13*). God threatens the false and greedy prophets with it, who prophesied for a piece of bread to please someone (*Micah 3:7*), giving it to be understood that they would be grieved, shamed, and rendered unable to prophesy any longer, or to speak with deceit and false flattery according to the heart of the people.

<margin>Observation regarding the lepers.</margin>
What concerns lepers and leprosy, and where they were struck, is not for me to discuss now: and therefore, standing only on the matter of muffling, I note that the clothes of the leper were torn, and sometimes burned. That his head was uncovered, or the hair shorn: being stripped of the usual ornament and covering, as if without honor and as an object of derision.

They had to muffle the upper lip: either to cover their face, or to practice mourning, or because of sadness and shame: or so as not to infect others with their breath.

A leper had to stay outside the camp, and during the inheritance of Canaan, outside the cities (*Leviticus 13*).

And if he heard or saw someone from afar, he had to cry out, "Unclean, unclean!" Or according to the gloss of the Chaldean translator <note>The Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, *Away from here, away from here, you who are clean: or you clean ones flee, flee from the unclean.* This was so that the clean might not be defiled by the unclean.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
We have just said that the leper, during his leprosy, had to remain outside the camp and the cities: therefore, one might ask with some difficulty, how then did the man covered in leprosy enter the city in *Luke 5*?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
To this it is answered: it may perhaps have been an unwalled city, an open village, or a hamlet, and in such places, it is said, the leper was permitted to enter. Yes, even in the synagogue there, it is said, though he had to sit in a sequestered place ten hand-breadths high and four cubits wide or broad: he had to enter before all others, yet be the last of all to leave. (*Negaim chapter 13, Lightfoot Harmony of the Four Evangelists, page 513, etc.*)

Some argue that this man was quite bold and did not strictly adhere to the laws and customs of the Jews because of the strong passion he had to be relieved of his miserable plague by Christ.

Others believe that the Savior went out to him, etc. However, I will not dwell on this.

For my part, since leprosy signified sin and the contagion of sin spread to all Jews and Gentiles—as must be shown in its proper place—it seems to me that the state of the unclean sinner is a state of dishonor, sadness, and mourning, in which he lacks all ornament of virtue and covering, and is deprived and ousted from all grace of God and from the fellowship of the saints and heavenly beings; yes, as if banished and exiled by God and the saints: with whom the clean must not associate or practice fellowship, so that they may not be defiled or gain any part in his unfruitful works: for the breath of the sinful leper stinks, and their—

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of symbolic "coverings" and uncleanness, transitioning into the legal and symbolic definitions of "Sowing" (Bezaaijen) in biblical law. It moves from the physical state of the leper to the agricultural laws of the Torah.</meta>

...their throats and tongues are inflamed, *Psalms 5:11, Proverbs 3, 11, and 12, Isaiah 59, 1 Corinthians 15, Ephesians 5,* etc.

They are covered and muffled at the lips, or as if entirely covered, because of concealment, shame, and grief before God: also having no tongues, lips, or ability—being unclean—to speak of the Holy One of Israel, His name, virtues, and works, or to engage in reasoning.

But more on one and the other later, when **LEPERS** and **LEPROSY** are to be discussed.

### S O W I N G, <term>Hebrew: *Zera* <note>זרע</note>; Greek: *Speiro* <note>Σπείρω</note></term>.

**R**egarding what this word entails and what should be noted about it, one can look under **SEED** and **SOWING**, where the matter is treated at length; here, we offer only a brief perspective on the word "Sowing" (or "Seeding over").

As for sowing a plowed field with any seed, it is well known that this is intended in the hope of profit and a favorable harvest when one entrusts seeds of various kinds to the earth.

It was something singular that the Lord gave this specific prohibition, *Leviticus 19:19. You shall keep my statutes. You shall not let your livestock breed with another kind. You shall not sow your field with mixed seed, nor shall a garment of mixed fabrics come upon you. Deuteronomy 22:9. You shall not sow your vineyard with diverse seeds, lest the fruit of the seed which you have sown and the fruit of your vineyard be defiled.*

I am inclined to believe that God’s will was to serve as a law for Israel, and that He is not obligated to give any reason for His pleasure to man. Yet, in the meantime, I also believe that one need not rest only in the outward and bare letter; indeed, one could express various reasons and insights as to why and for what purpose this prohibition was given.

Everyone has their own thoughts and observations. I will not expand upon the ideas of the ancients or the moderns, nor present them in great detail; it will be enough that I propose one or two, and leave the choice to the reader.

Some wish to see here, according to the letter, a reference to the superstitious practices of the **Sabians** <note>An ancient Middle Eastern religious group often associated by medieval scholars with star worship and magic.</note>, who used the mixing of animals, plants, and other things in the service of the planets.

Or that the Sabians honored Ceres <note>Roman goddess of agriculture</note> and Bacchus <note>Roman god of wine</note> together, and for this reason joined the grapevine and the grain.

Thus says **Maimonides** <note>Moses ben Maimon (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note>, that the Sabians had the habit of sowing wheat, barley, and raisins together, as if sowing them simultaneously with a single toss of the hand. See also **Spencer** <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a pioneer in the comparative study of religion.</note> and **Rabbi Josiah**.

**Cajetanus** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), an influential Italian cardinal and philosopher.</note> would gladly move past the literal prohibition and not view it as a strict ban, but rather think of it as a mere symbol and motto: that in the civil state, one must not sow seeds of novelty, strife, or discord, and other evils that cause the republic to decline rather than grow.

For my part, I judge that one must first hold to the letter—whether this should be understood as

<column-break/>

brought forward above from Maimonides, or whether the Lawgiver simultaneously intended to sketch for them that they should guard and protect themselves from vengeful greed, avarice, and exhaustion of the land. It seemed a matter of avarice and harshness to compel the cultivated ground, at one and the same time, to produce and bear two kinds of fruit; by which a subsequent depletion, consumption, and thinning of the land could also be caused.

One may also think that the Lord wished to keep the lineages and species of procreating things single and unmixed, just as He had created them and given them to man.

And certainly, what could be found more harmful to the grapevine and the springing grains, straw, and stalks, than that the vineyard be stifled by the high ears and stalks? Or that one crop oppressed the other and took away its nourishment? So that it happened not infrequently that in attempting to mow and harvest much from one and the same ground, one found themselves miserably deceived in their expectations.

Or one might think that the Lord intended to forbid that one should—as if owing Him two kinds of fruit—bring only one, thinking it was enough since they grew on the same ground.

This mixing of forbidden materials, animals, and such, could lend thoughts to the lustful heart of corrupted mankind toward carnal and forbidden mixtures.

It is perhaps likely that the Lord, being a great lover of simplicity of heart and of unadulterated and unmixed morals and commands, wished to imply that in all these things no mixture should be made; but rather that simplicity of heart, of faith, of love, of conduct, and of morals should be preserved in all parts, and His people should be consistent in all times and in everything.

<margin>The plowing up of a city.</margin>
The plowing up of a city or land and sowing it with salt was done as a hostile act to signify extreme infertility and desolation; more on this later under the words **SALT** and **SOWING**.

I cannot yet fully part from this word *sowing* until I have illuminated two more passages, namely *Jeremiah 31:27*. There, under the symbol of sowing Israel and Judah with the "seed of man and beast," it is implied that in the latter days—when He would establish a New Covenant, entirely distinct from the one He made with their fathers upon leaving Egypt—He would bring it to pass that they would expand and be more numerous than their ancestors, and He would bless them singularly in their livestock. Or, that He would bless and multiply them so that they would see brothers and sisters—the true offspring of Abraham—not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, who stood to be blessed in Abraham’s seed, even though they were formerly regarded or despised as beasts.

# B R O O M.
Q

->B R O O M,<-

BROOM, TO SWEEP, *to brush away, and to cast the filth outside*: <term>Metate <note>original Hebrew: מטאטא</note></term>, <term>Ya'um <note>original Hebrew: יעום</note></term>, <term>koros <note>original Greek: κόρος</note></term>, <term>karos <note>original Greek: κάρος</note></term>. *Broom, Broom <note>original Latin: Scopa, Scopa</note>*.

<margin>The use of brooms.</margin>
BROOMS are used to clean the house, the floor, and the rooms of the house of filth; in which shuffling about one sometimes indeed finds that which was lost.
Such scullery-drudges, kitchen-shufflers, and most despicable servants, called *Mediastini* <note>original Latin: lowest-ranking household slaves</note>, are found among the ancients. A Broom or a Scrubber was the mark of these people, also called *Scoparii* <note>original Latin: broom-bearers or sweepers</note>: *Horace* mentions them, *Book II, Satire IV.*

> *How much expense is there in cheap brooms,*
> *in napkins, and in sawdust?*
> <note>original Latin: "Vilibus in fcopis, in mappis, in fcobe quantus / Confiftit fumtus?"</note>

->That is:<-

> *What costs are there indeed hanging on your cloths,*
> *On your brooms, and scrubbers, on your sand?*

*Juvenal, Satire XIV.*

> *When a guest is about to arrive, no one of your household shall rest:*
> *sweep the floor, reveal the polished columns,*
> *let the dry spider descend with its entire web.*
> <note>original Latin: "Hofpite venturo ceffabit nemo tuorum: / Verre pavimentum, nitidas oftende columnas, / Arida cum tota defcendat aranea tela."</note>

->That is:<-

> *If you expect a guest, they wash at your place all day.*
> *Sweep, your wife wipes and brushes, leave neither dust nor cobweb.*
> *They try to rub the wood like gold until it shines.*

It seems that it was sometimes not a matter of indifference what the Brooms were made of. See *Euripides in Ion, Act I; Paschalius on Crowns, Book VIII, Chapter 8; Hofmann’s Lexicon under SCOPA.*

When the Word of the Lord speaks of Brooms, and of sweeping away with Brooms, I am inclined to believe that it is borrowed from what is achieved by Brooms—the sweeping and clearing away—and that it can thus depict heavy, righteous, and judicial judgments, through which God gives over the godless, and also His wicked and ungrateful people, to the utmost destruction, casting out, and most despicable state, even as in *Isaiah 14:23* <note>The source text says Isaiah 4:23, but the context of "the broom of destruction" is 14:23</note> where <term>Hashmed <note>original Hebrew: השמד; meaning to destroy or exterminate</note></term> corresponds to <term>exairein <note>original Greek: ἐξαίρειν; meaning to remove or destroy</note></term>, *to overthrow, exterminate, or cut off* <note>original Latin: profligare, exterminare, exfcindere</note>. This is a metaphorical way of speaking: just as one sweeps dust, dung, and filth forward and out the door with Brooms, to be rejected as something worthless, trampled, or thrown into a corner of filth. This can be applied literally to Babylon, and spiritually to the spiritual Babylon: as also *Isaiah 28:23* to the Jews, their city, and temple, who, though outwardly God's covenant people, would later be called "wild." *See Coccejus, Gulichius, Vitringa, etc.*

Some understand *Matthew 12:44* and *Luke 11:25* to mean by the Broom the Word of God, through which the house of the outward Jewish church was cleansed of idolatry and pagan abominations after the Babylonian captivity, but was later reoccupied by many sects and wickednesses.

At least, whatever the case may be, Jesus directed His speech to the Pharisees and the unbelieving and wicked Jews, such as those who belong to the house of Satan: they are an empty house, devoid of faith, grace, and true Christian virtues. Yet it is also a "garnished" house, with outward hypocrisy and that which is varnished over: at least prepared and fit for the reception of such a guest as the Demon is, since impurity serves as his ornament, slovenliness as his delight, and the foul-smelling as a pleasant fragrance to him. *See Gomarus, and Friedrich Spanheim the Younger in Biblical Vindications.*

<margin>Brooms applied to the preaching of God's Word.</margin>
Otherwise, I am inclined to believe that sweeping with Brooms signifies cleansing: and that through the preaching of the Word, one can cleanse the heart of errors, prejudices, misunderstandings, and many evil desires. Sinners are "found" thereby, like lost things, and brought to rights, over which one rejoices with right and reason, *Luke 15:8; 2 Corinthians 10:4, 5; Psalm 19; 2 Timothy 3:16, etc.*

Loose and unbound Brooms, *Scopae dissolutae* <note>original Latin: literally "dissolved brooms"</note>, is a name for loose, unruly "calves"—people of no fashion, understanding, or reflection, from whom nothing good or distinguished is to be expected. *See Cicero to Atticus, Epistles, Book VII; See Erasmus’s Adagia.* It also refers to unbound words and speeches, where no neatness, charm, spirit, nor power and order are found, and which are spoken unseasonably. *See Johannes Sartorius, Adagia, page 142.*

->R E E D, <term>Agmon <note>original Hebrew: אגמון</note></term>, <term>bryon <note>original Greek: βρύον</note></term>, <term>schoinos <note>original Greek: σχοῖνος</note></term>, *seaweed, rush <note>original Latin: alga, juncus</note>*.<-

REED appears in the holy scrolls in various places, though not everywhere in the same use or with the same imagery. One finds idioms and uses, especially of the Egyptians, who made small boats and shoes for the use of priests from reeds, etc. *Alexander ab Alexandro, page 349; Herodotus, Book II, Chapter 37.* Regarding reed boats which were sent across the sea, *Isaiah 18*, one can consult *Pliny, Book VI, Chapter 22; Dilherr, Truth, pages 149-167; Bochart’s Phaleg, page 213; Dietericus, Antiquities of the Old Testament, 580, etc.; Ursinus, Herbal, pages 157-160; Paralipomena, Book II, Chapter 16, etc.; Witsius, Egypt, page 67.* These reeds, canes, or papers <note>referring to papyrus</note> grew especially in Egypt, in the Nile. *Pliny, Book VI, Chapter 22; Lucan, Book IV.*

> *Thus when the Nile overflows everything,*
> *the boat of Memphis is woven together from thirsty papyrus.*
> <note>original Latin: "Sic cum tenet omnia Nilus / Conferitur bibula Memphitis cymba papyro."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Because the Nile floods everything there,*
> *Memphis fastens boats of paper tightly together.*

<margin>The use of reeds</margin>
Those reeds were directed to many uses, *Pliny, Book XXI, Chapters 18 & 20.* Therefore one may assume that they must have been sturdier and stronger than our common reeds, which are used for the mats of chairs, reed-bundles for learning to swim, and other things.

Of the reeds then, according to their different natures, their uses, and services, I shall not speak, satisfying myself merely by bringing forward what occurs in the holy scrolls by allusion and imagery.

I read in *Exodus 2:3* of the infant Moses, *But when she could hide him no longer, she took for him a basket of reeds, and daubed it with pitch,*

...with slime, and with pitch: *and she laid the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink.* <note>Quoting Exodus 2:3, describing the basket made for the infant Moses.</note>

The word <term>Gomeh <note>original Hebrew: גמא</note></term>, translated by our people as REED, is taken by Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish rabbi and grammarian</note> for a kind of the lightest wood, such as sea-reed: others understand it to mean paper <note>papyrus</note>, from which small boats were manufactured. *Isaiah XVIII.*

It is believed that this occurred around the Tanais, or Zoan. *Psalm LXXVIII. 12.* That the mother must have abandoned the child to Divine Providence, and perhaps expected that the Lord would take care of him, one might gather from *Hebrews XI.* That she placed it in the reeds at the edge, so as not to be rocked away or washed over by the water, but to be close at hand, is believable: perhaps intentionally brought to the place where the king's daughter was accustomed to wash. Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> calls this daughter THERMUTIS. The mercy, beauty, and impulse of the Lord will have moved her to take up that child and have him raised.

<margin>Comparison of Moses with Christ.</margin>
On this instance of Moses, I see that some have distinctively made several reflections and parallels: namely, just as Moses, the Lawgiver and redeemer of Israel, was in his youth with Pharaoh as one condemned to death and in mortal danger, so also the mediator of the better covenant, Christ, was in extreme mortal danger under Herod.

<margin>Remarks of the learned.</margin>
Meisnerus <note>Balthasar Meisner (1587–1626), a Lutheran theologian</note> has remarked upon this, *That just as the mediator Moses lay enclosed in the reed basket, so our mediator and Savior lay in His grave: but on the feast of Easter, He was drawn out of it by His heavenly Father to be the supreme leader and redeemer of His church, or congregation.*

Someone else has remarked, *that our burial places are like reed baskets, smeared with slime and the sap of the tree of life, Christ, so that they draw no water of destruction into themselves: they are committed to the water, but we are drawn out of them alive, and we are raised at the court of King Jesus, our Prince.*

Furthermore, one reads in *Job VIII. 11, 12, 13.* etc. *Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?*

According to the judgment of wise theologians, this depicts the state and condition of the godless and hypocrites, who indeed grow and flourish when the wind is in their favor, and temporal honor and profit flow into their mouths, but they fall away of themselves, quickly withering and fading when things go against them, unable to withstand the heat of visitation or the drought of misery or poverty: they fade, wither, and perish sooner than the low grass. Just as the Lord sometimes very suddenly cuts off and causes to perish the hope, growth, and bloom of the godless, and the mask is often suddenly ripped from the high-exalted hypocrite so that he has no permanence, having no strength or sap of grace, *Psalm LXXVII. 17, 18, 19.* etc. though it is entirely different with the righteous. *Psalm I. Jeremiah XVII. 7, 8.*

In *Job Chapter XL. verse 21* <note>In many English bibles, this is Job 41:2</note> it is asked, *Canst thou put a hook into his nose? or bore his jaw through with a thorn?* which is asked concerning the Behemoth, the water-horse or hippopotamus: which question implies a denial or negation.

<term>Gomeh <note>Hebrew: גמא</note></term>, a reed, grows in pools and rivers where there is mire. The word for standing water comes from

<column-break/>

<term>Gama <note>Hebrew root: גמא</note></term>, to drink in, to swallow, because the reed sucks in the water, and needs marshy mire and water for its growth. *Pliny in Book XIX, Chapter 2* says the Greeks use reeds for ropes and cables. The Talmudists <note>scholars of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> make mention of ropes and cables made of reeds, flax, and twigs, and of green and tough tree branches.

The 70 Translators <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, and common translators have *ring, circle, hook, barb*; Luther: *as a reed muzzle, or bridle:* also Junius, Cocceius, and others. This can now be applied and interpreted according to the explanation and interpretation of the Behemoth.

One reads in *Isaiah IX and XIX* of *head, branch, tail, and reed*, that is: since a reed is of little value, weak and powerless, and there is a proverb *more worthless than seaweed <note>original Latin: "vilior alga"</note>*, I can well imagine that here the reed signifies the lowest, weakest, and most despised sort of people: and that, since the Lord threatens a general judgment, this judgment would strike great and small, rich and poor, powerful and lowly people of every state and profession—namely, Magistrates, Priests, Prophets, and the common people.

And when *Isaiah XIX* speaks of the great destruction and misery in Egypt, through the destruction of the reed, flag, or paper-growth <note>papyrus</note>, it is understood to mean *that neither great nor small, neither judge nor old nor young will be capable of delivering Egypt from the Assyrian: indeed, that their state shall be so hopeless that nothing shall succeed for them, but that they shall be dejected, fearful, and cowardly, like women and children.* Now, some great men apply this to the "spiritual Egypt," and believe it depicts the withering and drying up of Christians in the Roman Empire, who had the name of being alive but were spiritually dead, and led astray by the love of the world and by human authority in the church, fell away and abandoned Christianity when the Muslims invaded their lands: in Asia, Africa, Europe, Syria, Palestine, etc. However, I shall not dwell on this.

One reads in *Isaiah XXXV. 7. and the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water: in the habitation of dragons, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes.*

If one pays proper attention to the preceding, it speaks of the days of the New Testament, the time of the Messiah, and the blessings of the New Testament, and almost everything is expressed through holy imagery, indeed of the pouring out of the Lord's Spirit on all flesh, *Joel II. Acts II.* in that abundant measure, *Isaiah XLIV. John VII. 37, 38, 39.* not drop by drop as of old, but in streams, so that the parched, dry, and unwatered Heathendom, through the word of the Gospel and the dew of the Spirit and grace, would be watered unto manifold fruitfulness, so that the dragon would have to leave his dwellings and endure the emergence of a fruitful growth—even those who would bring some shadow, shelter, and refreshment to the lowly, like reeds and rushes.

One reads in *Isaiah LVIII* of *bowing and hanging the head like a reed.* A reed, as it grows long, bends and lets its top crown hang, which is a sign of weakness. That the proud and those performing outward penance precisely bow and hang their heads, yet true penance and humiliation before God cannot be... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, likely continuing on the next page.</note>

### B E E. דבורה <note>Debora</note>, μέλισσα <note>melissa</note>, apis.

**A**S for the Bees, there would be infinitely much to say and write about them. Indeed, if only the writing of it pleased me, I could prepare an entire book on it, considering that there are many men who have made it their life's work: but I shall strive for brevity as much as possible, and note down what seems most important to me.

<margin>Naming of the Bee.</margin>

I find the Bee called *Debora*, as we are told, from דבר <note>dabar</note>, meaning not only *to speak*: but also, *to govern, to rule, to lead*. For they say it is a political animal: that constantly hums, and has a sort of sound and speech about it.

These little creatures are found called *Apes*, which some have interpreted to be as "without feet" <note>A-pes, a folk etymology suggesting they lack feet at birth</note>: whether because they seem to be born without feet: or that by the intertwining of their legs they seem to form a cluster. Unless one prefers that *Apis* comes from the old word ἀπω <note>apo</note>, in place of which ἀπλω <note>haplo</note> seems to have come, meaning, *I prepare, I weave, I fasten*, corresponding exactly to the activity of bees.

Whatever further distinct names the bees bear can be read in *Jonston* <note>John Jonston (1603–1675), a naturalist and physician of Scottish descent living in Poland</note>, in his learned work, the *Description of Animals*.

*Virgil* in the 4th Book of the *Georgics* <note>Lantgedichten</note>, has left this following summary of the bees' activity and nature:

> *They alone have children in common, and communal roofs*
> *Of a city, and pass their age under great laws,*
> *And know their fatherland and fixed homes:*
> *Mindful of the coming winter, they experience labor*
> *In summer, and store what they have sought for the common good.*
> *For some watch over the food, and by a settled pact*
> *Are exercised in the fields: part within the enclosures of their homes*
> *Lay down the Narcissus' tear and the slow glue from the bark*
> *As the first foundations for the combs, then hang the clinging*
> *Wax: others lead out the adult offspring, the hope*
> *Of the race: others pack the purest honey,*
> *And distend the cells with liquid nectar.*
> *There are those whose lot it is to guard the gates,*
> *And in turn they watch the waters and the clouds of heaven:*
> *Or receive the loads of those coming in, or, having formed a line,*
> *Drive the drones, a lazy herd, from the stalls.*
> *The work seethes, and the fragrant honey smells of thyme.*
> <note>original: Virgil, Georgics IV. 153–169. This passage famously describes the bee colony as a model for human society.</note>

<column-break/>

According to Vondel's translation <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679), the most celebrated poet of the Dutch Golden Age</note>, this sounds as follows:

> *They have mutual community of their goods*
> *And children, and collectively one single city.*
> *They spend their time, and live throughout,*
> *By fixed laws that are enduring: they learn*

> *The hope of her race: another pushes steadily*
> *The clear honey up, and fills with her load*
> *The cell with nectar: one must guard the gate*
> *By lottery, and she watches if the weather will clear,*
> *And attends to weather and wind, or takes in that space*
> *The load from the neck of the incoming ones,*
> *Or keeps in a troop the drones, foul animals,*
> *Out of the hive. It is busy here; the honey, amidst the swarming*
> *Of the bees, smells of thyme.*

> *Love of possessing urges each*
> *In its own duty. To the elders, the towns are a care,*
> *And to fortify the combs, and to fashion the Daedalian roofs.*
> *But the younger ones, tired, return late at night,*
> *Their legs full of thyme: they feed everywhere on strawberry trees*
> *And gray willows, and cassia, and blushing crocus,*
> *And the rich linden, and dark hyacinths.*
> *For all there is one rest from work: for all, there is one labor.*
> <note>original: Virgil, Georgics IV. 177–184. "Daedalian" refers to Daedalus, the mythical craftsman, implying the combs are intricate and skillfully built.</note>

->That is:<-

> *An innate desire thus drives them to nourish themselves,*
> *The bees of Hymettus, not sluggish in the honey-work,*
> *With strength and zeal. All the bands of old castle-soldiers*
> *Guard their wall, fortify the combs,*
> *And build the house with art. The weak youth alone*
> *Return late in the evening, with much thyme on the leg.*
> *They sniff steadily for bait on the country's wild apple trees,*
> *On gray willows, and rich linden, by streams,*
> *On brown May-flowers, and on cassia and saffron.*
> *They rest at the same time and set to work together.*

# BEES.

<margin>Origin of Bees from a rotten ox.</margin>On this account, it is held that they are named *Bougones*, as if coming out of and from a cow, or originating therefrom. And on this matter, one may consult *Antigonus (Mirabilia Historica 23), Varro (On Agriculture, Book II, Chapters 3 and 16), Columella, Pliny, Plutarch, Aelian, Ovid, Virgil*, as seen in *Bochart in Hieroz, Dieteric in Antiquities of the Old Testament, Jonston on Animals, etc.*
<note>The term "Bougones" (Greek: *Bougonos*) refers to the ancient "Bugonia" myth—the belief that honeybees were spontaneously generated from the carcasses of oxen.</note>

->Ovid in the 15th Book of the Metamorphoses:<-

> *Known by experience, flower-gathering bees are born here and there from rotting viscera; like their parents, they dwell in the countryside, favor work, and labor in hope of gain.*
> <note>original: "Cognita res usu, de putri viscere passim / Florilegæ nascuntur apes, quæ more parentum / Rura colunt, operique favent, in spemque laborant."</note>

->That is, according to Vondel's words:<-

> *Bury a fat steer; experience shall teach it.*
> *From rotting entrails a swarm of bees arises,*
> *Which sucks wax and honey from flowers, never poor,*
> *Loves the field, and works bravely in hope of profit,*
> *Just like their parents.*
<note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) was the preeminent Dutch poet and playwright of the Golden Age, often called the "Prince of Poets."</note>

---

->Virgil in the 4th Book of the Georgics:<-

> *But here they behold a sudden wonder, marvelous to tell: throughout the softened viscera of the oxen, bees hum within the entire belly and boil forth from the broken ribs; immense clouds are drawn along, and now they gather at the treetop and drop like a cluster of grapes from the pliant branches.*
> <note>original: "Hic vero subitum ac dictu mirabile monstrum / Aspiciunt, liquefacta boum per viscera toto / Stridere apes utero, & ruptis effervere costis..."</note>

->Vondel translates this again thus:<-

> *Here they see quickly, a matter too rare to believe,*
> *The bees hum in the prepared intestines, above*
> *The cattle a preparation. They burst forth warm*
> *From belly and ribs, with a thick swarm,*
> *Which, slung and wound high on a tree,*
> *Hangs like a cluster of grapes bound to a vine.*

Most among the ancients have said that they are not actually continued by mating or procreation. What can one say of this with much certainty? Let us hear the Prince of Latin Poets <note>Virgil</note> in the 4th Book of his Georgics:

> *You will wonder that this custom has pleased the bees: that they neither indulge in union, nor weakly relax their bodies for love, or bring forth young with labor.*
> <note>original: "Illum adeo placuisse apibus mirabere morem, / Quod nec concubitu indulgent, nec corpora segnes / In Venerem solvunt, aut fœtus nixibus edunt."</note>

->The prince of Netherlandish poets follows him thus:<-

> *You would often wonder at the bees,*
> *And their manners; never fond of wooing,*
> *Or pairing, nor ever through laziness*
> *Set upon gluttony, nor bearing young; but rather*
> *They breed with the mouth from the foliage and scent of herbs.*
<note>Ancient naturalists often believed bees gathered their young from flowers or "spat" them out, rather than mating.</note>

It is said that the king of the Bees <note>The "king" is what we now know to be the queen bee.</note> shoots seed into every cell, like a small white bladder, from which a little worm emerges, like a seed of a poppy. Around this bladder, a slimy dew-moisture, leaning toward white, is placed by the Bees. In this white lies the royal seed, like the yolk in the egg. Upon this, the little Bee goes to sit and broods it through its warmth, so that a little worm emerges from it. From this worm, its skin having

<column-break/>

burst, the Bee comes forth. But whatever others have said can be read at length in Jonston; I shall not dwell on it.

<margin>Another origin of Bees.</margin>It is said that they have a king among them, who reached the kingdom not through favor, succession, or inheritance, but chosen thereto by nature and Divine Providence because of his beauty, size, and gentleness.

<margin>The King’s feelings regarding his sting.</margin>Whether the king has a sting or not is argued variously. At the very least, it is judged that if he has one at all, he rarely or never uses it: because his subjects obey him with joy and love, and his safety lies in their protection; and furthermore, that he is not harsh, but carries out his rule with all gentleness.
<note>The Dutch word used here is "angel," which refers to the stinger of an insect.</note>

Furthermore, it is told that the king, remaining in the beehive, looks around with great diligence, taking care that everyone performs their duty for the common interest and well-being; and that the other bees who stay near the king, having experience and knowing what must be done or left undone, are as his courtiers and nearest councilors of the court and cabinet.

It is related that the king only oversees and sets everything in order, living from the income and fruits of his subjects, but in such a way that he does not waste the income to the poverty of his people.

<margin>His governance and the behavior of his subjects.</margin>That when the king is to go out, they are all in motion and stand in order, accompanying him with reverence. That if he should decline or weaken through old age or otherwise, they support him as if on their wings and provide him with all necessities.

That they make for him in their beehive a higher and more spacious place for his courtly household: and that if he should fall into a struggle with factions, they fight and battle lustily for him. Virgil in the 4th book of the Georgics:

> *...They offer their bodies to war, and seek a beautiful death through wounds.*
> <note>original: "--- Corpora bello / Objectant, pulchramque petunt per vulnera mortem."</note>

->That is:<-

> *They go at the risk of their lives, full of courage in the need of war,*
> *And, though wounded, still stand proud toward a famous death.*

Subsequently, it is said that they fly upon all sorts of flowers, yet only sweet and pleasant ones, and extract the honey from them through untiring industry. Thus they prepare wax, honey, etc., for support in the wintertime and for needy old age. Engelmodus in his *Poem in Praise of Saint Radbert*:
<note>Engelmodus was a 9th-century bishop and poet of the Carolingian Renaissance.</note>

> *And just as when the frosts are removed by the blowing west wind, when the flowery earth brings forth the budding herbs, painting the fields in the new spring with distinct colors, the youth of the bees is exercised, dispersed across the fields; fearing the past labors of winter, they gather purple flowers and sip from the streams: there is no delay, no rest, but that they either enclose the liquid honey in cells packed with thin nectar, or with clinging glue build the hard foundations of the combs, or arrange the saffron-colored wax in order. Their frequent care glows, as they offer up the purest honey.*
> <note>original: "Ac velut exemptis, zephyro spirante pruinis... Fervet cura frequens, adolent purissima mella."</note>

> *And the earth bears herbs and flowers above,*

### Corippus in the IV. book:
<note>Flavius Cresconius Corippus was a 6th-century Latin poet. This quote is from his epic poem *Iohannis*.</note>

> They settle upon various flowers and gather the moist dew 
> with their mouths; they load their shoulders, and they 
> fashion the liquid wax, and fix their sweet homes in the pumice-stone.
> <note>original: "Floribus insidunt variis roremque madentem. / Ore legunt, onerantque humeros, cerasque liquentes / Conficiunt, dulcesque lares in pumice figunt."</note>

->That is:<-

> They sit on the flowers, from which they lick the moisture,
> One sees them pull their legs, laden with their burden.
> Now they fashion out of wax, never weary of the labor,
> Their lovely little houses fixed in a pumice stone.

See Bochart’s *Hieroz.*, Dieteric’s *Antiq. V. T.*, Dilherr’s *Elector.*, etc.
<note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a famous scholar of biblical animals; the others are contemporary theologians and naturalists.</note>

<margin>Household of the bees.</margin>
It is testified that they divide their work fittingly among one another, so that some bring flowers with their legs: others water with their mouths, and that they carry drops in the rough wooliness of the hollows of their bodies. Those who are somewhat older work inside the hive. When the younger ones come home thus laden, they are received and unloaded by three or four who work inside.

<margin>Labor.</margin>
In the hive they work at their post, and according to order. Some build, others clean, others bring building and decorative materials, etc. See Jonston.
<note>John Jonston (1603–1675) was a naturalist known for his encyclopedic works on animals.</note>

As for poisonous herbs, they will have absolutely nothing to do with them.

<margin>Rest.</margin>
A proper order is established for the night's rest: for the rounds are made, a humming is caused around the hive, after which everything inside falls into a deep rest, Virgil in the IV. Book of the *Georgics*:

> When evening at last has warned them to depart from the pastures of the fields, then they seek their homes, then they care for their bodies. A sound is made; they buzz around the edges and the thresholds. Later, when they have settled themselves in their chambers, there is silence into the night, and their own sleep possesses their weary limbs.
> <note>original: "Vesper ubi pastu tandem decedere campis / Admonuit, tum tecta petunt, tum corpora curant. / Fit sonitus, mussant oras, & limina circum. / Post ubi jam thalamis se composuere, siletur / In noctem, fessosque sopor suus occupat artus."</note>

->Vondel follows this thus:<-

> When the evening finally blows the retreat, to peacefully
> Return from the meadow and the field, then they go home,
> Then they strengthen the body. One hears then a noise,
> A humming and a buzzing around the honeycombs.
> When they settle themselves to sleep in their cells, they dare 
> Not make a sound, and so the nights pass away:
> Then gentle sleep caresses their weary limbs.

<margin>Awakening.</margin>
And so in the morning they are awakened again by a buzzing or humming, to immediately either fly out or apply themselves to their internal work. Read Pliny, Bochart, Jonston, Dieteric, etc.

It is told that they place their waste in a special compartment, and that they

<column-break/>

cast it out of the hive during dark weather.

Also that they carry their dead out of the beehive, to prevent all internal stench, and hold a sort of funeral procession.
<margin>Funeral rites for the dead.</margin>

Virgil in the same book:

> ——— Then the bodies of those lacking light [the dead] 
> they carry out from the homes, and lead the sad funerals.
> <note>original: "——— Tum corpore luce carentum / Exportant tectis, & tristia funera ducunt."</note>

->That is:<-

> They bring the corpse, when its eye closes, unfortunately
> Out of the house; they walk in mourning from behind, sad and oppressed.

Pliny in the XI. book, 18. chap.

See further Bochart’s *Hieroz.* page 504.

<margin>Restraint and punishment of the drones.</margin>
If there be among them drones <note>The original Dutch uses "hommels," which can mean bumblebees, but in this context refers to male honeybees (drones).</note> who give no honey, nor have stings, which rob the hive too much and eat the honey, they practice gentle discipline for the first and second time; but upon persistence in this robbery, they fly at them, sting and kill them.

When the Bees have made a swarm, and are divided into parties and ranks, and seem about to leave the hive, a copper kettle, pan, earthen pot, or something else is struck: and it is related that they take a singular delight in that sound, a kind of music. Read Pliny, Aelian, Bochart, Jonston, etc. Ovid, speaking of Bacchus, in the III. Book of the *Fasti*:

> And now they had come to Rhodope and the streams of Panchaea, when the bronze-bearing hands of the companions clashed. Behold, new birds [bees] gather, driven by the tinkling, and the bees follow the sounds that the bronze makes.
> <note>original: "Jamque erat ad Rhodopen Panchaeaque flumina ventum, / Eriferae comitum cum crepuere manus. / Ecce novae coeunt volucres tinnitibus actae, / Quosque movent sonitus æra sequuntur apes."</note>

->That is:<-

> Now one had approached Rhodope on that journey.
> One saw the bees humming on Panchaean flowers.
> The company played there on copper clashing-cymbals,
> At which sound a swarm of bees, without number,
> Gathered, and followed wherever they went, everywhere.

Lucan in the IX. book:

> ——— As the sound of Phrygian bronze rattles, 
> the astonished ones cease their flight, and return to the 
> pursuit of their flowery labor and the love of sacred honey.
> <note>original: "——— Phrygii sonus ut crepat æris / Attonitæ posuere fugam, studiumque laboris / Florigeri repetunt, & sacri mellis amorem."</note>

->That is:<-

> As soon as they perceive the sound of the 
> copper clashing-cymbals, they stop their flight. Straightway they return
> To their flowers, and the honey-making.

See further regarding this the learned Bochart.

They are also by no means lacking in enemies, whom, being too much provoked, they attack hostiley, and defend themselves bravely with their stings. Virgil in the IV. Book of the *Georgics*:

> Their anger is beyond measure, and when hurt they breathe 
> poison into their bites, and leave their hidden stings 
> fixed in the veins, and lay down their lives in the wound.
> <note>original: "Illis ira modum supra est, læsæque venenum / Morsibus inspirant, & spicula cæca relinquunt, / Affixæ venis, animasque in vulnere ponunt."</note>

# BEES.

->That is, according to Vondel's translation:<-
<note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) was the most prominent poet and playwright of the Dutch Golden Age.</note>

> *Their anger and vengeance know neither rule nor measure:*
> *For if you hurt them, they will forgive you with a sting,*
> *And strike terribly, so that even the stinger remains stuck*
> *In the veins, and they die of revenge, quite enraged.*

<margin>Enemies of the bees.</margin>Their opponents and enemies are said to be wasps, hornets, swallows, frogs, toads, spiders, crocodiles, <note>In early modern natural history, "crocodiles" sometimes referred broadly to lizards or newts rather than the large reptiles we know today.</note> and night owls.

Smoke, thunder, lightning, etc., are very harmful to them, as are all foul vapors and smells. See *Jonston, Virgil* in the IV. Book of the *Georgics*:
<note>Jan Jonston (1603–1675) was a naturalist; Virgil’s Georgics is a classic Roman poem on agriculture.</note>

->*And hold forth the following smoke with your hand.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Fumosque manu prætende sequaces."</note>

->That is:<-

->*Busily smoke them out with a pot.*<-

*Ovid, Book I of the Remedy of Love,*
<note>Publius Ovidius Naso, Roman poet.</note>

> *What joy is it, when the swarms flee the smoke placed beneath them,*
> *so that the curved wicker-work of the hive may be relieved of the removed combs?*
<note>original Latin: "Quid, cum suppositos fugiunt examina fumos, / Ut relevent dempti vimina curva favi?"</note>

->That is:<-

> *What pleasure, what country delight can please you more,*
> *Than to drive the bees out through the thick smoke,*
> *And thus to plunder the sweet honeycomb?*

See *Bochart’s Hieroz. p. 507.* etc.

And so as not to bring everything here that can be read at length in other authors, this is noted about the Bees: that even if one had prepared a glass hive <note>term: glass hive (glaazen stok) — an observation hive used by early scientists like Jan Swammerdam to study bee behavior.</note> to observe their inner workings from the outside, they—so as not to be seen or disturbed in their freedom, or deceived—will smear and cover the glass from the inside with wax and sticky propolis.

Also, they leave a row or three of their hexagonal houses empty at the front, near the entrance of the hive, so that the hornet might not happen upon them by scent or sight and rob them of the honey and their stores.

<margin>The Bee, a symbol of man.</margin>Let the reader be satisfied with this brief extract, and consider the little Bee as a symbol of man in many and various respects and relationships: while I, from a wide field and rich harvest, shall only bind some sheaves together and share the tithes with the reader.

It seems to me that the honey bee, with its sweet honey and piercing sting, can sketch for me a man who gives sweet words but stings sensitively with his hidden barb.

Thus Hugo <note>Likely referring to the medieval theologian Hugh of Saint Victor.</note> writes of those who, being weary of court life, enter monasteries: *The little bee, which has honey in its mouth and its sting hidden in its tail, is a flatterer or a traitor who is in the land of Assur, that is, in the court of the great. There, Treachery reigns alongside Flattery. But now they reside in the cloisters of the Monks and the orders of the Canons.*

Because the aforementioned Bees sting so wondrously and sometimes come flying like a swarm, I can well believe that one may compare enemy troops and people, due to their hostile practices, to Bees: and so the Amorite enemies, attacking like swarms,

<column-break/>

are compared to Bees in *Deuteronomy 1:44*; and the surrounding and perishing enemies of David. Christ and the church are compared to bees in *Psalm 118:12*, *Isaiah 7:18*, and elsewhere, making a swarm and a multitude. *Justin, Book XXV, Chapter 2.*

<margin>Christ and the Church compared to bees.</margin>The Bee, being angered, flies at someone with a buzz; it stings him, but leaving its sting in the skin, it also dies. Thus Osiander <note>Lucas Osiander (1534–1604), a Lutheran theologian.</note> understood this regarding the *118th Psalm*, when he wrote: *The Bees are so zealous and vengeful that they would rather lose themselves than not take revenge: for having left their stings in the wounds, they die.* In the same way, the enemies of Christ (since their religion is evil and their morals are rebuked by the preaching of the Gospel) pursue Christ in his members with such insane rage that they would rather die than abandon their fury.

Theodorus Snepfius in *Comm. on Isaiah 7:18* expresses it thus: *The Lord compares the Assyrians to bees and the Egyptians to flies, and this for two reasons: first, because there are many insects in those regions, especially in the marshy lands by the Nile. Secondly, to make understood the vast number of the enemies; for the bees, when they leave their hives, fly in a powerful throng or swarm; and it is not to be doubted that it is the same with the Egyptian wasps and flies, which fly in entire troops and fill all places. The poet thus had his eye on the nature of bees and flies, wanting to convey that there would be no place in the kingdom of the Jews that could escape the danger of war.*

When one reads in *Judges 14:8* etc. about the dead lion in which Samson, after some time, found a swarm of bees and honey, and because of this made a riddle and gave it to the guests to solve, one does not necessarily have to think that they grew out of the decay: for it is only said that there were bees in it, but by no means how they got there.

<margin>Explanation by Burman.</margin>If it pleases us to hear the great Burman, <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> he will tell us this as an explanation of Samson's case and riddle: *His riddle first refers to the Philistines, who at that time dominated and devoured the children of Israel, but would later be conquered by them and serve as their food; and whereas they were now too strong for them, they would finally turn to sweetness and advantage. But it can be further applied to the Lord Christ. For when this lion from the tribe of Judah was dead, there arose from him—as the church teachers said—the bees, that is, the Christians, and the honeycombs of the Gospel, which with its lovely and wholesome moisture feeds and refreshes our souls. Yes, by a wonderful change, this lion has become a lamb, being slain on the cross, and so food has come forth from the eater, and sweetness from the strong: for this lamb feeds us with his flesh, gives us drink, washes, and redeems us with his blood, and clothes us with his wool (Romans 13:14, Galatians 3:27, Revelation 3:18). Indeed, just as it was a wonder in this riddle that food came from the eater (who otherwise takes food for himself and devours it, and sweetness from the strong), so this also depicts the spiritual transformation of all evil—in the devil, death, and oppressions—through the victory over them in Christ, who causes our good to come out of all evil (Romans 8:28).*

<summary>This page explores the natural threats to bees, such as smoke and predators, and then moves into a complex theological allegory. It uses the bee's sting and Samson's lion to symbolize the spiritual transformation of conflict and death into the "sweetness" of the Gospel.</summary>
