<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the nature of bees, shifting from their physical characteristics and enemies to their symbolic and moral significance in theology, statecraft, and personal virtue.</meta>

<page-num>131</page-num>
# BEES.
<columns>2</columns>

*...out of our bitterness a honey-sweet consolation, out of our infirmities strength, out of our sorrows joy, out of our wounds healing, out of our dishonor glory, out of the temptation of Satan godliness and power, 2 Cor. XII. 7-9, 10. indeed, out of bitter and all-devouring death, life itself, 1 Kor. XV. 54-56.*

<margin>The industry of bees is a symbol of diligence.</margin>
That the tireless industry of the Bees, providing food in the summer against the harsh autumn and barren winter, is a symbol of diligence for everyone in their profession and station in life, was already made understood by Solomon in his time in *Proverbs VI, as some would have it, if it does not rather speak of the ants.* <note>The author notes a common scholarly debate: while Proverbs 6:6-8 famously discusses the ant, some early commentators or translations associated these lessons on industry with the bee as well.</note>

At the very least, those who love literature and wisdom must strive to glean and gather the sweetness and the noblest parts from all good writers, to fill their own storehouse of learning. To this end, one must take advantage of one’s time of growth and bloom before the harsh winter and the unpleasantness of old age arrive, so as to have a treasure and a supply.

> *Lucretius, Book III.*
> <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), Roman poet and philosopher.</note>
>
> *Floriferis ut apes in saltibus omnia libant;*
> *Omnia nos itidem depascimur aurea dicta,*
> *Aurea perpetua semper dignissima vita.*
> <note>original Latin: "Just as bees sip from everything in the flowery glades, so we likewise feed upon all the golden sayings—golden, and always most worthy of eternal life."</note>
>
> That is:
>
> *Just as the bees gather flowers in the field,*
> *So we must also be busy with zeal everywhere*
> *In picking out all the golden and wise sayings,*
> *The sayings that no time or ages can wither.*

One can also observe in the king of the Bees, <note>Until the late 17th or early 18th century, the "Queen Bee" was often mistakenly identified as a "King."</note> the Bees themselves, and their conduct and work, how affairs ought to proceed in kingdoms and the states of nations. Thus writes *Ambrose:* <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan.</note> *The king is not chosen by lot, for the outcome of the lot is no judgment; for often, by an irrational chance of the lot, the worst is designated over the best. Nor is he designated by the outcry of the irrational rabble, which does not weigh the merits of virtue, nor scrutinize the welfare of the common good, but floats uncertainly through volatility. Nor does he ascend the throne by the privilege of lineage and royal descent, since in inexperienced hands the common intercourse cannot be wise and prudent; add to this the flatteries and wantonness which seem natural and innate to young years, and which tend to wound the understanding as if by a sharp edge, as well as the instructions or lessons of the chamberlains, who incline the king’s mind more toward their private interest than toward the utility of the public. But the bees receive a king who is famous for the gifts of nature, as one who surpasses others in the greatness and beauty of his body, alongside gentleness, which is the most excellent quality in kings.*

<margin>Comparison of kings with the king of the Bees.</margin>
That kings and princes have their palaces and courts—larger, loftier, and more magnificent because of their state and supreme authority—pertains as much to them as to the king of the Bees.

That he does not work himself, but oversees that all goes rightly and well everywhere and in everything, and that everyone performs their duty, is fitting and for the general good.

That he has his income for his state, household, the waging of war, and the protection of his subjects and freedoms, and lives, as it were, from the community, is seen even in the king of the Bees.

<column-break/>

Nevertheless, that he should not exhaust his subjects to the bone, but allow them to keep a sufficient supply, is in all respects just. *Oportet tondere pecus, sed non deglubere.* <note>original Latin: "It is necessary to shear the flock, but not to flay them." A maxim attributed to Emperor Tiberius regarding provincial taxation.</note> One must shear the sheep, but not skin them. That old, experienced, and aged men assist the king with counsel and deed, and are employed for the inner workings of the common good, seems to be a lesson learned from the conduct of the Bees.

That the king of the Bees either has no sting or does not use it, seems to give us this impression: that kings and princes govern more effectively through gentleness, good laws, and examples than through severity and violence.

That the infertile drones—the robbing, guileless Bees who consume the honey—must be driven away, or if they are stubborn, breaking into the hive at night or at improper times and hiding themselves, must be killed upon pain of banishment and fine, reminds me how the dead weight, the useless people, the pests of the republic—whoever they may be—who swallow up the country’s income, ought to be banished, cut off, and punished; each according to his state and the harm or danger brought thereby to the common good.

When I hear that the little Bees smear their glass hives and occupy the hive closely, not wishing to be spied upon, it seems to me that it can teach us that in a state government there must be a deep silence—that all matters ought to remain secret so that weakness is not discovered, and intentions and decrees do not leak out prematurely; that trade and alliances be kept silent as much as possible: *for so one reads in Velleius Paterculus, in the II. Book, that silence is the best and safest bond in the administration of affairs.* <note>Marcus Velleius Paterculus (c. 19 BC – c. 31 AD), a Roman historian.</note>

One can observe in the provoked Bee, which stings in such a way that it leaves its sting behind and dies, a representation of overly violent anger, which is harmful to the wrathful person.

Furthermore, one could compare the Bees in many respects as symbols of the believers: in labor, diligence, obedience to their heads, zeal, and otherwise. And when one finds that the Bees can endure no smoke or vapor, and that they provide sweet honey and feed their young therewith, and so forth; then one could be reminded that the faithful "Bees," filled with heavenly spirit and wisdom—being humble and far from pride and all windy wisdom and puffery—cannot well tolerate anything that is windy, inconstant, vain, or like smoke and vapor; and that their hearts and mouths being full of Divine honey, *Ps. XIX and CXIX,* they feed and strengthen their spiritual children with this honey.

Other transitions and applications I shall not make. Regarding HONEY and WAX, those shall be discussed in their own time.

### AX, <term>מַעֲצָד</term>, <term>צַרְזֹן</term>, <term>קַרְדֹּם</term>, <term>ἀξίνη</term>, <term>πέλεκυς</term>, *securis*. <term>בַּשִּׁיל</term>
<note>Hebrew terms: *ma'atsad* (hewing tool), *tsarzon* (hatchet), *qardom* (ax), *basshil* (felling tool). Greek terms: *axine* (battle-ax/pick), *pelekys* (double-headed ax). Latin: *securis* (ax).</note>

What kind of tool an AX is, is sufficiently known; made by the smith to serve for chopping, hewing, and rooting out.

These tools, being immobile in themselves, necessarily require the hand and strength, indeed the direction, of men.

# AXE.

When one considers a single person, or many together under one head—be they armies or otherwise—and observes that they all and each one live and move in God; and that without him, they can neither stir nor move: that the Lord also holds the hearts of kings in his hand; that he uses them as tools in his hand to punish or root out some wicked, unrepentant, and ungrateful people, then they are compared to an **axe**, because, although they have their own wills and activities, they are nevertheless dependent on God and fully under his direction and determination. Just as the Lord used the Assyrian and his army against his people in such a manner. *Isaiah X. 5.*

<margin>Comparison</margin>

It was therefore an foolish undertaking of the Assyrian that, completely ignoring the Lord, he attributed the outcome to his own wisdom, bravery, power, and foresight.

So lay the **Axe** of the Roman power at the root of the Jewish tree, of church and state, hacking steadily at their freedom, and soon to give the final blow under Titus. *Matthew III. 10. Luke III. 9. See under TREE and ROOT.* <note>The "Axe" here refers to the Roman siege and destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD led by Titus.</note>

When the word **AXE** is mentioned in *Psalm LXXIV. 5.* and *Jeremiah XLVI. 22, 23*, and hacking and hewing are added to it, it is intended to show how enemies would devastate everything and chop down and destroy with all violence, not even sparing the house of God, proceeding in such a way as if they were hacking and hewing in a wilderness or thicket. And so this figurative way of speaking carries with it a very heavy, righteous, and destructive judgment of God, carried out or to be carried out by the enemies.

<margin>Axe a symbol of power.</margin>

An **Axe**, being driven by a strong hand to hew, chop, and root out, can be a symbol of the highest power: since among many peoples an **Axe** is a symbol thereof. The kings of Libya had an axe instead of a scepter. Also among the Romans, the axe was a mark of honor for their highest power, and they added bundles of birch rods to it. <note>The author refers to the *fasces*, a bundle of rods with an axe, symbolizing a magistrate's power to punish.</note> Virgil in the VI. Book of the *Aeneid*, verse 819:

> *Consulis imperium hic primas sevasque secures*
> *Accipiet.*
> <note>original Latin: "Here he shall be the first to receive the consul's power and the cruel axes."</note>

->That is:<-

> *The strict justice-axe, and the Consul's power*
> *Is first rightly assigned to that great man.*

### BITING, <term>נשך</term> <note>Hebrew: nashak</note>, <term>δάκνω</term> <note>Greek: dakno</note>, *mordeo* <note>Latin: mordeo</note>.

This is usually done by dogs, mad, and wild beasts with their teeth. See under TEETH.

<margin>Metaphorical use of biting.</margin>

However, because of the result and the effect springing from a cruel, malicious, and hostile heart, it is transferred to humans, though they technically gnash their teeth more than they bite with them.

The **Biting** of someone can be understood as causing someone pain and smarting, a sensible cross and soul-sorrow, and spite.

*Terence in Eunuch, Act III. Sc. I.* <note>Publius Terentius Afer, a Roman playwright.</note>

> *Tu par pari referto, quod eam remordeat.*
> <note>original Latin: "Pay her back in kind, so that it may bite her back."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Pay her back, and bite in return.*

*The same in Adelphoe, Act V. Sc. 3.*

> *Si id te mordet.*
> <note>original Latin: "If that bites or gnaws at you."</note>

->That is:<-

> *If that bites or gnaws at you.*

**Biting** can also be understood in the sense of: out of hatred and envy, prejudices, partisanship, particular opinions, standing up for something with strong passions and vehemence, scolding, slandering, persecuting someone, making it anxious and bitter for someone, *Galatians V. 5.* <note>Likely a reference to Galatians 5:15: "But if ye bite and devour one another..."</note>

*Terence, Eunuch, Act III. Sc. I.*

> *Invidere omnes mihi,*
> *Mordere clanculum.*
> <note>original Latin: "They all envied me, and bit me in secret."</note>

->That is:<-

> *They all envied me, and bit me in secret.*

From this comes *Mordax carmen* <note>Latin: a biting song</note>, a biting satire or lampoon.

The Babylonians were to meet no better part than destruction and all hostility, *Habakkuk II. 7.* nor should the Jews imagine a better fate for themselves. *Jeremiah VIII. 17.* See regarding the adder's bite of Dan *Genesis XLIX. 17. Judges XVIII. 22.* under ADDER and DAN.

### BINDING, <term>אסر</term> <note>Hebrew: asar</note>, <term>δέω</term> <note>Greek: deo</note>, *ligo, vincio* <note>Latin: ligo, vincio</note>.

Mention has previously been made of Bands and Fetters, and figures of speech regarding these have been explained and illustrated. Now I shall deal somewhat more generally and extensively with **binding**.

The word occurs many times in the Sacred Scroll, though not always in a literal or physical sense, as will become manifest in this treatise.

**Binding**, as is known, is to secure a person with bands or fetters, of whatever material they might be, so that he remains under the power of the one who ensured he was bound; to restrain someone's power and freedom: to tie and fasten together things previously loose and free: to make someone a prisoner, and as a prisoner or criminal to secure, fetter, or lock them up; to bring someone under another's power and violence.

It is not always taken for an act and work of hostility or violence against someone's will, mind, or thanks, but it is sometimes an act of favor, love, conversion, and freeing from soul-destruction and misery, and so forth. But let us rather display the variety of meanings by opening many scriptural texts.

<margin>What Binding is taken for.</margin>

The word **Binding** is taken for having someone under one's violence and power, and making them unable either to resist or to escape. Thus we say, *his hands are tied*. That is, he is not his own master, he

-># BINDING.<-
<margin>R</margin>

...cannot do what he wants, and what would please him, if he were a free man and stood on his own.

In this sense, one may understand it when speaking of the binding, the shackles, and the bonds of our Savior, of Peter, Paul, Silas, etc. *Matthew 27, Mark 15, John 19, Acts 9, 12, and 21, Colossians 4, etc.*

This shall also apply to the strong man, according to the nature of his power and character—*Matthew 12, Mark 3, Luke 11,* etc.—to overcome him, overpower him, and prevent him from exercising his power or acting as before. <note>The "strong man" is a biblical metaphor for Satan being restrained by Christ.</note>

Otherwise, one also binds and shackles those who, through an ill condition of the body or mind, and other plagues and visitations—including those of the evil one—are unable to govern themselves properly but lie open to all kinds of danger and calamity: such as those possessed by madness, *Luke 13:16, Luke 8:29, Mark 5,* etc. For Satan can also be an instrument used to strangely torment and plague someone, without that person being able for a time to get free from him and his torments and plagues.

And although "binding," according to its usual and literal meaning, seems to involve shackles and bonds, these are nonetheless not always applicable. However, it signifies as much as saying of someone that he is bound and shackled—that is, effectively prevented from doing anything to cause harm, torment, seduction, or grief, which he would otherwise gladly do according to his inner nature and wicked desire. Concerning such matters are the expressions in *Revelation 9:14*: "Loose the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates." Likewise *Revelation 20:2*: "And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, and bound him for a thousand years."

Regarding the passage in *Revelation 9:14*, where the four bound angels at the Euphrates are spoken of: by these "angels," one understands not good but evil angels, sent out by the evil spirit to breathe wicked thoughts and desires into kings, princes, and peoples, and to incite them to wars and persecutions with no small rage.

By the Euphrates, some understand the peoples along the Euphrates—whether they be Mohammadens, Turks, Tartars, etc.—who were restrained for a time from carrying out their wicked undertakings and from disturbing and devastating the world through the force of arms to spread the teachings of Muhammad in all regions, for which they afterwards received a free and wide hand with a violent overflow and breakthrough. See *Mark, page 345,* etc.

<margin>Opinion of the Cocceians.</margin>
But Coccejus <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian who emphasized a "covenantal" interpretation of the Bible.</note> and his followers are of the opinion that one need not look here to the Turks, Mohammadens, Persians, Tartars, etc., but that one may figuratively take the Euphrates for the rivers of the "spiritual Babylon"—those kings and peoples upon whom the Roman Whore sits, such as Spain, France, Italy, along with a part of Germany. There those evil spirits have remained: the devil lives there, rules there, and stirs up evil, wicked, and destructive desires for wars, persecutions, and devastations, especially after the Reformation. But they were bound—that is, restrained for a short time by the Peace of Religion of the year 1555 <note>The text says 1563, likely a printer's error for the 1555 Peace of Augsburg or the 1552 Treaty of Passau.</note> at Passau. Yet these have subsequently broken loose with a joined hand and a common rage and persecution.

<column-break/>

As for the binding of the dragon, the serpent, in *Revelation 20:2* for a thousand years: it is generally agreed that this signifies that after the breakthrough of the Gospel, Satan and his instruments were restrained and prevented from deceiving and hoodwinking the nations and the gentiles as he did before. Whether one should begin this from the departure of the Gospel through the whole world, or from Constantine the Great—earlier or later—I see that there is much dispute back and forth; therefore, I shall not dwell on it, my aim being only to show that binding means to restrain, to prevent someone from doing something with craft or violence to which they would otherwise be strongly inclined.

<margin>Meaning of binding by the Spirit.</margin>
It must be understood somewhat differently when we read in *Acts 20:22*: "And now, see, I go bound in the Spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing what shall happen to me there: 23. Save that the Holy Spirit testifies from city to city that bonds and afflictions await me." What it means when Paul says he is "bound by the Spirit" requires some consideration.

Some take it as a prophecy of what was coming to him, as it was made known to him by the Spirit what was ahead: and through the testimony from city to city by the Spirit, he is already to be regarded as one bound, because of the well-assured prophecy of the Spirit, *1 Thessalonians 3:4*. But others have something else in mind—namely, that it is understood that Paul, foreknowing that bonds (that is, persecution) were coming to him, became saddened and anxious in the Spirit, all the more because he did not yet know what the end and the outcome of it would be.

But in my opinion, those have not understood it poorly who are of the mind that Paul means that the Spirit obligated him to go there, and that he was thereby so strongly inclined that he could not be moved by the prayers and tears of his good friends to change his purpose, or to release himself from the bonds of his obligation.

It is not to be taken literally when we read of "binding and laying burdens" on someone, *Matthew 23:4*; compare *Acts 15:10, 28*. It is, however, taken from the packs, burdens, and sacks that one binds onto yoke-bearing cattle so that they might not be able to cast them off, nor that they should slip, nor be taken from them, nor fall off.

<margin>Burden imposed on the Jews.</margin>
And such comprised all those human commands, institutions, and arbitrary rules which were imposed on the Jews by the Jewish clergy, and, supported by bold authority and threats, served as a pack and burden under which they went stooped and bent, and from which they could in no way release themselves. In *Matthew 16:19 and 18, John 20,* where "binding and loosing" appears, it is undoubtedly an allusion to the Jewish synagogues and customs, and even to the figures of speech used by the teachers, wise men, and scribes—namely, that "binding" shall signify to show and declare that this or that...

-># BINDING.<-
<meta>catchword: 'T zy</meta>

...a matter is forbidden, and one is not free to do it: indeed also declaring someone guilty, and by no means exempting or releasing them from the crime and punishment, but rather announcing and carrying out the punishment, *1 Cor. 5, 1 Cor. 16:22, etc.*

<margin>Meaning of loosing.</margin>
Thus "loosing" is to teach, declare, and show that this or that is permitted and allowed: to declare someone innocent or free from punishment, to declare that the sin or crime is forgiven. See Selden in *On the Sanhedrin* <note>original: "in Synedr." — John Selden was a famous 17th-century legal scholar and Hebraist</note>, Lightfoot, Spanheim, Burman, Hofman, etc.

It does not always appear as something joyful; indeed, it is not in all respects a benefit or blessing when the Lord says that He will bind someone: although in a certain respect, here and elsewhere, it can and may be interpreted for good, as in *Hosea 10:10*, "It is in my desire that I shall bind them," etc. where the Lord shows that He will visit His people—because they are not of one mind in doctrine and His pure service—and allow them to be bound and shackled by enemies; that is, to plague them with all kinds of hostile visitations.

Again, in *Psalm 105:22*, one reads of the unshackled and exalted man Joseph, that he had the power to *bind the princes according to his pleasure, and teach his elders.* I would think that "binding" there signifies placing them under his hand, making them submissive and dependent upon him: prescribing to them what they had to do or leave undone, with the power to reward and exalt, to rebuke, lower, and punish as an example to others.

Again, binding is attributed to the Lord in *Psalm 149:8*, *to bind their kings with chains, and their nobles with iron fetters.* The Jews apply this to their Messiah, who shall subject all kings and kingdoms to Himself, and cast the rebellious into bonds, fetters, and chains.

Unless it refers to the judgments which the Lord would execute against the enemies of the kingdom of grace of Prince Messiah—for which He always has enough instruments at hand—it may perhaps be an image of how the Lord will put kings and princes in the chains and bonds of His Law and subject them to Himself through the power of the convincing and enlightening Gospel, so that they shall pay Him homage and prostrate themselves before Him, *Psalm 2 and 97, Psalm 45, Isaiah 60, 2 Cor. 10:4, 5.*

When one reads that someone's soul is bound to another, *Genesis 44*, it is to be understood in a figurative and metaphorical way, meaning that one values someone so much that their presence cannot be missed without endangering one's life and health: in a word, the most heartfelt and strongest love of contentment and attachment, just as it is written in *1 Samuel 18:1*, *it happened now, when he had finished speaking to Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was bound to the soul of David: and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.*

When one reads in *Proverbs 22:15* that *folly is bound in or to the heart of the youth*, it signifies that there is a firm embrace and joining together between the heart and folly, both by nature due to corruption, and due to bad habit, association with corrupting company, evil conversations, and weak or blameworthy upbringing: so much so, that one requires earnest rebukes,

<column-break/>

sensible discipline, and unblemished examples to bring the youth to better thoughts and morals.

It means something entirely different when one reads in *Job chapter 12, verse 18*, *He looses the bond of kings, and He binds the girdle to their loins.* It seems to me that it signifies the Lord has the power to depose and appoint kings, to humble and to exalt: indeed, that He nullifies and breaks the laws, ordinances, conduct, and foresight of kings and princes, the stability of the kingdom and the state of the people, no matter how wisely or firmly they are woven together: so that one finds kings girding themselves to flee from their jurisdiction, to avoid—if possible—being caught and made prisoners of war, of which we have seen more than one example in our days, following the example of what happened to the Jewish leaders and powers when they sought to break the bands and cords, *Psalm 2.*

Almost the same, namely imprisonment and subjugation, is seen in *Job 36* <note>The OCR says chapter 26, but the context of "fetters" and "cords of affliction" matches Job 36:8.</note>: with which people it goes very poorly if, suffering all this because of their guilt, they do not come to repentance and reflection, but rather, pushing against the Lord and His striking hand, do not behave humbly and submissively as God's prisoners of war.

It seems, with reason, to involve more difficulty at first glance when it is said by Solomon in *Proverbs 26:8*, namely, *as one who binds a precious stone in a sling, so is he who gives honor to a fool.*

Regarding the allegories, the various thoughts, and explanations of both the Jews and the Christians, I shall not recount them all. One can look them up in *Selden, On the Syrian Gods, Book 2, Chapter 15* <note>original: "de dis Syris Lib. II. Cap. 15."</note>; *Dilherr, Demonstrations, page 427* <note>original: "Demonstr. pag. 427."</note>; *Gejerus, Cartwright*, etc. It can simply mean that just as a precious stone does not fit among common, poor stones, so a fool does not fit in the company of the wise, and that it is a senseless task to entrust a fool with honorable offices, important matters, and duties: that praise and elevation suit him just as poorly as if one threw a precious stone among a heap of common cobblestones: the precious stone does not belong with a heap of bad stones, and so neither does honor or any prominent office belong to a fool, etc.

To bind God's laws and ordinances to the neck, hands, between the eyes, and to fasten them to the doorposts, *Deut. 6, Gen. 11:18.* <note>Likely Deuteronomy 11:18, as it echoes the "binding" command of chapter 6.</note>

Also to bind those, alongside mercy and truth, to the neck and to write them on the tablets of the heart, *Proverbs 3:3, 6:21, 7:3, etc.*, must not—as the Jews are accustomed—be understood literally and according to the letter, but by figure and metaphor: that one must constantly keep them in one's heart and thoughts, look upon them, implement them with the utmost diligence in trade and conduct, make them habitual and entirely one's own, and hold them as one's ornamental garments, as something excellent and precious: not making oneself guilty of blameworthy forgetting or neglect, but imprinting everything in the heart.

It expresses quite a strong bond of love and urge when it is written of the Lover of the soul, King Jesus, in *Song of Solomon 7:5*, *The king is as if bound to the galleries.* <note>original: "de gallerie." In contemporary bibles, this is often translated as "tresses" or "corridors."</note>

# BITTER.
<sig>R 2</sig>

Whether one chooses to translate the root word <note>original: "grondwoort"</note> as "galleries" or "watercourses," and understands by it the public and usual means of worship—in the practice of which one walks toward an increase of knowledge, and grows in faith and strength until reaching the heavenly chamber—or whether one understands it as the conduits of Jesus' blood and Spirit in Holy Baptism, the Word, and the Sacraments in the unshakable kingdom; it can at the very least suggest how King Jesus is entirely enamored with and devoted to His bride, the Church. He is so captivated by her virtues and inner beauty that He cannot withdraw His eye, His love, or His tender-hearted care from her, desiring to make a permanent dwelling with her and to cover and favor the soul through faith, marital love, the overshadowing, and the assistance of the Holy Spirit.

Unless one should further think that, in translating the root words, *the king is bound between the water-trenches* or rivers, one could understand by this a certain prince or great ruler, bound for the sake of the name of Christ?

<margin>Application to the Elector John Frederick of Saxony.</margin>Thus, some remember the godly Elector John Frederick of Saxony, who, fighting knightly for the name of Christ, was bound and imprisoned between the rivers Elbe and Alster. <note>John Frederick the Magnanimous (1503–1554) was a leading protector of the Reformation who was captured by Emperor Charles V.</note> See Cocceius, Groenewegen, Ridderus, etc. <note>Johannes Cocceius was a famous 17th-century Dutch theologian known for "Covenant Theology."</note>

Finally, to take leave of this "Binding," I shall cast my eye once more upon such passages which, in distinction from the preceding, contain something unique and suggest a specific meaning, such as *Isaiah 49:9: to say to the bound, go forth; Isaiah 42:7: to bring the bound out of the prison; Isaiah 61:1: to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to the bound; Zechariah 9:11: bound as in a pit*, etc.

These passages promise a benefit of the New Testament: not only the unbinding, freeing, and releasing of those who were under the power of sin, the curse of the Law, and the dominion of Satan—as all people by nature, both Jews and Heathens, may be regarded—but also the unbinding and releasing of those who were bound and held in custody under the Law, the basic principles of the world, the heavy bondage, the fear of death, rulers, gods, guardians, powers, and taskmasters. One may consult Cocceius on the aforementioned passages, as well as Zwart in his *Sabbathschrift* <note>original: "Sabbath-writing"</note>.

### BITTER, BITTERNESS, BITTER HERBS: BITTER WATER, BITTER ROOT, etc. <term>מַר</term> <note>Hebrew: mar</note>, <term>πικρὸς</term> <note>Greek: pikros</note>. *amarum, amaritudo* <note>Latin: bitter, bitterness</note>.

Bitter and Bitterness is a quality and taste which is by no means desired by many, but is to most people unpleasant and repulsive, though sometimes not unwholesome, just as many bitter things and herbs are healthy and healing.

It is experienced that whatever is hard, heavy, and contrary to a person, causing them grief and pain, is called "bitter" or "bitterness." He who falls hard upon someone, who is sharp, stern, and cruel in his dealings, is called bitter, *Habakkuk 1:6, Judges 18:25*; indeed, such a one is said to be embittered, *Colossians 3:19*; to become angry or wrathful is to be in bitterness, *Genesis 26:35*; to be bitterly enraged, to be bitterly saddened, *Ezekiel 3:14, Hosea 12:15*. That is, to become exceedingly angry, embittered, wrathful, or sad: from whence comes "weeping bitterly," which is to weep very strongly, being grieved from the heart with very sensitive pain and emotion. *Genesis 27, Esther 4, Ezekiel 21 and 27, Matthew 26:75.* In a word, then, bitterness and that which is bitter is taken for everything that is distasteful and contrary to man, causing him pain, shame, harm, grief, and torment.

<column-break/>

<margin>Bitterness taken for pain.</margin>From this it is said, *to do someone bitterness; to satiate with bitterness; to write bitter things against someone*, etc. *Job 7:11 and 3:20 and 27:2 and 21:25 and 13:26.* Because of these aforementioned effects, something that is painful is compared to bitterness and that which is bitter in the Holy Scroll; indeed, it is named after it, just as envy is called bitter, *James 3, Colossians 3, Ephesians 4:31*; mouths full of bitterness, etc. *Psalm 10, Romans 3:14, Psalm 64:4.* This is understood as people who spoke sharply, so that it pierced the soul, undertaking and executing everything with a bitter spirit, without compassion—harsh, stern, and unmerciful in their encounters and dealings—burdening everything, magnifying things to the accusation of their neighbor, executing everything strictly without any softening or excuse.

This is bitterness in its derivative and figurative sense. But we must consider whether it should be taken literally or figuratively when "bitter water" is spoken of in *Numbers 5*—namely, the water that the woman suspected of unchastity had to drink. Regarding this, one finds among the learned those who are of the opinion that it was bitter water, caused not so much by the dust from the floor swept up and mixed into the water, as by the bitter juice of wormwood or the mixture of bitter herbs. Many Jewish masters hold to this, as do Fagius, Drusius, and others. <note>Paul Fagius and Johannes Drusius were renowned 16th-century Hebraists and biblical scholars.</note>

Others believe that it became bitter when the words of the curse were scraped into it, which must have been brought about by a divine miracle.

Again, some say that it only became bitter in the mouth and on the tongue of the woman, and that it was by no means bitter beforehand, nor did it become bitter by the scraping in of the curses.

For my part, I would most readily believe that it was literally bitter water; and that it must certainly have felt bitter enough when a woman, upon the simple suspicion and mere distrust of her husband, was forced into that public, shameful drink, accompanied by such curses, as an example to others. One may consult the second part of my *Holy Miscellanies* <note>original: "Heilige Mengelstoffen"</note> regarding this.

Certainly, the Lord demonstrated herewith how much chastity and honor pleased Him, and how much unchastity displeased Him: how pure He wished the marriage and the bed to be kept, or else that He would judge adulterers and adulteresses. *Hebrews 13:4, 1 Corinthians 6.*

He suggested how He would be jealous over Israel, as a man over his wife, if they made themselves guilty of spiritual adultery and harlotry, causing them to drink and pouring out over them all the bitter curses which He had written in His Law.

# BITTER.
<sig>R 2</sig>

...the law has thundered out against such people. *Deut. XXIII. 21. Rom. X. Deut. XXX. 15. and XXXII. 1. and XXXIX. 20. Ps. CIX. 17, 18, 19. etc.*

<margin>The Waters of Marah.</margin>But we must also consider the bitter draught at Marah, or the bitter waters of Marah, and how they were made sweet and drinkable; of which we read in *Exodus XV.* The text reads as follows in verse 22: *Then Moses led Israel from the Red Sea, and they went out into the Wilderness of Shur; and they went three days in the wilderness and found no water. When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water of Marah, for it was bitter; therefore the name of it was called Marah, etc.* <note>Marah means "bitter" in Hebrew.</note> and it is worth considering how it was made sweet and drinkable by a piece of wood thrown into it.

What kind of wood this might have been, I do not know; I know well that guessing leads to errors, and that the Jewish teachers <note>original: "Joodsche meesters"</note> attribute it to various trees.

Rabbi Joshua contends that it was a branch of a willow tree. Rabbi Eliezer says it was an olive branch. The son of Joshua believes it was <term>Harduphen wood</term> <note>Harduphen likely refers to the Oleander, which is naturally bitter or poisonous.</note>. Rabbi Nathan maintains that it was cedar wood. And Rabbi Simeon claims it was a branch from the Tree of Life—that is, that Seth planted a seedling from the Tree of Life (which had stood in Paradise) in the wilderness, from which Moses made his staff, and that he threw a piece or a branch of this wood into the water, whereby it turned from bitter to sweet and drinkable.

Some believe that the wood itself was bitter in taste, and that one bitterness was swallowed up by the other; others believe it was sweet in taste, and that through its sweetness, the bitterness was removed and tempered.

Whatever the case may be, it is clear enough that the Lord required Moses to use that outward means; but that such a vast quantity of water would actually and effectively become sweet and drinkable from a single piece of wood is not so easily imagined, understood, or believed. I believe much more that the Lord performed the miracle. And whether the water remained sweet and drinkable forever or not is not easily determined. It is a fact that Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (AD 23–79), a Roman author and naturalist.</note> testifies, as do many with him, that it was later found to have a bitter taste, in his *VI Book, Chapter 26.*

<margin>The miracle regarding this.</margin>This historical event, occurring in the Wilderness of Shur shortly after the Exodus, shows how the Lord provided Israel with bitter water before providing the sweet joy and peaceful possession of Canaan, and before He provided the twelve springs of Elim and the wells. This can remind us how the Lord is often accustomed to deal with His children and favorites in the wilderness of this world before He gives them the sweet water, initially here and perfectly hereafter in the heavenly Canaan: namely, following the example of their head and supreme captain, Jesus, He first gives them the bitter water of the cross and pain before providing the sweet water.

> *He has not earned the sweet, who has not tasted the bitter.* <note>original: "Dulcia non meruit, qui non gustavit amara."</note>

->That is:<-

> *No sweet did he deserve, who never tasted the bitter.*

<column-break/>

See *Matt. XX. 22. and XXVII. 34. Luke XXIV. Ps. CX. 7. Heb. XII. 1. Phil. II. 7, 8, 9.* But after that comes the sweet water, *Ps. XXXIV. and XXXVII. 37. and XCVII. 10.* Indeed, what shall I say? Christ’s wood of the cross—or His bloody, powerful, worthy, and meritorious suffering, the fruit and power of His obedience in the suffering of death—applied to the soul through the Spirit, makes that bitterness sweet and healthful. *Rom. That bitter water is certainly found in the wilderness of this world, but by no means in the promised land of Canaan that is above. *Rev. However, this bitter water of the cross is made sweet and drinkable by Jesus' strengthening rod and staff of His word, Spirit, and grace. *Ps. XLIV. Rom. VIII. Acts V. 2 Cor. XII.* etc.

There was undoubtedly some prefiguration in what we read in *Rev. XCIV.* But when it is rightly digested and ruminated upon internally, it brings forth bitterness, true sorrow, tears, and repentance—not according to the world, but according to God. *2 Cor. VII.* But to profess that openly, and to bring it forth from the belly and prophesy, that aftertaste and fruit is accompanied by bitterness of the belly, the inward parts, and the heart, because of mockery, scorn, slander, and persecution. One finds therein what judgments, rods, and plagues are forthcoming, causing sad and very painful weeping.

That bitter root brings forth gall and wormwood; so that one must take care that it does not bulge upward and bear foul fruits. *Deut. XXIX. and XXXII. Heb. XII. 15.*

All sin has death as its wages, *Rom. VI. 23.* and is therefore of a bitter aftertaste and entirely deadly fruit. So too is idolatry and spiritual adultery against the Lord, the end of which is bitterer than bitterness. All that man does, thinks, and wills, which actually springs from the root of the heart’s wickedness and corruption, *Gen. VI. and VIII. Matt. XV. Gal. V. 19-21.* is like a poisonous, nauseating, and entirely bitter fruit: bitter envy, *James III. 14.* bitterness, *Eph. IV.* *Amos V. 6. and VI. 12.* A root bearing gall and wormwood is an intention and thought which brings forth blasphemous words and evil deeds, as is subsequently made known; a thought leading to error and apostasy, says Cocceius. <note>Johannes Cocceius, a prominent 17th-century theologian.</note> However, Vlak <note>Abraham Vlak (1636-1710), a Dutch Reformed minister and author.</note> is of the opinion that it signifies a man or woman, household, or tribe, who turns their heart away from the Lord to serve the gods of the nations. # B I T T E R.
<sig>R 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: sun-</meta>

Regarding the passage from Paul in *Hebrews 12:15*, Vlak <note>Likely Abraham Vlak, a 17th-century Dutch theologian.</note> believes that the Apostle specifically refers to the root of envy and disturbance, such as the strange teachings of that time, which were entirely contrary to truth, grace, and Christian liberty (*Chapter 13:9; Acts 15:1, 2-19; Galatians 5:10*). This can be applied to all sins, but especially to envy, division, or anything from which some harmful, temporal, or eternal misfortune arises.

Thus, Gerardus <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a leading Lutheran systematic theologian.</note> writes concerning the *Hebrews*: See to it, *that there be no one among you who, like a bitter root which is accustomed to bring forth a cursed and bitter fruit like wormwood, shoots upward and causes the bitter fruits of sinful works and destructive doctrines to bulge or sprout out, through which your unity in Christ would be disturbed.* For here, particular attention is paid to the perversity of doctrine and the corruption of faith, as can be concluded or gathered from *Deuteronomy 29:18.*

Master Hoeke, in his explanation of the letter to the Hebrews, expresses himself thus: *This root of bitterness, which is a formed thought and sentiment in the heart from which the fruits of the bitter and harmful sprout, is the imagination and opinion of one's own righteousness. From this, as from a root, sprout all evil and harmful errors in religion—bitter, in no way comforting the mind but grieving it, causing the soul no sweetness but bitterness, not healing the conscience but leaving it diseased, and condemning the sinner.* This was the particular sin mentioned in *Romans 9:31, 32 and 13:3.* This now bulges and shoots upward; it makes the sinner puffed up and haughty, so that he swells up against the Lord, against His righteousness and grace, and against Christ and His kingdom. Of this, the *Pharisee provided a sample in Luke 18:9-12.* Sprouting upwards, it so disturbs the "work-holy" person <note>A term for those who rely on good works for salvation rather than grace.</note> that he, like a sea, cannot rest (*Isaiah 57:20, 21*). It disturbs the church in which he resides. And from this it arises that many are defiled and ignited by this, etc. (*Acts 15; Galatians 2; Nahum 1:11; Revelation 8:11*).

<margin>Bitter herbs</margin>
Finally, I must say something about the bitter herbs ordained at the time of the eating of the Passover lamb (*Exodus 12*). However, I shall not be long-winded in this, as they must be dealt with when the Passover lamb itself is discussed.

Some believe it was lettuce, but the wild variety, not unlike the sown kind but with longer stalks and on the bitter side; some believe it was endive, others chicory.

Bitter herbs—that is, perhaps more than one bitter plant—is called *merorim* <note>Hebrew: מְרֹרִים (merorim), literally "bitterness" or "bitter herbs."</note>. Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a famous French religious scholar.</note> mentions an *embamma* <note>original: "Embamma" (Greek: ἔμβαμμα), a sauce or dip.</note>, a soup or sauce of various bitter herbs, which the French call *mustardam* <note>mustard</note>, in which they dipped their unleavened bread. The 70 Translators <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> have *tōn pikridōn* <note>original: "τῶν πικρίδων", meaning "of the bitter herbs."</note>. Pliny says in Book 19, Chapter 8, that *Picrida* is one of the worst kinds of lettuce, notorious for its bitterness—that is, particularly bitter and unpleasant. Dalecampius noted from Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> that it is much the same as a type of chicory.

Sown lettuce was used in ancient times as a dessert, but later as an appetizer. *Martial 13, 14:* <note>Marcus Valerius Martialis, a Roman poet.</note>

> *Tell me, why does lettuce, which used to close the dinners of our ancestors,*
> *now begin our feasts?*
<note>original Latin: "Claudere quæ cœnas lactuca solebat avorum / Dic mihi cur nostras inchoat illa dapes?"</note>

-> That is: <-

> *Lettuce (so they say) was the appetizer for the ancients.*
> *Why is it kept by us as the dessert?*

Some make it out to be bitter wormwood; others *Intybum* or *Intubum*, which is endive or white chicory.

It is said that it sharpens the hunger; that it can still the passions and lusts so they do not swell up; and a healing virtue and power is attributed to it.

> *Now let the lettuce hasten with its healthy flavor,*
> *To relieve the sad weariness of a long illness.*
<note>original Latin: "Jamque salutari properet lactuca sapore, / Tristia quæ relevet longi fastidia morbi."</note>

-> That is: <-

> *Let one bring forth lettuce with its tastiness,*
> *So that the sad ailment may leave the limbs.*

See *Ursinus in Herbario, pages 114, 115.*

For my part, I can well recall that this order was given to make the Israelites remember that sadness and bitterness which was inflicted upon them in Egypt.

Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325 AD).</note> in Chapter 1 alludes to the bitterness of the law and asks, *What is bitterer than the law and its curse?*

On account of this, it is said that Christ does not taste right without the law (*Matthew 5:6; 9:12; 11:28*), as it awakens an appetite and hunger for Christ and His righteousness (*Matthew 5 and 6; Philippians 3; Galatians 3:24, etc.*), which can also be easily reconciled.

<margin>Christ symbolized by the Passover.</margin>
However, since the Passover is Christ (*1 Corinthians 5:7*)—that is, it looked toward Him and depicted His person and experiences—some have, in my judgment, not wrongly said that the bitter herbs represented not only Christ's tasted bitterness of suffering, but also the conformity to Him in and for His sake. This refers to the suffering of Christ in all who eat Him through faith; which suffering, however, is sweetened by the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, being made into a *hieron pikron* <note>original: "ἱερὸν πικρὸν", meaning "holy bitter."</note> and a healthy means for advancement in knowledge, love, faith, patience, etc. (*Matthew 16:24; Acts 14:22; Lamentations 3:15; 2 Corinthians 1:2; Romans 5:5; Romans 8; 2 Corinthians 4:17; Hebrews 12; Revelation 3; 2 Timothy 2:12; Philippians 1:29; Psalm 97:10; Psalm 37:37; 2 Timothy 3:12.*) But let us depart from this bitterness.

### LEAF, LEAVES OF TREES:
### Leaf <note>original Hebrew: עלה (aleh)</note>, Leaf <note>original Greek: φύλλον (phyllon)</note>, Leaf <note>original Latin: folium</note>.

<margin>Use of the leaves.</margin>
THE LEAF, or the LEAVES, are the ornament of the tree: which sometimes stand thick, sometimes thin; of all sorts of color, size, width, and power. Some fall off easily, others hang long on the tree, etc. Some wither, others remain green and juicy; some are for shade and covering, others for healing; others again are useful for nothing but external ornament, covering, and hiding the fruits against the cold and piercing heat—which is quite a lot and something good in natural tree leaves.

One reads in *Genesis 3:7* that our ancestors...

<margin>Fig leaves of Adam and Eve.</margin>Having sinned, they fastened fig leaves together and covered themselves with them: from this, one might conclude, following the Jews and some of the Church Fathers, that they had eaten from the fruit of the fig tree. Alcimus <note>Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus (c. 450–518 AD), a Bishop of Vienne and Latin poet known for his work on biblical themes.</note> writes:

> *The treacherous madness that fed them with the wretched apple* <note>original: "Quofque aluit mifero fallax infania pomo"</note>
> *Clothed them in leaves; those whom the cruel tree rendered naked,*
> *It now covered more heavily with its thin bark.*

->That is:<-

> *The madness that satisfied them with the apple,*
> *Immediately clothed them in a garment of leaves.*
> *The tree left them naked, but then covered them, burdened*
> *By their own crime, with a thin bark and foliage.*

Certainly, the blindness of their souls was sufficiently demonstrated here; while leaving the soul stripped of righteousness and holiness, they sought to cover the body and hide themselves from the Lord among the thick branches and leaves.

However, it seems that the fig tree, having broad leaves, appeared most suitable to them for covering the body; they chose the leaves over the fruits. Thus many cover themselves with appearances and words, while despising the fruits of righteousness and love, even as they tremble from inner remorse.

> *With the fruits lost, Adam clothes himself in leaves;* <note>original: "Fructibus amiffis, foliis fe veftit Adamus"</note>
> *He who is wise gathers the fruit and leaves the leaves aside.*

->That is:<-

> *When Adam with his bride had lost the fruit,*
> *He kept nothing to clothe himself but the leaf.*
> *He who is wise chooses the fruit and lets the leaves go.*

Sedulius <note>Coelius Sedulius (5th century AD), a Christian poet best known for his *Carmen Paschale*.</note> writes:

> *What does it help to be hidden? Since he who gathers [leaves]* <note>original: "Quid juvat abfcondi?"</note>
> *Nourishes his own crimes, and fears to lay bare his wound to the healer.*

->That is:<-

> *Why do you keep yourself hidden? The evil will draw nourishment,*
> *If you do not dare to reveal your wound to a healer.*

Confession of guilt, and by no means self-excusing, is salutary (*Proverbs 28:13; Psalm 32; 1 John 1*, etc.). *If you acknowledge it, God forgives it* <note>original: "Si agnofcis, Deus ignofcit"</note>, says Augustine: if you recognize your crime, God forgives you.

> *To cover guilt with sewn fig leaves* <note>original: "Confutis ficus foliis prætexere culpam"</note>
> *Is in vain. If you uncover it, God himself covers it.*

->That is:<-

> *Shall the fig leaf serve as a cover for your evil?*
> *It is in vain: if you reveal it, God shall cover it.*

<margin>Great personages compared to trees.</margin>There is nothing more common in the Holy Scrolls than for men, and especially great personages and human estates, to be compared to trees, and indeed to high trees. Yes, and sometimes to leaves.

Now it is clear that when roots, branches, fruits, blossoms, leaves, etc., are attributed to the children of men, it must be taken and explained as a figure and a parable.

Job compares himself to a driven leaf, withered by the wind, dried out, and as if falling, robbed of sap and nourishment, being tossed by the whirlwind, crushed, mixed with destructive and burning matter, decaying and rotting. Thus he prays that the Lord would not continue to act so harshly and severely with him, since he could not withstand the Lord's power.

Ovid:

> *You are lighter than leaves, then, when without the weight of sap* <note>original: "Tu levior foliis..."</note>
> *Being made dry, they fly on the shifting winds:*
> *And there is less weight in you than in the top of a grain-ear,*
> *Which, light and scorched by constant suns, grows stiff.*

->That is:<-

> *Much lighter are you than the leaves of the trees,*
> *When all their strength and their saps are taken away.*
> *Much lighter are you also, and you hold no more ground*
> *Than an ear of corn scorched by the sun’s fire.*

Homer <note>Referring to the famous passage in the *Iliad*, Book VI, comparing the generations of men to leaves.</note>:

> *Such is the fate of men, as that of falling leaves:* <note>original: "Tale hominum fatum eft..."</note>
> *The North Wind shakes these down and spreads them on the ground, but then*
> *The forest pushes forth others with new birth when spring is reborn:*
> *So is the lot of men, to be born or to die in turn.*

->That is:<-

> *Man is just like the leaves, taken from the trees*
> *By the powerful violence of the North Wind.*
> *These fall down. But when the spring comes,*
> *The forest receives new ornament upon its trees again.*
> *To be born and to die again is laid upon men*
> *By fate.* ———

And subsequently,

> *By the nod of the Fates <note>original: "Parcarum," referring to the Parcae or Roman Fates.</note> even youths are carried to their doom,*
> *Like leaves, which the turbulent South Wind carries away.*

->That is:<-

> *When it shall please the Goddesses of Fate,*
> *Even a youth is carried away from the earth,*
> *No differently than a leaf driven by the wind.*

> *As high beauty nourishes the burgeoning forests,* <note>original: "Ut alta fylvas forma vernantes alit"</note>
> *Which the mild warmth clothes in a naked grove.*
> *But when the North Wind <note>Boreas.</note> has driven out the loose South Winds,*
> *And cruel winter has shaken off all the "hair" [leaves],*
> *You see a grove deformed by its leafless trunks:*
> *So our beauty, running its long journey,*
> *Always loses something, and shines the less.*

->That is:<-

> *Just as a forest is overloaded with green leaves*
> *In the springtime,*
> *Which a balmy warmth brews.*
> *But when the North Wind lifts its head,*
> *And storms upon all the trees,*
> *Then their luster is immediately taken away,*
> *And the woods just now laden with leaves...*

> Let no one be enticed by their own beauty.
> Such is man in his elderly days.
> The beauty, which everyone with pleasure
> Beheld, loses its luster
> Through the envy of fleeting time.

*See Ursinus, Anal. Part I. page 288. Arboret. page 62. etc.* <note>Zacharias Ursinus (1534–1583) was a German theologian; "Arboret" likely refers to a botanical or emblematic treatise on trees.</note>

<margin>The rustling of trees.</margin>The leaves of the trees rustle slightly through the movement of the air and the wind. To be startled by this rustling, which is after all a common, natural, and minor thing, suggests through the imagination that the very least thing is enough for a remorseful conscience to instill fear, terror, and amazement, *Leviticus 26:36; Proverbs 28:1; Job 15:21; Isaiah 48:22 and 47:21.* Lucanus <note>Lucan (39–65 AD), a Roman poet known for his epic "Pharsalia."</note>, speaking of Pompey's flight:

-> He dreads the crash <-
-> Of the groves moved by the winds. <-
<note>original Latin: "Pavet ille fragorem / Motorum ventis nemorum."</note>

-> That is: <-

> He trembles whenever he hears the rustling of the leaves.

Horace in his 23rd Ode of the first book:

> For whether the arrival of spring has shuddered
> In the moving leaves, or green lizards
> Have moved aside the bramble,
> He trembles in heart and knees.
<note>original Latin: "Nam seu mobilibus veris inhorruit / Adventus foliis, seu virides rubum / Dimovere lacertæ / Et corde & genibus tremit."</note>

Which Mr. David van Hoogstraten <note>David van Hoogstraten (1658–1724) was a Dutch physician, poet, and scholar.</note> has translated thus:

> For whether the spring makes the leaves tremble
> By its arrival, or the green lizards
> Bore through the hedge in woods and wildernesses,
> The heart beats fast with fear, and she loses her courage.

The conscience of sin is the mother of fear, says Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an important Early Church Father.</note> on *Psalm 50.*

> Wounded limbs dread even a soft touch:
> And an empty shadow incites fear in the anxious.
<note>original Latin: "Membra reformidant mollem quoque faucia tactum: / Vanaque sollicitis incitat umbra metum."</note>

-> That is: <-

> A gentle touch affects even wounded limbs.
> One sees the worried oppressed by idle fear.

It is well known that leaves, due to a lack of nourishment, wind, and clattering, become bent, dry up, and fall off. It does not bode well for someone's state, behavior, outward appearance, and countenance before God or <margin>Application.</margin>men at all when their leaves wither and dry up, or even fall off, and so come to nothing: and yet such expressions are used in Holy Scripture, though here and there with some distinction. Therefore, I shall take them up one by one and try to explain them more closely.

*Isaiah Chapter 1:30. For you shall be like an oak whose leaf fades, and like a garden that has no water.*

Regarding an oak tree that lets its leaves fall, I shall speak of that more closely when I come to the entry for the Oak Tree.

It is clear enough to me that the Lord threatens a judg-

<column-break/>

-ment upon His people, whom He will punish, both for their whoredom and the idolatry practiced in the groves, under the oaks, on the heights, and in the gardens; as well as for their trust in the tall and strong oaks and the powers of the idolatrous nations: so that they would not only lose much of their bloom, strength, and outward prosperity, but would be severely punished.

The judgment of the Lord, threatened in *Isaiah Chapter 34:4*, would be no milder. Thus speaks the Lord's Prophet: *and all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll, and all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falls off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree.*

Here some wish to see this as a reference to the heavy, final judgment that was approaching the Jews in their civil and ecclesiastical state, particularly under and by the Romans, when the city and temple would be destroyed, and authorities and powers brought to naught and abolished, and everything that was glorious would perish. Some, who wish to interpret this as a later event, hold that it speaks of the hierarchy of Rome, the Papacy, belonging to the power of the Apocalyptic beast.

When one hears a lamentation regarding the decaying church, *Isaiah 64:6 <note>Note: The source text says 64:8, but refers to the content of 64:6</note>, that she fades as a leaf, and that her righteousnesses are like a discarded garment*, I would think that, concerning Christ's suffering in Edom *Chapter 63* and the calling of the Gentiles *Chapter 65*, it speaks here of the great decay of the Jews, both in terms of their godliness and works of faith, love, and inner holiness of mind, as well as the decay of state and luster in the commonwealth, which withered more and more and went to ruin. However, if some wish to cast their eye on the state and countenance of the Christian church after Constantine the Great—on that great decay, the failing of former zeal, sincerity, purity, and the intrusion of false zeal, mixing and falsification of the faith, etc.—we can allow it.

In *Jeremiah Chapter 8:13. I will surely consume them, says the Lord: there shall be no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; the leaf shall fade, and the things that I have given them shall pass away from them*, it is given to understand how justly the Lord would punish His people for their wickedness, stubbornness, and open godlessness, they being without true fruits of faith, love, and holiness. Yes, even so openly godless that their leaf fell off, so that they not only began to pine away and become like a tree in the waning of autumn, but were even without the leaf of such morals as one even found among the Heathen—namely, modesty, prudence, discretion, sincerity, compassion, helpfulness, sobriety, faithfulness, etc.—since they openly rejected the counsel, commands, and warnings of the Lord; just as one seems to have to understand the leaf when it falls off, when even the outward religion, the appearance of outward godliness, the external confession, and profession of truth is lacking, and the breach of covenant and uncontrollable godlessness is displayed, as is done here.

parable, along with the emblem explained and applied in the following.

When Jeconiah <note>Jeconiah (also known as Jehoiachin) was a king of Judah exiled to Babylon.</note> and his people were to be conquered by the Eagle, Nebuchadnezzar, and he left behind a small and weak kingdom, he, Nebuchadnezzar, would appoint Zedekiah as king. But because he would defect from the covenant and the loyalty of King Nebuchadnezzar, the first Eagle, he would turn to the second Eagle, the King of Egypt, imagining that he would fare much better with him; yet he would fail miserably, for he would wither more and more, weaken, and indeed be rooted out, and die without children; for Nebuchadnezzar would wage war against that ungrateful man, surround him, take him prisoner, and the second Eagle, Pharaoh, would by no means be able to deliver him.

<margin>Explanation and application.</margin>It stood piteously with the Jewish fig tree, when no fruits but only leaves were found upon it—namely, only outward virtues, verbal confessions of truth, a semblance of godliness, outward finery, and a civic life: common customs in which even many Heathens surpassed them: no faith, love, or knowledge of God in His Son, appearing to be what they were not. But more on this later under the word FIG TREE.

Certainly, it sounds much better when it is said that the leaf does not fall: that the leaves are for healing, even for the Heathens, *Psalm 1; Ezekiel 47:12; Revelation 22; Jeremiah 17:9;* that the foliage remains green, *Proverbs 11:28 <note>original: 29</note>,* etc. By these leaves, one can then understand all kinds of good and moral duties: dignity, modesty, sobriety, circumspection, uprightness, compassion, gentleness, friendliness, helpfulness, sedateness, etc. These do not fall off, because their nourishment is in the root of faith, love, and knowledge, if they be sincere: for even if the bleak autumn comes, the fierce winter of persecutions, slander, scorn, injustices, etc., yet faith working through love works according to the power of grace and sanctified knowledge of truth in such a way in them, and through their conduct and outward customs thoroughly, that they never fall away from their form, confession, and outward ornament of an irreproachable, inoffensive, and edifying walk, through which they are not only without offense to those who are around and outside them, but also capable of convincing and drawing others by their praiseworthy example: like the leaves of the cedars, the laurels, palm trees, etc., which always retain a lasting moisture and oiliness within themselves.

<margin>Application.</margin>Just as some leaves are not only for the covering of tree fruits and hiding against the burning heat and biting cold, but are useful in their application and capable of healing and curing boils, swellings, and the diseases of an extravagant and reproachable life, so must one let his light shine for the benefit of others, *Matthew 5.*

Since now every tree shall be spoken of regarding its leaves, blossom, fruits, etc., it seems to me that I have said and noted enough in general regarding the leaves.

WHITE <note>original Dutch: BLANK</note> set in contrast to Red, <term>צח</term> <note>Hebrew: Tsach, meaning dazzling or clear</note>, <term>λευκος</term> <note>Greek: leukos, meaning white</note>, *candidus, nitidus* <note>Latin: bright, shining</note>, etc.

When the WHITE, bright, clear ground of the outer skin, especially in the face, is tinged with a blushing red, it glows with a charming beauty upon the face, most lovely to behold.

The church, wishing to depict the soul-stirring beauty of the Fair Bridegroom Jesus, describes Him <margin>Song of Solomon 5:10.</margin> as white and ruddy. Jesus is described as the fairest among men. *Psalm 45.*

The root word <term>צח</term> <note>Tsach</note> signifies that which is clear, shining, pure white, glossy, and reflecting, like light, the glow of the moon, or the whiteness of snow.

Thus one speaks of a "white" <note>meaning "clear"</note> conscience, when one is conscious of no evil, but like a righteous man, free and frank, can and dares to lift up his head; the glory of a Christian. *2 Corinthians 1.*

> Horace *Book I. Epistle to Maecenas.*
>
> To be conscious of no guilt, to turn pale for no crime.
<note>original Latin: "Nil conscire sibi, nulla pallescere culpa."</note>

-> That is: <-

-> *To be conscious of no guilt, nor for one's misdeed* <-
-> *To turn pale with dread.* <-

In Christ, it expresses His perfect purity and holiness, both of His Divine nature and His human, His immaculate birth, His shining and irreproachable dealings and conduct: His triumphant glory, radiance, and luster, upon which I need not dwell, the more so because the words WHITE, LIGHT, and others are to be spoken of more closely elsewhere; and it is enough for me to have pointed out the grounds of agreement and the springs of the applications. The execution and elaboration I leave to those who seek to treat it in sermons.

### COSMETICS, WHITE-WASH.
### <term>פוך</term> <note>Hebrew: Phuk, antimony or eye-paint</note>, <term>φῦκος</term>, <term>φύκαγον</term>, <term>φυκάριον</term> <note>Greek terms for seaweed-dye or cosmetics</note>, *fucus, stibium* <note>Latin: cosmetic/dye and antimony</note>.

BY the ancients, <term>פוך</term>, <term>φύκαγον</term>, <term>φυκάριion</term>, <term>φῦκος</term>, *phucarum, phucarium, fucus, stibium* is called COSMETIC, or the means of WHITENING.

A distinction is made between *fucus*, or the root of *Anchusa* <note>Alkanet, used as a red dye</note>, described by Hesychius as being of a blood-red color, with which finicky girls and loose women smear their cheeks, lips, etc.; and between *stibium* <note>antimony</note>, which, after one had shaved [the eyebrows], was applied in a half-moon shape to make them black, whereby one seemed to have wider eyes, this being the doll-like finery of ancient times.

Now, art and the wicked inclination of the wanton and over-luxurious mind of many "little Venuses" <note>meaning vain or promiscuous women</note> have devised other finery and cosmetics: whereby the natural color is disguised and stifled. Propertius:

> And to destroy the beauty of nature with purchased ornament,
> Nor allow the limbs to shine with their own virtues.
<note>original Latin: "Naturæque decus mercato perdere cultu, / Nec sinere in propriis membra nitere bonis."</note>

One need not suspect anything else of such people than that they wish to ensnare someone through this lure, seeking a bedfellow; for which reason it is brought up as the work of paramours. *2 Kings 9; Jeremiah 4:30; Ezekiel 23:40.* De Bruine says in his *Wetsteen* <note>The "Wetsteen der Welsprekendheid" (Whetstone of Eloquence) by Cornelis de Brune, 1644.</note> on page 71:

Certainly Jerome <note>St. Jerome (Hieronymus), an early Christian priest and scholar.</note> pulls no punches when he writes to Furia regarding cosmetics: *It is a fire,* he says, *of the youth, a spark of foul lust, a sign of an unchaste heart.* For just as one who is covered with plasters, wrapped in poultices, and smeared with salve immediately suggests the decay of his limbs; so (says Clement of Alexandria in *The Instructor, Book 3, Chapter 2*) the painting and coloring of the face shows us that the soul is sick within: and just as branded marks show a runaway slave, so these borrowed colors show a harlot.

Thus says Kats <note>Jacob Cats (1577–1660), a famous Dutch poet known for his moral emblems.</note> in *Marriage*; and Jongtyts in the *Theater of Jealousy and Marital Zeal*,

<note>original Latin: "Maechis foliata parantur. / His emitur quicquid graciles huc mittitis Indi." Translates to: "Leafy ointments are prepared for adulteresses. With these is bought whatever you slender Indians send here."</note>

> Serves to please her paramour.
> For his delight is bought,
> Whatever the Indian ever brought us.

<margin>Cosmetics as a symbol of hypocrisy.</margin>
It can be regarded as a symbol of all kinds of hypocrisy before God and men, through which one adopts false colors to cruelly deceive and mislead another. For this reason, *fucus* <note>original: "fucus" (Latin for rock-lichen dye, and by extension, a pretense or sham).</note> is also used by the Latins to mean deceit; just as it was with the Pharisees, who were like beautifully plastered tombs, and with all varnished appearance of virtue and the form of godliness: when one appears beautiful, but hides a foul heart and wicked deformity beneath that decorated skin. Persius in *Satire 5*:

> Pelliculam veterem retinens, & fronte politus,
> Astutam vapido servas sub pectore vulpem.

<note>original Latin: "Pelliculam veterem retinens, & fronte politus, / Astutam vapido servas sub pectore vulpem."</note>

->That is:<-

> When you appear with a lamb-like brow,
> While a sly fox inhabits your cunning breast.

And Claudian in the second book on Stilicho:

> Blanda quidem vultu, sed qua non tetrior ulla
> Interius, fucata genas, & amicta dolosis
> Illecebris.

<note>original Latin: "Blanda quidem vultu, sed qua non tetrior ulla / Interius, fucata genas, & amicta dolosis / Illecebris."</note>

### BLIND, BLINDNESS,
<note>original Hebrew: "עִוֵּר, עִוָּרָה, עִוָּרוֹן" (ivver, ivvarah, ivvaron); original Greek: "Τυφλὸς, τυφλότης" (typhlos, typhlotes); original Latin: "caecus, caecitas"</note>

<margin>Blindness.</margin>
WE know that blindness is not only such a bad condition of the eyes and visual canals through which one can hardly see, and is cross-eyed, near-sighted, or dim-sighted, or has films and scales upon the eyes—as the word <term>the blind<note>original Hebrew: "העורים" (ha-ivrim)</note></term> in *Isaiah 42* can be understood in such a way—but that being blind and blindness can be taken absolutely for being completely blind, whether one is so from birth, *John 9*, or has become blind by some accident. Congenital blindness is incurable, as is blindness by accident; yet when caused by scales or films, and other minor ailments and causes, it is found that the same is sometimes helped by the lifting of the films and scales, or otherwise.

<margin>Blindness cured only by God.</margin>
Otherwise, the healing of absolute blindness is not the work of any man but of God, *Psalm 146; Isaiah 35 and 42; John 9*; by healing which, Christ proved His Divinity and His Messiahship.

Regarding the blind and blindness, there are already several commands and orders established in the Holy Writ, and ways of speaking, which one must consider not merely according to the letter: for example, one might not sacrifice a beast that was blind to God, though this was nevertheless done. *Leviticus 22; Deuteronomy 15; Malachi 1.* A blind man could not be a Priest or serve in the sanctuary: *Leviticus 21.* One was not to put a stumbling block before a blind man, or make him wander on the road, *Leviticus 19; Deuteronomy 27*, and so forth. The literal meaning is found there. There will undoubtedly be something secret <note>Meaning a hidden allegorical or spiritual meaning.</note> lying within this.

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
When a blind man is barred from the Priestly office and a blind beast from the altar, I believe it was shown that God wanted the best and most prominent in His service.

That it prefigured the perfection of the High Priest Christ, and the perfection of His sacrifice, which lacked nothing.

That no one who is blind in the soul, not understanding the good, holy, and pleasing will of God, is capable of being a Priest and being able to please God: just as one could not expect orderly service or proper watchfulness from a blind priest.

That one could not place a stumbling block before the blind, or make him wander on the road, had its reasonable purpose, both because of the danger it posed to the blind man, and to avoid all lack of love, wantonness, and wicked tricks, and to instill love, compassion, and mercy toward the weaknesses of one's neighbor.

# BLIND.

<margin>
Help to be shown to the blind.
</margin>
Much less should one ensnare the blind in soul—the ignorant and simple—or place a stumbling block to their ruin, causing them to wander in many detours and diversions. Rather, one ought to be an eye to them; being moved by their blindness and lack of understanding, one should lead them as if by the hand, with good counsel, deeds, and friendly instructions, warnings, and admonitions.

Thus it is said that Job was eyes to the blind, *Chapter 29:15.* Not literally, but figuratively, looking out for the blind in what they would have looked after for their own benefit had they been able to see; namely, that they were not misled or wronged by anyone in any matter, within or outside of court, so that he took their affairs to hand and heart as if he were handling and pursuing his own affairs.

It shall also depict how he instilled knowledge of God’s ways in the unwise, and those who had crippled gaits, and taught them to perfectly direct their path in the track of God’s commandments: just as someone is an eye to the blind, not only when he leads them on the right path and avoids all stumbling and ruin; but when he instructs the foolish and ignorant, and brings them to knowledge and prudence, so that in the future they can perform their own affairs themselves.

But if the blind lead the blind, they both fall into the pit of destruction. *Matthew 15; Luke 6:39.* For the blind person has no advantage over the blind; both are blind: both grope for the wall: both wander: neither can notice what stumbling blocks, bends, pits, and holes are at hand. The ignorant cannot give good and wholesome counsel to the ignorant: how shall he who does not understand the true wisdom and way of God present and show it to others?

<margin>
Application.
</margin>
Now it is subsequently a clear matter that natural blindness is a symbol of the ignorance of the soul: for understanding and judgment are the eyes of the soul, through which one wisely distinguishes between good and evil, wholesome and soul-damaging.

<margin>
Blindness a symbol of ignorance.
</margin>
The blindness of the soul, and the wretched ignorance in the matters and truths of God, even some Heathens <note>The author refers to pre-Christian Roman poets here.</note> were able to notice and somewhat describe. Lucretius in *On the Nature of Things, Book 2:*

> O wretched minds of men, O blind hearts!
> In what darkness of life, and in what great dangers
> Is passed this span of time, however long it be!
<note>Original Latin: "O miseras hominum mentes, & pectora caeca! / Qualibus in tenebris vitae, quantisque periclis / Degitur hoc aevi quodcunque est!"</note>

->That is:<-

> O miserable understanding of men! O concept
> Full of blindness! In what mist, alas, in what dangers,
> Where nothing is permanent, do we waste our years!

And Ovid in the 6th Book of the *Metamorphoses*: <note>Original Dutch text uses "Herscheppinge" (Transformations).</note>

> O gods above! How much of blind night
> Do mortal hearts possess.
<note>Original Latin: "Prob superi! quantum mortalia pectora caecae / Noctis habent."</note>

->That is:<-

> O Gods, what blindness has occupied the hearts of men!

This blindness, and ignorance in the matters and truths of God—ordained and established for salvation in the Messiah, yes, revealed in promises and doctrines, wound up in riddles, shadows, and examples, clarified, fulfilled, and brought about by Christ, and displayed in the Gospel—is indeed found in all people through the entrance of sin. But it was even more burdensome when this blindness was found even in those who had the word of life, heard it, and gave themselves out as teachers and leaders of the blind. For one speaks not only of the blindness and ignorance of the Heathens, but also of the Jews, regarding the main body of them. And not only this, but one heard that God’s servants, the Jewish leaders and teachers, were blind, *Isaiah 42 and 43; Isaiah 6; Isaiah 59; Matthew 15; Luke 6; Matthew 23; John 9; Jeremiah 5; Romans 2:19, 20.* etc. walking and stumbling, groping like the blind for the wall. *Deuteronomy 28; Isaiah 58 and 59; Lamentations 4; Zephaniah 1. etc.*

For even if (as they claimed) they sought the secret, hidden, and sublime sense of the Divine words, they did not seek on the right track: they had lost the key.

They occupied themselves mostly with the institutions and fables of men, with the sayings of the elders. At that time, one heard it said with a kind of general consent, *the science of traditions surpasses the practices in the law. Yes, the traditions of the elders are the key and the foundation of the Divine law.*

They did not know the state and condition of their souls before God, nor their own unworthiness and impotence. They sought a worldly Messiah: not a provider of salvation for the soul, but a king and redeemer of civil status. They sought righteousness from the works of the law, denying the righteousness of faith. They <margin>Blindness of the Jews.</margin> stumbled at Christ’s humility and death on the cross, which they themselves had brought upon him. And although the Messiah’s form was described in such a manner in *Psalm 22; Isaiah 53; Zechariah 9;* and though he performed the foretold wonders and signs mentioned in *Isaiah 35;* it could not help; they had the spirit of contradiction and blasphemed what they by no means understood.

When it is now said of God and the Messiah that they open the eyes of the blind, give them sight, uncover the eyes, or give enlightened eyes (*Ephesians 1 and 3; Psalm 119; Isaiah 35; and Psalm 146;* etc.), it gives to understand that God inwardly shines upon them through His word and spirit. He enlightens them and brings them to sufficient knowledge of His virtues, counsel, and ways in the Messiah. This knowledge of truth makes them free from errors, causes them to take root in the knowledge, love, and fellowship of the Triune God, and—with many comforts, boldness, desire, and joy—enables them to know, confess, and practice the truths of God to God’s honor, the neighbor’s perfection, and the pursuit of their eternal salvation.

someone who strikes with spiritual blindness of the soul—that which the Lord commanded *Isaiah* to do in *Chapter VI* when he had to announce to the carnal Jews what was approaching them; namely, that although they had and would enjoy the means of healing, they would nevertheless neither know nor accept the truth of God. They would by no means give faith to the preaching, *Isaiah LIII, John XII, Matthew XIII, Romans XI.* Indeed, all the means that could serve for healing would have as little grip, power, and hold on them as medicine has on the absolutely blind and deaf.
