<margin>Stubbornness of the Jews.</margin>
Certainly, when the Apostles preached the Jews' imminent rejection and the Gentiles' acceptance; the uselessness of circumcision; the powerlessness and vanity of sacrifices; and Christ the crucified *1 Corinthians II,* not a worldly prince or king, etc.; then the Jews were all the more hardened and blinded. They turned away, they stopped their ears, they blasphemed, persecuted, and conducted themselves incorrigibly.

The Lord refused His enlightening and softening grace as a punishment because they had not wanted to hear and had despised and neglected the means. Thus He let them go and proceed as a judge, so that they became more and more blind, senseless, and wandering in heart—even more so as they were supported and stiffened in their wandering concepts by the blind Priests and foolish Scribes.

### LIGHTNING, Lightning, Flash, Thunderbolt, *Thunderbolt*. <note>original: ברק (Barak), בָּזָק (Bazak), κεραυνὸς (Keraunos), *fulmen*</note>

<margin>Cause of Lightning.</margin>
What LIGHTNING actually is in nature does not need to be argued or explained by me in great detail. Generally, it is required that there be sulfurous, oily, and nitrous particles in the air, in which infinitely many fine fire-particles or spheres are contained, drawn up from the earth toward the upper air. These, being compressed and wonderfully moved by the movement and pressure of the clouds, either go without a crash (due to low resistance or the thinness of the clouds) or with a burst and crash of clouds bumping against one another, accompanied by a rapid, continued light and flame of fire. The first is called sheet lightning <note>In Dutch, 'weerlicht' refers to lightning flashes without audible thunder.</note>; the second is called thunder and lightning. In general, it is true that thunder and lightning are singularly terrifying, all the more because Lightning has wonderful, powerful, and often harmful effects.

<margin>Its power.</margin>
I would by no means agree with the ancients who imagined that those who were struck and killed by Lightning—heaven's fire—were made fit for immortality and promoted to the glory of heaven. So says *Artemidorus*: <note>An ancient Greek professional diviner and author of the 'Oneirocritica' (The Interpretation of Dreams).</note> *no one who is struck by Lightning is ill-reputed or held in contempt; from which he is also honored as a God.* Thus the place that was formerly struck by heaven’s fire was holy. *See Ursinus's Analecta, Book II, Chapter XXVIII; Alexander ab Alexandro, 353, etc.; Hofmann's Universal Lexicon; Balthasar Bonifacio's Ludicrous History.*

If it thundered and lightened on a wedding day, it was held to be a good omen: *Claudian, The Rape of Proserpina, Book II.* <note>Claudian was a Latin poet of the late 4th century.</note>

> *Acknowledge the son-in-law, Hymenaeus thunders from the*
> *gaping clouds, and the flames confirm the marriage as witnesses.*

->That is:<-

> *As proof of the son-in-law's status, there appears on that day*
> *The swift lightning, and it thunders strike upon strike.*

<margin>Thunder and lightning as a good omen among the ancients.</margin>
Regarding Lightning with its sudden, brief, and sometimes very harmful light and terrifying flame of fire: I believe that it appears as a sign of God's presence, power, and action to cause terror. At the very least, it was not a pleasant or joyful appearance in the sky, nor something that could give an impression of something beneficial and pleasant, when such a dismal crashing and flashing of thunder and lightning was heard at the giving of the law, *Exodus XIX.* and nearly everywhere this word appears in the Holy Scroll <note>The Bible.</note> where it cannot have a literal and natural meaning, I believe it is used as a symbol of God's judgments and visitations, especially for the punishment of the unholy and despisers of the Gospel teaching of grace, *Psalm XVIII and XCVII and CXIV, Psalm LXXVII, Revelation IV and VIII.*

<margin>Application of Lightning to the Gospel.</margin>
Meanwhile, because Lightning gives a sudden, fast, and penetrating light which shines through the Heaven in great haste, upon which one cannot keep an eye—coming after a dismal and eerie darkness, a strong light that is itself terrifying to many—I am willing to believe that in a certain respect the Gospel teaching of truth is compared to a Lightning bolt. This is because of its sudden and powerful radiation throughout the entire world, through the desired preaching followed by the power of the Holy Spirit. But since this is accompanied by thunder and terror—indeed, a very strong movement of the air—and since one often finds thunder and lightning together in the Divine mystery-scroll <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, I would think it most likely that one does not err in thinking that the Gospel would indeed have a swift course and breakthrough. Thus, those who had the dismal and deep darkness as a covering would see themselves shone upon by a clear light, enabling them to make right paths and see the prepared ways of the Lord. But it would also be to the terror of those who would be disobedient to the Gospel of God's Son. Just as Lightning sometimes has strange effects—more toward terror and sudden overwhelming, because the weak eye cannot endure such a fast and powerful light—by which many are dismayed and wonderfully, even leadly, struck. And so I would not be disinclined to join the one with the other, *Psalm XCVII:4, Revelation IV and VIII, Matthew XXIV, Psalm CX:2, Psalm XVIII, Psalm CXLIV, Zechariah IX,* etc. Lightning strikes and hits that which is high and hard and offers resistance; likewise God's hand and the fire of His wrath strike and fell the proud and the resistors. *Philotheus in Christian Symbols, page 116.*

### LIGHTNING, <note>Hebrew: *Barak*; Greek: *Keraunos*; Latin: *Fulmen*</note>

**W**hat LIGHTNING actually is in nature does not need to be argued and explained by me with extreme precision. Generally, it requires that there be in the air sulfurous, oily, and nitrous particles, in which infinitely many fine fire-particles or spheres are contained, drawn up from the earth to the upper atmosphere. These, being compressed and wonderfully moved by the motion and pressure of the clouds—either without a crash due to low resistance or the thinness of the clouds, or with a burst and crash of clouds bumping against each other—are accompanied by a rapidly moving light and flame of fire. The first is called "sheet lightning" <note>original: "weerlicht"</note>, the second is called "thunder and lightning." In general, it is a truth that thunder and lightning are exceptionally terrifying, especially since lightning has such strange, powerful, and often harmful effects.
<margin>Cause of Lightning.</margin>
<margin>Its power.</margin>

I would by no means side with the ancients who imagined that those who were struck and killed by lightning, the fire of heaven, were made fit for immortality and promoted to the glory of heaven. So says *Artemidorus: No one who is struck by lightning is to be held as ill-reputed or despicable; for which reason he is even honored as a God.* Thus, the place that had once been struck by heaven’s fire was holy. See *Ursinus, Analecta Lib. II. Cap. XXVIII; Alexander ab Alexandro 353, etc.; Hofmann, Lexicon Universale; Balthasar Bonifacius, Historia Ludicra.*

If it thundered and lightened on a wedding day, it was held to be a good omen: *Claudian, On the Rape of Proserpine, Book II.*

> *The Marriage-god, revealed as a son-in-law by the gaping clouds,*
> *Thunders, and the flames confirm the union as witnesses.*

> *The rapid lightning, and it thunders strike upon strike.*

<margin>Thunder and lightning as a good omen among the ancients.</margin>

Regarding lightning with its sudden, brief, and sometimes very harmful light and terrifying flame of fire, I would believe that it appears as a sign of God's presence, power, and action for the purpose of terrifying. At the very least, it was not a pleasant or joyful atmosphere, nor something that could give an impression of something beneficial and attractive, when at the giving of the law such a dismal crashing and flashing of thunder and lightning was heard, *Exodus XIX*. And almost everywhere this word appears in the Holy Scroll, where it cannot have a literal and natural meaning, I believe it is used as a symbol of God's judgments and visitations, especially for the punishment of the unholy and the despisers of the Gospel's teaching of grace, *Psalm XVIII, XCVII, CXIV, LXXVII; Revelation IV and VIII*.

Meanwhile, since lightning gives a sudden, fast, and piercing light which shines through the Heaven in a great hurry, and upon which one cannot keep an eye—coming after a dismal and eerie darkness, a strong light that is itself terrifying to many—I am inclined to believe that in a certain respect the teaching of Gospel truth is compared to lightning, both because of its sudden and powerful radiation throughout the entire world through the desired preaching followed by the power of the Holy Spirit. But since this is accompanied by thunder and terror, even a very strong movement of the air, and one often finds thunder and lightning together in the Divine secret scroll; I would most closely think that one does not err by thinking that the Gospel would indeed be of a rapid course and breakthrough, so that those who had dismal and deep darkness as a covering would see themselves shone around by a bright light, in order to be able to make straight paths and see the prepared ways of the Lord. But it would also be for the terror of those who would be disobedient to the Gospel of God's Son; just as lightning is sometimes of strange effect, more for terror and sudden overwhelming, because the weak eye cannot endure such a fast and powerful light, whereby many are struck down and wonderfully, even mortally, hit. And so I would not be disinclined to add the one to the other, *Psalm XCVII:4, Revelation IV and VIII, Matthew XXIV, Psalm CX:2, Psalm XVIII, Psalm CXLIV, Zechariah IX, etc.* Lightning strikes and hits that which is high and hard and offers resistance; likewise God's hand and the fire of His wrath strike and fell the proud and the resisters. *Philotheus in Christian Symbols, page 116.*
<margin>Application of Lightning to the Gospel.</margin>

> *From Parian marble rises a tall column, and turns its proud brow*

->That is:<-

> *The marble column lifts its head high*
> *With a defiant splendor toward heaven’s steep arch.*
> *It dares to boldly brave the hail, snow, and rain,*
> *And carries itself as if no calamity could ever harm it.*

> *Of angry Jupiter throws all its pride into the sand.*

One reads in *Luke 10:18*, compared with *Revelation 12:8, 9*: *And he said to them, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.* It is further specified in *Revelation 12* that he was cast down to the earth. I can imagine that this refers to the sudden and very powerful change which was to be brought about by the light of the preaching of the Gospel, through which Satan was to lose his power of deception, and in a remarkable way lose his service and worship among the Heathens—especially as the Gospel was to be accompanied by the power of miracles, signs, and the casting out of unclean spirits.

Because the light of Lightning is swift and piercing, and sometimes shines unexpectedly upon those who are in dreadful dark and gloom, so that they can see around them to go their way with some certainty: so I am willing to believe that in the dismal night and the pitch-darkness of ignorance, while the sinner walks in the dark, a Divine light of knowledge and grace <margin>Conversion.</margin> suddenly and very swiftly shines around him. But that light—being sudden, unexpected, and in deep darkness—causes consternation and bewilderment, because the eye is not prepared to receive such sudden, strong, and swift light. And when the Lord comes so suddenly and unexpectedly with such a strong light, shining in the darkness, I believe that at first it causes bewilderment, terror, and a transport outside of oneself: because the soul is not accustomed to being under such treatment. *Acts 8 and 9, 2 Corinthians 4, etc.*

Insofar as Lightning has the property of light, I shall not explain it further here: because what I have to say can be contained under the entry for LIGHT. Therefore, I will restrain myself and try to be more eloquent regarding this matter when I have come to the word LIGHT. For this reason, I shall break off here and limit myself to something else.

BLOOD, drunk with BLOOD: BLOOD *not to be eaten:* BLOOD-RELATIVE: BLOOD-AVENGER, etc. <note>Hebrew: דם (Dam - Blood), גאל (Goel - Redeemer/Avenger); Greek: αἷμα (Aima - Blood).</note>

<margin>Expressions derived from blood.</margin> **A**s I speak here of BLOOD, I shall try to briefly explain and illustrate all the principal names and expressions that relate to it, without needing to say that the soul of beasts consists therein, and that animal life depends on the circulation of the blood and the fluids.

<column-break/>

What blood actually is, whether of humans or of beasts, is known to us insofar as we know that one cannot live without it: and that upon the sufficiency, good condition, and the circular motion of the blood, our health, strength, and life chiefly depend: namely, the animal life which we have in common with all beasts.

Since the blood of beasts, and the life-spirits within it, along with the nimble fluids, are the only things in which their movement consists, and by which their movement, activity, and life are caused—and without which they otherwise lie soulless and motionless—it is therefore said in the Holy Scroll not only that the <margin>Blood, the life and soul of beasts.</margin> life and soul of beasts is in their blood, *Genesis 9, Leviticus 17:10–12*, but also the blood of sacrificial animals is held to be the most noble and excellent, as the soul of the sacrificial beast offered to God for the soul of the sinner. *Leviticus 17:11.* R. Salomo Jarchi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval French rabbi and author of comprehensive commentaries on the Talmud and Tanakh.</note> expresses himself on this passage thus: *The soul of every creature is in its blood: therefore have I given it for the atonement of your sins: one soul shall make amends for the other.* Aben Esdra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a distinguished Spanish rabbi and philosopher.</note> says: *the blood atones through the soul that is in it, one soul for the other.* R. Moses Ben Nachman <note>Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and philosopher.</note> says: *I have spared the soul of man, and given the blood upon the altar, so that the soul of the beast should make atonement for the soul of man.* R. Lipman <note>Possibly Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller (1578–1654).</note> says: *Since your soul is so bound to sin that you have deserved in your own person what is done to the beast: I have therefore given the soul of the sacrifice in the place of your soul.*

Regarding the blood of sacrificial animals, how it was received in <margin>Sacrificial blood.</margin> basins, poured out, or sprinkled; how the right earlobe, the right thumb, and the toe of the Priest were smeared with it, etc.; I shall also say something of that. But in general, one hears the great Apostle say, *Hebrews 9:22: and almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.*

The Apostle does not speak in absolute terms, but says *almost*, so that very little remained excluded; for one reads of holy things, and in a symbolic way, purifying through fire and water. *Numbers 31, Exodus 19, Leviticus 22.*

Regarding the offering of a poor person for sin <margin>Offering for sin.</margin> *Leviticus 5*, this brought no blood with it, but the soul, core, pit, and the marrow of the corn: the fine flour.

The Apostle had spoken previously of things belonging to the symbolic Tabernacle and the performance of service. Now he looks at things and ceremonies outside of it: writing thus of the purification of the flesh according to the letter of the commandment; that although this purification might occasionally be brought about by other matters, such nevertheless did not weaken or break the general rule and that which was most in use. For one could repeat the word *schedon* <note>original Greek: χεδὸν / σχεδόν, meaning "almost" or "nearly."</note> or "almost" here: generally, most all things (a few excepted) were purified by blood: and thus this small deviation and exception did not break the general principle and standard rule. For although the poor people brought fine flour, and the Lord might show His indulgence and mercy in these parts with some change in His...

# BLOOD

<sig>S 3</sig>

<margin>Connection of the meal offerings with the blood sacrifices.</margin> It pleased God to make His positive commandments depend solely upon His will and decree; nevertheless, these meal offerings <note>original: "meelbloeme," referring to the "fine flour" used in grain offerings</note> were brought into connection with the blood-stained altar, and were thus effectively united with the morning and evening sacrifices that were offered annually on behalf of the entire nation. As I have mentioned, it is certain that other means of purification were also found, though of a different nature: whether by water—as Israel had to wash and purify themselves and their clothes at Sinai (*Exodus 19*)—and <margin>Purifications.</margin> also for those who had touched any carcass (*Leviticus 16:26*); or as one reads of purification by fire (*Numbers 31:21-23*); and by oil (*Leviticus 8:10-12* and *14:16-18*).

Forgiveness through and upon the shedding of blood presupposes the transgression of the laws given through Moses: just as it also presupposes the death of some symbolic and mediating animal or bird in place of the transgressor.

Forgiveness here represents the pardoning of the physical punishments threatened against the transgressor. Otherwise, the spiritual and eternal punishment remained, as the Apostle previously stated; therefore, this forgiveness refers to the temporary, external physical punishments and penalties, such as being "cut off" <note>This refers to *kareth*, a biblical penalty of being excluded from the community or divine favor</note> from the people: being barred from the Tabernacle: having to forfeit social fellowship with Israel: and being deprived of the right to Canaan, etc. These held a symbolic power regarding the true and effective purifications and the cleansing of sin through better blood and sacrifice.

<margin>Anointing with the blood.</margin> One also reads of the anointing of the Priests' right ear, thumb, and the great toe of the hands and feet (*Exodus 29, Leviticus 8*). I am inclined to believe that he could be taught through this how he must take care to learn the law, to preserve the Holy Service and the ways of the Lord, diligently doing what he knew to be the Lord’s will. Thus says **Abravanel** <note>Don Isaac Abravanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and Bible commentator</note>: *all this was done to teach the Priests how industriously they must practice the law, and accustom their hands to the Lord’s service, and walk in the ways and commandments of the Lord: and so he had to direct his hearing, his works, and his conduct always toward the right hand—that is, toward perfection.* **Levi Ben Gerson** <note>Also known as Gersonides (1288–1344), a medieval Jewish philosopher and commentator</note> was of the same opinion.

Certainly, the Priest, having had his ear pierced <note>A symbolic reference to total devotion or "open ears" to God's command</note> and being entirely surrendered to the service of the Lord, had to hold fast to and take up the work of the Lord: hearing and listening to no other laws or statutes than those of God: choosing no other ways than those of the Lord. In this, the Priests were a type <note>In this context, a "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future reality, specifically Jesus</note> of the perfect High Priest, Jesus, who came for this purpose (*Psalm 40:7, Hebrews 10:5, John 4:34*). Truly, Christ's blood must be sprinkled on our members if we are to hear, work, and walk in God’s paths, doing what is pure, holy, and good; and when we are sprinkled with His blood, then what we hear, do, and preserve becomes acceptable to God through the power and value of His blood. See the entry for **PRIEST**.

<margin>Priests as a type of Jesus.</margin> Regarding the pouring out of blood and the sprinkling of the sanctuary, the altar, and the ark—so that almost everything was sprinkled with blood—see further under the word **SPRINKLING** (*Leviticus 4:6 and 16:12-15, 18, 19*).

I note that many Jewish masters did not understand this in such a way as if the blood actually had to be sprinkled *onto* the mercy seat, the ark, or the veil, 

<column-break/>

but rather *toward* the sanctuary, *toward* the Ark, and *toward* the veil—opposite it, near it, etc. **Bartenora** <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro (c. 1445–1515), a commentator on the Mishnah</note> says: *the blood drops do not reach the sanctuary, but fall upon the earth.* **R. Salomon Jarchi** <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator</note> on *Leviticus 16:16* says: *just as he sprinkles a portion of the blood from the sacrifices once upward and once downward in the inner sanctuary, so he sprinkles once upward and once downward against the curtain.*

Certainly, the frequent and annual repetition clearly demonstrated the powerlessness of these proceedings, for otherwise they would not need to be repeated (*Hebrews 10:1-2*). Because of this, sin remained more in the memory, and the conscience remained unpurified and imperfect; sin was still outstanding and the law retained its force. Therefore, a blood of greater power and more excellent value was symbolized and required by this, in order to cleanse the conscience of the sinner from dead works and to put away sins (*Hebrews 1:3 and 2 and 9, etc.*).

The Lord of Hosts is sanctified by right and righteousness (*Isaiah 5; Hebrews 9:12-14 and 10:19 and 13:12*), but more specifically in the sprinkling, alongside the sacrifice.

Since the blood was regarded as the soul <note>original: "ziel," meaning life-force or soul</note> of the beast—indeed, its most excellent part—no one should think it strange that blood is mentioned most often in the sacrifices as being shed for the soul of man for forgiveness (*Leviticus 17:11; Deuteronomy 12:27; Psalm 50:13; Hebrews 9:7-12, 13-18, 19, etc. and 10:4 and 13:11, etc.*).

Since blood was the most important thing in the sacrificial animal, serving as its soul in place of the soul of man, it should not seem strange to anyone that the Apostle Paul, when speaking of the purchase, redemption, and cleansing of the sinner, gives an account of Jesus’s blood. He passes from the symbol to the reality <note>original: "voorbeeld tot het tegenbeelt," literally "from the example to the anti-type"</note>, from the shadow to the body, from the powerless and low-valued to the powerful and infinitely worthy, borrowing the figures of speech from the symbolic rituals. By this, he most clearly and powerfully understands Christ’s love and obedience, as displayed in His bloody suffering unto death.

<margin>Blood, the most important part of the sacrificial animal.</margin> Now, that blood was for forgiveness and legal purification or sanctification. It is remarkable that sin, from which the covenant member had to be cleansed by blood, is itself compared to blood and said to be "as red as blood" (*Isaiah 1:18*) or like scarlet and crimson.

I believe this is because one cannot say that sin and the stains of sin cause any literal color in the one who is occupied and burdened by them; rather, the manner of comparison and naming follows the cleansing agents which were used in the past and were already known to the Jews, which were of a red color. Examples include the dust of the red heifer, the red bundle of wool with which the sprinkling was performed and which was burned with the red heifer. These were symbols of Christ’s blood and His bloody merits, and the value and power of the same—not only for justification but also for sanctification, to present His congregation to God the Father without spot or wrinkle (*Ephesians 5; Zechariah 13:1; 1 Corinthians 6:11; 1 Corinthians 1:30; 1 John 1:7; Hebrews 1:31 and 9:19, etc.*).

When one perceives that the blood of the sacrificial animals was the soul of the beasts and the most excellent thing that God reserved for Himself—that it was for the soul and sin of man—that the justification and sanctification were then not in Christ’s blood...

# BLOOD

<margin>Prohibition of eating blood.</margin> ...blood was brought in; and that the Pagans held fellowship with their idols in this; so one will easily understand for what reason the Lord forbade the eating of blood from of old. But a word on this.

I have already stated that the Lord forbade the eating of blood in *Leviticus 7 and 17*; one had to guard oneself against it, as seen in *Acts 15*.

I am quite willing to believe that man has no need of blood as a source of nourishment: I am willing to believe that in its use, it is not particularly healthy, but rather hard to digest.

I can well imagine that all cruelty and bloodthirstiness had to be prevented, and that one should not lightly step from shedding one kind of blood to another. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an important Early Church Father known for his preaching.</note> seems not entirely a stranger to this idea when he writes in his *Homilies on Genesis*: "He does this so that, from the beginning, he might restrain their impulse and inclination toward the shedding of human blood." <note>original Greek: "ταῦτα δὲ ποιεῖ, ἀνωθεν προαναστέλλων αὐτῶν τὴν ὁρμὴν τὴν περὶ τὴν ἀνδροφονίαν."</note>

And Mercerus <note>Jean Mercier (died 1570), a French Hebraist and commentator.</note> on *Genesis 9*: The eating of blood is forbidden so that, from the spilling of the blood of beasts, men might not easily be incited to the spilling of human blood; just as we see that slaughterers of beasts are almost all of a crueler nature and not entirely averse to human blood.

But that such is the actual reason for the prohibition in *Leviticus 7 and 17*, I can hardly think; at the very least, the Legislator clothes his prohibition with an entirely different reason.

I would much sooner believe the reason to be that the soul and life of the beasts consisted in their blood, which was given to God in place of the soul of man. And just as he was not permitted to eat of any atonement offering, so also not of the blood, as having itself the life—the soul forfeited through sin. As Ovid writes in *Fasti, Book 6*:

> This soul we give to you in place of a better one. <note>original Latin: "Hanc animam vobis pro meliore damus."</note>

->That is:<-

> We offer this soul to you, in place of a better.

In and through that sacrificial animal blood, the actual and true forgiveness or reconciliation of sins did not occur; it only brought the transgression to remembrance. It was a confession of a sin-guilt worthy of death; it pointed out that sin required another sacrifice, a worthier blood, of which this had to be given as a pledge.

<margin>No atonement through sacrificial blood.</margin> Since the atonement did not occur through that blood, no union or fellowship was to arise from eating it, so that one would not seem to rest his soul in that sacrificial animal blood.

Some would also have us believe that the Lord intended this prohibition to counter the rituals of certain Pagans. These people, imagining that blood was the food of the Demons <note>The author uses "Daimons," referring to spirits or pagan deities.</note>, ate of it to strike a covenant with them and to enter into their friendship and fellowship. For so writes Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note> in *The Guide for the Perplexed*: "Know that although blood was held to be unclean and forbidden in the eyes of the Sabians <note>A group of pagans often discussed in medieval philosophy.</note>, they nevertheless consumed it, because they imagined that this was the food of the Demons; and that he who consumes it, in this way obtains some fellowship with the Demons, so that—

<column-break/>

—they might interact familiarly with him and reveal future matters to him, just as the common sort of people are accustomed to attribute such things to Demons. There were, however, some among them to whom it seemed difficult and heart-wrenching to eat blood, a thing for which human nature has an abhorrence. These people, when slaughtering a beast, received its blood in a large trench or vessel; but the slaughtered meat they ate while sitting all around that blood in a circle. They imagined that while they ate the meat in this manner, the Demons consumed the blood—it being held as the food of Demons—and that in this way they entered into friendship, brotherhood, and familiarity with the Demons, because they all ate at one table and sat together in a circle. Besides this, they imagined that the Demons appeared to them in sleep, made future things known, and were exceptionally beneficial." Read in Spencer <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), author of *De Legibus Hebraeorum Ritualibus*.</note>, Part I, page 298, what he has brought forward from a book called *Zohar*; from Joseph Albo, etc., page 451, etc.

Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250–c. 325), an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine.</note>, *Book 9, Chapter 12*, regarding the rites of Bacchus <note>original: "Sacris Liberi," referring to Liber/Bacchus, the god of wine and frenzy.</note>: "The custom is such that once the goat is killed, all the initiates drink the blood." <note>original Latin: "Conſuetudo talis eſt, ut occiſo capro Sacrati omnes Sanguinem bibant."</note> In the ritual of Bacchus, the custom is that all the sanctified or consecrated ones drink the blood when the goat was slaughtered. See Spencer, Book II, Chapter III, page 465, etc.

With a sort of contrast to that prohibition, Christ introduced in the New Testament the commandment to eat His flesh and drink His blood in a spiritual and Sacramental manner (*Matthew 26*).

<margin>Christ's blood, the true blood of atonement.</margin> Certainly, Christ’s blood is the actual blood of atonement; we expect no other blood after He poured out His soul unto death. We, the Priests of the New Testament, must practice fellowship with the altar, and we must unite ourselves with Him to become partakers of the power and fruit of His blood.

The Great Burman <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> in his *Law and Testimony* writes thus: "So Christ proceeds by an entirely contrary command to bid us drink His blood; namely, for the same reason for which the Law had forbidden it. The Law forbids eating it because it made atonement for sins; Christ, on the other hand, commands us for that very reason to drink from the cup of the Holy Supper, because it was a sign of the blood of the New Testament, which was shed for many for the forgiveness of sins (*Matthew 26:28*). Namely, through the blood of beasts, true atonement did not occur, and therefore they were not permitted to have fellowship with that blood; but that atonement would occur only through the blood of Christ, fellowship with which is therefore now permitted to us." See further regarding this subject, Jan d’Espagne <note>Jean d'Espagne (1591–1659), a French Reformed theologian.</note>, page 261, etc.

It will, without doubt, suggest something entirely different when one reads that someone is given blood to drink, or that someone is drunk with blood; that arrows and the sword are said to be drunk (*Isaiah 49:26; Revelation 16:6 and 17:6; Deuteronomy 32; Isaiah 34; and Jeremiah 46*, etc.) with blood.

<margin>Drunk with blood.</margin> That someone is said to be drunk with blood signifies not only bloodthirstiness and an inclination to shed blood, but shedding it with madness, insanity, and rage in an overflowing measure—and that a very great slaughter is being carried out.

To give blood to drink to those who have shed it signifies not so much that someone thirsts for blood, but rather that he...

<meta>This page continues a theological exploration of the symbolism of blood, moving from the prohibition of its consumption to its deeper ritual and spiritual meanings in both Jewish tradition and Christian theology, focusing on blood as a symbol of sin and the necessity of Christ's redemption.</meta>

# BLOOD

...fades away, as it has done to others, through mutual factions, divisions, wars, internal disturbances, uprisings, and civil wars: or in the ecclesiastical state; just as it happened with the Roman power. See further Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian who developed "Covenant Theology."</note>, Groenewegen, Suicerus, and others.

That the flow of blood—whether the monthly periods or a long-term hemorrhage that became incurable over time—made one unclean according to the law of the fleshly command, required one to be set apart and not touched; such a person could not be mingled with, was unclean for seven days, and had to be washed. That Christ healed the extraordinary flow of blood (*Leviticus 5 and Numbers 5; Matthew 9, Mark 5, Luke 8, etc.*) seems to me to have illustrated the natural evil state of our nature, corrupted and offended by sin. Just as we are created from one blood, and receive it from the blood of women, and lie in blood, and wallow in it, so to speak, when we are born (*Ezekiel 16*), so it depicts our fellowship in that same blood—the same uncleanness in which we are conceived and born (*Job 14, Psalm 51*). Everything a woman touched became unclean when she was in the blood of her uncleanness: to the unclean, all things are unclean (*Titus 1*). Everything that comes from such a person is defiled—the person and all their belongings. Because of sin, uncleanness, blameworthiness, and imperfection hang over all their deeds (*Isaiah 64*). We are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousness is like a discarded garment <note>Often translated in Bibles as "filthy rags."</note>, or the garment of a menstruating woman.

<margin>The flow of blood as a symbol of sin.</margin>

This blood-flow and uncleanness came from within, and showed and spread itself outward, causing uncleanness through touch and infection. All sinful corruption, showing itself outwardly and infecting others, comes from the heart and reveals itself through many things capable of defiling (*Matthew 15:19, 20; Ezekiel 36:17*).

Such persons are not only turned away from God (*Isaiah 59, Ephesians 2*) but must also be avoided so that one does not share in their state or be infected by them, "hating even the garment spotted by the flesh."

That such laws existed in Israel, where the law of separation was maintained, I believe was intended to show that the true cleansing of sins had not yet occurred. Those who sought their purification only in external rituals, denying the only true means of cleansing—the blood of Jesus, embraced through faith, which cleanses the heart—would be declared unclean for many days and times. They would sit apart from God and the fellowship of those He has cleansed, still lying in their own blood and under the blood-guilt of Christ's death, which they called down upon themselves (*Hosea 3, Matthew 27*).

And when one saw such people separating, washing, and cleansing themselves; or saw the woman who was afflicted with a long-term flow of blood running to physicians and spending everything she had without help or benefit until she was healed in an extraordinary way by Jesus: it seems to me a picture of how the ailments of sin are not healed by the power, ability, or labor of man. For nothing one spends his money, and sells

<column-break/>

his labor (*Isaiah 55*). No physician, whether among the Jews or Greeks, was capable of this: it had to happen in an extraordinary way through the Christ, His blood, and His Spirit (*Psalm 51, Zechariah 13:1, 1 John 1:7, Hebrews 7 and 9, etc.*). No Jew or Jewess will ever be healed unless they gain fellowship with the garment—the mantle of Christ's righteousness. The power of His bloody merits must be effectively brought to their souls by the Spirit, which they shall only see and desire in the last of days, after they have found that they sought their healing from other masters and means in vain.

That the Jews in past days were not entirely ignorant of this can be concluded from what one can read in an old Jewish writing called the *Pesikta* <note>A collection of homiletic midrashim (Jewish commentaries).</note>: *When God created the world, He stretched out His hand from the throne of glory and created the soul of the Messiah, and said to her: "Will you heal and redeem My children after 6,000 years?" The soul answered: "I will." Then the Lord asked: "Will you also bear the chastisements to wash away their sins, as it is written: 'He has borne our sicknesses'?" She answered: "I shall bear them with joy," etc.*

The famous Wolzogen <note>Ludwig Wolzogen (1633–1690), a Reformed theologian and professor.</note> says regarding *Isaiah 53*: The prophet Isaiah uttered these words concerning the stains and diseases which Jesus had to undergo in His own body and soul for our sake. That *Matthew* now applies this to the people's physical ailments is because physical ailments are generally signs of spiritual ailments, which are sins, etc.

<margin>Physical ailments as signs of spiritual ones.</margin>

Thus speak the *Rabboth* <note>The Midrash Rabbah, ancient rabbinic interpretations of the Torah.</note>, Solomon Jarchi <note>Better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, and Rabbi Solomon on *Daniel 9*: the Messiah shall wipe away Israel's sins; they shall be redeemed and saved with an eternal redemption through the Messiah; for it is said: "And Israel shall be saved by the Lord with an eternal redemption" (*Isaiah 45:17*). And so one reads in the *Eshkol Ha-Kofer* <note>original Hebrew: אשכל הכפר; a 12th-century work of Karaite Judaism by Judah Hadassi.</note> that the Messiah is called *Ish Kol Kofer* <note>original Hebrew: איش כל כפר; a Hebrew pun on the book's title, translated here as "a man of full redemption."</note>, a man of full redemption. *The Messiah shall be a man of full redemption for the church, and He shall spring forth from the children of Abraham, and satisfy for sin, and He shall be able to say to the measure of judgment: "It is enough"; this one the Lord shall set as a pledge, and give up for His own.*

Blood is often taken to mean blood-guilt or manslaughter, and when it is shed innocently, it cries out for vengeance. If it is avenged, it falls upon the head of the guilty party: it is "demanded from someone's hands." One defiles their hands with it. If one is set upon revenge with mad rage, not resting until the one who offended us is "put aside," then one hears mention of "men of blood," "bloodthirsty" people, and "tyrants." If one withdraws from a grave violation and testifies against someone's wicked and raging undertakings, they wish for the blood to be "on that person's own head." One is said to be "clean of blood" when they wash their hands of it.

<margin>Expressions regarding blood.</margin>

Both concepts appear in the following places: *Genesis 42, Psalm 51, Exodus 22, Matthew 27, Acts 18 and 20, Isaiah 1, Ezekiel 3, Matthew 27,* etc.

According to the nature of the meaning of blood, the expressions in *Proverbs 1:11* and *12:6*—to "lie in wait for blood"—must be understood; this refers to a kind of cunning, readiness, and intent to...

# BLOOD

...indicates, with deliberation, counsel, cunning, to drag someone into ruin, being busy, a premeditated work, with intent and design.

<margin>City of Blood.</margin>
City of Blood (*Ezekiel 22 and 24, Nahum 3*) is so named because of blood, as one that has shed much blood, in which much innocent blood has been shed, and where many murderers reside. A symbol of the kingdom of the Antichrist, in which much blood is spilled, where one is, as it were, drunk with the blood of the saints.

To strive even unto blood (*Hebrews 12:4*) may perhaps symbolically signify venturing the utmost against one's adversary, even if one were to lose one's life in the process, and not only being beaten black and blue, but being faithful unto death, not holding one's life dear.

It had not yet come to that point with the Hebrews (*Hebrews 12:4*); they had had it quite easy and tolerable so far, because those of the circumcision <note>referring to Jewish traditionalists</note> were not allowed to do everything against them that they might have desired. Until then, the Romans did not rage within the vitals of the Christians; the times were mild, but it would not always be so.

<margin>Kinsman and Blood-Avenger.</margin>
But let us examine the Kinsman <note>original: *Bloetvrient* ("Blood-friend")</note> and Blood-Avenger a bit more closely and from nearby; we read of them in *Numbers 35, Deuteronomy 19, Joshua 20*, etc. (*Numbers 5, Leviticus 25, Deuteronomy 25*). He was also a redeemer <note>original: *losser*, meaning one who releases or unties a debt</note>, and he was permitted to marry his brother's childless widow and raise up seed for her, to keep his name and inheritance alive.

Such a person, as a close relative, had to redeem the properties, lands, fields, houses, etc., that had been sold or alienated through poverty, provided he paid the price that had been given for them (*Leviticus 25*).

The inheritance and goods that we had lost through sin, our Redeemer has redeemed and obtained again through his eternal redemption (*Hebrews 8:12*); he has found and paid the ransom (*Job 33*).

He had to redeem the enslaved and the bondservant and set them at liberty (*Leviticus 25*). We were slaves to sin (*Romans 7*); many under the law, which worked wrath, were in bondage and fear (*Hebrews 2*), prisoners of the strong one (*Isaiah 49, Luke 11*). Christ has delivered us from it (*Luke 1:74, 75, Luke 11, Isaiah 61, Zechariah 9, Romans 6*, etc.). This person [the kinsman] had to avenge blood with blood and, pursuing the guilty murderer, strike him down outside the city of refuge; the innocent person had to remain in one of the cities of refuge until the death of the High Priest. However, the slain person he left dead, being unable to make him alive.

The compass of the law seemed to have been given like a city of refuge for Israel's freedom and safety until the death of the true High Priest (*Galatians 3:23, Romans 3:25, Hebrews 9:15*). Christ attacked our enemies and conquered and crushed the murderer of men <note>a reference to the Devil, "a murderer from the beginning"</note> (*Genesis 3, Hebrews 2, 1 John 3*), taking away the sting of death (*1 Corinthians 15*), bringing those he redeemed into his fellowship unto life (*Galatians 2:20*, etc.).

He had to marry the childless brother's widow and keep his brother's name and lineage alive and in possession of the inheritance, so that the lineages remained undivided, and it would be known that the Messiah was from the promised house (*Deuteronomy 25, Ruth 3*). Thus he spread the corners of his garment <note>original: *flippen*</note> over them.

The one released from the husband of the law, by whom

<column-break/>

no children were begotten as free men, having died, or the church having died to that man, she has been united with Jesus through an unbreakable marriage bond (*Romans 7, Hosea 2 <note>original text says Hosea 21, likely a typo for Hosea 2</note>, Ephesians 5, Isaiah 61:10*). Through the seed of the living word, poured into the womb of the church, he has begotten many spiritual sons and daughters; and still the people who have been cast off for a long time and sit as a widow (*Hosea 2*) shall be shown mercy, and Jesus will spread the corner of his garment over them (*Hosea 3, Isaiah 60, Romans 11, 2 Corinthians 3*).

But before we take our leave of "Blood," we wish to consider some other testimonies and expressions.

Paul writes in *Hebrews 12:24*: "and to the Mediator of the New Testament, Jesus, and the blood of sprinkling, which speaks better things than that of Abel"; compare *Genesis 4:10* and *Hebrews 11:4*.

This passage is not understood and explained in the same way by all scholars.

It is known that the Hebrews had come to the sacrificial blood of sprinkling (*Exodus 21, 24:6, 7, 8*), but previously they had not come to the bloody sacrifice of Jesus' suffering and the obedience of suffering unto death. His sacrificial blood had not yet been shed as it was later, when they were brought to it through faith, confession, and imputation.

<margin>Blood of Abel.</margin>
By the blood of Abel, some understand his person and bloody death, because of his better sacrifice, having been killed by Cain.

Aretius <note>Benedictus Aretius (1505–1574), a Swiss theologian.</note> says of it (which speaks better things): that is, which cries for the forgiveness of sins and prays for its persecutors. The blood of these two is very aptly compared with each other: for Abel was a type <note>a prophetic symbol</note>; for just as Abel was innocently put to death by his brother, so also was Christ killed by the Jews, his brothers according to the flesh. Furthermore, God avenged Abel's death with the exile of the murderer, for Cain became a fugitive; in the same way, the Jews are also scattered. And I find in Sebastian Schmidt <note>17th-century Lutheran theologian.</note> on the Epistle to the Hebrews: (the opinion of Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early church father.</note> is followed by most of the ancients.) Abel's blood cries for vengeance, but the blood of Christ cries for mercy and forgiveness; the law works wrath and cries for vengeance, but the blood of the New Testament for forgiveness.

Others, however, have understood the blood of Abel not as the blood of his person shed by Cain, but as his sacrificial blood, shed by him for atonement, to which the blood of the legal sacrificial animals was later attached and followed. All that blood could not take away sin, nor cleanse the conscience; it was a mere painting, a representation of a worthier and more powerful blood, namely the blood of Christ, which speaks of atonement and forgiveness far better than the old—that is, it actually effects, establishes, and brings it about. See Knatchbull <note>Sir Norton Knatchbull (1602–1685), English biblical critic.</note> and others.

<margin>Flesh and blood taken from the constitution of man.</margin>
Flesh and blood is often used to mean man, and the human body with the weaknesses of animal life that spring from our nature. Human nature, insofar as it is fed and maintained by the circulation of blood, fluids, food, drink, rest, and sleep, struggles with many bodily attacks, weaknesses, pains, illnesses, etc., called *psychikon* <note>original Greek: *ψυχικον*, meaning the "soulish" or natural life as opposed to the spiritual</note>, the animal or natural body (*1 Corinthians 15:50*). See, if it pleases you, Cappel, Gomarus, Witsius on...

# BLOOD

...on faith, *page 493. Vitringa's Sacred Observations, Part 3, page 164, and my own Explanation, page 168, Part I.* <note>Referring to Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a famous Dutch theologian.</note>

Blood is taken to represent man, tribe, or lineage, living through blood as the support and strength of the body; it also represents the animal life. *Acts 17:26: created and sprouted from one blood.* On this, the work of Walæus on the *New Testament* can be consulted, who brought forth pleasant insights from Jerome, Lactantius, and Theodoret.

->Virgil in the 2nd book of the Aeneid:<-

> *Sprung from what blood.* <note>original: "Quo sanguine cretus."</note> This is explained by Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Virgil.</note> as: *From what parents he was born, that is, from what elders he was produced.*

->The same in the 4th book.<-

> *Let an avenger one day arise from our bones.* <note>original: "Exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor."</note>

->That is:<-

> *May a punisher rise up from our remains.*

Upon which Servius says:

> *The Carthaginians say that descendants arise from the bones, whom we say come from the blood. That is, the Carthaginians believe that posterity comes from the bone, whereas we say they come from the blood.*

->The same<-

> — *A race descended from the high blood of the Gods.* <note>original: "Genus alto à sanguine Divum."</note>

->That is:<-

> *A tribe sprouted from the exalted blood of the gods.*

->Also:<-

> *Thus the lineage of both branches from the same blood.* <note>original: "Sic genus amborum se sanguine findit ab uno."</note>

->That is:<-

> *The family of both thus springs from the very same blood.*

<margin>Leech.</margin>
But let us conclude this chapter with the leech, called *Sanguisuga* or *Hirudo* in Latin, of which we read in *Proverbs 30:15: the leech has two daughters, crying Give, Give.*

<margin>Applications.</margin>
I have noticed that various interpretations and applications have been made regarding this passage. Some think here of the bloodthirsty Devil, the murderer of men from the beginning (*John 8:44*); they attribute to him two daughters, Heresy and Godlessness: or Death and the Grave.

It is said that the leech is double-tongued, just as Satan thinks and pretends one thing, but means another (*Genesis 3:4, 2 Corinthians 11:3*).

<margin>Opinion of Jerome.</margin>
Jerome was partly in agreement with this when he said that Satan sinned insatiably and recommended sin: that his two married daughters among mankind were Squandering and Greed: for a greedy man never has enough, and a squanderer wastes even the fullest purses.

It is said that the Leech is a very small water creature, which, having attached itself to the body of a man by its snout, sucks blood until it is full—indeed, so full that it sometimes bursts from it.

<column-break/>

Horace, at the end of his *Art of Poetry*:

> *A leech that will not leave the skin unless it is full of blood.* <note>original: "Non missura cutem, nisi plena cruoris hirudo."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Whose skin he does not leave,*
> *Until first satisfied with their blood, like a leech.*

Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar.</note> in *Hierozoïcon 799*, etc., seems to understand this as God's eternal predestination and arrangement over man’s death and departure. However, Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a celebrated Hebraist.</note> in *Masoreth* is of the opinion that the leech is a symbol of a greedy person, who does not perform even the smallest service or kindness for the lowly without aiming for double profit in return, and who does not rest until he has sucked someone dry.

One would find many who share this opinion and judgment.

->FLOWER, FLOWERS, נִצָּנִים ,פֶּרַח ,עַיִן<-
<note>Hebrew terms for flowers: nitzanim (blossoms), perach (flower/bloom), and ayin (eye/appearance).</note>
->*ἄνθος, flos.*<-
<note>Greek *anthos* and Latin *flos* both mean flower.</note>

<margin>Nature of flowers.</margin>
Flowers, whether they come from seed, plants, or bulbs, are cultivated: whether they grow in the wild or are kept in gardens for pleasure, scent, and decoration, etc.; they possess, as fruits of the earth, more or less beauty, grace, scent, stature, and durability.

I shall not deal with them at great length, for various kinds will appear throughout this work.

In my opinion, it is also not necessary for me to deal extensively with the ceremonial uses of flowers.

What fuss was made over the plucking of pleasant little flowers with tender fingers!

Virgil:

> *Like a flower culled by a maiden's thumb*
> *Which mother earth no longer nourishes.* <note>original: "Qualem virgineo demessum pollice florem / Non jam mater alit tellus."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Like a May-flower, fading away,*
> *Snatched from its stem by a maiden's hand, so it seems,*
> *Since it is no longer nourished by the earth.*

<margin>Flower wreaths for feasts.</margin>
It was customary to weave them around the heads of guests: and sometimes the drinking cups were garlanded with them. See *Pascal on Crowns, Book 2, Chapter 2* and *Hofmann’s Universal Lexicon.*

<margin>Flower wreath as a sign of a maiden bride. Victors strewn with flowers.</margin>
A woven crown was the sign of a bride who was still a virgin but was about to be married. *Pascal, Book 2, Chapter 15, pages 118-125*, etc.

How victors were strewn with flowers on the road as a sign of joy and triumph can be seen in *Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 6, Chapter 6; Curtius, Book 5, Chapter 1*, and others.

<margin>Also the burial places.</margin>
Perhaps as a sign of frailty and transience, burial places were strewn with flowers in ancient times. *Virgil* in the *5th Book* of the *Aeneid, verse 79:*

> *Here he duly pours two bowls of pure wine to Bacchus,*
> *Two of fresh milk, two of sacred blood:*
> *And scatters purple flowers, and speaks such words.* <note>original: "Hic duo rite mero libans carchesia Baccho / Fundit humi, duo lacte novo, duo sanguine sacro: / Purpureosque jacit flores, ac talia fatur."</note>

# FLOWERS

->That is:<-

> Two jugs of wine he poured out as a holy duty on the ground,
> As an offering for the grave, raised high from the earth;
> Two more of fresh milk, two more, according to their worth,
> Consecrated and full of blood: and, scattering all around
> Roses upon the grave, he spoke while everyone stood nearby.

->The same in Book VI:<- <note>Referring to Virgil’s Aeneid, Book VI, where Aeneas sees the spirit of his young descendant Marcellus.</note>

> — — — Give lilies with full hands:
> Let me scatter purple flowers, and at least heap these
> gifts upon the soul of my descendant. <note>original: "Manibus date lilia plenis: Purpureos spargam flores, animamque nepotis His saltem accumulem donis."</note>

->That is:<-

> Bring lilies, yes, pluck whole beds of them,
> That I may strew the noble grave with purple hue
> And flowers, and adorn my descendant’s corpse with this gift.

<margin>Select expressions signified by flowers.</margin>
Flowers, *flores*, are the name given to choice words and reasons, selected, pleasant, and decorative expressions. *Paschalius on Crowns, Book II, page 119.* <note>Charles Paschal (1547–1625) was an author who wrote a famous treatise on the history and symbolism of wreaths and crowns.</note>

A *flower* is also the "bloom," the "pick of the crop," the most flourishing part: the strength of a person's youth, of the nobility, of manhood, etc.

<margin>Fragility of flowers.</margin>
To avoid further complexity and expansion, we generally observe this about flowers: they are usually of short duration and standing, and by heat, drought, excessive moisture, and strong winds, they easily wither, fade, and fall off. However, one flower possesses more beauty, pleasantness, scent, and permanence than another.

<margin>An emblem of human fragility.</margin>
In these various respects, it seems to me, one could regard flowers as emblems of human weakness, transience, vanity, and instability: and through the elegance which flowers possess more or less—the outward bloom, ornament, beauty, wealth, status, splendor, privileges, etc.—all of which also wither, fade, and perish together, *Job 14:1, 2; Psalm 103:15, 16.* These were put into verse by Buchanan <note>George Buchanan (1506–1582) was a Scottish scholar famous for his Latin paraphrases of the Psalms.</note> as follows:

> *Like the grass, the beauty of a nursing boy*
> *Comes forth, and matures in a hidden age,*
> *Until it falls like dried hay*
> *Under the scythe of old age.*
> *Or like a flower blooming with Tyrian*
> *Purple, when it has smiled with a modest, serene*
> *Countenance, it suddenly collapses*
> *At the breath of the warm South wind.* <note>original: "Herba ceu, lactens pueri venustas... Concidit Austri."</note>

In our Dutch language, Joan Six van Chandelier <note>A 17th-century Dutch poet known for his realistic and often somber verse.</note> expressed it thus:

> *Look closely at man: his best days are alike.*
> *They resemble the grass, which is quickly mown down.*
> *He blooms for a while, like a flower in the field;*
> *Which, should harsh winds pass over it,*
> *Is no more, its place knows neither flower nor leaf,*
> *Though it stood so proudly adorned just a moment ago.*

See *Isaiah 5:4, 28:1, and 40:6; James 1:10, 11; 1 Peter 1:24.*

Stobaeus shows the same. See *Paschalius on Crowns, page 130.* Pliny, *Book XXI, Chapter 1*: The earth produces flowers and scents daily, as is manifest, as a great warning to men, that those things which bloom most spectacularly wither most

<column-break/>

quickly. <note>original: "Terra magna... cele-riter marescere." Pliny the Elder was a Roman naturalist.</note> That is: *the earth daily brings forth flowers and scents, as is evident: as a great warning to people, that the things which bloom most proudly wither the soonest.* See *Clement of Alexandria, The Instructor, Book II, Chapter 8.* Ausonius: <note>A 4th-century Roman poet.</note>

> *Gather the roses, maiden, while the flower is fresh and youth is new,*
> *And be mindful that your own time hurries away just so.* <note>original: "Collige virgo rosas dum flos novus... ævum sic properare tuum."</note>

->That is:<-

> *O maiden, pluck roses, while it is permitted to you,*
> *And think on the approach of your old age.*

See *Propertius, Book II; Paschalius on Crowns, pages 131, 132.*

<margin>Flowers as symbols of the believers.</margin>
Setting aside the transience that all people have in common: one can regard beautiful, fragrant, and pleasant flowers as symbols of the believers, who grow while planted in the garden of the church—whereas weeds, thistles, and thorns are symbols of the ungracious. These flowers represent their beautiful gifts of grace, virtues, abilities, good words, and works, wrought in them by the Spirit of Christ as a spirit of faith, knowledge, rebirth, and sanctification. *Song of Solomon 2:12; Hosea 14:7; 2 Corinthians 2:15, 16.*

EXTINGUISH, TO QUENCH, *to be quenched, to go out*. <term>to put out</term> <note>original Hebrew: כבה</note>, <term>to be extinguished</term> <note>original Hebrew: נרעך</note>, <term>to flicker out</term> <note>original Hebrew: דעך</note>, <term>to quench</term> <note>original Greek: σβεννύω/σβέννυμι</note>, *exstinguo, exstinguor*.

These words and expressions, arising from their common use, undoubtedly presuppose that there are some burning materials: fire, candles, lamps, torches, which, while burning and giving off light and heat, are consumed, perish, are stifled, and are robbed of their warmth and light.

That such a thing is taken figuratively and applied to something else, I think no one will dare to deny. <margin>Application.</margin>

TO EXTINGUISH and QUENCH can at least mean to uproot, destroy, or cause something to cease and perish, as in *Isaiah 43:17*, where an allusion seems to be made to the fall and judgment of Pharaoh, with his army that pursued God's Israel as enemies, smothered in the Red Sea. See *Gulichius’s Compendium, Vitringa on Isaiah, etc.*

<margin>Dying signified by extinguishing.</margin>
This is also used when speaking of someone, not only who dies in general, but also of someone who, as they say, does not die their own natural death, but a violent death, and who is killed: *Terence in The Brothers, Act III, scene 2.* <note>Terence was a Roman playwright of the 2nd century BCE.</note>

> *I would first extinguish the light of life in that one,*
> *Who brought forth that wickedness.* <note>original: "Semi animam primum extinguereem ipsi..."</note>

->That is:<-

> *My wrath is not to be quenched.*
> *I would first extinguish the light of life of the old man,*
> *Who brought this rogue into the world.*

Again in *The Mother-in-Law, Act V, Scene 1:*

> *And because of that matter, he secretly wanted to extinguish*
> *The boy who was born.* <note>original: "Puerumque ob eam rem clam voluit... extinguere."</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of "flowers" as a symbol of fragility to the concept of "extinguishing" (Dutch: *blussen* or *uitbluffen*), specifically regarding the "light of life" and the symbolism of lamps and coals in biblical and classical texts.</meta>

# TO EXTINGUISH

->That is:<-

->*And therefore she wished to extinguish the life-light of the newborn child.*<-

<margin>The view of the ancients regarding souls.</margin> It has been noted by commentators that the ancients believed the soul was fire. Whatever the case may have been, the terms "to quench" and "to extinguish" do not always occur in their literal sense in various passages. In *2 Samuel 14:7*, we read: *And so they shall quench my coal which is left, and shall leave to my husband neither name nor remainder upon the earth.*

<margin>Note from Burman.</margin> On this history—in which the wise woman of Tekoa played her role so wonderfully before David to obtain a pardon for Absalom—Burman <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679) was a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> noted the following: "This woman, with all her wisdom, comes to the King and presents her case before him, which it pleased the Holy Spirit to include entirely in this history: which is also here and there somewhat obscure and confused, so that it must be considered carefully. She then, 1. coming to the king with proper reverence and prostrating herself, says to him with a *Hosanna*: 'Save, O King,' verse 4, which seems to have been the common formula for those seeking the King’s grace. *2 Kings 6:26* and *1 Chronicles 16:35.* 2. She arranges her speech in a parable, as a widow who consequently ought to be helped before others: who had two sons, one of whom killed the other in the field, without any mediator present, and thus without witnesses—that is, she means to say, in self-defense—verse 5, 6, just as Absalom had done to Amnon. She complains further that she stood in great danger from the whole family, or the blood-avenger within it, who demanded the death of her remaining son, unless the King provided help; as if wanting to *quench her coal which was still left*, to leave her husband no name or remnant on the earth, verse 7. She calls him her *remaining coal*—that is, her necessary helper and comforter, though very weak and small, just as a remaining coal in the midst of the ashes gives only a little fire and warmth, and yet is necessary to start a fire again."

*2 Samuel 21:17.* There, the men of David say to David—doubtless weary and exhausted from pursuing the Philistines, and having been in great danger of their lives—*You shall go out no more with us to battle, that you quench not the lamp of Israel.* (See under LAMP.) That is, says Burman, that you do not perish, you who are the light, the joy, and the glory of Israel, and who guides Israel with counsel and deed.

In *Job 17:1*, it is read: *My breath is corrupt, my days are extinguished, the graves are ready for me.* There Job seems overwhelmed with sorrow, that his desire, courage, and strength had vanished; that, being robbed of everything and exhausted to the extreme by sorrow, poverty, and mockery, he was as good as dead, counted among the deceased, and in short, was about to go to the grave.

"I shall *extinguish* you" means little less than to kill, to slay, or to cause to perish.

And in such an extreme sense of a person's eradication, it is not strictly necessary to understand the following texts; one can likely suffice in most cases by taking them in the sense of being deprived of a former state, luster, wealth, honor, esteem, or beauty—things which many value above life. # EXTINGUISHING. BOAZ. <note>Hebrew: *Boaz*</note>

...doubt is signified by this, that some Christian churches, sharing that name with others, would finally find that they lacked the true and right Christian doctrine and godliness. The oil here is a symbol of that which can be considered the substance of light—that is, the preaching of the Gospel truth and the practice of virtue, through which everyone can make themselves pleasing to Jesus Christ when He comes to perfect His church, and by which one can light the way for others toward eternal life. Thus, the oil here is a symbol of the true and pure Christian life. Some Christians will finally find that they lack this oil, such as the Socinians <note>The Socinians were a sect that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ, emphasizing rationalism.</note> and the Roman Catholics. They will see that they do not have as much oil in their lamps as they need to receive Christ. Indeed, there is a great lack and scarcity of thorough knowledge of the doctrines of faith among the Roman Catholics. The common people among them have no oil in their lamps; that is, they are stuck in a thick ignorance concerning Christian doctrine and are led astray by certain outward ceremonies that are idolatrous and superstitious, and in no way beneficial to salvation. The scholars among them decorate their lamps outwardly, as we are willing to admit. They publish excellent works for the benefit of Christianity. But they lack oil. Indeed, they do not have oil in such measure as is necessary to receive Christ. They do not have as pure a confession of the doctrine of truth as Jesus Christ requires of His own. They defend errors concerning the Holy Scriptures, justification, transubstantiation <note>original: "verzelfstandiginge"</note>, etc., and they cherish the people in a thick ignorance. The same must be said of the Socinians. They have something of Christ, but not such a doctrine by which they can make themselves pleasing to Him. They will realize this lack in due time, when the Lord shall come to judge the matter of pure religion, etc.

*Ephesians 6:16.* One reads of the *extinguishing of the fiery darts of the wicked.* Regarding this, see under ARROWS and under SHIELD.

It is written in *1 Thessalonians 5:19: Quench not the Spirit.* Paul, assuming that the Spirit—in a certain respect, like the fire on the altar in *Leviticus 6:12, 13*—could be dampened, stifled, and extinguished, exhorts the Thessalonians to ensure that they do not extinguish Him, neither in themselves, nor in their fellow Christians, nor in their teachers and leaders. Instead, by way of contrast, they should rather stir up, nurture, and fan the flame.

Scholars understand here (as often happens) that the finder, giver, and master-worker is the Holy Spirit, along with His operations, fruits, and gifts of grace, as in *Isaiah 35:4; Joel 2,* and as appears in *John 7:37, 38, 39; Isaiah 11:2; 2 Corinthians 4:13; 2 Timothy 1:7.* One may consult the learned writers on this: for my plan, regarding both the entire letter and this exhortation, would be too long to include here.

*Hebrews 11:34. quenched the violence of fire.* This divine biblical event is described at length in *Daniel chapter 3*, with singular emphasis, regarding Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, three of his companions. See Junius, Gejerus on Daniel; Cocceius, Strefo, Sebastian Schmidt, Gerhard, d’Outrein on the Epistle to the Hebrews. <note>These are prominent 16th and 17th-century biblical commentators and theologians.</note>

<column-break/>

This name we know from the book of *Ruth*; it was the name of a wealthy man in Bethlehem who, praising Ruth, chose her as his bride and wife, even though she possessed no worldly means and was a Moabitess.

It is also the name of one of the two pillars that Solomon built and had placed at the entrance of the sanctuary, *1 Kings 7; 2 Kings 25; Jeremiah 52,* etc. See under JACHIN.

This name signifies strength, "in him is strength," or power; and it is taken to mean ability or riches, and used for someone who is capable.

Thus, it was truly appropriate for this man, as one of the richest and most blessed in Bethlehem.

Of the occasion for the courtship, the awakening of love, and the marriage between Boaz and Ruth, one may read in the book of Ruth. See also under RUTH. I shall not mix everything together, lest I prematurely trim the material for the future. My intention here is to observe something of the relationship between Boaz and Christ; and to this end, I will first present the short reflections and elaborations of a few scholars.

<margin>Reflections of the scholars.</margin>
Burman, writing on Ruth, stated: "Boaz, like all the redeemers <note>original: "loffers," referring to the 'Kinsman Redeemer' or *Goel* in Hebrew law</note> of the Old Testament, presents to us our true Redeemer and blood-relative Jesus Christ, who became our neighbor (*Hebrews 2:14*) to redeem us as His own from our spiritual poverty and the distress of sin, the devil, and death, and to accept us as His own, His bride and beloved; He who also did not rest until He had finished this matter (*John 19:30*), to whom we, in all the gravity of temptation, in necessity and death, may say: *spread your wing over us, for you are the Redeemer* (*Job 19:25*)." Bierman noted it as a symbol of the calling of the Gentiles: saying in his *Moses and Christ* that just as Boaz was Ruth's redeemer, blood-relative, and *Goel*, so Christ is the Redeemer of both Jews and Gentiles. Thus He is called our brother in *Hebrews 2*, and particularly in the New Testament, He is the one who has betrothed them, who rescues them as His bride and people, accepts, protects, and comforts them; thus He makes them partakers of His goods and spreads the wings of His love over them to multiply them and to raise up spiritual seed.

I note then, as in Boaz, so in Christ, these things and practical applications.

<margin>Transferal of Boaz to Christ.</margin>
a. That the name Boaz, meaning strength or "in him is strength," is rightly applied to Christ the God-man, the strength of God (*Psalm 45; Isaiah 9:5; 27; 45; and 63*).
b. That He was rich and great, although He behaved very humbly on earth, as the King of all kings: the Lord and heir of all things.
c. Boaz, however rich, conducted himself humbly and poorly, sleeping on the threshing floor, on the straw, on a mat: Christ showed poverty and humility in all things, though He was rich (*Matthew 28; 2 Corinthians 8:9; Hebrews 1; Revelation 17 and 19; Psalm 45*).

Boaz was devoted to agriculture, and the Lord wonderfully blessed his labor.

Christ, although He never (to our knowledge) tilled a literal field, nonetheless cultivated that which I have represented as the field...

It was truly something remarkable that a rich man fell in love with a poor Moabite woman, whom he made rich by uniting her with him through marriage, acting as her redeemer and next of kin.

Certainly, just as Jesus's office of redeemer—through the assumption of our nature—is all the more wonderful because He, who was revealed in the flesh, was, is, and unchangeably remains God (*John 1, 1 Timothy 3:16*), so His love has fallen upon us children of men, who were sinful, deformed, poor, miserable, and wretched: for which reason He is all the more adorable and wonderful, *Psalm 69, 2 Corinthians 5,* etc.

Through this, He makes us—who had nothing but poverty and debt—rich (*2 Corinthians 8, Psalm 45, Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 3*) and raises us up to the most glorious and adorned state, *Psalm 45, 1 Peter 2:9, Revelation 1 and 5.*

But Boaz did not redeem Ruth until the nearest in blood, or the one first in the office of redeemer, had shown his unwillingness and inability in the presence of the elders. And so, the shoe was pulled off the first man, <note>This refers to the ancient "Halizah" ceremony described in Ruth 4, where removing a shoe symbolized the transfer of property rights or the refusal to fulfill a legal obligation.</note> leaving his right and power over everything to Boaz, *Ruth Chapter 4.*

Jesus began His office of redeemer before the weakness of the law, and of its advocates and drivers—indeed, of all flesh—had been openly revealed, *Psalm 40, Romans 1, 2, 3-8, Hebrews 10,* etc.

On which occasion He also "un-shoed" the Jewish Masters <note>original: "Bagnatim," likely a transliteration of the Hebrew *Be'alim*, meaning lords, masters, or legal possessors.</note> and took from them the fundamental cause of their claim, *Romans 7,* and made them all die, *Psalm 8:2,* not wishing that, on any grounds, any man should retain a right to claim His inheritance and promise, desiring to be, and to be held as, the only husband and Lord, *Colossians 2, 1 Corinthians 8:6.*

->BOOK, MEMORIAL BOOK, BOOK of LIFE, of the LAMB, etc.<-

<margin>Books of the ancients.</margin>It is known to the learned that the manner of writing, the materials of books, and the form of books in ancient times do not correspond at all with ours today. For in ancient times, people used to write on the bark of trees, leaves, on lead, in wax, on stones, ivory, and on the inner bark <term>inner bark (liber): the thin layer between the wood and the outer bark, from which the Latin word for book, "liber," is derived</term> or the thin membrane lying between the wood and the outer bark or rind of the tree: on parchments, etc., on the skins and fleeces of animals, and even on the intestines and guts of wild beasts. Thus, it is said that in the time of Emperor Basil, the verses of Homer, which make up his *Iliad* and *Odyssey*, were written on a dragon’s gut <note>This likely refers to a large serpent skin or intestine, a legendary artifact once kept in the Library of Constantinople.</note> of 120 feet long.

The shape of books, and their outward appearance and arrangement, was not the same as today's. One rolled the writing together into a circle. For this reason, one reads of the *Roll of the book*, or the rolled book, which was unrolled when it was to be read, called a *Megilla* <note>original: "Megilla," the Hebrew word for a scroll.</note>, *Isaiah 34, Psalm 40.* See *Salmuth in Pancirollus, Part II, Title XIII; Martianus Capella, On the Marriage of Philology, Book II; Saldenus, On Books, Their Use and Abuse, pages 5, 6, 7, etc.*

It is certain that one must first take the word BOOK in its literal sense, wherever one can with ground

<column-break/>

and reason: and in such a way, one can understand by it either the whole of Scripture or the specific parts thereof, according to whether one finds the distinct divisions made in the Word of God or in the writings of the Jews, sometimes understood narrowly and sometimes more broadly.

In which book of Holy Scripture, God has made known Himself, His nature, His counsel, will, and good pleasure, and what was necessary for the children of men to know, believe, practice, and avoid for their salvation, as in *Isaiah 34:16*; which was formerly obscure but is now presented more clearly through the Gospel, *Romans 1:2 and 2:12-16, 2 Peter 1:19, 20, 21, Exodus 24:7,* where it is taken somewhat more narrowly.

<margin>The Universe called a Book.</margin>It is quite metaphorical when one makes a book of the entire universe, in which one reads God's eternal power and divinity through larger and finer letters, just as even the smallest herb points to its Maker; so that if someone merely wishes to open their eyes, they cannot help but see, read, and find God and His virtues in the theater of nature, *Romans 1:19, 20, Psalm 19, Romans 10.* The comparison between a book and the heaven, or the heavens, is found in *Isaiah 34:4 and Revelation 6:14,* where there seems to be an allusion to the ancient rolling up of inscribed parchments and leaves, and the winding with a thread or other binding: or that they were rolled onto a long hand-stick of round shape. This is now applied by some to the end of the world, as in *2 Peter 3:10,* but others apply it to the figurative heaven of the Jewish ecclesiastical and civil state: others to that of the state of the Antichrist, about which I have no desire to dispute with anyone. But meanwhile, the point is that the entire universe has been regarded from olden times as a Book of God, and a theater of His virtues and perfections—indeed, as a textbook. Thus writes Basil: <note>original Greek: "παιδευτήριον τῆς θεογνωσίας, καὶ ψυχῶν λογικῶν διδασκαλεῖον"</note> *A school for the instruction in the knowledge of God, and a teaching-place for rational souls.* See *Visscher's Christian Thoughts, in folio, page 1063.*

I can certainly concede that one may call the created all, the visible world, the general textbook and instruction-book, insofar as one can observe many of God's virtues and perfections in His works and government, *Job 38, Psalm 19, Isaiah 40, Romans 1, Acts 14:17,* etc.

<margin>Book of life.</margin>But this is not the *Book of Life*, or *of the Lamb*, in which the actual names are written, on account of which inscription one can consider oneself truly blessed: that <note>referring back to nature</note> is a general textbook and instruction-book for all. There, one learns of one's absolute natural dependence on God: one's neediness: God's sufficiency, His government of and influence upon essential existence and actions.

But one does not find therein—nor does one read therefrom—how the God of all-sufficiency wills to be, and shall be, according to the propriety of His virtues and with the most extensive demonstration and revelation of them, a God of the sinful, miserable, damnable, and powerless sinner in His Son, the Lamb: to whom He has become such; and from which one can know it and know Him.
