# **BOOK.**

The book of the lamb: of the names written in the book of life; of the names to be blotted out from it; that sins are in God's memorial book; that the book is hung with seals; that it is closed and opened by the breaking of the seals; that it is written on the front and on the back, and much more besides.

That the all-knowing God—to whom all things are naked and open, and who is a pure and simple spirit—has no actual book or books, is not difficult to grasp. However, since it pleases God's Spirit to speak with us children of men as if by stammering, <note>The author uses "stamelen" (to stammer) to describe the concept of "divine accommodation," where God adapts His infinite nature into simple human metaphors so we can understand Him.</note> and to present what is in God and in His works under the image of what we perceive among ourselves in a certain respect, it will not be useless for us to investigate what these various terms mentioned above may give us to understand.

<margin>God's book.</margin>
In investigating such things, I find that by the "general book of Jehovah" one generally understands the internal, eternal, and firm science, or knowledge, which the Lord has of that which He has determined by the will of His decree shall or shall not be in time.

And since everything happens in time according to His counsel and will—not without His influence and active governance—so that the past, the present, and the future, man’s doing and leaving, even the inner depths of his heart are known to Him, so that nothing can escape Him (much less than him who records everything in his daily register and book, and strictly enters receipts and expenditures into the book), one sees that theologians call it "God's book." Holy Scripture likewise mentions God's memorial book and of something being written therein. *Psalm 56:8, Psalm 139:16, Matthew 3:16, Isaiah 65:6, and Jeremiah 17:1, etc.* <note>The author likely cites Psalm 56:8 regarding tears in a bottle/book and Psalm 139:16 regarding days fashioned before they existed.</note>

When one further observes that the Lord has from eternity in, by, and through Himself decided and firmly determined the outcome and the end of His rational creatures, then God's eternal counsel, decree, and purpose regarding some specific and certain persons (known to Him by name) to be brought to salvation—or to His fellowship in Christ His Son through the Holy Spirit—is called the **Book of Life**, and with further specification, the **Book of the Lamb**. *Daniel 12, Luke 10, Philippians 4, Revelation 13, 17, 20, 21, etc.*

<margin>Book of the Lamb.</margin>
Regarding what has been said, I further note that these expressions can indeed be compared to daily registers of events and the recording of things heard and seen (for man's head is no steel record-keeper), or to the books of merchants kept by their bookkeepers for receipts, expenditures, purchases, and sales—all to be closed at the set time and to strike a balance. But when this is applied to God, an infinite, pure, and simple spirit, it must represent the most perfect and intimate knowledge and consciousness, or the presence of all that has been, is, and shall be. *Psalm 139, Hebrews 4.*

<margin>Application.</margin>
I know well that one can call God's written Word, contained in the books of the Old and New Testaments, "God's book," in which the Lord has caused His counsel of peace, decrees, election, and rejection to be described and recorded. It is also like a daily register of what He has done from time to time in the world and concerning His people; one can also view it in part as a book of prophecy regarding the future; and it is a book of instruction in the world of great usefulness, both for true wisdom and godliness. *Psalm 12:6, 119, 2 Timothy 3:16, 2 Peter 1:19, 20, 21.*

<column-break/>

I would also be able to provide various reasons why that book may be called the **Book of the Lamb**, as it mentions the Lamb and the "antitype" <note>An "antitype" is the New Testament fulfillment of an Old Testament "type" or symbol. Here, Christ is the fulfillment of the sacrificial lambs of the Law.</note> of the lambs, *Psalm 40, John 1:29, and 5:39*; recording His life and conduct as God's Lamb, bearing and taking away the sins of the world; being the pit and marrow, the spirit of everything that appears in Moses, the Prophets, Evangelists, and Apostles; indicating how sinners, through faith in and obedience to Him, the Son, shall enter into eternal life, *John 3:16-36*. Nevertheless, despite these and other reasons, I do not believe that by "the Book of Life of the Lamb" one must understand the Bible, seeing as the explicit names of the elect, given to the Lamb, do not appear in it.

I have already said, and I repeat it once more, that if one properly awakens the idea of God within us, keeps it alive, and follows it accurately—as a simple, infinite, and most perfect spirit—one immediately understands that nothing material, physical, or finite serves or aids Him. Consequently, once one has rightly understood and presupposed that God's eternal and ever-remaining will is the root of all things, of their becoming, their qualities, etc., and that God is perfectly and most inwardly conscious of His will, then one also understands immediately that God, unlike forgetful man, in no way requires a memorial or record book.

However, one will perhaps not mismanage one's concepts regarding the Divine, and may be helped, when one imagines two books, namely:
> A. A Great and General Book.
> B. A Special Book.

<margin>General book.</margin>
By the Great and General Book, I understand God's eternal, internal, and most perfect knowledge of all that He has decreed and purposed to do Himself, and to command His creatures: of all that shall happen, along with the time, manner, and circumstances.

<margin>Special book.</margin>
<margin>List of names of the elect.</margin>
By God's Special Book, I understand the list of names, if I may speak thus, of the elect unto eternal life; <note>original: "ספרחיים" (Sefer Hayyim)</note> <gloss>the Book of Life</gloss>. For when one observes that all His works are known to God from eternity, then one can understand that He has firmly established in, by, and through Himself which persons He will bring out of the entire human race—through His Spirit, Word, and instrumental means—to knowledge, faith, and obedience in and to His Son, the fountain and cause of eternal righteousness and salvation.

These, now ordained unto eternal life in His Son, are said to be written in the Book of Life and of the Lamb, being known to God by name, as surely, firmly, and vividly as if He had them on a list and roll of names, and (so as not to forget them, as men do) read them daily and inspected them accurately; concerning which these following expressions also pertain, *Daniel 12:1. all*

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the "Book of Life." # **BOOK.**

1. *...all who are found written in the book, Malachi 3:16. A book of remembrance was written before His face; Luke 10:20. but rather rejoice that your names are written in heaven; 2 Timothy 2:19. the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are His.*

When we find that this eternal, divine, supreme, and sovereign election—the establishment of certain persons, determined by Him, to be brought to salvation and life in, with, and through His Son—bears the name of the "Book of Life" (and not of death), indeed the "Book of Life of the Lamb," it surely has one or more of the following reasons:

A. Because this list and prepared roll of names of those chosen in Christ for eternal life belongs to the Son as well as the Father, whose wills are one and the same, as they are one in essence. *John 5:10, Philippians 2, etc.*

B. However, one can also give these specific reasons for it, beyond the single, identical, eternal, and gracious—indeed, essential—will of the three adorable Divine Persons:

a. That God’s decree concerning these persons and their salvation is established in the Son. *Ephesians 4:5, <note>The author likely means Ephesians 1:4-5, which discusses election in Christ.</note> Matthew 25.*

b. Who, on behalf of these people, was recorded and promised to become the most perfect fulfillment <term>antitype|The person or thing represented by an earlier symbol or "type." In this context, the sacrificial lambs of the Old Testament are the "types" and Jesus is the "antitype."</term> of the sacrificial lambs, for their persons and their sins: just as He, being described and identified as such, conducted Himself. *Job 33, Psalm 40, Isaiah 53, John 1:29, 1 Corinthians 5:7, 1 Peter 1, etc.*

c. Just as no one actually receives or partakes in righteousness and life except through faith in and obedience to Him. *Psalm 36:20, John 14:6, Acts 4:12, John 3:16-36.*

d. This is why this union is so close, intimate, and mutual; He makes them alive by the Spirit of faith, in, with, and through Himself, and brings them into the possession of life within His union and fellowship. Therefore, He is called the "fountain of life," *Psalm 36:20,* the "way, the truth, and the life," *John 14:6.* It is said that our life is hidden in Him; that He is the "tree of life," *Revelation 3:22,* and that He gives His sheep eternal life, *Psalm 10, <note>Likely referring to the Good Shepherd passages in John 10.</note>* as His co-heirs. *Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 3, Hebrews 2, etc. Luke 12:32, Revelation 3.*

<margin>
Observation.
</margin>

e. And who could object if we follow with this observation: that the Son of God, being the Lamb on earth, served as a "Book," a portrait, a transcript, and an example to the world of how sinners—according to the will of God the Father—must and shall attain salvation and life as heirs of glory. Regarding this, see *John 14:6, Matthew 11:28, 29, Hebrews 12:12, 1 Peter 2:21.*

These reasons also pertain to the "Book of Life of the Lamb."

Now, I shall leave aside whether this naming occurred by looking at the actions of military commanders in picking out, writing down, and reviewing their soldiers—from which comes the phrase *to enroll soldiers* <note>original Latin: "conscribere milites"</note>—that is, to recruit people so as to read them out from the list and roll during the muster.

Or whether this is said with respect to those who were recorded among good friends, even the most exceptional ones, so as not to forget them and to receive them based on their motto or sign of hospitality. Or whether one might have in view here the list and roll of names of citizens who enjoyed the privileges of citizenship and were recognized as citizens; or the appointment by a last will and written declaration of someone as an heir; or the generations of Israel, according to their houses, to distinguish the families and ancestral estates in Canaan and keep them alive until the Messiah. And whether this is transferred to the spiritual military service under the supreme captain Jesus Christ, or to the inheritance of the heavenly Canaan, and those who were born in Zion, in the city of God, *Psalm 87:7, Hebrews 12, etc.*—I will not determine that here. Let each judge which may best apply.

In the meantime, however, certain parties <note>Refers to the Arminians or Remonstrants, who argued that believers could lose their salvation.</note> would gladly use some scriptural phrases concerning "books" to argue for the "falling away of the saints." For example: they bring up the wish and request of Moses, the man of God, in *Exodus 32*; the wish and prayer of David and the church in *Psalm 69:29*; and the threat in *Revelation 22.*

To demonstrate the immutability of God’s counsel and the stability of the state of the elect, I will not use the technical arguments of theologians; one can look those up elsewhere. I will stand on the passages themselves, such as *Exodus 32:32*, where Moses did not name the "Book of Life" or the recording for the inheritance of eternal life. Every "book of God" is not necessarily the "Book of Eternal Life." Much rather, he speaks of his temporal life, with which he sought to atone for the threatened punishment of temporal death and extermination; he wished rather to miss the entrance into and the co-inheritance of Canaan than that so many in Israel should perish by death as a punishment. For his offer may and must be judged as being in accord with the divine threat in *verses 10, 34-35*, as in another case in *Numbers 11:15.*

And here Moses expresses his burning and heroic sigh and love for the preservation of the people more strongly than he defines what is actually possible or not on God’s part with respect to His counsel and purpose. Certainly, Moses saw that if God destroyed His people, it would give Pharaoh and their enemies the opportunity to blaspheme the name of the God of Israel, which he wished to turn away as much as possible, so that they might not say: "The Lord could not help them; He was disgusted by them." The report of this miracle <note>The Exodus from Egypt.</note> would have completely vanished.

Furthermore, who has any ground to think of Moses—the most famous man and greatest prophet, so enlightened and intimate with the Lord—that while he knew beforehand that the counsel and divine purpose were firmer than any law of the Medes and Persians, he would nevertheless have believed (knowing it would never happen) that...

# **BOOK.**

The book of the lamb: of the names written in the book of life: of the names to be blotted out therefrom: that the sins are in God's book of remembrance: that the book is hung with seals: that it is closed, and is opened by the breaking of the seal: that it is written on the front and on the back, and so forth.

That the omniscient God—to whom all things are naked and open, and who is a pure and <term>simple spirit|In theology, "simple" means not composed of different parts; God is a singular, unified essence without internal division.</term>—has no actual physical book or books, is not difficult to grasp. However, since it pleases God’s Spirit to, as it were, <note>This "stammering" refers to the theological concept of "accommodation," where God speaks in simplified, human terms so that our limited minds can understand divine truths.</note> stammer with us children of men, and to represent what is in God and in His works under the symbol of what we perceive among ourselves, it will not be useless for us to investigate what these various terms mentioned above might signify.

<margin>God's book.</margin> In investigating this, I find that by the "general book of Jehovah," one understands the internal, eternal, and firm science, or knowledge, which the Lord has of that which He has determined by His decree shall be, or shall not be, in the course of time.

And since everything happens in time according to His counsel and will—not without His influence and active governance—so that the past, the present, and the future, man's deeds and omissions, and even the inner parts of his heart are known to Him, nothing can escape Him. This is even more precise than a man who records everything in his journal and book, strictly noting every receipt and expenditure. Thus, we see that theologians call it "God's book," and that Holy Scripture mentions God's book of remembrance and of things written therein, *Psalms 56:8 and 139:16; Matthew 3:16; Isaiah 65:6; and Jeremiah 17:1, etc.* <note>The author cites Psalm LIX. 9, which in many older Dutch bibles corresponds to the modern Psalm 56:8: "You keep count of my wanderings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book?"</note>

If one then observes that the Lord has from eternity—in, by, and through Himself—decided and firmly determined the outcome and the end of His rational creatures, then God's eternal counsel, decree, and purpose to bring certain specific persons (known to Him by name) to salvation or to His fellowship in Christ His Son through the Holy Spirit, is called the "book of life," and with more specific definition, the "book of the Lamb." *Daniel 12; Luke 10; Philippians 4; Revelation 13, 17, 20, and 21, etc.*

<margin>Book of the Lamb.</margin> Regarding what has already been said, I note further that these expressions can indeed be compared to journals of events and the recording of things heard and seen—for the human head is no steel ledger—or to the books of merchants, kept by their bookkeepers to track receipts, expenditures, purchases, and sales, all in order to close the books at the appointed time and balance the scales. However, when this is applied to God—an infinite, pure, simple spirit—it must represent the most perfect and intimate knowledge and awareness of all that has been, is, and shall be. *Psalm 139; Hebrews 4.*

<margin>Application.</margin> I know well that one can call God's written word, contained in the books of the Old and New Testaments, "God's book," in which the Lord has had His counsel of peace, decrees, election, and rejection written down and recorded. It is also much like a journal of what He has done from time

<column-break/>

to time in the world and concerning His people. One can also consider it in part as a book of prophecy regarding the future; it is a book of instruction in the world of great usefulness, both for true wisdom and for godliness. *Psalms 12:19; 109; 2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:19, 20, 21.*

I would also be able to provide several reasons why that book <note>Meaning the Bible itself.</note> may be called the "book of the Lamb," as it tells of the lamb and the <term>antitype|The historical reality or person that fulfills a symbolic "type" from the past; here, Jesus is the reality foreshadowed by Old Testament sacrificial lambs.</term> of the lambs, *Psalm 40; John 1:29 and 5:39*, and of His life and deeds as God's lamb, bearing and taking away the sins of the world. It is the pit and marrow, the spirit of everything found in Moses, the Prophets, the Evangelists, and the Apostles, showing how sinners shall enter into eternal life through faith in and obedience to Him, the Son, *John 3:16-36.* Nevertheless, despite these and other reasons, I do not believe that by *that* book [the Bible], one should understand the "book of life of the Lamb," for the explicit names of the elect given to the Lamb do not appear in its pages.

I have already said, and I repeat it once more: when one properly awakens, vividly maintains, and accurately follows the concept of God within us as a simple, infinite, and most perfect spirit, one immediately understands that nothing material, physical, or finite serves or aids Him. Consequently, when it is rightly understood that God's eternal and always-unchanging will is the root of all things—of their coming into being and their qualities—and that God is perfectly and most intimately aware of His own will, then one understands that God, unlike forgetful man, in no way needs a book of remembrance or a record.

However, one will perhaps not manage one's concepts of the Divine poorly, and will be aided, if one imagines two books, namely:
->A. A Great and General Book.<-
->B. A Particular Book.<-

<margin>General book.</margin> By the "Great and General Book," I understand God's eternal, internal, and most perfect knowledge of all that He has decreed and purposed to do Himself, or to command His creatures: of all that shall happen, along with the time, manner, and circumstances.

<margin>Particular book of the elect.</margin> By "God's Particular Book," I understand the "list of names," so to speak, of those chosen for eternal life—the <note>original: ספר חיים (*Sefer Chayyim*)</note> **Book of Life.** I say "list of names" because if one observes that all His works are known to God from eternity, then one can understand that He has established in, by, and through Himself which persons He will bring from the whole human race (through His spirit, word, and instrumental means) to knowledge, faith, and obedience in and to His Son, the fountain and cause of eternal righteousness and salvation.

These who are ordained to eternal life in His Son are said to be written in the "book of life" and of the "lamb," and to be known to God by name. This is as certain, firm, and vivid as if He had them on a list or a roll of names and, so as not to forget them (as humans do), read them daily and looked them over accurately. It is regarding this concept that the following expressions are used: *Daniel 12:1. all*

# **BOOK.**

When we find that this eternal, Divine, supreme, and sovereign <term>election|The theological doctrine that God chooses specific individuals for salvation before the beginning of time.</term>—the establishing of certain persons determined by Him to be brought to salvation and life in, with, and through His Son—is called the "Book of Life" and not the "Book of Death," and indeed the "Book of Life of the Lamb," there is surely a reason for this.

A. Because this list and prepared roll of names of those chosen in Christ for eternal life belongs to the Son as much as to the Father; their will, according to their being one in essence, is one and the same. <note>original: "Joh. V. 10. Philip. II. enz."</note>

B. However, one can also give these following specific reasons, besides the single, identical, eternal, and gracious—indeed, essential—will of the three adorable Divine persons:

a. That God’s decree concerning these persons and their salvation is centered in the Son. <note>Ephesians 4:5, Matthew 25.</note>

b. Because the Son spoke for these people and promised to become the most perfect fulfillment <note>original: "tegenbeelt" (antitype/counter-image)</note> of the sacrificial lambs for their persons and sins; just as He, being described and identified as such, conducted Himself. <note>Job 33, Psalm 40, Isaiah 53, John 1:29, 1 Corinthians 5:7, 1 Peter 1, etc.</note>

c. Just as no one actually receives or partakes in righteousness and life except through faith in and obedience to Him. <note>Psalm 36:20, John 14:6, Acts 4:12, John 3:16-36.</note>

d. Why this union is so close, intimate, and mutual that He makes them alive through the spirit of faith—in, with, and through Himself—and brings them into the possession of life through His union and communion. Thus He is called the "fountain of life" <note>Psalm 36:20</note>, the "way, truth, and life" <note>John 14:6</note>; our life is hidden in Him; He is the "tree of life" <note>Revelation 3:22</note>; He gives His sheep eternal life <note>Psalm 10</note> as His fellow heirs. <note>Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 3, Hebrews 2, etc.; Luke 12:32, Revelation 3.</note>

Observation.

See regarding this: John 14:6, Matthew 11:28, 29, Hebrews 12:12, 1 Peter 2:21.

These reasons also pertain to the "Book of Life of the Lamb."

Now, whether this naming occurred by looking at the practices of military commanders in selecting and writing down—and reviewing—their soldiers, from which comes the phrase <note>original: "conscribere milites"</note> "to enroll soldiers"—that is, to recruit people so as to read them from the list and roll during the muster—I shall leave aside.

# **BOOK.**

...that he could be blotted out from the Divine book of life? <note>Referring to Exodus 32:32, where Moses asks God to blot him out of His book for the sake of the people.</note>

Or must one think of Moses, that by the sight of God’s righteous wrath—which had to take its course as far as the actual execution was concerned—and through his sighing and love for the people's release, he was so overwhelmed by emotion that he did not reason soundly in all respects? That is to say, he did not properly consider that God would not leave the guilty unpunished nor punish the innocent, and that He would not change His arrangement regarding the <term>vessels of wrath and mercy|A reference to Romans 9, describing those destined for judgment or for God's favor.</term>.

Or must one think that Moses—in order to express the greatness of the committed evil and his strong impulse for the people’s preservation, and thus to move God to mercy—spoke this under a "silent proposition," namely: (if it be possible) "well then, forgive them, and punish me."

Furthermore, if Moses wanted to be blotted out of God’s eternal book of life for the sake of Israel, he must have firmly assumed that Israel stood with God in that book of life. Otherwise, his own blotting out could offer no benefit for their remaining in God's book. Now, the considerations would be: 1. How did Moses know this? On what ground? 2. Could Moses have had such favorable thoughts about all of these people? 3. And was it only so that Israel might escape the punishment of temporal death? What proportion was there, after all, between his eternal woe and their temporal death? What then? Moses does not even speak of God’s book for eternal life, nor of the <term>Book of Life of the Lamb|The specific record of those saved by Christ mentioned in Revelation.</term>, nor of being allowed to be blotted out of *that* book; rather, he speaks of such punishment and death which he foresaw could befall at least a portion of Israel. Consequently, this [argument for names being removed from eternal life] is an empty, deaf, and blind patch of arguments used by the unpracticed.

Regarding *Psalm 69:28*, <note>original: "Pf. LXIX. 23." Note: The OCR likely misread 28 as 23, as the text refers to being blotted out.</note> their names are not "removed" as if they had truly been inscribed by God in the book of life. To be sure, some "write themselves into it" through outward appearance and external confession. According to the nature and <term>judgment of love|The theological principle of assuming someone is a believer based on their outward profession, even if their heart is unknown.</term>, they are held to be true confessors, members of the church, and entitled to the goods of the covenant and testament, based on external probabilities (*Isaiah 44; Ephesians 1; Philippians 4*), giving up their names to Jesus’ army in the ancient manner. <note>See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, Book VIII, § 10; Dio Cassius, Books 5 & 6; Hugo Grotius, *On the Law of War and Peace*, Book II, Chapter 5; Kipp, *Roman Antiquities*, page 645.</note> Yet, in reality, they are not, and their actions are merely hypocrisy. Now, these are eventually revealed by God to have never been what they were held to be, or what they claimed to be, when He pulls away the mask of hypocrisy. They do not persevere in confession and glory, and they fall away from the name and the glory of being "children of the kingdom" and being entitled to the inheritance. And so, their names are wiped out from the number and the roll of worthy citizens and steadfast, pure confessors. They are no longer counted or reckoned. (*Revelation 3:4, 5 and 13:19; Psalm 69:28*).

<margin>Judgment on the Jews.</margin>
If one considers *Psalm 69:28*, it seems specifically to be a judgment that would strike the Jews—open enemies of the Christ, not coming to the righteousness of God but rejecting it. Upon them came a physical and spiritual judgment of rooting out, blinding, hardening, and a cessation of being the people of the Lord any longer. Thus, they are deprived of the goods of the kingdom, its inheritance and privileges, to which they were first invited and were, according to the outward appearance of their previous treatment, the first and nearest. They were removed from that "civil register" when the Gentiles were accepted in their place, and they were scattered among the heathens by public banishment and declared to be no longer God’s people. A separation from them was made with the destruction of the city and temple, which had for so long been God’s seat and the place of His court.

Besides this, it is requested that they "not be written with the righteous"; therefore, they were not yet written there. But through the execution of God’s judgment, it would be declared that they were *never* written there, even if they had passed themselves off as the people of God and children of the kingdom. This was according to the fulfillment of the Divine oracle in *Romans 11* and the prophecy of *Hosea 1*. However, I shall leave the [dogmatic] effects to the theologians, though I will remark further upon it for better understanding.

<margin>Further observation.</margin>
I say then regarding the "Book of Life" in *Psalm 69:28*, etc., based on what I have already noted: we primarily encounter two things in this Psalm. First, **a.** the very painful and shameful experiences of the Messiah, directly inflicted upon Him by the Jews and Romans. Second, **b.** the righteous and heavy punishments hanging over the heads of the Messiah’s enemies. When we now understand and correctly explain the latter—which is what it actually comes down to—we must pay attention to the subject of the conversation, their actions, and their character. These were public and stubborn sinners, willful people who were known for their evil deeds. As for the curses and speeches [in the Psalm], we must view them as prophetic announcements and proclamations, uttered through strong impulse and zeal for God’s honor, the innocence of the Messiah, and the interest of the Lord’s people, and to demonstrate the loathing and disapproval of the committed evil. When one has this impression of things, one can easily perceive that such evil souls were never inscribed in the book of eternal life.

It is not said that they were *already* inscribed in that book, but a heart-felt wish appears: that they may not be reckoned and inscribed with the righteous. And besides this, "all book of life" is not an "eternal book of life," and also not the "Book of Life of the Lamb." It is often a book of *temporal* life: a state and dignity of being reckoned among the outward people of the covenant, and enjoying prosperity and blessings in the land. This being said and noted, I think that the Psalmist (or whoever one judges is being introduced as speaking) here wishes and, in an impulse of the Holy Spirit, foretells and announces what was to happen primarily to the Jews—God’s accepted, recorded people, separated from the Gentiles (*Numbers 23; Deuteronomy 4; Psalm 147; Acts 17; Ephesians 2*)—by way of the covenant and by way of righteous punishment (*Hosea 1:3; Romans 9; Matthew 24*).

<margin>The book with seven seals.</margin>
One reads of a book written on the inside and the outside, closed and hung with seven seals. *Revelation 5:1.*

Here I perceive that some understand this—without any qualification—to mean the scriptures of the Old and New Testaments. This cannot be applicable in all respects, unless one wishes to fall into the opinion of the <term>Papacy|The Roman Catholic Church and its hierarchy</term>, which insists upon the obscurity and darkness of the Holy Scriptures and the necessity of an infallible interpreter and translator.

Certainly, things belonging to life and salvation are expressed clearly enough therein. It describes not only future matters but also past events. However, regarding future things, they are presented in the manner of riddles, through figures and symbols (as if they were closed), concerning what God has determined for the Church of the New Testament until the end, and what has been wound up in the prophecies. These same things are discovered, seen, and more clearly understood at the opening of each seal, so that no one may doubt them. As for the seals themselves, they shall be discussed under their own name and heading.

"Written on the inside and outside"—this refers to what happened when one could not write everything on the inside. Unless it signifies completeness—that nothing may be added or taken away—or that it contained matters already seen "on the outside" in their fulfillment and demonstrated truth, as well as matters not yet seen, but still to be fulfilled, heard, and seen at the opening of each seal.

<margin>Book of Life.</margin>
One reads in *Revelation 20:12* that the dead were judged according to their works, from what was written in the books; that the books were opened, and that another book, the Book of Life, was opened. There, the Book of Life is distinguished from the other books; and one sees a comparison made with *Daniel 7:10.*

Regarding this passage, some apply it to the general and judicial judgment of the Son of Man, sitting upon the clouds of heaven. They then understand the "books" which are to be opened as the Book of the Law and the Holy Gospel (*Romans 2*); the Book of God’s Providence (or His book of remembrance), having knowledge of all men’s deeds and 

<column-break/>

omissions; and the book of conscience, which men possess alongside the All-knowing One regarding their actions. Then the Lord shall open His Book of Life, and from the proceedings and the judicial verdict, it shall publicly appear whom He has appointed to life and whom He has not. *Matthew 25; 2 Corinthians 5; 2 Thessalonians 1; etc.*

Yet great and learned men are of the opinion that neither in *Revelation 20:12* nor in *Daniel 7:10* is the final and general judgment being discussed. Rather, they believe it refers to how the two witnesses of the Old and New Testaments—trampled by the <term>Roman harlot|A common Reformation-era polemic referring to the Roman Catholic Church</term> and shoved out of the hands of men—would become living. The power of truth would reveal itself to the consciences of men in such a way that lies and errors would be discovered and halted. Consequently, the authority of the Councils and the supposed infallibility of the Pope would no longer be allowed to prevail (to settle disputes). Instead, judgment would be made according to the rule of God’s Word (*Galatians 6:16*). This occurs when there is a spiritual resurrection through the Word and the Spirit of God, so that those dead [in sin] hear the voice of the Son of God and rise up from their state of error and sin (*Ephesians 5; John 5*). They receive the anointing of the Spirit to know the truth (*1 John 2*). On this occasion, it would become manifest—through the knowledge and confession of the truth and the rising from the death-state of sin, ignorance, and error—who has been given to the Lamb. These are recognized by their fruits (*Matthew 7:10*), as they call upon the name of Jesus and depart from iniquity (*2 Timothy 2:19, 20*).

If anyone is to rejoice that his name is written in the Book of Life, he must know it upon good grounds; otherwise, his imagination is empty and his joy unfounded. Since one cannot climb into heaven to look into God’s book, how and in what way does one reach such assurance? I answer that I view God’s Book of Life as a "wonder-tree," like Jacob’s ladder (*Genesis 28*). Its root is in heaven, in God Himself and in His will and good pleasure; but the branches and fruits of this divine wonder-tree are found and show themselves in man here below on earth. Therefore, we do not dig for the root, but we observe the branches and fruits (*Romans 9*). Those whom He has chosen, these He has also called, etc.

And does someone desire this to be presented even more simply? Then I say: you do not need to ask for a direct address from God, "Am I also one of your chosen ones recorded for eternal life?" That is not necessary. That is not the usual way of Divine revelation. there is a readier path, one more closely at hand.

If you then ask me, what is this path and certain track? I point the way to you—though it must be used properly, with earnestness and observation, without soul-coddling flattery.

*A.* Search in the Divine Book of the Bible for the specific and certain characteristics of the children of God: how they are, what they do, and by what means they are known (just as a tree is known by its fruits). Do not fashion characteristics in your heart or out of your own brain, but seek them in that Divine book.

*B.* Having done so, then descend into yourself...

...downward, search the book of your conscience, and pay close attention to the daily record of your conduct and way of life.

C. If you then find that your conscience and book of life correspond with the Book of Holy Scripture, you will notice that you are a tree and a plant, planted by the heavenly Father. You shall see this from the fruits within you (*Dan. VII. John XV. Matt. III. Eph. XLI. Philip. I. 27. Philip. III. 20. etc.*): your root is above.

If I am then asked what kind of fruits appear here on earth from this divine wonder-tree, I give the following as a reply:

a. The first fruit of this is (*Rom. VIII.*), through the calling by spirit and word, to bring the sinner on earth to the knowledge of the laws of the kingdom, and of Christ as the divine guarantor, mediator, High Priest, and sacrifice for our sins; to faith and to consent (*Isa. LIII. 11. John XVII. 3. and III. 16-36. Philip. III.*). Test and examine yourself, whether you are in the faith (*Acts XIII. 2 Cor. XIII. 5. Tit. I. Hab. II. Rom. I. Jas. II.*).

b. Strangers who are from far-off lands are generally recognized by their speech, clothing, manners, and customs. They usually speak with delight and praise for their homeland; and although they may have much in their exile, their heart nevertheless hangs upon their fatherland.

The <note>original: "Kanaäns taal"</note> language of Canaan shall be in your mouth because the words of God are in your heart. Your speech shall make you known, just as a worldling speaks of and from the earth.

Your manners and lifestyle shall be holy, pure, modest, humble, and temperate.

You shall choose as your companions those who are of your homeland and inner nature (*Ps. XVI. 27-119. 2 Cor. VI. Eph. V.*).

No matter how pleasant things below may be for the flesh, your heart shall itch and long for your fatherland; your heavenly origin shall pull you there like a <term>lodestone|A natural magnet used by sailors for navigation</term> (*Ps. XLII. 63-84. 2 Cor. V. Phil. I. Heb. XII. Col. III. Phil. III. 20.*).

c. Seeking to satisfy and satiate this pull and desire for your fatherland, you shall take your journey toward Heaven, your fatherland, along the shortest, paved, and well-secured path, and not at all along crooked, wandering, or side paths. You shall also not stand still, gape, or look backward on this road; you shall pull and detach your heart and senses from the world's Sodom, and always look forward and upward to where you seek to arrive and remain (*Rom. XII. 2. Col. III. 1. Ps. XVII. Phil. I. 3. 1 John II.*), thus going step by step (*Ps. LXXXIV. Prov. IV. 2 Cor. VII. 1, 2. Phil. IV. 2 Pet. I. 5, 6, 7. Heb. XII.*).

<column-break/>

### LOVER, LOVERS, TO DALLY
### <note>original Hebrew: רע (companion/paramour), עגב (to dote/lust)</note> Companion, Lust, <note>original: "fief, amator"</note> paramour, lover, <note>original Hebrew: עגב (to dote), אהב (to love)</note> to lust, to love, <note>original Latin: "amare, adamare"</note> to love, to love dearly, <note>original Hebrew: אהב (love), אהבה (affection)</note> love, affection.

Because this has a very great similarity with a whore, harlotry, and the practice of wicked and foul lust, as well as with idolatry, etc., I will not involve myself too deeply in this subject matter, so as not to <note>original: "my het gras niet voor de voeten af te maaien" — a Dutch idiom meaning to anticipate someone else's work or repeat oneself unnecessarily</note> mow the grass from under my own feet, but rather to be able to insert the essential details more closely in their proper time and place. Therefore, look under WHORE, HARLOTRY, TO WHORE, etc.

<margin>Description of a lover.</margin> A lover <note>original: "boel"</note> is a person with whom one practices the work of impure love in an illicit manner, answering physical love and lust with the appearance of mutual love. *Lamentations I. 19. Jer. XXX. 14. and XXII. 20. etc. Hos. II. 4-6-8. and IX. 10. Ezek. XVI. 15-33-36, 37. and XXIII. 5-9-12. etc. Jerem. III. 1. and IV. Hos. VIII. 10.* and elsewhere.

Now we know what these words mean literally as a forbidden work of the flesh.

By figure, allusion, and naming, this is now applied to two principal matters which can take place among a people who have entered into a covenant with God and are as if married to Him, being obliged to cling to Him alone, to love Him, to trust in Him alone, to pray to Him alone for protection against all enemies, and to wait upon His promise and His faithfulness in fulfilling the same.

This can be understood to happen in a state-wise or civil manner, according to one's civic status, when instead of relying on God's faithfulness, power, and help against enemies and praying to Him for protection and deliverance, one turns away from God with mistrust and unbelief and betakes oneself to kings and powers to desire their help. One buys this help and seeks to make oneself pleasing to them, flattering and caressing them, in order to lean on the arm of the flesh and be at ease. This is "hiring lovers for a reward," *Hosea VIII. 9.* When these lovers will not listen to promises and look away with contempt for those making the request, then it is said, "your lovers despise you," *Jer. IV. and Hosea VIII.*—which was not infrequently practiced by the outward people of God's name.

But when, as often happened, that civil turning away was accompanied by a departure from the Lord—or remaining attached to the Lord, His law, and covenant in appearance while meanwhile clinging to the idols of the nations—then such a thing was called "dallying" <note>original: "boeleeren"</note>, just as the idols were called "lovers" <note>original: "boelen"</note>. Israel of old made itself guilty of these sins, which break the love, faithfulness, and submission one owed to God alone, more than once. Indeed, one rarely saw the one without the other, and therefore one may generally understand it in the two aforementioned ways in the passages cited above. However, I shall deal with this more closely under the words WHORE, TO WHORE, and HARLOTRY; I will depart from this here and depict something else with my pen.

# BOSOM.

BOSOM, <note>Hebrew: ḥēyq, ḥēn, ṣallaḥat</note>, which is also translated as *lap*: <note>Greek: kolpos; Latin: sinus, gremium</note>.

Regarding the BOSOM, this is understood as the part of the human body between both arms, the upper chest, and the front surface of the body down to the lap, or the middle of the body. Sometimes the lap is included under it, according to the properties and meanings of the Hebrew and Latin words, *chest*, *lap*, *bosom*: <note>Latin: pectus, gremium, sinus</note> from which comes the designation for someone with whom one is very familiar and to whom one trusts a great deal, <margin>Bosom-friend.</margin> *a bosom-friend*, *a heart-friend*.

It is to be taken literally and according to the letter when the Lord commanded Moses to put his hand into his bosom, whereby it became leprous, and was healed again upon the second insertion, *Exodus* IV: 6, 7. This occurred when the Lord, through two miracles, <margin>God's promise to Moses.</margin> called him to his extraordinary undertaking and assured him of the legitimacy of his mission, and how He, the Lord, would be with him, protect him, and strengthen him.

<margin>Miracle of Moses' hand.</margin> Regarding what the miracle of Moses' hand—inserted into his bosom by divine command with the various outcomes to be read there—entails, it serves as a brief summary of time; based only on the movement of insertion and withdrawal, it cannot be attributed to any natural cause, but only to God's will and power.

I maintain that the observant Israel, through this miracle as well as further rare miraculous events, was able to notice not only that Moses had been sent for their deliverance, but that he was armed with the assistance of such a God who could and would deliver them by the hand of Moses.

<margin>Interpretation made by Augustine.</margin> Augustine, in his 86th sermon concerning the times, applied this miracle of Moses’ leprous and healthy hand by way of allusion to a two-fold view of the church, as scholars before me have already noted: namely, that the leprous hand of Moses refers to the Synagogue of the Jews, among whom not only did the physical impurity of leprosy take hold, but also the leprosy of their unbelief, through which they rejected Jesus. And by Moses’ healthy hand, he notes the Church of the Gentiles, which stepped into the place of the Jews—pure and healthy in the faith, once delivered to the saints.

<margin>Also by others.</margin> Yet others have focused on the person of Moses, seeing it as depicting or representing something in his own person, namely: that the leprous hand of Moses could represent and depict the state of Moses when he had fled from Pharaoh’s court and presence, and retreated to Midian, keeping himself withdrawn like a leper; or it could represent his inadequacy, like that of a leper, for performing the office assigned to him; for which reason he also said, *Lord, who am I? Send someone else.*

Moses' restored and healthy hand, cleansed of leprosy by God, is held by some to be a fitting symbol of how the Lord sometimes chooses the ignoble, weak, and powerless, and makes them capable—as happened with Moses—to serve as a leader and judge for the people, and to hold that great, very important, and perilous embassy at the court of Pharaoh.

<column-break/>

Others again have turned to a further outlook and higher mystery, viewing this impurity of leprosy and the following healing and purity in the mediator of the first covenant as a symbolic representation of what would later be perceived in the second and better Mediator of the Covenant, Jesus Christ. They apply this rare occurrence to Christ in this manner: namely, that Jesus Christ, who was truly pure and sinless in himself, was in the bosom of the Father, coming forth as the glorious one from the midst of Him to approach God as a guarantor and priest (*Jer. XXX: 21; Job I: 1, 2, 3-14*). Having appeared to the children of men on earth, he was seen, regarded, and treated as a leper—an unclean, sinful man—namely, as one occupied and burdened with the debt of his people's sins as a guarantor (*Ps. XL: 13; LXIX: 5, 6; Isa. LIII: 4, 5; Rom. VIII: 3, 4; 2 Cor. V: 21; Heb. IX: 28*). Yet that same Jesus, having risen from the belly and the bosom of the earth, is seen justified and without sin (*Heb. IX: 29; 1 Tim. III: 16; Rom. I: 4; etc.*).

In a moral and figurative way, one can derive from this miraculous event the expression, *put your hand in your bosom*; that is, return to yourself, examine and search yourself. Then even the sharpest Momus <note>A figure from Greek mythology representing mockery and criticism; here meaning a harsh critic.</note> and fault-finder will find that not only his hand and conduct, but also his heart and bosom, are leprous and unclean, according to *1 Kings VIII: 38-46; Job XIV: 4; Ps. XXXIX: 13; Ps. LI: 4-7; James III: 2; 1 John I: 8; and Isa. LXIV: 6* <note>Original text says Jes. LXXIV. 6, likely a typo for Isaiah 64:6.</note>.

It is figurative and very metaphorical when one sees that a bosom is attributed to God, who is a simple spirit, and it is said of Him that He puts his hand into his bosom, hides it, or draws his hand out of his bosom (*Ps. LXXIV: 11*) <note>Original text says Ps. XLVII. 11, but the context matches Psalm 74:11.</note>.

Since God's hand and arm are a symbol of God's power and help, I would believe that <margin>The hand, a symbol of His power.</margin> by the hiding of the same, it is suggested that He does not display His power and help for the good of His people as before—to strike the enemies, to withstand them, and to make them small—just as a warrior accomplishes nothing as long as he hides his hand in his bosom. On the contrary, to pluck the hand out of His bosom signifies the zeal and earnestness of God to take up the cause and the danger of His people, and to put His power and wisdom into action against the enemies for the good of His people, so that He may be glorified and magnified by those delivered due to the defeat of the enemy.

And again, regarding man, several expressions involving the bosom are in use which are figurative and symbolic, and cannot be taken according to the literal letter in all <margin>of the bosom.</margin> parts; as for example these following places and expressions, *Prov. XIX: 24*: *A sluggard hides his hand in his bosom*. It is a symbol of lazy and blameworthy idleness, and of rest, while one truly has a double need for the labor of his hands to exist honestly; a symbol of excessive filthiness, such that even the slightest labor is wearisome, and it is even an effort to bring the hand to the mouth: so that it is a depiction of the most base sluggard and of a foul idler. The Preacher [teaches] his pupils about anger and sud- <meta>catchword: sud- (likely "suddenness" or "rashness")</meta>

...warning against sudden outbursts of temperament, he brings forward as a reason *that anger rests in the bosom of fools. <note>original: "dat de toorn ruft in den boezem der dwaazen." This is a reference to Ecclesiastes 7:9, though the text cites "Spr." (Proverbs) VII. 9.</note>*

<margin>To avoid wrath.</margin> The fool immediately makes his outburst known, but a wise and cautious man hides the insult, *Proverbs XII: 16.* One must be slow to anger, *James I: 19 <note>The text says "Jakobus I. 10," likely a reference to James 1:19-20.</note>.* Horace does not speak poorly when he says in his letters:

> Anger is a brief madness: govern your mind, which unless it obeys, commands: restrain this with bits, this with chains. <note>original Latin: "Ira furor brevis eft: animum rege, qui nifi paret / Imperat: hunc frenis, hunc tu compefce catenis."</note>

One who is angry does not see the matter in its true form. As Cato said long ago in the second book of his *Distichs*:

-> That is: <-

No one is truly wise when he feeds his anger and lets it play the master. Persius says at the end of his third Satire:

> *Would swear that your head, like his, was failing.*

As long as reason does not stand above the inner self and bring the mind to calm, neither counsel nor external reason matters, as Plutarch has well said: *Just as in a tumult we do not hear what is said to us: so when angry we do not admit another's counsel, unless reason speaks within, which may restrain the tumult of the mind.* <note>original Latin: "Ut in tumultu non audimus quid nobis dicatur: ita irati non admittimus alienum confilium, nifi ratio loquatur intus, quæ tumultum animi compefcat."</note> That is: *Just as we do not hear what is told to us in a noise: so we do not listen to another's advice, unless reason speaks from within and subdues the commotion of the mind.*

A fool always wants to go against the stream and push through with his own head, but a wise man avoids the impulse of fury. Ovid, *Book I, Remedia Amoris (The Cure for Love):*

> While madness is in its course, yield to the running madness; every onset has difficult approaches. He is a foolish swimmer who, when he might depart sideways, fights to go into the opposing waters. <note>original Latin: "Dum furor in curfu eft, currenti cede furori; / Difficiles aditus impetus omnis habet. / Stultus ab obliquo, qui cum difcedere poffit, / Pugnet in adverfas ire natator aquas."</note>

-> That is: <-

> *If your mind is heated, you must not oppose it;*
> *One can hardly withstand a great force.*
> *The swimmer is not well-advised who, in the currents,*
> *Wants to swim against the stream, when he could save himself.*

<column-break/>

The "bosom," and "to rest in the bosom," signifies here that it is characteristic and habitual for fools to be angry, to reveal their anger, and to let it have its full course, by no means restraining themselves through right reason, but flaring up at the first and slightest opportunity.

Strictly speaking, the bosom is not the place to keep fire. One is ignited by it, and the clothes nearby easily catch fire. From this, Solomon borrows this question, this metaphor, to depict something else, *Proverbs VI: 27. Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?* I would certainly think that Solomon intends to depict here how dangerous it is to fix one's love upon a certain object, to familiarize oneself closely with a strange woman, to hide the love for her in one's heart, and to cast one's eye lightly upon a harlot or a stranger: for even if it is such that one does not immediately fly into a bright blaze, the desire and love smolder so long that one ends up in full flame, and cannot immediately extinguish it without sensible pain and damage, even shame.

The inner burning through love and lusts, directed toward an illicit object, is quite as disadvantageous and of harmful consequence as fire hidden in the bosom under the clothes, which smolders until it brings about a full flame.

Because of this, one sees that fire, flame, and burning, among both sacred and secular writers, are taken to mean both chaste and unchaste love. *It is better to marry than to burn,* says Paul, *1 Corinthians VII.*

Virgil, in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*:

-> That is, according to Vondel: <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) was a preeminent Dutch poet and playwright who translated Classical works.</note> <-

> *Too miserably struck by love, feeds that grief*
> *And wound in her breast, pining away secretly within*
> *From a fever of love.*

And:

> Loving Dido burns, and has drawn the madness through her bones. <note>original Latin: "Ardet amans Dido, traxitque per offa furorem."</note>

-> That is: <-

> *The flame consumes Dido's heart, stirs her senses.*
> *She quietly feeds a wound within her breast.*

And even if one wishes to hide and smother it, at the first opportunity it receives nourishment, shoots out new sparks, and burns all the more strongly.

> She cherishes the old fires in her bones. <note>original Latin: "Veteres cuftodit in offibus ignes."</note>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "bosom" as a metaphorical space for internal states. # BOSOM.

V 3
<meta>catchword: fels.</meta>

Ovid: <note>Publius Ovidius Naso, a Roman poet often cited by early modern authors for his insights into human passion.</note>

> *Meanwhile, silent flames creep into the vitals.* <note>original Latin: "Interea tacitæ serpunt in viscera flammæ."</note>

->That is:<-

*Meanwhile, the flames creep into her from within.*

The same author in the sixth book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> *The more the fire is covered, the more the hidden fire seethes.* <note>original Latin: "Quoque magis tegitur, tectus magis æstuat ignis."</note>

->That is:<-

*The more she covers the fire, the more it rages within.*

One must then be careful not to be seduced by a strange woman, and not to let the fire come too near: one should not hide these thoughts and desires in the heart, but rather cut off all opportunities and seek to extinguish the sparks in time.

Ovid in the second book of *The Remedy of Love*:

> *As when sulfur touches nearly extinguished ash, it lives again, and from the smallest thing comes a massive fire. So, unless you avoid whatever recalls love, the flame which was just now nothing will burn again.* <note>original Latin: "Ut pæne exstinctum cinerem si sulfure tangas, / Vivet, & ex minimo maximus ignis erit. / Sic, nisi vitabis quicquid revocabit amorem, / Flamma redardescet, quæ modo nulla fuit."</note>

->That is:<-

*When sulfur touches the extinguished glow,*
*It lives again, just as it blazed before.*
*If you do not shun what can awaken love,*
*A dead flame will be granted a new life.*

One is also said *to carry reproach in his bosom*. *Psalm LXXXIX. 51.* This is understood by some in this way: *Where I am, I who carry in my lap and bosom, as the Mother Church, the hope of the promise that many—indeed, all nations—would turn to my lap: which cannot be fulfilled for me in this state, seeing as my enemies despise the footsteps of your anointed.* Others understand it in this fashion: that it signifies *reproaches of every sort and kind, which neighboring nations and enemies brought in troops and heaps, mocking and scoffing at Religion, as well as the steadfast trust in the Lord, throwing many wicked deeds into the faces of the believers, of which they were in no way guilty nor had any part.*

Finally, it seems to me that others have not understood it poorly who believe that by *carrying reproaches in the bosom*, it is meant that one must bottle them up, endure them, hide them, and suffer them patiently and in silence. So judge Muis, Tirinus, and Campen. <note>These are likely Simon de Muis, Jacobus Tirinus, and Jan van Campen, prominent 17th-century biblical commentators.</note> Fesselius in *Sacred Adversaria* Book IV, Chapter 9, page 381.

That Nehemiah emptied his bosom, *Chapter V. 13.*—since one hides or can hide various things in one's lap and bosom—I would believe was a ceremony which he added to his charge and earnest testimony. It depicted God's punishment for all the wicked <term>usury</term> <note>Lending money at unreasonably high interest rates, which was legally and religiously condemned.</note> practiced against his brothers, the Israelites. He was not only testifying that he had no part in it, and that if he were held

<column-break/>

 to have had a part, he was unburdening himself of the unjustly swallowed goods, restoring them to their rightful owners; he wished that every person would act thus, or in case of transgression, that the righteous God—who forbids such usury in *Exodus XXII, Leviticus XXV, and Deuteronomy XXIII. 19*—would make their bosom or lap empty and bare, and in many ways and through many means, punish them tangibly in their temporal goods.

Otherwise, one could understand *shaking out one's bosom*, in a different context, to mean *pouring out one's heart*, as to a well-trusted friend, because it is difficult and distressing to hide longer that which has been suppressed and bottled up for a long time.

Yet, the phrase which appears in *Psalm XXXV. 13* will undoubtedly signify something else entirely: *My prayer returned into my own bosom.*

It is a great virtue to be moved through love with compassion for one’s miserable and needy fellow man: it is even greater if one can restrain one's passion so far as to be moved with love and compassion for one's enemies, blessing them and praying for them, *Matthew V. 44, Romans XII. 14.* David was able to achieve this in himself: *2 Samuel I.* The Messiah was a perfect pattern in this, *Luke XXIII. 34, Isaiah LIII,* and it was the constant practice of the early Christian church to pray for her enemies and to be inwardly moved with compassion. See Origen in the 3rd and 7th Books, Cyril in the 3rd Book, Tertullian’s *Apology* Chapter 39. Cave's *Primitive Christianity*, Kortholt on the *Life and Customs of the Early Christians*; Hornius and Spanheim’s *Ecclesiastical Histories*. Now, it is judged that this phrase signifies *praying frequently and inwardly in the heart for enemies, with manifold repetitions and reflections, with earnest and strong persistence: so that I wish that what I have prayed for my enemies might happen to me.* Or *that which I prayed for my enemies fell to my lot; I found the fruit, power, and effects of it in my innermost self.* Most interpretations essentially come down to this.

As for the phrase of *repaying into their bosom, or lap: measuring back the reward, Isaiah LXV. 6, 7; Psalm LXXIX. 12; Jeremiah XXXII. 18.* etc., I would think that such a phrase signifies a balanced retribution, according to the nature and character of someone’s previous actions, whether for favorable recognition and reward, or for righteous and weighty punishment: just as one sees someone measured—or wishes them to be measured—with the same measure with which he has measured out to others.

One also speaks likewise of <term>Bosom Friends</term>, <note>Extremely close, intimate friends in whom one confides everything.</note> or a friend, or a female friend in someone's lap, just as "lap" and "bosom" are sometimes exchanged and used for one another in our Dutch translation. *Deuteronomy XIII. 6: The wife of your bosom; the wife of his bosom; the husband of her bosom: Deuteronomy XXVIII. 54, 56. Slept in his bosom. 2 Samuel XII. Embracing the bosom of strangers, Proverbs V. 20. For her who lies in your bosom, Micah VII. 5. Who is in the bosom of the Father. John I. 18.*

Which places do not exactly all mean the lower lap, but also the upper lap or chest: and it does not always refer to lying in bed, for it also took place when reclining at tables.

<summary>This page discusses the metaphorical use of the 'bosom' in Classical and Biblical contexts, representing it as a place where hidden passions like lust are concealed, where reproaches are endured, and where heartfelt prayers or divine retributions are 'measured out.'</summary>

# GOAT.

...lessly. <note>The text likely completes the word "onbestraffelyks" (blamelessly) from the previous page.</note> Thus lay one of the Disciples, whom Jesus loved, in Jesus' bosom. <note>A reference to John 13:23.</note> Caius Caligula, loving his sisters above his wife, made them lie at the table in his bosom, but his wife above or behind him on the reclining couch, as can be seen in *Suetonius, Life of Caligula, Chapter 24.* <note>Gaius Caligula was a Roman Emperor notorious for his scandalous behavior.</note> Thus lay *Cythæris* in the bosom of *Eutrapelus*, according to the saying of *Cicero in Letters to Pætus*, etc. But more on this under the word BOSOM.

It signifies, at the very least, a friend or mistress, husband or wife, who is closest to us, whom one loves greatly, with whom one practices very close intercourse and even reveals one’s secret things: whether one does such things with right and reason, blamelessly, or culpably and with impure love.

That the Goat, being slaughtered and the blood used for sprinkling, etc., was clean according to the law is beyond all dispute; and since the offering and blood-pouring for ceremonial reconciliation and purity was a depiction of that which would happen to the Christ, and what he would achieve for the true and perfect justification and sanctification of his people, I hold it to be true—though Spencer <note>original: "Spencerus"; referring to John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian and Hebraist.</note> works against this view—that the Goat, especially the one for JEHOVAH, pointed toward the Christ. He appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, though without sin, like us in all things except for sin (*Hebrews 2:17 and 4:15; 2 Corinthians 5:21*). I will insert here the words of a learned man:

> *I feel then, that the Goat, which by lot was for Jehovah, was an illustrious symbol of the Lord Jesus, his entire person, and his perfect offering of reconciliation, through which he has perfected all those who shall be sanctified for eternity. That the Lord Christ had the honor of coming upon the altar of God, and like the Goat that was sacrificed—whose blood was brought into the Holy of Holies—so he also rightfully appeared before Jehovah as the true Ark of the Covenant: and that Jehovah, as if by lot—that is, by Divine decree, both in his word and through the deed and outcome—has declared that he had chosen King Jesus as the only true High Priest, not after the order of Aaron, but Melchizedek, and that the unique offering of his son alone pleased him, when he made him an offering of a pleasant scent to God his heavenly Father, and took delight therein, etc.* See Zwarts, *Dispensation of the Times*, pages 410, 417, 420, etc. <note>original: "Zwarts, bedeeling der tyden"; refers to Johannes Swart, a Dutch theologian.</note>

Among the offerings on the Feast of the New Moon, one also finds the Goat. This is called an offering for sin to the Lord, with that clear naming and designation so that one might not think it was offered to the Moon, as Jewish and other writers tell us (*Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed, Book III, Chapter 46; Rabbi Bechai on Parashah Phinehas, folio 184; Thomas Aquinas, Schook, Henricus Ursinus in Spencer, Part II, page 204*). But more on this under the Feast of the New Moon.

Since this animal will be handled more closely in the following under other names, I shall set aside my spade at the dike <note>A Dutch idiom meaning to finish a task for the time being.</note> and move to another subject: only showing the reader in the distance some similarities between the Goat of Jehovah and Christ. <margin>Parallels.</margin>
*a.* The Goat is frisky, stinking, prone to butting, an unpleasant animal: Christ was not so in himself, but as a surety burdened with our sins, he appeared so in outward appearance, regard, and treatment (*Romans 3; Hebrews 2 and 4*).

*b.* The Goat was determined by lot: Christ by God’s counsel, providence, and the decrees set forth concerning him (*Acts 2 and 4; Psalm 40; Hebrews 10, etc.*).

*c.* The Goat outside the camp, bearing the sins of the people, was slaughtered as a sin offering, burned, and its blood received for sprinkling: with this, the Priest entered the Sanctuary; and it served as a shadowy general reconciliation for the new year. Christ, because of and burdened with our sins, was outside the gate (*Isaiah 53; 1 Peter 2; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 12*), through the fire of God's wrath, glowing through the fire of love for his Father’s honor and the salvation of the world, on the general day of atonement, in the year of God's favor (*Isaiah 61 and 53; Isaiah 21:2; Hebrews 5*), with which he has entered, and by which we enter (*Hebrews 1:3, 9:12–14, and 10:8–19, 20, etc.*).

### BOW, <term>קשת</term>, <term>τόξον</term>, *arcus.*
<note>Hebrew: "keshet"; Greek: "toxon"; Latin: "arcus". All refer to the weapon used for shooting arrows.</note>

A BOW is, among other things, a weapon of war used from ancient times to throw arrows from afar at an enemy to strike him mortally: although bows were also used for the practice of hunting. One sees them mentioned quite early (*Genesis 49:24*), along with shooting and arrows (*Numbers 21:24; 2 Samuel 1; 2 Kings 9, etc.*).

<margin>Distinction of arrows.</margin>
Those arrows shot at the enemy with the drawn bow must be distinguished from those which one threw by hand.

<margin>Eastern peoples trained in archery.</margin>
It is said that the Parthians, Medes, Armenians, and most Eastern peoples were very skilled in archery, followed by the Cretans.

It is not difficult to believe that from ancient times they were made from copper, steel, iron, horn, and other materials. David (*Psalm 18:34; 2 Samuel 22:35*) <note>The Dutch text cites Psalm 19:3, but the reference to a "steel bow" is found in Psalm 18:34 (18:35 in some versions).</note> speaks of a steel bow that is broken.

It is believable that they could not be drawn too easily or lightly, and that one sometimes needed one's knees and feet to bend and tension them.

->Ovid:<-
<note>Ovid was a famous Roman poet; this line is likely from his *Amores*.</note>

> *He strongly curved the sinuous bow against his knee.*
<note>original Latin: "Lunavitque genu sinuosum fortiter arcum."</note>

->That is:<-

->*And against his knee he bent his bow with strength.*<-

I would believe that the sword, arrow, and bow are indeed among the most ancient instruments of war and violence: and that, although more weapons were devised over time, these being the most prominent, one might perhaps understand or include under them all sorts of weapons for defending oneself and for making enemy attacks (*Psalm 37:14, 15; 44:7; 46:10; 76:4*).

This being the case—that bow and arrows, to strike and pierce the enemy from afar, are the oldest and most common weaponry from antiquity—it is not hard to understand what it symbolizes when one reads *that someone's bow is broken*, as that expression appears in *Psalm 37:15; 46:10; 76:4; Jeremiah 49:35; Hosea 1:5*. Namely, either that peace is immediately established between peoples who were openly hostile and at war, or the destruction, breaking, and subduing of someone's power, through which they offered resistance, or sometimes heavy blows and destructive wars.

# BOW.
<note>original: "B O O G."</note>

...inflicted disasters and gave sharp stings to his enemies.

<margin>Israel compared to a bow.</margin>
When sinning and acting faithlessly, Israel is compared to a deceitful bow that turns back (*Psalm 78:57*). They do not turn to the Lord; they are like a deceitful bow (*Hosea 7:16*). A bow that is slippery and turns in the hand of the archer, with which one hits no mark or target, upon which one cannot rely, and which sometimes even harms the archer himself, may be called a deceitful bow. When Israel made a show of truly turning to God and repenting, yet meanwhile played the hypocrite and turned to faithless covenant-breaking—setting up high places and idols—they completely failed to hit the mark and goal of Jehovah's glory and the perfection of their neighbor in love. By not using their tongue and power to win over their neighbor through God's reason and to subject them to God, was this not, in a sense, a deceitful bow? As God's name was slandered among the Heathen through this, it inevitably led to destruction and ruin (*Hosea 13:9*).

A deceitful and perverse bow, says Jerome <note>Hieronymus (c. 347–420 AD), a prominent Church Father known for his Latin translation of the Bible (the Vulgate).</note>, is one that strikes and wounds the one who directs it. See Cyril, Theodoret, and others. Ursinus <note>Zacharias Ursinus (1534–1583), a German theologian and leading figure in the Reformed tradition.</note> says, *God turns the arrows against the archer.*

> *He obstructs opposing ranks, and turns the shot weapons*
> *Back against their authors, etc.*
<note>original Latin: "Obstruit adversas acies, revolutaque tela / Vertit in auctores, &c."</note>

->That is:<-

> He halts the troops, and the arrows they shoot,
> He turns back upon the archers.

They fell short and did not turn to the Lord their God; their zeal failed and broke off quickly, taking a sudden turn:

> *They turn themselves: but poorly! they are like a bow,*
> *Which deceives the archer with a treacherous strike,*
> *Or even while strained, fails as the string breaks.*
<note>original Latin: "Convertunt sese: verum male! sunt velut arcus, / Qui jaculatorem fallaci decipit ictu, / Aut etiam intentus nervo rumpente fatiscit."</note>

->That is:<-

> They turn, but all too prematurely, like a bow,
> That deceived its own archer in the very act of shooting,
> Or lost its strength as the string snapped.

<margin>The bow attributed to hypocrites.</margin>
When a bow is attributed to the wicked and hypocrites, and it is said in *Jeremiah 9:3* that they bend their tongue like a bow—that they bend the bow and aim in the dark, etc. (*Psalm 11:2, Psalm 58:8, and 64:4, 5*)—it is to be understood figuratively as the power, cunning, and artistry of the godless, through which they seek to harm the pious. This is particularly done with their "mouth-arrows" of lies, deceit, flattery, slanders, and such like. They aim to harm the pious through the power of seduction or to stir up heavy persecutions through lies, slander, and incitement, in order to do away with the upright and simple of heart. Yet, they do all this with a "quiet drum" <note>An idiomatic expression meaning "stealthily" or "without fanfare."</note>—in secret, so as not to be known, in order to strike more surely; and thus they play the part of hypocrites and feigned friends.

I have said above, that the sword, the bow,

<column-break/>

and the arrow are taken to represent all the weapons of war, for resistance and force. These are not to be trusted (*Psalm 37, 44, and 76*). Without doubt, it signifies not only that one should not rely on one's own power, courage, or martial skill—called the "arm of flesh"—but also, out of conviction that all such things are vain without the Lord, that one should place one's help, trust, and strength in the Lord, praying for His help and expecting His salvation and deliverance (*Psalm 27, 46, 56, etc.*).

It is well known that bow and arrow are found attributed to the Lord; that He bends it and shoots His arrows at the godless (*Psalm 7:13, 14; Lamentations 2:4; Habakkuk 3:9*).

For my part, I can see nothing else intended here but a figurative representation: that the long-suffering God, sufficiently provoked and taunted, exercises His power to judge and punish the godless and unrepentant sinners through the effects of His might. This sometimes leads to their physical and eternal ruin when He, as Judge of all the earth, does right (*Genesis 18; Romans 2:5, 6, 7; 2 Thessalonians 1:6, 7*) and repays everyone according to their works. Among the weapons of war of the reigning and triumphant King Jesus, one finds the bow and arrows (*Psalm 45:5; Revelation 6:2, etc.*). Now, Jesus is no worldly King (*Luke 17:20; John 18:36*); his weapons, though not fleshly, are nonetheless powerful and victorious (*2 Corinthians 10:4, 5*). I would not be averse to the idea that one may think and believe that these were symbols used by the wise to express how the Gospel—under the service of the spiritual archers (the Apostles, etc.) under the chief leadership of the Captain Christ and empowered by the Spirit—flew forth like lightning, like the swiftest arrows, and was preached through the whole world. It touched some in the heart unto conversion and subjection to King Jesus, while condemning others and threatening the ultimate fates and most miserable ruin. Meanwhile, this was even accompanied by terrible punishments and judgments, both upon the Jews and Romans, and all those who sought to break the bow of the Gospel (*Matthew 24:27; 2 Corinthians 2:15, 16; 2 Corinthians 10:4, 5; Hebrews 4:12; John 3:36; 2 Thessalonians 1:6, 7, 8; 1 Thessalonians 2:15, 16; Psalm 18:15; Joel 2:30, 31; Acts 2:17, etc.; Isaiah 43:3, 4, 5, 6*).

Through *Psalm 45:5, 6* compared with *Isaiah 4:2, Habakkuk 3:9, Zechariah 9:4-13, and Revelation 6:2*, it occurs to me that not only were chariots, horses, and swords used since ancient times, but also bows and arrows, to strike enemies and adversaries not just from nearby, but also from afar. I am of the opinion that God's Spirit, reporting the military campaigns of the Messiah among and against the Heathen to establish a kingdom for Himself in their midst, has introduced Him there as a heroic and well-equipped warrior provided with bow and arrows.

And perhaps one could translate *Psalm 45:5* ידרך <note>Hebrew: *yidrok*. While often translated as "tread," it refers to the act of stringing or bending a bow by stepping on it.</note> with different vowels, or without vowels, as: BEND the BOW.
