# BOW. TREE.

...and then they represented, through the arrows, all the excellent teachers who are held capable and sent out by Jesus.

But those who have considered the Apostles, Evangelists, Shepherds, and teachers to be represented by the bow give me more pleasure. <margin>Apostles and teachers represented by the bow.</margin> Through these, Christ has successfully employed blessed means and powerful instruments in the founding, establishing, and expanding of His kingdom among the Jews and Gentiles (*Zechariah 9:13, 14*).

He can be considered to span this bow when He provides and equips them through His Spirit with the necessary gifts and abilities, encouraging and moving them to speak without shame, fear, or terror—demonstrating the truth and revealing it to the conscience—before kings, princes, governors, judgment seats, philosophers, and the sages of this world, so as to plant the truth and overturn the seat of injustice. In this case, the arrows of the bow are also distinct. See under the word ARROWS, about which I could speak far and wide.

<margin>Meaning of the arrows.</margin>
The Masoretes <note>Jewish scholars who standardized the Hebrew text of the Bible between the 6th and 10th centuries.</note> on *Psalm 45* translate it as "the arrows of your words" or "of your armies." Rabbi Solomon <note>Also known as Rashi, a famed medieval French rabbi and author of comprehensive commentaries on the Talmud and Tanakh.</note> understands the arrows to be the teachings of the wise. For my part, I am somewhat more specific and think, with others, that one understands it on good grounds to mean the word of the Gospel, which is sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit (*Hebrews 4:12*). This word proceeded from the mouths of the Apostles and the first champions in their departure and advancement among the Jews, and especially among the Gentiles, being powerful in God (*Psalm 8:3, Romans 1:16, Romans 10:18, 2 Corinthians 10:4, 5, Hebrews 4:12*). Or one must interpret these arrows in a twofold manner regarding their effect, as Arnobius <note>An Early Christian apologist of the 4th century.</note> suggests: those arrows release the king’s favorites but kill the king’s enemies and adversaries (*2 Corinthians 2:14, 15, 16*).

One reads in *Psalm 127:4*, "Like arrows in the hand of a hero, so are the sons of one’s youth." Thus are the Apostles and other subsequent Shepherds and Teachers (*Psalm 110:3*) fathered by the Spirit of Christ—strong and mighty in the Lord and in the strength of His power, through which He establishes strength (*Psalm 8:3*) and brings about great things (*2 Corinthians 10:4, 5*). These go out with singular heroism and an undaunted lion-like courage against the enemies and adversaries of Divine truth, having girded themselves with the whole armor of God to stand firm in the evil day and to assault and storm the gates of hell.

This seems to be the focus of *Zechariah 9:13*. It appears to me that in the early Christian church, particularly the Apostles from Judah and Ephraim went out against the Greeks to cast down—through the power of truth, miracles, and signs, and by the assistance of the Holy Spirit—the wisdom, power, and following of the Greeks, which were famous throughout the whole world at that time. They did this to show the vanity, folly, weakness, and indeed the lifelessness of their religion (*1 Corinthians 1; 2 Corinthians 10*). See my notes on the first and second Epistles, where one finds the hand of the archers made strong through wisdom and power, being armed with the tools of God’s word and the church.

<column-break/>

### TREE, TREES; of KNOWLEDGE; of LIFE, etc. WONDER-TREE.

->Tree <note>original: "עֵץ, δένδρον, ξύλον, arbor"</note><-

What a TREE is, we know by sight and experience. Trees are of many types and kinds, each under its own name.

Because a tree stands in the earth, has roots within it, draws its moisture and nourishment from the earth, shoots out its branches, and gives its leaves, blossoms, buds, and fruits, it creates a shelter so that one often hides under it from the heat and the rain. Consequently, the designation of <margin>Tree used figuratively in Scripture.</margin> a tree in the Holy Scroll is not always taken literally, but frequently figuratively, in symbol and in imagination. Through this, either a particular man is sketched—such as a king, a chief of the people, a righteous man, or a wicked man—or a civil state and society of people that spreads far and wide, etc., is considered a "body politic." To this body, or tree of state, one can come from the outside and be sheltered and protected under it (*Daniel 4:10, etc.*; vine *Psalm 80:9, etc.*; fig tree *Matthew 21*; mustard tree *Matthew 13, Mark 4, Luke 13*).

Again, trees are brought forward as symbols of kings, monarchs, great <margin>Emblems of Sovereigns.</margin> and distinguished personages among the nations, yet in such a way that the people are usually included under them, even though they are the highest, greatest, and most prominent, together making up a tree or body of state under their rule, authority, and shelter.

Thus Abimelech is compared to a bramble bush and desired as head and king (*Judges 9:15*). See a tree reaching to heaven (*Daniel 4; Isaiah 10:19; Lamentations 4:20; Ezekiel 31:16-18; Revelation 7:1 and 8:7, etc.*) and explained in *Matthew 8:16*.

It appears sufficiently from all circumstances that John [the Baptist] speaks to and about the Jews, and that he compares the state of the Jewish citizenry and church to a tree, just as the Lord Jesus compared the same to a fig tree, a vineyard, etc.

A tree has a seed, the beginning of its coming forth. Likewise, all Israel is originally from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (*Isaiah 51:1, 2; Romans 11:16, 17*).

The height of these twelve sons, making up a stem of Jacob or Israel in Jacob’s house, later divided into various branches and ancestral houses, spreading into infinite side-branches and particular shoots, according to the prophecy (*Genesis 12:15-17, 19, 22, etc.*).

This tree began to grow in the land of pilgrimages; it wandered and was pruned, even oppressed in Egypt; it found itself without firm ground or planting in the wilderness; and finally, it obtained a firm ground in the promised Canaan (*Psalm 80; Isaiah 5*) and was there fertilized by blessings, watered by the Word and the Prophets, pruned by judgments and chastisements, and after much fruitlessness, uprooted by God.

John attributes a root to this Jewish tree, such as every tree must have to stand firm...

# BOW.

...gave and brought heavy disasters and sharp blows upon his enemies.

<margin>Israel compared to a bow.</margin>
When Israel sins and acts unfaithfully, it is compared to a **deceitful bow** that turns back on itself *Ps. LXXVIII. 57*. They do not turn to the Lord; they are like a deceitful bow, *Hos. VII. 16*. A bow that is slippery and twists in the hand of the archer—one with which no target or goal is hit, which cannot be relied upon, and which sometimes even harms the archer themselves—may be called a deceitful bow. When Israel made a show of truly turning to God and repenting, while meanwhile playing the hypocrite and committing unfaithful breaches of covenant by erecting high places and idols: completely failing to hit the target and goal of Jehovah's glory and the perfection of the neighbor in love with those actions; not using their tongue and power to win their neighbor through God's reason and subject them to God: was this not, in that regard, a deceitful bow? All the more so when God's name was blasphemed among the Heathens because of this, which inevitably had to be followed by destruction and ruin, *Hos. XIII. 9*.

A *deceitful and perverse bow* is, says *Jerome* <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the theologian best known for translating the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note>, one that strikes and wounds the one who directs it. See *Cyril, Theodoret*, and others. *Ursinus* <note>Zacharias Ursinus (1534–1583), a leading German Reformed theologian.</note> says, *God turns the arrows against the archer.*

For my part, I cannot see it otherwise than that it is given through imagery to understand that the long-suffering God, sufficiently provoked and taunted, exercises His power so that, through the effects of His power, He may appropriately judge and punish the wicked and unrepentant sinners—sometimes to their physical and eternal ruin—when He, as judge of the whole earth, does right, *Gen. XVIII. Rom. II. 5, 6, 7. 2 Thess. I. 6, 7.* and rewards everyone according to their works. Among the war gear of the reigning and triumphant King Jesus, one finds the bow and arrows. *Ps. XLV. 8. # BOW. TREE.

<margin>Apostles and teachers represented by the bow.</margin>
...and then they understood the arrows to be all the excellent teachers who are held as capable and sent out by Jesus.

However, I find more satisfaction in those who have viewed the bow as representing the Apostles, Evangelists, Pastors, and teachers. Christ successfully made use of these as blessed means and powerful instruments—as described in *Zechariah 9:13–14*—for the foundation, establishment, and expansion of his kingdom among both Jews and Gentiles.

He may be considered to "bend" or "string" this bow when he provides and equips them through his Spirit with the necessary gifts and abilities, encouraging and moving them to speak without shame, fear, or terror. By demonstrating the truth and revealing it to the conscience, they speak before kings, princes, governors, judicial benches, philosophers, and the wise of this world to plant the truth and overturn the seat of injustice. In this case, the arrows are distinct from the bow. See the entry for **ARROWS**, of which I could speak at great length.

<margin>The meaning of the arrows.</margin>
The Masoretes <note>Jewish scholars between the 6th and 10th centuries who standardized the Hebrew Bible text.</note> on *Psalm 45* translate it as: *the arrows of your words* or *of your armies.* Rabbi Solomon <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), a famed medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> understands the arrows to be the teachings of the wise. For my part, I speak more specifically and think, along with others, that there is good ground to understand them as the Word of the Gospel. This word is *sharper than a two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit,* *Hebrews 4:12.* It proceeded from the mouths of the Apostles and the first heroes of the faith in their departure and advancement among the Jews and, especially, among the Gentiles, being powerful in God, *Psalm 8:3; Romans 1:16 and 10:18; 2 Corinthians 10:4–5; Hebrews 4:12.* Alternatively, one might view these arrows as having a twofold effect, as Arnobius <note>An Early Christian apologist (died c. 330 AD).</note> did: those arrows deliver the king's favored friends but kill the king's enemies and adversaries, *2 Corinthians 2:14–16.*

One reads in *Psalm 127:4*: *Like arrows in the hand of a hero, so are the children of one's youth.* Thus are the Apostles and other subsequent Pastors and Teachers—begotten through the Spirit of Christ, *Psalm 110:3*—strong and mighty in the Lord and in the power of his might. Through them, he establishes strength, *Psalm 8:3,* and achieves great things, *2 Corinthians 10:4–5.* With singular heroism and an undaunted "lion-heart," they charge at the enemies and resistors of Divine truth, having girded themselves with the whole armor of God to stand firm in the evil day and to assault and storm the gates of hell.

This seems to be the focus of *Zechariah 9:13.* It appears to me that in the early Christian church, the Apostles from Judah and Ephraim specifically went out against the Greeks. Through the power of truth, miracles, and signs, and with the assistance of the Holy Spirit, they cast down the wisdom, power, and following of the Greeks—who were famous throughout the world at that time—bringing them to wonder and worship. They demonstrated the vanity, folly, weakness, and indeed the "juicelessness" <note>An archaic way of describing something as lacking life, substance, or spiritual nourishment.</note> of their religion, *1 Corinthians 1; 2 Corinthians 10.* See my notes on the First and Second Epistles, where one finds the hand of the archers made strong through wisdom and power, being armed with the equipment of God's Word and the church.

### TREE, TREES; of KNOWLEDGE; of LIFE, etc. WONDER-TREE.

->Tree (Hebrew: *Etz*, Greek: *Dendron* or *Xylon*, Latin: *Arbor*)<-

What a **TREE** is, we know through sight and experience. Trees are of many kinds and genera, each with its own name.

<margin>The tree as used in Scripture.</margin>
Because a tree standing in the earth has its roots within it, draws its moisture and nourishment from the earth, shoots out its branches, and produces its leaves, blossoms, buds, and fruits—and creates a shelter <note>Original: "belemmeringe," referring here to the protective canopy or shade of a tree.</note> so that one often hides under it from the heat and the rain—the name "tree" in the Holy Scroll is not always used literally. It is frequently used figuratively, in symbols and imagery, to sketch out either a particular person (such as a king, a leader of the people, a righteous man, or a wicked one) or a civil state and society of men that spreads far and wide. This is viewed as a "body politic," a state-tree which one can approach from the outside to find protection and shelter, *Daniel 4:10, etc.; the vine in Psalm 80:9, etc.; the fig tree in Matthew 21; the mustard tree in Matthew 13, Mark 4, Luke 13.*

<margin>Trees as symbols of Princes.</margin>
Furthermore, trees are presented as symbols of kings, monarchs, and great and prominent personages among the nations. However, the people are generally included under this imagery; although the leaders are the height and the greatness, together under their governance and authority, they constitute a single tree or "body of state."

Thus Abimelech is compared to a bramble bush when he is desired as head and king, *Judges 9:15.* See also the heaven-high tree in *Daniel 4; Isaiah 10:19; Lamentations 4:20; Ezekiel 31:16–18; Revelation 7:1 and 8:7, etc.; and Matthew 8:10* explained.

It is sufficiently clear from all the circumstances that John <note>John the Baptist.</note> speaks to and of the Jews, and that he compares the state of the Jewish citizenry and church to a tree, just as the Lord Jesus compared the same to a fig tree, a vineyard, etc.

A tree has a seed, the principle of its origin. Likewise, all Israel originates from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, *Isaiah 51:1–2; Romans 11:16–17.*

The higher part of these twelve sons, making up the house of Jacob like a trunk of Jacob or Israel, later divided into various branches and ancestral houses, spreading into infinite side-branches and particular shoots, according to the prophecy, *Genesis 12:15–17, 19, 22, etc.*

This tree began to grow in the land of "sojournings"; it wandered and was pruned, even oppressed, in Egypt; it found itself without firm ground or planting in the wilderness; and finally, it obtained a firm footing in the promised Canaan, *Psalm 80; Isaiah 5.* There it was fertilized through blessings, watered by the Word and the Prophets, pruned through judgments and chastisements, and, after much unfruitfulness, was uprooted by God.

John ascribes a "root" to this Jewish tree, such as every tree must have to sustain itself...

# TREE.
# X
<meta>catchword: compared to the sun.</meta>

...to unite firmly with the earth, to stand fast, to receive nourishment and moisture from the earth, and thus, in due time, to bear fruit.

A root is attributed to this tree, at which the axe already lay for the threatened uprooting. <note>Refers to Matthew 3:10: "The axe is already at the root of the trees."</note>

<margin>Messiah compared to a root.</margin>
It is not unknown to me how the Messiah is compared to a root, nourishing the members of His church toward true and excellent fruitfulness (*Isaiah 4, 11, 53, 55; Revelation 5, 22,* etc.).

I also well know how King Herod sought out the newborn <note>Jesus</note> as if with a slaughtering and vengeful axe, intending to cut Him down. And that the Jews attempted to kill and stone Jesus: and that He was finally, by the sword of judgment (so to speak) of the Romans, cut out from the land (*Daniel 9; Isaiah 53*), yet made alive again by His resurrection.

<margin>Faith compared to a root.</margin>
It is also not unknown to me that saving faith is frequently compared to a root, through which one is most closely united with Jesus: through which He dwells in the heart (*Ephesians 3*); through which one becomes like a plant with Him (*Romans 6:7*); through which one is immovably firm and becomes wonderfully fruitful, abounding in all good works (*Matthew 8:13; John 15; Galatians 2:20; Romans 11,* etc.).

Yet, because a divine sentence of vengeance and uprooting is revealed here due to bad fruits and a lack of good fruits—and because John <note>John the Baptist</note> threatens something not against Jesus, but against the Jews, not in the capacity of good trees but as bad and fruitless ones—and because faith is not uprooted but nurtured—and because that same faith makes a person fruitful in good works and virtues, etc.—it must follow by legal consequence that neither Jesus nor saving faith is meant here. Instead, it refers to something else that possesses the appearance and characteristics of a republic's root, contributing to the tree's stability, welfare, and growth.

That which has caused the Jewish republic, as God's people and government, to remain, stand, grow, and flourish, I hold to have been the **fundamental laws** <term>grontwetten: the constitutional or divine laws given by God</term> of that priestly kingdom, granted to them by God, their God, King, and Lawgiver. Furthermore, it refers to the government of this people through their judges and the Great Council <note>The Sanhedrin</note>: or the free government according to the divine fundamental laws of this kingdom. The tampering with these fundamental laws and the people’s free government was like an axe at this root.

The axe at this root must, by imagination, represent something suited to the nature of this tree and its root.

An axe is the creation of a blacksmith, made partly of wood and partly of iron, and sharpened. It is a carpenter's tool; it is also used by orchardists; and it is used in war to chop and hew (*Psalm 74; Jeremiah 46*).

<margin>The axe a symbol of powerful enemies.</margin>
The axe—an unreasoning and lifeless tool in the hand of a man for chopping and cutting out—can be a symbol and a figurative means of hostile men armed with power, who act as means and instruments in the hand of divine discipline and vengeance (*Isaiah 10:11*)...

<column-break/>

...(*Acts 14 and 17; Proverbs 21*) are used by Him to discipline, chastise, or even completely devastate, uproot, and scatter a people.

Now we can perceive various axes and blows at the root of the family tree of the Jewish people, planted by God in Canaan, both in respect to the fundamental laws and the free self-government of the people. Consider the various main sects and opinions among the Jews: the misinterpretations and violations of the divine laws (*Matthew 5:15–23*); the mutual bickering, strife, mutinies, and uprisings among the people, largely arising between those who claimed they ought to be free and those who favored the Emperors; the plot and existence of King Herod, a foreigner, regarding the ancestral genealogies and the members of the Great Council and the prominent citizens; the curtailment of the power to put criminals to death; the arbitrary removal and appointment of High Priests; the burden of a sort of head tax <note>poll tax</note>, etc. All of these were omens of even greater punishment. Therefore John says: *Every tree, therefore, that does not bring forth good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.*

The Orchardist, or the landowner, plants trees either for decoration or to gain good fruits from them.

Good fruits from a human being—as a rational tree and a covenant-partner of God—are all his deeds and actions arising from a living principle of faith, through burning love for God's glory, according to the precept of God's Word, for the edification, sharpening, and joy of one's neighbor (*Proverbs 16:4; Isaiah 43:21; Romans 11; 1 Peter 2:9*). These include godly reflections (*Psalm 2:14, 34; Romans 7:22*), edifying speech and conversations (*Ephesians 4:29 and Colossians 4:16*), Christian morals and virtues, godliness, righteousness, holiness, humility, etc., and subsequently all holy deeds (*Philippians 1 and 4:8; Titus 2:15; 2 Peter 1:5; 2 Peter 3:18*).

<margin>Bad fruits.</margin>
Regarding bad fruits, by way of reversal and evil contrast, one can look at *Psalm 81:15; Jeremiah 24; Ezekiel 16:49–50; Hosea 4:1, 2; Matthew 5:15–25; Galatians 5; Romans 3; Titus 3,* etc.

Such a corrupt tree of the Jewish civil and ecclesiastical state, and of each individual person for themselves, was to be uprooted and thrown into the fire.

<margin>Fire a symbol of love and hate.</margin>
Fire is an element that is hot and dry. Fire, however necessary it may be, is—when it is too hot and gains the upper hand—terrible, painful, harmful, and devastating.

Fire, according to its useful or harmful effects, has various symbolic powers in the Divine Scriptures: of love, hate, envy, bickering, strife, discord, war, devastation, God's indignation, wrath, hellish punishment, etc.

<margin>Tree of Judaism uprooted.</margin>
The tree of Judaism perished through mutual strife, civil and internal disturbances, the fire of war from the Romans, and the fire of judgment from the wrath of the avenging God, as one can read in Flavius Josephus <note>A 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian who chronicled the destruction of Jerusalem.</note> and elsewhere.

<margin>The body of state compared to a tree.</margin>
When one considers the body of the state as a tree, one encounters quite large and sweet similarities and correspondences between the two. Namely,

# TREE.
# X

<margin>Application.</margin>
a. Without a root in the earth, no tree can stand firm, grow, turn green, or produce foliage or fruit.
If one wishes to apply this specifically to the "Jewish tree"—their civil and ecclesiastical state, that great edifice of a people consisting of hundreds of thousands of Jews descended from Abraham and Sarah (*Isaiah 51:1, 2; Romans 11:16, 17,* etc.)—then from that root a stem grew in Isaac and Jacob. From this stem, twelve principal main branches emerged, and from these, infinite specific and smaller branches, main families, shoots, and offspring have sprouted.

<margin>Messiah called a root.</margin>
Furthermore, the Messiah is also called a "root" in *Isaiah 11* and *53*. The Hebrew word *shoresh* <note>original: "שרש"</note> is often understood as a spring or fountainhead, the beginning, the origin of a thing; also for the foundation and stability of any matter.

<margin>David's Root.</margin>
The Messiah is called the "Root of David" in *Revelation 5*, in whom the Gentiles were to be rooted or grafted (*Romans 11*). This root sprouted from the "hewn-down stump of Jesse" <note>The "Stump of Jesse" refers to the lineage of King David's father, which appeared politically "dead" before the coming of Christ.</note>, from Abraham and David. No one thought, judging by outward appearances, that He would ever have taken such a high leap or grown into a tree reaching toward heaven. Yet, in Him, all the promises were made to Abraham (*Genesis 12, 15, and 18*).
Otherwise, if the root is taken to mean the stability of the "tree of state" and that which makes the tree of the Jewish civil state grow and flourish, one would likely not be mistaken to think, as some do, of the Hierarchy or God’s government over that Jewish people: their fundamental laws, rights, freedom, and privileges upon which that civil and church state was founded, being governed by the Great Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and administrative council of the ancient Jewish people.</note>. To uproot this tree of free sovereignty and chop it down, the axe of God’s judgments—the axe and the hewing of the dominating, liberty-depriving, and devastating power of the Romans—was laid to that root (*Matthew 3:10*), a point upon which I shall not dwell.

b. The stem of that Jewish tree was to be sought in Isaac, then in Jacob and his sons, and thereafter in many branches among the twelve tribes and main families. These expanded into their various houses, spreading themselves throughout the land of Canaan, and afterwards far and wide into different cities, provinces, and colonies. Thus, one can view the tribes as the primary body and the rising essence of the state, extending itself more and more like branches into cities, provinces, colonies, and conquered territories, and so gradually becoming larger, higher, and more powerful (*Psalm 80:9, 10, 11, 12*).

c. What the branches are has already been heard. Among these, one finds those that shoot up very high and excel above all others. By these, one could understand either specific persons and families who, belonging to the "tree of state," excel above other lower branches in height, wealth, power, and luster; or some

<column-break/>

specific branches—parts of the body of state, such as conquered territories, principalities, duchies, etc.—which are found to have something special above the rest of the members and parts of the state. See an example of this in *Ezekiel 17:4, 22, 23, 24*, where one can see through the introduced symbols how Jeconiah, from the house of David, was plucked off like the topmost twig by Nebuchadnezzar and carried to Babylon. In his place was appointed Zedekiah, who, having made himself guilty of breaking a covenant with Nebuchadnezzar, turned toward the king of Egypt and made an alliance with him, expecting that the Egyptian would assist him with sufficient power against the king of Babylon—an effort that failed him and turned out very poorly. Now, from King Jeconiah, through Zerubbabel, a tender top-sprout and branch would come forth, which the Lord would plant on a high and lofty mountain, on Mount Sion: namely, the Messiah, the Christ (*Psalm 2*). He would become King, and His kingdom would extend itself far and wide in the world in and through His members, so that the Gentiles would take refuge in His kingdom—to such an extent that this kingdom would be exalted above all others (*Isaiah 2*). And the kings and princes, not having acknowledged Him and His governance but having rebelled against Him (*Psalm 2*) and having seen God's judgments, would have to submit to Him (*Isaiah 49*) or perish on the day of His wrath (*Psalm 2 and 110*).

<margin>Every person compared to a tree.</margin>
And to stay with the subject of a tree in general: every person may be compared to a tree, insofar as many things are found in man and in a tree that have some agreement. For:
1. All trees have their first origin from Creation, and thereafter through seed and sprouts, etc. So it is with men: from the first-created man, through the reproduction and sprouting of the seed.
2. Just as a tree grows from a small seed and a tiny, humble plant—according to its nature and kind—into height, thickness, and breadth, so it goes with a man over the years, some remaining small, others becoming of average or great height.
3. In the tree, on and upon it, one finds the bark, the stem, the branches, the crown, etc. In and on the man, one finds the skin, the rising stature of his body, the extending arms, the crown of the head, and the hair.
4. Without internal moisture and life-sap, and nourishment coming from the outside from the earth, no tree can grow. No man can live or grow without nourishment and moisture from food and drink coming from the outside, nor without his internal fluids which are spread throughout the entire body.
5. A tree brings forth its fruits according to its nature and kind. Every man produces after his own kind, and what one can expect from those adorned with a rational soul through thinking, willing, and working through and upon the body.

Indeed, I see that man is compared to an inverted tree <note>This philosophical concept, common in the Renaissance, suggests that man’s "roots" are his mind or soul, reaching toward heaven, while his "branches" (limbs) extend toward the earth.</note>, for the reason that with man...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical study of the "Tree," transitioning from the botanical and historical roots of the Jewish state to a moral and physiological comparison between trees and human beings, specifically focusing on the character of false teachers as described in the Epistle of Jude.</meta>

# TREE.

<margin>The difference between the nourishment of humans and trees.</margin>
In some respects, a human being functions quite differently in their nutrition than a tree does: for a tree draws its nourishment from below, through its roots in the earth, whereas a human receives food and drink from above. From the bottom upward, the tree distributes its saps; however, a human—through their natural soul—sends fluids, saps, and vital spirits downward from the brain, heart, and liver. The blood and vital spirits flow through the blood vessels toward the lower parts.

<margin>Metaphorical application.</margin>
Now, returning to a moral sense: insofar as a person is good or evil, or possesses good or evil intentions—what appears to be so but is not—they are compared to, or called, a good or evil tree, fruitful or unfruitful, and so forth. Thus, one speaks of a dry and withered tree, or of evil trees; and likewise of good and fruitful trees, as will now be more closely examined and demonstrated.

Regarding what constitutes an evil and unfruitful tree, something of this nature appears to us in the Epistle of Jude. By following this in our thoughts and discourse, we can arrive at a clear vision and understanding of the matter depicted. Jude writes in his letter, verse 12: *They are like trees in the fading of autumn, unfruitful, twice dead, uprooted.*

<margin>Explanation of the passage from Jude.</margin>
I believe that Jude is referring to godless, hypocritical, heretical, and deceitful teachers.

These appearing under the symbol of trees, I note they are so named:

a. Because they can be said to be planted in the external garden of the professing church or congregation through an outward calling, a certain enlightenment, and a confession of the truth—just as there is both wheat and weeds in a common field. *Matthew 13.*

b. The root is considered to be a historical "temporary faith" <note>Historical faith refers to an intellectual belief in the facts of the Bible without a personal spiritual transformation.</note> and a verbal confession of the truth; and outwardly, they are viewed as members of the congregation, belonging to the Lord's pleasure-garden.

c. Standing in this common soil and field, and being under the common fertilizing and pruning of the ministry of the Word and the Sacraments, they turn green and grow in knowledge and outward holiness. At times, they increase greatly in many outward matters beyond others who are truly planted by God. They are "professors" <note>In this context, "professors" are those who publicly profess their faith.</note>, giving exceptional hope that they will produce good fruit. One sometimes perceives in them great knowledge, extraordinary zeal, open confession, prominent modesty, compassion, helpfulness, and such things; one would think nothing else but that all was wonderfully well with them.

d. But because these people are not truly changed, nor are they sprouts of God’s planting, nor grafted and rooted in Christ, they merely retain their natural and animal life <note>original: "dierlyk, en ziellyk leven" — referring to the life of the physical senses rather than the spirit.</note>. Everything is more in appearance than in being. That which shows itself on their exterior never reaches its ripeness; their fruits, however beautiful in appearance, drop off, etc.

Jude calls them <term>δένδρα φθινοπωρινά</term> <note>original Greek: "dendra phthinoporina"</note> *trees in the fading of autumn.*

<term>Autumn</term> <note>original Greek: "Phthinoporon"</note> is that time of year which follows summer: and by common reckoning, it begins from

<column-break/>

the 15th or 22nd of August and lasts until the 22nd of December. In and around this time, when the fruits have been picked, the leaves also fall, and the trees lose all their beauty and pleasing appearance. For this reason, by <term>trees in the fading of autumn</term> <note>original Greek: "dendra phthinoporina"</note> is understood trees in that state in which they are <term>when the season is already declining</term> <note>original Greek: "phthinosis ede tes horas"</note> at the end of autumn: when they are no longer attractive due to the greenness of the leaves, nor pleasant due to the benefit of the fruit, but are as if dead. But among the Greeks, "autumn" also signifies as much as <term>a disease that spoils the fruit</term> <note>original Greek: "nosos phthinousa oporas"</note>, which causes them not to reach their ripeness, but to dry out, become sharp, harsh, and sour, rot, and fall off prematurely.

When this is applied to Jude's intent, it signifies and depicts such people who seemed to promise much, appearing beautiful to the eye, but when it came down to it, the leaves fell and the fruits were sour and harsh. They fell off prematurely against the autumn of surly storms and the winter blasts of adversity and oppression. They did not remain steadfast in the confession of the truth and the practice of godliness. Outwardly they appeared as tall and beautiful trees: exacting people with a form of zeal and godliness, yet without power. Their goal was profit, mastery, and reputation, acting as "belly-servers" <note>Those who serve their own physical appetites or greed rather than God.</note> and "men-pleasers," as in *Philippians 1* <note>The author likely intends Philippians 3:19, which mentions those whose "God is their belly."</note>. When the winter time arrived and the summer of prosperity was over, they "turned their coats" <note>A phrase meaning to change one's allegiances or principles to suit the circumstances.</note>; they let fall their leaf of confession and their buds of feigned virtue. Neither beauty, nor soundness, nor anything truly healthy, perfect, or ripe was to be found in them.

This is no wonder, for they did not have the true root of saving faith, which receives spiritual nourishment and communicates it to the tree, sending it properly through all the vessels.

They were not grafted or rooted in Christ: their root and branches were full of decay; they had a guilty conscience, a biting worm—the corruption not having been overcome by grace. It ate inward like a cancer; when the wind and cold arrived with chilly flakes, and the inner warmth was supposed to keep the tree in strength and standing, everything fell away, and nothing was brought to its ripeness.

The Apostle calls them <term>unfruitful trees</term> <note>original Greek: "dendra akarpa"</note>. Fruit-bearing trees are those which bear and produce something from which livestock or humans can derive some utility.

Trees are planted, fertilized, and pruned so that they might bear fruit.

Every tree has fruit according to its nature.

<margin>Man compared to a tree.</margin>
When a human is compared to a tree, one understands by their "fruits" their internal and external actions, virtues, and deeds toward God and men—their doing and leaving. These, when brought to the test of the Law (the rule of righteousness), are to be considered either good or evil.

Now, when Jude compares these base heretics—these deceptively beautiful, cunning frauds who spent grace in lewdness—to unfruitful trees, one must not think they were entirely without fruit; no, but they were without *good* and wholesome fruit. Certainly, they had their time, and behaved as though they were quite strongly zealous for Christian liberty, and for opposing—

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the "evil tree" metaphor from the Epistle of Jude, specifically analyzing why certain individuals are considered "fruitless" and "twice dead."</meta>

# TREE.

...left behind, as if they were the very cream of Christianity; yet their fruits were evil—they were "bad figs," <note>original: *Jerem. XXIV.*</note> *Jeremiah 24.* See them listed in *Galatians 5:19, etc.* They in no way sought the glory of God or the edification of their neighbors, but instead sought their own glory, a name, self-interest, a following, schisms, and the like. For several reasons, they were unfruitful, or trees without fruit:

- a. They did not purely intend the glory of God in everything. For according to the description by Jude, they achieved nothing less than that highest end: noting that they spent the grace of God in sensuality and denied the only mediator and ruler. They pursued "other flesh," living in impurity and base lustfulness, following their own desires and passions, serving their own bellies, *Philippians 3.* Indeed, they were not only without fruit but were also very harmful trees, since through their godless lives, God's name was blasphemed, and the early Christians were covered with a general stain of reproach because of them.
- b. And as for the neighbors of this generation—as has already been mentioned in a word—they drew no fruit from them. They did not seek to perfect them in love; instead, they led them with a bad example. They committed harlotry and adultery; they blasphemed authorities. They caused the Christians to be slandered and persecuted on their account, and they sought to draw the simple disciples away from following the Lord.
- c. Indeed, they were unfruitful for themselves, for surely they could draw no advantage from the "unfruitful works of darkness": from those things of which they should be ashamed, from that which had death as its wages, and from that which caused one to miss the Kingdom of God, *1 Corinthians 6.* In these things, they ruined and defiled themselves, foaming up their own shame.

<margin>
Twice-dead trees.
</margin>
The Apostle calls these trees <term>δὶς ἀποθανόντα</term> <note>original Greek: *dis apothanonta*</note> *twice dead*. *It is appointed for man once to die, and after that the judgment, Hebrews 9:27.* There lives no man who shall not see death. However, natural death—as the way of all flesh, brought about by sin, *Romans 6:23*—is not what is being spoken of here; for the people of whom Jude spoke were still in existence and would continue to manifest themselves further in the future. Those who have already died naturally are no longer "beacons in the sea" <note>This likely refers to being a warning sign or a guide for the living.</note> like the rest of mortals.

But there is another kind of death, inherent to all who come forth from the sinful womb, and that is spiritual death, *Ephesians 2*: death in sins and misdeeds, when one is by nature and through sinful corruption incapable of all spiritual endeavors, *2 Corinthians 3:5*; blinded and perverse, alienated from the life of God, *Ephesians 4*; when one is a servant of sin, *Romans 6*; and does not submit to the law of God, nor can they do so, *Romans 8.*

This is again the condition of all men by nature, and therefore what is common to all men is not specifically what is being addressed here.

This has led some to think of eternal death—the alienation from God, His blessed knowledge, and communion, accompanied by

<column-break/>

eternal horror, the precursors of which they feel in their consciences, more or less, in this life. However, since this shall be the lot and portion of all the godless, and not only of these of whom Jude speaks (whom he intends to be viewed as a specific example, providing an account of these people in the state of this life and not after their death), I agree with many theologians that Jude describes these base, heretical people—hypocrites and sham-professors—according to their nature, character, and state in this life.

To gain an understanding of Jude’s objective, one must properly observe the following: namely, a sinner who lives under the public ministry of the Divine Word can, through the use of these means, arrive at a knowledge of God, His counsel, and His will; how God can and will be merciful to a sinner in His Son and bring them into His blessed communion. He can give himself out to be a Christian and outwardly have the appearance of godliness. He can be viewed and held by others as an upright Christian. He may even lead others in profession and outward zeal. He can even preach the word of righteousness and speak of it to others with power and understanding. He can hear the word with joy and practice pure religiosity; being the first into the church and the last to leave; giving alms, being outwardly meticulous, and possessing a manufactured godliness—displaying a "painted fire"—and yet be and remain dead before God. He is not sanctified in truth nor changed in heart, but is swarming with evil lusts. For it is the knowledge of truth and virtue that causes one to embrace the truth in love, and which causes one to loathe, hate, and abandon evil; it is that which determines one's will and desire, intelligently and with steadfast joy, toward pure love and virtue.

Now these people, who seemed to live, who presented themselves as such, and were held as such by others—when they deny the truth and go against it after they have been transplanted into the external garden of the church and have come to the knowledge and profession of the truth, adhering to lies and destructive teachings, teaching them, advocating for them, and seeking to instill them in others—these, I say, are twice dead. See *Hebrews 7; 2 Peter 2:20, 21, 22.* Jude describes them as uprooted, <term>ἐκριζωθέντας</term> <note>original Greek: *ekrizōthentas*</note>: the word seems composed of <term>ἐκ</term> <note>original Greek: *ek* (out)</note> and <term>ῥίζα</term> <note>original Greek: *rhiza* (root)</note>, and it means *to root out, uproot, or pluck out of the earth*.

Trees whose leaves are withered, which languish, which produce unripe, sour, and bitter fruit, and which let their fruit and leaves fall, lack good and sufficient sap, or they do not have a good or healthy root, or their wood is cankered. They languish and die off gradually. When it then happens that a gardener or orchardist transplants the same into another soil, he prunes, manures, and cleanses it as much as he can of its evil and cankering wood. But if all is in vain, the fault must lie in the nature and the root. Therefore, he roots them out, not wanting them to occupy the ground uselessly any longer, only to be cast into the fire and burned afterward.

Uprooting presupposes a planting and a kind of taking root; when one applies this...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the metaphor of trees in the Epistle of Jude, moving from the description of "evil trees" to the nature of "good trees" and the process of spiritual planting.</meta>

# TREE.

Applying this to that sort of people of whom Jude makes mention, the nature of planting must be properly understood, as previously stated. Specifically, planting and rooting can be understood in two ways, just as "calling" is: namely, as a true planting and a powerful calling, where one—through saving faith, true conversion, and holiness—receives a share in Jesus and His acquired blessings, becoming a living member of His body, the church. Thus, one is rooted in Him <note>original: *Job. XV. Kol. II.* Note: The author likely refers to John 15 and Colossians 2.</note> for true spiritual stability and fruitfulness, living through faith. <note>original: *Habb. II. Gal. II. 20.*</note>

There is also an outward planting and rooting in the external church of those who profess the faith, through the general calling and the oral confession of faith, and by joining in the mutual fellowship of the signs and seals of the covenant of grace <note>This refers to the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper.</note>.

Of such a person, one would judge no differently than that he had roots, and that he drew nourishment and sap for spiritual growth and maturity, indeed, even an abundant fruitfulness.

And just as such people can seem to belong to the church—because they have, as it were, signed with their own hand that they belong to the Lord and stand openly recognized in the roll of names of those who profess the faith—nevertheless, their name can be crossed out and removed, either by themselves or by others. Consequently, they can be uprooted and cast out like a tree, either by their own doing or by someone else.

a. By themselves: when they, having presented themselves as good, well-rooted, and fruitful trees or members of the Christian church, demonstrate by their actions that they were hypocrites and never truly belonged to it.
b. This becomes known when they actually depart, leaving the fellowship of those who profess the truth, and go over to such gatherings where they deny, blaspheme, and persecute the truth they once confessed.
c. Or when they—having previously behaved offensively in their life, erring grossly in doctrines, and remaining stubborn in their opinions—are cast out of the church and no longer recognized as members of that society.
d. Or insofar as the Lord, through various righteous judgments, exposes such people, punishes them in an exemplary way, and—through a sudden death and exemplary punishment—makes an example of them to others. By this, He clearly makes it understood that, although they deceived men, He never recognized them as His own.

<margin>Good trees.</margin>
Until now, I have occupied myself and the reader with a genus of evil trees; now, if I am to complete my plan and the matter at hand, I must proceed and sketch how others are, and are called, "good and fruitful trees," just as specific things shall be said regarding various trees.

a. The righteous man is a good tree, planted by God, <note>original: *Pf. I. Jer. XVII.* (Psalm 1 and Jeremiah 17).</note> and grafted into Christ for spiritual fruitfulness, <note>original: *Joh. XV. 4, 5. Rom. XI. 17.* etc.</note> having become one plant with Him. <note>original: *Rom. VI. 5.*</note>

<column-break/>

Instrumentally, such trees are planted, grafted, and cared for regarding their fruitfulness and growth through the service of wise and faithful gardeners <note>A metaphor for ministers or apostles.</note>: although properly speaking, it is God who gives the growth. *See 1 Corinthians 3:6, 7,* where it is written that Paul had planted—that is, he had cast the good seed of the Word into their hearts. He had instructed the Corinthians regarding the fundamental doctrines of genuine Christianity and made them know and profess the truth, by which they were joined to the congregation of believers and planted into the Christian church.

Apollos had watered, further laboring upon what was planted and tending it for growth and fruitfulness; that is, he put everything into practice to subsequently teach, exhort, strengthen, and comfort them, building upon the first foundations of Christianity laid by Paul. He could do no more; but God had given the growth, which means God had blessed and empowered their labor in such a way that the Corinthians, being rooted in Christ through faith, increased more and more in knowledge, faith, love, hope, holiness, etc.

b. The righteous person has a root of knowledge, assent, and firm trust of the heart, <note>original: *Matth. XIII.* and *Marc. IV.*</note> through which Jesus dwells in his heart, <note>original: *Eph. III. 17.*</note> and through which he—love working with him—remains inseparably united with Jesus, provided he is firm and well-rooted. <note>original: *Eph. III. 17. Kol. II. 7.*</note> He is like one plant with Him, <note>original: *Rom. VI.*</note> and living in and through his union and fellowship, he draws the sap and the nourishment of life from Christ. <note>original: *Gal. II. 20. Joh. XV. 4, 5, 6.*</note>

<margin>The righteous compared to trees.</margin>
c. The righteous, like trees, are pruned of evil and destructive wood, of canker, and the eating worm—of sin and sinful corruption—through the circumcision of the heart and the pulling out and laying aside of the "old man," <note>original: *Deut. XXX. Ezech. XXXVI. Kol. III. 5. Gal. V. 24. 1 Kor. VI. 11. 1 Joh. I. 7.* etc.</note> through rebukes, threats, visitations, etc. <note>original: *1 Kor. XI. 32. Hebr. XII. 11. Openb. III. 19. Pf. CXIX. 67-71. Pf. XCIV. 12. Rom. V. 3, 4, 5.*</note>

d. The righteous, as trees, do not stand in parched or dry ground; they are fertilized and watered for fruitfulness, and thus planted by the streams of water of abundant means of grace. <note>original: *Pf. I. 3. Jer. XVII. 8. Jef. XLIV. 3.* etc.</note>

e. The righteous person is an ascending tree, growing tall: a tree that is fruitful, bearing leaves of profession, buds, and flowers of very good morals, giving hope for fruits, but also fruits and works of faith and pure love, etc. <note>original: *Pf. XCII. 13, 14, 15. Spr. IV. 18. 2 Petr. III. 18. Pf. LXXXIV. 8. 2 Theff. I. 3. 1 Theff. I. 3. Philip. I. 11 and IV. 8.*</note>

Vitringa, in his *Treatise on the Parables* <note>original: *Tract. de Parab. en Aug. p. 133.* Referring to Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian.</note> dealing with the mustard seed becoming a tree, compares the Church of the New Testament to it, writing in this manner:

> §. 39. *The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed,*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of botanical metaphors for the Church. # TREE.

<margin>The church compared to a mustard seed.</margin>
The seed, having been sown in the earth, has become a tree. *Matthew* states this clearly and with great emphasis: *and it becomes a tree.* Among the plants of the earth, a tree is the kind of plant that: 1. has a firmness and foundation upon which to stand and lean; 2. has a certain and fixed place in which to exist; 3. possesses a loftiness by which it excels among other plants and is seen by everyone; 4. is provided with foliage for beauty; 5. is divided into various branches which, through their leaves, create a shadow for the birds that are accustomed to nesting in those branches.

§. 40. All of this prompts us to think of that state of the Christian Church when, according to the ancient promises, it began to acquire a fixed and permanent dwelling place in the world—see *Psalm 107:7*—and began to become prominent and glorious. This occurred after the persecutions of Diocletian <note>Diocletian (r. 284–305 AD) led the last and most severe "Great Persecution" of Christians in the Roman Empire.</note> under Constantine the Great. During this time, all those characteristics we just mentioned regarding a tree applied very well to the Christian Church. For:

§. 41. Then, **a.** the church was visible in the world like a tall tree, and all people in the world were amazed at this sudden change in its state and fortune. Then the mountain of the house of the Lord was exalted above all the mountains. *Isaiah 2:2.*

Then **b.** it had a certain place where it took root and where, by Divine providence, it would remain for many years, having obtained a fixed place of residence in the Roman Empire. *Psalm 68:7.*

<margin>Jesus Christ the root of the church.</margin>
Then **c.** it had a foundation or root upon which it leaned in the world: namely, when the Roman emperors and princes, who had long before established their authority in the empire, supported and propped up the church. This happened as they themselves were accepted into the fellowship of the church—*Isaiah 49:23* <note>original: "13" – The text likely refers to verse 23: "kings shall be thy nursing fathers."</note>—for such princes and nurturing lords are truly like the roots of this tree of the church. they ensure that it has a fixed standing place in the world, and from them the church draws much benefit regarding temporal matters, just as a tree does from its root. I say regarding temporal matters, for regarding spiritual matters, no one is the root of the church except Jesus Christ.

**d.** When these princes brought their glory into the church, and alongside them, many men were found in the church who were famous for learning and virtue, the tree of the church displayed itself proudly with foliage and green leaves.

**e.** Then it could also grant shadow and refuge to those who, in other places, were stung by the heat of persecutions. This happened under Constantine the Great, in Persia, by King Shapur <note>original: "Sapores" — Shapur II, who ruled the Sasanian Empire and conducted long-term persecutions of Christians.</note>, who raised a heavy persecution in his kingdom against the Christians. Because of this, those Christians were forced to take refuge with Constantine, both by leaving Persia to live under the Roman Empire under the protection of the Christian emperor, and by pleading with him to be their advocate with the King of Persia. Constantine did so, although Sozomen <note>An early 5th-century historian of the Christian Church.</note> relates that the persecution continued until the time of Constantine—to say nothing of the persecutions of Julian <note>Julian "the Apostate," the last pagan emperor who tried to roll back Christian influence.</note>, as those were conducted within the Roman Empire. It also happened in the time of Theodosius, when the Persian kings Yazdegerd <note>original: "Isdigerdes"</note> and his son Bahram <note>original: "Gororanes"</note> raised heavy persecutions against the Christians, which forced many to take refuge under the protection of the Christian emperors.

§. 42. And this is then the fourth thing mentioned here in the parable: namely, that finally the kingdom of heaven has become a tree in whose branches the birds of the air nested. This indicates that the Christian Church would come to such a state in the world that even those living outside the church (as it was planted in the Roman Empire) would seek shadow and refreshment in the fellowship of that church. Or that they would join themselves to that church to have protection in its fellowship against the heat of persecutions and to enjoy a certain and safe dwelling place in the world.

§. 43. This occurred after the Christian Church, through God's providence, obtained a fixed dwelling place in the Roman Empire. Thus, even those living outside the Roman Empire, having been brought to the Christian faith, left their own fatherland and came to live under Roman rule to be participants in peace, rest, safety, and other privileges of the Christian Church. This could be proven with countless examples and has been taught by the experience of all times.

<margin>Birds, a symbol of all kinds of people.</margin>
§. 44. The birds of the air, then, are here a symbol of all sorts of people, whether good or evil (for in olden times there were clean and unclean birds), who would seek protection and refreshment in and through the Christian Church. This applies whether they only hypocritically subjected themselves to Jesus Christ, or whether they converted from Heathenism to Christianity with a true faith and joined the church to share with others in the outward benefits of the church, to which one may apply *Isaiah 60:8.*

<margin>Branches of the tree of the church.</margin>
For the branches of the tree of the church are a symbol of the great ones and authorities who can protect and refresh others. Compare *Ezekiel 31, Daniel 4:12-13, Revelation 19:17-18.*

§. 45. For whenever either a particular person or an entire society of people is compared to a tree, the birds—in relation to that tree—signify such people who seek their safety, protection, and refreshment with that person or society. Although in other circumstances birds may signify something else and something more—*Psalm 8:8*—nevertheless, under the symbol of the birds, the Philosophers are undoubtedly understood.

<margin>Birds, a symbol of the Philosophers.</margin>
§. 46. To clarify this parable, these remarkable passages should be compared: *Ezekiel 17:23-24, Isaiah 60:8, Daniel 11:35, Psalm 72:16, Ezekiel 47:1.*

Having spoken of trees in general, I shall now proceed to some specific trees, while sticking to my text.

One might think that if there were more of that species, it was not the entire species but only that tree, standing in the middle of the garden, that was forbidden. For one finds...

# TREE OF KNOWLEDGE.

No mention is made of any more trees: also, the word <term>כל</term> <note>Hebrew: *kol*, meaning "all" or "every"</note> "all" does not appear there.

It seems to me to have been a single tree, surrounded by the others, in the middle of the garden, perhaps standing opposite the Tree of Life.

If there had been more of that kind, what reason could Eve have had to want to eat from that specific tree, since she could have satisfied her desire elsewhere?

Unless one wishes to assume, without proof, that this tree was the most beautiful and attractive of its kind.

<margin>Investigation into this tree.</margin>
Regarding this tree, it is investigated what kind of tree and fruit it might have been.

I admit that one cannot speak with certainty or define anything here; however, since the Spirit of God has defined nothing in this matter—and human investigation often limits itself to the obscure—it has been found that scholars have cast their guesses in various ways.

<margin>Guesses of scholars.</margin>
Some have thought of the fig tree, because they took leaves from that tree to cover themselves. But it is not very likely that this tree would be so attractive to the sight, nor that our ancestors would want to cover themselves with the very thing that, by eating it, had plunged them and their descendants into infinite ruin.

Others think here of an apple tree, and an apple, because of what is written in *Song of Solomon 8:5.* <note>The text cites chapter VIII. 8, but the reference to the apple tree is found in 8:5.</note>

Others suggest a pomegranate, a "paradise apple" <note>likely a citrus fruit like the pomelo or a specific cultivar of apple</note>, a peach, an orange, a lemon, etc.; which, if anything may be guessed, cannot be entirely rejected.

Now, as to why this tree is called *the tree of the knowledge of good and evil*, scholars differ among themselves.

However, I believe that few will be found who would be of the opinion that it was so named because it possessed intellect, knew good and evil, and could properly distinguish between them; for that would be pure absurdity.

But some go so far as to believe, or at least deem it not unlikely, that the tree possessed the power to make the intellect, the use of reason, and the free will more ready, swift, and agile. This was the opinion of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, 1st-century Jewish historian</note>, *Antiquities Book II, Ch. 2*, Onkelos, the Jerusalem Targum, etc.

Yet I do not see how this follows so easily.

<margin>Difficulty raised by the author.</margin>
I know well that our spirit, being united with the body, gains or loses much in its operation depending on whether the body is well or poorly disposed—having swift and abundant spirits and juices, or few and corrupt ones—but I do not find that such a thing could take place in Adam in that first upright state at that juncture of time.

Nor do I see how something material in its nature could, through its use, add what was not already in the tree and the fruit itself, or enclosed within it.

I also do not notice at all that our ancestors became a hair's breadth wiser or more prudent, etc., by eating the forbidden fruit.

And if that tree had such power, then I do not

<column-break/>

see how God could have given a prohibition to man not to eat from that tree upon threat of death: for then Adam would have desired something for the further perfection of his spirit, and such a thing is surely not to be disapproved of; and how could he, knowing this beforehand, fail to direct his inclination toward it?

One might then wonder if the tree might not have been so named <term>ironically</term> <note>original Dutch: *spotsywyze*</note>, because of the promise and the shameful deceit of the serpent; as Rupert <note>Rupert of Deutz</note>, Alfonso Tostado, Pererius, etc., have thought.

But one must know that it was already so named before the temptation by the serpent, and that it is not likely that the tree would be so named after a lie and shameful deceit.

Nor do we see that they gained greater knowledge through the eating.

This then being rejected and passed over, I must come a bit closer: and then I notice that the thoughts of scholars arrive at two principal extremes, which are joined together by others.

<margin>Thoughts of scholars.</margin>
And since one expresses himself this way and another that way, I shall present the thoughts of the scholars more distinctly, using their own words or translations thereof.

> Such was it named, someone says, undoubtedly because it was presented by the will of God as a trial, by which it would appear whether man, according to the law of nature, would persevere in that uprightness or deviate from it: and in the outcome, if he persevered, he would experience what good he had chosen; if he deviated, what evil he had brought upon himself. Someone else writes thus: whether he would remain good or become evil; persevering in virtuous good, attaining useful good; choosing sinful evil, he would be ruined by calamitous evil. It was, says someone, a sign of the evil and the fault which would be in Adam and his descendants, or would dwell in them, consisting in the fact that he ate of it and, not being content with his portion and happiness, showed no obedience to God. God taught him, someone says, in a symbolic way, that he must receive instruction from God in and through this abstinence.

Thus, it is believed that this name was given to the tree in anticipation of the outcome and effect, so that Adam and Eve would find through the trial what and how great an evil they had brought upon themselves and their posterity by eating the forbidden fruit: what a great difference there was between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience: that it was, according to God's ordinance, the object of their obedience and a memorial of how great a good was to follow the obedient, and how great an evil the disobedient. God wanted to perform a trial here, it is said, whether man would persevere in the good or incline and turn toward the evil.

<margin>Opinion of Rivet.</margin>
Rivet <note>André Rivet (1572–1651), a French Huguenot theologian</note> believes that the tree was named such not before, but after the fall.

But one might wonder whether this trial and this tree were not more, and more properly, for man than for God.

And whether it was not already so named immediately before the temptation and the fall.

If so, Adam and Eve undoubtedly knew that beforehand. The knowing of good—

<meta>The previous page discussed various scholarly guesses regarding the physical identity of the Tree of Knowledge, such as the fig tree, apple tree, or pomegranate. # TREE OF KNOWLEDGE.

Knowing good and evil is not actually, as is often thought, the knowing of good and evil through trial and experience: but rather *knowing the nature of good and evil, and passing judgment according to that torch of knowledge, so that one chooses the good, rejects the evil, clings to the good, and turns away from the evil*, 2 Samuel 14:17; Isaiah 7:15; Job 28:28.

Certainly, God does not know evil through experience or practice; however, the promise lay therein, that in this way man would be made like unto God.

Indeed, when he had eaten, he knew evil by experience, but by no means did he know good by experience: for he was deprived of the true and supreme good—communion with God and true joy—and would have remained forever in a state of misery, had the Lord not had mercy upon him.

It seems to me then, that the tree, along with the Divine prohibition regarding that tree, can be viewed as a rule of what was good and evil by virtue of the explicit prohibition: thus, that tree had to be for them a cause for prudence, in a moral sense; that is, to teach them and bring to mind death and its cause, and to choose life: and such is the first and foremost rule of prudence, Proverbs 14:8, 16, 27 and Job 28:28.

One may consult regarding both points: Muis in *Various Sacred Matters* <note>original: *Variis Sacris*</note>, Rivetus, Dietericus in *Antiquities of the Old Testament* <note>original: *Antiq. V. T.*</note>, Leydekker's *The Torch* <note>original: *Fax*</note>, Witsius's *The Economy of the Covenants* <note>original: *Oecon.*</note>, Saldenus's *Leisure Works* <note>original: *Otia*</note>, Vitringa's *Sacred Observations* <note>original: *Observ. Sacr.*</note> page 4, etc.

<margin>God's purpose regarding the prohibition.</margin>
What end and purpose God had with this positive prohibition, I prefer to depict with the words of the pious Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for his "Federal Theology" or Covenant Theology.</note>. It was then to bring to the minds of Adam and Eve truths of the greatest and most weighty importance, namely: a. *That God was Lord of all.* b. *That Adam’s dominion was not absolute or independent.* c. *That true good is not to be found outside of God.* d. *That everything man desires, if it is not in and toward God, is evil; for no perishable thing, however pleasant and beautiful, is to be desired for itself as man's good, but that enjoying God in eternal life is man's highest and most eternal good; and that one ought to be satisfied and content with the things He provides for the flesh, or if circumstances dictate, with God alone.* e. *That God's will, as our Lord and sustainer, is alone the rule of all things to be desired or shunned outside of God.* f. *That man, in things to be desired outside of God, must not judge good or evil from his own heart, but only from God’s word, which makes known God’s good will.* g. *That the obedience through which man is justified is only this: that which is practiced with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the exertion of all of man's powers*, Deuteronomy 6:5. That is, *with a perfect judgment of the soul, with all inclination and desire, and with the highest earnestness and effort of all faculties.* Which obedience must be carefully maintained even in matters that seem smallest.

Add to this also h. *that man had not yet reached the pinnacle of happiness.* i. *That man should indeed strive for and desire that state, but that he had to keep to the path which God Himself had prescribed and pointed out.*

One might then think that this tree of the knowledge of good and evil, being forbidden by God as deadly to man, has allegorically

<column-break/>

sketched out all that which, as an object of irregular desire, could be the cause of death for man in its enjoyment: of all that which bears the fruits of death and has death as its wages, such as the world and that which is in the world—riches, pleasure, pride, status, 1 John 2:16, 17. These stand opposite the Tree of Life and must therefore not be irregularly desired, or it will lead to destruction; thus one must prudently arm oneself against them and guard against them. And yet these things are sweet and entice many, 2 Peter 1. Through this, man forsakes the love of God as his highest good, and thus inevitably casts himself into death and destruction. While the Tree of Life, Christ, offers Himself as the way and the means to life, <margin>Allurements of the world.</margin> the world does not cease to strongly recommend its sweetness and enticements for evil. Read the 7th and 8th chapters of Solomon's Proverbs: and that is the mind of the flesh and of the spirit, Romans 8:7-13.

Concerning desire, 1 John 2:16, 1 Peter 1:4, one is tested the most, as can be understood from the cases of Abraham, Genesis 22; Job chapter 1; Christ, Matthew 4. True self-denial is not to eat of the forbidden tree, Matthew 26:24, 2 Titus 2:12 <note>Likely intended as 2 Timothy 2:12 or Titus 2:12</note>. To bridle and regulate one's passions, to abstain from the forbidden, is true wisdom and prudence, Job 28:27.

In Paradise one found the trees of death and of life: it is true that Paradise was in a certain respect a figure of heaven; yet there one does not find the tree of death. <margin>Paradise a figure of heaven.</margin>

Paradise can be regarded as a place of fullness and abundance, a symbol of the Church of the Old Testament in Canaan, a land flowing with milk and honey: especially as a figure of the state of the Church of the New Testament, the Lord's garden and Eden, Isaiah 41:10-14 and 51:2. <margin>and of the church.</margin>

Moses set before Israel life and death, Deuteronomy 30:15—the two trees. From idolatry, fleshly lust, and self-righteousness from the works of the law, one had to guard oneself: for then one would not reach righteousness and life; then one would have to die in one's sins. That, alas, the Jews have experienced, following the desire for that fruit, with their expulsion from the Eden of Canaan. One had to taste and eat of the Tree of Life, Christ, believe in Him, and so live through faith in Him, as the cause of righteousness and life, with the renunciation of all that is in the world, and all that stands against the true means of life as a cause of death. See Vitringa's *Sacred Observations* <note>original: *Observ. Sacr.*</note> page 4, page 194, etc.

### TREE OF LIFE.

Regarding the TREE of LIFE, I shall, with the reader's permission, for the exercise of the understanding and for its opening, primarily bring forward Revelation 22:2: *And in the midst of its street, and on either side of the river, was the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit every month: and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.* Mention is also made regarding this tree of life in Genesis 2 and 3, to which Revelation 22:2 makes an allusion.

If we properly look at the Hebrew and Greek—

# THE TREE OF LIFE.

If we look at the Greek representation and expression, then this tree—this wood—appears to us in the plural or multiple number: *Genesis 2:9*, <term>the tree of life <note>original Hebrew: "etz ha-chayyim"</note></term>, the wood of life, or of the living; *Ezekiel 47:12*, <term>every tree <note>original Hebrew: "kol etz"</note></term>, all wood; *Revelation 2:7*, <term>the tree of life <note>original Greek: "xylon tēs zōēs"</note></term>, the wood of life: which will be more relevant in what follows.

<margin>Opinions of the learned.</margin>
Regarding the reason for this naming, all scholars do not hold the same understanding; I shall share various opinions with the reader.

One finds it said by some that <term>Augustine</term>, in *The City of God*, <term>Chapters 20 and 23</term>, might have been somewhat inclined toward the thought that this tree is called the "Tree of Life" because of the natural and medicinal powers placed therein by God. He suggested it possessed such inherent power that it could grant man immortality and preserve him forever from decay.

Luther, in his commentary on the book of *Genesis*, is said to have given this reason: *the tree of life was created for this purpose, so that man, by eating from it, might remain healthy in his body and exist without any fatigue.* And <term>Gerardus</term> on *Genesis 2:3* presented his thoughts in this manner: *1. This tree is named the tree of life because it would have provided man with a long-lasting life; 2. not only because it would have granted man long life, but also a peaceful and pleasant life; 3. it would not only have restored the "natural moisture" <note>An old medical concept referring to the essential fluids that maintain life and health</note> but also improved what was corrupted and lost.*

As for me, it seems to me that one goes quite far in this matter and asserts things that require proof. For if one ascribes power to this tree to make the Adam who eats from it live forever, or a healing and restoring power against weakness, sickness, and accident, etc., then it would also be necessary that this tree itself never weakened, aged, or died, but remained forever equally youthful, powerful, and full of sap. This is suggested to me neither by sound reasoning, nor by the word of life, nor by the purpose of Adam's gardening.

Then this tree alone would have been enough for Adam. What purpose, then, would the rest of the trees, the herbs, and plants serve? To what end was the tilling of the earth? It also seems to me that to wish to think of a healing, restoring, and improving power in this tree is very untimely and groundless, as it is not consistent with an uncorrupted nature—since all weakness and decay come from the sinful Fall and corruption.

<margin>Reflection on the naming of the Tree.</margin>
Since it is the case that the aforementioned opinions cannot be accepted on solid ground as the reasons for this naming and description, it further comes to mind what the most probable reason for this naming might be. In researching this, I have found that some have sided with Augustine, who says that while all other trees and fruits were intended for food, this tree served Adam and Eve as a <term>Sacrament <note>original Latin: "Sacramentum"</note></term>—a divine sign and pledge—that if they remained steadfast in their love and obedience, they would then, as a reward of recompense, live forever in God’s Paradise, in body and soul, both now and hereafter.

<column-break/>

It is known of God how God's Son is compared to a tree and wood of life, and how life, and the power, cause, and effect of life are attributed to Him: *Psalm 36:10*, for *with You is the fountain of life*; *Proverbs 3:19; Proverbs 13:14; John 14:6; John 1:4; Acts 13:15; Galatians 2:20; Philippians 1:21; Colossians 3:3, 4; Revelation 2:7*, etc. To bring this to my purpose, I would like my reader to observe with me Adam and Eve in two different states: before the Fall, not needing a mediator, guarantor, and God-Savior; but certainly needing one after the Fall. Meanwhile, we must also pay attention to and observe God's wise and eternal providence, and thus notice in what way one should consider the Son of God before and after the Fall.

<margin>Adam and Eve in two different states</margin>
a. Before the Fall, I note not only that the Father and the Son are one in essence and Divinity, but also that the Father regards the honor of His Son and does everything for the Son, whom the Father loves, just as the Son also regards the honor of the Father, *John 5:10-12, 17*; and from this fundamental principle, I subsequently derive everything.

b. When I now further propose that God placed this Tree of Life in the sight of Adam and Eve before the Fall, and he was permitted to eat of it, with the prohibition against eating from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil: then I imagine that God wanted to teach Adam before the Fall: 1. that Adam did not possess the animal life <note>The physical life shared with other living creatures</note> which he had from, out of, and through himself, but from, out of, and through the essential and self-existent Word, His Son, who had produced him and all else, *Genesis 1:2; Psalm 33; John 1; Colossians 1; Hebrews 2*. 2. That it was this Word, and the self-existent Wisdom of the Father, upon whose knowledge, love, and fellowship he must rely above all else, and in Him seek and place his happiness, life, and salvation, to "kiss Him" <note>A biblical expression for showing homage or devotion</note>, *Psalm 2:12*, to know Him, *John 17:3*, for *whoever finds me*, He says, *has and finds life*, *Proverbs 8:35*, and obtains favor from the Lord. 3. And to expect from the Son, who was his Creator, his fully blessed life, if he remained in His love, submission, and obedience. 4. And by logical consequence, that by turning away from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, he had to satisfy himself only with the Tree of Life. 5. If he did not do so and ate from the forbidden tree, it must necessarily follow that he sinned greatly, as one who lightly esteemed and despised the Tree of Life, the <term>symbol <note>original: "merk"</note></term> of the Son of God, the cause of all life, now and hereafter.

<margin>Tree of Life a symbol of God’s Son.</margin>
But after the sinful Fall and the apostasy of Adam and Eve, the Tree of Life was and remained a representational means and a <term>symbol <note>original: "zinnebeelt"</note></term> of the Son of God, yet it then appeared in another respect and relation: namely, as God-Savior, Redeemer, Healer, and Giver of Life to sinners, who were sick through sin and wounded unto death; which was by no means necessary before the Fall, of which more will be spoken in what follows.

And as for the question of whether there were more than one...
