<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Tree of Life, specifically debating whether it was a single unique specimen or a species of tree that existed in multiple locations within or beyond Eden.</meta>

# TREE OF LIFE.

there was but one tree of life; regarding this, I note that many will cast their votes for the singular number of this tree: observing that in quite many places, mention is only made of one God Savior, Redeemer, Deliverer, Fountain of Life, and Mediator, *Isaiah 43:11, Job 14:6, Acts 4:12, 1 Timothy 2:5-6,* and that the Old and New Testaments do not explicitly speak of more "life-wood" or trees.

Upon which, with appropriate modesty, the following should be noted:

a. That almost everywhere this tree and this "life-wood" are discussed, the naming appears in the plural and not in the singular, as was indicated above.

b. Here, in the naming of *tree of life* and *wood*, the type and the genus are presented, but by no means the specific number. In the same way, one might say "apple tree," "pear tree," "nut tree," or "grapevine": and then all sorts of individual specimens are understood under that name.

c. There may have been several types of trees of life, though perhaps the most excellent one stood in the middle of the garden and was shown to Adam.

d. And even if there is but one God Savior and Deliverer, it does not necessarily follow that there needed to be only one tree of life: for although the God Savior is but one, and no one is God Savior but He, and salvation is in no other, *Acts 4:12,* nevertheless, this God Savior imparts Himself to His own in various ways: and although He is a single person, He has nonetheless been represented by many persons and things, such as a *cloud, rock, fountain, sheep, lamb, priest, etc.* Now, who does not know that there are many of those kinds? Thus, there could also have been several trees of life in Paradise.

e. If I observe how God brought forth His blessing for multiplication of nearly everything—trees, herbs, and plants—*Genesis 1:11, 12,* then I find no appearance of reason to deny that blessing to the tree of life more than to other trees.

To further illuminate the matter, let me give my thoughts a bit more rein and propose a few scenarios: namely,

<margin>
Proposal
of several
cases.
</margin>

1. I propose that the tree of life was a <term>sacrament <note>A physical sign of a sacred reality</note></term>, a pledge, and a means of signifying and sealing life here and hereafter in the knowledge, love, and communion of the Son of God, provided Adam and Eve remained in Divine love and obedience.

2. Suppose that Adam and Eve had remained in the state of righteousness and in God's friendship.

3. Suppose also that they were to constantly behold, regard, and enjoy this tree of life as such a sacrament, sign, and pledge.

4. Suppose further that Adam's descendants, having multiplied and increased, would have populated the earth everywhere, as later happened:

From these observations and suppositions, one may lawfully deduce,

<column-break/>

1. That the tree of life standing in Paradise could not have been seen or enjoyed as a sacrament, sign, and pledge by thousands of Adam's descendants living everywhere outside of Paradise, which nonetheless seemed to be required.

2. From which it then seems to follow, to satisfy the purpose of the ordination of this tree of life, that it was the same with this tree as with the other trees and plants: that it could be cultivated, multiplied, and carried over by transplanting.

And if one does not wish to be too rigid in their position, then one will very easily perceive that here, and in *Ezekiel 47:12*, mention is made of more than one tree of life: for one should imagine a river that runs through the whole city: a row of trees through the city, by, next to, or along the river: indeed, a double row of trees on both sides of the river, as the most delightful walking path or the most beautiful sight for the eyes.

<margin>
Indian
wonder-tree.
</margin>

Or one must think that God's Spirit here had in mind the Indian wonder-tree, *Indi Dagheli* <note>Likely the Banyan tree (*Ficus benghalensis*), known for its aerial roots that grow into new trunks</note>, of which *Curtius*, *Strabo*, *Mandelslo*, and *Pietro della Valle* and others relate that it shoots its branches downward, which branches, uniting with the earth, make new shoots, and spread themselves so far and wide that a numerous army could shelter under it and hide against the heat of the sun.

But let this be noted only as a passing thought, from which I easily depart to proceed to another question.

It will not be entirely untimely to ask *whether Adam and Eve were free to eat from the Tree of Life. And if so: whether they actually did eat from it.* When I speak of one and the other, I will first say this: that some of the learned are on the negative side, and others on the affirmative and assertive side; however, I do not know of the clearest answer regarding this appearing to me in the Lord's word: therefore the answer must be derived from some probable principles. Stepping toward this, I say, it still seems by no means improbable to me that Adam and Eve were not only permitted to *eat* of the fruit of the tree of life, but also did eat. My reasons for probability are these:

a. God, in granting power and freedom, appears to do so with the sole exclusion of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. No other tree is seen to be denied in terms of use through exclusion in *Genesis 2:16, 17.*

b. When Adam had sinned, the Lord drove him out of Paradise so that he would not eat of the tree of life, *Genesis 3.* If this tree was, as noted above, such a sign, pledge, and sacrament, it is not only probable that he was allowed to eat from it, but that he did eat from it.

c. Yes, if this tree of life was a sign that the Son of God was the cause of physical life for Adam, and that He would bestow eternal life upon him if he remained obedient and in His love, then it seemed in every way—

# TREE OF LIFE.

<margin>Paradise as a symbol of heaven.</margin> it seems reasonable that he <note>Referring to Adam</note> was meant to eat from the fruit of this tree, and by his example and instruction, become a tree of life to his own descendants. Other reasons and reflections I shall pass by. 
I know well that Paradise, as a place of all fullness, is considered a very suitable symbol of heaven, *Luke 23:43, 2 Corinthians 12:4,* and that quite many points of agreement can be provided.

<margin>Places of pleasure compared to Eden.</margin> I know furthermore that places full of delight, and of singular pleasantness and abundance, are compared with Eden, a garden of the Lord, *Genesis 13:10, Isaiah 51:3, Ezekiel 28:13 and 31:9, Joel 2:3.*

<margin>The church compared to Paradise.</margin> And if there is anything, besides Heaven and the heavenly state, that can and may be compared to the famous Garden of Paradise, it would be the church of Christ, especially towards the latter times.
1. For did this garden have its designer, architect, and landowner? So too does the church, being frequently called a beautiful garden, full of fine trees and elegant fruits, as can be seen in *Song of Solomon 4:5, 6-8.* This garden exists because of the choosing, purchasing, calling, planting, and designing of the Father and the Son.
2. Did the Lord appoint Adam to guard and to labor in this garden? The Lord of old used for that purpose the patriarchs, Moses, the Prophets, the Evangelists, and the Apostles, and afterwards pastors and teachers.
3. Did God fence in Paradise? The Lord fenced in the Jewish church through His laws and statutes, and shut the Gentiles out; through "Gods" <note>likely referring to magistrates or divinely appointed leaders</note>, providers, and guardians: while in the New Testament, God Himself, through His protection and the "covering wing" of the powers, fences in His church, *Psalm 122 and 125, Isaiah 41, Zechariah 2, Isaiah 49,* etc.
4. Were very beautiful trees, tree-fruits, flowers, herbs, and spices found in Paradise? In the church they appear to us many times, especially in the Song of Solomon: *Psalm 50:91 <note>likely a misprint for Psalm 92</note>, Isaiah 35:44-51, Jeremiah 17, Song of Solomon 4:5.*
5. Was the Garden of Paradise intersected by various rivers and watered to a singular fertility? The garden of the New Testament church certainly has its share in this, both through the dew and rain of the Word, and the constant moistening and the fertilizing power of grace and the working of the Holy Spirit, *Psalm 1, Jeremiah 17, 1 Corinthians 3, Isaiah 35:44.*
6. Was the Garden in Eden not open to everyone? Did the defiled Adam have to leave it? The church and church communion is not for all and everyone: many are called, but few are chosen: some are shut out and cast out, *1 Corinthians 5 and 6, 1 Timothy 1, Revelation 21:8-27, etc.*

Now that this has been presented regarding the "Church-City" being compared with the ancient Paradise of God, it comes into further consideration: who is to be understood by this tree of life, or the trees by the river that intersects the city? This being brought into question, and having come to my answer, I say:

a. Jesus Christ, both in Himself as the

<column-break/>

true God and eternal life: as the Son of the Father: as <term>Surety</term> <note>Dutch: *borg*. A legal/theological term for one who takes on the debt or guilt of another</note>, Mediator, High Priest, God, Healer and Savior, the fountain of life, *Psalm 36:10,* who has life in Himself, *John 5:26,* the way, the truth, and the life, *John 14:6,* who gives the crown of life, *Revelation 2:10,* in whose knowledge is righteousness and life, *Isaiah 53:11, John 17:3,* He is primarily called the Tree of Life in and by the church and the true members of the Church-City.

<margin>Christ the tree of life.</margin> The first Adam, eating of the forbidden wood <note>The Dutch *hout* means both "wood" and "tree"</note>, brought death, curse, and punishment upon himself and his descendants, *Genesis 3, Romans 5:12, etc.*

<margin>Disasters caused by Adam.</margin> But the second Adam, Jesus Christ, has Salvation hanging on the wood <note>referring to the Cross</note>, having carried the sins and transgressions on the cross, suffered the curse and the punishment, reconciled and satisfied the Judge and the Debt-Claimant, and opened anew the heavenly Paradise, *Romans 5:8, 1 Corinthians 15, 1 Peter 2:3.*

<margin>Christ achieves.</margin> b. However, in another, fainter, subordinate sense, I also understand the matter thus: that in this Church-City, and along this running river of pure and crystalline water, many more trees of life are represented as standing, as seen by John according to his power of imagination: for
1. Indeed, it is too well known for one to dismiss it in ignorance, that believers and the righteous are compared not only to trees in general, but to the most prominent and fruitful trees: even the great princes, kings, and powers of the earth, when they bring to the church of God and the true church members a pleasant shade and a joyful and powerful protection: which they are not of, from, or through themselves, but as planted by God and grafted into the Tree of Life, Jesus Christ.

<margin>The righteous and princes compared to trees.</margin> 2. What has been said is so well known and clear that I will only—yet in abundance—add some texts: *Psalm 1:3 and 92:13, 14, 15; Proverbs 3:19 and 15:4; Isaiah 35:44-51; Jeremiah 17:8, etc.*
3. Which spiritual trees are living and fruitful through their grafting into Jesus, and the constant inflow of His fertilizing powers of grace. With such an allusion this matter is also presented to us in *John 15:4, 5; Romans 1:17; Galatians 2:20.*

<margin>Fruitfulness of the spiritual trees.</margin> This Tree of Life, God’s Son, and these living trees, the righteous, stand on both sides of the pure and crystalline river, flowing from beneath the throne of God and of the Lamb, through the Church-City.

When the Son of God is represented to us standing by this river, we must not think that He would necessarily need anything from outside Himself for a good state, standing, or fruitfulness, as a tree requires for its fertility: no, nothing less than that: for He is sufficient unto Himself: He has the fullness and the life in Himself: but just as the throne and the flowing waters from under the throne belong to Him, so He is...

# TREE OF LIFE.

...just as in the middle of the city [it is] compared to a tree of life, to satisfy the desires of souls through these two symbols, which are often presented in Holy Scripture as hunger and thirst; and thus he <note>Christ, the Tree of Life</note> is the food and drink of souls. Here, the church-city and its inhabitants are presented as being nearby and accessible, for the fulfillment of the soul's desires, the removal of hunger and thirst, and for spiritual refreshment and fruitfulness through his Spirit, Word, and grace.

But when we remember that this single tree of life, the *Son of God*, has made many into living—yes, life-giving—trees through being grafted into him; and when we most emphatically imagine how their state is depicted by the clear, living, crystalline waters, such that their roots are constantly moistened, and the inhabitants of this city can retreat and hide from the heat of the Sun by day under this refreshing shade, etc.; then it seems to me that this figure and pictorial representation can teach us that those who stand before Jesus' throne belong under his throne and dominion, and are grafted into him through faith. Being always in his proximity, under the reach, sight, and governance of his throne, they never lack the means of grace for inner refreshment and consolation, for proper growth and fruitfulness, nor for powerful protection in the day of wrath and heat.

And since it is already revealed from the preceding chapter <note>Revelation 21</note> that the kings and greats of the earth already brought their honor and glory into this church-city; and it is known that kings and princes are often compared to trees that provide high and strong shade—*Isaiah 10, Lamentations 4, Ezekiel 31, Daniel 4,* etc.—and since of old, when great and heavy heat came, people used to sit and walk under the shade of leaves and branches; so this symbol can also signify to us that very happy state and condition of the church-city and its citizenry, especially toward the later times: that alongside the throne of God and the church-city, there shall be kings, princes, and great personages belonging to and in the city, like a continuous river, so that under their oversight, protection, and cover, one may lead a quiet, peaceful, and godly life.

This tree of life yields twelve fruits, yielding its fruit from month to month.

<margin>Palm tree as a symbol of the year.</margin>
It is a strange thing that the Palm tree shoots out a new branch every month, and that for this reason (according to the report of Horus Apollo <note>Horapollo, an author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> and Pierius Valerianus <note>Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani, a Renaissance humanist known for his work on symbols</note>) it was held as a symbol of the year by the Egyptians.

In warmer lands, there are trees that are hung with fruit twice a year; but that trees should be found that give new fruit every month is something I do not recall hearing or reading anywhere.

<margin>Questions.</margin>
Here, several points fall under consideration and inquiry:
1. Different kinds of fruit every month?
2. Or the same kind, but always fresh fruit?
3. Or does it mean to suggest *never without fruit, throughout the entire year of Divine pleasure?* And are these fruits also of many kinds, powers, and natures?
4. Or fruits for the twelve tribes of Israel? Or from the twelve tribes of Israel? Since

<column-break/>

one later lives first from the Gentiles, and their healing?

<margin>And the author's suggestion.</margin>
For my part, I wish to suggest with the utmost modesty and submission whether one might understand these twelve fruits of Christ and his Spirit—produced by the grafted branch by virtue of being grafted into him—as those fruits presented in *Romans 14:17, Colossians 3, Galatians 5:22, Philippians 4:8, 2 Peter 1:4, 5, 6,* etc. Namely: *knowledge of Divine truth; faith and confession; love of God and neighbor; inward peace and rest; awakening conformity with God's image in holiness and purity; bearing joy and gladness in God; furthermore, kindness, longsuffering, humility, gentleness, patience, mercy, leading to active love and generosity.* These fruits would then be perceived in power when the Lord would stir the dead bones of the house of Israel and make them alive (*Ezekiel 37 <note>The original text cites chapter 17, likely a printer's error for the vision of dry bones in chapter 37</note>, Romans 9 and 11*). But I also wish to be mindful of the healing power of the leaves of this tree:

*And the leaves of the tree (wood) were for the healing of the Gentiles <note>Or "the nations"</note>.*

<margin>The state of the Gentiles.</margin>
The *Gentiles*, as such, are described as being outside the true knowledge and covenant-fellowship of God, and as having no active part in Christ, the tree of life (*Psalm 147, Acts 14 and 17, Ephesians 2,* etc.).

Yet they appeared to us in *Chapter 21* as flowing toward the church-fellowship and the church-city.

While still in their [fallen] nature, they have deadly ailments, maladies, sicknesses, and defects in their feelings, life, and morals; therefore, they must be made alive, cleansed, and healed by Christ's blood, Spirit, and Word (*1 Corinthians 6:11, Zechariah 13:1, 1 John 1:17*).

<margin>Leaves of the tree of life.</margin>
To which end the leaves of that living wood would also be found very useful and wholesome.

<margin>Usefulness of leaves on trees.</margin>
The leaves on the tree are proof of the tree's growing life. A tree without leaves seldom produces fruit—at least, seldom good and pleasant fruit. The leaves on the tree create a sweet ornament and a pleasant covering for the trees and fruit, providing shade against the scorching and drying heat, the night cold, sharp winds, and the pests falling upon them.

In hot countries, people used to seek the shade of trees by the rushing rivers and flowing streams.

<margin>Wholesomeness of tree leaves.</margin>
It is very rare that one chooses and seeks out tree leaves as healing food; they are often used to boil drinks, to prepare poultices, etc., for the ripening and driving away of hard swellings, fiery pustules, and inflammations.

This being the case, and speaking in a moral and spiritual sense regarding the defects and condition of the Gentiles and the peoples still foreign to the church (though flowing toward it and being taken in), one can easily understand how much can be contributed to the civilization and improvement of the life and morals of the wild, industrious, and unrefined Gentiles and nations. Besides the Word and heart-changing grace, much is contributed by the outward appearance with which the true trees of life are draped and adorned: namely, their moderation, dignity, friend-

## JONAH’S TREE.

<margin>Differences among scholars concerning Jonah's tree.</margin>
The learned differ wonderfully regarding this TREE; and certainly, its coming and its passing were wonderful and sudden.

Jonah, though unwillingly, having preached the approaching destruction at God’s command if those of Nineveh did not repent, went—after performing his duty—to sit outside Nineveh, having sought out a shelter and hiding place for himself against the burning rays of the Sun.

<margin>God’s delay of punishment vexes Jonah.</margin>
It seemed quite against his will that God delayed so long in punishing the inhabitants of Nineveh in an exemplary way; it appears he would rather not have preached to them at all than have his threat seem to come to nothing. He thought to himself that God could well have spared him this trouble, since He was merciful and compassionate enough to take pity on the Ninevites anyway.

<margin>A miraculous tree appears to him.</margin>
While he thus waited under his cover with the utmost displeasure and impatience to see what would become of Nineveh—wishing rather to die than to live in that sorrow and reproach, waiting with a heavy heart for what the Lord would do—God caused a miracle-tree to grow up over him in a single night. This tree shaded him pleasantly, so that he was wonderfully delighted by it and partially relieved of his sorrow. But when a worm and an east wind caused it to wither and fade in great haste, so that he no longer received protection from the burning heat, he became very angry. He wished this miracle-tree had been spared. On this occasion, God convinced him that there was not the slightest comparison between that tree, in its service to him, and the city of Nineveh, in which there were more than 120,000 children, besides the adults. Yet Jonah wanted the miracle-tree spared for his own sake, even though he should have judged it more fitting and consistent with Divine mercy to preserve and spare such a great city after its preceding humiliation and conversion.

<margin>Disputes regarding this.</margin>
As to what kind of tree this was, I confess I do not know. I know of no tree, sprout, or plant that naturally grows to such a height with such leaves and thick foliage—to create such a dense shade—anywhere in the ordinary course of nature. I hold it to be a miracle of God; yet regarding what nature or species this tree belonged to, people have argued for a long time.

Some take this growth to be Ivy; others a cucumber plant; others a type of Plane tree; others a white vine; others a fig tree; others a Colocynth, or wild gourd, called *Cucurbita* <note>Latin: "gourd"</note>.

Finally, others understand it to be the *Ricinus* <note>The Castor Oil plant</note>,

<column-break/>

the Wonder-tree, or mole-plant, called by some *Palma Christi* <note>Latin: "Palm of Christ"</note> or Christ’s Palm, whose leaves are broad and spread out like the palm of a hand with extended fingers.

<margin>Variations.</margin>
According to the variety of languages, regions, and peoples, it is named <term>Ki</term> <note>Greek: "Κι"</note>, <term>Kiki</term> <note>Greek: "Κικι"</note>, <term>Kroton</term> <note>Greek: "Κρότων"</note>, Elkeroa, Alkarva, etc. See Pfeiffer’s *Dubia Vexata Scripturae*, Dieterich’s *Antiquitates Veteris Testamenti*, Pliny Book XV Chapter 7, Dioscorides Book IV, Mattioli, Dodoens, and others.

Jerome <note>Hieronymus</note> relates that this little tree has broad leaves, like vine leaves, and provides a thick shadow; it stands on its own trunk, grows rapidly, and grows in Palestine, particularly in sandy places.

<margin>The power of this plant.</margin>
It is claimed that the word <term>Kikayon</term> <note>Hebrew: "קיקיון"</note> comes from <term>Kiah</term> <note>Hebrew: "קיא"</note>, meaning to spit out or vomit, and that Kikajon comes from "vomiting" or "vomit," because the *Ricinus* plant causes spitting and vomiting if one consumes a certain number of its seeds. It is said that much obstructing phlegm is cleared by it, that bile and water between the skin and flesh are driven off, and many obstructions and thickened, congealed fluids are thinned and expelled from both above and below. See Dodoens, Book XII, Chapter 11.

For my part, as to what kind of tree it actually was, I cannot say with any certainty, allowing everyone to make their own guess. However, I dare to take it upon myself to say that I believe no one will ever be able to determine and define it with full certainty.

<margin>Symbol of the Jewish people.</margin>
Furthermore, it is not unknown to me that some have viewed this miracle-tree, its stinging by a worm, and its sudden destruction as a symbol of the Jewish people. As Jerome writes, he found that some applied it to the Jews and their downfall, caused by the gnawing and judgment of the "worm" Jesus <note>Referring to Psalm 22:6, "I am a worm and no man"</note> and the service of the Romans. I have also noticed that some learned men of this time are not entirely a stranger to this view.

<margin>Jonah as a type of Christ.</margin>
It is certainly true that Jonah, in and out of the fish, was a glorious "type" <note>A prophetic symbol or foreshadowing</note> of Christ regarding his burial and resurrection (Matthew 12).

It is also certain that Jonah’s swallowing and spitting out was followed by his preaching to the Ninevites and their conversion and salvation. It is likewise known that after Christ’s resurrection, the Gospel, repentance, and conversion were preached to the Gentiles.

It is no less certain that Jonah did not want to go to Nineveh and would have preferred to see the destruction of the city. It seems there was an imagination among the Jews of an earthly and worldly kingdom of the Messiah, who would destroy and subjugate the Gentiles. And yet, to go and preach to them seemed not to fit their understanding at all. They expected the redemption of Israel and the destruction of the Gentiles in a short time. Therefore, like Jonah, they were envious and angry that the Gentiles converted. They would not enter themselves and hindered others (Acts 10, Luke 15, 1 Thessalonians 2:15-16, Acts 17:13, etc.). But while they waited fixedly for the destruction of the Gentiles—grumbling, sulking, and disparaging and contradicting God's dealings along with Jonah—they were stung as if by a consuming worm, and perished themselves.

<margin>The Law of Moses compared to the miracle tree.</margin>
The Law has many branches of various commands, much like the miracle tree <note>The "wonderboom" refers to the plant that shaded Jonah, traditionally identified as the castor oil plant (*Ricinus communis*).</note> which shaded the head of the Jew Jonah, and likewise overshadowed the Jews, under which they sought rest. It was given by God on Sinai on a dark and very cloudy day, having a shadow of the good things to come <note>original: *Hebr. VIII. en X. Kol. II.*</note>. Nothing was dearer to the Jews than that the Law should remain for eternity. Under it, they believed, there was sufficient shelter; they could tolerate nothing less than the Word being proclaimed to the Heathens, and the legal dispensation being set aside <note>The original Dutch idiom "agter de bank geraakte" literally means "placed behind the bench," signifying something discarded or forgotten.</note>, <note>original: *Hand. XVI. 1 Thess. II.*</note>. This Law was despised and trodden upon like a worm by Him who came in the fullness of time, as the dayspring from the east <note>original: *Gal. IV. 4, 5. Luc. I. 78.*</note>, bringing an end to the Law. He caused it to wither, fade, and pass away, leaving them without any covering or protection against the heat of God's righteous wrath and the unbearable curses and threats of the Law. This befell them just when they inevitably thought that the downfall and destruction of the estranged, god-forgetting, and idolatrous Heathens was brewing, while the Lord took pity on the Heathens and exposed the Jews to the heat of His wrath after long-standing disobedience and rebelliousness. All of this is very well known.

That Law, when used well and prudently, is quite as good and powerful as the *Ricinus* <note>The castor oil plant, used medicinally as a purgative.</note> to relieve man of the bitter gall of malice and envy; from the dropsy <note>An old term for edema; here used metaphorically for greed or an "over-filled" heart.</note> of an overly covetous heart; from the accumulation of evil fluids that cause stiffness and even a chalky buildup in the limbs of the body, greatly hindering the activity of our spirit in loving according to the rule of God’s law—the right reason, the lodestar to truth and virtue. Yet this purification in man does not occur without sensible pain, through the killing and crucifying of the self, etc. For this reason, it is compared with sorrow, etc. <note>original: *Gal. V. 24. Kol. III. 5. 2 Kor. VII.*</note>

### EMBROIDERY, EMBROIDERED WORK,
->the work of an embroiderer <note>original Hebrew: מַעֲשֵׂה רֹקֵם, *ma'aseh roqem*</note>, to paint with a needle <note>original Latin: *acupingere*</note>, embroidered <note>original Latin: *acupictum*</note><-

<margin>Frequent mention of embroidery in the Holy Scroll.</margin>
The words EMBROIDERY, EMBROIDERED, and EMBROIDERED WORK are read many times in the Holy Scroll <note>The Bible</note>. The French call it *Brodé*, and our people call it *Geborduurt*; the Germans say *Gestickt*—painted and stitched with a needle, or sewn onto something. This artistic work mostly consisted of flowers and foliage. Thus one reads of "the work of an embroiderer" <note>original Hebrew: מַעֲשֵׂה רֹקֵם</note>, whether made with the needle or through the art of weaving in many colors and hues, as if consisting of various parts and pieces, such as carpets, hangings, spreads, etc.

<margin>Embroidered covering.</margin>
Thus one reads of an embroidered covering, <note>original: *Exod. XXVII. and XXVI. and XXXVI. and XXXVIII.*</note>

<margin>Embroidered belt.</margin>
Of an embroidered belt <note>or girdle</note>, <note>original: *Exod. XXXV. and XXXVIII.*</note>
Of embroidery, <note>original: *1 Kron. XXIX.*</note>

<margin>Embroidery.</margin>
Of being "wrought as an embroidery," <note>original: *Ps. CXXXIX.* Referring to the complex knitting together of the human body.</note>
Of being led to the king in embroidered or stitched, multi-colored clothes, <note>original: *Ps. XLV.*</note> and more of the like.
That it was so in the Tabernacle, and especially in

<column-break/>

Solomon’s temple, where every part was precious, and everything shone with gold, silver, precious stones, and artworks, is a known matter. That such things not only accorded with the majesty and glory of the Heavenly King to provoke reverence and esteem, but were also an image of the richness of grace and the abundance of all desired things in the Church of the New Testament under the reign of the Prince of Peace, the Messiah, I can easily believe.

<margin>Girdle of the High Priest.</margin>
That the High-Priestly girdle was embroidered with gold and flowers, stitched or interwoven, is read in <note>original: *Exod. XXVIII. 3. and XXXIX.*</note>; compare <note>original: *Openb. I. 13. and XV. 6. Dan. X. 5.*</note> where the Savior appears to us. However, because it was not only a priestly garment but also belonged to kings and generals, etc. (as will be shown under the word GIRDLE), I might think that it depicted the honor, glory, and majesty of Christ’s person as King and Priest upon His throne. He bears the sign of power and truth to govern, <note>original: *Jef. XI. 5. and XXII. 21.*</note> and His dignity and readiness to fulfill His offices, <note>original: *Eph. VI. 14. 1 Petr. I. 13.*</note> all excelling through the gold and the flowers of His inner value, the ornament of His grace, and the virtues of His person, sufferings, and merits, righteousness and truth, or faithfulness in fulfilling His promises, <note>original: *Ps. LXXXIX. 15.*</note> etc.

<margin>Embroidered hanging.</margin>
Regarding the decorated cloth and hanging <note>original: *Exod. XXVI. and XXVII. and XXXVI.*</note>, Paul in <note>original: *Hebr. X. 22.*</note> points us to the garment and veil of Christ’s flesh, which had to be torn in His suffering and death so that one might enter—without fear, and with hindering bold freedom and the servitude of the yoke removed—into the innermost sanctuary, the throne and seat of grace.

That this same [veil] was embroidered and decorated with flowers and various figures, colors, and images has already been spoken of to some extent regarding the hangings. I would think that here one must look to the singularly beautiful virtues, gifts, and capacities of the Christ, not only as God’s Son but also as the Son of Man—the God-man who tabernacled among the Jews <note>original: *Joh. I.*</note>. These were poured out over Him, shared with Him, and shone forth in Him most beautifully and preciously. <note>original: *Ps. XLV. Jef. XI. 2. Kol. II. 3. 1 Kor. I. 24. Joh. III. 34.*</note>

# EMBROIDERY. CITIZEN.

...cited in his *Academic Disputations, page 404.* He says that these wedding garments are fine linen, stitched with a needle and adorned with gold ornaments. That stitched garments were customary among the Greeks at weddings is taught to us by *Spanheim in the Plutus of Aristophanes, pages 256 and 276,* from the beautiful edition by *L. Kuster, etc.* <note>Ezechiel Spanheim (1629–1710) was a noted Prussian diplomat and scholar; Ludolf Kuster was a famous German philologist.</note>

The origin of these magnificent garments is generally traced to the Phrygians, which is why they were called *Phrygian clothes*. I would rather derive them from the Phoenicians, not only because Holy Scripture precedes us there, stating that in the priestly garments, <term>רקם</term> <note>original: *rakam*</note> and <term>רקמות</term> <note>original: *rako-mooth*</note>—meaning *Phoenician*, or *stitched* and *embroidered work*—were used; but also because *Homer*, the founder and father of Heathen Antiquities, explicitly shows that this art was brought from the Sidonian women to the Phrygians. For he speaks thus in *Iliad VI, verse 288 and following:*

<note>original Greek: "Αὐτὴ δ’ ἐς θάλαμον κατεβήσετο κηώεντα, Ἔνθ’ ἔσαν οἱ πέπλοι παμποίκιλοι, ἔργα γυναικῶν Σιδονίων, τὰς αὐτὸς Ἀλέξανδρος θεοειδὴς Ἤγαγε Σιδονíηθεν ἐπιπλὼς εὐρέα πόντον."</note>

->That is:<-

> She enters the bedchamber, where sweet fragrance dwells,
> Filled with robes of pride, skillfully prepared
> By the practiced hands of Sidon’s maiden throngs,
> Whom Paris brought with him from Sidon through the waves.

Following this, the author shows with great proofs of wide reading and good judgment that stitched garments were usually outer garments; and his Reverence continues on page 346, etc., and intending to explain it further, writes as follows.

What is more, and primarily should be noted here, is that various garments showed the bride that she must place the pursuit of virtue above all else. Thus speaks *Antiphanes in Stobæus, Sermon 72.*

<note>original Greek: "Μὴ χρώμασιν τὸ σῶμα λαμπρύνειν θέλε, Ἔργοις δὲ καθαροῖς, καὶ τρόποις τὴν καρδίαν."</note>

->That is:<-

> Do not seek to spend your time and diligence on bodily finery;
> But rather adorn your soul with true virtue and character.

<margin>The magnificent garment of sanctification represented by stitched clothes.</margin>
Very fittingly, therefore, the magnificent garment of sanctification is represented by stitched clothes, which is always inseparable from the righteousness of the Savior. For:

1. Just as garments stitched with a needle are crafted with much skill, so too is sanctification the inimitable work of that heavenly artist, the Holy Spirit, *2 Thess. II:13, 2 Cor. III:18.*
2. Just as those garments consisted of many colors and depictions: so too are the gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit diverse, *Gal. V:22, 2 Peter I:5-7.*
3. Just as those garments were the specific attire of princesses and royal women: so too do those appear princely who are graced with the heavenly gifts of the saints, experiencing and proving how great a grace they receive from the heavenly bridegroom.
4. Just as those garments served more as ornament than as covering, and outwardly charmed the eyes: so too the fruits of the

<column-break/>

Holy Spirit produce no righteousness for men before the all-piercing eye of the Supreme Judge, yet they provide an excellent ornament to souls, being virtues worthy of praise even in the eyes of men.

And when it is said to the church—the bride of Christ to be gathered from Jews and Heathens and brought to the bridegroom and lover of the soul—through the preaching of the Word in *Psalm XLV*, that she is all-glorious within, and to be brought to the king with embroidered or stitched garments, I would think that the bride, who after all receives everything from Jesus since she has nothing of herself but frailty and guilt, is represented here not only as inwardly beautiful with the ornament of a humble, meek, and quiet spirit (precious before God), faith, hope, and love, but also in the outward matter of confession, conduct, and life—everything that is Christian and dignified. Having embraced by faith the gold of His righteousness and the prize of His merits, and having "put on Christ," she is filled with the fruits of righteousness, *Philip. I.*

<margin>Man compared to embroidery.</margin>
And that David compares man, in his formation in the mother's womb, to embroidery or embroidered work in *Psalm CXXXIX*, need not seem strange to anyone; for he who understands Anatomy finds how the human body is stitched through and, as it were, interwoven with nerves, bones, cartilage, tendons, veins, arteries, muscles, etc. And how the exterior, which presents itself to the sight of the eyes, is spread over with all kinds of colors: the skin, face, lips, cheeks, eyes, hair, etc.

## CITIZEN, CITIZENSHIP, <term>πολίτης</term>, <term>πολίτωμα</term>, etc. <note>original: *polítēs* (citizen), *polítōma* (citizenship/commonwealth)</note>

**O**f the Hebrew, Roman, Athenian, etc., citizens and citizenships, and their privileges, I do not care to treat at length.

Among the Romans, one found full citizens, and those who did not possess citizenship fully with every privilege.

Citizenship was obtained by birth, at first if one was born of two parents who were citizens; at least from a father who was a citizen; thereafter the right of citizenship passed to someone who had a mother who was a female citizen. One also obtained citizenship either by a sum of money, *Acts XXII:27, 28,* by gift, and adoption due to good service; or by passing from servitude to freedom.

It was granted either with full rights of citizenship, or without them, merely honoring one with the title and residency, as of citizens.

A full citizen could be elected to colleges and offices and give his votes in the *Comitia curiata* (assemblies of the wards), in the *comitia centuriata* (assemblies of the hundreds), and in the *comitia tributa* (gatherings of the tribes, districts, or families). No action could be taken against his life, his property, or his freedom except in the assembly of the Hundreds; one was not permitted to punish him with rods, shackles, or bonds without an order from a higher authority, as seen in the Apostle Paul in *Acts XVI and XXII*, etc. See here *Kipping, Goodwin, etc.* <note>Likely referring to Thomas Goodwin or similar contemporary scholars of civil and ecclesiastical history.</note>

# CITIZEN.

<margin>Privileges of Roman citizenship.</margin>
The Roman colonies and many nations enjoyed the privileges of Roman citizenship.

<margin>Given to foreigners.</margin>
The Romans were very careful with their citizenship, until they were so pressed and weakened by their neighbors that they were forced to admit foreign peoples to their citizenship as well, says Velleius Paterculus in Book 2, Chapter XVII. <note>Marcus Velleius Paterculus (c. 19 BC – c. AD 31) was a Roman historian; he describes the expansion of Roman rights following the Social War.</note>

<margin>Become a burden.</margin>
And however much one might have esteemed Roman citizenship in olden times, and however dearly it might have cost someone, in later times—because of tyranny and extortion—one would have considered oneself lucky if one could have been released from it entirely, says Salvian in his book *On Providence*, Volume V. <note>Salvian the Presbyter (c. 400 – c. 470 AD) wrote about the decline of the Roman Empire, noting that Roman taxes and bureaucracy became so heavy that citizens fled to the "barbarians" for relief.</note>

What has been said will provide me the opportunity to speak of a spiritual citizen, citizenship, and its privileges: of the citizens of Zion and Jerusalem, of believers in general, and particularly those of the New Testament, as the words CITIZENS, CITIZENSHIP, etc., appear several times, especially in the scrolls of the New Testament.

<margin>Citizens of Zion.</margin>
One reads of the citizens of Zion; of the New Jerusalem descending from Heaven; of a city of God; a kingdom of heaven; of the Jerusalem which is above, and so forth.

That these refer back to the old [Jewish] state is certain to me; that the state of glory above is the powerful fulfillment <note>original: *tegenbeelt*, or antitype</note> I believe; however, I consider it indisputable that one must not skip over or overlook the state of free citizens on earth, particularly in the Church of the New Testament.

<margin>New Jerusalem.</margin>
One finds a New Jerusalem, a city of God, as if descending from Heaven (Revelation 21; Galatians 4:26; Revelation 3 and 14), with the Lord as if descending from Heaven: heaven opened by His entrance, and the way to Heaven's sanctuary paved. In Him, heaven and earth are made as one: the heavenly spirit, with His grace and gifts, is richly poured out, whereupon the old heaven and earth of the Jewish civil and church state passed away, rolled up as it were. Through this, one is gathered to the heavenly state (Hebrews 12:18-24, etc.). This citizenship we do not have by nature or birth, from the will of the flesh or of man (John 1:13), but because of eternal election and rebirth (1 Peter 1:15), being called with a holy and heavenly calling (Hebrews 3; 1 Peter 2:9).

It is a precious price that brings us to that dignity and entitles us: the price of Jesus' blood. By right, and in Him the Head, we are seated in the heavens (Ephesians 2:6). It happens by His will and intercession (John 12 and 17:24).

Out of the citizenship of the world, which lies in wickedness, one is effectively given to Christ: one then belongs to the world no longer (John 17), having been drawn out of the world (Galatians 1; 1 Peter 2:9).

The principal part is above: the Holy Angels, Christ, and the believers who have fallen asleep in the Lord (Hebrews 12).

The inheritance, as the most important and perfect good, is in the heavens (1 Peter 1:3, 4).

<margin>Gentiles admitted to spiritual citizenship.</margin>
Meanwhile, the Jerusalem Above and the Jerusalem Below having been made one, many from among the Gentiles were added as citizens and to the enjoyment of citizenship in the Apostolic and early Christian church (Psalm 87:3, 4; Romans 11).

<column-break/>

17; Ephesians 2:19; Hebrews 12.

The true citizens thereof do not live according to the world (Galatians 2:20). They have not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God (1 Corinthians 2). They have died to the old things and the elementary principles of the world and live in freedom (Colossians 2:8-20). They seek the things above (Colossians 3:1, 2). Their conduct is ordered according to their citizenship and civil right (Philippians 3:20).

And although they travel about and journey, residing abroad for a time, their citizenship remains undiminished, as it is not tied to any Canaan, earthly Jerusalem, or earthly Zion.

Their names are in the citizen's roll (Luke 10; Hebrews 1:12; Revelation 22). God's name, and the name of the New Jerusalem, is written upon them as God's property and for His service. They receive the seal of the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 1:22; Romans 8; Ephesians 1). Through the engravings of grace and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and conformity with the heavenly Father, they are known by Him (2 Timothy 2:12). And by their heavenly-mindedness, holiness of life, boldness of confession, subscription to the truth, and surrender of themselves to the Lord, they are outwardly recognized as true citizens (Isaiah 44:5).

<margin>Privileges of spiritual citizenship.</margin>
Their privileges are briefly depicted by the highly enlightened Apostle in Romans 14:17: righteousness, peace, and joy through the Holy Spirit, which I shall not further embellish or expand upon.

Let this be a brief sketch of the Citizenship and civil rights of the children of God. I break off here and hasten to step into other material.

Here, commentators are not in agreement regarding the translation. Some believe that this refers to drawing true wisdom from Holy Scripture. # WELL.

<margin>
Application to the human body.
</margin>
...by which one leaves their legal wife <note>original: *1 Kor. VII* (1 Corinthians 7)</note> with whom one should be content, satisfying one's desires and properly quenching burning passions; by no means aiming for the lap of strange women, harlots, or concubines, I shall gladly leave the judgment of this to the sensible reader.

When one reads in *Ecclesiastes 12:6* of the wheel at the well <note>This refers to the "broken wheel at the cistern," a famous biblical metaphor for death.</note> which is shattered, I am inclined to think that here (as in the preceding text) we find a flowery, metaphorical, and figurative way of speaking, through which the condition of the body—along with its weakness and decay—is depicted.

One understands and explains this distinctly: by the "spring" one understands the human heart, which moves constantly and is, as it were, the principle of motion for almost all parts of the body. By the "pitcher at the spring," the heart-water <note>Likely referring to the pericardial fluid surrounding the heart.</note> enclosed in a small sac; by the "well," the left ventricle of the heart which gives up the blood; by the "wheel at the well," the greater and smaller blood vessels <note>The arteries and veins.</note> which receive the blood from the cavity of the heart and carry it, along with the "living and animal spirits" <note>A common early modern medical concept where "spirits" were thought to circulate in the blood to provide life and movement.</note>, through the entire body. These tubes and bodily instruments gradually weaken through mishaps, break, and are made entirely useless by death.

One reads in *Isaiah 36* of Rabshakeh’s <note>Rabshakeh was the chief messenger or field commander of King Sennacherib of Assyria.</note> advice and exhortation against the curse of Hezekiah, that "every man should drink from the water of his own well." It can be taken properly and literally (like the preceding), for Rabshakeh exhorts the people of the Lord to come to an agreement and alliance with the King of Assyria, so that it may go well with them, and every man may remain in his own place and thus be prosperous. And therefore, in addition to the literal meaning, it is a symbolic proverb to express peace, welfare, and a firm mutual trust under the rule of the King of Assyria.

One reads in *Isaiah 51:1-2* of the hollow of the well of Abraham and Sarah, from whom the people of the Lord were born.

I well know that the Messiah is from Israel's spring—from the fathers, as far as the flesh is concerned. *Psalm 68, Romans 1:3-4.* That the people of God according to the flesh have sprung from the fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (called Israel): just as all those who believe and do the works of Abraham—even those from the Gentiles—are from that well, *John 8, Romans 11, Galatians 6:16,* being made into one body. *1 Corinthians 12, Ephesians 4.*

<margin>
The small number of believers.
</margin>
However, I can also see that the Lord comforted His faithful people (though few in number, having sprung from the side of Christ alongside those from Abraham) regarding their loneliness and small numbers. To this end, He wants them to look to Abraham and Sarah, from and through whom they have come (though Abraham was very old and Sarah was past her time), *Romans 4,* as if hewn from that stone to build a family and a house. These were as if childless, barren, and lonely in their wanderings, yet they were multiplied like the stars of heaven: and therefore they ought to be properly mindful of God's deeds, promises, and pledged blessings for their comfort and encouragement.

The Lord wanted to show how righteous-

<column-break/>

-ly He would proceed to punish His people, and that their destruction came from their own bosom, *Jeremiah 6,* just as a well gives up its water, so she gives up her wickedness, etc. A well bubbles up constantly and provides those who draw from it with a new supply of abundant water: the situation with the people was just the same. Their evil and corrupt heart gave up one evil after another, *Matthew 15:19,* because love grew cold and iniquity was multiplied, *Matthew 24.* What this wickedness consisted of can be seen in the same verse in Jeremiah.

## BREAST: BREAST-CLOTH: BREASTS, etc.
### BREASTPLATE, <note>original Hebrew: חֹשֶׁן (*hoshen*), Greek: στῆθος (*stēthos*), Latin: *pectus*</note>.

The BREAST is the front and uppermost part of a human or beast, attached to the shoulders, containing several ribs under which the heart lies enclosed.

It is well known that the Lord our God took care in a singular way for His public servants who carried and performed holy duties.

<margin>
Offerings for the Priest.
</margin>
Grotius, <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> following the footsteps of Abravanel <note>Isaac Abravanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and biblical commentator.</note> and others, tells us that every Israelite slaughtering for his family was obliged to give to the Priest, as God's servant, the head, the shoulder, and the stomach: from the head, the jaws; from the shoulders, the right one; from the body, the stomach. And they could not buy their way out of this: for it signifies that one must sacrifice to God one's reason, deeds, and desires.

From the sacrifices, one had to give the Breast and the right shoulder to the Priest, God's servant and minister. These he was permitted to eat within Jerusalem with his wife and children. Thus the Priest had the right shoulder and breast of the sacrifices of individual Israelites; from the ram of the Nazirites, he also had the other shoulder, which was boiled. The rest of the peace offerings and thank offerings, which had to be consumed immediately, were for those who had sacrificed to God, who thus had fellowship with the altar and dined as if with the Lord—which did not happen except after the preceding sacrifice of atonement or for sin, *Exodus 29* and *Leviticus 3* and *7* and *8* and *9, Numbers 6,* etc.

Various reflections have been made upon these matters among the learned.

For my part, I am willing to allow the observation of how singular a care the Lord wished to take for His servants, so that they who spent and devoted their strength, service, time, and life for the good of the people in the established services of the Lord might also enjoy sufficient recognition and support, both for their persons and their families: just as the great Apostle seems to have alluded to this when he applies it to the ministers of the New Testament, who, preaching the Gospel, ought to be able to live from it. See what I have said on *1 Corinthians 9:13,* etc.

I find another application in Calovius: <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a prominent Lutheran theologian.</note> When the Priest received the right shoulder and breast from the people, it was shown that he stood in the place of God; and since the most prominent parts were assigned to him as God's servant, those noble parts ought to teach him that his duty was to surpass all others, to be like the breast and shoulder of the...

# BREAST.

...of the people, to take care of the people and to support them.

Certainly, one might well think that this breast and right shoulder could teach the priests how they were obliged to devote themselves with all their heart and all their might to carrying the holy things and performing the Lord's work in the Lord's house; indeed, to show them clearly <note>The original Dutch uses "dootverwen," literally to "dye thoroughly" or "color deeply," meaning to illustrate vividly or instill a deep impression.</note> how they must carry the entrusted people, as it were, in their breast and heart, and upon their shoulders. And on behalf of the people, or concerning what related to the people: certainly, it could represent their obedience and the love they owed, which they were to show to the servants of the Lord because of their faithful yet difficult services.

<margin>Observation of Jerome.</margin>
One may also recall Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a priest and theologian best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> in his 128th letter to Fabiola, saying that the heart being placed in the breast can represent pure thought and the knowledge of the Divine law in one's innermost self. That in and through the right shoulder and arm can be represented the pursuit of good works and the struggle against Satan, expressing through an armed hand and an exemplary life that which one has conceived in the heart.

<margin>From Gregory.</margin>
Also regarding what Gregory <note>Likely Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD), a significant influential figure in medieval theology.</note> has noted when he says: the Priests receive the breast and the right shoulder from the people to remind them that they owe their breast to God, so that they may think of nothing other than those things which are right; and the right shoulder, or arm, so that they might bravely perform God's business, despising both prosperity and adversity.

<margin>From C. a Lapide.</margin>
Upon this, Cornelius à Lapide <note>A Jesuit priest and renowned biblical commentator (1567–1637).</note> notes that the breast and right shoulder were given to the Priests on God's behalf, as God’s servants, to signify by the breast: faith, sound doctrine, and hearty wisdom; and by the arm or shoulder: a steadfast industriousness toward faithfulness and virtue, by which they must excel and instruct the people.

<margin>From Origen.</margin>
Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD) known for his allegorical interpretations of Scripture.</note> has proposed the following: that the breast and the shoulder signified that the breast and the heart must be filled with wisdom and knowledge—indeed, full of all kinds of Divine wisdom, indeed, filled with God. As for the shoulder or arm, it signified much care, labor, and vigilance, through which he might convert the sinner, who for this reason must offer a votive offering to God and give Him thanks. In this offering, the breast serves as proof to the Priest that the breast and the heart—which previously devised evil—is now converted through the Priest's service, receives good thoughts, and is purified in such a way that it can see God. Likewise, the arm is a symbol that it changes its evil and "sinister" <note>The original uses "flinxe," referring to the left hand or "clumsy/sinister" deeds, contrasted with the "right" hand of righteousness.</note> deeds into those of the right hand, so that they are according to God. Persius, in his second Satire <note>A reference to the Roman poet Persius (34–62 AD).</note>:

> *Compositum jus, fasque animi, sanctosque recessus*
> *Mentis, & incoctum generosum pectus honesto.*
> <note>original Latin: "A duty to God and man well blended, the soul's purity, the mind's sacred recesses, and a generous heart steeped in honor."</note>

->That is:<-

->*The piety of mind, and fairness, and right,*<-
->*Attached in the noble chamber of our mind.*<-

Furthermore, I can well allow that the people eating from the peace offerings after the sin offering was made, thereby practiced fellowship with God and the altar, and that it signified the friendship established with God:

<column-break/>

and that one thus, after the reconciliation of sins through the unique, true, and perfect sin offering of the Christ, now through faith in Christ the Priest, offering, and altar, practices fellowship, and through the working of His Spirit, becomes a partaker of the fruits of His reconciliation: righteousness, peace, and joy (*Romans 14:17*); and that for this purpose, one celebrates His memorial and has fellowship with Him (*1 Corinthians 10 and 11*).
<margin>Application to Christ.</margin>

<margin>Lessons to be drawn from the thank offering.</margin>
I can also see that from the thank offerings, which had to be eaten immediately, one can learn how—having tasted and seen how good and benevolent the Lord is in His Son—one must immediately accept His grace, apply it to the conscience, and immediately burst forth in gratitude, without forgetting to show benevolence to others, as Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher.</note> has pointed out, citing *Psalm 116:12, 13, 14*.

<margin>Statue of Nebuchadnezzar.</margin>
The Breast, as understood from the statue with its outstretched arms (*Daniel 2:32-39*), was known to signify merely one power—in distinction from the head, belly, thighs, and feet—and must be taken symbolically as a representation of the empire of the Persians and Medes.

<margin>Expressions regarding the breast.</margin>
The Breast applied to man, as the part of the upper body, especially the space and width between the two arms of the body, is subject to such expressions in Holy Scripture which cannot all be explained in one and the same manner.

As an example, one reads in *John 13:23-25, 20:2, and 21:20* <note>The text incorrectly cites Job, but the context clearly refers to the Gospel of John.</note> of the Disciple whom Jesus loved, who, reclining in Jesus' bosom and falling back against His breast, asked something important. The heart is hidden beneath it.

To lie in someone’s bosom, or before someone on the resting couch or table-bed, was a mark of honor and love, as can also be concluded from the aforementioned passages. At the signal from Peter, John turned around slightly and thus came with his head against Jesus’ breast to speak to Him secretly. As for what concerns the golden girdle around Jesus’ breast (*Revelation 1:13 and 15; Isaiah 11; Zechariah 6* and elsewhere), it has already been mentioned and said regarding the breast that it is a sign not only of His High Priestly and royal dignity, but also of His courage and readiness for the execution of His offices, as will be more closely noted under the word GIRDLE.
<margin>Golden girdle around Jesus' breast.</margin>

<margin>Beating the breast.</margin>
When someone beats their breast, it will undoubtedly signify heartfelt sadness and gloominess—indeed, the utmost embarrassment and heartache—as in *Luke 18:13 and 23:48*. This might be practiced upon someone’s death or a weighty accident, or to express one’s sadness because of their crimes and miserable state, as one will find various examples of this in Ravanel, Gejerus *On Mourning* <note>Referring to Martin Geier (1614–1680), a Lutheran theologian.</note>, etc. The hand was also sometimes placed on the breast as proof of sincerity when one swore an oath. See Lydius *On Oaths* <note>Referring to Balthasar Lydius (1576–1629).</note>.
<margin>Hand placed on the breast in swearing.</margin>

Subsequently, one reads of Breasts, and of various expressions that concern them.

-># BREASTS.<-

### BREASTS, MAMMÆ,
### <note>Hebrew: *shad*, *shadayim* (breasts); *dad*, *dadayim* (teats/breasts)</note> שַׁד, שָׁדַיִם, דַּד, דַּדַּיִם, <note>Greek: *mastos* (breast), *thēlē* (nipple), *brephos* (infant)</note> μασθὸς, θηλὴ, βρεφ, <note>Latin: *ubera* (udders/breasts), *mammæ* (breasts)</note> ubera, mammæ, &c.

Of the BREASTS, as natural parts and members of the female body, given by the Creator of all things to those of the female sex so that they might nurse their young children—I shall not write of their natural constitution, but of that which might be signified by them in the holy scroll <note>The Bible</note>, by way of comparison or imagination; sometimes more literally and closely, sometimes more figuratively and purely in the imagination.

<margin>Two breasts of the church.</margin>
Thus I read of two breasts attributed to the Church, Christ's bride, in *Song of Solomon I. 13.* and I note that one understands them to mean the scriptures of Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles: or the word of the living God, alongside the Sacraments. Between which one finds Christ, with all kinds of grace and nourishment, the rational milk for comfort.

Yet others understand it in this manner: namely, that because the heart lies beneath and between the breasts, and the bridegroom and lover of the soul stays there through the night like a bundle of myrrh, it is understood thereby how Jesus dwells in the heart through faith, *Eph. III. 17.* He is dear and precious to the soul, *Ps. LXXIII. and CX.* and the soul finds itself constantly strengthened, refreshed, and gladdened by remembering His love, suffering, death, and resurrection for her daily improvement and comfort, revealing Himself in His knowledge, fellowship, and love in the night of adversity.

Thus one reads in *Song of Solomon IV. 5. Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that graze among the lilies: and VII. 3.*

It is maintained that by the two breasts are understood either the Old and New Testaments or the entire Scripture, along with the Sacraments—equal to one another in essence, providing abundant nourishment for Jews and Gentiles; so much wisdom, grace, and warmth of love, etc., that the abundance cannot be sufficiently valued or comprehended, *Eph. III. 17, 18, 19.* the breasts being in whiteness and high swelling above the chest like lilies in color and elevation above other flowers.

Also, the Church can be viewed as having so much grace, power of faith, knowledge, and holiness, and the love of God poured out in the heart, that she can strive to nourish, edify, and perfect others through both her teaching and example, by the warmth of pure love.

Unless one wished to understand by the two breasts not only the Word of God in the Old and New Testaments, in which the spiritual and rational milk is enclosed; but also the Teachers and strongly practiced Christians, who nourish and refresh others through doctrine and example.

It is only to be understood figuratively when one hears Solomon say, *Prov. V. 19. A most lovely hind and a graceful doe: let her breasts satisfy you at all times: always be intoxicated with her love.*

It seems clear enough to me that Solomon intends to praise pure and matrimonial love, and to instill a horror of all strange, lustful, and fleshly mingling

<column-break/>

and practicing of impure love with harlots, and with all those outside of lawful marriage: and that through this figure he wishes to express that every man ought to be satisfied and delighted with the love, favor, endearment, and embraces of his wife, without longing for or aiming at the bosom of a strange woman.

One reads of a younger sister who as yet has no breasts, *Song of Solomon VIII. 8.* <note>The original text cites "Hand. VIII. 8" (Acts 8:8), but the quote "we have a little sister, and she has no breasts" is from Song of Solomon 8:8.</note> Some believe that the ancient believers are understood here, speaking of the Gentiles, still lying in nature—the Gentiles not yet called or converted, without covenants, testaments, word, and seals of grace, yet chosen according to eternal providence, destined to be called after Christ's coming in the flesh; which ancient believers wish for Abraham to become a Father of the Gentiles also, and that they may inherit the earth. *Matth. V. Gen. XV. and XVII.* etc.

<margin>Weak believers in great numbers.</margin>
But others look to the latter times, when Israel shall be converted and the fullness of the Gentiles shall enter. One notes that in Christendom there are "weak-believers," without the fullness of the milk of God's word, not yet in a position to nourish and edify others. The Jews and Gentiles, though converted, are small in number compared to those who are yet to be called and converted: and there are infinitely many weak-believers in Christendom, unpracticed in the word of righteousness.

When it is written of Joseph's tribe, *Gen. XLIX. 26.* that it is blessed with the blessings of the breasts and of the womb: I would most closely think that the fruitfulness of that tribe is depicted thereby: for the belly and breasts—to conceive, carry, give birth, and to nurse—are primarily suited to the fruitful continuation of the human race and the rearing of small children.

When the kings and princes, with their princesses, become Christians, and the Heathen nations are devoted to the Church and enlightened and converted by the word of preaching, then the Christian Church stands in no bad state, and her powers do not diminish in the least. She increases in number, honor, luster, riches, and prosperity, *Ps. LXXII. Isa. XLIX. 23. and LX. 16. and LXVI. 11.* and who doubts that such is signified by the sucking of the breasts?

When the Lord gives miscarrying wombs and dry breasts: it is a punishment *Hos. IX. 14.* the children must faint from thirst, and often perish because of hunger.

<margin>Firm breasts.</margin>
<margin>Slack breasts.</margin>
Firm breasts are a symbol of abundance and good health for providing nourishment, *Ezek. XVI.* unpressed, unbroken, firm breasts are a symbol of an unviolated virginity: but breasts that hang or are pressed are a sign of a robbed virginity, through lawful or unlawful love-play, *Ezek. XXIII. 3-34.* and in a bad sense, symbols of false teachers and instruments of spiritual harlotry.

One reads in *Hosea Chapter II. 1. Contend with your mother, contend, for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband: let her put away her harlotries from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts.*

Here I note that some understand the Jews' harlotry and adultery with the ceremonies of the law, without possessing faith, or

# BREASTS.

...or to regard them as the shadow of future goods, while renouncing Christ the true God and only Savior, and seeking their stability in a covenant with the Romans, relying upon them.
Others take this more generally to mean paramours, adulterers, seducers, and false teachers.
Some take it to mean the allurements, the finery, and the harlot’s charms used to attract paramours, to stir up lovers, and to entice them to fleshly lust, harlotry, and adultery—such as baring the bosom, coloring the nipples, using snares, and such things.
<margin>Spiritual adultery.</margin> Sanctius <note>Gaspar Sanctius (1554–1628), a Spanish Jesuit theologian</note> believes that by their outward finery and magnificent attire, they sufficiently signaled their spiritual adultery, as they wore the small images of idols on their foreheads and between their breasts. One may read about both of these views in Dieteric’s *Antiquities of the Old Testament*, Henricus Ursinus on *Hosea*, etc.
<margin>Breasts as a symbol of fertility.</margin> Among the Heathens, the breasts were a symbol of fertility and abundance, fullness for good, and the refreshment of man.
The Latins use the word *uber* <note>original: "uber" — a breast, teat, or richness</note>, a breast, or *Mamma*, for fertility. Virgil writes:
> *Terra antiqua potens armis, atque ubere glebæ.*
> <note>Latin: "An ancient land, powerful in arms and in the richness of its soil."</note>
->That is:<-
>An ancient region skilled in arms, fat
>And fruitful.
Homer calls a fertile land <gloss>the udder of the field</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ὗθαρ ἀρούρης" (houthar aroures)</note>, for the fertile parts of the earth are just like breasts.
The Goddess of the corn-crop, *Ceres*, was called *Ceres Mammosa* <note>Latin: "Ceres of the Large Breasts"</note>, well-breasted. And Diana was called *Multimammia*, the many-breasted.

### ->THE BREASTPLATE OF JUDGMENT, for ORNAMENT and GLORY, <term>Choshen</term> <note>Hebrew: חשֶׁן</note>, <term>Logion</term> <note>Greek: λόγιον — an oracle or speaking place</note>, *rationale* <note>Latin: the breastplate, often called the "Rationale" in older English and Latin bibles</note>, &c. <term>Choshen Mishpat</term> <note>Hebrew: חֹשֶׁן מִשְׁפָּט — Breastplate of Judgment</note>.<-

<margin>The High Priest's breastplate.</margin> Regarding this High-Priestly BREASTPLATE, the cloth of ornament and glory, we read in *Exodus XXVIII. 15-29.*
It was not so much a garment to cover and warm the limbs, for it did not have the proper size or shape for that; rather, it was a cloth for the chest, for ornament and glory.
It is called <term>Choshen Mishpat</term>, *a breastplate of judgment*. The 70 Translators <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> have *Logion*, *Logeion*, or *Kriseon*; Josephus in *Antiquities, Book III, Chapter 8* also translates it as <term>essen</term> <note>Greek: ἐσσὴν — a rendering of the Hebrew choshen</note>, the "reason" of judgments. The Chaldean Translator uses <term>Chouschau</term>; the Arabic says it is <term>Choshan</term>, meaning it was thick, coarse, hard, and heavy.
<margin>Disagreement over the origin of the root word.</margin> Concerning the origin of the root word, there is much disagreement, for some wish to derive it from:
1. <term>Chashah</term> <note>Hebrew: חשה</note> *to be silent, to be still, to be hidden*, because God's secret and hidden will lay as if enclosed within it, and one learned from it more by sight than by hearing; it being something like a silent oracle. Thus, it is named by "Antiphrasis" or contradiction; because the Priest, having been consulted and having obtained the Divine will,

<column-break/>

did anything but remain silent.
2. Or from <term>Choshen</term> *to understand, to notice, to perceive*: because the Priest, draped with the breastplate of judgment, became aware through it of what should be done or left undone in times of war and peace, and in other very weighty matters, according to the will of God.
3. Or from <term>Chazah</term> <note>Hebrew: חזה</note> *to see, to behold, to perceive*.
4. Or from the Arabic word <term>Chashan</term> *rough, coarse, weighty and hard*, due to the gold and stone materials.
<margin>Wisdom and knowledge required of the Priests.</margin> In any case, wherever the word may have its origin: knowledge and science were required to be with the Priests, *Malachi II. 7.* Especially must wisdom be with the High Priest to be able to judge in difficult and obscure matters, *Deut. XVII. 8, 9-10*. Coccejus <note>Johannes Coccejus (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist</note> noted this in his Lexicon regarding the word and this matter: *the breastplate of judgment was a character of the spirit that was with the High Priest, to judge and to prophesy: the High Priest was a Judge, and a proclaimer of the Divine will, or a regular Prophet.*
<margin>Materials of the breastplate.</margin> The materials of which the breastplate of judgment consisted are mentioned as being gold, sky-blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen: the same materials from which the Ephod <note>A vest-like priestly garment</note> was also prepared.
Maimonides <note>A famous medieval Jewish scholar</note>, and others with him, have understood the making or preparation of these materials in the following way; namely, that there were used:
1. Six sky-blue threads, and one continuous gold thread, made of wool and dyed.
2. Six purple threads, with a continuous gold thread: made of wool and dyed.
3. Six scarlet threads, the rest as before.
4. Six linen threads, the rest as before.
In total, then, it was made of 28 threads—of linen, wool, and gold—and thus was "seven-threaded" <note>likely referring to the composition of each strand</note>. And because the body consisted of seven-threaded materials woven together, the whole fitting—including the gold settings, chains, and the 12 inset stones—must have been somewhat coarse and heavy. It is for this reason we heard above how some derived the word *Choshen* from the Arabic word meaning *coarse, rough, hard*, and *heavy*. However, the authority of Maimonides carries little weight with others in this matter. Since the given order for the making of the High-Priestly breastplate mentions not seven-threaded, but doubled or twined linen: therefore, the threads, along with the body of the work, would have been lighter and not so heavy. Whether the linen threads alone were twined, and the others untwined, or all were twined, I shall leave undecided and consider the work itself.
The most artistic work, like the work of the Ephod, I interpret thus: it must be understood as being made of the finest and most precious materials, with the most permanent and vivid colors.
Also, in regards to the art and the labor, the arrangement of materials and their division, the weaving-in of the threads into flowers and figures—"Phrygian work" <note>intricate embroidery or needlework named after the Phrygians of Asia Minor</note>: not embroidered, and with...

<meta>The previous page concluded a symbolic discussion on "breasts" as representations of either spiritual adultery or fertility in the ancient world.
