# BREASTPLATE.

...not stitched with a needle, but woven through and through with changing colors, flowers, and figures, appearing equally beautiful on both sides.

> *Square it shall be, and doubled: a span shall be its length, and a span its width.*

The word <term>זרת (zeret)<note>Hebrew for "span," a unit of measure based on the distance between the tip of the thumb and the tip of the little finger</note></term> means a *span*, specifically in a square: not an entire cubit. Since it was folded double, it was half a cubit square; otherwise, the entire Ephod <note>The ornate vestment worn by the High Priest over his robe</note> would have been completely covered by the breastplate. A man does not need so much width just to cover his chest. It would not have been proportionate for the four rows, each row consisting of three stones. Instead, it was a quarter-cubit in width, and because it consisted of two layers—making four quarter-cubits in total length, or one full cubit—the length and width were counted twice toward each other. These two layers were undoubtedly sewn together in the manner of a pouch, left open on the right side so that something could be inserted and hidden within. Namely, as some have thought:
a. To hide the *Urim* and *Thummim* <note>Sacred objects or lots used by the High Priest to seek divine guidance</note> within it, and if necessary, to be able to take them out to consult with the "mouth of the Lord."
b. Or one might think that the *Urim* and *Thummim* and the breastplate with the twelve stones were one and the same ornament of the High Priest; I shall deal with this more appropriately when I come to the section on the *Urim* and the *Thummim*.
c. However, because a gold plate with twelve hollows for the twelve precious stones had to be attached to the breastplate—and this piece and its mounting were quite heavy—God commanded that the breastplate be made of two layers joined together, secured and fastened with pure gold hooks, eyes, chains, and clasps, to prevent it from tearing or pulling away. Whether the seams and edges of this double breastplate were sewn shut all around, or whether an opening was left on the right side to hide the *Urim* and *Thummim*, I do not dare to determine. Meanwhile, I will present what has been said by others.

<margin>Description of the breastplate by Arias Montanus.</margin>
Arias Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598), a Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible</note> says regarding Jewish Antiquities: *the breastplate was of the same workmanship as the Ephod and of the same art, yet it was not single but double, or folded over, so that the edges were brought together from three corners; and an opening remained on the right side, so that something might be placed inside the ornamental work itself. The same author, in his book regarding Aaron, says the breastplate was double, brought together and joined at the three extremities, but left open on one side. Between these two parts, or layers, the Urim and Thummim were hidden upon the breast of the High Priest, from which they were taken when one had to ask counsel from the Divine mouth.*

<margin>By Aben Ezra.</margin>
Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a major Jewish biblical commentator and philosopher</note> writing on *Exodus 28* says: *Choshen <note>Hebrew: חושן, the Breastplate of Judgment</note>, or the Breastplate, was folded over because the Urim and the Thummim were hidden within it until such time as they were needed, when they were brought out from the breastplate.*

This square Breastplate was intended to hold twelve precious stones for ornament and glory,

<column-break/>

and to fill the twelve prepared hollows with them.

*You shall set settings of stones in it, or fill it with four rows of stones, namely, in the following four rows:*
1. *Sardius, Topaz, and Carbuncle.*
2. *Emerald, Sapphire, and Diamond.*
3. *Jacinth, Agate, and Amethyst.*
4. *Turquoise, Onyx, and Jasper.*

Regarding each stone, I shall speak on each one's name and describe their colors, nature, power, and properties, and endeavor (as much as is possible for me) to interpret them spiritually.

<margin>Shape of the breastplate.</margin>
I imagine this High Priestly breastplate to consist of a square golden plate, a span long and wide. However, with twelve small cases or hollows in this square, flat, golden plate: four rows from top to bottom, three hollows in a row. And subsequently, the twelve precious stones were placed and set down into these twelve rows—three by three—in these hollows, placed so closely together, so fittingly and joined together, that when viewing the surface, it seemed to be a single stone, yet with many kinds of luster and shimmers.

These precious stones were not merely to be joined to the breastplate and united by their settings for ornament and glory; but for that same purpose, the names of the twelve sons, or tribes of Israel, had to be engraved upon them.

> *And these stones shall be with the twelve names of the sons of Israel, according to their names. They shall be engraved like seals, each with his name, for the twelve.*

<margin>Names of Jacob's children.</margin>
The sons of Jacob and their names cannot be strange or entirely unknown to us. They appear in Holy Scripture as follows: *Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin*, mentioned in the blessing of the tribes in *Genesis 49*. These names are engraved just as one cuts seal rings, carved into the hollows, representing all those particular families and houses that thereafter belonged under each tribe, the first fathers and heads of the tribes being taken for the entire tribe.

<margin>Uncertainty of the rank.</margin>
But in what rank and order these tribal names stood upon these twelve stones—who was first, second, and so forth—regarding that, I have not found the greatest agreement. For Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> maintains that they did not stand on these precious stones according to their age and birth, but according to divisions and rows:
1. *Judah, Issachar, Zebulun.*
2. *Reuben, Simeon, Gad.*
3. *Ephraim, Manasseh, Benjamin.*
4. *Dan, Asher, Naphtali.*

Others have divided them according to the mothers, namely:
a. *Those from Leah: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun.*
b. *Of the Maidservants: Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher.*
c. *Those from Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.*

Yet the simplest among the various opinions seems to me to be the opinion of *Josephus, Antiquities Book III, Chapter 8* and of *Maimonides, Laws of the Temple Vessels, Chapter IX* <note>original: "Halach Kele Hammichd"</note>, and best...

<meta>This page continues the technical and symbolic description of the High Priest's breastplate, moving from its physical construction to the engraving of the names of the twelve tribes and the theological purpose of the garment as a "memorial."</meta>

# BREASTPLATE.

...best to agree with *Exodus 28:9, 10,* according to their birth, just as they stood upon the Ephod <note>The Ephod was the outermost vestment of the High Priest, featuring two onyx stones on the shoulders engraved with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel</note>.

Whether the full names were engraved there, or only some letters of the names, I do not doubt. The command entails engraving the names, and not merely some initials, upon these twelve stones.

This Breastplate, with the twelve precious stones set within it, had to be attached and fastened to the Ephod, or the shoulder-mantle, by means of:
a. Two small eyes, or rings, at or on the Sardonyx stone settings <note>original: "Sardonyxsteenkasjes"</note>, on the shoulder-pieces of the Ephod.
b. Two eyes on the belt, or near the belt, by which belt the Ephod was tied and bound around the body of the High Priest.
c. Two eyes at the two corners of the breastplate: to which were attached two wreathed chains with hooks, which were inserted through the eyes of the Ephod at the upper side; being further fastened from below with two ribbons to the belt—namely, by two hyacinth or sky-blue <note>This refers to "tekhelet," a biblical blue dye of great significance</note> ribbons.

The reason why the High Priest, when he entered into God’s sanctuary, had to appear before God with this ornament and glory upon his breast, is presented in *Exodus 28:29.*

> *And Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart, when he goeth into the holy place, for a memorial before the Lord continually.*

<margin>Various opinions.</margin>
These words are understood and reasoned in various ways, according to whether one applies them to: a. God; b. Israel; or c. the High Priest. *For a memorial before the Lord continually:* these words are applied by some to:

A. The God of Israel, just as it is written in *Genesis 9:13* regarding the Rainbow, called the sign of the Covenant between God and Noah, because of the covenant of friendship that was made. God (speaking in a human manner) seeing the rainbow, would demonstrate through His actions that He was mindful of His covenant and His promises. Thus, the Lord would remember Israel for good when the High Priest solemnly appeared before His face in His sanctuary with Israel’s tribal names upon his breast.

B. Others apply it to Israel, whose names stood engraved upon these breastplate stones: and they wish it to be understood in this way—namely, that while the High Priest entered within on behalf of Israel, having brought their tribal names inside, those who were outside had to be attentive, with their souls intent and raised heavenward, joining their prayers and thanksgivings with those of the High Priest. Just as it is written of the people in *Luke 1:9, 10-21,* that the people stood outside praying at the time of the incense while the Priest was inside: for which reason prayer and thanksgiving have also been called an incense, *Psalm 141:2.*

<column-break/>

But as for me, if I may state my judgment—though I do not wish to reject or disapprove of the first or second opinions, as they are sweet and edifying—it seems to me, however (respecting everyone’s judgment and freedom), that this breastplate, like all the High Priest’s garments, was intended for his ornament and glory, according to *Exodus 28:2,* and that these words, *for a memorial before the Lord continually*, primarily refer to the High Priest, in consequence of the oversight and the relations of the high priestly office <note>original: "hooftkerkampt," literally "head-church-office"</note> which he held toward the twelve tribes of Israel.

And to explain my concepts in this matter somewhat more broadly and clearly, regarding why the High Priest wore this breastplate:

<margin>The High Priest's garment as a representation of dignity.</margin>
a. I am of the opinion and judgment that the High Priest, besides the other High Priestly garments, wore this breastplate in order to portray, through it as a garment of distinction, the excellence of his person, office, and dignity—not only above the people, but also above the common Priests and Chief Priests—as the same was for his ornament and glory, according to *verse 2.*

<margin>The High Priest as the first court-servant.</margin>
b. Being not only exalted above the common and Chief Priests, but also above all Israel, since it was a royal priesthood, *Exodus 19:6; 1 Peter 2:9.* For the High Priest was in the house of God as much as the first minister of state and courtier, a Prince and sovereign of the King of all kings, to whom the earth belongs with all its fullness, *Psalm 24; Haggai 2.* With reason, then, as God’s first and highest minister, the one closest to the King and His throne, he was thus richly, ornately, and gloriously attired.

c. One might also add the following, not without all ground of reason: that since all twelve stones each possessed their own particular virtue, power, and property; and since each stone represented a particular Patriarch and tribe, which also had something unique and virtuous about it; and since he had taken upon himself the care of all matters to be done before God; and since he was a leader and singular head: it would surely serve as a greater ornament and glory to him that he, having enclosed the praiseworthy virtues of them all not only in his heart and bosom, should carry them with him continually before God, but also manifest them upon the openness of his chest through a shining and sparkling radiance of confession and life.

<margin>To carry something on one's breast.</margin>
d. But there also occur to me, above all other things, these points: namely, that just as carrying something on one’s breast and heart represents and signifies close knowledge, union, love, regard, and care; it then follows that:
1. The High Priest had to give evidence that he knew his people.
2. That he must never forget his office and duty, acting in the name of the people and for the good of the people, occupying his high priestly office and this dignity of his, *Hebrews 5:2.*

3. By legitimate consequence, he had to be constantly mindful of the people before the king's throne in his offerings, intercessions, thanksgivings, blessings, etc.
4. In all important, difficult, and obscure matters and questions, he had to proceed with God and ripe counsel, so as to speak and act with justice.
5. And in matters of peace and war, acting as a Prophet and the mouth of God, he was not to advise for or against without having previously and properly consulted the mouth of God.
6. Finally, and this is where I primarily intend to go: since the writer of the Letter to the Hebrews, through constant comparison and with singular exaltation, has transferred the old High Priesthood according to the Order of Aaron to the one, true, and perfect High Priest, Jesus, according to the order of Melchizedek <note>The "Order of Melchizedek" refers to a priesthood that is eternal and superior to the levitical priesthood of Aaron, as argued in Hebrews 7</note>: I therefore maintain, without any doubt, that the old High Priest, with all his ornament and glory, prefigured the High Priest of our confession. Since demonstrating this serves for the instruction, glory, comfort, and joy of Christians, I shall proceed to present this matter more closely in its parts and members.

<margin>The author’s further presentation.</margin>
A. Considering the High Priest in his priestly equipment, with his costly breastplate and the twelve paternal tribal names, as the first minister of state—the one closest to and most familiar with the Lord as the head of the house regarding its administration—I consider him to prefigure the person of the Son of God, the man who is God's companion (*Zechariah 13:7*), the sworn Priest (*Psalm 110:4*), God's throne-companion and son (*Zechariah 6:12, 13; Psalm 110:1*), Lord, son, and heir (*Hebrews 1 and 3:6*). Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself. Having taken the form of a servant, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (*Philippians 2:6, 7*). For he, knowing the weakness and blameworthiness of all preceding Priests and their priestly works, had bound himself to the clothing of a much better Priesthood and the pursuit of a much better, worthier, and therefore more powerful priestly work (*John 33:23, 24 <note>The original text cites Job, likely a printer's error for John or a specific commentary reference</note>; Psalm 40:7; Hebrews 10:5, 6*), etc.

B. And when I look upon the old High Priest with his breastplate, having the twelve lineage names of the children of Israel engraved upon it, and consider the mutual relationship between the High Priest and the people, then there also arises in my heart that illustrious figure to whom 144,000 sealed ones from the twelve tribes are given. These twelve tribes of Israel are built upon the doctrine of the Prophets and the Apostles—the twelve foundation stones and founders of the New Jerusalem (*Ephesians 2:20; Revelation 21*) belonging to the Lamb, chosen from

<column-break/>

the world, according to the writing of their names in the Book of Life given to the Lamb (*Luke 10:20; Philippians 4:3; John 10:29; John 17:9-22; Revelation 3:5; 20:12; and 21:27*).

C. And when I have noted that each stone of these twelve breastplate stones, with which the High Priest used to enter the sanctuary, possessed its own nature, property, and a lesser or greater brilliance—though they were all radiant and glorious—then I apply <margin>Spiritual application.</margin> by spiritual transfer the idea that every believer is indeed an ornamental and precious stone (*1 Peter 2:4, 5; Isaiah 54:11: "I will make your gates of rubies, and your whole borders of pleasant stones"*). Each has a unique brilliance and light of knowledge and holiness; nevertheless, one surpasses the other. Every believer, as a living stone, has something unique about them (*1 Corinthians 12:4, 5, 6, etc., 27, 28, 29, etc.*). I will currently leave the further elaboration of this aside for the sake of brevity.

d. When I consider these twelve stones as distinct stones, yet set in one foundation—each in its own socket and hollow of that same foundation—I see that on the surface they were joined and united so closely and perfectly that they seemed to make up one body with many distinct names. Then it occurs to me very joyfully how the body of Christ's congregation is indeed composed of many persons, members, and distinct names; yet they are baptized and joined into one body and one spirit. They are all united as members of one body through the same Spirit, Baptism, Faith, Love, Hope, mutual harmony, and peace (*1 Corinthians 12:14; Ephesians 4*, etc.).

e. And when all these twelve stones come before my eyes—with the twelve tribal names of Israel upon them, enclosed in the hollows of the gold plate and firmly set in their sockets—then I am reminded of the firmness and sealing of the elect, the called believers, within God's unchangeable and irrevocable counsel and election. They are set in the hollows of the gold of Jesus' merits through the grafting in by faith, by which they have become one spirit with him through the sealing of the Holy Spirit. This priestly care and the support of Christ and God's power ensures that they are never moved from their firm standing (*Romans 8:38, 39 and 11:29; 2 Timothy 2:19; 1 Peter 1:5; 2 Corinthians 1:21, 22; Ephesians 1:13, 14 and 4:30*, etc.).

### BREASTPLATE (ARMOR), חחרא, סריון, שריה, תרה <note>original Hebrew: hakhra (likely 'achra'), siryon, shiryah, tirah. These terms refer to coats of mail or breastplates.</note>
->*thorax, θώραξ.*<-

->BREASTPLATE, called *thorax* <note>original Greek: θώραξ</note> by the Greeks,<-
->so we are told, from *thoro* <note>original Greek: θορῶ</note>, "I leap<-
->up," because in the region of the chest the heart<-
->moves constantly and, as it were, leaps up; it is a<-
->type of buckler to cover the chest.<-

<margin>The armor understood in broad and narrow senses.</margin>
I notice that some take the breastplate somewhat broadly, as covering the body from the chest to the thighs and private parts: but others have defined it more narrowly, such as Pliny, Celsus, Aristotle, and others, as being for the chest: Polybius holds it to have been only a hand-breadth, or a good span wide, to protect the right part of the chest, while the shield covered the left breast. Some covered the chest from the front and back. Some only from the front. Some only the right breast. *Kipping, Antiquities, Book III, Chapter 3.*

These were made from all sorts of solid and durable mined materials, chained, hooked, as if with overlapping scales. And one may read of both the one and the other in Hofman, Kipping, and others.

### BREASTPLATE (CUIRASS), <term>תהרא, סריון, שריה, טרה</term> <note>These are Hebrew terms for various types of breastplates or protective coats: tachara, shiryon, sharyah, and tarah.</note>
->thorax, θώραξ.<-

**B**REASTPLATE, called *thorax* by the Greeks, so we are told, from *Spara* <note>original: "Σπαρᾶ"; likely referring to the Greek σπαίρω (spairo), meaning to quiver or palpitate.</note> "to quiver," because in the region of the chest the heart constantly moves and, as it were, leaps up; it is a type of protective covering to shield the breast.

<margin>The term taken in broad and narrow senses.</margin>
I notice that some take the breastplate somewhat broadly, as covering the body from the chest to the thighs and genitals: but others have defined it more narrowly—such as Pliny, Celsus, Aristotle, and others—as being only for the chest. Polybius holds it to have been only a handbreadth, or a good span, to protect the right part of the chest, while the shield covered the left chest. Some covered the chest from front and back. Some only from the front. Some only the right breast. *Kipping, Antiquities, Book III, Chapter 3.*

These were made from all sorts of solid and durable minerals, chained or hooked, as if with overlapping scales. One may read of both types in Hofmann, Kipping, and others.

Virgil in the 11th Book of the *Aeneid*, concerning Turnus:

> Dressed in a Rutulian breastplate, he
> Bristled with bronze scales.
> <note>original Latin: "Rutulum thoraca indutus, ahenis / Horrebat squamis."</note>

And Vondel <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679), a preeminent Dutch poet and playwright.</note>, following him:

> The Rutulian armor, rough with scales of steel, closes
> Around his chest.
> <note>original Dutch: "’T Rutulisch panser, ruw van stale schubben, sluit / Om zyne borst."</note>

# THE BREASTPLATE.

*Statius in Thebaid, Book IV.*

> *But the linked breastplate, with its weave of countless steel, protects the expanse of the flanks and the broad chest.* <note>original Latin: "At laterum tractus spatiosaque pectora servat Nexilis innumera chalybum subtemine thorax."</note>

->That is:<-

> *But a breastplate thickly set with steel hooks* <note>The "hooks" refer to the interlocking rings or scales of chainmail or scale armor.</note>
> *Clothes the side and chest.*

Some, in order to be fully protected against stabs, blows, and shots, and to press more boldly against the enemy, put on a double breastplate.

*Valerius Flaccus, Argonautica, Book VI.*

> *But on the other hand, Sibotes, trusting in his double breastplate, withstood the blow, and with his sword strikes the very tip of the weapon.* <note>original Latin: "Contra autem geminis fidens thoracibus ictum Sustulit, & gladio Sibotes ferit ultima teli."</note>

->That is:<-

> *But Sibothes, emboldened by his breast-harness thickly*
> *Set with hooks, strikes the tip of the arrow.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Spiritual breastplate.</margin> The Apostle in *Ephesians 6:14* and *1 Thessalonians 5:8* speaks of a spiritual breastplate: whether he is looking at the customs of the wrestling arenas or has his eye on military armaments.

<margin>Faith called a shield.</margin> Paul in *Ephesians 6* calls faith a shield. With shields, one usually covers the left part of the body, using it to turn away the thrusts and blows of one's opponent, and from behind this, to deliver the heaviest blows.

I shall expand somewhat further regarding faith and love as a breastplate. Just as a proper breastplate is put on to turn away the enemy's attacks from the chest, heart, lung, and liver—which are enclosed and hidden behind it—so that no heavy and deadly wounds are inflicted: likewise, there must be and is a power within faith and love to turn away what is destructive from a person. Let us demonstrate this in several cases.

**A.** It is one of the most poisonous arrows and most dangerous swords for the soul of a Christian (or one who would appear to be such) not to believe that the Scripture is God's word, or to doubt it and remain hanging in uncertainty: for regarding such a person, the most essential and substantial truths collapse: all religion, hope of eternal life, fear of hell and punishment as incentives to virtue and deterrents from evil—and one insensitively becomes an atheist <note>original Dutch: "Gods loochenaar," literally "God-denier."</note>.

Faith, on the contrary, holding firm that the Holy Scripture is God's word: that God is a God of truth: that He is too good, just, and holy to want to deceive His creature and make them unhappy beforehand: seeing and believing with full certainty of the understanding that the most obvious marks of divinity lie within the Scripture; that it agrees with divine virtues and perfections to demand of man the things that appear necessary to be believed, done, left undone, or suffered

<column-break/>

upon His word: that faith is a Christian's breastplate, through which the arrows of an atheist, as well as the deceptive arguments of a doubter, cannot pierce into the very heart.

**B.** Let us bring forth another case anew:

The sharp arrow and dart of the evil one (*Ephesians 6*) consists sometimes in the attempt to make a child of God despondent and despairing, by constantly presenting to him divine justice, holiness, and the curse of the law: and by reminding him of his manifold and heavy iniquities. Faith—which makes a person believe and rely on God at His word and promises; which desires and accepts not his own righteousness, but that of the surety of the soul <note>original Dutch: "zielborg," referring to Christ as the guarantor or redeemer of the soul.</note>, and thus the divine grace in Christ—breaks the power of this arrow. For he who believes realizes wonderfully well that if he sought his own righteousness from the observations of the law, he could neither be covered before God nor be righteous before Him (*Romans 3*). Instead, his faith embraces God's righteousness: that which was devised and established by God Himself; which was brought forth by the Lord (the Righteousness) and came from God; presented to man by God Himself and revealed in His word, which man could not have known without divine revelation. It is therefore a righteousness which is in all parts divine. Upon this, the soul says to itself in reflection: 1. It is a divine, and not a human righteousness. 2. The Lord knows best how it becomes Him to deal with man. 3. The Lord directs everything to the glory of His name. 4. He who is perfectly good, holy, and just certainly does not intend, in so weighty a matter, to deceive His creature and hold them up with a false or vain appearance of hope. 5. So then, in this His righteousness, which my soul has taken hold of, there must be strength to cover me, deliver me, and bring me to the right and the possession of life. (*Isaiah 27:42-47; Romans 8:1-39; etc.; 1 Corinthians 1:30; Romans 3:25, 26.*)

**C.** Sometimes one tries to make a person despondent or doubtful by trying to make him believe that one may not place too firm a reliance on the promises and God's pledges, because many unfulfilled promises of God are found: and even assuming one could rely absolutely on the Lord, the Lord always knows well what to find in a person as a reason and cause for not fulfilling His word.

Against this fiery arrow, faith protects the heart and, relying on the divine word, breaks all hesitation and despair; for faith, having a lamp of the Lord, represents to the soul that which is written (*Deuteronomy 32:4; Numbers 23:19; Malachi 1; James 1*): God is faithful and does not deny Himself (*2 Timothy 2:12; Hebrews 10:23*); and realizing that He has fulfilled His promises in the Christ (*2 Corinthians 1:20; Luke 1*), the believing soul says with Paul (*2 Timothy 1:12*): I know...

# THE BREASTPLATE.

<margin>Power of faith.</margin>
...know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day. <note>original: "weet in wien ik gelooft heb..." citing 2 Timothy 1:12.</note>

**D.** Faith arms the soul against all accusations, on whatever ground they might arise and rest; because the believer finds that faith is a root within him of many good works and virtues (*1 Thess. 1:3; James 4*), with which he strives to be filled, and toward which he applies and exerts himself (*Philip. 1* and *4:8; 2 Pet. 1:4, 5, 6; Prov. 4; Ps. 84:8*). For he does not yield his members as instruments of unrighteousness (*Rom. 6:12, 13*); he turns away from all iniquity (*2 Tim. 2:19*); he has no fellowship with the wicked or wicked works (*Ps. 1; Eph. 5*). Therefore he has a good conscience (*Acts 24:16*); he clothes himself with his righteousness (*Job 29:14*); he is perfectly bold (*Prov. 28:1*) and challenges his accusers (*Isa. 50:8, 9; Rom. 8:1–38, 39*).

<margin>A Christian's breastplate.</margin>
But the Apostle also says that faith and love are the breastplate of a Christian. Faith and love frequently appear together (*1 Cor. 13:13; Gal. 5:6; Eph. 1:15; 1 Tim. 6:11*, etc.). Faith works through love (*Gal. 5:6*); it is powerless without love (*1 Cor. 13*); the noble essence of faith is love. Faith and love are a very fertile womb for all kinds of Christian virtues.

**a.** Love is a suitable breastplate to break and deflect the accusation that our faith is no good—as if one were to say: "You deceive yourself, making a false calculation regarding your faith and state; you shall die in your sins; you have no love," etc. For a person can best know how it stands within his inner self; thus, having an upright and fervent love for God, for Jesus, and for his neighbor (*Ps. 18:3; Matt. 22; 1 Cor. 16*, etc.), he finds that his faith works through love (*Gal. 5:6*).

<margin>Faith works through love.</margin>
**b.** Which faith, working in him through love, causes him to avoid everything in thought, will, deed, or omission that would lead him into Divine displeasure and His disfavor; he avoids the destruction and the pollution of the world (*Eph. 5:11; 1 Tim. 5:22; 2 Pet. 1:4*).

**c.** This Christian breastplate consists primarily of faith and love, yet one finds various attachments, like hooks and little chains, fastening everything into one body (*1 Cor. 12:14; Eph. 4*).

**d.** Love arms the soul against destructive thoughts, inclinations, attempts, and actions intended against one’s neighbor. And so the practitioner of love, and the neighbor, are covered by the neighbor's love against what is painful, harmful, and shameful (*1 Cor. 13*). This person neither thinks nor speaks evil; he is not embittered; he does not grieve his neighbor; he does not seek or wish for the other's sorrow or loss; he is no prick toward evil; but on the contrary, he seeks to gladden his neighbor; he wishes and brings him good according to his ability; he rejoices in the welfare of his neighbor and is to him a holy track and stimulus (*Ps. 122*).

<column-break/>

> *1 Cor. 13; Eph. 4; Col. 3; Philip. 2; Heb. 10:24.*

Here faith and love appear as a breastplate; in *Ephesians 6*, it is righteousness.

To avoid being overly verbose, I understand by this Christ’s righteousness, graciously imputed and embraced through faith, along with the inherent righteousness—or the manifestation of it—by yielding one's members as instruments of righteousness (*Rom. 6:13*) and by turning away from iniquity (*2 Tim. 2:19, 20*).

This is that through which one practices what is right toward God and neighbor: our thoughts, will, and works; our inner disposition and our outward deeds harmonizing with the rule of rectitude, truth, and virtue. This is what Job clothed himself with (*Chapter 29*); that good and blameless conscience (*Acts 24*) that makes a person bold (*Prov. 10 and 28*); the light and truth; a radiance like that of the <term>Urim and Thummim <note>The sacred objects on the High Priest's breastplate used for determining God's will; their names mean "Lights and Perfections."</note></term>, through which neither Law, nor Satan, nor the world can prevail against such an armed person with anything that might be deadly or destructive. Christ’s righteousness makes the enemy powerless (*Rom. 8*); faith overcomes the world; love cannot be extinguished (*Song of Sol. 8*).

It is a breastplate of an entirely different nature with which the locusts from the bottomless pit—the Jesuits and Monks—are armed (*Rev. 9:9–17*). They are armed not only with hardening of hearts and prejudices against the truth, or fleshly reasonings and deceptive arguments; but also with oaths, covenants, privileges, the power of the deceived or the furious, and even forced great powers and personages. They are armed with raging cruelty, burning lusts, and destruction by fire; a blind and perverted zeal, ignited by the fire of hell, through which they believe that by offering someone up to death, they do a service to God and the church, and so forth. Upon this they deflect everything. Truth, reason, love, and modesty find no place. Everything must yield to their insane rage, as these hellish soldiers judge only that they can and shall become the masters.

### FOREST, WOODS, <term>Ya'ar <note>Hebrew: יער</note></term>, <term>Drymos <note>Greek: δρυμὸς</note></term>, <term>Hyle <note>Greek: ὕλη</note></term>, <term>Sylva <note>Latin: forest</note></term>, <term>Eremus <note>Latin: wilderness</note></term>.

**I**t is known that a forest, whether it occurs naturally or is planted, signifies a collection of trees, specifically tall trees which bear no fruit and which create a very dense and heavy shadow and foliage, under which it is often dismal, lonely, dark, and gloomy; trees that are not pruned or tended as gardens, orchards, etc., usually are. Thus says Ovid in the *VIII* book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> *A forest crowded with trees, which no age had felled.* <note>original Latin: "Silva frequens trabibus, quam nulla ceciderat aetas."</note>
>
> ->That is:<-
>
> *A dense, grown forest, never yet notched by the axe.*

Also in the *III* book:

> *An ancient forest stood, violated by no axe.* <note>original Latin: "Silva vetus ftabat, nulla violata fecuri."</note>

<margin>The power of faith.</margin>
**D.** Faith arms the soul against all accusations, regardless of the grounds upon which they might arise or rest: because the believer finds that faith is a root within him of many good works and virtues, *1 Thessalonians 1:3; James 4,* with which he strives to be filled, and toward which he applies himself with diligence and industry, *Philippians 1 and 4:8; 2 Peter 1:4, 5, 6; Proverbs 4; Psalm 84:8.* For he does not present his members as instruments of unrighteousness, *Romans 6:12, 13;* he turns away from all iniquity, *2 Timothy 2:19;* he has no fellowship with the wicked or with evil works, *Psalm 1; Ephesians 5.* Therefore, he has a good conscience, *Acts 24:16;* he clothes himself with his 'righteousness,' *Job 29:14;* he is perfectly bold, *Proverbs 28:1;* and he challenges his accusers. *Isaiah 50:8, 9; Romans 8:1–38, 39.*

But the Apostle also says that faith and love are the breastplate of a Christian. Faith and love frequently appear together in *1 Corinthians 13:13; Galatians 5:6; Ephesians 1:15; 1 Timothy 6:11,* etc. Faith works through love, *Galatians 5:6;* it is powerless without love, *1 Corinthians 13.* The noble essence of faith is love: faith and love together form a very fruitful womb for all kinds of Christian virtues.

<margin>Faith works through love.</margin>
**b.** As this faith works within him through love, he avoids everything in thought, will, deed, and omission that would cause him to incur divine displeasure and disfavor: he avoids the destruction and the defilement of the world. *Ephesians 5:11; 1 Timothy 5:22; 2 Peter 1:4.*

**c.** While this Christian breastplate consists primarily of faith and love, one finds various attachments, like hooks and small chains, fastening everything into one body. *1 Corinthians 12:14; Ephesians 4.*

**d.** Love arms the soul against destructive thoughts, inclinations, attempts, and actions that might be conceived or carried out against one's neighbor. Thus, the practitioner of love—and the neighbor—are protected by that love against what is painful, harmful, or shameful, *1 Corinthians 13.* This person thinks and speaks no evil; they are not embittered; they do not grieve their neighbor; they do not seek or wish for their neighbor’s sorrow or loss; they are not a provocation to evil. On the contrary, they strive to gladden their neighbor; they wish for and, according to their ability, bring about good for them; they rejoice in their neighbor's prosperity and serve as a holy path and stimulus to them. *Psalm 132.*

*1 Corinthians 13; Ephesians 4; Colossians 3; Philippians 2; Hebrews 10:24.*

Here, faith and love appear as a breastplate; in *Ephesians 6,* it is righteousness.

To avoid being too long-winded, I understand this to mean Christ’s righteousness, graciously imputed and embraced through faith, alongside the inherent righteousness or the manifestation of it, by presenting one's members as instruments of righteousness, *Romans 6:13,* and by standing apart from iniquity. *2 Timothy 2:19, 20.*

This is what Job clothed himself with, *Chapter 29;* that good and inoffensive conscience, *Acts 24;* that which makes a person bold, *Proverbs 10 and 28.* It is the light and truth: a radiance like that of the <term>Urim and Thummim</term> <note>Ancient objects used by Israelite priests to determine God's will, often associated with "Light and Perfection."</note>, through which neither the Law, nor Satan, nor the world has power over one so armed in any way that might be deadly or destructive. # FOREST.

->That is:<-

*Here stood a growing forest, never finished in its building.*

Again in the second book of the *Fasti* <note>Ovid’s "Fasti" is a poetic calendar of Roman festivals</note>:

*Silvaque montanas occulere apta feras.* <note>original: "A forest well-suited to hide the mountain beasts."</note>

->That is:<-

*A forest, where the mountain beasts could hide themselves.*

Again in the sixth book of the same:

*Est nemus arboribus densum, secretus ab omni
Voce locus; si non obstreperetur aquis.* <note>original: "There is a grove thick with trees, a place secluded from every voice; were it not for the noise of the waters."</note>

->That is:<-

*There is a wood, densely shaded with trees,
A quiet place, where no noise troubles the ear.
One hears only the rustling of a brook.*

Another poet sings thus:

*Silva capax ævi, validaque incurva senecta
Æternum intonsæ frondis, stat pervia nullis
Solibus. &c.* <note>original: "A forest capable of ages, bowed with strong old age, with eternal unshorn foliage, it stands impassable to any suns."</note>

->That is:<-

*A forest of old years, bowed by the ages.
Fending off the power of the sun through thick leaves.*

Wherein also wild and cruel animals, such as lions, bears, wolves, tigers, and so forth, reside.

<margin>Forests suited for the service of idols.</margin>
That the woods and forests have been designated by nations since ancient times, or chosen for their idolatrous services—that they were dedicated to this or 그 godhood, such as to Pallas, Ceres, Diana, etc., to which last goddess almost all forests belonged, as Dempsterus noted on Rosinus—is a well-known matter. See Dilherr, *Verit.* page 127.

That since ancient times forests have been sought out to honor idols there through images, sacrifices, and otherwise, can be observed from many old passages: Exodus 34, Deuteronomy 12, Judges 6, 2 Kings 22 and 23, Isaiah 17 and 27, Ezekiel 7, etc. Whether the thick and heavy shade and shadows, as something alluring, could bring this about, I do not know; however, it is certainly held to be so. Virgil in the first book of the *Aeneid*:

*Lucus in urbe fuit media, lætiſſimus umbra:
Hic templum Junoni ingens Sidonia Dido
Condebat.* ——— <note>original: "There was a grove in the middle of the city, most joyful in its shade: Here Sidonian Dido was building a huge temple to Juno."</note>

<margin>Temple for Juno.</margin>
->That is, from Vondel’s translation:<- <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) was the preeminent Dutch poet and translator of classical works.</note>

*A wood shaded the city's center with trees.
Here Dido, when she came from Sidon, established a temple <gloss>original: "kerk," literally "church"</gloss>,
To the praise of Jupiter’s consort.*

However, that the sky-high trees, due to their shadow, darkness, gloom, and deep silence, could instill a kind of terror and fear, I am willing to believe; but that they could awaken reverence and piety in the heart,

<column-break/>

does not seem quite as plausible to me, although Seneca seems to want to give this impression in *Book V, Epistle 41.*

> *Si tibi occurrit vetustis arboribus & solitam altitudinem egreſſis frequens lucus...* <note>original Latin text provided in source</note> That is: *If you come across a grove with ancient trees that have grown taller than usual, and which, by the density of their branches covering one another, deprive you of the sight of the sky: then that loftiness of the woods, the silence of the place, and the wondrous shade, showing itself so thick and continuous in the open air, makes you think that there is some divinity in that place.*

Ovid in the third book of the *Fasti*:

*Lucus Aventino ſuberat niger ilicis umbra,
Quo poſſis viſo dicere, Numen in est.* <note>original: "Beneath the Aventine lay a grove black with the shade of holm-oaks; seeing it, you could say: 'A divinity is within.'"</note>

->That is:<-

*A sacred wood, shaded and enclosed all around
With oaks that almost touch the clouds with their crowns,
Lag at the ascent of the Aventine hill.
Whoever but looked at the wood said: a divinity must be here.*

Lucan, in the third book:

*————— Medio cum Phœbus in axe est,
Aut cælum nox atra tenet, pavet ipſe ſacerdos
Acceſſus; dominumque timet deprendere luci.
Hanc jubet immiſſo ſilvam procumbere ferro.
Sed fortes tremuere manus; motique tremenda
Majestate loci.* <note>original: "When the sun is at its zenith, or dark night holds the sky, the priest himself fears the approach; he dreads encountering the lord of the grove. He orders this forest to fall by the ax. But strong hands trembled, moved by the terrible majesty of the place."</note>

->That is:<-

*When Apollo completes half his journey,
And when the heaven is covered with darkness,
Then the priest himself shrinks from setting his feet
In the holy grove, for fear he might encounter the divinity there.
He commands this wood to be cut down to the ground.
But everyone’s hands are trembling at that moment.
The majesty of the place brings forth shivering and fear.*

I can well see that by "forests," one must not always and only understand that multitude of sky-high trees, but also the wooden images erected in the forests in honor of the Gods, called <term>אשרה</term> <term>Asherah</term>, closely corresponding to <term>עשתרת</term> <term>Ashtoreth</term> or <term>Ashtaroth</term>, translated by the 70 <note>The "70" refers to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> as <gloss>a grove, a forest</gloss>: by others as an image which was honored and served in the woods and forests. See Faber, *Semestr.* Book III, Chap. 1. Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, Synt. II, Chap. 2.

Rabbi Jochanan, Rabbi Kimchi on 1 Kings 21, and Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson, maintain that <term>Asherah</term> is a grove in honor of Baal: but Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>Also known as Rashi, a famous medieval commentator.</note> believes that it signifies an oak tree. See Isaiah 57:5, 2 Kings 17, Hosea 4:13, Ezekiel 6:13.

Rabbi Kimchi in his *Book of Roots* says that <term>אשרה</term> <term>Asherah</term> signifies not only a collection of trees, but also a single tree which is planted and dedicated to the service of the Divinity.

# FOREST.

And it appears that by *aserah* <note>original: "aserah"; a Hebrew term often translated as "grove" or "sacred pole," referring to the Canaanite goddess Asherah</note> one can understand not only a forest, but also a wooden image of a deity belonging to the forest, such as those that had to be rooted out and burned, as seen in 1 Kings 18, 2 Kings 21 and 23, Judges 6:25-28, Deuteronomy 7:5 and 13:3, Exodus 33:13, Isaiah 57:5, 2 Kings 17, Hosea 4:13, Isaiah 40 and 45, Jeremiah 10:3, etc.

And so some believe that by "forests" one must sometimes understand a temple, chapel, or a house of a God or idol, because it was customary to establish them in forests, 1 Kings 14:23, even if there was no plantation or grove nearby. At the very least, so writes Strabo in *Geography, Book IX*: *Poëtæ propter confitarum arborum juxta templum perpetuam consuetudinem, omnia templa lucos appellant, etiam arboribus carentia.* <note>original: "Poets, because of the constant custom of planting trees next to a temple, call all temples 'groves,' even those lacking trees."</note>
<margin>Temples called forests.</margin>
That is: *Because of the constant custom of planting trees next to a temple, the poets call all temples "forests," even though there are no trees around them.* And to this they add Virgil, *Aeneid VI*:

> Jam subeunt triviæ lucos, atque aurea tecta. <note>original: "Now they enter the groves of the crossroads and the golden roofs."</note>

->That is:<-

> Now they go together into Apollo's golden temple,
> Through the sacred grove of Diana.

One knows that there lies a Divine law, Deuteronomy 16:21, 22: *You shall not plant for yourself a grove of any kind of trees near the altar of the Lord your God, which you shall make for yourself: neither shall you set up any sacred pillar, which the Lord your God hates.*

I can well perceive that the reason for this, among others, is so that His people would not imitate the idolatrous and superstitious customs of the heathens, who early on appropriated the forests as places of service to their idols. For so writes Pliny in the *12th Book, 1st Chapter*: *Hæc fuere numinum templa priscoque ritu simplicia, rura etiam nunc Deo præcellentem arborem dicant. Primum lucos diis attribuerunt, tum & montes dicarunt, dein cuique suam arborem assignarunt.* <note>original: "These were the temples of the deities, simple according to the ancient rite; even now, the country districts dedicate an excellent tree to a God. First they assigned groves to the gods, then they dedicated mountains, then they assigned to each their own tree."</note> That is: *These were the temples of the gods, and the countrysides were very simple according to the old custom. Now they also dedicate a prominent tree to the god. First they appropriated the forests to the gods.* Pollux in *Onomasticon Book I*: *Dii vero consecrati sunt loci, nemora, luci, & sacra septa.* <note>original: "Indeed, the places consecrated to the gods are meadows, groves, woods, and sacred enclosures."</note> That is: *But to the gods are dedicated places, groves, forests, and sacred enclosures.* And it would indeed seem as if in the holy pages the forests and images were used interchangeably, says Spencer *part 1, page 371, on the laws of the Hebrews.*

Besides what has already been said, it seems to me that God wanted to cut off all opportunity for foul, fleshly uncleanness and lustful mingling, which used to happen in the hiding darkness under the tree shadows, as Cyril and others have noted on Hosea 4, etc. Compare 1 Kings 14 and 15; Dilherr's *Veritas page 129*; Henricus Ursinus, *Arbor. page 59-603*; Eusebius *regarding the grove in Phoenicia sacred to Venus, in the Life of Constantine Book III, Chapter 55*: *Erat illic schola quædam nequitiæ, omnibus impuris hominibus, qui corpus suum omni licentia corruperant, aperta.* <note>original: "There was a certain school of wickedness there, open to all impure men who had corrupted their bodies with every license."</note> And after that: *illegitimi mulierum concubitus, & adulteria, fœda & nefaria flagitia in luco illo, tanquam in loco ab omni lege & rectore vacuo, peragebantur.* <note>original: "unlawful intercourses with women, and adulteries, foul and wicked crimes were performed in that grove, as if in a place void of any law or ruler."</note> That is: *There was as it were a school of unchastity, opened to all foul people, who had*

<column-break/>

corrupted their bodies through all licentiousness. One found unlawful minglings with women, foul adulteries, and shameful deeds in that wood, as in a place where there was neither law nor governor. Horace in *Odes Book I, Ode 12* calls them *parum castos lucos* <note>original: "little-chaste groves"</note>, unchaste forests. See *Spencer on the Ritual Laws of the Hebrews, page 370, etc.*

Indeed, people fell so far that they publicly rendered Divine honor to the trees, either as being appropriated to a certain deity, or because this or that deity seemed to have a particular attraction to this or that tree, as a sort of divinity or divine manifestation. They wrote their name on the bark of the young tree, in hope and with the declaration that their love and reverence would grow along with it.
<margin>Trees honored as gods.</margin>
Curtius concerning the Indians, *History Book 8*: *Deos putant, quicquid colere cæperunt, arbores maxime, quas violare, capitale eſt.* <note>original: "They consider as gods whatever they have begun to worship, especially trees, which to harm is a capital offense."</note> That is: *They hold for gods whatever they have begun to honor, especially the trees, which one may not violate without capital punishment.* Theophylactus on *St. John Chapter IV*: *Eo dementiæ pervenerat hominum natura, ut & ſpecioſis arboribus, propter pulchritudinem, ſacrificarent, cupreſſis nempe, platanis, & ſimilibus.* <note>original: "The nature of men had reached such madness that they even sacrificed to beautiful trees for the sake of their beauty, namely to cypresses, plane trees, and the like."</note> That is: *So maddened had the nature of men become, that they also offered sacrifices to beautiful trees, and that for their beauty, namely to Cypresses, Plane trees, and the like.* See *Spencer page 371.*

They assigned this or that tree to such or such a deity; they hung it with veils; they made vows to it, they lit candles before it, they laid stolen booty by it: they wrote the name of the deity upon it, and to tear a branch or the bark from it was no small desecration: they buried heroes beneath them: they called upon them as representatives of the deity; they expected that they would give answers about future and secret things, says *Rabbi Maimonides* in *Guide for the Perplexed*. See *Henricus Ursinus in Arbor. page 606.*

And not only did they write the name of the deity, but also those of the people whom they honored and loved, upon the bark of the young and growing trees. Thus one reads in Theocritus, <term>σέβου μ’ ἑλένας φυτὸν εἰμὶ</term> <note>original: "sebou m' helenas phyton eimi"; Greek: "revere me, I am Helen's plant [tree]"</note>, honor me, I am Helen's tree!

> Quando ponebam novellas arbores mali, & pyri,
> Cortici ſummæ notavi nomen ardoris mei. <note>original: "When I was planting new trees of apple and pear, I marked the name of my passion on the top of the bark."</note>

->That is:<-

> When I planted the apple or the pear tree,
> I marked the bark with my burning love.

See *Lipsius Elector. Book I, Chapter 5. Virgil Eclogue 10.*

> — Teneris incidere amores Arboribus, <note>original: "To carve loves into tender trees"</note>

->That is:<-

> To write one's love upon the young and tender trees.

The same poet:

> ——— Creſcent illæ, creſcetis amores. <note>original: "As they [the trees] grow, so shall you grow, my loves."</note>

->That is:<-

> When the trees grow, then my love grows with them.

# BOZRA. BREAKING [FALLOW GROUND].

The Edomites, being governed by a king of that people, caused Edom and Bozra to become alike in life, customs, and various sentiments.

As for Edom, and the comparison of the Jews with Edom, that will be discussed in its proper place under that specific word.

<margin>Jerusalem as another Bozra.</margin>
That Jerusalem was another Bozra, although not in name, cannot be doubted in a certain respect.

Jerusalem was the seat and capital of Palestine, just as Bozra was of Edom—indeed, of the Jewish-Edomite land. There sat the Edomite king, Herod, in his court upon the royal throne; he who is said to have fortified Jerusalem wonderfully.

And if Bozra was the portion of the Levites, *Joshua 21:27*, certainly Jerusalem was the place where they had to reside for their services.

If "Bozra" comes from "binder" or "placing a hindrance" <note>The author is exploring the Hebrew etymology of *Batzar*, which can refer to fortifying, enclosing, or cutting off.</note> so that one does not rob or plunder; it was Jerusalem where one had to strive and keep watch against such desecration through Divine and civil laws and strict punishment. Yet, meanwhile, while forbidding stealing, they did it themselves and robbed the sanctuary, *Romans 2:21, 22.*

Indeed, where they should have furthered the course of the Gospel and the kingdom of heaven, both among their own people and among the Gentiles, they instead broke it off, placing great hindrances and obstructions, *Acts 4, 5, 9,* and *13:45-48; 1 Thessalonians 2:16, 17,* etc.; *Matthew 21* and *Psalm 119.*

And if anywhere the Christ trod the winepress—both of suffering unto victory and the finishing of His and our enemies, as well as of righteous vengeance—it was in Jerusalem, and just outside that city, in the garden, in the courtroom, on Calvary, the hill of skulls, etc., *Matthew 26* and *27.*

<margin>Particular opinion.</margin>
However, someone has recently appeared who, departing from the common opinion for several reasons his Reverence has given, suggests that this prophecy refers to later times, understanding "Edom" to mean Antichristendom and "Bozra" to be its capital, Rome. Bozra, meaning "vintage" or "grape-gathering," <note>original: "wynlezinge"</note> has its name from the nearby vineyards; likewise, the city of Rome, which was at first a pleasant vineyard of the Lord, later became a vine of Sodom, *Deuteronomy 32:32, 33.*

If we take it, secondly, as a fortress, then this place is rightly the stronghold of the entire Antichristian empire, and from there all laws are issued.

Thirdly, when one observes other derivations from the root word, it also signifies a barrenness, as seen in the word *BATZARAH* <note>original: "ניר"; likely a reference to *Batzarot*, meaning drought or dearth</note> in *Psalm 10:1.* Thus, this city is also entirely barren in works of righteousness and holiness, because it lacks the rain of true doctrine and the dew of the Spirit, so that it is impossible for anything else to arise but a great dryness and barrenness.

See also Vitringa on *Apocalypse p. 51* and on *Isaiah Chapter 63.*

<column-break/>

### ->BREAKING [FALLOW], FALLOW LAND, <term>Nir (ניר)</term>, <term>novare</term> <note>original: "novare"; Latin: to renew or plow up</note>, in the Hiphil form <term>Hanir (הניר)</term> <term>novellavit</term> <note>original: "novellavit"; Latin: renewed or plowed anew</note>, <term>agrum denuo proscidit</term> <note>original: "agrum denuo proscidit"; Latin: he cut the field again (plowed it)</note>, <term>aroo (άρόω)</term> <note>original: "άρόω"; Greek: to plow</note>. <term>Nir (ניר)</term> <term>novale</term> <note>original: "novale"; Latin: fallow land</note>, breaking land.<-

I am not speaking here of nausea or the vomiting that follows it, nor of "breaking out" or "spewing out"; but of an act and labor of husbandmen for the clearing of the arable land, to prepare the soil so that, in hope of greater fruit, the seed may be entrusted to the earth.

That word appears in two places, namely, *Jeremiah 4:3* and *Hosea 10:12.* The word <term>Nir (ניר)</term>, and <term>Nir</term> and <term>Mur</term> in the <term>Hiphil</term> <note>A Hebrew verb form usually indicating causative action.</note> form, <term>Hanir</term>, means *to be light, bright, clear, or shining*. The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> have <term>neosate neomata (νεώσατε νεώματα)</term>, from <term>neoo (νεόω)</term>, *to renew*. We say it is a "bright" land when it is pure of weeds, thistles, and thorns.

When one leaves some land that is exhausted to lie empty and still for a time—or land that is full of weeds and evil roots and unfit to be sown in that state—it is sometimes plowed and harrowed in the summer heat to purify it. This is done so that by the cutting of the plowshare and the loosening by the harrow, the roots of shrubs and bushes might wither and dry out through exposure to the summer heat, and thus the land is purified and becomes fit for proper cultivation and the raising of crops; that is called "breaking" the land, or "laying it fallow," etc.

<margin>Metaphorical Application.</margin>
It is used figuratively and metaphorically in the Holy Scroll when applied to the heart of man, or to the state of the church, compared to a field.

The Lord our God frequently uses the plow of His visitations and judgments; He cuts around and out to purge His people of wickedness, so that He may then, with better result, cast His teachings into the heart as a good seed, leading to fruitfulness in good works of conversion, holiness, and pure love.

But now we notice that the Lord gives the command to do such a thing in *Jeremiah 4:3* and *Hosea 10:12.*

> Rabbi Solomon <note>Also known as Rashi, a famous medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> understands it thus: *Be diligent and intent upon the law, and learn to walk in the good way, so that you may overcome and conquer your evil nature: in the manner of him who plows the field and turns the roots of harmful weeds upside down during the heat, long before the casting out of the seed.*

> And Rabbi David <note>Also known as Radak (David Kimhi), a medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note> understands it as follows: *Arouse your heart to receive the word of reproof, just as a field is prepared through plowing to receive the seed.*

I believe that everyone should purify the field of their heart from wickedness, resist evil, and uproot, kill, and subdue the roots and lusts, so that henceforth—as had previously happened—no foul, evil, and destructive fruits might come forth, but that it may be purified into a new and clean land. To this end the lessons tend in *Isaiah 16* and *55:7; Galatians 6:15; Ephesians 4:22,* etc.; *Hebrews 6,* etc.; *Colossians 3:5; Galatians 5:24;* for out of the heart comes all evil, *Genesis 6:5* and *5:2; Matthew 15:19, 20.*

If one wishes to apply it to the field of the church, well—

which has a great similarity to the heart? Certainly, nothing is more harmful than the delusion of self-righteousness derived from the works of the law. To wish to serve and cling to ceremonies after grace has been revealed and righteousness has been brought forth is harmful and loathsome; allowing the weeds of strife, quarreling, offense, and error to remain in the church prevents true fruitfulness in love and good works.

Creating factions and discord in the church, and binding oneself to established articles <note>The author likely refers to rigid dogmatic statements used to exclude others.</note> to feed strife and partisanship—rather than striving to be bound in truth through love, peace, and the unity of the foundation and sound doctrine in the unity of the spirit—springs forth from a bitter root that bears gall and wormwood.

<margin>Simple interpretation.</margin>
Simply put, I see it taken in this manner: One clears a field; one sweeps and cleanses it of weeds and evil roots through spading, plowing, harrowing, and turning it over, so that with a firmer hope of fruitfulness, one may cast in the good seed. *In the same way, you people, lay aside and cleanse yourselves of all evil desires, devious opinions, and thoughts; cleanse yourselves of the wicked roots whose fruits and shoots have been useless, censurable, evil, and loathsome, so that you may receive the good seed of the word and be filled with the fruits of righteousness, love, and mercy, to receive a gracious reward on the day of the Lord’s coming.*

## VOMITING, SPEWING OUT, SPITTING OUT, VOMIT, SPITTLE, etc. <note>original: קוא, ἀμέω. *vomere, evomere*. קיא, קיא, ἔμετος, ἔξεραma, *vomitus*. קיקליון</note> <note>The author provides the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin terms for vomiting and its products.</note>

<margin>Cause of vomiting.</margin>
**V**OMITING and SPEWING OUT happens after something troubles the stomach, or when, through one cause or another, a disordered movement is provoked within it; and nausea is often a precursor to vomiting. Vomiting is a violent movement or contraction of the stomach membranes and fibers upwards, so that whatever is troubling the stomach is cast out. It often comes from overly sharp acidic parts, bile, or foul juices that are poured into the stomach during fevers, smallpox, etc.; however, I leave that to the physicians. One also finds this spoken of by the secular writers:

> Virgil in the fifth book of the *Aeneid*:
> 
> *Illum & labentem Teucri & risere natantem,  
> Et falsos rident revomentem pectore fluctus.*
> 
> ---
> 
> ->**The Trojans laughed loudly**<-
> ->When he plunged into the water, and swimming, from the burden<-
> ->He had to save himself, and vomited the swallowed<-
> ->Salt water back out again.----------<-

> The same in the third book:
> 
> *------ Saniem eructans, ac frusta cruento  
> Per somnum commista mero.*
> 
> ---
> 
> ->That is:<-
> 
> ->There he lay stretched out, and vomited a flood of gore,<-
> ->And morsels mixed with wine, and flesh, and blood.<-

> Ovid:
> 
> *Non semel est stomacho nausea facta meo.*
> 
> ---
> 
> ->That is:<-
> 
> ->A nausea has gripped my stomach several times.<-

<margin>Vomiting taken figuratively.</margin>
Vomiting, spewing out, and spitting out are often taken figuratively and metaphorically, as in *Leviticus 18:28*, when the land vomits out its inhabitants. God allows Israel to be threatened that, by making themselves guilty of foul sins and heavy iniquities, they would be punished with heavy judgments, penalties, scattering, and exiles: the land being too holy to be able to harbor such foul and nauseating people.

In *Job 20:15*, it is given to be understood that ill-gotten goods, whether obtained by craft, deceit, or violence, seldom last; they very rarely pass to the third heir. "Easy come, easy go," and consumed: <note>original: *De male quæsitis non gaudet tertius hæres*</note> *the third heir does not enjoy ill-gotten gains*; as it came, so it goes.

In *Proverbs 25:16*, it is given to be understood that too much of anything, in whatever matter it may be, is unpleasant and harmful; that one becomes nauseated by it and finally develops a distaste and aversion to it—whether it be food, drink, pleasure, or lust. It eventually causes a man to "repeat" it <note>This refers to the "aftertaste" or "reflux" of a bad decision or overindulgence.</note>; therefore, to keep measure in all things is best: <note>original: *Sit modus in rebus*</note> *In all things let there be a measure.*

*Proverbs 26:11: As a dog returns to his vomit.* This will appear again below. Solomon seems to want to teach that a fool and unreformable sinner, according to his inner disposition and the nature that constantly remains with him, though he might have disparaged, rejected, and condemned something for a short time, nevertheless eventually returns to his former wickedness, evil dealings, and old whims, remaining beset with prejudices and carrying out what is unseemly. For even if he were pounded in a mortar, his folly would not depart from his heart; thus he is unreformable; there is no ointment to be smeared on him.

*Isaiah 19:14, 15* foretells and shows through a simile and metaphor how the Egyptian sages and rulers, throughout the entire kingdom, would confuse the people, the court, and the realm, bringing them into a whirlpool and maelstrom, into an extreme bewilderment and desperate predicament. They would be like someone who, having drunk a mixed and fermented drink poured for him, is thereby dazed, delirious, and light-headed. His head aches, his vision blurs, his head spins, he raves and stammers, he staggers, and he is entirely unable to do anything for which understanding and judgment are required. And by this is...

# BOZRAH. BREAKING [FALLOW GROUND].

Idumeans <note>The Edomites, descendants of Esau.</note>, and being ruled by a king of that people <note>Herod the Great, who was of Idumean descent.</note>, Jerusalem would have become like Edom and Bozrah in life, customs, and various sentiments.

As for Edom and the comparison of the Jews with Edom, that will be addressed in what follows under that specific entry in its proper place.

<margin>Jerusalem as another Bozrah.</margin>
That Jerusalem was another Bozrah, though not in name, cannot be doubted in a certain respect.

Jerusalem was the seat and capital of Palestine, just as Bozrah was of Edom, and indeed of the Jewish-Edomite land. There sat the Edomite King Herod in his court upon the royal throne; he of whom it is said that he fortified Jerusalem marvelously.

And if Bozrah was the portion of the Levites (*Job 21:27* <note>The author likely refers to Joshua 21:27, which mentions Golan in Bashan, though Bozrah is often associated with cities of refuge or Levitical cities in other contexts.</note>), certainly Jerusalem was the place where they were required to reside for their services.

*If Bozrah comes from "hindering" or "placing an obstacle" so that one does not rob or plunder;* it was Jerusalem where one had to strive and keep watch against such desecration through Divine and civil laws and the strict execution of punishment. Yet meanwhile, while forbidding stealing, they did it themselves and robbed the holy things (*Romans 2:21, 22*).

Indeed, where they should have advanced the course of the Gospel and the kingdom of heaven, both among their own people and among the Gentiles, there they broke it off, placing great obstacles and hindrances (*Acts 4, 5, 9, and 13:45-48; 1 Thessalonians 2:16, 17, etc.; Matthew 21 and Psalm 119*).

And if anywhere Christ trod the winepress—both of suffering unto victory and the finishing of His and our enemies, as well as for the exercise of righteous vengeance—it was at Jerusalem, and just outside that city, in the garden, in the legal proceedings, and on Calvary, the "Place of the Skull," etc. (*Matthew 26 and 27*).

<margin>A particular opinion.</margin>
However, someone has recently come forward who, departing from the common opinion for several reasons his Reverence has provided, believes that this prophecy refers to later times. By "Edom," he understands Antichristendom, and by "Bozrah," its capital, Rome. Since Bozrah means "vintage" or "grape-gathering," that city took its name from the nearby vineyards; likewise, the city of Rome, which at first was a pleasant vineyard of the Lord, later became a vine of Sodom (*Deuteronomy 32:32, 33*).

Secondly, if we take it to mean a "fortress," then this place is rightly the stronghold of the entire Antichristian empire, and from there all laws are issued.

Thirdly, if one observes other derivations from the root word, as can be seen in the word *BATZARAH* in *Psalm 10:1*, it also signifies "barrenness." Thus, this city is likewise entirely barren in works of righteousness and holiness, because it lacks the rain of true doctrine and the dew of the Spirit, so that it is impossible for anything else to arise from it but a great aridity and barrenness.

See also Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note> on *Revelation p. 51 & on Isaiah Chapter 63.*

<column-break/>

### BREAKING [FALLOW GROUND], FALLOW LAND, ניר, *to renew, in the Hiphil [Hebrew verb form] it means to make new or plow a field again; in Greek, ἀρόω [to plow]. ניר: newly tilled land, fallow ground.*

I am not speaking here of loathing or nausea, which is followed by vomiting <note>In Dutch, the word "Braaken" can mean both "to plow fallow land" and "to vomit." The author is clarifying he means the agricultural term.</note>, nor of outbursts, vomit, or spewing; but of an act and labor of husbandmen for the purging of the farmland, to prepare the land so that the seed may be entrusted to the earth in hope of greater fruit.

That word appears in two places, namely, *Jeremiah 4:3 and Hosea 10:12.* The word חכר and כור in the Hiphil, הכביר, means *to lighten, to be bright, clear, or shining.* The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> have *νεώσατε νεώματα* <gloss>plow up new fields</gloss>, from *νεόν*, to renew. We say it is a "clear land" when it is pure of weeds, thistles, and thorns.

When one leaves a piece of land that is exhausted to lie empty and still for a time—or land that is full of weeds and evil roots and is unfit to be sown in that condition—one sometimes "summer-fallows" it, plowing and harrowing it to purify it. This is done so that by cutting through with the plowshare and loosening with the harrow, the roots of shrubs and bushes might wither and dry out by being exposed to the summer heat. Thus the land is purified and becomes fit for proper cultivation and the growing of crops; this is called "breaking the land" or "laying it fallow," etc.

<margin>Metaphorical application.</margin>
It is used figuratively or metaphorically in the Holy Scrolls to apply it to the heart of man, or to the state of the church, compared to a field.

The Lord our God frequently uses the plow of His visitations and judgments; He chops around and out to purify His people from wickednesses, so as to then throw His sermons into the heart with better results, like a good seed, unto fruitfulness in good works of repentance, holiness, and pure love.

But now it is noted that the Lord, in *Jeremiah 4:3 and Hosea 10:12*, gives the command to do this.

> Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous medieval Jewish commentator.</note> understands it thus: *Be diligent and set upon the law, and learn to walk in the good way, so that you may overcome and conquer your evil nature: in the manner of him who plows the field and turns the roots of harmful weeds upside down during the time of heat, long before the casting out of the seed.*

> And Rabbi David <note>David Kimhi, also known as Radak.</note> understands it as follows: *Arouse your heart to receive the word of rebuke, just as a field is prepared by plowing to receive the seed.*

I am inclined to think that every individual must purify the field of his heart from wickedness, resist evil, uproot the roots and lusts, kill them, and bring them under subjection, so that henceforth—as had happened before—no foul, evil, and destructive fruits might come forth from it. This is so that it may be purified into a new and clean land, which is the goal of the lessons in *Isaiah 16 and 55:7; Galatians 6:15; Ephesians 4:22 etc.; Hebrews 6 etc.; Colossians 3:5; Galatians 5:24*, for out of the heart comes all evil (*Genesis 6:5 and 5:2; Matthew 15:19, 20*).

If one wishes to apply this to the field of the church, wel-

To wish to serve and cling to ceremonies after grace has been revealed and righteousness has been brought forth is harmful and detestable: allowing the weeds of strife, bickering, offenses, and errors to remain in the church prevents true fruitfulness in love and good works.

Creating factions and discord in the church, and binding oneself to established articles in order to feed strife and partisanship—rather than striving in truth through love and peace to be united in the foundation and sound doctrine, in the unity of the spirit—springs forth from a bitter root that bears gall and wormwood.

<margin>Simple transfer.</margin>
I see it taken simply in this manner. One strips a field; one sweeps and cleanses it of weeds and evil roots through digging, plowing, harrowing, and turning over, so that one may cast the good seed into it with a firmer hope of fruitfulness: likewise, you people, lay aside and cleanse out all evil desires, perverse opinions, and thoughts; cleanse yourselves of the wicked roots whose fruits and sprouts have been useless, reprobate, evil, and detestable, so that you may receive the good seed of the Word and be filled with the fruits of righteousness, love, and mercy, to receive a gracious reward on the day of the Lord’s coming.

### VOMITING, SPEWING OUT, VOMIT, SPITTLE, etc. <term>πτύω (ptyō)</term> <note>original Greek: to spit</note>, <term>ἀμέω (ameō)</term> <note>original Greek: to vomit</note>, <term>vomere</term> <note>original Latin: to vomit</note>, <term>evomere</term> <note>original Latin: to spew out</note>. <term>קיא (qi)</term> <note>original Hebrew: vomit</note>, <term>ἔμετος (emetos)</term> <note>original Greek: the act of vomiting</note>, <term>ἐξέραμα (exerama)</term> <note>original Greek: that which is vomited</note>, <term>vomitus</term> <note>original Latin: vomit</note>: <term>קלתון (qaltown)</term> <note>original Hebrew/Rabbinic: a basin or vessel for vomiting</note>, etc.

### VOMITING and SPEWING OUT occurs after the stomach finds something troublesome, or when for one reason or another a disordered movement is stirred up within it; nausea is often a precursor to vomiting. Vomiting is a violent movement or contraction of the stomach membranes and fibers upward, so that whatever is bothering the stomach is spewed out.

<margin>Cause of vomiting.</margin>
It certainly comes from overly sharp acidic parts, bile, or foul juices, which are poured out into the stomach during fevers, smallpox, etc.; however, I leave that to the physicians. One also finds it spoken of by secular writers:

> Virgil in the fifth book of the *Aeneid*:
> *Illum & labentem Teucri & risere natantem,*
> *Et falsos rident revomentem pectore fluctus.*
> <note>original Latin: "The Trojans laughed at him both as he fell and as he swam, and they laughed as he vomited the salt waves from his chest." This refers to Gyas, a ship captain who was thrown overboard during a race.</note>

->That is:<-

> — The Trojans laughed aloud
> When he plunged into the water, and swimming, from the burden
> He had to save himself, and vomited the swallowed
> Salt water out again. —

The same author in the third book:

> *...... saniem eructans, ac frusta cruento*
> *Per somnum commista mero.*
> <note>original Latin: "...belching gore, and bits [of flesh] mixed with bloody wine in his sleep." This describes the giant Cyclops, Polyphemus, after eating Odysseus's men.</note>

<column-break/>

->That is:<-

> There he lay stretched out, and vomited a flood of gore,
> And morsels mixed with wine, and flesh, and blood.

Ovid:

> *Non semel est stomacho nausea facta meo.*
> <note>original Latin: "Nausea has been caused to my stomach more than once."</note>

->That is:<-

> A loathing has seized my stomach several times.

<margin>Vomiting used figuratively.</margin>
Vomiting, spewing out, and spitting are often taken improperly and metaphorically, as in *Leviticus 18:28*, when the land vomits out its inhabitants. God allows Israel to be threatened that, if they make themselves guilty of foul sins and heavy iniquities, they would be punished with severe judgments and penalties of scattering and exile: the land being too holy to be able to harbor such foul and loathsome people.

*Job 20:15* gives it to be understood that ill-gotten goods, whether obtained through cunning, deceit, or violence, seldom last: that they very rarely pass to the third heir. Easy come, easy go, and consumed: <note>original Latin: *de male quæfitis non gaudet tertius hæres*</note> *the third heir does not enjoy things evilly acquired*: as it came, so it goes.

*Proverbs 25:16* gives it to be understood that too much of anything, whatever the matter may be, is unpleasant and harmful; that one becomes loathsome of it, and eventually gains a distaste and aversion to it: whether food, drink, pleasure, or lust: it repeats on a person in time: therefore, to keep measure in all things is best, <note>original Latin: *Sit modus in rebus*</note>: *In all things let there be a measure.*

*Proverbs 26:11. Like a dog he returns to his vomit.*
This will appear again below. Solomon seems to wish to teach that a fool and incorrigible sinner, according to his inner disposition and the nature that always remains with him, though he might have disparaged, disapproved, and rejected something for a short time, eventually always returns to his former wickedness, evil dealings, and old whims, remaining occupied with prejudices, carrying out that which is not becoming. For even if he were pounded in a mortar, folly would still not depart from his heart: therefore, he is incorrigible: there is no ointment to be smeared on him <note>a Dutch idiom meaning a situation is beyond repair</note>.

*Isaiah 19:14, 15* is foretold and shown through parables and metaphors, how the Egyptian wise men and rulers would confuse the entire kingdom, the court, and the realm, bringing and entangling them in a whirlpool and vortex, in an extreme bewilderment and desperate embarrassment: such that they would be like someone who, having drunk a mixed and spirited drink poured for him, is thereby dazed, delirious, and light-headed. His head aches, his sight flickers, his head spins, he raves and stammers, he staggers, and is entirely incapable of doing anything for which understanding and judgment are required. And by this
