### BURNING BUSH. <term>סנה (Seneh)</term> <note>Hebrew: thorn-bush</note>, <term>Rubus</term> <note>Latin: bramble</note>.

<margin>Vision of the Burning Bush.</margin>
Regarding the BURNING BUSH, and the Lord’s appearance within it—how it appeared to be all ablaze in flames without being consumed, etc.—one may read of this in *Exodus 3:2, 3, 4, Acts 7,* etc.
The vision appears to have come to Moses when he was eighty years old, having spent forty of those years with his kinsmen in Midian: after which he seems to have received a commission from God through this miracle,

<column-break/>

and to have been charged and sent by this Divine appearance and address to deliver and lead out his brothers, the oppressed Israelites in Egypt.
The place where the vision occurred was at and near Sinai, with its adjacent wilderness, where the Lord also appeared thereafter with his many thousands of Angels—as terrifying as it was awesome—to establish his covenant, bringing Israel into servitude and under the yoke <note>Referring to the Mosaic Law</note>, which would last until the appearance of the Lord in the flesh, and stand firm until the restoration and perfection of all things.
What species the Burning Bush was, I cannot precisely determine. I think it was of a short and low kind, and without doubt weak and fragile, a thorny and prickly growth.
The Burning Bush appears as if it were all ablaze, yet not being damaged at all, but rather illuminated by the fire, like a flame and an abiding light.
<margin>Burning bush on fire.</margin>
Whether this was caused by lightning, or by bandits, or by shepherds, or by erupted vapors and sulfurous substances, or immediately by God; I do not know that God’s Spirit, through the pens of his scribes, has determined it so precisely. At least, it is not stated exactly how the Bush had caught fire, but that the Bush appeared to Moses to be all ablaze without being consumed—even though fire easily ignites and destroys such dry fuel—was the cause of his very righteous wonder. Therefore, casting aside all fear, he was eager to investigate further what this matter might be. And upon this, he approaches the Bush.
The Lord seeing this (speaking in human terms), he who was in the Bush and is said to dwell there (*Deuteronomy 33*), called out to Moses, and was answered by Moses in return.
The Lord did not want him to come too close or penetrate too deeply; he commanded him to take the shoes off his feet, wanting him to show that the place, because of His presence and appearance, was holy ground, etc. Regarding both points, the aforementioned passages must be read with care.
As for Christians and non-Christians, as well as modern and ancient theologians and church teachers, they have designed various thoughts regarding this vision, some believing one thing and others another to be symbolized and sketched out by this.
I wish to suggest first that since Moses was about to be sent and used for the glorious work of Israel’s deliverance from the house of bondage in Egypt—which task could not be undertaken and carried out without great danger—the Lord intended to show through this vision, alongside the following address, that He who was so awesome and mighty to do wonders took the cause of the then-heavily oppressed Israel to heart. He showed that He would preserve Moses, though he was entering into great danger, so that no harmful or destructive injury would befall him; and that He would preserve, protect, and lead out His lowly, enslaved, and despised people of Israel by a mighty arm, even though they found themselves in a "burning furnace" (*Deuteronomy 4*), as if having His fire and light among them. Indeed, He showed that their oppression would lead to the...

What has been thought out regarding this, I shall briefly lay open to the reader, without, however, binding myself strictly to everything that has been thought and said about every single circumstance.

<margin>Reference to Christ.</margin> By the Burning Bush, springing from the common ground of the earth, close to the ground, low, insignificant, and of little value and esteem, etc., one observes a representation of Christ's human nature: a sprout and root out of a dry ground, low, humble, despised, having subjected himself to much pain, scorn, contempt, and poverty for sinners, having come in the form of a servant; not like the high oaks and cedars, or kings and greats among the Jews and Heathens. *Isa. 4 and 11 and 53. John 1 and 8.* Along with the union of his Divine and Human natures in the unity of his person, covering himself as if with flesh, without his human nature suffering any hindrance thereby, or being consumed and swallowed up; rather, it was much more glorified, perfected, and strengthened by it to endure the heat and the hotly stoked fire of God's wrath and the oppression, so that he was not devoured and entirely consumed by suffering and death. Thus one saw his glory, as of the only-begotten of the Father, *John 1:14.*

In this dwelt the Lord, the fullness of the Godhead, *Col. 2:9.* who otherwise dwells in an inaccessible light, *1 Tim. 6:16. Deut. 33:15.* He who is the Angel of the Covenant, *Mal. 3.* the Angel of God’s Presence, *Isa. 63.* in whose midst is the name Jehovah, Israel’s redeemer and leader, *Exod. 23. Acts 17:30. 1 Cor. 10.* He spoke out of that Bush; him one must hear. *Deut. 18:15-18. Matt. 3:17 and 17. John 1:18. Heb. 1.*

It is presumption to wish to sniff through the mystery of the Incar-

### FIRE, BURNING, to bring BURNING upon someone; BLASTED CORN; to have BURNING FIRE on one's lips; the HEART BURNS; BURNT OFFERING; BRANDING IRON, etc. <note>original Hebrew: לָהַט (lahat), יָקַד (yaqad), בָּעַר (ba'ar); Greek: καίω (kaio), πυρόω (pyroo); Latin: uro, incendium; Hebrew: עוֹלָה (olah - burnt offering), cauterium (branding), &c.</note>

Burning is caused by sparks of fire in dry fuels, capable of catching the flame and more or less feeding and preserving it.

When material fire and necessary fuels are spoken of, one may take burning more literally; and such is clear enough in itself.

<margin>Blasted corn.</margin> When blasted corn <note>term: "brandkoorn" - refers to agricultural blight, smut, or mildew that makes grain look scorched or blackened</note> is spoken of in *Deut. 28:22, 1 Kings 8:37, 2 Chron. 6:28 and 19:26, Isa. 37, Amos 4* and elsewhere, it is without doubt a punishment from God, with which he threatens a people, and which is justly sent home to a wicked and sinful people: called in Hebrew *shedaphah* and *shiddaphon*, meaning as much as *corn*, and *stalks of corn*, and *ears* that are withered by the strong wind, bent, and scorched due to heat and drought before they have come to their fullness and ripeness, so that they are useless and can give no nourishment.

The burning of the great city, *Rev. 18*, of fire and brimstone, *Rev. 19 and 21*, will perhaps be understood both literally and figuratively, just as the hellish fire and the most powerful stings of conscience and sorrows of the soul are often depicted through burning, a fire and flame: though I would also understand by it downfall and devastation, as once befell Sodom and Gomorrah.

Certainly when God's wrath burns, he indirectly sets the land and the cities on fire, *Isa. 10:16, 17 and 42:25, Ps. 97 and 106*; otherwise it is a name for a very hidden God

<header>B U R N I N G.</header>
<meta>catchword: because</meta>

To depict God when He consistently demonstrates the effects of His extreme displeasure, which are very painful and harmful to those deserving of punishment—because otherwise such things have no place in God. *2 Chronicles 23:26, Psalm 79:5, and 89:47, Jeremiah 4, 7, 15, etc.*

<margin>Metaphorical figure of speech.</margin>
It is also figurative and metaphorical when it is said of men that they "burn," or that they have "burning fire on their lips." *Proverbs 16:27, Ezekiel 21:36.* In a figurative sense, this undoubtedly refers not only to people who stir up the fire of strife, quarreling, and discord—from which fights, wars, and devastations spring—but also to people who, through the heat and rage of insane wrath, move against one another toward destruction in all manner of ways.

<margin>Burning in the Emmaus travelers.</margin>
There was a kind of burning that was not harmful, which was observed in the travelers to Emmaus, in *Luke 24:32*: "And did not our heart burn within us on the way, as He spoke to us," etc. This was undoubtedly a burning of love and high esteem for the person of the unknown traveler and teacher, Jesus, and for the word He spoke to them as He opened the Scriptures; it was also a burning with zeal because of their own great blindness and lack of understanding regarding the Scriptures, especially on that primary point concerning the Messiah, His suffering, and His resurrection. <note>The "Emmaus travelers" refers to the two disciples who met the resurrected Jesus on the road to Emmaus without recognizing him initially.</note>

"Who is offended, and I burn not?" asks Paul in *2 Corinthians 11:29*. When a stumbling block was placed before the weak in the race of truth, sincerity, and godliness—whether out of malice and intent, or out of weakness and ignorance—Paul took it very poorly. He was deeply affected by it; he had a "zeal of God." He sought to make the offended person walk uprightly, to lift them up, to help them; he exhorted, rebuked, or threatened the one who gave the offense, seeking to make amends for the damage suffered, the standstill, or the regression, and to remove the cause of the offense from their midst.

"Burning" is also used improperly <note>meaning figuratively or in a non-literal sense</note> in *1 Corinthians 7:9*, when Paul says, "it is better to marry than to burn." This means either being strongly in love with someone or having and nurturing within oneself a strong heat and provocation of the lusts of the flesh toward intercourse. One says of someone who is lovesick that "he burns," especially when he makes it sufficiently understood through his words, countenance, or deeds.

Virgil, in the 4th Book of the *Aeneid*, at the beginning:

> But the Queen, long since wounded by a heavy care,
> Feeds the wound in her veins, and is consumed by a hidden fire.
> <note>original Latin: "At Regina gravi jamdudum saucia cura / Vulnus alit venis, & caeco carpitur igni."</note>

Thus speaks Vondel: <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) was the preeminent poet and playwright of the Dutch Golden Age.</note>

> But Tyre's queen, now for a while in her heart
> Too miserably struck by love, feeds that pain
> And wound in her breast; she secretly wastes away within
> From a fever of love.

The same author in the same book:

> Dido burns in love, and has drawn the madness through her bones.
> <note>original Latin: "Ardet amans Dido, traxitque per ossa furorem."</note>

That is, according to the same poet's translation:

> The head of this community
> Blazes madly with love: the fever sits in the bones.

<column-break/>

Propertius in the 3rd Book:

> She keeps the old fires in her bones.
> <note>original Latin: "Veteres custodit in ossibus ignes."</note>

That is:

> She feeds the old fire of love in her bones.

Ovid in the 3rd Book of the *Metamorphoses*:

---

> --- Just as yellow wax is wont to waste away 
> by a gentle fire, and the morning frosts 
> by the sudden sun: so, thinned by love, 
> he melts away, and is consumed little by little by a hidden fire.
> <note>original Latin: "--- Ut intabescere flavae / Igne levi cerae, matutinaeque pruinae / Sole repente solent: sic attenuatus amore / Liquitur, & caeco paulatim carpitur igni." This passage describes the wasting away of Narcissus.</note>

This sounds like this in Vondel’s version:

> Just as a wax torch disappears by a little fire,
> And morning frost, upon which the spring sun shines,
> Gradually passes and melts; so one sees him change,
> And this fever of love gradually consumes his flesh.

Before I give an account of the fire on the altar of burnt offering, along with the burnt sacrifices, I shall speak a word about the branding iron.

The Apostle uses the word in *1 Timothy 4:2*: "having their conscience seared as with a branding iron."

No one can judge otherwise than that this is spoken figuratively and by way of comparison, the saying about branding irons and their use being borrowed and applied here.

<term>kauterion, kauter, kauteriazein</term> <note>original Greek: καυτήριον, καυτήρ, καυτηριάζειν</note>, *to brand with a cautery* <note>original Latin: "cauterio inurere"</note>—that is, to brand-mark—is used and applied when one sears and burns a cancerous limb so that the cancer does not spread; also when one wishes to staunch blood flowing from a wound and sear the veins; or when a hardness, calloused state, deafness, and insensibility comes into the affected limb. Those who have made themselves highly punishable by wicked deeds are often branded on the face, the hand, or the back.

Let this be said enough in passing regarding the branding iron. Now we come to the sense and meaning of the great Apostle in this metaphor, in which not all theologians are in complete agreement on how to track, grasp, and express it.

<margin>Opinions of the learned.</margin>
Since I am on this chapter, I shall serve the reader with what prominent men have left us regarding this matter.

Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and successor to Calvin.</note> has it as: "searched out and seared off with a branding iron, so that they have no conscience."

The common translation has: "having a burnt, or brand-marked conscience."

Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the famous Dutch humanist and theologian.</note> and Heinsius <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a famous scholar at Leiden University.</note> do not seem entirely foreign to this, for they have translated it as: "having a conscience identified by a branding iron."

Aretius <note>Benedictus Aretius (1505–1574), a Swiss reformer.</note> expresses his thoughts quite clearly when he writes: <term>kauter</term> <note>καυτήρ</note>, a branding iron, is a tool which physicians or masters of medicine use, sometimes cutting off certain body parts that are in bad condition by burning. It is also an instrument with which one used to mark cattle on the forehead, as well as slaves, so that they might be recognized by the branded mark. This the Apostle now transfers to the conscience. The conscience is said to be marked with a branding iron, which accuses and condemns the man.

### B U R N I N G.

for it is a household witness that one cannot deceive or mislead, as it is aware of all words, deeds, and resolutions—a witness whose judgment also carries weight before God's tribunal.

<margin>Explanation by Glassius.</margin>
Glassius, in his *Sacred Rhetoric* <note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656) was a German theologian; his *Rhetorica Sacra* explored the figurative language of the Bible.</note>, seems not entirely opposed to this view, for on page 245 this learned man writes as follows: *That word carries two meanings: a. the wounding or offending of the conscience; for they teach and compel the keeping of such things that they know are impossible to keep, which is why they are previously called* speakers of lies through hypocrisy: *thus their conscience rebukes them, knowing that the things they teach are false. b. It also carries the cause of this wounding or offense, being the heat of various lusts. These together (I say) are contained within that word: for it is derived from* a branding iron <note>Greek: καυτηρ / kautēr</note>, *an instrument with which one burns a brand-mark, in which is found both the injury to the skin and flesh, and the manner and way it occurred, through fire and heat. At the same time, the Apostle seems to look upon the spiritual shame which must necessarily follow the wounding of the conscience in matters of such weight and importance, just as in former times criminals marked by a branding iron were held in ill repute.* See further Flacius in *Key to the Scriptures* <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus, author of *Clavis Scripturae Sacrae* (1567).</note>, Part I, page 165; Balduin, *On Cases of Conscience*, Chapter XI.

Heinsius and Scultetus do not agree with Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and scholar.</note> that it refers to something cut off or scorched away; rather, they hold it to be a conscience marked as if with a branding iron through committed villainies: branded by a foul and shameful life.

Dietericus in *Antiquities of the New Testament* and Leigh in *Sacred Critiques* <note>Edward Leigh (1602–1671), an English lay theologian.</note> also maintain this, adding that through the habit of sinning, such people have become as if calloused and unfeeling, as if they had no sensation at all.

Furthermore, Dilherr writes in *On Monsters*, page 541: To be branded in the conscience is said of those whose minds are so covered and overcome with the callus of wickedness that in the foulest matters they feel no prick or remorse of conscience; rather, they are always greedy to commit all kinds of violations. Of such people, there is almost not the slightest hope that they will ever come to reflection or better senses.

Alternatively, as the learned Braunius writes in *System of Theology*, pages 101, 102: Those who flatter themselves to their utmost ability that they do not sin, or that their sins are not worthy of punishment; who place riches, offices, and power as their greatest delight; forgetting their villainies and throwing themselves into other and even more wicked acts—fornication, wantonness, and excess—so that what came before might be as if erased.

Suidas and Hesychius <note>Ancient Greek lexicographers.</note> explain the word "seared" <note>Greek: κεκαυτεριαμένοι / kekautēriasmenoi</note> as "those having their own conscience" <note>Greek: τὴν συνείδησιν ἔχοντες ἰδίαν / tēn syneidēsin echontes idian</note>, meaning those who do not have a healthy, wakeful, living, or active mind. Grotius interprets it as having the conscience defiled with the marks of villainies. Chrysostom translates it as "being of an evil life" <note>Greek: πονηρῷ ὄντες βίῳ / ponērō ontes biō</note>.

<margin>The author's conclusion.</margin>
I would then conclude from all this that the people of whom the Apostle speaks are those who say, teach, command, or do something which they cannot say, teach, command, or do with a good conscience; those who have no living, wakeful, and active conscience, but a corrupted mind. Because of their constant working against their conscience—through foul practices, devised tricks, sophistry, and other ruses—they

<column-break/>

have come so far that they have muffled their conscience. With such fair-seeming fallacies, excuses, cloaking, and distinctions, they have polished, advocated for, and covered their false teachings so that, in the end, they know no better than that they speak and teach the truth. They do it with such great earnestness; they speak with such fearlessness, without any suspicion, and with such boldness, as if they had truth and piety on their side, and as if everything they spoke, promoted, and defended was crystal-clear truth and pure godliness, while they hold lies in their right hand and make themselves hideous, tarnishing themselves with the foulest and most reprehensible lifestyle and morals.

<margin>Burning of corpses.</margin>
Regarding the burning performed over someone, which I mentioned above and which one reads about in 2 Chronicles 16:14 and 21:19, and Jeremiah 34:5: since I do not perceive it to be used as a figure of speech, I shall not give an account of it here. However, I must say it is well-evident that among the Romans it was customary to burn dead bodies, especially those of kings. For this purpose, fuel was gathered and piled up into a pyre upon which the dead corpse was laid, along with the state bed and many costly items. This pyre was then ignited with a burning torch by the closest friends, who kept their faces turned away, and finally, the bones were collected and buried. See Kipping’s *Roman Antiquities*, page 780, etc.; Jos. Cantel, *On Funerals*; Doughty in *Analects of the Old Testament*, page 196, etc.; Daniel Klaassen, page 150, etc.; Geier, *On Mourning*, page 107, etc.; Kirchmann, *On Funerals*, etc. But that such was the custom of the Jews, even regarding their kings, I—along with many others—do not believe. That it may have happened in an extraordinary case could be true, and it would have had its reasons: either because the body was already nearly decayed, or to prevent it from falling into the hands of enemies, or for some other purpose. But that it was a fixed custom of the Jews runs contrary to their usual practice of burial.

<margin>Not customary among the Jews.</margin>
However, that they did ignite and burn the bed, the usual household furniture, and the belongings of the king, along with many spices, is something I am not at all averse to. Read the aforementioned authors.

Having noted this beforehand and in passing, I shall begin something that will require more detailed elaboration, application, and transfer. Namely, I shall give an account of the

-> **Burnt offerings, with their circumstances, and the transmission of the burning, placed upon the altar of burnt offering, ignited by the holy fire, and consumed to ashes.** <-

As I treat this subject, I wish first to briefly review what pertains to the burnt offering and its principal ceremonies, before I step over to the symbolic meaning.

A "burnt offering" <note>Hebrew: עלה / Olah</note>, from a root meaning "to ascend" <note>Hebrew: עלה / alah</note>, was an offering that was entirely ignited by the fire on the altar; being consumed by the ascending flame, it flew upward as smoke and vapor.

Abrabanel <note>Isaac Abrabanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note> holds that this physical ascent was accompanied by the ascent of the mind to God the Creator, whether to give Him praise and thanks for His boun-

# 202 BURNT OFFERING.

benefits: whether it be to pray for a blessing from Him through humble prayers.

<margin>
Burnt offering for the atonement of sins.
</margin>
It was held that the burnt offering was brought and kindled for the atonement of sins—both internal and external—committed against the mandatory and prohibitive commandments of God.

<margin>
The best animals designated for the burnt offering.
</margin>
As for the sacrificial animals intended for the burnt offering, they were not the least of the beasts of the earth or the birds of the heaven: cows, calves, bulls, goats, rams, sheep, lambs, doves, and turtledoves. These were easily obtained in the land of Canaan as common and daily sustenance. As Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> says elsewhere, by offering these, they gave back to God what they had received from Him (2 Chronicles 29). But also, by setting aside their necessary daily food, they seemed to offer themselves up to the Lord.

The Egyptians spared many of these cattle, holding them sacred; it would almost seem as if the Lord wished to establish a divide between His people and the Egyptians.

Regarding the animal for the burnt offering: it had to be the best and noblest for the Lord, not too old, dry, or tough; a tame and useful animal, healthy, sleek, and without blemish. *Outramus* in *On Sacrifices*, Book I, Chapter 9 <note>William Outram (1626–1679), an English theologian known for his work on the Jewish sacrificial system.</note>, maintains it should not be more than two years old.

<margin>
Decline of the burnt offering.
</margin>
That a decline and corruption was observed among the Jews regarding this practice, alongside the fall of the city, temple, and morals, we learn from the Word of Life, *Matthew 1:7, 8* <note>Likely a reference to the criticisms of religious hypocrisy in the Gospels.</note>.

This ran directly contrary to the requirement and the law of God (Leviticus 9:3 and 19:20; Deuteronomy 15 and 17, etc.).

The Pagans were even more pious in this regard: they chose the noblest and the best.

Virgil, in the fourth book of the *Georgics* <note>original Latin: "Quatuor eximios præstanti corpore tauros / Ducit, & intacta totidem cervice juvencas."</note>:

> He leads four choice bulls of excellent body,
> and as many heifers with necks untouched by the yoke.

->This follows Vondel’s translation:<-

> He brings four bulls, the pick of the herd for sacrifice,
> To the altar, and a flock of two pairs of young cows,
> Not yet burdened by any yoke. --------

The same author in the fourth book of the *Aeneid* <note>original Latin: "Superoque nitentem / Cœlicolum regi mactabam in littore taurum." Note: This passage is actually from Book III.</note>:

> ------ I slaughtered on the shore a shining bull
> to the high king of the heavenly dwellers.

->This follows the same translation:<-

> I offer on the beach, and slaughter a white bull
> In honor of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note>.

The offerer had to bring his sacrificial animal to the door of the Tabernacle. There it was received by the priest and tied up (Leviticus 2:3). See also regarding the binding of the sacrificial animal with ropes to the horns of the altar in Psalm 118:27 <note>The text cites Psalm 119:27, but the reference to "binding the sacrifice with cords to the horns of the altar" is Psalm 118:27.</note>, or nearby, as if in attendance in the great courtyard. This was done perhaps to have it at hand so it would not run away, or so that one might see whether it was tame and gentle, or wild and fierce.

<column-break/>

Virgil, in the ninth book of the *Aeneid* <note>original Latin: "Et statuam ante aras aurata fronte juvencum."</note>:

> And I shall place before the altars a bullock with a gilded brow.

->That is:<-

> And I shall offer to you as a prize
> A young and snow-white calf with a gilded star.

And in the second book of the *Georgics* <note>original Latin: "Et ductus cornu stabit sacer hircus ad aram."</note>:

> And the sacred goat, led by the horn, shall stand at the altar.

->That is:<-

> Then we shall bring the goat, dedicated to his divinity,
> To the altar at the proper time of sacrifice.

After this, the offerer had to place his hands between the two horns upon the head of the sacrificial animal (Leviticus 1:4, 16:21, 3:2, and 4:4). Philo says this was as a testimony of the offerer’s innocence. And *Hesychius Presbyter* <note>A 5th-century theologian from Jerusalem.</note> says it was to testify that his offering was voluntary.

*Hugo Cardinalis* <note>Hugh of Saint-Cher (c. 1200–1263), a Dominican cardinal.</note>, and in part *Rabanus Maurus*, understood this to mean that the offerer was relinquishing the right he had over that animal—that he took it from his own ownership and designated it for the service of God. However, *Paulus in Festum*, *Ribera*, *Drusius*, etc., suggest that as he loathed his sins and prayed to avert the wrath of God, he laid those sins upon the head of his sacrificial animal, which took his place.

*Fagius* <note>Paul Fagius (1504–1549), a Renaissance Hebraist.</note> has taught us that this laying on of hands occurred with a confession of sins, alongside a prayer for forgiveness, in this manner:

> "O dear Lord, I pray thee, I have sinned, I have acted perversely, and have been rebellious before Thy face; thus and so have I done. Behold, I have remorse, I am ashamed of my actions, I shall not return to them." See *Franzius, School of Sacrifices*, Discourse 3; *Dilberr, Demonstrations*, page 248; and *Maimonides*: "I have sinned, done wrong, and rebelled, and have in this way strayed from Thy law; but I repent, and this offering is an atonement for me and my soul."

<margin>
Slaughtering of the sacrificial animal.
</margin>
After this, they set upon the sacrificial animal and cut its throat or slaughtered it (Leviticus 1:5). Whether the Levites and Priests alone were to do this, or whether the offerers were permitted to help to that extent, is a matter of debate; indeed, many believe it was permitted.

Concerning the slaughtering-knife and the rings through which the ropes were passed to secure the animal, etc., I leave it to others to write more closely.

See *Braunius* on the Epistle to the Hebrews, and *Biermans, Moses and Christ*. And among many others, *Buxtorff* on the word <term>shachat <gloss>to slaughter</gloss></term> (שחט), and *Johannes Baptista Villalpando*, Book III, Chapter 37, *On the Temple*.

The cutting of the throat or windpipe was done with a large and sharp throat-cutting knife, through and through, with two strokes, away from oneself and toward oneself, called by the Jews <term>halachah u-teva’ah <gloss>going and coming</gloss></term> (הלכה ותבאה).

The Pagans first struck the sacrificial animal on the head with an axe, much like our butchers do, and thereafter they cut the throat open, quite differently from the Jews. See *Homer, Odyssey Book 3*; *Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities Book 7*; *Sacrifices* by *Stukkius*; and *Dilberr, Demonstrations*, page 252.

<margin>Receiving the blood in basins.</margin>

->That is:<-

*And bowls with hallowed sacrificial blood.*

In the 1st Pastoral <note>Likely referring to Virgil's Eclogues, often called "Harderszangen" or Shepherd's Songs in Dutch.</note>:

> A tender lamb from our folds shall often stain his altar. <note>original Latin: "Illius aram / Sæpe tener nostris ab ovilibus imbuet agnus."</note>

->That is:<-

*I shall often bring him a lamb as an offering*
*From our fold, and with that blood sprinkle his table.*

Afterward, the beast was stripped of its wool and flayed, of which the Priests, and sometimes in part the Levites, received the hide; but here this did not apply: it was also burned, *Leviticus 6 and 7:8, 2 Chronicles 29, as well as Leviticus 4:11, 12, Numbers 19*, as they say, for purification and the detestation of the sin. The burnt offering was entirely for the Lord, as it was for sin. Whoever wishes to read more on this, see Burman, page 515, etc.; otherwise, the Priests kept the hide, *Leviticus 6:8*.

The Heathens also received the sacrificial animals. Homer, *Iliad 10*:

> They first pulled the animal's head back, then slaughtered and flayed it. <note>original Greek: "Ἀνέρυσάν μὲν πρῶτα καὶ ἔσφαξαν καὶ ἔδειραν"</note>

->That is:<-

*They hauled the animal on high. Then they slaughtered it, and pulled*
*The hide from it.*

Virgil:

> They strip the hides from the ribs and lay bare the entrails. <note>original Latin: "Tergora diripiunt costis, & viscera nudant."</note>

->That is:<-

*They strip the skin from the flesh and uncover the intestines.*

The [Jewish] Priests did not keep these hides and fleeces for themselves to sleep in or upon, in order to fall into dreams, to receive visions and revelations for prophecy, or for the discovery of the future or the hidden, as was claimed among the Heathen priests, as appears from Virgil's 7th book of the *Aeneid*:

> Hither the priest brought gifts, and when he lay down under the silent night upon the spread hides of slaughtered sheep and sought sleep, he saw many phantoms flying about in wondrous ways. <note>original Latin: "Huc dona sacerdos / Cum tulit, & cæsarum ovium sub nocte silenti / Pellibus incubuit stratis somnosque petivit, / Multa modis simulacra videt volitantia miris."</note>

And from Vondel's <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679), the preeminent Dutch poet and playwright, who translated Virgil into Dutch.</note> translation:

> When the priest brings his gifts
> And sacrificial offerings, and at night, through heaven’s impulses,

<margin>The Opening of the sacrificial animal.</margin>
Subsequently, the sacrificial animal was opened, the heart and the entrails taken out, and together with the feet or shanks, washed with water, etc., of which we shall speak as briefly as possible.

Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a foundational Sephardic Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note> in *Maase Korban* <note>The Procedure of the Offerings.</note>: *And they wash it with water, because it is said, he shall wash the entrails and the feet with water; namely, with water, and not with wine or mixed with any other liquid; but any kind of water is good for it. Yet, what do they wash? They wash the stomach until it is sufficient, but the intestines up to three times. They wash these upon the marble stone tables that stand between the pillars. However, because the intestines spread a foul odor, they are washed the first time secretly in the washing-chamber.*

After this, they placed it upon the stone tables to stiffen due to the cold, to prevent inflammation and rot, for which the sprinkling with salt was also very useful.

The Heathens also removed the entrails and laid them in dishes. Virgil in the 2nd book of the *Georgics*:

> On broad dishes we offer the steaming entrails. <note>original Latin: "Lancibus & pandis fumantia reddimus exta."</note>

->That is:<-

*Where we prepare the steaming entrails*
*For the gods in flat dishes.*

> And I shall cast the entrails into the salty waves. <note>original Latin: "Extaque salsos / Porriciam in fluctus."</note>

->That is:<-

*I shall plunge the entrails*
*Into the salt and foaming deep.*

One may consult Kipping's *Roman Antiquities*, page 227 <note>Heinrich Kipping (1623–1678), a German historian of Roman antiquities.</note>, regarding this.

# 202 BURNT OFFERING.

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>
Burnt offering for the atonement of sins.
</margin>
...benefits: whether by humble prayers to ask for a blessing from Him.
    It was believed that the burnt offering was brought and ignited for the atonement of sins—both internal and external—committed against the mandatory and prohibitive commandments of God. <note>The author refers to the "positive" (to do) and "negative" (to avoid) commandments in Jewish law.</note>
    As for the sacrificial animals intended for the burnt offering,
<margin>
The best animals designated for the burnt offering.
</margin>
they were not the least of the beasts of the earth or the birds of the heaven: cows, calves, bulls, goats, bucks, sheep, lambs, doves, and turtledoves. These were very easy to obtain in the land of Canaan as common and daily sustenance. As *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher.</note> says elsewhere, by offering these, they gave back to God what they had received from Him (*2 Chronicles 29*). Furthermore, by setting aside a portion of their necessary food, they seemed to offer themselves up to the Lord.
    The Egyptians spared many of these cattle, holding them sacred; thus it would seem as if the Lord wished to establish a dividing line between His people and the Egyptians.
    Regarding the animal for the burnt offering, it had to be of the best and noblest for the Lord—not too old, dry, or tough—but a tame and useful animal, healthy, sleek, and flawless. <margin>Outramus, *On Sacrifices*, Book 1, Chapter 9.</margin> <note>William Outram (1626–1679), an English theologian known for his work on the sacrificial systems of the Jews and Gentiles.</note> This author insists it should not be more than two years old.
<margin>
Decline of the burnt offering.
</margin>
    That a decline and corruption in this practice was observed among the Jews—alongside the decline of the city, the temple, and their morals—is taught to us by the Word of Life in *Malachi 1:7, 8.*
    This ran directly contrary to the requirement and law of God (*Leviticus 9:3; 19; 20; Deuteronomy 15 and 17, etc.*).
    Even the heathens were more pious in this regard: they chose the noblest and the best.
    *Virgil in the 4th book of the Georgics:* <note>A poem by Virgil concerning agriculture and rural life.</note>

> He leads four choice bulls of excellent body, and as many heifers with necks untouched by the yoke. <note>original Latin: "Quatuor eximios præstanti corpore tauros / Ducit, & intacta totidem cervice juvencas."</note>

->That is, according to Vondel’s translation:<- <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) was a preeminent Dutch poet and playwright.</note>

> *He brings four bulls, the choice selection laid out for sacrifice,*
> *To the altar, and a herd of two pairs of young cows,*
> *Not yet burdened by a yoke.* --------

    *The same author in the 4th book of the Aeneid:*

> ...And I was slaughtering a shining bull on the shore to the high king of the inhabitants of heaven. <note>original Latin: "------ Superoque nitentem / Cælicolum regi mactabam in littore taurum."</note>

->This reads according to the translation of the same:<-

> *I offer on the beach, and slaughter a white bull*
> *In honor of Jupiter.* <note>The original Dutch uses "Jupyn," a poetic variation of Jupiter.</note>

    The offerer had to bring his sacrificial animal to the door of the Tabernacle. There it was received by the Priest and tied fast (*Leviticus 2:3*). Regarding the binding of the animal with ropes to the horns of the altar, see *Psalm 119:27* <note>Commonly numbered as Psalm 118:27 in English Bibles.</note>, or binding it nearby in the great courtyard. This was done perhaps to have it at hand, so that it might not run away, or so that one could see whether it was tame and gentle, or wild and fierce.

<column-break/>

*Virgil in the 9th book of the Aeneid:*

> And I shall set a bullock with a gilded brow before the altars. <note>original Latin: "Et statuam ante aras aurata fronte juvencum."</note>

->That is:<-

> *And I shall offer to you as a prize*
> *A young and snow-white calf with a gilded star.* <note>The "star" refers to the gilding on the animal's forehead, a common practice in Roman sacrifice.</note>

And in the 2nd book of the *Georgics*:

> And the sacred goat, led by the horn, shall stand at the altar. <note>original Latin: "Et ductus cornu stabit sacer hircus ad aram."</note>

->That is:<-

> *Then we shall bring the goat, consecrated to his deity,*
> *To the altar at the proper sacrificial time.*

    After this, the offerer had to place his hands between the two horns upon the head of the sacrificial animal (*Leviticus 1:4; 16:21; 3:2; and 4:4*). *Philo* says this was a testimony of the offerer’s innocence. And *Isychius Presbyter* says it was to testify that his offering was voluntary.
    *Hugo Cardinalis*, and in part *Rabufensis*, understood this to mean that the offerer was relinquishing the right he had over that animal—that he took it from his own mastery and designated it for the service of God. However, *Paulus in Festum*, *Ribera*, *Drusius*, etc., argue that as he loathed his sins and prayed to avert God’s wrath, he laid them upon the head of his sacrificial animal, which took his place.
    *Fagius* <note>Paul Fagius (1504–1549), a German Renaissance scholar of Hebrew.</note> has taught us that this laying on of hands occurred with a confession of sins, alongside a prayer for forgiveness, in this manner:

> Oh dear Lord, I pray Thee, I have sinned, I have acted perversely, and have been rebellious before Thy face: thus and thus have I done. Behold, I have remorse, I am ashamed of my actions, and I shall not return to them. *See Franz, School of Sacrifice, Disp. 3; Dilberr, Demonstration, page 248; and Maimonides:* I have sinned, done injustice, and rebelled, and have in this manner strayed from Thy law; but I have remorse, and this offering is for me, and for my soul, an atonement.

<margin>
Slaughtering of the sacrificial animal.
</margin>
    After this, the animal was dealt with, and its throat was slit or it was slaughtered (*Leviticus 1:5*). Whether the Levites and Priests alone were required to do this, or whether the offerers were allowed to help to that extent, is a matter for consideration; indeed, many believe it was permitted.
    Regarding the slaughtering knife and the rings through which the ropes were pulled to secure the animal, etc., I let others write more specifically.
    See *Braunius* on the Epistle to the Hebrews, and *Biermans, Moses and Christ*. And among many others, *Buxtorf* on the word <term>שחיטה</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Shechitah," referring to the ritual slaughter of animals.</note> *shechitah*, and *Johannes Baptista Villalpando, Book 3, Chapter 37, on the Temple.*
    The cutting of the throat or windpipe was done with a large, sharp knife, through and through, with two strokes—away from oneself and toward oneself—called by the Jews <term>הולכה והבאה</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Holachah ve-Hava'ah," meaning "leading and bringing," describing the back-and-forth motion of the knife.</note> "going out and coming back."
    The heathens first struck the sacrificial animal on the head with an axe, like our butchers, and thereafter slit the throat—quite differently from the Jews. See *Homer, Odyssey Book 20; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities Book 7; Stuckius; and Dilberr, Demonstration, page 252.*

# 204 BURNT OFFERING.

<columns>

<margin>Division of the offering pieces.</margin> In the offerings for sins as a burnt offering, God received the whole; in others, the Priest and often the offerer had their portion. The entrails, the fat, and the divided pieces were arranged on the altar for burning, and so forth. We will discuss other offerings in due time, as well as the fat and the salt used in the sacrifices. Here we only sketch this in the background and in passing. *Leviticus* 1 and 3.

Regarding how many Priests were required to cut the burnt offering into pieces and parts, and then carry those parts to the altar of burnt offering, it does not seem necessary to insert that here. However, if one wishes to read modern authors on this, see Goeree <note>Willem Goeree (1635–1711), a Dutch bookseller and author on Jewish antiquities.</note>, in the third volume of the *Republic of the Hebrews*, page 366; Bierman, *Moses and Christ*, etc.

<margin>Woodpiles.</margin> There were also woodpiles on the altar, but there is no full agreement on how many, as appears from the *Mishna in Yoma* <note>A section of the Talmud dealing with the Day of Atonement rituals.</note> *Chapter 4.* Regarding the Day of Atonement, one reads: *on all other days there were four woodpiles of fire, and today five.* Rabbi Jose and Rabbi Meir say: *on all other days three and today four.* Rabbi Juda says: *on all other days two, and today one.* Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and scholar, also known as Rambam.</note> writes: *they make a triple woodpile every day on the altar: first, the large woodpile, on which they place the daily offering and other sacrifices; second, a small woodpile next to the large one, from which they take fire with an ash-shovel for the incense; the third pile was only to keep the fire burning, for it is written: The fire shall burn continually.*

It is clear enough that the Pagans also used to burn their offerings. *Dionysius* <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian.</note> *Book VII:* <note>original: "ὁι δὲ ἐπὶ βωμὸς ἐπιτιθέντες ὥπτων"</note> *they, having placed their offerings upon the altar, set them on fire.* *Virgil* in the 12th Book of the *Aeneid*:

> <note>original: "Admovitque pecus flagrantibus aris."</note>
> *He brought the cattle to the flaming altars.*

-> That is: <-

> *He brought the livestock to the altar that burned steadily.*

*Tibullus:*

> <note>original: "Cernite fulgentes ut eat facer agnus ad aras."</note>
> *Behold how the sacred lamb goes to the gleaming altars.*

-> That is: <-

> *See how the lamb joins itself to the burning altar.*

*Virgil* in the 6th Book of the *Aeneid*:

> <note>original: "Et solida imponit taurorum viscera flammis."</note>
> *And he places the solid entrails of bulls in the flames.*

-> That is: <-

> *He lays the entrails of the bulls into the flame.*

One has already heard from Maimonides by which woodpile the fire on the altar was maintained, for the Divine command lay there, *Leviticus* 6; though I read of only one fire.

After God had once given the heavenly fire, it had to be maintained by the Priests through the fuel of the fire, without neglecting to lay the wood on the altar in time, so that by maintaining the fire, they could also light the incense. For what happened to Nadab and Abihu <note>Sons of Aaron who were struck down for offering "strange fire" before the Lord.</note> for appearing with strange fire is learned

<column-break/>

from the holy history in *Leviticus* 10 and 16, etc. One may freely assume that there were woodcutters and carriers for this purpose; there would also have been woodsheds; and perhaps also some of the unclean Priests who, in their state of uncleanness, inspected the firewood and sorted out the decayed and worm-eaten pieces.

<margin>Eternal fire among the Pagans.</margin> One also reads among the Pagans and Romans of an eternal fire, and of the Vestal Virgins <note>Priestesses of Vesta in ancient Rome who tended the sacred fire.</note>, appointed to watch, preserve, and maintain that fire. If it went out, it was considered an omen of great approaching disasters; and if it was well maintained, a sign of blessing and prosperity, of which more will be said at a better opportunity. Meanwhile, one can look into this in Dilherr, *Demonstrations* page 266; Doughty in *V.T.* page 79; Goodwyn’s *Roman Antiquities*, page 90; Goeree’s *Republic of the Jews* page 2, page 406, etc.; Daniel Klaafsen page 4; Kipping, *Roman Antiquities*, and others. I will refrain from this now and will draft my thoughts on what has already been presented by way of figures, foreshadowing, and applications; yet in such a way that, looking to the Messiah, I shall also consider His mystical body, the congregation, and every living member, and having placed each in their rank, I will mix my applications therein.

<margin>Applications and symbols.</margin> **a.** It was noted that the burnt offerings had to be taken from cows, calves, bullocks, bucks, goats, sheep, lambs, doves, and turtledoves; all young, and in their greatest vigor and strength; pure, and perfect, all of which had to be entirely for the Lord.

The strength, industriousness, gentleness, purity, and innocence to be noted distinctly in these animals were symbols of Jesus, in the bloom of His life's strength, offered to God for the atonement of sins through the eternal Spirit—blameless to God, as a sweet-smelling savor. He who was industrious and busy with soul-delight in observing the will of God, *Psalm 40; John 4:34*, having a pure glow of love for God's honor and the perfection of His people; gentle and patient, upright in all His adversities, pure and without the least sin or contamination, *Hebrews 7; 1 Peter 1:19; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Matthew 11:29; Isaiah 53:7; Hebrews 12:3; 1 Peter 2:22, 23.*

Just as the believers are also made perfect in Him, *Colossians 2*, and are purified in and through His blood and Spirit, *1 Corinthians 6:11*, which they earnestly pursue, *Philippians 3; Hebrews 12; 2 Corinthians 7:1, 2; 1 Thessalonians 4.* They love and serve God with a perfect heart, *Matthew 22*, and offer themselves entirely to God as Priests of the New Testament, *1 Peter 2; Isaiah 66*, and dedicate themselves to service in soul and body, with delight and joy, *Psalm 110:3; Romans 12:1 and 14:7, 8; 1 Corinthians 6:20*, just as they are therefore frequently compared to that livestock. *Isaiah 53:6; Psalm 119:177; Hosea 7; Matthew 10:16; 1 Peter 2:25; John 10:4, 5, etc.*

**b.** When one sees that the sacrificial animal was brought to the door of the tent; that hands were laid upon the head of the sacrificial animal with confession of sins and prayer for atonement, etc., *Leviticus 16:21*, let one remember what was said.

# BURNT OFFERING.

Certainly Christ appears to us as the one upon whom our sins converged, upon whom they were laid, and who has borne them. *Isaiah 53:3, 4, 5-7. John 1:29. 2 Corinthians 5:21. 1 Peter 2:24.* For the sake of the Messiah, one had to pray for forgiveness, *Daniel 9:17,* and without this sacrifice and participation in it, as a door, one cannot approach God, or expect grace, salvation, and life with faithful boldness, *John 10:9. Romans 5:2. Ephesians 3. Hebrews 10:19.* etc. nor approach the sanctuary of the Lord, his tabernacle and temple in the spirit—the church—or belong to it.

c. When one considers how the burnt-offering animal was treated, namely killed, it could arise in the heart of the faithful Israelite that the Messiah—the counter-image <note>Original Dutch: "tegenbeelt," a theological term (antitype) meaning the reality that fulfills a symbolic shadow or "type."</note> and substance of these symbols—would be slaughtered and killed. To satisfy Divine justice, he would offer himself through the eternal Spirit to God for the sins of his people as an atonement. *Daniel 9:24. Isaiah 53:4, 5. Zechariah 3. etc. and 9.* It could portray how the sacrifice, coming in the place of the offerer for atonement and de-sinning <note>Original: "ontzondiginge," the process of being cleared from sin.</note>, allowed the believers in Christ to be regarded as crucified and killed, for the removal of guilt and punishment, and for their purification. *Romans 6 and 8. Colossians 3:5. Galatians 5:24.*

How the believers had to be prepared with him for suffering, even unto death, and be faithful unto death, not loving their own lives. *Matthew 10:38, 39. and 16:25. Revelation 2:10. Romans 8. Psalm 44. 2 Corinthians 4:10, 11.*

<margin>Meaning of the sprinkling.</margin>
d. The sprinkling with that blood for de-sinning, purity, and holiness—as I have stated regarding the word SPRINKLE—signified the power and worthiness of Jesus' blood, and the necessity of its sprinkling upon the sinner by the Holy Spirit and faith, for the true removal of sin and the cleansing of the sinner's conscience. *1 Corinthians 1:30. and 6:11. Hebrews 9:13, 14. 1 John 1:7. Revelation 1:5. Hebrews 12:24. 1 Peter 1:2.*

<margin>The stripping of the sacrificial animal.</margin>
e. That the sacrificial animal was undressed and stripped of its outer skin and hide, and was thus naked so that its bones could be seen and counted—especially as it was stretched and spread out—can bring to our minds how Christ, being robbed of his clothes, hung naked and exposed on the cross, *Psalm 22 and Matthew 27.* How he was stretched out on the cross and battered in such a way that one could count his bones, *Psalm 22,* so that he was exposed and opened before God and men, *Hebrews 4.* One could perceive his love and sincerity most closely and clearly in this, his obedience of suffering unto death, and see the blows, welts, and stabs received out of love with great patience for his own, for our healing. *Isaiah 53. 1 Peter 2:24.*

It also happens not infrequently that God’s rational sacrificial animals <note>The author is referring to the believers themselves.</note>, robbed of everything, are taken and drawn out naked, as a spectacle and mockery for Angels and men, *Micah 3.*

<column-break/>

*3. 1 Corinthians 4:11-13. 2 Corinthians 11:27.* through which they also more and more lay aside and pull off the skin and hide of corruption—that old man. *Ephesians 4:22, 23, 24. Romans 6:10. Colossians 3:10. 1 Peter 4. Colossians 2:11. 2 Corinthians 4:16.*

f. In the division and cutting of the members of one and the same body of the sacrificial animal—all of which were nonetheless suited for the service of the Lord and brought to the altar—one can note how Christ would be treated, and how his soul would be as if cut off from his body: how he, in and through all his parts and members, submitted himself to God and placed himself at His service. It could represent how one must serve God in various members, parts, and powers, *Matthew 22. 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Romans 6:12, 13, 14.* indeed, how it would go for the members of Christ on earth, how they would be scattered from one another, and yet brought back together and laid upon the altar of Jesus.

If the Apostle, in *2 Timothy 2:15,* with the words *rightly dividing the word of truth*, did not have his eye elsewhere, one might think—along with Beza, Hemmingius, Perkins, Dietericus, Flaccus Illyricus, Glassius, and Dilherrius <note>A list of prominent 16th and 17th-century Protestant theologians and Hebraists.</note>—that Paul borrowed this manner of speaking from the correct art of cutting and anatomy used by the Jewish priesthood. By this, they struck the sacrificial animal in its joints, knowing how to give to God, the offerer, and themselves each their due. This shows that Timothy, along with all other wise teachers, must wisely track and hit upon the sense and meaning of God's spirit, giving to each person distinctly what is theirs through instruction, admonition, rebuke, encouragement, and comfort.

g. Did one notice distinctly how some parts, external and internal, had to be washed and cleansed so that nothing unclean or tainted would come to the altar? That could bring to our minds how entirely pure and sinless the counter-image, Christ, would be—not only externally but also internally. *Psalm 40:9, 10, 11. Hebrews 7:26. and John 17:19.*

And how a sinner, by the power of the Covenant, through Jesus’ blood and the working of the Holy Spirit, would be washed and cleansed externally and internally, *Ezekiel 36:25. 1 Corinthians 6:11. 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Ephesians 5:26, 27.* so that the understanding, the will, inclinations, and intentions must be pure and before the Lord. *Matthew 22.* Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher.</note>, in his book *On Pure Animals* <note>Latin: "Libro de Animalib. puris"</note>, says: *It is a mystery that we are commanded to wash the entrails and the feet. For by the washing of the entrails, it is signified that desires must be washed away, and the stains which come from drunkenness, which fault is very harmful to human life. The washing of the feet signifies that one should no longer crawl upon the earth, but elevate oneself into heaven.* Paul may perhaps have looked upon this washing in *Hebrews 10:22.* Certainly, the heart, kidneys, and feet are the primary places of impurity. From the heart comes all good, or

# BURNING.

evil, *Matthew 15:8, 10, 20.* That must be purified through faith, *James 4:8, Isaiah 1:16,* and one must cleanse oneself from the wickedness and defilement of body and spirit, *2 Corinthians 7:1, 2.*

b. The heavenly fire, which always had to burn and be maintained upon the altar to ignite and consume the morning and evening sacrifices, and further the burnt offerings and incense, could not only portray Christ's eternal love—through which he glowed for his Father's honor and the salvation of the people given to him to be redeemed—but also his holy and steadfast love. Through this, alongside the fire of God, he was consumed and offered himself blamelessly to God through the eternal Spirit, *Psalm 69:10, Hebrews 9:10.* It showed his readiness in laying down his life, *Psalm 40, John 10:19 <note>The original cites Job 10:19, likely a printer's error for John 10:19, which discusses laying down one's life.</note>,* his suretyship and eternal will, *Hebrews 13:8, Revelation 13:18 <note>Original: Openb. XIII. 18.</note>, Job 33, Hebrews 10:10,* but also the eternity of his intercession based on his perfect sacrifice, which is of eternal power and infinite value, *Hebrews 10:14, Daniel 9, Zechariah 3.* Just as the sacrifice was burned in the morning and evening, so was Christ nailed to the cross in the morning and died in the evening, abolishing the shadowy symbols in and through himself, *Mark 15:25-34.*

And since the fire had to be kept burning to continually ignite the burnt offering and incense, it appeared from the purpose of maintaining the fire and the repetition of the sacrifices that everything was powerless in itself. Since the Lord could take no pleasure or satisfaction in these, *Psalm 40, Hebrews 10,* a sacrifice was surely desired and portrayed in which the Lord would rest and be reconciled with his people.

At the time of the morning sacrifice, the fire of the Spirit fell upon the Apostles, *Acts 2.* The fire of the Holy Spirit, with which Christ would baptize his own, is the love of God poured out into the heart and the holy zeal to serve God in Spirit and truth, *Romans 12:1, John 4:24.* The spiritual Priests of the New Testament must themselves be fervent, but also fan the flames: no one should extinguish the spirit, but nurture the holy fire and strive to offer themselves and others to God as a sacrifice, *Romans 15:16, 1 Thessalonians 5:19, Hebrews 10:24.* Indeed, no fire other than from Jesus's altar—that is, his Spirit which is from above—can ignite our souls and bodies to be a living, reasonable, and holy sacrifice to God, *Romans 12:1.*

<margin>
Salt with the offering.
</margin>

i. Finally, not to bring up everything, salt was found with this offering; and to prevent decay and rot, the sacrificial animal and its entrails were sprinkled with it.

Saving many observations and edifying applications until I come to the word SALT <note>The author intends to provide a full entry for "Salt" later in this alphabetical work.</note>, I shall only briefly note what I cannot entirely pass over on this occasion.

Certainly, Maimonides <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> erred when he

<column-break/>

wrote that the Heathens had no salt in their offerings. For the contrary is evident from their writings; as Ovid sings in the first book of the *Fasti*:

> Formerly, that which could reconcile the Gods to man,
> Was meal, and a shining grain of pure salt.
> <note>original: "Ante, Deos homini quod conciliare valeret, / Far erat, & puri lucida mica salis."</note>

->This is according to the translation of Hoogvliet:<-

> It was once enough, to appease the heavenly gods,
> When a little flour mixed with pure salt,
> Instead of costly incense, was poured on the altar of atonement.

Thus the Greeks speak of *olychytai* <note>original: ὀλύχυται — barley groats mixed with salt.</note>; and the Latins of a *mola salsa* <note>term: mola salsa — a mixture of toasted grain and salt used in Roman sacrifices.</note>; which Suidas calls barley meal mixed with salt, which was thrown upon the sacrifices. Eustathius says: barley meal with salt, which was added to the offerings. And Festus says: *MOLA* is roasted corn sprinkled with salt, with which, once ground, the sacrifices were strewn. Following this, I provide what Flaccus <note>The poet Horace.</note> has in *Book III, Ode 23.*

> If an innocent hand has touched the altar,
> Not more persuasive with a costly victim,
> It will appease the offended household gods,
> With pious incense and a crackling grain of salt.
> <note>original: "Immunis aram si tetigit manus / Non sumptuosa blandior hostia, / Mollibit aversos penates, / Thure pio, & saliente mica."</note>

->That is:<-

> If you touch the altar with pure hands,
> No costlier offerings
> Deserve the favor of the Gods more,
> Than salt with flour offered to them.

Thus Pliny relates concerning Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing religious rites.</note>, *Book XXX, Chapter 5.*

*Numa Pompilius* ordained that the Gods should be served solemnly with ground corn sprinkled with salt, and to supplicate them thus. This dough-cake had to be composed of corn, salt, and water; without which *MOLA* they judged no sacrifice to be complete.

Various reasons are given why salt had to be added to the offerings. The first is:

*Because the offering had to be preserved from corruption, for which salt is very capable.*

The second is:

<margin>
Reasons why the offerings were salted.
</margin>

*Since no feast was held without salt, it was fitting that no meal be prepared for God without salt.*

The third is:

*Since the sacrifices are signs and seals of the Covenant, it was customary to use salt in making covenants; and salt being a symbol of durability, friendship, and prudence, it is with good reason added to the sacrifice.*

Let me merely serve the reader with the thoughts of various famous men. Philo, concerning the sacrifices, writes thus: "Through salt [there is] a symbol of the permanence of all things; for what it is sprinkled upon, it preserves." <note>original: δι' ἅλες διαμονῆς τῶν τῶν συμπάντων σύμβολον. οἷς καὶ ἂν περιπασθῶσι, διατηρῶσι.</note> Cyril, in his first Easter sermon, expresses his judgment in this way: God commands the sacrifices to be sprinkled with salt; this is a symbol of prudence and of a good understanding. <margin>The reason for the salt and the sacrifices.</margin>
Finally, also Poole <note>Matthew Poole (1624–1679), author of the *Synopsis Criticorum*.</note> in his Annotations says thus: *Christ is the only sacrifice, who is the true heavenly salt, through whom both men and their works are presented to God as a food, savory and pleasant, who through sin were distasteful and unsalted; through whom also the believers, though deceased, are preserved from destruction and shall rise again.*

See, reader, here is a great and heaped dish full; here you may satisfy your desire. However, so that you, having an abundance of material, might not choose the wrong thing, I shall help you rightly and say what I think to be the reason why salt had to be added to the sacrifices.

Since the sacrifices formerly looked toward Christ—which, being brought to God in faith according to the requirement of the covenant, were means of strengthening, comfort, and sealing—I can well imagine that the salt was added to the sacrifice to be savory and well-pleasing to God, since it was His food, just as the altar was His table. And since salt is useful for steadfast duration, of which it was also a symbol, it may also have depicted the ever-enduring power and the incorruptibility of the Messiah's sacrifice. For this did not need to be repeated, as He once offered Himself blamelessly to God through the eternal Spirit, and now dies no more but lives in eternity to pray for us upon His sacrifice; whereby He has so ratified the covenant of grace and the New Testament <note>original: "N. T." (Nieuwe Testament)</note> that no repetition through any blood of sacrificial animals is necessary anymore: in consequence of which sacrifice and confirmed covenant (or the New Testament), He, through His indwelling Spirit, cleanses His own more powerfully than with salt, and preserves them from all destruction and defilement, and shall confirm them in the covenant in such a manner that they shall in no way waver, *Jeremiah 31* and *Ezekiel 36*, so that they are brought to a state of immortality, incorruptibility, and complete undefiledness through 

<column-break/>

Him. *1 Corinthians 15* and *Ephesians 5*. Meanwhile, they also do not neglect to guard themselves against "unsalted" <note>Meaning foolish or crude speech.</note> talk, and apply themselves to walk intelligently and prudently, to carefully preserve the close friendship between God and their souls, and to strictly fulfill the requirement of the covenant.

But more on salt hereafter, when the Meat and Drink offerings are to be spoken of.

### LETTER, ספר <note>Hebrew: Sepher</note>, ἐπιστολὴ <note>Greek: Epistole</note>, epistola <note>Latin: Epistola</note>.

<margin>Scripture regarded as a letter.</margin>
The word *Sepher* <note>original: "ספר"</note> among the Jews is taken broadly and widely, not only for a book consisting of many pages which one used to roll up (from which it is called the "roll of the book," *Psalm 40*, the "flying roll," etc., being thus a large writing), but also for a letter, a written narrative, and a draft of matters made for one who is absent; as one will find in Cocceius, Schindler, Pagninus, Buxtorf, Leigh, and others.

In this broad sense, one may regard the writings of the Old and New Testaments as a letter from God, wherein He has had drafted for us—who inhabit the lower parts—through His holy servants, the origin of all things, the generations of the nations, their propagations, dwellings, falls, states, and governments, in a historical style of writing. Many of these things in the early times were transferred and made known to others through oral tradition, as it is to be thought happened before Moses under the Patriarchs; to which belonged especially the promises of grace and salvation in the "seed of the woman," the points of faith, and duties toward God and neighbor to be practiced in love, and also what would happen to Abraham and his seed in the course of time. I would think that small notes would have been kept of these; but it seemed good to the Lord to have a history of the past, a prophecy of the future, points to believe, duties to practice, and things to avoid drafted more closely in writing through Moses and the following Prophets, Evangelists, and Apostles, and thus to be and remain well-assured of the Divine favor and the hope of healing and salvation.

Thus Augustine (*Sermon 56 to the Brothers in the desert*) and Chrysostom (*Homily 2 on Genesis*), etc., have called the whole of Scripture a letter from God to us who have the earth as a dwelling.

<margin>Truth of the Scriptures.</margin>
This letter is from God, delivered to the church by the holy writers. In the style, there is clarity, loftiness, and dignity; in the subject matter there is truth, and there are all the marks of Divinity, which can present themselves to the mind of the attentive and intelligent person for full persuasion: confirmed in many ways with wonders and signs, with the death and the blood of the writers and martyrs, as also by the wonderful effects, both in the heart and in the life and morals of those to whom this letter has come.

Before or after whose parts the Prophets and Apostles mostly placed their names.

One can also regard the Holy Scripture as a letter from God to His friends on earth, in which He makes known how, and in what manner, He [is] to His...

Various reasons are given as to why salt had to be added to the sacrifices. The first is:

*Because the sacrifice had to be preserved from corruption, for which salt is very well-suited.*

The third is:

*Because the sacrifices are signs and seals of the Covenant, and it was customary to use salt in confirming a covenant; and since salt is a symbol of durability, friendship, and prudence, salt is added to the sacrifice with good reason.*

Finally, Polus <note>Matthew Poole (1624–1679), an English nonconformist theologian famous for his "Synopsis" of biblical interpretations.</note> also in his *Annotations* says: *Christ is the only offering who is the true heavenly salt, through whom both men and their works are presented to God as a food, savory and pleasant, who were otherwise unsavory and unsalted through sin: through whom also the believers, though dead, are preserved from destruction and shall rise again.*

<margin>
Reason for the salt and the offerings.
</margin>
See, reader, here is a large and piled-high dish; here you may satisfy your desire. However, so that you, having a great abundance of material, might not choose the wrong thing, I shall help you aright and state what I think to be the reason why salt had to be added to the offerings.

Since the offerings formerly looked toward Christ—which, being brought to God in faith according to the requirement of the covenant, were means of strengthening, comfort, and sealing—I can well imagine that the salt was added to the offering to be savory and well-pleasing to God, since it was His food, just as the altar was His table. And since salt is useful for steadfast duration, of which it was also a symbol, it may also have depicted the ever-enduring power and the incorruptibility of the Messiah’s sacrifice. For this did not need to be repeated, since he once offered himself blamelessly to God through the eternal Spirit, and now dies no more, but lives in eternity to pray for us based on his sacrifice; whereby he has so empowered the covenant of grace and the New Testament that no repetition through the blood of sacrificial animals is any longer necessary. In consequence of this sacrifice and confirmed covenant (or the New Testament), he cleanses his own through his indwelling spirit more powerfully than through salt, and preserves them from all destruction and defilement, and shall confirm them in the covenant in such a way that they shall by no means waver, *Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36,* so that they are to be brought to a state of immortality, incorruptibility, and perfect undefiledness through

<column-break/>

him. *1 Corinthians 15 and Ephesians 5.* Meanwhile, they also do not neglect to guard themselves against "unsavory" words, and apply themselves to walking wisely and prudently, to carefully preserve the close friendship between God and their souls, and to strictly fulfill the requirements of the covenant.

But more of salt hereafter, when the Meat and Drink offerings are to be spoken of.

# LETTER, ספר, ἐπιστολὴ, epistola.
<note>The author provides the term "Letter" in Dutch (*Brief*), Hebrew (*Sepher*), Greek (*Epistolē*), and Latin (*Epistola*).</note>

<margin>
Scripture regarded as a letter.
</margin>
The word *Sepher* <note>Hebrew for "book" or "writing."</note> among the Jews is taken quite broadly, not only for a book consisting of many pages which one used to roll up (whereof it is called the "roll of the book," *Psalm 40*, the "flying roll," etc., being thus a large writing), but also for a letter, a written narrative, and a draft of matters made for those who are absent; as one will find in Cocceius, Schindler, Pagninus, Buxtorf, Leigh, and others.

In this broad sense, one may regard the writings of the Old and New Testaments as a letter from God, wherein He has caused to be drafted for us, who inhabit the lower regions, through His holy servants: the origin of all things, the generations of peoples, their procreations, dwellings, falls, states, and rule, in a historical style of writing. Many of these things in early times were brought and made known to others through oral tradition, as it is to be thought happened before Moses among the Patriarchs; to which belonged especially the promises of grace and salvation in the "woman's seed," <note>A reference to Genesis 3:15, traditionally viewed as the first prophecy of Christ.</note> the points of faith, and duties regarding God and neighbor to be practiced in love, and also what would happen to Abraham and his seed in the course of time. I would well think that small notes of these things were kept; yet it pleased the Lord to have a history of the past and a prophecy of the future drafted more closely in writing through Moses and the subsequent Prophets, Evangelists, and Apostles, in order to believe points of faith, practice duties, and avoid things, and thus to be and remain well-assured in Divine favor and the hope of salvation.

Thus Augustine *Sermon 56 to the Brothers in the Wilderness* and Chrysostom *Homily 2 on Genesis, etc.* have called the whole of Scripture a letter from God to us, who have the earth as a dwelling.

<margin>
Truth belongs to the Scripture.
</margin>
This letter is from God, delivered to the church through the holy writers. In the style, there is clarity, sublimity, and dignity; in the matter, there is truth; and there are all the marks of Divinity, which can present themselves to the mind of the attentive and understanding person for full persuasion. It is confirmed in many ways with wonders and signs, with the death and the blood of the writers and martyrs, as well as by the wonderful effects both in the heart and in the life and morals of those to whom this letter has come.

Before or after parts of which the Prophets and Apostles have mostly placed their names.

Regarded as a letter from God to his covenant-friends.
</margin>

<margin>h.</margin> The heavenly fire, which always had to burn and be maintained upon the altar to ignite and consume the morning and evening sacrifices, as well as the burnt offerings and incense, could not only prefigure <note>The author uses "afschetzen" (to sketch out), a common term in Reformed "typology," where Old Testament rituals are seen as artistic sketches or shadows of New Testament truths.</note> Christ’s eternal love—through which he glowed for his father's honor and the salvation of the people given to him to redeem—his holy and steadfast love, through which he was consumed along with the fire of God, and offered himself blameless to God through the eternal spirit, *Psalm 69:10, Hebrews 9:10*; his readiness in laying down his life, *Psalm 40, Hebrews 10:19*; his suretyship <note>A legal term (borgtogt) meaning Christ acted as a financial or legal guarantor for humanity's debt to God.</note> and eternal will, *Hebrews 13:8, Revelation 13:18, Job 33, Hebrews 10:10*; but also the eternity of his intercession based on his perfect sacrifice, which is of eternal power and infinite value, *Hebrews 10:14, Daniel 9, Zechariah 3.* Just as the sacrifice was burned in the morning and evening, so was Christ nailed to the cross in the morning and died in the evening, nullifying the "shadow-like" rituals in and through himself, *Mark 15:25-34.*

And since the fire had to be kept burning to continually ignite the burnt offerings and incense, it appeared from the purpose of maintaining the fire and the repetition of the sacrifices that everything was powerless in itself. Since the Lord could take no pleasure or satisfaction in these things, *Psalm 40, Hebrews 10,* a sacrifice was surely desired and prefigured in which the Lord would rest and allow himself to be reconciled with his people.

At the time of the morning sacrifice, the fire of the Spirit fell upon the Apostles, *Acts 2.* The fire of the Holy Spirit, with which Christ would baptize his own, is the love of God poured out into the heart, and the holy zeal to serve God in Spirit and truth, *Romans 12:1, 1 John 4:24.* The spiritual priests of the New Testament <note>A reference to the "priesthood of all believers," a core Protestant doctrine.</note> must themselves be fervent, but also fan the flames: no one should extinguish the spirit, but rather nurture the holy fire and strive to bring themselves and others to God as an offering, *Romans 15:16, 1 Thessalonians 5:19, Hebrews 10:24.* Indeed, no fire other than that from Jesus’s altar—that is, his Spirit, which is from above—can ignite our souls and bodies to be a living, reasonable, and holy sacrifice to God, *Romans 12:1.*

<margin>
i.
Salt with the offering.
</margin>
Finally, without citing every detail, salt was found with these offerings: to prevent decay and rotting, the sacrificial animal and its entrails were sprinkled with it.

Saving many observations and edifying applications until I come to the entry for the word SALT, I shall only briefly note here what I cannot entirely pass over on this occasion.

Certainly, Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note> erred when he wrote that the Heathens used no salt in their sacrifices. For the contrary is evident from their own writings; as Ovid sings in the first book of *Fasti*:

> Formerly, that which was able to reconcile the Gods to man; <note>original Latin: "Ante, Deos homini quod conciliare valeret;"</note>
> Was meal and a shining grain of pure salt. <note>original Latin: "Far erat, & puri lucida mica salis."</note>

->This is according to the translation by Hoogvliet:<-

->Once it was enough, to appease the heavenly gods,<-
->When a little meal mixed with pure salt,<-
->Instead of costly incense, was poured upon the altar of atonement.<-

Thus the Greeks speak of <term>olochytai</term> <note>original Greek: ὀλόχυται—barley groats mixed with salt, scattered on sacrificial victims.</note>: and the Latins of a <term>mola salsa</term> <note>salted flour/meal</note>: which Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> calls barley meal mixed with salt, which was thrown upon the sacrifices. Eustathius <note>A 12th-century scholar and archbishop.</note> calls it barley meal with salt, which was added to the sacrifices. And Festus says <term>MOLA</term> is roasted corn sprinkled with salt, with which, once ground, the sacrifices were strewn. Following this, I include what Flaccus <note>The Roman poet Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus).</note> has in *Book 3, Ode 23.*

> If a hand has touched the altar while free of guilt,
> It will appease the hostile household gods
> Not more effectively with a costly victim,
> Than with pious incense and a crackling grain of salt. <note>original Latin: "Immunis aram si tetigit manus / Non sumptuosa blandior hostia, / Mollibit aversos penates, / Thure pio, & saliente mica."</note>

->That is:<-

->If you touch the altar with pure hands,<-
->No more expensive offerings<-
->Deserve the favor of the Gods more,<-
->Than salt with meal offered to them.<-

Thus Pliny relates regarding Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many religious rites.</note>, *Book 30, Chapter 5.*
*Numa Pompilius ordained that one should serve the Gods stately with ground corn sprinkled with salt, and thus pray to them. This dough-cake had to be composed of corn, salt, and water: without which salted meal (<term>MOLA</term>) they judged no sacrifice to be complete.*

Various reasons are given as to why salt had to be added to the sacrifices. The first is:
<margin>Reasons why one salted the offerings.</margin>
*Because the offering had to be preserved from corruption, for which salt is very well suited.*
The second is:
*Since no feast was held without salt, it was fitting that one should not prepare a meal for God without salt.*
The third is:
*Because the offerings are signs and seals of the Covenant, and it was customary to use salt in making covenants; and since salt is a symbol of durability, the maintenance of friendship, and prudence, salt is added to the sacrifice with good reason.*

Allow me only to provide the reader with the thoughts of various famous men. Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher.</note>, concerning the sacrifices, writes thus: "That salt is a symbol of the permanence of all things, for whatever things it covers, it preserves." <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἅλες διαμονῆς τῶν τῶν συμπάτων σύμβοлон. οἷς καὶ ἂν περιπαθῶσι, διατηρῦσι</note> Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444 CE).</note> in his first Easter sermon expresses his judgment in this manner: *God commanded the sacrifices to be sprinkled with salt: this is a symbol of prudence and of a good understanding. It is fitting that the minds of those who bring an offering to God be filled with Divine*
