### LETTER, <term>sefer <gloss>Hebrew: ספר</gloss></term>, <term>epistole <gloss>Greek: ἐπιϛολὴ</gloss></term>, <term>epistola <gloss>Latin: epistola</gloss></term>.

<margin>Scripture regarded as a letter.</margin> **T**he word *sefer* among the Jews is taken broadly and extensively, not only for a book consisting of many leaves which one used to roll—of which it is said "the roll of the book," *Psalm 40*, "the flying roll," etc., being thus a large writing; but also for a letter, a written account, and a draft of matters made for those who are absent; as one will find in Coccejus, Schindler, Pagninus, Buxtorf, Leigh, and others.

In this broad meaning, one may regard the writings of the Old and New Testaments as a letter from God, in which He has had drafted for us—who inhabit the lower parts—by His holy servants, the origin of all things, the generations of the nations, their propagation, dwellings, downfalls, states, and governance, in a historical style of writing. Many of these things in the early times were brought to others and made known through oral tradition, as it is to be thought happened before Moses among the Patriarchs. To this belonged especially the promises of grace and salvation in the "seed of the woman," the points of faith, and duties toward God and neighbor to be practiced in love, and also what would happen to Abraham and his seed in the course of time; of which I would think that small notes were kept. But it pleased the Lord to have a history of the past, a prophecy of the future, points to believe, duties to practice, and things to avoid drafted more closely in writing through Moses and the following Prophets, Evangelists, and Apostles, so as to be well-assured of Divine favor and the hope of health and salvation.

Thus Augustine in *Sermon 56 to the Brothers in the Desert* and Chrysostom in *Homily 2 on Genesis*, etc., have called the entire Scripture a letter of God to us, who have the earth for a dwelling.

This letter is from God, handed over to the church through the holy truth of the writers. In the style, there is scriptural clarity, loftiness, and dignity; in the subject matter, there is truth; and therein are all the marks of Divinity, being able to present themselves to the mind of the attentive and understanding person for full persuasion. It is in many ways confirmed by wonders and signs, by the death and the blood of the writers and martyrs, as also by the wonderful effects both in the heart and in the lives and morals of those to whom this letter has come.

At the beginning or end of which parts the Prophets and Apostles have mostly placed their names.

<margin>Regarded as a letter from God to his testament-friends.</margin> One can also regard the Holy Scripture as a letter from God to His friends on earth, in which He makes known how, and in what manner, He [is] to His testament-friends <note>The term "testamentvrienden" refers to those who are heirs or beneficiaries of God’s "testament" or covenant.</note>.

# L E T T E R.
## Cc 2

<margin>This letter must be read frequently.</margin>
...made a testament <note>In a legal and biblical sense, a "testament" is a will that disposes of property and inheritance after death; here it refers to the New Testament of Christ.</note> for their benefit, along with the conditions for how to accept those goods and inheritance, etc.

And since this letter is of such importance, one must read it diligently, attentively, and reread it, to understand how the testament of our heavenly Father is laid out; how and in what manner we, as heirs, shall come into the possession of the inheritance. *John 5:39 <note>The original text cites Job 5:39, but this is almost certainly a printer's error for John 5:39: "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life."</note>, Psalm 1, Revelation 1, 1 Thessalonians 5:27.*

Does one find a difficulty here or there? The fault lies with us; we must read and reread it: comparing what appears obscure to us with what presents itself clearly to our understanding: praying for enlightenment, *Psalm 119:18*, consulting with the wise, yet without enslaving ourselves to any human authority as an infallible interpretation with blind consent and submission. Instead, we should suspend our judgment and consent until we have clearly and distinctly understood or grasped the sense and meaning of the Lord; for the interest is too great for us to depend on fallible men.

It is the work of dishonest men to either copy this letter of God with falsification, or to enlarge it, or to diminish it. It is the work of deceivers to twist and falsify the words and expressions of God through perverse explanations, in order to deceive and mislead the simple.

<margin>Corinthians a letter from Paul.</margin>
It is not exactly to be taken too literally, but by way of a parable <note>The author uses the word "gelykenisse," meaning a metaphor or comparison.</note>, when Paul speaks so broadly of the Corinthians, *2 Corinthians 3:2, 3*, calling them zynen brief <note>original: "his letter"</note>, and thereafter Christ's letter, etc., regarding which I shall note the following.

The Apostle had, in the preceding chapter, spoken—on account of the braggarts and blowers of their own fame who sought to bring him into contempt and to make his service useless everywhere—both of the fruit and power of his ministry among the Corinthians, as well as of his pure and blameless conduct among them. *2 Corinthians 2:14.*

And for that reason, he had no need at all to provide himself with letters of recommendation, to hear and understand from them who he was, what abilities he possessed, or how he had acquitted himself in his service and office.

<margin>Conduct of the Corinthians regarding Paul.</margin>
This the Corinthians knew thoroughly, and they could all give testimony of him, as one who had lived among them as an Apostle of Jesus Christ. Indeed, that which he had wrought and brought about in the Corinthians through God's Spirit and favorable illumination—in turning them away from dumb idols and from the most vile sins and abominations, to bring them over to the truth, virtue, and the living God, *1 Corinthians 6:11*—gave sufficient understanding of how he understood the matter of God and had acquitted himself.

This revealed itself clearly enough, and had spread everywhere: and since the work praised its master, he had no need of anything else, for he could appeal to the Corinthian witnesses and to what could be observed in them.

<margin>Corinthians, a letter of Jesus Christ.</margin>
For just as one can discern from a readable, clear letter its style, manner of writing, subject matter, delivery, and signature by the light of day—identifying from whom it comes and what matters it concerns—so one could clearly and distinctly see and notice from the Corinthians' confession, love, and holy conduct that they were a letter of Jesus Christ, prepared through

<column-break/>

Paul's service. For it was known everywhere that he had laid the first foundations of Christianity there; that they were Christ's own, and that they believed in Him. What they believed of Him, and of what power Christ's doctrine, death, and resurrection were, they showed sufficiently through their confession and conduct. See what I have noted on the second letter of the Apostle Paul to the Corinthians.

<margin>Remarks of the Writer.</margin>
On this occasion of the Corinthians being called a letter of Christ and of the Apostles, *2 Corinthians 3*, I note by way of short propositions that: **a.** Paul and his fellow laborers were in the place of a pen, speaking through their mouths and blessed instruction: the Holy Spirit was the writer: the Corinthians, inscribed by the Holy Spirit, were the letter. **b.** The Corinthians' understanding, will, and memory were in the place of the paper. **c.** The writing was the doctrine of Faith and of grace, unto the salvation of the sinner, according to the prescription of God's eternal counsel and will in, with, and through His Son. **d.** If one heard the inscription from the mouth of the Corinthians concerning God's counsel and purpose in His Son, it was as much as if one read it from a letter or heard it read aloud. **e.** And since it had brought Paul, along with his fellow laborers as rational pens, this far under the Lord's cooperation and blessing, they had no need of a letter or writing of recommendation.

While I find the way paved—by the occasion and the saying of Paul and of Jeremiah *Chapter 31:33* cited by the writer to the *Hebrews, Chapter 8:10*, who speaks of the writing of the laws in the heart, whereby the inscribed covenant-member <term>bontling: a person within a covenant relationship, here specifically the New Covenant described in Jeremiah</term> becomes a letter—to be able to treat more expansively of a letter and its necessary composition, according to the aim of Jeremiah and the Apostle Paul, I shall here give some free rein to my thoughts.

From of old, people used to write in or upon stone, lead, and wooden tablets covered with wax, on prepared Egyptian reed-leaves <note>The author refers to papyrus.</note>, on leaves and the bark of trees: prepared intestines of animals <note>The author likely means vellum or parchment.</note>: parchment, writing paper.

Neither of one nor the other do Jeremiah and Paul mention, but they speak of persons; Jeremiah also of the heart and understanding of the covenant-members.

That which shall be able to be inscribed, and inscribed clearly, distinctly, and vividly enough to be brought before the eye, must be:
1. Not too hard, cruel, fleeting, stiff, and unmanageable. It must be able to allow a pen, stylus, or engraving iron. If then the understanding, will, memory, and heart are to be the paper or subject, then it ought not to be too stony, hardened, rebellious, or obstinate.
2. That which shall receive the letters in or upon itself, so that they do not bleed through or run together but can be read distinctly, ought not to be too soft, damp, weak, soaking, and flowing: and likewise, man's understanding, will, and memory must not be loose, inconstant, fickle, changeable, quickly forgetting, nor mixing everything together.
3. It also ought not to be uneven, lumpy, dirty and

# L E T T E R.

...and sullied: but rather to be clean, white, smooth, level, or even.

<margin>Purity required in the souls of men.</margin>
The soul of man must be without prejudices: without imagined, self-made, and fleshly wisdom—heights and depths through which one exalts oneself against the knowledge of Christ—and free from all impurity and evil desires.

It is indeed true that such qualities and dispositions—which shall be described here in a fitting, distinct, clear, and plain manner—are required: and that the heart of man, intended to be written upon, ought to be so. However, in our sinful nature and unregenerate state, it is not so disposed: for *Romans 8:7* <note>original: "Rom. VIII. 7."</note> says it does not subject itself to the law of God, nor indeed can it. The sinner is a Nabal <note>Nabal is a biblical figure whose name means "fool"; his heart is described as becoming "like a stone" (1 Samuel 25:37).</note>, his heart has died within him, becoming like a stone, *1 Samuel 25:37*. The heart is like a rock. Whether one teaches, exhorts, rebukes, or threatens, it deflects everything and resists; *Acts 7:51* <note>original: "Hand. VII. 51."</note> "ye do always resist the Holy Ghost." Through the habit of sinning, this hardness grows, just as a stone in the bladder grows by the addition of new grit, *Ezekiel 3:7* and *7:12*.

Therefore, the unfit heart, in order to be capable of being written upon, must be made fit by someone who understands the craft.

This is done by the Lord, who has said, "I will write." Through art and labor, man knows how to skillfully prepare paper, parchment, and other writing materials; he knows how to form letters with a stylus in iron, lead, and stone. Would it then not be possible for the only wise and almighty God to remove all deformities from the heart? Could He not make it fit to be written upon by Him? Certainly, yes.

If one asks what the God of the Covenant does to the heart of His covenant-partner when He brings it to that state where it can be written upon by Him, I give this as an answer:

<margin>God prepares the soul.</margin>
a. Then the Lord removes from the heart the sinful, natural hardness, stubbornness, resistance, and unruliness: He makes the soul docile and manageable, to do with it as He pleases. Thus speaks the Lord in *Ezekiel 11* and *36:26, 27*:
> *A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh, etc.*

He brings it about that one allows the word to be implanted with meekness, *James 1:21* <note>original: "Jac. I. 21."</note>.
<margin>Of which Paul is an example.</margin>
How hard and bitter was Saul, how partisan, occupied with such deep and fixed prejudices, *Acts 9:6*! But how suddenly was his heart made docile, like clean paper! *And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?*

b. When the heart of the covenant-partner is thus made docile and trembling before the Lord's word and judgments, and has become manageable, then He brings it about that the understanding, will, memory, and passions do not remain as changeable and inconstant as before, but that truth and virtue take a stronger hold upon them, remaining more permanently, so that what is written stays in the soul, *Psalm 51:12* <note>original: "Pf. LI. 12."</note>: He gives a steadfast spirit;

<column-break/>

*Ezekiel 36:27*: He causes them to keep His statutes.

c. Then, after the heart has become docile, He removes—through His divine "chemistry" and purification—all roughness, unevenness, pride, and all heights and depths of worldly and fleshly wisdom. This work involves the circumcision of the heart's foreskin, *Deuteronomy 30:6*, so that there are "set highways" in the heart, *Psalm 84:6*. He casts down imaginations and every high thing, *2 Corinthians 10:5*; He makes them like weaned children, *Psalm 131*.

d. Finally, He immediately removes from the heart all impurity, defilement, evil impulses, lusts, and thoughts, through the spirit of Faith and purity, by the power of His Son's blood, *Acts 15:9; 1 Corinthians 6:11; Hebrews 10:25; Ezekiel 36:25*.
> *Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. Zechariah 13:1; 1 John 1:7; Psalm 51:12: Create in me a clean heart, O God.*

Since we have considered man's heart as being clothed and adorned with the qualities of fit writing paper, we still do not yet have a letter or a script. For that, one requires a stylus, an engraving tool, or a writing pen: ink, chalk, pencil, etc.

<margin>Writing pen.</margin>
Therefore, we must look for the writing pen through which the Lord writes His laws into the understanding and heart of the covenant-partner; and in this, we must proceed with caution.

1. The pen is by no means the writer himself, but the writer's tool.
2. The pen is a necessary instrument and must be prepared, cut, and guided by the master writer, otherwise it accomplishes nothing of or by itself.
3. Since a rational human being is not actually like literal writing paper—though his understanding, will, and heart take the place of paper—and since he must be handled through teaching, exhorting, and convincing by making the truth manifest to his conscience: it must naturally follow that in this respect, no literal stylus, pen, or engraving tool can be used.
4. Nevertheless, we should imagine something that resembles a pen and can occupy and fulfill the role and service of a pen.

Taking this to heart, I note how the Lord, in this earthly state, usually deals with men through other men. Coming to the matter, I understand by the writing pen (See further under PEN) in the hand of the Divine Master Writer, those God-consecrated men—Prophets, Evangelists, Apostles, pastors, and Teachers—who, being endowed with exceptional enlightenment, understanding, gifts, and zeal, and having received "the tongue of the learned," <margin>Teachers symbolized by the pen.</margin> *Psalm 45*, strive to make manifest to the consciences of men the Divine law (and not the traditions and ordinances of men, as the false pen of the scribes used to do, *Jeremiah 8:8* <note>The text says Jeremiah 6:8, but the reference to the "false pen of the scribes" is Jeremiah 8:8.</note>, *Matthew 5:15-23*) with simplicity and the demonstration of spirit and power.

And certainly, it has its basis and fitness, that

# L E T T E R.

...that one should compare such capable, faithful, and zealous men—in respect to the Divine Scriptures—to a writing pen, and view and regard them as writing instruments, and nothing more, in the Lord’s writing hand.
For:

1. If one is to make an untrimmed quill <note>original: "penneſchagt." Quills required precise cutting with a knife to create a functional nib.</note> into a capable writing pen, it must be trimmed; the rough and the blunt parts must come off, and it must be sharpened.
In every person, there is neither the capability nor the desire to let themselves be used as a pen, as described above. What prejudices, excuses, pretenses, and difficulties exist! Moses focused on his tongue and speech, *Exodus* 4. Jeremiah was not eager for it, for he could not well endure mockery and contempt, *Jeremiah* 20:7–9. And Jonah had no "sea-legs," <note>original: "ſcheepsvoeten," an idiom suggesting he was unwilling to travel by sea for his mission.</note> *Jonah* 1:3. All of that, and whatever else is in the way, must be removed and cut away by the Master Writer before a person can and will allow themselves to be used as a writing pen.

2. A writing pen must be in the Master Writer's hand and fingers, and be guided by him: for the pen alone, of and by itself, makes no letters, nor good and capable legible writing.
If someone is to be God’s speaking mouth and pen, if someone is to be capable of speaking and handling the Divine, in God’s name, and according to the mind of the Holy Spirit, he must be made capable, driven, and moved for it. *1 Corinthians* 4:7; *2 Corinthians* 3:5, 6; *2 Timothy* 3:16; *2 Peter* 1:18, 19.

3. The writing pen must be sharpened somewhat pointedly and sharply for a good letter-stroke and to touch the surface of the paper: the pressure must sometimes be lighter, sometimes heavier.
If teachers are to touch the surface of the human heart with their tongues, as if with pens, their words ought sometimes to be like sharp arrows, *Psalm* 45; like nails and goads, *Ecclesiastes* 12. That which is too blunt and soft does not touch the heart. If the soul is to be touched, the pen must have a sharp point, *Acts* 16. See this in the Jailer, <note>The "Stokwaarder" refers to the Philippian jailer in Acts 16 who was "cut to the heart" and asked what he must do to be saved.</note> and compare *2 Corinthians* 4:2; *Hebrews* 4:12.

4. The pen writes no differently than the Master Writer desires: the Prophets, Evangelists, Apostles, Pastors, and Teachers, being regarded as the pen and God’s mouth, may not speak anything according to their own impulse, sensuality, or thoughts, nor bring it upon the paper of human understanding and heart; but they must speak and write in the Lord’s name, speaking God’s words. *2 Corinthians* 2:4–6; *2 Peter* 1:20, 21.

5. Without capable ink and the required moisture, the pen does not write. And although no actual ink is required for the description of human understandings and hearts, nevertheless, the pen must be filled with the water of grace and the oil of the Holy Spirit, *2 Corinthians* 3:3. It is indeed true that one can write upon something that has a solid ground-color with

<column-break/>

white or black chalk, with pencil, red earth, ink, and other pigments—just as the Africans used to use a certain fluid from fish, and the Jews praised the ink in which olive oil was mixed. Yet, when I look closely, Paul in *2 Corinthians* 3 rejected writing-ink: for it is not suitable for the engraving of God’s law into the human understanding and heart. Furthermore, Jeremiah and Paul do not speak so much of writing on the surface of the understanding and heart—as one does with pen and ink on the surface of paper—but of inscribing and engraving with inward-going letters, as was the case with the Law, *2 Corinthians* 3; and Job wished that it might happen to his words, *Job* 19:23, 24.

<margin>Thus the Writer.</margin>
Since paper, pen, and ink can accomplish nothing without a writer and the hand of the Master Writer; and since we have already encountered the paper, pen, and ink according to the metaphor, proper order dictates that we look for the Master Writer, or for the hand of Him whom the God of the Covenant wishes to use for the inscription of His law into the understanding and heart of His covenant-people.

Little, indeed no effort is required to search out the Master Writer, for He makes Himself sufficiently known. *Jeremiah* 31; *Ezekiel* 36; *2 Corinthians* 3; *Hebrews* 8.

But I said just before that a writer, or one who wants something written or described, will use either his own hand or that of a practiced and experienced scribe, especially when he wants a text to be written clearly, understandably, meaningfully, and emphatically, in order to be all the better and more easily understood.

The hand, therefore, serves to be named here, which guides the pen and makes the image and design of the matters through the pen.

<margin>Stone tables written by God.</margin>
Paul gives this hand to us, *2 Corinthians* 3:3: *Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart.* Thus we read of stone tables written by the finger of God, *Exodus* 31:18; *Deuteronomy* 9:10. It is true that one can say in general, God was the writer: yet specifically I point to God the Holy Spirit, and that (if I have it right) not without all ground and propriety according to the course of the household of grace, since it is the Holy Spirit who teaches, enlightens, leads, comforts, seals, etc. Therefore, I find nothing up to now that opposes me in this.

a. From of old, by a "writer" or "scribe," one used to understand a wise and very skilled man. If this observation holds, then the Holy Spirit, as a Divine person and writer, is the most capable and the readiest writer, as one who searches and knows the depths of God, *1 Corinthians* 2:10, 11; as the Spirit of knowledge, and wisdom, of counsel, and of science. *Isaiah* 11:1 <note>original: "Jeſ. XI. 1."</note>.

b. From of old, by a "writer," one used to understand a teacher of the law: then the Holy Spirit is the supreme writer, the highest teacher, for the entire counsel of God has He...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical exploration of God as the "Master Writer." Having previously discussed the tools of writing (paper, pen, and ink), the author now moves to the "text" itself: the transformation of the human heart and mind through the New Covenant.</meta>

# L E T T E R.

He has drafted it in His Divine Scripture, *2 Peter 1:21*, and beyond that, He inscribes it into the human understanding and heart, *Jeremiah 31:34, 2 Corinthians 3:3*, and He enlightens the eyes of the understanding to grasp the inner meaning. *John 14:26* and *16:13*.

Even though we have already encountered the writing paper, pen, ink, the writer, and the writer’s hand: we still have to look toward the writing in the understanding and the heart. We must investigate what this writing actually consists of, and how—through that which is written of the Divine laws in the understanding and heart—the covenant-members <note>The Dutch "verbondlingen" refers to people who are part of a holy agreement or "covenant" with God.</note> are a letter, or as good and as much as a letter. Furthermore, we must understand whether the old covenant-members were also a letter. If so: how and in what respect the new covenant-members are a letter by excellence, possessing much more privilege and excellence, etc.

As for that which would be written in the understanding and heart as the subject matter, *Jeremiah 31, Hebrews 8:10*, etc., it is not a law of works, intended to enter into life through and according to one's own righteousness. For if there ever were such a law and covenant, they were broken and transgressed by our first ancestors; and for Adam and Eve, as well as their descendants, it became an impossible condition. Moreover, since the promise of grace and salvation—taking hold outside the sinner, in, with, and through the Son of God—is certain, it is not possible that one would unite the renewal of such a law, covenant, and impossible condition with that promise.

Next, when we look with proper earnestness and appropriate distinction at what shall constitute the writing in the understanding and in the heart, we cannot understand it to mean the taking up and following of the laws and order in the government of Israel’s civil state, nor the high prescriptions regarding the tabernacle and temple duties. For the Lord had already placed all these in the midst of Israel; they knew these. Although I will readily admit that very few in Israel understood the Lord’s true and real end and purpose concerning these, I do not think that such a lack of understanding would be the reason the Lord would wish to renew them to take hold in the New Testament or covenant-state. It is noted that they were only ordained for a time, and established and imposed as examples and shadows until the time of reformation and perfection. This is all the more so since the Lord is said to want to enter into and conclude a covenant with His people, not according to the old manner and the content of the previous covenant. And when one observes how extensively Paul in *Hebrews 8* has pointed out the faultiness, weakness, and powerlessness of the previous covenant, then one will not even think of or look back toward the old and the past regarding this internal inscription. This is even less likely because one would lose sight of this truth: that Christ is the end of the law, the body of the shadows and examples, the fulfiller of the law and all promises and pledges, the Surety, Mediator, Priest, and sacrifice.

However, if someone wishes to understand it in such a sense—that God would grace the children of the covenant, under the ministry of the Gospel, with such a light of knowledge that they would obtain a clearer and more distinct understanding and insight

<column-break/>

of God’s purpose in ordaining all those ceremonies, regarding them as examples and shadows; and how everything had obtained its fulfillment in His Son, and in His mystical body, the congregation—I shall have nothing against it, though not with the intent of maintaining and preserving them as before.

Therefore, this pruning, rejection, and exception seems to me to lead toward the law of faith, of conversion, and of love, which must be brought as a law of the Gospel, *Romans 3:27* and *10:6, 7-9; 1 Timothy 1:5; Romans 13*, etc. This prevents me from looking back to the old law as a husband and guardian, *Romans 7:8; Galatians 4:5*, because wanting to do so cannot well be reconciled with the law of faith and love, nor with the knowledge and acknowledgment of God as the powerful Covenant-God <term>Covenant-God: Originally "Bontgodt," an archaic spelling of "Bondgodt," referring to God in His role as a partner in a sacred contract with humanity.</term> and Father in His Son, made perfect through suffering.

This having been established beforehand, it further comes into consideration what it means that the Covenant-God shall give and set His law, or laws, in the midst of His people; indeed, in their understanding and hearts, and write them therein.

If we consider how the Lord, in the midst of old Israel at Sinai and subsequently, gave and set His law on stone tablets, to be locked in the Ark of the Covenant, preserved, and carried along in their military marches; then we can easily understand that this promise at least includes this: that He, as Covenant-God, would ensure that the law of faith, of conversion, and of love would be found—by means of the Gospel, or the word of faith, and by means of preaching by the Evangelists and Apostles—first among the Jews, and subsequently also among the Gentiles. *Psalm 110; Isaiah 2; Matthew 28; Mark 16; Daniel 10:6, 7, 8, 9.*

But when we observe how the stone tablets were the subject which was written upon by the finger of God, so that the Divine law was not outside and around them, but *in* and *on* the stone tablets, written and engraved with inscribed letters: then this writing in the understanding and heart implies much more than an outward appearance and a public manifestation of this law of God to both physical eyes and ears. Namely, it implies that the understanding and heart would be the subject of the description and of this Divine writing, just as the stone tablets were of the law.

Which promise and benefit enclosed in this promise, I shall present thus briefly and substantively, namely:

That the Covenant-God would grant to His covenant-members a much more abundant measure of His Spirit, to arrive at a clearer, more abundant knowledge and insight of His counsel, purpose, laws, promises, shadows, examples, and riddles; and from these, His virtues and perfections in His Son, Surety, Mediator, High Priest, God-Savior, etc. As foretold in *Psalm 68; Isaiah 35; 44; Joel 2* and as can be seen in *Acts 2; Ephesians 4; John 7:37, 38, 39.*

Which more generous outpouring in the children of the Covenant would bring about a convicting sight of their sin, damnableness, and impotence, *John 16:8*, and thereby bring them to a spiritual despair and true denial of themselves and all their own righteousness; in order to, with all the more strength...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical discussion of the "Living Letter." ### LETTER.

**Column 1**

he has drafted in his Divine Scripture, *2 Peter 1:21*, and beyond that, he writes it into the human understanding and heart, *Jeremiah 31:34, 2 Corinthians 3:3*, and he enlightens the eyes of the understanding to grasp the inner meaning. *John 14:26* and *16:13*. <note>The original text cites "Job," but the context of the Holy Spirit as a guide to truth refers to the Gospel of John.</note>

This now having been sent before, it further comes into consideration what it means that the Covenant God shall give and place his law, or laws, in the midst of his people: yes, in their understanding and hearts, and write them therein.

If we consider how the Lord, in the midst of old Israel, at Sinai and subsequently, gave and placed his law in stone tablets, to be enclosed in the Ark of the Covenant, to be preserved, and to be carried along in their military marches: then we can easily understand that this promise at least also included this: that the Covenant God would bring about that the law of faith, of conversion, and of love—by means of the Gospel, or the word of faith, and by means of the preaching by the Evangelists and Apostles—was found first among the Jews, and subsequently also among the Gentiles. *Psalm 110; Isaiah 2; Matthew 28; Mark 16; Daniel 10:6, 7, 8, 9.*

But when we observe how the stone tablets were the subject <term>subject: the physical material or surface being written upon</term> which was written upon by the finger of God, so that the Divine law was not outside of or around them, but written and engraved in and on the stone tablets with indented letters: then this inscription in the understanding and heart implies quite a bit more than an outward appearance and a public revelation of this law of God to both the physical eyes and ears; namely this: that understanding and heart would be the subject of the description and of this Divine writing, just as the stone tablets were of the law.

Which promise and benefit enclosed in this promise, I shall present briefly and essentially as follows, namely:

That the Covenant God would grant to his members of the covenant a much more abundant measure of his Spirit, to arrive at clearer, more abundant knowledge and insight of his counsel, purpose, laws, promises, shadows, types, and riddles <note>original: "schaduwen, voorbeelden, raatzelen"</note> and from these his virtues and perfections in his Son, Surety, Mediator, High Priest, God-Savior: etc. as foretold, *Psalm 68; Isaiah 35, 44; Joel 2* and as seen in *Acts 2; Ephesians 4; John 7:37, 38, 39.*

->Because<-

1. If an uncut quill shaft is to be made into a capable writing pen, it must be trimmed; the rough and the blunt parts must come off; it must be sharpened. <note>In the 18th century, pens were made from bird quills and required constant "cutting" or sharpening with a pen-knife to remain functional.</note> In every human, there is neither the capability nor the desire to allow oneself to be used as a pen, as stated above. What prejudices, excuses, pretenses, and difficulties exist! Moses focused on his tongue and speech, *Exodus 4*. Jeremiah was not eager for it, because he could not well endure mockery and contempt, *Jeremiah 20:7-9*. And Jonah had no "sea-legs," <note>original: "fcheepsvoeten," an idiom meaning Jonah was unwilling to travel or go where commanded.</note> *Jonah 1:3*. All of that, and whatever else is in the way, must be taken away and cut off by the Writing Master before a person can and will allow himself to be used as a writing pen.
2. A writing pen must be in the Writing Master’s hand and fingers, and be guided by him; for the pen alone, out of and by itself, makes no letters, nor any good and properly legible writing. If someone is to be God’s speaking mouth and pen—if someone is to be capable of speaking and handling the Divine in God's name and according to the mind of the Holy Spirit—he must be made capable, driven, and moved for it. *1 Corinthians 4:7, 2 Corinthians 3:5, 6, 2 Timothy 3:16, 2 Peter 1:18, 19.*
3. The writing pen must be sharpened somewhat pointedly and keenly for a good letter-stroke and for touching the surface of the paper; the pressure must sometimes be a bit lighter, sometimes a bit heavier. If teachers are to touch the surface of the human heart with their tongues, as with pens, their words ought at times to be like sharp arrows, *Psalm 45*, like nails and goads, *Ecclesiastes 12*. That which is too blunt and soft does not touch the heart. If the soul is to be touched, the pen must have a sharp point, *Acts 16*. See this in the Jailer, <note>referring to the Philippian jailer who was "cut to the heart" and asked what he must do to be saved.</note> and compare *2 Corinthians 4:2, Hebrews 4:12.*
4. The pen writes nothing other than what the Writing Master wants: the Prophets, Evangelists, Apostles, Pastors, and Teachers, being regarded as the pen and God’s mouth, may not speak anything according to their own impulse, sensuality, or thoughts, nor bring it onto the paper of human understanding and heart; rather, they must speak and write in the Lord's name, speaking God's words. *2 Corinthians 2:4-6, 2 Peter 1:20, 21.*
5. Without proper ink and the required moisture, the pen does not write. And although no literal ink is required for the description of human understandings and hearts, nevertheless, the pen must be filled with the water of grace and the oil of the Holy Spirit. *2 Corinthians 3:3.* It is true that one can describe something that has a solid ground-color with

white or black chalk, with pencil, red earth, ink, and other materials—just as the Africans used to use a certain fluid from fish, and the Jews praised ink in which olive oil was mixed. But when I look closely, Paul in *2 Corinthians 3* rejected writing ink, for it is not suitable for the human understanding and heart for the inscription of God’s law. Also, Jeremiah and Paul do not speak so much of writing on the surface of the understanding and heart, as one does with pen and ink on the surface of paper, but of inscription and engraving with inward-reaching letters, as was the case with the Law, *2 Corinthians 3*. And Job wished that his words might be so recorded, *Job 19:23, 24.*

Since paper, pen, and ink can accomplish nothing without a writer and the hand of the Writing Master—and as we have already encountered the paper, pen, and ink in our imagination—proper order dictates that we look for the Writing Master, or for the hand of Him who, as the God of the Covenant, wishes to use these for the inscription of His law in the understanding and heart of His covenant-members.

<margin>The Writer.</margin>
To seek out the Writing Master requires little, indeed no effort, for He makes Himself sufficiently known. *Jeremiah 31, Ezekiel 36, 2 Corinthians 3, Hebrews 8.*

But I have said just before that a writer, or one who wants something written or described, will use either his own hand or that of a practiced and experienced writer—especially when he wants a text written clearly, understandably, meaningfully, and emphatically, in order to be better and more easily understood.

The hand, therefore, serves to be named here, which guides the pen, and through the pen makes the image and design of the matters. This hand is pointed out to us by Paul, *2 Corinthians 3:3.*

<margin>Stone tablets described by God.</margin>
> Since you are being made manifest as a letter of Christ, prepared by our ministry, written not with ink but by the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of flesh in the heart.

Thus we read of stone tablets described by the finger of God, *Exodus 31:18, Deuteronomy 9:10*. While it is true that one can say in general that God was the writer, I specifically identify the Holy Spirit as the writer. And that—if I have it right—is not without foundation and propriety according to the arrangement in the dispensation of grace, since it is the Holy Spirit who teaches, enlightens, guides, comforts, seals, etc. Therefore, I find nothing thus far that opposes me in this.

a. From of old, it was customary to understand a writer or a scribe as a wise and very experienced man. If this observation holds, then the Holy Spirit, as a Divine person and writer, is the most capable and worthy writer, as one who searches and knows the depths of God, *1 Corinthians 2:10, 11*, as the Spirit of knowledge, and wisdom, of counsel, and of science. *Isaiah 11:1.* <note>The author uses "science" in the archaic sense of "systematic knowledge" or "learning."</note>

Consequently, when we look with true earnestness and proper discernment at what shall constitute the writing in the understanding and in the heart, we cannot understand it to mean the observation and following of the laws and order in the government of Israel’s civil state; nor the high prescriptions regarding the tabernacle and temple duties. For the Lord had already placed all these in the midst of Israel; they knew them. Although I am willing to admit that very few in Israel understood the Lord's right and true end and purpose regarding these things, I do not think that failing to understand them would be the reason the Lord would want to renew them to take hold in the New Testament or covenant state. This is even less likely because one would lose sight of this truth: that Christ is the end of the law, the body of the shadows and examples, the fulfiller of the law and of all promises and pledges, the Surety, Mediator, Priest, and Sacrifice.

It is certainly true that understanding, and thus the intellect, belongs to the soul: yet when the intellect—as it is here and elsewhere—is distinguished from the heart, it is generally held that the "heart" signifies the will, the soul's desires, and the passions, as distinct from the intellect.

If the Covenant God <term>Bontgodt; a term for God emphasizing His relationship through the Covenant of Grace</term> were to give His laws both in the intellect and subsequently in the heart: then the latter undoubtedly teaches that the Covenant God, having poured out such a measure of the Holy Spirit upon the covenant members, would lead them to judge that consenting to these laws—subjecting themselves to them with faith, love, and trust in obedience—contained a strong and eternal consolation, and a certain and eternal salvation. This would cause them to choose this standard and Divine order with inner delight, binding themselves to it most zealously and closely, and behaving accordingly, to find the goods of the intellect applied to their souls, both here and hereafter.

After all this, it may be considered whether the old believers and the old covenant members <note>referring to those living under the Old Testament/Mosaic law</note> had this inscription; and whether they were a "letter of Christ."

Regarding this problem and question, we are not among those who entirely deny the inscription of God's law in the intellect and heart to the believers of olden times. Yet we would also note that there is a preeminence and excellence in this inscription for the Church of the New Testament and Covenant.

I know well that David, Isaiah, and others were very great men; yet in comparison with the commonality and the bulk of the people, such individuals were generally few. They were extraordinary persons and prophets: first-fruits and examples of those who would later receive the Spirit more richly. John the Baptist was greater than all of these, and yet in the kingdom of heaven he was the least; and if the new covenant members did not have a distinguished advantage in this, then God would not have used so much preparation, ceremony, fanfare, and emphasis through Jeremiah, nor would Paul have made so much of that covenant and those promises in *Hebrews 8*. But I do not wish to expand further on this matter: the curious reader can find abundant information regarding the privileges of the New Testament and this inscription in the works of Coccejus, Burman, Witzius, Momma, Braunius, d’Outrein in his *Short Sketch*, and on the *Epistle to the Hebrews*, etc. <note>These were prominent 17th-century Reformed theologians, many associated with "Covenant Theology" (Cocceianism), which emphasized the historical progression of God's relationship with humanity.</note>

It is also believed, and is certain, that they were a "letter of Moses" and of the law: just as the veil of Moses remained, so too the letter of the laws—which were numerous and of various kinds—was in and upon their intellect and heart, and remained in them for a very long time, bringing about in them a spirit of servitude, serving God according to the oldness of these letters. Upon the upper surface of their intellect,

<column-break/>

and heart, one found the three-fold laws, and they were "baptized into Moses." This freedom of understanding could not be found among them; these covenant goods and privileges could not be so easily read or perceived in them. If one found the grievances of the Messiah in and among them, it was without an actual transfer to the person of Jesus, the Christ, noting that He had not yet been revealed to His people with the actual revelation of His identifying marks, and the "Yes and Amen"-ing of all God's pledges and promises in His person and His undertaken works of salvation, *2 Corinthians 1:23.*

# BROTHER and SISTER, <gloss>original: אחות, אח, ἀδελφός, ἀδελφή, frater, ſoror</gloss> <note>The author provides the terms for "brother" and "sister" in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin respectively.</note>

<margin>The name of Brother and Sister taken in a general sense.</margin>
It is well known that these words are sometimes used more specifically and sometimes more broadly, both among all nations and among us, as well as in the Holy Scrolls <note>the Bible</note>; namely, in the sense of humans with humans, as having sprung from the very first father and mother, Adam and Eve, from the same blood, possessed of the same stirrings, needs, and weaknesses; and therefore such a neighbor of ours is called "brother," *Matthew 5:22, 23, 24.*

Furthermore, in a closer degree, as having sprung from the same parents, *Matthew 1, Mark 1,* etc.; for male cousins, female cousins, and relatives by marriage or by blood, *Matthew 12,* etc.

For people of one and the same nation, city, covenant, religion, etc., among whom love can also play a part and have a place, as in *Matthew 23, Job 21, Acts 23, Romans 9 and 14,* etc.

<margin>Applicable to the pious.</margin>
The word and the designation of brother and sister is uniquely applicable to the elect, the called, the saints, the confessors of the word of righteousness—or, according to the judgment of love and the outward appearance of their confession and conduct, those held to be such; although there are also false and "seeming" brothers, *2 Corinthians 11, Galatians 2.*

Namely, they have not only one Father, *Matthew 23:8, 9, Ephesians 4:6*; one mother, the Church, *Galatians 4*; one seed of the Word, and birth from God; one elder brother, Christ; one household, *1 Timothy 3:15, 16, Ephesians 2*; one calling, one faith, confession, baptism, sacraments, inheritance, *1 Corinthians 12, Ephesians 4*; but are also joined together through love, peace, and likemindedness for each other's edification and perfection, *John 13:4, Acts 4:31, Romans 12:10, Psalm 33:1, 2.*

It is not brotherly or sisterly when people rise up against one another, and minds are scattered and torn apart by strife, envy, or otherwise incited to all kinds of hostilities, about which complaints have been made since ancient times. *Ovid, in Book 1 of the Metamorphoses:*

> Vivitur ex rapto, non hoſpes ab hoſpite tutus;
> Non focer à genero, fratrum quoque gratia rara eſt.
<note>original Latin: "People live on plunder; the guest is not safe from his host, nor the father-in-law from the son-in-law; even the affection of brothers is rare."</note>

Which is, according to Vondel: <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) was the preeminent Dutch poet and playwright of the Golden Age.</note>

> Men lives only by robbery. The host is in distress,
> And at his own hearth is not safe from the guest,
> No father-in-law is safe from the son; faithful brotherly love
> Is rare.

Manilius, *Astronomica, Book IV.* <note>original: "Ecce patrem nati perimunt, natosque parentes: Mutuaque armati coëunt in vulnera fratres."</note>

->That is:<-

<margin>The names "Brother" and "Sister" as used by the early Christians.</margin> It is evident not only from the Apostolic writings but also from those of the early Church Fathers that it was customary among Christians to use the names "Brother" and "Sister." 
Indeed, it is well enough known in the world that although the Pagans gave these names to their paramours and used them for wicked and carnal purposes, they nevertheless did not hesitate to suspect the pure confessors of the faith—who lived chaste and holy lives—of the foulest carnality and atrocities. Because of this mutual naming of "brothers" and "sisters," they uncharitably, godlessly, and untruthfully accused and blamed them.

<margin>Misused by the Pagans.</margin> Regarding the conduct of the Pagans, one may look at Martial, *Epigrams, Book 2, To Amianus*, where he speaks this language: <note>original: "O quam blandus es, Amiane, matri, Quam blanda est tibi mater, Amiane! Mater, quæ cupit esse se sororem, Nec matrem juvat esse, nec sororem."</note>

> O Amianus, how you smile upon your mother!
> Your mother never tires of your face.

> And do not wish to be what you truly are?
> Why do you seek to take such pleasure in this?

The Pagans, practicing such wantonness themselves, assumed (as we touched upon above) that the Christians lived with one another in the same manner. See Dougt. *In N. They charged the Christians with this violation under the names of brother and sister, a crime of which (as has now been shown) they themselves were guilty.

<margin>Christians falsely accused.</margin> But it was foul slander, for the Church Fathers gave the reasons for this naming quite distinctly, namely: *Because they acknowledged one God and Father; that they had been borne by one and the same Spirit of holiness; and that they had been brought forth from one and the same womb of ignorance into a single light.* Tertullian, *Apology, Chapter 39.* Also Octavius in the writings of Minutius Felix: *We, whom you envy, call each other brothers, as people of one and the same Father, God; as fellow-participants in the faith, and fellow-heirs of hope.* Jerome against Helvidius, *Chapter 8: We Christians are called brothers because we are humans born of one Father, and are bound to one another by a similar bond of brotherhood.* Lactantius in his *Divine Institutes, Book V, Chapter 6: Divine religion alone brings it to pass that one human loves another, and that he considers him to be fastened to himself by the bond of brotherhood, since God is the same Father to all.* And in his *Epitome, Chapter 11: If we*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Brotherhood" among early Christians and begins a new entry on "Breeches" (priestly undergarments), maintaining the encyclopedic and apologetic tone of the previous page.</meta>

# BROTHER. BREECHES.

The same God created them, and has brought forth every person to righteousness and eternal life upon the same conditions; thus, we are bound to one another by the necessity of brotherhood. *Ambrose in Book II, Chapter 6: <note>original: "Ambrofius... Alle menfchen zyn de vrugt van de zelve natuur..."</note> All men are the fruit of the same nature, received from the same inward parts, nourished and brought forth from one and the same womb. We are bound to one another as brothers by a right of kinship, created by one Father, and come forth from one mother as brothers of the same belly. Clement of Alexandria, Miscellanies 7: <note>original: "Clemens Alexandr. Strom. 7. Het zyn waarlyk broeders..."</note> They are truly brothers who, through an exquisite creation and agreement of character, do, think, and speak the same things—holy and good works, or things which God willed that they, as chosen ones, should feel. Prosper on Free Will: <note>original: "Profper van den vryen wille..."</note> The Church is the same mother to all, abundant through the consequences of her fertility: through her bearing we are born, by her milk we are nourished, and by her spirit we are inspired. Cyprian, On the Simplicity of Prelates.* <note>historically titled "On the Unity of the Church"</note>

They were thus not only brothers and sisters insofar as they had God for a Father and Nature for a Mother; that much they had in common with the Pagans, who for that reason were also called brothers, though they otherwise hardly deserved the name of men. (*See Minutius Felix page 26.*) But it was for more sublime reasons, namely, *that they had one and the same God as a Father, and all together drank from the same sanctifying Spirit; and that they were brought out of the same womb of darkness, or of ignorance, into the light of truth, sharing in the same faith, and heirs to the same hope of the heavenly inheritance.*

And even *Lucian in The Death of Peregrinus, page 764, Tome II* <note>a 2nd-century Greek satirist</note> had to admit that it was one of the greatest principles instilled in them by their master, *that they should all become brothers after they rejected the religion of the Pagans and embraced the service of their great crucified master, giving themselves over to live according to his laws. See Cave’s Primitive Christianity, page 519; Kortholt page 137, etc.; Henric. Ursin. part 2, page 144, etc. Anal. etc.*

Away then with the lies and slander of Caecilius, brought forward by Minutius, when he vomited the following from his cursed throat: <note>original: "uit zyn vervloekten ftrot uitbraakt"</note> *They call one another brothers and sisters among themselves, so that their habitual carnal mixing and incest might take place through the intervention of that holy name.*

That such carnal lusts and wicked works were in vogue and practiced among the Pagans, the Gnostics, and the rest of the scum <note>original: "fchuim"</note> is indubitable; but to smear the pure Christians and the Christian doctrine with evil for this reason, without having attended their assemblies or properly investigated their teaching, life, and morals from up close, was unreasonableness, lovelessness, and malice itself.

### BREECHES, UNDERPANTS, <term>miknasayim</term> <note>Hebrew: מכנסים</note>, <term>femoralia</term> <note>Latin: thigh-coverings</note>, <term>bracca</term> <note>Latin: trousers</note>.

<margin>Breeches, the attire of the Priests.</margin>
Since I here have my eye upon holy matters, and upon a portion of the Priestly attire wherewith the lower body and the private parts had to be honored and covered in the Tabernacle and Temple services, the Priests were required to wear linen under-breeches, just as the High Priest, on the Great Day of Atonement, was judged

<column-break/>

to have been clothed entirely in white linen.

As for the Breeches or Under-breeches, whether they have been in use for a long time or whether they belonged to daily dress, one might reasonably doubt. I shall provide an account of the Breeches and Under-breeches of the Priests.

One learns of the Divine command for them, as well as the practice, in *Exodus 28 and 29, Ezekiel 44, and Leviticus 6*, where they are called <term>miknasayim</term> <note>Hebrew: מכנסים</note>. The 70 Translators <note>the Septuagint</note> have called this garment <term>periskele</term> <note>Greek: περισκελῆ, "around the legs"</note>; the common translation calls them <term>seminalia</term>; Junius and others have called them <term>femoralia</term>. The breeches consist of fine and well-twisted linen of a very white and bright color, and indeed (as some will have it) of six threads, which is why the word <term>shesh</term> <note>Hebrew: שש, meaning "six" or "fine linen"</note> is added. Thus *Abrabanel* writes: <term>shesh</term> is Egyptian linen, which is the most precious among all kinds of linen; but when it is twisted from six threads into one thread, it is then called *SHESH*, or <term>shebesh moshzar</term> <note>twisted fine linen</note>. *See Braun, On the Clothing of the Priests, Book II, Chapter 1, page 435, & Book I, Chapter 17, page 410. Gemara Yoma Chapter 7.* Our Teachers teach that those things of which <term>shesh</term> is spoken must be taken for six-threaded. And in the *Zevachim Codex, Chapter 11: All garments made of fine linen must necessarily be of linen, new, twisted, and of six threads. Maimonides, Vessels of the Sanctuary, Chapter 8: Everywhere one reads "shesh" or "twisted" in the Law-book, it is necessary that the threads be six-fold.*

These breeches were woven, but not sewn or brought together from various panels; at least this was also feasible and not out of use. For since all garments had to be <term>ma’aseh oreg</term> <note>Hebrew: מעשה אורג, "the work of a weaver"</note> and not <term>ma’aseh mahshev</term> <note>Hebrew: מעשה מחשב, "the work of a designer/needleworker"</note>, that is, work of the needle or embroidery, it falls to us to believe that they were also woven Breeches. *Maimonides* is also of this opinion in *Laws of the Vessels of the Sanctuary, Chapter 8*, when he had spoken of the robe, breeches, and hat: *And all these garments of the Priesthood are not the work of the needle, but of the weaver, as it is said, "weaver’s work."*

I cannot see at all that they were breeches in the manner of women's aprons, but rather like ours, with two legs <note>original: "pypen," literally pipes</note>. And it is not unlikely that they were closed not just above the hips, but below the chest <note>original: "mammen"</note>, near the heart, *Exodus 28:42, Ezekiel 44:18*, not at the armpits but somewhat below them, because the upper body releases sweat more strongly. *Kimchi on Ezekiel 44*: The Teachers of blessed memory explain it in this way: *they shall not be girded where they sweat, according to the tradition. When they gird themselves, they do not gird themselves below the loins, nor above the armpits, but around the armpits.* The *Chaldean* <note>Targum</note> states: *They shall not gird by the loins, but by their heart.*

The extent, length, and hang of the breeches was not below the knees, as some have drawn and described them, but down to and just above the knees, "unto the thighs" <note>Hebrew: עד ירכים, ad yerekim</note>, to the point where the kneecaps begin.

*Maimonides, as above*: "to the end of the side, which is where the kneecaps are." So says *Rabbi Levi of Barcelona in Precept 99*: The form of the breeches is everywhere known,

# BREECHES.

of which some are as long as the knees. Jerome, writing to Fabiola, says: *From our people they are called pipe-sleeves, or breeches, which reach to the knees.* <note>original: "Van de onze worden pypmouwen, ofte broeken genoemt..." Jerome in Letter 64 (to Fabiola) describes the 'feminalia' or 'braccae' as tubular coverings for the legs.</note>

<margin>Breeches of the Easterners.</margin>
It is written that the Easterners formerly had breeches that were open in the front and back, so as to be able to perform their natural business, as one reads in the Code Niddah, Chapter 11, where the front opening is called the "place of shame," and the back opening is named <term>בית הכסא</term> <note>Hebrew: 'Beit ha-Kisse,' literally "House of the Chair," a common idiom for a latrine or toilet.</note> the place of the opening; which were nonetheless tied shut with bands or fastened, as Jarchi <note>The medieval commentator Rashi.</note> noted in the aforementioned place. See Braun’s *On the Hebrew Vestments, page 445.*

From this saying, one cannot conclude that the Priestly breeches were made in such a way; rather, it is probable that they were closed in the front and back, and that one stepped into them from the top and pushed the legs through the leg-pipes. They likely did not have a waistband stitched onto the top like our breeches, but rather a series of holes or eyelets in the upper part through which a string, drawstring-ribbon, or band was pulled, much like the way some drawstring purses are closed, in order to tighten them according to a person's thickness or thinness. As Maimonides writes in *Kele Hammikdash* <note>"The Instruments of the Sanctuary"</note> Chapter 8: *The breeches of the High Priest, as well as those of the other Priests, are let down from the loins to the end of the pipes (which extend to the private parts), which are the knees. And they have certain bindings. But they have no opening, neither in front nor in back, but are pulled together like a purse.* Thus one reads in the Tractate Niddah, Chapter 11: *To what things are the breeches of the Priests similar? They were like the breeches of the Pharisees <note>The term 'Perushim' here likely refers to those who lived lives of strict ritual separation and purity.</note>, from above to the intestines, and from below to the knee-pipes. They had bindings, but no opening on the front or back parts.*

This shall suffice regarding the Priestly breeches.

<margin>White garments.</margin>
As for the white linen clothes (whether one can actually include the breeches here would need closer investigation), it is well known that the same were found among the Pagans and their "popes," Priests, or holy ministers. They believed that garments of a white color, along with pure, stark-white linen, were uniquely pleasing to the Gods and belonged to the holy service. To confirm this, I shall bring forward just a few examples.

Suetonius recounts of Otho in Chapter 12 that he publicly observed the festival of Isis in linen and holy dress. And Silius Italicus describes the Priests of Ammon thus, at the beginning of the third book:

> -> No garment of a different color <-
> -> Before the altars: their bodies are veiled in linen. <-
<note>original Latin: "Non discolor ulli / Ante aras cultus: velantur corpora lino."</note>

-> That is: <-

> They cover themselves with linen before the altars,
> Where no one may appear in colored raiment.

Lucan introduces Magnus speaking thus in *Pharsalia*, Book IX:

> -> I shall now bring forth the goddess Isis from the tomb for the nations, <-
> -> And scatter Osiris, covered in linen, among the common people. <-
<note>original Latin: "Evolvam busto jam numen gentibus Isin, / Et tectum lino spargam per vulgus Osirim."</note>

<column-break/>

-> That is: <-

> I shall fetch Isis from the grave, now a goddess
> Of the peoples, and everywhere display Osiris
> Covered with linen. —

That the Egyptian Priests were dressed in stark white, Ovid seems to indicate quite clearly in the 4th Book of *The Festivals*:

> -> White suits Ceres; take up white garments for the Festival of Ceres; <-
> -> now the use of dark wool is absent. <-
<note>original Latin: "Alba decent Cererem, vestes Cerealibus albas / Sumite; nunc pulli velleris usus abest."</note>

Which Ovid’s translator follows thus:

> Dress in garments white and pure for Ceres' feast:
> For white becomes Ceres: and, as you approach the altars,
> Let the use of black coats be cast aside above all.

One may further consult Spencer, Part 2, page 54, etc., and Dilherr’s *Demonstrations, page 240, etc.*

Whether this custom was borrowed from the Egyptians—as Polydore Vergil (*Book IV, On the Discovery of Things, Chapter 7*), Josephus (*The Jewish War, Book VI*), Spencer, and others wish—or dates from Adam’s time, as Cluverius (*Ancient Germany, Book I*) suggests (See Spencer, page 55, etc.), I shall not venture to say. At the very least, Plato himself judged that the white color was pleasing to the divinity. Many have held the opposite view: namely, that the Egyptians and others imitated the Jews. As Bochart says in *Hierozoicon*, Part 1, Book II: *It shall suffice to note here that the Egyptians, emulating the Jews in many things, allowed no clothes but linen for their priests.* And after that: *Plutarch philosophized much about the linen of the Egyptians, with more finesse than substance, being unaware that many such things passed from the Hebrews to the Egyptians.* That is: *It will be enough to note here that the Egyptians, mimicking the Jews in many things, allowed no garments for their priests other than linen. Furthermore: Plutarch expresses himself on the linen of the Egyptians with more sophistication than weight, not knowing that many such things passed from the Hebrews to the Egyptians.* And Huetius in *Demonstratio Evangelica* says: "The linen-wearing priests of Isis imitated the linen coats of the Hebrew Priests."

The Lord our God willed that the private parts of the Priests should be covered and enclosed by breeches, which closed tightly and firmly enough around the body, so that modesty and shame in the pure Worship of God would be maintained and observed; and that no parts, which shame and modesty teach us to cover, might be exposed through the crouching and bending of the body, by intervening winds under the blue sky, while climbing the altar of burnt offering, or otherwise—which might otherwise have happened by an unexpected accident, just as it befell the Tuscan diviner while he was sacrificing.

Martial, Book III, Epigram 24:

> -> While he himself, leaning over the green altars, <-
> -> cuts the struggling necks with a knife and presses with his hand, <-
> -> a huge hernia appeared during the angry sacrifices. <-
<note>original Latin: "Ipse super virides aras luctantia pronus / Dum resecat cultro colla, premitque manu, / Ingens iratis apparuit hernia sacris." An epigram mocking a priest whose physical ailment was exposed during a ritual.</note>

<meta>Continuing from the discussion of the physical construction of the priestly breeches, this page explores the theological and moral necessity for these garments, contrasting the modesty of Israelite worship with the lewdness of pagan rites, and ultimately pointing toward a spiritual covering for sin.</meta>

# BREECHES.

->That is:<-

> When he bends forward to slit the beast’s throat
> For the offering with his knife, and presses it with his hand,
> A great exposure <note>original: "breuk" - a pun in Dutch between 'broek' (breeches) and 'breuk' (rupture or exposure)</note> shows itself, and defiles the sanctuaries.

Thus the common Priests, as well as the High Priest, were required to wear these linen breeches during the time of their service to cover the flesh of their shame: for nakedness, accompanied by shame and the need for concealment, is a fruit and a consequence of sin. When evil lusts and desires manifest in the external members, they then become the weapons of sin and unrighteousness, *Romans 6.*

One reads in *Exodus 20:26: Neither shalt thou go up by steps unto mine altar, that thy nakedness be not discovered thereon.*

<margin>Altar steps.</margin>
That there were steps at the altar is seen in *Leviticus 9:22, 2 Chronicles 4, and Ezekiel 43:17,* because it was impossible for any of the Priests to lift such heavy pieces of meat and lay them upon the burnt altar from above without some elevation; from which it seems to follow that these specific words, *neither shalt thou go up by steps unto mine altar,* should not be understood absolutely as a strict prohibition of any incline, but with a certain qualification. Namely, that you shall not use rungs or common ladder-steps to climb my burnt altar—no open, transparent, or un-enclosed steps, nor any that rise too steeply—but rather steps that are wide, enclosed, and rising slowly. This was so that the wind, the swift stirring and movement of the body, the leaning forward, or whatever accident might occur, would not reveal their shameful parts.

<margin>Service of Priapus.</margin>
When I compare one thing to another, I can well perceive that the God of Israel intended to teach and show thereby that He, loathing the filthy and stinking service of Peor <note>Baal-Peor, a Moabite god whose worship was associated with sexual license</note>, would in no way be honored or served in a similar manner, nor by anything that even resembled it. For Baal-Peor, or Priapus <note>The Greek god of fertility, often depicted with permanent arousal</note>, as we are told, used to be served by the uncovering of the shameful parts, and by urine, dung, and impurity. The God of Israel distinguished Himself from the "dung-gods," in whose images' presence things were practiced too shameful to recount. And in this regard, Maimonides <note>A renowned medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher</note> in *The Guide for the Perplexed, Book III, Chapter 49* [Latin: *More Nevochim*], is by no means wrong when he says that the God of Israel wanted to make and show a contrast between His service and the filthy service of Peor: *You have known from of old that the service of Peor formerly required one to openly uncover the shameful parts: therefore the Lord commanded the Priests to make breeches to cover their nakedness during the time of their service.* From this same principle arises the Divine covenant of not climbing to the altar by steps, so that their nakedness might not be discovered.

From which it must inevitably follow that Jehovah intended to teach His people and the Priesthood that He desired to be honored and served not only with the modest covering of the limbs and the warding off of all fleshly impurity, but also in purity of mind, with clean and chaste desires, thoughts, words, and gestures: and that in and during

<column-break/>

the performance of His public service, nothing should be found which could provide an opportunity or any fuel for fleshly thoughts, movements, and works of impurity.

Yet when I see both the High Priest and the common Priests clothed with under-breeches during their public services and their shameful parts covered, there does not arise in my heart this Jewish grievance or proposition: that there was any dignity, power, or ability located in this Priestly attire to take away natural impurity, or to atone for the crime of fornication, impurity, and adultery, whether committed by the Jewish people or by the Priesthood.

These are nothing but fantasies, in my opinion; since nowhere in the Word of the Lord does one find such inner dignity and actual power attributed to the Priestly garments. For if neither the living Priests nor the slaughtered sacrificial animals could bring such a thing about for the Priests and the people, what could linen breeches possibly achieve?

Better suited is what the Jews, by way of consequence, derive from this command regarding the Priestly breeches, namely: if the Priestly service was so exacting that they had to wear breeches when performing their duties, then those intending to perform the Priestly service must surely have descended from honorable parents and from a legitimate marriage, and not be bastards. *Deuteronomy 23:2.* This is the reason why, in the appointment of Priests, attention used to be paid to both their birth and descent, and to physical deformities and bodily defects. See *Maimonides, On the Manner of Entering the Temple, Chapters 6, 7, 8; On the Manner of Performing Sacrifices, Chapter 10; Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book III, Chapter 10 and Book XIV, Chapter 25; Selden, On the Succession of the Pontiffs, Book II, Chapter 5; Lightfoot, Volume I, page 691, etc.*

And when either the High Priest or the common Priests were thus covered regarding their shameful parts during their service, they could well see and learn from this necessary means of covering that, although they were sprung from an honorable marriage bed, they were nonetheless conceived and born in a sinful nakedness and exposure, and that the impure could not have produced anything pure or unblemished. *Job 14:4; Psalm 51:7; John 3:6.* <note>The text incorrectly cites Job 3:6; it likely refers to John 3:6 regarding being born of the flesh.</note>

<margin>Thoughts on the covering.</margin>
And seeing how Jehovah took care for the covering of the Priestly nakedness, they could, climbing higher in thought, well consider that Jehovah would no less provide a garment to cover spiritual nakedness and disgraceful shame; and this through a Priest according to another order, of greater excellence and more powerful effects. *Psalm 132:10; Isaiah 61:10; Jeremiah 23:5, 6; Jeremiah 30:21, 22.* See *Doctor Simeon, in the Babylonian Gemara.* Philo, especially in *Book III* concerning the life of Moses, finally concludes that the High Priest with his vestments portrayed the Son of the living God, the Supreme Priest: <note>original Greek: ἀναγκαῖον γὰρ ἦν τὸν Ἱερωμένον τῷ τοῦ κόσμου πατρὶ, παρακλήτῳ χρῆσθαι τελειοτάτῳ τὴν ἀρετὴν υἱῷ, πρὸς τὸ ἀμνησείαν ἁμαρτημάτων.</note> That is: *For it was necessary that he who was consecrated to the Father of the world, should have as a mediator His Son, most perfect in virtue, for the amnesty of sins.*

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the priestly breeches, moving from the physical requirements of the Old Testament law to its spiritual fulfillment in Jesus Christ. It contrasts the modesty required of Israelite priests with the lewdness of pagan worship and applies the concept of "covering shame" to the sinless nature of Christ.</meta>

# BREECHES.

entire world, brought offerings and religious services, necessarily to use the Son, through all virtues, as a perfect advocate or intercessor.

Subsequently, the entire company of priests <note>original: "Priesterrot" — 'rot' here refers to a formal troop or order of people, not decay.</note> had to carefully cover, keep covered, and preserve their private parts. This was done, without doubt, so that the onlookers might see and notice how great a distinction there was between the service of the God of Israel and that of Priapus and Baal Peor <note>Pagan deities often associated with fertility rites and public indecency.</note>.

It undoubtedly taught the priests that, while they were required to keep their external members covered and adorned, they were to conduct themselves chastely and honorably in all things.

<margin>Instruction for the Priests.</margin>
That in their hearts, eyes, and ears they were to tolerate nothing by which they could be defiled before God: that in all their actions, words, gestures, and conduct, they should be so modest and honorable that they would seem to provoke no lust or desire, nor even a single thought of impurity, in any of the onlookers. Not only were they to prevent desires and thoughts of vanity and impurity from arising and dwelling within their souls, but they were also to guard themselves closely, lest they should profane and defile God’s house and work through physical and spiritual whoredom, adultery, and unchastity.

<margin>Beginning of the application.</margin>
When I undertake to apply and transfer what has been said and handled thus far to the High Priest of our confession, Jesus—the only true and perfect Priest—I do not think anyone will expect me to assign a literal pair of linen under-breeches to Jesus. For everything in Him and His official performance is different and far more excellent: one must not seek it primarily in any garment outside of Him, but in Him Himself. Doing so will bring His excellence to light in the clearest and most powerful way.

a. No priest, though born of an honorable marriage and an undefiled bed, was born without the will of the flesh and of man: impurity was attached to him with and through his birth, and like his brothers, he had to be circumcised because of his impurity, as was previously heard from *Job 14*, *Psalm 51*, and *Job 3*.

But our priest’s birth, from a virgin by Divine overshadowing and not from the will of the flesh or of man, rendered Him sinless, spotless, holy, and pure, *Isaiah 7:14*, *Jeremiah 30:20, 21*, *Matthew 1:18, 20, 23*, *Luke 1:34, 35*.

b. And although the priests had to be pure, covering their private parts and ensuring above all that they gave no occasion for impure thoughts, lusts, words, and deeds; I nevertheless do not believe that they were all, in all cases, free from impure lusts, words, gestures, thoughts, and deeds, as they possessed the root of these things within themselves alongside other sinners.

<margin>Jesus the pure High Priest.</margin>
But our High Priest’s honor, chastity, and sinlessness in thoughts, lusts, words, and works are so well known and 

<column-break/>

praised from the Divine Bible that one may know that He—neither by imputation in Adam, nor by consent, nor by deed—had any fellowship with any sinful misconduct, *Psalm 16:10*, *Isaiah 53:11*, *Jeremiah 30:20, 21*, *2 Corinthians 5:21*, *Hebrews 7:26, 27*, *1 Peter 3:18*, *1 John 3:8*.

<margin>Priests not free from sin.</margin>
c. The High Priest and the common priests, though they kept their private parts covered by Divine order, nevertheless committed things, more or less, that were shameful; they needed the righteousness and holiness of the Messiah for their covering. Whatever they did or could do regarding Israel—whether they covered themselves or gave no occasion for internal and external impurity, or whether they sacrificed for the people, prayed, washed the people, and declared them clean—they could by no means remove the source and root of impurity from Israel's heart: they left them just as they had found them.

But besides the fact that our High Priest has nowhere transgressed, nor committed anything of which He need be ashamed, He has moreover sanctified Himself for His people as both Priest and offering, *John 17:19*, so that our sins—both innate and actual—might be covered and forgiven before God the judge, and that we might be washed and cleansed by His spirit in the fellowship and power of His blood. This results in the corruption, sins, and evil lusts no longer having dominion or reigning over us, *Isaiah 61:10*, *Romans 6:14*, *Luke 1:74, 75*, *1 Corinthians 6:11*, *1 John 1:7*, etc.

Yet if anyone wishes to be covered by this, if he wishes to be made clean by it, if he wishes to cover that which is shameful, etc., he must turn to this High Priest, lay hold of His righteousness, and strive to be found in Him: to put Him on: to become one spirit with Him: to let Him dwell in his heart through faith: *Isaiah 45:22*, *Isaiah 27:5*, *Philippians 3:9*, *Romans 13:14*, *1 Corinthians 6:17*, *Ephesians 3:17*.

Indeed, all the priests, even though they wore snow-white breeches, were impure before God; their breeches were stained by the flesh. These white breeches were a means of remembrance and admonition regarding their duty and efforts; they were a portrayal and a seal of the cleansing through the Messiah. They had to wash in that faith, praying for the spirit of de-sinning and cleansing. They had to wash and purify themselves in that faith, and see to it that they were defiled neither by themselves nor by others, and further ensure that they gave no occasion for the defilement of others. Certainly, none of us, though we may already be spiritual priests, *1 Peter 2:9*, can fitly belong to the generation mentioned in *Proverbs 30:12*, *that is pure in its own eyes, and yet is not washed from its filthiness*. *Isaiah 65:5*, *who say, "Keep to yourself, and do not come near me, for I am holier than you."* It will better suit us to confess, *Isaiah 64:6*, *James 3:2*, *1 John 1:8, 9*. It will suit us to keep ourselves and our members pure, and to cleanse ourselves daily, and to proceed toward holiness, *Isaiah 1:16*, *2 Corinthians 7:1, 2*, *1 Thessalonians 4:3*, *Hebrews 12*.

Ezekiel 36:25.* And just as it was unbefitting for a priest to cause offense to the people in the Tabernacle or Temple, or to show any sign of being under the influence of the service and conduct of Peor <note>original: "Peors dienft" — a reference to Baal-Peor, a pagan deity associated with shameful and lewd fertility rites in Numbers 25.</note>: so too is it unbefitting and harmful for us, as spiritual priests of the New Testament, to appear in God’s house with "exposed shame," <note>Referring to spiritual or physical indecency.</note> eyes full of adultery, a foul heart, and unchaste gestures. Modesty and decency, accompanied by recognizable signs of a chaste and honorable heart, wonderfully suit our priesthood.
