## BREAD, along with various names: UNLEAVENED BREAD; SHOWBREAD, etc. <note>original: "לחם, ἄρτος, panis" — Hebrew: lechem; Greek: artos; Latin: panis.</note>

<margin>Blessing located in the bread.</margin>
Bread <note>original: "לחם, ἄρτος"</note> is known to be composed with some distinction from wheat, rye, barley, etc.; after it is ground, it is mixed with water or other liquids, leavened or prepared with yeast, kneaded into a shape and lump of dough, mixed with some salt, and finally baked in a sufficiently hot oven. After this, it serves as a necessary, very useful, and suitable nourishment and food for mankind. It is the thing humans can least afford to miss, and it corresponds uniquely to our nature, being capable of tempering other foods and removing loathing <note>Bread was often seen as the "balancer" of a meal that prevented one from becoming sick of other richer foods.</note>. Truly, the Lord our God has placed a singular power and a hidden blessing within it. For this reason, Scripture speaks of a *stay and staff of bread, Psalm 105:16. Isaiah 3:1. Ezekiel 4, 5, and 14.* and it is a punishment when the Lord takes that away—whether we interpret this as that which a person eats but which does not satisfy or strengthen them, or as the Lord bringing extreme scarcity and lack of provisions upon a person, whereby they miss the strengthening power of bread.

<margin>Bread in a broad sense.</margin>
The word BREAD is not taken too narrowly in its naming within the Holy Scroll <note>The Bible.</note>, for it often signifies all kinds of provisions and needs, such as food, drink, clothing, etc. From this arise countless expressions: *Genesis 3:19. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread; Matthew 4:4. Man shall not live by bread alone, etc.; Matthew 6:11. Our daily bread, etc.; Luke 15:17. How many of my father’s hired servants have bread in abundance? etc.; Ezekiel 16:49. Fullness of bread, etc.*

<margin>Sayings regarding bread.</margin>
And when someone is invited to eat a morsel of bread, *Genesis 18. Judges 13. Ruth 2.* or when one is commanded to give their bread to the hungry, *Isaiah 58.* or when one eats with or of someone’s bread, *Psalm 41:10. John 13, etc.*—it is beyond dispute that it means something more than simple bread. In those instances, there was more than bread alone; it included a kind of friendship, hospitality, familiar social interaction, and care from a moved heart, and so forth.

Aben Ezra, commenting on *Proverbs 23:2,* says that <note>original: "לחם, lechem"</note> Bread signifies everything that belongs to human necessity, including food, drink, and clothing: because bread is, as it were, the foundation of a feast and of refreshment, and a summary of all foods.

<column-break/>

And Rabbi Levi on *Leviticus 21:17, 22.* <note>original: "כל סעودة נקרא לחם"</note> *Every meal is called bread:* and subsequently <note>original: "כל מאכל קרוי לחם"</note> *all food is called bread.*

<margin>Bread of adversity.</margin>
Again, other expressions regarding bread occur, such as *Isaiah 30:20. The bread of adversity:* whether this means they would eat their bread in distressing times with great sorrow and pain according to the state of the world; or that they would experience meager, expensive, and oppressive times, so that they, like someone in a prison or a besieged city, have a meager ration or can hardly obtain provisions. Or "bread of tears," *Psalm 80, etc.* to signify not only meager times but a miserable, very sorrowful state, such that all courage, desire, and joy vanish, because grievous sorrow is weighed out to them as their daily bread. And when distress, turmoil, plundering, and devastation by enemies sitting on their heels are meant, it is said figuratively: *to eat the bread of adversity with sorrow and trembling. 1 Kings 22. Ezekiel 2:18, 19.*

<margin>Canaanites as Israel's bread.</margin>
It sounds somewhat strange when one reads that the *Canaanites are called Israel's bread, Numbers 14:9.* With this, the saying of the royal harpist <note>King David.</note> seems to agree: *Psalm 14:4. Who eat up my people as they eat bread.* Regarding the first passage, it signifies that Israel should not fear but take heart, for they would snap up and subdue the enemies like a tasty dish, and be nourished and strengthened by their land and fortresses. And as for the second passage, it expresses the misfortune of the godly, who serve as "bread" to the wicked and restless, who not only oppress and persecute them with great lust, taste, and pleasure, but also swallow them up, root them out, and bring them down.

<margin>Bread of wickedness.</margin>
When the *bread of wickedness is spoken of, Proverbs 4:17,* it signifies either that they desire and perform wickedness and violence as tastily as food—being unable to rest until they have it, just as a hungry and thirsty person desires and consumes food and drink, so that it is like their very sustenance. In another sense, it was Christ’s food and drink to do the will of His heavenly Father, *John 4:34.* Or it means they do not rest until, like highwaymen, they have enriched themselves in a wicked and violent manner with another’s goods, and thus eat and drink, possess and use the goods they have obtained through violence and injustice.

<margin>Daily bread.</margin>
One also reads of daily bread, *Matthew 6:11 and Luke 11, etc.* <note>original: "ἄρτος ἐπιούσιος" — artos epiousios.</note> Regarding this, scholars dispute among themselves where the word comes from and what it means. Should it be understood as coming from <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ ἐπιέναι"</note> *to come upon, to follow, to approach*, much like <note>original: "מחר, Machar"</note> *the morrow, the future, the coming bread, the bread for the following day, or for our lifespan which might immediately follow*? Or should it be derived from *epi* <note>upon/for</note> and *ousia* <note>substance/essence</note>, meaning that which belongs to our physical essence—that is, what we need to remain in our being, strength, and activity; that which we cannot do without? Or does it come from *epion, epiousa, epion*: meaning as much as the "additional chief bread," the "added bread," being merely a throw-in, an extra gift, the least pre-

<meta>The catchword "voor-" at the bottom indicates the next page begins with "voorname" (prominent/principal).</meta>

# B R E A D.

<margin>Spiritual bread.</margin>
...principal bread, as a supplement to the bread of the soul—which is the most important—the Word, the Christ, the Divine grace, in the operation and strengthening of the Holy Spirit, *Matthew 4 and 6; John 6; Jeremiah 15:16; 1 Peter 2.* For without this, we cannot sanctify God’s name, come to Christ’s kingdom, or bring others to it, nor can we observe His will as subjects, nor remain steadfast against the wicked, etc.

<margin>Application of bread to the soul.</margin>
Because bread can nourish and satisfy, it is applied metaphorically to the soul, and is understood as that which can fulfill the soul's desires, remove its deficiency, and thus satisfy it. When there is mention of spending money and labor for that which is not bread and cannot satisfy, *Isaiah 55:2,* where previously water, wine, and milk were mentioned, it depicts the foolishness and vanity of the Jews and pagans. They uselessly wasted and spent all their understanding, effort, and even temporal powers and income in searching for the "heathen dross" of the moralists: self-righteousness from the works of the law, washings, purifications, manifold sacrifices, outward penances, abstinences, etc. All of these together could not cleanse the conscience, nor take away a single sin or stain of sin, but kept them occupied and obsessed with a completely fruitless and powerless way of life. Bread is taken to represent Christ, nourishing the heart, *Proverbs 9:5; John 6:23, 32, 35.*

<margin>Unleavened bread.</margin>
Thus one lives on unleavened bread, strictly observing the Lord's command regarding it, *Exodus 12:10, 15, 17, 20; and 13:6; and 29; Ezekiel 45:21; 1 Corinthians 5:7, 8,* in the eating of the Passover lamb, as well as throughout the entire festival, which for that reason is called the Feast of Unleavened Bread. From this arose much dispute between the Eastern and Western Churches as to whether Jesus served the Last Supper with leavened or unleavened bread—a dispute of not the slightest importance.

<margin>Dispute between the Eastern and Western Church.</margin>
It is certain—as will be said more fully under the words PASSOVER and PASCHAL FEAST—that Jewish men and women most scrupulously cleaned their houses and belongings, dishes, pots, pans, kneading troughs, etc., from the smallest to the greatest, so that no leaven might stick to them. They went so far as to search all cracks and crevices with a lit candle, and anything they found, even in appearance, as a remnant of leaven, they took outside and burned with fire, saying, it is said, these express words: *All the leaven and leavened bread, both what I have in my hand and what I have not been able to find, what I have leavened and not leavened, may all that remains of it be consumed and perish, like the dust of the earth.* The symbolic meaning of this will appear later in the following text.

<margin>Showbread.</margin>
Regarding the Showbread <note>original: "Toonbrooden"</note>, one reads of it in *Exodus 25; Numbers 4; Leviticus 24:7, 8, 9; Mark 2:26; Matthew 12; Luke 6; Hebrews 9:2.*

They are called: <term>Bread of the Faces</term> <note>original: "לחמי פנים" — *lachme pamin*</note>; <term>Bread of the Presence</term> <note>original: "ἄρτοι ἐνώπιοι" — *artoi enōpioi*</note>; <term>Bread before God</term> <note>original: "ἄρτοι ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ" — *artoi enōpion tou theou*</note>; <term>Bread of Presentation</term> <note>original: "ἄρτοι τῆς προθέσεως" — *artoi tēs protheseōs*</note>: bread of the faces, of the presence, "sight-bread," bread of presentation and showing, etc.

These Showbreads were prepared or made from fine flour, and as the Jews say, from very fine flour, finely sifted.

Some believe they had to be paid for by the Priests, but it seems to me that this is mis-

<column-break/>

understood: they had to be placed and prepared on behalf of the children of Israel, before the face of the Lord as an everlasting covenant, *Leviticus 24:8.* Therefore, it also seems to me that they were made from what all Israel had to contribute annually, head by head, *Exodus 30:13,* etc.

<margin>Bakers of the Showbread.</margin>
As for the mixers and bakers of these Showbreads, which were twelve in number, it seems to me they were not actually prepared by the Priests or Levites in general, but by the Kohathites. These twelve loaves (some say square, others round) were mixed, kneaded, and baked—not on the eve of the Sabbath, but as is judged, early on the Sabbath morning in the forecourt, where there was a bake-room—with oil or water (about which there is still dispute), and with some salt (which is not known for certain). While still warm, they were handed over to the Priests by these Levites. When the old showbread was removed every Sabbath, fresh and warm ones were put in its place on the golden show-table. Incense had to be placed by or on the loaves, it is said, in two golden bowls or platters, one golden bowl on each stacked row of six loaves. This incense was lit from the old showbread when the new was brought in, while the old showbread was for the service and use of Aaron and his sons, *Leviticus 2:16 and 24:7–9.*

Maimonides <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note> speaks on this matter as follows in *Tamid, Chapter 5*: *Four Priests entered: two of them had in their hands the two rows of bread, and two had in their hands the two bowls of incense. Before them, four Priests entered: two to take the rows of bread, and two to take the incense vessels that stood on the table. Those who carried them in stood on the North side, with their faces toward the South, and those who carried the bread out stood on the South side, with their faces toward the North. These took away the old bread, and the others put the new on the table.* Subsequently, he writes on the daily sacrifice, *Chapter 2*: *There were two of these incense bowls; in each was a handful of incense. Both had little rollers at the bottom so they could rest or stand on the table; and they were placed at the sides of the two rows of bread.*

These twelve loaves do not seem to me to have lain flat and spread out next to each other on the show-table, but were stacked in two heaps or rows, six upon six, between two stiff upright forks or rods to enclose them on both sides and keep them in balance so they would not slide off. Between each loaf—to prevent spoilage and mold, and indeed the stifling and overheating of the warm loaves—two split golden reeds were placed. All of this can be seen more closely in the illustrations by Witsius in *Miscellanea* and in Goeree’s *Jewish Republic*.

Regarding the exact quantity of fine flour for the weight of each showbread: each loaf is calculated at two-tenths of flour. Now, a tenth of an Ephah <note>An ancient Hebrew dry measure.</note> was a Gomer; thus, two Gomers for each loaf, totaling 24 Gomers for the twelve loaves. This makes 72 pounds of flour or baking material, which, when mixed with water or oil, could yield twelve loaves...

# B R E A D.

loaves, each weighing about 7 or 8 pounds.

These ancient "table-loaves" <note>original: "tafelbrooden," referring to the Showbread or Bread of the Presence</note> were for Aaron and his sons; they were required to eat them in the holy place, *Leviticus 24*. It is probable that they fell as a portion to those who were performing the service of the Lord throughout that entire week. See Goeree's *Republic of the Jews*, Part One, p. 359, etc. <note>Willem Goeree (1635–1711) was a Dutch author who wrote extensively on Jewish antiquities.</note>

<margin>Showbread eaten by David.</margin>
And although it was the property of the Priests, nevertheless, necessity and love seemed to set aside the law, since David, in his time of need, ate of the showbread. *1 Samuel 21. See Matthew 12, Mark 2, Luke 6.*

<margin>Transition to higher observations.</margin>
Let this now suffice regarding the literal sense; I shall proceed to higher matters.

In general, I can observe that through temporal and physical bread, one can see represented everything that feeds our souls: all means to practice fellowship with God, such as the bread of the Word of God's grace, the sacraments, and Christ Himself, preeminently. *John 6; 1 Corinthians 10:3, 4; Jeremiah 15:16; Romans 14:17; Hebrews 13:9.* <note>The original text cites "Job VI," but in this context, it clearly refers to the Gospel of John, chapter 6, the "Bread of Life" discourse.</note>

<margin>Christ, the bread of Life.</margin>
And in this regard, one can compare Christ to a grain of wheat—ground and baked in His suffering of soul and body by the fire of His love and the wrath of God—without which He could not feed our souls for eternal life; calling Himself bread, and indeed bread par excellence. *John 6.*

This Jesus, with His righteousness, must be accepted by those who hunger for His righteousness and must be "eaten" through faith. *Matthew 5, John 6.*

When a union with us is brought about—an attachment, a nourishment, a removal of hunger, life, strength, and activity—and the soul is fulfilled in its desire, then Christ dwells in the hearts through faith. *Ephesians 3:17, 1 Corinthians 6:7.* He who clings to the Lord is one spirit with Him; hunger flees (*John 6*), for from His fullness one receives grace upon grace (*John 1*). He gives something that can truly satisfy (*Isaiah 55, Proverbs 9*), so that they live, are active, and remain in grace to endure many heavy difficulties. *Galatians 2:20, 2 Corinthians 12:9.*

As for what follows regarding leavened and unleavened bread, it is well known that the Lord desired the Passover to be eaten without leaven—that is, unleavened bread—in likeness of the Jews' exodus from Egypt, when they had no time to leaven the bread and let it ferment, as everything occurred with the greatest haste.

More on this in the treatise on the Feast of Passover.

Nothing that was fermented or could ferment was allowed to be found in or near the offerings (*Exodus 23:10 and 24:25*), and therefore no honey was added to the offerings.

The great Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar.</note> cannot well hide that this specific commandment runs counter to the superstitious customs of the nearby Pagan peoples, who offered leavened or fermented bread to their Gods and chose sweet things as a gift for the Gods. And so Maimonides <note>The preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher (1138–1204).</note> writes in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "more Nevochim"</note>, *Part III, Chapter 46*: God commanded in *Exodus 23 and 34* that honey and leavened bread should be kept away from the sanctuary because idolaters offered nothing but raised bread and chose the sweetest things for their gifts, mixing honey

<column-break/>

among the offerings. But more on this later under the words HONEY and PASSOVER.

It is certain that Christ may be compared to unleavened bread, as being without the ferment and leaven of corruption, sin, contamination, malice, pride, and wickedness. *Isaiah 53:11; Hebrews 7:26; 1 Peter 1:18, 19 and 2:22; 2 Corinthians 5:21; etc. Psalm 40:9; John 8:46.*

<margin>The Requirements of the Passover.</margin>
It is clear enough that the great Apostle regarded our Savior as the antitype <note>A reality that fulfills a previous symbol or "type."</note> of the Passover (*1 Corinthians 5*). And since the Passover feast had to be celebrated with unleavened bread (*Exodus 12, etc.*), he desires that in the days of the New Testament, the Passover shall be celebrated by purging out the old leaven and, with Jesus as a "new dough," keeping fellowship in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

Thus, one shall put away the old leaven of the "shadow service" <note>Refers to Old Testament rituals seen as "shadows" of Christ.</note>: putting off and casting out the leaven of corruption and sin, which makes the heart swell, agitates the blood, causes the passions to rise and boil, through which one falls and bursts out into hatred, envy, wrath, greed for revenge, puffed-up pride, strife, brawling, and many scandalous sins and deeds contrary to love and godliness. One shall kill and crucify sin and the "old man" <note>The sinful nature.</note>; put off the body of sin and put on the "new man" (*Colossians 3:5; Ephesians 4; Galatians 5:24*); not offer the limbs to the service of sin (*Romans 6:12, 13*); cleanse oneself from the contamination of flesh and spirit (*2 Corinthians 7:1, 2*); pursue holiness (*Hebrews 12:21*); possess one's vessel in purity and honor (*1 Thessalonians 4*); and serve God with a pure heart and a clear love. Putting away hatred, envy, wrath, anger, and contentiousness, one shall practice the truth in love and perfect one another in love. If anyone desires, they may look further into what I have noted on *1 Corinthians 5*.

### BRIDE, BRIDEGROOM, WEDDING FEAST, or MEAL; WEDDING GARMENT, etc. <note>original: "νύμφιος (bridegroom), חתן (bridegroom), sponsus (bridegroom). כלה (bride), νύμφη (bride), sponsa (bride). etc."</note>

One would have to have completely emptied their understanding, or willfully closed their high mind to the Word of life, to not know that the fellowship between the Son of God (the lover of the soul) and the Church—indeed, the individual faithful members of the church—is presented through various symbols, idioms, and parables in the Holy Scriptures; and among others by the titles of Bridegroom, Bride, Husband, Woman, or Wife; Wedding, Wedding Feast, Meal, Clothing, Ornamental Garments, etc. *Song of Solomon 4:10, 11, 12; Hosea 2:18, 19; Matthew 9:15; Ephesians 5; Psalm 45; Isaiah 44; etc. 2 Corinthians 11:2; Revelation 19:9 and 21:9.*

In order to briefly record the most remarkable aspects of this state, which is as secret as it is spiritual and hidden, one may observe that both the Heavenly Father and His Son have, from before the ages of eternity, determined by way of a covenant and a counsel of peace to give Christ a certain heritage out of sinful and damnable humanity, though they were strangers to Christ. This was done to unite this heritage most closely with Himself in time, as His wife, under the condition of having assumed a nature equal to hers, the—

# B R I D E.

to purchase and redeem her through his blood: offering and giving himself to and for her; desiring to be accepted by her through faith, working through love, as Lord, husband, and bridegroom, with the intent that she should surrender herself entirely to his love, his presence, his guidance, and his protection in obedience: which was confirmed with an oath, *Zechariah 6:12, 13; Hosea 2:18, 19; Isaiah 54; Hebrews 6, 7, and 9.* This was formerly made known, promised, and sketched out, but with Jesus' incarnation, his obedience in suffering unto death, the payment of the purchase price and ransom, and the giving of his Spirit as a pledge of love, it was initially begun and continued, and shall be fully completed in the dwelling of the heavenly Father above, *Luke 1:74, 75; 1 Corinthians 6:20; Titus 2:14; Isaiah 41:14 and 54; Ephesians 5:25; 2 Corinthians 1:20; Romans 8; Ephesians 1 and 4, etc.*

She who shall fall as a portion to the bridegroom is called a stranger to him, *Ephesians 2:12*, and to cleave to his wife, Christ left the house of his heavenly Father and came to the earth; yet not to remain away from it entirely and forever, but to return there again and to take his bride and wife to himself, he going before to prepare her dwelling place, she following him and being taken up to where he is. Christ gives himself for and to her; she accepts him through faith, submits herself to him, and gives herself in return to him, as will be noted further on.

In marriage, those who were two become one, *Genesis 2:23, 24; Matthew 19:5; Ephesians 5; 1 Corinthians 6:16*, one flesh, as one flesh, being solely each other's property, for each other's service and physical fellowship, without being permitted to unite with others; the one having right, claim, and power over the other's body, to the exclusion of others.

<margin>The union of Jesus with the Church.</margin>
So it is between Jesus and the church, or the congregation of the living God: there is not only the shared nature which Jesus assumed, *Hebrews 2 and 4*, but also what concerns the soul, which is like a root through cleaving to him in faith, working through love, *1 Corinthians 6:16, 17.* Through faith Christ dwells in the heart, *Ephesians 3:17*; in this heart the Spirit of Christ lives and reigns. The will of both is one and directed toward one goal; for her, Jesus is everything: they are animated by the same Spirit, and that Spirit makes the union unbreakable: *Song of Solomon 6:3, "I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine; he browses among the lilies."* See my notes on *1 Corinthians 6:16, 17; Witsius in The Creed, page 432; Campegius Vitringa, Observations, Part 3, page 68, etc.* <note>Herman Witsius (1636–1708) and Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) were influential Dutch Reformed theologians.</note>

This is expressed by the vine and the branches, *John 15:2-5*; the head and the members; the root and the branches: *1 Corinthians 12, etc.; Ephesians 4:4, 5, 6.*

In marriage, because the Bridegroom and Bride bind themselves together, the woman loses her family and tribal name and takes on that of the Bridegroom. Eve was called "Woman" <note>original: "man-ninne," a Dutch construction mirroring the Hebrew *Ishah* (woman) derived from *Ish* (man)</note> after the Man, *Genesis 2.* The people of the Lord boast and appeal to the fact that they are called by the Lord's name, *Jeremiah 19:9.* The congregation, as one body, is also called "Christians" after the head, Christ, and as his many and distinct members, *Acts 11:26; 1 Corinthians 12:12.*

<column-break/>

And the Bride, the church, does not only take on the name of the Bridegroom, but also his status. If he is God’s son, she becomes the Lord’s daughter; if Jesus is King, she is his Queen; she is Priest and Prophet, etc., with, in, and through him, and anointed and made capable by his Spirit and oil, *Psalm 45; Isaiah 22:9, etc.; Revelation 1:6.*

Through marriage, she enters into the right to and the actual enjoyment of the Bridegroom's goods. She receives everything from his fullness, *John 1:16*; everything is her property, *1 Corinthians 3:22, 23*; she is a co-heir, *Romans 8:17, etc.*

<margin>The purification of the Bride by the Bridegroom.</margin>
The Bridegroom, for the sake of the most intimate unity, assumes the nature of the church, the Bride, *Hebrews 2 and 4*, and he knows what is sweet and sour, high and low, *1 Timothy 3:16.* It is true that the Bridegroom is *without the guilt of sin* and without blemish, *Hebrews 7:26; 1 Peter 1:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21*; however, since the Bride is burdened with both, he takes everything upon himself out of love, in such a way that he removes and pays off the guilt of sin, and washes away and purifies the stains through his blood and Spirit, *1 Peter 2:22-24; Isaiah 53; John 1:29; Zechariah 2:8; Isaiah 63:9; 1 John 1:7.*

Indeed, he enters into the deserved suffering for her; and he has a sensitive compassion for her pains, *Isaiah 53; Matthew 17:38; Acts 9:4; Zechariah 2:8; Isaiah 63:9.*

In this state of the Bridegroom and the Bride, one may imagine that there is mutual love—pure, strong, and inextinguishable—which allows no bitter strife, no rivals, or other suitors.

And to speak somewhat more distinctly for some regarding the love of the Bridegroom for his Bride, one should make these observations.

<margin>Observations.</margin>
a. The Bridegroom Jesus has loved her from eternity, before the Bride existed, and while she was in a very miserable and wretched state; he showed this in the eternal counsel <note>referring to the *pactum salutis*, a theological concept of a pre-temporal agreement between the Father and Son</note>, and the contract of his <term>surety-vow</term> <note>original: "borggelofte," referring to Christ's legal commitment to pay the debt of sin</note> and intercession.

b. To obtain her, he humbled and emptied himself in love, became her brother and kinsman *Isaiah 7:14; Jeremiah 31; Psalm 22:23; Philippians 2; Hebrews 2:4-11, 12, 14-17.*

c. He has shown his love powerfully and inimitably by placing himself for her and in her stead, fulfilling everything, bearing the punishment for sin, and purchasing and acquiring her for himself. *Psalm 22 and 69:40; Isaiah 53:4, 5-7; Daniel 9:26; Romans 5:4-8, 10; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Acts 20:21; Titus 2:14; 1 Peter 1:18, 19.*

d. This love knows no breaking. *Hosea 2:18, 19; John 12:1; Romans 8:38, 39.*

e. This love makes the Bride wonderfully beautiful and precious in Jesus’s eyes. *Song of Solomon 1:2, 3, 4; Isaiah 62:3-12.*

f. And it works out the utmost security, guarding, and preservation of her. *Isaiah 41:10-14 and 49:15, 16; Zechariah 2:10; Matthew 16; John 10; 1 Peter 1:15.*

The *Church-bride loves her Bridegroom*;
1. With a heartfelt, sincere love. *Psalm 18:3; Proverbs 23.*
2. With a grasping, embracing, holding, and clinging love. *Isaiah 27:5; Song of Solomon 3:4; 1 Corinthians 6:17.*
3. With a love of contentment, satisfied with him alone, and despising everything else compared to him. *Psalm 73; Song of Solomon 8; Philippians 3:8; 1 Peter 2:7.*
4. A constant love. *Psalm 44:18; Song of Solomon 8:6, 7; Matthew 16:24; Romans 8:38, 39; Revelation 2:10.*
5. Her love goes out so strongly with high esteem for Jesus that she cannot tolerate, and strikes as with a ban, those who do not love Jesus. *1 Corinthians 16:22.*

I admit, it is a very unequal marriage. Between the Bridegroom and the Bride, there is a very great difference in nature, status, descent, virtues, possessions, etc. It has well been judged that like with like, regarding a marriage, made for the best union,

> *Ovid, Book of Epistles IX, Heroides.* <note>Publius Ovidius Naso, Roman poet</note>
>
> *How poorly unequal oxen come to the plow:* <note>original Latin: "Quam malè inæquales veniunt ad aratra juvenci"</note>
> *So is the lesser bride pressed by the great husband.* <note>original Latin: "Tam premitur magno conjuge nupta minor"</note>
> *It is not an honor, but a burden likely to harm those who bear it:* <note>original Latin: "Non honor est, sed onus species læsura ferentes"</note>
> *If you wish to marry fitly, marry an equal.* <note>original Latin: "Si qua voles aptè nubere, nube pari"</note>

->That is:<-

> *No oxen can the plow, if they be unequal, endure.*
> *So is a lesser woman crushed by a greater man.*
> *It is no glory, but a semblance of worse suffering.*
> *Who wishes to marry well, marry one who is her equal.*

But here, between the Bridegroom and Bride, no displeasure, contempt, withdrawal, or divorce is to be expected, because he loves the Bride with a preventing <note>proactive or "prevenient" love that comes before any merit on her part</note> love, moved with compassion over her state, to glorify her in his fellowship and make her beautiful, and not strictly to become more glorious or happy etc. through marriage with her.

The Bridegroom is the son of the King of all kings: equal to God himself, the radiance of God’s glory, *Job 1 and 5; Hebrews 1; Philippians 2;* he is the most beautiful, *Psalm 65:3,* full of gifts and graces *Jeremiah 11:2; Psalm 45,* without faults or failings, *Isaiah 53:11; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 7:26,* the Lord and heir of all things, *Hebrews 1.*

She whom Jesus chooses as his Bride is in herself of low descent: especially the Gentiles after their separation from the holy seed, *Genesis 10; Ezekiel 16;* and at best, made of sinful, trifling, and damnable dust and ashes—mere flesh.

The Bride is in herself unclean, *Ezekiel 16; Isaiah 64;* dead through sins and loathsome *Isaiah 1; Ephesians 2;* and furthermore, before her heavenly calling and being brought to Christ, full of all kinds of sins and vices, *Titus 1:16 and 3:3;* for the rest, she possessed no true goods or essential riches, but she was poor, blind, naked, and full of debt, *Job 1:21; 1 Timothy 6:7; Matthew 16:26; Revelation 3; 2 Corinthians 8.*

For this marriage, she is prepared as a wife like a pure virgin, *2 Corinthians 11,* by the <term>companions</term> <note>original: "speelnoten," referring to bridesmaids or wedding attendants</note>, Prophets, Apostles, Shepherds, and Teachers, who are also friends and guests, and the Bride in another respect, *John 3:29; Psalm 45:15; Matthew 22; Proverbs 9,* and she has Bridal garments.

The Wedding garment of the Bride was usually white, a <term>wedding cloak</term>. <note>original Greek: "γαμικὴ χλαμυς" (gamikē chlamys)</note> *Aristophanes, The Birds, line 1692; Carpzovius, tenth Academic Disputation § 5; Euripides, Alcestis Act 4.*

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the "Bride" (the Church), shifting from the Bridegroom’s character to the nature of the Wedding Feast and the formal definition of the spiritual marriage between Christ and His people. # BRIDE.

<margin>The wedding feast.</margin>
The wedding feast takes place in the lower house of the church on earth <note>the "church militant," or the community of believers currently living in the world</note>, where both the good and the wicked are present, both with and without the wedding garment. *Matthew 22; Proverbs 8.*

<margin>Food and table.</margin>
The food and the table are also, in a certain sense, Christ the altar, insofar as He shares the fruits and power of His suffering with the soul for its life and joy. *John 5 and 6; Isaiah 55:2; Isaiah 12; Psalm 26:3; Psalm 23:1, etc.; Jeremiah 31:25.* Furthermore, this refers to the Word and the sacraments.

Jesus, the Husband and Bridegroom of the church, sows the seed of the Word into hearts, where it springs up and bears fruit. She was once filled with unrighteousness, but in this state, she is filled with the fruits of righteousness. *Philippians 1 and 4:8; Psalm 92; 2 Peter 3:18.* In her womb, or in her midst, both Jews and Gentiles are born through the seed of the Word. *Isaiah 54; Galatians 4; Isaiah 8:18; Hebrews 2:13.*

This state of grace is like a betrothal and a pre-wedding ceremony, accompanied by a "living away" from the Lord. *2 Corinthians 5.* Much frailty and imperfection remain, leaving the soul to look out, sigh, and long for the most intimate and perfect communion with the Lover of the soul. *Psalm 42, 63, and 74; Philippians 1; 2 Corinthians 5; Romans 8; Revelation 22.* However, this shall be changed into a completed marriage and a relocation into the house of the Heavenly Father. *John 14:2, 3.*

I shall here insert something from Professor Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian known for his work on prophecy and parables</note>, from his *Treatise on the Gospel Parables* <note>original: "Tract. de Evangel. Parab."</note>, concerning the Royal Wedding in *Matthew 22*, page 452, etc.

§. IX. This so great and mighty King has prepared a wedding feast for His Son. This wedding presupposes a marriage that has been entered into. This mystery must and can only be explained from Holy Scripture. For Scripture teaches us that there is a certain contract between these two persons of the Deity, the Father and the Son. According to this contract, it was the duty of that person whom the Holy Scripture calls the Son of the Father to essentially buy back all the elect from among sinners as free men. This was done through the ransom of His death and suffering, which He would undergo in His human nature, to make them His own and bring them near to Him, out of the power of Satan and sin, and to unite them to Himself through His Spirit, through true love and the obedience of faith. This multitude of the elect sometimes appears under the name of the Church and the Kingdom of Jesus Christ; and sometimes, and quite often, under the symbol of the **Bride**, or His wife. *Psalm 45:10-16;* and the *Song of Solomon* in its entirety; *John 3:29; Revelation 21:9; 2 Corinthians 11:2.* This occurs for clear and weighty reasons, which we shall only briefly state. For, 1. there is a true union between Christ and the Church through mutual love, with which Christ loves His congregation and she loves Him most fervently. *Ephesians 5:25.* 2. Yet, in that practice of love, there is such a relationship between Christ and the Church that the Church is subject to Christ, just as a wife is subject to her husband according to the order God established in the world after the Fall. She, who lacks every good thing and every salvation, desires the completion of her happiness from Christ alone, and expects it from Him, toward whom the desire of the Church goes out.

And since she also lacks help and counsel, she recognizes Jesus Christ as her only advocate and protector; she regards the law of Christ as

<column-break/>

the rule for all her actions. This subjection of the Church to Jesus Christ—since it consists in faith and love for Jesus—nevertheless has nothing difficult about it; on the contrary, it is sweet and pleasant. *Ephesians 5:23.* 3. The union that exists between Christ and the Church is a marriage union, that is, a voluntary union. By this, two persons, man and woman, between whom there was no natural bond or relationship, come into communion and society through a voluntary contract under certain conditions. Such is the union between Christ and the Church: Christ offers His fellowship to the elect, but under the condition that they are subject to Him in love. *Jeremiah 31:31, 32; Ezekiel 16:4.* 4. It is an inseparable union, like that of spouses; that which is once bound in this way cannot be loosened again. He who loves Jesus Christ, He loves unto the end. *John 13:1.* 5. The effects of this union are the same as those of a completed marriage. The joining of man and woman brings forth children (if God gives His blessing). This is also the fruit of the union between Jesus Christ and the Church. The Church is made fruitful by Jesus Christ, her husband, through His Word and Spirit, and brings forth abundant children in whom the image of Christ shines forth. *Psalm 87:4.* Now, she who is the wife of Jesus Christ also remains His bride because of the supreme purity and chastity of Jesus Christ in the practice of true love toward her; for it is a spiritual love, which is chaste, holy, and pure, defiling neither the soul nor the body.

§. X. This marriage between Jesus Christ was entered into and completed when He, being revealed in the flesh according to the promises, began to gather for Himself a people from Judaism who would be called the people and the congregation of Christ. For that is very clearly concluded from this parable, as well as from all those passages cited from the Old and New Testaments speaking of this marriage of Christ and the Church. Indeed, it is also evident from the matter itself: for no church could be called the wife of Christ (as the Christ)—that is, the church of the Son of God, the Mediator of the human race—before Christ (as such) existed in reality. This is not contradicted by the fact that Holy Scripture also presents the covenant established with the Jewish people under the symbol of a Marriage. *Ezekiel 16:8; Hosea 1:2, 3, 4.* For that marriage of God with the people was a "type" <note>a prophetic symbol or foreshadowing</note>, and God’s Son was the typical husband of the Old Testament church. In that marriage, there was a kind of prelude to that true marriage of Christ with His church, which is clearly made known in *Jeremiah 31:32* and *Hosea 2:19.*

<margin>Spiritual wedding.</margin>
§. XI. This spiritual wedding has now been celebrated, since the Son of God has sealed and confirmed His marriage covenant—that is, the covenant of grace of the New Testament—by a certain pledge <note>original: "onderpant," meaning a down payment or security deposit</note> of His love: the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which were shared with the Church after His ascension. For in the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the Church has had the love of God and of Christ poured out upon and into His true church. *Romans 5:5.*

§. XII. And what else shall the wedding feast—which the parable says honored the ceremony of this wedding celebration—signify, but the communion in the goods of grace which God offers to the sinner through faith in Jesus Christ? For the communion of those goods, especially the righteousness of Christ, is very often...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Bride" (the Church) and her preparation for the spiritual marriage. It specifically explores the metaphor of the Wedding Feast and the requirements for the Church to be fully "ready" for her Bridegroom, Christ.</meta>

# BRIDE.

*The Holy Scriptures, both of the Old and New Testaments, are presented under the image of a banquet at which many guests are seated, with a great abundance of all desirable foods. Proverbs 9:1; Isaiah 25:6, 7; Psalm 23:5, 6; Isaiah 55:1; and 65:13, 14; Matthew 8:11; Revelation 19:9. Indeed, because communion in the blessings of grace could not be depicted under a more fitting or illustrious symbol, the Lord willed that this communion in the church of the New Testament should be represented under this same display of a banquet, which is held in the <term>Holy Supper</term> <note>the Sacrament of Communion</note>. Through this seal of the covenant, the communion of the righteousness of Christ and of all the blessings of grace leading to joy and eternal life is sealed to all who believe.*

§. XIII. *This banquet has been prepared by the Father, the King, for the sake of His Son, the Bridegroom and husband. This is because the fundamental principle of the entire <term>Covenant of Grace</term> <note>the theological framework of God's promise of salvation through Christ</note>, with all its outcomes and consequences, according to the clearest teaching of Holy Scripture, must be sought in the will and purpose of the Father. From Him—that is, from God the Father—you are in Jesus Christ. 1 Corinthians 1:30. The Father has given a wife to His Son: a church, that is, the elect from among the Jews, the first bride of Jesus Christ. The Father has prepared a banquet for that church through the death of His Son. By the will of the same Father, friends and guests are invited to come and celebrate this wedding. In a word: from the Father, according to the Covenant of Grace, come both the Christ and the church.*

Regarding the "dishes" or blessings served, one may read in Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian</note> page 459, etc., and page 476, etc.

Also regarding the wedding garment, the *most elegant and best—namely white, Ecclesiastes 9:8—signifying the spiritual ornament fitting for the new dispensation. Galatians 3:27; Colossians 3:10; 1 Peter 3:4. This is the obedience and righteousness of Christ, granted and <term>imputed</term> <note>legally credited to one's account</note> to the naked and deformed sinner through faith. Revelation 3:18. See Vitringa page 478, along with the additions by Mr. d'Outrein <note>Johannes d'Outrein, another influential Dutch divine</note>, which are excellent.*

<margin>Seven days appointed for the wedding.</margin>
It was formerly the custom to hold a wedding for seven days, a continuous feast, yet greater on the first and last days. Thus the Feast lasts through the seven time-periods of the New Testament, but the first and last periods are the most distinguished and filled with the greatest joy. See the wedding of Jacob, *Genesis 29:27*; of Samson, *Judges 14*; Selden, *On Natural Law and the Law of Nations*, Book 5, Chapter 5; Heidegger, *History of the Patriarchs*, part 1, Book 15, etc. See also Lampe on *Psalm 45*, page 172, etc. Perhaps I shall express more regarding this matter in my sermons on *Revelation 21 to 22:6.*

When one pays proper attention to the vision in *Revelation 21:22* concerning the state of the Church-Bride, she is found in her perfect attire and ornament, prepared and ready to be brought by her Bridegroom from the lower house into the upper house, and to be presented to the Father.

Yet, when I observe the current condition of the church today, I do not yet perceive in any way that the Church-Bride is in a state to be taken up into the Father's upper house.

If someone asks me: what is still lacking? And what kind of ornament do you still expect for the further perfection of her state?

I give as my declaration and answer that something is still missing, both outwardly and inwardly, before the church in power and on firm ground shall

<column-break/>

be able to expect the fulfillment of her prayer and soulful sighing: *Come, Lord Jesus; yes, come quickly.*

<margin>Ornament of the church.</margin>
A. The church must still receive an external splendor and ornament arriving from without; in which ornament and splendor I understand the following to consist:
1. The multitude of people—of the great and the small, the noble, and the chosen of the people—in whom the king's glory and splendor consist, as does that of the queen. *Proverbs 14:28; Psalm 2:8, 9, 10, 11, 12; Isaiah 49, 60, etc.; Revelation 21:24, 25, 26, 27.*
2. For which purpose the Lord must once again lay His hand upon the Jews for their quickening and resurrection: with which shall be united the fullness of the Gentiles; and the closest union with these quickened Jews shall be observed, according to *Deuteronomy 32:21; Psalm 102:14, 15, 16; Isaiah 11:59; Ezekiel 27:1 to 14; Hosea 2:3; Romans 9 and 11:11, 12, 25, 26, 27.*
3. Furthermore, the truth, righteousness, and innocence of the oppressed, slandered, and suppressed Church-Bride must be made manifest through such judgments, plagues, and punishments falling upon the kingdom of the Beast and its supporters, as shall befit the God of judgments and His Son as a jealous husband and righteous judge. *Psalm 68:22 and 110:6; 2 Thessalonians 2:8; Revelation 18:21, 22.*

B. *And as for the internal form, splendor, and true beauty of the Church-Bride, it seems to me that quite a bit is still lacking there; and this can be presented distinctly in this manner:*
a. I look forward—if I may say so—to a much greater light of knowledge to be obtained:
1. Through a much stronger zeal and godly searching, both of the prophecies and of careful attention to the signs of the times. *Daniel 12:4; Matthew 16:3.*
2. Through the clear, lively, and practical realization that many prophecies and promises are about to receive their fulfillment. One generally views matters much better from behind than from the front; one sees the matter more clearly when it is present.
3. Through internal enlightenment, or the outpouring of the spirit of knowledge and wisdom in an extraordinary measure: so that all the children of the Covenant shall be endowed with a vast measure of knowledge. At the very least, I expect it, because I do not notice that as of yet the promises—being so great and so broad—have their fulfillment. *Isaiah 30:26; 54:12, 13; 60:2, 3; 65:20; Daniel 12:4.*
b. *And then I expect that from that light of knowledge, sanctified to the will, there shall be born a special light, ornament, and shine of holiness and unfeigned godliness, insofar as one...*

# BRIDE.

In substance, one can say of the glory and luster of the church: which I again understand as follows;
1. That with the purification of the <term>threshing floor</term> <note>a biblical metaphor for judgment and the separation of the righteous from the wicked</note>, *Revelation 21:8-21*, etc., there shall be joined a singular self-confirmation toward purity of heart and holiness of conduct: and that the pure, blank truth shall be found upon the lips of all the city's citizens, etc. *Isaiah 33:24 and 35:8.*
2. And that there being found peace and rest, one heart, and one mind, tears, mourning, weeping, persecutions, divisions, and schisms, human authority and titles, and such like, shall by no means be heard of as before, *Isaiah 11:6, 7-9 and 54, and 65:25. Revelation 21, etc.*

Suppose also that one of us might live when this desired and glorious state of adornment and flowering of the church were seen on earth. Even then he would experience that something would still be lacking, because

<margin>The state of the church on earth is imperfect.</margin>
1. Something is always lacking here below, *1 Corinthians 13:9, 10. Philippians 3:21.*
2. The perfectly satisfying good and portion is for the <term>upper house of the Father</term> <note>a reference to Heaven</note>, *Psalm 16:11, and Psalm 17:15, and Psalm 31. Romans 8:18. 2 Corinthians 4:17. 1 John 3:2.*
3. Furthermore, the bodies' humility, frailty, mortality, and corruptibility must be cast off and exchanged, *1 Corinthians 15:42, 43. etc. Philippians 3:21.*
4. Which, being rightly observed, can seem strange to no upright Christian—who has a foretaste of the good of the Father's upper house—that he perceives so many a sob and hot sigh of the soul for the good in the upper house, *Psalm 42:2, 3, and 63:2, and 64:3, 4. Romans 8:19, 20, 21. etc. 2 Corinthians 5:2-4. Philippians 1:22, 23. Revelation 22:17.*

Everything that is desirable and fit to fill the soul with such love that she desires to become the Bride of Jesus is in and with Him: for with Him is:
1. Beauty above that of the children of men: as God, God’s Son, image, and reflection: as God-man: Prophet, Priest, King, <term>Surety</term> <note>one who takes legal responsibility for another's debt; in this context, Christ's atonement for sins</note>, Mediator, etc. *Psalm 45:3. Job 1:5-10. Hebrews 1:7. etc.*
2. With Him is gentleness, peace-lovingness, the most sensitive compassion, and the sweetest and softest treatment and invitation, *Isaiah 45:22 and 55:1, 2. Matthew 11:28, 29. Isaiah 42:2, 3. Matthew 12:20. Revelation 3:18. etc.*
3. With Him is the highest nobility, the greatest lineage, Divine and Royal: being Himself the highest of all powers, *Isaiah 9:5 and 40:5-15-22-23. John 5:10. Matthew 3:17. Revelation 17:19; 14 and 16. Colossians 1:13-15, 16, 17. etc. Hebrews 1:4, 5, 6. etc.*
4. His wealth and power are incomprehensible and indescribable, *Psalm 8:6, 7, 8 and 24 and 72 and 50. Romans 8. 1 Corinthians 3. Hebrews 1:1.*

First, Jesus must be known as such, and the soul persuaded that to choose, will, seek, embrace, and possess Him, will make her

<column-break/>

state of happiness complete. Otherwise, "unknown remains unloved," <note>original: "onbekent, blyft onbemint," a common Dutch proverb</note> *Isaiah 53:11. Job 4 and 17:3. Philippians 3:8, 9, 10.*

Which having arisen and been born in the heart, then

<margin>Union of the soul with Jesus.</margin>
1. She turns herself, then she runs to Jesus, grasps Him through faith and love, and holds Him fast, *Isaiah 27:5 and 45:22. John 1:12. Philippians 3:7. Song of Solomon 3:4.*
2. Then she awakens love with love, and repays love with love, *Psalm 18. Proverbs 23. Song of Solomon 8. Matthew 22.*
3. Then she rejoices in Him and with Him, and with His love alone she is content, *Psalm 73:25, 26. Song of Solomon 1:2, 3. Isaiah 61:10. Luke 1:2. Philippians 3:4, 5.*
4. She accepts Jesus as her Husband, Head, Lord, and King: she willingly stands under Him; she loves, fears, honors, serves, and obeys Him in everything with love and humble submission, *Psalm 2:11, 12. Psalm 29 and 95:6, 7. John 3:16-36. 2 Corinthians 5. Ephesians 5:2.*
5. And she longs to be led by her Bridegroom into the innermost upper chamber of the Bridegroom's Father, *2 Corinthians 5. Philippians 1. Revelation 22.*

### ROARING, <note>original Hebrew: רגש (Regesh: "commotion/throng"), Greek: ἐμβριμάομαι (embrimaomai: "to groan/snort with anger"), Latin: fremere ("to roar/growl")</note>.

THE ROARING is properly characteristic of the sea and great waters when they are moved very strongly by the winds or other causes, so that they are tempestuous, uplifted, and incensed, striking and flinging the billows against rocks, cliffs, shores, and ships; stirring the sea strongly, causing silt, mud, foam, and spray. *1 Chronicles 16. Psalm 46:4 and 65:2 and 93:3, 4 and 96:11 and 98:7. etc.*

Since a mighty enemy in his processions—with his horses, chariots, trumpets, drums, and hostilities—causes a very great movement with the voice of the multitude, a great clamor and strong noise, and is terrifying in the first and hottest rage, overflowing everything: so it seems to me that by this, not unaptly, the power, the violence, and the efforts of the enemies are depicted—both against the cultivated and fruitful earth, the church, and the tossing little ship on the sea-waters of Heathendom, as generally of this wild world: also against Babel. This roaring also represents the spiritual, as appearing in this way by metaphor, in figure and image, the efforts of the dragon and the tyrannies of Heathendom, together raging and conspiring against the church, *Psalm 46:4 and 65. etc.* just as the nations rushing forth hostiley are compared to this. *Jeremiah 6:23 and 50:42 and 51:55 against Babel.*

Just as the church, standing firm in the Lord, mocks all the violence of the enemies, which is stilled by Him. *Psalm 65:8. Revelation 15:2 and 17:15. Psalm 46:4.* Such a violent, overflowing, and devastating roaring of war is presented to us by Virgil <note>a famous Roman poet from the 1st century BCE</note> in the Second Book of the *Aeneid* <note>an epic poem telling the story of Aeneas, a Trojan who travelled to Italy</note>, where he lets himself be heard thus:

### ROARING, <term>שאג — sha'ag</term>, <term>געה — ga'ah</term>, <term>μυκάομαι — mykaomai</term>, <term>mugio — to low/bellow</term>, <term>βρυχάομαι — brychaomai</term>, <term>μυκάω — mykaō</term>, <term>ὠρύομαι — ōryomai</term>.

ROARING belongs properly to lions and their kind, as one can know both from the writers on the nature of animals and from the Holy Scrolls: which they do particularly when they are hungry or enraged, seeking or devouring booty and prey: through which sound they strike terror into men and beasts, <term>Psalm 104:21; Isaiah 31:4; Judges 14:5.</term> This is also the reason that when roaring is attributed either to God or to men, one finds that the lion is mentioned alongside it. And since this subject will be relevant under the word LION, I shall treat the matter only briefly here.

<margin>Roaring applied to God.</margin>
Roaring is also applied to God, and since it cannot literally be applied to Him, who is an absolute Spirit, it certainly represents the Lord to us as being very incensed, and intending not only to carry out the weightiest judgments—with threats through His servants the Prophets—but also immediately executing them with terror upon sinners and the godless, <term>Job 37:4; Jeremiah 25:30; Hosea 5:14 and 11:10; Joel 3:16; Amos 1:2 and 3:8.</term> Or it refers to Him causing terrible stirrings in nature: or acting against His ungrateful people through enemies as instruments of His wrath; as also against the enemies of His people, when He, being zealous for His honor and mindful of His word, shall call and convert the Jews and Gentiles in the last days, <term>Hosea 11:10.</term> summoning them from far countries, when He shall cause the deserved plagues and threatened punishments to come upon the spiritual Edom and Egypt, <term>Joel 3:16.</term> etc. as well as the enemies of His church, justice, and truth. <term>Amos 1:2 and 3:4-8. etc.</term>

So too the voice and the sound of the roaring lion is attributed to the angel in <term>Revelation 10:3.</term> representing the terrible judgments which, to the amazement of the world and the exercise of vengeance upon the enemies of the church, were about to be

<column-break/>

carried out, <term>Revelation 10:3.</term> as a lion roars: where some read, as a lion lows, <term>mugit</term>: which is very improper, and is characteristic of oxen and cows.

However, John used the word <term>μυκάσθαι — mykasthai</term>, which among the Greeks means *Mugire*, to Low. Roaring is expressed by <term>ὠρύεσθαι — ōryesthai</term> and <term>βρυχᾶσθαι — brychasthai</term> by the Greeks. But this apparent difficulty has been removed by the most learned Bochart, <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar famous for his work on animals in the Bible.</note> <term>de Animalibus Sacris part 1. Book III. Chapter 2.</term> having shown from secular writers that for "Lowing," the "Roaring" of both lions and of cows and calves is taken. Plutarch <term>Book on Terrestrial & aquatic animals: κἂν λάβωσιν αἰτίαν, ἀνακαλενται μόσχῳ μυκημάδι τὸ βρύχημα ποιῦντες ὅμοιον :</term> <note>If they find cause, they call out to the young with a roar making it similar to a lowing calf.</note> if they catch something, namely, the parents of young lions, then they call their young, raising a lowing, almost as calves do.

John likely used this word rather than another for the sake of emphasis, to signify thereby that the voice brought forth by the Angel was very heavy and dreadful, like that of old lions, whether they be threatening defeat or possessing prey: and it seems to be taken from <term>Isaiah 21:8.</term> See Vitringa on <term>Revelation page 427. etc.</term> <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian and commentator on the Apocalypse.</note>

<margin>Roaring attributed to men.</margin>
When roaring is attributed to men, David, the Messiah, etc., as in <term>Psalm 22:2.</term> and <term>38:9; Job 3:24.</term> it signifies the extreme distress of the heart, the most violent agitations of the mind, either through a grumbling and murmuring of the mouth, or through dismal, distressed complaints, howling, or grim lamentation, brought forth with muffled, unformed outbursts of air and sobbing; which sound is dismal, dreadful, and very unpleasant.

<margin>To Princes.</margin>
Since roaring is characteristic of lions—not only dismal, dreadful, and a proof of their hunger, thirst, anger, etc., why everyone fears and trembles and imagines something evil at their coming and approach—so we observe that kings, princes, and those among them who love robbery and prey, are compared to lions, roaring lions, etc., like violent godless men who roar, bite, and devour, who shall be broken. <term>Job 4:10; Proverbs 19:12 and 20:2 and 28:15.</term>

The godless man does not always roar because he, being enraged, seeks the destruction of his neighbor. <term>Ezekiel 19:7; Zephaniah 3:3.</term>

A man does not always roar because of the torment, the grief, the piercing sorrow, and woe that comes to him from a stranger or from without. Someone can be the cause of it himself, if he has clung to the foreign woman, finds his strength and goods squandered, and has brought upon himself foul infections and pining diseases. <term>Proverbs 5:11. etc.</term>

<margin>To enemies.</margin>
So too the enemies are said to roar, who being famished, slaughter, kill, consume and devour everything, making it a prey, <term>Isaiah 5:29; Jeremiah 2:15.</term> just as Christ’s enemies appear as roaring lions, eating, tearing, possessed with an insatiable rage and bloodthirstiness, to destroy Christ and grind Him to dust, <term>Psalm 22:14.</term>

Just as the enemies are said to have roared in God’s sanctuaries, <term>Psalm 74:4.</term> when they are masters of the places of public worship, and everywhere make their voices hea-

## BOWING, BOWING DOWN, etc. <term>כָּרַע — kara</term>, <term>כָּפַף — kaphaph</term>, <term>כָּנַע — kana</term>, <term>κύπτω — kyptō</term>, <term>incurvare se — to bend oneself</term>, <term>παρακύπτω — parakyptō</term>, <term>συγκύπτω — synkyptō</term>.

<margin>Bowing taken in various senses.</margin>
This word appears several times in the Holy Scrolls, yet by no means in the same sense; for sometimes it is a word of politeness, an act of good breeding, reverence, and the showing of honor, especially among the Easterners. Thus one reads of Abraham, *Gen. XXIII. 7.* <note>The source text says XXII. 7, but refers to the purchase of the cave from the sons of Heth in chapter 23</note> that he bowed himself before the people of the land, before the sons of Heth. So did Jacob before Esau his brother seven times, *Gen. XXXIII. 3.* not only out of politeness and reverence, but also to steal and soften his heart through this submission.

In other instances, bowing and bowing down appear not only as a humble greeting and formal showing of honor, but as a mark of inferiority or submission to him before whom one bows. Thus Isaac's received blessing clearly suggested such a thing, *Gen. XXVII. 29. Let people serve thee, and nations bow down to thee: be lord over thy brethren, and let thy mother's sons bow down to thee, etc.*

That which appeared to Joseph in his dream regarding his sheaf was also a premonition of this, *Gen. XXXVII. 7, 8. And behold, we were binding sheaves in the midst of the field: and lo, my sheaf arose and also remained standing, and behold, your sheaves came round about, and bowed down to my sheaf. Then his brothers said to him, Shalt thou then indeed reign over us?*

<margin>Sign of submission.</margin>
When one now transfers this to God, or the King, Messiah, the Christ, who will understand it otherwise than that it depicts the submission of the mind, divine honor and service, in faith, love, humility, and lowliness? *Exod. XXXIV. 8. Ps. XCVII. 7. Hebr. I. 6. Philip. II. 10. Ps. XCV. 6. Mich. VI. 6. Isa. XLIX. 7--23.*

<margin>Bowing attributed to the soul.</margin>
Bowing down is sometimes attributed to the soul, whereas it actually takes place in some physical body, *Ps. XLII. 6. and XLIII. 5.* and that represents to us that state of the soul when faith and hope are greatly tossed about, and one hardly dares to claim divine grace, or cannot sufficiently strengthen oneself by the sight of divine truth and the promise of the assurances: when through sadness because of committed sins, faintness comes into the sun of God’s beaming favors: a struggle between flesh and spirit in heavy trials: a multiplication of enemies, when the understanding is dazed, the mind strongly disturbed, the former boldness weakens

<column-break/>

and passes away; which happens more than once to God’s children and the church, especially when the light of joy is extinguished and goes down through and behind a dismal and eerie cloud of heavy temptations and assaults by enemies, whether physical or spiritual, of which one finds many instances in the Holy pages, *Ps. XXXVIII. 7. and XIII. 3. and LXXVII. 3--10. and LXXXVIII. 15, 16. etc.*

When something cannot withstand some force, it is said to bow, *Hab. III. 6.* we say, it will have to bend.

When we wish to say that the young youth must be brought under discipline, who would otherwise gladly break out and fall into unbridledness, we are accustomed to say, *bend the twig while it is tender.* Those who are accustomed to the loose rein are brought under the bond with difficulty: an ingrained evil is hard to overcome.

> <note>original: "Quo semel est imbuta recens servabit odorem Testa diu." — Horace, Epistles I.2.69</note>
> The jar keeps for a long time the scent it first received.

-> That is: <-

-> *The pitcher holds long the scent it first received.* <-

To incline or bend oneself toward something: to be inclined or bent, whether it is applied to the ear or the heart, signifies the desire through which one sets and determines oneself toward something, wanting to hear or do it with consent, approval, pleasure, and submission: in contrast to turning away, stopping up, rejecting, etc. *Ps. XL. 2. and XLV. and XLIX. 5. Prov. II. 2. etc.*

This being the most important regarding this word, I shall prune the secondary work and advise moving on to something else.

## BELLY (OR WOMB), <term>בֶּטֶן — beten</term>, <term>κοιλία — koilia</term>, <term>venter</term>.

THE BELLY, as is known, is the lower front part of the human body, in which the intestines are specifically enclosed: a primary part, necessary to nourish and strengthen the body through the digestion of food and the preparation of nutrients.

But of that natural part of the body, I let the Naturalists speak and write. It does not go too well with its condition when it fluctuates greatly and rumbles with wind, and is strongly moved, or hard and tightly stretched: when sluggishness is felt in the thighs, melancholy in the loins, stiffness in the lower spine, or flabbiness of the loins: but let this be the subject matter of the physicians.

The fruit of the belly (or womb) is known to be taken for the children, offspring, and descendants of married persons, *Isa. XLIX. 15. Deut. XXVIII. 4. etc.* the first that opened the womb, the Lord desired for Himself.

It is known that the belly is often mentioned when someone's birth and first coming into the world is meant, at which occasion one is counted among the living and shows one's actual life to the outside: yes, sometimes even primary similarities, both in the natural and moral sense, with those from whom one reckons one's descent, and whose children one [is]...

# BELLY.

The term "belly" is used to express that which can be called natural or moral: as for example, David says in *Psalm 58:3: The wicked are estranged from the womb: they go astray from the belly, speaking lies.* <note>The Dutch text cites Psalm 58:4, following a different verse numbering common in older translations.</note>

This saying undoubtedly signifies not only the uncorrected and unremoved corruption of their hearts, *Ps. 51, Job 14,* through which their imagination is evil from their youth, *Gen. 6 and 8,* but also that their hypocrisy and blameworthiness is "dyed in the wool" <note>An idiom meaning a deep-seated, permanent characteristic.</note>.

Young scoundrels and hypocrites find parents whose children they can be called in terms of sentiments and morals. Thus ancient Pharisaism, old Babylon and Egypt, and the labor-focused and self-righteous Judaism live again in their children—the spiritual Babylon, Egypt, and Antichristendom.

<margin>Meaning of serving the belly.</margin>
To serve the belly—from which we get "belly-servers" <note>Gluttons or those driven by physical desires</note>—to have one's belly as one's God, and to be an enemy of the cross of Christ: to serve not Him, but one's own belly, *Rom. 16, Phil. 3,* etc., undoubtedly signifies seeking the temporal things of this world: pleasure, ease, goods, honor, and dominion. It means chasing these above all else to satisfy one's lust and greed, *Job 31:24, 25; Isa. 56:11, 12; 2 Pet. 2:3–13; Jude 11, 12; 2 Tim. 3:4; Ezek. 13:19; Ps. 16.* Such were also the Borborites, Nicolaitans, Gnostics, and in the present day, the "well-fed stallions" in the Papacy, and those who preach for the sake of bread: all those who turn grace into wantonness and uncleanness; who make more effort to follow their lustfulness, desire, and wantonness than to love God and observe His reasonable pleasure; who lead a luxurious and wanton life and are given over to pleasure; which Theognis calls "gratifying the belly" <note>original: "γασρὶ χαριζόμενος"—a Greek phrase for self-indulgence</note>: living to eat and drink, as Novius cites from Lucilius:

->Live, you gluttons, you big eaters, live, you bellies.<-
<note>original: "Vivite lurcones, comedones, vivite ventres."</note>

---

->That is:<-

->Live merrily, you gluttons, live you luxurious bellies.<-

Paul in *Philippians 3:19* seems to have had his eye on *Psalm 17:13, 14*: it would seem to me as if David, according to Paul's application, also placed this sort of people among the outward professors of the living words of God, yet he portrays them as haughty, earthly, and lustful; those who have a treasure of literal knowledge of the Word and enjoy the outward advantages of the Kingdom of God: drawing many treasures and earthly goods to their lustful pleasure under God's long-suffering and advantageous providence, which they chase entirely, though to their heavier judgment.

It does not sound very well when Paul, quoting a Heathen writer who knew thoroughly how matters stood with the Cretans, utters this in *Titus 1:12: One of them, being their own Prophet, has said, the Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.*

Whether one should understand "Prophet" here as a Heathen—namely, Callimachus or Epimenides—I leave undecided here. At the very least, it signifies that those of Crete

<column-break/>

were singularly greedy and obsessed with their gut, and did not care much for doing anything; they were lazy and idle, sluggish and lustful, which I shall not expand upon further.

It is undoubtedly by no means to be understood literally or strictly when the Church, the bride of Jesus, speaks of the belly of her Bridegroom, *Song of Sol. 5:14,* or Jesus speaks of the belly of the Church, *Song of Sol. 7:2.* Both passages read as follows: *Chap. 5:14: his belly is as bright ivory overlaid with sapphires. Chap. 7:2: your belly is like a heap of wheat, set about with lilies.* Because the heart and kidneys are found in the belly, to which thoughts and impulses are attributed, the belly is taken to represent the soul. In *Song of Sol. 5:14,* the thoughts of the Bridegroom are pure, steadfast, and heavenly, says Gürtlerus <note>Nicolaas Gürtler (1654–1711), a Swiss theologian.</note>.

The word in *Song of Sol. 5:14* can be translated as "entrails" or "bowels," as often happens: now the bowels and their rumbling are mentioned to represent inner compassion, sincere and very strong love; in Hebrew, <term>מֵעִים — me’ayim</term>, his bowels.

Certainly, ivory is smooth and snow-white; a sapphire is streaked with bloody, blue-spotted veins, according to the burning-blue color of the sky.

It could represent to me not only Jesus' preciousness and His Divine and human virtues, but also, among other things, Jesus' bowels of love and mercy, having excelled throughout His entire life in purity and unstained innocence. From this love and mercy flowed all those suffered blows, the dark and blue bruises in His flesh, sparkling with His precious blood of a high and costly price, because through this, among other things, He showed His highest love for His Father's honor and the salvation of mankind, by which He was consumed, *Ps. 69,* and gave Himself up for His congregation, *Eph. 5:25.*

<margin>Belly attributed to the church.</margin>
Again, one finds a belly attributed to the bride, the Church. *Song of Sol. 7:2: The church is fruitful and brings forth a great number of believers, just as many grains make up a heap,* says Gürtlerus.

I am inclined to think that, just as she is called a mother, being fruitful or unfruitful in certain periods and states is noted and described, *Isa. 54, Gal. 4,* that her belly or womb represents the innermost part, the center of the church, where one has the ministry of the Word and the sacraments: where the seed of the Word is cast, *1 Pet. 1,* where one is fed and fashioned according to the likeness of Christ: where one receives an internal and hidden life and grows up, as it were, to a sufficient size, *Gal. 4, 2 Cor. 4:16, Eph. 4:13, Gal. 4:19, 1 Cor. 3:1, 1 Pet. 2:2, Col. 3:3, 1 John 3:2,* etc.

However, I would understand this in such a way that in the midst of the church are living and flowing waters, *John 7:38,* of truth, comfort, grace, joy, and purification: that there is grain of spiritual food, such an essential bread of ever-abiding truths, that she does not go about pregnant with the wind of vain, loose, and unstable doctrine, but is in a state to feed, refresh, and strengthen herself and others, who come to her as lilies and place themselves around her as brothers in unity, *Ps. 133*: and all those to the mid-

<margin>Sayings about the Belly.</margin>
Furthermore, several sayings about the belly appear in *Job 15:2–35*. A wise man will not bring forth windy words or reasons—as if they were imprints of his own imagination or of boasting wisdom—nor words or things of no use, for his own stinking praise; nor will he keep his inward parts occupied or puffed up with foolish thoughts and windy self-imaginations.

Again, in verse 35: a hypocrite, and one who is out to deceive, conceives evil in his heart, feeds and nurtures base and unseemly thoughts in his inward parts, until the time comes that he brings them forth; then it becomes manifest that he has been pregnant with Nothing, and that he has deceived himself the most.

In *Job 20:15–20*, the life of the belly is also shown, where it is demonstrated that the godless and unjust are seldom long masters of what they have unjustly obtained by craft or force.
<margin>Misery of the miser.</margin>
And even if he has gathered much, he is never satisfied: he has no heart to enjoy it: he is always afraid that he will fall short, and so he receives as his lot and portion of retribution that he, who insatiably scraped everything together in all sorts of ways, in the midst of his abundance, like Tantalus <note>A figure from Greek mythology punished with eternal hunger and thirst despite being surrounded by food and water just out of reach.</note>, always thirsts and hungers.

When Job reports on his closed and pressured belly for the sake of speaking, to get air, in *Job 32:18, 19*, I would think that he uses this image to depict his strong zeal, uncontrollable impulse, and the movement of the Lord's Spirit, so that he could no longer restrain himself, but had to speak in the matters of God’s honor and his own.

<margin>Tongue and lips compared to a tree.</margin>
When Solomon in *Proverbs 18:19, 20* attributes to the tongue and lips that they can satisfy the belly with their fruit, etc., I almost think that the wise king imagines the tongue and lips as a fruitful tree, by which one can greatly—with good, wise, and edifying reasons—edify oneself and one's neighbor and bring benefit in all kinds of matters and cases, both regarding the world and the soul: just as, conversely, the tongue and the lips can bring about the greatest evil and the most remarkable damage, both to him who speaks and to the neighbor. *James 3*.

One also finds that something can be bitter in the belly. *Revelation 10*. See the words BITTER and BOOK.

BUNDLE, of Myrrh: of the living: enclosed in a bundle, etc. <term>צרور</term> <note>Hebrew: *tseror*</note>, *fasciculus* <note>Latin: a small bundle</note>.

<margin>A bundle of myrrh.</margin>
**T**he root word <term>צרور</term> signifies a *Pouch, Bundle, Purse, money-bag, Genesis 42:35, Proverbs 8*, or something that is tied together and enclosed, joined together, packed in a parcel, very tightly shut so as not to be scattered and lost.

Thus we read in *Song of Solomon 1:13* of a bundle of myrrh, which rests during the night between the breasts of the bride: to which she compares her beloved: consisting not of one, but several sprigs and twigs woven together.

> *I seem to carry a bundle of myrrh in my breast,*
> *While I recall the bridegroom put to death for me.*
<note>Original Latin: *Fasciculum myrrhæ videor mihi pectore ferre / Dum recolo sponsum pro memet mortificatum.*</note>

<column-break/>

-> That is: <-

> *It seems to me, as often as I remember my bridegroom's death,*
> *My bridegroom, who for me was stripped of life,*
> *That I carry a bundle of Myrrh by my breasts.*

Regarding Myrrh, its virtue, power, nature, property, use, etc., I will not give a full account at length, since the word itself appearing elsewhere will provide me with the opportunity.

However, I must say something of it for my purpose, and according to my plan of matters, so that I may hit the goal and target of God’s Spirit and of the speaker.

Whether myrrh takes its name <term>ἀπὸ τῇ μύρα</term> <note>Greek: *apo tē myra*, meaning "from the myrrh-oil or ointment."</note>, from the most excellent ointment and balsam oil, or from a Hebrew word which signifies bitter, that will do little for the matter here.

It is a bitter herb, of which we read as "myrrhed wine," *Mark 15*.

It has been a noble herb from of old, *Genesis 44, Mark 2*; it was an ingredient in the holy anointing oil, *Exodus 30*.

It is a spice, strong, and of a piercing scent, *Proverbs 7, Psalm 65:9*. Not only, as they say, strengthening and lovely—for which reason bundles and small bags of it were prepared—but it was also used, being mixed among ointments and spices, to preserve dead bodies against corruption. See MYRRH.

*Silius Italicus, Book 13.* <note>Silius Italicus was a Roman poet known for his epic on the Punic War.</note>

> *The people of Pontus make it a practice to empty the brains from the corpses,*
> *Which they smear with myrrh for the sake of lasting durability.*
<note>Original Latin: *Exhausto instituit Pontus vacuare cerebro / Ora virum, & longum myrrhata reponit in ævum.*</note>

-> That is: <-

> *The people of Pontus take the brains out of the corpses,*
> *Which they smear with Myrrh for durability.*

Prudentius <note>A Roman Christian poet of the late 4th century.</note> in the Hymn for the Deceased:

> *It is the custom to stretch out linens*
> *Shining with a clear whiteness:*
> *And sprinkled Myrrh with Sabæan*
> *Medicine preserves the body.*
<note>Original Latin: *Candore nitentia claro / Prætendere lintea mos est: / Aspersaque Myrrha Sabæo / Corpus medicamine servat.*</note>

-> That is: <-

> *In linen they clothe the corpses,*
> *Which they then smear with Myrrh,*
> *And thus preserve them from perishing.*

It is known that some, by the "bundle of Myrrh" in its weaving together, believe to be sketched out Christ’s Divine and human natures, united with each other in an incomprehensible way. Others understand it to mean the joining together of Christ’s threefold offices <note>The offices of Prophet, Priest, and King.</note>: yet it seems to me that they have not understood it poorly who understand it as Christ's death, and obedience in suffering unto death, as Haymo says, *Christ is compared to a bundle of Myrrh, as far as his death and burial are concerned.*

And Myrrh considered as such as a Bundle, tied together, as a sachet or spice-bag <term>riekerken</term> <note>A small scented bag or sachet used for its fragrance.</note> bound and wrapped together,
