<header>->LITTLE BUNDLE.<-</header>

<margin>Symbol of grace and truth.</margin>
...is noted as an image of the perfection of Jesus' bloody merits, of the fullness of grace and truth for the church, bound and enclosed within him so that its power can never vanish or evaporate. *Colossians 1:19 and 3:19, and John 1:16.*

<margin>Bitterness, a symbol of Jesus' suffering.</margin>
The bitterness symbolized his bitter suffering in soul and body, *Psalm 40:13, Isaiah 55, Matthew 26 and 27, Psalm 23,* through which sin and corruption are put to death, not without bitter sorrow. *2 Corinthians 7.*

The powerful and piercing scent symbolized the power and emotion of his lovely sacrifice, *Ephesians 5:2,* so much so that those who share in its fruit and proclaim his death through the preaching of the Crucified One smell strongly and pleasantly, the power of it spreading onto their garments, *2 Corinthians 2, Psalm 45,* etc. This can represent the strengthening power and the ability to prevent rot and decay, and to temper and remove the sluggish and foul vapors; so that not only does the power of Christ's obedience in suffering unto death strengthen the heart through the indwelling of Christ and the constant meditation on the cross and suffering, but it also tempers and removes the rot, stench, and venom of sin and impurity, whereby neither soul nor body remains under the power and bondage of sin, nor under the power of death. So says Origen on *Romans 6: where the death of Christ is carried in the heart, there sin cannot reign.* The Son makes the soul truly free, *John 8:36.* He puts away sin, death, and the ruler of the same, *Hebrews 2:14, 15, 1 Corinthians 15.* The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sins. *1 John 1:7, 1 Corinthians 6:11, 1 Corinthians 1:30, Zechariah 13, Hebrews 9:14, John 10 and 11.*

<margin>The effect of Christ's obedience.</margin>
The preciousness and worthiness—the royal gift—can represent the precious price of his obedience in suffering unto death, which cannot be weighed against gold, as it is the blood of the Son of God. *Acts 20:28, 1 Corinthians 6:20, 1 Peter 1:18, 19.*

Now, that this "little bundle" rests throughout the night between the breasts of the bride, the church (see the word BREASTS), we may perhaps understand this as the rational "milk-vessels" <note>A common metaphor in 17th-century theology where the breasts of the Church represent the Old and New Testaments which provide spiritual nourishment.</note> of the Old and New Testaments, in which Jesus' suffering and death for the church are enclosed; upon which word she is built, *Ephesians 2:20,* as her foundation, *1 Corinthians 3:11,* wherein is found for her the rational and unadulterated milk. *1 Peter 2, Isaiah 55:1, 2, 1 Peter 1:10, 11, 12, Luke 24:46.*

<margin>Meaning of staying the night between the breasts.</margin>
Or one can understand it as the heart, since the heart is placed there, where Jesus dwells through faith, *Ephesians 3:17,* which the Lord requires, *Proverbs 23:26.* And then Jesus, staying the night like a little bundle between her breasts, would mean that he is in her heart and upon her heart, an imprint of her love, *Psalms 18 and 73,* whom she values greatly, *1 Peter 1:8 and 1 Peter 2:7, Philippians 3:8;* her constant adherence, *1 Corinthians 6:17,* indeed, the constant meditation on his bitter suffering and death, especially in the night of heresy, persecution, need, and death. *Luke 22, 1 Corinthians 11, 1 Corinthians 2:2.*

We also read of a bundle in *Job Chapter 14:17: My transgression is sealed up in a bundle; you pack up my iniquity.* I would think that Job, in a figure and through an allegory,

<column-break/>

intends to convey that the Lord dealt strictly with him; that having gathered his sin and the guilt of his sin together, recorded it in his book of remembrance as if tied up and wound together, he even brought to light the misdeeds of his youth and made him inherit them, writing very bitter things against him. *Job 13:26.*

From this perhaps does not deviate what one can read in *Hosea 13:12: Ephraim's sin is bound up together, his iniquity is laid up, or hidden.* Some have understood it thus: *Ephraim's sin is laid away like a treasure against the day of wrath, to be dealt with all at once.* Just as God endures sin for a long time and sets it down with himself, yet does not forget, but when the measure and the tally-stick are full, he shows that he remembers it in order to settle it. Others have it: *Ephraim's sins are hidden, and their offensiveness taken away by judgment.* But Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> expresses it thus: *Just as when one binds something together in a small bag, it is preserved and not lost to the one for whom it is bound: so all Ephraim's iniquity, through which he sinned against God, is gathered together and hidden for him, being preserved as if in a purse.* The Chaldean <note>Refers to the Targum, the Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> has: *The sins of Ephraim are laid away, they are preserved in my heart.* And Rabbi Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a distinguished Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> as *in my chest of my memory.* Or as others say: *They are in the belly; they shall burst forth with pain and heavy woes.* *Deuteronomy 32:34, 35, Zephaniah 2:2, Romans 2:4, 5.*

Now I have found that some theologians apply this to the Eastern or Greek Church, whose heresy and sins were about to be reckoned with: in which visitation she behaved like a foolish woman and like a child, as one who, against the incursions of the Turks, requested help from the Latin or Western Church at the Council of Florence in the year 1438, subjecting herself to the Pope (though covertly and out of necessity) so far as to concede the procession of the Holy Spirit, for infallible assistance, and purgatory, alongside the Pope's supremacy over all of Christendom.

What the truth of this may be, I leave aside; for myself, I seek first the literal history and fulfillment, and then note whether there is any similarity in the course of time in those who, like Ephraim and Judah, are split and divided, yet still wish to bear the name of God's people and servants of the Lord.

<margin>Bundle of the living.</margin>
Among others, one also reads of a *bundle of the living, 1 Samuel 25:29. When a man shall rise up to pursue you, and to seek your soul: then the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living with the Lord your God, but the soul of your enemies he shall sling out from the middle of the hollow of the sling.*

<margin>Abigail’s intercession with David.</margin>
It is certain that these are the words of Abigail, seeking to reconcile the insulted and angered King David for the insult brought by her husband Nabal, wishing him—and as if prophesying—prosperity in his reign and length of days in Divine favor and protection against all the attempts and wicked counsels of Saul and his followers, if in this case he allowed himself to be entreated and showed mercy to Nabal for her sake.

Now, regarding this allegorical and symbolic way of speaking, and how and what should be understood by it, and what the Jewish masters in the course of time have understood by...

It explores various theological and literal interpretations of this phrase before transitioning to the definition of a "fortress" or "stronghold."</meta>

<page-num>231</page-num>
<header>LITTLE BUNDLE.</header>
<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Diversity of opinions.</margin>
...on this subject, there is no single opinion among Christians and non-Christians. For some maintain that it must be understood as the state of the souls of the pious after death, in the next life, contrasted with the state of the souls of the wicked and ungodly. They suggest that the souls of the pious are, as it were, hidden and enclosed under the throne of the Divine Majesty and grace; meanwhile, the souls of the wicked and ungodly are driven about, wandering from one end of the world to the other without any rest being granted to them, being tossed and moved like a stone in and out of the hollow of a sling. <note>This imagery is drawn directly from 1 Samuel 25:29, where Abigail speaks to David.</note>

This is, to cut short all the descriptions, the opinion of very many Jewish Masters, such as Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson <note>A prominent medieval philosopher and commentator also known as Gersonides.</note>; the Chaldean translator <note>The Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>; Rabbi Eliezar; the Talmud, Tractate <term>Shabbat <note>original Hebrew: שבת</note></term> Chapter 23; and in the book <term>Column of the World <note>original Hebrew: עמוד עולם (Amud Olam)</note></term> Chapter 23; Lipman, page 456, etc.

Others understand the "bundle of the living" as the Book of Life: the sealing of the elect; the number or registry of the names of the pious; God’s providence regarding life; God’s counsel and hand. Thus, it represents the firm and unchangeable arrangement which God has made within Himself concerning the state of the elect, both here and hereafter, from which their stability and security flows and follows.

<margin>Observations and applications.</margin>
In this regard, one finds these observations and applications being made, namely:

Just as a small bundle is woven together and squeezed; so too are the pious pressed down, and by this pressure are warned to take heed, to be on their guard, to stand and to watch, being preserved forever by the hand of the Redeemer—God taking care that their life is not snatched away against His will.

Just as a small bundle is bound and entwined together from many and various sprigs and twigs, so that none fall out or off; so do the pious and the church (consisting of many members as one body) remain bound and entwined together through faith, hope, love, and peace, by one and the same Divine oversight.

Just as a small bundle has certain and distinct twigs, shoots, and sprigs, which have been selected from many and innumerable others and brought into one body by being joined together; so, because of the election of grace, there is also a body of the elect, chosen from an infinite number, spread across the entire earth from the distinct races of men.

Just as in a small bundle there are smaller and larger, higher and lower twigs, each in its rank and order, yet all brought together into one body; so each member of the elect and the congregation has his distinct gifts and measure of grace in this life, and so shall there be grades and steps in the heavenly glory. *Daniel 12. 1 Corinthians 15.*

Be these applications and observations as they may; whether Abigail and God’s Spirit intended them here might be doubted with good reason, if not denied.

I have also noted that there are many who understand the "bundle of the living" to mean not only God’s singular providence and protection of David’s soul or his life against all the schemes and violence of Saul and his followers, but also after this life, so that the pious do not fall into 

<column-break/>

destruction, but according to the loving-kindness of God, are graciously rewarded. In life and death, they are and remain the Lord’s, without being separated from His love by any adversity, *Romans 8:35, etc. Romans 14:7, 8, 9. John 10:28. 1 Peter 1:3, 4, 5.* Thus, they are bound by the heavenly Master of the House like precious coins in a bundle, or like something precious and fragrant, so that it is not tossed away or lost.

Some look to the image of green cut branches, or those intended for transplanting, which one binds together and places in water to keep green and sap-filled, in order to transplant them later.

And finally, according to the letter and the thread of the history—as a remarkable event between David and Abigail in the matter of her husband Nabal—one might think, along with Franzius (*Oracle 69*), Kimchi, <margin>Explanation of the case of Abigail.</margin> Arias Montanus, Cajetanus, A Lapide, Bugenhagen, Mollerus, Sanctius, Hacfpan, and others, that Abigail actually means to say and wish that, as David forgives the foolishness and insult of Nabal because of her intercession and humble prayer, the Lord will (and indeed shall) take David into His care. He will protect him against all his enemies, among whom Saul and his followers were the most prominent; He will scatter and bring down his enemies; and in contrast, He will establish David's kingdom, increase his friends, and make him rule for length of days.

That seems to me, for now, to be the most accurate interpretation, flowing and following most easily from the way of speaking as well as the thread of the history. That one might, in the meantime, also apply it to other and higher matters, I can very well tolerate.

->FORTRESS, <term>Palace <note>original Hebrew: בירה (Birah)</note></term>, <term>Stronghold <note>original Hebrew: מצд (Metzad)</note></term>, <term>Tower <note>original Hebrew: טירה (Tirah)</note></term>, <term>Citadel <note>original Hebrew: ארמון (Armon)</note></term>, *citadel, palace, castle.*<-

**T**he aforementioned root words are translated in various ways, such as a fortress, castle, a royal palace, or a high, strong building, used both for ornament and for strength, to be secure within during times of need, raid, or attack by enemies, and from which one spies on the enemy and attempts to do them damage.

In the Sacred Scroll <note>The Bible.</note> this word is taken literally; but also improperly, in imagination, or figuratively, *Psalm 18:2, 3 and 31 and 71 and 141 and 144. Song of Solomon 8:9, etc.* <note>The original Dutch text cites CLI and CLXIV, but since the Psalms only go to 150, these may be typos or references to other numbering systems; I have adjusted to the likely intended Psalms of protection.</note>

And to say only in passing what this <margin>Explanation of the word Fortress, taken figuratively.</margin> implies, I believe that the singular, powerful protection of the Most High is signified by it, against all sorts of enemies of the figurative church in general, and of David, the Messiah, and every believer in particular. Specifically, it refers to the protection and steadfastness of the elect in faith unto salvation, which is brought about both by Christ and by the working Spirit, under and through the ministry of the Word, the sacraments, along with church discipline, and mutual strengthening, encouragement, and comfort. The following texts, with various distinctions, pertain to this: *Isaiah 26:1. Zechariah 2:5. Psalm 66:5, 6. Romans 1:16. 2 Corinthians 10:4, 5. Romans 16:25. Matthew 7.*

# BOXWOOD, <note>Hebrew: *te’ashshur* (תאשור)</note>, *buxus*.

<margin>Nature of the Boxwood tree.</margin>
This tree is found mentioned in *Isaiah 41:19 and 60:13* as one of the trees that was to sprout under the lovely and powerful ministry of the Gospel.
Some maintain that this tree grows tall and spreads wide with green branches. It is held by some to be oily. Kimchi <note>Rabbi David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish scholar and grammarian.</note> suggests that it is a species of cedar.
It is also thought that it is named *Te’ashshur* from the root *ashar* <note>original Hebrew: אשר</note>, meaning *he has walked, made movable, caused to go, or to move oneself*. From this comes "blessedness," as it is a "blessed tree," because blessedness, being desired, draws many toward itself. But whatever the truth of this may be, I leave it there; perhaps one could investigate other reasons for this naming.

<margin>Distinction of the Boxwood trees.</margin>
A distinction is made between a French Boxwood and others, which through pruning are given various shapes and appearances in height and width.
It is said there is a species that is somewhat oily, though of no use for food or medicine, but very heavy in scent.

<margin>Cultivated boxwood.</margin>
But there is a Boxwood, rendered "tame" (as it were) through sowing, which has broader and denser branches, is always green, and can be sheared.
It is recounted that this tree grows readily on mountains and thrives best in rough places.

<margin>Its fruit.</margin>
It has nuts that are not entirely unlike those of the myrtle, yet they are not desired by animals at all.
And although the fruit is unpleasant, the wood is nonetheless suited for various services—indeed, it is famous for its hardness, its incorruptibility, and its bitterness, because of which the woodworm does not gnaw through it.
Various forms are carved into it by the lathe; Virgil, *Georgics* 2:

->*Torno rasile buxum.*<-

->That is:<-

->*The boxwood turned by the iron tool.*<-

It is desired for its continuous grain; and spoons and handles for knives are turned from it; head-combs are also prepared from it. Martial:

->*Multifido buxus quæ sibi dente datur.*<-

->That is:<-

->*The comb of boxwood, which is given to him.*<-

<column-break/>

Juvenal:

->*Et caput intactum buxo.* ---<-

->That is:<-

->*And the head never touched by the boxwood comb.*<-

<margin>Boxwood, formerly a lucky tree.</margin>
It may perhaps have been called a "lucky" <note>In the sense of "auspicious" or "consecrated."</note> tree because of its idolatrous use, being suited for carving the images of idols and for making flutes used in the service of sanctuaries and festivals. Thus Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an Italian scholar.</note> cites from Theophrastus that Apollo’s statue was made of boxwood.

Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpine*, Book III:

> *If I wish to blow into the boxwood flutes, they groan a funeral sound;
> if I shake the drums, the drums return mourning to you.*
> <note>original Latin: "Si buxos inflare velim, ferale gemiscunt: / Tympana si quatiam, luctum tibi tympana reddunt."</note>

->That is:<-

->*If I play upon a flute made of boxwood,
A deadly sound is heard immediately.
If I strike the drum, a sad sound tires my ears.*<-

Virgil in the 9th book of the *Aeneid*:

> *Go to the heights of Dindymus, where the flute gives a two-toned song to those accustomed; the drums and the Berecynthian boxwood of the Idaean Mother call you: leave arms to men, and yield the sword!*
> <note>original Latin: "Ite per alta / Dindyma, ubi assuetis bimarem dat tibia cantum: / Tympana vos, buxusque vocat Berecynthia, matris / Ideæ: finite arma viris, & cedite ferro!"</note>

->That is, according to Vondel’s translation:<-

->*Run freely away
To your Mount Dindymus, to the cities,
Accustomed of old to hear your pipe piping most shrilly,
Which you know how to grip in turn with two fingers,
When you stop the air with a varying tone.
The mother of Cybele, the mother, calls you
From Ida with the flute of boxwood, fine and coarse.
Let men take their ease, leave the trade of weapons to them,
And lay down the blade.*<-
<note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679) was the preeminent Dutch poet and playwright of the Golden Age; the author is quoting Vondel's famous translation of Virgil.</note>

Propertius, Book IV, Elegy IX:

> *The dwarf himself, shortly compressed in his limbs,
> Tossed his stubby hands to the hollow boxwood flutes.*
> <note>original Latin: "Nanus & ipse suos breviter concretus in artus, / Jactabat truncas ad cava buxa manus."</note>

->That is:<-

->*The little dwarf, while he cramped and bent his limbs,
Lifted both his hands high during the flute-playing.*<-

Ovid seems to attribute it to Bacchus, with his blowpipe, in the 4th book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> *The cry of youths, and at once the voices of women, and the drums struck by palms, and the hollow brasses resound, and the boxwood with its long bore.*
> <note>original Latin: "Clamor juvenilis, & unà / Feminæ voces, impulsáque tympana palmis / Concaváque ærafonant, longoque foramine buxus."</note>

Followed thus by Van Vondel:

->*One heard a country-shout wherever you passed by,
The noise of women, the resonance of box-pipe and of drums,
And hollow cymbals, clarions, and kettledrums.*<-

Seneca in *Agamemnon*:

> *He strikes his breast, stirred by the hoarse boxwood flute,
> so that he may mourn for Phrygian Attis.*
> <note>original Latin: "Pectora rauco concita buxo / Ferit, ut Phrygium lugeat Attyn."</note>

->That is:<-

> She beats upon her breast as soon as the boxwood pipe sounds,
> To show her grief over Attis. <note>This refers to the mythological rites of Cybele, where flutes made of boxwood were played during lamentations for Attis.</note>

See Heinrich Ursinus in *Arbore Biblico*, Hoffmann’s *Universal Lexicon*, etc.

Indeed, people knew how to shear and prune this tree to create such forms that, when viewed from a distance in gardens and groves, they appeared as various animals—intended both for pleasant viewing and as an ornament, or even to strike fear. This can be seen in the aforementioned writer Ursinus, page 154, and further regarding this tree in the works of Matthias de Lobel <note>A famous 16th-century Flemish physician and botanist.</note>.
<margin>Shapes made from the Boxwood.</margin>

From the wood of this tree, people also turned whipping tops, which were called *Buxus* <note>The Latin name for the boxwood tree, also used to refer to items made from its wood, like tops or flutes.</note>, used as toys for children.

*Virgil, in Book VII.*
<margin>Also whipping tops.</margin>

> *As when a top, spinning under the twisted lash, which boys in a great circle round the empty halls, intent on their play, keep in motion: driven by the thong, it is carried in curving paths; the ignorant crowd stands amazed, and the youthful band wonders at the flying boxwood, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Ceu quondam torto volitans sub verbere turbo..."</note>

->That is, according to Vondel:<- <note>Joost van den Vondel was a preeminent Dutch poet and playwright who translated Virgil into Dutch.</note>

> *Just like the turned tops of the play-loving child, which quickly wind and roll before the crack of the whip, driven back and forth through the whole spacious hall, as often as the stroke gives them speed; there innocent and young lads marvel at the circling of the boxwood.*

And *Tibullus, Book I.*

> *For I am driven like a top spinning quickly over the level ground, which a swift boy turns with his practiced skill.* <note>original Latin: "Namque agor, ut per plana citus sola verbere turbo..."</note>

->That is:<-

> *I am hunted like a top, which, driven forward, runs quickly around once a child has given it a stroke of the whip.*

*Persius, Satire III.*

> *Nor was anyone more skilled at spinning the boxwood top with a whip.* <note>original Latin: "Neu quis callidior buxum torquere flagello."</note>

->That is:<-

> *And no one knew how to drive the boxwood top forward with more agility.*

<margin>Symbolism.</margin>
This tree is numbered among the wild trees that grow and thrive on mountains, on the slopes of hills, and in parched, dry places. When I see the Boxwood mentioned among the trees of the forest, the desert, and the wilderness—which, when not pruned, grow wild and often stand high and dry—as being brought into the spiritual temple and the garden of the New Testament, being watered and thus made fruitful and transformed into the nature of cultivated trees; then I can clearly see, in general, that this depicts the calling of unrefined, unpruned people. These were the people with whom the Heavenly Gardener in former

<column-break/>

times did not concern Himself, but who, early and late in the days of the New Testament, were to be graced and grafted into the congregation of Jesus Christ. This change among the wild, foreign nations—who were passed over by God in the past—would serve as a wonder to all and a sign that the Lord was God and King.

But to what specific category I should assign this, as distinct from other trees, I do not yet see. Meanwhile, I can find several similarities through symbolism, both in the people who are called and in those already graced.

The Boxwood grows in the wild, on parched and dry ground; but here it appears as watered and brought into the garden of God's church.

Truly, the Heathens grew up in the wild; God did not concern Himself with them, but let them walk in their own ways. They were previously without God in the world, without hope of salvation, alienated from the covenants of promise. They were in a land where the water of the Lord's Spirit and grace did not fall—just as one might call the state of the Jews, not only now under their blindness and hardening, but also by comparison to the church state of the New Testament, a parched and thirsty land. *Psalms 42:1, 2 and 63:1, 2; Zechariah 9, etc.; John 7:37, 38, 39.*

Yet through the powerful and gracious calling and transplanting, they find, under the Gospel, the poured-out Spirit—not in mere drops, but in downpours, in water-streams, and flowing brooks. *Psalms 1 and 23; Jeremiah 17:8.*

The fruits which these trees bore in their corrupt nature were, because of the bitter root and sap, bitterly foul-tasting, poisonous, deadly, and thus they were unfruitful trees. Such were the unfruitful works of darkness; no one could partake of them without losing health or suffering harm (Ephesians 5, etc.). But the transformation and watering by the Spirit with grace causes them to bring forth good, lovely, healthy, and manifold fruits, good and salutary for God and men (*Philippians 1 and 4:1; Psalms 1*). They retain their leaf of confession (*Psalms 1:3; Jeremiah 17:8*), being always green in virtues, able to show their life in and fellowship with Christ through the received and abiding saps of grace.

By nature, they were a very hard wood, and thus difficult to work; and so hardened and soaked in sin that they felt almost no worm of a gnawing conscience. But through grace, through true sorrow and conversion, that stony and unfeeling heart is so liberated (*Ezekiel 36; 2 Corinthians 7*) that they shall never be tormented by the worm of a bad conscience, nor ever be plagued by wretched passing away and destruction. *1 Corinthians 15; 1 John 3, etc.*

Was love written upon the external bark? Were the laws and ordinances of old written on planks and tablets of Boxwood covered with wax? They receive a new name (*Revelation 2*); they are named after their Lover and God (*Jeremiah 14; Acts 11*). The confession and marks of Christ make them sufficiently known (*Galatians 6:17; 2 Timothy 2:19; Revelation 7, 14, and 22*). Yes, the law of God is written on the tablets of their hearts (*Jeremiah 31; 2 Corinthians 3*), and thus they are a letter of Jesus Christ.

<header># BOXWOOD.</header>

Just as one could prepare various handiworks and vessels from boxwood; so every member of the **hidden body of the congregation** <note>This refers to the "mystical body of Christ," the spiritual union of all believers.</note> has their own gifts and their own use, *1 Cor. 12 and 14; 2 Tim. 2:20, 21. etc.* just as they previously had their distinct abilities and services under **Heathenism**, and even in the state of external **Judaism**, in their civil standing and various forms of religion.

If whipping tops <note>original: "dryftollen." Isa. 43:21. 1 Pet. 2:9.*

Eph. 4:23, 24. Col. 3:10.*

# CEDAR TREE, CEDAR WOOD, CEDARS OF LEBANON, <note>Hebrew: ארז, *Erez*</note>, <note>Latin: CEDRUS</note>, <note>Greek: Κέδρος, *Kedros*</note>.

<margin>Frequent mention of the Cedar in Holy Scripture.</margin>
Certainly, if any tree appears frequently in the Holy Scripture, whether in its literal sense or as a figure or likeness, it is the CEDAR or CEDAR TREE. Regarding the word *Erez* <note>original Hebrew: ארז</note>, there are those who derive it from a verb used by the Arabs which means to be firm and strong. Thus, it would signify a tree that possesses extraordinary firmness and strength (see *Stokkii Lexicon*). The renowned Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a famous French Protestant biblical scholar</note> in *Phaleg. lib. 1. cap. 35.* judges this to be a common name for all resin-bearing trees, following the Hebrews in this, and he is followed by Ursinus in *Arboret. Bibl. Sect. 2. cap. 19.*; yet it is not clear upon what ground this rests. The translators of the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek version of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> mostly translate this word as *Kedros* <note>original Greek: Κέδρος</note>, *cedar*, though sometimes as *kyparissos* <note>original Greek: κυπάρισσος</note>, *cypress*: however, the Hebrews have another word to express the Cypress, namely, *Gopher* <note>original Hebrew: גופר</note>. See under the word CYPRESSES. Lebanon is also said to be famous for its Cypresses, as they suppose from the translation of *Ezekiel 27:5* and *31:3*; but this is not to be gathered from either sacred or secular writers. For it is sufficiently understood that the Cedar tree must be meant there, because the aforementioned mountain range is established in the holy pages <note>original: "heilige bladeren," literally "holy leaves."</note> as the specific place for these excellent trees, and the describers of that mountain, both ancient and more recent, make mention of Cedar trees of extraordinary height and thickness found there; besides which, everything else said of this tree in the Scripture is applicable to the Cedar, as shall appear upon closer examination of the passages.

<column-break/>

<margin>Description of the Cedar tree.</margin>
As for the Cedar tree itself, the learned and industrious Johann Heinrich Ursinus, in *Arbor. Biblico*, has noted that the tree consists of an evergreen crown that never sheds; a bark that is somewhat rough and uneven from the lower base up to the branches, while the further shoots are smooth and even. Between the branches, it shines through with a heavenly blue color leaning toward brown; the orders or rows of the branches are very orderly, running in a circle around the trunk. Not too high above the earth, they leave the trunk bare of branches. The higher these trees grow, the more pointed and rounded they taper off, so that from afar they display and form the likeness of a pyramid. From the lowest branches, one climbs as if by rungs to the highest. They are very tall: they cast a thick shade: they give off a pleasant scent: the fruits look much like pineapples <note>In this period, "pynappels" referred to pine cones, not the tropical fruit.</note>, yet they are lighter; they do not hang downward, but on a stalk they point upward toward heaven. Some are found in Cyprus of 130 feet in length, and of such thickness that it is work for five men to encircle them with their arms. In Syria, they are of such thickness that they can hardly be embraced by three men.

Furthermore, they are durable, the wood is red, the roots are firm, and they are very tender in the beginning. Their bitter sap and oil protect them from the gnawing worm and from decay.

<margin>Which thrives best on Lebanon.</margin>
Because of the place where they flourished most, they are often called Cedar trees of Lebanon; (see the cited passages) and because of their greatness and beauty, Cedar trees of God. *Psalm 80:11.* Pliny, in the 16th book, chapter 11, and the 24th book, chapter 5, recounts: *That the oil prepared from the resin of this tree is of such power that in Egypt, the bodies of the dead being doused with it, they are preserved from decay. The large Cedars give a sap which could well be burned as oil, if it did not cause a pain in the head. If one smears anything with it, it is protected from moths and worm-stings.*

<margin>serves as an active agent.</margin>

<margin>Also for the purification of lepers.</margin>
<term>Cedar wood</term> was an ingredient in the cleansing agent for lepers: it was also used with the red heifer that was burned, etc. <term>Leviticus 14:49, 52.</term> <term>Numbers 19:6.</term>

The <term>Cedar tree</term> is also spoken of in <term>Numbers 24:6</term>, where one sees that <term>Bileam</term> <note>Balaam</note>, instead of cursing <term>Israel</term>, had to bless them; and for this reason the <term>Cedar tree</term> is named there, to be, among other things, a symbol of fertility and the blessing in <term>Jacob's</term> tents, which had spread far and wide, and were destined to be spread further, despite the enemies and nearby nations and powers.

In the book of <term>Judges 9:15</term>, <term>Jotham</term>, on the height of Mount <term>Gerizim</term>, demonstrates through a parable derived from certain trees not only the ungratefulness of the people toward the house of his father, but foretells the sad fates of the people, because king <term>Abimelech</term> would act according to his own will and lust, using great cruelty, without sparing great or small.

...wanted to root out the high Cedars, and hew down the choice fir trees; this can be understood literally, that he intended to bring about the destruction and loss of God's people, or figuratively, that he would make Jerusalem and the fortified cities of Judah bow before the power of his weapons and devastate them through the fire of war: and that he would by no means spare the kings and princes of the people.

<margin>Comparisons.</margin>
As for the passages and symbolic representations in *2 Kings 14:9 and 2 Chronicles 25:18*, they concern King Jehoash, king of Israel, regarding himself and King Amaziah, king of Judah, who had challenged him to battle. Jehoash compares himself to a Cedar tree and King Amaziah to a thistle, which had sought to enter into a marriage to bring the two kingdoms back into one. Jehoash mocks him and indicates through the symbol (for the Lord wanted to punish Amaziah for idolatry) that he, being content with the honor of having defeated the Edomites, should peacefully stay at home; otherwise, it was likely that he would be defeated by his army. See Burman on those two passages.

Regarding the passage and simile in *Job 40:12* <note>In modern Bibles, this is usually Job 40:17</note>, that the Behemoth lifts his tail like a Cedar: see the remarks on the word BEHEMOTH, and *Ursinus in Arbor. Bibl. page 356* etc., who takes it literally and applies it to the Elephant, citing *Pliny book 8, page 10.*

David in his 29th Psalm <note>original: "Snarenlied," literally a song for stringed instruments</note>, verses 5 and 6, also mentions the Cedars and Lebanon, saying that the Lord causes them to leap and move through upheavals.

On this, Bochart says in his *Hierozoicon, Volume 1, page 409:* Here we see the leaping caused by fear, which is attributed to Lebanon and the Cedars through a poetic exaggeration, as in *Psalm 114:4, 6.* Just as the terrible eruption and cracking of thunderclaps throw down not only the heaven-high trees but also the mountains, even the highest ones, from their roots and turn them upside down. And on page 288, judging that the word <term>וירקידם</term> <note>original Hebrew: "vayarkidem," meaning "He makes them skip" or "dance"</note> is well translated as *making them skip*, he says: for in the earthquake when the Law was given on Mount Horeb, God made the Cedars and mountains on which the trees stand skip and dance.

Alongside this, I will place what Johann Heinrich Ursinus in *Arbor. Bibl. page 304* has gathered from the ancients. Here, the power of the divine Word is spoken of first. Through it, the temples of idols were broken, being like the Cedars of Lebanon: which are highly exalted and are not accustomed to producing edible fruit. Basil and Theodoret believe that one should take it literally as God’s victory over Sennacherib and the Assyrians; and in a hidden sense, of Christ’s victory over the idols of the Heathens. Augustine says the voice of God, the breaking of the heart, humbling the haughty, will trample the proud who boast in the luster of nobility. Arnobius the Younger says: whoever has been rebellious and proud will be broken and diminished, like the Cedar of Lebanon. Those on Lebanon who to this day still sacrifice to the "fist-Venus" <note>likely a reference to a specific cultic practice or statue of Venus</note>, cut off the male parts of calves, and in that ritual, they offer such burnt offerings: they extend the reward of their error to their Goddess, a harlot; thus, he who has despised the purity and chastity of Christ shall be broken like a calf of Lebanon.

<column-break/>

<margin>Various interpretations.</margin>
I have noted that some understand this as thunder, through which the Lord, as proof of His power and majesty, overthrows the strongest trees and makes the mountains shake and tremble. Meanwhile, others understand Lebanon to mean the Jewish land, and thus its Cedars to mean the prominent rulers therein, and the breaking of the Cedars to mean the downfall of those notables. Compare *Zechariah 11:1 etc.*

<margin>State of the Jews after the exodus from Egypt.</margin>
*Psalm 80:11, 12* seems to suggest to me how the state of the Jews after their exodus from Egypt expanded to an extraordinary height, glory, power, and prestige, especially under David and Solomon, when the neighboring kings and princes were as nothing compared to them, indeed were made tributary. And this can satisfy the comparison in *1 Kings 4, 2 Chronicles 9, and Ezra 4.*

*Psalm 92:13:* <note>The source cites verse 14; in modern Bibles it is 92:12</note> *The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree, he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.*

<margin>Correspondence between the Righteous and the Cedar tree.</margin>
While referring my reader to the explanation of these words found in the writers on the Psalms, I am inclined, by the guidance of God's Spirit, to show the correspondence that can be made between the Righteous and the Cedar tree. Note then:

a. That it is said by God to be planted for His glory, and specifically on Lebanon *Psalm 104 and 148, Isaiah 41, etc.* So is the righteous man planted by God, *Psalm 1;* formed by God for His praise *Isaiah 43:21 and 60:21;* a sprout of His planting *Matthew 15:13;* on Lebanon His mountain, the church on earth. See under LEBANON.

b. The Cedar tree has a deep and firm root, through which it is deeply rooted in the earth. By the root, I understand here faith, through which he is very firmly and deeply rooted and united with Christ through love and close communion for nourishment; although one could also understand it as the close and firm communion with the church, its ground and place, where the soul-nourishing and strengthening means of the Word and the Sacraments are, as contrasted with the temporary believers who have no root. *Matthew 13:6, 21; Luke 8:13; Romans 11; Ephesians 3:17; and Colossians 2:7.*

<margin>Nature of the Cedar tree.</margin>
c. They shoot up very high, although being low at first. They are durable, they are very hard and firm of wood, they are full of sap and oily moisture, and they always have green foliage and fruits, and their fruits and crowns rise toward heaven, and at the same time they give off a lovely scent: their resin is fiery red, in a straight trunk, though rough and uneven toward the bottom, yet smooth and even toward the top.

<margin>Description of the Believers.</margin>
Here I observe that the believer is first low and small in faith and knowledge, but he grows in knowledge and grace, *2 Peter 3 and Proverbs 4;* he goes from virtue to virtue, from strength to strength, *Psalm 96;* first he is a child, then a youth, then a full-grown man and father in Christ. *1 John 2.*

The righteous, says Jansenius, always increase in good: they become higher in themselves until they reach the very heavens, toward which they, like the Cedars, always strive.

Hear Beza:

> But the righteous raise their heads
> Even to the clouds, like the palm;
> And their high peaks, like the cedars
> Of Lebanon, weigh heavy. <note>original Latin: "At justi adusque nubila, / Ceu palma, tollunt verticem; / Et celsa, tanquam Libani / Cedri, gravant cacumina."</note>

<header>CEDAR TREE.</header>

->That is:<-

They are hard and firm, possessing great strength and endurance, being strengthened by grace against every cross and sorrow (2 *Corinthians* 12; *Romans* 8). They are not easily moved, being firm in faith and having within themselves the living and incorruptible seed of the ever-abiding word (*Matthew* 16; 1 *Peter* 1). They are full of the oil of the Spirit (1 *John* 2). They have the anointing of the Spirit (2 *Corinthians* 1; *Ephesians* 4:22).

They are always green; their leaf does not wither (*Psalm* 1; *Isaiah* 17), filled with the fruits of righteousness (*Philippians* 1 and 4; *James* 2:18).

<note>original: "Anniculum, & binum, & trinum Phoenicia Cedrus Fert fructum: nunquam desidiosa fides."</note>
The Phoenician Cedar bears fruit in its first, second, and third years;
Faith is never idle.

->That is:<-
> *The Cedar gives in the first, second, and third year*
> *Its fruits: faith always attends to its duties.*

Their heads are turned upward, high with their hearts, conduct, and desires (*Colossians* 3:1, 2; *Philippians* 3:20). These are not fruits of the earth, but heavenly gifts and fruits (*Matthew* 6:20-27; *Philippians* 3:20). These spread a fragrant scent of knowledge, love, and blamelessness of conduct (2 *Corinthians* 1; *Philippians* 1 and 4; *Song of Solomon* 4). Their heart is always fiery red, as if burning and glowing through the fiery, upright, and strong-reaching love for God—the lover of their soul—Jesus, and their neighbor (*Matthew* 22; *Psalm* 18; 2 *Corinthians* 5; *Romans* 12, etc.).

It is true that in their behavior some unevenness appears in what is lowest and closest to the earth. Before one notices their spiritual fruitfulness, something uneven, hard, and rough appears in them; but the fruit sweetens it all, and the less refined part is immediately adorned and made perfect by the perfect part that yields fruit.

d. This tree has this quality: it must not lose its top or upper crown, or it will perish and die; and it is a miracle if it survives the danger of dying out. Faith, having cast its hope as a sheet-anchor into the inner sanctuary—if that were cut off, life would vanish and the tree would die (*Hebrews* 6:4, 5, 6, etc.).

<note>original: "Ut moritur Cedrus si forte cacumina tollas; Sic homo totus obit deficiente fide."</note>
As the Cedar dies if you happen to remove its crown;
So the whole man perishes when faith fails.

<column-break/>

->That is:<-
> *If you shear the high top of the Cedar, it is dead.*
> *Thus man dies, if he is stripped of his faith.*

e. In the Cedar tree there is something that kills and causes to consume and perish <note>The author refers here to cedar oil's natural pesticidal properties</note>, by which it is itself incorruptible and is not gnawed by the worm; it has the power to ward off serpents. Through the power of God's grace and the fruit of Christ's merits and spirit, the inflammation—the corruption that comes from sin, the foul poison brought in by the serpent's bite—is crucified, killed, resisted, and brought under (*Romans* 6; *Colossians* 3; 2 *Corinthians* 4; *Galatians* 5). The evil one flees from them, and they resist him (*James* 4; *Ephesians* 6; 1 *Peter* 5; *Romans* 16).

f. The Cedar tree served for buildings and for ships; so also the believers together make up that spiritual house and temple of the Lord (1 *Peter* 2:5; *Ephesians* 2:20-22, etc.), that little ship of the church that must toss upon the waves of this world (compare *Psalm* 107:23).

But let this be enough as a sample of what correspondence there is between a cedar and the righteous; I must yet consider and clarify more symbolic texts.

As for *Psalm* 104:16 and 148:9, these show us the works of God’s power, sufficiency, and wisdom in creation, preservation, and governance, with all things being urged to praise God. He provides the rational creature with the material for this, especially when one relates everything to the new creation, and in every day and era of the New Testament, attentively searches out the Lord’s works to recreate and perfect everything.

In *Song of Solomon* 1:17 one reads, *the beams of our houses are cedars, our rafters are cypresses.* See regarding this under the word BEAM.

*Song of Solomon* 5:15: *His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the Cedars.* Here is a figurative way of speaking by which the church, the bride, portrays the true Solomon <note>In mystical theology, Solomon in the Song of Songs is interpreted as a "type" or prefiguration of Christ</note>, so that his appearance and form, rightly considered and known, is as excellent as it is beautiful, capable in all parts of giving satisfaction to the soul, and of delighting in Jesus' loveliness and beauty, and standing in awe of his glory. Nothing in Judah was more lovely than Lebanon; no trees more excellent in height and pride than the Cedars. The church makes it understood how she blesses and prides herself in the Lord (*Isaiah* 45 and 65; 1 *Corinthians* 1:31).

<margin>Parallels between Christ and the Cedar.</margin>
This passage gives me cause to also point out what parallels can be thought of between Christ and the Cedar tree; who also, in *Ezekiel* 17:22, is compared to a tender twig of a Cedar tree, of which more will be said shortly.

a. The Cedar has its roots in the earth, is at first low and close to the ground, but grows high and seems to touch the heaven with its crown. The Messiah is from a dry ground (*Isaiah* 53), from humble beginnings (*Isaiah* 9 and 11; *Psalm* 2), though raised from a royal house to a heavenly height and majesty (*Philippians* 2), exceedingly exalted, and has his crown raised above all kings and powers in this present world (*Psalm* 2, 72, and 89; *Daniel* 2 and 7; *Luke* 6; *Matthew* 28; *Ephesians* 1; *Hebrews* 1; *Revelation* 17 and 19, etc.), just as he himself according to his Divine nature,

b. The Cedar tree is beautiful to behold, lovely in scent, and full of moisture and oil. Christ is the fairest of the children of men, *Psalm 45*; the scent of his merits and offerings, *Ephesians 5, Song of Solomon 1, Ephesians 1*, is very pleasant; his oil is abundant. *Psalm 45, Psalm 133, John 11* and *Isaiah 61.* <note>The original cites "Joh. c. However, the lower bark up to the branches that are fruit-bearing is rough, uneven, and not very handsome or desirable. Jesus's lowly human nature is close to the earth, and from the earth, insofar as he is our brother, *Hebrews 2* and *4*; he had little form or beauty, *Isaiah 53, Philippians 2*, especially not when he was so miserably scourged, mocked, spat upon, and crucified, and when his sweat ran down like drops of blood, *Matthew 26*, and he was made like a potsherd. *Psalm 22.* But when he began to manifest his power and spread the branches of his kingdom and domain—using for that purpose his sent and gifted Apostles, with the living word of the comforting Gospel among Jews and Gentiles—from then on, he was seen as that which was beautiful, most desirable, and healing.

d. The Cedar tree is always green, incorruptible, and full of fruits. Christ is the green wood, *Luke 23.* According to his Divinity, he is immortal, incorruptible, always of an infinite power and inexhaustible sufficiency. The First and the Last. And although he died, he did not decay. *Psalm 16, Acts 2.* He lives for eternity. *Revelation 1, Hebrews 7* and *9.* His fruits remain always and like themselves, being freshly plucked every month. *Revelation 22.*

e. Since the Cedar tree, with its sawdust and bore-dust <note>original: "zaag- en boorstoffe"</note> and with its oil, drives away snakes, overcomes worms, and prevents destruction and rot, what then shall we not think of the Christ? Indeed, he has crushed and finished the hellish Serpent. *Genesis 3:15, 1 Corinthians 15, Hebrews 2.* It is in his power to give life to the dead and to raise them to an incorruptible life. He kills those who think they live. He makes alive those who are dead in sins and sleep in the dust of the earth. He is the life and the resurrection. *1 Corinthians 15, Revelation 1, John 14:6.* He kills the worm of the accusing conscience of sinners. *Romans 5* and *8, 1 John 2, etc.*

One reads in *Isaiah 2:13*: "Against all the high and lifted up Cedars of Lebanon," etc. I will likely not be mistaken if I say that these are the same as in verse 12, and that the Prophet then expresses himself through symbols: unless one wants the phrasing of verse 12 to refer to all sorts and kinds; and that in verse 13 the Jewish greats, commanders, and authorities in the civil state and the church are primarily intended; which, if one regards it as a heavy judgment according to the civil and earthly state of this life, had its fulfillment before Christ’s coming in the flesh. For how the great ones lost their authority and highness around that time, both through Herod and the Roman Governors, is learned from divine and human histories, and preeminently from the destruction of the City and Temple.

If one takes it as a benefit and conversion, then it had its fulfillment in the humbling of the proud Jews—formerly swollen with the imagination of their own righteousness from the works of the law, as was seen before—and is seen from time to time in those who are converted; and which is to be expected once more in the subduing of the world, when the mountain of the Lord, in its preeminent power above all mountains and hills, shall have no heaven-high Cedars able to prevent the progress and the most excellent flourishing and adornment of the church.

*Isaiah 9:9, 10.* The sycamores <note>original: "wilde vygboomen" (wild fig trees/sycamores)</note> are cut down, but we will change them into Cedars. This metaphor seems to indicate the intolerable and God-provoking pride of the Israelites, who after God's judgments were still just as bold, unreformable, and proud, wanting to change the lowly into the magnificent, imagining that they were to increase incomparably in number, authority, and state.

As for *Isaiah 14:9*, from the content of this chapter it is clear that the fall of Babylon is seen there, and Babylon is openly mocked. Whether one must look at the worldly and old Babylon, or at the spiritual new-Testament Babylon, regarding that...

there is a dispute among scholars. Some relate it to ancient Babylon, suggesting that the Jews, seeing its fall, were now joyful and mocking, and that the "Jewish trees"—the great and exalted ones—were no longer afraid of any evil it might bring them. However, others believe one should by no means turn one's eyes away from the "Spiritual Babylon" <note>A common Reformation-era term for Rome or the Papal establishment.</note>, described so vividly, but rather think of how the Bishops in England, and the kings and princes in Germany and elsewhere, no longer fear the Pope (who already languishes and has taken to his bed due to the weakening of his power and authority, by which he once deposed and installed kings and emperors, making them all fear and bow before him), nor do they fear his "Vatican lightning" <note>original: "Vatikaanschen blixem"; a reference to papal bulls of excommunication</note>. Instead, they rejoice in their hearts and laugh at him because he has lost his power; and that Nebuchadnezzar's encounter and weakening until his final fall serves as an example of what shall befall the spiritual Babylon in the time of the Antichrist.

<margin>God's promise to His church.</margin>
In *Isaiah 61:19* <note>The author likely intends Isaiah 60:13 or a similar passage regarding the glory of Lebanon, as chapter 61 ends at verse 11.</note>, the Lord appears to strengthen the early Christian church in her persecutions and hard trials, promising that He would pour out and cause to flow the waters of His Spirit and grace, even in the desert of Heathendom. To the astonishment and spite of her enemies, He would raise up fertile trees within Heathendom—great and prominent persons, high in state and power—under whose branches and shadows the church might nestle and dwell.

*Jeremiah 22:7-14, 15-23.* Here, the Cedar is used either in magnificent architecture to represent loftiness in greatness, or is taken to represent the great and prominent, the proud and those exalted by their status, riches, and power in Judah—particularly under that king whom the Lord would by no means spare. For it is generally true that the Lord resists the proud.

<margin>A riddle in Ezekiel.</margin>
*Ezekiel 17:2-22, 23.* This is a riddle and a sign concerning an Eagle, who plucked off the highest twig of the Cedar with its young branches and carried it into a land of trade, etc.

This riddle is unraveled in the same chapter: the King of Babylon is compared to an Eagle who carried away the royal house in the person of Jeconiah and his household, along with his princes and nobles, to Babylon in Chaldea; setting his paternal uncle, Zedekiah, as king in his place. However, the latter, breaking the covenant, defected to the King of Egypt; this treachery did not go well for him, *2 Kings 24*, and his lineage was rooted out.

Furthermore, the Lord promises in *verses 22 and 23* that He would pluck a tender twig from the highest branch of the high Cedar, from the top of its young twigs, which would be planted on a high and lofty mountain and become a great tree. Understand here by the "high Cedar" the royal house of David; by the "highest branch" and the "top of its young twigs," Jeconiah, along with his lowly and powerless descendants. Thus, that tender twig shall be either Zerubbabel, as some wish, or, as others better judge, it <margin>Manifestation of the Messiah.</margin> represents the Messiah, who in that place is depicted in His upbringing, descent, lowliness, and the glory that follows. See *Cocceius on this passage, and Alting Hept. III. Diss. 4.* <note>Johannes Cocceius and Jacob Alting were prominent 17th-century Dutch theologians.</note>

<margin>Tyre, a merchant city.</margin>
In *Ezekiel 27:5-24*, Tyre appears, a famous merchant city which traded with the Promised Land and nearly all nations, taking fir trees from Senir and Cedars from Lebanon for its decks and masts. They also packed their merchandise in cedar wood.

This can be understood literally as it is written. However, many bring it home to the "Spiritual Tyre," which trades in God's word, grace, the forgiveness of sins, Christ, church offices, revenues, indulgences, etc. See **TYRE**.

Regarding *Ezekiel 31:3-8*, let the reader see what has been said under the word **CHESTNUT TREE**.

*Amos 2:9.* Israel's abominations and punishment are presented plainly and clearly in this chapter; and to demonstrate God's righteous dealing in this punishment, it is pointed out what benefits the Lord had done for this people—not only that He led them out of Egypt with a strong hand, but also, when the measure of the iniquity of the Amorites was full, He destroyed and drove them out, so that there would be room and a dwelling for Israel. Yet that people had been ungrateful, base, and adulterous.

<margin>Amorites compared to the Cedar.</margin>
The Amorites, well-known and famous among the Canaanites for their numbers and power, being a principal part of Canaan, are here compared to a Cedar tree.

As for the passage in *Zephaniah 2:14*, I cannot see it otherwise than that the Lord promises His people, on condition of conversion, that He will destroy the enemies He lists there, whether through temporal punishments or spiritual weapons; such that Nineveh, 그 "Cedar of Assyria," would become a desolation, with the destruction of its precious and magnificent buildings.

In *Zechariah 11:1, 2*, the fall of the great is presented as an example and terror to the lesser, and subsequently God's judgment against Jerusalem and its inhabitants is described and revealed, just as it was to be carried out by the Romans. This is not even rejected by Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi.</note> on this passage, who admits that this destruction is being looked upon. But by the "doors of Lebanon" and its "Cedars," he understands the doors and the wood of the Second Temple, which was likely cedar wood, just like that of the first.

<margin>Cedar tree a symbol of Christ, etc.</margin>
From all that has been said, the reader may conclude that the Cedar tree is a symbol of Christ, of believers, of fruitfulness and blessing, of princes, kings, and prominent persons of rank (both good and evil), of powerful nations, of those proud of their status and riches, of spiritual gifts, and so forth.

<note>original Latin: "Chamus membra sui ridet nudata parentis, In cruce nudatum ridet apella Deum." The term "apella" was a Roman nickname for Jews, referring to circumcision.</note>

->That is:<-
->Ham sees his father naked and makes sport of him:<-
->So does Jewry mock the crucified God.<-

Jerome expresses a similar view in his dialogue with a follower of Lucifer of Cagliari: The eldest son, who was a year older than Shem—as Rabbi Zacuto correctly judged—mocked his exposed father, while the younger son covered him. Similarly, the Jews laughed at the crucified God, while the Gentiles honored Him.

Polycarpus Lyserus makes this observation in his commentary on *Genesis 9*, page 357, etc.

But at the same time, let us remember that Noah was a Prophet, and that we are built upon the word of the Apostles and Prophets, which is still preached to us this very day. For wherever the "Hamites" and "Canaanites" are found—that is, those who despise their parents, the disobedient, and the mockers of the Son of God—this curse shall strike them. The Jewish Canaanites learned this: for when they followed in the footsteps of this Ham and mocked the Son of God appearing in the flesh, <margin>Titus Vespasianus</margin> *Titus Vespasianus* <note>The Roman Emperor who destroyed Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> came immediately and uprooted them. And in the present day, what does the Roman High Bishop—who bears the title of Ham and calls himself a "servant of servants"—do with his whole lineage other than mock the Son of God with his "merits" and persecute Him in His members? Therefore, we do not doubt that the divine curse remains upon him, though it has been deferred until now.

The learned Hulsius, in *The Shape of the Times*, page 492, etc., has the following on this subject:

The Jews, who are Canaanites and mockers of Christ and the Father, are cursed in the day of vengeance. This is due to the curse of the chosen Law, the hindrance they caused the Gospel, and their contempt for the Evangelical calling or invitation; but especially because of the violation committed against the Rock and Christ, whose members they did not cover in the aftermath, but instead exposed and despoiled. For this reason, the wrath of the Lamb now pursues them; because of this, they lie in those outer darknesses, cast out from the church of Christ and from salvation, by

<column-break/>

the power of the Law, the power of divine hardening, the wish of *Christ*, and the wrath of the Lamb. Combined with their unbelief, these factors ensure that God’s wrath remains upon them.

The rejected Jews are considered no different than Canaanites, partly because they largely sprang from that land, and partly because they were born from Jacob’s wives taken from the peoples of that land; for which reason it is said in *Ezekiel 16* that their birth is from Canaan. Furthermore, they resemble the Canaanites in their unbelief and godlessness. They are also subject to the descendants of Japheth <note>Traditionally identified as Europeans.</note> both physically and spiritually, scattered among them and dominated by them. From Ham and Canaan the Moors <note>Historically used here to refer to North and West Africans.</note> descended, etc., and that people is regarded as nothing other than despised slaves, and they are treated and sold as such.

<margin>Ham and Canaan live again in the Antichrist.</margin>
In many respects, one might say that Ham and Canaan live again in the Antichrist and his lineage: both because of his title, as he writes of himself as *servus servorum* (servant of servants), and because he is the Antichrist who opposes the true Noah—Christ, the perfect bringer of rest. He <margin>In what manner?</margin> mocks the single and perfect atoning sacrifice of Christ, robbing Him of His majesty, power, right, and authority. He does this by introducing the service of the tabernacle, the necessity and merit of the Mass, sacrifices, meritorious works, and the invocation of saints, as well as through his imagined highness and authority in heaven and on earth, etc. Thus, he leaves Jesus naked and exposed; though he praises Him with his mouth, he mocks and denies Him through his actions.

This figure dwells in the land of the spiritual Egypt: he is Canaan, the merchant of worldly and spiritual goods; he is Mercury, the patron and protector god of all the clergy who carry out this trade; he is honored and worshipped by his own as a god on earth, like Jupiter Ammon. He is Jupiter Ammon, from <term>αμμος (ammos)</term> <note>Greek for "sand."</note> sand, because his authority rests on a foundation of sand, just like everything he owns. He is cursed by the Lord, and his judgment shall dawn at the proper time, though he mocks it and says in his heart, "I shall see no sorrow."

### CHERUBIM, כרוב / Χερουβίμ.

<margin>Varying guesses about the Cherubim.</margin>
Many have "broken their heads" <note>An idiom meaning to struggle intensely with a difficult problem.</note> over the CHERUBIM. Much has been written about them by Christians and non-Christians alike; and since these are things that few have seen, it happens that guesses are somewhat inconsistent, and scholars sometimes differ among themselves.

I also begin to speak on this, and I shall inform my reader regarding what men of no small learning or reputation have said and left behind on this matter. Thus, I begin with a consideration of the Name.

Since some understand these CHERUBIM to be symbolic representations of the Angels, and people have imagined Angels as highly intelligent spirits—beings constantly in the presence of God—and as possessing great experience, they have found that the name *Cherub* or *Cherubim* was fashioned thereafter, deriving it from the word <term>נכר (nakhar)</term> <note>Hebrew root for recognizing or knowing.</note>, to know or recognize.

# CHERUBIM.

<note>original Hebrew: כרוב (Cherub)</note>, to discern, and <note>original Hebrew: רב (Rab)</note>, *much*; beings who know much, and are therefore "wise-knowers," wise, all-knowing spirits. *2 Samuel 14:20: But my lord is wise, according to the wisdom of an angel of God, to know everything that is on the earth.*

Others derive the word from <note>original Hebrew: כ (Kaph)</note>, meaning "like," and <note>original Hebrew: רב (Rab)</note>, a *rab* or *rabbi*: so that a Cherub is like a Teacher or Rabbi, who, in order to be fit to teach and instruct others, must themselves be wise, understanding, and practiced.

Yet some may find more satisfaction in the judgment that the word <term>Cherubiah<gloss>A variation of the word Cherub suggesting a great multitude</gloss></term> signifies "like a multitude," from <note>original Hebrew: כ (Kaph)</note> meaning "like" and <note>original Hebrew: רבוא (Ribbu)</note>, a great multitude, as they appear in great numbers in *Daniel 7:10, Revelation 5:11,* and *Luke 2:13.*

But because it is said that Angels have appeared in a masculine form, specifically as youths—fresh, strong, nimble, and swift—who are mighty heroes and angels of God's power, to whom great deeds are attributed (*Psalm 103:20, 2 Thessalonians 1:7*), just as the heavy slaughter in the Assyrian army is credited to an Angel; the rolling away of the stone in *Matthew 28*; and the opening of the prison in *Acts 12*: some have derived the word *Cherub* or *Cherubim* from the <term>Chaldean<gloss>An ancient Semitic language related to Hebrew, often used in biblical commentary</gloss></term> word <note>original Chaldean: כרוביא (Cherubiah)</note>, from <note>original: רביא (Rabia)</note>, meaning "to grow" or "to wax strong," just as children grow into the greatness and strength of youths. For this reason, the Cherubim on the <term>Mercy Seat<gloss>The gold lid placed upon the Ark of the Covenant</gloss></term> and elsewhere have been depicted as fresh and strong young men.

Since we sometimes find mention of God's chariot in *Psalm 18:11, 68:18,* and *104*, and the Angels are understood as God’s chariots, some have derived the name from <note>original Hebrew: רכב (Recheb) or רכוב (Rechub)</note>, meaning "he has ridden" or "he has been carried along"; from which comes *Recheb*, a chariot, and <term>Merchabah ha-Shekhina<gloss>The Chariot of the Divine Presence</gloss></term>, the chariot of the Divine Majesty.

Spencer argues that the word *Cherub* means *to be strong, mighty, or swift*, as it is applied to the King of Tyre in *Ezekiel 28:14*. He further says that whenever God wishes to manifest Himself beyond all visible and known human power—whether He uses angels or men as intermediaries to glorify Himself through great miracles—one or more Cherubs appear. *1 Samuel 4:4, 2 Kings 19:25, Psalm 18:11, 80:1-2, 99:1,* and *Isaiah 37:16.*

But to cut short further elaborations regarding the origin of the word, I say that those who link the word Cherub to the <term>Oriental<gloss>Refers here to Near Eastern languages like Hebrew or Arabic</gloss></term> word for *plowing* (<note>original: כרב (Karab)</note>) have likely not missed the mark, since oxen were formerly used for plowing as well as threshing.

> The sailor speaks of winds, the plowman of bulls,
> The soldier counts his wounds, the shepherd his sheep.
<note>original Latin: "Navita de ventis, de tauris narrat arator, Enumerat miles vulnera, pastor oves."</note>

->That is:<-

> *The sailor speaks of wind, whose power he has found,*
> *The shepherd of his cattle, the warrior of his wounds.*
> *So too the farmer speaks of bulls in his turn.*

See *1 Corinthians 9:8, Deuteronomy 25:4,* and *1 Timothy 5:18.*

This concludes the origin of the name.

<margin>Form of the Cherubim.</margin>
Regarding the form, shape, and appearance of the Cherubim, it is evident that they do not appear in a single way, but rather according to the context of the matters

<column-break/>

the Divine writer had in mind; for:
1. In Solomon’s Temple, they are depicted on the side walls in carved relief work, beautifully rendered on both sides, with two faces in front and two behind: with their wings stretched sideways along the walls.
2. But on the Ark of the Covenant and the Mercy Seat, they appear in a different form, with their faces and wings.
3. In *Ezekiel chapters 1 and 10*, they are different again, with four faces, with wheels and wings, full of eyes.
4. In *Isaiah chapter 6*, they are different again.
5. In John’s vision, each is like a living creature unto itself.

Because such a notable difference exists between the forms of the Cherubim, the question arises: in what likeness were they depicted on the Mercy Seat? To this, one might offer the following response:
a. Moses left behind little to nothing regarding this matter.
b. And we later Christians have never seen them.
c. Since they appeared twice in visions to Ezekiel, and he described the Temple very minutely in *Ezekiel 1, 10, and 40*, Moses’ account is very brief and broken, while Ezekiel’s is more detailed.
d. In *Revelation 5*, they appear as four living creatures; and in *Isaiah 6:2* and *Revelation 4:8*, they appear with six wings and full of eyes.

Thus, I would believe that since the Lord intended His symbolic sanctuary to be as complete an image of future things as possible (*Hebrews 8:5, 9:23, and 10:1-2*), He would have ensured that the symbolic Cherubim contained everything related of them in Holy Scripture, insofar as it agreed with the form of the Ark and could be most emphatically represented.

<margin>Differences of the Cherubim.</margin>
Most scholars believe the form of the Cherubim incorporated something of a man, an eagle, an ox, a lion, and wings; some emphasize one, others another, and thus they differ more or less. Some imagine them as two naked youths with only two wings. Others depict the Cherubim as having:

1. The face and body of a man.
2. The feet of an ox.
3. The chest, neck, and shoulders draped with a lion’s mane.
4. Furthermore, parts of an eagle. See Jerome, Pradus, Pererius, and Grotius.

*Witsius*, writing on *Exodus 24:18-20*, states: *They had their wings stretched upwards. With their outspread wings, they covered or overshadowed the Mercy Seat: their faces were opposite one another, both directed toward the Ark upon the Mercy Seat; from which one can conclude that they were winged creatures; but with how many faces, and what their actual body form was, Moses remains silent; either because this matter was already well enough known then, or because a higher reason and mystery lay hidden within it. Who can say?*

And as for the opinion of Jerome and Pradus...

<margin>Remarks of Witsius.</margin> Others, however, ascribe four types of heads to the Cherubim, and consequently many heads or partial heads; the front face being that of a human, on the right side that of a lion, on the left side that of a calf <note>or ox</note>, and from behind that of an eagle. It is argued that these were joined together into one head and one body, which corresponds most closely with the literal text. However, the form of the calf was most prominent, both because in *Ezekiel 1 and 10* it is called the face of a Cherub, and elsewhere the face of an ox, and because <term>כרב<gloss>Hebrew: k-r-b</gloss></term> means "to plow," which is specifically the work of oxen; also because Divine expressions and customs seem derived from this (*Psalm 68:18; Zechariah 6*). Furthermore, they are attached to the wheels, and these were what they drew forward.

And he concludes from all he has presented thus: *That the Cherubim were unusual animals, having the greater part of their body like an ox, provided with large wings—though it is uncertain how many—and equipped with at least two faces, namely those of a lion and a human.*

Spencer <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English scholar and Hebraist.</note> agrees with this: *The naming is based on the largest part; they came closest to the form of an ox, by virtue of which they received the name of an ox or calf.*

Flavius Josephus, in *Book 3, chapter 5*, describes the Cherubim as flying animals; others describe them in the form of flying birds.

However, let this be enough regarding the forms of the Cherubim in general.

Turning now to some particulars and various passages, I will subsequently present the thoughts of the learned on each specific place.

*And he drove the man out, and placed Cherubim at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming blade of a sword, which turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life. Genesis 3:24.* <note>The source text cites Gen. 3:3-4, but the quote is from verse 24.</note>

After the Lord had caused the man, who had sinned, to move from his desired resting place, He placed Cherubim or Angels—for there were no humans besides Adam and Eve—as visible signs of His presence, as watchmen of God, and executors of His justice at the entrance of the garden in the east, which likely provided the most suitable access to the garden. They were placed with a flaming blade, or a flame shaped like a sword, most closely resembling a glinting blade: a fire ready for vengeance to fall upon those who promise themselves peace outside the doctrine of the promise and the way of faith. Into this heat of wrath would fall those who fall away from the tree of life, who—along with Adam and Eve—seek fig leaves of their own righteousness to cover their sinful and shameful nakedness, and would try to excuse themselves before God.

Hermann Witsius, in his *Aegyptiaca* <note>A scholarly work comparing Hebrew and Egyptian rituals.</note>, writes: *It is a matter known and accepted by all that by Cherubim, Angels are understood; but in what form they appeared, in what outward shape, and why they are called Cherubim, is not stated. That there was something external and visible is evident from the gleaming sword—a form in which they appeared more than once (Numbers 22:22-23; Joshua 5:13; 1 Chronicles 21:6). It is well known that Moses wrote Genesis 3:24 some time after he was commanded to make the holy furniture, and he thus intended to name the Cherubim as symbols of the Angels, looking more at what was symbolized than at the form and specific*

<column-break/>

*kind of the symbol itself.*

And regarding the Cherubim in the Temple of Solomon in *1 Kings 6:23–28* <note>The source text cites 1 Kings 3:11-12, but describes the 10-cubit high statues in the Inner Sanctuary.</note>, Witsius has explained it thus:

> *As for the Cherubim in Solomon’s Temple, these did not have their faces opposite one another, but they stood side by side, both having their faces toward the east and the west, one behind the other. They spread their wings sideways across the width of the Most Holy Place, so that one Cherub touched the south wall with the tip of its right wing, and the other touched the north wall with the tip of its left wing, and they touched each other with their middle wings.*

§ Some matters are brought forward from Professor Campegius Vitringa <note>A prominent Dutch theologian (1659–1722) famous for his commentary on Isaiah.</note> regarding *Isaiah 6*.

<margin>Seraphim.</margin> Seraphim signifies burning, fiery, glowing bodies, from <term>שרף<gloss>Hebrew: s-r-p</gloss></term>, "to glow" or "to burn." The Seraphim in this passage are living beings, displaying the form of fire, a fiery appearance like the living creatures in *Ezekiel 1:13*.

One might ask whether Isaiah saw two or more. There could have been more, but divided into two rows, as can be concluded from their calling out to one another.

These stood above the throne. Did the servant then stand above his Lord? Some translate it in such a way that they do not apply it to the Lord, but to the throne. Others translate <term>ממעל<gloss>Hebrew: mimma'al</gloss></term>, "over," as "before him," "beside him," or "close by him" to serve him; yet the term everywhere appears with the meaning of "above" (*Genesis 22:9; Isaiah 35:4*).

The prophet wishes to imply that the Seraphim appeared to him in this vision as heavenly beings who came from an exalted place, and that they stood on both sides of the throne in such a way that they seemed a little higher than He who sat upon the throne—yet by no means protruding above the canopy of the throne—standing slightly to the side of the King to obey His command. To this end, they also appear winged, as those who would turn and set out from the exalted place to all others to execute the King’s orders with the greatest speed.

When the prophet spoke of six wings, he subsequently seemed to mention only one Seraph; but that is to be understood according to the property of the Hebrew language, which speaks of each one individually, referring to what belongs to every one among many (*Amos 6:9*), and thus to all of these.

Who shall we now judge is meant by these Seraphim? Some understand them to be all of God's holy servants. Origen, Jerome, and others understood them to be the only-begotten Son of God and the *Holy Spirit*. Cocceius and others say the Angels. Brentius says the Prophets and Apostles.

Vitringa distinguishes between a historical and a spiritual or prophetic sense. If one interprets and applies it to Isaiah, his time, and what appeared to him, then the Angels certainly come closest; but in a prophetic and spiritual sense, regarding the kingdom of the Son of God to be revealed in the world in His time, then we must understand two other choirs and rows. page 149.

Both views are briefly presented.
