<meta>This page continues the theological investigation into the nature of celestial beings, moving from the physical descriptions of the Cherubim on the previous page to their symbolic roles as divine servants and their representation in the visions of the prophets Isaiah and Ezekiel.</meta>

# CHERUBIM.

<margin>Angels as God's servants.</margin>
They appear surrounding Him as if with a retinue and bodyguard, as seen in *1 Kings 22:19, Daniel 7:10, and Revelation 5:11*. Angels are specifically and emphatically called "servants of God" in *Psalm 103:21*.

<margin>The nature of Angels.</margin>
Fiery bodies are attributed to them, not for their own sake, but to signify something else; this prompts us to consider the simplicity <note>In a theological sense, "simplicity" refers to being composed of a single substance, unlike humans who are a mix of body and soul.</note> of these angels, their swift activity, purity, and the excellence of their nature. As spiritual and heavenly beings, they are separated from the "filth of matter," *Psalm 104:4*. It also allows us to perceive their moral purity, holiness, earnestness, and zeal, through which they glow and burn for the glory of God, *Psalm 103:21*, as well as their speed and readiness in carrying out divine commands, *Psalm 104:4*.

<margin>Their standing by the throne.</margin>
When they are depicted as "standing" or "remaining standing" by the throne, it is a sign of the state of their ministry, to which they have been chosen and appointed by God—both in the realm of providence and especially in the kingdom of grace or the church. *Psalm 103:20, Daniel 7:10, Hebrews 1:14, 1 Kings 10:18, Job 1:5, 2.*

<margin>Above the throne.</margin>
When they are depicted as standing "above" the throne, or on both sides of the throne, this is understood to signify their origin or inclination: they are not of the earth, but from heaven. *Luke 22:43.*

<margin>Their wings.</margin>
They are provided with six wings for flying and covering. These wings undoubtedly signify the attributes natural to angels, through which the use and effect are provided to them, just as wings provide in this symbolic vision.

And although the angels "always see the face of the Lord," *Matthew 18:10*, natural attributes are nevertheless united with that "seeing of God," which could not be more aptly presented than by faces covered with wings, in order to portray:
1. The modesty, reverence, and sense of awe of the angels, with which they are moved before the Divine Majesty.
2. Their weakness, when considering the Divine glory.
3. And that they are, as it were, ready to stand at God's service with a "blind obedience," even though they do not yet see through the reasons or the ends of God's counsel. *Isaiah 40:13, Romans 11:33.* See Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a prominent Dutch theologian and commentator on Isaiah.</note> on *Isaiah*, page 150, etc.

They cover their feet; regarding which Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), the famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> noted that "feet" in Holy Scripture are understood to mean the bodily parts which modesty teaches us to cover; a point already noted before Grotius by Sanctius <note>Caspar Sanctius (1553–1628), a Spanish Jesuit scholar.</note> on *Job 7:20*: the lower part of the body, *Job 4:18 and 15:15*. Even though they have an excellent nature, they cannot be compared with God. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his covenant theology.</note> seems to have understood the covering of the feet as a symbolic means of showing they regard nothing but their duty, *Luke 17:10*; however, Vitringa says the feet here are not as fitting a symbol for the duty of a servant as the wings are.

<margin>Meaning of the covering of the feet.</margin>
Thus, the covering of their feet signifies more likely that they are holy and without defects, such that nothing shameful is seen or heard in the holy angels, neither by God nor by men. *Matthew 25:31, 1 Thessalonians 3:13.*

That they fly with two wings is not to be understood as if they flew 

<column-break/>

around and near the throne: but they are depicted with outstretched wings, as if ready at the first order to carry out the Lord's will; the power to follow orders with the greatest speed. *Psalm 18:11, Psalm 104:4.*

But in a secret and prophetic sense, the Seraphim signify the more excellent servants of Jesus Christ, regarded as King of the church; zealots for His glory, through whom Christ promotes His kingdom on this earth. For likewise:
a. Excellent servants are called "Angels." *Haggai 1:13, Zechariah 3:7, Malachi 3:1.*
b. He himself, whose tongue was touched with the fire of the altar, was counted among the Seraphim in verse 6.
c. God's will must be done on earth as it is in heaven, *Matthew 6:10, Psalm 103:21*. Vitringa page 153: the meaning is, "Bring it about that there are more on earth who may serve You with the same obedience, readiness, purity of inclination, earnestness, zeal, and steadfastness with which the angels in heaven perform service and honor to You." That is: bring it about that there are more angels and men of a heavenly inclination on earth.
d. The angels are but fellow-servants, *Revelation 19:10*. See Vitringa on Revelation.
e. Thus, faithful servants, princes, etc., are heavenly in inclination, and like a heavenly seed; both in the parables and in the prophecies, in a familiar and proper manner of speaking, they are "angels of the Son of Man" and "heavenly hosts." *Matthew 13:41 and 24:31, Revelation 12:7 and 19:14.*

Because Christ is presented as "perfected through suffering" <note>A reference to Hebrews 2:10.</note>, as King and Judge—not only by way of a history, like *Isaiah 31*, but also in a prophetic way—these servants cannot well be excluded. They are servants of the kingdom, in whom He has received gifts, *Psalm 68:19*; chosen ones among men, servants of Jesus Christ, whose service and help He uses to establish, advance, and preserve His kingdom among men.

The two rows are the Prophets and Apostles, upon whose teaching the church of the New Covenant is built. *Ephesians 2:20.*

How everything is applicable to these excellent servants, teachers, etc., shall subsequently be shown at the end, to which I direct the reader.

Furthermore, since many scholars have spent their labor on the vision in *Ezekiel 1 and 10* and have expressed their thoughts in writing—and I have shared with the reader the thoughts of Professor Vitringa just prior—I shall consider this vision in the same way. I do so the more willingly because many scholars' thoughts have been brought together by his reverence, the transcription of which I can thus spare. With much shortening, I make this following extract and proposition from *part four of Sacred Observations* <note>original: "part. quart. Observ. facrar." referring to Vitringa's "Observationes Sacrae".</note>.

The Cherubim were the Lord's carriage. The word <term>מרכבה<gloss>Hebrew: Merkabah</gloss></term> "wagon" or "chariot" does not appear there. Ezekiel also does not say that he saw the wagon apart from the Cherubim. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the Cherubim, specifically examining their role as the "wheels" and "living creatures" in the visions of Ezekiel and their symbolic connection to the architecture of Solomon's Temple and the governance of God's kingdom.</meta>

# CHERUBIM

...dare not, but upon the creatures to which the wheels were attached.

Therefore, according to *Ezekiel 1:22, 23*, the creatures support the Lord’s throne with their wings, and in this respect, they are also called God’s wagon and carriage in *Psalm 18:10* and *Psalm 99:1*. The wheels, being united with the wagon and the Cherubim, served as this support, just as wheels support a carriage.

Pintus <note>Likely referring to Jacobus Pintus, a Jesuit commentator known for his work on Ezekiel.</note> believes that this is an allusion to the great wash basin <term>Brazen Sea: a large circular basin in the Temple of Solomon used by priests for ritual purification</term> at the entrance of the temple, whose bases or pedestals—crafted with the highest skill—were supported by Cherubim and wheels, as described in *1 Kings 7:27, 28, 29*. And I believe one should look to the large copper wash basin standing in the temple, resting on a base or means of support upon which the images of Cherubim, lions, and oxen were carved with intermediate decorative work, and having four wheels below, joined to the supports, allowing the basin to be moved about.

In the Kingdom of Grace—which is founded upon the righteousness of Christ’s suffering and death, and which Christ obtained for Himself through these—Ezekiel saw in a vision: the Cherubim and wheels signify the same thing as the supports of the wash basin; the twelve oxen signify the same thing as the Cherubim.

<margin>God's kingdom viewed in two ways.</margin>
Since God’s kingdom can be viewed in two ways: 1. as the kingdom of His providence, in which He governs all worldly things, great and small; or 2. as a kingdom of grace, consisting of God’s care for and over the church; it has been found that some have interpreted this regarding the former, while others have applied it to the latter.

Those who apply it to the church and the Lord's government over it are particularly focused on the interpretation of the four creatures. Some apply them to the four Evangelists <note>Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, traditionally symbolized by the man, lion, ox, and eagle.</note>, though they differ in the specific application. Others apply the four creatures to four principal guardian angels of the Lord's people. By the wheels, some understand Apostles, Prophets, Evangelists, Pastors, and Teachers. Others understand the four creatures to be the New Testament church, inspired and made alive by God; and by the wheels, they understand the holy angels, performing their service to the church, in whom the same spirit dwells that is in the church.

I understand, says our learned author, by the throne of God among Israel, *the kingdom of grace, as a symbol of the spiritual and heavenly kingdom which the Lord was to establish in Christ in His own time; and secondly, the spiritual and heavenly kingdom that the Father governs through the Son, sitting upon the throne with majesty and glory; as in Isaiah 6:1, 2, John 12:41, and Hebrews 4:16.*

The exemplary kingdom <note>The earthly kingdom of Israel serving as a "type" or shadow of the heavenly reality.</note> under Israel is by no means excluded by his reverence, but included within it, which can be seen in his own work.

My hypothesis is then, *that the creatures and wheels signify instruments upon which God’s kingdom rests, and by means of which it is advanced.*

My next hypothesis is *that the creatures and wheels are rational and living instruments. Regarding the wheels, there is no difficulty, for they had the spirit of life, and they also had eyes. Ezekiel 1:18–21.*

From all which has been granted, I generally conclude that I understand them to be the ministers of the Old and New Testaments, whom the Lord uses

<column-break/>

for the founding, expansion, and preservation of His kingdom, acting as the supports and pillars of the same.

I do not understand the four creatures or Cherubim to be the general church, as Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian.</note> and Hofman <note>Possibly Melchior Hoffman or a similar contemporary commentator.</note> do. For not all the elect perform such singular services for the advancement of the kingdom. Furthermore, *the excellent virtues or gifts of knowledge of God’s ways, prudence, gentleness, purity, holiness, nobility, steadfastness in despising the world, constant occupation in the Lord's work, and strength in fighting and overcoming the world, etc., are not found collectively in all believers.*

God’s throne, with its pedestals and supports, is to be distinguished from the people over whom the Lord, sitting on the throne, exercises command and authority.

And in *Revelation 6:1*, etc., it is said that John was taught by the creatures. The church did not teach John; rather, John represented the church there, which was to be taught. Therefore, the creatures who instructed must be distinguished from the church, which was being instructed in the person of John.

And if the creatures are viewed as a symbol of the church in general, what then will the wheels signify? Not the angels, as Cocceius maintains, for the spirit of holiness, wisdom, and readiness does not pass from the church to the angels.

What shall we best make of the wheels in our imagination? God’s servants are either heavenly or earthly—that is, those who are on earth. Some apply the symbol of the wheels and creatures to the angels. Some to the angels above and ministers below. Some only to the ministers below who are conducive to the kingdom.

<margin>Symbolism of the wheels and creatures.</margin>
It is true that some, with some appearance of reason, are reminded of angels here, because in the writings of *Moses*, angels appear under the name of Cherubim, and because in *Isaiah 6*, the learned have understood Seraphim to be angels.

Yet, for the following reasons, that cannot easily be accepted or maintained by me. Namely:

1. The spirit passes neither from the church to the angels, nor from the angels to the church; the same spirit is in both of these.
2. In *Revelation 7:11*, the creatures are distinguished from the angels; and if the four creatures in *Isaiah 6* are angels, why then are they distinguished from the angel? If one should wish to argue that they are distinguished from common angels as being heads or chiefs, I shall answer: 1. This is a fabricated distinction; 2. In that case, they should not be distinguished from the angels in general; 3. Such a thing is of little use in a symbolic vision.
<margin>Instruments of God's kingdom.</margin>
3. Not the angels, but the ministers are the primary instruments of the kingdom of God and Christ Jesus. We find the names of the Apostles written as foundations, but by no means the names of the angels.
4. The four creatures and the twenty-four elders give thanks for their redemption in *Revelation 5:9, 10*. This does not apply to the angels, according to *Hebrews 2:16*.
5. The appearance of a man and an ox fits humans better than angels.

I conclude, therefore, that the creatures and wheels are all excellent ministers, whom God...

# CHERUBIM.

...and are in service to His kingdom: and that these servants are so closely united with one another that the spirit passes from one to the others, being helpful on earth, yet distinct from the angels in heaven.

The living creatures <note>The "living creatures" (Dutch: *dieren*) refer to the four beings described in Ezekiel 1 and Revelation 4.</note> are, in my view, extraordinary men, uniquely gifted with the Holy Spirit, in both the Old and New Testaments. *Moses, Joshua, Deborah, Gideon, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, etc. Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Haggai, etc. Apostles, Evangelists, Teachers in early Christianity.*
<margin>Meaning of the Wheels.</margin>
By the wheels, I understand the ordinary servants of the Old and New Testaments, such as the Priests, Shepherds, Teachers, etc.

Where it is said of the King of Tyre, *you were an anointed covering Cherub: and I had set you so, you were upon God’s holy mountain, you walked in the midst of the fiery stones,* although there are among the scholars those who apply this to the actual and literal Tyre and its king—as high, great, and awesome, having covered other powers, etc.—it seems to me, subject to correction, that in a hidden and prophetic sense, with allusion to the ancient Tyre, it can be applied quite as powerfully and meaningfully to the spiritual Tyre, the Roman domain of the Pope. This domain has degenerated and fallen away from the ancestors, among whom the pure faith and the defense of the pure doctrine of faith were once found. He presumes for himself the protection of the church, claiming that Jesus has established His throne upon him. He pretends to be the first and most prominent servant of God’s kingdom, through whom the King of Heaven speaks; he claims that the spirit of infallibility is housed within him, that he is a speaking God, whose spirit is also in the wheels—the Cardinals, Archbishops, Abbots, Priests, Jesuits, and Monks—whom he inspires to speak according to the spirit that is in him. See under TYRUS.
<margin>Application to the spiritual Tyre.</margin>

As for the vision in *Revelation IV* shown to John, many scholars have written about it, and as is often the case with such deep matters, not with the same understanding. In order not to report everyone's thoughts at length, I will provide the reader with what can be read in detail in the learned work on the Revelations by Prof. Camp. Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian known for his commentaries on Isaiah and Revelation.</note>. I shall trim my extract as much as is feasible for me.
<margin>Vision of John.</margin>

In the ring-like circumference of the throne stood 24 thrones, upon which the 24 elders are represented as sitting; something similar is depicted in *Isaiah XXIV. 22.*

Round about the throne <note>original: "Κυκλόθεν τοῦ θρόνου" (Kyklothen tou thronou)</note>, round about the throne of God, as if in a crescent-shaped circle, from both sides or corners of the throne.

If there is no allusion made to the seating of the *Synedrium* <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme council and tribunal of the Jews in Jerusalem</term> or the great and broad council of the Jews, (*see Selden, On the Sanhedrins, book xi. chap. 6; Vitringa, Sacred Observations, book xi. chap. 4. §. 11.*) then an allusion is made to the priestly assembly and seating in the priestly hall. This is because allusions are made to the temple and its holy things, and in the number of the elders, reference is made to the 24 priestly orders; and in describing the elders in white robes with crowns, allusion is made to the Chief Priests, whose signs of authority were crowns.

Through and under the title of elders, it is given to be understood: all rightful governors and faithful shepherds of the church of the New Testament reigning with God in Christ

<column-break/>

through the continuous passage of time of the New Testament church.

The white robes symbolize that they are justified and sanctified in the blood of Christ, *1 Corinthians VI. 11.* and that they are Preachers and Teachers of this doctrine of the true justification of the sinner.
<margin>Meaning of the white robes;</margin>

That they appear shining with crowns on their heads represents that they, having been promoted and raised to the dignity of the governance of the church, have entered into the portion and fellowship of Christ Jesus’s majesty and glory, of which the ornament of crowns was also a mark.

They reign principally with Christ, those who govern in the church—that is, those who govern and serve the church of God’s elect—if they have the spirit of Christ Jesus. See Vitringa, page 178.

By the four living creatures, some understand four archangels, princes in the heavenly household of angels, with regard to the four heavenly winds and regions, as De Launay <note>original: "Lanaeus"</note> and those who followed him have held.
<margin>Meaning of the four living creatures.</margin>

By the four living creatures, others understand the entire body and the multitude of believers of the New Testament, such as Mede <note>Joseph Mede (1586–1638), an influential English biblical scholar.</note> and Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian who developed Federal Theology.</note>, etc.

Many among the ancients understood them to be the four Evangelists. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), the famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> understood them to be Peter, James (the brother of Jesus), Matthew, and Paul.

Others desire that an allusion be made to the princely standards or main banners of the army of Israel around the tabernacle, namely, those of Judah, Ephraim, Reuben, and Dan. However, our learned author could by no means approve of these opinions.

Certainly not the first opinion of De Launay, because the Scripture does not speak of such four archangels in other places, and because the four living creatures in this entire vision are joined with the elders and are distinguished from the elders, yes, even from all the angels. Just as in *chapter VII*, the angels stood around the throne, the 24 elders and the four living creatures: they are absolutely distinguished from the angels, and form an entirely different rank, as can be seen in *chapter V. 9, 10, 12.* The entire heavenly assembly is split into two ranks and choirs: the living creatures and elders (verse 8) and the angels (verse 11). An entirely different song of praise and closing speech is attributed to the living creatures and elders (verse 9) than to the song of praise and closing speech of the angels (verse 12). Furthermore, the symbolism attributed to the living creatures better fits men—ministers of the kingdom of God that is to be expanded—than angels and archangels, as anyone will easily see for themselves.

Nor can the entire body of believers be well understood by them, because it is sufficiently manifest and clear that in all the believers who make up the New Testament church, those excellent virtues are not found whose symbolic representations are shown in these living creatures. Furthermore, I should say that the four living creatures in the visions to John are brought forward before the elders, placed above them, and serve as an example to the elders, and the hope of the elect is subsequently distinguished from these, *chapter VII. 9.* And these creatures taught and exhorted John, who in his person here replaced and represented the church. *chapter VI. 7.*

Consequently, it does not please me to understand by these four living creatures...

# CHERUBIM.

...the four Evangelists, or four prominent servants as Grotius, etc. understands in the N. T. <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch jurist and theologian who often sought rationalist or historical explanations for biblical prophecy.</note> and to pick them out from so many: for what reason is there to choose these few, since there are so many who have been promoted in office, dignity, and other qualities in the kingdom of God, making them equal and standing together, and to pull others ahead and above them?

Therefore, nothing else remains for us than that we understand by these four creatures the highly excellent servants of God, whose help God has used to ground, preserve, and raise up His church throughout the world during the entire time of the new dispensation: those who, being powerfully called by God, have given themselves entirely to God and to the utility of the church, and have steadfastly and bravely endured all adversities for His name, honor, and truth: those who have been diligent in labor, watching, with contempt for all worldly comforts: and have allowed themselves to be led and moved by the Lord’s Spirit; and in a word, all those in whom a singular and remarkable grace of God has shone forth, such that they are chosen out from the common sort of believers, and have been advanced closest to the perfection of the true servants of Christ and Teachers of the church: among whose number I primarily place the Apostles and Apostolic men of the first time: thereafter also Prophets, Evangelists, Teachers, provided by God’s singular grace above the common in the first church age: subsequently, those who may have been lower than these, yet are by no means to be excluded from this rank, such as for example Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, Origen, Athanasius, Gregory Nazianzen, Chrysostom, Augustine, Bede, Bernard, Calvin, Oecolampadius, Ussher, Martyr, etc.

In order to now give my Reader a view of the thoughts of the most prominent scholars, who have viewed the Cherubim as symbolic representations of the angels, since they appear more often under this name: and the Lord appeared with these on Sinai, and they are in His service, and around His throne, *Deut. 33 <note>Original: XXX; likely referring to the blessing of Moses in Deut 33:2</note>, Ps. 68:18, Acts 7, John 1:52, Dan. 7 and 10, etc.* and they were primarily placed in the temple and on the mercy seat <term>mercy seat: the golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant where God's presence was said to dwell</term> by divine order; so I shall consider them as they appeared on the mercy seat and elsewhere in this treatise.

<margin>Material.</margin>
The general material, especially of those that stood on the Ark of the Covenant <note>Original: "bontkift," a variant for "bondskist" (Covenant Box/Ark).</note>, was pure gold, and the others were of precious workmanship.

<margin>Image of the form of the Angels.</margin>
A fitting mark and symbol of the angels' precious, glorious, pure, incorruptible nature, glorious form, and gifts.

Their attachment, union, state, and position, as emerging from the mercy seat, and very closely joined and united with the same and the ark, has been noted to be a symbol of this: that even if they were not bought and set free by Jesus Christ, *Hebr. 2:16,* they were nevertheless created by Him, are maintained, and are carried in His power, *Ps. 30:6, John 1:4, Col. 1:16,* and *Hebr. 1:2, Rev. 4:11,* being His servants who must pay Him homage, *Psalm 97:7, Hebr. 1:6,* having made the elect on earth and the angels of heaven and earth into one citizenship *Hebr. 12:22, 23, Col. 1:20, etc.*

<margin>Cherubim with human faces.</margin>
The Cherubim are shown with a human face. This belongs more to the

<column-break/>

things to which they have regard and relation, than to their nature and actual inner essence, as they are simple spirits who have no outward appearance of face, flesh, or bones. *Luke 24:39.* And therefore it is a symbol, not only of their close connection and interaction with men, having been brought into one community and citizenship: but additionally of their wisdom, prudence, understanding, humanity, and gentleness, as being appointed for the service of those among the elect who shall inherit salvation.

They appeared in the essence and with the face of a lion. Not with lion’s paws, teeth, and claws toward the elect, to terrify, devour, or harm them—such fits better for the godless—but to serve, protect, etc., the elect.

It is a fitting symbol of their fearlessness, strength, and bravery, mentioned in *Psalm 103:20, 2 Thess. 1:7,* because of their works *Isa. 37:36 <note>Original: Jef. XXXVII</note>, Matt. 28:2, Acts 12:7,* and their watchful guard-duty and powerful protection. *Psalm 34:8, 35:5, and 91:11, 12, Hebr. 1:14.*

They appear with the face of an ox; an animal formerly accustomed to plow and help promote the work of the fields; thus serving as a sign of the angels' activity, untiring nature, willingness, steadfastness in their state, love, and service, which they perform toward those chosen for salvation according to the will of God.

They appear to us in God’s Word as having the face of an Eagle; to depict the angels' nature, character, and properties; as being not earthly but heavenly, nesting as if on high, therefore also called the heavenly host, heavenly armies, *Psalm 33:6, Luke 2:13,* constantly busy around the high God, the divine, and those who are destined for the heights of God, *Isa. 6:3, Hebr. 1:14 <note>Original: Hebr. XIV; likely Hebr. 1:14</note>, Rev. 4:8-11,* having eagle eyes of a sharp understanding, *2 Sam. 14:20,* performing divine orders, swift as with eagle wings, *Psalm 103:20, 21, and 104:4, Hebr. 1:7,* always striving toward the heaven-heights, and flying up like eagles, *Job 39:30, Psalm 103:5,* with a renewal of their heavenly zeal and passion. *Isa. 40:31.*

Furthermore, they appear with wings, through which movement is made wonderfully hurried and faster, by which they show themselves active in various ways; as a symbol of the angels' proper acknowledgment of God, and reverence for His highly-dreaded majesty, to willingly obey and observe His high and pure throne-orders with readiness. *Psalm 104:4, Hebr. 1:7.*

<margin>Wings of the Cherubim.</margin>
Of their six wings, two appeared stretched out and raised upward; as being from above, as wanting to go upward, having in all their activities the honor of God as their aim, in the performance of service according to the divine will, toward those whose names are written in the heavens; just as if they pointed upward with their wings, and wanted to carry them with themselves to God’s throne.

With two wings they covered their faces, the mercy seat, and the Ark of the Covenant. By this one can consider the angels' modesty to be depicted, their very deep humility, and the evident fear of God's supreme majesty and incomparable glory and highness, as being nothing compared to the Lord: that they are as if blind, without the reasons and...

# CHERUBIM.

...to perceive and see through the ends of Jehovah's counsel, following his commands as servants, knowing that nothing can or shall come from him except that which is good, holy, wise, righteous, and fitting for him.

In the time of their ministry, the doctrine of the promise was covered as if with a wing, creating shadow and darkness, becoming wrapped in examples, shadows, and riddles, *2 Cor. 3; Heb. 2:5, etc.* while they also occasionally cover and protect the ark as if with a wing. *Psalm 34:8; 35:5, 6; 91:11, 12.*

<margin>Explanations.</margin>
With two wings, one finds their hands, body, and feet as if covered; which has been noted by some as a symbol of their humility, as they do not exalt themselves in their deeds, *Luke 17:10.* However, since they are depicted as performing their primary work with their wings, this can certainly serve to some extent as a mark of modest reverence. But it can also signify that, regarding what they do, they are covered in such a way that no fault or impropriety is found in their actions by God or men; and that the nature of angels is invisible. The hands are a symbol of skill, and these, being united with wings, could illustrate that great speed and haste—if not paired with skill and dexterity—would cause a person to fall into great difficulties by birthing over-hastiness.

*When they are depicted flying with two wings;* this can be held as a very fitting symbol of the angels' inner disposition, readiness, desire, and joy to be able and willing to always be obedient to the Lord, and in that very obedience, their mindset, flying from the high order upwards, being heavenly spirits and heavenly hosts.

*When they are depicted as looking toward the mercy seat;* <note>original: "verzoendexel"</note> one can view it as a symbol of their inner and abiding desire to be allowed to see God’s plan of peace in the actual reconciliation and redemption of sinners through the Son of God, with the glorious rays of God's virtues, in the power and emphasis of his name, *Exod. 34:5, 6, 7; Ephes. 1:6, 7, 1.* and *3:10; 1 Pet. 1:12.* looking as if toward the high orders and handiwork of him who sat upon the mercy seat, like servants looking to their masters. *Ps. 123:2; Rev. 19:10.* <note>The Dutch text cites Psalm 133:2, likely a scribal error for Psalm 123:2, which describes servants looking to the hand of their masters.</note>

*When they are described elsewhere as being full of eyes all around, in front and behind, over the whole body;* then one could take this as a symbol that one should imagine in the angels and their actions a great understanding, singular wisdom, and a close foresight and circumspection, observing everything accurately; seeing the past and the future, insofar as it can pertain to them as created and finite spirits—to angels who always stand before God's face as his throne-messengers.

*They are also portrayed with ox or calf feet, with straight feet, with round feet;* which has been held and viewed as a symbol of the angels' stability and surefootedness, and the humility and purity of their conduct and walk; that all their intentions are good, virtuous, and right, being according to God's will and command, directed as if by a rule: an activity they can perform without difficulty, and everywhere, because round feet have no front or back.

<column-break/>

*Furthermore, it says that they go straight forward.* Due to the roundness of the feet, there is no crookedness or deviation. They do not stray from the path of God's commandments, doing nothing outside of or against their duty; the difference and distinction between nations is now gone; God now has his chosen ones everywhere; in the way of God, one does not turn back; there is also no crooked path; all the ways of the angels are straight, though they are dispatched and used for many things by him who sits upon the throne; in them, no deviation is seen, nor is any side-track to be found in their inner nature.

*When they appear with feet of fiery red, glistening like red and glowing copper;* then it is viewed as a symbol of their holiness and glowing zeal for the honor of God, coming closest to the divine virtues. *Dan. 10:6; Rev. 1:15.*

*In such a way that in this description one encounters two types of animals: two tame ones, namely man and ox; two wild ones, namely lion and eagle; the former to be a help, service, and comfort to the believers; the latter to terrify the disobedient; the lion to track down the enemies on the earth, the eagle to resist the spiritual enemies.*

Both of the tame animals are on the earth, because the protection of angels is necessary for us on earth, but not in heaven.

<margin>Cherubim as symbols of the Angels.</margin>
Let this serve as a small sample of how the Cherubim have been viewed as symbols of the angels of God.

Going further, I shall show how the Cherubim and Seraphim have been primarily viewed as representing the prominent servants of God in establishing and propagating his kingdom in the world below, as was already noted above; it being observed here that Christ Jesus does not take on the nature of angels, but the seed of Abraham, *Heb. 2:16.* that the spiritual blessings earned by the Messiah are prepared and obtained for the elect: that Christ Jesus is the actual <term>Caphoreth: the Hebrew term for the "Mercy Seat," the gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant where atonement was made.</term>, not for the angels, but for sinners, etc.

And it should be observed while reading the following applications and comparisons, that it must be understood in a lower and fainter sense for all common Christian believers, and in a more exalted and powerful sense for the exceptionally gifted and zealous teachers and men whom the Lord has raised up, does raise up, and shall yet raise up, to uniquely advance the interests of his kingdom through them: in such a way that one may allow it to be said that there is an emphatic depiction in the Cherubim of how one ought to be, and what one must strive for. But pruning further preparations, I come to the matter itself, proceeding with the same arrangement of topics as used before.

<margin>Application.</margin>
The Cherubim consisted of pure gold, a solid, heavy, pure, precious, lasting, and radiant substance. This is applied in this manner to believers in general, and with emphasis to the excellent among them—the prominent heads and blessed instruments in God’s kingdom and right hand. That in these, one contemplates the glorious nature which they share through rebirth: the precious purchase-price and ransom by which they are redeemed, bought, and obtained; their noble and very precious faith, along with the gold of knowledge; Christ's imputed righteousness and shining garments of internal and external purity...

<meta>This page continues the symbolic interpretation of the Cherubim, moving from their general nature to the specific meanings of their connection to the Mercy Seat and the significance of their four faces—human, lion, and ox (with the eagle to follow).</meta>

# CHERUBIM.

and holiness, along with many kinds of beautiful gifts and virtues, for which reason they are dear and precious in the Lord's eyes. *1 Corinthians 6:20; 1 Peter 1:7, 18, 19; Job 28:12, etc.; Psalm 45; Isaiah 61:10; Psalm 16:3; Isaiah 62:3, 4.*

The **Cherubim** appear in the vision as emerging and protruding from the <term>mercy seat<note>The 'mercy seat' (Dutch: *verzoendeksel*) was the gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant, representing the place where God’s mercy meets human sin through atonement.</note></term>, firmly united with it, and rising above the Ark of the Covenant. This is interpreted in this way: that believers are members and the body of Christ; His people, seed, portion, and inheritance, whose origin and beginning is from Him, dwelling through Him, with Him, and closely joined and united through the Spirit, faith, and love. This is represented through symbolic language and parables taken from natural things—of head and members, vine and branches, *Isaiah 15; 1 Corinthians 12 and 14*—that Christ dwells in the heart through faith, *Ephesians 3:17;* that he who clings to the Lord becomes one spirit with Him, *1 Corinthians 6:17;* that we are God’s workmanship in Christ, *Ephesians 2:10;* His people and creation and new creatures, *Psalm 100:3; 2 Corinthians 5:17.*

Excellent teachers—chosen instruments in Jesus's right hand—have this in common with all other members; yet they protrude, stand out, and excel above the common members of the Ark like heads or governors of the people. They receive their calling, qualification, and mission from Him who is the mercy seat, though in varying measures of gifts, *1 Corinthians 14;* not out of or from themselves, *2 Corinthians 3:4; 12.* They are authorized and tempered to preach Him as the mercy seat, *Matthew 28; Mark 16; Romans 10:15; 2 Corinthians 5:18, 19, 20.* They share with Jesus in His power, authority, and glory, insofar as they have governance in the church in His name, with and under Him, sitting as if on thrones.

*We have seen and heard that the face of the Cherubim was like the face of a man.* This was intended to impress that all who have communion with the mercy seat, Christ Jesus, spring from Him, are and remain united with Him, and also partake of His Spirit and His anointing. Thus, they must be of the same nature as He was; not beasts, horses, mules, or animalistic men who do not have the Spirit; wise to do evil, but too foolish to do good, *Psalm 3; Isaiah 1; Psalm 32; Jeremiah 4:22 and 5:21.* No, but those who possess the Spirit of Christ, the anointing of the saints, enlightened eyes, being taught by the Lord, *1 John 2:20; Isaiah 54;* which befits and suits the "new man," *Ephesians 4:24; Colossians 3;* with the gift of prudence, love for God, and toward one another, etc. *Ephesians 4; Colossians 3; 2 Peter 1:4, 5, 6, 7.*

Particularly, human understanding is very fitting for leaders, that they—like Apollos—be mighty in the scriptures, able to teach, and capable of "rightly dividing" the word of truth. *1 Timothy 3:2; 2 Timothy 2:15.* That a peaceful nature becomes them, *Isaiah 60:17; Matthew 5:9; 1 Timothy 3:2, 3;* that they ought to use understanding, circumspection, and gentleness, making distinctions in their treatment of others according to a person's state and nature. *1 Thessalonians 2:17; Galatians 6:1, etc.; 1 Corinthians 3:2.*

We have also learned that the Cherubim had a lion’s face. Not biting and roaring lions with biting teeth and tearing claws; no, but all the righteous must be heroic and undaunted to resist the world and Satan; standing for truth and righteousness in divine matters, the honor of God, and the interests of Jesus's kingdom,

<column-break/>

this is bravery and courage, an eminent and healthy state of mind, *Proverbs 28:1 and 30:29.* It befits them, along with David and the church, not to be fainthearted. *Psalm 23:4 and 27:1 and 46:4, 5, 6.*

It especially befits teachers and leaders to heroically and undauntedly wage the wars of the Lord against the world and Satan; not to be "dumb dogs," *Isaiah 56:10 <note>The OCR reads "L. 10," but this is a likely reference to the "silent watchmen" of Isaiah 56:10.</note>;* not to be afraid, *Joshua 14:27;* to deny themselves, *Matthew 16:24;* and not to count life or anything else as dear. *Acts 20:24 and 21:13; Romans 8:36.* It is testified of lions that they sleep with open eyes; Christians must be sober and watch, and constantly keep their eyes open, never laying aside all oversight through carelessness. Danger sometimes comes suddenly. *Song of Solomon 5:2; 1 Thessalonians 5:5, 6, 7, 8; 1 Peter 5:8.* Especially, since the overseers are watchmen, watching and having oversight over the congregation befits them singularly. *Ezekiel 3:17, etc., and 33:7, etc.; Acts 20:28; Hebrews 13:17.*

The nature of the lion is not like some cowardly animal that outwits someone from behind or leaps from the side; but rather to meet someone face-to-face and grapple with them directly.

It does not befit any Christian, much less any heroic and noble-minded teacher, to grapple with someone as their opponent using lies, deceit, craftiness, slander, abuse, or suspicion; no, their weapons must be direct—weapons of light and of the dawn, weapons of righteousness, true weapons, the manifestation of the truth to the conscience. *2 Corinthians 4:2 and 10:4, 5.* See further under **LIONS**.

*We have seen above how the Cherubim had the form and face of an ox.* A symbol, without doubt, of those who are ready, steadfast, capable, and industrious, singularly well-disposed and suited to undergo and carry heavy works and burdens; being at the same time a clean animal that <term>chews the cud<note>In period theology, "chewing the cud" was a common metaphor for meditation—slowly "digesting" and reflecting on God's Word.</note></term>, which has a firm and certain gait and step; which clean livestock was anciently brought to God’s altar, though in a certain respect it eats grass, and in certain cases gores with horns.

As oxen, it does not belong to or befit the righteous to eat grass with the transformed Nebuchadnezzar—meaning they should not seek the low and trivial things of the world and primarily prey upon them, *Psalm 17; Philippians 3;* nor should they be wanton and unruly oxen who throw off the yoke of the Lord, for whom serving the Lord would be a yoke and a burden: to be as stupid as an ox or donkey, which neither knows nor shows it knows its duty. *Psalm 78:8; Hosea 4:16; Malachi 1:13 and 3:14; Isaiah 1:2, 3, 4.*

But in general, it befits and suits the chosen and called, as God’s household, to be tame, composed, and well-disposed; constantly preying upon the clean and living words of God and "chewing the cud" of what they consume. *Psalm 1:2 and 119:11, 15, 19; Jeremiah 15:16; Luke 2:19.*

It befits them to be industrious and hardworking in the Lord's work, *1 Corinthians 15:58;* to be firm in the Word of God for believing and confessing, *Romans 10:10; 2 Corinthians 4; Psalm 116:10;* and to offer themselves up to God. *Romans 12:1; 1 Corinthians 6:20.*

Before and above all others, this accords with the state, calling, and office of the plowing and the Lord's...

# CHERUBIM.

working in the fields, shepherds and teachers, being at one, peaceful, not fighters nor strikers <note>The Dutch *smiyters* refers to those prone to violence or "strikers," following the requirements for bishops in 1 Timothy 3:3</note>, not being filthily defiled, but keeping themselves purely exemplary in everything, *Isaiah 60:17; 1 Timothy 3; Titus 1.* And since they must teach others, *1 Timothy 3,* they must be learned, teachable, and capable in it, so that as those experienced in the word of righteousness, they may speak the words of God. To this end, they must indeed read, reread, and meditate upon the word of God, so that the treasures of wisdom and knowledge may be found within them.

It suits them, before and above all others, to be willing and industrious in the Lord’s plowing and fieldwork, *1 Corinthians 3:9, 10; 1 Corinthians 9:16, 17, 18, 19.*

It suits them to stand in the breach before the Lord, sacrificing their lives and everything, *Acts 20* and *21,* as was noted above.

<margin>Fighting for the truth recommended to the teachers.</margin>
And although—preserving a good conscience, truth, and righteousness—peacefulness and gentleness are wonderfully becoming to them, cases do arise where they must bite back and butt with horns to silence opposing parties, to make the truth manifest to the conscience, and to move the godless to conversion through the fear of the Lord; for not all spiritual weapons have a single use. *Ephesians 6; 2 Corinthians 5:10, 11; 2 Corinthians 10:4, 5; Titus 1, etc.*

<margin>Cherubim with the face of an Eagle.</margin>
It was also seen and heard above that the Cherubim appear with the face of an eagle. I do not think this is with an eagle’s beak and claw to tear and devour after making a kill; no, but I believe that the Spirit of God, among many other things, intended to depict for us through this symbolic means the understanding, power, and loftiness of the soul. This belongs to all the righteous who have opened and enlightened eyes, so that they might contemplate the wonders of God's law and the mystery of faith, *Colossians 2:2; Colossians 1:27; Ephesians 3:1-18, 19.* Indeed, He wished to portray that the chosen, called saints do not have closed eyes, that they are not blind in divine matters, but have cleared and bright eyes of understanding, *Ephesians 1:3; Isaiah 54; 1 John 2:20.* They must be "heaven-winged" eagles, in no way hovering low to the earth with their thoughts, desires, and conduct, but lifting themselves upward and heavenward in all these things. *Daniel 7; Colossians 3:1; Philippians 1 and 3:20, etc.*

If one applies this to the guides, heads, and rulers, I believe that in the course of time there have been highly enlightened understandings in God's church—heaven-winged eagles. Remember what was cited above from <term>Vitringa<note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist known for his commentaries on the prophets.</note></term>; how wretched and harmful to the church’s soul everything was in the time of the Savior, and before Him, *Isaiah 42:18, 19, 20; Matthew 23:16.* It is no wonder, since they had taken away the key of knowledge, *Luke 11:5-21;* therefore, being exemplary and excelling and outshining all others, the shepherds and teachers must be like guides and beacons at sea, upon whom people primarily look. *Matthew 5:14, 15, 16; 1 Thessalonians 2:10.*

<margin>Cherubim with wings [stretched] upwards.</margin>
The Cherubim appear with wings stretched upwards. I like to think of all chosen, called saints that, just as their separation, calling, and change of state is from above, and their principle, head, and future inheritance is above, so too their thoughts, desires, and efforts are stretched upward toward heaven. I further wish to think and believe that in everything they have the aim of God’s

<column-break/>

honor and glory, *Isaiah 43:21; 1 Corinthians 10:31; Colossians 3:17; 1 Peter 2:9,* and that such can be represented by these symbolic images.

Yet, to have such a disposition, to be so situated, and to act accordingly, belongs to the leaders of God’s people who stand out above the <term>Ark of the Covenant<note>The Dutch *bondkist* refers to the Ark of the Covenant, the sacred chest described in the Bible as the dwelling place of God's presence.</note></term>: and this must be found in them to an excellent degree. What lesson or example of heavenly-mindedness can there be in those who are set upon <term>Mammon<note>A biblical term for wealth or profit, often personified as a false god.</note></term>, are greedy for money, and who preach Jesus for the sake of worldly interest—just as the Pharisees and those of their kind are described, *Luke 16:14; Matthew 23:14*—or in those who seek their own honor and esteem more than the honor of God and the interests of their Lord and Master? Quite different are the Cherubic teachers. *2 Corinthians 5:5; 2 Corinthians 10:17; 1 Thessalonians 2:6, etc.*

When the Cherubim are shown to us in this active exercise, it can serve as a symbolic and doctrinal image for all upright Christians: that humility and reverence are wonderfully becoming to their persons, state, and calling, since before God they are nothing other than sinful, impure, and imperfect. *Genesis 18:27; Isaiah 40:15-17; Isaiah 6; Psalm 64; 11:11; Philippians 2:12; Hebrews 12:28; 1 Peter 3:17.*

<margin>Humility suits the Teachers.</margin>
But for the Teachers, Predecessors, and Guides of the people above all others, humility and reverence before God and the holy are fitting. For otherwise, what impression can it give when wild fierceness, uplifting boldness, and pride in handling the divine shine through in such "Cherubim"?

When the Cherubim appear to us as covering their hands and feet—even though their nature and essence is invisible, and nothing deficient or blameworthy is found in their actions before God and men—it can at least teach this, based on firm ground and public proof as well as experience: that certainly all believers, whoever they may be, have reason to cover themselves and be ashamed before God. This is both because of their staining and impure origin, the impulses and actions of soul and flesh springing from this ignited and corrupt fountain, and because of imperfect and defiled deeds, *Job 14:4; Psalm 51:7; Job 3:6; Isaiah 64:6; James 3:2; 2 John 1:8.* Consequently, they have not the slightest reason or ground to boast before God of their actions, since they are but duties, *Luke 17:10,* and all the good in them is not to be regarded as from themselves, but as a gift of God's generous goodness, and as something initially wrought by the Lord's Spirit. Above all this, it is singularly fitting for the Teachers to acknowledge this, seeing that their gifts, along with the blessing and fruit of their labor, depend entirely on the Lord, *2 Corinthians 3:6, 7, 9; 2 Corinthians 3:5, 6;* while in the meantime they are obliged to ensure that, being blameless, they make their ministry glorious, and show in everything that they pursue the Lord's service and work with wings of willingness. *2 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6; Romans 11:13; 1 Corinthians 9:16, 17, 18.*

<margin>Cherubim flying.</margin>
When the Cherubim are depicted flying with two wings, this was to be held as a mark in the angels of God's throne of their inner disposition and readiness, desire, and lust to always obey the Lord, and of their swiftness, speed, and that they [reach] upwards...

We have reason to think that it represented the inner disposition, zeal, desire, and readiness of all the elect, called, and holy ones, along with the haste and speed they ought to make, *Psalm 110:3; 109:32, 68, 162; Titus 2:14,* which should especially take place in the Church-Seraphim <note>original: *Kerkferafynen*; likely referring to the most fervent or highest-ranking ministers</note>. *1 Corinthians 9:16.*

The Cherubim had their faces toward one another, and both their eyes were cast down and fixed upon the mercy seat. However this may or may not have been applied to the angels previously, it is certainly true that since Jesus does not take on the nature of angels, but the seed of Abraham, *Hebrews 2:16,* it was truly beyond the duty and interest of the angels to look out for the Messiah, just as the same faith and the same love caused the believers of the old and new times to look out for Jesus; the coming and the present one, who in the essence of the blessed interest is the same today and yesterday, *Genesis 49:18; Matthew 13:17; Luke 10:24; John 1:29.* It suits them to look toward one another in love, for each other's sharpening toward good and perfection. *1 Corinthians 10:24; Philippians 2:4; Hebrews 10:24.*

<margin>
Obligation of believers.
</margin>

And so every believer is obliged to look to and toward Jesus, not only like the bitten Israelites at the bronze serpent to be healed, *John 3:14, 15; John 1:29,* but also to embrace and hold him fast in faith and love, *Song of Solomon 3:4; Isaiah 27:5; John 1:12,* to watch for his eye and nod from the sanctuary for observation, *Psalm 123:2; John 14:21, 23, 24; 1 John 2:3, 4, etc.,* and to follow in his footsteps, *Matthew 11:29; 16:24; Hebrews 12:2; 1 Peter 2:21.*

And if it suits anyone to observe this in everything, it fits and suits the leaders, who excel above all others in power and official dignity in God's sanctuary; just as it suits them in their teaching and lifestyle, love, zeal, and earnestness, to follow their master's footsteps as much as possible, always pointing to Jesus, *John 1:29,* preaching him, *1 Corinthians 2:2,* and always keeping a watchful eye on the congregation, *Ezekiel 3:17, 18, etc. and 32:8; Psalm 32:8; Acts 20:28; Colossians 4:17.*

<margin>
Cherubim with eyes.
</margin>

The Cherubim appear in the vision covered everywhere with eyes: in front, in back, on their bodies, and if one wishes, also on their wings. How this is applicable to the angels we have heard before: now it must be considered by us with another eye and outlook for application.

Those are not entirely wrong who have thought of these two wings with eyes as faith and hope. One sees the past, and one stretches out toward the future, toward the prize of the high calling of God, which is from above.

Whatever one does or leaves undone, wherever one is, one must be cautious and circumspect, and walk not as unwise, but as wise, *Ephesians 5:17,* in, with, through, and toward that which is from above, *James 3:15, 17,* in all circumspection and prudence, *Colossians 4:5.* One has need of Argus-eyes <note>A reference to Argus Panoptes from Greek mythology, a giant with a hundred eyes, signifying extreme vigilance</note> here: the world lies in wickedness, and is more base and skilled in cunning to do evil than the children of light. *Jeremiah 4:22; Luke 16:8.*

In particular, the leaders need eyes of wisdom and circumspection everywhere, to be shown in their manner of teaching and treatment, and church government, to keep everything in edifying order. He who wins souls is wise, *Proverbs 11:30.* To do that, the word of Christ must dwell in them richly and with all wisdom, *Colossians 3:16.*

<column-break/>

Since they sometimes fall among a generation of wolves, Jesus's lesson is useful to them, *Matthew 10:16:*
> Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves: be then wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.

One could meet with a contemptuous reception by throwing heavenly banquets to dogs and swine, and without observing how and where one spoke or remained silent, one could fruitlessly spend their labor, *Matthew 7:6; Proverbs 9:7.* Sometimes one must pray and kindly admonish, *Romans 12:7; 2 Corinthians 5:19;* sometimes one must employ a holy shrewdness, *2 Corinthians 12:16;* and with rough and stubborn minds, hard words and means are appropriate. *2 Corinthians 5:11; Jude verse 23.*

If they appear in the depiction with bovine, straight, and round feet, walking straight: it is noted regarding the heavenly spirits as a symbol of establishedness and firmness in walking; purity of conduct, ease and perfection of movement, <term>the permanent</term> <note>original: *τὸ μόνιμον* (to monimon)</note>, <term>the steadfast</term> <note>original: *τὸ ἐυσταθὲς* (to eustathes)</note>, that which is quite firm and established: not crooked or distorted, but walking and wandering straight. It signifies at least this: how the saints called by God should apply themselves to walk worthily of God, *1 Thessalonians 2:12,* to walk honestly and without deceit in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, *Philippians 2:15; 1 Peter 2:12,* to walk according to God's Law and Word with love, without deviating from it. Then one has straight feet, and then one is blameless and keeps his path pure, *Psalm 119:3, 9, 21, 59, 60, 102, 167, 168; Hebrews 12:13.* One makes straight paths for one's feet, but steadfastness belongs with it. *1 Corinthians 13:58.*

That is characteristic of the noble Cherubim, Shepherds and Teachers, who strive to excel and to show that they keep the faith in a good conscience, *1 Timothy 1:19 and 3:9.* They stay with and persevere in the doctrine of faith, fighting the good fight of faith in a good conscience, *1 Timothy 4:16 and 5:11, 12, 13, 14–20,* not being ashamed of this, *Romans 1:16; 2 Timothy 1:8,* but fulfilling their ministry in all faithfulness, *Colossians 4:17,* when they have boldness and can and dare appeal to God and men, both regarding their conduct and the discharge of their office and duty, *Acts 23:1 and 24:16; Romans 1:9; 1 Corinthians 4:2, 3, 4; 2 Corinthians 1:23; Philippians 1:8; 1 Thessalonians 2:4–10.* And in all this, they are straightforward and impartial, among both Heathens and Jews: for they discern the course of the kingdom of heaven, and they know that everyone is their neighbor, whom they must strive to give birth to in love through the Gospel, so that Christ may take form in them.

When they are subsequently presented to us with glistening feet like the burnish of polished copper; I have noticed that it has been judged that this represents the firmness and steadfastness of faith and love, and furthermore the bright and clearly shining virtues, which spring from both of these like daughters and fruits, like a radiant and pleasant light. *Which faith is sometimes tested by suffering as by a fire; and which love, in the heat of persecution and the waters of distress, is neither cooled nor extinguished, but is and remains steadfast. Psalm 44:10–21; Romans 8:36; Song of Solomon 8:6, 7; Romans 5:3, 4.*

## CHRYSOLITE, <term>Tarshish</term> <note>Hebrew: תרשיש</note> <term>chrysolithos</term> <note>Greek: χρυσόλιθος</note>, Gold-stone.

IN Greek, <term>chrysolithos</term> is composed of <term>lithos</term>, a stone, and <term>chrysos</term>, gold, signifying as much as a <term>gold-stone</term>, a stone through which gold runs, and one as worthy as gold. According to the opinion of many eminent men, it is called <term>Tarshish</term> <note>Hebrew: תרשיש</note>. It is one of the stones of the breastplate, *Exodus 28:20,* and is included among the foundation stones in the walls of the holy city. *Revelation 21:20.*

Regarding what concerns the name *Tarshish* or CHRYSOLITE, Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> in his *Phaleg* seems to want to derive this name from Tarshish, a city in Spain built and established by the Phoenicians after they were driven from their regions by Joshua. He supports this by citing a certain Bocchus, mentioned by Pliny, who testifies that Chrysolites are found in Spain. On this basis, making a conclusion, he says: *Tarshish lies in Spain; Tarshish also signifies a Chrysolite stone, therefore the Chrysolite coming from Spain takes its name from Tarshish.*

<margin>Bochart speaking against the Hebrew scholars.</margin>
However, Professor Braunius <note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708), an expert on biblical textiles and gems</note> in his *Book on the Vestments of the Hebrews* <note>original: *libro de vest. Hebræor.*</note> says very rightly that such a conclusion does not follow, because this stone was known by that name for a long time and was placed in the High Priest's breastplate before the Phoenicians were driven out and built this city in Spain. Consequently, there must be another reason for this naming, for that which is newer in time cannot have given a name to that which is older. And even if there is some similarity in the name, it does not provide a firm conclusion that one was named after the other; for then the probability would be greater for a free people under Tarshish in Phoenicia.

Yet it may likely have some probability that a Tarshish or Tarshish-land lay in the Indian Ocean, Ophir, or Taprobana <note>likely referring to modern-day Sri Lanka</note>, where Solomon’s fleet sailed from Ezion-Geber, *1 Kings 10:22; 2 Chronicles 9:20,* and that trade was driven in that region by the Phoenicians from ancient times. These Phoenicians, after they were driven out, later built a city in Spain to which they gave the name of that Indian Tarshish, being as it were "New Tarshish," while continuing their trade so that they transported this stone, along with other merchandise, from the Old Tarshish in the Indies to the New Tarshish.

<margin>Various kinds of Chrysolites.</margin>
It is held that there are several kinds of Chrysolites, more or less valuable, pure, brilliant, hard, and enduring. It is said that the Indian and Bactrian <note>from Bactria, an ancient region in Central Asia</note> ones are the best. That they are reported to be found on Ceylon and Cambaya near the Bactrians and in Arabia is evident from the writers. Also, that the Chrysolites of Spain, Germany,

<column-break/>

Bohemia, Meissen, etc., are the most common and poorest, being much darker, softer, and of a more brittle and crumbly nature.

It is easy to think that the best stones having been used for the breastplate, the Indian Chrysolite would certainly have been chosen.

As often happens with precious stones, they do not all have exactly the same color and "water" <note>clarity or luster</note>; thus I have found that the colors and lusters have been categorized: 1. To a purple and sky-blue color. 2. To a sea-green luster. 3. Reflective, as if gold ran through this stone. 4. Furthermore, clear, pure, very hard, and solid.

Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish scholar and grammarian</note> says that this stone is of a sky-colored hue and appearance. Onkelos <note>author of the famous Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> makes it a <term>Tarshish</term> or Turquoise. The translators of the Septuagint, Theodoret, Symmachus, Luther, Cocceius, and our own translators seem to have intended this as well in *Ezekiel 1:16, 10:18, 28:13; Song of Solomon 5:14; Daniel 10:6.* However, Junius and Deodatus seem to relate it to the Beryl.

Pliny, in the 37th book, chapter 5, attributes to this stone that it tends toward green and sea-green. And in the same book, chapter 9, he says that a golden ray runs through it. Epiphanius also says: "The chrysolite is golden" <note>original Latin: *Chrysolithus est aureus*</note>; the chrysolite stone is a gold-stone, with gold radiating through it.

And since it has appeared to me that most translations have understood <term>Tarshish</term> <note>Hebrew: תרשיש</note> to be the Chrysolite, I shall join them and leave all further dispute on this to the learned.

It is easy to understand that not all Chrysolite stones are of the same size, purity, and luster, and consequently, regarding value, they also differ greatly from one another. It is said they commonly reach the size of an almond kernel; and if it is believable, then it is certainly something extraordinary when they are found weighing 12 pounds, two cubits long, and half a cubit wide, as Boetius <note>Anselmus Boëtius de Boodt, a famous 17th-century mineralogist</note> relates. Tavernier <note>Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, a renowned 17th-century gem merchant and traveler</note> reports a Chrysolite found and sold to the Great Mogul for two hundred and seventy-two thousand guilders, having weighed 158 carats. That would likely have been an extraordinary stone, as we are told that some are found on Ceylon the size of a man’s palm and the thickness of a man’s arm.

<margin>Healing uses of this stone.</margin>
Regarding the medicinal uses of this gold-stone, I will report these as I have found them described; namely, that one knows how to prepare water from it—perhaps they are first crushed into powder—which is very useful for many eye ailments: weakness, darkness, tearing, and dimness; also to open the clogged bronchial tubes and thus improve burdened breathing, from which heart-oppression and anxiety in sleep are often born. Should anyone be seized by the desire to have further information, he may consult Psellus, Rueus, Pliny, Braunius, de Mey, etc.

What has been said should satisfy the natural properties of this stone.

<margin>Scriptural application.</margin>
I will next turn to the Scriptural application; and though the <term>Tarshish</term> <note>Hebrew: תרשיש</note> might be translated by some as Turquoise, it would likely not have been bad if it had been translated as Chrysolite. However, looking more at the word than the translation, I shall [discuss] some places in which the...

*Exodus 28:20.* one finds the *Tarshish* in the high-priestly breastplate, the tenth in order; according to the opinion of *Rabbi Solomon Jarchi* <note>Better known as Rashi (1040–1105), a famed medieval French rabbi and commentator</note>, *Josephus*, *Braunius* <note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708), a theologian who wrote extensively on the clothing of Hebrew priests</note> etc., it is a symbolic sign of the tribe of Zebulun. This *Tarshish*, as already shown, has been translated by many scholars as a Turquoise. However, a certain learned man has convincingly shown that it is a *Chrysolite*. Regarding Zebulun’s tribal blessing, one may read *Genesis 49* and *Deuteronomy 33:18, 19.* On this, one may consult *Burman*, *Huisinga* <note>Johannes Huisinga, a Dutch theologian</note> and others, and subsequently that which is noted in this work regarding the Tribes. Insofar as this stone belonged to the high-priestly breastplate, one may look under <term>BREASTPLATE</term>. Furthermore, Zebulun also had his "sealed ones" in *Revelation 7*, and these stones together—each having its own charm and particular, diverse qualities in common with one another—can represent what believers, as living and precious stones, have in common with each other, and also what they possess individually, *1 Corinthians 12:14*, *Ephesians 4.* Thus I can remark regarding Zebulun that they possessed something of preeminence. I do not speak now of Jesus as a *Chrysolite* and *Tarshish*, the Father's brilliant image, reflection, and glory; but also of Him in His humiliation and exaltation, *Matthew 4:13, 14, 15, 16.* *Isaiah 8:23.* and *9:1.* concerning which places I will not expand at length now; noting only that this *Tarshish* represented Zebulun, *Leah’s* son, yielding 60,500 fit and combat-ready men at the counting of Israel’s manpower upon entering *Canaan*, though at *Sinai* there were 57,400 men.

To this stone is attributed a hue, color, form, or "water" <note>A jeweler's term for the luster and transparency of a gemstone</note> of sea-green, with gold rays running through it. The inheritance of Zebulun was located by the inland sea, *Gennesaret*, stretching to the Great Sea <note>The Mediterranean</note>. Because of this, Zebulun was situated for maritime trade; yet she had not only the sea-green, the occasion of the sea, but also a light, luster, golden shine, etc., like the *Chrysolite*. See *Isaiah 8:23.* and its fulfillment, *Matthew 4:15, 16.* See also *Vitringa* <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist</note> on *Isaiah 8* and *9.*

*His hands are as gold rings, filled with Turquoise*, or rather *Tarshish*, *Chrysolite* <note>A quotation from Song of Solomon 5:14</note>. It appears to me thus: the church is compelled, and as if sworn, to describe her beloved, upon whom she was so strongly set and enamored. She describes him, therefore, and having come to his hands, she gives forth what our words report.

Wishing to explain these symbolic manners of speaking according to their imaginative nature, I must then show what the hand signifies, and subsequently the ornament of the hand, consisting of Turquoise, or rather *Chrysolite*. For what the hand signifies, see under <term>HAND</term>.

<margin>
The hand is a symbol of power.
</margin>
The hands on the human body are capable and useful means and instruments to execute skillfully and with strength what the human understanding has conceived: and therefore the hand is a symbolic means of power, understanding, judgment, and actual activity; from which come the expressions "to have a hand in something," "to have it in one's hand," "to lend someone a hand," etc. How some have been able to understand nails <note>original: "nagelen"</note> by *Tarshish*, 

<column-break/>

or still think here of a "flesh-coal" <note>original: "vleeschkolen"; perhaps a reference to the glowing color of a carbuncle or ember</note>, I do not understand. Nor how some have been able to satisfy themselves with this explanation of this symbolism. All sublunary <note>Earthly things subject to change</note> things are very changeable, but Jesus the Unchangeable, who is and remains always the same, has all these things in His power and hand, *Hebrews 12:26, 27.* It also strikes me with some wonder how men, otherwise truly learned and cautious enough, could satisfy themselves with the explanation that it represents how all creatures, being in Jesus' hand, are illustrious and transparent to the very bottom, like a glassy sea, *Hebrews 4:12.* which is how a *Tarshish-stone* also is. In general, the application of the symbol could give me much more satisfaction in the heart of the matter when I noticed how others related Jesus' hand to His works, powerful government, direction, and exercise of power: for if one looks closely, the creatures being in Jesus' hand and power are not described, but rather the hand of Jesus, and that which made His hand appear very precious and ornate, so that it shone remarkably, etc.

For me, the hand of the Lover of the Church, Jesus, is a symbol of His power and authority given to Him over all things in heaven and on earth, He being appointed as Head over all things, and especially the congregation. *Psalm 8:7.* *Matthew 28:18.* *Ephesians 1:20, 21, 22.* *Colossians 1:18.* and *2:10.* *Hebrews 1.* etc.

Through the hand one actually executes what is one's intention, the decided and firmly deliberated plan. Jesus, Son of God, Surety, Mediator, High Priest, Prophet, and King, has, according to the will of the Father, also His work in the aforementioned respects, *John 17:4.* and *4:34.* and *19:30.*

In the work of redemption and governance, something shines forth which adds quite as much beauty, luster, and rays to Him and His government, deeds, and actions as any ornament of Turquoise or *Chrysolite* ever brought to someone's hand and finger; for in this dealing, works, and government, He has revealed, and constantly reveals, how He is the only-begotten of the Father, the glory, full of grace and truth, *John 1:14.* the image of the invisible God, *Colossians 1:15.* in whom all fullness dwells, *Colossians 1:19.* the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, *Colossians 2:3.* the fullness of the Godhead, *Colossians 2:9.* the radiance of His glory, and the express image of His person, and upholds all things by the word of His power. And then this ring represents to me not merely and alone His right, power, legal title, and dignity to redeem, govern, and direct, and to apply the salvific and heavenly goods to His own; to thwart, resist, punish, and bring down the enemies, etc. (see under <term>RINGS</term>) but also the glorious virtues, matchless rays of wisdom, understanding, strength, holiness, righteousness, goodness, mercy, love, faithfulness, etc., which radiate from all His works, dealings, and government, making the same known as formidable, full of majesty, etc., as in *Psalm 111:2, 3.* "The works of the Lord are great: they are sought out of all them that have pleasure therein: His work is majesty and glory, and His righteousness endureth for ever." *Luke 24:19.* "Who was a Prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people." *Revelation 15:3.* "Great and marvelous are thy wor-"

# CHRYSOLITE.
### (C) 3

> ...works, Lord, you almighty God: just and true are your ways, you King of saints. <note>original: "regtvaerdig en waaragtig zijn uwe wegen, gy koning der heiligen." This is a quote from Revelation 15:3.</note>

In both of these places <note>Referring to the visions in Ezekiel and Revelation</note> wheels appear, whose color, shape, and appearance were like the turquoise stone or Chrysolite. See the entry for <term>CHERUBIM</term> <note>The "Living Creatures" or winged beings described in the visions of Ezekiel and Revelation</note>. Some have attributed these wheels to the angels in their thoughts; however, others have imagined, not without foundation, that in both of these places one sees not only the realm of God’s general governance and providence, but emphatically the administration of the church in the world of men below. This administration He establishes, continues, and moves through "living creatures" with wheels full of eyes, into which the wind of the Lord’s Spirit breathes, animating and guiding them. This makes them wise, holy, zealous, active, prudent, circumspect, kind, and full of love for the glory of God and the propagation and support of that kingdom. Thus, this Turquoise or Tarshish-color <note>The author uses "Tarshish-color" to refer to the specific yellow-green hue of the Chrysolite</note>, shape, and appearance can represent for me the excellence, purity, constancy, cleanliness, virtues, and brilliance of the Prophets, Apostles, Evangelists, Pastors, and Teachers (especially in the early times) in their doctrine and conduct. See further on Revelation 21:20.

For my part, I do not wish to argue with anyone over even the smallest matter, nor to dwell particularly on what every tiny detail in the vision might represent on its own. I will not insist on whether the fine linen garment was so transparent that one could see the entire body through it, nor whether the midsection was revealed so that one could draw a conclusion about the whole body from a single part. I believe that from the entire composition of that vision, one can conclude that the whole appearance was fiery, shining, clear, and steady, like gold and polished copper.

These various partial appearances in the same person are, without doubt—according to the diversity of the imaginative power—means of representing Christ’s heavenly descent, His pure, incorruptible, glorious nature, and His incorruptible state, power, glory, majesty, etc.

<margin>Chrysolite is one of the twelve foundation stones of the New Jerusalem.</margin> This passage can be understood and explained according to the letter, and first in a historical manner regarding the commerce of ancient Tyre; and then it may be applied spiritually and prophetically to the "spiritual Tyre." See the entry for <term>TYRUS</term> <note>Tyre, the ancient Phoenician city often used in the Bible as a symbol of worldly pride and commerce</note>.

In Revelation 21:20, the Chrysolite clearly appears as one of the twelve foundation stones of the New Jerusalem, descending from God out of heaven.

As I have said many times, and will say in what follows: I know that the Messiah, Jesus par excellence, is a ground-stone and foundation stone; that no other can be laid, even though the Jewish builders rejected and despised Him, Psalm 118:22 <note>The original text cites Psalm CX. 22 (110:22), but this is likely a printer's error for Psalm 118:22, the famous "cornerstone" verse</note>, Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16, Matthew 21:42, 1 Corinthians 3:11. See the entry for <term>FOUNDATION</term>.

<margin>Application of the Chrysolite to Christ.</margin> I maintain that everything that can be represented by these twelve foundation stones is to be found in Christ Jesus. And to cut through all the preparation, I shall take what has been said of the <term>Chrysolite</term>, pull it briefly together, and apply its symbolic state to Christ, the Foundation.

One finds in the Chrysolite stone: 1. A pleas-

<column-break/>

-ant sea-green; 2. A heavenly color and form; 3. Golden rays and reflections appear in it; 4. A fiery-flaming, glittering red; 5. It is united with singular purity and clarity; 6. It is to be valued all the more for its powers and healing effects; as such, it is a stone of great value.

a. To me, the appearance of the pleasant sea-green stands out; because of what is testified in the divine Book of the Bible regarding God’s Son, Surety, Mediator, Prophet, High Priest, etc., it reminds me of the "tender mercies" <note>original: "innerlyke ingewanden van ontferming," literally "inner bowels of mercy," a common Hebraism for deep compassion</note> with which the "Dayspring from on high" <note>Luke 1:78</note>, or the East, even Jesus becoming man, has visited us out of love and kindness, assuming human nature so as to be able to practice brotherly compassion, Luke 1:78, Hebrews 2:17, and 4:15. This He has demonstrated in various ways:

1. In His general help and compassion toward so many who were sick, infirm, and miserable, Matthew 4:23, 24, Luke 8:27, etc.

2. His tears are of inner compassion, John 11:33-35, Luke 19:41.

3. In His inviting call, His love and compassion shine through, Isaiah 45:22, 55:1, 2, Matthew 11:28, 29, John 7:37, 38, Revelation 3:18.

4. In His friendly, lovely, and soul-refreshing treatment, Psalm 23:2, 3, Isaiah 40:11, and 42:3, Isaiah 49:10, Matthew 11:29, 30.

b. In this stone, a heavenly form and hue appear to me according to the description; this currently provides me the opportunity to remember:

1. Jesus’ heavenly descent, nature, and gifts, Jeremiah 30:21, Matthew 1, Luke 1, Isaiah 7: born of a virgin mother through the power and overshadowing of the Lord; Jeremiah 3: the Lord of Glory, 1 Corinthians 2; the Lord is from heaven, 1 Corinthians 15:47, John 3:13, and 6:62.

2. His heavenly-mindedness, His prayers in solitary communion with His heavenly Father, His heavenly conduct, etc.

3. That He came from heaven to earth for no other end, and with no other insight, than to do the will of His heavenly Father, according to Psalm 40:9, John 4:34, and 17:4, and 19:30.

4. How He, after the work was finished, ascended again to heaven, Acts 1:9, 1 Timothy 3:16, according to Psalms 47 and 68.

c. It being named for its golden rays, or because it is worth its weight in gold, brilliant and durable; then it occurs to my heart that nothing too precious or too glorious can be thought or said of the Messiah, Christ Jesus:

1. As God, of one being with the Father, the Father’s Son, the image and glorious reflection, in whose innermost being the name Jehovah resides; God with us, Isaiah 7:14, Exodus 23:21, John 1:1-14, Colossians 1:15, Hebrews 1:3, etc.

2. As the Mediator between God and men, buying His congregation with His precious blood, which no amount of gold can equal. Matthew 20:28, Acts 20:28, 1 Corinthians 6:20, 1 Peter 1:18, 19, Revelation 5:9.
