<margin>Psalm 45:3-9. Isaiah 11:2 and 61:1. John 3:34. Colossians 1:19. Colossians 2:3.</margin>
3. To this are added his most beautiful gifts and virtues, which are mentioned in *Psalm 45:3-9, Isaiah 11:2 and 61:1, John 3:34, Colossians 1:19, and Colossians 2:3.*

<margin>d. Psalm 69:10. Isaiah 43:1, 2, 3. Zechariah 2:5-8. John 10:11, 15-28. Psalm 50:2, 3. etc.</margin>
When it is described as fiery and burning—qualities that gold and polished copper display in color and form—I am reminded of Jesus's love and the fire of his zeal for His Father's honor and the redemption of His people, *Psalm 69:10*; fiery and zealous to protect His people, *Isaiah 43:1, 2, 3; Zechariah 2:5-8; John 10:11, 15-28*; and fiery and zealous in righteous judgment and vengeance upon His enemies and adversaries. *Psalm 50:2, 3. etc.*

e. When the pure, clear, and radiant light—and the sparkling, flickering rays of this so precious "gold-stone" <note>The author uses the literal translation of the Greek "Chrysolite" (chrysos = gold, lithos = stone).</note>—shine and shimmer in my eyes, then something comes to mind compared to which the fame of the aforementioned stone is nothing at all, namely:

<margin>1. Psalm 84:12. Malachi 4:2. John 1, 3, and 8.</margin>
The matchless light, the purity, the radiant and divine brilliance of Christ Jesus, in whom we see the light, *Psalm 36:10*; *a sun and shield* *Psalm 84:12; the sun of righteousness, the actual, right, and true sun, Malachi 4:2; the light and life of the world. John 1, 3, and 8.*

2. And he is to be considered as such, having:
a. One essence with the Father.
b. A pure, holy, and spotless birth.
c. A pure and holy life.
d. Matchless prophetic light and miracles.
e. Incomparable gifts.

3. Unspeakable radiance of majesty and glory after his resurrection, ascension, etc.

<margin>f. Isaiah 35:5, 6. Matthew 4 and 11.</margin>
And as for the healing powers and effects mentioned above regarding the eyes, the heart, and chest ailments, etc., it gives me cause to remember what Jesus did for almost all kinds of diseases and ailments, as was noted earlier regarding Jesus's "greening" <note>The author likely refers to a previous section on the Emerald or Jasper, linking green to life and mercy.</note> love and compassion, according to *Isaiah 35:5, 6; Matthew 4 and 11.* It reminds me of what He has done for the ailments of the soul—concerning the dark and blind eyes of the understanding, the distress of the soul, and faint-heartedness—and how He, regarded as such a "gold-stone" in His offices and the fruits of salvation, can be applied by spiritual physicians against all kinds of soul-sicknesses, anxieties, and spiritual faintness. It would lead too far afield and require too great a collection of scripture passages if I undertook to work this out in full detail.

<margin>g. Proverbs 8:30, 31. Matthew 3:17. John 3:16. Psalm 18:3 and 72:25, 16. Song of Solomon 5:9, 10. etc. Philippians 3:7, 8, 9. 1 Peter 2:7.</margin>
Therefore, I believe that regarding what has already been said about Christ in comparison with the Chrysolite stone, I may conclude on fair and firm grounds that He—being held and valued by His Father as well as by the chosen out of the world who know Him as the most excellent and choicest Chrysolite stone—is set at a very high price. *Psalm 16:10; Proverbs 8:30, 31; Matthew 3:17; John 3:16; Psalm 18:3 and 72:25, 16; Song of Solomon 5:9, 10. etc.; Philippians 3:7, 8, 9; 1 Peter 2:7.*

Next, just as I have noted with the previous foundation stones of the New Jerusalem—

<column-break/>

<margin>Application to the Apostles.</margin>
—I can certainly allow that these various stones, in view of their various qualities, properties, and virtues, may generally be regarded as symbols of the Apostles: their persons, high church offices, gifts, powers, and works, and the excellence, purity, and firmness of their doctrine. But since each Apostle was an Apostle in his own right, and each laid the foundation individually, and also in different places, and each had his particular gifts, qualities, and way of life, it seems to me that what fits all Apostles fits one of the Apostles. And although all the stones on the High Priest’s breastplate may well have belonged to the bulk and body of Israel, yet each stone was also a particular representation of this or that tribe. Thus I consider that it can also be understood here in this way, and I will therefore take the liberty to apply it.

<margin>To Thomas.</margin>
In a lesser, lower, fainter, and subordinate sense to Thomas, an Apostle, the seventh in rank and order of counting. And on this occasion, it will not be in vain that I briefly recount what pertains to his Apostolic deeds, as far as I have been able to receive some light and report regarding him, both from Divine and human records.

Thomas was one of Jesus’s twelve Apostles, named *Θωμᾶς, δίδυμος* <note>original Greek: "Thomas, didymos"</note>, *תאום תאומו* <note>original Hebrew: "Te'om Te'omo"</note>, *Didymus*, a twin, born alongside another from the same mother in one birth.

He did not actually have two names, but they were the same name, yet in two different languages and pronunciations, in Syriac and in Greek.

I do not know that his parents are mentioned by clear name and lineage in Divine history; but that he understood fishing seems to be concluded from John chapter 21.

<margin>Nature of Thomas.</margin>
As for the nature of Thomas, he appears to me as rather sudden and hasty, allowing himself to be quite confident in his own bravery. For a certain time, having not yet faced a "hot fire" <note>A metaphor for intense trial or danger.</note>, he urged the disciples to resolve to suffer and go to death with Jesus, *John 11:8-16*; but when it seemed it would come to that, he was like the rest and took the "rabbit's path" <note>An idiom meaning to flee in fear.</note>. *Matthew 26.*

Thomas was—whether due to fear or something else—by no means the first to attend the Apostolic gathering after Jesus’s resurrection; he was also just as hard and slow to believe Jesus’s resurrection as any of the Apostles. Therefore, he bound his faith and agreement to a condition that was neither in his power nor was he given assurance that it would be granted to him; but this having been given to him through Jesus’s extraordinary indulgence, he also brought forth a beautiful confession, *John 20:28: My Lord and my God:* and that (as it still stands before me and comes to mind) is the essential account that the Divine history has given regarding Thomas.

<margin>Travels.</margin>
Origen relates that Thomas preached in Media, Persia, among the Carmanians, Bactrians, and Hyrcanians; and that from there he traveled to Sumatra or Taprobana <note>An ancient name for a large island in the Indian Ocean, usually identified as Sri Lanka, but here associated with Sumatra.</note>, where the choicest Chrysolites are found; and that while there, wishing to convert the Brahmans, a singular...

...showed an uncommon passion for love, gentleness, kindness, and modesty; and that, when he had almost lost courage—because he had little success among the souls of the wild, savage, barbaric Parthians, Moors, and other Indians—God miraculously and singularly uplifted and strengthened him. Thus, having performed many signs and wonders in the name of Jesus, he is said to have converted many Indians to Christianity, who are still known today by the name of St. Thomas Christians.

<margin>St. Thomas Christians.</margin>
And to bring this particular history to a close, it is further said that Thomas, having come to Kalamina <note>Kalamina (or Calamina) is the traditional site of St. Thomas's martyrdom, often identified with Mylapore in India.</note>, where the erected sun-idol was publicly honored and worshipped, forced Satan to shatter that sun-idol. When the sun-priests realized this, their raging fury went so far that they tortured him with glowing plates; and when he remained unharmed, he was thrust or thrown into a glowing oven. Being preserved by God in this oven as well, finally the dehumanized people of Kalamina attacked him at the very place where he was accustomed to pray and to teach and instruct the people. They stoned him with stones and pierced and miserably murdered him with spears, arrows, lances, and javelins.

This account being as it is, who can doubt that Thomas—both as a singularly faithful man and especially as a founder of the Christian church in so many parts of the world, and indeed as a martyr and blood-witness alongside the other Apostles—was a foundation stone of the church and a most excellent Chrysolite stone?

<margin>Every believer is a Chrysolite stone.</margin>
Indeed, every excellent believer is a very elegantly placed and living "egg-stone" <note>original: *eiersteen*; likely referring to the smooth, oval shape of certain river-worn gems</note>, a Tarshish <note>A biblical term (*Tarshish*) often translated as chrysolite or beryl, referring to gemstones from the Mediterranean trade port of the same name.</note> or a Chrysolite; namely, one:

a. Who possesses the greenness of love: kindness, an inner heart of gentleness, mercy, and benevolence, having shown this,
1. Toward God and the lover of the soul, *Psalm 18:3, Song of Solomon 1:16.* Also, our bed is *green*.
2. Who always fervently practices love toward their neighbor, not letting it grow cold, but always fanning the flame and practicing it without hypocrisy. In seeking the neighbor's good—whether teaching, exhorting, instructing, or rebuking—everything is mixed with the "green" of loving-kindness, humility, gentleness, and friendliness. *1 Corinthians 10:24, Philippians 2:2-4, Hebrews 10:24, Colossians 3:12, Ephesians 4:32, Galatians 6:1-2.*
3. Who, always acting from the fundamental principle of the love of God infused into their heart through living faith, their engrafting into Jesus, the dew of the Spirit, and the testing of heavenly doctrine and its preaching, is always "green" in all good works. *Psalm 1:3 and 92:13-14, Jeremiah 17:8, John 15:5, Philippians 1:9 and 4:8, 2 Peter 1:5-7.*

b. He is an outstanding and most elegant Chrysolite or "gold-stone"; in which gold is mixed and which displays pure gold.

<column-break/>

1. One who possesses something more excellent than this natural gold-stone is, which is compared to the most precious things, such as the knowledge of divine truth and the wisdom which is from above. *Job 28:12-13* etc., *Psalm 12:7, Proverbs 3:13-14* etc., *Psalm 19:8-9.*
2. One who possesses the saving faith which causes him to grasp and hold fast to Jesus's righteousness, more excellent than gold and silver. *1 Corinthians 6:20, 1 Peter 1:18-19, 2 Peter 1:7.*
3. And displays the shining and virtuous elegance of Christian virtues and gifts of grace, of which *Psalm 45* speaks, as does *Song of Solomon 1:10* and chapter 4 throughout, and *6:4-5* etc., *1 Peter 3:3-5, Philippians 4:8.*

c. He is a Chrysolite of a heavenly color, displaying his heavenly birth, descent, and fellowship with the divine nature. He clearly portrays this through the heavenly-mindedness of his heart and the conformity of his will and deeds to the will and law of God. Specifically, one who:
1. Is not of the world in his heart, conduct, and meditations, belonging to the world or acting like worldlings. *Psalm 17:14, Romans 12:2, Philippians 3:18-19, 1 John 2:15*; but
2. Shows his heavenly origin and inner nature with his heart, thoughts, mind, desire, and conduct, like one who is from above. *Philippians 3:20, Hebrews 13:14, and Daniel 7:18.* Therefore, as a traveler and foreigner of the Lord, he looks out for, sighs for, and longs for heaven. *Psalm 42, 63, and 84, 2 Corinthians 5, Philippians 1, etc.*
3. To which end he—as a called saint, called with a holy calling, called to holiness, etc.—strives to show here on earth a certain resemblance to heaven, the God of heaven, and the heavenly state. *1 Peter 1:15-16, Leviticus 11:44-45, Hebrews 12:14, 2 Corinthians 7:1-2, 1 John 3:3.*

d. He is a truly virtuous Chrysolite, who, having the light within him and being enlightened by it, gives off a pleasant radiance; namely:
1. In the possession of the light of knowledge.
2. In the communication of his light.
3. In the emphatic practice of truth and virtue, in purity and exemplary holiness. *Matthew 5:16, 1 Peter 2:12, Ephesians 5:8, Proverbs 4:18.*

e. He is a fiery, burning, and glittering Tarshish or Chrysolite, who, in all his godly meditations, allows the divine, pure fire of love and earnestness to shine through and glow like a Seraph <note>The word "Seraph" literally means "burning one" in Hebrew.</note> (*Isaiah 6*), is fervent in spirit (*Romans 12:11*), and is a willing subject and soldier. *Psalm 110:3, Titus 2:14.*

f. Finally, every called saint shows himself to be a Chrysolite with respect to healing, refreshing, restoring, and strengthening powers. This is seen when he employs and applies his received gifts of grace and spiritual powers to the enlightenment of the eyes, the purification of the mind, and the strengthening, joy, comfort, and perfection of his neighbor—anointing him with the true eye-salve (*Revelation 3:18, Psalm 32:8, 1 Thessalonians 5:11*), comforting, uplifting, and strengthening the faint-hearted. *1 Thessalonians 4:8, 2 Thessalonians 4:18, Isaiah 40:1, Luke 22:32.*

# CHRYSOPRASE. 24

<margin>
Isaiah 54:11, 12. and 62:3, 4. Psalm 16:3. 1 Peter 2:4, 5-9. Psalm 87:3.
</margin>
All that has been said, falling more or less within a believer, truly makes him into a precious and choice Chrysolite stone.

### CHRYSOPRASE, <note>original: χρυσόπρασος (chrysoprasos)</note>,
### LEEK-STONE, GARLIC-
### STONE.

<margin>
Chrysoprase, the tenth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem.
</margin>
As for the name of this stone, it is composed of two words: from *gold* <note>original: χρύσος (chrysos)</note> and *leek* <note>original: πράσος (prasos)</note>, a Prase-stone; it appears as the tenth among the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21:20.

<margin>
The beautiful greenness of this stone.
</margin>
Pliny, in his thirty-seventh book, chapter 8, places it among the stones of a green color and compares it with emeralds; and since there are emeralds of various colors and values, it remains to be seen whether this stone might also be a species of emerald. Indeed, Pliny in the 5th chapter of the same book testifies that, above all green herbs, it provides the strongest and most pleasant green—marvelous, pleasing to the eye, and awakening and strengthening the sight.

Isidore, in the sixteenth book, chapter 7, testifies regarding the emerald that it surpasses all precious stones in greenness, and because of its grass-green color, it is called an emerald. Epiphanius, in the twelfth book, says that the prase-stone is also called an emerald, as it possesses a green color. Some call them Neronian stones, others Domitian stones; however, the Neronian is smaller, yet possesses a very strong and shimmering green.

Therefore, these testimonies lead me to imagine that the green of this Chrysoprase most closely resembles the pressed juice or the foliage of leeks. Among us, when we wish to express a strong green, we have this saying: *as green as a leek.*

This stone and its luster must be all the more precious and pleasant because it is a "gold-stone," containing many light golden particles within itself, and displaying golden specks and rays; see Psellus, and Braun's *On the Vestments of the Hebrews* <note>original: de vest. Hebraeor.</note> page 657, etc.

Hofman, in his *Universal Lexicon* <note>original: Lex. Univers.</note> under *Chrysoprase* <note>original: Χρυσόπρασος</note>, mentions that Chrysoprase appears in Ezekiel 27:17 and 28:13; however, I have not found it in our Dutch translation. He has noted from Solinus in his 51st book and Pliny in his 37th book, chapter 8, that it might well be a type of Beryl. Junius and Tremellius were of the opinion that the Chrysoprase is the same as the <term>Nopech <gloss>Hebrew: נֹפֶךְ, often translated as turquoise or carbuncle</gloss></term>. The <term>Septuagint <gloss>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</gloss></term> translators have *anthraka* <note>original: ἄνθρακα (carbuncle or glowing coal)</note>; the common translation has carbuncle.

<margin>
Symbol of spiritual gifts.
</margin>
It is told of this stone that it shines much brighter by night than by day, and for this reason was called *Chrysolampis* <note>meaning "golden lamp"</note> by the Ancients; consequently, it has been used by moralists and in symbolic language to represent humility in the possession of exceedingly beautiful gifts.

Caussinus (page 528) recounts from Isidore's *Etymologies* <note>original: Origin. (Etymologiae)</note> in his sixteenth book, chapter 7, that *the Ethiopian Chrysoprase hides its rays in bright daylight, but shoots them out in the dark.* And he has translated and applied it thus: *The humble are bright before God in the night, but in the light of the human crown of fame, true virtues usually lose their luster.*

<column-break/>

<margin>
Birthplace of this stone.
</margin>
It is said that Arabia and Ethiopia are the birthplaces of this stone.

As for the internal virtues, powers, and effects of this stone: I do not believe that it has such a hold on the soul that it can turn a greedy heart into one content with its lot, as some have dreamed; but I can better agree with the following.

<margin>
Its powers.
</margin>
That one can use this stone to refresh the heart and to awaken the life-spirits. That by its beautiful and choice green, it can strengthen the eyes and the sight; and that something can be prepared from it against the inflammation and clouding of the eyes, to cool and refresh them.

<margin>
Revelation 21:20.
</margin>
Furthermore, it is not known to me that this stone appears anywhere else in God's word than Revelation 21:20, where it is counted among the foundation stones. That it might also have been found among the stones of the <term>breastplate <gloss>The ceremonial breastpiece worn by the High Priest of Israel</gloss></term> has not yet become clear to me.

Coming to the hidden meaning, metaphor, and application, I do not wish to repeat what has already been said more than once in the treatment of the preceding Apocalyptic foundation stones, and in what sense it is applicable in the most excellent way to Jesus. I shall only follow what I have noted regarding this stone in its natural state; and following that, there appears to me:

**a.** The very green color and appearance. Regarding the imaginative power of the green—both in the rainbow and in precious stones—one may look back at what I have already noted concerning the Chrysolite and other stones, which I shall list here for better memory:
1. Eternal and prevenient love and mercy.
2. For actual manifestation and powerful practice, the human nature being assumed in time.
3. In which the Word of God, having appeared, expressed Himself generally and physically toward men afflicted with all kinds of evils.
4. Singular movements and stirrings of compassion over the state of mankind.
5. Entirely friendly and gentle invitations to tender and weak men; yet His treatment was stern and sharp in punishing and rebuking hypocritical, hard, and bold sinners. *Matthew 5:15-23.*

**b.** The gold color, golden specks, and rays. Regarding the power of the imagination and the hidden sense, one may look to GOLD, and that which has already appeared in the Chrysolite and other noble foundation stones. For the sake of memory, I shall merely record it without further elaboration or proof:
1. The gold and the golden rays of Jesus' divine nature, very closely united with the human.
2. The gold of His virtues and gifts, shining forth preciously.
3. The gold of His obedience and priestly sacrifice, as the purchase and price of praise.

**c.** The purity, clarity, and radiance are also sufficiently indicated in the imaginative power and hidden sense of the other stones; and therefore one can find it in the treatment...

# C H R Y S O P R A S U S, 25

...searching and finding the treatment of the other stones.

<margin>Gold-lamp.</margin>
d. This stone has been called *Chrysolampis*, meaning **gold-lamp**, as it gives light in the darkness; it sparkles more strongly in the dark than in the clearest and strongest daylight.

<margin>Symbol of humility.</margin>
It has been regarded as a representation of true humility, even when possessing exceedingly beautiful virtues and gifts, without exalting oneself beyond measure.

<margin>Humility of Christ.</margin>
Something concerning this will appear regarding the Topaz. In passing, I only note that our foundation stone, Christ—though he did not think it robbery to be equal with God, *Philippians 2*, and though he was the most beautiful of men, *Psalm 45*—nevertheless gave no lesser signs than those of vain greatness and winding exaltation, *Matthew 11:29; Zechariah 9*; he covered his glory with a cloud of humbled flesh, took on the form of a servant, and in outward appearance he resembled nothing less than a king, *Isaiah 53:2, 3; Philippians 2:7, 8*; nonetheless, he revealed his rays of light at the time when the evening and night of the Jewish civil and ecclesiastical state, and of the heathen idolatry and blindness, were there: just as he shall let them be seen gloriously once more in the late evening of the world.

e. What may subsequently be told concerning the healing powers and effects of the Chrysoprase; it is clear and evident enough that our Jesus can work within the soul and the soul's struggles <note>The original Dutch 'zieltogten' refers to the passions or movements of the soul.</note> what the Chrysoprase cannot do in such a way.

1. It is certain that where Jesus dwells in the heart through faith, there his spirit possesses soul and body as his temple: where the word of Christ dwells richly and with all wisdom, *Ephesians 3:17; 1 Corinthians 6:19; Colossians 3:16*; such a person is and walks without greed; seeking before and above all the kingdom of God with his righteousness, and is content with his portion. *Hebrews 13:5; Matthew 6:33.*

<margin>Jesus the true Chrysoprase.</margin>
2. Granting that art made use of nature and brought the natural elements in the Chrysoprase to the clarification and strengthening of the eyes and of weak sight, removing harmful conditions and averting certain injurious occurrences; what can this possibly compare to what is found in our Chrysoprase, Jesus? If one desires it concerning physical eyes, it is far greater to give sight to the blind than to heal some weakness or ailment of the eyes. See the prophecy, *Isaiah 35*, and compare it with the fulfillment. It goes even further when it also touches the soul, and he brings about the opening of the soul's eyes, so that one understands. *Luke 2:32; Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6; Luke 24:45.*

3. Let art prepare something from the Chrysoprase that can strengthen and gladden the heart; in Jesus, through and from Jesus—in him as Prophet, as Priest, as Lord, Head, and King; in his doctrine, sacrifice, intercession, protection, sealing, etc.—is that capable of gladdening the most mournful,

<column-break/>

encouraging the most faint-hearted, and making them lively and joyful? *Isaiah 61:1, 2, 3-10; Luke 1:47; 2 Corinthians 12:9, 10; Philippians 4:4.*

In the treatment of the preceding foundation stones, I have applied and transferred each stone in a lower sense to one of the Apostles: so I shall also do here and in what follows, and <margin>Application to the Apostle Jude.</margin> apply this one to the Apostle Jude—not the traitor, but the Jude surnamed Thaddeus and Lebbaeus; in doing so, it is necessary that I speak of his person, calling, life, deeds, and end: concerning which I shall call to aid divine and worldly history, as well as linguistics.

The Apostle Jude, as can be seen from his letter, verse 1, was a brother of James the Less, who was perhaps a half-brother of Jesus, a son of Jesus <note>The OCR reads 'voorzoon van Jesus', but historical context suggests the author likely meant 'son of Joseph' (from a previous marriage), a common 17th-century view on the 'brothers' of Jesus.</note>, or a sister's son, and thus a cousin of the Savior.

Yet this Jude seems to have had as a father, and thus as a brother a certain James, and so both were sons of an Alphaeus, *Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6; Acts 1.* His mother seems to have been a certain Mary, called Mary of Clopas, *John 19:25*; whether Clopas was also called Alphaeus, or whether Clopas was her first and Alphaeus her second husband. His given name <note>The Dutch 'besny-naam' literally means 'circumcision-name'.</note> seems to have been JUDE or JUDAH.

<margin>Explanation of the name.</margin>
It is one and the same name as father Judah, *Genesis 29:35 and 49:8*, and it signifies someone who confesses God's name and truth, magnifying the Lord, from <term>Judah (יהודה): to acknowledge, confess, praise, or boast</term>. Chrysostom has said very well and emphatically on *Matthew 10*:
> This Apostle is named Jude, not only because he possessed the godliness and steadfastness of the patriarch, but also because he was a confessor and magnifier of God, both in his life through his teaching of the church, and after his death, through the report of his letter.

And to distinguish this Apostle from his namesake—and to keep him far from his wicked deed and abominable act—he is called not Iscariot, but THADDEUS.

There is no complete agreement on how this name should be understood, for some maintain that Thaddeus, <term>Thaddaios (Θαδδαῖος)</term>, comes—just like Jude or Judah—from <term>Judah (יהודה)</term>, confession, praise, and thanksgiving, and thus indicates someone who confesses, speaks praise, and gives thanks. Others would prefer to see it derived from <term>Shad (שד)</term>—in Syriac, <term>Tad (תד)</term>, in Arabic, <term>Tada / Tadi (תדא / תדי)</term>—a breast, *mamme*, from which root milk is sucked; just as is spoken under this symbol in *Isaiah 66; Song of Solomon 8:1.* See under BREAST, BREASTS.

<margin>Milk: symbol of the Doctrine of Grace.</margin>
It could be that this Apostle received this name with no small foresight: for milk is a symbol of the doctrine of grace, *Isaiah 55:1; 1 Peter 2:1*; singing <note>The OCR says 'zingen' (singing), but context suggests 'zuigen' (sucking), which aligns with the nursing imagery of Isaiah 66.</note> is a representation of communion in this comforting doctrine of salvation, *Isaiah 66, etc.* Jude, appearing as "breasted," can signify how he, being full of divine truth and wisdom through mouth and writing, would be accepted and as it were "sucked in" by others.

<margin>Various considerations regarding the name Lebbaeus.</margin>
Subsequently, the same person appears under the name or surname of <term>Lebbaeus (Λεββαῖος)</term>; regarding which name there are also various considerations, namely whether he might have been so named like Joseph of Arimathea, from a certain place...

# CHRYSOPRASUS.

...in Galilee, called Lebba: then whether he might be named *Lebbaeus* with a certain allusion to the description of Judah, *Genesis 49:9* (Judah is a lion’s whelp), for <note>original: לביא (labi)</note> **a lion**, to represent such lion-like courage and steadfastness. Unless it perhaps serves to be derived from <note>original: לב (leb)</note>, **the heart**: indeed finding this, that <note>original: לב (leb)</note> signifies **a little heart** <note>original Latin: *corculum*</note>; and that people used to be called such for whom one had not only love, but also singular high esteem, because of their understanding, wisdom, prudence, and bravery, which our Apostle was by no means lacking, as he displayed eyes of understanding, alongside the bravery proper to the righteous and the prudence proper to the holy.

<margin>Life and deeds of Jude.</margin>
It is now time that I treat the Apostolic life, deeds, and departure of this Man.

If this Apostle had not made himself known through his letter and made a name for himself in God’s church, one could say little of him in particular from the divine book.

He is known as an Apostle. *Matthew 10, Mark 3, Luke 6, Acts 1.*

He is presented as one asking a question, *John 14:22, 23*, and as far as the subjects of his letters are concerned, they correspond wonderfully with those of the Apostle Peter.

For the rest, one must observe what the ecclesiastical writers have noted and recorded concerning the Apostle.

<margin>Uncertainty of his death.</margin>
Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century Byzantine church historian.</note> has written that he did not die a violent death, but died of natural causes; yet with what certainty this is known is not clear to us.

Otherwise, writers mostly agree on this: namely, that at the beginning of his preaching ministry, he proclaimed the word of the Lord with singular zeal and much fruit in Judea, Samaria, Idumea, Syria, and Mesopotamia; that he subsequently departed for Edessa, and converted the king of the Edessenes and Abgarids <note>Refers to King Abgar V of Edessa.</note>.

And finally, that in Persia, together with Simon the Canaanite <note>Also known as Simon the Zealot.</note>, he was put to death by the heathen priests in a cruel and unnatural manner.

All of which, being well-considered, may lead us to conclude that this man was a precious stone, not only regarded as a believer—as has been heard several times from *Isaiah 55:1, 1 Peter 2:4, Proverbs 10:30*—but especially as an Apostle, as a divine writer, and as a Martyr and blood-witness.

<margin>Application to the believers.</margin>
And although not all believers are Apostles and foundation stones, it is nevertheless fitting and proper for them to be a Chrysoprase, and to demonstrate such in their deeds.

a. Certainly the green of unfading love toward God and neighbor: not with words alone, but in deed and truth; kindness, gentleness, and friendliness especially suit these, *Colossians 3:12, 13, 14.* Look to the preceding stones and the writers on Christian virtues and duties; and take to heart what has been said regarding Jesus, in which he must be followed by his members.

b. As for the gold color, rays, dots, and particles of gold in this stone; every believer certainly has more or less of this, according to the measure of knowledge he possesses of the divine, according as his faith in him is great, strong, and fruitful, and the Covenant God has wished to adorn and grace him with

<column-break/>

beautiful gifts, habits, and virtues: which is frequently compared with gold in Holy Scripture. See again regarding Christ above, and what was said concerning **CHRYSOLITE** and elsewhere pertaining to this subject.

c. It was heard above that the Chrysoprase has been brought forward as a symbol of humility of heart, even though one might have received great and precious goods and gifts of grace from God. If there is anything that ought to be found in a Christian Chrysoprase, it is this ornament of the heart, alongside the evident display of it in words and works. The Lord desires to dwell under a low soul-roof; through the high gates, the exalted doors, to the heart hoisted as high as heaven, the Lord does not wish to enter, *Isaiah 57:15, Luke 1:51, 52, James 4:6, 1 Peter 5:5.* To acknowledge what one possesses as a received gift of God, and therefore to boast in the Lord and of the Lord, is found in a Christian Chrysoprase, *1 Corinthians 1:28, 29, 30, 31, 1 Corinthians 4:7, 2 Corinthians 3:5, 6.* Under **TOPAZ**, something regarding this will appear.

It is indeed such that a Chrysoprase always has light within itself and gives off rays of light, yet they are most noticed when it is dark.

It is certain that a believer, a living and precious stone, is always light, has light, and walks as a child of light, *Ephesians 5, 1 Thessalonians 5:5-8*; that for such a one it is day, and such a one is a child of the day; but in the time of the day, it is evening and night for others; there come times of ignorance, idolatry, and superstition. To provide light then, like Chrysoprases, through confession and conduct is a beautiful thing, *Matthew 5:16, 1 Peter 2:12, Philippians 2:15, Proverbs 4:18.* Who knows when it shall please the Lord, who said that light should shine out of darkness, to shine in many hearts, to give the blinded of mind enlightenment of knowledge through the rays of the Gospel to the knowledge of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God? *2 Corinthians 4:4-6.*

Just as the Chrysoprase, because it shoots singular rays in the dark, is helpful to some, and according to the rules of the art, when properly applied, helps dim and weak eyes. See what was said regarding **CHRYSOLITE**.

By the preceding observation, it is already given to be understood that a believer, himself enlightened in the Lord and being light, provides light; yet then he must be no Cain, and as a believer and righteous man, he cannot be so; and therefore he surely concerns himself with his brother, he gladly wishes to rub him with the right eye-salve and honor him; he very gladly wishes to rid his neighbor of prejudices and make the shadows depart from him; he recognizes his neighbor in love as being as excellent as himself. *1 Corinthians 10:24, Philippians 2:3, 4.*

I could have expanded my thoughts further: however, the reader will find mention of the same matter in the other noble stones. To say one and the same thing in the same way and to the same end many times, and so close together, is not very tasteful. I will therefore step away from the Chrysoprase and take the following subject in hand.

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of the Chrysoprase and the Apostle Jude to a broader exploration of the concept of "Ornament" or "Adornment" in a biblical and linguistic context, particularly its figurative applications to children and the Messiah.</meta>

ORNAMENT.

# ORNAMENT, ADORNMENT, DECORATING, etc. <note>original Hebrew: תפארת / פאר / צבי / הוד / הדר / עדי</note>.
# Adornment, ornament, beauty, glory. <note>original Latin: Ornatus, ornamentum, decor, gloria</note>

The subject of ORNAMENT in general will be treated here, and I shall stay as close to the Dutch word as I can. One may meanwhile look at what has been said regarding BRACELETS, ARM-ORNAMENTS, etc. Specific means of decoration will likely be found elsewhere under their own headings.

The root words appearing in the Hebrew text are primarily the following:

<term>Tsebi</term> <note>original: צבי</note> *swelling, puffing up, a growth,* from <term>Tsabah</term> <note>original: צבה</note> *to swell, is swollen*; because an elevated state, wealth, etc., usually cause the heart of man to swell and rise up through pride. <term>Pa'er</term> <note>original: פאר</note> comes from <term>Pa'er</term> <note>original: פאר</note> *he has adorned, made glorious, or distinguished, dressed up*; <term>Pe'er</term> <note>original: פאר</note> refers to that which belongs to this, and what arises and follows from it.

<term>Hadar</term> <note>original: הדר</note> comes from <term>Hadar</term> <note>original: הדר</note> *he has glorified, shown honor.*

<term>Hod</term> <note>original: הוד</note> signifies *honor, praise, beauty, dignity, glory, majesty.*

<margin>Ornament used figuratively.</margin>
The word ORNAMENT sometimes replaces everything that contains honor, glory, beauty, and majesty. This is applied and transferred distinctly: *a.* to God and a divine person; *b.* to an individual or many; *c.* to any city, place, region, power, or state. Furthermore, it can be distinguished such that one can seek and find it in the natural, physical, or external—likewise in the domestic and civil—or in the spiritual and internal. Taken generally, it is either natural to a subject or added to it, thereby making the subject or object appear to us as beautiful, ornate, lovely, pleasant, desirable, great, rich, powerful, formidable, etc.

The matter will appear with more distinction in the following.

The word ORNAMENT is used figuratively when it is understood to mean children, who, like sprouts from the tree of marriage, are for the glory, fame, ornament, and luster of the parents, as it seems to be taken in *Hosea 9:11, 12; Job 19:9; Psalm 127:5; Proverbs 17:6.* So Claudianus <note>Claudius Claudianus, a Roman court poet (c. 370–404 AD).</note> calls Proserpina the crown and pride of Ceres; and so the fame and glory of the deified Augustus is named.

*Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and theologian.</note> in Poem to his father Nicobulus, 49.*

> For the glory of a father is the reputation and honor of his children. <note>original Latin: Gloria namque patris natorum est fama decusque.</note>

-> That is: <-

-> *The fame of children is glory for the father.* <-

And someone else,

> It is a blessed thing to raise an orderly son. <note>original Greek: Μακάριόν ἐστιν, υἱὸν εὔτακτον τρέφειν.</note>

-> That is: <-

-> *How blessed it is to nourish a child who is virtuous?* <-

<column-break/>

*Hosea 9:11, 12.* Ephraim would not bear holy seed for God; and even if it had many beautiful children, and a numerous people and lineage, through which it was formerly formidable to enemies, the Lord would cause these to melt away and become thin: the city, temple, kingdom, and the name of being the Lord’s people would disappear and pass away, and so its ornament and glory would have an end.

In times of sadness, mourning, and humiliation, one laid aside one’s ornament; one clothed oneself in sackcloth and ashes, and all kinds of signs of sadness and humiliation were perceived. To put on the ornament, the decorative garment—to be draped, adorned, and girded with it, to receive beauty for ashes, *Isaiah 61:3-10,* etc.—signifies receiving cause for joy, to be beautifully arrayed with gifts, especially with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, to possess that internal ornament before God and to display it externally through the practice of all kinds of virtues. This holds a special place in the New Testament, in the acceptable time, the day of salvation, *2 Corinthians 6:1, 2,* but more on this ornament hereafter.

<margin>Ornament applied to the Messiah.</margin>
The word ORNAMENT is also found applied to a man, namely the Messiah, and he is called a Branch of the Lord, of righteousness, a righteous Branch, who would be for ornament and glory, *Isaiah 4; 11; 23;* and *33; Zechariah 3; 6:12, 13.* This is true in himself, in comparison with others, according to his descent as man from a royal house; as God-man, because of his inner virtues and qualities, the sprouting and climbing to the highest peak and step of honor and glory, happiness and salvation, both for himself and for his people, of which more under the word BRANCH.

*Isaiah 4:2: In that day the branch of the Lord shall be for ornament and for glory, etc.* It has been noted that in *Chapter 3,* many and various threats of judgment appear because of many sins and heavy iniquities prevalent among the Jewish people, which judgments would strike persons of every kind, state, office, and rank.

It would be somewhat too literal, physical, and carnal—and too common to the good and the evil—if one were to think here only of some beautiful and abundant fruits of the earth, by which the Lord would refresh and favor the survivors after the times of such a heavy and long-lasting visitation and punishment.

It also turns out rather meager when one understands this "branch for ornament and glory"—presented as a single person, yet to be understood in a representative and collective way—as referring to many great, honorable, and distinguished men who would be found among God’s people after the Babylonian captivity, namely, Zerubbabel, Ezra, Nehemiah, Prophets, a congregation of the saints, and of wise and prudent men.

They have understood it best, in my judgment, who here think of God’s son, the Messiah, and of his excellent servants in the New Testament. He, being glorious as has been said in many parts and respects in himself, would also be for ornament and glory to his father, church, and people, in and through his ascension, in elevation to majesty, honor, and glory and the highest rule as their Head, Lord, Lawgiver, King, etc.; in and through the outpouring of his spirit, abundant gifts, powers, and workings; by effectively advancing his kingdom everywhere among Jews and Gentiles, through righteous and exemplary judgments.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Ornament" (Cieraad), moving from general definitions to the specific priestly and royal ornaments of the Messiah and His people, drawing heavily on the commentary of Vitringa and Van den Honert.</meta>

ORNAMENT.

...and to bring punishments over his and his people’s enemies. Even the elect, who would make up the church, would choose, appoint, and make this Sprout—as Prophet, Priest, King, Lord, Rock of salvation and blessedness, the foundation of the church—into the cause and substance of their glory, joy, and rejoicing. See Campegius Vitringa <note>A prominent Dutch theologian (1659–1722) known for his commentaries on Isaiah.</note> on this passage.

Of the Priestly garments, and that which the High Priest wore, with which he showed off and paraded—his miter, gold plate, the breastpiece, etc.—all are called garments for glory and ornament, certainly making one glorious and magnificent. Regarding the most excellent depictions—elegant, glorious, and precious garments, shining because of the snow-white or variegated or other colors, gold, silver, gemstones, embroidery, etc.—more is to be seen under their specific names.

Whereupon I also believe, among other things, that *Zech. VI. 12, 13* is being considered, when it speaks of this Sprout, who shall be King and Priest at the same time upon his throne, and therefore exalted above all *Philip. II. 9, 10, 11*. Not only as Priest, but as a royal Priest, Priest and King, whereby the ornaments of both converge and sparkle brilliantly. And I believe those same ornaments and garments, as fruits of Jesus' righteousness and the communion with him and his spirit, have made us into Kings and Priests, yes, *into a royal Priesthood, 1 Pet. II. 9. Rev. I. and V.* which ornamentation is called holy ornamentation, decoration, and adornment; the robe of salvation and mantle of righteousness, the gold, etc. *Psalm XLV. and CX. 3. Isa. LX. 10. Rev. III.* etc. as demonstrations and symbols of their state, dignity, inner gifts, virtues, deeds, etc., of which more will be said below.

*Psalm CX. 3. in holy ornaments* <note>original Hebrew: בהדרי קדש / be-hadre qodesh</note>: translated by *Tako Hajo van den Honert* in his *Treatise on Psalm CX* <note>original Latin: Tract. in Pf. CX.</note> as "the armors of the sanctuary." The word *haadaar* <note>original Hebrew: הדר</note>, he says, signifies something that is awesome: that evokes reverence and awe. It is of common usage. One sees it used for old age, *Prov. XX. 29*; of the kingdom, *Dan. II. 20*; of God and his kingdom, *Psalm CXLV. 5-12*; but mostly of precious and elegant garments, *Lam. I. 6. Ezek. XXIII. 26. Prov. XXXI. 25.* from whence it is also transferred to the armor in which heroes are accustomed to appear, and which makes them not a little awesome in the eye of the beholder and of their enemies, *Ezek. XXXIII. 6-12-15-24 and XXVII. 10*.

Since it speaks here of the Messiah's people in relation to the day of the Messiah’s muster: there is nothing simpler than to understand by the ornaments mentioned here the military equipment and weapons in which the Messiah’s people were to present themselves on the day of the Messiah’s muster. Now, of these armors it is said that they were armors of the sanctuary. For the Oracle says, *through the armors of the sanctuary*.

<margin>Armors of the Sanctuary.</margin>
1. That they are holy, not fleshly, but powerful through God, who has sanctified them. These weapons consist in the holiness of the people, *2 Cor. X. 4.* weapons of light and of righteousness *Rom. VI. 13. and XIII. 12*. Which holiness of the people is frequently called <note>original Hebrew: הדרת קдש / hadrat qodesh</note> *the ornament or the glory of the sanctuary. John IV. 24. Ps. XXIX. 2. LXIX. 9.*

The armors are kept in all well-regulated

<column-break/>

kingdoms in armories, to be ready for the day of the muster, and to be brought forth from there. *Song of Sol. IV. 4*.

*Qodesh* <note>original Hebrew: קדש</note> certainly signifies holiness, yet because armors are kept in an armory, the question arises whether *qodesh* ought not be translated as *armory*. *Qodesh* (holiness) is used not only to signify the earthly sanctuary, but also to signify heaven, which is prefigured by the earthly sanctuary, *Psalm LXVIII. 6.* and so nothing is simpler than that we consider the heavenly sanctuary, in which the Messiah would sit at the Father’s right hand, as the true armory here. *James I. 5, 6, 17*.

The courage of the soldiers, which makes them very willing on the day of the muster, is indeed a virtue that is properly housed in their hearts: but it is nonetheless greatly encouraged by very good armor, and so it is here as well. For they could rely on these armors on the day of battle, *Song of Sol. IV. 4.* because they were armors of the heavenly sanctuary, etc.

It says in *Isa. XLV. 11. And I will lay your stones most ornamentally.* <note>The author likely means Isaiah 54:11</note> Regarding the stones and living stones, more will be explained under the word STONE.

Those the Lord would lay down, <note>original Hebrew: מרביץ / marbits</note>; the word is also applied to cattle, which lie down in the grassy pastures, and with good reason: for the cattle and these stones are the same persons, though in a different respect and type of imagery.

*Be-puk* <note>original Hebrew: בפוך</note> suffers various translations. Some want it to mean a carbuncle, others a ruby; yet because these stones are listed in what follows, others translate it for distinction as *stibium, fucus* <note>original Latin: terms for antimony or cosmetic pigments</note>, taken for white and red Antimony, used as makeup for beautifying and coloring the eyes, eyelids, cheeks, lips, etc. *2 Kings IX. 3.* And since these are not used in architecture for the setting of stones—and makeup serves for ornament and finery—our translators have rendered the word as *most ornamentally, in, with, or for ornament laying*.

But in the application and "bringing it home," all the learned will not be in full agreement.

<margin>General application.</margin>
> The learned Commentators understand it thus: *I will rebuild you, O Jews, who have been captive in Babylon and greatly devastated by Antiochus Epiphanes, yes, make you more glorious than you were before.* Or one can understand by it, *the spiritual rebuilding of the elect, which begins in this life through the Gospel and the glorious gifts of the Holy Spirit, Eph. IV., and will be perfected in the future life, Rev. XXI.*—an application and transfer which is quite indefinite and general.

For my part, it seems to me that the Prophetic thread, and the power and meaningfulness of the imagery—pertaining neither to the Jews after the return from Babylon, nor after the devastation by Antiochus Epiphanes—calls me to the calling of Jews and Gentiles, to be living stones for the building up of the spiritual temple, the church of the New Testament, to be bound and united together through faith with Jesus, in the confession of the doctrine of truth, and in brotherly love. *Eph. IV.*

*Be-puk* in *precious ointment*, used for ornament and coloring. Thus would the Lord lay them ornamentally, just as the stones for the temple building were of such quality and form; so are these living stones

# O R N A M E N T.

...precious, dear, immovable, the holy ones on earth *Psalm 16*. a *chosen generation, 1 Pet. 2:9.* resting through a firm covenant in Jesus' blood, upon his righteousness or upon him, the righteousness of his people—that decorative, precious, and well-tested stone, Jesus—firm, immovable, well-suited for a spiritual temple structure; without the "whore's ornament" <note>original: "hoerencierziel"</note> of varnished virtues, which are merely beautiful on the outside, with a pretense of godliness but without its power; but rather with the form and power of godliness, love, peace, humility, gentleness, tolerance, lowliness, etc., as will be shown more closely in what follows; the light of wisdom, holiness, and love as gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Isaiah *54:11* in general, and in its broader scope, teaches through that imagery that God would make his church wonderfully decorative, very shining, and of a spiritually pleasant appearance: just like the sight of some city which is built and composed of precious, shining, red-colored, and white-glittering stones.

<margin>Ornament of the Church.</margin>
The ornament of the church lies in her gifts, such as knowledge, wisdom, and faith, alongside the extraordinary miraculous gifts joined with these in the early and first church; and in her virtues, such as purity, holiness, spirituality, goodness, gentleness, lowliness, love, and works consistent with these, as well as in the privileges of the church, etc. One can also consult Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a famed Dutch theologian whose commentary on Isaiah was standard in this period.</note> on this.

When Ephraim’s ornament is spoken of in *Isaiah 28:1-4* as a kingdom separated from the kingdom of Judah, much of its light would have been situated in the temple, capital city, king, power, etc. In the Assyrian inundation and the deportation to Chaldea, this went to ruin. Popery <note>original: "Papendom"</note> with its ornament, pomp, splendor, head, and luster, shall also be brought down, the preparations for which we have already been able to see the beginnings.

<margin>Thoughts of Vitringa.</margin>
Regarding *Isaiah chapter 28:1-4*, where the proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim is spoken of—whose glorious ornament is a fading flower, which is there upon the head of the very fat valley of those overcome with wine, etc.—I shall present the following from Campegius Vitringa. In the first sense, the city of Samaria is understood, and not the territory and kingdom. This city was built by Israel's king, Omri, the father of Ahab, on the mountain of Samaria, purchased by him from Shemer, after which Shemer the city of Samaria is named. *1 Kings 16:24.*

At the foot of this mountain lay a fat valley of very fertile ground.

Later, having been somewhat rebuilt by Herod, it was named Sebaste, situated on a mountain of an oval roundness, surrounded by a fertile valley and a circular ring of hills.

This was a proud crown; in respect to the city, and the ornament and proud buildings in which this city, when it was still in its bloom, exalted itself.

Which ornament is compared to a fading flower. This city—though compared to a flower because of its fame, luster, ornament, and elevated location (since a flower displays its beauty and ornament on high)—was nevertheless close to its downfall, and already the land all around had been almost entirely dug up, stripped, and devastated, *2 Kings 17:3, 4, 5.* Therefore, it was like a fading flower that is on the head, on the crown of the mountain, by which that fat valley and region lay.

<column-break/>

<margin>Allusion to the wreaths of the ancients.</margin>
*Those overcome with wine, the drunkards of Ephraim.* Here an allusion is made to the customs of the ancients, who in their feasts and drinking bouts used to encircle their heads with little crowns and wreaths of interwoven flowers.

Some believe that the wantonness, flightiness, "bread-drunkenness" <note>A Dutch idiom meaning being "spoiled by prosperity."</note>, and gluttonous excess of Samaria and the ten tribes of Israel before their devastation and depletion by Shalmaneser is meant and held against them, as in *Amos 6:6*.

<margin>Spiritual drunkenness.</margin>
But the Prophet here does not only, nor primarily, have his eye on physical abundance and the wantonness caused by it. Rather, the Prophet takes it in a secret significance and conceptual sense <note>original: "zingreep"</note> for a defect of a troubled judgment, being afflicted with which they are like drunken people. By the force of the divine judgment resting upon them, they took foolish resolutions in a matter of the utmost importance, on which the preservation and welfare of their state depended; and to interpret this thus in a secret conceptual sense and meaning should seem strange to no one, since in this same way the straying of the leaders and teachers of both Jewish kingdoms is depicted, *Isaiah 29:9.* It becomes manifest from *chapter 28:7-13* that the Prophet is dealing with spiritual drunkenness; for if he had his eye on physical drunkenness in such a way that he primarily intended it, he would have made a further expansion and more detailed proposal of the same, in which they used to practice and perform it.

The drunkards of Ephraim, in the metaphorical transference to another sense-meaning, will primarily fit the rulers, the most prominent of Ephraim, and belong with them; as those who, in matters of faith and religion and points of state interest, peace, and security, deviating from sound reason, were like drunken people—deprived of the use of senses, judgment, and reason, brought to mindlessness by a judgment of God, as it is used several times. *Isaiah 29:9, 10* and *51:21. Hosea 4:11.*

Regarding the established form of religion, they were drunk, and by no means of a sound mind; they resisted the convictions of the true prophets and the divine judgments.

They sought help against the Assyrian from the king of Egypt, in a matter of such uncertain and perilous outcome.

In a second, indirect sense, this applies to the Jews, and specifically to those who were inhabitants of Jerusalem, who followed the foolish institutions and council-decrees of the Ephraimites.

The unholy hypocrites, being without divine reverence and regarding God’s help little or not at all, looked out and about for the human assistance of the Egyptians, who lay enclosed under the same divine judgment of spiritual drunkenness; whose proud crown was Jerusalem, and the fading and withering flower of their ornament was the temple, the fame and glory of that nation, situated on the top and crown of a fat and oil-rich valley, which separated the hill of Moriah from the Mount of Olives—namely, Gethsemane, the valley of fatness. *Matthew 26:36.* Drusius <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant Hebraist and theologian.</note> can be consulted on that passage.

<margin>Comparison of Jerusalem to Samaria.</margin>
It is no strange paradox, nor something entirely unusual, that one should compare Jerusalem to Samaria. The Prophets lead us in this, and we—

# ORNAMENT.

indicate to us that both these cities [Jerusalem and Samaria] shared the same failings, deviations, institutions, and the same fate, *2 Kings 21:11, Ezekiel 16:46, Micah 1:1, etc.*

Shall the church see the ornament of Carmel and Sharon, even God’s ornament? *Isaiah 35:2.* This undoubtedly represented the flowering of the Christian Church in knowledge and virtues, when Jews and also Gentiles flocked to her bosom at the Gospel calling; when the old "shadow-heaven" <note>A theological term referring to the Old Testament types and ceremonies which were "shadows" of things to come.</note> disappeared, the [pagan] gods and powers were stripped away, and that unprofitable and darkness-inducing religion was changed into a gentle yoke, a clear ministry, and a day without clouds or darkness. *2 Corinthians 3; see also under CARMEL.*

*Isaiah 49:3.* In the first verse, says Gulichius <note>Abraham Gulich (1642–1679), a Dutch theologian.</note>, the supernatural birth of Christ and the mention of his name before or during his conception is presented to Zechariah and Elizabeth, when John [the Baptist] was about to be born. *Luke 1.*

The making of the mouth like a sword is the word *Hebrews 4:12* heard from the mouth of Christ and his Apostles.

Under the *shadow of his hand he has hidden me*; he has so sheltered and protected himself that no one could bring him harm: this must be understood as his mystical body, the church, especially when the church gained emperors as protectors.

Verse 3 suggests the separation and emergence of the church, when it obtained the name of the Reformed or Evangelical church, God providing peace unto the same.

But let us hear the frequently mentioned writer, Professor Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), an influential commentator on Isaiah.</note>, on *Isaiah* regarding this.

The first turn of phrase or address is from the Messiah, Jesus the highest Teacher and Savior, to the nations, *verses 1-6.*

The second is from God the Father to the Messiah, whether in himself or in his mystical body, the church from the believing Jews, protected in the early time of grace, *verses 7-13.*

The third is from God the Father through the Holy Spirit to the entire body of the elect, in their oppression, in the early administration of grace, *verses 14-26.*

This Master [Vitringa] concedes that by "Israel," in a healthy sense, one can understand the mystical body of the elect, *Isaiah 46:3*; yet here Israel is distinguished from the old Israel, *verses 5, 6.* His Reverence understands "Israel"—applying it to Jacob, who was named Israel—as the same person, the Messiah, Christ, the most excellent one out of Israel; Israel par excellence, who uniquely was a servant to the Father, and in fulfilling his assumed office of Helper and Savior, has been a glory and an ornament: just as he likewise received ornament and glory from the Father, *page 566, volume II.* It is well worth examining His Reverence's work with attention.

But as for *Isaiah 49:18*, at this place Master Vitringa has noted that where <term>ornament <gloss>original Hebrew: עדי (adi)</gloss></term> is mentioned, the application seems to be made to the long mantles, the low-hanging outer garments of women, in which women living in the East—preparing them from costly and choice fabrics—placed great ornament and splendor: also to necklaces, bracelets, and ornaments, and further to whatever served as ornament for the hands and feet.

His Reverence brings this in a secret [spiritual] sense to the

<column-break/>

literati, scholars, philosophers, orators, or masters of eloquence, who were formerly held in singularly high esteem among the Pagans, and who would embrace the Christian religion, defending Christian truth with their books and apologies, clearing the blame and slander of the Pagans from the Christians and Christian doctrine, and adding no small luster and ornament to the church and the truth. His Reverence can be consulted on *page 591, etc., volume II.*

The promised ornament in *Isaiah 49:18* speaks of something good for the church, not only in its beginning but also in the progress of the Christian Church, after the greats of the earth should have done homage to the reigning King Jesus: it will likely have its most excellent fulfillment in the calling of the Jews in later times. Indeed, for the later time, a very great ornament seems to be set aside, *Isaiah 60:19*, but such shall take place when the supposed Sun and Moon—the Pope with his vassals who worship his highness—are no more, or are in no way recognized.

When the ornament of Zion’s daughters is gone, *Lamentations 1*, she sits piteously mourning because of the destruction of the city, temple, ark of the covenant, freedom, the rule of her own people, freedom of religion, and what is more, because of foul stains of sin and defilement through many reprehensible deeds. And so as not to pass by many other places "with dry feet" <note>An idiom meaning to pass over something quickly or superficially.</note>, in the Prophet *Isaiah 13:19*, one reads that Babylon, the ornament of kingdoms, the shining star, the head, the golden head, would be annihilated.

<margin>Babylon the most beautiful city in Asia.</margin>

*Isaiah 13:19.* Babylon was the most beautiful city in all Asia, the most magnificent, the richest; even at that time when she was destroyed and humbled, the excellence and the ornament of the Chaldeans consisted in resources, powers, wisdom, bravery in war, splendors, strengths, and fortified places of the territory, vastness, and especially in Babylon itself, with its temples, palaces, strongholds, and sturdy buildings, etc. See Vitringa.

Thus one reads in *Isaiah 23:9* of the punishment of proud Tyre, the desecration of its ornament, and of places that are more of this nature.

This happened to Babylon in due course, and Tyre received it as her portion; but the spiritual Babylon and Tyre <note>A common Protestant identification of the Roman Catholic Church with the "Babylon" of Revelation.</note>, where the Pope has presumed to be the head of the whole world, deposing and appointing Emperors and Kings, giving hats, miters, etc., to Cardinals, Bishops, Abbots, and Prelates; where everything glitters with gold, silver, precious stones, costly garments, hangings, images, altars, churches, chalices, etc., shall also receive its due. See further also *Isaiah 60:7, 13, 21 and 61:3.*

*Isaiah 60:7, 13, 21. I will decorate my church, and she, being decorated by me through me, is an ornament to me,* says Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his federal theology and covenant emphasis.</note>. The ornament of Lebanon is undoubtedly the Cedars, those very high and beautiful trees of oily and durable wood.

<term>Sanctuary <gloss>original Hebrew: מקדש (miqdash)</gloss></term> signifies a standing place in and on a height, a set-apart place which serves as a castle and protection to those who turn there in times of need and difficulty. I understand it to mean the temple, in which the Lord had placed his throne, and which made that place ornamental and magnificent by his presence. The Lord wished to make the place of his feet ornamental; that is, the ark of the covenant, upon which the Lord rested as if with his feet. To bring this to...

# ORNAMENT.

concerning the building and decorative materials of the tabernacle and temple, brought from the tall trees of Lebanon, is a somewhat low interpretation and possesses little spirituality or loftiness. There were many such buildings in those times; therefore, the Lord Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist known for his commentary on Isaiah.</note> elevates this to a mystical sense. *p. 812.*

Isaiah 60:21. The believers and the saints—all that they are in the state of grace—they owe to God and His grace, *Matthew 15:13, John 15:1, Psalm 92:14.* Considered apart from the root from which they have their origin, they grow over time according to degrees and steps, up to the height determined by God; and this is to the glory and ornament of Him who has planted, created, prepared, and made them into a spiritual garden, *John 15:8, Ephesians 2:10.* Meanwhile, the saints—the greening and blooming ones—lifting their heads high, are an ornament to the church and to Him who has appointed, nurtured, and raised them to be a spiritual garden and an ornament. One may consult Vitringa on this.

Isaiah 61:3. According to Gulichius <note>Abraham Gulich (1642–1679), a Dutch theologian of the "Covenant Theology" school.</note>, this refers to the granting of voluntary gifts of grace from heaven, through which they shall stand out and be distinguished in the world. And the garment and covering of glory, *verse 10,* or of renown and praise *verse 3,* he says, refers to the renown and joy regarding salvation and the hope of the glory of God *Romans 5.* He made them into new creatures, so that He might make Himself ornamental in them and be glorified, and show to them the riches of His grace.

Therefore, says Vitringa, the Messiah would not only be a preacher and teacher, but also a distributor of God's grace, bringing about in hearts—along with the benefits of grace—inclinations and affections corresponding to those benefits. See my *Sacred Miscellany*, Volume III.

When it is said of Canaan that it is the ornament of lands *Ezekiel 20:6, 15,* it refers to the abundance of all things and its favorable location; and it is no small matter that it received its ornament in greater part because it was called Immanuel's land, was a sacrament and pledge of the heavenly realm, the Lord dwelt there, the temple stood there, and the worship of the saints of Israel was practiced.

Moab also had its ornament *Ezekiel 25:9,* being the choice part of its land through which it excelled. Ar and Kir, great, fortified, and populous cities, along with the rest, were also quite firm and distinguished, etc.

Judah’s ornament and abundance, when turned toward idolatry, caused her to fall under the heavy judgment of extermination; no luster remained after the destruction by the Romans, for the temple, city, civil government, and all that was holy went missing, *Ezekiel 7:20.*

In *Ezekiel 26:20, 21,* the Lord threatens, among other enemies of His people, Tyre, which rejoiced over Jerusalem’s fall and destruction.

<margin>Rejoicing of the spiritual Tyre.</margin>
This has also become the lot of Tyre. Although the spiritual Tyre <note>In the Protestant tradition of this era, "spiritual Tyre" or "Babylon" often referred to the Roman Catholic Church or worldly powers opposing the Reformation.</note> laughed in its sleeve, seeing that the City of God, the New Jerusalem that descended from heaven, suffered quite a setback—just as it is joyful in its heart the more Jerusalem's beauty and greatness decline. It shall happen, however, that this Tyre will be destroyed, and the Lord will rebuild the fallen Jerusalem. When the Lord shall fully deliver His inheritance from Babylon's 

<column-break/>

violence and destruction, and Tyre shall perish with all its pride, pomp, and splendor, then there shall be a life from the dead, and the church shall be like Jerusalem, the city of the living God in a spiritual life, with many beautiful gifts and perfecting peace.

Things did not go well at all when the Lord was heard to complain, *Micah 1:9,* etc., that the Jews were not only exploiting, oppressing, or abusing women and widows; but also when they harmed the children—the simple and inexperienced—not only in body but also in soul, since they were instilling in them principles of religion and doctrine that ran contrary to all the right teachings of the Lord, His service, acknowledgment, submission, and reverence.

Of the harlot’s ornament of spiritual Babylon, one reads in *Revelation 17 and 18,* and that she adorns herself quite magnificently; yet whatever beauty and excellencies she may pretend to have to entice her lovers and keep them subservient to her, she shall receive Babylon’s fate, *Jeremiah 4:30,* and will no more escape the reckoning than the adulterous people did when they rejected their lawful king, Jesus, and clung to the Roman hills and highness. *Hosea 2:12.*

<margin>Ornament of women.</margin>
We have touched upon Babylon's harlot-ornament with a word; the true ornament of women is not found in costly clothing, gold, silver, pearls, braiding and hair-powdering, and what the intolerable pomp, pride, and arrogance formerly brought with it, being indescribable what all belonged to this. See *Isaiah 3:18, 19.*

Often it was a prostitute's dress, meant to make the eyes sparkle and to move the mind to impure passions through exposed and barely covered limbs; called by Petronius <term>ventus textilis</term> <gloss>a woven wind</gloss>; <term>nebula linea</term>, <gloss>a linen mist</gloss>; by Nazianzenus, <term>vestis aëria</term>, <gloss>an airy garment</gloss>; by Varro, <term>toga vitrea</term>, <gloss>a glassy gown</gloss>; by Seneca, <term>vestis non tegens</term>, <gloss>a garment which does not cover.</gloss>

# ORNAMENT.

Constantijn Huygens <note>Constantijn Huygens (1596–1687) was a celebrated Dutch Golden Age poet, diplomat, and polymath.</note> already took aim in his time at finery and foreign luxury.

->O Holland, old fame of simple dignity,<-
->Where shall we find a shield for your righteousness,<-
->In the painful tale of overseas splendors?<-

<margin>Distinction of dress according to the person.</margin>
Nevertheless, it is true that slovenliness is neither a virtue nor holiness: according to 1 Timothy 2:9, it must *be a modest apparel*; there may also be some distinction between people of higher or lower standing.

The word *Katastolē* <note>original: "Καταστολή"</note>, used by Paul in the aforementioned passage, is said by Pasor <note>Matthias Pasor (1599–1658), a German mathematician and theologian who taught in Groningen.</note> and others to mean a low robe or garment hanging down to the feet. *Salmasius* <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a renowned French classical scholar who lived in the Netherlands.</note> is of the opinion that translating it in such a way is quite a mistake, since it signifies lowliness of mind, humility, and smallness. Others take it for a humble garment, representing modesty and sobriety, because *kosmos* <note>original: "κόσμος"</note> is added to it—well-ordered and well-arranged—from which comes *kosmiōs* <note>original: "κοσμίως"</note>, meaning a modest, well-ordered, and dignified life.

And this being so, the Apostle would desire of women that they should adorn themselves in, with, and through a well-ordered, fit, and well-mannered modesty of mind, with which the outward appearance of their behavior must correspond, serving as a proof and sign thereof.

*Justinus* <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Latin historian.</note> says in his 20th book concerning Pythagoras, that he instilled moderation in everyone as the nurturer of virtues, and by constantly reasoning upon this, he brought it about that the women laid aside their golden clothes and other ornaments of their status as instruments of wantonness, judging that not clothes, but the chastity of women, was the true ornament.

One may say what one wishes, but Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an Early Christian writer.</note> in *On the Dress of Virgins* put it well when he wrote: The finery of ornaments and clothes, and the allurements of decked-out beauty, suit none but unchaste women who put themselves up for sale, etc., and no women are more strongly set upon it than those for whom shame is of little value. And Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquence.</note> in his 17th homily on Matthew: If any woman allows herself to be adorned and decked out so that she might draw the eyes of all to herself, even though she can seduce no one with her beauty, she shall nonetheless suffer final punishment; for she has prepared the poison, mixed the venom, and offered the cup, even if no one was found who drank from it.

Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), a Roman playwright.</note> in *Mostellaria* also put it not poorly,

> *A woman smells right when she smells of nothing.* <note>original: "Mulier rectè olet, ubi nihil olet."</note>

->That is:<-

->A woman smells good when she smells of nothing at all.<-

And after that:

> *She is afterwards adorned well in vain, if she is ill-mannered.* <note>original: "Poſtea nequicquam ornata eſt benè, ſi morata eſt malè."</note>

->That is:<-

->She dresses herself up in vain if she is ill-behaved.<-

<column-break/>

Cats <note>Jacob Cats (1577–1660), a hugely popular Dutch poet and moralist often called "Father Cats."</note> writes quite shortly and succinctly,

->Avoid with earnestness, through any lustful ornament,<-
->To hatch unrest and to show off for everyone,<-
->Or that you might, through any loose expression,<-
->Kindle lustful sparks in any person;<-
->But rather strive to adorn your fresh youth,<-
->For your own comfort, inwardly:<-
->And let your radiance, arising from virtue,<-
->Be a track for all young thieves.<- <note>In this context, "thieves" likely refers to those who would steal one's virtue or heart through vanity.</note>

<margin>The right ornament.</margin>
The most principal beauty and excellent ornament is humility, gentleness, chastity, a quiet spirit, good works, and holiness. Psalm 93:5, 1 Timothy 2:9, Titus 2, 1 Peter 3.

And to fill the measure for the reader on this, though briefly, I shall fill a little more paper with the lessons of the Church Fathers. Namely:

Tertullian <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155–220 AD), a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note> in his 9th chapter *On the Apparel and Ornament of Women*, lets himself be heard thus.

If any are forced to such splendor and outward show by wealth, birth, honor, and dignity, being quite old and gray as having received wisdom, take care that you guard yourself against these, or moderate yourself, lest under the pretext of necessity you give free rein and bridle to liberty. And in the 13th chapter: Come now with the remedies and Apostolic ornamental garments, taking from simplicity the white or blank color, from modesty the red blush, having painted the eyes with honorable shame and silence of spirit, fastening in or to your ears the twisted linen of holiness, with the purple of shame; and being thus painted, you shall have the Lord as a lover.

Just as Alcimus Avitus <note>Saint Avitus of Vienne (c. 450–518 AD), a Gallo-Roman bishop and poet.</note> spoke to his sister,

> *Strip off the delights of this world, and put on Christ.* <note>original: "Exue delicias mundi hujus, & indue Chriſtum."</note>

->That is:<-

->Cast off all the luxuries of the earth, and put on Christ.<-

->Manners, not gold, are the ornament of a woman.<- <note>original Greek: "Γυναικὶ κόσμος ὁ τρόπος, κ' οὐ χρυσία."</note>

->That is:<-

->The character, not the gold, adorns a woman.<-

->It is beautiful to see a woman adorned with good manners.<- <note>original Greek: "Καλὸν γυναικὸς ἐισορᾶν καλὸς τρόπος."</note>

->That is:<-

->It is fine to see a woman decorated with good morals.<-

<margin>Virtue is the best ornament.</margin>
Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Burgundian abbot and influential mystic.</note> in his *Apologia*: A vain heart transfers the signs of vanity to the body; the excess which is outward is a proof of the vanity and emptiness within. Soft clothes indicate the softness of the mind. One would not be so strongly set upon the ornament of the body, unless first the soul were neglected, unpracticed, and unadorned by virtues.

Nothing is more excellent than virtue; the beauty of virtue is the best ornament.

# ORNAMENT. CYMBAL.

<margin>Horace, Book 1, Epistles to Maecenas <note>Horace (65–8 BCE) was a leading Roman lyric poet. This quote is from Epistles 1.1.52.</note></margin>
> *Silver is of less value than gold; gold is of less value than virtue.* <note>original: "Vilius argentum est auro: virtutibus aurum."</note>
