### CYMBAL, CYMBEL, צלצלים [Tzilttzilim] / Κύμβαλον [Kymbalon], ששנים [Shoshannim] / Cymbalum, Schosohannim.

**C**YMBALS are musical instruments. The root
<margin>he has tinkled; thus</margin>
word comes from *tzalal* <note>original: "צלל"</note>, meaning "he has tinkled" or "rung"; so
named because of the sound they produce when
clashed against one another, and by the tinkling
upon them.

Some believe that *shoshannim* <note>original: "ששנים" - often translated as "lilies" in the Psalms.</note> are CYMBALS, being a charming and shrill-sounding
instrument for playing and singing; perhaps shaped like
a lily with six petals, having a hollow bowl
or calyx: *shoshanna* a lily, Song of Solomon 2:1, Hosea
14:6. Perhaps it is named after Susa <note>Shushan</note>, the capital
city of the Persians; which among the Phoenicians means *souson*, a lily. And that Susa was named for the multitude and pleasant
scent of the lilies there, as testified by
Stephanus, the author of the *Etymologicum*, and Bochart in *Phaleg*,
book 2, chapter 14. And as far as I have
found thus far, one should consider the *shosho-hannim* to have been a musical instrument
with six strings, perhaps shaped like a
hollow lily with six petals, or otherwise adorned
with images and foliage-work of lilies;
or perhaps it signified a well-known tune,
perhaps sung with six voices, so that
the Psalms where *shoshan* and *shoshannim* appear—such as Psalm 45, 60, 69,
and 80—could be sung in this manner
and with that many voices.

Hopfnerus <note>Heinrich Höpfner (1582–1642), a German Lutheran theologian.</note> believes one could interpret this
regarding the power and pleasantness of the content
of the Psalm, as if blowing a very strong
and lovely lily-scent toward a pious soul.

And Bugenhagen <note>Johannes Bugenhagen (1485–1558), a primary reformer under Luther.</note>, says Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow (1562–1633), a German orthodox Lutheran theologian.</note>, on the *shoshanna* or *shoshannim*, "upon or over the lilies": that is, on account of Christ the Bridegroom of the Church.

And it seems to have been a musical instrument
 of very pleasant and sweet melody, to
harmonize with the lilies, which
wonderfully affect both the ears and nostrils
pleasantly.

And the great Coccejus <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his covenant theology.</note> on Psalm 45, speaking
of this, writes: *The ancient Hebrews do not
deviate far from this when they say that it
refers to the request in Psalm 44: that the deliverance
shall have come like a lily, which is open at the top,
when they shall have their hearts open toward
heaven, toward God, and toward His
grace.*

It is said that cymbals were made of steel or copper;
they gave a loud sound, Psalm 150:5.
They were used in the Lord's service, in joy:
1 Chronicles 13 and 15, and 2 Chronicles 5, 2 Samuel 6, Psalm
150:5.

In the Treatise *Shekalim* <note>A tractate of the Mishnah regarding the half-shekel temple tax and temple administration.</note>, chapter 5, § 1: These were placed over
the service in the sanctuary: the son of
Babi over the lashings, the son of Arsa over the
Cymbals, Hugdam the son of Levi over the
songs.

They were struck, beaten, shaken, etc.

<margin>Propertius, Book 3 <note>Sextus Propertius (c. 50–15 BCE), a Roman elegiac poet.</note></margin>
> *He will beat the hoarse cymbals to the sounds of Ida.* <note>original: "Tundet ad Idaeos cymbala rauca sonos." Mount Ida was associated with the worship of Cybele.</note>

-> That is: <-

> Upon his cymbal he shall play the tune
> of Ida.

From Catullus and Propertius, book 3, elegy 15,
one learns that the priests of Cybele <note>The "Mother of the Gods" in Greek and Roman mythology, whose rites were famous for wild music.</note>
had them in use.

> *The cymbals clashed for the Theban God.* <note>original: "Cymbala Thebano concrepuere Deo." The "Theban God" is Bacchus (Dionysus).</note>

-> That is: <-

> The cymbal sounded for the Theban God.

Claudian, in *Against Eutropius*, in his first book,
speaks of it:

> *Or if sacred rites please you, take Cybele instead of Mars;
> learn the Celænean furies to the sound of hoarse drums:
> let it delight you to carry cymbals, to beat your breast with pine wood,
> and to cut away the remainder of your manhood with Phrygian knives.* <note>original: "Vel si sacra placent... Inguinis & reliquum Phrygiis abscindere cultris." This refers to the self-castration of the Galli, priests of Cybele.</note>

-> That is: <-

> *If you desire to offer sacrifice, choose Cybele over Mars,
> And learn to fetch frenzy and mad passions
> At the Celænean rumbling and clashing of Cymbals,
> To beat your breast against the pine tree, and the part
> Of your manhood to cut off from the whole.*

By striking and tinkling upon them, they gave sound.
<margin>Ausonius, Epistle 25 <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius (c. 310–395 CE), a Roman poet and rhetorician.</note></margin>
> *Dindyman songs answer from the Gargaric grove;
> cymbals give sound by their clash.* <note>original: "Dindyma Gargarico respondent cantica luco, / Cymbala dant flictu sonitum." Dindyma and Gargara were mountains in Asia Minor.</note>

-> That is: <-

-> That is: <-

> One hears the sounds of the Dodonaean basin,
> And one after the other, through the knocking, they
> provide an answer.

<margin>Form of the / cymbals.</margin>
Rhabanus Maurus <note>Rabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), a Frankish Benedictine abbot and scholar.</note> says: *Cymbals are
very small bowls, fashioned together from mixed metal,
having their bellies in the sides or rims, which,
by a skillful guidance, being struck against
one another in measure, restore the sharp sound with a
pleasant resonance.*

# ORNAMENT.

Constantijn Huygens <note>A renowned Dutch Golden Age poet, diplomat, and polymath (1596–1687).</note> already took aim in his time at ornament and foreign luxury.

> O Holland, old fame of simple dignity,
> Where shall we find a shield for your justice,
> In the painful tale of overseas splendors?

Nevertheless, it is true that slovenliness is neither virtue nor holiness: according to 1 Timothy 2:9, there must be "decent apparel"; there may also be some distinction in dress between people of higher or lower station.

<margin>Distinction of dress according to the person.</margin>
The word *Katastole* <note>original: "Καταστολὴ"</note>, used by Paul in the aforementioned passage, is said by Pasor <note>Matthias Pasor (1599–1658), a German mathematician and linguist.</note> and others to mean a low-hanging skirt or garment reaching to the feet. Salmasius <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a famous French classical scholar.</note> is of the opinion that translating it in such a way is quite mistaken, as it signifies lowliness of mind, humility, and smallness. Others take it for a humble garment, representing modesty and sobriety, since it is accompanied by the word *kosmos* <note>original: "κόσμος" — meaning order, the world, or ornament</note>, meaning well-ordered and well-arranged; from this comes "to live modestly" <note>original: "κοσμίως ζῇν"</note>, to live a sober, well-arranged, and dignified life. And this being so, the Apostle would desire of women that they should adorn themselves in, with, and through a well-ordered, suitable, and well-mannered modesty of mind, with which the outward appearance of their behavior must agree, and be a proof and sign thereof.

Justinus <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a 2nd-century Roman historian.</note> says in his 20th book of Pythagoras <note>The famous Greek philosopher and mathematician (c. 570–495 BCE).</note>, that he instilled moderation in everyone as the nurturer of virtues, and by constantly reasoning upon this, he brought it about that the women laid aside their golden clothes and other ornaments of their status as "tools of wantonness," judging that not clothes, but the chastity of women was their true ornament.

One may say what one wishes, but Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258), Bishop of Carthage and an Early Christian writer.</note>, in *On the Dress of Virgins*, had it right when he wrote: *The finery of ornaments and clothes, the allurements of decked-out beauty, suit none but unchaste women who offer themselves for sale, etc., and no women are more set upon them than those for whom shame is of low price.* And Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father known for his powerful preaching.</note> in Homily 17 on Matthew: *If any woman allows herself to be adorned and painted so that she might draw the eyes of all to her, even though she can seduce no one with her beauty, she shall nonetheless suffer punishment in the end; for she has prepared the poison, mixed the venom, and offered the cup, even if no one was found who drank from it.*

Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BCE), a Roman playwright of comedies.</note> in *Mostellaria* also did not have it wrong:

> *A woman smells right when she smells of nothing.* <note>original: "Mulier rectè olet, ubi nihil olet."</note>

That is:

->*A woman smells well when she smells of nothing at all.*<-

And after that:

> *She is adorned in vain if she is poorly mannered.* <note>original: "Postea nequicquam ornata est benè, si morata est malè."</note>

That is:

->*She dresses herself up in vain if she is ill-mannered.*<-

Cats <note>Jacob Cats (1577–1660), a hugely popular Dutch poet and moralist often called "Father Cats."</note> writes quite shortly and concisely:

> Avoid with earnestness, through any lewd ornament,
> Breeding unrest and parading for everyone,

<margin>The true ornament.</margin>
The principal beauty and most excellent ornament is humility, meekness, chastity, a quiet spirit, good works, and holiness. Psalm 93:5, 1 Timothy 2:9, Titus 2, 1 Peter 3.

### CYMBAL, צלצלים / Κύμβαλον, שושנים Cymbalum, shoshannim.

Cymbals are musical instruments. The root word comes from the Hebrew *tsalal* <note>original: "צלל"</note>, meaning "he has tinkled"; so named because of the sound they make when struck against each other, and by the clanging upon them.

Some believe that *shoshannim* <note>original: "שושנים" — literally "lilies"</note>, are CYMBALS, a stroking and shrill-sounding musical and vocal instrument; perhaps following the form of a lily with six petals, having a hollow bowl or chalice: *shoshanna* a lily, Song of Solomon 2:1, Hosea 14:6. Perhaps named after Susa, the capital of the Persians; which among the Phoenicians, *souson* <note>original: "σουσον"</note>, means a lily. And that Susa was named so from the multitude and pleasant scent of the lilies, as testified by Stephanus, the *Etymologicum* <note>A 12th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of Greek words.</note>, and Bochart in *Phaleg* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar.</note>, book 2, chapter 14. And as far as I have found until now, one should feel that the *shoshannim* was an instrument with six strings, perhaps shaped like a hollow lily with six petals, or otherwise adorned with images and foliage of lilies; or perhaps it signified a well-known tune, perhaps sung with six voices, so that the Psalms where *shoshannim* appears—such as Psalms 45, 60, 69, and 80—were sung in this musical style and with that many voices.

Hopfnerus <note>A reference to a 17th-century theologian or commentator.</note> believes one could interpret it regarding the power and pleasantness of the Psalm's content, like a pious soul breathing out a very strong and lovely scent of lilies.

And Bugenhagius <note>Johannes Bugenhagen (1485–1558), a primary figure in the Protestant Reformation.</note> says (according to Tarnovius <note>Paul Tarnow (1562–1633), an Orthodox Lutheran theologian.</note>), on the *shoshan-na*, *shoshannim*, "upon or over the lilies": that is, on account of Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church.

And it seems to have been an instrument of very pleasant and sweet melody, to harmonize with the lilies, which wonderfully delight both the ears and the nostrils.

And the great Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his covenant theology.</note>, speaking of this in Psalm 45, writes: The ancient Hebrews do not stray far from it when they say that it refers to the request in Psalm 44 that deliverance might come; and that it is given to understand that this deliverance will come when they, the Jews, shall have become like a lily, which is open at the top, when they shall have their hearts open upward toward God and toward His grace.

It is said that cymbals were made of steel or copper; they gave a loud sound, Psalm 150:5. They were used in the Lord’s service and in joy: 1 Chronicles 13 and 15, 2 Chronicles 5, 2 Samuel 6, and Psalm 150:5.

In the Treatise *Shekalim* <note>A tractate of the Mishnah regarding the temple tax.</note>, chapter 5, section 1: These were placed over

<note>original: "Nec Dodonaei cessat tinnitus aheni..." refers to the bronze cauldrons at the oracle of Dodona that rang when struck.</note>

->That is:<-

->One hears the sounds of the Dodonaean basin,<-
->And one to the other, by knocking, serves as<-
->an answer.<-

<margin>Form of the Cymbals.</margin>
Rhabanus Maurus <note>A 9th-century Frankish Benedictine monk and scholar (c. 780–856).</note> says: The Cymbals are very small bowls, composed of mixed metal, having their "bellies" in the sides or borders, which, through a skillful guiding, being struck against each other in measure, restore a sharp sound with a delightful resonance.

# ORNAMENT.

Constantijn Huygens <note>A celebrated Dutch Golden Age poet and diplomat (1596–1687) known for his wit and moralizing verse.</note> already had his sights set on ornament and foreign luxury in his time.

> O Holland, old glory of simple dignity,
> Where shall we find a shield for your justice,
> In the painful tale of overseas splendors?

<margin>Distinction of dress according to the person.</margin>
Nevertheless, it is true that slovenliness is neither a virtue nor holiness: according to 1 Timothy 2:9, it must be "modest apparel"; there may also be some distinction between people of higher or lower station.

The word <term>Καταστολὴ</term> <note>original: "Katastolē"</note>, used by Paul in the aforementioned place, is said by Pasor and others to mean a low-hanging robe or garment reaching to the feet. Salmasius <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a French classical scholar.</note> is of the opinion that translating it in such a way is quite mistaken, since it signifies lowliness of mind, humility, and smallness. Others take it for a humble garment, representing modesty and sobriety, because <term>κόσμος</term> <note>original: "kosmos" — meaning order or ornament</note> is added to it, meaning well-ordered and well-arranged; from this comes <term>κοσμίως</term> <note>original: "kosmiōs"</note>, a modest, well-arranged, and dignified life.

And this being so, the Apostle would desire of women that they should adorn themselves in, with, and through a well-ordered, fit, and well-mannered modesty of mind, with which the external aspect of their behavior must correspond, being a proof and sign thereof.

Justinus <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a 2nd-century Roman historian.</note> says in his 20th book concerning Pythagoras, that he instilled temperance into everyone as the nurturer of virtues, and by constantly reasoning upon this, he brought it about that the women laid aside their golden clothes and other ornaments of their status as "instruments of wantonness," judging that not clothes, but the chastity of women was their true ornament.

One may say what one will, but Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an Early Christian writer.</note> in *On the Dress of Virgins* had it right when he wrote: *The finery of ornaments and clothes, the allurements of made-up beauty, suit no one but unchaste women who offer themselves for sale, etc., and no women are more set upon them than those for whom shame is of low value.* And Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Christian preacher.</note> in his 17th Homily on Matthew: *If any woman allows herself to be adorned and painted so that she might draw the eyes of all to herself, even though she can seduce no one with her beauty, she shall nonetheless suffer final punishment; for she has prepared the poison, mixed the venom, and offered the cup, even if no one be found who has drunk from it.*

Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), a Roman playwright.</note> in *Mostellaria* also put it not poorly:

> *A woman smells right when she smells of nothing.* <note>original: "Mulier rectè olet, ubi nihil olet."</note>

->That is:<-

->A woman smells well, when she smells of nothing at all.<-

And thereafter:

> *She is adorned in vain if she is ill-mannered.* <note>original: "Poſtea nequicquam ornata eſt benè, ſi morata eſt malè."</note>

->That is:<-

->She dresses herself up in vain, if she is ill-mannered.<-

<column-break/>

Cats <note>Jacob Cats (1577–1660), a Dutch poet and politician famous for his moral emblems.</note> writes quite briefly and concisely:

> Avoid with earnestness, through any lewd ornament,
> Brewing unrest or parading for everyone,
> Lest you might, through any loose countenance,
> Kindle lewd sparks in any person;
> But rather strive to adorn your fresh youth
> Inwardly for your own comfort:
> And let your radiance, arising from virtue,
> Be a spur for all young thieves. <note>In the context of the time, "thieves" often referred to suitors or those who would "steal" one's heart.</note>

<margin>The true ornament.</margin>
The most important beauty and excellent ornament is humility, gentleness, chastity, a quiet spirit, good works, and holiness. Psalm 93:5, 1 Timothy 2:9, Titus 2, 1 Peter 3.

And to measure out the full portion for the reader on this subject, though briefly, I shall fill a little more paper with the lessons of the Church Fathers. Namely:

Tertullian <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155–220 AD), a prolific early Christian author.</note> in the 9th chapter of *On the Apparel of Women* speaks thus:

> *If any are forced to such splendor and outward show by wealth, birth, honor, and status—being quite old and gray, having received wisdom—take care that you guard against these things, or moderate yourself, so that under the pretext of necessity, you do not give free rein and bridle to liberty. And in the 13th chapter: Come now with the remedies and Apostolic ornaments of the day, taking from simplicity the white or blank color, from modesty the red blush, having painted the eyes with modest shame and silence of spirit, fastening in or on your ears the twisted linen of holiness, with the purple of shame; and being thus painted, you shall have the Lord as a lover.*

Just as Alcimus Avitus <note>A 5th-century Bishop and Latin poet.</note> spoke to his sister:

> *Strip off the luxuries of this world, and put on Christ.* <note>original: "Exue delicias mundi hujus, & indue Chriſtum."</note>

->That is:<-

->Strip off all the luxuries of the earth, and put on Christ.<-

> *A woman’s ornament is her character, not gold.* <note>original: "Γυναικὶ κόσμος ὁ τρόπος, κ' οὐ χρυσία."</note>

->That is:<-

->Manners, not gold, adorn a woman.<-

> *It is beautiful to see a woman adorned with good manners.* <note>original: "Καλὸν γυναικὸς εἰσορᾶν καλὸς τρόπος."</note>

->That is:<-

->It is fine to see a woman adorned with good manners.<-

<margin>Virtue the best ornament.</margin>
Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153).</note> in his *Apologia*: A vain heart transfers the marks of vanity to the body; the excess which is outward is a proof of the vanity and emptiness within. Soft clothes indicate the softness of the mind. One would not be so strongly set upon the ornament of the body, unless the soul were first neglected, unpracticed, and unadorned by virtues.

Nothing is more excellent than virtue; the beauty of virtue is the best ornament.

<margin>
Horace, book 1, Epistle to Maecenas.

->That is:<-

# CYMBAL, צִלְצְלִים <note>Hebrew: "Tziltzalim"</note>,
# *κύμβαλον* <note>Greek: "Kymbalon"</note>, שֹׁשַׁנִּים <note>Hebrew: "Shoshannim"</note>, Cymbalum <note>Latin for "Cymbal"</note>.

CYMBALS are musical instruments. The root word comes from צָלַל <note>Hebrew: "tzalal"</note>, meaning he has tinkled; so named because of the sound they give when struck against one another and by the tinkling upon them.

Some believe that *shoshannim* <note>A term appearing in the titles of several Psalms, literally meaning "lilies."</note> are CYMBALS, a stroking and shrill-sounding musical and vocal instrument, perhaps shaped like a lily with six leaves, having a hollow bowl or chalice: *shoshanna* a lily, *Song of Solomon 2:1, Hosea 4:6.* Perhaps it is named after Susa, the capital of the Persians; which among the Phoenicians means *souson*, a lily. And that Susa was named after the abundance and pleasant scent of lilies, as testified by *Stephanus, the Etymological Author, and Bochart in Phaleg, book 2, chapter 14.* And as far as I have found until now, one should feel that the *shoshannim* was a musical instrument with six strings, perhaps after the shape of a hollow lily with six leaves, or otherwise adorned with images and foliage of lilies; or perhaps it signified a well-known tune, perhaps being sung with six voices, so as to sing the Psalms where *shoschan* and *shoshannim* appear—such as *Psalm 45, 60, 69, 80*—in this manner of singing and with as many voices.

Hopfnerus believes one could interpret it regarding the power and pleasantness of the content of the Psalm, *as a pious soul breathing forth a very strong and lovely lily-scent.*

And Bugenhagius says, according to Tarnovius, regarding the *shoshanna, shoshannim*, "upon or over the lilies": *that is, on account of Christ the Bridegroom of the Church.*

And it seems to have been a musical instrument of very pleasant and sweet melody, to harmonize with the lilies, which wonderfully delight both the ears and the nostrils.

And the great Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian.</note> speaking of this on *Psalm 45*, writes: *The ancient Hebrews do not deviate far from this when they say that it refers to the request in Psalm 44, that the redemption shall have become like a lily, which is open at the top, when they shall have their hearts open upwards toward God and toward His grace.*

It is said that cymbals were made of steel or copper; they gave a loud sound, *Psalm 150:5.* They were used in the Lord's service, in joy, *1 Chronicles 13 and 15, and 2 Chronicles 5, 2 Samuel 6, Psalm 150:5.*

In the *Tractate Shekalim, chapter 5, § 1:* These are appointed over the service in the sanctuary: *the son of Babi over the lashings, the son of Arfa over the Cymbals, Hugdam the son of Levi over the songs.*

They were struck, beaten, shaken, etc.

ORNAMEΝT. CYMBAL.
(E)
<meta>catchword: Kory-</meta>

<margin>Horace, Book 1, Epistle to Maecenas.</margin>
*Silver is worth less than gold; gold is worth less than virtue.* <note>original Latin: "Vilius argentum est auro: virtutibus aurum."</note>

->That is:<-

> Match the value of virtue.

# CYMBAL, CYMBEL, *Tsiltselim*, *Kymbalon*, *Shoshannim*, Cymbalum. <note>The author provides the name in Dutch, Hebrew (צלצלים), Greek (Κύμβαλον), and Latin. *Shoshannim* (שושנים) literally means "lilies," which the author explains below.</note>

CYMBALS are musical instruments. The root word comes from *tsalal* <note>Hebrew: צלל</note>, meaning "it has tinkled" or "clanged"; so named because of the sound they produce when struck against one another, creating a ringing tone.

Some believe that *shoshannim* <note>original: "schofochannim"</note> are cymbals, described as a pleasant and shrill-sounding instrument for playing and singing; perhaps shaped like a six-petaled lily, having a hollow bowl or calyx. *Shoshanna* means "a lily" <note>Song of Solomon 2:1, Hosea 14:6</note>. It is possible the name comes from Susa, the capital of the Persians; which among the Phoenicians, *souson*, signifies a lily. That Susa was named for the abundance and pleasant scent of lilies is testified by Stephanus, the *Etymologicum Magnum*, and Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> in *Phaleg*, Book II, chapter 14. As far as I have discovered thus far, one should consider the *shoshannim* to have been an instrument with six strings, perhaps shaped like a hollow lily with six petals, or otherwise adorned with images and foliage of lilies. Alternatively, it might signify a well-known tune, perhaps sung with six voices, to which the Psalms titled *shoshannim*—such as *Psalm 45, 60, 69, and 80*—were sung in this specific musical style and with that many voices.

Hopfnerus suggests one could interpret this regarding the power and pleasantness of the Psalm's content, as if a pious soul were breathing out a very strong and lovely scent of lilies.

And Bugenhagius, says Tarnovius, regarding the *shoshanna* or *shoshannim* (upon or over the lilies): says it refers to Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church.

It seems to have been an instrument of very pleasant and sweet melody, to harmonize with the lilies, which wonderfully delight both the ears and the nostrils.

And the great Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian</note>, speaking of this in *Psalm 45*, writes: *The ancient Hebrews do not stray far from this when they say it refers to the request in Psalm 44 that deliverance might come; and that it is given to understand that this deliverance shall come when they, the Jews, shall have become like a lily, which is open at the top, when they shall have their hearts open toward God and toward His grace.*

It is said that cymbals were made of steel or copper; they gave a loud sound <note>Psalm 150:5</note>. They were used in the service of the Lord during times of joy <note>1 Chronicles 13 and 15; 2 Chronicles 5; 2 Samuel 6; Psalm 150:5</note>.

<margin>In the Treatise Shekalim, chapter 5, § 1.</margin>
These men were appointed over

<column-break/>

the service in the sanctuary: the son of Babi over the lashings <note>disciplinary scourging</note>, the son of Arsa over the Cymbals, and Hugdam the son of Levi over the songs.

They were struck, beaten, shaken, etc.

*He shall strike the hoarse cymbals to the sounds of Ida.* <note>original Latin: "Tundet ad Idaeos cymbala rauca sonos." Mount Ida was sacred to the goddess Cybele.</note>

->That is:<-

> Upon his cymbal he shall play the tune
> Of Ida.

From Catullus and Propertius <note>Book III, elegy 15</note>, we learn that the priests of Cybele <note>The "Great Mother" goddess of Phrygia</note> used them.

*The cymbals clashed for the Theban God.* <note>original Latin: "Cymbala Thebano concrepuere Deo." Referring to Bacchus/Dionysus.</note>

->That is:<-

> The cymbal gave sound for the Theban God.

<margin>Claudian, in his first book against Eutropius, speaks of it:</margin>

Inguinis & reliquum Phrygiis abscindere cultris." This refers to the self-castration of the Galli, the priests of Cybele.</note>

> The Cymbal gives sound through the striking.

->That is:<-

> One hears the sounds of the Dodonean basin,
> And one after another, through the knocking, they serve as an answer.

<margin>Rhabanus Maurus says: Cymbals are very small bowls, composed of mixed metal, having their rounded bellies in the sides or rims, which, when struck against each other in rhythm by skillful management, produce a sharp sound with a delightful resonance.</margin>

# ORNAMENT.

<note>original Dutch: "CIERAAD."</note>

Constantijn Huygens <note>1596–1687, a celebrated Dutch Golden Age poet and polymath</note> already had his sights set on ornament and foreign luxury in his time.

> O Holland, old fame of plain dignity,
> Where shall we find a shield for your justice,
> In the painful tale of overseas splendors?

<margin>Distinction of clothing according to the person.</margin>
Nevertheless, it is true that slovenliness is neither virtue nor holiness: according to 1 Timothy 2:9, it must be "modest apparel"; there may also be some distinction between people of higher or lower standing.
The word *katastole* <note>Greek: καταστολὴ</note>, used by Paul in the aforementioned passage, means—according to Pasor <note>Matthias Pasor (1599–1658), a German linguist and theologian</note> and others—a low gown or garment hanging down to the feet. Salmasius <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), an influential French classical scholar; OCR reads "Samasius"</note> is of the opinion that translating it in such a way is quite mistaken, since it signifies lowliness of mind, humility, and smallness. Others take it for a humble garment, representing modesty and sobriety, because it is accompanied by *kosmos* <note>Greek: κόσμος</note>, meaning well-ordered and well-arranged; from this comes *kosmios* <note>Greek: κοσμίως</note>, a modest, well-ordered, and dignified life.
And this being so, the Apostle would desire of women that they should adorn themselves in, with, and through well-ordered, suitable, and well-mannered modesty of mind, with which the outward appearance of their behavior must correspond, serving as a proof and sign thereof.
Justinus <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian</note> says in his 20th book concerning Pythagoras, that he instilled temperance in everyone as the nurse of virtues, and by constantly reasoning on this, he brought it about that women laid aside their golden clothes and other ornaments of their status as instruments of wantonness, judging that not clothes, but the chastity of women was the true ornament.
One may say what one will, Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage</note> in *On the Dress of Virgins* <note>Latin: "De habitu virginum"</note> had it right when he wrote: The finery of ornaments and clothes, the allurements of decked-out beauty, suit none but unchaste women who offer themselves for sale, etc., and no women are more set upon them than those in whom shame is held at a low price. And Chrysostom <note>Saint John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an Early Church Father noted for his oratory</note> in Homily 17 on Matthew: If any woman allows herself to be adorned and painted so that she might draw the eyes of all to herself, even though she can seduce no one with her beauty, she shall nevertheless suffer final punishment; for she has prepared the poison, mixed the venom, and offered the cup, even if no one was found who drank from it.

Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), a Roman playwright</note> in *Mostellaria* also did not have it wrong:

> *Mulier rectè olet, ubi nihil olet.* <note>Latin quote from Plautus</note>

->That is:<-

->A woman smells well when she smells of nothing.<-

And after that:

> *Postea nequicquam ornata est benè, si morata est malè.* <note>Latin quote from Plautus</note>

->That is:<-

->She dresses herself up in vain, if she is ill-mannered.<-

<column-break/>

Cats <note>Jacob Cats (1577–1660), a hugely popular Dutch poet and moralist known as "Father Cats"</note> writes quite shortly and concisely:

> Avoid with earnestness, through any lewd ornament,
> To breed unrest and to show off for everyone,
> Lest you might, through any loose expression,
> Ignite lewd sparks in any person;
> But rather that you strive your fresh youth,
> For your own comfort, to adorn inwardly:
> And that your luster, risen out of virtue,
> Might be a spur for all young creatures.

<margin>The true ornament.</margin>
The foremost beauty and most excellent ornament is humility, gentleness, chastity, a quiet spirit, good works, and holiness. Psalm 93:5, 1 Timothy 2:9, Titus 2, 1 Peter 3.
And to fill the measure for the reader on this, though briefly, I will fill a little more paper with the lessons of the Church Fathers. Namely:
Tertullian <note>c. 155–c. 220 AD, a prolific early Christian author</note>, on the finery and ornament of women, in the 9th chapter, speaks thus:
*If some are compelled to such splendor and outward appearance by wealth, birth, honor, and dignity—being quite old and gray, having received wisdom—take care that you guard yourself against these, or moderate yourself, lest under the pretext of necessity, you give free rein and bridle to liberty.* And in the 13th chapter: *Come now with the medicines and Apostolic ornamental garments, taking from simplicity the white or blank color, from modesty the red blush, having painted the eyes with modest shame and silence of spirit, fastening in or to your ears the word of God, and binding to your necks the yoke of Christ. Clothe yourselves with the silk of piety, with the twisted linen of holiness, with the purple of shame, and being thus painted, you shall have the Lord for a lover.*
Just as Alcimus Avitus <note>c. 450–518 AD, a Bishop of Vienne and Latin poet</note> spoke to his sister:

> *Exue delicias mundi hujus, & indue Christum.* <note>Latin quote from Avitus</note>

->That is:<-

->Cast off all the luxuries of the earth, and put on Christ.<-

> Γυναικὶ κόσμος ὁ τρόπος, κ' οὐ χρυσία. <note>Greek aphorism often attributed to Menander</note>

->That is:<-

->Manners, not gold, adorn a woman.<-

> Καλὸν γυναικὸς εἰσορᾶν καλὸς τρόπος. <note>Greek aphorism</note>

->That is:<-

->It is beautiful to see a woman adorned with good manners.<-

Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a French abbot and mystic</note> in *Apologia*: *A vain heart transfers the marks of vanity to the body; the superfluity which is outward is a proof of the vanity and emptiness within. Soft clothes indicate the softness of the mind.* <margin>Virtue is the best counsel.</margin> One would not be so strongly set upon the ornament of the body, unless the soul were first neglected, unpracticed, and unadorned by virtues.
Nothing is more excellent than virtue; the beauty of virtue is the best ornament.

Horace <note>Quintus Horatius Flaccus (65–8 BC), a Roman lyric poet</note>...

# CYMBAL, CYMBAL, <term>Tziltzalim</term> <note>Hebrew: צלצלים, meaning clanging or whirring instruments</note>, <term>Shoshannim</term> <note>Hebrew: ששנים, meaning "lilies," likely referring to an instrument shaped like one</note>, <term>Kymbalon</term> <note>Greek: Κύμβαλον</note>, <term>Cymbalum</term> <note>Latin</note>, <term>shoshannim</term>.

<insert>C</insert>YMBALS are musical instruments. The root word comes from <term>tzalal</term> <note>Hebrew: צלל</note>, meaning *he has tinkled*; so named because of the sound they produce by being struck against one another, and by the ringing tone they give.

Some believe that *shoshannim*—cymbals—are a soothing and high-pitched playing and singing instrument; perhaps named after the form of a six-leafed lily, having a hollow bowl or chalice: *shoshanna* means a lily, *Song of Solomon 2:1, Hosea 14:6* <note>The OCR cites Hosea 4:6, but the context of lilies suggests 14:6</note>; perhaps even named after Susa, the capital city of the Persians; which among the Phoenicians means <term>soson</term> <note>Greek: σόσον</note>, a lily. And that Susa was named for the abundance and pleasant scent of the lilies there, as witnessed by Stephanus, the *Etymologicum Magnum*, and Bochart in *Phaleg, Book 2, chapter 14.* And as far as I have found until now, one should understand the *shoshannim* to have been a musical instrument with six strings, perhaps shaped like a hollow lily with six petals, or otherwise adorned with images and foliage-work of lilies; or perhaps it signified a well-known tune, maybe sung with six voices, so that the Psalms preceded by *shoshan* or *shoshannim*, such as *Psalm 45, 60, 69, and 80*, were sung in this musical style and with that many voices.

Hopfsnerus believes one could interpret it regarding the power and pleasantness of the Psalm’s content, as *a pious soul exhaling a very strong and lovely scent of lilies.*

And Bugenhagius, says Tarnovius, regarding the *shoshanna, shoshannim*, "upon or over the lilies": that is, on account of Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church.

And it seems to have been an instrument of very pleasant and sweet melody, to harmonize with the lilies, which wonderfully delight both the ears and the nostrils.

And the great Coccejus <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian</note> speaking of this in *Psalm 45*, writes: *The ancient Hebrews do not stray far from it when they say that it refers to the request in Psalm 44 that deliverance might come; and that it is suggested that this deliverance will come when the Jews have become like a lily, which is open at the top, when they shall have their hearts open toward heaven, toward God, and toward His grace.*

It is said that cymbals were made of steel or copper; they gave a loud sound, *Psalm 150:5.* They were used in the Lord’s service and in times of joy, *1 Chronicles 13 and 15, 2 Chronicles 5, 2 Samuel 6, Psalm 150:5.*

In the *Tractate Shekalim, chapter 5, § 1*: These are set over

<column-break/>

the service in the sanctuary: the son of Babi over the lashings <note>referring to the temple overseer responsible for discipline/shame</note>, the son of Arza over the Cymbals, and Hugdam the son of Levi over the songs.

They were struck, beaten, shaken, etc.

<margin>Propertius, Book III.</margin>

> *He shall beat the hoarse cymbals to the sounds of Ida.* <note>original Latin: "Tundet ad Idaeos cymbala rauca sonos." Mount Ida was associated with the worship of the goddess Cybele.</note>

->That is:<-

> *On his cymbal he shall play the tune*
> *of Ida.*

From Catullus and Propertius *Book III, elegy 15*, one learns that the priests of Cybele <note>The "Great Mother" goddess of Phrygia</note> used them.

> *The cymbals clashed for the Theban God.* <note>original Latin: "Cymbala Thebano concrepuere Deo." Referring to Bacchus/Dionysus.</note>

->That is:<-

> *The cymbal gave sound for the Theban God.*

Claudian in *Against Eutropius*, in his first book, speaks of it:

> *Or if sacred rites please you, take Cybele instead of Mars,*
> *Learn the Celaenean furies to the sound of hoarse drums:*
> *Let it please you to carry cymbals, and strike your breast with pine,*
> *And cut away the rest of your manhood with Phrygian knives.* <note>original Latin: "Vel si sacra placent, habeas pro Marte Cybellen, / Rauca Celaeneos ad tympana disce furores: / Cymbala ferre juvet, pectusque illidere pino, / Inguinis & reliquum Phrygiis abscindere cultris." This refers to the ecstatic and self-mutilating rites of the Galli priests.</note>

->That is:<-

> *If it pleases you to sacrifice, choose Cybele over Mars,*
> *And learn to find madness and wild passions*
> *By the Celaenean drumming and the clanging of the Cymbals,*
> *Beating your breast against the pine tree, and the part*
> *of your manhood cutting off from the whole.*

By striking and clanging them, they made a sound. *Ausonius, Epistle 25.*

> *The Dindymene songs respond through the Gargaric grove,*
> *The cymbals give a sound by being struck.* <note>original Latin: "Dindyma Gargarico respondent cantica luco, / Cymbala dant flictu sonitum." Dindyma and Gargarus were mountains associated with Cybele.</note>

->That is:<-

> *The song of Dindyma resounds through the Gargaric wood:*
> *The Cymbal gives sound through striking.*

And a little after,

> *Nor does the tinkling of the Dodonaean bronze cease,*
> *Whenever, struck by the hitting rods, the rhythmic*
> *And docile basins respond to the measured stroke.* <note>original Latin: "Nec Dodonaei cessat tinnitus aheni, / In numerum quotiens radiis ferientibus ictae / Respondent dociles, moderato verbere pelves." Dodona was famous for its oracular "brazen kettles."</note>

->That is:<-

> *One hears the sounds of the Dodonaean basin,*
> *And one after another, through the knocking, they serve as an answer.*

<margin>Form of the Cymbals,</margin>
Rhabanus Maurus <note>c. 780–856, a Frankish Benedictine abbot and scholar</note> says: *Cymbals are very small bowls, fashioned together from mixed metal, having their "bellies" in the sides or rims, which, being struck against each other by skillful management according to the rhythm, produce a sharp sound with a pleasing resonance.*

<header>CYMBAL.</header>

<language>English</language>

<term>Kotyledon</term> <note>Greek: κοτυληδὼν, commonly known as navelwort or pennywort</note>, of which Pliny writes in the 25th book, chapter 13, that it is thin, with a tender stalk, a small and fatty leaf, and a hollow leaf like navel flowers and leaves. See Matthias de Lobel, *On Plants*, page 164, etc. He shows its shape to be very close to the image provided by Pfeiffer in *Difficulties of Scripture*, page 561. See also Lampe, *On Cymbals*.

One might think that Paul, in 1 Corinthians 13:1, when speaking of a clanging cymbal, <term>kymbalon alalazon</term> <note>Greek: κύμβαλον ἀλαλάζον</note>, had this in mind for his purpose.

It is well known that metal rings out, whether it be a bell, trumpet, cymbal, or any other artistic and musical instrument; and when moved with skill, it produces various and not unpleasant tones.

It is said that *kymbalon* means a round copper tool, a round ball or sphere that gives off a sound through impact. *Alalazon*, it is said, signifies a dull and irregular sound, a confused noise like that of a crowd marching against an enemy or returning with shouts of victory.

If Paul did not have love: even if he brought fruit to others, stirred them to their duty, woke them and made them rise from their sleep and carelessness; even if he tickled their ears and performed a service by speaking and preaching with a tongue of eloquence and charm—if his goal was not to build them up in love, he would be speaking, in his own view, in an unknown language. He would merely be showing off his learning and knowledge of languages; he would be letting his "chatter-tongue" be heard while not being understood. What else was he then but sounding brass and a clanging cymbal? It profited him nothing, because through love he did not seek the glory of God or the edification of his neighbor. And his neighbor gained nothing, for though the sound was heard, being unaccustomed to such tones and words, they heard the sound only as a cymbal or clanging bell. For the rest, they had no more use for it than the sound of a cymbal or sounding metal, which is not understood or indicates nothing certain. See Poole, Lightfoot, Hammond, Adrianus Junius in *Analecta*, our *Notes on 1 Corinthians*, Delrio, Roa, etc., *Selected Dissertations*, book 1. Compare this with the saying of Timon in Diogenes Laertius regarding Zeno:

> *Now [he] has less sense than a stringed instrument.* <note>Original Greek: Νῦν δ' ἔχειν ἐλάσσονα σκινδαψὸν. Timon was a skeptical philosopher mocking Zeno, the founder of Stoicism.</note>

->That is:<-

->To have less understanding than a stringed instrument.<-

<margin><term>Skindapsos</term> <note>Greek: Σκινδαψὸς</note></margin> A *skindapsos* is a type of musical instrument with four strings, which was primarily used by women.

Timon means to say that Zeno was a chatterbox whose words made a sound without meaning. One could make nothing of it. And Cleanthes used to say of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle who taught while walking</note> that they *suffered a fate similar to lutes, which, though they sound beautiful, do not hear themselves.* <note>Original Greek: ὅμοιόν τι πάσχειν ταῖς λύραις, αἳ καλῶς φθεγγόμεναι αὐτῶν οὐκ ἀκούουσιν.</note>

Quintilian calls a senseless orator a clanging cymbal. For when puffed-up boasters,

<column-break/>

shouters, clanging cymbals, and their like commit errors through a false zeal, I am certain that they fail not through an abundance of strength, but through weakness, just as bodies swell not from health, but from illness.

And Juvenal, in *Satire 6*, line 440 <note>The OCR says "m. 63," likely a local reference or misreading of the line number</note>, is also not mistaken when he aims at a talkative woman whose mouth almost never stays still, saying:

> *Grammarians yield, rhetoricians are defeated, the whole*
> *crowd is silent; neither the lawyer nor the herald may speak,*
> *nor any other woman; such a force of words falls.*
> *You would say so many basins and bells*
> *were being struck at once; now let no one tire the trumpets or brass,*
> *she alone can come to the aid of the laboring moon.* <note>Original Latin: "Cedunt Grammatici, vincuntur rhetores... Una laboranti poterit succurrere lunae." In antiquity, people made loud noises with brass to "help" the moon during an eclipse.</note>

Thus Master Gargon translates this in the translation of Adolf Lampe, *12th Exercise on Psalm 45*:

> *The linguists fall silent, along with all the orators,*
> *The lawyer is hushed, the loudest criers give way.*
> *No other woman is here, no chatterer is missed,*
> *No basin or bell can match that cackling mouth.*
> *Stop the beating of drums and the blowing of trumpets,*
> *She alone helps the Moon when it has fainted away.*

And so we can conclude how much "useful Roman-ness" there is in the Roman Masses and speeches to the people in unknown languages.

I am willing to think that these cymbals, like other musical instruments in the Tabernacle and Temple, were intended for the glorification of God, and that harmony was made upon the temple heights to the sound of David’s songs on strings; but I would also think that the Lord intended to compensate for and sweeten the harshness and costliness of that legalistic worship, and to show that the gloom and melancholy of His service should be far removed.

And since everything in the Mosaic religion was shadowy and exemplary, why should one not think that such things prefigured the joyful sound at the time when the Gospel of the fulfillment and triumph of Christ would be preached throughout the whole world? In that most pleasant time and day of salvation, when everyone would recognize the sound. *Psalm 89:15* <note>The OCR cites verse 16, following some Dutch numbering conventions</note>.

Lampe, in *Psalm 45, part 1, page 109*, etc., has the following: for although Paul in 1 Corinthians 13:1 uses the image of the Cymbal in a negative sense, nevertheless that explanation provides a certain ground to establish the meaning of the secret sense in the temple service. For it appears from the context that those who received many extraordinary gifts in the early Christian church to promote the course of the Gospel are being addressed, though they misused them because they did not have the true sanctification of the heart. Thus, having entirely wrong intentions—seeking not God's honor and the conversion of souls, but their own fame among men—it is clear from church histories that those uncommon gifts of the early church were not always paired with true conversion of the heart, and that Christianity had to struggle with such people early on, etc.

Let us now, from the Apostle's allusion, leave out and set aside that which is of bad omen and serves his specific purpose; then we shall find, under his guidance, that the cymbals in the Levite worship very aptly prefigured in the church of the New Testament those who, with extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit...

graced, have spread the sound of the Gospel far and wide throughout the whole world.

<margin>Pleasant sound of the cymbals.</margin>
The comparison of the symbol also shines through clearly when one considers not only: 1. that the shape of the cymbals was round like the earth, but also 2. that the sound was sharp, penetrating, and far more pleasant than that of drums, etc.

So too has the preaching of the Gospel doctrine, presented by men of exceptional heavenly gifts, a special power to stir the whole world to attention and to the contemplation of such great wonders, and to prepare souls through its novelty and unheard-of truth to receive the Gospel. 3. And since the singing in the temple began with the cymbal players, these may have represented those who, endowed with special gifts of grace, are choir leaders and precursors in the New Testament.

And if one allows that the *schoshamina* <note>original: *schoshamina*, a musical term often found in the Psalms, likely referring to an instrument or a melody</note> are cymbals, then the chief musician "over-schoshamini" must be an example of the Apostolic men and Teachers of the church. These men excel through heavenly gifts and spiritual foresight, ensuring that the gifts shared with others are devoted to God's honor and the edification of the congregation; for the spirit of the prophecies was subject to the Prophets (1 Corinthians 14:32). To such Teachers, the title of honor <term>menatzechim</term> <note>Hebrew: מנצחים, meaning "Chief Musicians" or "Overseers"</note> is preeminently suited. This means they are not only leaders but also zealots who prudently, wisely, and industriously urge and advance the work of the Lord, which is one of the most perfect virtues by which Teachers in God’s congregation must shine.

Meanwhile, all of this is also an example of that joy and singing that shall be heard in the heavenly temple above, just as it could be applied to many instances of the church’s victories and triumphs.

However, I shall stop here and leave further matter for reflection to the consideration of the learned and the godly.

### CYPRESS, <note>Hebrew: *kopher* / *beroth* / *gopher*</note>, *Cupressus* <note>Latin</note>, Κυπάρισσος <note>Greek</note>.

<margin>Origin of the name.</margin>
Regarding the Hebrew names appearing here, the learned have not produced a unanimous testimony concerning their meanings.

<margin>Gopher, a word of obscure meaning.</margin>
As for "Gopher"—Genesis 6:14, *make yourself an ark of gopher wood*—it has become clear to me that there is still no full agreement on defining which tree and wood should be understood here. Drusius, in his commentary on Sulpitius Severus, says that *Gopher* is an obscure word, and all the more obscure because it appears only once in the Bible. Some consider it to be a pine tree. Others a fir tree. The Chaldean, Aben Ezra, Kimchi, the Rabbi, Buxtorf, and others hold it to be a type of cedar wood. Augustine, Ambrose, and Munster take it for a pine tree. Others for a cypress tree or a kind of cypress; cypress wood is light in substance, floating very well on the water, yet incorruptible.

<margin>Also Borith.</margin>
Regarding *Borith* <note>Hebrew: *berothim*</note>, there is likewise much disagreement, and it has not yet been proven what kind of tree etc. should be understood by it. Song of Solomon 1:17: *The beams of our houses are cedars, our galleries are cypresses.* Some identify it as a type of pine, fir, cedar, or ash; a name, some say, which is common to various kinds and species, because several trees growing in the wild have a great resemblance to one another.

Regarding the word *Copher*, one reads in Song of Solomon 1:14: *My beloved is to me a cluster of cypress <note>often translated as henna</note> in the vineyards of En-Gedi.* And 4:13: *Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with noble fruits, cypress with nard.*

In Genesis 6:14, the ark had to be "pitched" <note>Dutch: *bepekken*</note> inside and out, as if with a covering or a garment, so that the water would not penetrate into the ark. Thus <term>copher</term> <note>Hebrew: כפר</note> is a means of covering or a garment. How this signified a "price of atonement" or "praise," as it can be viewed as a cover or lid, is clearly shown by the great Cocceius in his Lexicon under the word *Copher*.

However, the same word also signifies a type of tree that bears clusters that are fragrant and spicy.

Yet one might almost think that in 1 Kings 4:13, "cypress" joined with "nard" should be understood as a kind of fragrant and sweet-smelling rush, <term>juncus odoratus</term> <note>Latin: "sweet rush" or camels-hay</note>. See Pliny, Dioscorides, Lobel, etc.

Having said this regarding these three names, I shall report what I have found regarding the cypress or cypress tree itself.

<margin>Description of this tree.</margin>
Pliny, in his 16th book, chapter 33, says: "It is a tree that grows slowly, produces fruit abundantly, has a bitter leaf, bears harsh and sour berries, has a strong scent, and its wood is thin, like that of a spruce." Bernard, in Sermon 46 on 1 Kings 1:17, says: "The cypress tree has a very good scent and is made of incorruptible wood." And Gregory of Nyssa, on the same passage, says: "The cypress tree smells pleasant by nature; it is not subject to decay or rot; it is a light wood, very suitable for use as timber, decorative work, galleries, and walkways."

Pliny and others testify of this tree that it stands exceptionally well, lives a very long time, and remains very youthful; it does not crack or split, is not subject to crumbling because of its bitterness, is not bitten by any worm, and grows toward the height.

> *Statius, Thebaid, book 6.*
>
> ->The cypress is unhurt by the winter cold.<-
>
> ->[Cypress of no cold offended.]<-

> *And Thebaid, book 4.*
>
> ->And for him alone, a cypress stands, stripped of its leaves,<-
> ->with a sharp point fixed to its tip.<-
>
> ->That is:<-
>
> *Beside him stood a cypress, of its leaves bereft,*
> *Which he could use, with iron at the base*
> *Fastened; none but he would dare to take it.*
> *That tree he used as a throwing-spear.*

Matthiolus, writing of this tree, says: "That one distinguishes between the male and the female varieties."

# CYPRESS.

...alike in stature; the male forms a pointed crown at the top, and the female spreads its branches upwards; both being tall and straight plants with a smooth stem, bearing branches towards the top; always green of leaf, longer than the oak or the seed-bearing Savin tree <note>The Savin tree, or *Juniperus sabina*, is a species of juniper known for its evergreen foliage</note>: yielding three times a year pointed and oblong fruits, resembling—as Matthias de l'Obel <note>A famous 16th-century Flemish physician and botanist whose Latin name was Lobelius</note> says—oak-knobs and galls, yet harder, firmer, thicker, and more compressed, in which small and fine seed is enclosed; the trunk allows a certain kind of resin to seep out, though not abundantly, strong in both scent and power, not unlike Terebinth <note>A resinous tree known as the turpentine tree</note>; the wood is firm, tight-grained, beautiful, and smells as lovely as sandalwood.

<margin>Origin of these trees.</margin>
Regarding the birthplace of these trees, I have found that they are attributed to Crete. Peter Martyr d'Anghiera <note>An Italian-born historian for Spain who documented the Age of Exploration</note>, in his *Babylonian Embassy*, book 11 (according to the excerpt by Fuller in *Miscellanea*, page 438), says: "The Cretans possess cypress forests to such an extent that from them they carve all beams, ceilings, and partitions for houses, as well as ships and vessels."

Diodorus testifies they are also found in Phoenicia, near Tripoli, Byblos, and Sidon; in Babylonia, Alexander the Great is said to have built his naval fleet from them, according to Arrian (Alex. book VII) and Strabo (book XVI). See also Adrianus Cocquius in *Philological-Physiological Observations and Exercises*, page 127.

<margin>What these trees were used for.</margin>
Regarding the uses of cypress trees, they are varied. It is known that because the wood was not subject to worms, wormholes, or further decay, it was used for writing tablets and small boards, as if to immortalize what was written upon them; a point perhaps observed by Martial in *Epigrams*, book V, 49.

> But born from living cypress,
> Which neither fears a hundred passed centuries,
> Nor the long decay of old age.
<note>original Latin: "Sed viva generata de cupresso, / Quae nec secula centies peracta, / Nec longe cariem timet senectae."</note>

-> That is: <-

> Grown from living cypress,
> Which preserves its form,
> Nor fears the wearing of the years.

<margin>The incorruptibility of this wood.</margin>
And in *Epigram* 37:
> With eternal cypress that shall never die.
<note>original Latin: "Perpetua nunquam moritura cupresso."</note>

-> That is: <-

> Never subject to death because of the cypress.

<margin>The folding doors of the temple at Ephesus made of Cypress wood.</margin>
Because of the incorruptibility of this wood, according to the testimony of Pliny in *On Plants*, book V, chapter 5, the folding doors of the temple at Ephesus—which lasted over four hundred years—were made from it.

<margin>Idols made of Cypress wood.</margin>
It is likely the same reason that encouraged idolatrous nations to make their idols from this and other indestructible wood. Pliny, book XVI, chapter 4; Livy, book VII; Isaiah 44:14.

Furthermore, it is for the same underlying reason that firm wooden chests, boxes, and coffins were made of this wood, to enclose and preserve writings, laws, historical records, and the bodies of the dead, etc.

I have noticed that this tree and its wood, because of its incorruptibility, constancy, and smooth, ever-green, and uniform appearance,

<column-break/>

has been taken as a symbol <note>The author uses the term "zinnebeelt," referring to an emblem or allegorical image</note> of someone's steadfastness and constancy of mind, standing firm in prosperity and adversity, and remaining consistent with oneself; it is quite a grand undertaking which Philotheus <note>A pseudonym for Karl Ludwig von der Pfalz in his work of religious emblems</note> presents in *Christian Symbols*, page 67. However, I shall include it here for its charm, singular meaning, and edification;
<margin>Symbol of resignation.</margin>

> Therefore, Kind God, you subject me again to your wrath,
> And a terrible punishment falls upon my trembling head.
> Ah, you inflict a great wound, you take away my joys,
> Even that which was dearer to me than my own eyes.
> Yet I shall endure, and in hard times, patience alone
> Shall bind me more strongly to you, O God.
> Live long, O Cypress. But a greater constancy
> Preserves me through late days after my losses.
> They show no signs of failing youth:
> So too, minds that care for heavenly things
> Preserve a perpetual and endless glory.
> Greedily devouring time consumes all, and destroys all:
> Whatever men possess, and whatever the world holds.
> Only the soul consecrated to God shall endure; it never
> Fears the envy of time, nor evil fates.
<note>original Latin poem translated above</note>

-> That is: <-

> You expose me once more, O God, to your anger,
> And place your punishment before me as you did before.
> You deal me a heavy wound with your arrow,
> You take from me that which was dearer than the light.
> I shall nevertheless endure everything with patience,
> In hope that my endurance might one day please you.
> Cypress, live long and bloom. Cypress, I envy you not.
> My tough patience preserves me long after my sorrow.
> Cypresses last long, and spread their scents.
> No approaching old age makes them mourn with sadness.
> So is the soul that always turns toward heaven.
> It has a luster and a beauty without end.
> The gluttonous age corrupts whatever has received life,
> Whatever man has here, whatever the world has embraced.
> The mind consecrated to heaven lasts forever,
> And fears neither injustice nor the plagues of envy.

One was also accustomed to see cypress trees at the houses of the rich and esteemed, and not so much at those of the lowly and impoverished: also that its wood and branches were employed when someone had died, as a sign of a deceased person there, and a token of deep mourning and funeral processions, etc. This is what this verse testifies:
<margin>used.</margin>

> And the cypress, witnessing no common griefs.
<note>original Latin: "Et non plebejos luctus testata cupressus."</note>

-> That is: <-

> Also the cypress tree, which bears testimony
> Of the death that has taken away no ordinary person.

Whether this happened merely for the sake of ceremony, or to show that the deceased would return to life as little as a cypress tree whose top has been cut off—to represent the common lot of mortality—or to guard against defilement, etc., I shall leave aside and not investigate further, but rather present something that should make us think of one or the other. Horace, *Odes*, book 2, ode 14.

> You must leave your land, and home, and pleasing
> Wife, nor shall any of these trees you tend
> Follow you, their short-lived master,
> Except the hated cypress.
<note>original Latin: "Linquenda tellus, & domus, & placens / Uxor, neque harum quas colis arborum / Te praeter invisas cupressum / Ulla brevem dominum sequetur."</note>

Furthermore, one may consult Lucan *Book* III *On the Civil War*, Alciat <note>Andrea Alciato, a famous Italian jurist and author of the first emblem book</note> with notes, Claude Minois pages 672-674, and Meurs in *Sacred Trees* page 48.

Causinus <note>Nicolas Caussin (1583–1651), a Jesuit famous for his works on symbols and emblems</note> presents the cypress tree as a teaching symbol of mortality for constant reflection, writing on page 481: The cypress tree is a funeral tree and belongs to the graves of the deceased. Furthermore, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist and author</note> says that it is subject neither to moths nor worms, and for this reason, statues were often made of such wood

<column-break/>

to preserve them as if for eternity. This he applies as follows:

> The memory of death brings down the moths and worms of sin which gnaw at the soul; it is therefore necessary that man, according to the lesson of Augustine, daily performing penance and contemplating perfection, should so conduct himself that he may be deemed worthy in the end to be free: to that end always mindful of the passing away, nor forgetting the day of judgment.

<margin>Harmfulness of sin.</margin>
The fact that the cypress tree, as is told, cannot endure filth, and that stinking manure causes it to wither, can serve as a teaching symbol: that the filth of sins—the foul and fleshly lustfulness that stinks before God and the pious—certainly cannot provide good nourishment to the godly; therefore they hate rotten, evil, and stinking words, arguments, foolish chatter, and mockery: and further, everything that, being tainted by the flesh, might ignite them. 2 *Peter* 2; *Jude verse* 23; *Colossians* 4:6; *Ephesians* 4:29, etc.

<margin>Instruction for parents and authorities.</margin>
When it is noted in the Cypresses that they extend their branches equally on all sides, and therefore spread an equal amount of sap for nourishment everywhere, this has been brought forward as a teaching and symbolic image: that parents and authorities must treat their children and subjects equally. It is fitting for neither princes nor monarchs to give more ear to flatterers, courtly "pan-lickers" <note>A term for sycophants or freeloaders</note>, and such people than to others, since they are generally the pests of the human race. See Claude Minois on *Alciat page* 462; *Camerarius Emblems* 15, *Century* 1.

As I would now undertake to open some places in the Bible where the cypress is mentioned, it would bring me great peace of mind if I knew what the proper meaning of the Hebrew words was, and if I had not noticed such a marked difference in the views of the learned. Now everything appears quite obscure to me, and it falls even harder upon me to bring out the explanation properly.

*Song of Solomon* 1:14 has *kopher* <note>original: כפר, likely referring to henna or cypress</note>, and verse 17 has *beroth* <note>original: ברות, likely cypress or fir</note>. See above regarding the meaning of these words.

A cluster <note>Dutch: *troffe*</note> consists of many grapes or berries on a stalk, joined together by various small branches and sprouts, through which they draw their sap for nourishment.

A cypress cluster is counted among the noble fruits produced in clusters, or among the fragrant spices that seep from fragrant trees; whether such clusters might grow atop the sprouted stem of the cypress plant or cypress tree.

Yet it must indeed be wood if one is to make galleries from it, *Song of Solomon* 1:17, unless one posits that there is more than one kind, and if that is so, the use can also be varied.

<margin>Engedi.</margin>
Engedi is held to have been a city and region not far from the Dead Sea, in the inheritance of Judah, *Joshua* 15:62. According to calculations, it was located three hundred stadia from Jerusalem, situated between two cliffs; it was a very precious region, wonderfully fertile, planted with exquisite trees, whether palm trees, vineyards, balsam trees, etc. Rabbi Jarchi relates that the trees there bear fruit four or five times a year. See *Lightfoot, Chorographical Century, page* 174.

Some believe that fragrant and cluster-bearing cypresses may have been transported from Cyprus to Engedi and planted there, or one must assume a Cyprus...

# CYPRESS, CITHER.

...wanting to be understood as a Prussian grapevine <note>original: "pruswynstok"</note>; yet what wood from that might be suitable for making galleries <note>Likely referring to pergolas or covered walkways in a garden.</note>, I do not yet understand: unless it were to be used for covering and shading the galleries, as it has beautiful grapes and large clusters.

<margin>Christ's blood is the ransom of mankind.</margin>
In *Song of Solomon 1:14*, the word כפר <note>original: "kopher"</note> is used, meaning ransom and atonement money—a metaphorical naming of something that covers, overspreads, or acts as a veil or means of concealment, as *Cocceius* says in his *Lexicon* on that word. For just as a covering hides or covers that which is displeasing in a subject, or as the letters by which a debt is recorded are painted over and hidden, so too by a price is the debt or crime removed, so that it is no longer noticed by men and no longer appears before God's sight. God’s ransom is not something perishable, but only the blood of Christ, through which the righteous judge and holy God could be justified and sanctified, as he forgives sin and grants the right to life (*Romans 3:25, 26; Isaiah 5:16 and 1:27; Romans 8:3*). This bloody sacrifice alone is well-pleasing to Him, and a sweet fragrance (*Ephesians 5:2; Psalm 40; Hebrews 10*).

And in this way *Durham, Oldenburg*, and others who have written on the Song of Solomon have attributed it to Christ's blood and his price of reconciliation and redemption. *Oldenburg* may be consulted on this. And here it appears that Abbot *Willeramus* already preceded him:

> *He is like the cluster of grapes produced by the Cyprian vine,* <note>original: "Hic Botro similis quem profert Cypria vitis,"</note>
> *standing out in the vineyards of En-Gedi with heavy fruit.* <note>original: "Prominet Engaddi vinetis ubere gravi."</note>
> *He who had troubled me with his death for a brief hour,* <note>original: "Qui me morte suâ modica turbaverat hora,"</note>
> *let him be a sweet-smelling wine to me, rising from death.* <note>original: "Suave mihi redolens sit vinum morte resurgens."</note>
> *Whose sweet scent, more pleasant than balsam,* <note>original: "Cujus odor dulcis, & plus quam balsama suavis,"</note>
> *gladdens the pious and cleanses even the wicked.* <note>original: "Laetificatque pios, sed & ipsos mundat iniquos."</note>

->That is:<-

->*This hangs, like a cluster of Cyprus, bravely on display,*<-
->*And adorns the vineyard foliage at En-Gedi like a crown.*<-
->*He unsettled me for a time when He had died,*<-
->*But refreshed me again when He had regained life,*<-
->*Like a sweet wine which, through its power and virtue,*<-
->*Purifies the wicked and gladdens the pious folk.*<-

The scent of which must be fragrant and powerful, and no less pleasant, considering that even the Preachers become sweet-smelling from it, and pleasant upon the mountains (*2 Corinthians 2:15, 16; Isaiah 52:7*).

As for the galleries of cypresses, see under GALLERY. Also *Groenewegen, Oldenburg, Durham*, etc.

Since there is such uncertainty regarding the meaning of the root word, I shall not attempt a broad metaphorical interpretation until I have found firmer ground, and therefore I leave the subject.

### CITHER, כנור ,קתרוס <note>Hebrew: Kinnor; Aramaic: Qathros.</note>
### Chaldean: Cithara; Greek: κιθάρα <note>original: kithára</note>.

**T**his musical instrument appears many times in the sacred scrolls. I find that the *LXX* <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translators, *Luther*, and our own translators have rendered the word כנור <note>Kinnor</note> as *harp*; and it seems to me

<column-break/>

as if they found little distinction between the CITHER, harp, psaltery, etc.

I have found that *Mersennus* <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French polymath who wrote extensively on music theory.</note> in his work on *Genesis* has given us the depiction of CITHERS, both modern and ancient, on page 1527. However, these differ significantly from the form and shape in which *Jerome* <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> and others present them to us—namely, like a Delta Δ, with 24 strings stretched across; and as far as the number of strings is concerned, whether made of brass wire, sinew, etc., *Mersennus* is inclined to agree.

Nevertheless, this author says that one cannot know for certain what fashion, shape, or make it was, seeing as they have not been seen (page 1518; *Jerome, volume IX, epistle 28*).

*Josephus* (*Antiquities, Book VII, chapters 10 and 12*) and other Jewish masters, as *Mersennus* (page 1704, etc.) and *Picus Mirandula* in his *On the Kabbalah* wish to show, maintain that it was an instrument with ten strings, corresponding to the *Sephiroth* <note>In Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah), the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> or ten Virtues, or emanations of God and His throne, and ten different representations of the celestial signs which were marked on David's cither; and that upon the stirring, pressing, or striking of a particular string, he had in mind and brought forth a specific emanation and celestial sign for the healing of King Saul, who was tormented by an evil and restless spirit. See on this, and Saul's healing, *Mersennus* pages 1704–1708, etc. That the art of singing and playing has wonderful effects on the passions of the soul can be seen in *Lampe* on *Psalm 45, part 1, page 71*, etc., and page 103.

<margin>Obscurity regarding the shape of the Cither.</margin>
What kind of instrument it was, with how many strings stretched across, etc., seems to me to have sunk into a pit of ignorance due to its antiquity; and I believe that whatever shape one might attribute to it, it is uncertain to say, "The shape of the ancient Cither was thus or so."

I see indeed that *Pfeifferus* in *Difficulties of the Sacred Scriptures* <note>original: "Dubiis Vex. scr."</note> presents it in the shape of a Delta Δ with fourteen strings stretched across; but whether he has hit upon the true form, I would not dare to say; at the very least, it does not quietly agree with the string counts of *Jerome, Mersennus*, or that of the Jews.

But this seems more likely: that it was an instrument of lovely tone, capable of moving the soul, soothing the brain, stirring joy, calming the mind, and providing lovely relaxation. Indeed, the fact is that this lovely instrument seems to have been used in times of joy and cheerfulness in worship, at festive meals, and in general public rejoicing for victories won or other deeds (*Genesis 31:27; 1 Samuel 10:5; 1 Samuel 16:23; 2 Samuel 6:5; Psalms 33:2, 92:1, 2, 98, 110, and 150; 1 Corinthians 14:7; Revelation 5:8, 14, 15, and 18*).

<margin>The silence of the Cithers is a sign of mourning.</margin>
And when, among other instruments, this one stops, it is considered a sign of adversity, sadness, defeat, and ruin (*Isaiah 24:7; Ezekiel 26:13; Revelation 18:22*).

Thus one reads in *Psalm 137* of hanging the cithers upon the willows. Whether this should be taken literally as a historical event, I doubt very much; for these were of little use to the sorrowful and the captives. They did not have the festivals and holy days; therefore they were as if hung up and without use. Sadness had the upper hand. And it was with them as with those of old who, when departing from somewhere, dedicated the same to some deity or hung up their weapons. See *Ursinus, Analecta, part I, pages 36, 37*.
