# CITHER.

<margin>
The Cither was used by the Greeks in times of sadness.
</margin>
What might cause some difference in its use here is what Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> relates in *Phaleg, page 908*, stating that the Greeks played the cither during times of sorrow.

<margin>
Highly esteemed since antiquity.
</margin>
It is clear enough that from ancient times there were great lovers of the cither and its sound, blended with the human voice; for Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A Renaissance scholar known for his work *Genialium dierum* (Genial Days)</note> notes regarding Nero, the Roman Emperor, that at the end of his banquets, he would summon the most prominent cither players. Suetonius, in his *Life of Nero*, chapter 12, relates that *Nero was so obsessed with the cither that he worshipped the instrument when it was brought to him by the judges.*

The harp and cither must have been held in quite high regard as symbols of song and musical art, since Mercury gave a cither to Apollo, the God of the Sciences.

<margin>
Symbol of wisdom.
</margin>
It seems the Pagans regarded the cither as a portrait of a wise man. Aristophanes describes a wise man as one who understands the playing of the cither.

<margin>
Nero's passion for cither playing.
</margin>
Nero must have been an immense lover of cither playing, as he is depicted on some coins as a cither player, according to Alexander ab Alexandro, *book iv, chapter 4.* Certainly, those who understood cither playing must have been held in great esteem in ancient times. So relates Cicero in *Tusculan Disputations, book 1.*

The Greeks placed the greatest learning in the exercise of voice and strings. Therefore Epaminondas, the most prominent man of all Greece in my judgment, is said to have been very skillfully practiced in stringed instruments. And Themistocles, some years earlier, was considered unlearned when he refused a lyre to play. Indeed, that art was so highly regarded that a statue of honor was erected in the Greek games for one who triumphed in this skill. See Xiphilinus in the *Life of Nero*, Julius Caesar, and Bulenger, *On the Theater, book 11, chapter 25.*

In order not to collect everything concerning the *kinnor* <note>The Hebrew term for the lyre or harp</note> or the cither—which is often used in a mystical sense in *Psalm 81:3, 92:4, 98:5, 108:3, 149:3, and 150:3*—I shall further say that in most of those Psalms, the events and blessings of the New Testament are recounted. It is indisputable that the cither was lovely, sweet-sounding, and wonderfully soothing; and who can reasonably object to my thought that it may metaphorically represent that part of the Divine Evangelical Scripture which shows us God's name and virtues with the greatest emphasis in the work of grace and salvation, and the praise and revelation thereof in the midst of His congregation? One should consider whether this emphasis does not also lie in the "cither of God" in *Revelation 15:2*. And for what purpose did the Messiah and David use the cither, etc., if not to attribute to the Father the praise of His name and deeds? See *Psalms 49:52, 71:22, 43:4, 18:50, 40:4, and 69:31.*

Would the Hebrews have spread the glory of their God any less than the Pagans, who honored their gods through cither, harp, and lyre? See Reland and Muller, and Virgil in the 1st book of the *Aeneid*:

> *Cithara crinitus Iopas*
> *Personat aurata docuit quae maximus Atlas.*
> *Hic canit errantem lunam solisque labores:*
<note>original Latin: "Long-haired Iopas makes the hall resound with his golden cither, which greatest Atlas taught. He sings of the wandering moon and the labors of the sun."</note>

That is, according to Vondel’s <note>Joost van den Vondel (1587–1679), the preeminent Dutch poet and playwright</note> translation:
> Iopas touches the strings:
> That singer, long of hair, plays all that the experienced
> And courageous Atlas taught. He sings the moon's course.
> He sings of the sun’s eclipse—

<column-break/>

It is certain that in ancient times much importance was attached to the decoration of cithers, whether they were heavily gilded or made entirely of gold. We also read of cedar and ebony wood being used for cithers. Homer mentions golden cithers.

Let this be said of cither playing: it provided the euphony and sweetness of harmony created by the movement of the strings, which strings are held to have been ten in number, according to Josephus.

<margin>
Metaphorical application.
</margin>
The soul that is to praise God rightly must possess the instrument of faith and precious godliness. In all that the Lord's word mentions of God—His virtues, His counsel, and His works—there is revealed a perfect harmony. This must also be found among godly men in the utmost concord and with the sweetest agreement, *1 Corinthians 12:14, Ephesians 4:3-16*, even though one may surpass others by more than one tone according to the degrees and levels of the gifts he has received; for one possesses more talents than another. *Luke 19.* I pass over allegorizing on the occasion of the ten strings as the ten living words <note>The Ten Commandments</note>; nor do I play further upon the number ten, nor upon the fragility of the strings, nor upon other things which could provide sweet thoughts and allusions. Whoever has the desire may read the work of the learned Lampe <note>Friedrich Adolph Lampe (1683–1729), a German pietist theologian</note> on the 45th Psalm; and if he is studious and godly, no regret shall seize him.

It is true that Horace, in *book 1, ode 15*, calls the cither *imbellem* <note>Latin: "unwarlike" or "peaceful"</note>, as there is nothing masculine in it; it is suited to soothe and please the feminine senses but not the masculine ones, and thus it was not used in war, as he sings:

> *Grataque foeminis*
> *Imbelli cithara carmina divides.*
<note>original Latin: "And you shall share songs pleasing to women on your unwarlike cither."</note>

That is:
> You shall on your timid lyre
> Play melodies for the women,
> And wail out songs of love.

Therefore, this instrument served more for sweet, pleasant, and joyful occasions than for the extolling of heroic deeds. Likewise, Horace calls his songs Lyric songs or Cither songs for this reason, as they differ from the Epic Poem, through which dignified deeds of war are spread and blown into the ears of all the world as if by a trumpet. The same Venusian poet <note>A reference to Horace, who was born in Venusia</note>,

> Whose lyre, if you dare to reach for the crown,
> You challenge, like Pan, Apollo’s highest throne,
> And receive in the end your well-deserved reward
> Of Midas's ears; <note>Refers to the myth where King Midas was given donkey ears for judging Pan's music better than Apollo's</note>

The same Venusian poet, I say, warbles thus:

> *Nolis longa ferae bella Numantiae,*
> *Nec dirum Hannibalem, nec Siculum mare*
> *Paeno purpureum sanguine, mollibus*
> *Aptari citharae modis.*
<note>original Latin: "You would not wish the long wars of fierce Numantia, nor dreadful Hannibal, nor the Sicilian sea purple with Punic blood, to be set to the soft measures of the cither."</note>

That is:
> To play the Numantine war upon the lyre,
> Or proud Hannibal who glows with the fire of war,
> Or the Sicilian sea, swollen with Punic blood,
> Has neither fitness nor grace.

Also, Clement of Alexandria, in *The Instructor, book 4*, does not count the cither among the instruments of war, although Alexander ab Alexandro, in *Genialium dierum, page 178*, mentions that the Cretans among

# CITHER.

...others have carried it with them into war: and **Erasmus** <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the famous Dutch humanist</note> in his *Adages* under the entry for *The Sun* <note>original: "Sol"</note>, page 987, also brings up the contrary view, arguing that it can strongly stir the mind to bravery and other passions, depending on how it is played.

I have recounted that at the end of banquets, cither players were summoned. They would play there in praise of the Gods and heroes. **Virgil** <note>The Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro</note> has an example of this at the end of the first book <note>of the *Aeneid*</note>, which we have already mentioned. Also **Silius** <note>Silius Italicus, author of the epic *Punica*</note> in book 11.

At Delos, cither players were allowed to compete for the palm wreath, says **Alexander ab Alexandro** <note>A Renaissance scholar</note> on page 262.

Cither players were dressed in long, hanging robes to best represent Apollo. See **Hofmann’s** *Universal Lexicon*. <note>Johann Jacob Hofmann’s massive 17th-century encyclopedia</note>

Regarding the magnificence of **Ptolemy**, **Paschalius** testifies in *On Crowns* <note>original: "de Coronis"</note>, page 120, that gilded cithers and garlanded cither players were found there; the cithers were made of cedar wood, ebony, or wood brought from India, as in *1 Kings 10:11*. Golden cithers are mentioned in *Revelation 5:8*. See **Sperling**, cited by **Adolf Lampe** <note>Friedrich Adolph Lampe (1683–1729), a prominent German pietist theologian</note> in his work on *Psalm 45*, page 94.

It even appears that from ancient times, by praising the cither, people sought to exalt the art of music to the heavens, as **Dieterich** <note>Conrad Dieterich (1575–1639)</note> noted in *Antiquities of the Old Testament* <note>original: "Antiq. V. T."</note>, page 352, concerning **Pindar** in his *First Hymn*.

To now proceed toward my purpose and plan, I need only remind the reader that in various Psalms of David the cither is introduced when speaking of God's fame, praise, and the exaltation of His virtues and mighty deeds, and when mankind is urged to observe these things rightly. *Psalms 33:2, 92:4, 98, and 150.*

**Paul** also gave an account of it in *1 Corinthians 14*, and **John** in the *Revelation, chapters 5:8, 14:1, 2, 15:1-18, and 18*, speaks of these musical instruments.

<margin>Instruments useful for the glorification of God.</margin>
It is generally certain that through the playing of instruments, if the heart is truly involved, one has a good and holy purpose and can glorify God.

But I also believe that in many instances musical instruments are named where they serve as nothing other than signs and holy symbols <note>original: "zinnebeelden"</note> of something else, as in *Revelation 5, 14, 15, and 18*, etc.

Namely, they represent speeches of praise, thanksgivings, songs of joy, holy ecstasies, and raptures, to the glory and acknowledgment of God's virtues and deeds.

<margin>Transference of the instruments.</margin>
I must admit that I find the observation of **Johannes Draconites** <note>A 16th-century German reformer and colleague of Luther</note> (cited by **Dieterich** in *Antiquities of the Old Testament*, page 351) to be quite clever. He transfers the meaning of musical instruments not only to the Gospel but also to the Apostles, Evangelists, Pastors, and Teachers, who brought forth one and the same truth, yet in different ways and tones.

Would one then compare the Gospel—here soft, sweet, and lovely; there sharp, stern, and strongly striking—to various instruments? So be it. The Pastors and Teachers shall be the players: meanwhile, they are wise and happy if they understand the art of playing and strike the tone according to the subjects they must handle.

If one wishes to think that the Gospel, for the conversion of the sinner, sometimes terrifies like thunder, wakes one up like a trumpet, and like a cither lovely caresses and lifts up, calms, and refreshes the anxious and dejected heart—it shall have its own ingenuity and charm.

<column-break/>

If one wishes to allow this observation with **Mersenne** <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French polymath and "father of acoustics"</note> in his work on *Genesis, page 784*, I have nothing against it. *Just as music,* he says, *has its silences, hushing, and rests, which it allows so that the other parts may be heard all the more clearly and the entire melody may come to light more elegantly;*

> *so the Lord allows the fall of some, so that the virtues of the pious might shine all the more beautifully; for the harmony of the pious and the sounding out of their virtues seems to strike through more pleasantly amidst the silence of sinners; and to what end is this? So that we might steer the cither of our soul after the divine example; whose strings—I mean the passions—the hand of prudence should guide according to reason, so that the passions being restrained by the virtue of prudence and arranged according to God's law and will, we might sing the song of the new life to our God.*

In the meantime, if one wishes to distinguish the instruments, thinking that in the Church of God one has spoken, played, or sung in a sharper, harder, or softer and more lovely way according to how the times passed and what spiritual profit was seen therein, I have no objection. Then **Henricus Groenewegen** <note>A Dutch theologian known for his commentaries on Revelation</note> in his *Apocalypse*, page 673, may not have been wrong to place the cither-playing in the time of the Waldensians <note>A medieval Christian movement often seen by later Protestants as precursors to the Reformation</note> within the rank and order of the times and the naming of instruments. One may read him for oneself.

If one wishes to interpret the ceasing of the instruments in *Revelation 18:11* in "Spiritual Babylon" <note>A term often used by Protestant authors to refer to the Roman Catholic Church</note> as a proof of sadness and great mourning over its decline—as also seen elsewhere in *Isaiah 24* and *Ezekiel 26*, etc.—it will not be a mistake. And when one remembers that Spiritual Babylon has all sorts of instruments in its idolatrous worship, Masses, Festivals, etc., it follows naturally that in its fall and destruction, such wicked uses—meant to stroke and entice the people and bind them firmly to itself—will be heard no more.

<margin>Observations of Adolf Lampe.</margin>
I shall with the utmost brevity bring together some sweet and learned observations on the cither from Professor **Adolf Lampe**, from his exercises on *Psalm 45* in the first volume.

Page 50. I confess beforehand to be of the opinion that not only all the temple authority of the Levites, but also all string, flute, and musical instruments were symbols <note>original: "zinnebeelden"</note> that must have their fulfillment in the New Testament: because:

1. They are not presented according to the pleasure of men, but according to the pleasure and specific instruction of God, and commanded in the temple, being used by men driven by God's spirit, *2 Chronicles 29:25, 26, 27.* Therefore, belonging to the other symbolic things, they had to be abolished with the old service. *Amos 5:23.*

2. They are all the more symbolic and exemplary because passages occur which necessarily refer to the New Testament, such as *Psalms 68:26, 47:6, 98:2, 3, etc.*

3. And no one can deny that the singing and musical instruments outside of the service of God and sacrifice were symbolic and full of mysteries, as in *Exodus 15:20*, spiritually transferred to the joyful shouting of the church over the spiritual plagues of "Spiritual Egypt." *Revelation 15:2, 3.*

4. Of no less weight is that now and then, in that context, vocal harmony and musical instruments appear in the New Testament, *Luke 15:25, Colossians 3:16.* And what is clearer than that the cithers and cither players in *Revelation chapters 5:8, 14:2, and 15:2* and elsewhere refer to this? See **Braun** <note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708), a Dutch theologian and professor</note>.

Braun in *Selected Various Sacred Books, Volume II, chapters 3, 9, and 10.* <note>Johannes Braun (1628–1708) was a Dutch theologian and professor known for his works on Hebrew antiquities.</note>
d'Outrein in his treatise *On the Sound of the Gospel*, the 8th Oration. <note>Johannes d'Outrein (1662–1722) was a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note>

5. This was by no means unknown to the ancients, as is proven on page 57 from Ignatius, Augustine, Theodoret, Ambrose, etc.; see Lampe, pages 58, 59. <note>Friedrich Adolph Lampe (1683–1729), a prominent theologian mentioned on the previous page.</note>

6. Even the pagans, whether through natural instinct, a faint rumor of truth, or a wicked imitation of true religion (which seems characteristic of Satan), attributed something secret to singing and musical instruments: as his reverence <note>Referring to d'Outrein or Lampe</note> demonstrates extensively on page 60, etc.

At this point, his reverence continues on page 64, showing what these instruments represented: 1. as supplements to the **doctrine of salvation**, both in terms of its internal quality and content, and in relation to the outward duties that would be in practice according to the variety of places and times in which that doctrine was to be portrayed. This is especially true regarding the gracious gifts of the Holy Spirit, in which the holy messengers who were to proclaim this doctrine would excel, and finally, regarding the effects of that truth in the hearts of those who would be enticed and brought over to the spiritual worship of the New Testament.

On page 67, etc., the learned author shows the parallels between musical instruments and the Holy Gospel, which is demonstrated in 14 observations. After dealing with several specific instruments, he speaks on page 91, etc., of the **cither**: and says further: "But when I let my thoughts go more deeply into the secret meaning of the cither, which the Holy Spirit Himself points out, I find indeed that the Gospel doctrine must be represented by it, just as it is by other instruments. However, I believe that one may distinguish the cither from the others in this: that it primarily represents that part of the Gospel which demonstrates God's virtues and perfections in the work of grace, and the manner in which these must be praised in the congregation, and what fruit that praise would have in the New Testament." I am moved to this conclusion because in *Revelation 15:2*, these instruments are called, with special emphasis, the **cithers of God**, etc., and one almost everywhere finds God’s praise and glory joined to the cithers: *Revelation 5:8; Psalm 49:5, 71:22, 43:5,* and *57:9, 10*. This can be further clarified from the customs of the pagans, who used to report the praise of their gods and heroes with the cither, examples of which are seen on page 93, etc.

<margin>Lyre and lute on old coins.</margin>
For this reason, a lyre and lute are shown on some old coins of the Hebrews, representing God's glory and honor in religious worship. See Reland, Muller, and Conrad Dieterich Koch. <note>Hadrian Reland (1676–1718) was a famous Dutch Orientalist and cartographer.</note>

Subsequently, he brings forward various comparisons on page 44, beginning by presenting the matter.

<margin>Cithers of precious material.</margin>
1. The material of the cithers is entirely uncertain; it is certain, however, that it was precious. See what has been said above regarding this. 
   There is nothing more certain than that precious souls are required for God's praise and honor, decorated with the gold of faith and godliness.

<margin>Transfer.</margin>
2. It is certain that a variety of strings and harmony were characteristic of the cithers, and therefore they must hold the first place in secret significance; which he demonstrates from various writers regarding the whole instrument on page 94, etc., and on page 95, by **transfer** <note>Meaning the symbolic application or spiritual interpretation</note>, he says: "How much higher must the holy cithers lead us when we consider the subjects of which they consist!"

<column-break/>

If one pays attention to the content, it describes to us the truth of God’s ways and works, and the miraculous harmony of His virtues, decrees, and purposes. If one looks at the subjects, one finds men of various spiritual gifts, places, and times, who were nevertheless driven by one Spirit to proclaim the great miraculous works in unison. *1 Corinthians 12:4-30; Ephesians 4:3-16.*

<margin>Number of strings as a symbol of perfection.</margin>
3. One may and must also think of the number of strings, which is made greater in some than in others; this can, not unpleasantly, represent the various degrees and ways of proclaiming God's virtues and perfections.

<margin>The number ten as a symbol of perfection.</margin>
A ten-stringed arrangement is most commonly recognized. The early teachers piously thought that the ten commandments of the law were represented by them, but that is a bit of a stretch. In general, the number ten is in itself a symbol of perfection because it contains all single numbers within it. Nothing prevents us from understanding by this the perfection of God's honor and praise, which must take place in the worship under the New Testament. This perfection of God's praise relates to: **a.** The subject of glory, which includes all God’s virtues as they shine through the great work of grace, which among the ancient Jews were contained in the **ten sephiroth**. <note><term>Sephiroth</term>: In Jewish Kabbalah, these are the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals Himself.</note> **b.** The manner, because the perfect measure of the gifts of grace, which God's Spirit distributes to His congregation, is represented by **ten pounds**. *Luke 19:13.* **c.** The time, because the true and spiritual Hallelujah is reserved for its fullness; and therefore the great Day of Atonement fell, if I am not mistaken, on the **tenth day** of Tishri. <note>The seventh month of the Hebrew calendar.</note> **d.** The place, because the fullness of the Gentiles, who shall sound out these hymns of praise, was often presented under the number ten. *Zechariah 8:21; Luke 19:13.*

4. The cither strings were touched with a plectrum or with fingers to give sound: so we also must be touched by the **finger of God** to proclaim His praise. *Psalm 51:17; Isaiah 6:7.*

5. The strings were struck or bowed; because they were made of fragile material—namely, sheep guts (*Homer, Odyssey 21*)—they would burst and break if they were stretched too tightly. So too do the proclaimers of the Lord's praise, though they strain all their powers of soul and body, carry that treasure in **earthen vessels**, and are consumed while they serve others. *2 Corinthians 4:7.*

6. The sound of the cithers was clear and pleasant, which is why a certain type was nicknamed *gnazavim* <note>original: "ענגים" (anagim)</note>, meaning **delights**. For this reason, the sweetest comforts of human life are expressed with that word. *Ecclesiastes 11:8.* And these instruments were used on the most joyful occasions, especially at banquets. *Plutarch, Symposiacs 7, chapter 8.* But nothing can be more pleasant to hallowed souls than to know God's virtues, who has made Himself known as a Covenant God, and to delight in the proclamation of His praise. *Psalm 104:33.*

7. Cither playing required a special and greater skill than any other instrument, which is why those who excelled in it were held in high esteem. See what was cited above from Cicero. But of incomparably greater value is the proclamation of God's praise in His congregation. No one can learn this except he who is taught by the Holy Spirit and shares in His gifts.

# CITHER.

<margin>
The silence of the cither is a prelude to sadness.
</margin>

9. Regarding its use, it corresponded with its sound, so that the cither was never used except during the most joyful occasions. The ceasing of the cither and harp was a prelude to overwhelming sadness, as seen in *Isaiah 24:8, Ezekiel 16:13, Psalm 137:2, and Job 30:21*. See also *Bochart in Canaan* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a French Protestant biblical scholar; "Canaan" refers to his work *Geographia Sacra*.</note>, part 1, book 11, chapter 7. Nothing stirs the spiritual joy of believers more than the proclamation of God's praise; that is truly being joyful in the Lord.

<margin>
Special use of David's cither.
</margin>

10. But before we depart from this, we must mention a special use of David's cither or harp—namely, how the evil spirit of Saul was restrained by its sound (*1 Samuel 16:14, 16, 23*). It was previously stated <note>Referring to page 103 of the source author's work.</note> that the art of singing generally has the power to calm rising passions; see page 103 for some examples. Likewise, the proclamation of God's name often has the power to still the rage of the church's enemies, especially in those centuries following the "ten days of tribulation" <note>A reference to the ten periods of Roman persecution of the early church.</note>, which mostly correspond to the reigns of Saul and David.

<margin>
The esteem of the cither.
</margin>

11. Finally, the cither was esteemed above all other instruments. *Philo, in "On the Creation of the World" <note>original Latin: "De Opificio Mundi"</note>, page 28, says that the cither is almost the leader of all stringed instruments.* Thus, the primary occupation of men of God is the proclamation of God's virtues. For through this, they are like the angels and have fellowship with the triumphant church above, even while they are still on earth.

Following this, I include what Professor Campegius Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian and professor at Franeker.</note> has written regarding the cither and cither players.

*Revelation 5:8.* John saw that each of the elders had a cither in their left hand and a censer in their right, not playing and offering incense at the same time (for the cither requires both hands to play), but playing after the incense had been brought to the altar, just as occurred in the Temple. When the priest had lit the incense and the sacrificial portions were laid upon the altar of burnt offering, and the priest was busy sacrificing, then the signal was given to the players, upon which everyone began their work. See *Liturgy of the Codex Taanit <note>A tractate of the Mishnah regarding fasts.</note>, chapter 7, section 3.* However, it is no new thing here that the priests, who were to prepare the incense, handled the cithers (for in the Temple services this was commanded of the Levites; see *Maimonides, Laws of the Temple Vessels <note>original Latin: "Maimonides, Hilchot Kele HaMikdash"</note>, chapter 3*) and men of distinguished descent in Israel (*1 Chronicles 25:1, 2 Chronicles 20:19, Nehemiah 12:19*). The priests handled only the trumpets or rams' horns.

<column-break/>

It pleased the Lord that those duties divided in the Temple between the priests and Levites should be joined together in the elders of the New Testament; for their task is to lead the congregation in prayer and in spreading the virtues of their God and Savior. Prayer and thanksgiving are represented by the bowls <note>The original Dutch uses "violen," which can mean violins, but here refers to the "vials" or shallow bowls of incense described in Revelation.</note> of incense (*Psalm 141:2, Malachi 1:11*). Just as burning incense spreads a pleasant fragrance that delights us, so too the prayers which the saints pour out to God, and all the acts of rational worship which they <margin>Application.</margin> present to Him, are praised as pleasing to Him and judged as good by His decree. However, He does not desire such things from everyone without distinction, nor in every manner, but rather that it be done by priests washed in and with the blood of Jesus, and adorned with the garment of the "new man," who have obtained the right of access to the throne of grace through Christ. Therefore, they bring the incense of their worship to God in golden bowls—that is, in and with pure and clean souls, imbued with true concepts regarding religion and provided with the firm faith through which they take hold of Christ's precious obedience. See the section on INCENSE.

The true priests in the New Testament do not approach God only with prayers and thanksgivings, but they also report and boast of His virtues and majesty. Also, the cithers are symbolic means of the soul's disposition and readiness to be able to report God's praise, according to how they are distinctly moved by the Spirit. It is the teachers and leaders who, in the public gatherings of the believers, lay open before God the desires, wishes, prayers, and thanksgivings.

If one looks for these cither players, history will show you men of distinguished merit who ought to be mentioned with esteem: such as John Wycliffe in England, along with the learned men among the clergy in England and the University of Oxford who stood with him; in Bohemia, Jan Hus, who followed in Wycliffe’s footsteps; and subsequently those who followed his example, Jerome of Prague, Matthew of Paris, Jacob of Mies, etc. See *Vitringa on the Apocalypse, pages 643–644*, etc.

*Revelation 15:1, 2.* Such people appeared to John holding cithers: holy confessors, fit for the reporting of the Lord's praise and dedicated to God, representing persons who possessed the ability to spread God's praise with an appropriate manner of song, and to aptly demonstrate the doctrine of the Gospel for the delight and comfort of others.

When the priest had lit the incense, and the sacrificial portions were placed upon the altar of burnt offering, and the priest was busy with the offering, then the signal was given to the musicians, upon which each began their work. *See Liturgy of the Code Ta'anit, chapter 7, section 3 <note>original: "Liturgia codic. Thanith c. 7. §. 3." A tractate of the Mishnah.</note>.* Yet it is no new thing here that the priests, who were to prepare the incense, handled the citterns (for in the temple services, such was commanded to the Levites, see *Maimonides, Laws of the Vessels of the Sanctuary, chapter 3 <note>original: "Maim., Hilcoth, Kele, Hammikdaich kap. 3."</note>* and to men of noble descent in Israel, *1 Chronicles 25:1, 2 Chronicles 20:19, Nehemiah 12:19.*) The priests alone handled the trumpets.

<column-break/>

It pleased the Lord that what was divided between the priests and Levites in the temple should be joined together in the elders of the New Testament; for their task is to lead the congregation in prayer and in spreading the virtues of their God and Savior. For praying and giving thanks are represented by the vials with incense, *Psalm 141:2, Malachi 1:11.* For just as ignited incense spreads a pleasant fragrance that delights us, so also the prayers which the saints pour out to God, and all the acts of rational worship which they present to God, are praised as pleasing to Him and judged as good by His decree. However, He does not desire such from everyone without distinction, nor in every way: but that it be done by priests washed in and with the blood of Jesus, and adorned with the garment of the new man—those who in Christ have obtained the right of access to the throne of grace. These, therefore, bring the incense of their worship to God in golden vials; that is, in and with pure and clean souls, clothed with true concepts regarding religion, and provided with steadfast faith, through which they lay hold of Christ's precious obedience. See **INCENSE**.

<margin>Application.</margin>
The true priests in the New Testament do not approach God with prayers and thanksgivings alone: but they also report and boast of His virtues and majesty. Also, the citterns are symbolic means of the soul's disposition and readiness to proclaim God's praise, according as they are distinctly moved by the Spirit. It is the teachers and governors who, in the public assemblies of the faithful, lay open desires, wishes, prayers, and thanksgivings before God.

If one looks for these cittern-players, history will show you men of distinguished merit: spiritual men in England, along with the learned men under Wycliffe <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320s–1384), an English reformer.</note> in England and the University of Oxford who stood with him; in Bohemia, Jan Hus, who followed in Wycliffe's tracks; and subsequently those who followed his example, Jerome of Prague, Matthias of Paris <note>Matthias of Janov, though the text says "Parificnfis."</note>, Jacobel of Meissen <note>Jacobellus Misnensis, a follower of Hus.</note>, etc. See *Vitringa on Revelation, pages 643-644, etc.*

*Revelation 15:1, 2.* There appeared to John those who had citterns: holy confessors, prepared for the proclamation of the Lord's praise and as if dedicated to God, representing persons who possessed the ability to spread God's praise with a fitting manner of song, and to aptly demonstrate the teaching of the Gospel for the delight and comfort of others.
